Indeed, since I judge that these *Dissertations* should be compared with such *Lamps*—which, as they say, enjoy a perpetual light, or were at least hung or hidden away as evidence of perpetual light—I offer them to you, Benevolent Reader. II. As for authenticity, this opinion has been held by certain most learned men: that those titles were added to the books as "God-breathed" <note>original Greek: Θεοπνευςοις (theopneustois), meaning divinely inspired.</note> by the Authors, and that this was done by divine inspiration. DAVID SCHRAMM <note>David Schramm (1572–1620) was a German Lutheran theologian.</note>, a Theologian and Court Preacher of Neuburg, defended this cause to the best of his ability, not only in the Colloquy <term>Colloquy</term> <note>A formal academic or ecclesiastical discussion, in this case, the Colloquy of Ratisbon (1601) between Catholics and Lutherans.</note> which the Lutheran Theologians held at Ratisbon with TANNER <note>Adam Tanner (1572–1632), a Jesuit professor and controversialist.</note> and other Papists, but also in a specific book published thereafter. ### III.
On the other hand, most Interpreters have moved in the opposite direction and have admitted that these inscriptions originated from another hand. This matter has been treated specifically by RICHARD SIMON <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712) was a French priest and a pioneer of modern biblical criticism.</note> in his *Critical History of the New Testament*, chapter 11; by J. H. MAJUS <note>Johann Heinrich Majus (1653–1719), a German Lutheran theologian and Hebraist.</note> in his *Examination of Simon’s Critical History*, chapter 11; and by GOTTFRIED OLEARIUS <note>Gottfried Olearius (1672–1715) was a professor at Leipzig known for his work on the Gospel of Matthew.</note> in his *Observations on Matthew*, observation 1. Since their arguments seem to carry more weight, we will present their reasons here, though augmented by our own observations.

### IV.
First, therefore, it must be conceded that it was generally not the custom of the sacred Writers to place titles at the front of their books. Nor is there any reason to doubt that the titles of the Pentateuch <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>The first five books of the Bible (Genesis through Deuteronomy).</note>, the Psalms, and the other Prophets owe their authorship to the Jewish Church rather than to the sacred writers themselves. And who would dare to deny that even in the New Testament, the titles of the individual Apostolic Epistles—which differ from the common habit of Apostolic writing—were prefixed through the diligence of others? The same may be conjectured regarding the Acts of the Apostles, which in certain manuscript codes is immediately joined to the Gospel of Luke and has no other name prefixed to it; this arose because they recognized a single Author for both the Gospel and Acts. Regarding the *Revelation of John* <note>original Latin: "Apocalypsin Joannis"</note>, the most learned men hold the same opinion, as defended by CHRISTIAN PFÜTZNER in his elegant dissertation on the *Inscription of the Johannine Apocalypse*.

### V.
Added to this, *secondly*, is a certain necessity imposed upon us to decide the same regarding the Inscriptions of the Gospels after considering the beginnings of the Gospels of Matthew and Mark. For these books contain their own authentic general titles within themselves, and thus they do not allow for others originating from the hands of the authors. Matthew’s Gospel begins thus: *The book of the generation of Jesus Christ* <note>original Greek: Βιβλος γενεσεως Ιησου Χριστου (Biblos geneseos Iēsou Christou).</note>, where the word "generation" <note>original Greek: γενεσεως (geneseos)</note> should be translated not as "genealogy" but as "history," or as the Ancients put it, "origins" <note>original Latin: "origines"</note>. This is in the same sense as CATO called his books on the ancient deeds of the peoples of Italy *Origins*, and DIONYSIUS OF HALICARNASSEUS <note>A Greek historian (c. 60 BC – 7 BC) who wrote a history of Rome.</note> along with JOSEPHUS <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), the famous Romano-Jewish historian.</note> called their histories *Antiquities* <note>original Greek: Αρχαιολογιας (Archaiologias)</note>. This has been abundantly proven by JACOB ALTING <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679) was a Dutch philologist and theologian.</note> in his *Heptas III, dissertation III*, by comparison with the Hebrew word *Toledot* <note>original Hebrew: תולדות, meaning generations, descendants, or the history of a family.</note>.

§. 2. **Campegius Vitringa** <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a prominent Dutch theologian and Hebraist.</note> in *Sacred Observations*, Book 1, Dissertation 1, chapter 4, section 4; and **Gottfried Olearius** in *Observations on Matthew*, chapter 4. By the same reasoning, **Mark** also prefixed a specific title to his book: *The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.* <note>original Greek: "Ἀρχὴ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, υἱοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note> Since, therefore, it is not at all likely that these Evangelists prefixed another title beyond what was necessary, a reason arises for us to conclude the same regarding the two remaining Evangelists <note>Luke and John</note>.

VI. *Thirdly*, we can appeal here to the faith of the ancient Fathers, whose sufficiently old tradition we respect. **John Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) was the Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the most prolific authors of the early Church.</note> in his *First Homily on the Epistle to the Romans*, not only provides testimony for us but adds a reason worth considering as to why the names of the Authors were not placed at the beginning of the Gospels: *Moses, having written five books, never placed his own name on them, nor did those who followed him, who composed the histories after him. But neither did Matthew, nor John, nor Mark, nor Luke. However, the blessed Paul prefixes his name everywhere in his letters. Why so? Because they [the Evangelists] were writing to those present, and it was superfluous to declare themselves present; but he [Paul] sent letters from a distance, and in the form of an epistle. Therefore, the addition of the name was necessary.* <note>original: "Μωσης μεν πεντε βιβλια γραψας ουδαμου το ονομα το εαυτου τεθεικεν... Διο και αναγκαια ην του ονοματος προθηκη"</note>

However, Chrysostom is not entirely consistent with himself; for in the Preface or first Homily on Matthew, he says: *He aptly called his work "The Gospel."* <note>original Greek: "Εὐαγγέλιον δὲ αὐτοῦ τὴν πραγματείαν εἰκότως ἐκάλησε"</note> It is easily apparent that the venerable Father’s memory failed him in this latter passage.

Regarding the Evangelists, **CHRYSOSTOM**, in words which **EUSEBIUS** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339) was the first major historian of the Christian Church.</note> preserved in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 7, chapter 25: *“For the Evangelist nowhere writes his own name alongside his work. VIII. Two other arguments are added by **MALDONATUS** <note>Juan de Maldonado (1533–1583), a Spanish Jesuit scholar known for his influential biblical commentaries.</note> in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 1, and **JANSENIUS** <note>Cornelius Jansen (1585–1638), a Dutch bishop and the namesake of Jansenism.</note> in the *Preface to the Four Gospels*. The first is sought from the very similarity of the titles. For if they [the Evangelists] had added them themselves, they would not have stuck to the exact same words, *“The Gospel according to N.”* <note>The "N" here serves as a placeholder for the name of the Evangelist.</note> just as in other matters, when they narrate the same thing, they do not use the same words. This is more likely than the second argument, sought from the difference between the Greek and Latin titles, since in Greek it is *“The Gospel according to N.”* <note>original Greek: "Ευαγγελιον κατα N."</note> but the Latins, in most manuscripts, read: *“The Holy Gospel of Jesus Christ according to N.”* **MALDONATUS** thinks this difference arose from the fact that the Greek Church added the Greek title, and the Latin Church added the Latin one. Naturally, this is so he might not miss any opportunity to elevate the authority of the Latin Church. But who told him that in the Greek Manuscript which the Latin Translator used, this discrepancy existed? Or would it not have been proper for the Translator to adhere closely to the words of the copy he had before his eyes?

IX. From whatever hand this <term>inscription</term> <note>In this context, 'inscription' refers to the title or heading written at the top of the manuscript page.</note> originated, it cannot be doubted that it was extremely ancient, since frequent mention of the Gospels occurs in the writings of the Fathers of the second century. Indeed, **DIONYSIUS**, the Presbyter of Alexandria from around the year 232, mentions this title specifically <note>original Greek: "κατα ρητον," meaning 'expressly' or 'according to the text'.</note> as something accepted in his own time, saying: *“The Gospel inscribed 'According to John'.”* <note>original Greek: "Το ευαγγελιον το κατα Ιωαννην επιγεγραμμενον"</note> **TERTULLIAN**, writing around the end of the second century, not only throws in mentions of the <term>Gospel Instrument</term> <note>Tertullian used 'instrumentum' to refer to the official, authoritative record of the Christian faith.</note> and the *Gospels* elsewhere, but also disputes against **Marcion** <note>Marcion was a 2nd-century teacher who rejected the Old Testament and edited the New Testament to fit his own theology.</note> from their inscriptions in Book 4, chapter 2: *“Marcion, of course, ascribes no author to his Gospel, as if it were not permitted for him to also forge a title, when it was no sin for him to destroy the body of the text itself.”* And I could now halt my step here, contending that a work should not be acknowledged which does not show its face, which

XI. But one may even ascend to the beginnings of the second century or the end of the first, when we observe that already at that time certain various *Pseudo-Gospels* <note>Literally "False Gospels"—writings that claimed apostolic authority but were not accepted into the official Bible.</note>, or narratives about the life of Jesus Christ, began to be published. The name "Gospels" was undoubtedly bestowed upon them in imitation of the evangelical commentaries. Such was the *Gospel according to the Hebrews*, mentioned by CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA in book I of his *Miscellanies*, page 380, as well as by ORIGEN <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was one of the most prolific and influential early Christian scholars and theologians.</note> in his 15th Homily on Jeremiah and in Volume II of his *Commentary on John*, page 58, and others after them. The most learned J. A. FABRICIUS <note>Johann Albert Fabricius (1668–1736) was a German classical scholar and bibliographer famous for cataloging ancient texts.</note> has treated each of these at length and with great erudition, following others, in his *Pseudepigraphal Code of the New Testament*, volume I, page 335 and following. From this, we rightly conclude that the titles of the Gospels were prefixed to the commentaries of the Evangelists immediately after they were published, and thus were already in place during the Apostolic age. Indeed, MILLIUS <note>John Mill (c. 1645–1707) was an English theologian famous for his critical edition of the Greek New Testament.</note>, in his *Prolegomena to the New Testament*, section 347, thinks that *the very founders of the New Testament Canon attached the names of the authors to each individual Gospel, like public seals, by which it would be known among all posterity that these alone were the true and authentic records.*

Among these is the author of *New Thoughts on the First and Second Adam*, published anonymously, but known to be Samuel CRELLIUS, the grandson of the famous Socinian <note>The Socinians were a rationalist Christian group in the 16th and 17th centuries who denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ.</note> Johannes CRELLIUS, in section 122, page 88. However, this is by no means elicited from the words quoted. The argument is being made against Marcion <note>Marcion (c. 85–160 AD) was a famous heretic who rejected the Old Testament and most of the New Testament, creating his own shortened version of Luke's Gospel without a title or author’s name.</note>, who had either substituted some new Gospel or was selling an interpolated one as new. Hence, the author rightly demands of him, not that he show a title prescribed by the original author himself, but only that he himself at least provide a title for the book and reveal its author. For from this, one could easily gather what should be held regarding the <term>genuineness</term> <note>original Greek: γνησιοτητι (gnēsiotēti) — referring to the authenticity or legitimate authorship of a text.</note> of the entire book. Therefore, nothing else follows from this passage than that titles and the names of the authors had already been prefixed to the <term>genuine</term> <note>original Greek: γνησιοις (gnēsiois)</note> Gospels by the time of Tertullian.

X. Furthermore, moving closer from the end to the middle of the 2nd century, not a few testimonies of this same thing occur. IRENAEUS <note>Irenaeus (c. 130–202 AD) was the Bishop of Lugdunum (modern Lyon) and a major early Christian theologian who defended orthodoxy against Gnosticism.</note>, in *Against Heresies*, Book III, Chapter II, explicitly mentions not only the four Gospels but also indicates the form of their inscription. In section 1, he says, *that John began thus in that doctrine which is ACCORDING TO the Gospel: In the beginning was the word.* And in section 7: *The Ebionites <note>A Jewish-Christian sect that insisted on following Jewish law and used only one Gospel.</note> using only that Gospel which is ACCORDING TO Matthew, etc.* And again: *But those who follow Valentinus <note>A prominent Gnostic teacher in the 2nd century.</note>, using most fully that which is ACCORDING TO John, etc.* It is certain that the particle "ACCORDING TO" <note>original: KATA (κατὰ) — the standard Greek preposition used in Gospel titles to indicate authorship.</note> was expressed by the translator, especially since in the Greek fragment of Irenaeus from the same chapter, section 8, it is still read: <term>And the Gospels are in agreement among these, in which Christ is seated: for that which is ACCORDING TO JOHN, etc.</term> <note>original Greek: Και τα ΕΥΑΓΓΕΛΙΑ ἐν τουτοις συμφωνα, ἐν οἷς ἐγκαθεζεται ὁ Χριστος το μεν γαρ ΚΑΤΑ ΙΩΑΝΝΗΝ</note> CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA <note>Clement (c. 150–215 AD) was a scholar who headed the Catechetical School of Alexandria.</note> makes explicit mention of the fourfold nature of the Gospels. For while he cites a certain passage from the *Gospel according to the Egyptians*, he immediately adds in Book III of his *Miscellanies*, page 465: <term>First of all, in the four Gospels handed down to us, we do not have this saying, but in that [Gospel] according to the Egyptians.</term> <note>original Greek: Πρωτον μεν ἐν τοις παραδεδομενοις ἡμιν τεταρσιν Ευαγγελιοις οὐκ ἐχομεν το ῥητον, ἀλλ’ ἐν τῳ κατ’ Αἰγυπτιους</note> That is: *First, indeed, in the four Gospels delivered to us we do not have this saying, but in that which is*

Furthermore, there is a well-known passage by JUSTIN MARTYR in his *Second Apology*, page 98: "The apostles, in the memoirs produced by them, which are called Gospels <note>original Greek: Οἱ ἀπόστολοι ἐν τοῖς γενομένοις ὑπ’ αὐτῶν ὑπομνημονεύμασιν, ἃ καλεῖται εὐαγγέλια</note>." I will not dwell now on similar remarks in his work against *Trypho* <note>Justin Martyr's "Dialogue with Trypho" is one of the earliest Christian defenses against Jewish objections.</note> or other passages excerpted from the *Apostolic Constitutions*, since the authority and antiquity of those books are still a matter of debate.

XI. But we may even look back to the beginning of the second century or the end of the first, when we observe that various <term>Pseudo-Gospels</term> <note>original: Pseudo-Evangelia — apocryphal or "false" gospels that were not included in the official Bible.</note>, or narratives about the life of Jesus Christ, had already begun to be published. These were undoubtedly given the name "Gospels" in imitation of the evangelical memoirs. Such was the *Gospel according to the Hebrews*, mentioned by CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA in the first book of the *Stromata*, page 380, as well as by ORIGEN in his *15th Homily on Jeremiah* and in the second volume of his *Commentary on John*, page 58, and others after them. This work is of such great antiquity that PAPIAS <note>Papias (c. 60–130 AD) was an early Christian bishop said to have heard the Apostle John speak.</note>, a hearer of John, in his books on the *Interpretation of the Oracles of the Lord*, explained a story about a woman accused of many crimes before the Lord, which he had taken from that book, according to EUSEBIUS in book 3, chapter 39. There is also that *Gospel according to the Egyptians*, which CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA mentions in the passage just cited. Not to mention the *Gospel of Judas* mentioned in IRENAEUS, book 1, chapter 35, and the twenty-four books written by *Basilides* <note>Basilides was an early Gnostic teacher in Alexandria who claimed to possess secret Christian wisdom.</note> on the Gospel, according to EUSEBIUS's *Ecclesiastical History*, book 4, chapter 7. There is also the *Gospel of Basilides* specifically labeled with his own name, "according to Basilides" <note>original Greek: κατὰ Βασιλείδην (kata Basileidēn)</note>, as ORIGEN asserts in his preface to Luke; Basilides boasted that he had received this from his master Glaucias, the interpreter of Peter, according to CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA in the seventh book of the *Stromata*, page 764. The most learned J. A. FABRICIUS has treated each of these individually and with great erudition in his *Apocryphal Codex of the New Testament*, volume 1, page 335 and following. From this, we rightly conclude that the titles of the Gospels were prefixed to the memoirs of the Evangelists immediately after they were published, and thus were already in place during the Apostolic age. Indeed, MILLIUS <note>John Mill (1645–1707) was an English theologian famous for his critical edition of the Greek New Testament.</note> in his *Prolegomena to the New Testament*, section 347, believes that the very compilers of the New Testament Canon attached the *names of the authors* to each Gospel as *public seals*, by which it would be recognized by all posterity that *these alone are the true and authentic instruments*.

history. The same author believes that the names of the Evangelists were inscribed on the Gospel of Matthew by Christians of the first or second century. But unless I am mistaken, one can guess from the proven <term>malicious imitation</term> <note>original Greek: κακοζηλία (kakozēlia) — a term used to describe how heretics or rival writers poorly or deceitfully mimicked the style and titles of the authentic Gospels to gain credibility.</note> of the heretics that this title was already in use before the official collection of the Gospels (the Canon) was even established.

XII. From this great antiquity of the titles, it is clear that the lie of the **Manicheans** <note>Followers of Mani, a 3rd-century religion that was a major rival to early Christianity; they often claimed the New Testament had been corrupted.</note> was far too recent; they falsely claimed in the fourth century that the authors of the Gospels were someone other than those whose names are prefixed to them. On this matter, see **AUGUSTINE’S** *Against Faustus*, Book 33. To us, the authenticity of the Evangelists seems to shine forth from their very silence. For it was a mark of their modesty and humility that they did not wish to expressly name themselves as the writers of such excellent commentaries. Since these titles were nevertheless attached immediately by others, we conclude that at the very time these writings were being published, they were universally recognized in the Church as the works of holy and **divinely inspired** <note>original Greek: Θεοπνεύστων (theopneustōn) — literally "God-breathed," a term emphasizing that the scriptures were produced under the guidance of the Holy Spirit.</note> men.

XIII. Truly, *Richard SIMON* <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712) was a French priest and scholar whose critical methods in studying the Bible were controversial among both Catholics and Protestants.</note> wanders far from the mark when he seeks to use the titles prefixed to the Gospels to establish the authority that the **Roman Catholics** <note>original: Pontificii — a term used here to refer to those who support the supreme authority of the Pope and the institutional Church.</note> ascribe to the Church. He asserts that *one must always return to the authority of the ancient ecclesiastical writers to demonstrate that this title and this Gospel truly belong to the author whose name is inscribed.* However, the testimonies of certain individual Fathers that we possess cannot be considered "public" testimony of the Church (as the Catholics define it); nor do they have more authority than what other trustworthy historians provide concerning the writers of their own age. Unless, of course, you wish to believe that every individual Father was immediately inspired by the Holy Spirit, which would be most absurd. Indeed, anyone knowledgeable in these matters easily notices the whole "barns" of blemishes—both historical and theological—with which the writings of the Fathers abound, showing how far they were from the spirit of infallibility.

XIV. However, in the reading of these titles, a certain variety occurs which we believe should be examined more closely. Regarding the word **Gospel** <note>original Greek: Ευαγγέλιον (Evangelion)</note>, there is total harmony. This is proven by passages from the first centuries...

->### CONCERNING THE TITLE ###<-

<meta>catchword: evangelical</meta>

They have called the commentaries of the Evangelists "Gospels" <note>original Greek: Ευαγγελια (Euangelia)</note> in the plural number, the instances of which **SUICER** <note>Johann Caspar Suicer (1620–1684), a Swiss German theologian and author of the *Thesaurus Ecclesiasticus*.</note> noted in his *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus* under the entry "Gospel" <note>original Greek: Ευαγγελιον (Euangelion)</note>. Thus also among more recent scholars, **GROTIUS**, **HAMMOND**, **RICHARD SIMON**, **ERASMUS SCHMID**, and countless others. Others are convinced that through this word, the subject matter of the entire book is presented in summary; as this yields a fuller and more proper sense, we also conclude it to be the most fitting. From this, we also gather that this use of our word is by far the most frequent, both when it is placed alone—as in Mark 1:15, 8:15, 10:29, 13:10; Romans 10:16, 11:28, etc.—and in compound phrases. Thus, we often see "the Gospel of the kingdom" <note>original Greek: ευαγγελιον της βασιλειας (euangelion tēs basileias)</note> in Matthew 4:23, 9:35, 24:14; Mark 1:14. Likewise Romans 1:9, "The Gospel of His Son" <note>original Greek: Το ευαγγελιον τυ υιυ αυτυ (To euangelion tou huiou autou)</note> and verse 16, "The Gospel of Christ" <note>original Greek: Το ευαγγελιον τυ Χριςυ (To euangelion tou Christou)</note>. Add to these 1 Corinthians 9:12, 2 Corinthians 2:12, 9:13, 10:14, Galatians 1:7, and 1 Thessalonians 3:2. There is no reason why we should depart from this more common usage. I will not even press the point of the pronoun "the" <note>original Greek: το (to) — the definite article.</note>, which, when placed before nouns used absolutely, indicates that they should be understood in their accustomed and fuller sense: and all the more so because otherwise, this article is plainly unusual in the titles of books, whether Hebrew or Greek.

XIX. This notion also prevailed among the Fathers of the primitive Church. For among them, "Gospel" did not refer solely to the history of Jesus Christ contained in the Evangelists, nor just to the proclamation of Him, but to the very doctrine of salvation, even when it was set forth in the Epistles of the Apostles. We safely refer to this passage—though some dispute its meaning—from **CLEMENT OF ROME** in his *First Epistle to the Corinthians*, section 47: *Take up the epistle of the blessed Paul the Apostle. What did he first write to you in the beginning of the Gospel?* <note>original Greek: Αναλαβετε την επιϛολην τυ μακαριυ Παυλυ τυ Αποϛολυ. Τι πρωτον υμιν εν αρχη τυ ευαγγελιυ εγραφεν;</note> For I cannot persuade myself that "the beginning of the Gospel" <note>original Greek: αρχην τυ Ευαγγελιυ (archēn tou Euangeliou)</note> designates here the first times of the Evangelical preaching; since not only is the very beginning of the cited Epistle brought forward by Clement, but it is also well established that this Epistle was not written to the Corinthians at the very start of the Evangelical preaching. For this reason, that passage in Philippians 4:15 cannot be compared, where Paul truly speaks of the beginning of the Evangelical Preaching...

# ON THE TITLE

...which the faithful decided after these things to call Gospels, as being truly the Gospel—that is, containing the doctrine of Christ. <note>original Greek: εὐαγγελια οἱ πισοι μετα ταυτα ἐδικαιωσαν καλειν, ὡς το ὀντως εὐαγγελιον, τουτεσι την του Χριστου διδασκαλιαν περιεχοντα; original Latin: i. e. quæ postmodum fideles Evangelia appellanda esse censuerunt, utpote revera lætum nuncium, hoc est, Christi doctrinam, continentia.</note>

XXI. Let us now take this opportunity to indulge our inclination for a while and wander a little into a deeper meditation on both the emphasis and the sweetness that the word GOSPEL encompasses. We find a path already trodden by many; yet it will not be entirely useless to present the scattered thoughts of others gathered in a convenient order and increased by our own diligence, offering a "gleaning after the harvest." <note>The author uses the phrase "spicilegium post messem," a metaphor for collecting small details that earlier scholars might have missed.</note>

XXII. The origins of this word, in the use that the New Testament writers employ it, are rightly traced from the Hellenistic style <note>The form of Greek used by Jewish scholars in the Septuagint and later by New Testament writers.</note> by **ALEXANDER MORUS** in his *Notes on the New Testament*, page 3. For among the Alexandrians <note>The translators of the Greek Septuagint in Alexandria.</note>, "to bring good news" <note>original Greek: εὐαγγελιζεσθαι</note> corresponds to the Hebrew <term>basar <gloss>בשר</gloss></term> and "good news" <note>original Greek: εὐαγγελιον</note> corresponds to <term>besorah <gloss>בשורה</gloss></term>. Its proper meaning is to designate the announcement of a matter that is not only new, but also joyful; furthermore, it is delivered by specific messengers sent for that purpose, who expect rewards for their news. Thus in 2 Samuel 4:10: <note>The text cites verse 17, likely a printer's error for verse 10.</note> "He was like one bringing good news before me" <note>original Hebrew: והוא היה כמבשר בעיניו; original Greek: Αὐτὸς ἦν ὡς εὐαγγελιζόμενος ἐνώπιον μου</note>, because he seemed to himself to be bringing a good thing to David and expected to carry back rewards—an error which David refutes. Compare also 2 Samuel 18:20–27. And from this, the word for "good news" <note>original Hebrew: בשורה; original Greek: εὐαγγελια</note> occurs metonymically <note>A figure of speech where the name of one thing is used for another associated with it.</note> for the rewards themselves given to such a messenger in 2 Samuel 4:10.

XXIII. Only one passage is urged to the contrary by those who judge that the Hebrew word <term>basar <gloss>בשר</gloss></term> has a "middle" or neutral meaning <note>Meaning it could refer to either good or bad news depending on context.</note>, namely 1 Samuel 4:17. Where **KIMCHIUS** <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a highly influential medieval Jewish rabbi and grammarian.</note> says: "And the messenger <term>Hammebasser <gloss>המבשר</gloss></term> answered; that is, the messenger of news: for <term>Mebasser <gloss>מבשר</gloss></term> is said of both good and bad things." **DRUSIUS** <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish scholar of the Old Testament and Hebrew.</note> follows him on this passage. **SEBASTIAN SCHMID** <note>Sebastian Schmidt (1617–1696), a Lutheran theologian and Bible translator.</note> tried to resolve this doubt with a new translation, in this way: "Furthermore, Eli answered: Are you a messenger of good news? And he (the messenger) said: Israel has fled." We would gladly admit this translation, unless it seemed to be hindered by the fact that this messenger had just said in the preceding words that he had fled from the battle line, from which Eli could already gather that it was not good...

# THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

...the good news that he brought. **GOUSSET** <note>Jacques Gousset (1635–1704) was a French Protestant theologian and Hebrew scholar known for his work on Hebrew roots.</note> thinks that since this is a unique example, it might be considered an "abusive" or improper use of the term. However, such a conclusion shouldn't be easily accepted in the sacred style of the Scriptures without an urgent necessity. Therefore, another response from the praised **SCHMIDT** <note>Sebastian Schmidt (1617–1696) was a prominent Lutheran theologian and commentator.</note> regarding this passage seems better to us: namely, that this messenger is called a <term>mebasser <gloss>מבשר</gloss></term> <note>A bringer of tidings, usually good ones.</note> improperly, because the news was *thought* to be good before it was actually heard. This is just like David: when he was told a single man was running toward him, he thought the news would be good and joyful because the man was running alone. But he soon found the news to be bad. Similarly, in this passage, although Eli was anxious about the Ark, he still hoped for better things. And perhaps others tried to hide the disaster in the presence of the old man. Thus, the meaning would be: "He whom others tried to persuade Eli was a bringer of good news, and whom Eli himself almost hoped was such, answered," etc. Furthermore, since this is not only the sole instance but also the first place in the Holy Scriptures to feature this word, we commit nothing <term>out of place <gloss>ἄτοπον</gloss></term> if we suggest that perhaps from the beginning the word enjoyed a "middle" meaning <note>A "middle" sense (Latin: *medio sensu*) refers to a word that is neutral, potentially meaning either good or bad news depending on the context.</note>, but over time it shifted toward a better meaning and was determined as such by actual usage.

XXIV. The word occurs at least in the most joyful occasions, such as the birth of a young son in Jeremiah 20:15, and especially a victory reported over enemies in 1 Samuel 31:9 and 2 Samuel 18:21, 26. From there, it is quite frequently transferred to that future proclamation of the Gospel, which announced the birth of the Messiah and the salvation gained through him. It is used specifically regarding the announcement of the Lord’s coming in Isaiah 40:9. Furthermore, it refers to the announcement of salvation and the justice acquired after the victory reported over the enemies of the chosen, which first had to be performed by the Lord himself in Psalm 40:10 and Isaiah 61:1. Then it was also carried out by other ministers of the Gospel in 1 Chronicles 16:23, Psalm 68:12, Psalm 96:2, Isaiah 52:7, Isaiah 60:6, and Nahum 2:1.

XXV. The Greek word <term>Euangelion <gloss>Ευαγγελιον</gloss></term> is clearly equivalent to this Hebrew word <term>besorah <gloss>בשורה</gloss></term> in all its parts. For the very composition of the word <note>From the Greek *eu* (good) and *angello* (to announce).</note> sufficiently teaches us that it is used for *news* and indeed *good* news. **ORIGEN** <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 185–253 AD) who wrote extensively on the Gospels.</note> in his commentary *On John*, page 6, says: <note>original Greek: Εςι το ευαγγελιον λογος περιεχων ἀπαγγελιαν πραγματων κατα το ευλογον δια το ὠφελειן εὐφραινοντων τον ἀκουοντα ἐπαν παραδεξεται το ἀπαγγελλομενον</note> "The **Gospel** is a discourse containing an announcement of things which, as is reasonable, gladden the hearer because of their benefit, once he accepts what is reported." That is, *Gospel*...

# CONCERNING THE TITLE
<meta>catchword: has,</meta>

[The Gos]pel is a speech that contains a good announcement that is appropriate to the nature of the events; it makes the listener joyful because of the benefit of the news as soon as the things being announced are received. Regarding news that is good, new, present, and unexpected, **PHAVORINUS** <note>Varinus Phavorinus (c. 1450–1537) was an Italian scholar and bishop who compiled a massive Greek dictionary.</note> testifies in his *Lexicon*: "A Gospel is a proclamation of a new salvation, or a word containing abundant good things. It is called 'gospel' because it announces the most beautiful things and brings good messages." <note>original Greek: Ευαγγελιον ἐςι κηρυγμα της νεας σωτηριας, ἡ λογος περιεχων ἀγαθα πλεσιαν. Λεγεται δε εὐαγγελιον παρα το τα καλλισα ἀπαγγελον, το ἀγαθας ἀγγελιας φερον.</note> In **JOSEPHUS** <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a famous Jewish historian.</note>, *Antiquities of the Jews* (Book 5, Chapter 10), the Angel announcing the birth of Samson is said to be <term>bringing good news <gloss>εὐαγγελιζομενος / euangelizomenos</gloss></term>. **VITRUVIUS** <note>A Roman architect and engineer (1st century BC).</note> (Book 10, Chapter 7) is the source for the fact that Pixodorus was called "Evangelus" <note>The "Good Messenger."</note> because he announced the discovery of marble. It is well known that a public message is called by this name from **ARISTOPHANES** <note>The most famous playwright of Old Greek Comedy.</note> in *The Knights* (lines 639–640):

->- - - O Council, bearing good words,<-
->I wish to be the first to bring you joyful news.<-

That is: *O Senate, bearing good words, I want to tell you joyful news first.* **HESYCHIUS** <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian who compiled a dictionary of rare and difficult words.</note> defines "Gospels" <note>original: Ευαγγελια</note> as "messages" or "proclamations." Indeed, it is clear that the term is used for a message sent from the divine based on what follows immediately in Hesychius, where he asserts that Mercury <note>The messenger of the gods in Roman mythology (Hermes in Greek).</note> is called the <term>Good Messenger <gloss>Ευαγγελον / Euangelon</gloss></term>. In a very specific sense, however, this word is proper to messengers announcing a victory obtained or the liberty of a people restored after the enemy has been defeated. **LUCIAN** <note>A satirist and rhetorician of the 2nd century AD.</note> in *A Slip of the Tongue in Greeting*: "Announcing the victory and the capture of the Spartans." <note>original Greek: Ευαγγελιζομενος την νικην και την των Σπαρτιατων ἁλωσιν.</note> The same author in *The Tyrannicide*: "I am here bringing you democracy and announcing liberty." <note>original Greek: Παρεμι κομιζων ὑμιν την δημοκρατιαν, και την ἐλευθεριαν εὐαγγελιζομενος.</note> From this, the rewards given to messengers—especially crowns—and the sacrifices offered for victories were called "gospels" through <term>metonymy <gloss>a figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it</gloss></term>, as has been noted abundantly by **MEURSIUS** in *Miscellaneous Observations* (Book 3, Chapter 22) and *Greek Festivals* (Book 3), **TARNOVIUS** in his *Introduction to John* (Chapter 1), **CYPRIANO** in the *Preface to Schmidt’s Concordance*, and **JENSIO** in *Literary Bundles* (Volume 1, pages 2–3). This last meaning [of a reward], though it is very frequent in Greek authors, is nonetheless less common in the New Testament. In the meantime, it seems that light can be shed on it from 1 Corinthians 9:14: "The Lord ordained that those who announce the Gospel should <term>live from the Gospel <gloss>ἐκ τε εὐαγγελιε ζην</gloss></term>,"—that is, live from the reward of the labor spent on this announcement.

XXVI. From these observations it is clear how much power this word has,

# OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN
### C

[...it] has, when it designates not only the doctrine of salvation in a general sense—where anything opposed to it is called **another gospel** <note>original Greek: ἕτερον Ευαγγελιον</note> (Galatians 1:6; 2 Corinthians 11:4)—but also more specifically that doctrine of the New Testament which indicates that Christ came into the world and fully acquired salvation and life for the sinner. This is the constant use of this word in the New Testament. I do not think any example can be brought to the contrary. We do indeed read in Galatians 3:8 that the promise concerning *all nations being blessed in Abraham’s seed* is called a <term>pre-gospel <gloss>προευαγγελισμος / proeuangelismos</gloss></term>. However, the very form of the word and its composition with the prefix "pre" indicates clearly enough that a distinction is being made by the Apostle between the promise made to Abraham and the doctrine of the fulfillment of this promise, which is called **Gospel** <note>original Greek: ἁπλως Ευαγγελιον</note> in the strict sense. This is also the reason why he distinguishes the **Gospel of God**, of which the Apostle was a minister, from the "prior promise" in Romans 1:1–2, and from the "promise" in Ephesians 3:6 and Acts 13:32. Similarly, Romans 16:25–26 implies that *his Gospel contains a mystery kept silent for long ages, but now made manifest.* Compare 2 Timothy 1:10.

XXVII. Certainly, no clear example exists in which the word **Gospel** <note>original Greek: Ευαγγελιον</note> is used for any message other than that of present salvation. The passage in Hebrews 4:2, 6 might be raised as an objection, where it is said of the Israelites that they also were <term>given the good news <gloss>εὐηγγελισμενοι / euengelismanoi</gloss></term> in the desert, and they are therefore named <term>those who formerly had the good news preached to them <gloss>οἱ προτερον εὐαγγελισθεντες / hoi proteron euangelisthentes</gloss></term>. But this does not seem to extend further than to the announcement of a symbolic rest through the liberation from Egypt opened to them. In that case, there is nothing in that saying which contradicts the proper meaning of "Gospel." 

Regarding the passage in 1 Peter 4:6, *For to this end was the gospel preached to the dead, so that they might be judged according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the Spirit*; I know that our theologians everywhere understand "the dead" to mean those who perished in the flood, and consequently they take this "evangelizing" to mean the preaching of Noah. However, the connection of Peter's reasoning becomes quite tangled if interpreted this way, since the Apostle's intent is to urge that tribulations must be borne holily—a point for which the example of those before the flood does little service. That preaching would even be called a "Gospel" <term>misleadingly <gloss>Catachrestice</gloss></term>, as it put forward the gravest threats, as is clear from the prophecy of Enoch preserved by Jude.

<summary>This page argues that the term "Gospel" refers specifically to the fulfillment of salvation in Christ, distinguishing it from the "pre-gospel" promises of the Old Testament. The author also disputes the idea that Noah's warnings to the antediluvian world should be strictly categorized as "Gospel" preaching.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion regarding whether the term "Gospel" can be applied to the Old Testament. It concludes a point regarding the "preaching to the dead" mentioned in 1 Peter 4:6 and then provides supporting evidence from the Church Fathers (Origen, Eusebius, and Justin Martyr) to argue that "Gospel" specifically refers to the fulfillment of salvation in Christ, not just its promise.</meta>

# ON THE TITLE

[...having been] observed. Therefore, I agree thus far with the opinion of **GROTIUS**, who understands "the dead" to refer to those who were already deceased when Peter wrote these things—the pious martyrs, such as Stephen, James, and others. Although these men were judged <note>original Greek: κατ’ ἀνθρωπες / kat’ anthropous</note> "according to men"—that is, *as far as it lay in the power of men, who can kill the body* <note>original Latin: quantum in hominibus fuit, qui corpus interficere poffunt</note> (referencing Matthew 10:28), or even according to the opinion of men—and were judged <note>original Greek: σαρκι / sarki</note> "in the flesh," so that they suffered the loss of the physical body, yet they *lived by the Spirit*, which returned to God. Thus, the phrase itself agrees with the wording that Peter used in the proposition he intended to prove here in verse 1: *for he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin.* <note>original Greek: ὁτι ὁ παθων ἐν σαρκι πεπαυται ἁμαρτιας / hoti ho pathon en sarki pepautai hamartias</note> I am uncertain, therefore, whether, speaking accurately, the doctrine of grace before Christ can be called the **Gospel**, or even the <term>Proto-Gospel <gloss>Πρωτευαγγελιον / Proteuangelion; the "First Gospel" or earliest promise of a Savior</gloss></term>.

XXVIII. On our side once again stand the Church Fathers, from whom I may be permitted to transcribe a few passages. ORIGEN, in his commentary on John, page 4, says: *The Old Scripture is not the Gospel, for it does not show the one who is coming, but rather announces him in advance. But all the New Scripture is the Gospel; not only because it says, as at the beginning of the Gospel, "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world," but also because it contains various praises and teachings concerning him, through whom the Gospel is the Gospel.* <note>The Latin text provides a translation of Origen's Greek: "Veterem Scripturam non effe Evangelium..."</note> EUSEBIUS agrees in his *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 1, page 3: *The Gospel announces to all men the presence of the highest and greatest goods, which were predicted long ago, but have recently shone forth upon all.* <note>The Latin text translates Eusebius: "Evangelium omnibus hominibus præfentiam..."</note> Add to this JUSTIN in his *Questions and Responses to the Orthodox*, page 457: *As far as learning is concerned, the Gospel does not differ from the Law. But as far as the promise and the fulfillment are concerned, they do differ. For what is the Law? It is the Gospel announced in advance. And what is the Gospel? It is the Law fulfilled.* <note>The Latin text translates Justin: "Evangelium nihil a lege differt..."</note> That is to say: the Gospel differs nothing from the Law; but as for the promise and the per-

### OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.
<page-num>19</page-num>
->C 2<-
<meta>catchword: XXXI.</meta>

*...pertains to the delivery of salvation, this matters a great deal. For what is the Law? The Gospel foretold. What is the Gospel? The Law fulfilled.* <note>original Latin: "Quid enim lex? Evangelium prænuntiatum. Quid Evangelium? Lex completa."</note>

XXIX. This at least we must confess: it is necessary that, in its highest emphasis, the name "Gospel" belongs solely to the doctrine of the New Testament, and that the meaning of the word is fully exhausted in that doctrine alone. For (1) it was preached by the most excellent and heavenly Messenger, namely the Son of God himself, who was sent into the world for this purpose <note>referencing Matthew 11:5, Luke 4:18, 4:43, 8:1, 20:1, and Ephesians 2:17</note>. In his footsteps followed the entire company of Apostles and Evangelists. (2) Its subject matter was most joyful, insofar as it encompasses a certain good that is new, present, and supreme—namely, *that the Savior of the world has been born* <note>Luke 2:20</note> and that *God has fulfilled for their children the promise made to the Fathers, by raising up Jesus* <note>Acts 13:32</note>. Primarily, it announces that victory has been won over all enemies, *death is abolished, and life and immortality are brought to light, which is said to be made manifest through the Gospel* <note>2 Timothy 1:10</note>. This is the foundation of that glorious Kingdom, from which it is absolutely <note>original Greek: ἁπλῶς / haplōs</note> called the *Gospel of the Kingdom* in the passages already cited. In this Kingdom, true and spiritual goods—salvation, grace, and peace—are possessed. For this reason, it is also known as the *Gospel of grace* <note>Acts 20:24</note>, the *Gospel of salvation* <note>Ephesians 1:13</note>, the *Gospel of peace* <note>Ephesians 6:15</note>, and the *Gospel of glory* <note>1 Timothy 1:11</note>. (3) Nor were there lacking results suitable for such a great Gospel: the most ample rewards for those who announced it—crowns of righteousness and life—as well as *sacrifices of praise* offered by the people of God, which there is no need to discuss at greater length here.

XXX. Therefore, when the commentaries of the Evangelists are called the *Gospel*, it indicates that the saving doctrine preached in the New Testament is most fully contained within them. This is true not only insofar as it is the *doctrine about Christ*—concerning his birth, life, death, and resurrection—but also insofar as it is the *doctrine of Christ himself*, revealed by him as the <term>Chief Messenger <gloss>Archangelo</gloss></term> <note>The author uses "Archangelo" here in its literal Greek sense of "Chief Messenger" to describe Christ's role in delivering God's final word.</note> and brought forth to men *from the bosom of the Father*. In this way, the Apostolic writings are set in opposition to the writings of the Prophets as being far more perfect and sweet. This is not only because many of the prophetic writings are titled <term>Burden <gloss>משא / Massa</gloss></term>, as **GROTIUS** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> notes, but also because they are called a <term>Vision <gloss>חזון / Chazon</gloss></term> of a future thing, whereas the Gospel shows salvation as a present reality.

<summary>This page argues that the term "Gospel" belongs uniquely to the New Testament because it records the fulfillment of God's promises through Christ, contrasting the "joyful news" of the Apostles with the "burdens" and "visions" of the Old Testament prophets.</summary>

<page-num>20</page-num>

XXXI. Since, therefore, it is abundantly clear from this how excellent and majestic is the name of the Gospel, which distinguishes Christian doctrine, we rightly feel grief at the <term>hardness of heart</term> <note>original Greek: σκληροκαρδία / sklērokardia</note> of the Jews. By this hardness, they have not only stubbornly rejected such a saving message—which was offered to them in the first place—but they even wickedly insult this sweetest name with a most unfortunate "abortion of wit." For some of them break down this word in Hebrew as <term>Iniquity of the Scroll</term> <note>original Hebrew: עון גליון / Aven Gilyon; a mocking pun on the Greek 'Euangelion'</note> or "revelation of iniquity." How these blinded Teachers delight in these blasphemies drawn from the Talmud can be seen in the works of <term>Münster</term> <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a German cartographer and Hebrew scholar</note> on Matthew 1:1, and especially <term>Eisenmenger</term> <note>Johann Andreas Eisenmenger (1654–1704), whose "Judaism Revealed" was a famous, though highly polemical, critique of Jewish literature</note> in *Judaism Revealed*, part 1, chapter 7, page 275 and following. We pray from our hearts for the uncovering of their eyes so they may perceive the truth of the testimony concerning Christ which the Gospel presents, so that in its light they might finally acknowledge their own vanity and iniquity with sincere repentance.

XXXII. We must still examine the word <term>According to</term> <note>original Greek: KATA / kata</note>, through which the Gospel is attributed to various authors. Learned men feel that the Vulgate version, which renders this as *secundum*, is using poor Latin, since examples are lacking where this particle is used to describe someone who commits something to writing. However, the Greek construction is equally unusual. The fact that other spurious Gospels appear in ecclesiastical antiquity, called the "Gospel <term>according to the Hebrews</term>" or "<term>according to the Egyptians</term>," does not really apply here; in those cases, the "According to" designates not those who wrote them, but those who used them. Nor would anyone easily give an ear to <term>Simon</term> <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712), a pioneer of biblical criticism who suggested the Gospels were later collections of Apostolic preaching</note>, who regards the Gospels merely as collections of Apostolic preaching—without regard for time or order—suggesting they were collected by disciples from what they had received from the Apostles or Apostolic men, and were thus titled *according to Matthew* rather than *of Matthew*.

XXXIII. Most interpreters agree on this: that this particle denotes the Gospel as committed to writing by Matthew, John, etc., and thus it is the same as if one said: *The Gospel of Matthew, of John, etc.* Hence, the <term>Syriac translator</term> <note>Refers to the Peshitta, the standard Syriac version of the Bible</note> renders it <term>The Proclamation of John, etc.</term> <note>original Syriac: קריאותא דיוחנן / keryota d'Yuchanan</note>. Other versions—the Ethiopic, Arabic, and Persian—agree with this. Nor does it stand in the way that in the fuller...

...is usually said with emphasis: *The Gospel of Jesus Christ* <note>original Greek: Ευαγγελιον Ιησε Χριςε / Euangelion Iēsou Christou</note>, since Paul also calls it *his Gospel* in Romans 2:16, which he announced with his own mouth; hence he also explains his meaning in Romans 16:25: *according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ*.

XXXIV. There is debate, however, over which dialect this expression flowed from. <term>Drusius</term> <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish scholar of biblical languages</note> maintains it is a <term>Hebraism</term> <note>An idiom or grammatical structure derived from Hebrew</note> in *Questions*, Book I, 23, and in his notes on Matthew 1:1, suggesting it corresponds to the prefixed letter *Lamed* [ל], which is used to denote a Sacred Writer. For example: *A Psalm of David* <note>original Hebrew: מזמור לדוד / Mizmor le-David</note>, which <term>Aquila</term> and <term>Symmachus</term> <note>Translators who produced Greek versions of the Old Testament in the 2nd century AD</note> render according to the Vatican manuscript as: *A Psalm to David* <note>original Greek: Ψαλμος τω Δαυιδ / Psalmos tō Dauid</note>. For it is well known that this *Lamed* is sometimes rendered as "according to" <note>Greek: κατα / kata</note> by the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> interpreters. One could also think here of the particle *as according to* <note>original Hebrew: כפי / k'phi</note>, which is likewise rendered as "according to" [KATA] among the Hellenists, and which was used by the author of the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew which <term>Sebastian Münster</term> <note>A German cartographer and Hebrew scholar (1488–1552)</note> published, placing this title before it: *The New Law, which is the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the mouth of Matthew the Evangelist* <note>original Hebrew: תורה חדשה והיא בשורת האדונינו ישוע המשיח כפי מתי המבשר / Torah Chadashah ve-hi Besorat ha-Adoneinu Yeshua ha-Mashiach k'phi Matai ha-Mevasser</note>. Others believe it is a pure <term>Graecism</term> <note>A style or idiom belonging to the Greek language</note>, and examples which strive to confirm this have been brought forward by my most celebrated and very dear friend <term>Elsner</term> <note>Jakob Elsner (1692–1750), a Prussian theologian</note> in *Observations on Matthew*, pages 1 and 2. It is quite difficult for us to sit in judgment here because the examples brought forward on both sides are not so perfectly matched as to settle the matter. For so far, no example has been brought from either Hellenistic or purer Greek where "according to" [KATA] is used specifically for the author of a book. From this, it follows at least that, from wherever this phrase was taken, it was quite unusual.

XXXV. Various reasons are offered as to why those who wrote these titles used an unusual phrase. <term>Grotius</term> <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note> gives a grammatical reason: namely, because the old inscription, according to him, did not simply have *The Gospel*, but *The Gospel of Jesus Christ*; therefore, the name of the writer could not be put in the genitive [possessive] case. For instance, we do not say *The Life of Caesar of Plutarch*, but *written by Plutarch*. But here, memory failed this most eminent man while he was busy with other things. For people do say *Xenophon's Education of Cyrus* and *Cyrus’s Expedition*; and *Philostratus’s Life of Apollonius*, as <term>Eunapius</term> <note>A Greek sophist and historian of the 4th century</note> testifies this work was inscribed in the preface to the *Lives of the Sophists*; also *Porphyry’s Life of Pythagoras*, and so six hundred <note>Latin: fexcenta; an idiom meaning "countless" or "innumerable"</note> [others].

...six hundred other things. A more mystical reason is the one given by <term>Beza</term> <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant reformer and scholar</note>, which <term>Schmidius</term> <note>Erasmus Schmidt (1570–1637), a Greek scholar and lutist</note> borrows from him: namely, to indicate that the Evangelist is only the *writer*, while Christ himself is the true author of the Gospel. This reason does not suit the critical palate of <term>Simon</term> <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712), often called the father of modern biblical criticism</note>. It is certainly true that Beza speaks awkwardly when he distinguishes between *author* and *writer*, since these terms are used with equal breadth among Latin speakers.

XXXVI. Therefore, it would be sufficient for me that the particle *according to* <note>Greek: κατα / kata</note> is frequently used by the Greeks when they wish to distinguish the words, opinions, and deeds of one person from the words and deeds of another. To this point belongs that formula *according to Thucydides* or *according to Plato* <note>Greek: κατα Θουκυδιδην, κατα Πλατωνα / kata Thoukydidēn, kata Platōna</note>, meaning *so that I may use the words of Thucydides or Plato*, as noted by <term>Stephanus</term> in his Lexicon. Likewise, <term>Aelian</term> in *Various History*, Book XIV, 8, says of Polycletus: *He changed something according to each of those entering* <note>Greek: Καθ’ ἑκαστον των εἰσιοντων μετετιθει τι / Kath’ hekaston tōn eisiontōn metetithei ti</note>; *that is, he changed it based on their opinion, etc.* And from this usage, the Latin word *according to* <note>Latin: secundum</note> does not really seem to me to be as far removed as is commonly thought.

Nevertheless, while we admit this distributive sense of the word *according to* here, we do not want it understood in any way other than the nature of the subject permits. <term>Maldonatus</term> <note>Juan Maldonado (1533–1583), a Spanish Jesuit theologian</note> seems to have correctly distinguished this for us on this passage: *It is signified both that others have written and that they did not write in the same way.* Therefore, that *according to* does not declare a *different doctrine or opinion—as when the Greek philosophers say "according to Aristotle" or "according to Plato"—but rather declares only different authors and a different manner of writing.* 

Certainly, since those who wished to mark the commentaries of the Evangelists with a <term>rubric</term> <note>A title or heading, traditionally written in red ink for emphasis</note> had several writers of the Gospel before their eyes, they decided the name of the writer should be prefixed in such a way that they simultaneously hinted that there were also other *divinely inspired* <note>Greek: θεοπνευςους / theopneustous</note> men who had handed down the same doctrine in writing. These men were distinct in their manner of handling the material, but they agreed in the substance and goal of the matter. These accounts ought to be compared because, in the book then before the reader's eyes, the testimony of only one Evangelist was presented. Indeed, the early scribes were held by a certain necessity of giving this warning, since the writings of the Evangelists existed separately before the <term>Canon</term> <note>The final, official collection of books recognized as the Bible</note> was yet completed. ALBERT FABRICIUS deserves to be added, specifically his *Greek Library*, Book IV, chapter 13, where he provides a catalog of ancient authors who wrote on the interpretation of dreams.

V. Meanwhile, some element of true tradition remained among them, because they derived their method of interpreting dreams from the School of the Patriarchs <note>The "School of the Patriarchs" refers to the inherited wisdom of biblical figures like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</note>. JUSTIN, at least, in Book XXXVI, chapter 2, records that Joseph in Egypt was the most skilled in portents and *was the first to establish the understanding of dreams.* <note>original Latin: "Somniorum primum intelligentiam condidisse."</note> With this, one may compare what SUIDAS <note>A 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note> says regarding *Abraham*: *From him also the Greeks claimed the books of dreams for themselves.* <note>original Greek: Εκ τουτου και τα ονειρων βιβλια εφετερησαντο Έλληνες.</note>

VI. Regarding the reason why it pleased God to use this mode of Revelation with men, various reasons are offered by various theologians. Let the interested reader see ANDREAS RIVETUS on *Genesis*, Exercise CXXIV; FRIEDRICH SPANHEIM in *Evangelical Doubts*, Part II, Doubt 59; HERMAN WITSIUS in *Miscellanies*, Volume I, Book I, chapter 5; and JOHANN HEIDEGGER in *History of the Patriarchs*, Part II, Exercise XVI, § 4. However, because some of those reasons are not sufficiently clear or compelling, while others that could be mentioned are not touched upon, we shall explain our own opinion regarding this matter in a few words.

<page-num>26</page-num>

### DISSERTATION

VII. Many place this reason at the very forefront as the most important: that the nighttime, which is intended for rest and silence, is the most suitable for receiving Revelation, as the mind is more tranquil, the soul more composed, and thus better fitted for the reception of spiritual things. They add that at this time, the soul is less distracted and less divided by the variety of objects that usually affect it in different ways during the day. They also consider it a certainty that during the night, all objects appear larger and the mind is more powerfully affected by them. A tiny noise is thought to be louder, and a small light appears great; hence, this time is more suitable for affecting and striking a person with awe. Indeed, they even argue that fear is instilled through the darkness of night when dealing with sacred matters. They claim the pagans were not ignorant of this, as they insisted that the Sacred Rites of Iacchus and the Eleusinian Mysteries <note>original: "Sacra Jacchi & Eleusinia"; these were famous secret religious rites of ancient Greece.</note> be celebrated only at night, as CICERO testifies in book 2 of *On the Laws* <note>original: "de leg." (De Legibus)</note>. However, these arguments, drawn from the shallow pools of pagan philosophers, seem poorly suited to our purpose, because they assume a greater capacity in a sleeping person to receive divine Revelations than in one who is awake. This not only seems to bind the most free grace of God too closely to a certain human disposition—a foundation upon which SPINOZA <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a philosopher who applied rationalist criticism to the Bible.</note> peddled the idea in his *Theologico-Political Treatise* <note>original: "Tract. Theolog. Polit."</note>, chapter 11, that *Prophets were more suited to these or those revelations according to the varied temperament of their bodies*—but it is also contrary to the nature of the matter itself, since a sleeping person is much less suited to perceive divine truths clearly and distinctly than one who is awake. Additionally, God himself has sufficiently indicated that he has no regard for such circumstances, because far more Revelations occurred to those who were awake.

VIII. There is even less solidity in what some think: that this choice of nighttime can be attributed to that supreme reverence which is owed to God when he reveals himself. Specifically, they argue that just as the Seraphim <note>A high-ranking order of angels described in the vision of Isaiah.</note> cover their faces with their wings because of the splendor of the Supreme Majesty, which they cannot look upon with uncovered eyes, so too does a person taught by God at night receive heavenly Revelations as if with a covered face. However, I do not perceive how a person sleeping and lying flat on their back <note>original: "supinus jacens"</note> can exhibit a symbol of reverence.

IX. Closer to the matter are those moral observations suggesting that God...

### CONCERNING THE LADDER OF JACOB

<note>original: "DE SCALA JACOBI"</note>

D 2
<meta>catchword: Sometimes</meta>

...[God] thus wishes to teach that there is no time unsuited for sacred meditations: that God requires a student who is composed and teachable, not argumentative, and who receives divine Revelation without contradiction. He shows that God takes account of us even when we are unable to do so ourselves, and is present with care and affection even for those who sleep. In this way, His power is demonstrated to far exceed our own strengths, because while we can only speak to those who are awake, God can speak even to those who sleep. Moreover, the true nature of our soul becomes known—that it can understand, act, and be taught even without the help of the senses. Indeed, dreams serve as proof that all knowledge of heavenly things in this life is shrouded in darkness. All these things can be piously contemplated and fruitfully deduced as corollaries from this mode of action which God has established, even if they do not express the primary purpose.

X. It is right to establish that primary purpose, which is common to all divine dreams and follows most closely from the nature of the matter. And unless I am much mistaken, it is clearly contrary to the theory I refuted in the first place <note>The author refers to the theory on page 26 that nighttime is naturally "better" for the soul's tranquility.</note>. For since by nature we are all most unfit and unworthy to receive divine light, no one is more unfit than he who lies buried in deep sleep, which is nothing but the "cold image of death" <note>original: "gelidæ nisi mortis imago"; a common classical poetic description of sleep, often attributed to Virgil or Ovid.</note>. When, therefore, the Lord reveals His counsel to a sleeper as easily and clearly as to one who is awake, He most clearly indicates that it is all the same to Him which instruments He uses for His glory. There is nothing in humans that cooperates with His grace; it depends solely on His good pleasure what He wishes to reveal, to whom, in what state, and in what way. No part is left for man except to admire the ways of the Lord; and regarding the prerogative <term>prerogative: here meaning a special privilege or divine favor</term> which God has granted him, all glory must be referred solely to the Author. That aim of God has been constantly present in all kinds of Revelations, and in all Gifts and spiritual endowments <note>original: "Charismatibus"; from the Greek 'charismata,' referring to supernatural gifts given by the Holy Spirit.</note>. And how fully He obtained that aim in this present case, let our own Jacob be an example, who testifies in **verse 16** that this revelation happened to him while he was completely unaware and unsuspecting: *Truly the Lord is in this place; and I did not know it.*

XI. From this general aim, we must distinguish the most specific purposes peculiar to individual divine dreams, which God intends most directly. Sometimes...

<page-num>28</page-num>
<header>DISSERTATION</header>
<meta>catchword: liberans</meta>

...Indeed, sometimes in this way He wished to confirm the divine mission of the true Prophets. He achieved this through Dreams with which He deigned to favor the Gentiles themselves—not so much for their own sake, although it also carried some weight in convincing them, but for the sake of other holy Men whose cause He was championing. Thus, Abimelech’s Dream pertained to the honor of Abraham; Laban’s to the justification of Jacob; that of the Midianite soldier to the glory of Gideon; and the dream of Pilate's wife to demonstrating the innocence of Christ Himself. In the same way, Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar were led by their Dreams to seek their interpretation from Joseph and Daniel, so that it might be even more clearly evident how divine was the Spirit that dwelt within them.

XII. At other times, by infusing Dreams into His Saints, He took their frailty into account. For, as <note>Friedrich Spanheim (1600–1649), a prominent Reformed theologian.</note> SPANHEMIUS rightly notes here, *during the time of night and sleep, God glides into a person without terror, without 그 consternation that the Majesty of God wrests from those who are awake—whom heavenly revelations so strike that, out of awareness of their own weakness and sins, they cannot help but be deeply affected and moved when that supreme Majesty of God offers itself to be beheld more closely.* This was perhaps the reason why the Dreams of the Saints were more frequent under the Dispensation of Promise and the Gospel, and rarer under the Law. This much is certain: if Jacob, who had hitherto been less accustomed to divine visions, had seen this same sight while awake in that vast wilderness, a much greater fear would have seized him.

XIII. Sometimes even the very state of the dreamer had a mystical purpose and belonged to the "type" <note>A 'type' is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic foreshadowing of something in the New Testament.</note> which the entire nocturnal vision displayed. That this also applies here will become clear from the unfolding of the mystery.

XIV. Therefore, the pagan philosophers were mistaken when they judged that no Dreams are divine. ARISTOTLE, in *On Divination through Sleep, Chapter 1*, rejects them because <term>μη τοις βελτιστοις και φρονιμωτατοις, αλλα τοις τυχουσι πεμπειν, ατοπον</term> <note>original Greek: "mē tois beltistois kai phronimōtatois, alla tois tykhousi pempein, atopon"</note>, *it would be absurd to send them not to the best and wisest, but to common and ordinary people.* This can be easily refuted by so many examples of Saints in the Scripture. Epicurus also held a distorted view of Dreams. TERTULLIAN, in *On the Soul, Chapter XLVI*, writes: *Epicurus judged Dreams to be entirely empty.*

<summary>The author explains that God uses dreams to validate his prophets to outsiders and to protect his servants from the overwhelming terror of His direct presence. He refutes Greek philosophers like Aristotle and Epicurus who dismissed the divinity of dreams based on the perceived unworthiness of the recipients.</summary>

<header>CONCERNING JACOB'S LADDER</header>
<sig>D 3</sig>

...freeing the divinity from [earthly] concerns. <note>The author refers to the Epicurean philosophy, which argued that gods were indifferent to human affairs and did not send dreams.</note> In this same spirit, PETRONIUS wrote in his *Satyricon*, chapter 104:
> Dreams, which mock the mind with flitting shadows,
> are sent neither by the shrines of the Gods nor by divine powers from the sky,
> but each person creates them for himself — — — — —

And TIBULLUS in Book III, Elegy IV, verse 7:
> Rash dreams play during the deceptive night,
> And command fearful minds to dread false things.

However, examples found in the sacred scriptures wipe away all this alleged uncertainty regarding divine dreams; these examples flowed into the minds with such clarity that no opportunity remained for doubting their divine origin.

XV. Truly, Jacob’s dream was so arranged that he was most certain of its divine origin. For whether he considered the nature of the dream itself—shining around him with such light, the appearance of Jehovah <note>The personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible, often rendered as "the LORD."</note> being seen and His voice being heard impressing their traces so deeply on his soul—it did not leave him even when he was awake, but urged him to cry out: *How awesome is this place! This place is none other than the House of God, and this is the Gate of Heaven!* (Genesis 28:17). Or, if he compared the substance of this dream with the Revelations that had happened to his Fathers, it agreed so closely both with the manner of their Visions and the things revealed that he easily perceived that the same Jehovah who had spoken to his Fathers had now opened his own eyes. Finally, if in the time following he compared this vision with the eventual outcome—even though he could not have presumed such success in his then-meager state—he could be made as certain as anyone could be of the Divinity of his Dream by its very fulfillment.

XVI. The vision itself, which was presented to him, consisted of three parts. The first was that a Ladder was set up upon the earth and its top reached to heaven. The fancies of the Jews regarding this Ladder are quite fertile. They believe that while its feet rested in Beersheba, the summit touched Bethlehem, but the middle part was over Jerusalem. They measure its width from above as being equal to the world and a third part of it. Some count four steps on the Ladder, others seven, others 180. See JARCHI <note>A common Latinization for Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, 1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> on this passage and MAIMONIDES <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the influential Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note>

<summary>The author refutes the skeptical view of Roman poets who dismissed dreams as mere imagination, using Jacob's Ladder as the primary evidence for truly divine revelation. He describes Jacob's certainty in the vision's origin and begins detailing various Jewish Rabbinic traditions regarding the ladder's physical dimensions and location.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the detailed analysis of Jacob’s dream at Bethel. <page-num>30</page-num>
<header>DISSERTATION</header>

In Maimonides’ *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "More Nevoch"</note> Book II, Chapter 10, and in the *Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer* <note>original: "Pirke R. ELIESERIS"</note> Chapter 35, Hugo Grotius <note>A Dutch jurist and theologian (1583–1645) known for his biblical commentaries.</note> compares this to a passage from the third book of Aristides’ *Sacred Tales*, though it has little relevance to our dream. For nothing occurs in that dream except "ladders that mark the boundary between the things under the earth and those above the earth" <note>original Greek: "κλιμακες, αἱ το ὑπο γης τε και ὑπερ γης ἀφοριζουσι"</note>, that is, steps separating the subterranean and celestial realms. Perhaps, however, Artemidorus took the opportunity from Jacob’s travels to write in his *Interpretation of Dreams* <note>original: "Oneirocritic."</note> Book II, Chapter 47: "A ladder is a sign of travel and transition" <note>original Greek: "Κλιμαξ, ἀποδημιας ἐσι σημαντικη και μεταβασεως"</note>. *A ladder is a sign of pilgrimage and of transition to another place.*

XVII. Our ladder is described as *upright* or *established* <note>Hebrew term: מצב (mutzab)</note>, which indicates not only that it was stretched out toward the heights, but also that it was placed in a stable position on the ground. Hence, Onkelos <note>The author of a famous Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> translates it as *fixed* <note>Aramaic: נציבא (netziba)</note>; Jonathan <note>Refers to the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan.</note> as *standing firm* <note>Aramaic: קיימא (kayama)</note>; and the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> as *firmly set* <note>Greek: ἐστηριγμενη (esterigmenē)</note>, a reading which Philo also follows in his work *On Dreams*.

XVIII. The *head* of this ladder designates its highest part, a concept commonly found in both sacred and secular writers. This head touched *heaven*. The celebrated Heidegger <note>Johann Heinrich Heidegger (1633–1698), a Swiss theologian.</note> understands "heaven" here as the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest part of heaven, believed by ancient and medieval scholars to be the dwelling place of God and the angels.</note>, since it is inhabited by Jehovah and the Angels. Regarding the spiritual mystery, this interpretation can be admitted; however, regarding the literal sense, it is sufficient here to understand the "aerial heaven," which elsewhere is called the *expanse* <note>Hebrew: רקיע (rakia)</note>. Without a doubt, it was similar to what the Elders saw in Exodus 24:10 and Ezekiel Chapters 1:22–23. I would also think that heaven appeared to Jacob as if open or *split*, because Jacob afterwards calls this place the *House of God and the Gate of Heaven*. There would have been an opening, therefore, which bore the likeness of a Gate leading into a majestic Temple; whence also Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Portuguese Jewish statesman and philosopher.</note>, in his commentary on this passage, seems to have perceived the Temple of Jerusalem under this figure. To this opening, as if to the door of a heavenly Palace, the ends of the Ladder were neatly fitted. The same held true in other visions and aligns with the passage in John 1:52. When, however, the Ladder merely "touched" heaven—which was purely emblematic and imaginary—it is suggested that its summit did not enter or penetrate heaven, but only reached it from below.

XIX. Furthermore, there appeared *Angels of God ascending and descending.*

# ON JACOB’S LADDER.
<meta>catchword: XXVIII.</meta>

XIX. Scripture names these Blessed Spirits *Malakhim* <note>Hebrew: מלאכים</note>, from the root *la’ak* <note>Hebrew: לאך</note>, meaning "to send" or "to delegate." This root still survives in the Ethiopic language <note>The author refers to Ge'ez, an ancient Semitic language of Ethiopia used extensively in early biblical scholarship.</note> to designate the office they perform in the economy of salvation <note>A theological term for God's management of the world and the plan for human redemption.</note>. They already fulfilled this role in the time of the Promise <note>The era of the Old Testament Patriarchs before the giving of the Law to Moses.</note>, as is apparent from the history of Abraham and Lot. From this, it is clear that the doctrine of angels could not have been unknown to the Patriarchs; this knowledge was the means by which Jacob recognized the figures he was seeing as being angelic.

XX. For the sake of distinction, these *Angels* are called *Elohim* <note>Hebrew: אלהים</note>. This divine name seems here to express the Triune God Himself, and thus has a broader significance than the name *Jehovah*, which we immediately attribute specifically to the Son <note>The author reflects a common early modern Christian view that the specific name "Jehovah" or the "Angel of the Lord" in the Old Testament often referred specifically to the pre-incarnate Christ.</note>. By this addition, these angels are usually contrasted in the Holy Scriptures with evil angels (as seen in Job 4:18, Psalm 103:20, 104:4, Matthew 22:30, John 1:52, etc.). This contrast is not regarding their origin of essence from God—which they share with demons—but regarding those properties by which they are distinguished from evil angels. They are like "Sons of God" (Job 1:5, 38:7) who, as "Angels of light" (2 Corinthians 11:14), are clothed in the image of God (who is Light). They fulfill His will, devote themselves entirely to His glory, and must be considered as God's ambassadors in the work of salvation.

XXI. The *form* in which they appeared was undoubtedly *human*. We gather this from their ascending and descending on the ladder. They had already appeared in this way to Abraham and Lot, and the same occurred frequently thereafter. This human shape foreshadowed their wisdom and love for humanity <note>original Greek: φιλανθρωπια (philanthropia)</note>. However, their appearance usually breathed something more majestic, which Josephus <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> also records as having been seen here in his *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 1, Chapter 19: "He seemed to see a ladder reaching from the earth to heaven, and through it figures descending, having a more august appearance than belongs to human nature" <note>original Greek: Κλιμακα γηθεν εδοξεν εφικνουμενην του ουρανου βλεπειν, και δι' αυτης οψεις κατιουσας, σεμνοτερον η κατα ανθρωπου φυσιν εχουσας</note>. This is very probable, because their appearance was undoubtedly such that it was easy for the dreaming Jacob to judge the appearing figures to be the shapes of angels. That "more august" quality, when we compare other visions, undoubtedly consists in the bright and fiery aspect they presented. Hence we read of "horses and chariots of fire" (2 Kings 6:17) and an "appearance like lightning" (Matthew 28:3).

<summary>This page discusses the linguistic roots and theological nature of the angels in Jacob's vision, emphasizing their human-like yet majestic and fiery appearance as messengers in God's plan for salvation.</summary>
