->DISSERTATIO<-

XXVIII. 3. Ancient painters imitated this [the angels' brilliance], a practice for which Gregory Nazianzen <note>Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390 AD), an influential theologian and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers" of the early Church.</note> provides the reasoning in his 23rd Oration: *The wearing of bright clothing and radiance is angelic; when they are depicted in bodily form, I believe this is a symbol of their natural purity.* <note>original Greek: Ἀγγελικὸν ἡ λαμπροφορία καὶ φαιδρότης, ὅταν τυπῶνται σωματικῶς, σύμβολον οἶμαι τοῦτο τῆς κατὰ τὴν φύσιν αὐτῶν καθαρότητος. The author provides a Latin translation: "Angelis, quotiescunque corporaliter effigiantur, competit splendidae vestis cultus & nitoris minime vulgaris hilaritas; quod symbolum esse arbitror naturalis illorum puritatis."</note>

XXII. The text indicates that these angelic forms were many in number. The Rabbis restrict this to a group of four. Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar.</note> writes in *The Guide for the Perplexed* (Book II, Chapter 10), from the version by Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a famous Christian Hebraist who translated Maimonides into Latin.</note>: *All the Midrashim* <note>Jewish homiletic commentaries on the Bible.</note> *and all the manuscripts agree on this: that there were four angels whom he saw ascending and descending, and no more; specifically, two ascending and two descending. They were gathered together on one step of the ladder, standing in a single row as two went up and two came down. From this, they taught that the width of the Ladder in the prophetic vision was equal to the world and a third of the world. For the width of a single angel in a prophetic vision was like a third of the world, as it is said: "And his body was like Tarshish."* (Daniel 10:6) <note>Tarshish is often translated as beryl or chrysolite; here, the size or brilliance of the gemstone is used to calculate cosmic proportions.</note> Therefore, if this is the case, the width of four angels would be like the world and a third part of it. And in the parables of Zechariah (Zechariah 6:1), where he describes four chariots coming out from between two mountains of bronze, they expressly say: *These are the four spirits of heaven, who go out from the presence of the Lord of all the earth and are the cause of all things that are renewed.* Similar views occur in the writings of Jarchi <note>Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, 1040–1105), the most famous medieval commentator on the Tanakh.</note> and others. It would have been more successful to compare them to the four living creatures of Ezekiel. These ideas savor of typical Jewish ingenuity. We, however, believe that nothing can be defined with certainty regarding the number.

XXIII. Their activity is described as *ascending and descending*. Whether the same ones ascended and then descended, or whether these different movements belonged to different individuals, is also difficult to determine. The latter seems more likely to the Jews, who, assigning specific angels to individual provinces, believe that those to whom Canaan was committed—and from which they had led Jacob—ascended, while those responsible for Mesopotamia—which Jacob was now entering—descended. See Fagius. <note>Paul Fagius (1504–1549), a German Renaissance scholar of Hebrew.</note>

# ON JACOB’S LADDER.

**E**
<meta>catchword: be</meta>

Fagius <note>Paul Fagius (1504–1549), a German Renaissance scholar of Hebrew and a reformer.</note> on this passage [notes the following]. However, at first, the simplicity of the history seems more persuasive. Generally, this figure indicated the activity of heavenly spirits, specifically in those affairs that concerned both heaven and earth. Plato also attributed such an ascent and descent to his own <term>Daemons</term> <note>In ancient Greek philosophy, "daemons" were not evil spirits, but benevolent intermediary beings between gods and humans.</note>. Plutarch <note>A Greek-Roman philosopher and historian (c. 46–120 AD).</note> writes in *On Isis and Osiris*: <note>original Greek: Ὅτε Πλατων ἑρμηνευτικον το τοιουτον ὀνομαζει γενος, και διακονικον, ἐν μεσῳ Θεων και ἀνθρωπων, εὐχας μεν ἐκει και δεησεις ἀνθρωπων ἀναπεμποντας, ἐκειθεν δε μαντεια δευρο και δοσεις ἀγαθων φεροντας.</note> *And Plato also says that this class of beings performs the duty of interpreters and ministers between men and Gods: who carry the vows and prayers of men from here to the Gods, and bring back oracles and the gifts of good things from there to men.* Apuleius <note>A Roman philosopher (c. 124–170 AD) best known for his Platonist writings and the novel *The Golden Ass*.</note> teaches the same in *On the God of Socrates*: *Furthermore, there are certain divine intermediate powers, between the highest heavens and the lowest earths, situated in that space of air, through which our desires and merits travel to the Gods. These they call by the Greek name <term>daimones</term>; they are carriers between mortals and the inhabitants of heaven, of prayers from the former and gifts from the latter.* A similar point is suggested by a passage from Hesiod <note>An ancient Greek poet, often cited alongside Homer.</note> in *Works and Days*, Book I, verse 124, where he says of the Daemons:
> *Clothed in air, they travel everywhere upon the earth.* <note>original Greek: Ἠερα ἑσσαμενοι, παντη φοιτωντες ἐπ’ αἰαν. Latin: "Aerem induti, passim venientes in terram."</note>

Pfanner <note>Tobias Pfanner (1641–1716), a historian of theology.</note> in *Theology of the Gentiles* (Chapter VI, Section 2) and Vossius <note>Gerardus Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar and theologian.</note> in *On Idolatry* (Book I, Chapter 7) teach that this was consistent with the doctrine of Osthanes, Zoroaster, Orpheus, Thales, Pythagoras, and other most ancient philosophers among the nations, to whom this dogma could have flowed from Patriarchal tradition.

XXIV. The most important part of the Dream remains: *And the Lord [Jehovah] stood above it.* Without any reason, Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian often known for his literalist and rationalist approach to scripture.</note> departs from the simplicity of the literal text—to which he otherwise clings more than is right—when he understands the name **JEHOVAH** to mean *a more distinguished Angel who represented the person of God.* Clericus <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a Genevan theologian and biblical critic who followed Grotius's methods.</note> follows in his footsteps, even adding on his own that wherever we read in the Old Testament of Jehovah being seen, nothing prevents us from understanding them to be Angels. He argues this is to avoid violating the grammatical sense of John 1:18, which says *that no one has ever seen God.* He believes this is confirmed by the fact that Jehovah is said to have *stood* (in Hebrew: <note>original Hebrew: נצב - nitsav</note> *nitsav*), a posture proper to the human form...

# DISSERTATION

-> 34 <-

...[he] thinks it is, with which God is not clothed. <note>This likely refers to a specific scholarly opinion mentioned on the preceding page regarding the "form" or "clothing" of the divine presence.</note> To refute this opinion, it was not necessary to prove two theses which we consider to be most true, and which, once established, cause all doubt in this matter to vanish. One is that the name **Jehovah** is never attributed to any creature, neither metonymically nor metaphorically <note>Metonymy is using the name of one thing for another it is associated with; a metaphor is a symbolic comparison. The author argues "Jehovah" is a name reserved exclusively for the Creator.</note>. The other is that a human form was often the representation of God in Visions. We would be spread too thin if we wished to dwell on these points, which we believe have been abundantly proven and demonstrated by others against the enemies of the **Deity of Christ**.

XXV. Nor do we have need of these evasions, since the present history contains within its heart various arguments which place it beyond controversy that Jehovah, seen at the top of the Ladder, represented the true God Himself. For **first**, in the figure itself, being placed above the Angels, He is excluded from their number. He is the one to whom they ascend and from whom they descend; they are, therefore, His attendants and ministers. **Second**, He speaks such words as belong only to the Most High God in verses 13, 14, and 15: *I am Jehovah, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Ego Jehova Deus Abraham, Patris tui, & Deus Isaaci, &c."</note>

XXVI. So that the force of this argument might be evaded, it is usually claimed that it was a settled custom for the **Ambassadors of Princes** to speak as if the Prince himself were present. For this matter, examples are brought forward from 1 Kings 5:2-3: *Solomon sent to Hiram, saying: "You know that David my father could not build a house to the name of Jehovah his God."* <note>original Latin: "Misit Salomo ad Hiramum, dicendo: nosti Davidem patrem meum non potuisse ædificare nomini Jehovæ Dei sui."</note> Also Luke 7:6: *The Centurion sent friends to Christ, saying: "Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof."* <note>original Latin: "Centurio mittit ad Christum amicos, dicens: Domine noli vexari, non enim sum dignus, ut sub tectum meum intres."</note> And 1 Samuel 25:40, where Abigail speaks to the messengers of David as if he were David himself: *Behold, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.* <note>original Latin: "Abigail ad Legatos Davidis, ac si ipse Davides esset, loquitur: En famulam tuam, in ancillam, ad abluendos pedes servorum Domini mei."</note> Exodus 6:6 and 7:17 are also cited. Furthermore, similar examples from secular authors are added for illustration. Thus **Quintilian** <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus (c. 35–100 AD), a Roman rhetorician.</note> in *Institutes of Oratory* 4.4 says: *A Roman Knight, to whom Augustus sent someone while he was drinking during the games to say to him: "If I want to eat lunch, I go home."* <note>original Latin: "Eques Romanus, ad quem cum in spectaculis bibentem misit Augustus, qui ei diceret: Ego si prandere volo, domum eo." This illustrates a messenger using the first person ("I") to speak for the Emperor.</note> In the same way, a King is said to have written what a royal Scribe penned, because the King used the Scribe's hand as if it were his own; hence it happens that the Scribe in a decree or letter speaks as the King himself would speak if he were writing with his own hand. Similarly, when patrons among the Greeks and Romans [presented] themselves...

XXVI. ...they spoke of the defendants, and spoke in the same manner as the defendants themselves could have; yet no one suspected for that reason that the advocate was being called the "defendant" or was attributing the defendant's deeds to himself. <note>The author is using a legal analogy: just as a lawyer says "I did not do this" on behalf of a client without people thinking the lawyer is the criminal, some argue an angel says "I am God" without being God.</note> Theodor Hackspan <note>A 17th-century Lutheran theologian and Orientalist.</note> proves that the Jews also favored this opinion in his notes on Lipmann’s *Nizzachon* <note>original: "Nizzachon Lipmanni"; a famous Jewish polemical work by Yom-Tov Lipmann-Muhlhausen intended to refute Christian interpretations of the Bible.</note> p. 361. See Jean Le Clerc on Genesis 16:13, Crellius *On God* chapter 11, Episcopius’s *Theological Institutes* book II, chapter I, and the anonymous author in *Bilibra Veritatis et Rationis* p. 188 and following.

XXVII. Although these arguments are presented plausibly, we are moved by fundamental reasons to withhold our approval. <note>original: "pollicem præbeamus," literally "to give the thumb," a Roman expression for approval.</note> For even if it is granted that these examples are appropriate, the proponents of the opposing view will gain nothing from it. There is nothing preventing men from performing the role of other men and making the words of others their own, because of the common frailty of the human condition. But God has never imposed His own role upon any creature. The *Prophets*, although they speak in the name of God, always insist that *“God has said.”* *God has not given His glory to another* (Isaiah 42:8). And certainly, if He had given it, He would have led the faithful into the danger of idolatry <term>idolatry: the worship of a created thing instead of the Creator</term>. Nor would it have been absurd to offer divine worship to those who acted in the place of God Himself; yet this honor is expressly denied to Angels in Revelation 19:10 and 22:9.

XXVIII. Furthermore, the examples cited are many miles apart <note>original: "longissimis parasangis," using an ancient Persian measure of distance to mean "vastly different."</note> from our passage and similar ones. For **1.** although sometimes the words of others are uttered by someone else as if they were their own, never in a narrative of an actual event is the name of the Sovereign given to the Ambassador, as is supposed to happen here. **2.** In the passages cited, the distinction between the speakers and those in whose name the speech is made is evident, whereas here no such distinction appears. **3.** In most places, the speech is elliptical <note>meaning some words are omitted but understood from context.</note> and must be filled in from the context. For I have no doubt that the ambassadors of Solomon and the Centurion <note>References to 1 Kings 5 (Solomon's messengers to Hiram) and Matthew 8 (the Centurion sending friends to Jesus).</note>, who brought words from Solomon and the Centurion—spoken just as they appear in the text—to Hiram and Christ, even if they had kept the same syllables, which however...

### DISSERTATION

-> 36 <-

...it is difficult to prove that they [messengers] always prefixed the names of those who sent them. It was certainly necessary, for instance, that the envoys of Solomon should speak in this way: *King Solomon said: You knew my father David, etc.* Without this, it would not have been clear to Hiram in whose name the envoys were speaking. The same holds true in the passage of Exodus 6:5–6, where Jehovah commands Moses: *Say to the children of Israel, I am Jehovah, etc.* When Moses reported these words to Israel, he undoubtedly prefaced them by saying that these were the words of Jehovah. And since such a preface is explicitly expressed in another passage, Exodus 7:17, that case clearly does not apply here. The words of Abigail are likewise irrelevant <note>original Greek: "ἀλλότρια" (allotria); meaning "foreign to the matter" or "beside the point."</note> to this argument. For even if we were to grant that her words were a kind of apostrophe <note>A rhetorical figure where a speaker turns away from the immediate audience to address an absent person or personified object.</note> to the absent David as if he were present, they would still have been directed only to David, not to the envoys. But the context clearly shows that Abigail was committing herself to the service not only of David but also of these servants of his, and thus she was directly addressing the one who was the head of this delegation. As for other examples drawn from common usage, they prove nothing; for here we are discussing formulas peculiar to the sacred style regarding the God of Israel, and they can easily be dismissed by these same observations.

XXIX. Now comes the *Third* point: the declaration of Jacob’s faith, displayed immediately after he woke up, from which it is clear that the Patriarch was most firmly convinced that Jehovah Himself had appeared to him. For in verse 16, he says at once: *Truly Jehovah is in this place.* It is suggested here in vain that Jacob spoke this way out of ignorance or error. For it would be too meager a judgment of the Patriarchs’ faith to think they were ignorant of the fact that God is present everywhere on earth. And could it not be considered that God Himself confirmed Jacob in this error, who in Genesis 31:13 says to him in another dream: *I am that strong God of Bethel, where you anointed the pillar, where you vowed a vow to me?* Or how could Jacob be cleared of the crime of idolatry, he who built an altar to that very God <note>original Hebrew: "אלהים" (Elohim)</note> who had revealed Himself to him? Genesis 35:7: *And he built there an altar to the strong God of Bethel, just as he had named that place: because there God had revealed Himself to him, when he fled in fear of his brother.* This faith of Jacob is most clearly defended in Hosea 12:4–5: *At Bethel he found him (namely, the Angel) and there he spoke* <note>The text ends mid-sentence with the catchword "loque-" from the Latin "loquebatur" (he spoke).</note>

-> 37 <-

...was speaking with us. *And Jehovah, God of hosts, Jehovah is his memorial.* <note>The author concludes a citation from Hosea 12:4–5, arguing that the figure who spoke to Jacob is identified directly as the Lord (Jehovah).</note>

XXX. Our fourth argument in favor of our position is the very nature of this revelation, which was nothing other than a *Vision*, and indeed one offered not to the external senses, but to the imagination alone through sleep. In that vision, only emblematic appearances of various subjects were shown, not the subjects themselves. Therefore, there is no reason to introduce an Angel here speaking in the name of Jehovah, since divine power alone was active here to display to Jacob an emblem of the great mystery of godliness. I need not mention that Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note>, Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC – 50 AD), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who used allegorical interpretation.</note>, and various other Jewish and Christian interpreters generally agree with our opinion.

XXXI. The arguments brought forward to the contrary, however, are easily struck down. For as to what is urged from the passage in John 1:18, *that no one has ever seen God*, however this saying is understood—whether of physical or spiritual vision—it has no bearing on this matter. For he who sees an emblem, by which God displays certain of His works and certain divine perfections to be demonstrated in their execution, can in no way be judged to have seen God in His essence with his physical eyes. But if those words refer to spiritual vision, or a more excellent degree of knowledge, then even he to whom some riddle of the virtues and ways of God is shown has not yet known God adequately or in the most excellent way. We will shortly indicate what force the word <term>נצח</term> <note>original Hebrew: "nitzach"; often translated in this context as "standing" or "overseeing," referring to God's position at the top of the ladder in Genesis 28:13.</note> carries in this connection.

XXXII. Furthermore, it is most clearly established, not only from the words of the Savior in John 1:52, but also from the Patriarchal history itself, that the *Jehovah* who appears to Jacob here is none other than the Son of God himself. Thus, in Genesis 31:11, 13: *Moreover, the Angel of God said to me in a dream, "Jacob"; and I said, "Here I am" — — — "I am that strong God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar, etc."* Hence, in Genesis 48:15–16, Jacob himself speaks in this way: *May the God in whose presence my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked without ceasing, the God who has fed me from my beginning even to this day, the Angel who delivers me from all evil, bless—* <meta>catchword: the boys (pueris)</meta>

-> 38 <-

...**these boys.** Anyone who compares this description of God with the words of Jehovah in our dream (verses 13 and 15) cannot doubt that Jacob is speaking of the same subject. Furthermore, in the passage from Hosea just cited, the one whom Jacob found at **Bethel** is described as an **Angel, whose memorial is Jehovah.** Now, Christian interpreters have abundantly proved that this Angel of God and Redeemer <term>Goël: a Hebrew term for a kinsman-redeemer, one who recovers or vindicates the rights and property of a relative</term>—who is called at once the God of Abraham and Isaac and the mighty God of Bethel—is none other than the Son of God. Consult, among others, Johann Jacob Cramer <note>Johann Jacob Cramer (1673–1702) was a German Reformed theologian who wrote extensively on the concept of the "Goel" as a type for Christ.</note> in *On the Redeemer*, book 2, chapter 1, and *Theology of Israel*, part 2, pages 35–36.

XXXIII. That this was not unknown in ancient Jewish teaching is proven even by a passage from Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC – 50 AD), a Jewish philosopher who blended Greek philosophy with biblical study.</note> in his work *On Dreams* (p. 599) regarding the words of Genesis 31:13: **He now calls God his most ancient Word** <note>original Greek: Καλεῖ δὲ τὸν Θεὸν τὸν πρεσβύτατον αὐτοῦ νυνὶ λόγον (Kalei de ton Theon ton presbytaton autou nyni logon). In Philo’s thought, the "Logos" or Word is the intermediary between God and the world.</note>. He understood the same thing regarding the Redeeming Angel in book 2 of his *Allegorical Interpretation of the Law* (p. 93). There is an excellent passage on this matter by Rabbi Moses Gerundensis <note>Also known as Nachmanides or Ramban (1194–1270), a prominent Spanish Sephardic rabbi and scholar.</note> on Exodus 23:20–21: **And according to the truth, this Angel is the Vindicating Angel, in whose midst is that great Name. And he is the one who said: "I am the God of Bethel." For it is the custom of a King to dwell in his house. And our Masters have said that he is the Metatron.** <term>Metatron: A high-ranking angel in Jewish mystical literature, often described as the "Prince of the Countenance" or a divine mediator who carries the name of God.</term> And am I mistaken? Or does the praise of **Wisdom** found in the *Book of the Wisdom of Solomon* (chapter 10, verse 10) apply to the same: **She guided the righteous man [Jacob], a fugitive from his brother’s wrath, along straight paths; she showed him the kingdom of God [specifically in this dream] and gave him knowledge of holy things.** <note>original Greek: Αὕτη φυγάδα ὀργῆς ἀδελφοῦ δίκαιον ὡδήγησεν ἐν τρίβοις εὐθείαις ἔδειξεν αὐτῷ βασιλείαν Θεοῦ, καὶ ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ γνῶσιν ἁγίων (Autē phygada orgēs adelphou dikaion hōdēgēsen en tribois eutheiais edeixen autō basileian Theou, kai edōken autō gnōsin hagiōn).</note> This observation is of the greatest importance, because it establishes that the God who appeared so frequently to the Patriarchs in visible form was consistently the Son of God, and that even then He was marked by the name **Jehovah**.

XXXIV. And certainly, the emphasis of this name belongs preeminently to the Son of God, because the truth, faithfulness, and constancy of God—which God specifically wished to bear witness to through this name—is most fully manifested through Him and will be demonstrated at the completion of salvation. We may speak more on this in another place. For our part here, especially...

XXXIV. We particularly congratulate ourselves on the consensus of the Jews, who in great numbers and in many passages of the Old Testament understand the "Son of God" through the name *Jehovah*. This has been demonstrated by very many scholars, among whom we praise here Raymundus Martin <note>Raymundus Martin (c. 1220–1285) was a Dominican friar and author of *Pugio Fidei* (Dagger of Faith), a work that used Jewish texts to argue for Christian truths.</note> in *Dagger of Faith*, part III, book 3, chapter 2; Edzard <note>Esdras Edzard (1629–1708) was a German Hebraist known for his efforts to convert Jews in Hamburg through Rabbinical scholarship.</note> in *Berachot*, volume 1, page 235 and following; and Cramer in *Theology of Israel*, part II, dissertation 1, chapter 8. This supports our point all the more because of the great reverence—verging on superstition—that the Jews show toward this name, and because they occasionally admit that it is attributed to the Messiah by way of excellence. Thus, in the **Midrash Tehillim** <note>A Rabbinic commentary (Midrash) on the Psalms, also known as *Midrash Shocher Tov*.</note>, folio 19, on Psalm 21:

<note>original Hebrew: מלך בשר ודם אין קוראים לסגן שלו בשמו וגו׳ והקב״ה קורא משיח על שמו ומה שמו יהוה איש מלחמה ומלך המשיח וזה שמו אשר יקראו יהוה צדקנו :</note>
*It is not common to call the deputy of a mortal king by the name of the King himself. But God, the Blessed One, calls the Messiah by His own name. And what then is the name of God? **Jehovah, a Man of War** (Exodus 15:3). And what is the name of the King Messiah? **This is the name by which they shall call him: JEHOVAH our righteousness.** (Jeremiah 23:6).*

XXXV. Although the text does not indicate in what form Jehovah appeared, we are nevertheless easily inclined to believe that it was a human form. Indeed, the name of "Angel" <note>The author argues that because the figure is called an "Angel" elsewhere, and angels typically appeared as men, the figure must have looked like a man.</note>—which is given to the Jehovah appearing here in parallel passages—insinuates this. For it was the constant custom of angels to appear in human form. Additionally, the Fathers <note>The "Patriarchs" or early biblical ancestors.</note> had been accustomed to this pattern ever since Paradise, and it was preserved in the times that followed. It is perhaps from this that Jacob, in the place cited, calls the Jehovah who had appeared to him the <term>Angel ha-Goel: The Redeeming Angel; "Goel" refers to a kinsman-redeemer who acts on behalf of a relative</term>, a name which, likely even before the Law of Moses, noted a "closeness of flesh" <note>An allusion to the Incarnation—the idea that the Redeemer would become "kin" to humanity by taking on a human body.</note>.

XXXVI. Since we have already proven that the other angels were also clothed in human form, it is easy to imagine that, besides the form which he held in common with the rest of the angelic host, there was some sign in this vision by which Jehovah could be distinguished from the others. According to Le Clerc <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Swiss theologian and biblical critic known for his rationalist approach.</note>, all inquiry into this matter should be dismissed as useless. However, we do not give up hope so easily. Indeed, it seems very probable to us that this human form was surrounded by a certain bright cloud, shimmering with a fiery splendor, and rising in the manner of a pyramidal column.

<meta>This page continues the author’s argument that the various appearances of God to the Patriarchs were unified by a consistent physical symbol—specifically a cloud of fire—to ensure they recognized the speaker as Jehovah, the God of their fathers.</meta>

### DISSERTATION

-> 40 <-

XXXVII. It was certainly very fitting that Jehovah, appearing so frequently to the Patriarchs, would constantly use some certain symbol known to them through both tradition and their own subsequent experience. This would allow them to be certain from the very beginning that no one other than Jehovah, the God of the Fathers, was addressing them. Now indeed, there are many things that suggest that the most constant symbol of the divine presence—not only later under the Law, but already under the Promise—was such a cloud. Immediately after the Fall, we believe something analogous to this appearance occurs in that vision described in Genesis 3:24, where joined with the Cherubim is <note>original Hebrew: להט החרב המתהפכת</note> **the flame of a whirling sword**, or as others prefer, a double-edged or self-turning sword (meaning inverted), which the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translates as *strephomenēn* <note>original Greek: στρεφομενην, meaning "turning" or "revolving."</note>. Behold: 1.) a flame surrounded by Cherubim, just as later appeared above the Ark of the Covenant; 2.) a flame having the likeness of an upright and inverted sword, which closely resembles a pointed pillar. 

Nor is the symbol in Genesis 15:17 dissimilar, where Abraham *saw* <note>original Hebrew: לפיד אש</note> **a torch of fire passing between those pieces**, which in a unique way served as a prelude to the manifestation of God among Israel. For this reason, Borrhaus <note>Martin Borrhaus (1499–1564), also known as Cellarius, was a Protestant reformer and commentator known for his works on the Pentateuch.</note> rightly thinks, in his commentary on this passage, that the same symbol occurs here as was later exhibited on Mount Sinai. Yet nothing relates more closely to this matter than the vision of Moses in Exodus 3:2, where the *Angel of Jehovah* appeared to him <note>original Hebrew: בלבת אש</note> **in a flame of fire**, who said to Moses in verse 6: *I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob*; by this very statement, he was implying that he was appearing to Moses in the same manner as he had been seen by the Patriarchs. 

Rabbi Meir ben Gabbai <note>A significant 16th-century Spanish-Jewish Kabbalist whose work *Avodat HaKodesh* (Holy Service) explores the relationship between God and the world.</note> acknowledges in *Holy Service*, Part III, chapter 31, that it is indeed the same one who appeared to Jacob at Bethel and to Moses at Horeb:

<note>original Hebrew: מה שכתוב ויאמר אלי מלאך האלהים בחלום יעקב ואמר הנני אין זה מן הנפרדים אבל הוא המלאך הגואל אותו מכל רע ולוה אמר אנכי האל ביתאל ונקרא מלאך לסוד שאבאר במה שיבא במ"ד והוא הנאמר בו וירא מלאך יי' אליו בלבת אש מתוך הסנה :</note>

### ON JACOB’S LADDER

...he is called the *Angel in Mystery*, which, with God’s help, I will explain in what follows. And it is of him that it is said: *And the Angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire in the middle of the bush.* The description of this vision in the writings of PHILO (in the first book of *The Life of Moses*) is not irrelevant <note>original: ἀπροσδιόνυσος (aprosdionysos), a Greek idiom meaning "beside the point" or "unrelated to Dionysus."</note> here: *From the midst of the flame there shone forth a most beautiful form, unlike any visible thing, a most god-like image, flashing with a light more brilliant than the fire itself, which one might suspect to be the Image of Him Who Is.* <note>original Greek: Κατα δε μεσην την φλογα μορφη τις ην περικαλλιστατη, των ὁρατων ἐμφερης οὐδενι, θεοειδεστατον ἀγαλμα, φως αὐγοειδεστερον του πυρος ἀπαστραπτουσα, ἡν ἀν τις ὑπετυπησεν εἰκονα του Ὀντος εἶναι.</note> Why then should we not believe that in other visions, even though no explicit mention is made of such a form, it nevertheless appeared?

XXXVIII. In our current passage, this becomes even more probable because those visions which were displayed from the clouds—as if heaven were opened—were everywhere joined with a shining cloud (Exodus 24:10; Ezekiel 1:4, 10:1–2; Daniel 7:9–10; Matthew 17:5). Indeed, one may suggest that Jacob wished to create some representation of this vision when, in memory of it, he set up the *stone* which had served as his pillow as a <term>cippus<note>A small pillar or memorial stone used by the ancients to mark a sacred or significant site.</note></term> or *column* (verse 18). <note>original Hebrew: מצבה (matzevah), referring to a standing stone or pillar.</note> Since that first memorial was quite rough, Jacob substituted another in Genesis 35:15 which more closely resembled a column. From this, it happened that the *column* became a symbol of divinity among most nations from the most ancient times; we have already discussed this in our dissertation on the "horn of salvation" inserted in the *Bremische Bibliothek*, Class II, page 686 and following. 

Nor should I now overlook the <term>Baetylia<note>From the Hebrew "Bethel," these were sacred stones or meteorites worshipped in the ancient Near East as dwelling places of a deity.</note></term> stones mentioned by SANCHUNIATHON <note>A Phoenician author whose fragments are preserved by the historian Eusebius.</note> in EUSEBIUS’S *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book I, chapter 10: *The god Uranus invented Baetylia, having fashioned animated stones.* <note>original Greek: Επενοησε Θεος οὐρανος βαιτυλια, λιθους ἐμψυχους μηχανησαμενος.</note> Many learned men have perhaps exercised their wits on these stones more than was necessary. It is easily seen that the word *Baetylia* is formed from *Beth-el* <note>original Hebrew: בית אל (House of God).</note>. As for the notion of them being "animated" <note>original: ἐμψυχων (empsychon), meaning "having a soul" or "living."</note> stones, if I may offer my own conjecture after so many others, the idea could easily have arisen from the root *bsm* <note>original: בשם</note>, which among the Syrians signifies not only *to breathe* but also *to smell*, from which comes a certain kind of ointment among the Chaldeans. Nevertheless, since Sanchu—

# DISSERTATION

-> 42 <-

Since it has been proved by others that the work of Sanchuniathon <note>An ancient Phoenician author whose writings were claimed to be discovered by Philo of Byblos, though many Enlightenment scholars, as noted here, suspected they were a "Jewish fraud" or a later invention.</note> is a forgery and reeks of Jewish deception, we will gain little from it for our purpose. However, regarding the anointing of this stone pillar—the reason for which ritual is not entirely clear—it is possible that through that oil, the fiery splendor of that same column could be somehow represented. But lest we seem to indulge too much in conjecture here, we will "roll this stone" <note>A Latin idiom (*saxum hoc volvere*) meaning to labor over or dwell on a specific problem.</note> no further.

XXXIX. This seems to have been the reason why the CHALDEAN <note>Referring to the Aramaic Targums, which were Jewish paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translated our passage: *And behold, the glory of the LORD was established above it.* <note>original Aramaic: והא יקרא דיי מעתד עלוהי</note> For it is well known that "the glory of the LORD," in a stricter sense, is used to denote such a physical sign of the divine presence. To this same point belongs the fact that the Jews—who, following the Aramaic Paraphrasts, call this sign the **SCHECHINAH** <term>Shekhinah<note>From the Hebrew root "to dwell," referring to the divine presence or "settling" of God among humanity, often depicted as a cloud or light.</note></term>—believe on this basis that the Shekhinah was not unknown to Jacob. Thus REKANATENSIS <note>Menahem Recanati, a 13th-century Italian rabbi and kabbalist.</note> writes on Genesis 31:13:

*The Angel mentioned above in verse 11 said to Jacob: "I am the God of Bethel." This implies the SHEKHINAH, who is called "Angel," because it was she who appeared to the Patriarchs, and it was to her that his vow was directed; therefore it says in verse 13, "to whom you made a vow there." She is also called "Angel" because this world is governed by her command.* <note>original Hebrew: המלאך הנזכר למעלה אמר לו אנכי האל בית אל כי היא הנראות לאבות ואליה היה הנדר וע'כ אמר אשר נדרת לי שם נדר ונקראת מלאך יען היות הנהגת העולם הזה על פיה:</note>

Add to this Rabbi BECHAI <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish commentator.</note> in his commentary on the Law, folio 95:

*Now this Glory is the one who said to Jacob: I AM THE GOD OF BETHEL (Gen. 31:13), because this Glory is the God of his father, just as it was said to Moses (Exodus 3:6): "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob."* <note>original Hebrew: והכבוד הזה הוא שאמר ליעקב אנכי האל בית אל כי הכבוד הזה הוא אלהי אביו מכן אמר לו אנכי אלהי אביך אלהי אברהם ואלהי יצחק ואלהי יעקב</note>

Rabbi MANASSEH BEN ISRAEL <note>A famous 17th-century Portuguese rabbi and diplomat based in Amsterdam.</note> in *The Conciliator*, question 64 on Genesis, page 87:

*I say that Jacob directed his prayers in Genesis 48:15–16 to the First Cause, but he directed his understanding most perfectly to that one through whom God was intended to act.*

And as Rabbi Bahre learnedly says, he began with *Elohim* <note>God</note> and ended with *Angel*, that is, the *Angel who is the* **SCHECHINAH**, *as Rabbi Joseph Gikatilla says, who unites the entire structure and the world of the ten illustrious lights <note>Referring to the ten Sefirot, or divine emanations in Kabbalah.</note>, as anyone skilled in this doctrine will be able to note there.*

...is. Hence the words of Genesis 45:27, *And the spirit of Jacob revived*, were interpreted by RABBI SOLOMON <note>Rabbi Solomon Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah.</note> as: "The Shekhinah rested upon him" <note>original Hebrew: שרתה עליו שכינה</note>. WAGENSEIL <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil (1633–1705), a Christian Hebraist and theologian.</note> noted this in his work *Sota*, page 83.

XL. Regarding the *location* of this illustrious phenomenon, it is noted that it *stood above the ladder*. Here the word *nitsab* <note>original Hebrew: נצב, meaning to stand, be stationed, or be established.</note> occurs again; since it is used for anything standing tall and stretched upward, it refers not only to a human figure but also to the bright cloud itself. The place where it stood was "over it" <note>original Hebrew: עליו</note>, *above the ladder*, so that the ladder seemed to support it like a column. Hence the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> says: *The Lord was firmly established upon it.* <note>original Greek: Ὁ κυριος ἐπεστηρικτο ἐπ’ αὐτης</note> Those who wander from the path here are those who, like SANTE PAGNINO <note>An Italian Dominican and leading Hebraist of the Renaissance (1470–1541).</note>, translate the Hebrew word *alav* as "beside," or those who, like ALCASAR <note>Ludovicus ab Alcasar (1554–1613), a Spanish Jesuit theologian.</note> in his commentary on Revelation 4:1, believe the Lord stood by this ladder on earth rather than in heaven, arguing that Jehovah could only speak to the sleeping Jacob from nearby on the ground—a reasoning so empty that it seems to belong to a dreamer rather than one who is awake.

XLI. The little word *behold* <note>original Hebrew: הנה (*hineh*)</note> must not be overlooked here. Its general use—to indicate something new, wondrous, joyful, or noteworthy, and to demand the close attention of others—is too well known to dwell on explaining it. Therefore, we note here only its threefold repetition for each part of the vision. This repetition commands us: 1. to pause with renewed attention at each stage of this vision, in which the scenes are arranged so that the later part is always more illustrious than the former. It was already a great thing to see heaven opened and a ladder reaching it; it was greater to see the Angels ascending and descending on the ladder; and it was greatest of all to see Jehovah at the summit. Furthermore, 2. the history intends to express that these scenes were presented to Jacob not all at once, but successively. First he saw the sky split and the ladder erected. After a short interval, the Angels appeared on the ladder. Finally, he gazed upon the Lord above the ladder.

The place of its stationing was *alav* <note>original Hebrew: עליו</note>, *above the ladder*, such that the ladder appeared to support it like a column. Hence the **SEPTUAGINT** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> renders it: *The Lord was firmly set upon it.* <note>original Greek: Ὁ κυριος ἐπεστηρικτο ἐπ’ αὐτης</note> Those who wander from the path here include **SANTE PAGNINO** <note>An Italian Dominican and leading Hebraist of the Renaissance (1470–1541).</note>, who translates the Hebrew *al* as "beside," and **ALCASAR** <note>Luis del Alcázar (1554–1613), a Spanish Jesuit theologian.</note> in his commentary on Revelation 4:1, who thinks that the Lord stood by this ladder on the earth rather than in heaven, because Jehovah could only have spoken to Jacob—who was sleeping on the ground—from a nearby position. This reasoning is so empty that it seems more like the thought of a dreamer than one who is awake.

XLI. The little word *hinneh* <note>Hebrew for "Behold" or "Look!"</note> should not be neglected here. Its general use—to indicate something new, wonderful, joyful, and worthy of observation, demanding the close attention of others—is too well known for us to dwell on explaining it. Therefore, we note here only its triple repetition for each part of the vision. This repetition commands us: 1. To pause with fresh attention at each individual stage of this vision, in which the images are arranged so that the later part is always more illustrious than the former. It was already a great thing to see the heavens opened and a ladder reaching toward them; it was greater still to see the Angels ascending and descending on the ladder; but it was greatest of all to see **JEHOVAH** at the very top. Furthermore, 2. the history intends to express that these images were presented to Jacob not all at once, but successively. First, he saw the sky split and the ladder erected. After a short interval, the Angels appeared on the ladder. Finally, he gazed upon the Lord standing above the ladder.

XLII. There have been some who compared this vision to the fiction of **HOMER** in the *Iliad*, book 8, where Jupiter calls together all the Gods and Goddesses—

### III.
## THEOLOGICAL DISSERTATION
### ON THE
# MYSTERY
# OF JACOB’S LADDER.

### I.

That the dream of Jacob breathes a mystical sense and is a representation of something more sublime is denied by certain men who cling too closely to the literal letter, among whom are Franciscus Junius <note>François du Jon (1545–1602), a Huguenot theologian and professor at Leiden.</note> and Sebastian Schmidt <note>Sebastian Schmidt (1617–1696), a prominent Lutheran theologian and commentator.</note>; which is something we wish they had not done. For who would judge it consistent with Divine Wisdom to present images signifying nothing to the imagination of men? Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers.</note> rightly says in *Sermon 122, § 2*: *A man’s dream would not be described unless some great mystery were figured in it, and some great truth of the Prophets were understood in that vision.* For what purpose was such a great preparation made? To what end was the Ladder shown?

->## ON THE MYSTERY OF JACOB’S LADDER.<-

[F 3]

...to what purpose were there visible forms of Jehovah and the Angels, which are so fundamentally different from spiritual natures? How false a conception of them would Scripture produce, if these were not figures of spiritual things? The same is confirmed by the analogy of so many other dreams, to which the Holy Spirit added a clear explanation. And this has been the common opinion of nearly all Interpreters, both Jewish and Christian, who have labored competitively—though with unequal success—in interpreting this dream. It would be a fruitless labor to review their various opinions, especially since others have already taken up that task. A full measure <note>original: "Lancem saturam," literally a full dish, referring here to a comprehensive or overflowing account.</note> will be provided by PERERIUS <note>Benito Pereira (1535–1610), a Spanish Jesuit theologian.</note> and CORNELIUS A LAPIDE <note>Cornelis Cornelissen van den Steen (1567–1637), a Flemish Jesuit and influential biblical commentator.</note> in their commentaries on Genesis at this passage; SCOTANUS in *Biblia Sacra*, Volume I, Part II, page 318 and following; HEIDEGGER in *History of the Patriarchs*, Book II, Exercise 16, section 7 and following; PFEIFFER in *Vexing Doubts*, Century I, Location 57, etc.

### II.

Many of the ancients stumble in this: they hardly progress beyond the general governance of divine providence in explaining the meaning of this dream, even though that would provide little comfort for Jacob in his present state; and because they do not properly build their interpretations upon the analogy and sacred emblems found in other places, nor on the parts of this dream considered in their own connection—by which means every interpretation of sacred symbols is rendered vague.

### III.

Even those who seek here the mystery of grace and the future redemption promised to the Fathers through the Seed <note>A reference to the "Seed of Abraham," traditionally interpreted by Christians as the coming Messiah or Christ.</note>, are nonetheless often occupied by the prejudice that they take the *Ladder* itself as a *type* <note>In biblical studies, a "type" is a person, event, or object in the Old Testament seen as a prophetic symbol of something in the New Testament.</note> of *Christ*, even though they differ greatly in other circumstances. By examining the meditations of some of them in advance, we shall pave a convenient path for proposing our own opinion.

### IV.

The commentary of RIVET <note>André Rivet (1572–1651), a French Huguenot theologian.</note> in his *Exercises on Genesis*, Exercise 124, page 482, has pleased many; he writes: *We refer this vision to the perpetual administration of the Kingdom of Christ on earth, so that the Ladder is Christ, who touches heaven with his head because he is God eternal with the Father, and stands upon the earth because he assumed human nature. The continuity of the Ladder from heaven to earth shows that the separation has been removed, and that Christ, because he is the Mediator, joins God with men. Therefore the Father presents himself to be seen, as if leaning upon the Ladder, because he was God* <meta>catchword: erat (was)</meta>

<summary>The author argues that Jacob's ladder must have a spiritual meaning rather than a literal one, critiquing those who see it only as "providence" and introducing the common view that the ladder represents Christ as a mediator between God and man.</summary>
<keywords>Jacob's Ladder, Biblical interpretation, Typology, Christology, André Rivet, Divine Providence, Mediator, Genesis 28</keywords>

<page-num>46</page-num>
->### THEOLOGICAL DISSERTATION<-

*God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not counting their sins against them* <note>original: "erat in Christo, mundum reconcilians non imputando eis peccata eorum," a translation of 2 Corinthians 5:19.</note>. For this reason, *heaven is said to be opened* in the Gospel of *John* [1:51], which is otherwise closed to sinners. The *angels ascending and descending* signify God’s special care for the Church, and they indicate that the angels have come together with us into the same fellowship under one head, Christ, etc. CREGUTUS <note>Jacques Cregut (1623–1663), a Reformed theologian.</note> in *The Revelation of Secrets*, chapter 12, page 513 and following; ALTINGIUS <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679), a Dutch philologist and theologian.</note> in *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, chapter 10, Volume 3, page 170; PAREUS <note>David Pareus (1548–1622), a German Reformed Protestant theologian.</note> on Genesis at this passage; BURMANNUS <note>Frans Burman (1628–1679), a Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> on Genesis at this passage, and others, hold views that do not differ much from this.

### V.

There are, however, fundamental reasons—at least as it seems to us—which do not allow for such an interpretation of the Dream. Indeed, the Ladder itself creates the greatest difficulty here. For:

I. Nowhere in the Holy Scriptures is a *Ladder*, or anything analogous to it, such as *Steps* <note>original: "Gradus," referring to the steps of a staircase or degrees of ascent.</note>, used as an emblem for the person of Christ.

II. Nor will you easily find the Divinity represented by something man-made <note>original: "arte factum," something made by human skill or artifice.</note>, such as a Ladder.

III. Nor would it certainly be fitting for the very same continuous body, with no distinction added, to represent the Divinity of Christ with its upper part and his Humanity with its lower part.

Added to this is IV. that Jehovah standing at the top of the Ladder is taken to be God the Father, whereas it was sufficiently proved in the preceding dissertation that this Jehovah was the Son of God himself.

V. And since we have also made it probable that this Jehovah not only used a human voice but also appeared in human form, we therefore consider it entirely redundant if the same mystery of the incarnation were expressed not just twice, but even more obscurely in the Ladder, when it was exhibited far more clearly in that illustrious sign of the Lord’s presence. Those who take the burning bush, in whose flame the *Angel of Jehovah* appeared to Moses in Exodus 3:2, as a symbol of Christ’s humanity, stumble over a similar stone <note>original: "In similem lapidem impingunt," a Latin idiom meaning to commit a similar error or face the same logical obstacle.</note>, since that humanity was recognized far more clearly from the appearance of the Angel who was seen.

### VI.

Therefore, the most acute JOSUA PLACÆUS <note>Josué de la Place (c. 1596–1665), a French Protestant theologian known for his work on original sin.</note> set out another path in his *Works*, Volume 2, page 783, writing: *That ladder was not the starting point or the destination of the ascending and descending of the Angels, but the medium and the cause, and that upon which all that communication relied; it had Jacob sleeping at one end and God at the other.*

Indeed, God seen in heaven and at the summit of the Ladder was the divine person of the Son of God; but Jacob lying on the ground at the feet of the Ladder was a type of the human nature, united to the Son of God by a personal union <term>unio personalis: the theological doctrine that in Christ, a divine nature and a human nature are united in one single person.</term>. The complete vision of the Ladder, of God, and of Jacob was a type of the Son of Man or Christ the Mediator between heaven and earth, coalescing from the divine and human nature, joined by a personal union. For just as in the symbolic vision God and the Man Jacob, joined by the Ladder in the middle, merged into one, by which heaven and earth, God and Man, were seen to be joined in a friendly and wise manner: so that while God was in heaven, He was simultaneously in the man Jacob on earth; no differently also in Jesus the Son of Man, or Christ, God and man, heaven and earth were bound by so close a union that while the Son of Man moved on the earth, He was at the same time in heaven.*

In this hypothesis likewise we find various things lacking.

V. The union of the divine and human natures of Christ does not seem aptly expressed by a Ladder placed between the Lord and Jacob. The union was the purpose for which He willed to be incarnated, but the connection between these natures was actually the effect of pure divine power, which took a created nature into such a close fellowship with itself.

Or certainly, they ascend when they themselves cross over in their minds to contemplate heavenly things; but they descend when they instruct their listeners how they ought to live on earth.*

## THEOLOGICAL DISPUTATION

<page-num>50</page-num>

<meta>catchword: Aro- (original Greek: Αρω-). This is likely a reference to the beginning of a name or word on the following page.</meta>

...contains two things: first, the possession of the land of Canaan: *The land on which you sleep I will give to you and to your seed*; second, the multiplication of the offspring of Israel in that land: *And your seed shall be as the dust of the earth: for you shall be multiplied to the West and to the East and to the North and to the South.* The second benefit is the inheritance of the nations and their blessing in the **Seed** <note>As noted previously, this refers to the promised Messiah who would descend from Jacob.</note> of Jacob, so called by excellence: *And in you and in your seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed.* The third is the protection of Jacob on his journey along with his return. This benefit is not only promised—*And behold, I am with you, and I will keep you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land*—but the reason is also subjoined: *because I will not leave you, until I have done what I have spoken to you.*

### XIII.
Now I would like careful attention to be paid to the connection and the relationship that these different benefits have with each other. The last benefit differs from the preceding ones because those regarded the posterity of Jacob, while this one concerned his person and present circumstances specifically. Furthermore, the last benefit is placed in the final position, even though it was to be fulfilled first in execution; this is because it is considered only as a means that paves the way for the fulfillment of the former promises, and therefore it had to be granted for their sake. This is also declared by the reason added: *because I will not leave you, until I have done what I have spoken to you.* For that which **Jehovah** <note>The personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible, often rendered as "The LORD" in English translations.</note> had spoken to Jacob—since it is distinguished from the promise of protection and his return—contains nothing other than the previously mentioned promises, which could not have been fulfilled if Jehovah had abandoned Jacob on this journey. 

Regarding the phrase <term>ad asher|A Hebrew particle phrase (עד אשר) usually translated as "until."</term>, it should be noted that it sometimes designates not a limit of time, but the end of a work, to which the preceding work is subordinated as a means. In such cases, it is translated as *because*, *for the reason that*, or *so that*. We see this in Joshua 17:14. **Noldius** <note>Christian Noldius (1626–1683), a Danish theologian and author of a famous concordance on Hebrew particles.</note> shows that this phrase has the same power in other combinations. A particularly notable passage for the present matter is 1 Chronicles 28:20: *Jehovah God, my God, will be with you; he will not fail you, nor forsake you, (<term>ad l’kallot|A Hebrew phrase (עד לכלות) meaning "until the completion."</term>, until or rather) so that you may finish all the work for the service of the house of Jehovah.* The **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, often abbreviated as LXX.</note> translates this with <term>heos|The Greek word for "until" (ἕως).</term>, which is shown to have the same usage in **Homer’s** *Odyssey*, Book 19, line 367.

Thus, in our passage, God declares He will be present with Jacob for this reason: because He was going to perform—or so that He might perform—those greater works at the appointed time, about which He had spoken to Jacob. From this we now infer that our vision was so analogous to the added Promises that it looked primarily toward those things which were most noble, and which were the goal of all the ways of the Lord that He took with Jacob.

### XIV.
When, however, we look more closely at these promises regarding the *Seed of Jacob* <note>In this context, "Seed" refers specifically to the promised Messiah who would descend from Jacob’s line.</note>, we then discover in them two *Testaments*, whose benefits—already granted to Abraham and Isaac for their Seed—are here confirmed by a new repetition. For under the *possession of the land* in which Jacob slept, and the multiplication of his offspring within it, the sum of the entire *Old Testament* is contained; while under the *blessing of all the families of the earth in his Seed*, all the benefits of the *New Testament* are included. Since, indeed, the Old Testament was nothing but a preparation, a prelude, and a shadow of the New Testament, it follows again from this that the most important part of this promise was that concerning *all the families of the earth being blessed in the Seed of Jacob*. To this, both the preceding and subsequent events were subordinated. It was vital that this point be repeatedly emphasized and confirmed both by words and by signs, especially given the meager state of affairs in which the Patriarchal family lived for so long a time. Therefore, we conclude again that, although we do not wish to completely exclude the other parts of the divine words, the promise concerning the *Seed of Jacob*—the source of the blessing of the nations—is by far the most significant, and was the primary thing foreshadowed by our dream.

### XV.
Furthermore, the matter itself speaks to the fact that the promise concerning the *blessing in the Seed of Jacob* properly describes the Kingdom to be administered by the Messiah after his exaltation. For it concerns that time in which all the families of the earth were to follow in the footsteps of Jacob’s faith and adhere to that illustrious Seed of Jacob. Moreover, the *Blessing* itself in Jacob and his seed designates nothing other than that full measure of Grace and Salvation which Jacob desired and foretold,

### XVI.
The same will be clear from the indication of the Lord himself—who appeared here in the vision—when he was subsequently seen in the flesh, if only it is established that he referred to our passage in John 1:52. Indeed, not only the constant consensus of interpreters but also the facts themselves suggest this. That Jesus alludes to some Vision can hardly be doubted. For he speaks of *heaven opened*, of *Angels appearing*, and of the very act of *Vision*. Now, indeed, no Vision occurs in the writings of the Old Testament in which the opening of heaven is joined with the ascent and descent of Angels, except for this dream. XVIII. Pierre Du Bosc <note>A famous 17th-century French Reformed theologian.</note> substitutes another conjecture: namely, that Jesus was referring to the Vision of Daniel, chapter 7:10, where both the *Son of Man* and the *Angels* appear around the throne of the Father. Furthermore, according to Du Bosc’s own hypothesis, they surround the throne of the Father, not the Son. And can we not turn his own weapon back against him here? There is no clearer reason in Nathanael's preceding words to point toward the Vision of Daniel than toward the Vision of Jacob.

XIX. Since it is clear, therefore, that nothing occurs in the entire Old Testament that is more similar to the words of our sweetest Savior than our Vision of the Ladder, we will now easily arrive at the point we were aiming for. For Jesus’ goal was to describe the glory of the Kingdom of Israel—a title Nathanael had just granted him in his confession—and which Jesus was to occupy at the right hand of God after his suffering and exaltation. We will show this extensively and with invincible arguments, God willing, in our own future explanation of the Gospel of John <margin>a) For this Dissertation was publicly defended in the year 1721 at the University of Utrecht <note>original: "Academia Trajectina"</note>, before the author's own commentary on the Book of John was published.</margin>.

heavenly throne, whose edges reached down to the earth, accompanied by Angels. Such was that vision of Ezekiel in the place cited <note>original: "l. c." (loco citato)</note> which the scholar Peter Martyr <note>Pietro Martire Vermigli (1499–1562), a significant Reformed theologian.</note> recognized in this passage as not being far removed from our own. In that vision, a sight occurs that fills the entire space between heaven and earth, with the *wings of the Cherubim spread out and touching (verse 23), above which was the likeness of a throne, and upon the likeness of the throne was a likeness like the appearance of a man (verse 26); the wheels, however, moved upon the earth along with the living creatures (verses 15, 19).* Here, the Cherubim took the place of the Angels. Nor does the vision of Isaiah (chapter 6:1 and following) differ much. For Isaiah saw *Jehovah sitting in human form.* He saw him sitting on a *throne elevated far above the earth, high and lofty*, that is, a heavenly one. He undoubtedly saw the throne occupying the middle space of the air with its footstool, *the hem of the Lord’s robe filling the temple.* He saw angelic forms in the Seraphim. From this, the *four living creatures of the Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation</note> (Revelation 4:8) imitate the *doxology* <note>A short hymn of praise</note> *of the Seraphim.*

XXI. For since the Temple was built on the high summit of a mountain and was of such a height that, according to the testimony of Josephus in *Jewish Antiquities* (Book 8, Chapter 6), *eyes grew dim at the sight*, its peak certainly seemed to those standing below in the valley to be hidden among the clouds. The steps leading up to it, rising gradually from the courtyards all the way to the Sanctuary itself, increased its majesty. The pagans also seem to have imitated this, elevating the entrances of their temples so that they were ascended by steps. Thus, one approached the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus <note>The most important temple in Ancient Rome, located on the Capitoline Hill.</note> by a hundred steps, which however do not seem to have been continuous, but rather had their own landings <note>original: "retractiones"</note>. See Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius, a famous Renaissance humanist.</note> *On the Magnitude of Rome*, Book 3, chapter 5, and Ryckius <note>Theodorus Ryckius, a 17th-century historian.</note> *On the Capitol*, chapter 12.

The same principle held true in the Temple of Delphi, which Augustus Buchner <note>August Buchner (1591–1661) was a German philologist and rhetorician who often sought parallels between classical and biblical antiquity.</note> compared in many circumstances with the Temple of Jerusalem in his *Festal Oratory VI: On the Mimicry of the Devil*. Other authors here and there testify to the same thing regarding other Temples, using engravings of coins as evidence. Virgil writes of the temple of Juno in the *Aeneid*, Book 1, verse 452:

> *Bronze thresholds rose up with steps - -* <note>original: "Aerea cui gradibus surgebant limina"</note>

In this way, the steps of Solomon’s Temple correspond to the Ladder. The Priests and Levites who occupied themselves upon those steps daily do not differ much from the Angels of our Dream. Indeed, it is so clear that it requires no proof that the Throne of God in the earthly Sanctuary, that Aaronic retinue <note>The "Aaronic retinue" refers to the priests descended from Aaron who served in the Temple.</note>, and that entire system of worship exhibited a magnificent <term>type</term> <note>In theology, a "type" is an Old Testament person, event, or object that foreshadows a New Testament reality.</note> of the spiritual Kingdom of the Messiah in the New Testament.

<margin>AMOS 9:6.</margin>
XXII. I believe light can be shed on this from that illustrious passage in AMOS 9:6: *He builds His steps into the heavens and has founded His vault upon the earth.* <note>original Hebrew: הבונה בשמים מעלותו ואגדתו על־ארץ יסדה (*Ha-boneh ba-shamayim ma’alotav va-aguddato al-eretz yesadah*)</note> The <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, often abbreviated as LXX or οἱ ὁ.</note> did not translate the first part poorly: *The one building his ascent into heaven.* <note>original Greek: Ὁ οἰκοδομῶν εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν τὴν ἀνάβασιν αὐτοῦ</note> For it is more fitting to the metaphor of *steps* to translate *bashamayim* as *into heaven* rather than *in heaven*. It is supposed, therefore, that heaven is the throne of Jehovah, and in order that free access might be opened to it from the earth, He erected His steps, through which His Ministers can strive upward into heaven. 

In the second clause, interpreters waver regarding the word *aguddah* <note>אגדה</note>. The Septuagint rendered it as *promise*, and they are followed by the Syriac and Arabic versions. Most of the more recent scholars interpret it as a *bundle*. Certainly, by the nature of the root word, it designates something that is bound together with a firm bond. Yet none of those whom I have consulted observed that in this context, the subject is a building whose parts are joined together. Therefore, we prefer to translate it as *joining* <note>original Latin: "coagmentationem"</note> or *vaulted structure*, such as that of a building with its foundation. Among the Arabs, *agada* means *he strengthened*, *agād* refers to an *arch of firm joining and structure*, and *mu-agjad* means a *building firm in its joining*. Thus all things cohere properly: the first clause indicates the summit of this building ascending into heaven, and the latter indicates its foundation joined upon the earth. That this refers to the building of the Temple in Zion is gathered from the context of the entire vision, in which the Lord appeared to AMOS standing by the altar, undoubtedly in the accustomed symbol of His glory.

XXIII. Just as this comparison of other figures makes us more certain of the goal of Jacob’s Vision, so also it will contribute much to the correct unfolding of the individual parts of our Vision, which we shall arrange in the following theses.

> **A.** Jehovah appearing in Glorious light, and conspicuous in human form in heaven, represented the heavenly Glory of the Messiah, which was to be occupied at some time according to both natures and revealed on earth.

This sight, therefore, involved: (1) that humanity was to be received into the closest union with the divine nature. (2) That human nature was to be transferred into celestial glory, and thus the Son of God, according to both natures, was to be crowned with glory and honor. (3) That the Kingdom of Heaven was to be erected through and after this exaltation, such as is described in Psalm 103:19: *Jehovah has established His throne in the heavens.* Compare Isaiah 57:15 and 66:1. From this, it was also celebrated among the Jews themselves under the name of the *Kingdom of Heaven*. ### XXIV. B. The ladder fixed on the earth and reaching to heaven designates the path of life, through which first the Messiah would ascend the throne of glory, and then lead His elect into blessed communion with Him in glory.

This interpretation of the LADDER, though it might seem novel, is so consistent not only with the context of this Vision but also with the nature of the subject itself, that we trust the fair-minded reader will be easily convinced of its truth. A Ladder serves as a *path* leading to an elevated place and fulfills that same purpose. Furthermore, in the Holy Scriptures, that active effort by which the chosen and the faithful strive for heavenly glory and the enjoyment of God is compared to such a path leading upward. Proverbs 15:24 states: *The path of life leads* **upward** <note>original Hebrew: "למעלה" (le-ma’alah)</note> *for the wise.* Ecclesiastes 3:21 asks: *Who knows the spirit of the sons of man, whether it ascends upward?* Indeed, nothing is more common even in the Philosophy of the heathens than to compare the practice of virtues—the means by which true happiness is reached—to a *path leading upward*. <term>Hesiod</term> <note>Hesiod was an ancient Greek poet active around the same time as Homer; he is known for his "Works and Days," a poem of moral instruction.</note> writes in *Works and Days*, Book 1, line 286:

> Before virtue the immortal Gods have placed sweat; the road to it is long and steep, and rough at first. But when one arrives at the summit, it then becomes easy, however difficult it was before. <note>The author provides both the Greek and a Latin translation of Hesiod’s famous lines on the "Path of Virtue."</note>

<term>Cebes</term> <note>Cebes of Thebes was a disciple of Socrates. The "Tabula" or "Tablet of Cebes" is an allegorical dialogue describing the journey of human life and the path to true virtue.</note> says in the *Tablet*: *Does there not seem to be a certain high hill there, and a very narrow ascent with deep cliffs on both sides? I see it. This, then, is the way, he said, leading to true Education <note>original Greek: "Παιδειαν" (Paideia), referring to the cultivation of the mind and soul.</note>, and it is very difficult even to look upon.*

One may also compare the title of the *Psalms* of the <term>Ascents</term> <note>original Hebrew: "המעלות" (Ha-Ma'alot), often translated as the "Songs of Degrees" or "Songs of Ascents," comprising Psalms 120–134.</note>, or of the STEPS. *Anagogically, it signifies that they guide us onto the path of virtue; for some have understood them in this way. For the road that leads there is like steps, gradually carrying upward the man endowed with virtue and wisdom, lifting him and placing him in heaven itself. Others, however, say that through these [psalms] the LADDER OF JACOB is hinted at, which was shown to him reaching even to heaven. For in this way, places that are inaccessible and higher become accessible when steps and ladders are placed beneath us.* 

Similar interpretations occur in the writings of **Augustine**, **Hugh of St. Victor**, and others.

XXVII. C. The **Steps**, of which the Ladder consists, are symbols of events that, according to the counsel of God, are distinguished by their specific intervals of time, through which the Church emerges into heavenly glory after the coming of Christ.

It is surely obvious that the greater increases of honors or virtues, by which the summit of either earthly happiness or true blessedness is more closely reached, are called *Steps*. Regarding the increase of honors, many interpret 1 Timothy 3:13 as referring to this: "a good standing" <note>original Greek: *βαθμον καλον* (bathmon kalon), literally "a good step" or "degree."</note>, which those who have served well as ministers acquire for themselves. In this way, the *Steps* of both civil and military honors were distinct among the Romans. **Cicero** writes in *Against Catiline*, Book I, 11: "To be advanced through all the STEPS of honors." **Suetonius**, in his life of *Otho*, chapter 1, says: "Nor did he exceed the STEP of the Praetorship, although for that very reason he knew others had been promoted to a higher STEP by Claudius." Compare the same author in his life of *Claudius*, chapter 4, and the notes provided there by **Pitiscus** <note>Samuel Pitiscus (1637–1727), a Dutch scholar known for his detailed commentaries on Roman history.</note>. **Apuleius** writes in book 10: "As his lineage and dignity required, having passed through honors STEP BY STEP <note>original Latin: *gradatim*</note>, he had been destined for the five-year magistracy." **Vopiscus** <note>One of the six authors of the *Augustan History*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies.</note> writes in his life of *Carus*: "This man, advancing through civil and military STEPS, as the inscriptions of his statues indicate, was made Praetorian Prefect by Probus." An ancient inscription reads: RAISED THROUGH THE STEPS OF MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MILITARY SERVICE TO THE PEAK OF ETERNAL GLORY. Compare **Cuper's** *Observations*, book 3, chapter 20, and **Price** on 1 Timothy, at the place cited.

It is no less common to speak of the steps of virtues. **Cicero** says in *On the Nature of the Gods*, book 1: "I see that you have come to the blessed by steps—reaching toward virtue, and from virtue to reason." Add to this what **Barth** <note>Caspar von Barth (1587–1658), a German philologist and polymath.</note> has in his notes on Claudian, pages 88 and 89, and in his *Adversaria*, book 5, chapter 12.

XXVIII. However, a doubt may be raised: do these individual steps designate individual virtues, or should they be understood as progress in virtues taken collectively through intervals of time? The former view pleased certain mystics, for whom **Basil** <note>Basil of Caesarea (c. 329–379), a Greek Father of the Church known for his monastic rules.</note> led the way. His words on Psalm 1, lest we be too wordy, we give here in English: "The Ladder is the ascent to perfection, the summit is charity [love], and the steps are the ten stages of renunciation, of which the first is to renounce earthly things. 2. To forget them. 3. To hate and turn away from them as dung. 4. [The renunciation] of parents..."

...and to cast off the improper love of relatives. 5. *To hate one’s own life for Christ’s sake.* <note>original Latin: *Odisse animam suam propter Christum*—a reference to Luke 14:26.</note> 6. *To deny one’s own judgment and will.* 7. *To always mortify one’s desires.* 8. *To follow Christ and learn from Him, for He is gentle and humble in heart.* 9. *To love one’s neighbors constantly and effectively, even enemies.* 10. *In which the Lord is seen, is to cling to God and be united with Him in one Spirit.* We could gather more of this kind from other authors; however, they do not meet our approval, both because the historical account of the Ladder does not number the steps, and because the connection of Christian virtues is so intertwined from the very beginning of grace that whoever possesses one virtue radically possesses them all. In this way, the *Steps of Solomon’s Throne*, the mystery of which we briefly indicated in Exercise VI on Psalm 45, sections 4 and 5, can designate as many shifts through which the Messiah is carried to the highest glory in the Church. **Johann Gerhard** <note>A prominent 17th-century Lutheran theologian.</note>, in his *Theological Commonplaces*, Volume IX, "On the Final Judgment," section 18, thinks that the six steps of Solomon’s Throne designate the six millennia of the world; once these are completed, Christ will ascend the judgment seat and judge the world in justice. But since the kingdom of Solomon was a shadow of the Messiah’s kingdom in the days of the New Testament, it is more fitting to understand six more noble periods, which, having passed, the <term>millennial Kingdom|The "thousand-year reign" of Christ mentioned in Revelation 20.</term> itself will follow, representing the seventh period. Nor is it unusual for other authors to call the revolutions of ages *steps*. **Lucretius** <note>A Roman poet and philosopher.</note> writes in Book II, line 1121:

> — — Whatever you see growing with happy increase
> And gradually climbing the STEPS of adult age.

Hence, six steps of age were commonly numbered according to **Isidore of Seville** in *The Etymologies* <note>original: *Origines*</note>, Book XI, chapter 2. And the <term>climacterics|Critical turning points in a human life or history, often thought by ancients to occur in cycles of 7 or 9 years.</term> of years are mentioned when they are distinguished by weeks and nines, according to the "climbing law of years," as **Pliny** says in *Natural History*, Book VII, chapter 49. These climacteric years are called *gradarii* <note>original: *gradarii*, meaning "proceeding by steps."</note> by **Firmicus**. See **Stephanus** in his Lexicon under the word *Klimax* <note>original Greek: *Κλιμαξ*, meaning a ladder or staircase.</note> and **Salmasius** in his specific treatise *On Climacteric Years*.

### XXIX. D. The lowest part of the ladder, fixed firmly on the earth, suggests that the habitable world will be brought under the Messiah's kingdom.

One may compare here the passage in Isaiah 66:1: *Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool.* <note>original Latin: *Cœli sunt thronus meus & terra scabellum pedum meorum.*</note> For what is a *footstool* <term>scabellum: a low stool or step placed before a throne</term> but that lowest part of the throne which corresponds to the steps? This description corresponds beautifully to the description of God's Majesty which **Clement of Alexandria** <note>A Christian theologian of the late 2nd century known for blending Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note> attributes to the mythical poet **Orpheus** in his *Stromata* <note>Or "Miscellanies," a major work by Clement exploring the relationship between Greek philosophy and Christianity.</note>, book V, Potter edition, page 723:

> For He Himself is established in the bronze heaven
> Upon a golden throne. And He walks with His feet upon the earth.
> *He sits upon a golden seat, which the bronze-colored sky sustains;*
> *Indeed, He fixes His footsteps upon the earth.*
<note>The first two lines are translated from the original Greek; the following two are the author's Latin translation of the same verse provided in the text.</note>

Compare also the work of **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian famous for his biblical commentaries.</note> on Matthew 5:35. Furthermore, it is clear from 1 Chronicles 28:2 that this is an allusion to the Temple in Jerusalem, which with its steps was once the typical footstool of God's Throne: *That I might build a house of rest for the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord, and for the footstool of our God.* From there, the same phrase is transferred to the Church of the New Testament in Isaiah 60:13 <note>The original text cites Isaiah 61:13, but the verse quoted is 60:13.</note>: *To beautify the place of my sanctuary; and I will make the place of my feet glorious.* It is also applied to the Temple of Ezekiel, which depicts the Church of the latter times in Ezekiel 43:7. Therefore, when the "shadowy" <note>Meaning the Old Testament rituals and structures that served as a "shadow" or precursor to spiritual realities.</note> Temple is replaced by the entire earth as the *footstool of the Lord’s feet*, it indicates that the whole earth will be subject to the Kingdom of the Messiah. In this way, that which had already been predicted so often to **Abraham** and **Isaac** would be fulfilled with all emphasis—and was confirmed in this vision—namely, *that all the nations of the earth would be blessed in their Seed.* 

And since the Patriarch <note>Jacob</note> saw this ladder fixed in such a firm and stable place, he learned from it that this Kingdom would be confined by no limits, not only in terms of its extent but also its duration. Hence, stability was promised to the Throne of David before the Lord in 1 Kings 2:45. The Throne of the Lord is described as firm in Psalm 93:2 and *as remaining forever and ever* in Psalm 45:6 <note>The text cites Psalm 45:7.</note>. *Its foundation is in the holy mountains: the Most High himself shall establish her* in Psalm 87:5. *Your eyes will see Jerusalem, a quiet habitation, a tabernacle that shall not be taken down, of which...* <note>Isaiah 33:20.
