### XXX. E. The top of the Ladder touching heaven represents the communion of the "church militant" with the "church triumphant" and its excellence over all the kingdoms of the world.

For since the highest step of the Ladder reaches the firmament, the step and the footstool of the Throne are joined with its seat; in this way, the closest possible bond is expressed which exists between the Church on earth <term>Church militant: the body of believers currently living and "struggling" on earth</term> and the blessed inhabitants of Heaven <term>Church triumphant: the believers who have died and are now in the presence of God</term>. However, this bond will be fully revealed only when heaven is opened through the "torn veil of the flesh" <note>An allusion to Hebrews 10:20, suggesting that Christ's body is the veil through which we enter God's presence.</note> and *the Bride is introduced by the King into his inner chambers. Song of Solomon 1:4.* Furthermore, by the very height of the Ladder, it is shown how the Sanctuary of the Church—which is the FOOTSTOOL of the Messiah’s feet—was to be raised in glory above all worldly kingdoms. *Isaiah 2:2: And it shall come to pass in the last days, that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established in the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and all nations shall flow unto it.* Compare *Micah 4:1.* In this way, the Church actually achieves that height which the King of the mystical Babylon <note>Often interpreted by theologians of this period as a symbol for the Antichrist or worldly pride.</note>—the rival of the builders of the Tower of Babel (*Genesis 11:4*)—strove for with a vain and Phaëthon-like <note>Phaëthon: in Greek mythology, the son of Helios who attempted to drive the sun-chariot but fell to his death; used here to describe overreaching pride.</note> daring, saying in his heart: *I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north. Isaiah 14:13.*

### XXXI. F. Jehovah standing upon the Ladder displays in various ways the image of His unchanging communion with the Church on earth.

For while the highest step of the Ladder is trodden upon by JEHOVAH STANDING THERE, it is elegantly implied that He Himself has gone before us on the same path by which He introduced His people into the communion of heavenly glory. *Psalm 16:11: You will make me know*—that is, to experience and to initiate for all the saints—*the path of life.* *Ezekiel 10:18, 19: And the glory of the Lord departed from off the threshold of the house and stood over the cherubims. And the cherubims lifted up their wings and were lifted up from the earth.* *Song of Solomon 1:4: Draw me after You, we will run: the King has brought me into his inner chambers.* *John 12.* <note>Likely referring to John 12:32: "And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me."</note>

# THEOLOGICAL DISSERTATION

XII. 32. *And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto myself.* <note>John 12:32</note> Therefore, He stands out at the summit of the Ladder as a glorious Victor, who has overcome all difficulties, temptations, and dangers, and has ascended to a place so high that no engines of the enemy <note>The author uses "machinae," likely referring to siege engines or metaphorical weapons of spiritual warfare.</note> can reach Him.

XXXII. Moreover, while He leans upon the Ladder by **STANDING**, He also demonstrates His provident and constant care for the kingdom subject to Him. In this way, the metaphor of **STANDING** is used for those who rule in Daniel 11:2, 3, 20 and Amos 4:15. <note>original: "Amos IV. 15." This may be a scribal error or a reference to an older verse numbering, as Amos 4 ends at verse 13. It likely refers to God's presence or judgment.</note> Rulers *sit* when they are displaying their majesty and enjoying a state of peace; however, they **STAND** when they are keeping watch for the good of the Commonwealth, and are ready to defend it against enemies and imminent dangers. VIRGIL, *Aeneid* VIII, line 678:
> *Hence Augustus Caesar, leading the Italians into battle,*
> **STANDING** *on the high stern* — — — — — —
> <note>original: "Hinc Augustus agens Italos in prælia Cæsar / STANS celsa in puppi"</note>
The same author in *Aeneid* XII, line 565, regarding present care and help:
> *Let there be no delay to my words. Jupiter* **STANDS** *on this side.*
> <note>original: "Ne qua meis esto dictis mora. Juppiter hac STAT."</note>
SENECA, in *Consolation to Helvia*, chapter 5: *They ordered me to* **STAND** *constantly, as if placed in a guard-post, and to look out for all the attempts of fortune and all its attacks long before they might strike.*
The Messiah is frequently introduced in this sense, after having taken possession of His kingdom, as one **STANDING**. Isaiah 11:10: *The root of Jesse shall* **STAND** *as a sign to the peoples.* Daniel 12:1: *At that time Michael shall* **STAND**, *that great Prince, who* **STANDS** *for your people.* Micah 5:3: *And he shall* **STAND** *and feed <gloss>shepherd</gloss> in the strength of the Lord, in the majesty of the name of the Lord our God.* Zechariah 14:4: *And his feet shall* **STAND**, *on that day, upon the Mount of Olives.* Revelation 14:1: *Behold, the Lamb* **STANDING** *upon Mount Zion.* And especially deserving of comparison here is the passage in Acts 7:56: *Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man* **STANDING** *at the right hand of God.* It is clear that in these places there is a specific allusion to the position of the Column of Cloud <note>The "Shekhinah" or divine presence that guided the Israelites in the desert.</note> over the Ark of the Covenant in the Sanctuary, which we hinted above was analogous to our Vision. Wherefore also in Ezekiel 10:1, the glory of the Lord is seen **STANDING** above the Cherubim. Compare Amos 9:1 and Exodus 33:21.

XXXIII. Furthermore, to **STAND** in such circumstances is a symbol of constancy. Psalm 111:3, 10; 119:89; Daniel 12:13.

Amos 7:2, etc. Seneca, *Consolation to Polybius*, chapter 25: *Fortune has placed you in a great light; all will know how you have behaved in this wound of yours: whether, having been struck, you immediately laid down your arms, or whether you* **STOOD YOUR GROUND**? <note>original: "in GRADU STETERIS." -> — — — For perhaps — <-
-> Fortune, advancing slowly, will stand well. <-

*For perhaps fortune, progressing more slowly, will beautifully* **STAND**. <note>The author provides a Latin translation of the Greek verse, here rendered into English.</note> Hence, when antiquity wished to express the immutability <note>The quality of being unchanging or eternal.</note> of the Divine Power, it named Him the **STANDING ONE** <note>original: "ἙΣΤΩΤΑ" (Hestota).</note>. Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who used allegory to fuse Greek philosophy with Jewish scripture.</note>, in *On the Confusion of Tongues*, page 324: He called God the **ALWAYS STANDING** God. The same author, in *On the Change of Names*, page 1054, explains this title in this way: *Because He Himself,* **STANDING** *in the same state, moves all that exists.*

If we listen to Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444 CE), a major figure in early Christian theology.</note>, this very concept was accepted in the school of Plato. For in Book 3 of *Against Julian*, he writes that Plato established two Gods, the first of whom is called the **STANDING** <note>original: "ἙΣΤΩΣ" (Hestos)</note> One, and the second the one **WHO IS MOVED**. It did not escape Simon Magus <note>A figure mentioned in the Book of Acts who practiced sorcery; in early church tradition, he is often depicted as the first great heretic.</note> himself, based on Jewish tradition, that this name applies particularly to the Son of God, if those things are true which are passed down in the *Clementine Homilies* <note>A 4th-century Christian work that purports to be written by Clement of Rome, often containing debates between Simon Peter and Simon Magus.</note>, Book 2, chapter 22: *This Simon, having trained himself thoroughly in Alexandria and possessing great power in the magic arts, being puffed up, wished to be thought a certain supreme power, even superior to God the creator of the world. Sometimes, also hinting that he himself was the Christ, he called himself the* **STANDING ONE**. *He used this title as if he were one who would always exist, and having no cause for decay, his body would not fall.*

Indeed, Clement of Alexandria <note>A Christian theologian (c. 150–215 CE) who sought to unite Greek philosophy with Christian faith.</note>, in *Stromata*, Book 2, chapter 11, confirms that the followers of Simon worshipped **THE STANDING ONE**. On this point, let Potter <note>John Potter (1674–1747), an English scholar and Bishop who published a famous edition of Clement’s works.</note> be consulted in his notes. And Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> recognizes that the word *nitsav* <note>original: "נצב," the Hebrew word used in Genesis 28:13 to describe God "standing" above the ladder.</note> also has this meaning in our passage, in *The Guide for the Perplexed*, Book 1, chapter 15, where he says *nitsav* and *yatsav* <note>original: "נצב & יצב" — Hebrew roots meaning to stand, station oneself, or endure.</note> ...

### THEOLOGICAL DISSERTATION

<meta>catchword: this</meta>

[This signifies] existence and persistence: *Your word stands in the heavens* <note>Psalm 119:89</note>, that is to say, it is established and standing; and everything that derives from this name <note>The Hebrew root N-Z-B, meaning "to stand" or "be stationed."</note> in the Holy Scriptures <note>original: "בהק' הבר'" (be-ha-qodesh ha-barukh), an abbreviation referring to the Holy One, Blessed be He.</note> relates to this matter. Thus: *Behold, the Lord stood upon it*—He was established and standing upon it, that is, upon the ladder. [This implies] **stability, firmness, and perpetuity:** as in the phrase *Your word STANDS in heaven* (Psalm 119:89), which means it remains **stable and firm.** This is the usage whenever these terms occur concerning God, the Blessed One: as in *Behold, the Lord STOOD upon it* <note>Genesis 28:13</note>, which means He remains **firm and stable upon it**, namely the Ladder, whose one end is in heaven and the other on earth. By this ladder anyone who desires to ascend must climb, so that they may take hold of Him who stands above it; for He **REMAINS** firm at the very highest peak of the Ladder. Indeed, the stability both of the Messiah’s kingdom in general and of His faith and care regarding the Church in particular are celebrated everywhere in the sacred pages. Psalm 93:2; 102:27, 28; Isaiah 9:7, etc. Specifically relevant here is Psalm 89:3: *Mercy shall be built up forever: in the heavens themselves You shall establish Your truth.*

-> XXXIV. G. By "Angels," we understand the primary ministers <-
-> of the Messiah in the administration of His heavenly kingdom, <-
-> both celestial and terrestrial. <-

**A question arises** <note>original: "Dubium"</note> whether we should understand "Angels" here only in the common sense as heavenly Spirits—to whom the name "Angels" is most properly applied—or also in the sense often found in the Prophets, as Ministers of the Gospel? Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> certainly thinks that mystical Angels are to be understood in the place cited. He says: *What I am saying is clear, namely that these words—"Behold, the Lord stood upon it"—are to be understood according to this parable or metaphor, as is clear from what follows: "And the Angels of God were ascending."* For by these, nothing else is understood than the Prophets. The same opinion is held by Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 CE), a pivotal Father of the Church.</note> on Psalm 119, and by Pelargus <note>Christoph Pelargus (1565–1633), a German Lutheran theologian known for his commentaries.</note> on this passage. Nor is this meditation unsuitable; not only because the nature of allegory favors a mystical sense more than a literal one, but also because the Angels in this vision correspond to the Cherubim, Seraphim, and Living Creatures <note>The "Hayyot" or four living beings in Ezekiel’s vision.</note> in the Sanctuary and other prophetic visions. We are led by foundational reasons to interpret these images as referring not only to celestial angels but also to earthly ones. Indeed, they strive to be like **ANGELS** in wisdom, readiness, holy zeal, and other virtues. We would expand further into this field of thought, were it not already abundant.

The most celebrated **VITRINGA** <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a famous Dutch theologian and Hebraist known for his massive commentary on Isaiah.</note> discussed this matter in his excellent *Commentary on Isaiah* at chapter 5, verse 3. XXXV. H. The ascending and descending of the Angels on the Ladder indicates how these Ministers of the Messiah are active in matters pertaining to His kingdom.
The interpretation of **TERTULLIAN** <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD).</note> wanders too far from the truth here; in his work *Against Marcion*, book III, chapter 24, he says *that this ladder demonstrates a journey to heaven, by which some arrive and others fall away.* Compare the same author in *On Flight in Persecution*, book I. Although this view also pleased **GERHARD** (following **BERNARD** <note>Referring to St. Bernard of Clairvaux and the Lutheran scholastic Johann Gerhard.</note>) in his commentary on 2 Peter 3, page 486, it does not sit well with us; it seems to be drawn from the depths of **PHILO’S** book *On Dreams*. For both the ascent and the descent are directed toward Christ, according to John 1:51 <note>"You shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man."</note>. Rightly refuting this [Tertullian's] opinion, **AUGUSTINE**, in his commentary on Psalm 119, section 2, observes: *It is not for nothing that the text does not say "falling," but "descending." There is a great difference between descending and falling.* Therefore, **ORIGEN** <note>An influential and controversial early Greek Church Father (c. 184–253 AD).</note> thinks it better that the ministry of the heavenly Angels is shadowed forth through ASCENT and DESCENT in his work *Against Celsus*, book V: <note>The author provides the following quote in both Greek and Latin; it is translated here into English.</note> *We confess that the angels are ministering spirits, sent into service for the sake of those who shall inherit salvation. They ascend to offer up the supplications of men in the purest places of the universe, in the heavens, or in those places even purer than the heavens. They descend, in turn, from that place to bring to each person, according to their merit, something of those things which they are commanded by God to administer and bestow upon those who receive His benefit.*

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the interpretation of Jacob's ladder, specifically rejecting the idea of angels acting as necessary intermediaries for prayer or belonging to two different natures (mortal and immortal). ->### THEOLOGICAL DISSERTATION<-

I 2

But these things also seem less suitable to us, if only because the prayers of the faithful do not require such intermediaries. Equally far from reason are those who imagine two kinds of Angels here, thinking that the immortal and incorruptible ascend, while the mortal and corruptible descend. But, as **MARTYR** <note>Peter Martyr Vermigli (1499–1562) was a significant Italian-born Reformed theologian whose works were foundational to the development of Protestant thought.</note> rightly says, *these are human inventions; for Scripture does not teach more than one kind of Angels, and what those men say, they have drawn from the books of the Platonists.* Therefore, the ASCENDING Angels, as I think, more aptly foreshadow the exultant choirs of celestial Spirits accompanying or following Christ in his ascension. They had descended with him onto Mount Sinai; they had descended to him at his birth in Luke 2:13 and had been his Ministers on earth. Now they leave the earth with him, sounding the trumpets in Psalm 47:6 <note>The verse reads: "God has ascended with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet."</note>, and presenting themselves before his Throne, attentive to his commands. Having received these commands regarding the present state of the Church and the faithful, they soon DESCEND again. Hence, once the heavenly throne of Christ is described in Psalm 103:20, it is added: *Bless the LORD, you His angels, mighty in strength, who do His word, obeying the voice of His word.* For this reason, immediately after the Lord's ascension, they stand by the disciples, comforting them in Acts 1:10. However, this angelic movement is reciprocated in each triumph of the people of God. As often as they are introduced into a closer communion with the glory of Jesus Christ, so often do the ASCENDING angels accompany them. Thus they carry Lazarus into Abraham's bosom in Luke 16:23. But as often as they go out *like the winds* (Psalm 104:4) to summon others, sent out for the sake of ministry because of the heirs of salvation (Hebrews 1:14), so often do they DESCEND again. And thus they form <term>מחנים</term> <note>original: *machanayim*, meaning "two camps" or "two hosts."</note> *two camps*, as companions of the Church both in its triumph and in its warfare. They are to DESCEND for the last time on the day of judgment, when the Son of Man comes with his glory and all the Holy Angels with him (Matthew 25:31), so that they may adorn the supreme and universal triumph of Christ and the Church.

Those who advance toward spiritual understanding. Who are those descending? Those who, although they enjoy spiritual intelligence as much as humans can...*

...counsel, nevertheless they descend to the little ones, so that they may tell them such things as they are able to grasp, and having been nourished with milk, they might become fit and strong to receive spiritual food. **BEDE** <note>Bede the Venerable (c. 672–735) was an English monk and scholar known as the "Father of English History."</note> and **LYRANUS** <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349) was a Franciscan teacher whose literal interpretations of the Bible influenced later Reformation scholars.</note> follow this view. There is again a descent when they are presented as returning from heaven, and living again in those who follow in their footsteps in *Revelation 20:4*; also the whole *new **Jerusalem** will one day **DESCEND** from God out of heaven, Revelation 21:2*.

Thrice indeed it is redoubled: BEHOLD! BEHOLD! BEHOLD! The **raising of the Ladder** or the **Steps** comes first, through the founding of the Throne of the Messiah in justice and judgment, which are the supports sustaining both sides, as it were, of this Throne (*Psalms 89:14; 97:2*). There follows the **activity of the Angels of the Lord** for manifesting the Glory of the heavenly King to men. And this is the means through which the King himself becomes visible in his Glory, so that *all the ends of the earth may see the salvation of our God (Isaiah 52:10).* Truly, the faithful soul is deservedly swept up in wonder at each detail. The **raising of the Ladder** recalls all the treasures of all-sufficiency, wisdom, and divine love spent in the construction of a new way to heaven and the founding of Zion <note>In this context, Zion refers to the spiritual Church or the kingdom of God.</note>. The **ascent and descent of the Angels** bids us contemplate the care and faithfulness of the Lord in applying salvation through stages, as well as the incredible happiness of the Church, raised to such sweet fellowship with the Angels. Nothing truly drives the soul into deeper amazement than that **Jehovah himself** desires to complete this work of communion between heaven and earth, and especially that he wishes the glory of his divine perfections to **be manifested** in it and celebrated by Angels and men.

### XXXVIII. K. Jacob, perceiving such an illustrious Vision in a dream, is a <term>type</term> <note>A "type" is a person, event, or institution in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow or symbolize something in the New Testament (the "antitype"), such as Christ or the Church.</note> both of the Son of God himself wandering on the earth, and of the Church tending toward the heavenly homeland through various trials.

Although we do not think Jacob can be viewed quite fitly as a part of the Vision itself, nevertheless in his person, and in his singular fates noted by the Holy Spirit, he bore an excellent type of both Christ and the New Testament Church; we assume this here, lest we spread our argument too thin. Among the parts making up this type, his **pilgrimage** is deservedly mentioned, which has a singular analogy <note>A "singular analogy" here means a specific and remarkable point of comparison.</note> first with Christ himself, living as a resident alien on the earth, and *not having where to lay his head (Matthew 8:20);* then also with the New Testament Church consisting of *strangers and pilgrims (1 Peter 2:11)* <note>Original Greek: ἐκ παροικων και παρεπιδημων (ek paroikōn kai parepidēmōn)</note> and *not having a lasting city (Hebrews 13:14)* <note>Original Greek: μενουσαν πολιν (menousan polin)</note>. Just as, therefore, the Patriarch was refreshed amidst the troubles and difficulties of his journey

By gazing upon these, He was sustained through all temptations, sufferings, and death itself. This is excellently shown in the Messiah’s soliloquy during His passion, where He sets before Himself His inheritance and future joys in **Psalm 16**. Hence it is stated in **Hebrews 12:2** that He endured the cross <note>original: "ἀντὶ τῆς προκειμένης αὐτῷ χαρᾶς"</note> "for the joy that was set before Him." No less does the Church, in all its dangers, anxieties, and persecutions, take heart whenever it looks upon that Prince of salvation and life—now perfected and brought to the helm of the heavenly Kingdom—standing ready for the defense and help of His people. The Church is strengthened in faith and ignited with constancy to finish the race. Thus is it strengthened in the Lord, *so that they may walk continually in His name* (**Zechariah 10:12**). Thus the faithful have *the hope set before them as an anchor, reaching even into the things within the veil, where the forerunner has entered for us* (**Hebrews 6:18-20**). With the same argument, the Savior fortifies His disciples against imminent temptations in **John 14:3**.

### XXXIX.
It is also not without reason that a Vision offering such great comfort is presented in the form of a **Dream**. Insofar as a Dream bears the image of death, it alludes both to the death in which the Lord Himself was about to fall asleep—though the hope of imminent glory never perished from His soul—and to the mystical death the Church must undergo in its most grievous afflictions. This mystical death, likewise, will never extinguish trust in the Lord, for the faithful even glory in their afflictions (**Romans 5:3**) and say: "*Do not rejoice over me, O my enemy; though I sit in darkness, the Lord shall be a light to me*" (**Micah 7:8**). Furthermore, insofar as a Dream is often regarded among the vain mockeries of men, it foreshadows how the hope of Christ was to be torn apart by the jeers of His enemies (**Psalm 22:8-9**) and how the trust of the Church, placed in His promises, was to be mocked as if it were a vain thing (**Psalm 42:11, Psalm 94**). XL. From these considerations, it is easily seen what an excellent support for his faith and hope Jacob obtained from this very Vision. For the salvation of the Lord <note>original: "Jehova"</note>, to be brought through that Seed *par excellence* <note>original: "κατ’ ἐξοχὴν"</note> expected from the descendants of the Patriarchs in the promised land, was the sum of all the prayers of both the Fathers and Jacob himself. This hope was weakened in no small way by the fact that Jacob seemed to be an exile, poor, alone, exposed to the dangers of an uncertain journey, and thus abandoned by God and men—not only from his father's house but even from that land for which such a great good was destined. Thus, he could have remained in a doubtful state of mind—if not about the core of the matter, then at least about whether such a great promise specifically looked to his own offspring, and whether any benefit would return to him from the right of primogeniture <term>birthright</term> bought from Esau, and the blessing of the Father shrewdly snatched away; or whether he himself, by fleeing from that region, was about to lose such a great prerogative for himself and his seed. Therefore, divine mercy timely settled these waves of his mind, while the Lord appearing in that vast solitude indicated that Jacob enjoyed the perpetual care of the God of his fathers. He taught him that both Testaments <note>covenants</note> pledged to Abraham remained ratified and firm in Jacob and his descendants, and He set before him, by adding the Vision, the most excellent manner in which these promises would one day be most fully fulfilled. <meta>This page continues the linguistic analysis of the term "bosom" (Greek: kolpos; Latin: sinus) as applied to God. ...designates the **womb**, the **lap**, or the **knees**. Therefore, just like other human body parts, the term <term>BOSOM</term> <note>original Greek: "ΚΟΛΠΟΣ" (kolpos)</note> is attributed to God in John 1:18 only through a **metaphor**; it is our pleasure to explain the elegance and power of this imagery more closely here.

II. Since the **BOSOM** expresses the front and simultaneously the interior part of the human body, it is for this reason sometimes a figure for things pertaining to someone’s nature or essence. **Job 19:27**: *My kidneys <note>Often used in the Bible to represent the inmost heart or emotions</note> are consumed within my* **BOSOM** <note>original Hebrew: "בחקי" (be-cheyqi)</note>. **MARTIAL** <note>A Roman poet known for his epigrams</note>, *Epigrams* I. 16: *Often joys flow, having slipped from the depths of the* **BOSOM**. From this, the Church Fathers were convinced that the communion of the very same essence with the Father is indicated by this phrase. **CHRYSOSTOM** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching</note>, *Homily XV on John*:

> He placed him who is in the bosom of the Father, so that he may be understood as being the Son from Him and in Him by nature; by saying "bosom" instead of "essence," he was using a physical example.

When this Venerable Father says: *from Him and in Him*, he seems to allude to that notion of "bosom" which signifies the **mother's womb**. It is as if it were indicated that, just as an infant in the mother's womb is of the same nature as the mother, so the Son, when he is said to be in the "womb" of the Father, is of the same essence as the Father. **CYRIL OF ALEXANDRIA** <note>A 5th-century Patriarch of Alexandria and major figure in Christological debates</note> certainly conceived of the matter in this way:

> That the Father generates the Son as if in a womb, clearly, as he shines out in a certain radiance and in a certain unutterable progression toward his own <term>hypostasis</term> <note>A technical theological term referring to a "person" or distinct individual existence within the Trinity</note>; yet the Father has the Son within himself again, since that Divine <term>Offspring</term> <note>original Latin: "Genimen"</note> came forth from the Father not by any cutting or physical partitioning.

I am not sure, however, whether the imagery of the "womb" is applied aptly here. This is partly because the text speaks of the **"bosom of the Father"** <note>which is male, making the "womb" metaphor biologically mismatched</note>, and partly because the existence of the Son in the Father cannot be compared to the existence of an embryo in the womb. The latter precedes birth, whereas the Son is considered "born" from all eternity, such that any idea of "before" or "after" is excluded. I would prefer therefore to consider the...

### ON THE BOSOM OF THE FATHER.

...a better analogy, by which the Son is also asserted to be in the Father because of the unity of essence, as seen in **John 14:10**.

III. Furthermore, to be **IN THE BOSOM** refers to that which lies closest to the body. Consequently, this phrase is often used to express the closest **union of persons**, through the joining not only of bodies but also of minds that feel and will the same things. Thus, a wife is placed in the **BOSOM** of her husband in **Deuteronomy 13:6**, **28:54**, **2 Samuel 12:8**, **1 Kings 1:2**, and **Micah 7:5**; likewise, the husband is in the **BOSOM** of the wife in **Deuteronomy 28:56**. Imitating this sacred style, **SIRACH** <note>Also known as Ben Sira, author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus</note> says in **Ecclesiasticus 9:1**: *Do not be jealous of the woman of your* **BOSOM** <note>original Greek: "γυναῖκα τοῦ κόλπου σου" (gynaika tou kolpou sou)</note>. The poet **TIBULLUS** <note>A Roman elegiac poet (c. 55–19 BC)</note> writes in *Elegies* I. 3, lines 39–40:

> *How it pleases to hear the harsh winds while lying down*
> ->*And to have held the mistress in a tender* **BOSOM**.*<-

The same author in Book III, Elegy 3, lines 7–8:

> *But that with you I might share the joys of a long life*
> ->*And that our old age might fall in your* **BOSOM**.*<-

From the marriage covenant, this same expression passed into any covenant of close friendship. **PERSIUS** <note>A Roman satirist (34–62 AD)</note> in *Satire* V, line 36:

> *I placed myself under you: you take up my tender years*
> *In a Socratic,* **BOSOM**, *Cornutus* - - - <note>Referring to the intellectual and moral protection provided by his teacher, Cornutus</note>

**VIRGIL** <note>The famous Roman epic poet</note> in *Aeneid* VII, line 233:

> *Nor will it shame the Ausonians <note>Ancient Italians</note> to have received Troy in their* **LAP** <note>original Latin: "gremio" (lap/bosom)</note>.

**PLUTARCH** <note>A Greek biographer and philosopher (c. 46–120 AD)</note>, in his life of *Cato the Younger* (page 775), calls Gabinius *a man from the* **BOSOM** *of Pompey* <note>original Greek: "ἄνθρωπον ἐκ τῶν Πομπηΐου κόλπων" (anthrōpon ek tōn Pompeiou kolpōn)</note>. From this, intimate friends are themselves called **BOSOMS**. **TACITUS** <note>A Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD)</note> in *Histories* IV: *New* **BOSOMS** *are sought*, which is to say, new friends. Consult **MARCELLUS DONATUS** in his clarifications on Tacitus at this passage; **BARTHIUS** in *Adversaria* Book 38, Chapter 11; and **FESSELIUS** in *Adversaria Sacra* IV. 9, sections 3 and 4. Thus, according to **CHRYSOSTOM** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD)</note> in *Homily IV on the Incomprehensible*, when the Son is said to be *in the bosoms of the Father* <note>original Greek: "ἐν κόλποις τοῦ Πατρός" (en kolpois tou Patros)</note>, *by the name of the "bosom," he understood the proximity and familiarity of the only-begotten with the Father.* **ORIGEN** <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD)</note> has similar things to say in his commentary on John (Huet edition, page 406).

> ->Whatever fortune and faith I have,<-
> ->I place in your **LAPS**<- <note>The Latin *gremium* is a synonym for *sinus*, often meaning "lap" or "bosom."</note>

**TACITUS** in *Histories* III. 69: *Therefore, as if the whole republic had passed into the **BOSOM** of Vespasian.* The same author in *Histories* IV. 74: *Soon after obtaining power, [Domitian] dedicated a massive temple to Jupiter the Guardian, and himself **IN THE BOSOM OF THE GOD**.*

V. But that which is hidden is also said to be **IN THE BOSOM**. In this way, it is used to refer to the secret recesses of the mind in **Ecclesiastes 7:9** <note>Cited in the text as verse 10</note>: *Anger rests in the bosom of fools.* <note>Original Hebrew: כעס בחיק כסילים ינוח</note> The **SEPTUAGINT** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> renders this: *Anger will rest in the bosom of the foolish.* <note>Original Greek: Θυμὸς ἐν κόλπῳ ἀφρόνων ἀναπαύσεται</note> With this we can compare what **PERSIUS** in *Satire* V calls the "sinuous heart" (*sinuosum pectus*), referring to the more secret part of the soul; and in **GELLIUS** Book XII, chapter 5, "sinuous" is used in opposition to "open." Thus **PROPERTIUS** in Book II, Elegy 25:

> ->Keep your joys enclosed in a silent **BOSOM**.<-

More examples will be provided by **FESSELIUS** in the cited work, **PASSERATIUS** on the passage by Propertius, and **ERASMUS** in his *Adages*, page 674. This is what **AUGUSTINE** meant in *Tractate IV on John*: *What is 'IN THE BOSOM OF THE FATHER'? In the secret of the Father. For God does not have a bosom as we have in our garments; nor should He be imagined to sit as we do; nor perhaps is He girded so that He might have a bosom; but because our bosom is within, we call the secret of the Father the 'bosom of the Father'.*

VI. **HAMMOND** <note>Henry Hammond (1605–1660), an English churchman and scholar</note> in his commentary on **Matthew 8:11**, believes that there is a specific allusion here to the custom of reclining at meals among the ancients. In this custom, the most honored guest reclined in the middle place, while the one who was next in honor and love occupied the space immediately following, and in this manner appeared to lie in the **BOSOM** of the other. **JUVENAL** in *Satire* XI:

### CONCERNING THE BOSOM OF THE FATHER
<center>K 3</center>

> ->*The dinner is set; the new bride lay in the **LAP** of her husband.*<-

**ZONARAS** <note>Joannes Zonaras, a 12th-century Byzantine chronicler</note> says of the Emperor Heliogabalus: *his beloved dined in his bosom.* <note>Original Greek: ἐν κολποις ἀυτου ἡ ἐρωμενη ἐδειπνησε</note> **PLINY THE YOUNGER**, in *Epistle 22* of Book IV: *Nerva was dining with a few guests; Vejento was reclining very close and even in his **BOSOM**.* <note>In ancient Roman dining, guests reclined on couches; to be "in the bosom" meant reclining immediately in front of someone so that one's head was near their chest.</note> **APULEIUS** in *The Golden Ass*, Book VI: *The husband reclined at the head of the couch, embracing Psyche in his **LAP**.* **LIVY**, in Book XXXI, criticizes the banquet of the Consul Quinctius Flamininus because *he placed a harlot at the foot of the couch in his **BOSOM**, contrary to the dignity of the fasces, as if she were his lawful wife.* <note>The "fasces" were a bundle of rods and an axe symbolizing the high judicial and executive power of a Roman magistrate.</note> This is expressed clearly regarding the Apostle John in **John 13:25**: *he was reclining in the bosom of Jesus, and falling back against the chest of Jesus.* <note>Original Greek: ἦν ἀνακειμενος ἐν τῳ κολπῳ Ιησου, και ἐπιπεסων ἐπι το στηθος του Ιησου.</note> Consult on this custom **SALMASIUS** in *Plinian Exercises*, pages 886–887; **CIACCONIUS** in *On the Dining Room*, page 50; and **LIPSIUS** in *Antiquarian Readings*, Book III. It is also the opinion of **DELRIO** in *Sacred Adages*, Book I, adage 125, that our phrase refers to this custom.

VII. While all these examples add an excellent emphasis to the phrase when applied to the Son of God, there remains something more specific which involves the preceding points. For it must be observed that the text here does not speak of the "bosom of God" in a general sense, but pointedly of the **BOSOM OF THE FATHER**. From this we gather that the **BOSOM OF THE FATHER** designates that state in which the first person of the Trinity manifests Himself as the Father of the Son. Consequently, **TO BE** in that *bosom of the Father* primarily expresses the Filial relationship of the second person to the first.

VIII. It is certainly well known that children are usually carried by their parents in their **BOSOM**, and that this is a sign of the care they have for them and the love with which they embrace them. This is evident from **Numbers 11:12**: *Did I conceive all this people? Did I give them birth? That you should say to me, "Carry them in your **BOSOM**, as a nurse carries a sucking child?"* I do not think the word <term>ha-amen</term> <note>Original Hebrew: האמן</note> here designates a "pedagogue" or a "porter," such as were slaves among the Romans (as some believe), because this "carrying" is considered a consequence of *begetting*. Therefore, the <term>ha-amen</term> is the Father himself. And the interpretation of **ABARBANEL** on this passage is entirely to our taste: *Am I like the mother who takes upon herself the burden of her children, or did I beget them, that I should be to this people like the father who begets sons and labors for them, as a father has compassion on his sons?* <note>Original Hebrew: האם אני כמו האם שתקבל טורח גול בניה אם אנוכי ילידתיהו והייתי לעם הזה כמו האב המוליד הבנים שיטרח עליהם כרחם אב על בנים</note> *Am I...*

# DISSERTATION
<page-num>78</page-num>

*“Am I like a mother who exhausts herself with unbelievable labor for the sake of her children? Or did I give birth to this people, so that I should be in the place of a father to them, who for their sake swallows every hardship, just as a father has compassion for his children?”* <note>The author is likely paraphrasing the spirit of Moses' complaint to God in Numbers 11:12 regarding his burden in leading the Israelites.</note> Thus Metabus speaks of his daughter Camilla in **VIRGIL**, *Aeneid* Book XI, line 544:

> *He himself, carrying her in his **BOSOM** before him, sought the long mountain ridges.* <note>original Latin: "Ipse SINU præ se portans juga longa petebat."</note>

Compare the distinguished **ELSNER**’s <note>Jacob Elsner (1692–1750), a Prussian theologian known for his philological commentaries on the New Testament.</note> *Observations on the New Testament* regarding John 1:18. Fathers are accustomed not only to carry their children, but also to cherish and hold them tenderly in their **LAP**. Hence Phoenix says in **HOMER**, *Iliad* Book IX, line 455:

> *“Never to set upon my **KNEES** a dear son born of myself—”* <note>original Greek: Μήποτε γούνασιν οἷσιν ἐφέσσεσθαι φίλον υἱὸν Ἐξ ἐμέθεν γεγαῶτα</note>

And the same is said immediately after regarding Achilles, whom he adopted as a son (line 484):

> *“—I, placing you upon my **KNEES**—”* <note>original Greek: Σ' ἐπ' ἐμοῖσιν ἐγὼ γούνασσι καθίσας.</note>

**ENNIUS** imitated this earlier when introducing Medea speaking to Jason, as cited in **CICERO**'s *The Orator*: *“Nor shall you ever lift up into your **LAP** the offspring of children born of you.”* <note>original Latin: "Neque tuum in GREMIUM unquam extollas liberorum ex te genus."</note> To this belongs **Genesis 50:23**: *“And Joseph saw the great-great-grandchildren born of Ephraim; also the sons of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were born upon the **KNEES** of Joseph.”* In our opinion, this designates nothing other than that Joseph remained alive when the grandsons of Manasseh were born, so that he was able to place them upon his knees or his lap and delight in them. On this point, the distinguished **LE CLERC** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Genevan theologian and biblical scholar.</note> rightly compared a passage from **HOMER**, *Odyssey* Book XIX, regarding Autolycus (the father of Laertes), who received Odysseus on his **KNEES** shortly after he was born:

> *“Euryclea placed him upon his dear **KNEES**, just as he was finishing his supper—”* <note>original Greek: Τόν ῥα οἱ Εὐρύκλεια φίλοις ἐπὶ ΓΟΥΝΑΣΙ θῆκε Παυομένῳ δόρποιο</note>

**CARTWRIGHT** <note>Thomas Cartwright (c. 1535–1603), an English Puritan divine.</note> thinks this indicates that they were formally adopted into the house and family of Joseph; others, following the **CHALDEAN** <note>A reference to the Aramaic Targums (Jewish translations and paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible).</note> translation, believe they were educated by Joseph. In this sense, the “**BOSOM** of the grandfather” appears in **TACITUS**, *Annals* Book VI, chapter 45: *“Even if he was moved in his nature, however, through simulations—”* <meta>catchword: however</meta>

**IX.** Specifically, sons would sit upon the knees of their Father when they took their food. **HOMER** says in the *Iliad*, Book XXII, line 500:

From this practice comes the tradition that the place at a banquet closest to the Father—and thus in his **BOSOM**—belonged to the wife or the children. **PLUTARCH** <note>A Greek-Roman philosopher and biographer (c. 46–120 AD).</note> writes in *Table Talk*, Book II, question 3: *The first place is most suitable for the host... The place below him belongs to his wife or children.* <note>original Greek: Ὁ πρωτος τοπος μαλιστα του ἐσιωντος ἐσιν - - Ὁ μεν γαρ ὑπ’ αυτον, ἡ γυναικος ἡ παιδων ἐσιν.</note>

**X.** From these observations, full light is shed upon the passage in Luke 16:23, where *Lazarus* appears in the **BOSOM OF ABRAHAM** <note>original Greek: ἐν τοις ΚΟΛΠΟΙΣ ΑΒΡΑΗΑΜΙ.</note>. The reality of the situation, the connection with the preceding parables, and the Lord’s own purpose—to strike down the pride of the Pharisees (verse 15, compared with chapter 15:2)—all point to this. Nor do we disagree with those who think this alludes to the custom of reclining at a banquet, since such hungry and thirsty paupers are promised fulfillment in the Kingdom of the Messiah (1 Samuel 2:5, Psalm 22:27, Psalm 107:5, 9, Isaiah 55:1, Luke 1:53). And thus, in the preceding parables in Luke 14:13, 21, the *beggars*...

...to the **beggars, the maimed, the lame, and the blind** <note>original Latin: *mendicis, mancis, claudis, caecis*. **XI.** However, the emphasis of this phrase becomes much fuller when we investigate the primary reason why **Lazarus** reclines specifically in the **BOSOM OF ABRAHAM**. This reason is none other than that he is to be considered a genuine Son of Abraham according to the Spirit, excluding those who were sons only according to the flesh and who boasted in that physical prerogative. The authors of the **Tosephtot** <note>Additional legal commentaries on the Talmud.</note> for the tractate **Kiddushin** <note>The section of the Talmud concerning "Betrothals" or marriage law.</note> seem to favor this view. They explain this phrase—which occurs in the Babylonian Talmud—as follows:

*On that day he reclined in the bosom of Abraham. Some explain this to mean he died on that day. And if that does not apply here, this Rabbi Ada would be the one mentioned in the Gemara <note>The part of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary.</note>. However, it seems to be claimed that he rests in the bosom of Abraham because he was circumcised.*

For through circumcision, one entered into the covenant of Father Abraham. Meanwhile, **Saubertus** <note>Johann Saubert (1638–1688), a German philologist and theologian.</note> in his *Palæstra*, pages 278 and 279, proves from the context that the phrase refers to death, not to circumcision. Compare also **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a renowned English Hebraist who used Jewish tradition to explain Christian scripture.</note> on this passage. Whatever the case may be, it is certain that in sacred matters, Abraham is considered the mystical Father of all believers under the New Testament. We have illustrated this more extensively in our discussion of Psalm 45, Exercise 12, § 13. To the authors cited there who recognized the same point, it is helpful to add **Maldonatus** <note>Juan de Maldonado (1533–1583), a highly influential Spanish Jesuit biblical scholar.</note>, who says the following regarding this passage after citing the opinions of others:

*They have a better understanding who think the cause is that Abraham was the Father of all believers: and so all the saints were received into his **BOSOM**, just as sons are received into the house of a Father.*

Thus **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most significant Latin Church Fathers.</note>

XII. I am led all the more to believe that the same relationship is hinted at in our passage <note>Referencing John 1:18: "the only Son, who is in the bosom of the Father."</note> because the Evangelist undoubtedly looked back to the passage in **Proverbs 8:30**: *And I was beside him, a son carried in his bosom, and I was his delight daily, playing before him at all times.* <note>original Hebrew: ואהיה אצלו אמון (*ve-ehyeh etzlo amon*). This verse describes Wisdom (interpreted by Christians as the pre-existent Christ) being with God during creation.</note>. For although many interpret the name *Amon* <term>Amon (אמון): Usually translated as "master workman" or "nursling."</term> actively as **one who nourishes and cherishes all things**, it is more appropriate that it be taken passively for a **nursling**—one who is nourished and educated—as it seemed correct to **Mercer**, **Noldius**, **Cocceius**, and **Gousset**. So also **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval commentator on the Hebrew Bible.</note>: *brought up with him.* <note>original Hebrew: גדלה עמו (*gedelah immo*)</note>. This sense is supported by the passage in **Lamentations 4:5**: *those brought up in scarlet.* <note>original Hebrew: האמונים עli תולע (*ha-emunim alei tola*). The author is showing that the root of the word *Amon* refers to being raised or carried.</note>. And—

---

*a)* There are learned men who also compare **Jeremiah 46:25** and translate it as *the nursling of No.* <note>original Latin: *alumnum de No*. Most modern Bibles translate this as "Amon [the god] of Thebes."</note>. So says **Gousset** in his *Lexicon* under the word *Amen*, and **Crinesius** in his *Exercises*, part 1, page 2. But **Cocceius**, along with others, correctly observes that this is the name of an Egyptian idol called **Amun**, which also appears in **Nahum 3:8**. Yet, even this is not far removed from this name of the Son of God, not only in the sound of the letters but also in its very meaning. **Plutarch** <note>A Greek-Roman historian and philosopher (c. 46 – 119 AD).</note> in *On Isis and Osiris*, page 354, says: *Furthermore, since most people think the specific name of Jupiter among the Egyptians is* **Amun** <note>original Greek: Τον Αμουν (*Ton Amoun*)</note>, *which we, by drawing out the word, call Ammon; Manetho of Sebennytos* <note>An Egyptian priest and historian from the 3rd century BC.</note> *thinks that* **the hidden thing** <note>original Greek: το κεκρυμμενον (*to kekrymmenon*)</note> *and "concealment" are indicated by this voice.* **Hecataeus of Abdera** <note>A Greek historian and skeptic philosopher (4th century BC).</note>, however, says the Egyptians use this word with one another when one calls another; for it is an invocative word. And since they think the principal God is the same as the Universe, being obscure and **HIDDEN**, he is called and prayed to by them saying **AMUN**, so that he might bring himself forth and allow himself to be seen. Here, the word *AMUN* is explained not only passively but also in such a way that it agrees with the notion of the **BOSOM** <note>original Latin: *sinus*</note>, because the ancients used that term to express whatever was **HIDDEN**. Hence, Plutarch also compares this name in the cited passage with the veil of **Isis**, concerning which the inscription at Sais says: *No mortal has yet uncovered my veil.* <note>original Greek: Τον ἐμον πεπλον οὐδεις πω θνητος ἀπεκαλυψεν (*Ton emon peplon oudeis po thnetos apekalupsen*)</note>. **Fuller** <note>Nicholas Fuller (1557–1626), an English philologist and orientalist.</note>, in *Miscellany* II.4, understands Hecataeus’s explanation to mean that *Amun* is a common noun *which the Egyptians use in mutual gatherings whenever one kindly addresses another.* If this is the case, *Amun* expresses one whom we, loving most tenderly, also carry in our bosom. **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD).</note> explains *Amun* slightly differently in *On the Egyptian Mysteries*.

and so it is correlated with the word *ha-omen* <note>original Hebrew: האמן, meaning a guardian or nursing-father</note> in **Numbers 11:12**, **Esther 2:7**, **2 Kings 10:1, 5**, and **Isaiah 49:23**; and with *omenet* <note>original Hebrew: אומנת, meaning a nursing-mother or governess</note> in **Ruth 4:16** and **2 Samuel 4:4**. This refers to a man or woman who cares for little ones in such a way that they *carry them in their BOSOM* as their most beloved. And certainly the entire context supports this meaning. For (1) the word *amon* <note>nursling</note>, when connected with *etzlo* <note>original Hebrew: אצלו, meaning "beside him"</note>, expresses the manner in which Wisdom was with the Father: which manner (2) is in the likeness of a *daughter*, or a son, who had said *he was born* <note>original Hebrew: חוללתי (*cholalti*)</note> before the depths existed, according to verses 24 and 25. To this is added that (3) Wisdom immediately testifies that *he was his delight and played before the Father*, by which words the allegory of the *nursling* is clearly continued. Let it be permitted here to compare that saying of **Euripides** <note>A famous Greek tragedian (c. 480–406 BC).</note> in *Danaë*, found in **Stobaeus**, *Sentences*, Sermon 76.

VIII. 3. <note>This citation refers to Iamblichus, *On the Egyptian Mysteries*, Book 8, Chapter 3.</note> where he distinguishes this idol from the highest God, *Hmeph*, or rather *Kneph*, and considers it as the hidden principle of all creation and generation: *For the creative Mind, the presiding authority of truth and WISDOM, when it descends toward generation and brings the unseen power of hidden reasons into the light, is called Amun according to the language of the Egyptians.* <note>original Greek: Ο γαρ δημιουργικος νους, και της αληθειας προστατης και ΣΟΦΙΑΣ, ερχομενος μεν επι γενεσιν, και την αφανη των κεκρυμμενων λογων δυναμιν εις φως αγων, Αμων κατα την των Αιγυπτιων γλωσσαν λεγεται.</note> It is clear that these ideas do not stray far from Solomon’s description of WISDOM, BORN before all things, and the beginning of every creature. 

Whether this idol was the same as **Jupiter Ammon**, as **Plutarch** maintains, is doubtful. At least if his opinion is accepted, the name of Jupiter Ammon should no longer be derived from *Cham* <note>The son of Noah, traditionally associated with Egypt (Ham/Khem).</note>, but from the same root *aman* <note>original Hebrew: אמן, meaning to support, foster, or trust.</note>. Compare **Wolf**, page 72 and page 75. Furthermore, the name *Amanos* also agrees with this name, which **Strabo** mentions among the Persian demons in Book XI, and which is written as *Omanos* in the same Book XI. This similarity of letters is surely closer than the *chammanim* <note>original Hebrew: חמנים, often translated as "sun-pillars" or cultic idols.</note> which **J. C. Bulenger** considers in his *Notes on Arnobius*, page 314, and **Selden** in *On the Syrian Gods*, Synthesis II. 8; or *Aban* or *Acman*, which is the conjecture of the celebrated **Reland**, *Dissertation* VIII, page 117. 

Hence also the illustrious **Hyde**, in *The Religion of the Persians*, Chapter III, page 95, compares the Egyptian *Amun* with this *Amanos*, although he is mistaken in thinking that *Amun* was corrupted from *Ammon* or "The Sandy One," as if it designated the one who was worshiped among the sands of Libya. For the word *Amun* is of Egyptian origin, and that corruption was an invention of the Greeks.

**XIII.** Furthermore, it seems to me that we should hardly doubt that this passage of Solomon <note>Referring to Proverbs 8.</note> was clearly before the eyes of the Evangelist <note>The Gospel writer, John.</note>, especially since in his entire Prologue <note>John 1:1-18.</note> he alludes more than once to that excellent description of supreme Wisdom. The very names **Word** <note>original Greek: Λογος (*Logos*)</note> and **Wisdom** <note>original Hebrew: חכמה (*Chokmah*)</note> have a remarkable agreement, as we have pointed out elsewhere. And from where could that phrase—by which the Word is said to have been **with God** <note>original Greek: προς τον Θεον (*pros ton Theon*)</note>—be better derived than from that very word **beside him** <note>original Hebrew: אצלו (*etzlo*)</note> which occurs in the present passage? Where did that phrase **in the beginning** <note>original Greek: ἐν ἀρχῃ (*en arche*)</note> come from, if not from verse 22: *Jehovah possessed me as the beginning of his way, etc.*? It is added that, just as Wisdom in Solomon's writing commends his teaching by recalling his eternal generation, so here also the prophetic office of the Son of God is established from the same argument.

**XIV.** From all these points gathered into one, we conclude that the foundation of the metaphor which the Apostle <note>John</note> applies here is that adorable mystery of the **SONSHIP** <note>original Latin: *filiationis*</note> of the second person [of the Trinity]. The metaphor itself is so constructed that, although it does not fully exhaust the mystery—which is true of any human or physical comparison—it can nonetheless suggest some concept both of the properties and of the consequences or acts of those relationships by which this sonship is demonstrated in the work itself.

**XV.** Regarding the properties, it pertains first to the fact that just as a Son, who is carried **in the bosom**, is not only of the same nature as the Father, but is also from the Father by a natural order; so the second person—while maintaining his independence and co-eternity or co-existence with the Father—is a sharer of the same essence with the Father. Indeed, he is so in such a way that is peculiar to the second person, so that it does not allow for alternation: hence, according to the **analogy of faith** <note>A theological rule that individual Bible verses should be interpreted in a way that is consistent with the whole of Christian doctrine.</note>, it can be said that the Son **is from the Father**, but not conversely that the Father **is from the Son**. This is the true reason why it is said

-> ### DISSERTATION <-

...is called the **proper son** <note>original Greek: ἴδιος υἱὸς (*idios huios*)</note> in Romans 8:32. This is the formal reason why this name is said to be **more excellent** than that of the Angels, even though they are likewise called **Sons of God** in a clearly distinguished sense in Job 38:7. This agrees with the name **Only-begotten** <note>original Greek: Μονογενὴς (*Monogenēs*)</note>, which excludes any sharing of this excellence with any creature. For just as a son who is **in the bosom of the Father** fills that space entirely, so that there is no room for any other in that same bosom, in the same way the second person of the Trinity fills the entire "bosom" of the Father, as it were, and admits no partnership of any creature alongside himself in this honor.

Hence, it is never said of any Angels or Believers that they are **in the bosom of God**; rather, it is affirmed of the elect only that they are **in the bosom of Abraham** <note>A biblical expression referring to the place of comfort in the afterlife, named after the patriarch Abraham</note>. They are capable of this honor only because of a communion of essence <note>Meaning they share a human nature with Abraham, whereas only the Son shares a divine nature with the Father</note>. Therefore, **Clement of Alexandria** <note>A prominent Christian theologian and teacher in Egypt (c. 150–215 AD)</note> is not accurate enough in his treatise, *Who is the Rich Man that Shall Be Saved?*, when he interprets the **BOSOM OF THE FATHER** as the eternal life to be inherited by the faithful, writing: *leading into the bosoms of the Father, into eternal life, into the kingdom of heaven* <note>original Greek: ὁδηγῶν εἰς τοὺς κόλπους τοῦ Πατρὸς, εἰς τὴν αἰώνιον ζωὴν, εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν</note>.

**Faustinus** <note>A 4th-century priest and theologian</note> correctly writes in chapter 2 of his book to Flaccus: *Adopted sons are in the bosom of Abraham; but he who is the true and only-begotten Son is in the bosom of the Father.* Therefore, we whole-heartedly subscribe to the Catechetical expression by which Christ is said to be THE ONLY CO-ETERNAL AND NATURAL SON OF THE ETERNAL FATHER.

**XVI.** The same image confirms, **secondly**, the personal distinction of the second person from the first, while preserving the most absolute unity of the divine essence. For a **nursling** <note>or "foster-child"</note> carried in the bosom is someone other than the one carrying him, although through paternal embraces he is so united with the Father that he seems to be **in him**, or rather to be **one** with him. Thus, Scripture presents the Son to us as **another** <note>original Greek: ἄλλον (*allon*)</note> in John 5:32, and nonetheless **one** in John 10:30 and 17:21.

**XVII.** The **relative acts** <term>Relative acts: actions or relationships that define how the persons of the Trinity relate to one another (e.g., loving, protecting)</term> which this image displays are of two kinds: some **alternate**, and some **do not alternate**. To the mutual or alternating acts belongs **mutual love**, and the resulting mutual delight of the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father, as seen in John 14:10 and 17:21. Among the **non-alternating** acts, however, we include the protection, guardianship, and defense which the Father provides to the Son.

<meta>catchword: XVIII.</meta>

<summary>This page argues that the title "Only-begotten Son" and the image of being in the "Father's bosom" signify a unique, essential divine relationship that cannot be shared by angels or human believers. It distinguishes between the "bosom of Abraham" for the saved and the "bosom of the Father" for Christ, emphasizing the distinction of persons within the unity of the Trinity.</summary>

# ON THE BOSOM OF THE FATHER.

XVIII. These acts, according to Scripture, are displayed in an illustrious manner in the work of grace and salvation. There the Father demonstrates the most tender love toward the Son. *For the Father loves the Son* (John 3:35), as the **Son of His love** <note>original Greek: Υἱὸν τῆς ἀγάπης αὐτοῦ (*Huion tēs agapēs autou*)</note> (Colossians 1:13); indeed, *He seeks the glory of the Son, and glorifies Him* (John 8:50, 54). The Son, in turn, loves the Father from His innermost being <note>original Latin: *ex intimis visceribus*, literally "from his innermost bowels," a common idiom for deep, heartfelt emotion</note> (Psalm 18:2), *and honors Him* (John 8:49). Hence, *the Son delights in the Father and in doing His will* (Psalm 40:9), *and He blesses Him because He gave Him counsel* (Psalm 16:7). The Father truly testified from heaven, *that this is that Son of His, that beloved one, in whom He is well pleased* (Matthew 3:17). Finally, the Father provides help to the Son, and proves His devoted faithfulness by action while He *is at His right hand* (Psalm 16:8). Whence the Father is called a *shield around the Son* (Psalm 3:4); indeed, *His rock, and His fortress, and His deliverer, and the cliff of His refuge, and so forth* (Psalm 18:3). There is no room here to draw these points out at greater length.

XIX. It is helpful to add this one thing: since hidden and secret things are said to be **IN THE BOSOM**, nothing is more remote or concealed from all human knowledge and conception than that mystery of the Father and the Son, in which *all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden* (Colossians 2:3). Here even the sharpest eyes grow dim. Whatever academic terms, whatever reasonings of human wit are brought in to help, these are generally put together in such a way that they complicate the matter rather than explain it. Therefore, it would be better to abstain from all of them and nobly profess ignorance, than to bring forth things that are **inconsistent** <note>original Greek: ἀσύστατα (*asustata*)</note> and unintelligible even to their own authors, things which lie outside of Scripture. The failure to observe this has been—alas!—an all-too-fertile source of quarrels, which have often been tossed back and forth in such a way that the reverence due to so wonderful and terrifying a mystery seems rather to have been shaken out of minds than provoked within them.

XX. I think it should not be neglected, however, that the Evangelist <note>The author refers to the Apostle John</note> affirms in the present tense that the only-begotten Son **IS** <note>original Greek: εἶναι (*einai*), Latin: *esse*</note> in the Bosom of the Father. Without necessity, those who translate the phrase **the one who is** <note>original Greek: ὁ ὤν (*ho ōn*)</note> as "who was" establish a grammatical shift <term>enallage: the substitution of one grammatical form for another, such as a change in tense</term>; this is done not only by the **Socinians** <note>A group of 16th- and 17th-century thinkers who denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ</note>, but even by some of the orthodox. For the present tense suggests that He is **returning to the Father's House** (John 14:2-3) and is as **Manna** in the sanctuary <note>The original Latin *adyto* refers to the innermost, most sacred part of a temple, equivalent to the "Holy of Holies" where the manna was kept in the Ark of the Covenant</note>

He declares that he had already been there, as a *Nursling* <note>original: *Alumnum*; a term implying one who is nourished, cherished, or brought up in a close, dependent relationship.</note> in the bosom of the Father. For there is a unique analogy between that honor which the Son then had with the Father and that which he received after his ascension. Thus our Savior asks in John 17:5: *Now therefore, Father, glorify me with yourself, with that glory which I had with you before the world began.* Regarding that passage, we shall provide the reasoning for this analogy, God willing.

XXIII. Indeed, this description of Christ corresponds excellently with the context and purpose of the Evangelist. For *firstly*, it contains the argument that makes it clear with what great emphasis he called him THAT ONLY-BEGOTTEN SON. *Secondly*, within it lies the reason for the title that is added: namely, that he is the supreme <term>Exegete</term> <note>original Greek: Εξηγητης (Exegetes); someone who interprets, explains, or reveals hidden mysteries.</note>, or INTERPRETER, of the Father’s entire will. For such a Son, who is so closely united with the Father and who has such an intimate experience of the Father's love, faithfulness, and help, perfectly and adequately knows the essence, virtues, will, and ways of the Father; he is able to provide a testimony regarding them that is beyond all doubt. > *No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him* Matthew 11:27. *The Father loves the Son and shows him all things that he himself does* John 5:20. From this comes the remarkable privilege of the New Testament: that *God in these last days has spoken to us in his Son* Hebrews 1:1. For the same reason, the Supreme Wisdom <note>A common reference to Christ or the personified Wisdom of God in the Old Testament.</note> used the same argument to commend her teaching in the cited passage of Proverbs. CHRYSOSTOM <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), a prominent Early Church Father known for his preaching and biblical commentary.</note> hit the mark here in his 15th Homily and in the *Catena on John* page 40: <note>original Greek: Ορα μεθ’ ὁσης φθεγγεται της περιουσιας ὁ Ευαγγελιστης. Ο μεν γαρ ἁπλως ὁρων ου παντος ακριβη του φαινομενου την γνωσιν εχει. ‘Ο δε εν τοις κολποις διατριβων ουδεν αγνοησει ποτε. > *See with how much authority the Evangelist speaks. For after saying that no one has ever seen God, he did not say that the Son, having seen Him, explained Him. But he who dwells in the bosom will never be ignorant of anything. Through this one word, he has shown us everything: that the closeness of their being is great, and that his knowledge is exact.*

### DISSERTATION ON THE BOSOM OF THE FATHER.
<meta>catchword: V.</meta>

[The Evangelist] substituted something more excellent than mere vision. For *to dwell in the bosom of the Father* is much more perfect than *to see*. *For he who only sees does not always have an accurate knowledge of the thing seen; but he who dwells in the bosom will never be ignorant of anything.* He has thus explained everything to us in a single word: both the intimate closeness of substance and the highest certainty of knowledge. Thirdly, this description indicates how great is the excellence of this Interpreter and <term>Mediator</term> <note>original Latin: *Internuncius*; literally an "inter-messenger" or go-between who carries news between two parties.</note> compared to Moses, the mediator of the Old Testament, to whom he had been opposed in the preceding verse. For although Moses was *with the Angel on Mount Sinai* <note>Acts 7:38. The original text cites Act. VIII, likely a scribal error for chapter VII.</note>, yet he is never called the *Son of the Father*, but only the *Servant of God*, a contrast which the Apostle emphasizes in Hebrews 3:5-6. He was so far from having a place in the very BOSOM OF THE FATHER.

XXIV. From this, we gather how impiously the <term>Anti-Trinitarians</term> <note>Various groups who rejected the traditional doctrine of the Trinity, arguing instead for the singular personhood of God.</note> pervert the full emphasis of this phrase. Some of them, following in the footsteps of the <term>Arians</term> <note>Followers of Arius (4th century), who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being, distinct from and subordinate to God the Father.</note>, believe that *being in the bosom of the Father* means nothing other than being most dear to God. Truly, no passage can be produced in which *being in the bosom* signifies nothing else. It always includes some close relationship which is the foundation of that love. <term>Schlichtingius</term> <note>Jonas Schlichting (1592–1661), a leading scholar of the Socinian movement.</note> devises something else: *When God,* he says, *uniquely loved his only Son, he took him to himself into his bosom and revealed to him all the secrets of his will concerning grace and truth, and the salvation of the human race.* These words evidently refer to that <term>Socinian</term> <note>A non-trinitarian movement that emphasized Jesus's humanity; they often claimed Jesus was literally "taken up" to heaven for instruction before his earthly ministry began.</note> fiction, in which they claim that the Son was caught up into heaven after his baptism and instructed by the Father. However, everyone sees that these ideas diametrically oppose the analogy of faith, the much broader significance of the natural imagery, Solomon’s proclamation of Wisdom <note>Referring to the personification of Wisdom in Proverbs 8:30, often interpreted as the pre-existent Christ.</note> occupying the Father's bosom like a nursling from eternity, and the present participle <term>who is</term> <note>original Greek: ὁ ὤν (*ho ōn*); a grammatical point used to argue that Christ is *currently* and *permanently* in the Father's bosom, rather than being "taken up" there later.</note>, which we have defended.

### ON THE
## BIRTH FROM WATER AND SPIRIT.

### I.
In Christ’s discourse on the Birth from *Water and Spirit (John 3:5)*, interpreters have wavered chiefly concerning the meaning of WATER. Some have understood it *literally*, others *metaphorically*. Both groups have, in turn, been pulled in various directions. It is helpful, therefore, to attempt to see if something certain can be found amidst such a great diversity of opinions. To this end, before we put forward our own view, we must examine the opinions of others in advance.

II. Among those who adhere to the literal letter, none is more absurd than the ANONYMOUS author whom SANDIUS <note>Christoph Sand (1644–1680), a Dutch Socinian scholar known for his controversial and "paradoxical" interpretations of Scripture.</note> follows in his *Paradoxical Interpretations of the Four Gospels, p. 189 and following.* For he understands the *new birth* as the sending of pre-existing souls into bodies, and thus as a carnal or physical birth. For this reason, he <term>paraphrases</term> <note>original Greek: παραφράζει; to restate a text in different words to clarify its meaning.</note> the third verse, which precedes our passage, in this way: *Unless one is born in the flesh, he cannot enter the kingdom of God, because it is not permitted to them by God to be born a second time—specifically in the flesh—for they are the authors of all sin; but because of the soul seduced by the Devil, God created the world and established the flesh as contrary to the spirit. Therefore, by the mercy and grace of God, the soul is incarnated and becomes man, so that it might recover its former state.* Having supposed these things, he claims regarding our verse that Christ is here explaining more closely what he meant by the second birth in *verse 3*, namely that it is indeed carnal, or that it occurs from water and Spirit—that is, from flesh and spirit. [...the soul is incarnated and becomes human so that it may] be the principle of carnal generation, from which many modern and ancient philosophers have believed all bodies consist. **Sandius** himself <note>Christoph Sand (1644–1680), a scholar associated with Arianism who proposed controversial interpretations of the New Testament.</note> adopted this error—drawn from the pits of certain pagan philosophers—in his treatise *On the Origin of the Soul*, page 97.

III. It is hardly worth the effort to seriously refute this crude concept. For it is not only *unscriptural* <note>original Greek: "ἄγραφος" (agraphos); literally "unwritten," meaning not found in holy writ</note>, but clearly *anti-scriptural* <note>original Greek: "ἀντίγραφος" (antigraphos); meaning directly contradicting the written word</note>, since the sacred pages teach the immediate creation of the soul in the body in Genesis 2:7 and Zechariah 12:1. Furthermore, nothing is more opposed to the true doctrine regarding the way sin resides in a corrupted body. It should be added that the entire context of our passage is diametrically opposed to this heresy. For Jesus is discussing a generation that makes one fit for communion with the kingdom of God—a birth which **Nicodemus** and his companions lacked, and which Jesus emphasizes in verse 7: *It is necessary for you to be born again.* It will become clear to those who investigate that the writings of some Church Fathers are cited in support of this [Sandius's] view with very poor faith <note>The author suggests Sandius is misrepresenting or misquoting the early Church leaders.</note>.

IV. The opinion of those who understand the "water" in this place to mean the *sacramental water in Baptism* carries greater weight. This was the view of most of the Church Fathers, especially from the time around the end of the second century when some of them began to fight for the necessity of baptism as a *means* <note>term: "medium"; here referring to a "means of grace," a necessary instrument for salvation</note> to regeneration and salvation. You might think **Irenaeus** <note>A 2nd-century bishop of Lyons and a major early Christian theologian.</note> already felt this way, if you were to trust the translation by **Billius** <note>Jacques de Billy (1535–1581), a French scholar known for translating Greek patristic texts into Latin.</note> of *Against Heresies*, book I, chapter 21, section 1: *"And indeed, regarding the denial of that Baptism through which we are reborn to God, and thus the rejection of the entire faith, we shall report in its proper place that this kind [of heresy] was suggested by Satan."* However, in the original Greek text, *Baptism* and *regeneration to God* are distinct: <note>original Greek: "ὅτι μὲν εἰς ἔξαρνησιν τοῦ βαπτίσματος τῆς εἰς Θεὸν ἀναγεννήσεως, καὶ πάσης τῆς πίστεως ἀπόθεσιν ὑποβέβληται" — "Because it [this heresy] has been suggested for the denial of the baptism of regeneration unto God, and the putting away of the whole faith..."</note>. Nevertheless, it is clear from the *Second Apology* that **Justin Martyr** <note>An early Christian apologist (c. 100–165 AD) who wrote defenses of the faith to the Roman Emperor.</note> had already spoken somewhat less carefully about this matter: *“Then they are led by us to where there is water, and they are regenerated in the same manner of regeneration by which we ourselves were regenerated... For in the name of God the Parent and Lord of all things, and of our Savior Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, they then receive the washing in water.”* Which hypothesis,

**Tertullian** expressed this opinion more openly when, in chapter 12 of his work *On Baptism*, he concedes *that it is a rule that salvation belongs to no one without Baptism, especially based on that pronouncement of the Lord, who says: Unless a one be born of water, he does not have life.* <note>A reference to John 3:5. Original Latin: "Niſi natus ex aqua quis erit, non habet vitam."</note> Hence also in the same work, chapter 1, he thinks the name "little fish" <note>original: "piſciculorum"</note>—which the Pagans gave to Christians in mockery based on the acrostic <note>An acrostic is a word formed from the first letters of other words. The Greek word for Fish is *ICHTHYS*, which stands for *Iēsous Christos, Theou Hyios, Sōtēr*—Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.</note> of the words **Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior**—should not be rejected, since from this hypothesis he obtains a convenient explanation: *We little fish, following our "Ichthys" [Fish], Jesus Christ, are born in water.*

The same is professed by **Cyprian** (Letter 1 to Donatus), **Augustine** (Letter 28; *On the Origin of the Soul*, Book II, ch. 12; *Against Julian*, Book V, ch. 8; *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, Book I, ch. 16, 23, 27), **Ambrose** (*On the Holy Spirit*, Book III, ch. 2), **Jerome** (Volume II, Letter 83 to Oceanus), **Basil** (*Exhortation to Holy Baptism*), **Chrysostom**, **Cyril**, and **Theophylact** in their commentaries on this passage, **Athanasius** (*Oration on the Holy Passover*), **Cassiodorus** (*Commentary on the Song of Songs* 7), etc.

From this, **Leo the Great** likens the water of Baptism to the womb of the Blessed Virgin in his fourth *Sermon on the Solemnity of the Nativity*: *The water of baptism is like the virginal womb, with the same Spirit filling the font who also filled the Virgin.* And in Sermon 5: *The origin which He took from the womb of the virgin, He placed in the font of Baptism: He gave to the water what He gave to His Mother.* Indeed, others have added that this was the very purpose for which Christ himself wished to be baptized: so that the water of Baptism might receive such great efficacy. **Ambrose** in Book II of his *Commentary on Luke 3*: *The Lord was baptized, not wishing to be cleansed but to cleanse the waters, so that having been washed through the flesh of Christ, which knew no sin, they might have the right of Baptism.* For which cause

V. We, however, do not hesitate to place this interpretation among the *misinterpretations* <note>original Greek: *παρερμηνείας* (parermēneias)</note> with which the records of the Church Fathers abound. To be sure, the **Council of Trent** <note>The 16th-century ecumenical council of the Catholic Church held in response to the Protestant Reformation.</note> in Session VII on Baptism, Canon 2, defined it thus: *If anyone says that true and natural water is not of the necessity of Baptism, and thus distorts those words of our Lord Jesus Christ, "Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit," into some metaphor, let him be anathema.* <note>An "anathema" is a formal curse by a church or council, excommunicating a person or denouncing a doctrine. Original Latin: "Si quis dixerit, aquam veram & naturalem non eſſe de neceſſitate Baptiſmi atque illo verba illa Domini noſtri Jeſu Chriſti, Niſi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu Sancto, ad metaphoram aliquam detorſerit, Anathema ſit."</note> But the truth does not fear these hollow clatterings <note>The author uses the phrase "strepitus ex pelvi," literally "noises from a wash-basin," an idiom suggesting the Council's threats are empty or superficial.</note>. And the authority of the Fathers constrains us even less, because their practice was clearly contrary to their theory. For if they had been convinced of the absolute necessity of Baptism, they themselves would not have delayed Baptism so often until adult age. We do not, therefore, bow to authorities but to reasons, which are strongest against this opinion.

For 1. To set aside other arguments with which the "necessity of means" <note>A theological term (*necessitas medii*) referring to something that is an indispensable instrument for achieving salvation.</note> (as they call it) ascribed to Baptism is attacked by our theologians, we note this: that by *water* is designated such a principle of the new generation that precedes it by nature. For this reason, it is placed in the first position before the Spirit, as a principle anticipating the saving operations of the Holy Spirit. However, the very nature of the matter requires that the water of Baptism suppose and follow the grace of the Holy Spirit. For whoever approaches to be received into the communion of the people of God by being washed in the sacred font, it is required of him that he be touched by a living desire for his salvation; no one can be so touched unless he has already come into possession of the beginnings of spiritual life.

Furthermore, faith is required before Baptism (Mark 16:16, Acts 8:37, Ephesians 4:5). It is most certain that faith holds its place among the first acts of the new life. **Peter** also requires conversion itself before Baptism (Acts 2:38). The same is clear from the examination of examples—not only the house of **Cornelius**, upon whom the Holy Spirit was poured out before Baptism (Acts 10:44, 47), but also of many others who, before they were baptized, showed by their very actions such movements as were a very clear [sign]...

VI. But the text provides other reasons against this opinion. II. For "to be born of water and spirit" <note>original Greek: *τὸ γεννηθῆναι ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ πνεύματος*</note> is equivalent to "to be born from above," <note>original Greek: *τῷ ἄνωθεν γεννηθῆναι*</note> which was not only used in the preceding third verse, but is also repeated in verse 7: *Do not marvel that I said to you, you must be born again.* Therefore, the Savior intended only to urge the necessity of regeneration considered in itself and its own nature.
