In these words, Jesus not only expresses the present tense but also prescribes a path for Nicodemus, outside of which the way into the kingdom of God was not open to him at that very moment. VII. Some seek to soften this opinion by attributing the use of baptismal water to a necessity of **command** rather than a necessity of **means** <note>original: *necessitatem non medii sed præcepti*. In theology, a "necessity of means" implies an act is essential for salvation, whereas a "necessity of command" means it is required because God ordered it, but exceptions (like the thief on the cross) may exist.</note>. This opinion is championed by FORBES <note>John Forbes of Corse (1593–1648), a Scottish theologian</note> in his *Historical and Theological Instructions*, book 10, chapter 9, section 2. SCALIGER <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a renowned French scholar</note> understands "water" as the visible sign and "Spirit" as the invisible grace and **the rebirth in Christ** <note>original Greek: *καὶ τὴν ἐν Χριστῷ παλιγγενεσίαν*</note>. ERASMUS SARCERIUS favors this same view in his commentary on this passage, as do ROBERT ROLLOCK and GATAKER <note>Thomas Gataker (1574–1654), an English Puritan scholar</note> in his *Posthumous Miscellaneous Works*, chapter 28, saying: *that he thinks, along with all the ancient writers, that the discourse concerns sacramental water; however, he considers water here only as a symbol and seal of the operations of the Holy Spirit, which he believes is joined here with the thing signified.* 

And this was indeed the opinion of some of the Church Fathers, although they are often dragged into a harsher interpretation by those who wish to make the text serve their own theories. Thus GREGORY OF NAZIANZUS <note>A 4th-century theologian and Doctor of the Church</note> in his 40th Oration, speaking of Baptism, says: **"Since we are twofold—I mean of soul and body, and of a nature both visible and invisible—the cleansing is also twofold: namely, through water and the Spirit; the one received visibly and bodily, the other concurring invisibly and incorporeally; the one being typical, the other being true and cleansing the depths."** <note>original Greek: *Διττῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν... τὰ βάθη καθαίροντος*</note> *Just as we consist of two parts—that is, soul and body, one of which is seen and the other escapes the sense of the eyes—so also Baptism consists of two things: water and the Spirit; the former accepted in a visible and corporeal way, the latter concurring in an incorporeal and invisible way: THE FORMER IS TYPICAL, the latter is true and purges the innermost reaches of the soul.* The same opinion is found in CYRIL OF JERUSALEM’S *Catechesis* 3, section 2, and others. 

GATAKER, however, is inconsistent with himself in this theory; for in the place cited, he immediately adds *that it is perhaps only an allusion to the water of Gospel Baptism or even to the Mosaic rites of washing*, and he compares it to John 6:53, where he correctly determines that the sacrificial feast is alluded to <note>In John 6, Jesus speaks of eating his flesh; Gataker argues this is a metaphor, just as "water" in John 3 is an allusion rather than a literal requirement.</note>. These claims are **inconsistent** <note>original Greek: *ἀσύστατα*</note>. For he who judges that Jesus speaks of water merely through an "allusion" has already conceded, by that very fact, that the word must be understood metaphorically.

### OF REBIRTH FROM WATER, ETC.

I deny that God has anywhere so strongly asserted the necessity of any ecclesiastical or sacramental rite without any limitation or distinction. It will never be proven—Divine Wisdom intervening—lest the idol of the **work performed** <note>original: *operis operati*. A theological doctrine suggesting that sacraments are effective purely by the act being performed, regardless of the recipient's faith. The author here argues against this "automatic" view of salvation.</note> should seem to find some support in the sacred pages. The way of speaking that Jesus uses in the command for baptism in Mark 16:16 is quite different: *He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned.* For here, he not only places Baptism after the saving grace of faith, but he also takes care not to link the danger of condemnation with the omission of Baptism. For although he joins Baptism with faith as a seal of salvation in the first part of the sentence, in the second part he did not want to add the omission of Baptism to unbelief. He did this lest anyone think that condemnation depends on the omission of Baptism viewed in itself, and conclude that Baptism is a necessary means in its own right for escaping condemnation. This error could not have been prevented if Jesus had pronounced that the unbaptized were certainly to be damned. 

Therefore, I cannot be led to believe that Jesus intended to link exclusion from the kingdom of God with the lack of baptismal water. Nor is it enough to point out that sometimes in Scripture things of different degrees of necessity are joined in the same breath; for example, *prayer and fasting* for the casting out of demons in Matthew 17:21, or *faith and confession* for the attainment of salvation in Romans 10:9-10. For everyone sees that these examples, although they are brought up everywhere against the **Catholics** <note>original: *Pontificios*. A term used by Protestant writers to refer to those who follow the Pope/Pontiff.</note>, are clearly not adequate. The connection between those things (faith and confession) is naturally much closer than the connection between a physical element (water) and the operations of the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, although a saving effect is ascribed to those things in a certain order, the opposite is not affirmed without any restriction regarding the omission of fasting or confession. Thus, it will be better to completely abandon the literal sense—as it conflicts with the nature of the subject—rather than opening ourselves up to our opponents by admitting it.

Therefore, just as to baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire is to confer the Holy Spirit, who in regeneration has the office and nature of fire, so to be born again of water and Spirit is nothing other than to receive that power of the Spirit, which does in the soul what water does in the body.* He holds similar views in his Commentary on this passage.

The same view was held by **Hugo Grotius**, who at the same time answered an objection that could be raised: *Nor does it stand in the way that one word precedes the other as if limiting it. For thus in Acts 17:25, "Life and breath" <note>original: *Ζωὴ καὶ πνοὴ*</note> is the same as "breath of life" <note>original: *πνοὴ ζωῆς*</note> elsewhere, as in Genesis 2:7; and in Mark 7:23 <note>Likely a citation error in the original text for John 6:63.</note> "spirit and life" <note>original: *πνευμα καὶ ζωὴ*</note>. So in Genesis 3:16, "conception and pain" means the pain resulting from conception. So in Colossians 2:8, "through philosophy and empty deceit" <note>original: *διὰ τῆς φιλοσοφίας καὶ κενῆς ἀπάτης*</note> means through the empty fallacies of philosophy. And in Matthew 4:16, "in the region and shadow of death" <note>original: *ἐν χώρᾳ καὶ σκιᾷ θανάτου*</note> the Arabic version translates as "in the region of the shadow of death."* 

Besides our own [theologians], this same opinion is embraced by **Daniel Chamier** in his *Panstratia Catholica*, Volume IV; **Franciscus Gomarus**; **Herman Witsius** in *The Economy of the Covenants*, Book III; **Jean Daillé** in the place cited; **Johannes Piscator**; **David Pareus**; **Moïse Amyraut** in the *Saumur Disputations*; and others. **Simon Episcopius** also takes this view, as do **Jonas Schlichting** and **Ludwig von Wolzogen** from among the Socinians <note>A rationalist Christian movement that emerged during the Reformation, often criticized by the orthodox for their views on the Trinity.</note>.

# DISSERTATION

...becomes a frequent and elegant symbol of the operations of the Holy Spirit. However, there are things that prevent us from agreeing with this. For I. A <term>hendiadys</term> <note>original: *Hendiadys*. A figure of speech where two words linked by "and" are used to express a single complex idea, like saying "cups and gold" to mean "golden cups."</note> is not to be admitted in the <term>Sacred Style</term> <note>original: *stylo sacro*. The specific literary and linguistic conventions used by the authors of the Bible.</note>, except where necessity demands it, which occurs when a fitting distinction cannot be made. But where such a distinction is readily available, the sense of the Sacred Scriptures is rendered much richer if we prefer the distinction over the conjunction. Whoever more accurately weighs the passages referred to the category of <note>original: *των εν δια δυοιν* (tōn hen dia dyoin), "one through two."</note> hendiadys by **GROTIUS**, **GLASSIUS**, and other philologists, will find that most of them do not require this grammatical figure. It is a figure that should be admitted all the more rarely because it was formerly more common among poets than among orators. **SERVIUS**, in his commentary on Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book I, verse 65 (*"A mass and mountains"*), says: *That is,* he says, *the mass of the mountain. And it is the figure of hendiadys, so that one thing is divided into two, with a conjunction placed between them FOR THE SAKE OF THE METER,* as elsewhere: *We pour libations from bowls and gold, that is, from golden bowls.* Compare **VOSSIUS**, *Institutes of Oratory*, Book V, chapter IV, paragraph 4. II. There is no available example in the Sacred Style where a sign has been distinguished from the thing signified, or a symbol from the thing symbolized, by the intervening conjunction "AND." For while in other contexts this figure can sometimes have a certain emphasis for intensifying, or distinguishing, or limiting, in such a case it would be plainly useless.

XIII. Most of those, therefore, who think the metaphorical sense should be preferred, distinguish water from the Spirit. But they themselves go in different directions. **HOTTINGER** in *Heidelberg First-fruits*, dissertation III, paragraph 3, page 78, thinks this phrase can be illustrated from the Jewish school in such a way *that the sense is: We must not only be born of water (for so semen is called <note>original: *κατ’ ευφημιαν* (kat’ euphēmian)</note> "by euphemism," as elsewhere in Isaiah 48:4), that is, naturally; but we must be reborn of the Spirit.* He modestly leaves this, however, to the judgment of others. And in his *Philological Treasury*, Book I, chapter 2, page 246, he declares himself in favor of the hendiadys, which I was just examining. I noted in paragraph IX that such an <term>ellipsis</term> <note>The omission of words needed for a full grammatical structure.</note> is indeed unusual. And the Savior himself, in the very next verse, calls natural generation not generation *from water*, but *from flesh*, and he does not assume it, but opposes it to that which is spoken of here.

### DISSERTATION
<meta>catchword: candi (likely from the Latin "significandi")</meta>

...which therefore cannot be considered as its *principle*. The latter opinion is favored by the fact that elsewhere the Word is joined with the Spirit as his primary instrument, as in Isaiah 59:21, and that *water* is a frequent emblem in sacred scripture for the divine word; for this purpose, passages such as Psalm 23:2, Isaiah 11:9, 12:3, 41:17-18, Ezekiel 47:1 and following, Joel 2:23, 3:18, Zechariah 14:8, etc., are brought forward. Although this opinion is pious and elegant—so much so that it has sometimes caused my own mind to waver—one primary difficulty remained for me when weighing it more deeply. Namely, those cited passages in which *water* is held as a symbol of the divine word are so constructed that they do not designate the *external word* on its own, but rather joined with the operation of the Holy Spirit, and it is only because of that conjunction that it is compared to water. The word, considered in itself, has no vital power. This power belongs to the Holy Spirit alone, who drives the truths proposed in that word into the soul in such a way that its faculties are simultaneously disposed to consider them attentively, perceive them correctly, and receive them eagerly. Since, therefore, the word joined with the Spirit is the regenerating water, it would follow that *by water and Spirit*, taken in this sense, one and the same thing is signified; thus, according to this opinion, a <term>hendiadys</term> <note>original: *Hendiadyn*. A figure of speech where two words connected by a conjunction (and) are used to express a single complex idea, such as "grace and favor."</note> would actually be established, which we rejected above as being less appropriate.

XVII. There remains the opinion of those who believe our Savior indicated his own obedience and merit through the "water." **JOHN WYCLIFFE** <note>Jan Wycliffe (c. 1320s–1384), an English philosopher and precursor to the Reformation.</note> led the way for these thinkers; among his errors, it is recorded by **NATALIS ALEXANDER** <note>Noël Alexandre (1639–1724), a prominent French Dominican theologian and church historian.</note> (*13th & 14th Century, Part I, p. 465*) that he held *that the Baptism of water is not necessary for salvation, but the Baptism of the Spirit <note>original: *Baptismus Flaminis*. A theological term for the "Baptism of the Breath" or Spirit, often contrasted with the water rite.</note> through the merits and the flow of water from the side of the crucified Savior suffices.* This same view appealed, not without cause, to the celebrated **COCCEIUS**, **BURMAN**, and other most learned men <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) and Frans Burman (1628–1679) were major figures in Dutch "Covenant Theology."</note>. For in this way: I. A real distinction is established between the water and the Spirit, which provides the fullest sense of the text. II. This distinction agrees with the very nature of the matter, because the merit of Christ is truly the cause of regeneration—and indeed, a cause that precedes the operations of the Holy Spirit. For Christ, through his obedience, acquired the right of giving the Holy Spirit and of bringing the elect to life through him.

->DISSERTATION<-

*...which it is clear that the Lord himself explains in the cited chapter of Ezekiel, verse 26.* Truly, with all due respect to such a Great Man <note>original: *pace tanti Viri*. A polite Latin formula used by scholars when they are about to disagree with a respected authority.</note>, whose name is venerable in the Christian Church and especially in this Academy, we are fully persuaded that these passages refer to the merit of Christ. Ezekiel 36, verses 25 and 26, do not explain each other, but rather exhibit two different benefits of the New Testament. And we shall immediately show that the former cannot designate anything other than the obedience of Christ. In Hebrews 10:22, a clear mention of **sprinkling** <note>original: *aspersio*. This refers to the ritual sprinkling of blood or water in Jewish law, symbolizing purification.</note> is made, which in the Levitical worship <term>Levitical worship: the system of sacrifices and rituals performed by the tribe of Levi in the Old Testament</term> constantly foreshadowed the obedience of Christ. Nor do we think that 1 John 5:6, 8 refers to anything other than the water of sprinkling mixed with blood, with which the water and blood flowing from the side of Christ elegantly corresponded. Thus, the same reasoning that applied in the previous passage holds true here as well.

XIX. But there are also men, whose names we look up to, who think there is some difficulty in the fact that the particle **from** <note>original: the Greek particle *ek* ($\epsilon\xi$)</note> in the text denotes not so much the **meritorious cause** <term>meritorious cause: the legal or moral basis that earns a result (here, Christ's death earning salvation)</term> as the **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause: the primary agent or force that produces an effect (here, the Holy Spirit's power)</term>. To this exception, we first oppose those passages in which "from" is used for a meritorious cause, or as a means of acquisition or justification, such as Matthew 27:7, Romans 1:4, and Matthew 12:37. And there are plenty of writers, both Greek and Latin, for whom *EK* or *EX* <note>the Greek and Latin forms of "from" or "out of"</note> signifies *by* and *on account of*. Not to mention the prefix **beth** <note>original: $\beth$. The Hebrew preposition meaning "in," "with," or "by."</note> of the Hebrews, which the writers of the New Testament imitate. Truly, we do not dwell on this, because, secondly, we judge that in this very passage not only the meritorious cause but also the **instrumental cause** is designated. For the focus here is not so much on the obtaining of salvation through the obedience of Christ on the cross (although that is presupposed) as on its application in the consciences of the elect through the remission of sins. Moreover, this application is the medium through which spiritual life is produced; for when the elect are enlightened by the Holy Spirit to recognize such immense grace granted to them, then simultaneously their heart is bent and moved by that same Spirit to present themselves to God as a living sacrifice of gratitude, which is the beginning of the activity in which the new life exerts itself.

XX. However, so that the strength of this expression may be more deeply recognized, we believe we must inquire into the origin from which it was taken. The author is referencing Thales of Miletus, a Greek philosopher who claimed water was the fundamental substance of the universe.</note>

Whatever the case may be, we do not think that such mystical waters considered in general are aptly referred to here, even on the grounds that they everywhere foreshadowed the operations of obedience and the Spirit of Christ simultaneously. For in our passage, water is distinguished from the Spirit, and therefore we must seek a "water" which distinctly represented only the obedience <term>obedience: here meaning the "active obedience" or merit of Christ’s life and sacrifice</term> of Christ, separate from the Spirit.

It is manifest that he uses this allusion to support his own hypothesis, which we have already refuted. And even if that theory were set aside, the allusion would still be unsuitable. For the *water* over which the Spirit hovered during creation was the subject and matter upon which the Spirit operated, and it behaved purely passively toward Him. However, in our specific passage, *water* and the *Spirit* are considered as coordinate and concurrent causes leading to regeneration <note>The theological term for "being born again" or spiritual rebirth.</note>.

XXI. Therefore, those reflections are more relevant which consider the waters used for various mystical washings. Some of these scholars focus generally on the ritual washings required by the Law of the Old Testament; others take into account the water of Baptism itself, suggesting it is probable that the Savior alluded to it. Here, LIGHTFOOT <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675) was an English churchman and Hebraist known for using Talmudic knowledge to explain the New Testament.</note> fosters his usual peculiar conjectures. He considers it likely that the Nicodemus of the Gospel history is the same as a certain Nakdimon <note>original Hebrew: נקדימון</note>, about whom a short story exists in the Talmud <note>A central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note>. From this story, one might conjecture that he was a Priest and held the office of *Inspector of Waters* <note>original Hebrew: ממונה על המים; an official responsible for the water supply</note> for the use of the people during festival times. Thus, Christ would be arguing from Nicodemus's own professional element when He *discourses on being born of water*. The same author finds it credible that Christ, during this Passover in which He conversed with Nicodemus, performed certain miracles at the pool of Bethesda, just as He did in the one immediately following. From this, He could have pointed a finger toward the effect of those waters, where the first person to descend after the water was stirred by an Angel was restored to new health and was, as it were, "reborn." Whatever the case may be, we do not think that such mystical waters, considered generally, are aptly referred to here—if only for the reason that they would everywhere represent the combined operations of obedience and the Spirit of Christ. In our passage, however, water is distinguished from the Spirit; hence, we must seek a "water" that, distinct from the Spirit, depicted only the obedience of Christ.

XXII. THOMAS CARTWRIGHT <note>A prominent 16th-century English Puritan theologian.</note> provides another thought in his *Gospel Harmony, p. 142*. *Perhaps*, he says, *He alludes to that washing applied to infants as soon as they are born, by which the blood they are covered in is washed away.* He could have illustrated this opinion from Ezekiel 16:9, where the Lord is introduced wash... <margin>to wash</margin>

XXV. SPENCER <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), an English theologian and pioneer in the comparative study of religion.</note> rightly observes in his *On the Laws of the Hebrews* (Book III, dissertation III, ch. 4) that the Hebrews performed purifications with water in three ways: by *immersion of the body*, by *washing of the hands and feet*, or by *sprinkling of water*. Of these, the first two methods could prefigure the purification of the soul through obedience and the Spirit of Christ in various circumstances more generally. But the last, by sprinkling, never bore any other archetype than the obedience of Christ. I prove this from the very clear explanation of Paul in Hebrews 9:13, 14; 12:24; and Peter in 1 Peter 1:2, which constantly compare the *blood of Christ* with *sprinkling* <note>original Greek: ῥαντισμῷ (*rhantismos*)</note> or *legal sprinkling*. Hence also in Hebrews 10:22, people are introduced *having their hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience* <note>original Greek: ἐῤῥαντισμένοι τὰς καρδίας ἀπὸ συνειδήσεως πονηρᾶς (*errantismenoi tas kardias apo syneidēseōs ponēras*)</note>. For since an *evil conscience* is nothing other than one which, convicted of sins and their guilt, justly dreads the punishment due to them, the *sprinkling of the heart* from such a conscience can designate nothing other than the remission of those sins and justification through the blood of Christ.

XXVI. The very nature of the matter adds to this. In this regard, we wish to observe two primary kinds of legal sprinklings. Some were *ordinary*, performed with blood alone, such as were required in all sacrifices whose blood was offered to God—whether it was to be scattered at the altar, or toward the sanctuary, or in the sanctuary itself, and that again either in the outer or inner shrine. Compare OUTRAM <note>William Outram (1626–1679), an English clergyman noted for his scholarly work on the Jewish sacrificial system.</note> *On Sacrifices*, Book I, ch. 16, § 2 ff. There are some who think that water was also mixed with this blood, among whom is LIGHTFOOT <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a renowned Hebraist who provided deep Jewish context for the New Testament.</note> in his commentary on John 19:34, to illustrate the passage in Hebrews 9:19 where the Apostle asserts that Moses took the *blood of calves with water*; "Either my memory fails me," he says, "or I have read somewhere among Hebrew writers—though the location unfortunately escapes me—that since some delay had to be interposed between the slaughter of the victim and the sprinkling of the blood upon the altar (such as the delay while Moses read the law—

XXVII. Namely, there were other extraordinary sprinklings of various kinds. Some of these were performed with blood alone, such as the sprinkling of the Passover blood on the doorposts and the lintel <note>original: "in poftes & fuperliminare"</note> in Exodus 12:7. These sprinklings agreed in that they were all performed using an <term>aspergillum</term><note>A ritual brush or instrument used for sprinkling liquid.</note> made of *hyssop*, which was bound to *cedar wood* with *scarlet wool* in such a way that the cedar wood served as a handle. For in this way, these three parts are most aptly combined, all of which are mentioned when those sprinklings are described in Leviticus 14:6–7 and Hebrews 9:19. They also shared the same logic in that *water* was required for them, and also that the water was used only for sprinkling people or impure things, but never for a sprinkling to be made "before the face of God" to directly <term>propitiate</term><note>To appease or satisfy the requirements of a deity.</note> God. Meanwhile, they differed in that the *persons* or *things* which were purified by these waters were of different kinds, and that depending on their variety, sometimes *blood* and sometimes even *ashes* were mixed with the water.

XXVIII. The *first occasion* in which they were employed was when the Sinaitic covenant was ratified. Moses describes this sprinkling in Exodus 24:8: *Moses, taking the remaining blood (of which a part had indeed been sprinkled upon the altar), sprinkled it upon the people themselves, and said: Behold the blood of that covenant, which Jehovah has struck with you...*

## XXXII. ##

There is less difficulty in the passage of Numbers 31:19–20, where the army returning from the slaughter of the Midianites is commanded: *“Stay outside the camp for seven days; and whoever has killed a person or touched one who was slain, purify him on the third day and then on the seventh day, both you and your captives. You shall also purify every garment, every leather vessel, everything made of goat's hair, and every wooden vessel.”* And in verse 22: *“Moreover, the gold, silver, bronze, iron, tin, lead, and whatever is accustomed to be put into the fire, you shall pass through the fire and it shall be clean. Nevertheless, it shall also be purified with the waters of impurity”* (<term>מי נדה</term> <note>Hebrew: *Mei Niddah*, usually translated as the "water of separation" or "water of cleansing." It refers to the water mixed with the ashes of the Red Heifer.</note>). Since that phrase "waters of impurity" is specific to the waters mixed with the ashes of the red heifer, and because the passage concerns the cleansing of an army polluted by the corpses of the dead, we can rest satisfied with this interpretation.

## XXXIII. ##

From a review of all these passages, it will be evident that those lustral waters <note>Water used for ceremonial or religious purification.</note> could not conveniently signify anything else than the obedience of Christ applied to the sinner for righteousness before God—and indeed, in such a way that it is distinguished from other operations of the Holy Spirit. For:

I. Those waters did not have the power of cleansing through themselves, but received it from the admixture of either blood or ash, by which it will be easily granted to us that the bloody passions and death of Christ were being aimed at.

II. Furthermore, *sprinkling* was a rite in the Levitical worship through which the power of Christ's sacrifice was figured in various ways. Insofar as it was done toward God, it indicated how He was to be appeased through the sacrifice of Christ. Therefore, insofar as the *lustral water* with blood and ash was *sprinkled* externally upon men, it must have figured how that same power of Christ's obedience was also to be externally applied to the sinner for righteousness.

III. The operations of the Holy Spirit, by which the purification of souls is completed, were figured by other rites joined with sprinkling, namely the distinct and separate washings of both the clothes and the body itself.

## XXXIV. ##

We add the most elegant [analogy] between those *sprinklings* and the justification of the sinner through the application of the righteousness of Christ

analogy. We shall present it in summary, lest we be too wordy. **I.** *River water*, being living, clear, and fresh, designates a perfect, most pure, most pleasing to God, and constant holiness of the whole of life. **II.** *Blood*, or ash added to the water, indicated that the perfection of the most absolute holiness and obedience of Christ would be demonstrated and fulfilled primarily in his *passion* and *death*. **III.** The *earthen vessel*, which contained the cleansing water, can be compared to the Apostles, to whom the testimony of such a great mystery was directly entrusted, and who thus held such a *treasure in jars of clay* <note>original: *thesaurum ἐν ὀστρακίνοις σκεύεσιν*; a reference to 2 Corinthians 4:7, emphasizing the contrast between the glory of the Gospel and the human frailty of its messengers.</note>. **IV.** The *sprinklers* were either Moses, or the Priest, or any other pure man. The application of Christ’s righteousness is made partly internally by Christ himself through his Spirit, and partly externally, both by the Ministers of the Gospel and by any of the faithful whose labor the Lord uses to *justify* many. **V.** The *sprinkler* <note>The instrument, usually a bundle of hyssop, used to flick the water during the ritual.</note> signifies the preaching of the Gospel itself. And so, the parts making up the sprinkler represented the chief virtues of Christ, which the Gospel emphasizes everywhere, not only as *satisfactory* <note>In this theological context, "satisfactory" refers to Christ's work satisfying the demands of divine justice for the forgiveness of sins.</note> but also as *exemplary*. *Cedar* represents the constancy of a mind savoring heavenly things; *hyssop* represents humility; *scarlet wool* represents patience and love; these are the same virtues that the Preachers of the Gospel must exercise in following Christ. In the cleansing of the leper, a *Little Bird* <note>Based on Leviticus 14, where two birds were used; one was sacrificed and the other released.</note> was added, so that communion with Christ through the exercise of the virtues that made up his *image* might be more clearly expressed, and at the same time to suggest how that communion involved not only *death* but also *resurrection with Christ*. **VI.** In the *persons* who were *sprinkled*, the misery and foulness of the sinner is depicted in various ways, showing one who is made a sharer of such great grace. He served in spiritual Egypt, cast out from the covenant of God, like Israel. By birth from impure parents, he is a child of wrath and worthy to pay for sin in his own person—just like the *Levites*, who were descended from a father whose deed the dying Jacob had detested <note>A reference to Genesis 49:5-7, where Jacob curses the violence of his sons Simeon and Levi.</note>, yet were substituted in place of the firstborn. He is like a *leper*, because he is stained with the foulest sins; furthermore, he is contaminated by *dead* works. Each of these had their own specific emphasis in those who were introduced into the Kingdom of the Messiah when he established it. But

we continue. **VII.** Just as those to be sprinkled, although they were merely passive <note>In the sense that the person being sprinkled does not perform the action themselves, but receives it.</note>, nevertheless had to be present and willingly submit themselves to the divine order; so nothing happens in justification on the part of the sinner, except that he hungers and thirsts for righteousness, and hands himself over to the Lord to be justified according to his word. **VIII.** Although those sprinkled might appear defiled before the world by *blood and ash*, they were nevertheless pure before God. To those whom the power of Christ's death is applied, although they are *crucified to the world*, they are nevertheless beautiful in the eyes of Jehovah. **IX.** The *sevenfold* number observed in the sprinklings foreshadows the perennial power of Christ's righteousness through all times of the Church. **X.** Not only persons, but also *things, houses, vessels*, etc., were purged by the cleansing <note>original: *lustralibus*, referring to the water used in the ritual of purification.</note> waters. The power of Christ's merit removes the uncleanness not only of the sinner but also of all creatures polluted by misuse, and restores their true use.

**XXXV.** This, however, is especially relevant to our subject: that those cleansing waters had the power not only to release one from legal impurity, but also, as it were, to return life from death, and thus to regenerate, at least in a symbolic way <note>original: *in typo*</note>. This was observed by the most celebrated VITRINGA <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent Dutch theologian known for his work on biblical prophecy and typology.</note> in his *Sketch of Practical Theology* <note>original: *typo Theol. Pract.*</note>, chapter III, section 6, where he writes: *The leper was considered to be dead, because his flesh was dead and void of the movement of life, so much so that the leper presented the appearance of a corpse walking among the living. Therefore, the purification of the leper was his vivification [bringing back to life]. Likewise, he who had touched a dead person was considered dead according to the Law of the Old Economy, that is, through contact with the dead he had come into the communion of death. Therefore, the cleansing of the unclean from contact with the dead presented the appearance of vivification.* The same can be said concerning the sprinkling of the Israelites in the ratification of the Sinaitic Covenant. For this introduction into external communion with God also bore the likeness of generation. Hence the Old Testament is compared to *Hagar* GENERATING for slavery <note>original: *Gal. # DISSERTATION

**CHRISTOPHER SAND.** <note>A scholar known for Arian views.</note> **JONAS SCHLICHTING** composed a *Dissertation on the Word of God* <note>original: "Dissertationem de Verbo Dei"</note> at Raków <note>A Polish city that was a major center for the Socinian movement, which denied the Trinity.</note> in the year 1644 against Vechner. Two anonymous authors should also be referred to here. One is the *Author of the Bible of Truth and Reason concerning the Word of God, to which is prefixed a debate on the Word of God, of which frequent mention is made among the Chaldean Paraphrasts* <note>The "Chaldean Paraphrasts" refers to the Targums, Aramaic translations/interpretations of the Hebrew Bible.</note> (Freistadt, 1700). **JOHANN CHRISTOPH WOLF** accurately proved that the author of both was **WILLIAM HENRY VORST**, son of **CONRAD**, in the second part of the *Hebrew Library* which recently appeared according to the wishes of the learned (pages 1187, 1188). In the same year, another author put forward a book in French: *Platonism Unveiled, or an Essay touching upon the Platonic Word* <note>original: "le Platonisme devoilé, ou Essai touchant le Verbe Platonicien"</note>, against which a certain **BALTUS**, a Jesuit, sharpened his pen.

II. And indeed, after the labors of so many others, and among them most learned men, it might seem superfluous for us to begin "rolling this stone again" <note>A reference to the myth of Sisyphus, meaning to redo a task already completed by others.</note>, were it not that our proposal to illustrate the entire Gospel of John to the best of our ability not only grants us this pardon but also imposes a necessity upon us. Furthermore, new controversies concerning the **LOGOS** <term>Logos: The Greek word for "Word," "Reason," or "Discourse," used by John to describe the pre-existent Christ.</term>—as the subject of John’s Prologue—have been stirred up by new enemies of the truth, especially in the island opposite our shore <note>Likely referring to England, where Unitarian and Deist ideas were gaining traction at the time.</note>. This requires that we continue to fight against them with the same weapons that the orthodox Church has used most successfully from its very cradle against other attackers of the Supreme Divinity of Jesus Christ.

III. So that we may follow a certain path in our meditations on this admirable Name, the order that seems most fitting to us is: first, to determine the *Subject* which Scripture points out simply through the **LOGOS**; then, to draw out the true meaning in which it is attributed to that Subject, according to the analogy of faith from the very clearest fountains of Divine Revelation. However, before we descend to these particulars, we consider it necessary above all to inquire whether, besides our own passage, other places of Scripture occur which treat of a certain **DIVINE & HYPOSTATIC** <term>Hypostatic: Relating to the "hypostasis" or individual personhood of the Godhead; here meaning the Word as a distinct, living Person rather than just a spoken command.</term> **WORD**. For when we find those, we promise ourselves no small assistance from a careful comparison of them, both for certain knowledge of the Subject itself and for establishing the origin and true emphasis of this Name.

<meta>This page continues a theological discussion on the use of the term "Logos" (the Word) in the New Testament. ->### ON THE WORD IN THE NEW TESTAMENT.<-

IV. In the Gospel itself, after the Prologue, this name [the Word] is read nowhere else. For we have refuted those who, in Chapter 5:38 and 10:35, understand the Son by the "Word of the Father" <note>original Greek: "λογον Πατρος" (logon Patros)</note>. And although AUGUSTINE, and after him BEDE, the *GLOSSA ordinaria* <note>The "Ordinary Gloss" was a standard medieval collection of biblical commentaries.</note>, and SALMERO understand the "Word" to mean Christ in Chapter 17:17, in the words: *Thy word is truth* <note>original Greek: "ὁ λογος ὁ σος ἀληθεια ἐστι" (ho logos ho sos alētheia esti)</note>, this interpretation is nevertheless too far-fetched. For since in this whole context the "Word of the Father" <note>original: "Λογος Πατρος" (Logos Patros)</note> recurs quite often—which the disciples kept and which Christ gave to them in verse 14—it cannot be called into doubt that those words designate the "spoken word" <note>original: "λογον προφορικον" (logon prophorikon); a technical term in theology for the externalized word or speech of God, as opposed to the internal, eternal Word/Son.</note>. Therefore, since no distinction occurs, and the predicate easily admits the same sense, that same notion must also be kept in verse 17. Moreover, it is clear that the predicate matches, because the Gospel Word is an effective means of sanctification, and is also called "Truth" in the abstract elsewhere. Thus, Psalm 119:142: *Thy Law, or Thy Doctrine, is truth* <note>original Hebrew: "תורתך אמת" (Toratcha emet)</note>. Furthermore, our Savior, as far as we read, never used this name for Himself; whence an even smaller suspicion remains that in the prayers he poured out in the presence of his disciples, he would have wanted to use an unusual name that was less perceptible to them.

V. We find the Personal WORD <note>original: "ΛΟΓΟΝ Perſonalem"</note> more clearly in 1 John 1:1. SOCINUS, VORSTIUS, and GROTIUS <note>Scholars often associated with Socinianism or Arminianism who favored more rationalist or metaphorical interpretations of scripture.</note> indeed struggle against this, understanding it to mean the Doctrine of the Gospel. But he who does not recognize that the beginning of John’s Epistle points its finger toward the beginning of his Gospel must be closing his eyes to the light of the sun. Added to this are the predicates proper only to the Personal WORD <note>original: "ΛΟΓΩI Perſonali"</note>, such as that he was not only *heard*, but also *seen with eyes and touched with hands*: because the same is named *Life*, and indeed *eternal life, which was with the Father and was made visible to us.* CALOVIUS <note>Abraham Calovius, a leading 17th-century Lutheran orthodox theologian.</note> can be consulted on this passage, as he professedly refutes GROTIUS.

VI. Most evidently this relates to Chapter 5:7 in the same Epistle, if only it were first established that this comma <note>The "Johannine Comma," a famous disputed clause in 1 John 5:7-8 that explicitly mentions the Trinity.</note> was not inserted by a foreign hand—a sea which we are not stirring up now. No one is unaware with what great effort this has been disputed on both sides. Nor can it be denied that those attacking it produce arguments that have a remarkable appearance [of truth]. But even stronger ones seem to be required by us. It is certainly easier

<meta>This page continues the defense of the authenticity of the "Comma Johanneum" (1 John 5:7), specifically arguing that the verse was likely omitted by accident in some early manuscripts rather than fraudulently added to others.</meta>

-># DISSERTATION<-
->### VII.<-

...it is more conceivable that a whole verse fell out of certain manuscripts than that it could have been inserted into them. For the latter could hardly have been done in its entirety without fraud, a suspicion with which no one should be burdened except on the basis of primary evidence. On the other hand, the former <note>referring to the omission of the verse</note> could have happened without malicious intent, by mere chance and pure negligence of a scribe. Perhaps while writing, he raised his eyes at the phrase *those who bear witness* <note>original Greek: οἱ μαρτυροῦντες (hoi martyrountes)</note> in verse 7, and soon after, his eyes falling upon the same phrase in verse 8, he passed over the intermediate words, *in heaven... And there are three* <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ. - - Καὶ τρεῖς εἰσιν (en tō ouranō... Kai treis eisin)</note>, leaving them untouched <note>This describes a common scribal error known as "homoeoteleuton," where a scribe's eye skips from one word to a similar-looking word later in the text, accidentally deleting the text in between.</note>. Furthermore, no other example of a similar <term>interpolation</term><note>A passage or word added to a text by a later hand, often viewed as a corruption of the original.</note> occurs in the Holy Scriptures. In this matter, just as we rightly revere God's unique providence regarding His Word, piety scarcely permits us to allow that providence to be called into question in this single passage, which is still under debate.

Moreover, those who have taken up the defense of this passage have the claim of antiquity on their side. Since in matters of fact, older testimonies brought forward by trustworthy witnesses carry more weight than more recent ones, it is most significant for our case that our opponents produce no evidence that reaches or exceeds the age of **TERTULLIAN & CYPRIAN**. It is clear from their citations that our <term>comma</term> <note>The "Comma Johanneum" is a short clause in the First Epistle of John (5:7–8) that provides a scriptural basis for the Trinity: "For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one." Its authenticity has been debated for centuries.</note> was read in their manuscripts: for the former, in his *Book Against Praxeas*, chapter 25; for the latter, in his *Book on the Unity of the Church* and his *Letter to Jubaianus*. These precedents seem so strong to us that a mighty battering ram would be required to destroy them. <meta>This page continues the defense of the Comma Johanneum (1 John 5:7), specifically addressing objections regarding the specific vocabulary used in the verse, such as the title "The Word" (Logos).</meta>

->## ON THE LOGOS IN THE NEW TESTAMENT.<-
->### Q 2<-
-><meta>catchword: VIII.</meta><-

VII. Our purpose does not permit us to leave this point at least untouched: that SOCINUS <note>Faustus Socinus (1539–1604) was a prominent Italian theologian whose followers, the Socinians, denied the traditional doctrine of the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ.</note>, in his commentary on this passage, argues against our text using the name of the LOGOS <note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΟΣ (Logos), translated as "The Word."</note> itself among other arguments with which he fights against it. But the arguments he draws from this are clearly made of straw. His first point is this: *Although it may have been unique to John in some places to call the Son of God or Jesus Christ by that name, there were reasons for doing so elsewhere, yet there seems to be no reason why he should have done so in this place.* However, reasons can exist even if Socinus is ignorant of them. He argues against those who would want to allege this reason: *because it would seem absurd to say that the Son of God himself or Christ would testify about himself, and indeed that he is the Son of God, or Christ.* I do not know who holds such a view. Another reason is ready at hand for me. For who does not see that, since the Son is introduced here as a *Witness*, John most aptly employs that name of his which had a singular relationship to his testimony? But even if we confessed to be ignorant of the reason, what would SOCINUS gain from that, unless he simultaneously proved that the use of this name clashed with John's purpose in the present passage?

He attempted that indeed, but produced nothing except this one point: that *the FATHER and the WORD are not well joined together. For there is not the same relationship of the Father to the Word as there is to the Son, by which name Jesus Christ seemingly ought to have been named in this place, where God is signified by the name of the Father; or if that title of Word was to be used to signify Jesus Christ in this place, it seems it clearly should be said that God ought to have been called not by the name of Father, but by the name of God himself, since God and the Word have a relationship to each other.* But there was no necessity that the individual words used regarding the three divine Persons should have a special relationship among themselves. It was enough that there was a relationship between this name and the predicate. Furthermore, his denial of any relationship between the name of FATHER and WORD is entirely without grounds. We will teach the contrary in its proper place, showing that within the meaning of the WORD there also lies something analogous to the <term>eternal generation</term><note>A theological term describing the relationship within the Trinity where the Son is eternally "begotten" or "generated" by the Father, rather than created.</note> of the Son. Nor should the observation of KETTNER <note>Friedrich Ernst Kettner (1671–1722), a Lutheran theologian who wrote extensively defending the authenticity of the Comma Johanneum.</note> in the place cited, page 152, be despised: *The name "Word" was more suited to indicating the Trinity than "Son": for the Word brought forth includes three persons: (1) the speaker, (2) the Word or the power of the speaker, and (3) the Spirit of the mouth.*

-># DISSERTATION<-

VIII. Nor does this same name occur any less evidently in REVELATION XIX. 13. He is called *his name is the Word of God* <note>original Greek: Ο ΛΟΓΟΣ του Θεου (Ho Logos tou Theou)</note>. And the reason why he employs this name there seems to coincide with that which we just noted regarding the passage treated against SOCINUS <note>Faustus Socinus, who argued against the divinity of the Word.</note>, because the same one who is here called the WORD <note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΟΣ (Logos)</note> was called *faithful and true* <note>original Greek: πιστος και αληθινος (pistos kai alēthinos)</note> a little before in verse 11, which no one will deny refers to his *Testimony*. Furthermore, because this expression agrees with that in REVELATION I. 2, *Who bore witness to the word of God, and the testimony of Jesus Christ* <note>original Greek: Ος εμαρτυρησε τον λογον του Θεου, και την μαρτυριαν Ιησου Χριστου (Hos emartyrēse ton logon tou Theou, kai tēn martyrian Iēsou Christou)</note>, ZEGERUS, GRELLOTUS, and others have thought that one must also consider the personal WORD <note>Referring to the <term>Hypostatic Word</term>, or the person of Christ as the Word, rather than just a spoken message.</note> in this passage. The latter scholar [Grellotus] ingeniously observes that the same title of the Savior is found at the beginning of the three principal writings of John, and the reader is silently sent back to the beginning of the Gospel and the first Epistle, indicating that one and the same Spirit was the inspirer and author of these writings. This meditation would easily lead one to agreement by its own sweetness, were it not for two obstacles:

I. If that had been John’s intention, he would not have distinguished between *the word of God* and Jesus Christ, but would have said, *and his testimony*. GRELLOTUS, indeed, to avoid this weapon, observed that when *And the Testimony of Jesus Christ* is added, it should be taken as an explanation of what preceded, with the particle *and* <note>original Greek: και (kai)</note> being accepted as the relative *which*. But even if this notion were admitted, we do not see how it could have a place here, since it would not then be said that the <term>Hypostatic Word</term> is *Jesus Christ*, but rather the *Testimony of Jesus Christ*, which would establish a completely foreign sense. 

II. It is added that the verb *to bear witness* <note>original Greek: μαρτυρειν (martyrein)</note>, when used by the New Testament writers regarding a testimony given to a certain person, is never constructed with the *accusative* case, but either with the preposition *concerning* <note>original Greek: περι (peri)</note> or with the *dative* case.

IX. Whether other New Testament writers besides John also employ this mystical name must now be examined. Some simply deny it, among whom are GROTIUS <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch legal scholar and theologian.</note> and MALDONATUS <note>Juan Maldonado (1533–1583), a Spanish Jesuit theologian.</note> on Luke I; as well as HILDEBRANDUS, cited by SAUBERTO in his dissertation on the word *Logos* §. 9; and GLASSIUS, Book I, Tract IV, Section 3. To these we add, from our own ranks, PISCATOR <note>Johannes Piscator (1546–1625), a German Reformed theologian.</note> on Luke I. Among the ancients, EUSEBIUS <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), a historian and bishop.</note> asserts it in his work against Marcellus.

### ON THE LOGOS IN THE NEW TESTAMENT.
<note>original Greek: DE ΛΟΓΩΙ (Logōi) — "On the Word"</note>

-># DISSERTATION<-

[Eusebi]us in *Ecclesiastical Theology*, Book II, chapter 10, writes: *Since only the Evangelist John called him the Word* <note>original Greek: Μονου του Ευαγγελισου Ιωαννου λογον αυτον αποκαλεσαντος (Monou tou Euangelistou Iōannou logon auton apokalesantos)</note>. Since, however, there are not a few who maintain the affirmative—that other authors did use this title—the passages themselves to which they appeal must be examined in order.

**X.** In **LUKE I. 2.** it is said of the Apostles that *from the beginning they were eyewitnesses and ministers of the WORD*. Among the ancient fathers, ORIGEN (in his commentary on John, Volume XXI), AMBROSE, and EUTHYMIUS (on this passage) judged that the Son of God should be understood here. JEROME, in his *Preface to Matthew*, provides a version that sounds like this: *Just as they delivered to us, who from the beginning saw the Word and ministered to him*. ATHANASIUS also supports this in *Oration III against the Arians*. These have been followed by more recent scholars such as VALLA, BUDÉ, SALMERON, GOMARUS, CAMERON, HAMMOND, LOUIS CAPPEL, THOMAS CARTWRIGHT, JACOB ALTING, and others. The distinguished WITSIUS presents their arguments in his *Miscellanies*, Book II, Exercise 3, § 38, which come down to these points:

1.  Because that phrasing is a twin to the expression used by John in 1 John I. 1: *That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, concerning the word of life*.
2.  Because the reality of the situation fits, since the Apostles both saw Christ with their own eyes and were his ministers <note>or servants</note> from the time he presented himself as the Messiah.
3.  Because the explanation offered by others is awkward. For if you understand "the word" to mean the "message of the Gospel," they were not *eyewitnesses* <note>original Greek: αυτοπται (autoptai)</note> of it—which the nature of things forbids—but were rather listeners first, and then later heralds. If, on the other hand, you think the events narrated in the Gospel are meant, there are many things the Apostles explained of which they were neither eyewitnesses nor *ministers* <note>original Greek: ὑπηρεται (hypēretai)</note>, such as the miraculous conception, the birth, and so on.

**XI.** Nevertheless, others have preferred a more common-sense interpretation. Some of them explained *the word* <note>original Greek: τον λογον (ton logon)</note> as *the matter itself* <note>Latin: rem ipsam</note>, corresponding to the Hebrew term *davar* <note>Hebrew: דבר (davar) — a word that can mean both "speech" and "event" or "thing"</note>. Among these scholars are MALDONATUS, JANSENIUS, FLACCIUS ILLYRICUS, STELLA, and others. Others, however, understand it to mean the *Message of the Gospel*. TITUS OF BOSTRA mentions this opinion. This is the view held by CALVIN, GUALTHER, GROTIUS, and LE CLERC. And this last view is the one that most commends itself to me. For 1. it signi-

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding Luke 1:2. The author is arguing against the idea that Luke used the term "Word" (Logos) to refer personally to Jesus Christ, suggesting instead that it refers to the "word of the Gospel" or the preached message.</meta>

-># DISSERTATION<-

This meaning of **the word** <note>original Greek: του λογου (tou logou)</note> when used by itself is quite common among the New Testament writers. For example: Matthew 13:20 and following; Mark 2:2, 4:14 and following; Philippians 1:14; 2 Timothy 4:2; and it is especially characteristic of Luke in Acts 6:4, 8:4, 10:36, 11:19, 14:25, and 16:6. It will therefore be simpler to stick to the more well-known sense that was so frequently used by the writer, especially since there is nothing in the text to limit or change its meaning. This is even more the case because:

**II.** It is entirely unusual for Luke to use the term **WORD** <note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΟΥ (Logou)</note> in its "excellent" or divine sense <note>The "excellent sense" refers to using "The Word" as a title for the divine person of Christ, as seen in the Gospel of John</note>. **GOMARUS** <note>Franciscus Gomarus (1563–1641), a prominent Dutch Calvinist theologian</note> objects (in his *Works*, Volume I, page 152) that there is no necessary reason why a single word cannot be used with one specific meaning in just one book, while signifying something else in all other writings. He cites Matthew 8:22, where "the dead" refers to "unbelievers," and Luke 16:2, where **word** <note>original Greek: λογος (logos)</note> signifies a "mode of administration" <note>often translated as an "account" of stewardship</note>.

However, that distinguished scholar does not pay sufficient attention to the force of the argument. We do not deny that a **multi-meaning word** <note>original Greek: πολυσημον (polysemon) — a term with multiple possible definitions</note> is sometimes used by the sacred writers in a sense that does not appear elsewhere, provided that the context, the goal of the passage, and the descriptive details clearly require it. Our point is simply this: when there is a question between two different ideas, both of which seem to fit the coherence and the descriptions of the text, then that idea is to be preferred which is simpler and which occurs most frequently elsewhere in the same writer’s work, especially when the alternative meaning never appears in his writings at all. We believe this principle will be easily granted to us.

Therefore, the point added by others—that the term **Word** <note>original Greek: Λογος (Logos)</note> appears in this disputed sense in Acts 20:32—would carry more weight against us. One might reply that the passage there presents the words of Paul, not Luke’s own words. But that will not be necessary, as we are about to reject that hypothesis as well.

**III.** The style of Luke in his **Preface** <note>original Latin: Proœmio — the introductory section of the Gospel</note> also requires a simpler interpretation; it is clearly historical and breathes nothing of the sublime or mystical, in which everyone can see he differs as much as possible from the prologue of John.

**IV.** Finally, it cannot be proven that the name **WORD** <note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΟΣ (Logos)</note> was used in this "excellent" sense either by our Savior himself or by the Evangelists who wrote before Luke. Therefore, when Luke set about writing, it would have been a completely new concept in the Church. If, then, Luke had wished to use a name not yet well-known or explained in the Church for the primary subject and argument of his writing...

...to designate his own, who would not think that he would have used the name **Holy Spirit** more *demonstratively* <note>original Greek: δεικτικως (deiktikos) — pointing out directly</note> and with some qualification that would immediately rouse the reader's mind to conceive such an illustrious subject of Gospel history? 

**V.** Finally, we believe that the Evangelist’s own purpose favors our view quite significantly.

**XII.** To make this last point clear, we assume that Luke’s **Prologue** refers not only to the *Gospel* but also to the *Acts of the Apostles*. This is shown by:

**I.** The connection in Acts 1:1, which is made through a transition indicating that Luke turned immediately from writing one book to the next. Since no new or specific preface was placed before this second part, we rightly refer the prologue of the Gospel to this part as well.

**II.** In that same transition, it is declared that Luke has so far presented only the *beginning* of those things he had undertaken to write about, because he says he composed the first book about all the things that Jesus "began to do and teach" <note>original Greek: ηρξατο ποιειν και διδασκειν (erxato poiein kai didaskein)</note>. By this, he implies that he would now add the second book about those same matters as they were brought to completion after the Lord’s ascension.

**III.** In the Gospel Prologue itself, the summary of what is to be said is called a "narrative of the things that have been fulfilled among us" <note>Luke 1:1; original Greek: διηγησις περι των πεπληροφορημενων εν ημιν πραγματων (diegesis peri ton peplerophoremenon en hemin pragmaton)</note>, and the goal of these things is designated here so that the reliability of these accounts "about which you have been instructed" <note>Luke 1:4; original Greek: περι ων κατηχηθης (peri hon katekhethes)</note> might be recognized. 

These things, however, look more broadly than to the doctrine and life of Christ alone; they also encompass the outpouring of the Holy Spirit and the establishment of Christ's kingdom. However far the history Luke was about to write extended, so far also the *knowledge* of the witnesses Luke appealed to had to extend. Therefore, it would not have been sufficient to have *Eyewitnesses* and *Ministers* of Christ himself, because they could not, by themselves, testify to the events that occurred throughout the full thirty years after the Lord’s ascension unless they had also been **Ministers of the Gospel Word**. 

And this is what Luke’s words mean, in which two different types—or at least attributes—of the witnesses he cites to confirm the reliability of his history are expressed. The first was that they were *Eyewitnesses* <note>original Greek: Αυτοπται (Autoptai)</note>, namely in relation to the preceding "things fulfilled among us." The second was that they were also *Servants of the Word* <note>original Greek: Υπηρεται του Λογου (Hyperetai tou Logou)</note>, *Co-workers* in preaching the Gospel, "in the ministry of the word" <note>Acts 6:4; original Greek: εν διακονια του λογου (en diakonia tou logou)</note>, "the ministers of the..."

### CONCERNING THE WORD IN THE NEW TESTAMENT.

...must be seen <note>The text continues from the previous page: *videndum esse*</note> by metonymy <term>metonymy: a figure of speech where a thing or concept is referred to by the name of something closely associated with it</term> for "one emitting a voice." But why, then, would the same metonymy not fit our passage? Furthermore, the reasoning of **PHILO** in his book *On the Migration of Abraham*, page 395, is clearly not to be despised: *“For this reason, since the voices of mortal beings are judged by the sense of hearing, we learn from divine oracles that the words of God are seen in the manner of light. For it is said that 'all the people saw the voice' <note>referring to the giving of the Law at Sinai in Exodus 20:18</note>, they did not 'hear' it; because this was not air struck by the tools of the mouth and tongue, but a most radiant splendor of virtue, no different from a rational fountain.”* Therefore, since even the voices of mortal creatures are judged by the sense of hearing, we learn from divine oracles that God's words are seen in the manner of light. For they say that the whole people saw the voice, they did not hear it: because this was not air struck by the "plectrum" <note>a pick or tool used to strike a stringed instrument; here used metaphorically for the tongue</note> of the tongue, but a most brilliant splendor of virtue, differing in no way from a rational source.

However, **GOMARUS** <note>Francis Gomarus (1563–1641), a Dutch theologian famous for his opposition to Arminianism.</note> insists that we produce an example of the word **Eyewitness** <note>original Greek: Αυτοπτης (Autoptes)</note> as it pertains to the "voice" itself. He cannot demand this from the Sacred Scriptures, since the word is a *hapax legomenon* <term>hapax legomenon: a word that occurs only once in a particular body of literature (in this case, the New Testament)</term>. But look, here is a passage from **POLYBIUS**, in which he designates not an eyewitness in the literal sense, but one grasping a matter with the intellect from a certain experience, *Histories*, Book I, page 4: *“If some, looking at the scattered parts of a body that was once animate and beautiful, believe they have become sufficient **EYEWITNESSES** <note>original Greek: ΑΥΤΟΠΤΑΙ (Autoptai)</note> of the power and beauty of the creature itself.”* <note>Polybius argues that one cannot understand a whole system or history just by looking at isolated parts; one must see the whole "living" connection.</note> This is for the sake of those who think that the term **eyewitness** in our passage <note>Luke 1:2</note> should not be separated from **the Word**. We, however, do not even need those arguments, since according to our construction, the natural meaning of the word can be preserved.

**XIV. ACTS 10:36.** Regarding "the Word" <note>original Greek: Λογον (Logon)</note> which God sent to the children of Israel, **ATHANASIUS** understood this to be the *Personal Word* <note>meaning the second person of the Trinity, Jesus Christ</note> in Volume I, *Oration V against the Arians*. He was followed by **THEOPHYLACT**, **HUGO**, **DIONYSIUS**, and among more recent writers, **HEINSIUS** in his *Sacred Exercises*, page 289. Since the construction of this verse seems somewhat intricate, that most famous man <note>Heinsius</note> thinks the matter can be best explained through an **Atticism** <term>Atticism: a grammatical construction characteristic of the elegant Greek of Athens</term>, which is very common. Namely, that "the word which he sent to the sons of Israel" is the same as: "the word which he sent to the sons of Israel, this one is Lord of all." Thus—

->DISSERTATION<-

it seems the words of the ancient translator can be understood in this way: *The Word God sent to the children of Israel, announcing peace through Jesus Christ: he is Lord of all.* <note>The author is quoting Acts 10:36, where Peter begins his speech to the Roman centurion Cornelius.</note> Among more recent scholars, this interpretation has also found specific supporters. However, it was examined and rejected by **STOLBERG** in his work *On Solecisms of the New Testament*, chapter 9, and by **J. HENR. MAJUS** in *Sacred Observations*, book III, pages 47–48. Let us therefore, while maintaining the respect due to the names of such famous men, modestly profess our disagreement. 

**I.** Because "the Word" <term>original Greek: Λογος (Logos)</term> is clearly distinguished as the subject of the announcement from *Jesus Christ*, through whom the announcement of peace was made. For unless one thing is understood by "the Word" and another by "Jesus Christ," those words *preaching peace through Jesus Christ* would have been added redundantly; it would have been better to say: *preaching peace through it*, namely, through "the Word." 

**II.** Although we admit—not only from <term>Hebraism: a linguistic usage or idiom peculiar to the Hebrew language</term> but also from <term>Atticism: a style of Greek characteristic of the city of Athens, often considered the refined standard</term>, as **JAC. PERIZONIUS** has proven in his notes on Aelian's *Various History* and **RAPHELIUS** from Xenophon in his notes on Luke 21—that the accusative case <note>The "accusative" is the grammatical case usually used for the direct object of a verb, but the author notes it is sometimes used as the subject.</note> often designates the subject of a speech, we do not think that usage can be applied to this passage. For such an accusative carries the force of a relative pronoun, and thus assumes that the subject was mentioned previously, or that a question had been raised about it, or that it is being contrasted with another subject. This is why the Greeks, when using this accusative, usually add the little words <term>original Greek: μεν (men)</term> or <term>original Greek: δε (de)</term> or another of similar value. Therefore, according to this hypothesis, it would have to be translated: *As for that Word which he sent.* But nothing can be pulled from the preceding text to suggest that Peter was referring back to such a thing. 

**III.** This also gives us pause: it seems less probable that Peter would have used the title "the Word" <term>Logos</term> right at the start of an address to the Gentiles <note>non-Jewish people, specifically the Romans in this context</note>, as it does not appear that this term for our Savior was yet in common use among Christians. The instruction of the Gentiles required a greater simplicity of language; they needed to be educated in the history of Jesus Christ before they were ready to perceive the mystery of **THE WORD** <term>original Greek: ΛΟΓΟΥ (Logou)</term>.

**XV.** These difficulties are completely avoided by those who connect our verse with the preceding one, in such a way that Peter would be declaring that the truth he proposed as an introduction—concerning the removal of the distinction between nations—is the very word that God sent to the children of Israel.

XVIII. ACTS 20:32. In the same way, Paul commends the Ephesians to God "and to the word of his grace" <note>original Greek: τῷ λόγῳ τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ (tō logō tēs charitos autou)</note>. Here again, **FRANCISCUS GOMARUS** <note>A strict Calvinist theologian (1563–1641) known for his role at the Synod of Dort.</note> (Theological Works, pages 152–153), **JACOB ALTING** (on the Epistle to the Hebrews 4:12), **HERMAN WITSIUS** (Miscellanea, vol. 2, in the place cited), and other most learned men argue in favor of the personal **WORD** <note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΩΙ (Logō), meaning Christ himself</note>. The principal arguments with which they fight are: I. because it is far more fitting for the faithful to be commended to Christ than to the Gospel. For the Gospel is commended to the faithful (2 Timothy 1:18, compared with 2 Timothy 2:2). II. Because the words that follow immediately can neither be referred to God without the fabrication of an unnecessary transposition <term>hyperbaton: A rhetorical figure where the natural order of words is shifted for emphasis or style.</term>, nor do they suit the Gospel, which neither builds us up upon a foundation nor gives us an inheritance—things which belong to Christ with far greater emphasis.

XIX. But the counter-arguments are no weaker. For: I. It cannot be proven that the Apostle Paul ever used the term *Word* in that higher sense <note>the theological sense of the "Logos" as the Second Person of the Trinity</note>. We have already examined the one passage cited to the contrary, Acts 13:26, and we shall see about the rest immediately. II. Luke, the companion of Paul, uses the same phrase in Acts 14:3 when he introduces the Lord "bearing witness to the word of his grace" <note>original Greek: μαρτυροῦντα τῷ λόγῳ τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ (martyrounta tō logō tēs charitos autou)</note>. According to the common consensus of interpreters, he means nothing other than the Word of the Gospel, for which it was said earlier in verse 23 <note>Likely referring to Acts 20:24</note> "the Gospel of the Grace of God" <note>original Greek: τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον τῆς Χάριτος τοῦ Θεοῦ (to Euaggelion tēs Charitos tou Theou)</note>. III. Although we grant that pious and suitable reasons could be brought forward as to why the Son of God might be called the *Word of the grace of God*, nonetheless, no example of this phrase can be produced in Scripture, whereas we have brought forward a most evident one for our own opinion. Indeed, no similar example occurs. For the Word is always found in simple relation either to God as the Father—when He is called the "Word of God" <note>original Greek: λόγος Θεοῦ (logos Theou)</note> in Revelation 19:13—or to life and salvation as the effect flowing from Him as the principal cause—when He is named the "word of life" <note>original Greek: λόγος τῆς ζωῆς (logos tēs zōēs)</note>. He is *not*, however, called the "Word of the life of God," lest anyone should argue from there that He is not the source of that life in the most excellent sense, but merely an instrument through which that life is communicated by God.

# DISSERTATION

<page-num>134</page-num>

XX. These objections present no delay. Nothing prevents the faithful from being commended not only to God but also to the **Word of His grace**. For the word of the Gospel is frequently introduced under the figure of a person through a <term>prosopopoeia: A rhetorical device where an abstract thing or inanimate object is represented as a person.</term> familiar to Holy Scripture. *It is the messenger of God, who performs that for which it is sent* <note>original: "Est legatus Dei, qui facit id, ad quod mittitur"</note>—Isaiah 55:11. *His testimonies are the counselors of the faithful* <note>original: "Testificationes ejus sunt consiliarii fidelium"</note>—Psalm 119:24. *Sent to the earth, it runs swiftly* <note>original: "Missum in terra velociter currit"</note>—Psalm 147:15. It also dwells in the faithful—Colossians 3:16. And what is more, all divine operations—which nevertheless have God alone as their Author—are ascribed to His Word. *It restores the soul, makes the fool wise, gladdens the heart, enlightens the eyes* <note>original: "Restituit animam, sapientem facit fatuum, lætificat cor, illuminat oculos"</note>—Psalm 19:8–9. *It breaks the cedars, strikes with flames of fire, shakes the desert* <note>original: "frangit cedros, cædit flammis ignis, percellit desertum"</note>—Psalm 29:5, 7, 8. 

And so that the faithful might be more aptly commended to it, a preserving power is ascribed to the same Word. In turn, they not only keep the word of the Lord, but are also kept by it. Proverbs 4:6: *Do not forsake her (wisdom) and she will preserve you; love her and she will keep you.* And Proverbs 6:20, 22: *Keep, my son, the commandment of your father and do not let go of the teaching of your mother. When you walk, it will lead you rightly; when you lie down, it will watch over you; and when you wake, it will talk with you.* From these examples it is clear that when the **Word of God's grace** is also considered by the Apostle as the fortress of the faithful in the New Testament, he does not consider it nakedly and in itself, but insofar as it is joined with the Spirit and vivified by Him as the *power of God unto salvation*. 

Although in this way the strength of the Evangelical Word is the strength of God Himself, the Apostle nevertheless wisely distinguishes these from one another. He does this to teach what is properly that medium through which the faithful are preserved by God, and toward which they ought to direct their first refuge, so that through it they may move God Himself to their guardianship. That medium, however, is nothing other than the **Evangelical promises**, which, when seized through faith, cannot fail; they give <term>parrhesia: A Greek term for "boldness" or "candid confidence," especially in prayer before God.</term> to appeal to those promises before God and to comfort oneself in them against all the assaults of hell. Therefore, *to commend to God and the word of His grace* is in reality nothing else than to commend to God for the purpose that He may act according to the Word of His grace and faithfully fulfill all His promises. Thus, one reads in **CICERO** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the Roman statesman and orator often cited by post-Reformation scholars for linguistic parallels.</note> of being commended to someone's *faith, authority, and prudence*...

WITSIUS and HAMMOND) <note>Herman Witsius (1633–1708) and Henry Hammond (1605–1660) were influential Dutch and English theologians, respectively.</note> they cannot persuade themselves that this passage concerns the **Personal Word** <note>The *Logos* or the Person of Jesus Christ</note>. Or is it credible that, while treating a matter which had a singular relation to the meaning of the Personal WORD (such as the commendation of the doctrine brought forth by him), he would have used this name only once, and that so ambiguously, if he had intended to use it in that way?

XXIV. When we now *Secondly* consider the predicates <note>the descriptive terms applied to "the Word"</note>, it is certain that by the emblem of the *sword* or *double-edged sword*, the Person of Christ is never designated, but rather the Word or the Doctrine of the Gospel is constantly intended. Under this figure, the Word is even distinguished from Him in Revelation 1:16, 2:12, 16, 19:15, 21; Isaiah 11:4; and Psalm 45:4, at which place we have more extensively illustrated the emphasis of this symbol. Our Apostle himself gave the most evident explanation of this emblem of all in Ephesians 6:17: *And the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God* <note>Greek: *rēma Theou*</note>. Since, therefore, every author is the best interpreter of his own words, should we think the Apostle would have departed from this given description unless he had indicated it with equal clarity? This point is even more compelling if the most elegant hypothesis of the celebrated BRAUN <note>Johannes Braun (1628–1708), a Dutch theologian</note> is adopted. Following in the footsteps of GROTIUS, CAMERON, WITTICH, and others, he thinks the Apostle specifically alludes here to the sacrificial knife, which cuts the sacrificial victim in such a way that all the intestines can be accurately seen and examined, to see if perhaps some hidden defect might lie anywhere that would render it unfit for the altar. Indeed, he shows that the individual Pauline phrases correspond so well to such a knife that he has easily won my own assent in this matter. I add only for the sake of illustration that among Greek authors, the word *machairan* <note>sword or large knife</note> also frequently refers to a sacrificial knife. See ARISTOPHANES in *The Peace*, verse 948.

Where the SCHOLIAST <note>An ancient commentator on classical texts</note> compares a verse of Plato from *The Little Child*:

XXV. I am not unaware that there is also a place where the sword is a personal emblem. For it is said of Zion in Zechariah 9:13: *shaping you like the sword of a Hero.* But it is clear enough here that Zion, or the Church, is considered as an instrument and medium which Christ himself uses to pursue his victories. This, however, cannot be applied to the Son of God, who is not the instrument of his operations, but the Lord of them.

XXVI. Only one saying remains, therefore, which seems to add some weight to the opinion of those who disagree, namely Isaiah 49:2, where the Messiah is introduced speaking: *And he made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand he hid me, and he made me a polished arrow: in his quiver he concealed me.* But from the beginning of this saying, it is visible that not the Person of Christ itself, but only his Mouth or his Doctrine is being considered, which alone is proclaimed here to be like a sword. When it is added that the Messiah himself was made into a polished arrow, that must undoubtedly be explained from the preceding phrase, and thus likewise refers not to the Person but to the preaching of Christ. This is even more so because, while the former phrase can simultaneously refer to the doctrine of Christ delivered orally in the days of his flesh, the latter...
