## ON THE LOGOS IN THE NEW TESTAMENT.
<note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΩΙ (Logōi). This refers to "The Word," a title for Christ or the Gospel.</note>

S 2

...nevertheless [this image] directly regards that preaching which was to be established by the Apostles and other teachers of the New Testament. For there occurred a *hiding in the shadow of Jehovah’s hand* <note>original Latin: occultatio per umbram manus Jehovæ; a reference to Isaiah 49:2</note>, while all the schemes of the enemies of truth, especially the Jews, were dashed against the doctrine of Christ; an *appointment as a chosen arrow* <note>original: constitutio in sagittam electam</note>, through the granting of legal authority, so that he might send forth the scepter of power from Zion and rule the nations with a rod of iron; and a *hiding in God’s quiver* <note>original: absconsio in pharetra Dei</note>, through his exaltation to the right hand of God, above all the rages of his enemies. With these things having been carried out in order, this weapon could be drawn from the quiver, which happened when *those sharp arrows began to fly, which pierced the hearts of the King’s enemies* <note>quoting Psalm 45:5 in the English numbering, 45:6 in the Latin Vulgate</note>. 

The following verses prove that this is the aim of this emblem <note>a symbolic image or figure</note>, showing that the Jews did not feel the force of this weapon as long as Christ lived in the flesh among them (verse 4), but that its power would be demonstrated even more strongly in the conversion of the Gentiles (verses 6 and 8). This conversion, however, was not so much the work of Christ himself in person, as the work of his Spirit through the ministry of the Word, which reveals the glory of Christ. And the very nature of the emblem requires this. For a *sword* is used for fighting hand-to-hand, but an *arrow* is used for fighting at a distance. Thus, the word preached by Christ himself among the Jews in the Holy Land is elegantly described by the first symbol [the sword]; but by the second symbol [the arrow], the same word is described as being carried far more effectively to the most distant nations with the swift motion of an arrow. 

Therefore, Christ is said here to be *made into a weapon* <note>original: in telum constitutus</note> not so much by a *metaphor* <note>a direct comparison</note> as by a *metonymy* <note>a figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it; here, Christ is called the "weapon" because he is the source and subject of the Gospel-weapon</note>, since he was the author and the subject of that Word which, like a weapon, was meant to strike the world with the rays of his glory. It is for this same reason that later in verse 8 it is said of the same Messiah that he is to be given <term>as a covenant for the people</term> <note>original Hebrew: לִבְרִית עָם (le-berit am)</note>. This does not mean his very Person should be considered under the form of a legal contract or covenant, but rather that by his intercession, authority, and the power of his Word, the people were to be led into the covenant. Thus, this passage does nothing to help those who contend that the person of the Son of God—viewed as distinct from the Word of the Gospel—is called the "Logos" <note>the Word</note> by Paul and as such is compared to a sword.

XXVII. I do not think, therefore, that anyone will depart from the usual meaning of *the Word* <note>original Greek: του λογου (tou logou)</note>, if only the difficulties regarding its attributes can be removed. As for those attributes drawn from verse 12...

# DISSERTATION

[...having been] performed, those things are quite small. SCHMIDT <note>Likely Erasmus Schmid (1570–1637), a Lutheran theologian and Greek scholar.</note> suffered a human lapse when his memory failed to provide the locations in which "living" <note>original Greek: ζων (zōn)</note> is also said of that which does not formally possess life within itself. For "living oracles" <note>original Greek: λογια ζωντα (logia zōnta)</note> explicitly occur in Acts 7:38. This is not to mention "living water" <note>original Greek: ὑδωρ ζων (hydor zōn)</note> in John 4:10–11 and 7:38. Nor does the "judicial" <note>original Greek: κριτικη (kritikē); meaning the power to judge or discern</note> force attributed to the Word constrain us further, as it must be understood according to the subject matter; it is no different than an instrumental power, such as that of the *knife* in the hand of the Priest, or like that attributed to the *rod of the mouth* of the Messiah, which in Isaiah 11:4 *strikes the earth* as an instrument of judicial power which he was destined to exercise. Compare also Isaiah 2:4, where it is said of the Law and the Word of Jehovah: *And he shall judge among those nations and shall provide conviction for many peoples.* Hence, the distinction between the judgment of this life and the future life is entirely irrelevant here. For in both cases, the Word of God is the instrument and the standard of judgment. Therefore, everything will be on solid ground if the predicates of verse 13 can themselves be connected to our passage without any violence to the text.

This is primarily established in two ways. GROTIUS <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a foundational Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> finds no difficulty in this verse being understood as referring to the Gospel itself. Others, however, generally prefer that different subjects be designated, and thus they believe the Son of God himself and his omniscience are described in verse 13. These latter scholars avoid the inconvenience that arises from the fact that "faces" and "eyes" would otherwise be attributed to the Gospel through an excessive use of <term>catachresis</term> <note>A figure of speech in which a word is used in a strained or non-literal way, such as "the eye of the needle."</note>. Nor are they lacking in significant reasons. For *First*, it is well-known among the learned that the Pauline style loves <term>hyperbata</term> <note>The transposition or inversion of normal word order for emphasis.</note>. *Second*, in our passage we do not even need a hyperbaton, since nothing prevents us from referring those words: *And no creature is hidden from his sight* <note>original Greek: Και οὐκ ἐστι κτισις ἀφανης ἐνωπιον αὐτου</note> to *God*, concerning whose *Word* the Apostle had been treating; this is surely the nearest noun to which this relative pronoun could refer. For from the connection of the preceding verses, it is clear that through the word *God* in verses 4, 9, and 10, the Apostle intended to specifically designate the Son of God. For he deals with him who, as the <term>antitype</term> <note>A person or thing in the New Testament that is foreshadowed by a "type" in the Old Testament.</note> of Joshua, also rested from his perfect work of salvation and led his people into rest, and whose voice *was heard today*, who was signally the Son of God—the very one whom the Church had named *their God* in Psalm 95:7: *Since he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture.*

### CONCERNING THE WORD <note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΩΙ (Logōi)</note> IN THE NEW TESTAMENTO.

...and the flock led by Him; *today if you hear His voice, do not harden your heart.* **Thirdly**, so that no one may go astray, the true subject of this verse is pointed out by those final words: *with whom we have to do* <note>original Greek: προς ὁν ἡμιν ὁ λογος (pros hon hēmin ho logos). This phrase is famously ambiguous, meaning either "to whom we must give an account" or "concerning whom we are speaking."</note>. I know indeed that CHRYSOSTOM <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching.</note> and other ancients paraphrase these words as: *to whom we must give an account of our deeds* <note>original Greek: ᾧ ἐχομεν δουναι εὐθυνας των πεπραγμενων (hō echomen dounai euthynas tōn pepragmenōn)</note>. The *Glossa Ordinaria* <note>A standard medieval collection of biblical glosses or commentaries.</note> expresses it thus: *To whom it is necessary for us to render an account of our works.* This is particularly pleasing to JAKOB ALTING <note>1618–1679, a Dutch linguist and theologian.</note>. But why should we assume a rather harsh ellipsis <note>A grammatical omission of words.</note> here without necessity? Much less does the VULGATE <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note> find agreement, which ERASMUS follows, rendering it: *To whom our speech is directed*, that is, whom we invoke. For it is plainly unusual for prayers to be called "the Word" <note>original: λογον (logon)</note> in an absolute sense. Therefore, everything flows most easily if "with" <note>original: προς (pros)</note> is translated as "concerning," as GROTIUS <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a foundational Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> asserts from Chapter 1:7, and as WITTICH <note>Christoph Wittich (1625–1687), a Dutch Cartesian theologian.</note> has illustrated more fully at this location.

The Apostle therefore guards against the ambiguity which could have arisen from the connection of this verse with the preceding one, specifically because a certain judicial power was ascribed to the Word of the Gospel. From this, a suspicion was close at hand: whether the Apostle might be continuing to discuss the same subject in verse 13. **Fourthly**, in this way, a suitable transition to the following verse was constructed. For since in that verse the Son of God is proposed as the High Priest <note>original: Summus Sacerdos</note>, in our verse His excellence above all the priests of the Old Testament is taught by this: while they, by means of a sacrificial knife, could only examine the hidden parts of the intestines, before our High Priest all creatures and all secrets of the heart are naked and *laid bare* <note>original: exenterata. This word literally means "disemboweled" or "eviscerated," maintaining the metaphor of a priest inspecting a sacrifice.</note>. Since this phrase proves not only His divine omniscience but also His widely extending kingdom, it is manifest from here why Paul, in the immediately following verse, considers Jesus not merely as a Priest, but as one *who has passed through the heavens*, and who in verse 16 established a *throne of grace*, to which all the faithful have the right to approach with *boldness* <note>original Greek: παρρησια (parrhēsia); meaning "freedom of speech" or "bold confidence" before God.</note>.

**XXVIII.** We trust that these observations will gain even more agreement if it can only be shown that, according to this hypothesis, a connection between our verses and the preceding ones can be demonstrated that is both easy and suitable to the Apostle’s goal. Regarding this matter, we observe that the Apostle is here concluding the refutation from Chapter...

# DISSERTATION

Chapter III. 7. from Psalm XCV. is established to demonstrate the necessity of providing the obedience of faith to Christ as the Apostle and High Priest <note>This refers to Hebrews 3:1, where Jesus is uniquely titled "Apostle," meaning one sent by God, alongside his role as High Priest.</note> of our Confession. To that end:

**I.** The statement itself is proposed in Chapter III. 7—11.
**II.** From this, various arguments binding one to the obedience of faith are deduced in Chapters III. 12 to IV. 13. These are sought:
**A.** From the foulness <note>original Latin: *foeditate*</note> of the crime itself described in the Psalm (Chapter III. 12–14).
**B.** From the horrific judgment (Chapter III. 15 to IV. 13) which:
**1.** Is explained in Chapter III. 15—19.
**2.** Is applied to the Hebrews in Chapter IV. 1—13.
**a.** Through a general admonition (Chapter IV. 1).
**b.** Through its demonstration (Chapter IV. 2—13), which is arranged so that:
**α.** It is proved that this judgment must still be feared by unbelievers in the New Testament <note>The author uses "N. T." to refer to the "New Testament" era or covenant.</note> (verses 2–11).
**β.** The equity <note>meaning the fairness or justice</note> of this judgment, and likewise the necessity of providing the obedience demanded by Psalm XCV. 7—*Today if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts*—is proven by two arguments.
**$\aleph$.** <gloss>Aleph (the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, used here as a bullet point)</gloss> The first (verse 12) is taken from the efficacy of the *voice heard*; for the *Voice of God* and the *Word of God* <note>original: *Vox Dei* and *Verbum Dei*</note> are synonyms here. Since, therefore, that *Voice* or that *Word* revealed itself as such not only in the preaching that was done generally at the beginning of the New Testament, but also in the very conscience of the Hebrews, what is more equitable than to persist constantly in its obedience?
**$\beth$.** <gloss>Beth (the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet)</gloss> The second (verse 13) is sought from the omniscience of *God* himself—whose *Voice* or *Word* was heard in that "today"—and from His kingdom extended over all creatures, especially after He placed His throne in heaven.

**XXIX.** Either I am very much mistaken, or attentive judges will easily recognize this connection as natural and clear. Therefore, there will be no need for us to inquire whether the connections proposed by those who disagree are quite so convenient.

-># ON THE WORD IN THE NEW TESTAMENT.<-

We have sufficiently fulfilled our role if we have cleared that single difficulty which could be opposed to our view, so that it might appear from this that there is no reason to depart from the more common meaning of both the subject and the predicate occurring in Verse 12. We cling to this all the more because that meaning—which our words provide when explained according to our hypothesis—is no less sublime and emphatic. For whatever efficacy and perfection is attributed to this instrument of the glory of the Son of God, the praise for it redounds upon the Hero <note>The "Hero" here refers to Christ, depicted as a warrior or judge using the "sword" of the Word.</note> himself, who uses that blade so aptly and successfully. And in this way, it is possible for both meanings to be joined, as our venerable D'Outreinius <note>Johannes d'Outrein (1662–1722), a Dutch theologian highly regarded for his detailed commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews.</note>—a man who served the Christian Church most excellently—observes in his outstanding commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews (which he wrote in the vernacular), following Zegerus <note>Tacitus Nicolaus Zegerus (died 1559), a Flemish scholar known for his notes on the New Testament.</note>. For we do not understand the Word to be anything other than that which is animated by the Spirit of Christ. We only mean that there is a single subject in this verse, and that is not so much the Person of Christ revealing Himself through His word, as it is the Word being made effective through the power of Christ. And this unity of the subject is especially required by the phrase "of God" <note>original Greek: Θεου</note>, with which "Word" <note>original: *logos*</note> is constructed. For otherwise, that phrase would take on a double meaning: in the first sense it would designate God the Father, but in the latter sense it would designate God the Son, which seems quite clumsy.

XXX. In **1 Peter 2:8**, those who are rebellious against Christ and His Gospel are described as *those who stumble, being disobedient to the word*. <note>original Greek: *οἱ προσκοπτουσι, τῳ λογῳ ἀπειθουντες*</note> Here, Drusius <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616) was a renowned Flemish Protestant scholar and Hebraist.</note> thought of the *Substantial Word* <term>Substantial Word: A theological term for Christ Himself as the eternal "Word" (Logos), as opposed to the spoken or written word of Scripture.</term>. If the name "LOGOS" had been commonly used in that sense before this time, it would not be absurd to understand it that way here as well. But I believe the Apostles intentionally abstained from it in the flow of their speech to avoid obscurity. Therefore, I judge that learned men have observed soundly that in this passage, "to the word" <note>original Greek: *τῳ λογῳ*</note> should be connected not with "stumble" but with "being disobedient." For this is the same phrase that recurs *according to the letter* <note>meaning, the exact wording</note> in 1 Peter 3:1.

XXXI. In **2 Peter 3:5**, Placæus <note>Josué de la Place (1596–1665), also known as Placæus, was a French Protestant theologian at the Academy of Saumur.</note> (in his work *On the Divinity of Jesus Christ*, part 1, disputation 21, section 1) includes this among those passages which indicate the personal WORD. For it is said there that *the heavens were of old, and the earth standing out of the water and in the water*, *by the WORD of God*. <note>original Greek: *τῳ του Θεου ΛΟΓΩΙ*</note> To this same...

# DISSERTATION

To the **Word** <note>original: "λογῳ" (logō)</note> also in verse 7, the *preservation of heaven and earth* is attributed. And I truly confess, if anywhere outside of the Gospel of John the name **LOGOS** is attributed to the Son of God, then it happens in this place [2 Peter 3]. For it cannot be denied that the Apostle here looks back to the history of creation, in which God is described as having produced all things from nothing by speaking—which in Psalm 33:6 is declared to have been done through the **WORD OF THE LORD**. Now, in what follows, God willing, we shall prove that these passages refer to the Son of God. If, therefore, Peter had not been referring to Him, then a foundational reason <term>caussa fontica: a reason derived from the very source or origin of an argument</term> ought to be provided as to why the Apostle, while pointing his finger toward those Old Testament passages, nevertheless used this word with less emphasis than it carries there. However, I do not see how such a reason could be offered, unless one wished to argue that Peter is discussing those who *willfully ignore* this truth, and thus he seems to speak of a matter that is sufficiently manifest through the light of conscience itself. 

But from verse 4, it is clear that those mockers were either Jews, or at least people to whom the prophecies of the Prophets—and thus the books of the Old Testament <note>original: "V. T." (Vetus Testamentum)</note>—were not unknown; by paying attention to these, they could have easily learned the truth. However, those who understand the *Word of God* here simply as a command, a will, or a counsel of God, must produce examples to prove that when the discussion concerns that *Word of God* through which the world was founded, nothing except His will is understood, without any reference to the Son of God.

### XXXII.

And so we consider the path to be cleared for us to observe a certain synonym of the personal **LOGOS** in the writings of the New Testament <note>original: "N. T." (Novum Testamentum)</note>. As such, we hold **THE WORD** <note>original: "TO PHMA" (to rhēma)</note> in Hebrews 11:3: *By faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the* **WORD OF GOD** <note>original: "PHMATI ΘΕΟΥ" (rhēmati theou)</note>. Among the Church Fathers, Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century theologian known for his Christological works</note> understood this passage as referring to the Son of God in his *Treasuries*, page 293. I gather that many at that time felt the same from the dispute of the Semi-Arians <note>A 4th-century group who held a middle position between the Arians and the Nicene Christians regarding the nature of Christ</note> against Paul of Samosata <note>A 3rd-century bishop whose views on the divinity of Christ were condemned as heretical</note>, which occurs in Epiphanius’s *Against Heresies* <note>original: "Hær." (Haereses)</note>, No. 73, Section 12. ### VII.

## THEOLOGICAL DISSERTATION
## ON THE PASSAGE
# PSALM 33:6.

->**I.**<-

The mystical names that the writers of the New Testament give to the Son of God are drawn from various places in the Scriptures. This was done for the purpose that, for Jews searching the writings of Moses and the Prophets, those passages might be called to mind in which the Mystery of Salvation and the Glory of the Messiah were clearly described. Since, therefore, the name of the **Word** <note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΟΥ (Logos)</note> shines with a singular brightness among them, it is easy to imagine that it was drawn from the same source as the others. And indeed, such a passage occurs in **Psalm 33:6**: *By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their host* <note>original Hebrew: בדבר יהוה שמים נעשו וברוח פיו כל צבאם</note>. If it can be demonstrated in this place that none other than the Son of God is to be understood by the **Word of the Lord**, we believe we will gain much light for the phrasing used by John <note>Referring to the opening of the Gospel of John, "In the beginning was the Word..."</note>. Therefore, it is pleasing to meditate on this matter deliberately.

->**II.**<- The differences of opinion regarding the **Word of the Lord** <note>original Latin: *Verbum Jehovae*</note> mentioned here by the Psalmist can be divided into three main classes. For some think that the Mystery of the Trinity should not be considered here at all, but they stop at a simpler meaning. However, even these do not agree among themselves. Some, sticking to the literal letter, seem to understand it as the **uttered word** <term>prophorikon</term> <note>From the Greek *logos prophorikos*, referring to the spoken word as an external expression of internal thought</note>. **Didymus** <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398) was a famous theologian in Alexandria who lost his sight at age four but became a master of grammar, rhetoric, and theology</note>, if I am not mistaken, tends toward this view when he interprets the "heavens" mystically as the saints who are established through the *Word of the Lord*. Most, however, judge that His "Word" is spoken of metaphorically as the decree and will of the Lord. The **Anti-Trinitarians** <note>Groups who reject the doctrine of the Trinity, often viewing "Word" as a personification of God's power rather than a distinct person</note> hold this view everywhere, but so do some of those who otherwise embrace the doctrine of the Trinity, among whom we find not only **Franciscus Vatablus** <note>François Vatable (d. 1547) was a renowned French humanist and Hebrew scholar whose annotations on the Bible were highly influential</note>,

III. The second class consists of those who contend that the **Personal Word** <note>The "Personal Word" refers to the Son of God, the second person of the Trinity, as described in the Gospel of John.</note> is hinted at by the Psalmist. These scholars look to the most ancient of the Church Fathers as their leaders. Among them is Irenaeus in *Against Heresies*, book 1, chapter 19 and book 3, chapter 8. Cyprian follows these in *Against the Jews*, book 2, chapter 3, along with many others cited by Lorinus on this passage. *Just as there is no spoken word in God, but one living and subsisting, and active over all things; so in God there is no diffused breath, no dissolved air, but a sanctifying power, consubstantial, inherent, and subsistent.* <note>original Greek: Ὥσπερ οὐ προφορικὸς Λόγος ἐν τῷ Θεῷ, ἀλλὰ ζῶν καὶ ὑφεστηκὼς, καὶ τῶν ὅλων δραστήριος; οὗτος ἐν τῷ Θεῷ οὐ Πνεῦμα διαχεόμενον, οὐ διαλυόμενος ἀὴρ, ἀλλὰ δύναμις ἁγιαστικὴ ἐνούσιος, ἐνυπαρκτος, ἐνυπόστατος. Basil is arguing that God's "Word" and "Breath" are not temporary sounds or physical air, but eternal, divine realities.</note>

Among more recent scholars, by far the greatest part embraces this opinion.

IV. To the third class I refer those who strive to join both senses together. Such is the Old Commentator, who is thought to be Theodore of Heraclea in the *Chain*, on this passage:

*In order to say that by a single decree he produced such a great work and instilled the power to endure, needing neither time nor labor. For just as the earth would not have stood firm if the mercy of the Lord had not been in its midst, so neither would the heaven have been established if it were not held together by the divine Word. This is the obvious sense; however, true theology points to the Word of God along with the Holy Spirit, who created both the heavens and the heavenly powers—both the divine and the rational ones.* <note>original Greek: Ἵνα εἴπῃ ὅτι μόνῃ ἀποφάσει τοσοῦτον ἔργον παρήγαγε, καὶ πρὸς διαμονὴν ἰσχὺν ἐνεποίησεν, οὐ χρόνου, οὐ πόνου προσδεηθείς. Ὡς γὰρ ἡ γῆ οὐκ ἂν συνέστη, μὴ τοῦ ἐλέους κυρίου μέση τυγχάνουσα, οὕτως οὐδὲ οὐρανὸς ἂν ἐστερεώτο, εἰ μὴ θείῳ Λόγῳ διεκράτειτο. Τοῦτο μὲν ὁ πρόχειρος νοῦς, ἡ δὲ ἀληθὴς θεολογία, τὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ ὑποδείκνυσι Λόγον σὺν τῷ ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι, καὶ τοὺς οὐρανοὺς καὶ τὰς οὐρανίους δυνάμεις, καὶ θείας, καὶ λογικὰς δημιουργήσαντα.</note>

# DISSERTATION

*...requiring neither time nor labor. For just as the earth would not have stood firm unless it had been full of the Lord's mercy, so also the heaven would not have been established unless it had been sustained by the divine Word.* This is indeed what the obvious meaning signifies; yet true Theology demonstrates that *the Word of God, together with the Holy Spirit, created both the heavens and the heavenly, divine, and rational powers.* <note>original Latin: *divinas & rationales virtutes*. In medieval and early modern theology, "virtues" or "powers" often referred to specific ranks of angels or the spiritual capacities of the soul.</note> Thus **Origen** <note>An influential early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) from Alexandria.</note> held in his *Commentary on John*, Volume I, page 43; and among more recent authors, **Jansenius**, **Cajetan**, and **Lorinus** adopt the same opinion. **Corderius** adds this observation: *In that former and simpler sense, the Holy Spirit feeds the unrefined—such as the Jews—in these and similar passages; but in the latter sense, He feeds the more perfect—such as the Christians.* <note>This reflects a common historical perspective in 17th-century Christian scholarship, which viewed the Old Testament as containing "hidden" Christian truths that were only fully understood after the coming of Christ.</note> **Theodore Hakspanius** <note>A 17th-century German scholar of Hebrew and Oriental languages.</note> gives his approval to the same sentiment in his *Philological Notes*, Part II, pages 142 and following, adding for the sake of illustration that *it is not a new thing in Scripture to join that double sense. For example, in Exodus 20 with the Passover Lamb, which is understood immediately, Christ himself is simultaneously denoted; just as through the bone which must not be broken, the bone of the Passover Lamb is immediately understood, but the bone of Christ is understood through a mediated sense, as in John 19:36.*

**Calvin** <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the French reformer and influential theologian.</note> was pleased with the same interpretation on this passage: *By saying the heavens were created by the word of God, he amplifies His power even more; because, being content with a mere nod, He neither summoned help from elsewhere, nor even spent much effort or labor on such a splendid and noble work. However, although the Prophet contrasted the Word of God and the Breath of His mouth against all external means and difficulty, it is truly and certainly gathered from here that the world was fabricated through the eternal Speech of God, who is the only-begotten Son.* I have decided these words ought to be transcribed here all the more so that the bad faith of **Vorstius** <note>Conrad Vorstius (1569–1622), a controversial theologian often accused of holding unorthodox views on the nature of God.</note> may appear in his *Balance of Truth*, page 169, where he numbers Calvin among those who believe the Psalmist designated nothing but the command of God through the "Word of Jehovah."

### ON THE PASSAGE OF PSALM 33:6.

There is plainly no weight to this wavering <note>original: *fluctuationis*. The author refers to the hesitation some feel in applying New Testament doctrines to Old Testament texts.</note>. For although the mystery of the Trinity was to be more clearly revealed in the Administration of the New Testament <note>The "Economy" or "Administration" refers to the different ways God relates to humanity across history, specifically the era of the New Testament.</note>, that it was not unknown to the Fathers <note>The "Patriarchs" or early leaders of the faith.</note> from the beginning of the world is both suggested by the importance of this article of faith and proven by the writings of Moses. And even if this doctrine had remained largely in the dark, it would nevertheless have been an appropriate time—when this Psalm was being delivered to the Church (the author and age of which are unknown)—to instruct the people more closely on a matter of such great weight. Therefore, nothing hinders us from embracing the second opinion without hesitation, which we consider to be the most consistent with the *aim* of the Psalm, the *meaning* of the words, their *connection*, and the *analogy* of the faith of that time.

VI. The *aim* of the entire Psalm is easily perceived: namely, that the chosen people of Jehovah might be stirred up to celebrate His name in faith and trust. To that end, it describes the mutual encouragement of the faithful to celebrate the name of the great Jehovah and to recognize the happiness of those whose God He is. Various phrases prove that it specifically looks toward the times of the Messiah: for instance, in verse 3, a *new song* <note>original Latin: *carmen novum*</note> is required, an expression which constantly designates the praises of the Lord to be composed in the New Administration <note>See Psalms 96:1, 98:1, Isaiah 42:10, and Revelation 5:9, 14:3.</note>; and in verse 5, where the *earth is said to be full of the grace of Jehovah*; and in verse 8, where *all the earth and all its inhabitants* are introduced as *fearing and trembling before Him*. These and similar descriptions do not fit the Mosaic Administration. It may be added that the first verse of this Psalm, by repeating the same words with which the preceding Psalm ends, shows that these two Psalms are connected in matter and subject. Now, we are persuaded that Psalm 32 is to be referred to the Administration of the New Testament, both from other arguments and especially from the Apostolic citation in Romans 4:6 <note>Where the Apostle Paul quotes David regarding the blessing of the man to whom God credits righteousness apart from works.</note>. Specifically, however, it points toward such a time of the Kingdom of the Messiah *when the nations had already been converted, because the earth was full of the grace of Jehovah; yet when it was still expected in the future that all the earth and all its inhabitants would be touched by the fear of Jehovah; when the plans and thoughts of various enemies of the truth had been rendered useless; when Jehovah, looking out from heaven and seeing all the sons of man, was striving for a certain general change of things in the world and the Church:*

### VIII.

From this outline <note>original: "schediasmate"</note> it is clear that the entire Psalm deals with the divine administration of the **Kingdom of Grace** <note>a theological term for God's spiritual rule and mercy toward believers</note> in preserving and liberating the Church. Therefore, verse six describes the ***work of creation*** specifically in its relationship to the ***work of salvation***. It is common in the prophetic Scriptures for the faithful to be lifted up during their afflictions by considering the creation of the world. (See, for example, Psalm 95:4, 5; 96:5; 102:26; 121:2; 136:5 and following; Isaiah 40:28; 42:5; 45:12; 48:13; Jeremiah 10:12, 16; 31:35; 32:17). 

This is done not only so that God's power might be revealed—the power by which he can fulfill all his promises to the Church—but also because the work of creation is, by a certain logic, subordinate to the plan and Kingdom of Grace. For the world was founded for this end: that in it, this Kingdom might be established for the eternal praise of glorious grace. Furthermore, the very process and order of creation was a type and a shadow <note>a symbolic foreshadowing or "typology"</note> of the more notable turning points of the Church. Because of this, those parts of creation are frequently cited which [demonstrate] that [work] of God in the Church...

->### ON THE PASSAGE OF PSALM 33, VERSE 6<-

V 3

Thus, in our passage, *the perfection of the heavens and their host* serves as a symbol and sign that **Jehovah, that Rock, whose work is perfect** (Deuteronomy 32:4), will undoubtedly bring to completion the *heavens* of the Church—that *Kingdom of Heaven* which had already been founded through the eternal justice described in the preceding Psalm. And when, in the following verse, the **separation of the waters from the earth and their gathering within their boundaries** is added, it brings to mind that most elegant emblem, frequently found in the Prophets, which is used to represent the empty waves and violent rushes of the Church's restless enemies.

### IX.
Having weighed these matters, it is clear that mention is most aptly made of the **Holy Trinity** <note>original: "SS. Triados"</note> in the present text. I will not dwell now on the traces of this mystery occurring in the creation itself, nor on the custom of Scripture to speak of the Creator of the world in the plural number (Ecclesiastes 12:1; Isaiah 54:5). This especially pertains to the *aim* of the Psalm: that the mystery of the Father and the Son is the primary object of faith in the **Covenant of Grace**. This mystery was intended to be more fully revealed under the Kingdom of the Messiah; furthermore, there is a singular analogy in this very matter between the work of Creation and Redemption, as the same order of divine operations occurs in both works. The same **Father** is in both cases the fountain and origin of all divine activity for producing a work outside of God; the same **Son** is the executor of the divine will; and the same **Spirit** is the adorner and perfecter of the work produced.

### X.
But to draw the knot even tighter <note>meaning to make the logical argument more compelling</note>, let us more closely examine the phrase **Word of Jehovah** <term>Hebrew: *Dabar Yehovah*</term>, and let us investigate all the places in which it occurs. Although these are many, we find none in which the *Word of Jehovah* is used merely for a "nod" of His will—whether decreeing or commanding—or for His own effectiveness in producing something. It consistently designates a **spoken word** <note>original Greek: *prophorikon*, referring to a word that is physically uttered or expressed</note>. This is sometimes produced by God Himself through a voice externally sounded in the air (Deuteronomy 5:5; 1 Samuel 3:7); sometimes through a prophetic vision (Genesis 15:1, 4); and finally, dictated through inspiration or any other manner, whether preached to others in the name of God by Prophets and **divinely inspired men** <note>original Greek: *theopneustous*, meaning "God-breathed"</note> or recorded in writing (Exodus 9:20, 21; 1 Kings 2:27).

<meta>This page continues the theological argument from page 157, where the author began defending a Trinitarian reading of Psalm 33:6. -># DISSERTATION<-

II. 27. Psalm 147:19, etc. In this sense, the *Word of Jehovah* is mentioned in the nineteenth verse of this Psalm. There are those who, to the contrary, bring forward Psalm 107:20 and 147:15. But we will show in the proper place (a) that those passages deal with the Word of the Gospel. **SCHLICHTINGIUS** <note>Jonas Schlichting (1592–1661), a prominent Polish theologian of the Socinian tradition, known for arguing against the Trinity.</note> adds Psalm 148:8: *Fire and hail, snow and vapor, stormy wind, fulfilling his Word.* But that passage indicates nothing other than that all these creatures are subject to the Governance of the Church according to the Covenant and the eternal *promises* of God, as the entire context of the Psalm shows. Some also incorrectly interpret the *Word of Jehovah* in 1 Kings 22:5 and 2 Chronicles 18:4 as His mere "will," when it is clear from the context that an oracle of God sought from the mouth of the Prophets is what is meant. In Joel 2:11, it is said of the locusts that they would carry out the *Word of Jehovah*, but this undoubtedly refers to that which was set forth through God's threats. Deuteronomy 8:3 is also cited, where Moses testifies that *man does not live by bread alone, but by every thing that proceeds from the mouth of Jehovah.* For this is explained as *every Word of his* in Matthew 4:4. However, the very term "proceeding" <note>original: "egressio"</note> leads us by the hand toward the external Word—namely, the promises made to the Fathers—as is evident by comparing Psalm 89:33: *My covenant I will not profane, and the utterance <note>original: "egressio," literally "that which goes out"</note> of my lips I will not change.* Hence, in 1 Timothy 4:5, it is said that *every creature is sanctified by the Word of God and prayer.* For the Word of promise and prayer have a very close relationship to one another. Psalm 105:19 is also mentioned without any justification, because the *Word of Jehovah* there refers to the divine revelation made to Pharaoh in a dream. We pass over other similar points of lesser importance.

XI. ...[breathing or] inspiration. Indeed, **VALENTINUS SMALCIUS** <note>Valentinus Smalcius (1572–1622) was a prominent German-Polish Socinian theologian who denied the Trinity and the deity of Christ.</note> argues this against Smiglecius <note>Marcin Smiglecki (1563–1618), a Polish Jesuit philosopher and fierce opponent of the Socinians.</note> in chapter II. However, in the proper place, God willing, we shall prove that a far deeper mystery lies hidden when God is introduced as "speaking" in the history of creation. For now, we only note that since we believe no tautologies <note>original: "tautologias"; redundant repetitions of the same idea</note> should be admitted in the words of the Holy Spirit—especially in prophetic ones—a singular confirmation of our opinion arises from this very passage. 

For while the word "said" is here distinguished from "commanded," it also indicates something different. How the Psalmist distinguishes these concepts appears from the text itself. For the complete verse reads: *For he spoke, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast.* <note>Psalm 33:9</note> The first <term>section <note>original: "tmema"; a Greek term used to describe a segment or clause of a verse</note></term> here regards the work of Creation, in which a command had no place, because there was not yet an object toward which a command could be directed—unless we wish to say that God spoke to nothingness. 

But the second division—which **SCHLICHTINGIUS** <note>Jonas Schlichting (1592–1661), another key Socinian thinker.</note> in his *Commentary on Hebrews*, p. 84, deceitfully renders as: *he commanded and they were created*—describes the work of divine Providence concerning things already existing, so that they might be established in a fixed order. Specifically, it describes the manifestation of the "Counsel of Peace" through the Covenant of Grace, by which God restored, as it were, all things that had been founded, and laid a firm foundation for the governance of the whole world. 

The passage in Psalm 148:5 seems to oppose us: *He commanded, and they were created.* However, it can be countered not only that this does not speak of the first production of matter, but of its "digestion" <note>the ordering and arrangement of pre-existing elements into a structured world</note>, regarding which a command at least metaphorically had a place; but also that this word <term>tzivah <note>Hebrew: צוה; to command, ordain, or give a charge</note></term> should not be restricted to the words immediately following, but extended also to those added right after: *And he made them stand forever and ever*, and thus to the entire Kingdom of Nature, insofar as it is subordinated to the Kingdom of Grace.

### XII.

Although this might not please certain defenders of the Holy Trinity—among whom we admit **JOHN CALVIN** himself stands—it is nevertheless most convincing to us. For why would the Psalmist, in the description of creation, [attribute to] the Spirit of Jehovah...

# DISSERTATIO

<meta>catchword: tus</meta>

By attributing the name *Spirit*, he understood that very *Spirit* who is commemorated as the **efficient cause** <note>The "efficient cause" is a philosophical term for the primary agent that brings something into existence.</note> in the history of creation in Genesis 1:2. Moreover, we believe it has been abundantly demonstrated by others that only a **Divine Person** is indicated there by Moses. For it is absurd to think that at that beginning of things, it refers to *air* or *wind* (which is nothing but motion, and thus only an **accident** <note>In traditional logic, an "accident" is a property that can change without changing the nature of the thing itself—like the movement of air.</note> of air), since no distinction of things had yet been made—not even of air from water and earth. 

Furthermore, since the Spirit is described in explicit words as מרחפת על פני המים <note>original Hebrew: "merachephet al pnei ha-mayim"</note> *moving itself or brooding over the waters*, just as a bird broods over its chicks, he must be considered not as an effect or the motion produced, but as the **moving cause**. To bring out the emphasis of this phrase, it is worth comparing what **HOTTINGER** <note>Johann Heinrich Hottinger (1620–1667), a Swiss philologist and theologian.</note> writes in *Examination of the History of Creation*, page 40 and following, and **GATAKER** <note>Thomas Gataker (1574–1654), an English scholar and theologian.</note> in *Cinnus* II. 2, though he is not entirely consistent with himself. 

Besides, that *Spirit moving itself* over the terrestrial-aquatic globe is undoubtedly distinct from that globe, and thus cannot be reduced to the category of created things. Therefore, God the Creator himself must necessarily be understood. And since it is nonetheless called the *Spirit of God*, a certain person in the divine essence who is distinct from the others is simultaneously hinted at—specifically from the one who is considered the primary source of all divine activity directed outward. 

Nor do others understand it any less ineptly when they interpret it as a "divine power," because the power of nourishing and moving is ascribed to the Spirit itself by the word מרחפת <note>original Hebrew: "merachephet," often translated as hovering or fluttering.</note>. For it would be "absurd to attribute power to a power" <note>original Latin: "absonum esset, virtutem tribuere virtuti."</note>. And why then did Moses not say immediately from the beginning: *In the beginning the Spirit of God created the heavens and the earth?* Was more power required to produce motion than to produce matter? And if not, what need was there that the creation of the former be attributed more to a "divine power" than the latter? 

Additionally, anyone to whom effective action is attributed in a simple and historical style must be recognized as an active and acting principle. This is further confirmed by the fact that **Job**, dealing with the same work of creation, likewise presents the *Spirit of God* as an acting and producing substance in chapter 33:4: *The Spirit of the Almighty made me, and the breath of the All-Sufficient gives me life.* On this passage, the **BERESCHIT RABBA** <note>Genesis Rabbah, an ancient Jewish commentary on the Book of Genesis.</note> judged more soundly than many Christian interpreters: ורוח אלהים וגו׳ זה רוח המשיח שנ׳ ונחה עליו רוח יהוה <note>original Hebrew: "Ve-ruach Elohim... zeh ruach ha-Mashiach she-ne'emar ve-nachah alav ruach Adonai."</note> *“And the Spirit of God [hovered]... this is the Spirit of the Messiah, as it is said: And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him.”* <note>Referring to Isaiah 11:2.</note>

### CONCERNING THE PASSAGE IN PSALM 33:6

...and we may suspect that phrases on this matter were borrowed and twisted from Moses. Nevertheless, we must not overlook this remarkable passage by **PORPHYRY** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who was often critical of Christianity but respected ancient wisdom.</note> in *On the Cave of the Nymphs*, where he records these words from **NUMENIUS**: *“For this reason, he says that the Prophet also stated that the Spirit of God is borne above the water, and for the same reason the Egyptians do not place any of their deities on solid ground, but all of them upon a ship.”* <note>original Greek: "Δια τουτο λεγων και τον Προφητην ειρηκεναι ἐμφερεσθαι ἐπανω του ὑδατος Θιου πνευμα..." This refers to Numenius of Apamea, a philosopher who famously asked, "What is Plato but Moses speaking Attic Greek?"</note> *He says, therefore, that the Prophet (the context shows this refers to Moses) said that the Spirit of God is carried over the waters; and for that same reason, the Egyptians place all their lesser gods not on dry land, but in a boat.*

XIV. Indeed, those slight arguments by which our interpretation of the Mosaic "Spirit of God" is attacked are plainly empty. **RIVETUS**, in his *Exercises on Genesis*, II, has already professionally refuted the objections of **ENJEDINUS** <note>George Enyedi (1555–1597), a Unitarian theologian who argued against traditional interpretations of the Trinity.</note>, which we will not copy out here. But other excuses have also been brought forward by others. For instance, **ATHANASIUS** in his *Six Days of Creation*, Book III, contends that this Spirit is a "wind," because it is not called *the spirit* <note>original Greek: το πνευμα</note> but simply *spirit* <note>original Greek: πνευμα</note> without the definite article. **JACQUES CAPPELLUS**, in his *Observations on Genesis*, page 582, has already replied to this, noting that this distinction never holds in Hebrew grammar, and not always even in Greek. **CLERICUS** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous biblical critic.</note> especially insists on the passive meaning of the word *merachephet* <note>original Hebrew: מרחפת</note>, from which he translates it as: *it was moved*. But since he produces no examples, and the lexicographers—especially **GOUSSET**—prove by examining all known examples that it always designates motion from an internal principle, this "wedge" is easily blunted. As for the objection others raise—that the word *God* <note>original Hebrew: אלהים (Elohim)</note> joined to a noun indicates the "highest" or "greatest" <note>This is the theory that "Spirit of God" just means "a very mighty wind."</note>—this is likewise a ruinous argument. For it has not yet been proven that the divine names are used in such a way in the Sacred Scriptures. Much less can such an unusual and strained way of speaking be admitted here, where the subject matter itself contradicts it. There are even those who appeal to Psalm 147:18: *He shall blow <term>his Spirit</term><note>original Hebrew: רוחו (rucho), which can mean "his wind" or "his spirit."</note>, and the waters shall flow*; where they argue "Spirit" should be understood as wind, and "His" as referring to God. Even if this were granted by most, those who disagree gain nothing from it. For that passage looks at the work of divine providence, which assumes a wind that has already been created. Moses, however, is dealing with the very first beginning of creation, when neither air, nor vapor, nor any motion had yet been produced, but was first to be produced through this Spirit of God. Truly...

<meta>catchword: synony-</meta>

We add that it is an injustice for that Psalm to be restricted solely to the work of external providence. For the connection of the text abundantly teaches that a unique <term>Economy of the Kingdom of Grace</term> <note>Latin: *Oeconomia Regni gratiae*; a theological term referring to the way God manages his relationship with humanity regarding salvation and spiritual life.</note> is described here. Therefore, there is no reason why we should not also understand the divine and <term>hypostatic Spirit</term> <note>From the Greek *hypostasis*; referring to the Holy Spirit as a distinct person within the Trinity, rather than just an abstract power or "wind."</note> to be present here.

But even more trivial is the argument devised by **WITTER** <note>Henning Bernhard Witter (1683–1715), a German theologian who was an early pioneer in the critical study of the Pentateuch.</note> in his *Commentary on Genesis*, where he says: *"I marvel that those men have been so deceived that, in order to gather from this the specific action of the Holy Spirit, they entirely desert the common opinion of the orthodox, which truly attributes creation to God the Father alone, redemption to the Son, and sanctification to the Spirit—not the work of creation—from a unique (as they say) approximation of Scripture."* Will orthodoxy then finally be called into danger if we understand the **Spirit of God** <note>original Hebrew: *Elohim*</note> as the third person of the Trinity?

With even greater right, we marvel that this learned man does not know that that specific order of the works of God <note>The Father as Creator, Son as Redeemer, Spirit as Sanctifier.</note> was established not so much by the nature of the reality itself, but by the occasion of the <term>Apostles’ Creed</term> <note>Latin: *symbolum Apostolicum*.</note>. Truly, that Creed, in attributing creation to the Father, by no means intended for it to be considered the personal work of the Father alone. Rather, it sought to claim that glory for the Father which was being taken from Him by the heretics of the early Church, who imagined a certain <term>Demiurge</term> <note>In Gnostic belief, a lesser deity who created the physical world, often viewed as inferior or even hostile to the supreme God.</note> inferior to the highest God. Otherwise, the Son and the Holy Spirit are equally Creators, just as the Father is the Redeemer, as anyone who handles the basics of religion knows. 

For the Economy of **Nature and Grace**, or if you prefer, of Creation and Redemption, are so compared to one another that the same order of operations that holds among the divine persons recurs in both. This is the foundation of that most wise and delightful analogy by which the Work of Creation is considered as a <term>type</term> <note>A "type" is a historical person, event, or thing in the Bible that foreshadows a future reality (the "antitype").</note> of the Work of salvation. Therefore, the truth of the opinion remains on firm ground: it maintains that the hypostatic Spirit of the divine essence is intended in the beginning of creation; and since the <term>Psalmist</term> <note>Latin: *Psaltes*; referring to the author of the Psalms.</note> looked back to this, he also must not be understood in any other way.

XV. And we embrace this all the more eagerly because, if this hypothesis is set aside, a suitable and forceful sense cannot be given to the Psalm. For to think of a material wind here would be just as absurd as in the history of creation. Nothing is less satisfying than the literalists who, to cloak their error, take the *Spirit and Word of Jehovah* here for synony- <margin>synonyms</margin>

<meta>This page continues the logical defense of the Holy Spirit’s distinct personhood in the act of creation, specifically addressing arguments surrounding Psalm 33:6. It follows a critique of theologians who attempt to reduce the "Spirit" to a mere metaphor for God's power or breath.</meta>

# ON THE PASSAGE OF PSALM 33:6.

<sig>X 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: the wicked (Hebrew: רשע)</meta>

they treat them as synonyms. For we do not dwell here on **Calvin’s** *blindness* <note>original Greek: *ἀβλεψία* (*ablepsia*); meaning a lack of insight or a spiritual "oversight."</note>, who, since he understood the *Word* as *personal* <note>Referring to the 'Logos' or the Second Person of the Trinity.</note>, had no reason why he should not also have wished to interpret the *Spirit* in the same way. Whatever the case may be, it is highly inconvenient to understand the *Spirit of Jehovah* as merely His will or His command. For no example occurs in the sacred scriptures from which it can be proven that the *Spirit of Jehovah* ever designates His mandate. And even if it were so, this could not be granted in this passage to those who had already understood His will through the *Word of Jehovah*. 

For although <term>elaborations</term> <note>Latin: *Exergasiae*; a rhetorical figure where a thought is repeated in different words to provide more detail, clarity, or emphasis.</note> frequently occur in the sacred writings—to which we also refer our passage—they are nonetheless composed such that even if the same subject is treated in both parts of a sentence, something more specific or significant is designated in the latter part, or something from which the nature of the subject is more clearly revealed. That, however, would clearly have no place here. For granted that the same will of God is called first the *Word of Jehovah* and then the *breath of his mouth*, what, I ask, will there be in the latter designation that differs from the former? What would explain it or determine it more specifically, and from which the nature of the divine will might be more clearly known? Does not he who says *Word* already simultaneously include the *breath of the mouth*, through which the word is formed and which is, as it were, the material of the word modified by the mouth? Would he not then be judged to say much less, and to use a less emphatic figure of speech, if he compared the will of Jehovah to the *breath of his mouth* rather than to the *Word*? And would not this text consequently incur the mark of *tautology* <note>unnecessary repetition of the same idea.</note> if such a repetition were admitted? 

It can be added, as **Gousset** <note>Jacques Gousset (1635–1704), a prominent French Hebraist and theologian.</note> timely advised in his Lexicon under the word **Spirit** <note>original Hebrew: *Ruach* (רוח)</note>, that one cannot admit an identity of meaning between the "Spirit" and the "speech" or "command" of God as if it were an allusion to human speech (which is made by emitting breath and air). This is because in Genesis 1:2, in the history of the creation, mention of the *Spirit* is made before God is introduced as speaking. Since that only happens in verse 3 through the word *and he said* <note>original Hebrew: *wayyomer* (ויאמר)</note>, it cannot be denied that by the *Spirit of Jehovah* in the mystery of creation, something distinct from His *Word* and subsisting in its own proper person is implied.

XVI. Lest the adversaries seem entirely destitute of any example for their interpretation, they appeal to Isaiah 11:4, where it is said of the Messiah: *And he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth*, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked <note>original Hebrew: וברוח שפתין ימית רשע (*u-be-ruach sefatav yamit rasha*)</note>.

<margin>the wicked <note>Hebrew: רשע (*rasha*)</note></margin> *...and with the Spirit of his lips he shall slay the wicked.* <note>Original Latin: *Spiritu labiorum suorum occidet impium*; a reference to Isaiah 11:4.</note> But those who here understand the *Spirit of the lips* to mean merely the "external word" (the spoken scripture) must first remember that they gain nothing by this interpretation. This is because such a notion cannot be admitted in our current context, which deals with the act of creation. Furthermore, by using this <term>rhetorical elaboration</term> <note>Latin: *exergasia*; repeating a thought in different words for emphasis.</note>, they create a redundancy; they see nothing more or more specific in the *Spirit of the lips* than they do in the *rod of his mouth*.

Meanwhile, it is clear from the very actions the Prophet mentions that there is a progression in the means of the actions attributed to the Messiah. For just as *slaying* is a more powerful act than *striking*, so too the medium of *slaying*—called the *Spirit of the lips*—is more illustrious than the instrument of *striking*, which is compared to the *rod of his mouth*. We are right, therefore, to understand the *Spirit of the lips* of the Messiah here as the Holy Spirit himself. For the Spirit, joined with the *word*, grants it all its life and efficacy. In the <term>Economy of salvation</term> <note>The historical unfolding of God's plan for humanity.</note>, the Spirit is so subordinated to the Son that he establishes the Son’s Kingdom and overthrows his enemies according to the Son’s good pleasure (Isaiah 63:10; Psalm 110:2; Zechariah 4:6). This same Spirit is appropriately called the *Spirit of the lips* of the Messiah for several reasons:
1. Because, like the *breath of the mouth*, he is intimately united in essence with Jehovah and proceeds, as it were, from his inner being in his activity.
2. Because he was poured out upon the Messiah’s lips and promised through them.
3. Because he works according to the word of the Messiah's lips, and being joined with the word of those lips, he brings that word to life.

This is also why our Savior chose to foreshadow the granting and pouring out of his Spirit through the symbol of *breathing from his mouth* in John 20:22.

XVII. With little effort, we can now refute the argument that **Enjedinus** <note>György Enyedi (1555–1597), a theologian known for his "Explications" of scripture which argued against the Trinity.</note> seeks to draw from this passage against the <term>personality</term> <note>The status of being a "person" (a distinct, self-aware individual) rather than just an abstract force.</note> of the Holy Spirit. He argues as follows: *The spirit (or breath) of the mouth is not a thing that exists as a person in its own right. The Holy Spirit is called the "spirit of the mouth." Therefore, the Holy Spirit is not a person,* etc.

We respond:
**I.** The one discussed in our passage is indeed a <term>self-subsisting entity</term> <note>Latin: *res per se subsistens*; a technical term for a "person" in Trinitarian theology.</note>, because a personal action is attributed to him—namely, the creation of the *host of the heavens*.
**II.** Even the breath of the mouth is, in a sense, a distinct thing. For it is nothing other than vapor. Vapor is a specific part of the air modified by the movement of the mouth and lungs, and it is distinct both from the mouth and from the surrounding air.
**III.** In foreshadowing the mystery of the Trinity, Scripture most wisely employs such emblems, which...

...they represent the distinction of persons in such a way that they simultaneously indicate their essential union. XVIII. But the thought might easily occur to anyone: are we not "cutting down our own vineyards" <note>A Latin idiom, *propria vineta caedere*, meaning to undermine one's own argument or act against one's own interests.</note> by defending the most perfect unity of essence among the Persons of the Holy Trinity, while nonetheless believing that distinct works should be ascribed to the Son and the Holy Spirit? Specifically, that to the Son is ascribed the *firming of the heavens*, while to the Spirit is ascribed *their host*. And since we assert that all things *were made through the Personal Word, and without him nothing was made that was made* <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 1:3; "Personal Word" refers to the *Logos* or the Son.</note>, it might seem strange that the *host of the heavens* is, as it were, excepted from this number by the Psalmist and attributed to the Holy Spirit. Caspar Bolerus <note>A 17th-century Lutheran theologian.</note> raises this objection in the work cited by Hakspanius <note>Theodoricus Hackspan (1607–1659), a noted Lutheran theologian and scholar of Oriental languages.</note>. Hakspanius himself retorts *that because of the rhythm in the Old Testament, certain predicates are often distinguished and some are attributed to certain persons, even though they are actually common to all the persons.* For example, in *Psalm 99:6* <note>The Latin text cites verse 5, following a different numbering system.</note>: **Moses and Aaron were among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name.** Here, the sense seems to be as if Moses and Aaron were not among those who called upon the name of God, because those descriptions are separated into different clauses. *But this is done only for the sake of the rhythm.* This response seems quite weak to us, both because the nature of Hebrew poetry <note>original: *poëseos Hebraicæ*</note> is still a matter of uncertainty, and because it does not seem likely that the Holy Spirit would be so concerned with rhythm as to separate things that are naturally joined without a specific reason.

XIX. Therefore, to fundamentally remove this difficulty, one must remember that we believe in such a unity in the divine essence as does not destroy the distinction of persons. And so that we might be more fittingly instructed regarding this mystery, it pleased the most wise God to establish in his external works a certain order of operation that agrees with and foreshadows the natural order of the divine Persons themselves. This order is such that, while individual works are indeed attributed to the entire divine essence because of its unity, nonetheless certain more specific parts of those works...

# DISSERTATION

...these [works] have a certain definite relation to the individual Persons, because of which they can be attributed more closely and more properly to one Person than to another. This is true not only in the work of **Redemption**, but also in the work of **creation**, which is a "type" <note>A "type" is a person, event, or thing in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic foreshadowing of something in the New Testament.</note> of the former. Therefore, although the Son, according to the Father's decree, is the Creator of the universe—and this in communion with the Holy Spirit—nevertheless, the *perfection of the heavenly host* can be elegantly attributed to the Spirit as distinct from the Son. This is especially true if by that *host* one understands the rational inhabitants of heaven, the **Angels**, whose *perfection* includes their sanctification <note>The process of being made holy.</note>.

Thus, the Holy Spirit was engaged with the Angels in the same manner as He entered into the human soul. *For the breathing of the breath of lives into Adam's nostrils (Genesis 2:7), following the constant emblem of the breath and wind of Jehovah in the sacred writings, designates a certain singular operation of God through the mediation of the Spirit regarding the creation of Adam. Through this, his soul received the breath of lives—that is, of every kind of life and the most perfect life according to its nature—not only physical but also moral, which properly constituted the likeness to God.*

In this arrangement <term>dispensation; the way God orders his dealings with humanity</term> of God, we recognize a shimmering shadow of the **Economy of Grace**. For since here, too, the Son is the founder and builder of the entire Kingdom of Heaven, the task is nevertheless given to the Holy Spirit to perfect the host, or the inhabitants of this mystical heaven, by giving life to their hearts, purifying them, and furnishing them with those gifts which make them fit to take up the inheritance of the saints in light.

Certain Church Fathers also recognized this mystery. **EUSEBIUS**, in his commentary on this passage (page 125 of Montfaucon’s edition), says: *For nothing is sanctified without the presence of the Spirit. To the angels, therefore, the Creator Word, the maker of all things, provided the passage into existence; but the Holy Spirit brought along their sanctification at the same time; for the angels were not created as infants.* <note>original Greek: "ου γαρ νηπιοι κτισθεντες οἱ ἀγγελοι" — meaning they did not begin in a state of spiritual immaturity but were created fully formed in holiness.</note>

**BASIL**, in his work *Against Eunomius*, book III, citing our passage, adds: *Just as God the Word is the creator of the heavens, so the Holy Spirit provides what is firm and solid to the heavenly powers.* <note>original Greek: "το ςερεον και παγιον"</note>

XX. This same commentary gives us an opportunity to examine an objection that could be raised against our argument based on "tautology" <note>The unnecessary repetition of the same idea using different words; the objection suggests that "Word" and "Spirit" are just two ways of saying "God's power" rather than referring to two distinct Persons.</note>. For it mentions an opinion that distinguishes the *Word* and the *Spirit* in this way: *By the Word, that is by the decree; and by the Spirit of the mouth, that is by the power.* <note>Original Greek: *Λογῳ, τη ἀποφασει, πνευματι δε στοματος, τη δυναμει.*</note> We would require those who wish to adopt this distinction to provide examples; they would have to prove from the sacred pages that they understand the *Word* to mean a "decree" and that they use the *Spirit of Jehovah’s mouth* to express His "power." This is all the more reasonable because there is a clear distinction between an internal decree <note>A thought or decision kept within the mind of God.</note> and an external word—the latter being the means by which the content of a decree formulated in the mind is manifested outwardly to others. Additionally, according to this hypothesis, no reason could be given why the creation of the heavens is ascribed to the *Word* and the creation of their host to the *Spirit*, since the creation of the heavens is undoubtedly also a work of *Jehovah's power*, and the arrangement of the heavenly host depends just as much on God's most free decree as the former does. Since it is clear from what has been said that no well-founded objection can be made against those who understand the *Spirit of Jehovah’s mouth* to be a divine Person, we declare with the highest justice—because the logic for equals is equal—the same regarding the *Word of Jehovah*.

XXII. There is also a passage in Isaiah 48:13 which approaches the words of the Psalm so closely that one seems to reflect the other: *Even my hand founded the earth, and my right hand spanned the heavens.* For here again, it is clearly evident to Christians from the New Testament that the Son of God, a Person distinct from the Father, is designated; where the words immediately preceding—*I am the first, and also the last*—are applied to Christ in Revelation 1:8, 17. But the context itself also suggests this, since in verses 16 and 17 the same person continues to speak; and although He is Jehovah Himself, the *Redeemer and Holy One of Israel*, He nonetheless confesses that He was sent by the Lord Jehovah along with His Spirit.

XXIII. It is clearly a parallel to what occurs in Isaiah 51:13: *You forget Jehovah your Maker, who stretched out the heavens and founded the earth.* For here likewise, it appears from the context that we must think of the Son of God. From Him *the Law had to go forth, and judgment be brought out into the light of the peoples* (verse 4). Coming into the world, He could say: *My righteousness is near, my salvation has gone forth, and my arms shall judge the peoples.*

### VIII.

## THEOLOGICAL DISSERTATION
->CONCERNING<-
### Passages of the Old Testament,
->Which it is Doubted, whether they<-
# Deal with the HYPOSTATIC WORD <note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΩΙ ΥΠΟΣΤΑΤΙΚΩΙ (Logōi Hypostatikōi). In theology, "hypostatic" refers to the "Word" as a distinct, living Person within the Godhead, rather than just a metaphor or a spoken sound.</note>.

### II.

Setting aside the passage in Judges 13:17—which I will mention below in sections 17 and 22, noting that GALATINUS <note>Pietro Galatino (1460–1540), a scholar of Hebrew and theology.</note> and FAGIUS <note>Paul Fagius (1504–1549), a prominent Hebraist and reformer.</note> argue it was applied here by certain Jews without justification—I first encounter the passage found in 1 Samuel 3:21: <note>original Hebrew: כי נגלה יהוה אל שמואל בשלו בדבר יהוה (ki niglah Yehovah el Shemuel be-Shilo bi-dvar Yehovah)</note> *“For the Lord revealed himself to Samuel in Shiloh by the word of the Lord.”* Regarding the phrasing, this should be compared with the passage in 1 Kings 13:17, where that Prophet who came from Judah had announced divine threats to Jeroboam *“by the word of the Lord”* <note>original Hebrew: בדבר יהוה (bi-dvar Yehovah)</note> in verse 2, accompanied by a remarkable miracle. When he was invited by another Prophet living in Bethel, he excused himself by saying: <note>original Hebrew: כי דבר אלי בדבר יהוה לא תאכל וגו (ki davar elay bi-dvar Yehovah lo tokhal...)</note> *“Because the Word [spoke] to me by the word of the Lord, saying: ‘You shall not eat bread,’ etc.”* 

FR. JUNIUS <note>Franciscus Junius the Elder (1545–1602), a Reformed theologian.</note> believed these passages should be understood as referring to the **substantial WORD**, *“who in earlier times was called the ANGEL OF THE LORD; but thereafter, as he revealed himself more clearly over time, is called the SPEECH OF THE LORD.”* This opinion is appealing because it makes nothing in the text appear redundant, and it provides a clear reason why, in the passage from Samuel, *the Lord* is distinguished from *the Lord*. TARNOVIUS <note>Paul Tarnow (1562–1633), a Lutheran theologian.</note> follows this view in his commentary on Haggai 2:5.

### III.

However, there are factors that prevent full agreement. First, it appears from the context that the phrase *“Word of the Lord”* is used by the sacred writers in those histories to mean a divine revelation. This is evident regarding the first passage from 1 Samuel 3:1: *“The word of the Lord was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision.”* Here, the *“Word of the Lord”* is placed in the same category as a prophetic *“vision.”* In the second history, the phrase *“Word of the Lord”* recurs frequently in 1 Kings 13:1, 5, 9, 18, 20, and 32. The connection of events shows that the same thing is being discussed throughout; and yet, it would be very harsh <note>original Latin: durissimum (meaning difficult or forced in interpretation)</note> to understand the **hypostatic WORD** <note>The "hypostatic Word" refers to the Word as a distinct person of the Trinity (the Son), rather than just a spoken command.</note> in every single instance. From verse 20, the opposite is most clearly evident.

*Secondly*, there is the fact that the Lord who appeared to Samuel was indeed the Son of God himself. We gather this from the fact that the Lord offered himself to be seen by Samuel in a visible form. This is how we must understand what is said in 1 Samuel 3:10: <note>original Hebrew: ויבא יהוה ויתיצב ויקרא (wayyabo Yehovah wayyityassab wayyiqra)</note> *“And the Lord came, and stood, and called.”* The Jews acknowledge this...

Schmid <note>Sebastian Schmidt (1617–1696), a prominent Lutheran theologian and commentator.</note> has noted on this passage: Le Clerc <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a theologian known for his critical approach to biblical texts.</note> thinks that here, perhaps, only a sound of feet was heard—first as if someone were approaching, then as if they were standing still. But if the sound of feet was heard, why was an appearance not also seen? This is certainly suggested by the first segment of verse 21: <note>original Hebrew: ויוסף יהוה להראה בשלה (*Vayosef Yehovah lera'oh be-Shilo*)</note> *“And the Lord continued to reveal himself in Shiloh.”* Now truly, that Lord who appeared in Shiloh was without doubt the **Shekinah** <note>The "Divine Presence" or "In-dwelling" of God among humanity.</note> itself, the **Angel of the Presence** <note>original Latin: *Angelus facierum*. A term for a divine messenger who carries the very presence or "face" of God.</note> himself, who lived in Shiloh above the Ark of the Covenant. It is well established from other sources that this was the Son of God. Therefore, while that Lord—who is the Son of God himself—is said to have revealed himself to Samuel *through the Word of the Lord*, it necessarily follows that this "Word of the Lord" was distinct from the Son of God. 

Therefore, it seems much easier to me that *through the Word of the Lord* we should here understand a certain specific mode of divine revelation, distinct from a Prophetic Vision. In this mode, the Lord himself, appearing in his customary symbol, spoke to certain Prophets in a familiar way without any state of ecstasy. And this is exactly what the deceptive prophet intended when he said to the Prophet from Judah in 1 Kings 13:18: *“I also am a prophet like you, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the Lord.”* With these words, he boastfully advertises that he possesses no lesser degree of prophecy, since the "Word of the Lord" was also communicated to him through an appearing angel. In this way, nothing is redundant in either passage. For in the first, it is said that the Lord revealed himself to Samuel through that more excellent mode of revelation which was emphatically called the *Word of the Lord* at that time. And in the second passage, the prophet asserts that he is all the more certain that the *Word* he was to obey was divine, because it had come to him neither while dreaming nor in an ecstasy through the power of imagination, but *through the Word of the Lord*—through such a mode of revelation that left the least possible room for doubting its divine origin.

IV. Among the primary passages cited here is 2 Samuel 7:21: <note>original Hebrew: בעבור דברך וכלבך עשית את כל הגדולה הזאת להודיע את עבדך (*ba’avur devarkha ve-khalivkha asita et kol ha-gedulah ha-zot le-hodia et avdekha*)</note> *“For the sake of your Word and according to your heart, you have done all this greatness, to make it known to your servant.”* Here, many believe that by the *Word of the Lord* we should understand the **Messiah**, relying on these arguments: 1. that in 1 Chronicles 17:19 <note>The source text mistakenly cites verse 20.</note>, the words of David are reported this way: *“O Lord, for the sake of your Servant...”*

*For your servant's sake, and according to your own heart, you have done all this greatness, to make known all these great things.* <note>original Latin: "Servum tuum & juxta cor tuum fecisti omnem magnificentiam hanc, ut notas faceres omnes magnificentias." This is a translation of 1 Chronicles 17:19.</note> From this, they infer that the *Word* and the *Servant of the Lord* are synonyms in these passages. Since, therefore, the *Servant of the Lord* is understood emphatically to be the Messiah, they think that for this reason the *Word of God* is also the Messiah. To this is added: II. That God truly bestows benefits upon David and all his people in view of his Servant, the Messiah (Psalm 80:15–16). However, this cannot be said of *David* himself, who entirely removes any consideration of his own merit from the causes of such great kindness and beneficence (verse 20 and 2 Samuel 23:5). III. Furthermore, there would be no reason for the difference in the accounts of David's prayers among the sacred historians <note>The "sacred historiographers" refers to the different authors of the books of Samuel and Chronicles, who record the same events with slightly different wording.</note> if this interpretation were not admitted, as the discrepancy seems to be resolved by it. Following Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the Church Father famous for translating the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note>, this view is defended by Abraham Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a champion of Lutheran Orthodoxy.</note> in his *Illustrated Bible* on this passage; Glassius <note>Salomon Glassius (1593–1656), a theologian known for his work on biblical philology.</note> in *Onomatology of the Messiah*, Class VIII, § 1; Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian who emphasized the covenantal structure of the Bible.</note> on Haggai 2:5; and Witsius <note>Herman Witsius (1636–1708), a leading Dutch theologian.</note> in *Sacred Miscellanies*, II. 3. § 18.

V. But other men of outstanding learning intervene—among them Peter Martyr <note>Peter Martyr Vermigli (1499–1562), an influential Reformed theologian.</note>, Johannes Brenz <note>Johannes Brenz (1499–1570), a prominent German Reformer.</note>, and explicitly Sebastian Schmidt <note>Sebastian Schmidt (1617–1696), a Lutheran theologian mentioned on the previous page.</note> on this passage—whose reasons are so strong that, regarding the first difficulty, we cannot doubt that David meant himself by the *Servant of the Lord* in the latter passage. For (a) in the entire context of his prayer, besides our passage, David calls himself the *Servant of the Lord* nine times—three times immediately before and six times after this statement. Therefore, it can only seem harsh and difficult if, just once in that connection and without any mark of distinction, David had intended that name to refer to a completely different and far more excellent Person. We add that although the name *Servant* in a very illustrious sense is often attributed to the Son of God by the Father in those prophecies regarding his actual obedience and humiliation *in the form of a servant* <note>original Latin: "in forma servi." This refers to the "Servant Songs" in the prophets and the concept of Christ's humility.</note>—such as Psalm 35:27, Isaiah 42:1, 43:10, 49:6, 50:10, 52:13, 53:11, Ezekiel 34:23, 37:24–25, and Zechariah 3:8—nevertheless, this name is never used by the godly, and much less in prayers, who are accustomed to use more illustrious names to testify to their sublime perception of Christ. Nor was it sufficiently fitting that a believer of the Old Testament <note>original Latin: "V. T." (Vetus Testamentum).</note> should claim that past benefits had been shown to him simply on account of the *Servant of God*...
