...would testify [to the point], since in truth the Son of God did not become the *Servant of the Father* through his self-emptying <note>The original Latin *exinanitionem* refers to "kenosis," the theological concept of Christ setting aside his divine attributes to take on human form.</note> until his arrival in the flesh.

**VI. $\beta$.** The connection of the passage itself also works against those who interpret the *Servant* as the Son of God. For the Lord is praised because, for the sake of his Servant, he has performed *all this greatness* (or *magnificence*) *to make known all these great things*. To understand these words, we must distinguish between the *benefit itself* which the Lord showed to David—namely, *that he performed all this magnificence*—and the *purpose of that benefit*: *that he might make known all these great things*. The term *gedulot* <note>original Hebrew: גדלות</note>, "greatnesses," the manifestation of which is God's purpose, primarily designates his divine perfections, which constitute his divine excellence and majesty. It is in this sense that David attributes *magnitudo* <note>original Hebrew: גדולה, meaning greatness</note> to God in 1 Chronicles 29. From this, God is sometimes called absolutely *The Great One* in Exodus 18:11, Psalm 86:10, and Psalm 96:4, etc. This title is occasionally applied to specific perfections of God; for example, when he is called *Great in counsel* <note>original Latin: Magnus consilio</note> in Isaiah 28:29 and Jeremiah 32:19; *Great in grace* <note>original Latin: Magnus gratia</note> in Nehemiah 1:3; and *Great in kindness* <note>original Latin: Magnus benignitate</note> in Psalm 145:8.

Consequently, by a figure of speech <note>The author uses "metonymy," where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it.</note>, those ways and works in which God exerts and demonstrates his greatest perfections are also called the *Greatnesses* of God. Since this occurs most prominently in the <term>Economy of Salvation</term> <note>The "Economy of Salvation" refers to God's management of the world and his historical plan for the redemption of humanity.</note> and the Kingdom of Grace, the wonderful deeds of Jehovah pertaining to these are called *his greatnesses* <note>original Hebrew: גדלותיו</note> in Psalm 145:6. This is the meaning of the *mighty works of God* <note>original Greek: τα μεγαλεια του Θεου</note> which the Apostles spoke of in new tongues in Acts 2:11, which can designate nothing other than those illustrious works by which the hope of the Fathers was fulfilled and perfect salvation was obtained. The translators of the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as "the Seventy" or "O."</note> use this same word *megaleion* <note>original Greek: μεγαλειον</note> for "greatness" in Psalm 70:21 and in our present passage. The same usage is found in Sirach 17:7, 18:3, 45:33, etc.

I would particularly like to compare this with the Song of Mary in Luke 1:49, where she celebrates *God her Savior* because *he has done great things for me* <note>original Greek: ὁτι ἐποιησε μοι μεγαλεια</note>. We can infer that Mary, the daughter of David, is looking back at these very words because the Angel in verses 32 and 33 had indicated that the promise made to David was now about to be fulfilled. For further illustration, it may be observed that among the *Sephiroth* <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Jewish Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note> of the Kabbalists, "Greatness" <note>original Hebrew: גדולה, or *Gedulah*</note> also appears, and indeed in such a way that among the seven...

[...seven] lower Sephiroth <note>In Jewish Kabbalah, the *Sephiroth* are the ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite reveals himself. The "seven lower" ones are often associated with God's actions in the world.</note>, it occupies the first place as the primary virtue that the Lord exercises in His Kingdom. This *Gedulah* <note>original Hebrew: גדולה, meaning "Greatness"</note> is diametrically opposed to *Gevurah* <note>original Hebrew: גבורה, meaning "Power" or "Severity"</note>. For this reason, the Hebrews consistently translate the former as *Chesed* <note>original Hebrew: חסד, meaning "Grace" or "Loving-kindness"</note> and the latter as "rigor and severity."

Given these premises, it is clear that by the revelation of all the "magnificences" of the *Lord* in relation to David, nothing else is meant than an instruction regarding the most complete demonstration of divine perfections in the finished, glorious work of redemption. The specific object of this instruction is omitted in the book of Chronicles, but is clearly indicated in the book of Samuel: *to make it known to your servant*.

The benefit was subordinated to this goal as a *means*, in that God performed a certain magnificence for David—that is, He granted David a certain illustrious *splendor*. In this splendor, David placed all his glory—or as he says in 2 Samuel 23:5, *all his salvation and all his desire*. What exactly this great *magnificence* was, in which David rejoiced to be clothed, is clear from verse 17: *You have spoken of your servant’s house for a great while to come, and have regarded me according to the estate of a man of high degree*.

In this, David established the very peak of his greatness: that he was chosen as the ancestor of the Messiah. This was the *means* subordinated to that great end, namely the execution of the work of redemption. Through this special promise, a seal (as it were) was given to David regarding the certainty of this salvation to be manifested in the future. From this it appears evident that the *Servant* mentioned in Chronicles *is no other than David himself*, to whom the Lord wished to *make known all His greatness*, so that he might be confirmed in his faith in an illustrious manner. This person was David himself, and thus distinct from the *Word* <note>The "Logos" or pre-incarnate Christ mentioned in the parallel passage in 2 Samuel</note> mentioned in the books of Samuel. Once this is proven, the primary foundation of those who disagree collapses.

**VII.** Furthermore, from this explanation of the words, the remaining objections vanish. For the *second* objection has no place here, since David’s intention is clearly not to attribute anything to his own merit. Rather, at most, he intends to declare that the excellence God had given him—by placing him at the head of the family line of the Messiah—tended toward his own greatest good. ### ON THE WORD IN THE OLD TESTAMENT.
Z 2

...rendered him fit for true faith in all the magnificences <note>The "magnificences" refers to the great and glorious deeds of God, particularly those related to the promise of a future savior.</note> of the Lord and to rejoice in them. Thus in 2 Samuel 5:12, it is said that *David perceived that the Lord had established his kingdom* <term>propter</term> <note>original Hebrew: בעבור (*ba'avur*), meaning "for the sake of" or "on account of"</note> *his people Israel*, that is, for their good. Compare 1 Chronicles 14:2. But in another sense, David could suitably say that God had applied this revelation *on his account*—namely, that he might look back at the preceding promises which God, though more obscurely, had presented regarding this matter. For not only had the house of David already been destined for such great happiness through the prophecy of Jacob in Genesis 49:8, 10, but David himself had also sensed from God’s various ways that he had been set apart for this end. Hence, even before he ascended the throne of Israel, he had declared his faith regarding this matter in various Psalms, such as Psalms 18 and 52, which are beyond dispute. Nothing is clearer for establishing this sense than the words of Psalm 132:10: <note>original Hebrew: בעבור דוד עבדך אל תשב פני משיחך</note> *For the sake of your servant David, do not turn away the face of your Anointed*. In that place, *for the sake of David* is nothing other than "for the sake of the promises given to David and about David," as is evident from the immediately following verse: *The Lord swore a truth to David from which he will not turn back*.

**VIII.** The third objection raised, however, is much more in our favor. For in this way, both passages are equally broad in scope. For **I.** while in the passage from Samuel, David, the *Servant of God*, is clearly considered as the object to whom all the magnificences of the Lord were to be revealed, this same object is also mentioned in Chronicles, albeit with an inverted construction; otherwise, it would have been completely omitted, so much so that if this were neglected, the later words would yield a far more general sense than the former. **II.** It is clear from the sense given to the words in the preceding paragraph in Chronicles that, although David is understood there by the phrase *Servant of the Lord*, nothing has been omitted; rather, the very same thing found in Samuel has been said. This is because *for the sake of the servant of the Lord* there means nothing other than "for the sake of the Word of the Lord," spoken both through the Prophets concerning David and to David himself.

**IX.** PSALM 33:4. <note>original Hebrew: כי ישר דבר יהוה</note> *For the Word of the Lord is upright, and all his work is done in faithfulness*. ### DISSERTATION

...believes it is proven that the *Word is neither a created work nor merely one of those singing, but is sung along with the Father and is the Architect of all works.* <note>The author is quoting an opponent who argues that the "Word" is a divine co-creator rather than a spoken promise.</note> But it is clear that this is said without grounds, both from the analysis of the entire Psalm shown in the previous Dissertation, and from the fact that the faithfulness of Jehovah is proclaimed in his work, which has a singular relation to the Word of promise.

X. PSALM 45:2. <note>Hebrew: רחש לבי דבר טוב (*rachash libbi davar tov*)</note> *My heart overflows with a good word.* This is a remarkable example of <term>misinterpretation</term> <note>original Greek: παρερμηνεία (*parermēneia*), meaning a false or distorted interpretation</note> by the Church Fathers, in that they found in this passage not only the hypostatic WORD <note>The "hypostatic Word" refers to the "Word" (Logos) as a distinct person—Jesus Christ—rather than a message or promise.</note>, but even the mystery of eternal generation <note>The theological concept that the Son is eternally "born" from the essence of the Father.</note>. This interpretation is found in the commentaries attributed to THEOPHILUS OF ANTIOCH, a writer of the second century: *God is the Beginning, the Word is the Son of God, Christ, of whom the Fatherly voice says in the Psalm: My heart has brought forth a good word, that is, Christ, through whom all things were made.* Although it is doubted whether he is their actual author, it is certain that he—and perhaps he was the first—understood this passage in this way in Book II of *To Autolycus*, on which matter Jean Le Clerc may be consulted regarding the year 168 AD.

TERTULLIAN, at least, in *Against Praxeas*, chapter 7, says: *Christ is begotten before all things and is the only-begotten: and he alone was properly begotten by God from the womb of his heart, according to what the Father himself testifies, saying: My heart has brought forth the best word.* Many followed him in this view, including CYPRIAN, AMMONIUS, AMBROSE, ATHANASIUS, CYRILLUS, EPIPHANIUS, and others. One may consult the author of *The Balance of Truth* <note>Latin title: *Bilibra veritatis*</note> pages 82–83, and DANIEL WHITBY in *On the Interpretation of Scripture according to the Commentaries of the Fathers*, pages 75–76. 

However, JUSTIN MARTYR seems to have been wrongly included in this list by those authors in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, pages 256–257. For although it is said there, *likewise in the forty-fourth Psalm* <note>In the older Vulgate numbering, Psalm 45 is counted as Psalm 44.</note> *these things are said regarding Christ: My heart has brought forth a good word, etc.*, it is not necessary for us to refer this to these words alone, since the entire Psalm is being considered. The more learned of the Fathers were not persuaded by this interpretation, among whom were ORIGEN, BASIL, THEODORET, and JEROME. VORSTIUS, in the place cited, falsely accused the latter [Jerome] of this error, since he wrote explicitly in his *Letter to Damasus*: *Certain people, more out of superstition than truth, think these things should be understood as being spoken from the person of the Father.* It is not necessary, however...

...it was necessary to seriously refute this interpretation, since there is no longer anyone who doubts that it is completely inconsistent with the goal and context of the words. # DISSERTATION
->Z 3<-
<meta>catchword: de</meta>

...widely <note>original: *late*; continuing the sentence from the previous page</note> it becomes probable to many interpreters that in this Psalm are described the various liberations of the Church of the New Testament to be performed in succession. The renowned **D'OUTREIN** <note>Johannes d'Outrein (1662–1722), a prominent Dutch theologian and author</note>, a man so illustrious for his merits toward the Church and so conspicuous for the remarkable bond of his vigorous piety with distinguished erudition, proved this expressly in his commentary on this Psalm. It is not without singular grief of mind that we, along with all good men, must groan as we write these things, for he has been taken from human affairs.

However, it cannot be consistent with that hypothesis to say that the **PERSONAL WORD** <note>the *Logos* or Christ as a person</note> was sent to heal them. For such a *sending* <note>original: *missio*</note> is supposed to occur precisely at that time when the fools had approached the gates of death and were crying out to Jehovah, and He was saving them from their distresses. Therefore, this passage does not concern the **obtaining of salvation** <note>the act of Christ winning salvation on the cross</note> but rather its **application**, and that in a specific case pertaining to the Economy of the Kingdom of the Messiah.

Indeed, only one *Mission* of the Son of God is recorded for the purpose of saving—namely, through His coming in the flesh—which was prefigured by various typical missions. But I do not recall anywhere that the administration of the Kingdom of the Messiah, and the manner in which He was to be revealed in it, is called a *mission*. Regarding the **Word of the Gospel** <note>original: *Verbum Evangelii*</note> as the instrument of Christ’s Governance, however, this metaphor does occur. *So shall it go forth from the mouth of Jehovah and prosper in that for which it is sent,* as stated in Isaiah 55:10. The phrases in Psalm 110:2, Isaiah 2:3, and Psalm 147:15 can be compared.

It may be added that **Jehovah**, who is introduced here as *sending the Word*, and whose kindness and grace are proclaimed, is undoubtedly the Son Himself, the true <term>Goel</term> <note>Hebrew: גואל; a "Kinsman-Redeemer" who rescues or ransoms a relative</note> or Redeemer (verse 2). He is the one *satisfying the weary soul and filling the hungry soul with good* (verse 9; compare Luke 1:53, Jeremiah 31:25, and John 6:35), *bringing them out of darkness and the shadow of death and breaking their bonds* (verse 14; compare Isaiah 42:7, 61:1, etc.). Given this, nothing else can be understood here but the **Word of the Gospel**. And such a *healing* through the saving doctrine of the Word rightly suited those who, through the neglect of the path of virtue, had fallen into "folly," which was the cause of all their evils.

XIII. The sole support for the opinion of those who fight for the **Substantial WORD** <note>the Word as a divine substance or person</note> in this passage is that the Messiah is, with emphasis, the spiritual **Physician** of His people. But who does not know that the Son of God uses the **Word of the Gospel** as the means for healing hearts, and that...

# CONCERNING THE WORD IN THE OLD TESTAMENT.
->Z 3<-

...for the same reason, is a healing power likewise attributed to it? From this, those words are called **wholesome words** <note>original Greek: ὑγιαινοντες Λογοι (*hygiainontes Logoi*)</note> in *1 Timothy 6:3* and *2 Timothy 1:15*. Hence *Proverbs 12:18*: *The tongue of the wise is health.* <note>The source text cites Proverbs 12:12, but the quote corresponds to verse 18 in modern Bibles.</note> Compare *chapter 15:4* and *16:24*. For this reason, the Ministers of God are also called **healers** <note>original Hebrew: רפאים (*repha'im*); Latin: *Medici*</note> in *Jeremiah 8:22* and *51:9*. This is a common metaphor for any discipline or instruction, even among secular authors. Note the epigram of **Diogenes Laertius** <note>A biographer of Greek philosophers from the 3rd century AD.</note> regarding Plato in *Book III, § 45*:

> Just as Asclepius, born of you, is the healer
> Of the body, so Plato is the healer of the immortal soul.
> <note>The original text provides this in Greek followed by a Latin poetic translation.</note>

To the same point is what is found concerning **Pythagoras** in **Aelian’s** *Various History, IV. 18*: *When he traveled through the cities, a rumor spread that Pythagoras had arrived not to teach, but to heal.* **Plutarch**, in his book *On the Education of Children*, calls philosophy *the medicine for the diseases and passions of the soul.* But what I believe should be especially observed in our passage is that the act of healing is not attributed to the *Word*, but to **Jehovah the Savior** himself. For the phrase **and he healed them** <note>Hebrew: וירפאם (*vayirpa’em*)</note> should not be grammatically linked with the "Word," but with the "Sender" of the word, who is called *Jehovah* in the preceding verse, and by whom it is promised that He would save them from their distresses.

### XIV.
Our interpretation would suffer some disadvantage if the version of those who translate our text in the past tense were to stand: *He sent his word.* For in this way, it might seem that the mission of the Son into the flesh <note>The Incarnation</note> is hinted at as preceding this liberation of the Church. However, just as we believe it is consistent with the sacred style that the <term>interchange of tenses</term> <note>original: *enallage temporum*; a grammatical phenomenon where one tense is substituted for another, often found in Hebrew prophecy.</note>—which through the carelessness of interpreters has accumulated immensely, especially in the Prophets—should be more and more eliminated, so we specifically wonder that even the most excellent interpreters in our passage and its context have taken no account of the tenses, almost as if there were no longer any distinction of tenses among the Hebrews. Let us take an example from the commentators of lesser renown, and even from the celebrated **Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a highly influential Dutch theologian known for his federal theology and linguistic expertise.</note> himself.

He <note>Referring to the commentator or translator discussed on the previous page, likely Johann Crell.</note> renders verses 19–21 in this way: *And they cried out to Jehovah, when they were in trouble: From their distresses he **saved** <note>Latin: *servabat* (imperfect tense, implying ongoing past action)</note> them. He **sent** <note>Latin: *mittebat*</note> His Word, and **healed** <note>Latin: *sanabat*</note> them, and **caused them to escape** <note>Latin: *evadere faciebat*</note> from their pits. They **confessed** <note>Latin: *confitebantur*</note> to Jehovah his grace and his wonders to the sons of men.* Nevertheless, the text itself holds thus: *And they **cried out** <note>Hebrew: *vayi’zaqu* (perfect/past tense)—that is, when they had cried out, their cry preceding the action</note> to Jehovah, when they were in trouble; from their distresses he **will save** <note>Latin: *servabit* (future tense)</note> them. He **will send** <note>Latin: *mittet*</note> His Word and **will heal** <note>Latin: *sanabit*</note> them and **will cause them to escape** <note>Latin: *evadere faciet*</note> from their pits. They **will confess** <note>Latin: *confitebuntur*</note> to Jehovah his grace, etc.*

### XV.
Furthermore, **Crellius** <note>Johann Crell (1590–1633), a prominent Socinian theologian who argued against the traditional doctrine of the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ.</note> exercises his ingenuity in the cited passage when he wishes to claim that John, in Revelation 19:13, was alluding to this saying when calling Christ **that Logos of God**. He does this especially because he introduces the Savior appearing in a special manner for the healing and liberation of his oppressed people from their corruptions. These ideas savor of too much cleverness, because in Revelation one reads nothing regarding either the "mission" or the "healing" of the Word; for Christ is introduced there not as a Physician, but as a Hero, and because the Revelation deals with times much later than these. Far more futile is the observation that occurs in § 142: that in the Psalm it is not simply said **he sent his Word** <note>Latin: *misit Logon suum*</note>, but rather **he sent forth** <note>original Greek: ἐξαπέστειλεν (*exapestelen*)</note>, which he interprets as: *he sent from himself—namely, he sent from heaven itself and the place of his residence—so that even the Psalm itself, albeit obscurely, indicated that before Christ was to appear publicly among men with the doctrine of the Gospel, he was to be taken up into heaven, and sent forth from heaven itself by the Father himself.* If this is not **laborious trifling** <note>Latin: *operose nugari*</note> in order to seek defenses for an impious error from every side, then what is? You may wonder, Reader, where this thought originated for this paradoxical man, since neither the Hebrew text nor the editions of the Septuagint version give any occasion for it? Only **Origen** <note>An influential early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) whose Greek transcriptions often varied from the standard Septuagint.</note> supplied it, who, citing our passage, used the word **sent forth** <note>Greek: ἐξαπέστειλεν (*exapestelen*)</note> in place of the Hebrew **sent** <note>original Hebrew: שלח (*shalach*)</note>.

# CONCERNING THE WORD IN THE OLD TESTAMENT

<meta>catchword: Vol.</meta>

...the phrase, *In the beginning was the Word, saying.* <note>original Greek: *Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ Λόγος, λέγων*</note> *In his progression, he touches upon more sublime dogmas, making mention of the eternal Word of the Father and saying almost exactly: In the beginning was the Word.* <note>The author is likely quoting a commentary on the Gospel of John or a patristic source comparing it to the Psalms.</note> This same view is pleasing to **Hilary**, **Ambrose**, **Athanasius**, and others. **Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his "federal theology" and focus on the covenants.</note> himself concedes that the Son of God can be understood here. **Lorinus** <note>Jean Lorin (1559–1634), a Jesuit biblical commentator known for his voluminous works on the Psalms.</note> also favors this opinion, mentioning this reasoning: that *a human word neither lives nor subsists, but is merely a movement of a living and subsisting breast.* It also seems that in this way one can best find the reason why this Word is said to *stand* or *be established in the heavens* <note>Referring to Psalm 119:89: "Forever, O Lord, thy word is settled in heaven."</note>, whereas the spoken word <note>original: *verbum προφορικον* (logos prophorikos), a philosophical term for the "word uttered" as opposed to the "word within the mind."</note> sounds equally upon the earth, where, despite the Devil, it is preached, fulfilled, and believed.

Nevertheless, one who considers how many times in the preceding and following parts of this Psalm the "Word of Jehovah" designates Evangelical doctrine—alternating with terms like Law, Commandments, and Testimony of Jehovah—will find it difficult to be persuaded by this. No distinction of a more emphatic or distinct notion appears in our specific verse. Indeed, the small arguments brought forward do not necessitate such a distinction. For that "Word" is most aptly said to *stand* or *be established* because Scripture compares it to a pillar for its perennial constancy, and a parallel phrase is used immediately in verse 152 of this same Psalm: *Of old I have known from your testimonies, that you have founded them forever.* As for the fact that this establishment is said to be done *in heaven*, it coincides with that found in Psalm 89:2: *Mercy shall be built up forever: In the heavens! You shall establish your truth in them.* For heaven is the foundation of the Word, which receives all its strength from the supreme majesty, the powerful will, the firm decree, and the unshakable fidelity of Him who dwells in the heavens. Heaven is also the theater in which the proofs of the constancy of that same *Word* are exhibited through the glorification of Christ and the Church.

Volume V, p. 6. On this same matter, **Galatinus** <note>Pietro Galatino (c. 1460–1540), an Italian Franciscan friar and theologian who wrote *De Arcanis Catholicae Veritatis* (On the Secrets of Catholic Truth) to defend Christianity using Jewish texts.</note> praises **Libertas Cominetus**, a Spanish former Jew, a man exceptionally learned in divine literature and skilled in fourteen languages, who offered this conjecture on these words:

*He will send His word and melt them.* <note>original Hebrew: ישלח דברו וימסם; quoting Psalm 147:18.</note> I should have said: *He will speak His word*, and not: *He will send His word*, because the act of speaking is more appropriate than sending. This is just as it is written: *And God said: Let there be light and there was light.* <note>Genesis 1:3</note> He did not say: *God sent His word to make or create light*, because the language of "sending" cannot be fulfilled without a messenger. 

After a few intervening remarks, he continues: 

How then does it fit, what the Prophet says: *He will send His word*? The answer is this: As far as I can perceive, David in this place prophesied the coming of Jesus the Messiah, our Righteous One, who is rightly called His "Word." And the truth is: Jesus is the Word of God, and is the messenger of God’s words. And just as God's word is not something distinct from the essence of God, so also the Messiah is not entirely distinct from the divine substance. And this is what is written in Judges 13:17: *When your word comes, we will honor you.* <note>Cominetus argues that "Word" here refers to a person (Christ) rather than a message.</note> For if he were entirely divided from God, it would have said: *And we will honor IT*, etc. 

But here, the same things we have already warned regarding the statement in Psalm 107, § 10 and following, may suffice. For it seems clear enough to us that in this Psalm as well, the **Governance of the Church** and those paths which are connected to the building of Jerusalem (verses 2 and 13) are being foreshadowed by similarities drawn from the providence by which the world is governed. Therefore, the "sending of the Son in the flesh" <term>Incarnation</term> is not the primary focus here. 

It does indeed seem to favor those who understand the Son of God by the "Word" here that a mention of the "Spirit" is added. Nor do we resist those who wish the **Holy Spirit** to be designated here. But has not God joined the proclamation of the Word with the operations of the Holy Spirit in an eternal covenant? (Isaiah 59:21).

# ON THE WORD IN THE OLD TESTAMENT.
Aa 2

**Clement of Alexandria**, <note>Titus Flavius Clemens (c. 150 – c. 215 AD), a prominent Christian theologian who sought to unite Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note> bringing forward this passage in his *Exhortation to the Heathen*, Chapter 1, Section 2, adds: *The heavenly Word, the genuine champion crowned in the theater of the whole world.* <note>original Greek: Λογος οὐρανιος, ὁ γνησιος ἀγωνιστης ἐπι τῳ παντος κοσμου θεατρῳ στεφανουμενος.</note> The author of the *Excerpts from the Prophetic Scriptures*, which are appended to the works of Clement, Section 58, writes: *The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls. Both Law and Word refer to the Savior himself, as Peter asserts in his Preaching. And the prophet says: "For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the Word of the Lord from Jerusalem."* <note>original Greek: Ο νομος του Θεου ἀμωμος, ἐπιστρεφων ψυχας. Νομος και Λογος αὐτος ὁ Σωτηρ λεγется, ὡς Πετρος ἐν κηρυγματι. Και ὁ προφητης: Εκ γαρ Σιων ἐξελευσεται νομος, και Λογος Κυριου ἐξ Ιερουσαλημ.</note> Add **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquence and biblical commentaries.</note> in the *Catena on Psalm 1*. 

This interpretation, however, not only lacks a foundation but also cannot be sustained. For the *Law and Word of Jehovah* going out from Zion and Jerusalem are distinguished from *Jehovah, the God of Jacob*, the supreme *Teacher*, to hear whom the people ascend the *mountain of Jehovah* in this very verse. This would not be necessary if the heavenly Teacher himself were to be conceived here as having gone out from Zion. Furthermore, pointing his finger toward this passage, the Apostle [Paul] in 1 Corinthians 14:36 says: *Did the Word of God go out from you? Or did it come to you only?* <note>original Greek: Ἢ ἀφ' ὑμῶν ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐξῆλθε;</note> In that context, I think no one will deny that the "Word of the Gospel" is what is understood.

XIX. ISAIAH 9:7. *The Lord sent a word into Jacob and it fell upon Israel.* <note>original Hebrew: דבר שלח אדני ביעקב; modern Bibles usually list this as Isaiah 9:8.</note> A certain very famous man <note>Likely referring to Johannes Cocceius or a similar contemporary scholar of the author.</note> proposes this passage as a problem: whether it too might be understood as the **substantial Word** <term>substantial word: the Word as a living person (Christ) rather than just a spoken message</term>? 

For: 
I. Although these words are commonly considered the beginning of the prophetic section that follows, nothing prevents them from being viewed as the conclusion of the verses immediately preceding, in which the birth, excellence, and dominion of the Messiah are most fully described. 

II. In this way, the *Child and Son born* [from Isaiah 9:6] would be declared by the name of the *Word*; thus his mission from Jehovah himself would be clearly expressed; thus the first boundary of his mission would be designated (who is nevertheless to receive a vast kingdom without end among all nations); and finally, through the "falling" of this *Word*, his descent for a divine mission and his manifestation among the Jewish people would be emphatically noted, with this phrase being adapted to the concept of the Word.

**XX.** Although we acknowledge that these points have been brought forward learnedly and sharply, they still suffer from their own difficulty, which compels us to stick to the accepted opinion. For *first*, the natural *sound* and *connection* of the words does not admit what is being suggested. The sound itself points to the preface of a new prophetic section. No sign of a connection with the preceding verse is present. However, it hangs together with the following verse, not only regarding the words through a conjunction, but also regarding the subject matter. For it concerns those who *knew this Word*, yet held it in low esteem, and for that reason exposed themselves to the most severe judgment of God. It is most evident that these were the subjects of the kingdom of Samaria, or the Ten Tribes, who were soon to be led away into the Assyrian captivity because of their contempt for the prophetic speech. *Secondly*, the observations regarding the phrase could be admitted if by "mission" <note>referring to the "sending" of the Word</note> one understood the arrival of the Messiah in the flesh, so that he might prepare souls for the receiving of his kingdom by his heavenly doctrine. Meanwhile, the interpretation of those who think here of the *falling* of the prophetic Word is less harsh, insofar as it is usually compared to *arrows* or *rain* rushing down from above. We have already dealt with the *third* point in the discussion on the passages of the New Testament which seem to treat the "Word." <note>original: λογῳ (Logos)</note> Section XIV and following.

ISAIAH 10:23.** Likewise, this majestic name would have to be sought here, if one were to believe **Cyprian** <note>Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus (c. 210–258 AD), Bishop of Carthage and an early Christian writer.</note> in Book 2 of his *Testimonies against the Jews*, Chapter 3, and **Evagrius** in the place cited in his *Altercation with a Jew*, page 6: *Isaiah says: I have heard of matters completed and shortened, for God will make a shortened Word in all the earth. This is the Word who healed our stripes, etc.* This is unsuccessfully brought against the Jew, contrary to the original sources. For in those sources it is said: *For a destruction and a decree, the Lord Jehovah of Hosts performs in the midst of all the earth.* <note>original Hebrew: כי כלה ונחרצה אדני יהוה צבאות עשה בקרב כל הארץ</note> The **Septuagint** <note>The "LXX," the influential Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible used by early Christians.</note> translators provided the occasion for this error, as they translate: *Because the Lord will make a shortened word in the whole world.* <note>original Greek: Οτι λογον συντετμημενον Κυριος ποιησει ἐν τῃ οἰκουμενῃ ὁλῃ.</note> The Apostle cited this version in Romans 9:28.

counted among this number. The first is **JEREMIAH 17:15**: *Behold, they themselves say, <note>Hebrew: *Ayeh debar-Yehovah*</note> Where is the Word of the Lord? And this is what is said: "Your word shall come and we will honor you" (Judges 13:17). Certainly, when the Word of God comes, which is His messenger, then we will honor him. Rabbi Saul said: "Did the Prophets not come, and we killed them and shed their blood? How then shall we now receive His Word, or how shall we believe Him?" Rabbi Samuel answered him: "Because He will heal them and free them from their plagues; because of these signs, I say, we will believe and hold Him in honor." Then he said to him: "Why, I pray, did He not say, 'He will send His word and heal *you*,' but rather said, 'and heal *them*?' This is because, as I perceive it, He was speaking of a part—of some only, and not of all." (This is marked, of course, according to the property of the Hebrew language, in the choice of the word "them.") He said to him: "You certainly speak the truth, for His Word came to heal all universally, not just some in part. However, it was not received except by some individuals, who were considered among all others to be of a cruder nature—fishermen, and those laboring upon the sea. And this is what was said: 'Those descending into the sea in ships, doing work in great waters, they have seen the work of God.' (Psalm 107:23). Those indeed who (if you consider rightly) did not seem fit to be able to admit anything intellectual, or pertaining to the intellect, because of the rudeness of their senses—those, I say, received the truth of prophecy and vision, because they believed."*

-># DISSERTATION<-

...they believed **in his word. And this is what was said: he believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.** <note>The author is finishing a quote attributed to a Jewish source that suggests the "Word" is an object of faith leading to justification.</note> It is scarcely believable that such a book and passage exist in Jewish writings, both because no one has yet come across it, and because it is unheard of for Jews to appeal to the authority of the New Testament to confirm a thesis. Rabbi **ISAAC ARAMA** wrote a book called *The Binding of Isaac* <note>original: *ligatio Isaaci*; Hebrew: *Aqedat Yitzhaq*</note>; which is an extensive commentary on the Law and the *Megilloth* <note>The five scrolls of the Hebrew Bible: Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, and Esther</note>. Whether **PAUL FAGIUS** <note>A 16th-century Hebraist</note> intended to refer to this specific work, I cannot say, since these words are sought in vain in the common editions. **LAURENTIUS WEGER** in his *Dissertation on the Word of God* <note>original: *de Verbo Dei*</note>, section 36, judges this passage to be spurious and believes that Fagius was deceived by **GALATINUS** <note>Pietro Galatino (1460–1540), a friar who claimed to find Christian truths in Jewish texts, often accused of forgery</note>, who produced a similar passage—namely, that one from which we presented some words in section 17. However, the authors are different and the sayings themselves also vary. As for the matter itself, it does not deserve a refutation, since anyone who looks at the preceding verse even with fleeting eyes will immediately discover that the "Word" in question is that which the Prophet—in whose power the Word of Jehovah is—was obliged to speak as the **Word of Jehovah**, and which would demonstrate its efficacy through its effects.

XXIII. **HOSEA 1:1.** *The Word of the Lord <note>Hebrew: *debar-Yehovah*</note> that came to Hosea, etc.* **ATHANASIUS** in his *Third Sermon against the Arians*, **JEROME**, and **BEDE** (as cited by **DIONYSIUS THE CARTHUSIAN**) explain this as referring to the **substantial Word** <note>The personal "Logos" or Christ, rather than just a spoken message</note> of the Lord. Athanasius certainly thinks that not only this passage, but also generally the phrase itself that recurs so often among the Prophets, should be understood this way: *And while the Prophets say: "And the Word of the Lord came to me"; John says: "In the beginning was the Word," etc. For all these things everywhere denounce the Arian heresy and signify the eternity of the Word.* <note>original Greek: Και των μεν Προφητων λεγοντων, και εγενετο Λογος Κυριου προς με; του δε Ιωαννου, εν αρχη ην ο λογος &c. Ταυτα γαρ παντα την μεν Αρειανην αιρεσιν στηλιτευει πανταχου, την δε του Λογου αιδιοτητα σημαινει.</note> Even before Athanasius, **ORIGEN** felt the same way in his *Commentary on John*, Volume 2. It is a wonder how light the armor was that the Church Fathers sometimes used against such deadly enemies as the Arians <note>The Arians argued that Christ was a created being; the author suggests the Fathers' biblical proofs here were weak</note>. Truly, nothing departs more from both the proper meaning and the usage of this phrase.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether the "Word" (Logos) mentioned in the Old Testament refers to the pre-incarnate Christ (the "Substantial Word") or merely to spoken prophecy or divine decrees. <header>ON THE WORD IN THE OLD TESTAMENT.</header>
<meta>catchword: III. 1.</meta>

### XXIV. HAGGAI II. 4, 5.
->Jehovah of hosts says: **For I am with you; according to the word that I covenanted with you when you came out of Egypt, and my Spirit remaining in your midst, do not fear.**<- <note>original Latin: *Quia ego vobiscum sum; cum verbo, quod pepigi vobiscum in exitu vestro ex Ægypto, & Spiritu stante in medio vestrum, ne timeatis.*</note>

This passage is utilized by the most learned interpreters, following the tradition of **JEROME**, to prove the mystery of the Trinity. For this purpose, it is believed that the Prophet intended the "substantial Word" <note>The Word as a living person or divine essence—the pre-incarnate Christ—rather than just a spoken message</note> to be understood here. **CORNELIUS A LAPIDE** <note>A prominent 16th-century Jesuit exegete</note> praises various authors for this view, including **ATHANASIUS** in his *Letter to Serapion*, **GREGORY OF NYSSA** in his *Book of Testimonies against the Jews*, **CYRIL OF JERUSALEM** in *Catechesis 19*, **THEODORET**, and others. Even the **TARGUM OF JONATHAN** <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> is thought to favor this hypothesis, because it translates: **My Word shall be a help to you, says the Lord of hosts.** <note>original Aramaic: *Memri be-sa'adekon amar YHWH tseba'ot*</note>

However, this is merely an interpretation of the final words of the fourth verse, "I am with you." The Paraphrast <note>The author of the Targum</note>, by separating the fifth verse from the fourth, understands the "word" not as the substantial Word, but as the *uttered* word <note>original Greek: *prophorikos*; a word spoken or a decree issued</note>. He renders it thus: **The word which I decreed with you when I led you out of Egypt, and my Prophets who teach among you, do not fear.** <note>original Aramaic: *yat pitgama di gezrit imekon...*</note> Consequently, far from this interpretation favoring the Trinitarian hypothesis, it actually adds weight to the opinion of those who argue that the Aramaic term **Word** <note>original Aramaic: *Memra*</note> used by the Chaldean Paraphrasts should not be understood as the **Personal Word** <note>original Greek: *Logon hypostatikon*; the Word as a distinct person of the Trinity</note>. If it were otherwise, it would have been much easier for the Paraphrast to translate "the word" <note>Hebrew: *et ha-davar*</note> using the term *Memra*.

Among more recent scholars, **TREMELLIUS** embraced this view. **HAKSPANIUS** rashly asserts that Tremellius's exposition was unheard of in all previous centuries; nevertheless, many among the Lutherans arrive at the same conclusion. **TARNOVIUS** <note>Paul Tarnow, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> paraphrases the passage in this way: *I am with you together with the **Word** or the essential and eternal **Logos**, by whom the heavens were established (Psalm 33:6), in whom I revealed myself to the fathers (1 Samuel 3:21; Hebrews 1:1), and because of whom I perform the greatest things (2 Samuel 7:21; 1 Chronicles 17:19). It was also through his intervention and mediation that I struck that perpetual covenant with you, that I would be your God and you would be my people (Exodus 6:4; 19:6). This promise, like all others, is only made firm in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20), who for that reason is called the Messenger of the Covenant (Malachi 3:1).*

It contrasts the views of early Church Fathers and Lutheran theologians against Aramaic Targum translations that suggest a more literal, prophetic meaning.</summary>

### XXIII. HOSEA I. 1.

Ταυτα γαρ παντα την μεν Αρειανην αἱρεσιν στηλιτευει πανταχου, την δε του Λογου αϊδιοτητα σημαινει.</note> Before **ATHANASIUS**, **ORIGEN** <note>A 3rd-century theologian from Alexandria</note> already felt this way in his *Commentary on John, Volume II*. # CONCERNING THE WORD <note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΩ (Logos)</note> IN THE OLD TESTAMENT.
<meta>catchword: III. 1.</meta>

XXIV. HAGGAI II. 4. 5. The Lord of hosts says: *For I am with you; according to the word that I covenanted with you when you came out of Egypt, and my Spirit remains in your midst; do not fear.* <note>Haggai 2:4–5. The author provides the original Hebrew: "כי אני אתכם את הדבר אשר כרתי אתכם בצאתכם ממצרים ורוחי עמדת בתוככם אל תיראו"</note> This passage is used by the most learned interpreters, following **JEROME**, to prove the mystery of the Trinity; for this purpose, they believe the "substantial Word" <note>The personal Word of God, i.e., the second person of the Trinity</note> is intended by the Prophet. **CORNELIUS A LAPIDE** <note>A renowned 17th-century Jesuit biblical commentator</note> praises authors such as **ATHANASIUS** in his *Letter to Serapion*, **GREGORY OF NYSSA** in his *Book of Testimonies against the Jews*, **CYRIL OF JERUSALEM** in *Catechesis XIX*, **THEODORET**, and others. Even the **TARGUM OF JONATHAN** <note>An ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> is thought to favor this hypothesis, because it translates: *My Word shall be your help, says the Lord of hosts.* <note>original Aramaic: "מימרי בסעדכון אמר יי צבאות"</note> But this is merely an interpretation of the last words of the fourth verse, "I am with you." Among more recent scholars, **TREMELLIUS** <note>Immanuel Tremellius (1510–1580), a Jewish-born Italian Reformed theologian and Hebraist</note> embraced this view, whose exposition **HAKSPANIUS** <note>Theodor Hackspan (1607–1659), a Lutheran orientalist</note> rashly asserts was unheard of in all previous centuries. However, many among the Lutherans agree with this same view. **TARNOVIUS** <note>Johann Tarnow (1586–1629), a Lutheran theologian</note> paraphrases the passage in this way: *I am with you together with the essential and eternal WORD <note>original Greek: Λογῳ (Logos)</note>, by whom the heavens were established (Psalm 33:6), in whom I revealed myself to the fathers (1 Samuel 3:21; Hebrews 1:1), on account of whom I perform the greatest things (2 Samuel 7:21; 1 Chronicles 17:19), and by whose intervention and intercession I had struck that perpetual covenant with you, that I would be your God and you would be my people (Exodus 6:4; 19:6). This promise, like all others, is made firm only in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20), who for that reason is called the Messenger of the Covenant (Malachi 3:1).*

->DISSERTATIO<-
<meta>catchword: OF THE WORD</meta>

III. 1. *And because the law brought through Moses could achieve nothing due to the weakness of the flesh, but possessed the letter that kills <note>original Latin: "literam occidentem"</note> (Romans 8:3, 2 Corinthians 3:6), the Gospel through Christ and the grace given and provided through him succeeds it; it is the ministry of the life-giving Spirit (Jeremiah 31:31, Ezekiel 36:26). Moreover, this eternal Christ—the Word, the Speech, or the <term>Logos</term> <note>original Greek: λογος</note> (John 1:1)—was also with you when you went out of Egypt (1 Corinthians 10:4, 9). And with my Holy Spirit standing in you, enduring firmly among you, and standing in my sight to intercede for you with groanings... so he shall yet give you understanding and skill in your actions as you proceed in your work; and therefore, do not fear.*

XXV. Above others, the most celebrated **COCCEIUS** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian known for Federal Theology</note> undertook the serious defense of this hypothesis in his commentary on this passage. His primary reasons are:
I. That the Hebrew particle <term>et</term> <note>את</note> should be translated as *with*, so that the Father says He is present to them *with His Word and His Spirit*. He argues it is quite rare for this particle to serve as a marker for the nominative case <note>the subject of a sentence</note>. But even if it were conceded that <term>et</term> here denotes the nominative, it should then be understood in the manner of the Rabbinic <term>oto</term> <note>אותו</note>, which signifies <term>these very things</term> <note>original Greek: ἀυτα ταυτα</note>. He argues no disadvantage would arise if it were explained <term>without conjunctions</term> <note>original Greek: ἀσυνδετως (asyndetōs)</note> in this way: *I am with you, that very Word which I promised you when you went out of Egypt, and my Spirit stands in your midst.* 
II. No other example can be cited in which the phrase <term>karat dabar</term> <note>Hebrew: כרת דבר, literally "to cut a word"</note> is used instead of <term>karat berit</term> <note>Hebrew: כרת ברית, "to cut a covenant"</note>, and for a similar reason, it cannot be said that way. For a covenant—that is, friendship and peace—is made by "cutting" <note>Referring to the ancient ritual of cutting sacrificial animals in two to seal an agreement</note>, but a "word" is not.

XXVI. Although these arguments have persuaded many others, there are factors that hold back our assent. *First*, it is less favorable to this view that the *Jehovah of hosts* who is introduced here as the speaker is the Son himself. For there follows immediately in verse 6 and those following: *For thus said Jehovah of hosts: Yet once more (it is a little while) I will shake the heaven and the earth and the sea and the dry land, etc.* The subject matter itself suggests that the same person is speaking here who spoke to the Fathers on Mount Sinai; the Apostle confirms this, citing these words as the words of the Son of God himself speaking from heaven in Hebrews 12:26: <note>The author provides the Greek text from Hebrews</note> *Whose voice then shook the earth, but now he has promised, saying: Yet once more I shake not only the earth, but also the heaven.* *Second*, it is added that when the Lord led Israel out of Egypt, he never gave the name <term>Word</term> <note>Hebrew: דבר (Dabar)</note> or...

### ON THE WORD IN THE OLD TESTAMENT.

Bb

<meta>catchword: of its-</meta>

...of the **WORD** [God] might have given, which nonetheless seems to be assumed here, and without which the present promise labored under a certain obscurity. Specifically, it is thought to refer to Exodus 23:20 and Deuteronomy 18:19, where God promises that He will send an Angel to Israel, "in whose midst His name shall be," and that He will raise up for them a Prophet, into whose mouth He will put His word. However, not only does the name of the "Substantial Word" <note>original: "VERBI substantialis" — referring to the Logos, the second person of the Trinity</note> not appear in those places, but also those promises did not at all concern the current state of Israel when Haggai was prophesying—a state which is shown to be intended by him by the use of the present participle *standing* <note>original Hebrew: עומדת — 'omdet,' suggesting a present, enduring reality</note>.

XXVII. The reasons at least brought forward for the "Substantial Word" carry no weight. For regarding the *former* reason, however the little word <term>et</term> <note>the Hebrew particle את (et), which can mark a direct object or mean "with"</note> is taken, nothing is lost for those who believe it refers to the *uttered word* <note>original Latin/Greek: "Verbo προφορικῳ" — the spoken word or promise of God</note>. For if you translate it as a connective *with* along with the preceding clause, there is no difficulty in the fact that the *Lord of Hosts* is said to be present with His people *with His word*, because in this way the manner of the divine presence is determined—a manner which differed quite a bit from the way He had been with them in the Tabernacle and the Temple of Solomon. For since that visible sign of the divine presence—the pillar of cloud and fire, the typical glory of *Jehovah*—was no longer seen in the Temple of Zerubbabel <note>The Second Temple, built after the Babylonian exile</note>, the Lord had decided to honor it with His presence in another way: namely, with the **Word** of the covenant, which was to find its fulfillment in this Temple. Yet nothing prevents us, following the punctuation <note>original: "accentuationem" — referring to the Hebrew cantillation marks which guide the meaning</note>, from considering the statement of the fifth verse as a separate sentence, since without any gap it sounds like this: *According to that word which I covenanted with you when you came out of Egypt, and my Spirit standing in your midst, do not fear.* In this version, the <term>et</term> <note>את</note> forms an ablative <note>a grammatical case indicating "by means of" or "according to"</note>, as in Leviticus 8:7 and 1 Kings 7:14. **NOLDIUS** <note>Christian Nold (1626–1683), a Danish theologian and author of a famous concordance on Hebrew particles</note> will provide more examples.

XXVIII. The *latter* difficulty is greater only in appearance. But we reply: I. There is nothing harsh in the word *dabar* <note>original Hebrew: דבר — "word"</note> being used by <term>metonymy</term> <note>a figure of speech where a related term is used to stand in for another</note> for *berit* <note>original Hebrew: ברית — "covenant"</note>. The reason that this phrase is supposedly "uncomfortable" is clearly non-existent. For peace is not "made" by cutting; rather, once made, it is merely confirmed through an external ceremony, and thus it presupposes a covenant already made. Furthermore, the federal "cutting" <note>refers to the ancient practice of "cutting a covenant" by dividing animals in two</note> refers specifically to the *word of the covenant*...

<summary>The author argues that the "Word" in Haggai 2:5 refers to God's spoken covenant from the Exodus rather than the person of Christ (the Logos). He explains that the Second Temple's glory was not a physical cloud but the presence of God's Word and Spirit.</summary>

# DISSERTATION

...and had regard for its *stipulation*, which he asserted would be made firm through a certain sacramental rite, just like an oath. II. Another distinguished example, in which the Hebrew term for "cutting" a covenant <note>original: כרת (karat)</note> is paired with the term for "word" <note>original: דבר (davar)</note>, is found in Psalm 105:8–9: *He remembers his covenant forever,* <note>original Hebrew: דבר צוה לאלף דור אשר כרת את אברהם — "the word he commanded to a thousand generations, which he pledged to Abraham"</note> *the word which he commanded to the thousandth generation, which he pledged to Abraham, and his oath to Isaac.* From this, the word for "cutting" or pledging also occurs in construction with the word for "oath" <note>original: אלה (alah)</note> in Deuteronomy 29:11–13, and alongside the tablets of the covenant in 1 Kings 8:9. To this we can also refer the passage in 2 Chronicles 7:18, where God is said to have "cut" a pledge for David. In this way, the phrase is parallel to the one in Jeremiah 31:31, where the Lord mentions the *covenant which he had made with the Fathers on the day he took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt.*

XXIX. So far, then, nothing prevents us from understanding the prophet Haggai as speaking of the *Word of the Covenant*, especially since this expresses the best and most natural sense. For the *Covenantal Word* given to the Fathers after they were freed from Egypt was no different from the one God had pledged to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in Exodus 3:6, 6:2 and following, and Deuteronomy 29:13 and 30:20. As such, it simultaneously included the very promise concerning that "Seed" who was to be the source of all blessing. Furthermore, this "Word" is elegantly joined with the Spirit because of the unbreakable bond that exists between the *Covenantal Word of God and His Spirit* in Isaiah 59:21. Because of this connection, the Hebrew term *standing* <note>original: עמדת (omdet) — meaning to remain, abide, or stand firm</note> refers equally to the *Word* as it does to the *Spirit*. For the Word of the covenant was established by God himself in Psalm 105:10. For this reason, the *Fear of the Lord* (or the doctrine that instills it) is said to be *abiding forever* <note>original: עומדת לעד (omdet la-ad)</note>. Compare Psalm 111:8 and the notes we made in section 16.

XXX. At the very least, the connection fits our interpretation excellently. For the words immediately preceding—*I am with you, says the Lord of Hosts*—seem to us to suit the "Substantial Word" <note>The "Substantial Word" refers to the Logos, the second person of the Trinity</note> much better than the words of the fifth verse. For to Him belongs the symbolic name *Emmanuel*—meaning *God with us*—given to the Son of God in Isaiah 8:14 <note>The author cites Isaiah 8:14, though the name Emmanuel is famously introduced in Isaiah 7:14; both chapters discuss the concept.</note>. The power of this name had to be fulfilled within this Second Temple, because the Word pledged to the seed of Israel could not be rendered void. Nor was there any reason to fear, because the grace and gifts of the Spirit...

# ON THE LOGOS IN THE OLD TESTAMENT.

[...of the Ho]ly Spirit had remained conspicuous among them until now. In this way, the passage in verses 6–9 also fits perfectly, describing the manifestation of the Glory of the Lord Messiah at his coming and the establishment of his Kingdom; this section is connected to our previous discussion by the small particle *ki* <note>original Hebrew: כי; a conjunction meaning "for" or "because"</note>: *For thus says Jehovah, God of hosts: once more I will shake the heavens and the earth... and I will fill this house with glory, etc.* From this, it seems clear to us that the future manifestation of the Messiah's Glory during the time of the Second Temple is regarded as proof that the Word of the covenant made with the Fathers stands unshaken. This is because that "Word" included the clear promises regarding the appearance of the Son of God in the flesh. The fulfillment of these promises during the era of this Temple would certainly prove the Lord's singular care and providence regarding it. If anyone nevertheless prefers to understand the *hypostatic Word* <note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΟΝ ὑποστατικον; referring to the Word as a distinct Person of the Trinity, i.e., Christ</note> in this passage, we will not strongly oppose them. Of all the passages we have cited, this one presents the least difficulty for that view. Meanwhile, it is clear from what we have presented that our hypothesis recommends itself by its greater simplicity, without in any way weakening the force of the prophetic language.

XXXI. Since the word *imrah* <note>original Hebrew: אמרה; meaning "utterance" or "saying"</note> is, in its common sense, a synonym for *davar* <note>original Hebrew: דבר; "word"</note>, we must also consider those passages where some interpreters take the word *imrah* to refer to the personal Word <note>the Logos/Christ</note>. For example, in **PSALM 138:2**: *You have magnified your word above all your name* <note>original Hebrew: הגדלת על כל שמך אמרתך</note>; Jerome <note>an influential 4th-century scholar and Bible translator</note> interprets this as referring to the Son of God. We add another passage, **PSALM 147:15**: *Sending his word to the earth, his word runs swiftly.* <note>original Hebrew: השלח אמרתו ארץ</note> Here, Origen <note>an early Christian scholar</note> (in Corderius’s *Catena* <note>a "chain" or collection of traditional commentaries</note>, page 821) understands this—at least allegorically—as the Son of God joined with the earth in the flesh. However, it is clear from section 12 that this latter passage plainly rejects such a meaning. The context also argues against the interpretation of the former passage. In that psalm, David's purpose is to celebrate the grace and truth of the Lord as seen in the results of the preached Gospel. Hence, verse 4 says: *All the kings of the earth shall praise you, Jehovah, for they have heard the words of your mouth* <note>original Hebrew: אמרי פיך (imre picha)</note>. Therefore, since no other example occurs in which the word *imrah* is used for the *substantial Word* <note>referring to Christ as the divine "Word" or "Logos" in his essence</note>, there is no reason why we should depart from the usual meaning in this passage.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring floral and vine motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>Among those who have obscured the true mystery of the Johannine Word <note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΟΥ; referring to the "Word" (Logos) as described in the Gospel of John</note> through distorted interpretations, we must first mention those who have denied that a "person" in the true sense of the word is designated by this name. II. Since there are different classes of those who stumbled at the very threshold of this matter, we rightly mention first those who considered the LOGOS <note>original Greek: ΤΟΝ ΛΟΓΟΝ</note> to be the supreme and essential REASON <note>Latin: *RATIONE*</note> of God Himself. ### IX.
## THEOLOGICAL DISSERTATION
### ON THE
# PERSONALITY
# OF THE WORD.

->I.<-

Among those who, through perverse interpretations, have obscured the true Johannean mystery of the Word <note>The "Johannean mystery" refers to the theology of the "Logos" or "Word" found in the opening of the Gospel of John</note>, we must first mention those who have denied that a person in the true sense of the word is designated by this name. For this error not only contaminated the Church earlier than others, but it also overthrows the entire foundation of the Deity of the Word—which we shall, God willing, present at another time. For once the divine Subject, who exists in Himself, is removed, all divine attributes are also taken away.

II. Since, however, there are different classes of those who have stumbled at this very threshold, we rightly mention first those who held the Word <note>original Greek: ΤΟΝ ΛΟΓΟΝ</note> to be the supreme and essential Reason <note>original Latin: RATIONE</note> of God itself, whether considered generally, or specifically as a certain essential attribute, such as divine wisdom or omnipotence. Among these is numbered the man who, in the second century under Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, manfully defended the Christian religion: Athenagoras <note>An early Christian apologist known for his philosophical approach to the faith</note>. Dionysius Petavius <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a prominent Jesuit theologian who often criticized the early Church Fathers for imprecise language regarding the Trinity</note> brought this charge against him in his *Theological Dogmas on the Trinity*, book I, chapter 3. The occasion for the accusation was provided by a passage occurring in his *Apology*, sections 9 and 10: *The Son of God is the Word of the Father in idea and in operation <note>original Greek: ἐν ἰδέᾳ καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ</note>; for by Him and through Him all things were made, since the Father and the Son are one; so that the Son is in the Father, and the Father is in the Son, through the unity and power of the Spirit: the Mind and Word of the Father <note>original Greek: νους καὶ λογος του Πατρος</note> is the Son of God.*

HEADER: DISSERTATION

<meta>catchword: EUSEBIUS</meta>

...who, though he was a mere man, was dwelt in [by the Word]. Thus, he says, there is one God; and neither is the Father truly Father, nor the Son truly Son, nor the Holy Spirit truly Holy Spirit. Rather, the one God is the Father, and his Son is within him, just as the Word <note>original Greek: λογος (logos)</note> exists in a human being. And although others differ in defining Paul’s concept—as we note in Section 6—they nonetheless agree on this: that he denied the personal distinction <note>original Latin: hypostaticam distinctionem; "hypostatic" refers to the distinct, individual existence of the persons of the Trinity</note> of the Word from the Father. Nevertheless, Garner <note>Jean Garnier (1612–1681), a Jesuit scholar and church historian</note> calls this into question in his *Dissertation on the Heresies and Books of Nestorius* (Diss. I to Mercator, Vol. II, p. 307). He does so partly because the testimony of the authors asserting this is not sufficiently ancient, and partly because something quite different is evident from the letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Paul himself. From the words of Paul which Dionysius quotes, it seems one must conclude that Paul distinguished between two Sons of God: *one by nature, who existed before the ages, and one "by a shared name"* <note>original Greek: κατ’ ὁμωνυμιαν (kat' homonymian)</note>, *namely Christ and the Son of David, who did not exist before the ages but came into being in time, and received the name of Son according to God’s good pleasure.* The following words clarify that he understood the former Son to be the *Word*, where he declares: *that Christ is a different man besides God and the Word, differing in substance and dignity from the other Christ.* Deciding this difficult controversy is a challenge because it is doubtful whether that Letter of Dionysius—which appears in Greek and Latin in the *Auctarium Ducaeanum* (Vol. I) and in Labbe's *Councils* (Vol. I, p. 849)—is genuine. It is defended by Tillemont <note>Sébastien le Nain de Tillemont, a famous 17th-century French ecclesiastical historian</note> in Note 8 on the life of Dionysius, Stillingfleet <note>Edward Stillingfleet (1635–1699), an influential English theologian and Bishop of Worcester</note> in his *Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity*, Noël Alexandre in his history of the third century (p. 614), Garner in the work cited, and Fabricius in his *Greek Library* (Book V, ch. 1). However, others attack it as spurious with strong arguments, including Valesius <note>Henri Valois, a French classical scholar</note> in his commentary on Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* (VII. 30), Louis Ellies du Pin (Vol. I, p. 516), William Cave, Hardouin in his notes on Chrysostom’s *Letter to Caesarius* (who attributes the letter to a follower of the Eutychian heresy <note>Eutychianism was the 5th-century view that Christ had only one nature, his humanity being absorbed by his divinity</note>), and Basnage in his *Annals* for the year 247 (Section 11), who has no doubt that its author lived after Nestorius <note>Nestorius was a 5th-century bishop who emphasized the separation of Christ's two natures; Basnage suggests the letter is a later forgery trying to link Paul of Samosata to Nestorius's later ideas</note> and confused Nestorius's views with those of Paul.

V. Leaving these matters behind, then, and descending to the fourth century, we find that Marcellus, Bishop of Ancyra, was accused of the same heresy. At least, Eusebius accuses him on that account...

### ON THE PERSONALITY OF THE WORD.

[EUSE]BIUS, in the books written against him, asserts that he [Marcellus] professed **"that God and His Word are one and the same"** <note>original Greek: ἑν και ταυτον ειναι τον Θεον και τον ἀυτου Λογον</note>. It is also true that MARCELLUS used these and other inconvenient expressions, both in those words which EUSEBIUS quotes throughout **literally** <note>original Greek: κατα ῥητον (kata rheton)</note>, and in the Letter (or profession of faith) presented to Pope Julius, which EPIPHANIUS preserved in *Against Heresies*, Book 72. For from these it is clear that he was accustomed to calling the Word <note>Greek: Λογον (Logon)</note> the "power of God," and the **"Word by which He reasons,"** <note>original Greek: ᾧ λογιζεται (hō logizetai)</note> nor did he wish for it to be considered as a **person** <note>original Greek: ὑποστασιν (hypostasin); a term used to denote a distinct, individual existence within the Trinity</note> different from the Father. For this reason, BASIL, HILARY, CHRYSOSTOM, MARIUS VICTORINUS, and THEODORET held him to be a heretic. Among more recent scholars, those who rely on their authority include PETAVIUS (*Dogmatic Theology on the Trinity*, book I, ch. 13), SCHELSTRATE (*Dissertation III on the Council of Antioch*, ch. V), PAGI (*Criticism on the Annals of Baronius*, Year 347, § 2 ff.), LARROQUE (*On the Photinian Heresy*, p. 24 ff.), ITTIG (*History of Photinus*, § 3), and BASNAGE (*Annals*, Year 347, § 13).

Nevertheless, much can be said in defense of MARCELLUS: first, that the phrases he employs are such that other Orthodox Fathers used similar ones; second, that they were used in the heat of disputation not only against the Arians <note>followers of Arius, who argued the Son was a created being</note> but also against the Semi-Arians. When the Fathers wished to distinguish themselves accurately from the errors of those groups, they often seemed to crash into the opposite rock <note>a reference to the "Scylla and Charybdis" of theology—avoiding one heresy only to fall into its opposite</note>, as could be proven with many examples. Furthermore, the first authors of these accusations were the "Eusebians" <note>the party of Eusebius of Nicomedia, who favored Arian views</note>, whom Marcellus had attacked as supporters of Arianism; for that reason, they became his most bitter enemies, not only launching the most unjust persecutions against him but also seeking to blunt his arguments by striking back at him. 

It should also be noted that he was a distinguished member of the Council of Nicaea; that not only Pope Julius but also the Synod of Sardica <note>a council held in 343 AD to address the Arian controversy</note> cleared him of the suspicion of error; and finally, that ATHANASIUS <note>the champion of Nicene Orthodoxy</note>, a companion in Marcellus's labors and persecutions, provides most excellent testimony regarding him. It seems one should trust Athanasius's explicit words more than the uncertain conjecture of EPIPHANIUS, which was derived from some sort of "silence and a nod" from Athanasius. What weighs most heavily against MARCELLUS, [is...] <note>The text ends here; the catchword "mit," completes the Latin word "premit" (weighs against).</note>

-># DISSERTATION<-

[pre]mits <note>The text continues from the previous page's final word "premit," meaning "forces" or "presses."</note>, to be quite frank, it is established from HILARY in his *Fragments* that Athanasius subsequently *separated Marcellus from his communion* on account of *ambiguous preaching*. But who will dare to affirm for certain—if they compare what we have already noted with the spirit of that century—that the enemies of Marcellus (among whom he had the most hostile "hidden Arians" <term>Crypto-Arianos; people who outwardly accepted the Nicene Creed but privately held Arian views</term>) did not twist certain ambiguous expressions into a worse sense? Who can say they did not alienate the mind of Athanasius from Marcellus through various tricks and schemes, so that, by breaking the friendship between these two Prelates who were so burdensome and feared by them, they might more easily crush them individually? Indeed, around the time when Marcellus died, EPIPHANIUS himself testifies that he had no fewer great defenders than attackers. Compare the arguments made expressly in favor of MARCELLUS by NATALIS ALEXANDER <note>original: NAT. ALEXANDER; a prominent 17th-century Dominican church historian</note> in his *Ecclesiastical History*, 4th Century, dissertation 30.

VI. To the second class of errors regarding the WORD <term>LOGON; the Greek term for the "Word" or "Reason" of God</term> we refer those who likewise believe that the Word does not really differ from God himself, but with this distinction observed: they do not think the "Word" refers to God as he is in himself, but in relation to his creatures, insofar as he either determines his own will toward them or manifests himself to them. Since there are various modes of this divine determination and manifestation, they believe that each and every one of these, depending on the circumstances, is called the *Word*. Thus, regarding an outward determination, they think the *command of God* is called the Word—which is the first cause of all things—whether they consider it "internal" (which is the decree) or "external" (through the actual production of things). And because the *command of God* is joined with efficacy, they soon call the productive *Power of God* itself the *Word*. In fact, they claim that all instruments of divine manifestation, such as the Angels and Christ himself, are only called the *Word* by way of metonymy <term>metonymice; a figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it, like using "the crown" to mean "the king"</term>.

VII. The enemies of the Trinity strive to make many Fathers of the primitive Church guilty of this concept. But they labor in vain. An example of this—as it would be a long task to go through every instance—is CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA. He was accused on this basis because he teaches that the *Angels* under the Old Testament were also the *Word of the Lord*, when he says in *The Instructor*, Book I, chapter 7: "To the older people..." <note>original Greek: το μεν νυν προτερον τῳ πρεσβυτερῳ λαῳ (to men nyn proteron tō presbyterō laō)</note>

### ->ON THE PERSONALITY OF THE WORD.<-
<note>original header: DE PERSONALITATE ΛΟΓΟΥ</note>
Cc

"The old covenant existed, and the law educated the people with fear, and the Word was an angel; but for a new and recent people, a new and recent covenant has been granted, and the Word has been born, and fear has been transformed into love, and that mystic Angel, Jesus, is born." <note>This is a quote from Clement of Alexandria's *Paedagogus* (The Instructor). Clement argues that the same Word who appeared as an angel to the Israelites has now become human.</note> *Therefore, for the old people there was an Old Testament, and the Law instructed the people through fear, and the Word was an Angel: but to the new and recent people, a new and recent Testament has been given, and the Word was brought forth, and fear has been turned into love, AND THAT MYSTIC ANGEL OF JEHOVAH IS BORN.* But anyone who examines these final words will easily perceive that it was **CLEMENT'S** settled opinion that the same divine person who was made flesh and manifested himself in the flesh had previously assumed the form of an Angel as a prelude to his mission into the world. For he clearly declares that he is speaking not of *angels* in the plural, but of one specific *Angel*, who is named by him with emphasis as the *Angel of Jehovah*, and that he speaks not of a literal angel but of a "mystic" one. And so, **BULL** <note>George Bull (1634–1710), an influential Anglican theologian who defended the orthodoxy of the pre-Nicene Fathers</note> showed in his *Defense of the Nicene Faith*, Section I, chapter I, paragraph 12 and following, that **CLEMENT** is consistent not only with himself but also with other early Church Fathers.

VIII. With much greater probability, according to many, this was the opinion of **PAUL OF SAMOSATA** <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Antioch who was condemned for heresy; he taught that Jesus was a mere man who was "inhabited" by the Word, rather than being the Word incarnate</note>. **MARIUS MERCATOR** <note>A 5th-century Latin writer who opposed the Nestorian heresy</note> writes in his *Letter on the difference between Paul and Nestorius*, number 1: *Regarding the Word of God, Nestorius does not indeed think as Paul does, who defines the Word not as a substantive thing, but as a "prolative" <term>prolatitium; something spoken out or emitted like a sound</term> and effective power of God.* The same author says in his *Dissertation on the Twelve Anathemas*, number 19: *Paul understood the Word of God to be a "prolative, practical, and energetic word" <note>original Greek: προφορικον και πρακτικον λογον και δε ενεργετικον</note>, that is, a word that is spoken and effects power, but not a substantive word, which the Greeks call "essential" <term>ousiodes; having its own being or substance</term>.* Similar accounts are held by **JOHN OF DAMASCENUS** in *Heresies* 65, **LEONTIUS** in *On Sects* Article III, and others. **PHILASTRIUS** in *Heresy* LXIV adds that *he established the Word as "prolative," that is, as if it were a kind of air*, a conclusion which Philastrius perhaps draws only as a logical consequence of Paul's view.

IX. **EUSEBIUS**, in *Against Marcellus* Book II, chapter 2, transfers a similar error to the reasoning of **MARCELLUS**, accusing him of making the Word a "naked word" <note>original Greek: ψιλον λογον</note>, like some sort of command for things to be made, a *naked word,*

from the words of **MARCELLUS**, which we read in the following passages in **EUSEBIUS**: *“Before the production of all things there was, as it is right to believe, a rest in God, since the Word was in God,* <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ Θεῷ του Λογου ὀντος</note> *when the Word was (internally) in God.”* For if **ASTERIUS** <note>Asterius the Sophist, an early Arian theologian.</note> believes that God is the creator of all things, it is necessary that he simultaneously confess that absolutely nothing else existed besides God. *The Word, therefore, had its own glory, being in the Father.* <note>original Greek: Ἐιχεν ὀυν την ὀικειαν δοξαν ὁ λογος, ὠν ἐν τῷ Πατρι.</note> The sense of these words clearly escaped the previous translator. X. Regarding **PHOTINUS**, whom many (based on a false understanding of Marcellus’s <term>hypothesis|A fundamental proposition or theological starting point</term>) establish as his disciple, the matter is clearer. The **Synod of Antioch** in the year 344 strikes at both of them, as recorded in **ATHANASIUS** (*On the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia*) and in **SOCRATES** (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, Chapter 15), defining it thus:

> “We furthermore detest and curse with <term>anathema|A formal curse by a church council, excommunicating a person or denouncing a doctrine</term> those who name the Son merely the ‘bare Word of God’ without substance in a made-up fashion, and who hold that His existence is within another; and who understand Him now as a voice which is brought forth from the mouth, and now as a speech that dwells within thought.” <note>This refers to the "Logos Prophorikos" (uttered word) and "Logos Endiathetos" (internal thought).</note>

**AMBROSE** says in *On the Faith*, Book I, Chapter 5: *“This Word is not, therefore, an interpretation of speech, but is found in that designation of celestial power, so that Photinus may be refuted.”* **BALSAMON** <note>Theodore Balsamon, a high-ranking 12th-century Byzantine lawyer and commentator on church law.</note> writes in his notes on the first Canon of the Second Council of Constantinople (found in **BEVEREGE’S** *Pandects*, Vol. I, p. 86) regarding Photinus: 

> “...holding the opinion that the Word was ‘uttered,’ and was a kind of divine command, serving God in the production of the universe like some mechanical tool.” <note>original Greek: τον δε Λογον προφορικον φρονουντος, και θειον τι προσαγμα, ὑπουργουντα τῷ Θεῷ εἰς την παραγωγην του παντος ὡς ὀργανον τι μηχανικον.</note>

XI. A third form of errors concerning the Personality of the Word <term>Logos|The Greek term for "Word" or "Reason," used in the Gospel of John to describe the pre-existent Christ.</term> is shown by the **GNOSTICS**, for whom the Word is a certain *emission* in that marvelous chain of causes or <term>Aeons|In Gnostic mythology, these are divine beings or emanations that flow from the ultimate, unknowable God.</term> which they invented.
