## ON THE PERSONALITY OF THE WORD.

Cc 3

<meta>catchword: eternally</meta>

...the letter, where it is said concerning Jesus Christ, *who is His eternal Word, not proceeding from silence.* <note>original Greek: ὅς ἐστιν αὐτοῦ Λόγος ἀΐδιος, οὐκ ἀπὸ σιγῆς προελθών; original Latin: qui est Verbum ejus æternum, non à silentio progrediens. This is a famous passage from Ignatius's Letter to the Magnesians.</note> This passage, at least—regardless of the <term>authenticity<note>original Greek: γνησιότητι (gnēsiotēti)</note></term> of the entire Epistle—is justly doubted to have come from the hand of **IGNATIUS** <note>Ignatius of Antioch (c. 35–107 AD), an early Church Father and martyr.</note>, especially when one weighs the arguments against **PEARSON** <note>John Pearson (1613–1686), an English bishop who defended the authenticity of the Ignatian letters.</note> which **LARROQUE** <note>Matthieu de Larroque (1619–1684), a French Reformed theologian who challenged the authenticity of the letters.</note> discusses at length after others in his *Observations on the Defense of Ignatius, p. 220 ff.*

XII. Furthermore, it is extremely difficult to define what the Gnostics specifically intended by the monstrous <term>Syzygies<note>From the Greek word for "pairings" or "unions," referring to the male-female couples of divine beings in Gnostic thought.</note></term> of their <term>Aeons<note>From the Greek 'Aion,' meaning ages or eternal beings that emanate from the divine source.</note></term>. For not only is the word *Aeon* itself ambiguous, but it is also clear from the testimonies of **IRENAEUS**, **TERTULLIAN**, **THEODORET**, and others that the opinions of all Gnostics regarding the *Aeons* were not the same. There is also debate concerning the sources from which the Gnostics drew their system of *Aeons*. To me, indeed—to speak my own opinion while hastening to other matters—it seems most likely that although the Gnostics plundered the writings of others as well, they followed for the most part the teachings of **Platonic Philosophy**, which flourished in the Alexandrian school at 그 time. This is something which **MASSUET** <note>René Massuet (1666–1716), a Benedictine monk and scholar known for his edition of Irenaeus.</note> established with singular diligence after others in his *First Dissertation on Irenaeus, Article 1, Chapter 5.* Compare also what I mentioned in my *Prolegomena to John, Book II, Chapter 3, Section 48.* Indeed, one egg is hardly so similar to another as the doctrine of the Platonists regarding **Ideas** is to that of the Gnostics regarding **Aeons**. Nor does a groundless suspicion rest within me that these men changed the names of things rather than the things themselves, affecting a peculiar obscurity so they might avoid the resentment of their attempt to twist and pervert both Jewish and Christian Theology according to pagan Philosophy. Therefore, he who has gained an insight into what the **system of Platonic Ideas** signifies will pull back the veil here considerably. But even here the water will be held back <note>A Latin idiom, "haerebit aqua," meaning to be stuck or at a standstill.</note> as long as it remains controversial whether Plato established that *Ideas* were substances and essences existing by themselves—distinct from material bodies and even from God Himself (even if they were joined with the essence of God and subsisted in Him from all eternity, and gradually proceeded and were, as it were, unfolded from Him)—or whether he believed instead that *Ideas* were merely the thoughts and notions of God, insofar as He [conceived] visible things to be created from eternity...

If we were to follow these authors, the Gnostic opinion regarding the **Word** <note>original Greek: Λογῳ (Logō)</note> would not differ much from the second error, except that they intended the **Word** to signify not God’s entire will concerning the existence of things, but only that part of His will which concerns a certain class of things. 

Meanwhile, no less strong arguments seem to support those who prefer the former concept, following **ARISTOTLE**, **PLUTARCH**, **PHILOPONUS** <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570), an Alexandrian philosopher and grammarian who sought to reconcile Greek philosophy with Christian thought.</note>, and others. It is certain that Plato was understood in both senses by his disciples: in the former sense by **PROCLUS** and in the latter by **PLOTINUS**. 

Whatever the case may be regarding Plato's own opinion, it seems hardly doubtful to me that his more prominent disciples understood those "ideas" in a "lower" or more literal sense, and that the Gnostics primarily followed the sect of these followers. From this twofold and contradictory understanding of the Platonic system, it is easily gathered how Platonic philosophy could be held in high esteem both by the most ancient heretics and by the Orthodox at the same time, and be twisted by each into their own beliefs—since the Orthodox followed the better concept, while the Gnostics followed the cruder one.

# ON THE PERSONALITY OF THE WORD.

<note>The author uses the Greek term "Logos" (Λόγος) to refer to the "Word" or the second person of the Trinity.</note>

...although they speak of "persons," it might seem doubtful from this whether the Gnostics actually recognized the personality of the Word. But anyone who examines more closely their depiction—especially as found in the writings of **IRENAEUS** <note>Bishop of Lugdunum (c. 130–202 AD) and author of *Against Heresies*.</note>—will discover that the Gnostics consider the **Aeons** <term>divine beings or emanations that represent various attributes of God</term> as certain parts or emanations of the divine essence. This is not because it can be directly proven that they conceived of a "material" God, but because, although they separated God from matter (following Plato), they nonetheless lacked a pure concept of the nature of the mind. Hence, they proposed the divine essence to themselves as the **Pleroma** <term>original Greek: πλήρωμα, meaning "fullness" or "totality"</term>, that is, the source of all Spirituality, or if you prefer, the *universal thought*, from which all "modes of thinking" flowed forth in a certain order. To these modes, they used to refer not only the Aeons but even the higher part of the soul itself, which they called the *spirit*. For they felt that the lowest of the Aeons, which they called **Achamoth** <term>a gnostic term for a lower form of Wisdom, derived from the Hebrew word for Wisdom, *Chokhmah*</term> and **Enthymesis** <term>original Greek: ἐνθύμησις, meaning "thought," "intent," or "impulse"</term>, produced spiritual and animate substances, and that these would eventually return to the Pleroma of the Deity according to certain cycles or "revolutions."

### XIV.
I hardly doubt that **TATIAN** <note>An early Christian writer and apologist (c. 120–180 AD) who eventually joined the ascetic Encratite sect.</note> proposed the **Word** to himself under such a concept of "emanation" or "emission" when he says in his *Address to the Greeks*, sections 7 and 8: "I will now more clearly reveal the secrets of our religion. God was in the beginning, and we have received that the 'beginning' is the power of the Word. Indeed, the Lord of the universe, since he himself is the substance of all things, was alone before the world was established. But if you look at his power, in which all things visible and invisible consist, all things were with him. For by the power of the Word, both he himself and the Word that was in him existed. But when he willed, the Word sprang forth from his simplicity. And the Word, not brought forth in vain, became the first-born work of the spirit itself. This we know to be the 'beginning' of this world. **It came into being by division, not by cutting off.** <note>original Greek: Γεγονε δε κατα μερισμον, ου κατα αποκοπην (Gegone de kata merismon, ou kata apokopēn)</note> For that which is severed is separated from the first; but that which is divided, being endowed with its own function, does not diminish him from whom it took its power. For just as many other torches are lit from one torch, yet the light of the first torch is not diminished because many are lit from it, so also the Word, having proceeded from the power of the Father, does not leave the one who begat him devoid of the Word." It is well known that there is much dispute among learned men about this passage, with some [arguing that] **TATIAN**...

Whether he is guilty of denying the Deity of Christ—as some assert, among them **PETAVIUS** <note>Dionysius Petavius (1583–1652), a highly influential Jesuit theologian.</note> in *Theological Dogmas on the Trinity*, book I, chapter 3, section 5, and the **ANONYMOUS** author of the dissertation on Tatian added to the very elegant edition by Worth—while others defend him, such as **GEORGE BULL** in *Defense of the Nicene Faith*, Section III, chapter 6, and **NICOLAS DE NOURRY** in his dissertation on Tatian, chapter II, section 2: I believe a middle path must be held here. For since it is abundantly clear from the testimonies of **IRENAEUS**, **EUSEBIUS**, **EPIPHANIUS**, and others that after the death of **JUSTIN MARTYR** (whom he had followed during his life), **TATIAN** surrendered himself to the delusions of the **Valentinians** <term>followers of Valentinus, a major Gnostic teacher who proposed a complex system of divine emanations</term>, I do not doubt that he collaborated with the Gnostics in his general concept of the **Word** <term>the *Logos*</term>, and therefore this passage must be explained according to their system. 

For this reason, I believe the **SCHOLIAST** <term>an ancient commentator or annotator</term>—a fragment of whose work from the Royal Manuscript is cited by the aforementioned anonymous author—rightly remarked on those words, *it came to be by division* <note>original Greek: "γεγονε δε κατα μερισμον"</note>: *For even this they dared to say, as we have mentioned, men being driven by the trifles of Plato.* <note>original Greek: "Επει και τουτο ετολμησαν, ως ειπειν εφημεν, οι ανθρωποι εκ των του Πλατωνος ορμηθεντες ληρων."</note> Indeed, some have dared to assert this, as we said before, led on to it by the nonsense of Plato. Now, although the doctrine of the Gnostics thought crudely regarding the Deity of the Son, it cannot be said that they simply denied it; rather, we have proved in the *Prolegomena to John*, book II, chapter 3, note o, that their doctrine was more opposed to his **personality** <term>his existence as a distinct, individual person</term> than to his **Deity**. **TATIAN**, along with his associates, might easily have conceded the Deity of the Word as existing within the Father from all eternity; but it is clear that they denied the *eternity of his personality*. Because the ancients did not distinguish this well, they regarded the Gnostics as precursors to **Arius** <note>Arius (c. 256–336 AD) taught that the Son was a created being, not co-eternal with the Father.</note>, when in fact they were more like precursors to the **Sabellians** <note>Followers of Sabellius, who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons but merely three "modes" or "masks" of a single divine person.</note>, at least regarding the person of the Word.

XV. Those who nevertheless attempt to clear **TATIAN** of all guilt of heterodoxy <term>holding beliefs different from the established church</term> primarily emphasize that his opinion is not different from that of **JUSTIN MARTYR**, his teacher. Nor do they seem to appeal without some significant appearance of truth to those words from the *Dialogue with Trypho*: *In the brief remarks above, I explained the **Word** <note>Logos</note>, saying that this Power was begotten from the Father, by his power and will; but not by excision, as if the essence of the Father were partitioned off, in the way that all other things are partitioned and cut, not the...* <note>original Greek: "αλλ’ ου κατα αποτομην, ως απομεριζομενης της του Πατρος ουσιας, οποια τα αλλα παντα μεριζομενα και τεμνομενα, ου τα"</note>

### ON THE PERSONALITY OF THE WORD <note>original: "DE PERSONALITATE ΛΟΓΟΥ"</note>

<meta>catchword: Wherefore</meta>

*"They are the same things as they were before being divided."* <note>original Greek: "ἀυτα ἐσιν, ἁ και πριν τμηθηναι"</note> But this is not by a cutting away, as if partitioned from the essence of the Father; for other things, once divided and cut, are no longer the same as they were before they were split. *“And for the sake of an example, I have taken those things which are lit by fire: we see another fire produced, while the original is not diminished but remains in the same state, from which many fires can be lit.”* <note>This "fire from fire" metaphor was used by early Church Fathers to explain how the Son could be begotten from the Father without the Father losing any of His divine nature.</note> Truly, it is all too clear and transparent from the writings of **JUSTIN MARTYR** that he often incautiously blurred Platonic concepts with Christian doctrines. Indeed, nothing more crude could be proposed than this simile of "fire from fire," or as **TATIAN** expresses it even more harshly, *"one torch lighting another torch,"* <note>original Latin: "facis facem accendentis"</note> regardless of what others may say. Those who do not rest in the simplicity of Scripture, but instead wish to adapt the mysteries of faith to human understanding and the jargon of the schools, end up obscuring the inherent majesty and light of those mysteries far too much.

It must be admitted, meanwhile, that although **JUSTIN** sometimes seems to approach the Platonic fictions of the **Gnostics** <term>members of early mystical sects who believed in secret knowledge and divine emanations</term> through the use of careless phrases, he nevertheless did not wish to appear to have anything in common with their errors. This is especially evident from those words which immediately precede our passage:

“I know there are those who wish to seize upon these things and say: That the **Power** <term>Latin: *Virtus*; here referring to the divine energy or the Logos</term> proceeding from the Father of all things—which appeared to Moses, or Jacob, or Abraham—is called an **Angel** when it goes out to humans to announce the Father's commands; but is called **Glory** when it is shown in an incomprehensible vision; and is named a **Man** or a **Human** when it appears in whatever form the Father wills; and is called the **Word** <term>Logos</term> because it carries the Father’s speech to mortals.”

“They claim this Power can in no way be disjoined or separated from the Father, just as the light of the Sun on earth cannot be cut off or segregated from the Sun in heaven; and when the Sun sets, the light is taken away with it. In this way, they say, the Father—when He wills—makes His Power leap forth, and when He wills, He retracts it back into Himself. They teach that He makes Angels in this same way. However, it has been demonstrated that Angels exist and always remain as such, and do not return through dissolution back into that from which they were begotten.”

Therefore, just as when two people do the same thing, so also when they write the same thing, it is not actually the same. <note>This is a variation of the legal/philosophical maxim: *si duo faciunt idem, non est idem* (if two do the same thing, it is not the same), implying that the intent and context change the meaning of the act or word.</note>

# DISSERTATION

### Why **JUSTIN** and **TATIAN**, though using similar words, must be understood differently according to the distinct systems they embraced.

XVI. We have chosen to review these three erroneous concepts of the ancients regarding the Word <note>original Greek: Λόγῳ (Logō)</note> all the more willingly because they reveal the true origin of so many similar errors defended by more recent writers. Through a more accurate distinction of these errors, we intend not only to cause those "old wives' tales" of the ancient age to collapse but also to pave the way for establishing a sounder concept of the **hypostatic Word** <note>original Latin: Verbo hypostatico. This refers to the Word as a distinct, personal subsistence or individual reality within the Trinity, rather than just an abstract power or thought.</note>.

XVII. The first concept—though we leave it undecided for now whether it ever truly entered the minds of any of the ancients—has found many supporters among the moderns. Among these we must count **GUILLAUME POSTEL**, as is clear from his book *On the Generation of the Mediator*, chapter 13. The followers of **SPINOZA** <note>Baruch Spinoza, a philosopher known for "monism," the idea that everything is part of one single substance (God or Nature).</note> defend the same view, as is evident from the preface attached to his posthumous works; they do this because they believe it fits perfectly with that monstrous system of *one substance*. Nevertheless, various so-called "mystic" writers wander off playing the same tune. It is enough to name here the author of the book *Seder Olam* <note>Hebrew: "The Order of the World."</note>, who is thought to be **VAN HELMONT**; and **PIERRE POIRET**, who in his *Divine Economy* (Book I, chapter 4, section 4) provides this paraphrase of the beginning of our Gospel:

"**In the beginning** (meaning, in eternity) **was the Word** (the idea, form, or speech of God within Himself regarding Himself). **And the Word was with God** (meaning, it was in the essence of God, and was nothing else but God). **And the Word was God Himself** (that is, that which God saw in Himself—that internal form and thought, that Representation in which He was eternally occupied—did not display the ideas of creatures, natures, and essences which differ from the divine essence: but was God Himself: **the Form and Idea of God Himself**). **All things were made through Him**, that which they are: (here you see the origin not only of existing things, but of the Ideas of all things, and of all notions, truths, possibilities, goodness, and everything whatsoever that concerns both the intelligible and the existing world and creatures). **And without Him nothing was made that was made**: (Nothing was made intelligible, thinkable, or possible without Him..."

XVIII. This is not the place to fully dissect Poiret’s entire system regarding the Holy Trinity. In that system—following the work of **GUILLAUME POSTEL** <note>original: POSTELLO; a French Renaissance polymath known for his universalist religious theories.</note> cited previously—the *Son of God* is understood as nothing more than *God’s Idea of Himself, or the Knowledge of simple Intelligence*. Nor shall we dismantle it here with the same weapons usually deployed against the **Sabellians** <note>A 3rd-century group who believed the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons, but merely three "modes" or "masks" worn by one God.</note>. Furthermore, we shall not stir up the famous question entangled in this reasoning concerning the *Idea of possible things*. Poiret, along with many others, distinguishes this "Idea of possible things" from "God’s Idea of Himself" in a way that seems to us quite unphilosophical <note>original Greek: ἀφιλοσόφως (aphilosophōs)</note>. In truth, that idea is nothing other than the Idea of the divine Power itself, a point we believe has been brilliantly settled by the most celebrated theologian of Herborn, **ABRAHAM PUNGLER**. For our present purpose, it is enough to point out how poorly this concept fits the sketch of the **Word** <note>original Greek: Λογου (Logou)</note> provided by our Evangelist <note>The author refers to John the Apostle, author of the fourth Gospel.</note>, and how much violence is openly done to the words of the Holy Spirit through him.

XIX. I will not dwell now on the fact that Poiret understands *the beginning* to mean *eternity* itself. Not only can he produce no example of such a meaning, but the very nature of the matter plainly overthrows it; for "beginning"—whether it denotes the cause of a dependent existence or its starting point—is diametrically opposed to eternity. Even more removed from all reason is Poiret’s claim that *to be with God* is equivalent to *to be in the essence of God*. Not only is this notion forced upon the text without any authority from the small word *with* <note>original Greek: προς (pros); the author argues this preposition implies a relationship between two distinct entities, not just being "inside" one.</note>, but it would also make the grand style of the Holy Spirit guilty of "saying the same thing twice." If we accept this explanation, *to be with God* and *to be God* mean exactly the same thing. Anything conceived as being within the essence of God, because of God's simplicity <note>A theological term meaning God is not "made of parts," so His attributes are identical to His being.</note>, is God Himself. Added to this, the entire second verse would be nothing but a useless repetition if no deeper meaning lay beneath the phrasing. Consequently, Poiret took no account of that verse in his paraphrase.

XX. But there are also so many subsequent attributes and qualities assigned to this **Word**...

...it would be permitted to strangely twist the works written about him, unless he were personally distinct from God. What suitable reason, I ask, can be given for why the *Idea* or *Form of God* should be called his *Son* and *Only Begotten*? It does not escape my notice how **POIRET** <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719) was a French mystic and philosopher who tried to combine the rationalism of Descartes with mystical Christianity.</note> explains these things. For he considers the Divinity in the abstract, apart from this *Idea*; as if the Divinity, in order to think directly, seeks a luminous and calming object, and since in this respect it exists in darkness and restlessness, it would urgently desire to be liberated from them. And since this same Divinity is most active, he considers this *activity* as the *Father*. This Father—through a dark *desire*, through a restless *activity*, through vivid *efforts*, and through the impulse of his own power—produces the one who is the essential *Image of the Father*, the *Idea, Light, Truth, Eternal Word*, and *Beloved Son*, etc. See *The Divine Economy*, Book I, chapter 14, section 15 <note>original: *Oecon. div. Lib. I. cap. 14. §. 15.*</note>.

We hear here the sounds of words that are not only completely unknown to Scripture but also contain something repugnant to the supreme Majesty of God, unless you wish to soften them through a very harsh metaphor. If, however, anyone thinks that fairness requires us to assume the Author spoke allegorically rather than literally (which would be too crude), then he should have been required to explain what *darkness, desire, restlessness,* and *effort* in the depths of the <term>Deity</term> <note>The essential nature or essence of God.</note> could possibly mean in a way that is fitting for God's dignity. Since he did not do this, we rightly pronounce all these ideas to be unintelligible. They are not fit for explaining the concept of <term>generation</term> <note>In traditional theology, "generation" refers to the eternal relationship where the Son originates from the Father without a beginning in time.</note>—which was their intended purpose—but rather for plunging that concept into even deeper Cimmerian darkness <note>A common scholarly reference to the Cimmerians of ancient myth, who were said to live in a land of perpetual mist and gloom; it signifies total obscurity.</note>.

XXI. Setting aside these words and examining the matter itself more deeply, we conclude most clearly that there is no appearance of truth in the notion that *God's Idea of himself* can be considered as a *Son* produced by God. This is because we cannot imagine anything in God prior to the *Idea of Himself*, even in our simplest conceptualizing. For if the essential *activity* of God is to be named the *Father*, then that *Idea* would necessarily constitute the essence of the Father; and thus, the same *Idea* would be both *Father* and *Son*, which is a contradiction. For what is *Activity* but *Thought joined with consciousness*? And how can God be conceived as being perfectly conscious of Himself, except by possessing an adequate *Idea* of Himself? Furthermore, it is certain that the order of thinking, which

...[the process of thinking as it] occurs in us has no place in God, and much less can such a series of thoughts be attributed to God, through which one is produced from another, like a *Son* from a *Father*. But let us grant that we are permitted, because of the weakness of our intellect, to distinguish and arrange the thoughts of God—which is especially useful in the matter of the [Divine] Decrees <note>The "Divine Decrees" refer to God's eternal purposes or plans, such as the decree to create the world or to save humanity.</note>, because of the diversity and order of the objects they concern—nevertheless, all that distinction vanishes when the *Thought of God about Himself* is taken into account. For that thought falls under no distinction, but rather constitutes the deepest and most inward depth, so to speak, of the divine essence and the internal root of all its activity. For absolutely no thought in God can be placed before the *thought of Himself* by any abstraction. 

That very fabricated *desire, activity, and effort* [described by Poiret] will not only require an object but will pre-require it. Since, however, this pre-required object cannot be anything other than the *Idea of God*, it follows that either the alleged desire, activity, and effort of God is directed toward nothing, or that Idea must already be assumed to exist in act before we conceive of God as being active concerning it. This can be further deduced through those arguments by which our theologians prove that the *Knowledge of Simple Intelligence* <term>Scientia simplicis Intelligentiæ: A technical term in Scholastic theology referring to God's knowledge of all possible things that could exist, considered independently of His will to actually create them.</term> must be considered as the foundation of the most perfect Will. Therefore, since this knowledge appears to us in God as the first source of all divine thoughts, every reason vanishes why this *Idea* or *Form of God*, which **POIRET** understands as the *Word*, can appear to us as the Son; since it is rather the Principle, and thus in a certain way the *Father*, of that *Activity* which **POIRET** calls the *Father*.

To adapt this phrase to his own hypothesis, **POIRET** flees to a gross error—claiming that the essence of divine life is communicated to souls themselves. What of his *coming*, what of his *incarnation*? Will this be the work of the *Idea of God* considered abstractly from his activity? ...will there be an end to the distortions in this matter if Poiret is to be listened to? XXIII. Therefore, the empty boasting of this most sharp-witted man departs quite far from both modesty and truth. He does not hesitate to claim that among the "teachers of the letter" <note>Poiret's dismissive term for traditional theologians who focus on the literal text rather than mystical insights.</note> there will be many who judge by human reason that he interprets John's words in a sense too sublime to apply to the Apostle and his contemporaries; he argues that judgment regarding the thoughts of those who have attained the light of the Holy Spirit should not be made from the "carnal state of men." Yet Poiret’s interpretation breathes anything but that pretended sublimity. For if you remove the hypotheses he has fashioned "without scriptural basis" <note>original: <term>ἀγράφως</term> (agraphos)</note>, nothing more remains hidden under the Apostle’s magnificent opening than what any Gentile philosopher could learn from the light of Reason alone: namely, that God, as the most perfect Mind, possesses an Idea of Himself which pertains to the essence of God and was thus co-eternal with God. How much more sublime are the thoughts of those who—following the thread of Scripture itself—show that in these words are revealed the most hidden foundations of the Mystery of Redemption? These foundations are things which no Reason attains, which "flesh and blood" does not teach, and which will be the eternal subject of the deepest admiration and celebration.

### DISSERTATION

...came forth. We rightly look for examples of this improper <note>original: <term>catachrestici</term>; referring to a word used in a strained or non-literal way</note> usage. Therefore, SERVETUS <note>Michael Servetus (c. 1511–1553), a Spanish physician and theologian whose radical views on the Trinity led to his condemnation by both Catholics and Protestants.</note> argues in vain in the passage cited on folio 50, contending that *the sound doctrine of Christ understands the "Word was with God" to mean that this Mystery <note>original: <term>Sacramentum</term></note> was from the beginning hidden in the divine mind until the fullness of time came.* Without provided examples of such a meaning for these words, his claim is rejected with the same ease with which it is asserted.

XXVI. But it is even more compelling that the same Word <note>original: $\lambda o \gamma o \varsigma$ (Logos)</note>, who was *with God*, is established as being *God* himself. No one would interpret this as referring to any kind of relationship between God and His creatures, unless they intended to introduce an absolute necessity into divine decrees, creation, and all modes of divine revelation.

XXVII. Add to this that John, in his Prologue, speaks in such a way that it clearly appears that he who is first called the **Word**, and afterwards the **only-begotten Son of God, distinct from the Father**, is the very same person he eventually names **Jesus Christ**. To blunt the force of this "battering ram" of an argument, Servetus distinguishes between the *Word* and the *Son of God* in such a way that he denies that the *Word*—which existed from the beginning, indeed from eternity—was the *Son of God*. For he says that the Son was "assumed" by the Word; or rather, that the Word was like an eternal seed by which the Son of God was generated in time. From this it follows that he completely denies that the only-begotten Son of God existed at all before Jesus was born of Mary. For this reason, it is incorrectly asserted in Volume II, Part I of the *English Library* <note>original: *Bibliothecæ Angl.*, likely referring to the *Bibliothèque Angloise*, a 18th-century journal that reviewed scholarly works.</note> that SERVETUS believed in the pre-existence of Jesus Christ, since he carefully distinguishes the pre-existing Word from the "Son of God" or "Jesus Christ." Hence, in the passage cited on folio 7, he says: *They have philosophized poorly, those who deny that the man is the Son so that they might make a Son out of the Word; however, the truth of the matter is otherwise, and John thought it more fitting to say "the Word" than "the Son"; indeed, by reason of the Word, the flesh is called the Son.* This exception is opposed not only by everything that argues for the Deity of the Son, but also by the entire context of John’s Gospel, from which it is clearer than the midday sun that one and the same Subject is being described throughout the whole Prologue.

XXVIII. To destroy this connection, SERVETUS devises two points. First, he attacks it directly and tries to make it appear absurd, pretending that if the Word were the Son of God, then "generation"—and indeed "eternal generation"—would have to apply to the Word as well. However, he is willing to concede neither. He acknowledges no generation of the Word...

### ON THE PERSONALITY OF THE WORD.

...or the powerful command of God, through which the ages were founded, and then also that it was applied to Christ: and on that foundation the work could be ascribed to Christ, which through the Word—even before it was united to Christ—was performed of old. How great a train of the most perverse sense, good God, lies hidden here? Can it really be said of one who, a long time later, possesses as his own the sword with which some Hero once performed stupendous deeds, that those things were carried out by him which the sword accomplished in the hand of the Hero? By the same logic, would not the world also have been made through the Angels or the Prophets or any other reborn persons in whom the same Word is said to be manifested?

XXX. But also, although he boldly asserted that generation does not apply to the true Word but only to the flesh of Christ, he nevertheless thinks that this generation—long before it happened—can be improperly joined with the very utterance of the Word, insofar as a preparation for the future generation of Christ was contained in it. This is illustrated on leaf 67b by this absurd simile: *Just as among legal experts one is said to be dead from the day the wound was inflicted that caused his death, so the Son of God Jesus is said to be born and begotten from the day the Word was uttered, from which he essentially has his every manner of being; and the Son of God was made the Son of Man because, having been eternally born of God, he is afterwards born in time of man, although there is only one thing.* Who is not weary of such trifles? Where do legal experts speak like this? And even if they did, what would that expression have in common with this phrase of Scripture? The wounded person exists as an individual and begins to die from the lethal wound received. But here, "generation" is understood of a subject that will exist long afterward—hardly a situation where he could even *begin* to be generated. Add to this that he begs the question <note>original: *principium petatur*, a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premises.</note> when the Word or Wisdom is considered not as the begotten *Son* but as the generating *Father*, which we have proved to be not only clearly unwritten in Scripture <term>ἄγραφον (agraphon): "unwritten," referring to doctrines not found in the Bible</term>, but also contrary to Scripture <term>ἀντίγραφον (antigraphon): "counter-written," or directly contradicting the biblical text</term>. Finally, by this reasoning, such an "eternal generation" is attributed to the Son as could be ascribed to any creatures whatsoever, whose existence was the effect of the eternal will and divine power.

# DISSERTATION

Let us briefly summarize and touch upon his arguments, which are scattered with strange confusion throughout that poisonous book <note>The author refers to Michael Servetus’s "On the Errors of the Trinity" or "The Restoration of Christianity," which were considered heretical by both Catholics and Protestants.</note>. **First, he argues from the word itself**, the <term>Logos<gloss>The Word</gloss></term>. Who will endure it, he says on leaf 47, when people pull Scripture in a direction other than what the proper meaning of the word allows? For *Logos* does not signify that "philosophical entity," but rather the oracle, the voice, the speech, or the utterance of God. Indeed, it is derived from the verb *lego*, which means "I speak." He adds: To investigate the meaning of a word, one must examine the passages where the Holy Spirit produced that same word, and there is not a single letter in the entire Bible that proves that imaginary meaning of "the Word" <note>Servetus argued that "Logos" only meant a spoken word of God, not a pre-existent divine person.</note>.

But should not words be understood according to the subject matter they describe? Therefore, when Scripture speaks of the <term>Word</term> and assigns to it both spiritual attributes and actions, and simultaneously distinguishes it from the Father, is this not a sufficient foundation for understanding the *Logos* as a specific person distinct from God the Father? Is it not impudently proclaimed that this never happens in the sacred pages, when the *Word as a heavenly witness* is introduced in 1 John 5:7? Or when the *Word of God* is asserted to be *the name of him who sat upon the white horse, who was called Faithful and True, who judges and fights in justice*, etc., in Revelation 19:11 and following? Or when the entire <term>Prologue of John<gloss>The first chapter of the Gospel of John</gloss></term> is nothing but a linked review of the personal attributes and operations of the Word? Or when this Word is the same as the <term>Solomonic Wisdom<gloss>The personification of Wisdom in the Book of Proverbs</gloss></term>, which I have formally proven in my discourse on "Supreme Wisdom" to designate a personal subject distinct from God the Father? We can therefore be certain of the notion we assign to the Word, as we closely follow the Scripture, in which that profane guest is a stranger.

His blindness—not only in his barbaric style but also in his empty observation regarding the <term>etymology<gloss>The origin and history of a word</gloss></term> of *Logos*—demonstrates that he is equally dim-sighted in matters of grammar and rhetoric. Let us grant that *Logos* properly designates "speech." Is it then unusual for attributes to be put in place of the subjects themselves? Has not the very word *Logos* passed into this usage among approved writers, as we shall show in due time? Indeed, is he not himself forgetful of his own observation when, in chapter 2, leaf 26b, he wants "the Word" to be understood as God himself—and thus the subject from whom the Word is produced?

XXXIII. Thirdly, he fights against us from a distance through consequences, slanderously objecting to *polytheism* <note>The belief in multiple gods</note>—as is the custom of men of that sort <note>original: "istius furfuris hominum" — a disparaging idiom for heretical groups</note>—because we distinguish the Word from God, with whom He was, and we assert that He was indeed with the Father, but not with the *divine essence* or with the *Holy Spirit*. This consequence, if it is valid, burdens not us but Scripture itself, whose assertions we simply adhere to. What, however, is more unjust than this objection, when Scripture, while distinguishing the Word from the Father and the Holy Spirit, nevertheless hammers home the Unity of God in the same breath and at every given opportunity? From this so often repeated testimony, it is clear that whoever places such a distinction between *these three* as if it were a distinction of *three individuals* divided in number, has least of all grasped the sense of Scripture, which cannot so openly contradict itself. While our Church adheres to this testimony of Scripture, no charge of *Polytheism*—which tears the divine essence into several separately existing individuals—can be brought against us with any appearance of truth. Just as they rest on no foundation, they also plainly destroy the idea of a Most Perfect Being. For while they imagine "emanations" or "emissions" from the divine essence—which are themselves said to participate in the divine essence, albeit in a lesser degree—among which **Boehme** <note>Jacob Boehme (1575–1624), a German mystic and philosopher whose complex, idiosyncratic theology often drew the ire of Lutheran orthodox scholars.</note> specifically names the *Word* and *Sophia* <note>The Greek word for "Wisdom," often personified in mystical traditions.</note>, both of which he considers distinct from the "ground" of the Trinity, who does not see that such things are diametrically opposed to the supreme perfection, simplicity, and immutability of the divine essence? Therefore, although according to the sound of the words, "Deity" might seem to be attributed to the **Logos** through this error, in reality, while he is subordinated to the one supreme and primary God, that same Deity is overturned.

XXXVI. Let the *primary error* <note>original: "πρωτον ψευδος" (proton pseudos), the fundamental false premise of an argument.</note> alone be noted, from which these monsters of "linkages"—whether Platonic or Cabbalistic <note>Referring to the Jewish mystical tradition of the Kabbalah, which describes the divine as a series of emanations (Sefirot).</note>—flow. It consists in the idea that among the attributes of God there is included a certain fertile power of begetting beings similar to himself out of himself. In this way, the Gnostics long ago learned from the Platonists, who, as **Proclus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD).</note> testifies in Book V, Chapter 29, asserted: *Generating, producing, and providing are characteristic of gods, insofar as they are gods.* <note>original: "το γεναν, και παραγειν, και το προνοειν, θεων εςιν ιδιον, καθοσον εισι θεοι."</note> From this the Valentinians <note>Followers of Valentinus, a 2nd-century Gnostic teacher who taught that the divine realm consisted of pairs of male and female "Aeons."</note> took the opportunity to divide the <term>Aeons<gloss>In Gnostic systems, these are the various emanations or powers that come from the ultimate divine source.</gloss></term> into males and females, from whose marriage others would spring forth. And since the "Enthusiasts" adopt this same principle, it is clear that they form a plainly crass and corporeal concept of the divine essence. They are not even afraid to profess this more openly when they make it their habit to compare the order of emanations they imagine with **Chemical** <note>Referring to Alchemists (*Chymici*), who used laboratory processes as metaphors for spiritual or divine transformations.</note> processes. But I have no desire to stir this stagnant marsh <note>original: "camarinam hanc movere" — a classical proverb referring to a marsh that, if drained or disturbed, released a foul stench; it means to avoid making a bad situation worse by meddling with it.</note> further now, since there is nothing to fear from it that would prejudice the personality of the **Logos** which we are defending here.

->I.<-

Among the enemies of the supreme Deity of our Savior, there are those who—while recognizing that the subject described in the Prologue of the Gospel of John is indeed a personal subsistence <note>original: "suppositum personall," a technical term in scholastic theology referring to an individual existence or person.</note> distinct from God the Father—strain every nerve of their intellect to obscure the testimony given there regarding the divine excellence of the **Logos** <note>The "Word" (Greek: *Logos*), referring to the second person of the Trinity.</note> through their distortions. Therefore, lest a testimony of such weight—which has always been rightly and deservedly esteemed among the primary arguments for the Deity of the Son—should waver in any part, it will be helpful to flush out their hiding places as well. In doing so, we aim to cut off every opportunity for even the slightest hesitation regarding the *Subject of our Prologue* and his true excellence. 

While we do this, I think no one will expect us to speak here formally <note>original: "ex professo," meaning to treat a subject as one's primary profession or in great detail.</note> about the Son's Deity, or feel that we ought to, since our only intention is to defend the thesis proven in our Commentary on the Prologue of John from the nature of the words and phrases: namely, that the supreme Deity of the Word, equal to the Father, is most clearly described therein, against the tricks of our adversaries. We undertake this with all the more eagerness because the Emperor **Julian** <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363 AD), the last pagan Roman emperor, who wrote "Against the Galileans" to critique Christian doctrine.</note> himself, when arguing against the Christians, recognized the force of this logical consequence. In order to treat this matter more distinctly, we shall establish two classes of those who each strive to twist our passage <note>Referring to the Prologue of the Gospel of John.</note> to suit their own hypothesis. A judge of these matters is far too harsh if he expects such refined purity and **precision** <note>original: "ἀκρίβειαν" (akribeia).</note> in the expressions of the Fathers of the primitive Church as might now be rightly required after so many centuries of practice, with scholarship more highly cultivated, and resources provided in far greater abundance. Nevertheless, a defense of him was undertaken by **George Bull** in *Defense of the Nicene Faith*, part II, chapter 4, section 10; **Ellies Du Pin** in *Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*, Volume I, page 67; and **Jean Le Clerc** under the year 168 AD. For my part, however, I harbor a not insignificant suspicion that neither side has fully grasped **Theophilus**. Regarding the *Deity of the Son*, there occurs at least no reason for doubting in his words that he thought correctly. For he confesses his existence in express words before he was begotten or produced; fairness forbids interpreting these words in a worse sense without a weighty cause. Truly, however, on the article concerning the *generation of the Son*, he wanders from the [orthodox] line, as he denies it is eternal, while he joins it with the beginning of all things. Thus, through that "generation," he seems to understand nothing other than a certain mode of manifestation of the **Word** <note>The Logos</note> which previously subsisted within the essence of God. We are confirmed in this opinion by his own words occurring in the following passages, where he speaks thus:

> God indeed and the Father of all things (note here the restriction of the word **God** <note>original: "Theos"</note> by the addition of **Father of all things** <note>original: "patēr tōn holōn"</note>, which was a title proper to the First Person in the most ancient Church, as is clear even from the Creed) is neither enclosed in a place, nor is he found in a place. For there is no place in which he himself might rest. But his **Word** <note>The Logos</note>, through which he created all things, existing as the power and wisdom of the Father, assumes the person of the Father and Lord of all things; he is the one who came into Paradise. And do not think, as the poets and writers of myths claim, that the sons of God were born from sexual union, but understand that in this place is described the **Word** <note>The Logos</note> perpetually existing and implanted in the heart of God the Father. For before any of those things which were made had come to be, he had this counselor, as one who was his mind and prudence. But when he had already decided to establish those things he had deliberated upon, he brought forth <note>original: "genuit prolatum"</note> this **Word**, the firstborn of all creation; nor in the meantime was God emptied of his Word, but [He was] begetting the Word and always conversing with his Word.

Thus he clearly declares that he indicates such a "generation" of the **Word** <note>original: "Logos"</note> which was contrary neither to his pre-existence nor to his personal union with the Father. He further proves this by a citation of our Prologue <note>The beginning of the Gospel of John.</note>, adding: "Wherefore the holy scriptures teach us, and all the spirit-bearing men <note>original: "pneumatophoroi," a term for divinely inspired writers</note>, among whom John says: *In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.*" <note>original Greek: "Ὅθεν διδάσκουσιν ἡμᾶς αἱ ἁγίαι γραφαὶ, καὶ πάντες οἱ πνευματοφόροι, ἐξ ὧν Ἰωάννης λέγει· ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν Θεόν."</note>

IV. **TERTULLIAN** <note>An influential North African theologian (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) known for his prolific Latin writings.</note> is brought into this same line of interpretation. We do not deny that he may have stirred a just suspicion against himself through various obscure statements. Thus, a passage from *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 45, is cited against him, where he says: *The Prophets and Apostles do not hand down that the world was made by God merely by His appearing and approaching matter, because they named no matter at all: but first that Wisdom* <note>original: "Sophia"</note> *was established, the beginning of His ways for His works; then also the Word* <note>original: "Sermo"</note> *was brought forth, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. Therefore, the "bringing forth" of the Word in these words is not the production of the *essence* of the Word, but the production of things through the Word in that manner which He had previously defined with the Word. This sense is clear from his words in *Against Praxeas*, chapter 5: *Even if God had not yet sent His Word, He nonetheless held him with and in Reason itself within Himself, by silently thinking and arranging with Himself those things which He was soon to say through the Word.* And again in chapter 6: *As soon as God willed those things,*

*...which He had arranged within Himself by the reason of Wisdom <note>original: "Sophiæ"</note> and the Word <note>original: "Sermone"</note>, to bring forth into substances and species; He indeed first brought forth the Word itself, having within it its own inseparable principles, Wisdom, so that through Him all things might be made, by whom they had been conceived and arranged—and indeed already made, so far as God’s mind was concerned. For they lacked this: that they might also be known and held openly in their own species and substances. Then, therefore, the Word itself also took on its own form and ornament, sound and voice, when God said: "Let there be light." This is the perfect birth of the Word, when it proceeds from God: created by Him first for thought under the name of Wisdom: "The Lord created me as the beginning of His ways." <note>Proverbs 8:22</note> Then generated for the purpose of action: "When He prepared the heaven, I was there with Him."* <note>Proverbs 8:27</note> From these words it is clear at once that the system of **TERTULLIAN** <note>An early Latin theologian from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD).</note> is quite consistent with **THEOPHILUS**, as he likewise considers the revelation of the Son in the creation of the world as His "perfect birth," distinguishing it from an "imperfect" state which he supposes existed during the arrangement of this work. There is no time now to confirm this with other parallel passages.

V. With easier effort, those claims can be wiped away which have been made against other Fathers distinguished for their praised orthodoxy. Let **IRENAEUS** <note>Bishop of Lyon (2nd century AD) and famous defender of the faith against Gnosticism.</note> suffice as an example. **DANIEL ZWICKER** <note>A 17th-century Unitarian who argued that the early Church did not believe in the Trinity.</note>, growing insolent through the concessions of **PETAVIUS** <note>Denis Pétau, a Jesuit scholar who admitted some early Fathers wrote ambiguously about the Trinity.</note>, tries with every effort to claim Irenaeus for his own (*Irenicum Irenicorum*, p. 42 sq., and in its new confirmation § 166, p. 361 sq.). How impudently this is done is evident from the most eloquent passages in which Irenaeus roundly confesses the Word to be one with the Father through essence. **MASSUET** <note>René Massuet, a Benedictine editor of Irenaeus's works.</note> accumulated these in his preliminary dissertation on Irenaeus, III, Article V, § 49 seq. Let that passage from Book IV, chapter 20 suffice: *“For God did not need these (Angels) to make the things which He Himself had pre-defined to be made, as if He did not have His own hands. For the Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, are always present with Him, through whom and in whom He made all things freely and spontaneously, to whom He also speaks, saying: 'Let us make man in our image and likeness'; He Himself receiving from Himself the substance of creatures, and the pattern of things made, and the figure of ornaments in the world.”* See also **NOURRY**’s *Apparatus for the Second Century*, Dissertation VI, Article 6, and **NATALIS ALEXANDER**, Second Century, Dissertation VII.

Perhaps, however, he allowed such things to slip out not with the intention of refuting the Deity of Christ, but because, enticed by the tenets of **Platonic Philosophy** and swept away by the fervor of refuting **Sabellius** <note>A 3rd-century priest who taught that the Father, Son, and Spirit were merely different "modes" or masks of a single person, rather than three distinct persons.</note>, he did not recognize the obviousness of the contradiction. ...we could establish with [evidence], because the **Arians** <note>A 4th-century theological movement that held that Jesus Christ was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> often impiously trifled with the term <term>Logos</term> <note>Greek for "Word," referring to the Second Person of the Trinity as described in the Gospel of John.</note> on the occasion of this distinction. In demonstrating the absurdity of this distinction, various Church Fathers go into exhaustive—and in our view, perhaps unnecessary—detail. For it matters little to the heart of the matter whether the "Word of God" is used with different meanings in different passages of Scripture. The only question was whether in those specific passages, such as our Prologue <note>Referring to the first chapter of the Gospel of John: "In the beginning was the Word..."</note>, where the Arians conceded that the "substantial Word" was being discussed, it was to be understood as an absolutely divine substance rather than a created one. IX. The **Semi-Arians**, for their part, spoke more cautiously and rejected that distinction used by the "crasser" or more extreme Arians. This is evident from the confession of **Basil of Ancyra** and his associates, which **Epiphanius** included in *Against Heresies* 73, section 12. It is also seen in the formula known as the <term>Macrostichos</term> <note>original: "μακροϛιχος," meaning "the long-lined [creed]," a detailed theological statement produced by Eastern bishops in 344 AD to explain their position to the West.</note>, which Bishop **Eudoxius** presented to the Bishop of Rome after it was composed in the Eastern Council of the Semi-Arians; it is included in the *Volumes of the Councils* for the year 344, to say nothing of other records. Nevertheless, their underlying intent was the same: they denied that the Son enjoys absolute independence, eternity, and unity of essence with the Father. **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the famous church historian whose views on the Trinity were often seen as subordinating the Son to the Father.</note> alone will prove this point; along with **Origen**, he is the greatest hero of the Neo-Arians. Despite the ambiguity of his phrasing, the most learned men—such as **Natalis Alexander** (in *Dissertations on the 4th Century*, 17), **Jean Le Clerc** (writing against Cave, especially in *Critical Epistle* 2), and **Bernard de Montfaucon** (in the *Preliminary Discourse on Eusebius's Commentary on the Psalms*, chapter 6)—have proven that he was imbued with the errors of Arius.

-># DISSERTATION<-

It is plainly evident that **John Campanus**, **John Silvanus**, the **Sandians**, and others who have stuck in the same mire, as well as the **Neo-Arians** <note>A term for 17th and 18th-century theologians who revived the 4th-century Arian view that Jesus was a created being subordinate to God the Father.</note>, **William Whiston**, **Samuel Clarke**, and others in Britain—who teach this heresy more subtly and plausibly than was done in the past—leave no stone unturned to weaken the illustrious description of the Johannine **Word** <note>original: "Verbi Joannei," referring to the Logos in the Gospel of John.</note> by similar reasoning. The former [Whiston], in his response to the observations of **Allix**, declares his faith regarding the **Logos** <note>original: "ΛΟΓΩΙ," the Greek term for "Word."</note> among other things as follows: *VI. Jesus Christ is the pre-eternal Word of God, the firstborn of all creatures, the beginning of the creation of God, a divine person created or begotten by the Father before all ages, or before all subordinate creatures, visible and invisible. VII. God the Father first created, made, ordered, and arranged, and still governs all subordinate creatures, visible and invisible, through the Word and His Son as through a minister and active instrument. VIII. Jesus Christ, the Word and Son of God, is a divine person, much inferior to his Father in nature, attributes, and perfections, etc.* Nevertheless, he does not wish to be numbered among the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arius (c. 250–336 AD), who held that the Son was not co-eternal with the Father.</note>, because he claims that <term>Arius</term> <note>A priest in Alexandria whose views on the nature of Christ sparked the first major Trinitarian controversy.</note> went too far in using the phrases "there was a time when he was not" <note>original: "ην ὁτε οὐκ ην"</note> and "he was from nothing" <note>original: "ἐξ οὐκ ὀντων ην"</note>. **Clarke** is in agreement with him, explaining his views with similar reasoning in *The Scripture-Doctrine of the Trinity*, Part II. There, on one hand, he distinguishes himself from those who want the Son to be **God-of-Himself** <note>original: "αὐτοθεον" (autotheon), meaning possessing divinity independently rather than derived from the Father.</note>, independent and without origin; but on the other hand, he blames the Arians for declaring the Son to be "from nothing" or "first-created" <note>original: "πρωτοκτισον"</note>. In the same work (section 17), he expresses his mind more clearly: he does not believe the existence of the Son should be derived from the Father *by a mere necessity of nature*, but *from an act of the Father’s incomprehensible power and will*. By this reasoning, he clearly shows that he differs from the "crass" Arians only in words, not in reality. He essentially identifies as a **Semi-Arian**, repeatedly explaining his opinion using the words of **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century bishop and historian who held a middle-ground position in the Arian controversy.</note>.

However, since its defenders claim that the **Prologue of John** <note>The opening section of the Gospel of John (1:1-18), which identifies Jesus as the Word made flesh.</note> favors them in more ways than one, it will be our duty to show how empty this boast is, since this very "fortress" can most successfully be used to fight against them. This is a matter that should not be neglected, because in today’s controversies with the **Anti-Trinitarians**, the views of the *Socininians* <note>Followers of Fausto Sozzini, who denied the pre-existence of Christ and the Trinity.</note> are usually given the most—or even the only—consideration. # DISSERTATION
<meta>catchword: retor-</meta>

...the version of the **Seventy Translators** <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> passed into the usage of the Writers of the New Testament especially, in which it most frequently occurs in place of the name **Elohim** <note>original: "אלהים" (Elohim)</note>. From this, all the arguments by which we are accustomed to provide proof—both that **Elohim** designates, abstractly and properly, the Most Perfect Being, and that it is used for the three persons of the divine essence taken together—militate against our Opponents.

XV. But let us proceed to the application of this alleged notion to the matter at hand. **CLARKE** <note>Samuel Clarke (1675–1729), an English clergyman and philosopher whose book *The Scripture-Doctrine of the Trinity* was accused of Arian tendencies.</note>, whose footsteps we follow here most closely, deduces from this (in the place cited, § 25) *that the reason why the Son is sometimes named "God" in the New Testament is not so much to be placed in the divine substance, metaphysically understood, but in his relative attributes and the divine authority which was communicated to him over us by the Father.* We reject this hypothesis as being contrary to reason and *faith*, and indeed, according to the very principles of its Defender, *contradictory*.

XVI. When we consult reason, it teaches us: I. That *divine majesty* cannot be attributed to anything except a divine nature. For to exercise that majesty requires <term>omniscience</term> <note>The state of knowing everything.</note> and <term>omnipotence</term> <note>The quality of having unlimited power.</note>, which must have an infinite nature as their subject and foundation, and by the very nature of the thing, these are incommunicable. II. That such a distinction between a "supreme God" and a "subordinate God" is the pure and simple <term>polytheism</term> <note>The belief in or worship of more than one god.</note> of the pagans. III. That there are only two kinds of things. For whatever presents itself to us under the idea of a Being is either <term>necessary</term> <note>Something that must exist and cannot not-exist; specifically, God.</note> or <term>contingent</term> <note>Something that exists only because something else caused it; a created thing.</note>. The former is uncreated; the latter is created. Here, however, while reason and revelation remain silent, a new class of Beings is imagined, as a being that is neither necessary nor contingent, neither uncreated nor created, is brought onto the stage.

XVII. Regarding the latter argument, he replies in **An answer to the Author of some considerations** (p. 227, 228): **A.** That Orthodox Theologians accept a third kind, namely, a thing produced not through *creation*, but through *generation* <note>The theological concept that the Son is "begotten" of the Father's essence rather than "made" from nothing.</note>. However, the Orthodox derive this *generation* not from a free choice of will, but from the very necessity of the *nature* of God; by this means, that which is established through generation is exempt from the number of all contingent and created beings, so that it is regarded as something uncreated and necessary. **B.** Furthermore

**Gg 2**
<meta>catchword: God</meta>

[The opponent] wishes to turn the weapon back against us while arguing in this way: *Since the Creator of the world is the same as the Father, who established all things through the Son, if there could only be two types of being—Creator and Creature—it would follow from this either that the Son is the Father himself, or a mere creature; both of which are absurd.* But that which is brought forward here as a logical consequence is a mere <term>begging of the question</term> <note>original: "principii petitio"; a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premise.</note>: because we defend, along with the orthodox Church, that the Son is the Creator of the world in the unity of essence with the Father, and is directly called such in the Holy Scriptures.

XVIII. How much this error departs from the *analogy of faith* <note>The principle that individual Bible verses should be interpreted in accordance with the whole of Christian doctrine.</note> is clear from the following:

I. Because Scripture expressly calls the <term>Son</term> <note>original: "Filius"</note> <term>God</term> <note>original: "Deus"</note> with the highest emphasis, and ascribes to him every divine excellence that can be conceived in the mind, such that nothing can be brought forward as belonging to the Father alone, except for the personal relationship of being the *Father*.

II. Because if this were not so, the foundation of all hope—resting uniquely on the infinite value of the merit of Christ—would waver.

III. Because it attributes such excellence to the Son as to be the source of honor and worship equal to that given to the Father.

IV. Because specifically, such <term>divinity</term> <note>original: "Θεοτης" (Theotes)</note> is attributed by John to the <term>Word</term> <note>original: "ΛΟΓΩΙ" (Logoi)</note> which he already possessed with the Father before created things existed. Through this divinity, a majesty relative only to creatures cannot be understood, since creatures did not yet exist.

V. Because God protests so many times that he will not give his glory to another, which he would nevertheless do if he communicated his own majesty to a contingent being <note>A being whose existence is not necessary but depends on something else.</note> and established that same being as the object of worship.

XIX. We conclude that this entire system dissolves into a mere contradiction, because on one hand, true and properly so-called Deity is ascribed to the Son, and he is exempted from the number of created things; yet, on the other hand, in the place cited (Section 12), it is asserted: *the Son derives his essence and all his attributes from the Father as from a supreme cause; which is to be understood not as a necessary cause, but as an arbitrary one.* Hence we also read in Section 35: *Every action of the Son, both in the production of the world and in all other operations, is nothing but the exercise of the Father's power communicated to him in an ineffable way.* These statements destroy one another for a twofold reason. First, because he who is acknowledged to be without a beginning is nonetheless deprived of the necessity of existence, even though nothing...

If matter were produced through the eternal operation of the divine will and power, it would no more be necessary and independent than when it was produced through a temporal operation.* But we answer that the question here is not about a duration extended to a very great length, but about an infinite duration, which excludes every first moment of time, and is therefore free from succession; such a duration cannot apply to a thing produced outside of God. The second point, which involves a contradiction, consists in this: that he who is proposed as an object of divine worship is reduced to the same rank as *Angels and Prophets*, from whom he differs only by degree. For the same things ascribed here to the Son of God are entirely true regarding their own extraordinary works. Despite this, they [the Angels and Prophets] removed even the shadow of divine worship from themselves as far as possible. To avoid the appearance of this contradiction, he seeks to hide behind the term "ineffable mode." But the same could also be said of the power communicated to the Angels and Prophets over the whole universe—for example, Joshua’s power over the Sun and Moon, Moses’ over the sea and winds, and the Apostles’ over the dead, and even over Devils. And *if the mode is ineffable* <note>original: "ineffabilis"; something that cannot be expressed in words.</note>, why are so many terms used in explaining it which the Scripture does not know? Where does Scripture assert that the Father is the supreme Cause of all the attributes of the Son? Or that the name of <term>God</term> <note>original: "Θεου" (Theou)</note> is restricted only to relative attributes? Or that the Son created the world not by his own power but only by the Father’s? and so forth.

Specifically, there is a distinction concerning the person of the **WORD** <note>original: "ΛΟΓΟΥ" (Logos). How inappropriately **HERMAS** and **CLEMENT OF ROME** <note>Two of the "Apostolic Fathers," the earliest generation of Christian writers after the Apostles.</note> are brought in is clear from the fact that not even the name of the **WORD** [Logos] is found in the records attributed to them. Whatever the case may be, both can easily be cleared from the stain of this error. Although the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arius who believed that Jesus, the Son, was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> long ago cited **HERMAS** in support of their opinion—according to **Athanasius** <note>A 4th-century bishop of Alexandria and chief defender of Trinitarianism against Arianism.</note> in his *Letter to the African Bishops* and **Theodoret** <note>A 5th-century bishop and church historian.</note> in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 8—it is clear that they twisted the words of Hermas into a foreign meaning. XXVIII. With what right **Clement of Rome** <note>Bishop of Rome in the late 1st century.</note> is referred to here, no one will easily guess, unless he has observed the previously cited treatise (page 33) concerning the *Apostolic Constitutions*, which are said to be attributed to him. Furthermore, **Whiston** <note>William Whiston (1667–1752), an English scholar who famously defended Arian views and the authenticity of the *Apostolic Constitutions*.</note> gave a singular example of a fanatical mind when he struggled to claim canonical authority for this "miscarriage" of a work with the same intent—namely, to aid his own cause. Following others, and specifically the famous **Le Clerc** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a prominent theologian and critic.</note> in the first dissertation of the *Appendix to the Apostolic Fathers*, the most learned **Nonnius** <note>likely Marcellus Nonnius.</note>—who is "mine" on more than one account—taught this point abundantly in his inaugural dispute regarding the *Canonical Authority of the Song of Songs*, chapter 1, section 13, page 81 and following.

XXIX. Concerning the *Letters* attributed to **Ignatius** <note>Ignatius of Antioch (died c. 107 AD), an early Christian martyr and bishop.</note>, various passages can be brought forward from them which, if taken in a negative sense, are not far removed from Arianism. Indeed, it was from this very fortress that **Ussher** <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh.</note> fought to prove these letters were interpolated, while **Daillé** and **Larroque** fought to prove they were entirely fake. **Cotelier** showed in his notes on individual passages that the places cited for this purpose allow for a milder interpretation. It cannot be denied that such excellent testimonies for the supreme **Deity of Christ** occur in these very Letters that either tampering must be admitted, or a favorable explanation must be granted regarding the other parts. But there is also no small difference between the letters of Ignatius that are called the *shorter* and the *longer* ones; the latter provide a paraphrase of the former that more openly favors Arianism. This was also the reason why Whiston argued that the later [longer] versions were the genuine ones. But Le Clerc, in the second dissertation of the cited *Appendix*, most successfully drove back this wedge after others had done so.

XXX. Meanwhile, lest the accumulation of so many testimonies—which derive the Son’s subsistence from the Father in explicit words—should be a source of dread to anyone, this must be firmly held: the Orthodox Doctors of the Church who speak in this way attribute to the Son a mode of subsistence from the Father that does not exclude, but rather presupposes, the **necessity of existence** <note>In this context, "necessity" means that God exists by His own nature and cannot *not* exist; the author argues the Son shares this same essential necessity.</note>, which constitutes the formal nature of the Deity. This could be corroborated by six hundred testimonies, were it not superfluous to wander so far into a well-known matter.

XXXII. To be sure, lest I should seem to intentionally hide anything of importance, certain passages of the Fathers could be objected against this assertion, such as those excerpted by **Clarke** <note>Samuel Clarke (1675–1729), an English clergyman whose work "The Scripture-Doctrine of the Trinity" was accused of Arian tendencies.</note> in the cited book (§17, p. 249 ff.), which derive the generation of the Son from the **will** of the Father. From this, Clarke infers that they by no means deduced the Son from the mere necessity of the divine nature. But beyond the fact that we do not make all the <term>ἀφιλοσόφως</term> <note>original Greek: "unphilosophically"; here meaning without technical or metaphysical precision.</note> statements of the Fathers our own, nor would we wish to acknowledge all the witnesses brought forward as "Orthodox," it is at least manifest that these two predicates do not destroy one another. For by the necessity of His own nature, God wills to be such as He is. And since [He acts] according to His nature...

# ON THE DEITY OF THE WORD. <note>original: "DE ΛΟΓΟΥ DEITATE." The Greek word *Logos* refers to the "Word" of God as described in the Gospel of John.</note>

## Hh 2

<meta>catchword: BASI-</meta>

Since the personal relationship also belongs to the nature of God, it cannot be doubted that He *willed* this very thing most freely. Nor is this will a mere approval, but an effective activity that can be viewed as the principle of the generation of the Son. Hence, most of those who are cited—either in the context of the passages produced or in other places—have abundantly taught that they conceived of the generation of the Son as *voluntary* in such a way that they nonetheless recognized it as being simultaneously *necessary*. This is especially true since they were unaware of that subtle distinction between *necessary existence* and *eternal existence*. <note>The author suggests that the early Church Fathers did not see a conflict between something being "willed" by God and "existing eternally/necessarily."</note>

XXXIII. Thus, to illustrate this matter with a few examples: although **Novatian** <note>A 3rd-century Roman theologian; his work *On the Trinity* is one of the first major Latin treatments of the subject.</note> writes in *On the Trinity*, chapter 31: *From whom, when he himself willed, the Word was born as Son*; nevertheless, in almost the same breath he asserts that *the Father is always Father*. Since that which *always is* must surely belong to His essence, does it not follow that this very thing is necessary? **Alexander of Alexandria** <note>The Bishop of Alexandria who first opposed Arius; his writings were preserved by the historian Theodoret.</note>, in the excellent Letter that is cited and which **Theodoret** preserved in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, chapter 4, fights most strongly for the necessary existence of the Son, writing among other things:

> *It must necessarily be said that the Father is always Father. But He is Father because the Son is always present, on account of whom He is called Father. Therefore, since the Son is always present to Him, He is always a perfect Father, lacking nothing in goodness. — For he who denies that the splendor of glory exists, simultaneously removes the primary light of which it is the splendor. And if the image of God was not always there, it is clear that He whose image it is was not always there either, etc.*

For this reason, **Arius** <note>The priest whose teachings led to the Council of Nicaea; he argued the Son was a created being and not eternal.</note> in the following chapter 5, in his *Letter to Eusebius, Bishop of Nicomedia*, blames Alexander for publicly preaching:

> *God is always, the Son is always; Father and Son together; the Son coexists with the Unbegotten God* <note>original Greek: "ἀγεννήτως" — the author notes this should likely be read as "ἀγεννήτῳ" (with the Unbegotten One) to avoid a contradictory meaning.</note>; *He is always begotten, He is begotten of the Unbegotten; NB: NEITHER IN THOUGHT nor in any point of time does God precede the Son; always God, always Son; the Son exists from God Himself.*

The same may be said regarding **Hilary** <note>Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), a defender of the Nicene Creed against Arianism in the West.</note>,

<summary>This page argues that early Church Fathers viewed the Son's generation as both voluntary and necessary, using Novatian and Alexander of Alexandria as examples. It highlights Arius's own complaints as evidence that the orthodox position has always maintained the Son's eternal coexistence with the Father.</summary>

# DISSERTATION

<meta>catchword: nature-</meta>

By citing **Nazianzen** <note>Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390 AD), one of the "Cappadocian Fathers" known for his defense of the Trinity.</note>, **Nyssen** <note>Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–395 AD), another Cappadocian Father and younger brother of Basil the Great.</note>, and other most vigorous opponents of **Arianism** <note>A 4th-century belief that the Son was a created being, not equal to the Father.</note> and **Semi-Arianism** as if they favored their own cause, they make a mockery of a serious matter. When they add to these the principal Doctors of the Protestant Church—**Luther**, **Calvin**, and who else?—who can doubt that they have lost all sense of shame? Who would judge it out of character for such people to do what the journals of the learned report: that many of this sect, even though **Whiston** <note>William Whiston (1667–1752), an English theologian and scientist who was expelled from Cambridge for his Arian views.</note> disapproved, have subscribed their names to the Confession of the Church of England? And yet, that document begins as follows: *We believe that there is one certain nature and divine power, which we call God, and that it is distinct in three equal persons: in the Father, in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit; of the same power, the same majesty, the same eternity, the same divinity, and the same substance. And although these three persons are so distinct that the Father is not the Son, nor the Son the Holy Spirit or the Father, yet God is one, and that one God created heaven and earth and all things contained within the embrace of the heavens.*

XXXI. Meanwhile, lest the accumulation of so many testimonies—which derive the **subsistence** <note>A technical term in theology referring to the individual existence of the Persons within the Trinity.</note> of the Son from the Father in specific words—should be a source of dread to anyone, it must be firmly held that the Orthodox Doctors of the Church who speak this way attribute such a mode of subsistence from the Father to the Son in a way that does not exclude the **necessity of existence** (which constitutes the formal nature of Deity), but rather presupposes it. This could be corroborated by six hundred testimonies, were it not superfluous to wander so far into a well-known matter.

XXXII. To be sure—lest I should intentionally conceal anything of importance—certain passages of the Fathers excerpted by **Clarke** <note>Samuel Clarke (1675–1729), an influential philosopher and clergyman accused of Arianism for his book "The Scripture-Doctrine of the Trinity."</note> in the cited book (§ 17, p. 249 ff.) could be objected against this assertion, as they derive the generation of the Son from the "will" of the Father; from this, he infers that they by no means deduced it from the mere necessity of the divine nature. But besides the fact that we do not wish to adopt every "unphilosophical" statement of the Fathers as our own, nor to acknowledge all who are brought forward as witnesses for the Orthodox, this much at least is manifest: these two predicates do not overthrow each other. For from the necessity of His own nature, God **wills** to be such as He is. And since...
