->### DISSERTATION ON THE DEITY OF THE WORD <note>original Latin: *De ΛΟΓΟΥ (Logou) Deitate*</note><-

...it would be an extensive task to prove the views of **BASIL**, **ATHANASIUS**, and the rest, were we not hurrying toward the end. One may simply compare what **PETAVIUS** <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a highly influential Jesuit theologian whose work *Dogmata Theologica* (Theological Doctrines) organized the views of the Church Fathers.</note> has proved more extensively regarding this concept of the Orthodox Church in his *Theological Doctrines on the Trinity*, book 5, chapter 4.

XXXIV. A brief word must be added regarding the self-professed **Arians** <note>Followers of the 4th-century priest Arius, who taught that Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> who follow in the footsteps of **SANDIUS** <note>Christopher Sandius (1644–1680), a scholar who argued that the early Church Fathers were actually Arian in their beliefs before the Council of Nicaea.</note>. Against them, one can most successfully argue from the same points in our Prologue <note>Refers to the opening of the Gospel of John.</note> by which we have unraveled more subtle webs. For if the person of the **WORD** is of such great excellence that not even a shadow of any imperfection or dependency falls upon him; and if it is clear from the entire connection of the Prologue that the name **God** is attributed to him by John in the fullest emphasis; then what further room for grumbling is left for those who blaspheme with an open mouth—saying what others we have dealt with at least dread to speak—while they reduce the **WORD** to the *order of created things*? But besides this, both in the text itself and in the comparison of it with Proverbs 8 <note>A passage often interpreted by theologians as describing the eternal wisdom of God as a person.</note>, a whole arsenal is found from which weapons can be drawn to directly strike down Arianism, as our own interpretation shows throughout.

XXXV. Hence the Fathers frequently and successfully used our passage against the Arians. As a sample, it will be helpful here only to hear **ALEXANDER** <note>Alexander of Alexandria, the bishop who first excommunicated Arius.</note> in the letter cited just now, in which he held out the signal, as it were, for the others in this deadly controversy: >*That the Son of God was not made from nothing, and that there was no time when he did not exist, is abundantly taught by John the Evangelist, writing of him thus: The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father. For since the Divine Teacher wished to show that the Father and the Son are two realities inseparable from one another, he said that this one is in the bosom of the Father. Now, that the Word of God is not contained among the things created from nothing, the same John testifies when he says that all things were made through him. For he declared the Word’s own hypostasis* <note>original: *hypostasin*. A technical term for "individual subsistence" or "personhood" within the Trinity.</note> *by saying: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him, and without him was made nothing that was made. For if all things were made through him, how could he, who provided the very existence of created things, not have existed himself at some time? For the Word that creates is understood to be by no means of the same nature as the things created. Inasmuch as he himself was indeed in the beginning, while all things were made through him and established out of nothing, etc.*

# DISSERTATION #

...with the Father, and was manifested to us <note>original Greek: προς τον Πατερα, και εφανερωθη ημιν—a reference to 1 John 1:2</note>. Therefore, the *manifested life* mentioned here is not merely an effect of the **WORD** <note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΟΣ (*Logos*)</note> manifesting it, but is the *manifested Word* himself.

**XI.** Let us pass to the predicates of the **WORD**, which are of two kinds. First, he is directly named **God**. Secondly, lest the name **God** <note>original Greek: Θεος (*Theos*)</note> be understood in any way other than with its full weight and emphasis, various divine attributes and truly divine works are attributed to him. To weaken the force of the name **God** in relation to the **WORD**, our opponents devise various excuses. **Socinus** <note>Fausto Sozzini (1539–1604), a theologian who argued that Jesus was a highly exalted man but not eternally God.</note> rests his argument on the claim that the name *God* is not a *proper* name (denoting a specific being), but an *appellative* <note>a descriptive title</note> denoting authority, power, and benevolence. It is not necessary for us to dwell on this objection, since **Coccejus** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian.</note> examines it thoroughly in the cited work, chapter V, following the work of others. Furthermore, the **Arians** <note>followers of Arius, who believed Jesus was a created being subordinate to the Father</note> form the same argument, to whom I have already given a response in the preceding disputation.

**XII.** Another point occurs to an **ANONYMOUS** writer in the same cited work (pages 255 and following): namely, that the names of the *sign* and the *thing signified* are often swapped with one another. He argues that this is how we explain the words of the Eucharist—*This is my body*—against the Papists <note>Roman Catholics</note>. By this same logic, he claims it is said, *the Word was God*, only because the Word was the image of the Deity, since all the characteristics of the Deity shone out from every part of his person. He argues that all the fullness of the Deity dwelt in him **bodily** <note>original Greek: σωματικως (*somatikōs*)</note>, not in a **riddle** or **figure**, but in a **sensible** and **palpable** manner. Hence, he claims Paul asserts that Christ was **in the form of God** <note>original Greek: εν μορφη Θεου (*en morphē Theou*)</note>, etc. Therefore, he believes Christ is called God in the same figurative sense that he is called the *door*, the *way*, or the *vine*.

**Response 1:** This is a clearly distorted interpretation. The word **was** <note>original Greek: ην (*ēn*)</note> occurs so many times in this context—and three times in the same breath in the very first clause. Indeed, it is contrasted with singular emphasis against the word **became** <note>original Greek: εγενετο (*egeneto*), referring to the incarnation</note>. It is a pretense to claim that "was" should be understood here in such a wildly different [metaphorical] sense.

**2.** When the concepts of a "sign" and the "thing signified" are swapped, it happens in two specific ways which this debater should not have confused. Either the sign is the **subject** (the thing being talked about), as in the Eucharistic formula ["This bread is my body"], or it is the **predicate** (the description), as in the other examples he added at the end ["I am the vine"]. The latter has nothing to do with our passage, because the **Word**—and thus, according to the opponent's hypothesis, the *sign*—functions as the **subject** in this statement. Therefore, the Eucharistic formula would be a more relevant comparison, as it shares the same grammatical structure. However, even this comparison is useless, because (a) it is contradicted by all those passages in which...

253

...in which the names **God** <note>original Hebrew: *El*, *Elohim*; Greek: *Theos*</note> are simply applied to the person of Christ. However, it is clearly unusual for the name of the thing signified to be attributed simply to the sign. Although the thing signified may take the name of the sign, this is not easily reversed. Thus Christ can indeed be called the *bread of life* or *spiritual bread* in an abstract sense, but Christ is never called the *Eucharistic bread* in an absolute sense. (b) The cited passages clearly support us. In Colossians 2:9, the word *bodily* <note>original Greek: σωματικῶς (*sōmatikōs*)</note> is clearly contrasted with the *shadow of the Law* <note>original Latin: *umbræ Legis*; referring to verse 17</note>; and so the Apostle teaches that the fullness of the Deity was in Christ not according to a type or image, but according to the antitype <note>the actual reality represented by a symbol</note>, that is, in reality. In Philippians 2:6, *in the form of God* <note>original Greek: ἐν μορφῃ Θεου (*en morphē Theou*)</note>, when compared with the *form of a servant* <note>original Greek: μορφῃ δουλου (*morphē doulou*)</note>, indicates not a mere scheme or external appearance, but the *nature of God*. Christ is the image, the *exact representation of his being* <note>original Greek: χαρακτηρ της ὑποστασεως (*charaktēr tēs hypostaseōs*)</note>, that is, of the divine *essence* itself (Hebrews 1:3). This prerogative belongs to him above all creatures and requires a subject who shares in the divine essence itself.

**XIII.** Among the divine attributes given to the **Word** <note>original Greek: Λογῳ (*Logō*)</note>, the first is eternity, which we demonstrate in our Commentary from the words: *In the beginning was*. Consequently, the arguments brought forward by **Socinus** <note>Fausto Sozzini (1539–1604), who denied the pre-existence of Christ.</note> and others fall apart on their own—arguments where they try to prove that *beginning* <note>original Latin: *principium*</note> is never used in the Holy Scriptures to mean eternity. For even if we grant this, the logic remains binding as long as it stands that *beginning* here is understood as the beginning of the creation of the universe. Those who hold the opposing view not only attack this notion with frivolous little objections (which the famous **Coccejus** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian.</note> has abundantly refuted in the cited work), but also think of another "beginning," namely the beginning of the *new creation*, or the proclamation of the Gospel. In establishing this, however, they show no small amount of uncertainty.

**XIV.** **Socinus** understands it as the *start of John the Baptist's preaching*, at which time Jesus already existed (before he became known to the Jews through the Baptist's preaching) and had already been destined by God for this office—namely, to reveal His will. **XV.** We add a few points as extra weight. (1) Since **Socinus** thinks the "beginning" of *mystical creation* <note>A Socinian term referring to the "new creation" or the start of the Christian era, rather than the literal creation of the universe</note> is to be understood here, he joins the precise start of this creation with the beginning of the Baptist’s proclamation. However, we do not perceive on what foundation he does this, since he regards not the Baptist but Christ as the *Author* of that alleged new creation. Therefore, the formal beginning of that era could only be placed at the inauguration of the Lord’s own ministry. If it is objected that this beginning was merely *preparatory*, why should it not rather be dated from the birth of Christ and the illustrious angelic and human testimonies joined with it? (2) From the interpretation of the second verse, it is clear that a "beginning" is hinted at in which he was known to God alone. For that is how they explain *being with God*. And yet, from his first birth he was known to many witnesses—indeed, even before that, if not to John in his mother’s womb, certainly to his parents. (3) Such a "beginning" must be understood in which the **Logos** <note>The Word; the divine person of Christ</note> already existed. For, by a comparison with verse 14, that time precedes the moment in which he *became flesh*. For if the **Logos** *became flesh*, then it follows that he *was* the **Logos** before he became flesh. For the evasion of **Socinus**—that *became* <note>original Greek: ἐγένετο (*egeneto*)</note> here denotes not "became," but simply "was"—**Enjedinus** <note>George Enjedinus (1555–1597), a prominent Unitarian/Socinian theologian</note> and others did not dare to adopt as their own. Even if, therefore, we were to refer his "becoming flesh" (along with them) not to the assumption of human nature, but only to his lowly and contemptible form, he was nevertheless "flesh" even from the cradle. And yet, already before that beginning of humility, contempt, and afflictions, he was the **Logos**.

This argument is drawn from various passages of Scripture in which they claim that the **beginning** <note>original: *ἀρχὴν* (archēn)</note> denotes the *beginning of the Gospel*. CALOVIUS <note>Abraham Calov (1612–1686), a staunch defender of Lutheran orthodoxy</note>, that most diligent opponent of the **Socinians**, has examined these passages accurately, among others, in his *Anti-Socinian Writings*, Volume II, page 461 and following. To settle the matter briefly, we refer these passages to different classes:

1. Some are falsely transferred to this argument, since they clearly deal with the beginning of the first creation, such as 2 Thessalonians 2:13, 1 John 1:1, and Chapter 2:13–14.
2. Others, although they indicate the beginning of a certain specific era after the origin of the world, must be applied to a different *beginning* than that of the Gospel and the **New Economy** <term>The "New Economy" or "New Dispensation" refers to the era of the New Testament and the Christian church</term> because of the evident signs in the text itself: for example, Isaiah 52:4, 60:9; Matthew 19:8; and Daniel 8:1.
3. Furthermore, there are those which indeed regard the beginning of the New Economy, but by no means refer to the preaching of John the Baptist; rather, they must be restricted by the context to other circumstances according to the various stages of that beginning. For example, to the beginning of the preaching of Christ himself (John 6:64, 15:27, 16:4; Luke 1:2; 1 John 2:7, 24, 3:11; and twice in 2 John); or to the outpouring of the Holy Spirit (Acts 15:11); or to the Gospel as preached by the Apostles (Philippians 4:15).
4. Finally, some are plainly irrelevant, such as the passage in John 8:25.

Consequently, there remains only the saying in Mark 1:1, where the Gospel history begins thus: *The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ* <note>original Greek: *Ἀρχὴ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ*</note>. Yet even this contributes nothing to the present case, both because the limitation of the **beginning** in this place is manifest, and because this is a title prefixed to the history written by Mark. Moreover, from the fact that Mark began the Gospel history from the preaching of John the Baptist, it does not follow that the entire New Economy must be precisely dated from that point.

XVIII. Not only *was the Word in the beginning*, but he was also intimately united with the Father in a manner worthy of himself, which is why it is added, *that he was with God*. Nothing is more lifeless here than the interpretation of **SOCINUS** <note>Faustus Socinus (1539–1604), a primary figure in the development of Nontrinitarianism</note>: *that is, Jesus, insofar as he is the word of God, was known to God alone before he was revealed by the preaching of the Baptist.* For (1) its defenders have so far been unable to produce any example in which "to be with God" denotes "to be known to Him." For when they cite the passages John 17:5 and 1 John 1:2, they are **begging the question** <term>A logical fallacy where the premise of an argument assumes the truth of the conclusion it is trying to prove</term>. (2) Even if that were granted, it would still not be established that "to be with God" indicates knowledge belonging to **GOD ALONE**. **SOCINUS** was forced to stuff in that restriction because otherwise his explanation would have appeared completely weak and tasteless at first glance. For what special thing would be predicated of the **Word** <note>original: *ΛΟΓΩI* (Logōi)</note> if nothing else were asserted than that he *was known to God*, to whom all His works are known? Therefore, so that the Evangelist would not seem to have asserted absolutely nothing, that word "ALONE" had to be added.

Compare what **PLACEUS** <note>Josué de la Place (1596–1665), a French Protestant theologian known for his views on original sin.</note>, though adhering to the received opinion, discusses solidly, as is his custom, in the cited work, disputation XXVII.

He proves this from the prophecy of Zechariah 9:9, where the coming of the King is promised to the *daughter of Zion*; and from Luke 1:33, where the Angel Gabriel indicates to Mary that *Jesus would reign over the house of Jacob forever*. From this, he thinks the resulting sense is that *that Jewish world still existed for the sake of the Messiah, and, notwithstanding so many rebellions, was preserved through so many miracles and liberated from the Babylonian captivity; and that Christ, for the same reason, tolerated their unbelief for a notable time, and even interceded for them on the cross itself, because they knew not what they did.* Hence, their ingratitude was all the more shameful, in that they refused to recognize Him. against this interpretation, it will suffice to note: (1) that they depart without cause from the common meaning of the phrase **of "it was made"** <note>original: *του ἐγένετο* (tou egeneto). In the Greek text of John 1, this usually refers to physical creation, but Socinians argued it meant a "new creation" or moral change.</note>, which recurs frequently in this very prologue; and this is all the more notable because a different meaning is substituted that is supported by no other example. For "to become" is rendered not simply as "to be," but as "to continue to exist" or "to be preserved"; nor is the past tense respected, while "it was made" is referred to present preservation, and even to a continued lack of recognition after a failure to acknowledge what was owed. (2) The Kingdom of the Messiah, as the **SOCINIANS** <note>Followers of Fausto Sozzini who denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ, viewing Him as a man who was later granted divine authority.</note> imagine it for themselves, was not of such great importance that so many miracles should be spent on preserving the Jewish nation through so many centuries for its sake. (3) There was no link between such a Kingdom of the Messiah and the preservation of the Jews, since that Kingdom concerned only a few of the Jews, and the nations [Gentiles] would make up by far the greater part of it. It adds to this that, under the Socinian hypothesis, it could have happened that the entire Jewish nation rejected the Messiah. (4) The purpose of the Messiah’s coming and the establishment of His Kingdom was not the unbelieving part of the Jewish people—who are here, and very often in the Gospel, strictly understood by the term **"the world"**—but only the elect and the believers among them. These are precisely whom **Zechariah** understands by the **"daughter of Zion"** and **Gabriel** by the **"house of Jacob."** Regarding them, however, it can in no way be said that they did not know the light coming into the world.

XXVII. To the work of creation, another no less divine work is joined to demonstrate the divine glory of **THE WORD** [the Logos], namely the work of Redemption, for the sake of which He is described as the light, the author of spiritual life, and the giver of **"authority"** <note>original: *ἐξουσίας* (exousias). This refers to John 1:12, the right or power to become children of God.</note> to the Sons of God. Lest **SOCINUS** should have to admit defeat to this most powerful argument, he employed every effort to weaken the genuine force of these phrases. Thus, he says that "life was in Christ" for a twofold reason: both because he who believes in Him will obtain eternal life, and because He will raise the dead on the last day. How foolishly these things are invented is clear from the fact that this is a discussion of the life that was in Him even before He became flesh. **SOCINUS** himself ought to have shown from his own hypothesis how this life was already in Christ during the preaching of the Baptist. But we can set these matters aside, since we are convinced that "to believe in someone" designates divine honor according to the emphasis of Scripture, and that no one can raise the dead unless...

XXVIII. XXIX. For now, let it only be observed that in this way, Christ is again turned into a mere instrument through which God will raise the dead. And thus, once again, the phrase *that life was in Him* is stripped of its genuine emphasis.

XXX. Since the work of salvation has various stages—among which stands out that by which the *Word coming into flesh* accomplished it—a new and peculiar argument for His Deity arises from it. This stronghold can be used to fight for the Deity of the Word in a twofold manner. First, the incarnation itself speaks for it, of which it is said: *And the Word was made flesh*. From this, it is gathered that the Word possesses a nature: (1) different from *flesh* or human nature; (2) opposed to flesh in that it was not *made* <note>The author argues the Word *became* flesh but was not *created* as a creature.</note>; (3) existing *before the incarnation*. Second, there is the most majestic and truly divine manner by which the Word was revealed in the flesh and completed the work of Redemption, which the following sections describe with most emphatic <note>original: *ἐμφατικωτάτοις* (emphatikotatois)</note> phrases.

XXXI. They raise two primary objections: first, that from the fact that *the Word became flesh* <note>original Latin: "Verbum caro factum est"</note>, it does not follow that the Word existed beforehand; and second, that the Greek word *egeneto* <note>original Greek: "ἐγένετο"</note> should not be interpreted as "became" or "was made," but rather as "was." These objections were so fully addressed by **PLACEUS** <note>Josué de la Place (1596–1665), a French Protestant theologian known for his work on the imputation of Adam’s sin and Christ’s divinity.</note> in the work cited (Disputation VI) that there would be no need for us *to add our two cents* <note>original Latin: "teruncium nostrum addere," literally "to add our smallest coin."</note>, were it not for the fact that **WOLZOGEN** <note>Ludwig von Wolzogen (1632–1690), a theologian often associated with Arminian or Socinian tendencies.</note> has devised certain new maneuvers with which he seeks to attack the translation of the word *became* <note>ἐγένετο</note> that we defend. To stir up ill-will against this translation, he has used the pretext that it favors both *Apollinarism* and *Eutychianism*. <note>**Apollinarism** was the 4th-century belief that Jesus had a human body but a divine mind instead of a human soul; **Eutychianism** was the 5th-century belief that Christ’s human and divine natures blended into a single, new third nature.</note>

XXXII. We do not deny that some have seized upon this saying as an opportunity to think that the Son of God did not assume a human *soul*, but only human *flesh*, and that the Word took the place of a soul. To leave the ancients aside, **WHISTON** <note>William Whiston (1667–1752), the successor to Isaac Newton at Cambridge, who was famously accused of Arianism (denying the full divinity of Christ).</note> still remains stuck in this mud. But by what torture of logic can this be extorted from our hypothesis? Wolzogen indeed bursts forth into these questions: *Why did the Most High God need a human soul, when He Himself could perform all those things that a human soul performs in a body much more perfectly? And how could it be that there were not two persons in Christ, if the second person of the Trinity assumed not only a human body, but also a human and rational soul?* We easily meet these little questions: the first, because the nature of the *ransom of souls* <note>original Latin: "lytri animarum," referring to the theological concept of Christ's death as a payment or ransom to redeem human souls.</note> demanded it; the second, because we derive this from the mere good pleasure of His most powerful will. Meanwhile, this entire line of reasoning goes up in smoke. It would have to be shown that our interpretation actually produced this error.

XXXIII. *Eutychianism*—which is said to teach that a "third thing" was made out of the Word and the flesh—will gain just as little from that interpretation. He [Wolzogen] deduces it from our opinion in this way: *He who is both God and man at the same time, and is only one person, is neither perfectly God nor perfectly man, but something third composed of the two. For such a person cannot be perfectly God, because he is mortal and has other human properties which cannot be predicated of the Most High God; nor can he be perfectly man, because he is immortal and endowed with other divine properties which do not belong to a man.* This is a straw man argument <note>original Latin: "Straminea sane argumentatio," literally "an argumentation of straw."</note> indeed, which we shall blow away with a single breath by opposing it with this syllogism: he who [is composed] of body and soul at the same time...

XXXIV. But those phrases describing the manifestation of the divine glory of the *Word* in the flesh which he assumed are also attacked. Thus **SOCINUS** <note>Faustus Socinus (1539–1604), the founder of a movement that denied the pre-existence and essential divinity of Christ.</note> does not want the *Word* to be called *only-begotten* <note>original: "unigenitum"</note> on the basis of being God's Son by nature, but only *because he is most acceptable to God and excels others in dignity*. His arguments are: (1) because otherwise he would have contradicted himself, having said shortly before that those who trust in Christ were "born of God"; (2) because otherwise much of the weight of the sentence in *John 3:16*—*that God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son*—would be lost, since that passage alludes to the offering of Isaac, who is called the *only-begotten* son of Abraham, even though Isaac was the unique son of Abraham not by birth but by *love*. 

But the first argument falls apart on its own, because the Evangelist intended to use the name <term>only-begotten <note>original Greek: "μονογενὴς" (monogenēs). This term implies being the sole offspring of a specific kind.</note></term> to distinguish the Word—as the unique Son by nature—from all those who are adopted. Regarding the latter point: (a) we do not reject the allusion to Isaac, nor to Solomon, but we subordinate it to the orthodox interpretation, since both were clearly illustrious types <note>In biblical studies, a "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows a person or event in the New Testament.</note> of the Word. From this it follows that the Word is called "only-begotten" in a far more excellent sense—inasmuch as the reality surpasses the symbol—than Isaac and Solomon ever were. (b) Although Isaac is called "only-begotten" because of love and preference, it is not for that reason alone. That very love assumes a shared nature with the Father and a natural birth. (c) How we wish they would open their eyes and notice the analogy between the offering of Isaac and that of Christ! It is certain that there would be absolutely no emphasis in this allusion if Isaac had not been the natural son of Abraham. **ENJEDINUS** <note>György Enyedi (1555–1597), a Unitarian bishop and influential Socinian writer.</note> insists: "The divine nature was not given for the world, but the man Jesus; therefore it follows that the term <term>only-begotten <note>original Greek: "μονογενὴς"</note></term> is attributed not to the divine nature, but to the man." XXXV. When the same Word <note>original: ΛΟΓΟΣ (Logos)</note> is said to have been full of grace and truth, **SCHLICHTINGIUS** <note>Jonas Szlichtyng (1592–1661), a leading Socinian theologian who argued against the Trinity and Christ's pre-existence.</note> deceitfully makes the Apostle teach that *all the effects of divine grace toward men were in the "speech" [or Word]—namely, eternal life, the imputation of faith for righteousness, adoption, freedom from the Law and consequently from all the rituals of the Law, the Spirit of adoption, more effective than any law; and all these things without distinction toward all who believe in the name of the Word, etc.* Who, reading such things, would not think that the highest and truly divine things were being attributed to the *Word*? Is this the fullness from which all have actually received? Foreseeing this objection, **SCHLICHTINGIUS**, on verse 16 <note>John 1:16: "From his fullness we have all received."</note>, says: *“All received, insofar as all drew and embraced the same doctrine of God's grace and truth from Jesus.”* But how meagerly are "receiving doctrine" and "receiving grace" confused here? The former occurs by knowledge and assent alone; the latter occurs by the very embrace and possession of that grace. The former requires only a Teacher; the latter requires the Fountain and Author of grace, who counts that grace among his own possessions, and has the right and power to actually communicate it to others and assign it as their own.

### XII.
## THEOLOGICAL DISSERTATION
### ON
# THE PRODUCTION
# OF TRUE FAITH.

->I.<-

Although the PRODUCTION OF FAITH in the chosen sinner is the goal of the entire Divine Revelation recorded in Holy Scripture, there is no book in the entire Canon of the Bible in which mention of Faith occurs more frequently, its necessity is more fully demonstrated, and its practice is more effectively urged, than the Gospel of John. I have kept this Gospel before my eyes for several years and placed it among my greatest delights. For since that Divine Apostle directed his chief effort toward rescuing from oblivion certain key discourses of our Lord and Savior that had been omitted by the other Evangelists, he chose—under the guidance of the Holy Spirit—those specific words in which the command of Faith fills every page <note>original: *utramque paginam implet*—literally "fills both sides of the page," an idiom meaning the theme is found everywhere</note>. He did this either to stir up faith in those who were previously unbelieving, or to strengthen it in those who already believe.

II. The weightiest reasons lay behind this purpose for the Divine Writer. Considering the matter generally, saving faith <term>saving faith: in Protestant theology, this refers to a heart-felt trust in Christ's merits that results in salvation, distinguished from "historical faith" which is mere intellectual agreement with facts</term> is the "prow and stern" <note>original: *prora & puppis*—a Latin idiom meaning the beginning and end, or the most essential part of a thing</note> of the entire Christian Confession. It is the key to the entire mystery of grace and the unique bond of union between God and the sinner—from the sinner’s side—and thus it is the most certain means of righteousness and eternal salvation. From this it follows that anyone who is ignorant of the true nature of Faith, or is mistaken in their concept of it, remains stuck in the mud of harmful ignorance and faces the most immediate danger to their supreme happiness. Whoever strives to turn away this danger should be considered to possess a healthy care for the human race and to be fulfilling the role of an Evangelist...

<summary>This page introduces a new theological dissertation focused on how "true faith" is produced in a person, highlighting the Gospel of John as the preeminent scriptural source for understanding faith's necessity and function.</summary>

...to be defended. But more specifically, this **economy** <term>economy: in this context, the "divine economy" refers to God’s plan or arrangement for the salvation of humanity</term> was suited to the peculiar goal that John set for himself in his Gospel. For he declares in express words in Chapter 19:35 and 20:31 that this goal was the awakening of Faith in the Jews and its confirmation in the disciples. ->III.<-

Therefore, lest we rashly neglect anything that might pave the way for a full understanding of John’s Gospel, we have deemed it advisable to collect into a single system, as it were, those things concerning Faith which appear scattered throughout his work and are so frequently and zealously preached. We intend to compare these not only with one another but also with other testimonies of Scripture so that it may become clear, with as much evidence as possible, what exactly the Holy Spirit calls *Faith*. And we believe this opportunity for a more detailed discussion on a matter of such importance should not be overlooked, because—alas!—we live in times when this most holy fundamental doctrine of our religion is not only continued to be attacked by enemies cast out from our communion, but there are even those arising from our own midst who strive to twist it into a fleshly sense with every possible device <note>original: *fidiculis*; literally "torture-strings" or "pulleys," used here metaphorically to describe the forceful twisting or manipulation of a text's meaning</note>, burdening it with the foulest suspicions, and all but exposing it to the mockery of profane men.

->IV.<-

Therefore, so that the unwary may be warned of this danger threatening truth and piety, and so that weapons may be provided to avert it, we—mindful of the Apostolic command in Jude verse 3, *that we should contend earnestly for the faith which was once delivered to the saints*—will not so much repeat what has been said about Faith in all theological systems or what can be said about it in general. Instead, we will specifically select those questions that seem to possess more difficulty or are most exposed to the distortion of certain people. We shall do this with that modesty and reverence which befits those discussing divine matters, so that in this respect also we may show ourselves unlike our opponents. For we are not trying to sow quarrels here, but to turn away those that have been stirred up and, if possible, to extinguish them at their very birth. For this reason, we will pursue the matters themselves rather than attacking persons (even if their insolence in hurling insults seems to have richly deserved to be exposed in the open <note>original: *in aprico sistatur*; literally "to be set in a sunny place," meaning to be publicly exposed</note>), being burdensome to no one...

...without looking down on anyone with a haughty frown, driven by no partisan zeal, and no desire for revenge, but intending solely that its own strength be preserved for this most weighty truth. We also desire that the erring themselves—for whom we earnestly long—might be taught to think more humbly of themselves and be led back into the path of truth.

V. We trace back whatever might seem to be clouded with some difficulty regarding the nature of true Faith to three articles. For it either concerns the *manner* by which Faith is *produced* in each of the elect, or its *saving act* itself, or finally the relation it has to other good works, of which it is the *root* and *origin*. By proving our opinion on each of these from the Sacred Scriptures and the very nature of the matter, and by freeing them from the objections of certain individuals, we hope to easily prove ourselves to the consciences of those seeking the truth that is in Christ. 

However, since those who agree with us are also burdened by a prejudice among the common people—as if they were divorcing themselves from the Confession of the Reformed Church <note>The "Reformed Church" refers to the Protestant tradition following the theology of figures like John Calvin.</note> and crossing over into the camps of adversaries, specifically the Roman Catholics <note>original: *Pontificiorum*, literally "the Pontificians," referring to those following the Pope.</note> and the Arminians <note>A group that broke from the Reformed tradition, emphasizing human free will in the process of salvation.</note>—it would follow that they should no longer be recognized as members of the orthodox Church, and thus not even tolerated in its communion. The weight of this most atrocious accusation imposes a necessity upon us to demonstrate, as a counter-weight, how well the most excellent Reformed theologians agree with one another on this cause, and how greatly they differ from the erring groups on this point.

VI. Regarding the *Production of Faith*, we take as a starting point those truths asserted by all the theologians of our Church and called into doubt by none of them. These are: *First*, that the *efficient cause* <note>In philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the primary agent that brings something into being.</note> of Faith is God alone (John 6:26; Ephesians 2:8; Philippians 1:29) and specifically the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 4:13) according to the good pleasure of the Father (John 6:37) on account of the merit of the Son (Ephesians 1:11, 12). Furthermore, this happens not through some ordinary operation, but through a plainly extraordinary and always effective operation of divine power (Ephesians 1:19). *Second*, that the *subject* in whom Faith is produced is the sinner elected to this grace (2 Thessalonians 2:13), for which reason it is called the *faith of the elect* (Titus 1:1) and it is declared that *faith is not for all* (2 Thessalonians 3:2). This is confirmed by all the promises of Faith, especially those found in the Prophetic Word...

# DISSERTATION

[...pro]phetic <note>Continuing the word "Prophetico" from the previous page's catchword.</note> promises regarding the reward for the **Messiah’s** <term>Messiah: derived from the Hebrew word for "Anointed One," referring to Jesus Christ</term> labors, which could not fail, and are restricted to the circumstances of certain **Times**, **Peoples**, and **Persons**. Compare, among others, Psalm 22:27, 40:4; Isaiah 45:23-24, 49:22-23, 52:6, 55:5, 65:1, etc. *Thirdly*, that the medium through which **Faith** is produced is solely the Word of the **Gospel** and its Ministry; hence, where this is not revealed or preached, no capacity or fitness for **Faith** can even be imagined (Romans 10:14-15). *Fourthly*, that the first point in time of that gracious moment in which **Faith** is effected is the same as that of **Regeneration** <term>Regeneration: the theological concept of being "born again" or spiritually renewed by God</term>, so that whoever lacks **Faith**—until its beginning is instilled into the soul—ought to be considered as hitherto dead in sins and alienated from the life of God (Ephesians 2:12, 1 John 5:10).

VII. Although it must therefore be acknowledged that ***Faith*** and ***Regeneration*** are such benefits of **Grace** that they are communicated to the **elect** <note>In Reformed theology, the "elect" are those chosen by God for salvation.</note> in one and the same moment of time, it can nevertheless be investigated in what order they should be arranged according to our way of conceiving them—that is, *whether, according to the very nature of the thing, Faith should be thought to precede Regeneration, or rather to follow it?*

VIII. To satisfy this question, a certain distinction must be strictly observed, the neglect of which we believe to be the primary cause of confusion in this matter. Namely, ***Regeneration*** is sometimes understood *more broadly* and sometimes *more strictly* in the schools of **Theologians**. When it is taken *more strictly*, it designates the very work of Divine **Omnipotence** and **Grace** through which the first beginning of a new life is stirred up in the elect. However, it is often used *more broadly* for the effect itself, and that either the *proximate* effect, encompassing spiritual life or the faculty for performing actions pleasing to God in Christ, or the *remote* effect, namely the actions themselves in which that life expresses itself more and more. Indeed, it is clear from Psalm 51:12 <note>Psalm 51:10 in modern English Bibles: "Create in me a clean heart, O God."</note> that the restoration of the Saints from various lapses and the new renewal of a new life can be considered as a **Regeneration** and a new birth.

IX. Everyone perceives that the first sense, since it lacks all figurative language <note>original: *tropo*, referring to a rhetorical figure or metaphor</note>, is the simplest. Nor is it understood otherwise in the Sacred Scriptures. According to that sense, however, **Regeneration** must be ordered before **Faith**...

->### ON THE PRODUCTION OF TRUE FAITH.<-

...[th] <note>original: "dam"; continuing the word "Fidem" or "concepi-dam" from the logic of the previous page.</note> cannot be doubted. The very nature of the matter implies this. For ***Regeneration*** is the first ***Work of God*** in the sinner, while ***Faith*** is truly the ***Work of the sinner***—and indeed a work that is morally good, pleasing to God, and honoring to Him. Just as it is certain that God's work in a human must anticipate any human effort, and that the sinner suffers from a total natural impotence <term>Total Impotence: the theological doctrine that fallen humanity is completely unable to contribute to their own salvation or perform spiritual good without divine grace</term>—being clearly ***dead*** in sins before his regeneration—it is equally certain that the sinner cannot believe until God has regenerated him. Furthermore, we take it as granted (a point to be more fully demonstrated in its proper place) that ***Faith is an act of the will***. An act cannot be drawn forth unless a capacity is first assumed. Capacity requires life. Just as all life presupposes a birth, so ***Regeneration*** is a prerequisite for the new life. Nor is it less reasonable to assume—as many will grant us and as will be taught later—that Faith involves ***Love***. For Faith strives toward union with Christ, who presents Himself to the soul as a desirable good. Who would dare deny that this love is legitimate? But from where does it come, unless the production of a new life has preceded it? Finally, our theologians agree that when a sinner is regenerated, no prior "fitness" for regeneration should be imagined in him; yet such fitness would necessarily have to be admitted if faith (as the root of regeneration) preceded regeneration strictly speaking.

X. Sacred Scripture indicates this same order whenever it ranks ***Resuscitation from spiritual death***, ***New Creation***, ***Circumcision of the heart***, ***Conversion***, ***Regeneration***, and ***Sanctification***—which are all synonymous terms—before faith. 

**RESUSCITATION.** <note>The act of bringing someone back to life.</note> *Ephesians 5:14: Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you.* <note>The Latin text cites this as Eph. IV. 14, following a different chapter numbering or a scribal error; modern Bibles place this at Ephesians 5:14.</note> Upon whom does Christ shine, if not the one who, being irradiated by the knowledge of Him, is led into union with Him through Faith? But for that to happen, the awakening of the sleeper and the resurrection of the dead must come first. For the one whose eyes are closed by sleep—indeed, by death itself—light will shine in vain. 

**NEW CREATION.** Hence in *Galatians 5:6 and 6:15*, the terms *Faith effective through love* and *new creature* are treated as equivalent. And in *2 Corinthians 5:17*, whoever *is in Christ*—namely through Faith—is called a *new creature*. If Faith constitutes the essence of the *new creature*, then [creation] <note>The catchword "creatio" indicates the start of the next page.</note> must surely precede...

...creation. <note>original: "creatio"; this completes the thought from the previous page that faith cannot be a self-generated creation of the sinner.</note> We see this in the **CIRCUMCISION OF THE HEART** described in Deuteronomy 30:6: *The LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your descendants, to love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, so that you may live.* It will be seen below that the love of God is Faith itself; this is evident from this very passage, because it is considered the means to life. Truly, for that love to occupy the heart, the circumcision of the heart is a prerequisite. <term>Circumcision of the Heart: a biblical metaphor for the spiritual purification and transformation of a person's inner will by God.</term> We also see this in **CONVERSION**, as in Mark 1:15: *Repent and believe the Gospel.* See also Acts 20:21. Likewise in **REGENERATION**, 1 John 5:4: *Whatever is born of God overcomes the world.* This is because faith is produced through that birth from God, and by that faith the world is conquered. Hence the passage adds: *And this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith. Finally, in **SANCTIFICATION**, 2 Thessalonians 2:13: *Because God chose you from the beginning for salvation through sanctification by the Spirit and Faith in the Truth.* Here, the sanctification of the Spirit, as the work of God, comes first, and Faith in the Truth follows as the effect of that work.

XI. Nowhere is this more clearly emphasized than in the Gospel of John. For example, we read in Chapter 1:12: *But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become children of God, even to those who believe in his name.* But from where do they get this ability to believe? Behold the cause in verse 13: *Who were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.* In Chapter 3, before Christ teaches Nicodemus about the necessity of faith, he first establishes the necessity of regeneration; indeed, he declares with a repeated oath: *unless one is born again, he can neither see nor enter the kingdom of God* (verses 3 and 5). <note>original: "nisi quis genitus sit iterum..."</note> What is Faith, if not the eye by which the Kingdom of God is seen, and the foot by which one enters it? Thus, "seeing," "coming," and "believing" are used interchangeably, as even students of the Word know. <note>original: "tyrones norunt"; referring to those beginning their theological studies.</note> Yet no one happens to be so fortunate unless they have first been born again. In Chapter 5:21–23: *The Son gives life to whom he will... so that all may honor the Son,* specifically through faith. Likewise in verse 44: *How can you believe, when you accept glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only* <meta>catchword: solo (alone/only)</meta>

XII. So that the strength of this argument may be perceived, we cannot pass over that controversy with a "dry foot" <note>original: "sicco pede"; a Latin idiom meaning to pass over something quickly or without getting involved in the details.</note>: *whether the command of Faith pertains to the elect alone?* This is something that must be affirmed, at least by those who defend the doctrine of particular grace. <term>Particular grace: the theological view (often associated with Calvinism) that saving grace is offered by God specifically to the "elect" rather than to all of humanity generally.</term>

XIII. It is apparent that all men generally are not bound to the duty of Faith for this reason: *because faith comes from hearing*, which so many nations lacked in ancient times and still lack today. This is undoubtedly the meaning of the Apostolic saying in which he declares that the nations will perish <term>ἀνόμως</term> <note>Greek: anomōs</note>, *without the law*—meaning without the written [law] of Faith, which differs from the law of works implanted in the hearts of all men. Romans 2:12 and following. But even among those who hear the preaching of the Gospel, it cannot be admitted that others besides the elect are strictly invited to faith. For Faith is a requirement of the Covenant of Grace, and thus it concerns no one except those who are admitted into it through an efficacious calling. <term>Vocatio efficax (Efficacious calling): the internal call of the Holy Spirit that effectively brings a person to salvation, as opposed to a general outward invitation.</term> Just as efficacious calling is determined only for the elect and the redeemed, so also the requirement of Faith, which is proposed in that calling, supposes these benefits. Furthermore, whoever is obligated to believe is at the very least obligated to suppose the possibility of his own salvation; yet, in regard to the reprobate <term>reproborum: those not chosen by God for salvation</term>, this is possible neither on God’s part (because of His immutable decree) nor on their own part (due to the total [corruption] of the heart).

XVI. From this it seems necessary to infer that if unbelief is not only the greatest *sin* but also aggravates judgment, then Faith was also a *duty* for those very people who incur the crime of unbelief, because every sin presupposes a law and an obligation to it. XVII. But the matter having been more carefully weighed, a distinction must be made between the *formal act of unbelief itself*, which properly constitutes its action, and other depravities which are its *root* and *adjuncts*. Just as the *formal nature of Faith* is fulfilled through the union of the will with Christ as the sole author of salvation and justice, so the *formal nature of unbelief* consists in this: that the sinner refuses this union and is unwilling to be saved through Christ according to the will of God. This resistance proceeds from an impure source in the sinner—namely, from a hatred of the light and a neglect of one's own salvation. Furthermore, it is joined with most atrocious crimes. For it either exerts itself through obstinacy against the truth, contempt for God and His Son, disregard for the blessings of God’s people, opposition to the Gospel, blasphemy of the Son and the Holy Spirit, a vain presumption of one's own powers, and the establishment of a false justice contrary to the holiness of God (all of which coincided in Judaism); or it exerts itself through a hypocritical confession of the truth, false boasting in God, and the opposition to the holiness of God arising from that, just as it holds sway in all false members of the true Church.

Just as the *formal nature of Faith* is fulfilled through the union of the will with Christ as the sole author of salvation and righteousness, so the *formal nature of unbelief* consists in this: that the sinner refuses this union and is unwilling to be saved through Christ according to the will of God. This *resistance* <note>original: renitentia</note> proceeds from an impure fountain in the sinner, namely, a hatred of the light and a neglect of one's own salvation. Furthermore, it is joined with the most atrocious crimes. For it either exerts itself through obstinacy against the truth, contempt for God and His Son, disregard for the blessings of God's people, opposition to the Gospel, blasphemy against the Son and the Holy Spirit, and a vain presumption of one's own strength and the erection of a false righteousness contrary to the holiness of God (all of which converged in <term>Judaism: referring here to the religious leadership that rejected the early Christian message</term>); or it exerts itself through a hypocritical confession of the truth, a false boasting in God, and an opposition to the holiness of God arising from that, as is the case in all false members of the true Church.

XVIII. These things having been established, that *Resistance*, even if it is not against an express Law, and suffers from a notable defect regarding its formal act...

# DISSERTATION

<margin>Mm</margin>

...to work out <note>original: *elaborare*; completing the thought from the previous page regarding the duty to work toward salvation</note>, and regarding its secondary circumstances, it cannot be denied that this sin is more atrocious than other crimes. The act is **in itself** vicious because, although it may not be certain to the sinner who externally hears the proclamation of the Gospel that the **Law of Faith** was written specifically for him, he nevertheless cannot assert that it was *not* written for him. The invitation of the Gospel is restricted to no particular persons. Whom God has chosen is not made public, but is manifest only in the consciences of the faithful. Whom He has rejected, He has kept entirely hidden. There is nothing that cuts off all hope for the sinner who is externally invited, except for the hidden <term>good pleasure of God: the theological concept of *beneplacitum Dei*, referring to God's sovereign and independent will</term>, of which he has no knowledge.

On the contrary, he sees a certain path to hoping for better things opened to him when he hears the invitation of God proposed without any distinction of persons. Therefore, he ought to have tested whether this so-salutary command pertained to him as well. Those who find themselves in the greatest danger will never neglect to pursue even uncertain remedies. Whoever neglects to do this, he also **judges himself unworthy of eternal life** (Acts 13:46). Based on this foundation, it is said in John 3:18: **he who does not believe is already condemned**. Thus, this unbelief and perseverance in it is an external sign that such a person is already condemned in the judgment of God. 

Added to this is the fact that such unbelief implicitly runs afoul of the <term>Law of Works: the original moral obligation for humanity to obey God perfectly, established before the fall</term> itself, by which man was held to burn with a zeal for acknowledging God’s glory and celebrating it in all His works. Likewise, man was bound to pay attention to those things which God reveals—and was to reveal in the future—concerning His good pleasure, according to which He wills to exert His perfections. Furthermore, man was obligated to cherish a care for his own salvation, and if any damage should come to it, to neglect nothing that might pertain to its restoration. While he holds all these things in contempt, the one who does not examine and urge himself toward the Testimony of the Gospel regarding the saving of believers—even if God does not say to him individually in the <term>Covenant of Grace: the promise of salvation through faith in Christ rather than human effort</term>, "believe"—nevertheless, his unbelief deserves the highest punishments even according to the Covenant of Works.

XX. Now, as an additional weight to the argument, we add that those whose error we strive to correct here place the saving act of Faith in **trust** <note>original: *fiducia*</note>—specifically, the belief that Christ shed his blood not only for others, but also for me as an individual, and became the cause of righteousness and salvation for me specifically. Those who hold this view, although they form a confused concept of the nature of Faith (as will be demonstrated in its proper place), must nevertheless agree with us on this point: that they should establish Faith as prescribed only for the elect. For since Christ died only for the elect, and the merit of Christ’s death is applied to no one but them, it is certain that if anyone besides them cherishes this trust or glories in it, he not only lacks any command to do so, but also acts in a most Vitious manner. This is because through <term>will-worship: from the Greek *ethelothrēskeia*, referring to religious practices or beliefs self-imposed rather than commanded by God</term> he believes that which God does not want him to believe, and deceives himself with a vain confidence.

XXI. Let us now tighten the knot of the argument. If God prescribes the **Law of Faith** to the elect for the purpose of it being fulfilled, should he not be considered to prescribe it to those who are not only able to recognize it and be persuaded of its fairness, but are also supposed to have already received the aptitude to fulfill it? Since this aptitude necessarily presupposes some vital principle, who would dare to deny any longer that **Regeneration**—or the production of that vital principle—must be conceived as occurring before Faith?

XXII. However, when the term *Regeneration* is used in a broader sense to include its entire *effect*—namely, the *activity* and *actuality* arising from that new principle—it must be held above all else that Faith itself is also to be reckoned among those acts. For although in many theological systems the treatment of Faith occupies its own separate chapter, and for that reason Faith is not commonly named among the parts of Regeneration or the actions in which it exerts itself, yet in the matter itself all theologians agree who confess (following the lead of Scripture) that Faith is, in every emphasis, a **Good Work**. To this latter class <note>i.e., the things that lead up to faith</note> must necessarily be referred the acknowledgment of sin, sorrow for it, and a sincere desire for true salvation. However, since these very acts cannot be produced by the powers of nature <note>The author argues that human effort alone, without divine help, cannot even produce the initial sorrow for sin.</note>, it follows again that, although the actions constituting the form of the **New Life** (or if you prefer to speak so, **Regeneration**) proceed from Faith, there are nevertheless one or two among them which must precede as a means to Faith. Thus, **Regeneration** properly so-called must be conceived as being *before* Faith, even though all **Good Works** strictly speaking—which belong to the pursuit of true holiness <note>original: *sanctimonia*</note> and through which the elect are renewed more and more into the image of God and show themselves grateful to God in their rational worship—have Faith as their root.

# ON THE PRODUCTION OF TRUE FAITH.

...is formed against the order indicated by us, an objection as if that order contradicts the nature of true *Conversion*. For since conversion is supposed to be the fruit of faith, they infer from this that the same must be thought regarding **Regeneration** <note>The theological concept of being "born again" or spiritually renewed by God.</note>.

XXV. To show the emptiness of this objection, we observe at the outset that although the terms *Regeneration* and *Conversion* are used interchangeably, they are not so synonymous that they do not each have a specific emphasis that distinguishes them. For *Regeneration* properly designates a divine act within the elect, while *Conversion* more so expresses the act of the elect through the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is the *effect* of Regeneration. Although conversion appears once or twice as a divine act (1 Kings 18:37; Jeremiah 31:18), in six hundred other places it expresses a human act, which is entirely different from the concept of Regeneration. Sinners are urged, *Turn yourselves, repent,* etc., but never *Regenerate yourselves*. It follows, then, that although Regeneration (strictly speaking) is ordered before Faith, this does not prevent Conversion—as a secondary effect of Regeneration—from being subordinate to its primary effect, which is Faith.

XXVI. Furthermore, those who reason this way seem to have forgotten that, although there are a few passages where Conversion is distinguished from Faith, in most cases Faith is included under the name *Conversion*. To this category belong all those sayings in which Conversion is considered as the unique means to salvation and constitutes the entire requirement of the **Covenant of Grace** (Jeremiah 3:14; Joel 2:12, 13; Zechariah 1:3; Malachi 3:7; Matthew 3:2; Acts 26:20). It is described as the source of healing (Isaiah 6:10), the forgiveness of sins (Isaiah 55:7), and life (Ezekiel 18:32). Hence it is also called *Conversion to Jehovah*, and—in a way that presents God even more fully as a covenant-partner and merciful in Christ—*Conversion to Jehovah your God* (Deuteronomy 4:30; 30:2, 10; Joel 2:13).

XXVII. And the matter itself confirms this. For it belongs most strongly to the effective conversion of the heart that the soul—accustomed to seeking and placing its salvation in goods that only falsely appear to be so—should renounce them, and through **self-denial** <note>original: *abnegatio*</note> of itself and the whole world, seek its salvation from here on...

# DISSERTATION

...from here, one begins to seek solely in Christ, which is certain to constitute the act of Faith itself. And so, in Faith, two acts of conversion meet. Insofar as it presupposes or involves self-denial and the renunciation of all dominion of sin, to that extent it belongs to the **mortification of the old man** <note>The theological process of "killing off" sinful nature and selfish desires.</note>. Insofar as it speaks of conversion to Christ as the unique Savior of the world—connected with the desire for true sanctification through Christ and producing joy in the Lord—it is the most principal part of the **vivification of the new man** <note>The process of being "made alive" or spiritually renewed in character and purpose.</note>. Truly, the Lord must be understood in this way when sending Paul: *To open their eyes and turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God, so that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith, which is in Jesus* (Acts 26:18). For here, Faith and Conversion alternate, and Faith is included under the term **Conversion**. This is gathered not only from the object of this act, which is **Light**—the perpetual symbol of saving grace and its Author, the Son of God—but also from the fruit of conversion, namely that through Faith they receive *forgiveness of sins, etc.* This could not be said unless Faith also belonged to the very essence of that Conversion of which the Lord speaks.

XXVIII. From what has been said, we conclude that those who consider Conversion as the *fruit and effect* of Faith take the word *Conversion* in a narrower sense than is common in the Holy Scriptures. For that term is so broad that it encompasses: 
1. Certain acts of **Repentance** <note>original: *Refipifcentia*, a "coming to one's senses" or changing one's mind.</note> which precede Faith, as shown in §XXIII (on which basis we saw in §X that it can also be ordered before Faith); 
2. **Faith** itself, into whose formal nature it enters; 
3. The **beginnings of Sanctification and Renewal** <note>The lifelong process of becoming more holy and like God.</note> according to the image of God through the struggle against sin and the pursuit of Good Works. 
Hence, when Orthodox theologians place Conversion after Faith as its effect, they must be understood as speaking of Conversion in this third and final sense.

XXIX. From this same source, it can be understood what Peter means when, in Acts 15:9, he testifies that the hearts of the Gentiles were **purified by Faith**. For in a certain respect, Faith itself is a **pure heart**, namely insofar as it moves with self-denial and the rejection of all created things toward a sincere purpose in Jesus, as the unique Savior of the world,

XXXI. ->## DISSERTATION<-

...it is carried, *that it is impossible for those who are grafted into Christ through Faith not to bring forth fruits of gratitude*; this is mentioned entirely wide of the mark <note>original: "extra rhombum"; a Latin idiom meaning "off-target" or irrelevant to the point.</note> in this case. XXXIII. And then the will, now renewed, is not only driven and moved by God, but being acted upon by God, it also acts itself.* For which reason also MAN HIMSELF THROUGH THAT GRACE RECEIVED...

For in a stricter sense, he indicates by that term the moral actions in which the life of faith is demonstrated. I admit that CALVIN holds Regeneration and Conversion or Repentance as synonyms, but it is clear to the eye from the provided definition of repentance that he then uses "Regeneration" in a sense that looks primarily at its effects.

...He gave us birth voluntarily, that is, through His free love. From this it follows, first, that FAITH does not come from ourselves, but IS THE FRUIT OF SPIRITUAL REGENERATION. I respond that both views fit together perfectly: because through faith we conceive the "incorruptible seed" by which we are reborn into a new and divine life, and yet Faith itself is already the work of the Holy Spirit, who lives only in the children of God. Therefore, from different perspectives, Faith is a part of our Regeneration and our entry into the Kingdom of God, so that He might count us among His children. For the fact that the Spirit enlightens our minds already belongs to our internal renewal. IN THIS WAY, FAITH FLOWS OUT OF REGENERATION AS IF FROM A FOUNTAIN. But since we receive Christ by this same Faith—and He is the one who sanctifies us by His Spirit—faith is therefore said to be the beginning of our adoption <note>In this context, "adoption" refers to the theological status of a believer being legally and spiritually made a child of God.</note>.

### XIII.

## THEOLOGICAL DISSERTATION
## ON THE
# FORMAL ACT
# OF TRUE FAITH.

->I.<-

Although Orthodox Theologians agree and are of the opinion that *Saving Faith* is a disposition <term>habit: from the Latin 'habitus', referring to a semi-permanent internal quality or state of the soul produced by God's grace</term> produced by the Holy Spirit in the elect which occupies the whole soul—and thus encompasses various interconnected affections and actions—they nonetheless rightly teach that among these, one must especially note a certain most eminent *Act*, which they call the *formal* act <term>formal act: the specific, defining action that makes faith what it is, as opposed to its preliminary stages or its fruits</term>. To understand this thesis, one must observe both what is *presupposed* by it and what it *comprehends*.

II. It is presupposed that the proper and immediate subject of Faith is not the *intellect*, but the *will*. The very notion of *Faith* teaches this abundantly. For in its simplest and primary sense, it means nothing other than the *Reception of Testimony*, a phrase commonly used regarding Faith in John 3:33 <note>original: "Joh. III. 33." The verse says: "Whoever has accepted it has certified that God is truthful."</note> and 1 John 5:10. Now, the reception of Testimony first signifies a *judgment* regarding the proposed Testimony, through which it is acknowledged as true and certain. Since *judgment* is rightly numbered among the *acts of the will* by Philosophers, even on this account *Faith* must already be referred to the *will*. But there is also the fact that for the full *reception of a testimony*, it is not enough to declare it as true, to approve it, and to acknowledge it as most certain and most fitting; especially when that Testimony concerns a matter that has a specific relation to us, and the presentation of which requires a certain unique care and activity in the perceiving subject...

## THEOLOGICAL DISSERTATIO

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring floral and vine motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>Although Orthodox Theologians agree and hold that **Saving Faith** <term>Saving Faith: The specific belief and trust in Christ that leads to salvation, as distinguished from a mere intellectual belief in facts.</term> is a **habit** <term>habit: from the Latin 'habitus,' meaning a settled or regular tendency or state of the soul, rather than a fleeting thought.</term> produced by the Holy Spirit in the elect <note>original: "electis," referring to those chosen by God for salvation.</note>, which occupies the whole soul and thus encompasses various interconnected emotions and actions; these same thinkers rightly teach that among these, one must especially note a certain preeminent *Act*, which they call the *formal act* <note>The "formal act" is the essential core action that defines what faith is at its most basic level.</note>. <meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section, specifically completing the thought that while the intellect judges a testimony to be true, it is the will that must act upon that truth when it concerns one's salvation. ...requires from the recipient. For if such a Testimony concerns some remarkable good or evil regarding us, then it cannot be denied that he fully receives such a Testimony who not only assents to it by judgment, but also inclines the **will** according to that judgment toward choosing, pursuing, and seizing the good, and toward rejecting the opposite evil, fleeing from it with every effort along the prescribed path. This is the situation with the *Testimony of the Gospel*, which is the *object of Faith*, because it concerns the Sinner’s Highest Good and the manner, worthy of God, through which one can arrive at communion with and possession of Him. Therefore, its *Reception* necessarily requires that the *will*, following the tribunal of judgment, desires this Good, seizes it, and enters into possession of it. Hence, in the sacred pages, the heart is considered the seat of Faith (Romans 10:9; Acts 8:37), by which we have more fully demonstrated—in our commentary on *Psalm 45, Exercise II, Section 8*—the will and its inclinations and desires are most frequently designated. We believe this to be self-evident, and the points we will soon raise regarding the *form of Faith* itself will further confirm it.

III. I am not unaware that there have been certain theologians of no small reputation who wished to brand Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian famous for his "Covenant Theology" and his emphasis on the emotional and volitional aspects of faith.</note> and his disciples with the mark of dangerous novelty for this reason. See P. Allinga, *Questions*, page 148 and following. The cause of the disagreement seems to us to be twofold: first, that those who oppose this view have less accurately attributed the assent of judgment to the intellect; and second, that they have too greatly separated that same assent from the determination of the will which follows that assent.

However, since a believer determines himself in various ways regarding the testimony of the Gospel—whether by generally approving and loving the Good offered in it, or by desiring it, or by seizing it and uniting himself with it, or by resting, rejoicing, and glorying in it—the question has been raised: which of these acts is to be considered the *principal* or *formal* one? <note>The "formal act" is the core essence of faith—the specific moment or action that turns "believing about God" into "saving faith."</note> To this question...

-># ON THE FORMAL ACT OF TRUE FAITH.<-

To understand and resolve this matter, we note that by the *Formal Act* <note>In scholastic philosophy, the "formal act" is the specific action that gives a thing its essential character or "form."</note> we mean one: I. Which so constitutes and, as it were, exhausts the essence of Faith that if it is present, Faith exists, and if it is removed, Faith is taken away. II. Which so spreads itself through all other acts of Faith that it serves as their Principle and Root. III. Which is the immediate and unique means of our Justification before God. IV. Which can be considered the fountainhead of all other good Works.

V. These points being admitted—which no one among our theologians could doubt are most justly required—by the *Formal Act* of Faith we understand that determination of the will by which the person who is chosen, called, and regenerated **EFFECTIVELY WILLS** <note>The author emphasizes that faith is not a passive wish, but an active, effective movement of the will.</note> that the whole *Testimony of the Gospel be fulfilled in himself*; that is, that through Christ as the unique Redeemer of the World, and in that way most worthy of God which the *Gospel reveals*, he may be enlightened, justified, sanctified, and perfectly saved.

VI. Concerning the *object of Faith*, as we have expressed it here, there is little need for us to delay. No one will deny that this object is generally Christ, the Redeemer of the world. However, it must not be overlooked—so that a barrier may be placed against all the deceptions of the flesh—that Christ, when He is established as the object of Faith, is not to be torn apart, but must be considered according to all those relationships which were required for the redemption of the sinner. For it is clearly evident that Christ is the *Rock*, whose *work is perfect* (Deuteronomy 32:4); He who *is able to save to the uttermost* <note>original: "σώζειν εἰς τὸ παντελὲς δύναται" (sōzein eis to panteles dynatai)</note> (Hebrews 7:25). To this belongs the fact that He not only acquires Salvation through His Blood, but also applies it through His Spirit; thus He is encountered not only in the role of Priest, but also as Prophet and King. From this it is clear that, although at first glance Faith recognizes Christ as the High *Priest*, by whose obedience it wills to be cleansed from all guilt of sin, it is nevertheless simultaneously carried toward Him as *Prophet* and *King*, by whose instruction and leadership it may be fully introduced into the salvation He has prepared. From which it further follows that, although *Knowledge* <term>Notitia: the intellectual grasp of facts or doctrines</term> cannot enter into the *formal act* of Faith (since it is not even an *Act* of the will and belongs solely to the *intellect*), it is nevertheless required—and indeed, such a knowledge as accurately perceives the Testimony of the Gospel and its essential parts in their true connection and order...

->### DISSERTATION<-

[...to be] clearly understood according to the mind of the Holy Spirit testifying in the Word. For unless it is clearly established by what path God wills to become the "God of the sinner," our will is unable to subject itself to the divine will or unite with it. Indeed, every reception of a Testimony occurs only according to that part which is known, and regarding whose truth and fitness a judgment can be made—but certainly not according to that part which remains unknown.

VII. Therefore, the *Act* of Faith itself is nothing other than the determination of our own will according to the determination of the divine will expressed in the Testimony of God. Thus, whatever God declares Himself to will concerning the salvation of a sinner, the sinner also wills, once he perceives the will of God and recognizes it as being certainly revealed by God and consistent with His holiness. Since, therefore, God declares that He wills to be merciful only through the Son, the believer wills that very thing. When God testifies that for this purpose He has not only entrusted the *Priesthood* to His Son, but has also given Him the *Kingdom* and *power* over all flesh, and has appointed Him as *Wisdom, Righteousness, Sanctification, and Redemption* <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 1:30, where Paul describes the multifaceted role of Christ in the life of the believer.</note>; every believer not only approves all this as being suitable to Divine fitness and sufficient for his salvation, but also *wills* it in relation to himself. He desires nothing more than that this great work of Redemption may, according to this order, achieve its effect in him more and more.

VIII. And we believe this is the reason why *Faith* in Scripture is expressed simply by the word "to will" <note>original Greek: $\theta\epsilon\lambda\epsilon\iota\nu$ (*thelein*)</note>. Since we find that the emphasis of this word has not been so well observed by others, it is pleasing to "thresh this ear of grain" <note>original: *aristam fricare*. A Latin idiom meaning to examine a specific point or detail with great care.</note> for a moment. An evident passage for this matter is Revelation 22:17: *Let him who thirsts come; and whoever WILLS, let him take the water of life freely.* That "TO WILL" here is nothing other than "to believe" is clear not only from the context of this passage—where the promise of righteousness and life is joined with this *will* as a condition (which applies only to Faith)—but also from a comparison with the prophecy of Isaiah 55:1, to which our passage alludes. For in that prophecy, through the terms "to come" and "to buy"—for which we here have "to come" and "TO WILL"—likewise nothing other than the justifying act of Faith is designated.
