VIII. One must also compare the words of the Savior Himself in John 7:37–38. For it is common for the Apostle John to imitate the manner of speaking used by his Master. In that passage, "thirsting" and "coming" are immediately linked with *believing*; consequently, it must be established that "believing" alternates with "WILLING" in our present context.

IX. We believe that the saying in Isaiah 1:19 must be explained from this same source: *If you are WILLING and obedient* <note>original Latin: *Si VOLETIS & auscultabitis*; original Hebrew: *im to’vu u-sh’ma’tem*</note>, *you shall eat the good of this land.* Excellent interpreters everywhere identify a "hendiadys" here <note>A "hendiadys" is a figure of speech where two words are used to express a single complex idea—in this case, "willingly obeying" rather than two separate actions.</note>, as if it were said, *if you are willing to obey*—that is, if you listen to me gladly, promptly, and with readiness <note>original Greek: *prothymos*</note>. This is the force found in the Hebrew word *’avu* <note>meaning "to be willing" or "to consent"</note>, which implies "willingness with pleasure" <note>original Greek: *eudokia, prothymia*</note>, as the famous Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a prominent Dutch theologian and scholar famous for his massive commentary on the Book of Isaiah.</note> notes. Nor is this contrary to our opinion, because *willing to obey* also pertains to the "form" of Faith; for while Faith wills to be saved through Christ, it does not only desire to be justified through Him, but also to be sanctified <note>In theology, "justification" refers to being declared righteous before God, while "sanctification" refers to the ongoing process of becoming holy in one's life.</note>. However, it is more emphatic if we divide the terms, just as the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> did: *If you are willing and if you listen to me* <note>original Greek: *Ean thelete kai eisakousete mou*</note>. The Chaldean, Syrian, Arabic, and Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible translation of the era.</note> versions have all consistently maintained this same distinction. And thus the sense will be: *if you believe, and demonstrate this Faith through listening or obedience.* We are confirmed in this explanation by the opposition that follows immediately in verse 20, which is distinguished in the same way: *But if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword.* Just as *rebelling* is the opposite of *listening*, so *refusing* <note>original Hebrew: *ma’an*</note> is the opposite of "willing." Now, "refusing" refers to the Testimony proposed in the Word of God, which the one "refusing" does not want to receive; and since this constitutes the essence of unbelief, the Prophet has therefore defined the "form" of faith through the word "willing."

X. The emphasis of this particular observation is to strip away every defense from those passages used by the supporters of free will <note>original Latin: *liberum arbitrium*</note>. For if "to will" here designates nothing other than "to believe," then it is clear how uselessly it is inferred from the proposal of this condition that it lies within everyone’s power whether they will or not—since Scripture in so many other places considers Faith to be a gift of God and the effect of His Holy Spirit.

XI. Indeed, even in other places where "the ACT OF WILLING" <note>original Greek: *to VELLE*</note> seems to have a broader meaning, this significance of Faith must always be included.

<summary>The author argues that in biblical language, "willing" or "desiring" God is synonymous with faith itself. By interpreting "willing" as a gift-based act of faith rather than an exercise of independent human choice, the author challenges the doctrine of free will.</summary>

->### DISSERTATION<-

...should be weighed. Matthew 23:37 and Luke 13:34. In these passages, the Jews are accused because they **WERE UNWILLING** <note>original Latin: *NOLUERINT*</note>, which is to say, they did not believe. For this is specifically the sin by which they resisted Christ when He sought to gather the children of Jerusalem, and through it, they became ripe for all the punishments predicted by the Prophets. When the Apostle witnesses in Romans 7:18: *To **WILL** is present with me*; and in Philippians 2:13: *It is God who works in you both to **WILL** and to do*, there is no doubt at all that this involves Faith itself.

XII. Specifically in the Gospel of John, the essence of Faith is expressed through the act of **WILLING**. Thus, in chapter 5:6, when Jesus asks the paralytic: *Do you **WILL** to be made whole?* <note>original Greek: Θέλεις ὑγιὴς γενέσθαι? (*Theleis hygiēs genesthai?*)</note> He is undoubtedly looking for Faith, because in similar cases He was accustomed to demanding Faith, as seen in Matthew 9:28, Mark 5:36, 9:23, and Luke 8:50. When the same Lord reproaches the Jews for their unbelief in chapter 5:40—through which they were losing out on life—He says: *And you do not **WILL** to come to me, that you may have life*; from which He immediately substitutes the idea in verses 44 and 46 that *they do not believe in Him*. And what is clearer than the words in chapter 7:17? *If anyone **WILLS** to do His will, he shall know concerning the doctrine, whether it is from God, or whether I speak from myself.* For what does "the will of the Father" signify here other than what was stated in chapter 6:40: *This is the will of Him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in Him may have everlasting life?* Whoever believes effectively "wills" this will, and thus conforms his own will to the divine will expressed in the Word of God regarding the manner of salvation. And because righteousness <term>justitia: the state of being right with God</term> and life are joined with such an act of "willing faith," the one who "wills" this is convinced by inward experience that the doctrine of the Son is from God. For the sum of His entire doctrine is this: that he who believes in Him has eternal life. A person is made fit to know the truth of this doctrine not only through Faith—which dispels the clouds of ignorance, prejudice, and fleshly perception—but he also knows it as if through an undeniable experiment; while he wills the same thing that God wills, he is introduced into the possession of the promised good.

XIII. With this definition of Faith agree those passages in which its formal act is described as delight <note>original Hebrew: רצון (*ratzon*)</note>, good pleasure <note>original Greek: εὐδοκία (*eudokia*)</note>, *well-pleasing*, *delight*, or **will**—

->## ON THE FORMAL ACT OF TRUE FAITH.<-

...a joyful will, combined with a full persuasion of the propriety of the Testimony of Jehovah and the highest pleasure, is so named. Hence, the blessed man is proclaimed in Psalm 1:2: <term>whose delight is in the law of Jehovah</term> <note>original Hebrew: בתורת יהוה חפצו (*be-torat Yehovah chephtzo*)</note>. And in Psalm 35:27: *Shouting and joy are promised to those who take pleasure in the righteousness of God.* So too David, in 2 Samuel 23:5, commemorating the object of his Faith, says: *All my salvation* <term>and all my delight</term> <note>original Hebrew: וכל־חפץ (*ve-kol-chephetz*)</note> and *all my good pleasure* <note>original Greek: εὐδοκία (*eudokia*), referring to God's gracious will or favor</note> *shall be.* Add also Psalm 107:30.

XIV. There is no doubt, therefore, that Scripture considers Faith as an *inclination of the will to unite itself with the will of God revealed in the Gospel.* When we call this will *effective*, we distinguish it from all "velleity" <note>a weak or passive desire that does not lead to action</note> or "double-heartedness," as Scripture speaks, because it is joined with inward sincerity. It occupies the throne of the soul in such a way that it dominates all other volitions, expels those that are contrary, and subordinates the rest to this one goal. In this way, the soul is considered to *will to live through this will*, and to do whatever it does by this impulse. By this very fact, *true Faith is distinguished from all hypocritical, false, or dead faith.* But there is no need to dwell on this matter at present.

XV. That this determination of the will is the *chief act of Faith* is evident to us because all the attributes mentioned above in Section IV, which are required for its <term>formal act</term> <note>the specific, defining action that makes a thing what it is</note>, coincide here.

XVI. That the aforementioned disposition of the will *primarily constitutes the essence of Faith* is clear from the fact that this Act corresponds to the *object* of Faith, tends immediately toward its next *End*, and is habitually present in all believers at every place and time.

XVII. That this Will—which, according to the proposal of the Gospel, wills what God wills regarding its own salvation—possesses the proper fitness for the *Object* of faith, is clear because the Gospel takes the form of a <term>Testimony</term> <note>original Latin: *Testimonium*, meaning a formal witness or legal declaration of truth</note>. Now, a testimony requires *reception* from the one to whom it pertains. This act of "receiving" is the specific relative response to a Testimony, for without it, the testimony would be given in vain. And from this, the basis of the phrasing found elsewhere and in the writings of John is readily available, by which he defines believing as <term>to seize or grasp</term> <note>original Greek: καταλαμβάνειν (*katalambanein*)</note> and <term>to receive or take to oneself</term> <note>original Greek: παραλαμβάνειν (*paralambanein*)</note>,

# DISSERTATIO

...to receive, to take <note>original Greek: βανειν, λαμβανειν (*banein, lambanein*)</note> [John 1:5, 11, 12; 3:33], which we have sufficiently illustrated—following the work of others—both in our vernacular Commentary on the Covenant of Grace (Book I, chapter VIII, section 10) and in the homily on Colossians 2:6. But what is it *to receive the Testimony*, other than to approve of it and to *will* it to be true? And when that Testimony specifically concerns my own state and its perfection, what will it mean *to receive such a Testimony*, if not to will that it be fulfilled in me as well? Indeed, one must will it in no other way than that which is defined in that very Testimony.

XVIII. Nor is it less clear that the will, when composed in this way, tends by its own nature toward the *proximate end of Faith*. No one will easily doubt that the closest goal of Faith is *union with Christ*, since faith is proposed as the *bond of union* between Christ and the believers in Ephesians 3:17 and Colossians 2:7, 12. Among the many metaphors by which Scripture loves to sketch the *mystery of this union*, that of *betrothal* stands out, and specifically a betrothal *through faith* [Hosea 2:20]. From this, faithful souls obtain the right to consider Christ as their *Groom* and *Husband*. 

Hence it is clear that this union is *relative*—existing by way of a <term>covenant</term> <note>a formal, binding agreement between two parties</note>—which cannot occur except through a formal <term>agreement</term> <note>original Latin: *adstipulatio*, a legal term for a formal verbal agreement to conditions</note> to all the conditions of that Covenant. On this foundation, Scripture is accustomed to establish the "form" or essence of Faith in this *agreement* or <term>confession</term> <note>original Greek: ὁμολογια (*homologia*)</note> mentioned in 2 Corinthians 9:13: *honoring God* <note>original Greek: ἐπι τῃ ὑποταγῃ της ὁμολογιας ὑμων εἰς το εὐαγγελιον του Χριστου (*epi tēi hypotagēi tēs homologias hymōn eis to euangelion tou Christou*)</note> *through the obedience of your agreement to the Gospel of Christ*. Now, what can that *agreement* to the Covenant of God designate other than the submission of our will under the will of God? By this, we declare that we approve and receive the entire proposal of the Covenant of Grace, and *will* nothing else than to practice communion with God in precisely that way. When a *Bride agrees* to the marriage covenant, what else does she do but testify that she *WILLS* to be united with this groom according to the proposed conditions?

XIX. To this also pertains what has been placed in such clear light by many excellent theologians that it does not require our further explanation: namely, that *Love* enters into the very essence of *Faith*. For God in Christ is presented to the sinner called to Faith as a *good* thing to be desired, toward union with which the sinner tends. And from the concept of Love...

# ON THE FORMAL ACT OF TRUE FAITH.

<meta>catchword: XXII.</meta>

If faith is separated from it, every concept of a covenant perishes. Now, what else is it to *love* than to be inclined in mind, or to *WILL*? For every determination of the will can be categorized into only two kinds. For it either wills just as the nature of the object requires, or it wills otherwise. To will otherwise is to disapprove, to turn away from, to hate, or to separate oneself; therefore, to approve, to be inclined toward, to love, and to join oneself is nothing else than to *WILL*. And so, to *love*—or to embrace God in Christ with true faith according to the prescription of the Gospel—will be nothing else than to *WILL* that God be glorified in me through Christ.

XX. That this act of Faith must be, and is, habitually present to each and every believer at all times follows from what has been said. *It must be present.* For take away this will: what remains except a turning away from that path in which alone God wishes to be found? But experience also teaches that it is present in practice; because whatever changes the faithful soul must undergo, it is never deprived of this inclination of the will, by which it seriously wills to be reconciled with God in Christ. The chief things that cast darkness over Faith are *afflictions and sins*. From these sources all doubt and the obscuring of <term>parrhesia</term> <note>original Greek: παρρησία, meaning a believer's "boldness" or "freedom of speech" in the presence of God</note> draw their origin. And when these troubles coincide, faith often seems to be in its final death-struggle. No light flickers for it. All sense of grace has perished. Hope has been cut off. But although all other things may have perished, the will nevertheless persists, which is carried toward Jesus as the only Redeemer.

XXI. *Afflictions* are so far from suppressing this will that they actually confirm and inflame it further; for this reason, they are compared to fire, which melts and purifies the gold of faith. This is truly that <term>testing</term> <note>original Greek: δοκίμιον (*dokimion*), referring to a "proving" or "trial" of character</note> of *Faith* mentioned in 1 Peter 1:7, which endures in the furnace of tribulation. This is that love, *unconquerable as death, and a zeal hard as the grave; its sparks are sparks of fire, a flame of God, which many waters cannot extinguish* [Song of Solomon 8:6, 7]. This is that Faith *which conquers the world* [1 John 5:5]. For that will to seek salvation solely in Christ never perishes from the soul, even when the waves of temptations rush in; it endures against them all like a <term>Marpessian rock</term> <note>original Latin: *Marpesia cautes*, a classical reference to the hard marble of Mount Marpessos; used here to describe a will that is unshakable and firm</note>.

<summary>This page argues that the essence of faith is a "will" or "love" directed toward God, which defines the believer's part in the Covenant. Crucially, the author asserts that while a believer may lose their feelings of hope or grace during times of sin and suffering, this fundamental will toward Christ remains as an unshakable core.</summary>

<meta>catchword: to have</meta>

XXII. And how could this purpose of the mind perish in afflictions, when no inherent corruption of nature can stifle it, and no lapses can extinguish it? Although Paul did that which he did not want to do, yet *the will for good* <note>original: "velle tamen bonum"</note> did not cease in him. Although Peter faithlessly denied [Christ], yet his *Faith* persisted, because the intercession of Christ could not be in vain. *I have prayed for you, so that your faith may not fail* (Luke 22:32). Without a doubt, in such a heavy fall, the internal sense of divine grace failed, especially given the memory of so many benefits received. But while all the fruits ceased, this root nevertheless remained. Peter’s mouth spoke one thing, driven by the violence of his emotions, while his heart thought another. In the denial itself, there was no settled purpose of deserting Jesus. Even then, he continued to hold his doctrine as true and life-giving, and he cherished the sparks of love toward Jesus, which soon burst into flames again.

XXIII. *The second requirement of the formal act of Faith—namely, that it produces from itself all the other acts attributed to Faith and serves as their foundation*—is most evidently found in this same inclination of the will. Scripture expresses the "Work of Faith" through various phrases, which we have reviewed more at length in *On the Covenant of Grace* <note>original: "de Foed. Gratiae," referring to the author's other work, *Economy of the Covenants*</note>, Book I, Chapter VIII, Section 29 and following. But there is no phrase that does not involve or presuppose this union of the will with the testimony concerning Christ. When the Scripture speaks of *hunger and thirst for righteousness* or the *desire for Christ*, it means nothing other than this very will, which from the first moment of sincere desire already tends toward union with Him. *What is it to come to, to flee for refuge, to receive oneself unto Jesus, and to grasp Him*, if not a more effective exertion of that same will? *What is it to place trust in Him, to rejoice in Him, to boast, to be satisfied, to find rest, and to be secure*, other than a fuller demonstration of that same will? If you take away this will, none of these acts will have any place anymore.

XXIV. But we also find here, in full emphasis, what we placed in the *third* place. For regarding that act *which is the medium through which we can be certain of the remission of sins before the Tribunal of God in our conscience*, it is required that it precedes the sense of the remission of sins; this is because the "medium" <note>the means or instrument</note> must be exercised before the *end* <note>the result or goal</note> can be attained. This takes place in this inclination of the will toward Jesus...

XXIV. No one fails to see that it is necessary to have this. In the very nature of things, *willing to be justified* <note>original: "velle juſtificari"</note> comes before *actually being justified*. Indeed, it would be unbecoming of God to justify a sinner before he had instilled a desire for this justification within them. If He did otherwise, He would be thrusting a benefit upon someone who did not want it. For this reason, He grants no gifts of grace except to those who ask. Thus, no one will rejoice in the gift of the forgiveness of sins except the one who has sought it. And what is "asking," if not expressing the sincere vows of the will before God?

XXV. Furthermore, the justifying act must possess a certain *aptitude* <term>aptitudinem: a fitness or readiness to receive something</term> for receiving and applying God's verdict to oneself. Among all the actions in a sinner that precede justification, what is it that possesses this aptitude, other than that striving of the will by which a person seeks to unite themselves so closely with Christ that, immediately upon exercising this act, they can be considered to be "in Him"? For when the Father justifies a sinner because of Christ’s merit, He does so in view of the close relationship that is now understood to exist between Christ and such a sinner. This relationship can be viewed from the side of Christ and from the side of the sinner. On Christ's part, it consists in that most free and gracious will by which He chose to take away the sins of His elect; and certainly, because of that, the justification of all the elect was decreed from eternity in the Court of Heaven <term>Foro Poli: literally the "Court of the Pole/Sky," referring to God's divine or celestial court</term> and confirmed through the justification of Christ. On the sinner's part, however, a *will* is likewise required, which unites itself with Christ according to the testimony of the Gospel. As soon as that will is present, from that very moment, the person is held by God to be a *member* of Christ, and is therefore fit to enter into the communion of all His goods, and thus also into His merit.

XXVI. Let us illustrate this with the analogy of *betrothal* <note>original: "deſponſationis"</note>, which we have already noted most effectively foreshadows the act of Faith. Through betrothal, the Bride gains a right to the person and the property of the Groom—a right she clearly did not have before the betrothal. But what is that betrothal, if not a full surrender of the Bride's will to the will of the Groom? Therefore, just as the *means* through which a Bride acquires a right to the Groom's goods is, on the Bride’s part, nothing other than a serious determination of the will to unite herself with him; so also the *means* through which the elect in...

### DISSERTATIO

...they come into the possession of Christ and, through Him, all His benefits—of which **justification** <term>justification: the legal act where God declares a sinner righteous through Christ</term> occupies the primary place. This occurs solely through that conformity of the human will with the will of Christ, who invites us in the **Gospel**.

XXVII. From this same analogy, it is clear how this same act can be the source of all **Good Works**, which was our final requirement. Just as the will by which a **Bride** <note>original: "Sponsa"</note> is drawn toward her **Groom** <note>original: "Sponsum"</note> and desires to be united with him fundamentally contains the intention of pleasing him and doing things that are agreeable to him; so too the soul that betroths itself to Christ, by that same will through which it tends toward union with Him, simultaneously embraces Him with love. It stands ready to produce the fruits of **gratitude** for the greatest benefits it expects from Him—a point we shall demonstrate more fully in another dissertation.

XXVIII. What has been presented is sufficient to refute the error of those who *deny that the desire or hunger and thirst for Christ, and the act of taking refuge in Him, are contained within the formal act of faith*. They go so far as to decree that those *who consider people to be true believers if they hunger and thirst for Christ’s righteousness—and so desire to be found in Him that they simultaneously renounce their sins and begin a new life for the glory of God*—are departing from the **Reformed Church** and clearly returning to **Papism** <note>original: "Papismus"; a period term for the Roman Catholic Church, used here to suggest a return to a "works-based" salvation</note>. Hence, they dismiss it as "vain consolation" if someone tries to persuade those who possess nothing but these qualities that they already possess the beginnings of saving **Faith**.

XXIX. Those who reason in such a way reveal themselves to be complete strangers to the ways of God, which He follows while leading the souls of the **Elect** <term>the elect: in Reformed theology, those chosen by God for salvation from eternity</term> into His communion. No doubt they would speak differently if they had applied more careful study to their interactions with those in whom the first beginnings of a new life are breaking forth. For they would have experienced that many souls, precious in the sight of God, detect nothing further within themselves—not only for a long time, but even until the very end of their lives. Yet, in the meantime, they bring forth such excellent fruits of this faith (however weak it may be), that anyone who would decree that such people die in their sins could not excuse themselves from a cruel and rash judgment of their brothers and of the tender lambs whom the **Heavenly Shepherd** Himself carries in His bosom. Christian modesty and charity suggest otherwise.

->### CONCERNING THE FORMAL ACT OF TRUE FAITH<-

->Pp 2<-

...they urge. If only those who have been warned would remember the words of Christ, which apply nowhere more appropriately than here: *Judge not, so that you may not be judged!* (Matthew 7:1). Although this argument will carry the greatest weight with those who are concerned with faithfully performing **pastoral care** <term>pastoral care: the practical guidance and shepherding of a congregation, as opposed to abstract academic study</term>—which is distinct from, and in dignity stands far above, scholarly teaching—and who have had the opportunity to know more deeply the various spiritual states of individual believers, it will nevertheless be undervalued by others, and perhaps even received with contempt. Therefore, we do not linger on it, since other arguments are available which will be sufficient for those men, if they are willing to pay attention.

XXX. Indeed, we have already taught in section 23 that the essence of faith must be placed entirely in **desire, hunger, and taking refuge in Christ**. <note>original: "desiderio, fame, confugio ad Christum"</note> We have all the less doubt about this because this act of Faith is so general that it extends through the entire life of a Christian, who, as long as he lives, never ceases to *desire* Him and to *come* to Him. For even though he has already experienced the beginnings of union with Jesus, he nevertheless always longs for further communion with Him and a full introduction into salvation through Him; he comes to Him continually through prayers, takes refuge in Him in all temptations, and seeks His face in all his sins. From this it is clear that there is no other exercise of Faith more general or more extended to all states of a Christian than that which consists in desire and the resulting seeking of Christ.

XXXI. Truly, the Holy Spirit also fights on our behalf as often as He connects the promise of righteousness, life, and blessedness with such a **desire for Christ** and **refuge** in Him. We will select only a few passages out of many on this subject. XXXII. One might add this by way of an extra argument <note>literally "in the place of an over-weight," an idiom for a bonus or conclusive point</note>: our Savior, in Matthew 5:6, is so far from excluding true believers when He speaks of *those who hunger and thirst*, that He rather wishes to designate by this very phrase all those who were waiting for the kingdom of God in His days. For He alludes precisely to those passages of the Prophets in which the desire to embrace the Messiah in the flesh, and to obtain true redemption through His provided righteousness, was described under these emblems: 1 Samuel 2:5; Psalm 42:2; Psalm 63:2; Isaiah 55:1, and so on. These are specifically *those pursuing righteousness* (Isaiah 51:1) and *those knowing righteousness* (Isaiah 51:7); *those fearing the name of Jehovah, for whom the Sun of Righteousness shall rise* (Malachi 4:2). Anyone who wished to remove these people from the number of the Faithful would have to conclude that the Church had perished by the time Jesus arrived.

XXXIII. Nowhere is our cause pleaded more strongly than in the Gospel of John, in which our Savior himself explains *coming to him* as *believing* in chapter 7:37–38: *If anyone thirsts, let him COME to me and drink. He who BELIEVES in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his heart.* Anyone can see that verse 38 contains the reason why the thirsty ought to be persuaded to come to Jesus and drink. Since He draws this reason from the promise made to those who believe, we conclude that *to thirst, to come, and to believe* are interchangeable according to the Lord’s phrasing. In this interpretation, we enjoy the support of **Calvin** <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the influential French theologian of the Reformation</note>, who notes on this passage: *Christ calls no others to obtain the riches of the Spirit except those who burn with a DESIRE for them; and: TO COME IS NOTHING OTHER THAN TO BELIEVE.* And what is more evident than the words of John 6:35: *I am that bread of life: he who COMES to me shall by no means hunger; and he who BELIEVES in me shall never thirst?* From which chapter also...

even coming to Christ is considered a consequence of the Covenant of Grace <note>original: "Testamenti gratiæ"; a central theological concept in which God promises eternal life through faith in Christ</note> and an act that can never be in vain, as seen in *verse 37: Whatever the Father gives me will come to me; and the one who comes to me I will certainly not cast out.* Let those who try to make us clash with **CALVIN** read here again what he noted regarding *verse 35: He who comes to me.*) *He now defines the manner of feeding: namely, when we receive Him by Faith. For it does the unbelieving no good that Christ is the bread of life, because they always remain empty; but then Christ becomes our bread,* **WHEN WE COME TO HIM HUNGRY**, *so that He may fill us.* **COMING TO CHRIST AND BELIEVING ARE THE SAME** *in this passage: but in the former word, the effect of Faith is expressed—namely, that* **DRIVEN BY THE SENSE OF OUR OWN STARVATION, WE FLEE TO CHRIST FOR THE SAKE OF SEEKING LIFE.** Furthermore, those who conclude from this passage that the "eating" of Christ is nothing other than Faith do not reason quite appropriately. I certainly confess that we do not eat Christ in any other way than by believing; but *THE* **EATING ITSELF IS THE EFFECT AND FRUIT OF FAITH, RATHER THAN FAITH** *itself.* For Faith does not merely look at Christ as if from a great distance, but *we* **EMBRACE HIM, SO THAT HE MAY BECOME OURS** *and dwell in us: it brings it about that we grow together into His body, have a common life with Him, and finally that we are one with Him.*

XXXIV. Another point of no less importance for our case occurs in *verses 27-29* of the same chapter: *Work for the food, not that which perishes, but the food that remains unto eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you; for God the Father has sealed Him. They said therefore to Him: What shall we do, that we may work the works of God? Jesus answered and said to them: This is the work of God, that you believe in Him whom He has sent.* It is most evident that Jesus, in prescribing to the Jews that they "work for" the food that lasts forever, is commanding nothing other than that they believe. For He explains Himself in this way when the Jews ask Him. Therefore, Faith stands in relation to Christ just as the "working for" food stands in relation to its use. Now, what is it to work for food, except to be set on fire by hunger, to be carried toward the food by desire, and to move every stone <note>an idiom meaning to leave no stone unturned or to make every possible effort</note> so that you may become a partaker of it? Here again, we congratulate ourselves on the agreement of **CALVIN**:

->DISSERTATION<-

*This is the work of God*) <note>original: "Hoc est opus Dei"; a reference to John 6:29</note> *They had spoken of works: Christ calls them back to a single* WORK, *that is, to* FAITH, *by which he signifies that whatever men strive for outside of Faith is useless and vain, and that Faith alone suffices: because this is the one thing God demands of us, that we believe. And a little later: Faith brings nothing to God; rather, it presents a person as empty and destitute before God, so that he may be filled by Christ and his grace.*

XXXV. These testimonies of Scripture have all the more power because this desire and the resulting *flight for refuge* <note>original: "confugium"; the act of fleeing to Christ for safety and salvation</note> to Christ must necessarily be counted among the first effects of saving grace. Anyone who would want to establish that these things could take place even in the reprobate <note>those not chosen for salvation</note> and be produced through the powers of nature alone, would clearly show that he is ignorant of the impotence of the flesh. Hence, among the promises of grace, these also occur: Psalm 36:8; Isaiah 45:24. From this category, the Messiah is elegantly named the *desire of the nations* <note>original: "desiderium gentium"</note> (Haggai 2:7). Unless, therefore, God provides these requirements, they cannot be fulfilled. For by nature, sinners are a nation devoid of *desire* (Zephaniah 2:2). Whence Jesus most truly says again in John 6:44: *No one can come to me, unless the Father, who sent me, draws him.* On this point, CALVIN speaks plainly in favor of our opinion: *Christ declares that the doctrine of the Gospel, although it is preached indiscriminately to all, cannot nevertheless be perceived by all, but there is a need for a new mind and a new sense.* Faith, therefore, is not within the choice of men, but is conferred divinely, because COMING TO CHRIST IS PLACED HERE METAPHORICALLY FOR BELIEVING. Since, therefore, it cannot be denied that the desire for Christ and the *flight for refuge* to him born from it must be held as the first effects of grace and acts of the new life—and since even those with whom we disagree seriously defend the idea that Faith precedes all good acts in the elect—on what grounds will they deny that the hunger and thirst for the righteousness of Christ belongs to the formal <note>the essential or defining characteristic</note> act of saving Faith?

XXXVI. Our case having been thus proven, the opposing petty arguments will easily collapse. It is truly a weak excuse <note>original: "ficulneum," literally "made of fig-wood," meaning flimsy or worthless</note> that is held out: that *the act of a soul seeking Jesus as it departs [from sin] is not true Faith, but only a consequence of Historical Faith:* <term>Historical Faith (Fides Historica): A belief that the facts of the Bible are true without a personal, life-changing trust in God.</term> *because it is not the seeking, but the finding, that reconciles comfort, rest, and the hope of eternal life. For it is in vain to seek unless you find, whence he who [does not find] cannot worship God with a grateful mind...*

<meta>This page continues the author’s refutation of an opponent who argues that the early stages of spiritual seeking are not yet "true faith." # ON THE FORMAL ACT OF TRUE FAITH.
<meta>catchword: XXXVIII.</meta>

*...who does nothing but seek.* <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely quoting an opponent's description of a person who has not yet reached "full" faith.</note> These things are said plainly against the nature of the <term>Covenant of Grace</term> <note>the theological framework where God promises eternal life through faith in Christ</note> and the express word of God. For since the act of *seeking* itself is an effect of saving grace, under what pretense shall it be considered a consequence of <term>Historical Faith</term> <note>original: "Fides Historica"; a mere intellectual agreement with biblical facts that does not lead to salvation</note>? Is it not this very thing in which *Historical Faith* differs from <term>Saving Faith</term> <note>original: "Fides Salvifica"; the faith that truly unites a person to God</note>: that the former leaves a person idle, while the latter impels them to seek? Should it then be thought that God has given the promise of certain discovery to such an act which is nothing but a consequence of Historical Faith? Is not the entire requirement of the Covenant of Grace included under the word *seeking*? (Psalm 27:8; Isaiah 55:6). Do not those who enter this Covenant agree to this condition? (2 Chronicles 15:12, 13). Is not the people of God named from this, as an attribute proper to those in the covenant? (Psalm 24:6). I admit that the *seeker* lacks all comfort, *unless he hopes that he will find*. But to want to enroll all those who are not refreshed by the comfort of the Gospel into the number of unbelievers—oh, what great rashness and harshness! Meanwhile, it is enough that this *seeking*, in which we place the beginnings of true Faith, is so composed that it carries the source of all consolation in its bosom, because the Gospel promises create an unbreakable bond between serious seeking and certain finding. *God does not want to be sought in vain* <note>original: "Deus non vult frustra quæri"</note> (Isaiah 45:19). *He who seeks, will find* (Proverbs 8:17; Jeremiah 29:13, 14; Matthew 7:7, 8).

XXXVII. Nor is it of any better quality when *conversion to Christ, hunger and thirst for righteousness, and the desire to be found in Christ* are asserted—by a distinction hitherto unheard of in the Reformed schools—to be *steps to Faith, but not steps in Faith*. For either these steps are proper to those in whom saving Grace is already working, or they are also common to those who are established outside the Covenant of Grace. That the latter cannot be said has been abundantly proven through what we have discussed. If, however, no one stands upon these steps except one who is actually passing into the Covenant of Grace and has been made a partaker of new life, they must necessarily be joined with Faith, unless you wish to deny that Faith is the principle of all actions of a truly <term>regenerate</term> <note>original: "regeniti"; those who have been spiritually "born again" by God</note> person. How can those acts be called *steps to Faith* when true Faith is so joined with them that they presuppose at least the infused <term>habit of Faith</term> <note>original: "habitus Fidei"; the internal capacity or disposition for faith given by God's grace</note> before they can even be brought forth?

<summary>The author argues that "seeking" God and "hungering for righteousness" are not merely preparatory steps taken before faith begins, but are the first active expressions of true saving faith itself. He contends that such desires are only possible through the work of divine grace and are thus inseparable from the state of being a believer.</summary>

# DISSERTATION
<meta>catchword: with,</meta>

XXXVIII. Truly, nothing is more full of holes than the scriptural passages that those who disagree with us cite in their favor; as these passages are produced far less frequently than is proper, they are most unfortunately selected. Such is the saying in Romans 9:16: *It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.* <note>original Latin: "Non est ejus, qui velit, neque ejus, qui currit, sed ejus, qui miseretur, Dei."</note> Who would think that anything could be elicited from this passage against our opinion? Whether you wish to understand by *will* and *running* here generally any effort or endeavor of the will, or specifically that *will* and *running* which constitute the <term>formal act of Faith</term> <note>the essential, defining action that makes faith what it is</note>, it is all the same; nothing that opposes us can be extorted from it by any means. 

The former sense is not inconsistent, because it can happen that even an unregenerate person—driven by the force of conscience or the fear of hell—may want to be saved, and may begin to "run" through certain external acts of repentance, or at least seem to want to begin; all of whose effort is declared here to be in vain. But who could carve out from this that Faith cannot be situated in <note>original Greek/Latin: "$\tau\tilde{\omega}$ velle"</note> the act of willing or running? For at most, nothing else follows from it than that there is some "willing" and "running" which does not deserve to be called Faith. This we concede wholeheartedly <note>original Latin: "utroque pollice," literally "with both thumbs," a Roman idiom for complete agreement</note>, because we do not refer just any "willing" or "running" to Faith, but only such a kind that consists in a sincere desire according to the Testimony of the Gospel. 

But neither would it be absurd to establish that the Apostle understood true Faith by *willing* and *running* here. For then he would be teaching that, although *willing* and *running* according to the promise of the Gospel cannot be in vain if rightly instituted, nevertheless that act should by no means be held as the <term>efficient or moving cause</term> <note>the primary force or "trigger" that produces an effect</note> of our salvation, because that glory belongs entirely to the mercy of God. For although a will filled with sincere desire must precede the enjoyment of salvation, and a "run" is required to reach the goal, yet these things merit nothing by themselves; both because there is no proportion between these means and the end, and because these very things could not have been performed unless that same mercy of God had given all the capacity for willing and running.

XXXIX. The reasoning is exactly the same for the saying in Luke 13:24: *Many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.* <note>original Latin: "Multi, dico vobis, quærent intrare & non poterunt."</note> For how, I ask, does this pertain to that question which we described as the formal act of Faith? Are those whom the Savior describes by this saying...

<summary>The author argues that Romans 9:16 does not exclude "willing" from faith, but rather emphasizes that human effort is not the cause of salvation. He asserts that while true faith involves a sincere desire (willing and running), the ability to do so is entirely a gift of God's mercy.</summary>

This same one regenerates those believing in Him from the seed of His word and restores them with new strength, so that, having been made a new creature in Him, they can do all things and, animated by His Spirit, may bear abundant fruit in Him.* Examples confirming these things occur everywhere in the Scriptures. The ancients hungered and thirsted for Christ, as many as rejoiced with Abraham to see His day: and all these saw through faith and were satisfied. The sinful woman came, inflamed by this hunger and thirst, and washed His feet with her tears, and wiped those washed feet with her hair; and soon she was satisfied when He said: *Your faith has saved you, go in peace.* Tax collectors came to Him, driven by that same hunger, who also found that which satisfied their burning consciences. Finally, amid the dire and terrible tortures of his punishment, that truly blessed thief turned himself to Christ, feeling pains from the consciousness of the crimes he had committed sharper than from the cruel torture of the cross...

### XIV.

## THEOLOGICAL DISSERTATION
## REGARDING
# A S S U R A N C E.

### I.

Since the very beginnings of the Reformation, a famous controversy has existed among the most prominent Reformed Theologians regarding the subject of Faith: whether its *essence* <note>original Latin: *essentia*</note>, or its formal act, includes **Assurance** <note>original Latin: *Fiducia*. In this context, it refers to the personal certainty or heartfelt trust that one's sins are forgiven.</note>, or whether that Assurance should instead be regarded as an *effect* of Faith? 

Early on, many sixteenth-century theologians, specifically in Germany and Switzerland, held the former view, describing Faith through the lens of **Assurance**. However, a disagreement was soon voiced by **PERKINS** <note>William Perkins (1558–1602), an influential English Puritan theologian.</note> and many other theologians of Britain. This is the reason why **RICHARD BAXTER** <note>A prominent English Puritan (1615–1691) known for his efforts at church unity.</note>, in a certain note to his book written in the common tongue, *The Saints' Everlasting Rest*, laments that the greatest overseas theologians—namely **TESTARD**, **CHAMIER**, and **CALVIN**—define Faith as **Assurance**. He argues they most wrongly assert that no one truly believes in Christ who does not also believe that their own sins are forgiven and that they are justified. 

He congratulates the Church of England, however, because its teachers used greater caution regarding this article of doctrine. Yet, in the following century, this praise did not remain exclusive to the English Church, especially after **FRANCIS GOMARUS** <note>A Dutch professor (1563–1641) famous for his role in the Synod of Dort and his opposition to Arminianism.</note> published his singular *dissertation on the nature of Faith, through which we are justified*, which appears in his *Collected Works*, Volume I, page 654 and following. In that work, he addresses the question: *Is the Faith through which we are justified (that is, the faith commanded by the Gospel for the receiving of the remission of sins) properly the assurance of sins having been forgiven?* He so vigorously defends the side of those who say "No," that from that time forward, almost all the theologians of the Netherlands have gradually moved toward his opinion; to whom <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "bus," likely continuing "quibus..." (to whom/among whom) on the next page.</note>

II. Among these controversies, this one is considered to be among those about which one may disagree without suspicion of **heterodoxy** <note>The state of holding beliefs that differ from the established or "orthodox" standards</note>, and no one has been a burden to another because of it, especially since those who affirm it often speak so ambiguously that they seem to disagree more in words than in reality. In the meantime, experience has taught us that the description of *Faith* through *Trust* is not only less convenient in itself, but is also subject to multiple distortions. It has been twisted by the **Antinomians** <note>A group who argued that under the gospel of grace, moral law is not binding on Christians</note> who seek out paradoxes in the Church of England, by the **carnal** men in our own confession, and even by those craftily attacking the very foundations of our religion—specifically the **Hebraeans** or **Hattemists** <note>Followers of Pontiaan van Hattem (1641–1706), a Dutch theologian accused of fatalism and Spinozism</note>. This state of affairs has caused our theologians to begin to **speak with greater precision** <term>ἀκριβολογεῖν: to use scrupulous accuracy in language</term> even more than before. They have deemed a correction and a kind interpretation of those who, in our Church, judged *Trust* to be the *justifying act* of Faith, to be more necessary than ever.

III. Since, however, there remain those who view this caution as a crime, and cry out that because of it the camp of the Reformed Religion is all but being abandoned, it will be highly opportune to bring back "under the anvil" <note>An idiom meaning to re-examine or rework a piece of writing or an idea</note> that opinion which **GOMARUS** <note>Francis Gomarus (1563–1641), a famous Dutch theologian and strict defender of Calvinism</note>—whom our Church rightly and deservedly numbers among its greatest Doctors—once so successfully defended, and to free it from the chief objections of both the ancients and the moderns.

IV. Lest any crack for a **war of words** <term>logomachiæ: an argument about words rather than the underlying concepts</term> should open up, it must be observed beforehand that since the name *Trust* is used in different ways, it is claimed by both sides. Here it is understood in the same sense in which it occurs in the **Heidelberg Catechism**, *Question XXI*, where Faith is also described as: *a certain Trust kindled by the Holy Spirit through the Gospel in my heart, by which I rest in God, establishing for certain that not only to others, but to me also, remission of sins, eternal righteousness, and life have been granted.*

V. If one looks at this description at first glance, it seems clear enough. And yet, a significant ambiguity lies hidden in the relative pronoun **BY WHICH**, when it is said: *By which I rest in God.* For it can be taken in two ways...

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the definition of Faith. The previous page ended by suggesting that theologians in the Reformed tradition began to speak with greater precision—an approach called <term>akribologia</term>—concerning whether "Trust" (<term>Fiducia</term>) is the act that justifies a person or merely a result of faith. This page examines the grammatical and historical nuances of "Trust" in the works of Zacharias Ursinus and classical Greek authors.</meta>

<page-num>313</page-num>
<header>ON TRUST.</header>
<sig>Rr</sig>
<meta>catchword: VII.</meta>

...for this relative term <note>The Latin text discusses the grammatical function of the word "quo" (by which), referring to how "Trust" relates to the soul's rest.</note> admits of two meanings: either it is said that Trust is the medium **by which** or **through which** that peace of mind <term>acquiescentia: a state of rest or quiet satisfaction in the soul</term> is produced, or it is the very act **by which** we find rest—that is, the formal nature of Trust consists in and completes that peace. No one will deny to us that these two meanings differ considerably from one another, and therefore the words of the Catechism <note>The Heidelberg Catechism (1563), a foundational teaching document for the Reformed churches</note> are not sufficient to correctly settle the state of this controversy unless the author's intent is established from other sources.

VI. From where, then, can we more safely seek an explanation of the Catechism than from **Zacharias Ursinus** <note>1534–1583, a German theologian and the primary author of the Heidelberg Catechism</note> himself, who played the most significant role in its composition? In his explanation of this question, he not only places something in the definition of **Trust** that necessarily precedes peace of mind, but he even distinguishes the peace itself from **Trust** as if it were a consequence. He does the former when he says: *Trust is a movement of the heart and will pursuing some good, and both rejoicing in it and leaning upon it.* <note>original: "Fiducia est motus cordis & voluntatis persequens bonum aliquod, eoque gaudens & nitens."</note> From this we conclude that he is discussing the kind of **Trust** that does not yet rejoice in the full possession of the good, because according to him, it is *a movement of the heart and will pursuing some good*, which is presented under the terms of desire, hunger and thirst, seeking, and so on. Therefore, when it is added, *and both rejoicing in it and leaning upon it*, Ursinus must be understood as referring either to a second and greater degree of Trust, or to the kind of Trust that **rejoices** because the good is most certainly attainable through Faith and leans upon its sufficiency. Indeed, the illustration of this word which is immediately added favors this latter meaning: for **Faith** <note>original Greek: Πίστις (Pistis)</note> and **to believe** <note>original Greek: πιστεύειν (pisteuein)</note> come from the word meaning **I have been persuaded.** <note>original Greek: πέπεισμαι (pepeismai)</note> Hence, even among secular authors, **to believe** signifies to place one's trust or to lean on a thing. As found in **Phocylides**: *Do not trust the people; the crowd is fickle.* <note>original Greek: Λαῷ μὴ πίστευε, πολύτροπος ἐστὶν ὅμιλος. Phocylides was an ancient Greek gnomic poet.</note> And in **Demosthenes**: *You trust in yourself* <note>original Greek: Σαυτῷ πίστευεις</note>—meaning, you rely on yourself. In such cases among approved Greek authors, **to believe** designates nothing other than one who, having the highest expectation regarding the sufficiency of a thing or person and rejoicing for that reason, entrusts themselves to it so that they may be delivered or defended by it; it does not mean that one believes they are *already* delivered in the actual moment. Therefore, such **Trust** in the relationship of the faithful to Christ designates nothing other than the very refuge of the soul, fully persuaded of His all-sufficiency, which by the nature of the thing precedes peace of mind.

<summary>The author argues that "Trust" (Fiducia) should be understood as the act of seeking refuge in Christ based on His sufficiency, rather than the feeling of peace that follows. He supports this by citing the Greek etymology of "faith" and the writings of Zacharias Ursinus, the primary author of the Heidelberg Catechism.</summary>

# DISSERTATION

VII. The same **Ursinus**, a little later, enumerating the various successive acts of **Faith** <term>Fides: the general term for religious belief</term> among themselves, proposes them in this order: "Indeed, every believer finds these things in himself, which he can also explain to others:

> 1. He believes that everything contained in **Scripture** is true and divine.
> 2. He feels himself obligated to firmly believe and embrace those things. For if we confess them to be true and divine, it is right that we should assent to them.
> 3. He chiefly looks upon, embraces, and applies to himself the **promise of grace** <term>Promissio gratiae: the theological concept that God offers forgiveness and life freely through Christ</term>, or the promise concerning the free remission of sins, righteousness, and eternal life, through and because of Christ; just as it is said: *He who believes in the Son of God has eternal life.* <note>original: "Qui credit in Filium Dei, habet vitam æternam." - John 3:36</note>
> 4. Relying on this **Trust** <term>Fiducia: the specific act of personal reliance on God’s promise</term>, he firmly finds rest in the present grace of God, and from it he concludes the following about future grace: Since God already loves me and gives me such great goods, He will also save me for eternity; because He is immutable, and His gifts are without repentance.
> 5. **Joy** regarding these goods follows, along with a peace of conscience surpassing all human understanding.
> 6. He possesses the will and a serious desire to obey God.

From these words, three things are clear: 
1. **Ursinus**, in his preceding explanation of **Trust**, does not mean by the "joy" ascribed to it a **joy** concerning the possession of salvation <term>Salus: being saved from sin and its consequences</term>, because he places such a joy in this list *after* the act of finding rest; therefore, it must be explained as the joy which the very sight of the all-sufficiency of Christ can produce in a soul sincerely desiring salvation. 
2. The **Trust** which the **Catechism** <note>The Heidelberg Catechism</note> discusses according to **Ursinus**, *consists in this: that one looks upon, embraces, and applies to himself the promise of grace*; and thus it does not consist in one believing *that the promise of grace has already been actually given to him individually*. For such Trust presupposes the looking upon, the embracing, and the application of the promise of grace. 
3. The **finding of rest** <term>Acquiescentia: the state of quiet confidence or "resting" one's case in God's hands</term>, by which one certainly determines that the promises of grace have been given to him as well, does not belong to the formal nature of that Trust of which the Catechism speaks, but is a consequence of it; because the believer, relying on this Trust,

...relying [on this promise], and even presupposing it, *he rests in the present grace of God*, and from it he forms a **Syllogism of Faith** <term>Syllogismus fidei: A logical deduction where a believer concludes they are personally saved based on the evidence of God’s promises and their own internal faith</term>.

**VIII.** Therefore, those who typically present the state of this controversy using the words of **Question 21 of the Heidelberg Catechism** <note>The Heidelberg Catechism (1563) is a foundational Protestant document; Question 21 defines true faith as both knowledge and a deep-rooted assurance</note> without observing this distinction, do so not without the deception of ambiguity. For there is no general controversy regarding that certain **Trust** <term>Fiducia: personal reliance and confidence</term> *kindled in my heart by the Holy Spirit through the Gospel*, which the Catechism discusses. This trust consists in our pursuit, contemplation, embrace, and application of Christ to ourselves as the "highest good" through an impulse of the will—which we admit, with total approval <note>original: "utroque pollice," literally "with both thumbs," a Roman idiom meaning "hearty approval"</note>, to be the essential nature of **Faith**. Instead, the dispute is solely about that specific Trust which is placed in that *rest and assurance which establishes for certain that the remission of sins, eternal righteousness, and life have been granted not only to others, but to me as well.*

**IX.** Regarding this assurance, however, we pronounce our position in a way that allows us to concede the following: 

*   **First**, that such assurance <term>acquiescentia: a state of resting or being satisfied in a truth</term> is indeed an act in which true Faith is exercised. Thus, it not only cannot occur in a saving way except in true believers, but it is also a work of Faith itself—the **Testimony of the Holy Spirit** <term>Testimonium Spiritus sancti: the internal conviction given by God to a believer</term> in the heart of one who recognizes it, approves of it, and rejoices in it. 
*   **Second**, that it is the duty of every one of the **elect** <term>electi: those chosen by God for salvation</term> and the **called** to strive with every effort to reach this *assurance*. 
*   **Third**, that it is a sign of a disordered weakness in Faith if it has not yet been raised to this level. This is because it is not impossible for any faithful person—whenever they examine themselves according to the Word of God with prejudices set aside—to find the criteria of true Faith within themselves; and because, before they are granted this assurance, they cannot yet fully glorify God for the benefit of grace offered to them. 
*   **Fourth**, that God often works this so effectively in the hearts of the elect that they become sharers of this fuller consolation immediately after the first beginnings of their new life.

**X.** This, then, is the only thing that remains in which we profess our disagreement: namely, that we maintain such assurance should not be regarded as an *essential attribute*, or if you prefer, a *formal act* of Faith in such a way that it is necessarily required and found in all believers, and that consequently all who lack it, without exception, must be condemned as those who have no beginnings of true Faith...

...they have or can have thus far, but rather that it is the **effect and fruit of Faith**, which is granted to some sooner and others later, according to the diverse manner of the Holy Spirit's operations. This is easily established if we only compare those four requirements which we indicated must concur in the **formal act of Faith** in § 4 of the preceding dissertation.

**XI.** **First**, for that **resting assurance** <note>original: "acquiescentia," referring to the internal peace or "resting" in the certainty of one's own salvation</note> is not of the **essence of Faith**, since it is not an act such as the *nature of the object* necessarily demands, nor is it absolutely required *to obtain the end of Faith*, nor is it *always found in true believers*.

**XII.** We have already taught, and no one disputes, that the **Object of Faith** is the **Testimony of God** regarding our salvation. Since, therefore, the act of Faith consists in the **reception** of that Testimony, it follows that the nature of the *object* of Faith requires nothing else than that this Testimony be admitted with full assent in all its parts; it by no means requires that we receive that which is not clearly expressed in that Testimony. Hence it follows that no one can certainly determine that *not only to others, but to me also, the remission of sins etc. has been granted*, unless they clearly perceive that this truth is contained in the Testimony of God.

**XIII.** If we now examine the **Testimony of God** concerning the salvation of the sinner, it is issued either **externally** in the **Word of the Gospel**, or **internally** through the Holy Spirit in our **consciences**. The **Testimony of the Word** manifests God's counsel regarding the salvation of believers only in a general sense. Nowhere do I find my name written among those to be saved. Nowhere is this resting assurance proposed as a criterion of true Faith. Nowhere is it declared in express words that he who lacks this resting assurance is not to be held as a true Believer. If this were to be expected anywhere, surely such a precept for Faith—which, at the **SAME MOMENT** the Gospel was heard, ought to have been persuaded of the already received remission of sins and righteousness—should have been proposed at least once in the sermons of the Apostles. On the contrary, the famous **Van der Waeyen** <note>Johannes van der Waeyen (1639–1701), a Dutch Reformed theologian and professor at Franeker</note> against **Van Hattum** <note>Pontiaan van Hattum (1641–1706), a Dutch pastor whose followers, the Hattemists, were accused of fatalism and downplaying the need for personal struggle in faith</note> on page 10 and following, has exposed the opposite so clearly through a detailed induction of passages from the *Acts of the Apostles* that there is no need to "hold a lamp to the sun" <note>original: "Soli ipsi lucernam accendere," an idiom meaning to provide a useless explanation for something already perfectly clear</note>.

**XIV.** By the same logic, one might think that if it belonged to the **object of Faith** <note>In theology, the "object" is what the faith is directed toward or what it must believe to be true.</note> to believe that **the remission of sins, etc., has been granted to me**, then there would be at least one passage in the Gospel of John where this truth is commanded to be believed. But such a thing occurs nowhere, even in those passages that deal specifically with the object of Faith, such as chapter 1:12, 49, 50; 3:18, 36 (compared with 32, 33); 4:42; 6:29; 10:38; 11:25, 26; 12:36, 44; 14:1; and so on. In all these, the object of Faith is considered to be *outside* of the person who believes, and it concludes in the acknowledgment of Christ’s **all-sufficiency** and His divine mission. Nowhere is even the slightest bit <note>original Greek: "gry," literally a grunt or a tiny speck, meaning "not a single syllable."</note> added from which it might be clear that it belongs to the essence of Faith, right from the beginning, to believe that "Jesus has saved you." On the contrary, this alone is urged as sufficient for salvation in chapter 8:24: *Unless you believe that I am <note>referring to Jesus's divinity or His role as the Messiah</note>, you will die in your sins.*

**XV.** However, an appeal is made to 1 John 5:9, 10, 11: *If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater; for this is the testimony of God which He has testified of His Son. He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself; he who does not believe God has made Him a liar, because he has not believed the testimony that God has testified of His Son. And this is the testimony: that God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son. He who has the Son has life; he who does not have the Son of God does not have life.* 

Yet, there is nothing in this saying that could provide even a shadow of proof that the certainty of one's own salvation is part of the object of Faith, except for that part which declares the sum of the Gospel Testimony to be: *That God has given US eternal life.* 

But I respond <note>original: "R." standing for "Responsio"</note>: 

1.) 2.) For in a Testimony, it is the Witnesses who speak. He is therefore speaking of himself and the others who constituted the foundations and members of the **primitive Church**, who were handing down this Testimony to others—and in whose name John was able to testify that eternal life...

**XVI.** Regarding the **Testimony of the Holy Spirit** in the *consciences of the elect*, this is either *immediate* or *mediate*. <note>"Immediate" testimony would be a direct, mystical whisper from God; "mediate" testimony comes through looking at evidence, such as one's own changing character or "fruits of the Spirit."</note> The latter cannot be considered here because it presupposes the criteria of true Faith, and thus Faith itself. *...rather we say that the faithful are in a constant struggle with their own distrust. We are far from placing their consciences in some peaceful quiet that is never interrupted by any disturbances. On the other hand, however they may be afflicted, we deny that they fall away or defect from that certain trust which they have conceived concerning the mercy of God.*

XX. It is clear that this exception is of no consequence, because doubting and **being certain** are so diametrically opposed to one another that those who allow for even the slightest *fluctuation* regarding a matter immediately destroy the whole concept of certainty. For what else is doubting but **being uncertain**, and what is **becoming certain** but to cease **from doubting**? Since our mind is not capable of holding even two distinct thoughts (which do not exclude each other) at the same moment of time, how much less will it foster contrary thoughts and think at the same moment: *I am certain of my salvation*, and: *I doubt it*. Either we are no longer dealing here with *Trust* or that *CERTAIN resting* of the soul which the Catechism <note>The author likely refers to the Heidelberg Catechism, a standard Reformed instructional manual, which defines faith as "assured confidence."</note> discusses—and thus we are merely **beating the air** <note>A metaphor for wasting effort or arguing pointlessly.</note>—or it must be admitted that whenever faithful souls begin to doubt their salvation, they have left that certainty behind. This is true even if, through the strength of the Faith remaining in them (which at that moment must be something quite different than *certainty*), they repeatedly struggle out of these doubts. This point applies much more forcefully to those who, in the midst of the most serious temptations, imagine themselves to be guilty of **blasphemy against the Holy Spirit** <note>In this period, the "unforgivable sin" (Matthew 12:31) was a source of profound spiritual terror; many believers feared they had committed it and were thus beyond God's mercy.</note>, or believe they have no part in the inheritance of the saints, and so on. Everyone can see that such people plainly deny that they belong to the redeemed.

For he does not wish to place the consciences of the faithful in a state of peaceful quiet; he even allows that this *resting* can sometimes perish. Generally, he speaks only of the *trust which the faithful have conceived concerning the mercy of God*, leaving it undecided whether the faithful considered this mercy as something already granted, or as something yet to be granted. ...the words with which Calvin <note>The author is quoting John Calvin’s *Institutes of the Christian Religion*, likely Book 3, Chapter 2.</note> concludes this subject? XXII. We cling to this argument all the more because the Gospel history itself praises the Faith of those who nevertheless did not yet have the certainty of being heard. Concerning the Centurion, Jesus testifies in Matthew 8:10: <note>original: "Amen, dico vobis, ne in Israële quidem tantam Fidem inveni."</note> *Truly, I say to you, I have not found such great Faith even in Israel.* But what was it that the Centurion believed? Surely nothing other than what he had said in verse 8: <note>original: "Solum loquere, & sanabitur puer meus."</note> *Only speak the word, and my servant shall be healed.* These words indicate a recognition of the <term>all-sufficiency</term> <note>The theological concept that Christ possesses all power and grace necessary for salvation and healing without need for physical presence or other aids.</note> of Christ, joined with a desire for help and a fleeing to Jesus for refuge; they do not, however, indicate a certain hope of being heard. Nothing more occurs in the example of the Canaanite woman in Matthew 15. Nevertheless, Jesus testified in verse 28: *O woman, great is your Faith!*

XXIII. *According to the criterion of a formal act—namely, that it should influence all the remaining acts of Faith and be their root*—this [subjective trust] is plainly absent. For how could that Assurance be the foundation of the other acts of Faith, when it supposes most of them and is their effect? This clearly follows from the preceding points, in which we showed that Assurance concerning salvation requires a clear Testimony, by which the Gospel promise is applied to me individually. Since, however, no other Testimony can be given except from some indubitable criterion of the operations of the <term>Holy Spirit</term>, as was established in § XII, the question here is: what is that criterion which I can consider as the Testimony of God in my heart, proving that I myself have a place among the redeemed? That criterion must necessarily contain within itself some such attribute that makes an evident distinction between the <term>regenerate</term> <note>One who has been "born again" or spiritually renewed by God.</note> and the <term>unregenerate</term> <note>One who remains in their natural state, without spiritual renewal.</note>. This attribute will be either...

<summary>The author argues that faith is defined by a persistent seeking of God rather than a feeling of certainty, citing the biblical examples of the Centurion and the Canaanite woman. He concludes that subjective assurance is a result of faith's operations, not the root of faith itself.</summary>

...it will be something besides Faith, or Faith itself. The former cannot be admitted by the dissenters themselves, because they would then be arranging some good <term>habit</term> <note>In scholastic theology, a "habit" (habitus) is a stable internal disposition or quality of the soul.</note> before Faith. The latter is confirmed by the sum of the whole Gospel proclamation, in which salvation is assigned to whoever believes, and *it is declared impossible that anyone can please God without Faith.* <note>original: "impossibile esse declaratur, ut quis sine Fide Deo placere queat." A reference to Hebrews 11:6.</note> If indeed Faith is the first criterion from which I am able to be certain of my salvation, then it is written as if by sunbeams <note>A Latin idiom meaning "it is as clear as daylight."</note> that Faith must necessarily precede the certainty of salvation. Our theologians agree that this certainty rests upon this <term>Syllogism</term> <note>A form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises. Here: 1. All believers are saved. 2. I believe. 3. Therefore, I am saved.</note>: *He who believes shall be saved. I believe, therefore I shall be saved.* To those who wish to call this into doubt, the burden falls on them to produce another testimony on which trust can be founded. Since they neither do this, nor are they able to do so, it follows that true Faith must already be present before any "acquiescence" <note>A state of rest or peace in the soul regarding one's standing with God.</note> worthy of the name can be produced through this conclusion. Compare on this argument the triumphant GOMARUS <note>Francis Gomarus (1563–1641) was a strict Dutch Reformed theologian famous for his opposition to Arminianism.</note> in the place cited, pages 654 and 655.

XXIV. From this, however, it is clear how empty is the evasion of those who think they will gain something by this distinction: that the *duty of believing* is one thing, but the *persuasion regarding faith* is another. From this they infer that *everyone can and ought to believe immediately as soon as the Gospel is announced to them, even if AT THAT MOMENT they have lived most wickedly. But that no one can or should presume that they truly possess Faith unless that Faith regenerates them.* This thesis—especially when proposed by someone who admits <term>particular grace</term> <note>The doctrine that God’s saving grace is intended only for the "elect" (those chosen by God) rather than for every individual.</note>—suffers from multiple absurdities. First, we proved in the first dissertation (§ 13 ff.) that it is contrary to the Reformed system of election, the merit of Christ, and <term>effectual calling</term> <note>The belief that when God calls a person to salvation, His grace is powerful enough to ensure they respond with faith.</note> for everyone hearing the Gospel to be obligated to believe that Christ died for them. Furthermore, what could be more unworthy of the holiness of Christ's merit, or what more composed to foster "carnal security" <note>A state of false spiritual confidence or spiritual laziness.</note>, than to wish to persuade the most wicked sinners—not even excepting those who have spent their whole lives in adultery, robbery, and other more atrocious crimes—that they ought to believe they are righteous before God WITHOUT ANY PREPARATION at the VERY MOMENT they hear the Gospel? Must there not first precede a serious [repentance] for sins...

...repentance and a desire for true salvation? At least these same opponents admit this elsewhere. Must not a sense of sincerity be added to this sorrow and desire? Or will these affections of the soul, and this reasoning gathered from them, not require at least some **MOMENTS**? <note>In this context, "moments" refers to stages of logical or temporal progression.</note> How, then, will it remain true that they ought to apply this salvation to themselves at the **SAME MOMENT** in which they externally hear the testimony of the Gospel, without any preparation? Finally, who does not notice that those who press this distinction are "pruning their own vines"? <note>original: "propria vineta cædere." A Latin idiom meaning to undermine one's own argument or cause oneself harm.</note> For we grant that some do believe in act, even if they are not yet persuaded of their own faith. But from that very fact we conclude that the essence of Faith does not consist in a certain acquiescence. <note>A state of internal rest or peace regarding one's standing with God.</note> For this cannot exist where one is not persuaded of the <term>genuineness</term> <note>original Greek: <term>γνησιοτης</term> (gnēsiotēs), referring to the authenticity or sincerity of one's faith.</note> of their faith.

XXV. Let us pass to the *third criterion*. Indeed, nothing more absurd can be said about this Trust which rests in the certainty of salvation than that it is the immediate and unique *antecedent* means of *Justification* before God. For since the means suited for sharing in this good is nothing other than the apprehension <note>The act of "grasping" or "taking hold of" something mentally or spiritually.</note> of Christ's righteousness, it cannot be perceived what a "fiducial act" <note>An act of trust or assurance.</note> would do in this cause. Furthermore, Faith is the means to the *Remission of sins*, and the means must be placed before the end; this order is clearly perverted if one thinks it belongs to the essence of Faith for someone to suppose that Remission of sins has already been granted to them.

XXVI. The Sacred Pages certainly order these things differently, whenever they arrange Faith as a <term>condition sine qua non</term> <note>A Latin legal and philosophical term meaning "a condition without which it could not be."</note> before the Remission of sins. **Acts 26:18**: *That you may open their eyes and turn them from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive remission of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by Faith, which is in me.* **Romans 3:26**: *That he himself might be just and the justifier of him who is of the Faith of Jesus.* **Romans 5:1-2**: *Justified by Faith, we have peace toward God through our Lord Jesus Christ: through whom also we were brought into this grace by Faith.* **Acts 2:38**: *Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins.* **Galatians 2:16**: *We also have believed in Christ, so that we might be justified.* Hence Jesus, about to defend that he remitted the sins of the female sinner, in **Luke 7:50**...

His first argument is that the words <term>faith</term> <note>original Greek: <term>πίστις</term> (pistis)</note> and <term>to believe</term> <note>original Greek: <term>πιστεύειν</term> (pisteuein)</note> are often used by good authors to mean *Trust* and *to place one's trust*, which he illustrates with examples. <gloss>Response 1.</gloss> From the frequent use of this word among secular authors, a conclusion cannot be made regarding its use in sacred matters: even less so because nothing similar to saving Faith occurs anywhere outside the revelation of the divine word. <gloss>2.</gloss> The passages cited prove nothing else than that "to believe" among secular authors is the same as *to trust oneself to someone* from whom you expect help. Trust regarding help already provided is clearly another thing entirely. <note>The author distinguishes between trusting God *for* salvation versus the assurance that one *has* already been saved.</note>

XXXII. For his second argument, he produces passages of Scripture in which *to believe* is used for *to trust*, such as Luke 16:11, John 2:24, and Romans 3:2. The response is not only the same as before, but these passages are even less binding; for in them, <term>to believe</term> <note>original Greek: <term>τὸ πιστεύειν</term> (to pisteuein)</note> indicates nothing other than to entrust something to someone’s care, or to have a certain persuasion regarding someone's faithfulness and truthfulness. The Trust <note>original Latin: *Fiducia*</note> being discussed here, which presupposes all those things, is as distant as the whole of heaven.

XXXIII. The third argument is sought from the phrase by which we are commanded to *believe in Christ* or *in His name*. For this, he argues, must necessarily signify Trust, because *to believe in God* and *in Christ* is something more than simply *to believe God*. <gloss>Response 1.</gloss> Learned men dispute whether the observation of this distinction has a solid foundation. <gloss>2.</gloss> Even if we granted that, it would not yet follow that *to believe in Christ* is the same as being certain of one's own salvation through Christ. It is enough that we understand more than a theoretical assent by this phrase.
