# ON TRUST.
### Sf 3

...what is brought forward by today's antagonists, but also omitted by them; and what was once brought forward by others, let us subject to a brief examination.

XXX. Against our opinion, **ANTONIUS WALAEUS** <note>Antonius Walaeus (1573–1639) was a prominent Dutch Reformed theologian and a professor at Leiden. He was known for his moderate tone at the Synod of Dort.</note> long ago disputed formally in his *Common Places*, page 413 and following. He did so with the modesty that is fitting, not insulting those with whom he disagreed with insults or slanders, but holding them as orthodox *Writers* and Brothers, and leaving a free judgment to them.

XXXI. His first argument is because the word <term>pistis</term> <note>original Greek: πίστις, "faith" or "belief"</note> and <term>pisteuein</term> <note>original Greek: πιστεύειν, "to believe"</note> among good authors <note>Refers to classical Greek writers like Homer or Plato.</note> is often used for *Trust* and *placing trust*, which he illustrates with examples. <gloss>Response 1.</gloss> From the frequent use of this word among secular authors, a conclusion cannot be made regarding its use in sacred matters: even less so, because nothing similar to saving Faith occurs anywhere outside the revelation of the divine word. <gloss>2.</gloss> The cited passages prove nothing else than that "to believe" among secular authors is the same as *to trust oneself to someone* from whom you expect help. Trust regarding help already provided <note>The author distinguishes between the act of trusting someone for help and the assurance/confidence one feels after the help has arrived or been promised.</note> is clearly something else.

XXXII. As a second argument, he produces passages of Scripture in which *to believe* is placed for *to trust*, such as Luke 16:11, John 2:24, and Romans 3:2. <note>In these verses, the Greek verb for "believe" is used in the sense of "entrusting" something to someone—for example, in Romans 3:2, the Jews were "entrusted" with the words of God.</note> The response not only returns to the same point, but these passages are even less binding, because in those, the act of <term>believing</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ πιστεύειν</note> indicates nothing else than to entrust something to someone's care, or to have some persuasion regarding someone's faithfulness and truthfulness. The Trust being discussed here, which presupposes all those things, is as distant as the whole sky.

XXXIII. The third argument is sought from the phrase by which we are commanded *to believe in Christ or in his name*. For this necessarily designates *Trust*, because to believe in God and in Christ is something more than *to believe God*. <note>Theologians often distinguished between *credere Deo* (believing God’s words are true) and *credere in Deum* (placing one's heart and trust in God).</note> <gloss>Response 1.</gloss> Learned men dispute whether the observation of this distinction has a solid foundation. <gloss>2.</gloss> Even if we were to grant that, it would not yet follow that *believing in Christ* is the same as being certain of one's own salvation through Christ. It is enough that we understand more than a theoretical assent by this phrase.

XXXIV. The fourth argument is provided by the word <term>batach</term> <note>original Hebrew: בטח</note> *to trust*,

<meta>This page continues the logical dismantling of arguments that equate "faith" entirely with "trust" or "assurance." The author is responding to theological opponents by examining specific biblical proof-texts and philological evidence from the Old and New Testaments to show that trust is often a result or a higher degree of faith, rather than faith itself.</meta>

<header>DISSERTATION</header>

*to trust* <note>original Latin: fidere</note>, for which in the New Testament *to believe* <note>original Latin: credere</note> is used in Psalm 31:1 compared with Romans 10:11, and Proverbs 3:5 compared with Acts 8:37. For this reason, in the Old Testament, the terms <term>batach</term> <note>Hebrew: בטח, meaning "to trust" or "be confident"</note> and <term>he’emin</term> <note>Hebrew: האמין, meaning "to believe" or "to stand firm"</note> are placed for the same things in Micah 7:5 and Psalm 78:22. 

<gloss>Response 1.</gloss> The answer comes back that it is one thing *to trust that one is to be saved by someone*, and another *to believe that one has been saved by him*. 
<gloss>2.</gloss> The passage in Romans 10:11 is brought from Isaiah 28:16 or 49:23, where not <term>batach</term> <note>trust</note> but <term>he’emin</term> <note>believe</note> and <term>kawah</term> <note>Hebrew: קוה, "to hope" or "wait for"</note> occur. 
<gloss>3.</gloss> It is assumed without evidence that the passage in Acts 8:37 is quoted from Proverbs 3:5. 
<gloss>4.</gloss> In Micah 7 and Psalm 78, *to believe* and *to trust* are distinguished in such a way that, by the usual literary elaboration <note>original: exergasia, a rhetorical figure where an idea is repeated with different words</note>, *to believe* precedes, and *to trust* follows as something more emphatic.

XXXV. Fifthly, passages are produced where Faith is called <term>pepoithesis</term> <note>Greek: πεποίθησις, "confidence" or "reliance"</note>, <term>kauchēma</term> <note>Greek: καύχημα, "boasting" or "glorying"</note>, <term>tharsos</term> <note>Greek: θάρσος, "courage" or "confidence"</note>, <term>plērophoria</term> <note>Greek: πληροφορία, "full assurance" or "fullness"</note>, <term>parrhēsia</term> <note>Greek: παῤῥησία, "boldness" or "openness"</note>, and <term>hypostasis</term> <note>Greek: ὑπόστασις, "substance" or "assurance"</note>. 

<gloss>Response 1.</gloss> Even if it were granted that "Trust" (about which we are debating) is expressed by all these words, nothing else would follow from the passages in which they occur than that many of the faithful in the New Testament arrived at this measure of Faith in its early stages, and that every believer ought to strive for it; however, it does not follow that Faith which has not yet been raised to that point is not to be considered true Faith. 
<gloss>2.</gloss> Certain of these words do not necessarily designate the *Trust of acquiescence* <note>A theological term for the restful assurance that one's salvation is already secured</note>.

**Confidence** <note>original Greek: Πεποίθησις</note> sometimes indeed denotes confidence regarding a *good already received* in 2 Corinthians 1:15 and 3:4, but also occasionally confidence regarding a *good that is still expected* in 2 Corinthians 8:22. However that may be, in Ephesians 3:12, it is clearly distinguished from Faith as its fruit, because the Apostle says: *In whom we have boldness and access with confidence <note>original Greek: ἐν πεποιθήσει</note> through his Faith.*

**The boasting of hope** <note>original Greek: Καύχημα τῆς ἐλπίδος</note> in Hebrews 3:6 is an act of Trust, but the kind that requires *that a person should prove his own work* in Galatians 6:4. Since Faith belongs to that work, it is clear that such boasting is not Faith itself, but its **effect**.

**Confidence** or **Courage** <note>original Greek: Θάρσος</note> in Matthew 9:2 and 22 is a consequence of Faith. For in verse 2, Jesus rouses the man whose Faith he had seen just as clearly as he had seen the faith of those carrying him. And in verse 22, he says explicitly: *Take heart, daughter, your Faith has saved you.* Therefore, she believed even before that confidence.

**Fullness** or **Assurance** <note>original Greek: Πληροφορία</note> can designate a fuller degree of Faith...

The author contends that a believer can have true faith even before achieving the state of full assurance or "acquiescent" trust.</summary>

The author is responding to theological opponents by examining specific biblical proof-texts and philological evidence from the Old and New Testaments to show that trust is often a result or a higher degree of faith, rather than faith itself.</meta>

### ON TRUST.

we easily grant [this point]: however, nowhere is it proposed as a criterion of true faith. In Hebrews 6:11, the *fullness of hope* <note>original Latin: plenitudo spei</note> is considered as a consequence of the pursuit of holiness. In Hebrews 10:22, that <term>plerophoria</term> <note>Greek: πληροφορία, meaning "full assurance" or "conviction"</note> is understood not so much *subjectively* <note>referring to the internal feelings of the believer</note> as *objectively*, insofar as it denotes the fuller object of Faith in the New Testament, which is the actual expiation of sin through the blood of Christ. In Colossians 2:2, Paul wishes to stir this up in the Colossians, who were already believers. In 1 Thessalonians 1:5, those who had reached that point are praised; while this may be proposed as an example to others, those who have not yet advanced to that degree are not excluded from Faith.

<term>Parrhesia</term> <note>Greek: Παῤῥησία, meaning "boldness" or "freedom of speech"</note> in Ephesians 3:12 is clearly distinguished from Faith as an effect. This is also proven by the nature of *parrhesia* itself. Specifically, it designates freedom of speech. This, however, presupposes a consciousness of Faith, according to that saying: *I believed, and therefore I have spoken* <note>Psalm 116:10 and 2 Corinthians 4:13</note>.

<term>Hypostasis</term> <note>Greek: Ὑπόστασις, translated here as "Subsistence" or "Substance"</note> is used in Hebrews 11:1 <note>The original text cites Hebrews 1:1, likely a scribal error for the famous definition of faith in 11:1</note>, not to propose a general definition of Faith, but to indicate an effect of true Faith, which is that things hoped for are made present—whether through a full persuasion of their certainty or through a living foretaste of them.

XXXVI. Sixthly, the thesis is confirmed by examples. <term>Response.</term> We do not deny that the Faith of many—and specifically of Abraham, who is praised in Romans 4—involves a Trust regarding the certainty of the promises given to him. We concede the same for others who show an example of certain Trust in Paul’s writings. However, it does not follow from this that such must be the Faith of everyone, especially since immediate revelations have ceased. See <term>Van der Wayen</term> <note>Johannes van der Wayen (1639–1701), a Dutch Reformed theologian</note> against <term>Van Hattem</term> <note>Pontiaan van Hattem (1641–1706), a Dutch theologian accused of Spinozism</note> in his Preface, where he thoroughly dismantles this argument.

XXXVII. In the same argument, it is added that in our prayers we ought to believe that those things we ask for will happen to us. Mark 11:24: *Whatever things you ask when you pray, believe that you receive them, and you will have them.* Add Matthew 21:22, 1 John 5:14, and James 1:6. But <term>Response 1.</term> Although it is the duty of every believer to strive for that strength of Faith, so that they may be certain of their right to those things they ask for, it does not follow that where there is a lack of this certainty, Faith is not present.

<header>->DISSERTATION<-</header>

Faith. 2. When it is said in James 1:7 that *one who doubts should not expect to receive anything from the Lord* <note>original Latin: dubitanti non putandum esse, quod accepturus sit quicquam à Domino</note>, this refers to doubt regarding the *object* of faith <note>The "object" refers to the truth of God’s promises itself</note>, rather than the *subject* <note>The "subject" refers to the internal state or worthiness of the person asking</note>, which is very clear from the fact that such a person is called in verse 8: *A double-minded man* <note>original Greek: Ανηρ διψυχος; Latin: Vir duplex anima</note>, which is to say, according to James 4:8, *one who does not have a pure heart*. 3. The strengthening of Faith is among those things which ought to be prayed for, as seen in Luke 17:5 and 2 Thessalonians 2:11.

XXXVIII. Seventh, an argument is made from opposites—namely, that doubt and fear are blamed and forbidden in Matthew 14:31 and Luke 8:50, etc. **Response:** 1. We grant that doubt and fear are "diseases" within Faith for which a cure must be sought. 2. Doubt concerning the *object* of Faith is more contrary to its nature than doubt concerning the *subject*, and it is this [doubt of the object] that is primarily intended in the passages cited.

XXXIX. The eighth argument is drawn from the "object," which is the divine promise in Christ; this promise is accepted not only as *true*, but also as *good* and salvific for us. **Response:** This holds weight only against those who define Faith as a mere *theoretical assent* <note>A "theoretical assent" is a cold, intellectual agreement with facts without any personal engagement or emotional response</note>. Since we have maintained that love belongs to the very essence of Faith, we already assume that the promise of Christ presents itself to the sinner as a certain *good*.

XL. In the last place, this <term>Syllogism</term> <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note> appears: *Trust either belongs to Faith, or to Hope, or to Charity [Love]. It does not belong to Charity, as is well known; nor to Hope, because hope is only concerned with future goods. Therefore, it belongs to Faith.* **Response:** This line of reasoning is quite obscure and, to have any relevance to the matter, it relies on this proposition: *Whatever does not constitute the essence of Love and Hope must constitute the essence of Faith.* Anyone can see how false this is. For Love and Hope have many "accidental fruits" <note>Results or side-effects that are not part of the core definition</note> which do not belong to the essence of Faith. Furthermore, *Love* and *Hope* are not to be essentially separated from Faith, because they certainly enter into the essence of Faith in a specific way: *love* insofar as the Gospel promises are viewed as a "good," and *hope* insofar as they are viewed as a "good" that can be obtained.

XLII. The **APOSTLES’ CREED** <term>Symbolum Apostolicum; the most ancient and widely used statement of Christian belief</term> itself is the first thing brought into this debate. For when Faith in the *forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body, and eternal life* <note>original Latin: remiffionis peccatorum, refurrectionis carnis, & vitæ æternæ</note> is declared in it, the claim is made that the Church’s intended meaning was that whoever holds to this creed must believe that his sins are already actually forgiven, and that he has thus become an heir to the resurrection of the righteous and to eternal life. 

But this assumption is rejected with the same ease with which it was put forward. If the Church had such a mind, why did it pass over a matter of such great importance? Should we not rather praise its prudence <note>prudence or "circumspection" in choosing words carefully</note> for expressing itself indefinitely in such a way that it can be applied to different degrees of Faith? In this way, one and the same formula can be prescribed not only for those strengthened in Faith, but even for infants. 

Or is it believable that this could have been the intention of those who composed the Creed, when they had just professed the *Holy Church and the communion of saints*? By this very act, they provided sufficient precaution so that no one might, through empty boasting, seize for themselves the following blessings—which encompass the *inheritance of the Saints*—without any prior foundation. If that was indeed the Church's opinion, as it is falsely attributed here, then it would have to be concluded that it was unknown to all those men whom we have already presented as sharing our view <note>original Greek: ὁμοψήφους (homopsēphous) — "of the same vote" or "unanimous"</note>, and whom we will continue to present. 

**Zacharias Ursinus** <note>A 16th-century German theologian and a primary author of the Heidelberg Catechism</note> himself, in his explanation of this article, places Faith and repentance before the actual forgiveness [of sins], saying: *“The decree of God concerning the forgiveness of sins is eternal, but its execution happens when we apply to ourselves through Faith the forgiveness of sins offered in the Gospel. Thus God always loves His elect: but this love of God is not poured out into the hearts of the elect before repentance. For only those who truly repent have that certain testimony of conscience from the gift of the Holy Spirit—that they are loved by God, and that their sins are therefore forgiven.”* He reasons in exactly the same way regarding Faith in eternal life. Hence, all the best interpreters of the Creed carefully distinguish the various degrees of Faith occupied with these blessings...

XLIII. In no testimony, however, is there more triumphing than in the testimony of the **HEIDELBERG CATECHISM** <term>A Protestant instructional document written in 1563, used to teach the core tenets of the Reformed faith</term>. This document not only responds to many other questions in a way that assumes a certainty of salvation in the one issuing the confession of truth, but in Question 21, it describes Faith in such a way that this certainty enters into its very definition. The **Hattumists** <term>Followers of Pontiaan van Hattem, whose views on the "finished" nature of salvation led to accusations that they disregarded the need for personal struggle or growth in faith</term> boast greatly in this argument. Consequently, Johannes van der Wayen <term>Johannes van der Wayen (1639–1701), a Dutch professor of theology</term>, Johannes d'Outrein <term>Johannes d'Outrein (1662–1722), a Dutch preacher and author</term>, and other men—whose "good aroma" <note>a biblical allusion to a good reputation or godly influence</note> regarding their love for orthodox truth is well established—wrested that argument from them with such a weight of reasoning that anyone who continues to "play the same lyre" <note>original: eadem lyra oberrare; a Latin idiom meaning to repeat the same old, failed argument</note> before refuting their points is simply wasting his time and effort <note>original: operam & oleum perdat, literally "wasting work and oil"</note>.

XLIV. Regarding the general custom of the Catechism—that it introduces a speaker who is fully persuaded of his own salvation—they have wisely noted two things in particular. The *first* is that it would be unfair to demand of every **catechumen** <term>a student of the faith receiving basic instruction</term> that he precisely answer everything the Heidelberg Catechism provides as if speaking from his own personal experience. For the Catechism provides nothing but a summary of truths in which the student is to be more broadly educated. Thus, nothing prevents an unbaptized person from reciting the words of the baptized, or an orphan the words of one who still has parents, and so on. Just as one who sings a Psalm does not have to apply everything to himself personally, even though the text of the Psalm uses the first person.

XLV. *Secondly*, there is the fact that the authors of this Catechism had deep-seated reasons for introducing a respondent who is strengthened in Faith. This is done so that every believer, even if not yet established in that degree of faith described by the Catechism, might nevertheless clearly perceive—through that beautiful image of perfection in Faith—how far true Faith can reach through the grace of the Holy Spirit, and may be increasingly inflamed with a desire to strive toward that goal. # CONCERNING TRUST <note>original: *DE FIDUCIA*</note>

Tt 2
<meta>catchword: BAPTI-</meta>

In this summary of Christian doctrine, they aimed above all to distinguish themselves from the **Roman Catholics** <note>original: *Pontificiis*</note> and to place the excellence of our Confession in a full light. Since the most powerful defect of the Papal error is that it offers no true *consolation*, while it removes all certainty of salvation, nothing was better composed to achieve this goal than to treat our doctrine in such a way that it is clear to the eye that the true springs of consolation are opened within it. This, indeed, could not be demonstrated more clearly or brilliantly than by presenting a Christian who, through the foundations of our religion, is raised to the highest level of firmness in Faith and certainty concerning salvation.

XLVI. Regarding Question 21 specifically, it is sufficient to note that it presents a far fuller definition of Faith than the dissenters desire. For it does not only stop at marking the *formal* <note>the essential or technical definition</note> act of Faith, but also includes all the *degrees* of Faith; it shows not only what is necessarily required in Faith and what it truly is, but also what it can become, and how far it eventually carries the believer. It presents not only its first beginning but also its final consummation and perfection here on earth, as I think is so evident from the analysis of **Ursinus** <term>Zacharias Ursinus (1534–1583), a German theologian and the primary author of the Heidelberg Catechism</term> in Section VII that there is no need to dwell on this matter. It is true that the vernacular <note>referring to the original German or Dutch translations used by the people</note> text does not propose these degrees of Faith so distinctly. However, it is enough that the authors of the Catechism, in that Latin version, proposed more explicitly those things which were more intricate in the vernacular text, and that Ursinus himself wished to illustrate that very unfolding with a fuller explanation. This is all the more true because the Catechism cannot be understood otherwise unless one wishes to introduce an absurd meaning into it, as the most celebrated **Antonius van Driessen** <term>Antonius van Driessen (1684–1748), a Dutch professor of theology known for his orthodox and sometimes polemical defenses of Reformed doctrine</term> demonstrated more abundantly in another vernacular writing, where he manfully championed this same cause. For while he ascribes *certainty* to **Trust** <note>original: *Fiducia*</note>, he also presupposes the foundation of this certainty. Moreover, we have shown in Section XII and following that this foundation, regarding the *subject of Faith*, can be nothing other than the internal consciousness of Faith based on its own criteria.

<meta>catchword: differ</meta>

BAPTISM IS administered to adults as well as to infants. The *Formula for the Baptism of Adults* <note>original: *Formula circa Baptismum adultorum*</note> carries the greatest appearance of evidence for the opposing view; in this formula, the candidate is asked: *Do you believe that Christ — — — was given to you by God as a Redeemer, and that through this faith you receive the forgiveness of sins in his blood, and that you have been made a member of Jesus Christ and his Church through the efficacy of the Holy Spirit?* <note>original: *An credis, Christum - - - tibi in Redemtorem à Deo donatum esse, teque per hanc fidem accipere remissionem peccatorum in sanguine ejus, teque membrum Jesu Christi & Ecclesiæ ejus per efficaciam Spiritus Sancti factum esse.*</note> But we respond: 1) this question cannot be twisted to serve our opponents' cause, because in adults who are received into the bosom of our Church, a greater power of Faith is already assumed to exist, and because in order to draw full consolation from Baptism, it is necessary that one considers it as a seal of their justification before God. 2) This phrase should not be pressed too strictly, as is clear from the <term>analogy of Faith</term> <note>the principle that individual passages of scripture or doctrine must be interpreted in harmony with the whole of Christian teaching</note> which we have already abundantly demonstrated, and according to which this formula must undoubtedly be explained. From this it follows that the statement *to believe the Redeemer was given to you by God*, when it designates a formal act of Faith absolutely necessary for salvation, involves this silent condition: *if you embrace him with a sincere faith*. Indeed, we conclude that the very authors of this Formula did not wish to be understood as rigidly as our opponents noisily claim, because it is added: *And that through this Faith you receive the forgiveness of sins*. For if their opinion were to stand, then the past tense would have had to be used: *That you have received the forgiveness of sins* <note>original: *Te accepisse remissionem peccatorum*</note>. For he who believes absolutely that *Christ was given to him as a Redeemer* is also persuaded that *he has already received the forgiveness of sins*. Since, therefore, the authors speak of the forgiveness of sins in the present tense, they indicate that they are speaking of the kind of forgiveness that Faith precedes. Faith that precedes the forgiveness of sins establishes that Christ was given as a Redeemer not absolutely, but only conditionally.

XLVIII. Much less relevant to this matter is the *Formula for the Baptism of Infants*, in which Parents and Sponsors are asked: *Do you not confess our children to be sanctified in Christ, and therefore as members of his Church they ought to be baptized?* <note>original: *Annon confitemini liberos nostros in Christo sanctificatos esse, & propterea tanquam membra Ecclesiæ ejus debere baptizari?*</note> Those who think that by this question all Parents are bound—such that they should not offer their children for Baptism until they are certain of their own union with Christ—stray far from the true and orthodox sense of this question. ...would have differed, had the authors of this Formula phrased the question not in the first person, *our children*, but in the second person, *yours*. Since they speak indefinitely of *our children*, we must believe they were referring only to the true members of the internal <term>Church</term> <note>the "internal" or "invisible" Church refers to the collective body of true believers known only to God, as opposed to the "visible" Church of all baptized members</note>; for the Pastor speaks in the name of the Church and receives the children offered into its communion. It is no wonder, then, that some people—upon whom is forced an interpretation of this question that is so crude and so contrary to the true nature of Faith—remain stuck in hesitation regarding it. They would certainly do so less often if the same effort used to urge the necessity of this Formula for maintaining union were also applied to providing an explanation of it—one that would clearly remove any suspicion of a hidden, monstrous meaning.

XLIX. Allow me on this occasion to offer my opinion regarding this Formula (about which various investigations are currently being conducted in many places) with appropriate freedom and modesty. In the words in which it is composed, nothing occurs that cannot be reconciled with the nature of Christian Baptism when understood in a healthy sense. For we hold it as certain that the Formula refers only to the children of the truly faithful, who possess that relative *holiness* <note>original: *sanctitas*</note> discussed by Paul in 1 Corinthians 7:14. <note>In this Bible verse, Paul suggests that the children of a believing parent are "holy," a concept used by the Reformers to justify the baptism of infants.</note> In the meantime, what keeps many faithful Ministers of the Church anxious is that this specific question is prone to so many distortions; they worry that among those who present their children for Baptism, there are many who either do not understand the proposed question at all, or understand it in that perverse sense which we refute. Furthermore, this Formula relates to a holier and more precise exercise of <term>Church discipline</term> <note>the practice of overseeing the conduct and beliefs of church members</note>. By the strength of such discipline, no parents or witnesses should be admitted to Baptism unless they are the kind of people who can be presumed to understand the question in a healthy sense, and whose Faith is such that the children can be considered sanctified within it. Therefore, we believe that for all who urge the preservation of this Formula—whether they be political or ecclesiastical leaders—this duty also rests upon them: that out of a sincere love for public edification, they should apply all their labor to removing these difficulties. In this way, they may show by their actual deeds that they are concerned not only for external *union*, but also for the *communion of SAINTS* <note>original: *communionis SANCTORUM*</note> and the internal splendor of the Church.

...that its preservation and promotion are close to their hearts. L. To continue weaving our thread <note>original: *telam nostram pertexamus*, a classical metaphor for continuing a complex argument</note>, with the same rigor by which those weaker in Faith are barred from the water of Baptism, these same people—if it should happen that our opponents were so successful as to seize the Tribunal of the Church for themselves—would be kept away from the **HOLY ASSEMBLY** <note>original: *SACRA SYNAXI*, a Greek-derived term for the gathering of the faithful for Holy Communion</note>. For it is declared that those who do not yet enjoy that "certain persuasion" that all their sins are forgiven have **NO RIGHT WHATSOEVER** to the seals of communion of the Reformed Church. For this purpose, they appeal to the very words of the Savior at the institution of the Holy Supper: **This is my body, which is given FOR YOU.** 

But what would stop someone from arguing that this was a clearly unique privilege for the disciples, because they heard it from the mouth of Jesus himself? Thus, it was easy for them to embrace this comfort with Faith, since they could know from this clear declaration of Jesus, without prior inquiry, that they already belonged to his own people <note>the "peculium" or special possession of God</note>. Does this remove the necessity of a prior scrutiny of the sincerity of Faith for those to whom such an infallible and immediate Testimony of the Lord is not shown? What if even this declaration was only hypothetical, since it was offered not to individual disciples but to the whole college <note>the "college" refers to the group of the twelve Apostles together</note>, and thus was not to be applied by individuals to themselves without a previous self-examination? Certainly, those who believe they can prove—for reasons not to be despised—that Judas himself received the sacred signs <note>the bread and wine</note>, must conclude this. Whatever the case, it is certain that even the faithful disciples did not yet fully understand this declaration of the Lord, nor did they rightly apply it to themselves; despite this, Jesus offered them the seals of this truth, which would be more clearly revealed after his resurrection.

LI. But they insist that the **FORMULA** prescribed for the administration of the Holy Supper nevertheless condemns such people. If that were true, it would have to be examined according to the nature of the Gospel by what right this is done.

...would happen. But this is superfluous, since the authors of that <term>Formula<note>Likely referring to the "Form for the Celebration of the Lord's Supper" used in the Dutch Reformed Church.</note></term> do not allow us to doubt their intention. The only question is whether those who do not yet enjoy the certainty of the remission of their sins, even if they earnestly long for it, have **NO PART** in the right to the Eucharist? From where will those who disagree establish this? Is it from what is added: *That all who feel this way are worthy guests; but those who do not find this Testimony in their heart—namely, that they feel this way—eat and drink judgment upon themselves?* 

But who does not see that an ambiguity lies hidden in that phrase: *Those who are so minded* <note>original: *Die alsoo gesint zyn*</note>? For "to be so minded" in a fuller sense would designate here having a certain persuasion of the remission of one's sins; yet in a narrower sense, it can also be said of those who are convinced that such persuasion belongs to the fullness of Faith, and who, for that reason, sincerely strive toward it themselves. And that this latter sense was the one in which the authors understood these words is clearer than the midday sun, because they subsequently testify that *these things are not proposed for the purpose of terrifying the contrite hearts of the faithful: whence those also, who **SEEK** their life in Christ but do not yet have a perfect Faith, and who must fight daily with the weakness of their Faith, ought to be certain that no sin or infirmity, which remains in us **AGAINST OUR WILL**, can prevent God from graciously receiving us, and **RENDERING** us **WORTHY** of this heavenly food and drink and partakers of it.* 

Compare the right of those weak in Faith to the Holy Gathering in the defense against <term>van Hattum<note>Pontiaan van Hattem (1641–1706), a Dutch theologian whose views on grace and assurance were often condemned as fatalistic or Spinozistic.</note></term> by <term>Van der Waeyen<note>Johannes van der Waeyen (1639–1701), a prominent Dutch Reformed theologian.</note></term> in the place cited, page 135 and following, where he cites an excellent passage from <term>Huysinga’s<note>Jacobus Huysinga, author of popular Dutch devotional works.</note></term> vernacular ascetic book on the Holy Gathering in support of this cause.

LIII. We do not deny that they and others following them did not always distinguish the degrees of Faith with enough accuracy. For in the first dawn of Evangelical Light arising through the Reformation, <term>Metaphysics<note>The branch of philosophy dealing with the nature of reality and being.</note></term> had not yet been so fully cleansed from <term>Scholastic<note>Referring to the medieval "Schoolmen" whose complex, logical systems were often rejected by Reformers as overly dry or confusing.</note></term> obscurity that they were always accustomed to clear and distinct concepts of things. A proof of this is that, here and there, in describing Faith as *certain knowledge*, they wished its seat to be the intellect. Yet these same men explained themselves in other places so that it is abundantly clear that they truly recognized the beginnings of Faith in those who sincerely desire Christ and flee to him. Compare what we have noted from them in the preceding dissertation (§ 33, 42) and in this one (§ 6, 7, 21, 42). To all of which we add here CALVIN himself (*Institutes* Book III, chapter 2, § 6) declaring *Confidence* to be an *effect* of Faith: *This is the PRINCIPAL HINGE ON WHICH FAITH TURNS, lest anyone [of those things which] the Lord offers of his mercy*...

# ON TRUST.

V v

<meta>catchword: granted</meta>

...we should not think the promises are true only for others and not at all for ourselves: but rather that we should make them our own by embracing them within. *FROM THIS AT LAST IS BORN THAT TRUST<note>original: *Fiducia*, a key theological term referring to the personal assurance or "heart-trust" that one is saved.</note>*, which the same author elsewhere calls peace: unless one prefers to derive peace from that source. From this act, Trust is born—specifically through an intimate consciousness of that act. This is the very point we are defending here against those who disagree.

LIV. Nothing remains except that we demonstrate our agreement with the Orthodox Faith on this point as well, in order to remove every prejudice of the common people. We therefore congratulate ourselves immensely on the public testimony of the **FATHERS OF DORT<note>Referring to the Synod of Dort (1618–1619), an international gathering that defined the "orthodox" Reformed position on salvation and predestination.</note>**, who in their *Judgment on the Five Articles* (at Article I, § 16) say no less piously than solidly: *Those who do not yet effectively feel in themselves a living Faith in Christ, or a certain Trust of the heart, peace of conscience, the pursuit of filial obedience, and glorying in God through Christ, but who nevertheless use the means<note>The "means of grace" typically refer to the preaching of the Word and the administration of the Sacraments.</note> through which God has promised to work these things in us, should not be terrified at the mention of Reprobation<note>Reprobation: The theological concept of being passed over by God's saving grace; the opposite of election.</note>, nor count themselves among the reprobate. Instead, they should diligently persist in the use of these means, ardently desire the hour of more abundant grace, and wait for it with reverence and humility. Much less should those be terrified by the doctrine of Reprobation who seriously desire to be converted to God, to please Him alone, and to be rescued from the body of death, yet cannot yet reach the point they wish for on the path of Piety and Faith; for the merciful God has promised that He will not quench the smoking flax and He will not break the bruised reed.*

LV. We equally congratulate ourselves on the agreement of the **CHURCH OF ZURICH**, which the entire Reformed Church venerates as its mother. In her Catechism, established by public authority even before the Heidelberg Catechism, Faith is defined in Question XXXII as follows: *True Faith is not only a true knowledge of God and His word, but also a filial trust of the heart in God the Father, that to me, out of mere grace without any merit of works, solely because of the satisfaction of Christ* (all my sins are forgiven, and eternal righteousness is granted...<note>original German: *alle meine sünden vergeben, und ewige gerechtigkeit schenken*. The sentence cuts off here as a catchword for the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the author's defense against theological critics who claim his definition of faith contradicts the established Reformed doctrine on Good Works and Justification. The catchword "flee" from the previous page completes the verb "confugio" (to flee for refuge).</meta>

[I] flee for refuge. They now judge that true Faith is active, and those who wish for <term>Regeneration</term><note>The theological concept of being "born again" or spiritually renewed by God.</note> to be conceived before Faith, strike against the orthodox opinion of the Reformed Church regarding Good Works. They attempt to prove this in two primary ways.

*First*, they think this view is opposed to <term>justification</term><note>The act of God declaring a sinner righteous.</note> by Faith alone, with all works excluded. They argue that those who stand with us must necessarily establish that *no one is justified by God before he has fled to God through Faith with a sincere hunger and thirst for righteousness, has become a suppliant to God with true sorrow for sins, has begun to cease evil works, and has in some way begun a new life.* This, however, seems to them to be diametrically opposed to the Christian Confession expressed in the **Synod of Dort**<note>An international council held in 1618–1619 to settle disputes in the Dutch Reformed Church.</note>, which defines in Article XXIV: *We are justified by Faith in Christ, and indeed before we have performed Good Works.*

*Second*, they urge that nothing is more contrary to the nature of Good Works than this hypothesis, because works cannot be considered "good" unless they proceed from gratitude. Since the sole purpose of such works is *that we may show ourselves grateful to God for the benefits bestowed upon us through Christ*, this can be expected from no one except the person who believes that he has already actually become a partaker of these benefits. From this it further follows, according to them, that those who do not believe this are *active not out of Faith, but only out of fear of hell and a desire for heavenly glory.*

These consequences are of great weight because those who link them together theatrically exaggerate<note>original: "paratragœdiantur," meaning to speak in an overly dramatic or tragic style.</note> their foul outcomes. Not only do they place us in the same rank as the **Papists**<note>A common term used by Protestant reformers to refer to Roman Catholics.</note> and other heretics, but they also proudly define, as if speaking from an oracle, that *as long as we persevere in this opinion, no greater hope of salvation appears for us than for the Papists themselves; and that it is a marvel that we still wish to be considered members of the Church and practice the communion of public worship with it*, along with other things that a pen dipped in the bitterest black bile<note>According to the theory of the "four humors," black bile was associated with a melancholy or bitter temperament.</note> pours forth.

II. Therefore, in the last place, I have reserved the wiping away of this stain—which is surely shameful and should be tolerated by no sincere member of the Church. I shall do this in such an order that, beforehand, I will explain the true nature of the connection between Faith and Good Works somewhat more carefully; especially since most theologians here and there are not only too brief on this matter of the greatest importance, but also somewhat obscure.

# ON FAITH AS THE ROOT OF GOOD WORKS

<note>original: "DE FIDE RADICE BONORUM OPER."</note>

...than it really was, let us find out. Once this is done, it will be easy to see by what right those consequences are attributed to us.

III. Before all else, we must remember the distinction we touched upon in Dissertation I, sections 22 and 23. Specifically, sometimes **Good Works** are understood in such a broad sense that they include Faith itself; at other times, however, they designate moral actions that agree with the <term>Divine Law</term><note>The moral requirements revealed by God in the Bible, particularly the Ten Commandments.</note>, through which Faith is exercised and demonstrated. In this sense, they include any exercise of the Christian virtues that are distinct from Faith and presuppose its existence. We are using the term in this latter, stricter sense here. Although this stricter sense is not as common in the Sacred Scriptures as many believe—since in many places nothing prevents Faith itself from being included under the name of **Good Works**—nevertheless, these two things are often distinguished. *Titus 2:8: "I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works." 2 Corinthians 9:8: "That you may abound in every good work." Colossians 1:10: "That you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord; pleasing Him in all things, bearing fruit in every good work."* Add also *Acts 9:36, 1 Timothy 2:10, etc.*

IV. That these **Good Works** have such a relationship to true Faith that they are not only connected to it by an unbreakable bond, but also take their origin from it, is taught so clearly by Scripture that nothing else is more plainly revealed. *Without Faith it is impossible to please God (Hebrews 11:6).* Add also *Romans 14:23, Acts 15:9, 1 Timothy 1:5, Galatians 5:6, John 15:5.*

V. Indeed, to form a clear concept of the manner in which **Good Works** are produced from **Faith**, nothing seems more appropriate to us than the emblem of the **Root**, which the Sacred Scriptures are accustomed to use regarding Faith. Job surely understood this when, in chapter 19:28, he boasts that the *Root of the word* <note>original Hebrew: "שרש דבר" (shoresh davar); the Latin text reads "Radicem verbi." This is often translated in modern Bibles as "the root of the matter."</note> *is found in himself.* For while in verse 10 he had complained that God, like a tree whose branches are cut off, had driven away his hope, he nevertheless feels that the root remains. In this way, he opposes himself to the wicked man, of whom Bildad had affirmed in the preceding chapter that not only *the firstborn of death devours his branches (verse 13), but also that his roots dry up from beneath,*

<summary>This page defines "Good Works" in both a broad and strict sense, establishing that while they are distinct from Faith, they are inextricably linked to it as their source. The author introduces the biblical metaphor of Faith as a "Root" from which the fruits of Christian virtues grow.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 341 regarding the nature of Good Works. Having previously distinguished between Faith and the moral actions that follow it, the author now uses the biblical metaphor of the "Root" to explain how Faith provides the essential foundation and stability for a Christian life.</meta>

->DISSERTATION<-

...and his harvest is cut off from above [Job 18:16], where "the roots of the wicked" refers to his false confidence, as is clear from comparison with verse 14. In the same way, Proverbs 12:3 says: *The root of the righteous will not be moved.* Again, in verse 12: *The wicked man desires* <note>original Hebrew: "מצוד רעים" (matsod ra'im)</note> *a stronghold of evils* (namely, so that he may act securely away from divine judgments); *but the root of the righteous will give* that refuge against evil which the wicked man desires in vain. 

Now, what is it in the righteous that is not moved, and which provides a firm fortress against all the attacks of the world and of Satan, if not **Faith**? Hence the righteous man, *who puts his trust in the Lord, is compared to a tree extending its roots by a river* (Jeremiah 17:8). Thus the faithful are said to be <note>original Greek: "ἐῤῥιζωμένοι" (errizomenoi)</note> *rooted in Christ* (Colossians 2:7), specifically through **Faith**, which "puts on" Christ; for this reason, Ephesians 3:17 says, *rooted and grounded in love.* Whether you understand "love" here as the love of Christ (mentioned in verse 19), which is the foundation in which Faith takes root, or the love of the faithful toward Christ, it constitutes the very form of **Faith**. And in this way, we can explain the phrase where those who have only a <term>temporary faith</term><note>A theological term for a shallow belief that does not last under trial, often referencing the Parable of the Sower.</note> are said to *have no root* (Matthew 13:6, 21). See also Jude, verse 12.

VI. **Polycarp** <note>An early Christian bishop and martyr who was a disciple of the Apostle John.</note> imitates the elegance of this metaphor at the beginning of his *Letter to the Philippians*: <note>original Greek: "Καὶ ὅτι ἡ βεβαία της πίστεως ὑμῶν ῥίζα..."</note> *And that the firm root of your faith, announced from ancient times, remains until now and bears fruit in our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom you believe without seeing Him,* etc. 

So also the author of the **Book of Wisdom**, which carries the name of Solomon, says in chapter 15, verse 3, regarding the knowledge of God: <note>original Greek: "Τὸ γὰρ ἐπίστασθαί σε ὁλόκληρος δικαιοσύνη..."</note> *For to know You is perfect righteousness, and to know Your power is the root of immortality.* See also the same book at chapter 3, verse 15, and the **Son of Sirach** <note>Also known as the Book of Ecclesiasticus.</note> in chapter 1, verse 20: <note>original Greek: "Ῥίζα σοφίας φοβεῖσθαι τὸν Κύριον..."</note> *The root of Wisdom is to fear the Lord, and her branches are long life.* There can be no doubt that this is drawn from Proverbs 1:7 and 9:10, where theologians have abundantly demonstrated that the <term>Fear of the Lord</term><note>In this context, a reverent and living faith that leads to obedience.</note> refers to true **Faith**.

VII. The sweetness of this symbol is enhanced by the frequently recurring allegory of well-rooted trees and plants full of sap, applied to the pious in Psalm 1:3, 52:10, 92:13, Isaiah 44:5, and 61:3. The Creator stretched the roots of this soul into heaven and attached them to the outermost orbit of the so-called fixed stars; for among the creatures on earth, God made man alone to be a heavenly plant.* <note>original Greek: "Ἀνθρωπου δὲ ψυχὴν... οὐράνιον ὁ Θεὸς ἄνθρωπον εἰργάσατο."</note>

...and his harvest is cut off from above <note>Job 18:16</note>. In this passage, by the "roots of the wicked," their **confidence** is understood, as is clear from a comparison with verse 14. In the same way, Proverbs 12:3 says: *The root of the righteous shall not be moved.* And again in verse 12: *The wicked desire* <term>the fortress of evil men</term> <note>Hebrew: *matsod ra'im*, referring to a defense or a hunter's net</note>; (namely, so that he might act securely, shielded from divine judgments); *but the root of the righteous shall yield* that very asylum against evils which the wicked man longs for in vain. IX. And certainly there are many things in which **Faith** can be compared to a **Root**. Just as the beginning of a Root is the seed, entrusted to prepared soil with the necessary combination of heat and moisture; so Faith is born from the seed of the Word of the Gospel, preached in the Church, with the added efficacy of divine grace and the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, just as the Root lies hidden under the earth and exerts a wonderful power there, upon which the growth, preservation, and fruit-bearing of the plant depend—and which, even when the leaves fall or the branches are cut off, nevertheless preserves its vigor—so it is clearly established with Faith. It lies hidden within the heart and is not known externally except through its fruits. It is the medium through which spiritual life is nourished, increased, and abounds in the fruits of the Spirit. No winter of temptations, no violence of persecutions can suppress it.

# ON FAITH AS THE ROOT OF GOOD WORKS
### Xx
<meta>catchword: all [original: totam]</meta>

but they are even made fruitful. In the same way, Faith is engaged with Good Works. For in one part, through a power implanted from heaven, it is the immediate <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The "efficient cause" is a philosophical term for the primary agent that brings something into being—like a carpenter is the efficient cause of a table.</note> of Good Works. In another part, it ought to be regarded as the <term>instrumental cause</term>, <note>An "instrumental cause" is the tool used by the agent—like the carpenter's saw.</note> which repeatedly draws from elsewhere those aids and supports which it needs to bring Good Works to their maturity and to give them their proper form. We will attempt to pursue and explain both of these aspects more accurately.

XI. First, therefore, we consider Faith as the *efficient cause* and as an internal principle of all activity in the spiritual life, which is unfolded more and more through the constant exercise of Good Works. Hence, it is regarded as a Fountain of *living water* in the hearts of the chosen in **John 7:38**: *He who believes in me, as the Scripture says, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.* From the same source, the *issues* or emanations of *lives* are attributed to the heart in **Proverbs 4:23**. **Philo** <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher.</note> comes close to this in the first book of *The Life of Moses*, comparing Israel divided into twelve tribes with the twelve springs in the desert, since each one has the character of a spring <note>original Greek: εὐσεβοῦσα, χορηγούσης εὐσεβείας ἀεννάους καὶ ἀνελλιπεῖς καλὰς πράξεις</note> *cultivating piety, and producing through that piety perennial and unfailing good actions.* 

But even the pagans sought the fountain of virtue in the heart. Hence that saying of **Marcus Aurelius** <note>The Roman Emperor and Stoic philosopher, often called "Antoninus" in older texts.</note> in the seventh book of his *Meditations* (7.59): <note>original Greek: Ἔνδον βλέπε, ἔνδον ἡ πηγὴ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ, καὶ ἀεὶ ἀναβλύειν δυναμένη, ἐὰν ἀεὶ σκάπτῃς.</note> *Look within; within is the fountain of good, which is always able to bubble up if you always dig.* Add to this the same author in book eight (8.51) and the things gathered for both passages by the most diligent **Gataker**. <note>Thomas Gataker was a 17th-century English scholar famous for his commentary on Marcus Aurelius.</note> Thus, while they remained close in their wording, in reality they remained very far apart, because they did not understand how Faith properly turns the heart into such a fountain. 

But let us return to the emblem of the **root**. Just as a tree and its fruit can be thought to be contained in a root in two ways—either insofar as it lies hidden secretly within it, or insofar as it is produced from it successively—so the matter stands in the relationship of Faith to Good Works. For these works are partly *enfolded* <note>The author uses "involvuntur" to suggest they are folded inside the seed of faith like a blueprint.</note> within Faith from its first beginning, and partly *produced* by degrees from its various acts, which succeed one another in a rightful order.

# DISSERTATION
### XIII.

the whole chain of all Good Works shines forth from the formal act of Faith, which must be present immediately from its beginning. For since Faith is the first act of the **will** <note>In this context, the "will" refers to the human capacity for choice and desire, which the author argues is fundamentally redirected during a religious conversion.</note> renewed through <term>regeneration</term>, <note>Regeneration, or spiritual rebirth, is the theological concept of a person being "born again" or internally transformed by divine grace.</note> it follows that the transformation of the entire will—and its conversion from a deceptive goal to the true one—is already contained within the very nature of that Faith. This becomes very clear if one only considers what the very first movements of a will are when it has conceived faith from the "divine seed." 

From that moment in which a person is regenerated, they feel a sincere desire to have communion with God again and to live for His glory, especially after sensing the foul and sorrowful state into which they had fallen through sin. Behold, here are the first seeds of every virtue! For the entire Law of God is encompassed in the single word **LOVE**. *That is the end of the commandment* (**1 Timothy 1:5**). *That is the fulfillment of the Law* (**Romans 13:10**). Who could deny that the *beginning of Love* is already present there, where God appears to the sinner not only as a Good that can be *obtained* <note>original: "impetrabile"</note>—which the sinner has heard from the word of the Gospel—but also as a Good that is *desirable*? <note>original: "appetibile"</note> If the sinner dared to hope for communion with God, they would, from that first moment, trade all the riches of the world for it. 

Since it is true that whoever wills the goal also wills the means to get there, should we not also judge that whoever sincerely begins to desire communion with God also sincerely desires all the **means** that can lead to it? Furthermore, since the presence of one thing is the destruction of its opposite, does not the person who begins to love God as the true and supreme Good declare, at that very same moment, that all the "Goods" they sought outside of God are false? Do they not condemn themselves for the highest folly, having deluded their immortal soul with the desire for such things? Do they not begin *not to will* them? And when they cease to will those false Goods, must they not also be judged, at that very same moment, to no longer will all those impure and disordered *means* through which they pursued worldly gain? 

Who, then, can fail to recognize that in this first determination of the will—which is the beginning of belief—the pursuit of every virtue and the flight from every vice already lie hidden? Just as an infant, at the moment it is brought into the light of the world, possesses all the integral parts of a human being, so too does the person who places Faith as the first product of Regeneration simultaneously establish all the essential parts of the "internal and new man."

<summary>This page argues that the first act of Faith contains the seeds of all future Good Works because it fundamentally redirects the human will toward God and away from worldly "goods." The author uses a logical argument to show that desiring the "end" (God) necessitates desiring the "means" (virtue).</summary>

->### ON FAITH AS THE ROOT OF GOOD WORKS.<-

### XIII.

Furthermore, the means by which this first movement of Faith is most closely stirred is the Testimony of the Gospel. For through the Gospel alone, the soul perceives that God—though offended by sin and thus separated by His own holiness far from the company of the sinner—is nevertheless all-sufficient. Thus, God is an unfathomable Good <note>original: *impenetrabile*; likely suggesting a Good that is beyond human reach or understanding until revealed by grace.</note> for the sinner. Before this was established for the sinner, it was impossible for the desire for communion with God—which is the very beginning of true Faith—to be stirred. Therefore, when a person begins to believe, they embrace this Testimony as something that is both true and good for them.

However, one cannot embrace the Testimony of the Gospel unless they do so in the exact way it was revealed by God. Now, that Testimony declares that **God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all** (**1 John 1:5, 6**), and thus He has chosen a path that agrees with His perfect justice and holiness. To that end, He designated that Redeemer who would deliver us not only from the curse of sin, but from sin itself—the one **who would save His people from their sins** (**Matthew 1:21**). He would not fulfill this perfectly if He left those whom He redeems in the slavery of sin. 

Therefore, that Redeemer **gave himself for us, that He might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify for Himself a peculiar people, zealous for Good Works** (**Titus 2:14**). Thus, through His obedience, He did not only take away the curse, but also acquired power over all flesh, so that He might transfer the elect—once freed from the slavery of sin—into His own kingdom. Consequently, Christ cannot be embraced as the Author of salvation by anyone who is unwilling to be fully saved by Him—that is, to be released equally from the *stain* <note>The internal corruption or "dirtiness" of sin.</note> as from the *guilt* <note>The legal liability or "debt" of sin.</note> of sin. 

Finally, the ultimate goal of the entire plan of grace explained through this Testimony is nothing else, nor can it be anything else, than **the praise of His glorious grace** (**Ephesians 1:6**) and **the proclamation of the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light** (**1 Peter 2:9**). Anyone who desires the "means" (salvation) must also desire this "end" (God’s glory), and all the more so because the highest Good and the true perfection of man consist in that very goal. From all this, it is as clear as day that one cannot conceive of any serious inclination of the will toward God stirred by this Gospel Testimony, unless there already exists within that will an actual state of holiness...

<header>DISSERTATION</header>

...the sense and fear of God and the desire for liberation from all slavery of sin, with a readiness to give oneself to Christ as His own possession <note>original: *peculium*; a technical term in Roman law for property held by a subordinate, here used to describe the believer as Christ's own treasure.</note>, and to glorify God and show oneself grateful to Him through one's whole life for such a great salvation. Who, then, does not see that in a will so composed there lies hidden a rejection of all vices belonging to the slavery of sin, as well as a desire for every virtue? Hence the Savior says in John 14:23: *If anyone loves me, he will keep my word.* And from this source, **Good Works** are considered as an essential attribute of **Faith**; he who does not perform them boasts in vain of Faith, since it is dead without works, as stated in James 2:14, 17, 18.

### XIV.

Faith contains in its bosom not only the matter but also the *form* of a **Good Work**, because without Faith, a work would be done neither from the true *principle*, nor according to the just *norm*, nor toward the proper *end*. 

The **principle** of a Good Work is undoubtedly the rational persuasion of the soul regarding the will of the Legislator <note>The "Legislator" refers to God as the source of moral law.</note>. Through Faith alone is the will of God established, by which He willed in Christ not only to become the object of the sinner's worship, but also to allow a worship so halting and imperfect to be offered to Him, and to be able to find pleasure in it—which is a mystery hidden without Faith. 

Through Faith, no other *norm* is accepted than that which the Testimony of the Gospel presents, of whose perfection the soul is persuaded, and which it considers as the condition of the **Covenant of Grace**, from which it would not voluntarily depart by a hair's breadth <note>original: *latum unguem*; literally "a fingernail's breadth," an idiom meaning the smallest possible distance.</note>. And thus Faith shrinks from all <term>self-imposed worship</term> <note>original: *ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ* (ethelothrēskeia); often translated as "will-worship," referring to religious practices and devotions devised by human ingenuity rather than commanded by God.</note>. 

Faith also ensures that the work is performed in true *humility*, while it teaches about the false and true *end*. For on the one hand, Faith recognizes that it is impossible for the reborn to merit anything before God through their work, because it perceives the imperfection of even its best work. Indeed, nothing makes that work more unworthy than the very magnitude of divine love shown in Christ. Hence the **Seraphim** use the service of their *wings*—which best represent the movements of Faith and love—not only for flying but also for *covering their feet* in Isaiah 6:2 (just as the **Cherubim** use their hands and bodies in Ezekiel 1:8, 11) before the throne of grace. Meanwhile, however, through that same magnitude of divine love, Faith is urged and, as it were, constrained...

<meta>catchword: ...strained (Latin: gitur)</meta>

# ON FAITH AS THE ROOT OF GOOD WORKS

->Xx 3<-

[Therefore,] according to 2 Corinthians 5:14, the soul strives to show itself grateful in some way to so gracious a God.

### XV.
Just as a plant hidden in the seed gradually unfolds itself and spreads its fibers, so from this beginning of love—which the very start of **Faith** already possesses—all other actions gradually emerge. Hence **Faith** is said to be *working through love* <note>original Greek: *δι᾽ ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένη*; original Latin: *per amorem operosa*</note> in Galatians 5:6. This is because Faith first contains love within itself, from which all other virtues and actions emerge in their proper order. 

This is also the foundation of the admonition in 2 Peter 1:5–7: *Supplement your faith with virtue, virtue with knowledge, knowledge with self-control, self-control with patience, patience with godliness, godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love.* Regarding this passage, the celebrated **Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a prominent Dutch theologian known for "Covenant Theology," which emphasizes the organic unfolding of God's relationship with humanity.</note> writes in total agreement with our view: 

> Faith is the seed of God, which sprouts with every good fruit. Therefore Faith, at least as the Root, contains every virtue. Indeed, it contains love for God and neighbor. For God: because it possesses knowledge of Him who called us by glory and virtue. We cannot know Him as the cause or quality of our calling and not love Him. For the neighbor: because it is impossible to wish God to be glorified in oneself and not wish Him to be glorified in one's neighbor.

### XVI.
So that the wisdom of this most elegantly linked <term>Petrine admonition</term> <note>Referring to the "ladder of virtue" described by the Apostle Peter.</note> might appear more clearly, it should be noted that the virtues listed there are not only joined as diverse fruits of Faith derived from the same principle, but also as operations so intertwined that one follows from the other and buds forth as the **Root of Faith** repeatedly stimulates them. 

To make this even clearer, note that Peter progresses gradually from the internal and more general habits of the soul toward the external demonstration of these habits in more specific parts of virtue. He begins with the most general, which is **VIRTUE** <note>original Greek: *Ἀρετὴ* (Arete)</note>. Under this name, Greek authors sometimes include the whole of practical philosophy. The translators of the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> use this Greek word to translate the Hebrew terms for *splendor* <note>original Hebrew: הוד (*hod*)</note> and *praise* <note>original Hebrew: תהלה (*tehillah*)</note>. This is to let you know that whatever pertains to the splendor and praise—and thus to the perfection of our nature—is understood here by "virtue."

# DISSERTATION

Through [virtue], nothing else is designated here than a sincere purpose of living and acting according to the norm of the Gospel. This purpose, just as it is contained in **Faith**—in the manner we demonstrated in sections 12 and 13—in turn contains everything that follows.

### XVII.
The first quality in which **Virtue** begins to unfold itself is **Knowledge** <note>original Greek: *Γνωσις* (Gnosis); Latin: *Cognitio*</note>. Since there is already in virtue a sufficient awareness of one's obligation and a serious inclination of the soul to fulfill it, nothing will be more primary to the cultivator of Christian virtue than—with **Faith** itself holding out the lamp—to *look into that perfect Law of liberty* (James 1:25) and *prove what is the will of God, that which is good, pleasing, and perfect* (Romans 12:2). 

To this belongs not only the recognition of the duties themselves, but also the proper understanding of their foundations, arguments, and goals. This cannot happen without a more diligent investigation of the whole mystery of God, the Father, and Christ. Such a result is not to be expected, however, before **Faith** has occupied the depths of the heart; for without Faith, the sinner flees from the terrifying murmur of the Law and can hope for nothing from the Law except conviction, confusion, and condemnation. Thus, a new branch grows from the tree of **Faith**, yet one which is also the origin of all that follows. Because the Law of the Gospel contains the general standard for those who are subjects in Christ’s Kingdom, the knowledge of it grants a general fitness for performing all **Good Works** according to this standard.

### XVIII.
The first fruit springing from the knowledge of the Gospel Law, in which we are instructed through **Faith**, is called **Self-Control** <note>original Greek: *Εγκρατεια* (Enkrateia); Latin: *Continentia*</note>. By this term, we do not mean a specific virtue, elsewhere called "temperance," which concerns abstaining from bodily pleasures—a concept treated at length by **Suicer** <note>Johann Caspar Suicer (1620–1684), a Swiss theologian famous for his *Thesaurus Ecclesiasticus*, a massive dictionary of Greek Church Fathers.</note> in his *Ecclesiastical Treasury*, Vol. I, p. 998 and following. Rather, we mean a more general quality that demonstrates the *kratos* <note>Greek for "strength" or "power," the root of the word for self-control.</note> or strength of **Faith** in its victory over oneself and the entire world. 

Hence, it is said in **Xenophon’s** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and student of Socrates.</note> *Memorabilia*, Book I: *Self-control is the foundation of virtue* <note>original Greek: *Εγκρατειαν αρετης ειναι κρηπιδα*</note>. Imitating this, **Clement of Alexandria** <note>A prominent Christian theologian of the 2nd century who sought to bridge Greek philosophy and Christian faith.</note> in *Stromata*, Book II, calls self-control the *foundation of the virtues* <note>original Greek: *θεμελιον αρετων*</note>. **Aristotle** describes it quite elegantly in his *Ethics*, Book VII, Chapter 2: *The self-controlled man, knowing that his desires are base, does not follow them because of his reason.* <note>original Greek: *Ο εγκρατης, ειδως οτι φαυλαι αι επιθυμιαι, ουκ ακολουθει δια λογον*</note>

-># CONCERNING FAITH AS THE ROOT OF GOOD WORKS<-

### XVIII. (continued)
*A self-controlled person is one who, knowing their desires are evil, does not follow them because of reason.* <note>original: "Continens est is, qui sciens, malas esse concupiscentias, eas non sequitur propter rationem." This is a classic definition of self-control or "continence" often found in moral philosophy.</note> A similar example is drawn from athletes, who, in order to gain strength for the contest, carefully avoid everything that could weaken the body. Nothing is more suitable for describing the true <term>self-denial</term><note>The practice of setting aside one's own impulses to follow God's will.</note> of oneself and of all things outside of God in Christ. That self-denial is the genuine work of **Faith**. For as long as **Faith** regards nothing as a "True Good" except for communion with God through the reconciled Christ, it rejects by that very act whatever might hinder that communion with God. Furthermore, **Faith** produces this self-denial directly from its knowledge of the Gospel Law, because the first requirement of that Law is *self-denial*, through which the heart must be emptied before it can be filled with Christ and heavenly gifts. And from this it is again clear how this *denial* is the embrace of all the fruits that follow, because it is done for the purpose of making the soul more fit to pursue <term>sanctification</term><note>The ongoing process of being made holy or being set apart for God's purposes.</note>.

### XIX.
The next effect of this self-control or self-denial is *Patience* <note>original Greek: Υπομονη (*Hupomone*); Latin: *Patientia*</note>. Although this virtue might seem to be more specific, it actually has the broadest application. This is because it involves both *Constancy*—or the firmness of purpose in living according to the Gospel, having set aside all adversities and temptations that make the path of virtue difficult—and also *Hope*, which Paul numbers among the three cardinal virtues of Christianity in 1 Corinthians 13:12 <note>Likely referring to 1 Corinthians 13:13.</note>. This is evident both from the nature of the thing itself, because the hope of certain liberation is the foundation of all patience, and from Romans 8:25: *But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience.* See also Romans 5:4 and James 5:7–8. Such patience is the genuine daughter of **Faith** (James 1:3), which involves not only a firm purpose of virtue but also perceives that **Hope** is awakened in the sinner who desires salvation through the testimony of the Gospel. Moreover, it is produced directly through *self-denial*, because that denial gives one the strength to endure and is a criterion for a hope that is by no means deceptive. Hence, Jesus immediately connects the *endurance of the cross* with self-denial in Matthew 16:24. Scripture considers this same **Patience** to be the "womb" or source of all the remaining good fruits in Luke 8:15 and James 1:4. For the one who has thus steeled their mind against all obstacles to virtue, and is filled with the hope of a successful outcome,

### XX.
A soul prepared in this way is adapted for the exercise of more specific virtues, among which the first place is held by **Piety** <note>original Greek: Εὐσέβεια (*Eusebeia*); Latin: *Pietas*</note>. Here rises the second order of the "fruits of knowledge" in the faithful. For the two preceding virtues <note>Self-control and patience.</note> were required for conquering evil; the three following virtues contain the pursuit of the opposite good, and this according to both <term>tables of the Evangelical Law</term> <note>A reference to the Ten Commandments, traditionally divided into two "tables": the first four regarding duties to God, and the final six regarding duties to neighbors.</note>. For **Piety** here encompasses all duties pertaining to the true worship of God, both internal and external. Its deepest root is once again **Faith** itself, which, while it is carried by love toward God, longs to declare this love through reverence and appropriate worship; hence it is also distinguished by the name **Fear of Jehovah** <note>original: *Timoris Jehovae*. This "fear" refers to a holy awe and respect rather than terror.</note>. Furthermore, **Piety** is most closely linked to **Patience** joined with **Hope**, because the believer endures all things for the sake of God alone, and perceives that He, from whom they hope to be fully delivered, must be worshiped. Since the first table of the law is the root of the second, it is clear from this how the remaining fruits spring forth from **Piety**.

### XXI.
The next work of piety is **Brotherly Love** <note>original Greek: Φιλαδελφία (*Philadelphia*)</note> toward those born of the same God and heavenly Father. He who seeks to be united to God through **Faith** is ready for this duty. For while he loves God, he also loves God’s image <note>See 1 John 5:1.</note>. Indeed, he considers this very thing as a part of divine worship or **Piety**, which does not end only with the heavenly Father, but through Him spreads itself to all the offspring descended from Him.

### XXII.
Once **Brotherly Love** is established, all acts of **Charity** <note>original Greek: Ἀγάπη (*Agape*); Latin: *Charitas*</note> are established at the same time, in which that love is expressed in various ways. This **Charity** most immediately designates the duties of love owed to the Brothers, yet it is such that it spreads itself to other people as well, whom the believer seeks to entice into the bond of the same brotherhood, and thus to expand that bond as much as possible. # ON FAITH AS THE ROOT OF GOOD WORKS.

...to understand it most broadly as the exercise of any specific virtues flowing from the love of God and His people. This sense of <term>love</term> <note>original Greek: ἀγάπη (*agape*)</note> is evident in Romans 12:9, 1 Corinthians 14:1, 2 Corinthians 6:6, Ephesians 5:2, Colossians 1:8, Philemon verse 5, and elsewhere. Hence, among the outward fruits of the Spirit—which are opposed to the outward fruits of the flesh—**love** is mentioned in the first place (Galatians 5:22). 

And this very activity lies hidden in the root of Faith: 
1) regarding love of neighbor, both because it belongs to the Law of Faith to win others for Christ, and because he who is himself convinced of the greatness of that good which the proclamation of the Gospel proposes, burns with a desire to make others partakers of that good along with himself; 
2) regarding whatever virtuous actions are encompassed under the name of <term>love</term> in a broader sense. 

Whence Peter immediately adds: *If these things are in you and abound, they will make you neither idle nor unfruitful* <note>2 Peter 1:8</note>. Paul also foreshadows this under a most elegant image in Colossians 3:14, commanding us to put on **love** over all virtues, which is the <term>bond of perfection</term> <note>original Greek: σύνδεσμος (*syndesmos*), meaning a fastening or ligament that holds things together</note>. It is like a precious and most ornate belt which is added over the rest of the garments; it binds them together and makes the wearer ready and unencumbered for work. And so the love of Faith forms that link in the "chain of virtues" which connects their beginning and end together, since not only does every virtue proceed from that love, but it also ends in the same, having this as its immediate goal: to actually demonstrate that love in individual actions.

### XXIII.
However, although it is certain from what has been said that Faith itself contains all Good Works within its bosom as a root—works which gradually emerge from there—this would still not be enough unless Faith also possessed and exercised a singular fitness for drawing that power from elsewhere. It is by this power that the life of Faith is preserved, and Faith is unceasingly stimulated, sharpened, and repeatedly "impregnated," as it were, to bring forth the mature fruits of Good Works. Hence in James 2:22, it is said that Faith <term>works together with works</term> <note>original Greek: συνεργεῖν τοῖς ἔργοις (*synergein tois ergois*)</note>. In this matter, we must attend both to the *source* from which Faith draws, and the *manner* in which Faith pulls the life-sap from that source, which makes it fertile in Good Works.

### XXIV.
That source is none other than Christ himself,
