->### DISSERTATION<-

...the <term>Savior</term> <note>original: *Servator*</note> himself excellently teaches in John 15:4–5: *Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, unless it abides in the vine; so neither can you, unless you abide in me. I am the vine, you are the branches: he who abides in me, and I in him, this one bears much fruit: for apart from me you can do nothing.* For this reason, the pious soul calls the Lord the **strength of his life** <note>original: *robur vitae suae*</note> in Psalm 27:1. *For the life of the godly is hidden with Christ in God*, according to Colossians 3:3. From this, Paul graphically boasts in Galatians 2:20: *I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh, I live through that Faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.*

XXV. The faithful soul ought to be always occupied in drawing from this fountain. Indeed, it often pauses in this work, whether through carnal sloth and a sense of security—by which it does not pay enough attention to the necessity of the influence of Christ and the Spirit of his life for the preservation and growth of the <term>new man</term>—or through faint-heartedness. This faint-heartedness is usually a consequence of neglected duty; after a new staining of one's "garments" <note>a metaphor for committing new sins</note>, the soul does not dare to appear before the pure eyes of the Lord, or at least does not dare to use its usual freedom of access. Truly, the longer one persists in such a state, the more the numbness of the soul often grows, its strengths decrease, and the spiritual life is seized by a kind of slow wasting disease. A living image of such a state is presented in **Psalm 32:3–4**: *When I kept silent, my bones grew old, while I groaned all day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me. My moisture was turned into the drought of summer. Selah.* 

For what could better foreshadow that silence joined with groaning than such a state of the soul? In this state, the soul indeed sends out a complaining voice, but it remains "silent" before God because it does not perceive how perfect that **everlasting righteousness** <note>original: *justitia seculorum*, referring to the enduring justification provided by God</note> is, which was described in verses 1 and 2 of that Psalm. It is this righteousness which gives everyone in whose heart there is no deceit the right to approach the **throne of grace** with <term>boldness</term> <note>original Greek: παῤῥησία (*parrhessia*), meaning free and confident speech</note>. Therefore, while the soul—through ignorance and the waves of doubt by which it is hedged in (contrary to the nature of the New Testament)—neglects to embrace the merit of Christ for the forgiveness of sins with a firm Faith, nothing else can follow but both a sense of divine wrath and a **drying up** of the vital sap needed to bear the fruits of sanctification.

It is so necessary that the soul continues to embrace the <term>merit of Christ</term> <note>The "merit of Christ" refers to the theological idea that Jesus's perfect life and sacrifice are credited to the believer</note> again and again with true Faith, if it wishes not only to have a sense of divine favor, but also to acquire ever-new strength for walking before the Lord.

XXVI. Scripture most vigorously compares this occupation of Faith with eating and drinking. From many passages we will extract only that of *John 6:53, 56, 57*: *<note>original: "Amen, amen, dico vobis, nisi ederitis carnem Filii hominis, & biberitis ejus sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis. Qui edit carnem meam & bibit sanguinem meum, in me manet, & ego in eo. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. As the living Father sent me, and I live through the Father, so also he who eats me, he himself will live through me.* The emphasis of these words is such that they refer the fruits of *eating and drinking* through Faith not only to the right to eternal life, but also to the preservation of <term>spiritual life</term> itself in those who have already received its beginnings. This is something that nature itself suggests by analogy. For we require food and drink if we wish not only to keep life going, but also to be active in it. And just as we repeatedly make use of new food and drink to refresh our failing strength, so too a continual activity of Faith is required to acquire new spiritual strength through a union with Jesus that is renewed daily.

XXVII. However, so that the manner in which Faith must restore strength for producing good fruits without ceasing may be more deeply understood, we must distinctly consider both what means Faith employs to draw new strength from Jesus again and again, and *how* it proceeds internally in the *use* of those means.

XXVIII. Among the means that Faith employs, the principal one is *Prayers*, by which the Father is petitioned in Christ, and this for a double reason. For since it belongs to Faith to acknowledge the unworthiness of one's own work (as we noted in § XIV), both because of the omission of various duties and because of the imperfection of what has been performed, Faith repeatedly lays hold of the merit of Christ for the remission <note>forgiveness or wiping away</note> of those offenses and imperfections. This cannot happen without a renewed sorrow and shame over their foulness. From this, it naturally follows that the soul considers this sad sense of sins as an evil rendering life itself troublesome—as in *Romans 7:24*—and so, with a new desire and zeal, it is <insert>filled</insert> <note>The catchword "implea-" at the bottom suggests the word "impleatur," meaning "is filled" or "may be filled."</note>

### 354

Our Savior himself teaches this excellently in **John 15:4-5**: *Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, unless it abides in the vine; so neither can you, unless you abide in me. I am the vine, you are the branches: he who abides in me, and I in him, he bears much fruit: for apart from me you can do nothing.* <note>original Latin: "Manete in me, & ego in vobis. Sicut palmes non potest ferre fructum à semetipso, nisi manserit in vite; ita nec vos, nisi in me manseritis. Ego sum vitis, vos palmites: is qui manet in me, & ego in ipso, hic fert fructum multum: nam seorsim à me nihil potestis facere."</note> For this reason, the pious soul calls Jehovah the **strength of its life** in **Psalm 27:1**. For the **life of the pious is hidden with Christ in God**, according to **Colossians 3:3**. From this, Paul gloriously boasts in **Galatians 2:20**: *I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh, I live by that Faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.* <note>original Latin: "Vivo, non amplius ego, sed vivit in me Christus: & vitam, quam nunc vivo in carne, vivo per Fidem illam Filii Dei, qui dilexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me."</note>

XXV. The faithful soul must always be occupied in drawing from this fountain. Indeed, it often neglects this, either through sluggishness and carnal security—whereby it does not pay enough attention to the necessity of the influence of Christ and the Spirit of his life for the preservation and growth of the "new man"—or through faint-heartedness, which is usually a consequence of neglected duty. In this state, after a new staining of its garments <note>A metaphor for committing new sins or failing in moral duties.</note>, the soul does not dare to appear before the pure eyes of the Lord, or at least does not dare to use its accustomed freedom of access. Truly, the longer one persists in such a state, the more the soul's numbness often increases, its strengths decrease, and the spiritual life is seized as if by a slow wasting disease. 

A living image of such a state is presented in **Psalm 32:3-4**: *When I kept silence, my bones grew old, while I roared all day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me. My moisture was turned into the drought of summer. Selah.* <note>original Latin: "Quum tacerem, senuerunt ossa mea, quum rugirem toto die. Nam interdiu & nocte gravis erat super me manus tua. Vertebatur succus meus in siccitatem æstatis. Selah."</note> For what could more aptly shadow forth that silence joined with roaring than such a state of the soul? In it, the soul indeed emits a complaining voice, but it is silent before God, as it does not perceive how perfect that **righteousness of the ages** <note>original: "justitia seculorum," referring to the eternal or everlasting righteousness provided by God.</note> is, which was described in verses 1 and 2, and which gives everyone in whose heart there is no guile the right to approach the **throne of grace** with **boldness** <note>original: "parrhesia," a Greek term used in the New Testament to describe the confident, outspoken freedom of speech believers have before God.</note>. Therefore, while the soul—through ignorance and the waves of doubt with which it is hedged in, contrary to the nature of the New Testament—neglects to embrace the merit of Christ for the remission of sins with a firm Faith, nothing else can follow but both a sense of divine wrath and a drying up of the vital juice needed to bear the fruits of **sanctification**.

XXXV. From such a vast heap of means, which are offered to the faithful through Christ, the supreme <term>goodness</term> <note>original Greek: *χρηστότης* (chrestotēs); refers to God’s moral excellence and kindness.</note> and <term>love for mankind</term> <note>original Greek: *φιλανθρωπία* (philanthrōpia); the benevolent affection of God toward humanity.</note> of God shines forth more clearly than the noonday light. By these means, He shows that He has no less care for preserving and promoting the spiritual life in grace than He has for the care with which He nurtures the natural life of men. For here there is an equally great abundance and variety of heavenly nourishment that serves this saving purpose of God. These means follow one another in a pleasing diversity, so that if one should be lacking, another is available, and there is no time in which Faith does not have something by which it can be sustained. And although sometimes winter may set in and a scarcity of spiritual grain may prevail, nevertheless the promise always remains certain and fixed: *His bread is given, his waters are sure* <note>Isaiah 33:16</note>. And Faith, turning this abundance of divine grace—which provides so many helps—to its own use, acts again like a root split and spread into many fibers. These fibers collect various kinds of sap from different parts of the surrounding earth and carry them toward the sustenance and fertilization of the plant. Yet, this happens in such a way that, according to the different nature of the sap and the arrangement of the fibers, some fruits are formed more abundantly and excellently than others; those fruits come closest to perfection which are produced by the most suitable sap flowing through the best-disposed fibers.

XXXVI. What has been said concerning the general relationship of Good Works to Faith can easily be applied to individual Christian virtues and their exercise. It most willingly prepares itself for those services in which it can testify to the promotion of God’s honor, and show how sincerely it is carried toward the preservation and promotion of communion with Him. [...Faith] employs all things that God has granted, turning them to its own use, so that this specific <term>Good Work</term> <note>original: *Opus Bonum*; in this theological context, it refers to actions performed by a believer that are considered pleasing to God through faith.</note> which it contemplates may receive its proper form and tend toward the praise of the glorious divine grace manifested in Christ.

XXXVII. The boundaries and specific scope of this disputation do not permit us to demonstrate this in a detailed review of the Christian virtues. For that would require a proper commentary on Christian virtues—a work that is all the more desirable because, if it is permitted to speak the truth, almost all writings that have hitherto professionally treated *Moral Theology* <note>The branch of theology focused on how a person should live and the nature of their actions.</note> suffer from this notable defect: they deal too generally with the nature of individual virtues. For although they occasionally treat the duties in which those virtues ought to manifest themselves with accuracy, and do not neglect the motivating arguments and appropriate means, they are nevertheless everywhere lacking in that they do not show how the proof of such fruits flows *from Faith*, and how Faith is active in bringing them forth. 

This defect ought to be remedied all the more because, through the properly demonstrated bond between Faith and the individual Christian virtues, two things would be achieved: first, one would more clearly perceive what renders an externally good work truly acceptable before God, distinguishing it from the "splendid actions" of all heathens and hypocrites; second, the excellence of Christian Ethics above all the dictates of reason and the decrees of philosophers would be set in full light. Allow us, therefore, on this occasion to indicate by at least one example the order in which, in our view, the treatment of individual virtues can be undertaken with the greatest fruit.

XXXVIII. Among the Christian virtues, a prominent place is occupied by *liberality toward those who need our help, especially the poor*, to be exercised through <term>almsgiving</term> <note>original: *eleemosyna*; from the Greek *eleēmosunē*, meaning mercy or pity, specifically referring to the giving of money or food to the poor.</note>. One who is about to treat this subject will best exhaust everything to be observed regarding this virtue if he presents it to be viewed first *in itself*, and then *in relation to Faith*. To the first part will belong the task of providing an accurate definition and reviewing the various circumstances of persons, places, and times in which this virtue ought to be practiced, and prescribing what proportion and measure should be prudently observed in each case.

To that communion belongs both the requirement to regard all members of that body as one's own and all subjects of this kingdom as brothers, and to contribute all one's resources to the expansion of this kingdom. Finally, the person who receives a benefit beholds a living image in the generosity of the benefactor, and indeed feels it; from this, he can gather how solid, certain, and excellent are the effects that **Faith** <note>original: *Fides*</note> has in the chosen ones. **XLI.** Thus it is certain that whoever establishes **Faith** also establishes generosity. But through that same Faith, the use of "means" is simultaneously provided, by which the habit of that virtue can be preserved and expressed more and more. All *prayers* <note>original: *preces*</note> tend toward this, in which a person seeks through the blood of Christ the forgiveness of sins—often committed through the neglect of this virtue—and desires to be filled more and more with His Spirit. Only this Spirit can suppress the depravity of *self-love* <term>original: *philautia*; a Greek-derived term used by theologians to describe a disordered or excessive love of oneself that blocks love for others.</term> which is contrary to the exercise of this virtue; and this generosity must also be counted among the fruits of that Spirit. Hence Paul considers the generosity of the Macedonians as a grace of God granted to them. <margin>2 Corinthians 8:1. See also 2 Corinthians 9:14, 15.</margin>

**XLII.** The same fruit comes from the various *meditations* <note>original: *meditationum*</note> of **Faith**, through which the believer cultivates communion with Christ, and in which various arguments frequently recur that insist upon this duty of generosity. For Faith not only assumes those arguments already known through nature, but also presents them in full light and adds many others. Considering the beauty of his Savior in the word of grace, the believer perceives that care for the wretched and the needy also belongs to Christ's beauty—a care not neglected by Him, even though He was poor. <margin>John 13:29.</margin> The believer sees that he must imitate this example, so that he may become more like the One with whom he longs to be most intimately united. From this same source, he learns that the constant practice of the faithful has always been occupied with exercising this virtue: that the very Church of Israel was bound to this generosity <margin>Leviticus 19:9; 25:35, 39; Deuteronomy 15:7.</margin> and that the faithful themselves who lived before Christ produced excellent examples of this virtue. <margin>Job 31:16; 1 Kings 18:19.</margin> How much more will this befit a member of the New Testament Church, who, the greater the benefits he has received, the more promptly...

<summary>This page argues that faith is the necessary foundation for true generosity, using prayer and meditation on Christ's example as the means to overcome self-love. It highlights how the generous actions of believers serve as a "living image" of faith that inspires others to join the religious community.</summary>

<meta>catchword: XLVI.</meta>

...ought to be used for the relief of others: especially since the possession of bodily goods is not to be considered the primary "good" of the **New Covenant** <note>original: *Novi Fœderis*</note>, and the number of those from the people of God who are called to want and poverty is far greater—whom we must assist as members of Christ. On this basis, that particular and prescribed benevolence was assigned to the faithful of the New Testament among the Prophets. <margin>Psalm 112; Isaiah 58:6, 7.</margin> Hence, from the very first beginnings of the New Testament Church, the **Faith** of the new Christians shone forth in this generosity in a singular way. <margin>Acts 2:45; 4:34; 11:29; Romans 15:25ff; 2 Corinthians 8:3, etc.</margin>

**XLIII.** Whoever reflects upon themselves will soon discover how bountifully they have experienced God on various occasions, especially if they find enough of a foundation within themselves to hope that, without any merit of their own, they have been enrolled into the inheritance of eternal life. The more clearly one perceives this, the more strongly they will feel incited to imitate divine generosity, lest they become guilty of that ingratitude by which the debtor of ten thousand talents lost the full benefit of that gift which he imagined he had already obtained. <margin>Matthew 18:24ff.</margin>

**XLIV.** In the very **theater of nature** <note>A common theological metaphor of the time, suggesting the physical world is a stage where God's attributes are put on display.</note> one finds a spur to their own generosity. This happens not only when a person recognizes that other men share the same origin and nature as themselves, but also when they observe that great benevolence of the Heavenly Father toward everyone, who *makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust.* <margin>Matthew 5:45.</margin> The believer deems that this example of the Father—whom **Faith** regards as its own Father—must be imitated.

**XLV.** Furthermore, **Faith**, having been raised to the contemplation of the future goods for which we hope, weighs how great those things are which God, according to His most free good pleasure, has promised in His word as a gracious reward for generosity rightly spent. <margin>Galatians 6:9; Proverbs 22:9; Isaiah 58:8ff; Matthew 10:42; 25:34ff; Luke 14:13, 14.</margin> For the one who believes without hesitation that these promises will come true—and that within a very short interval of time—would they not notice that any slowness in giving (where Christian love and prudence require it) is contrary to a full assent of **Faith** in these promises?

<summary>This page argues that Christian generosity is a natural outcome of faith, motivated by the biblical examples of the early Church, the imitation of God’s universal providence, and the certain hope of future eternal rewards.</summary>

# ON FAITH AS THE ROOT OF GOOD WORKS.

<page-num>365</page-num>

## XLVI.
From what has been said, the vanity of the conclusions with which our opinion regarding the formal act of **Faith** is burdened will now be easily established. For it is most true that *God justifies no one unless they have begun to cease from evil works and have, in some way, started a new life*, because He justifies no one except the believer. Indeed, whoever denies that the ceasing of evil works and the beginning of a new life are joined with the very first rise of Faith must be ignorant of how Faith itself is a **Good Work** in an emphatic sense <note>original: *in emphafi*; meaning it is the quintessential good work from which others flow</note>, and how, as the first act of a new life, it involves all subsequent acts. 

Meanwhile, it is frivolous to accuse us on that ground of colluding with the **Papists** <note>original: *Pontificiis*; a term used by Protestant writers to refer to the Roman Catholic Church</note> and others who teach that we are justified *because* of **Good Works**. For it is one thing for Faith—viewed even as a Good Work and joined from its first moment with the love of God—to precede our justification; it is quite another thing for it to be, in any way, the **meritorious cause** <term>meritorious cause: the legal or moral basis upon which a reward is deserved</term> of justification. We are all the more free from this charge because we attribute it to the very nature of Faith itself that it alone is capable of recognizing **without delay** <term>ἀνυπερθέτως (anyperthetōs): a Greek term meaning immediately or without hesitation</term> the worthlessness of any Good Work for meriting anything before God, and therefore it becomes a suppliant to Christ, so that through His merit, the stains clinging even to the best works may be washed away. 

However, when the **Fathers of Dordrecht** <note>Referring to the Synod of Dort (1618–1619), which defined key doctrines of the Reformed tradition</note> affirm that *we are justified by Faith before we have performed Good Works*, this must be understood either generally regarding such *legally Good Works* which could be the matter of justification before God, or more specifically according to the distinction of the concept of Good Works which we provided in §. 3.

## XLVII. 
Nor does the second objection have more weight—namely, that we take away the very essence of **Good Works**, *to which essence it belongs that they proceed from gratitude, from which it is argued they cannot proceed unless they are done by someone who believes himself already in possession of all the benefits of grace*. Let it be well noted here in what matter we differ. For the question is not whether it is required for a Good Work (which according to the **Gospel** must please God in Christ) to proceed from gratitude; nor whether that work lacks its due perfection which is offered to God from a Faith raised so high that it applies all the Gospel promises to itself with sole confidence. In this—

The author clarifies his position against both Roman Catholic views and potential misinterpretations of the Synod of Dort.</summary>

# DISSERTATION

<page-num>366</page-num>

...for we indeed agree, and we maintain that **Faith** <note>original: *Fidem*</note> remains imperfect for as long as it has not yet grown into that strength. As long as the **Root** <note>original: *Radix*</note> is imperfect, the fruits will also be imperfect. But the question is this: does no hope of salvation appear for those who indeed strive for **Good Works**, yet do not yet dare to rejoice in the benefits of **grace** as if they were already granted to them—even if all other requirements, and specifically a hunger and thirst for the **righteousness of Christ**, are present? We pronounce those who affirm this <note>that is, those who say there is no hope for such people</note> to be injurious to many, and perhaps the majority, of faithful souls at this time. 

For how many are found in whom **Faith** lies hidden for some time, like a root in winter, and is not conspicuous by any external good works? This is so even though some vital sap glows in secret, which is so faint that it is not perceived even by those who truly possess it. How many, perhaps, are there who are brought to true **Faith** so late that it could not be demonstrated through the fruits of **Good Works**? How many others, in the beginnings of **grace** or under heavy temptations—even after they had already been filled with the full assurance of **Faith**—do not dare to claim the **Evangelical** promises for themselves? How rash it is to place all these people in a damnable state!

## XLVIII.
But they <note>the theological opponents</note> insist: Why not? It is enough that they are not grateful toward God, and thus God does not reach the goal of His glorious **grace** in them. I respond that God, in this life, expects nothing except the beginnings of gratitude; and for the sake of the **obedience of Christ**, He tolerates this weakness just as He does other infirmities of **Good Works**, until eternity begins, in which a full *Hallelujah* <note>original: *Hallelujah*</note> will be sung to Him. He also holily bears this weakness because it does not proceed from a vice of the will, but from an intellect that has been so obscured thus far that it cannot recognize the benefit given to it. It is not as if the person distrusted the all-sufficiency of God, but rather because in their own **sinfulness** <term>peccaminositas: the state of being prone to sin or the quality of one's sinful nature</term> they cannot yet distinguish the criteria and foundations of this hope.

## XLIX.
And any attentive person will admit this all the more easily when we establish, by the following arguments, that gratitude itself is present from the very first beginning of even a weaker **Faith**—which desires Christ and seeks to be united with Him. 

**I.** That the soul, which is carried into union with Christ according to the testimony of the **Gospel**, from...

From the first moment this desire arises, it holds the intention of consenting to this condition: that it wishes, if Jesus admits it to the **marriage covenant** <note>original: *foedus conjugale*; a common theological metaphor for the union between Christ and the soul</note>, to show itself pleasing to Him throughout all of life. This purpose of the will is already a part of **gratitude**.

II. Because the soul already considers it a great benefit just to hear in the **Gospel** <note>original: *Evangelio*</note> that a way of escape from the curse and power of the Devil lies open; that its **carnal security** <note>original: *securitatem carnis*; a state of false spiritual comfort or indifference</note> has been driven away; and that it feels itself filled with a desire for Christ. For although the soul may still doubt whether it should consider this an effect of saving **grace**, it nevertheless values this feeling so highly that it prefers it to all the treasures of the world. Therefore, it already possesses something for which it can be grateful.

III. Moreover, there is the hope of finding [God], which, although it may sometimes be faint, is able—because of the greatness of the goal—to ignite the soul with a zeal for **gratitude** even in the smallest spark.

IV. Finally, if anyone still seems to doubt the truth of our argument, let him consider: can there be more than two driving causes for a **Good Work** <note>original: *Boni Operis*</note>? Namely, is it done either to earn **merit** <note>original: *mereantur*; to earn salvation by one's own efforts</note>, or to show **gratitude**? Can a third cause be given? Does it not then follow that all **Good Works** that reject the first goal must be done from the second? Such are the works of those "weak in **Faith**" whom we are defending. They acknowledge no **merit** in their own work. They feel its unworthiness and inadequacy, not only for the purpose of **justification** <note>being made right before God</note>, but even for offering the thanks due to God. It is from this very feeling that their inner struggles and fluctuations arise. Why, then, should those who so completely reject all **merit** in their works not be judged to bring forth whatever good they do from the true fountain of **gratitude**?

L. But if we wished to burden those who so virulently insult our opinion with the consequences of their own views, what would be easier than to raise a most just complaint about the "wide gate" <note>a reference to the "wide gate that leads to destruction" in Matthew 7:13</note> which is opened to **carnal security** by their contrary hypothesis? How dangerous is that persuasion—the belief that "Christ died for me"—before I have seen the criteria of the sincerity of my **Faith**; this was already cautioned in the preceding dissertation, section 24. Specifically, the fallacy of this **Confidence** <note>original: *Fiducia*; here used to mean a premature or false sense of assurance</note> is seen in the sick and in those at the point of death. After a whole life spent in sin, some would wish to command these people—without any prior self-examination—that at the **SAME MOMENT** they hear the **Gospel**, they should apply it to themselves...

# DISSERTATION ON FAITH AS THE ROOT, etc. #
XVI.

If they [ministers] soothe them regarding the **certainty of salvation** <note>original: *certitudinem salutis*</note>, what else will it be but to miserably deceive them at the very moment of eternity, causing irreparable loss? It gives them cause to later complain in hell about those who deluded them with false comfort, as if they were the most shameful seducers. To these ministers, the description of the Prophets who speak vanity in Ezekiel 13:18-19 applies. I do not repent of the assertion which I, along with other truly **Reformed Theologians** <note>original: *Theologis vere Reformatis*; scholars belonging to the Calvinist tradition</note> in the *Covenant of Grace* <note>original: *Fœd. Grat.* (Foedus Gratiae); a central doctrine in Reformed theology regarding God's promise of salvation through Christ</note> (Book I, ch. V, §. 24 and Book VIII, §. 42), have indicated: the danger of such **Confidence** <note>original: *Fiduciæ*; here meaning a bold assurance of one's own salvation</note>, by which thousands of **False Christians** <note>original: *Pseudo-Christiani*</note> perish eternally. My opponents may declare this assertion to be vain and worthless, *intending nothing else than that the **Way of Truth** <note>original: *via Veritatis*</note> and the pure **Reformed doctrine** <note>original: *Reformatorum doctrina*</note> be blasphemed.* How rashly they judge is most evident from the examples of Holy Scripture itself. In these texts, people are introduced who, puffed up by this false confidence, will discover on the day of judgment *that they have made a lie their refuge, and hidden themselves in falsehood* (Isaiah 28:15). Such are those *who say, "Lord, Lord," although they do not do what the Father in heaven wills*, and who will say to Jesus on that day: *"Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and perform many miracles in your name?"* To whom it will be answered: *"Truly, I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity"* (Matthew 7:21-23). See also Matthew 25:44 and 2 Peter 2:2.

LI. Nor is the force of this conclusion broken by the admission *that **Faith** <note>original: *Fidem*</note> which is devoid of works is not true Faith.* Therefore, if someone were to boast of true Faith but did not demonstrate it through its fruits, he would simply be showing the vanity of his own boasting. For since those fruits follow from Faith, according to my opponents, I would be required to believe that Christ died for me at the very moment when those fruits are not yet visible—when it is still uncertain whether they will ever follow. In such a case, it is possible that the faith is not true Faith, and consequently, by the very nature of the matter, it is uncertain whether it is true that Christ died for me. How close this is to the **Implicit Faith** <note>original: *Fide Pontificiorum implicita*; a Catholic doctrine suggesting one can have faith simply by agreeing with the Church's teachings, even without personal understanding</note> of the Papists, and what a ruinous foundation for Faith it lays down, is self-evident.

<summary>The author warns against granting "certainty of salvation" to those who lack the evidence of good works, comparing such false assurance to the "implicit faith" of Catholicism. He argues that true faith must be validated by its fruits (works) to avoid the eternal tragedy of being a "False Christian."</summary>

### XVI.

## THEOLOGICAL DISSERTATION
### ON THE
# ORIGINE OF THE NAME
# LOGOS. <note>original Greek: Λ Ο Γ Ο Σ; meaning "The Word"</note> $^a)$

->I.<-

To understand the Mystery of the **LOGOS** <note>original Greek: ΤΟΥ ΛΟΓΟΥ</note>, a singular importance is added if one is able to attain the first origin of this Name used for the Son of God. A large crowd of ancient and modern interpreters has determined that this origin must be sought in the Mosaic history of Creation itself. And the Prologue of the Gospel of John particularly favors this opinion, which, speaking of the **Hypostatic LOGOS** <note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΩΙ; "Hypostatic" refers to the Logos as a distinct person or substance within the Trinity</note>, ascends to the very **Beginning** <term>Bereshit <note>Hebrew: "In the beginning," the first word of Genesis 1:1</note></term> of Moses. It happens also that the unique passage of the entire *Old Testament* <note>original: *V. T.* (Vetus Testamentum)</note> in which we have otherwise judged the Son of God to be designated by the *Word of Jehovah*—namely Psalm 33:6—likewise looks back to the very Creation of the Universe.

->II.<-

Following this clue while we unfold the history of Creation, a new strength is soon added to our preliminary judgment. For illustrious traces of the Mystery of the Trinity shine forth from it everywhere. The plural name <term>Elohim <note>Hebrew: אלהים; the plural form of the name for God</note></term> is given to the Creator of the World. The divine conversation in the production of Man in Genesis 1:26 [indicates] a personal distinction... <note>The text on this page ends mid-sentence as the author begins to discuss the "Let us make man" passage</note>

requires. It is suggested that the entire Deity belongs to each individual person, since <term>Elohim <note>original Hebrew: אלהים; a plural name for God used in the Hebrew Bible</note></term> is used in Genesis 1:2 for the first and second persons as distinct from the third, not only **essentially**, but even **hypostatically** <note>meaning as a distinct person or individual existence within the Godhead</note>. But it will also be shown in §. 24 that very often the **Elohim** who speaks is distinguished from the **Elohim** who is the effect. Furthermore, the third person of the Holy Trinity, the Holy Spirit, is not only distinguished here specifically from the others, but also appears in that same order of operation which the <term>Economy of Grace <note>the theological concept of how God manages the salvation of humanity through the different roles of the Trinity</note></term> assigns to him. Add to this that the same order recurs where the creation of man is described in Genesis 2:7. Supposing these things, lest we be scattered right at the threshold—since for the most part they have already been abundantly exhausted by other theologians—we do not think we will be wasting our effort if we also seek traces of the Second Person in the history of Creation itself. Scripture directly attributes the Glory of Creation to him so many times. Why would Moses not have already indicated this Creator? And if Scripture proposes the work of Creation to us as a <term>type <note>a symbolic foreshadowing or pattern</note></term> of the work of Redemption, which is most evident, who would think that this sketch was expressed with such a rough brush that no prelude of the Redeemer himself occurred in it?

III. Why say more? Since a clear indication of a certain divine **Word** in the history of creation becomes manifest in that formula recurring so often in Genesis 1, **AND ELOHIM SAID** <note>original Hebrew: ויאמר אלהים, *Wayyōmer Elohim*</note>, we can presume here, if anywhere, that he who is **strictly** <note>original Greek: κυρίως, *kyriōs*</note> defined by the **WORD OF JEHOVAH** has been pointed out to us. Let us then rub this ear of grain <note>a metaphor for examining a subject closely to extract the "nutritional" truth, like rubbing grain to remove the husk</note> for a little while, and in such a way that, *first*, we prove that this phrase breathes the Mystery of Christ; *second*, let us attempt to see by what reason and to what extent it is permitted to reach the knowledge of him through this expression.

IV. That Moses intended to include the doctrine of the Son of God in the cited expression has already been demonstrated with many sound arguments by André Rivet in *Exercises on Genesis* III; Sebastian Schmidt in *Collection of Theological-Philological Disputations*, disputation I; Moïse Amyraut in *On the Mystery of the Trinity*, part IV, page 163 and following; Josué de la Place in *On the Divinity of Jesus Christ*, Volume I, disputation XXI, section 10 and following; and Johannes Leydecker—at one time my colleague and a most learned man—in *Sacred Archaeology*, dissertation IV. We shall follow in their footsteps in such a way that we use the freedom not only to supplement them but also to modestly disagree with them in certain matters.

<page-num>371</page-num>
## ON THE ORIGIN OF THE NAME **LOGOS** <note>original: ΛΟΓΟΣ; Greek for "Word" or "Reason," referring here to the Second Person of the Trinity</note>.

<sig>Aaa 2</sig>

V. We shall not dwell long on the argument that **Amyraldus** <note>Moïse Amyraut (1596–1664), a French Protestant theologian known for his views on the "Economy" of salvation</note> places at the forefront: that a specific reasoning occurred to the sacred Writer because *in the production of matter from nothing, no such mention of speech is made, whereas in the creation of other things, speech is not only used but even repeatedly stated. For [he argues] the creation of matter was more difficult than the formation of other things from matter, and thus its history had to be set forth somewhat more laboriously.* The strength of this reasoning is slight. For it does not appear that Moses is dealing plainly with the production of matter out of nothing [in the very first verse], since the first verse seems rather to be understood as the structure of the Universe in the most general sense, considered according to both *matter* and *form* <note>the author uses the Aristotelian distinction between "matter" (the raw substance) and "form" (the specific structure or identity of a thing)</note>. In the second verse, however, it is merely the *imperfection* of existing matter that is described, not its first *production*. Furthermore, it is no more difficult for the most powerful Cause to *produce matter* than it is to produce *form*. For even form, before it is introduced, stands as *nothing* before its Maker, and it requires infinite power for it to be introduced. Moreover, one must not conclude that some things which cannot exist without infinite power are more difficult to produce than others, since *infinite power acknowledges no limits, no degrees.* Failing to attend to this truth has been a stumbling block for many philosophers. Besides, since the work by which *form* is introduced into matter is actually more perfect—without which matter could not be directed toward suitable ends worthy of God—than the work by which the bare *existence* of *matter* is given, this could be a sufficient reason why the sacred Writer would follow the creation of form more fully. But another mystical reason is also hinted at by the Holy Spirit, which favors us especially, though we do not use it here lest we commit a circular argument, so long as the hypothesis of the true Mystery of Creation is not proven.

VI. The reasoning of **Placaeus** <note>Joshua de la Place (1596–1665), a colleague of Amyraut at the Academy of Saumur</note> carries more weight: *if by that Word <note>original: Sermo</note> which God used for the Creation of the world, the <term>Hypostatic Word</term> <note>the Word as a distinct Person of the Trinity, rather than just an audible sound or a metaphor</note> is not hinted at, then it cannot be understood what that speech was.* This would be absurd, because in a history of such importance, nothing should be considered to have been placed in vain, much less repeated seven or nine times—which would not have been done by the Best and Wisest Author, God, if He either did not want that thing, whatever it is, to be understood, or if it were not worthy...

<summary>The author critiques Moïse Amyraut’s idea that the lack of "speech" in the creation of raw matter was due to the difficulty of the task, arguing instead that infinite power knows no degrees of difficulty. He supports Joshua de la Place's view that the "speech" in Genesis must refer to the Personal Word (Christ) to avoid being a meaningless repetition.</summary>

VII. To make this argument tighter, we must briefly review the opinions of those who do not recognize the mystery of the **hypostatic WORD** <note>original: *VERBI hypostatici*; referring to the Word as a distinct, "hypostatic" person within the Trinity</note> in this Mosaic phrase. Three possibilities can be considered here. For either a mere *pleonasm* <note>a linguistic redundancy</note> must be established—as if Moses intended to say nothing else than that *God created light*—or a literal sense must be assigned to the phrase, or we must look for a *figurative* meaning. The first opinion, due to its impiety, and the second, due to its absurdity, will have hardly any declared defenders. Among the latter group, however, those who "dream" with **Petersen**, **Whiston**, and others will easily claim the name; they imagine that the Son of God already existed as the **God-man** <note>original: $\Theta\epsilon\alpha\nu\theta\rho\omega\pi o\nu$ (*Theanthrōpon*)</note> during the Creation of the world. In this way, He could have received and executed the command of the Father through an external voice. This opinion falls along with the error it presupposes. **Petavius** <note>Dionysius Petavius (1583–1652), a Jesuit theologian</note> noted in *Theological Dogmas* (Book II, ch. 6, sec. 7) that **Lactantius** and **Theodore of Mopsuestia** were stuck in this same "mire." **Augustine** declares in his book *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* (ch. 5) that only the "carnal-minded" think this way. Furthermore, **Theodoret**, in the *Catena* <note>a "chain" of biblical commentaries from various Church Fathers</note> of **Aloysius Lippomannus** on Genesis, says: *If God created light by some voice, He did it for the sake of the invisible powers [the angels], so they might know that by God’s command, those things which are not are brought into being.* As if those invisible powers could have been invited to contemplate the works of God through an external sound, when neither air existed nor did they possess bodies to hear it!

VIII. Those who argue for a figurative meaning stop at the idea that God is presented by Moses **anthropopathically** <note>original: *$\alpha\nu\theta\rho\omega\pi o\pi\alpha\theta\omega\varsigma$*; a term for attributing human emotions or physical actions to God for the sake of human understanding</note>—that is, He is introduced speaking in the same way He is elsewhere introduced as seeing, hearing, etc. This is the view of **Steuchus Eugubinus** in his *Cosmopoeia* on Genesis 1, and others like **Huet** and **Le Clerc** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Genevan scholar and biblical critic</note>. Le Clerc deals with this matter specifically not only in his Commentary but also in the *Bibliothèque Choisie* (Vol. X), where he presents and annotates a letter from the Bishop of Avranches. The opinion of **Henry More** <note>1614–1687, an influential Cambridge Platonist</note> tends in a similar direction. Although More recognizes the *Mystery of the Son* in the work of creation, he thinks it should be sought more in the word **Beginning** <note>original: <term>ראשית</term> (*Reshith*; the first word of Genesis 1:1)</note> than in our current phrase ["And God said"]. Consequently, he attributes an *internal word* to the entire Deity, by which he understands the *Wisdom and Power which had then been sharpened by the actual will [of God] for the purpose of a greater...*

-># ON THE ORIGIN OF THE NAME <term>LOGOS</term> <note>original: ΛΟΓΟΣ; the Greek term for "Word" or "Reason," central to the Gospel of John</note><-

<sig>Aaa 3</sig>

*...facility with which we represent any notion or idea to our minds, as described in the working of **Cabbalistic Philosophy**, chapter 1.*

IX. To examine their hypothesis more accurately "under the anvil" <note>a Latin idiom (*sub incudem vocemus*) meaning to scrutinize or refine an idea through rigorous testing</note>, we note that it has two parts. When **bodily affections** and **actions** are attributed to God in the Holy Scriptures, this can be understood in two ways. It is either through **metaphor**, or, as others put it, through <term>synecdoche</term> <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole or vice versa</note>—where a certain perfection, faculty, quality, or action of God Himself is meant; or through <term>metonymy</term> <note>a figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it</note>, where an effect produced outside of God and the manner of its production is considered. In the first sense, for instance, "to see" ascribed to God can designate His knowledge; in the latter sense, it can designate His providence and His care for His covenant people. The authors cited in our passage combine both senses. Others, however, embrace only one or the other. Let us, therefore, examine each part individually; once these are dismantled, the entire **system of the figurative sense** will collapse of its own accord.

X. Those who claim this is a matter of metaphorical speech are again divided into different camps. Some understand the **internal word** <note>original: *sermonem ἐνδιάθετον* (*endiatheton*); a philosophical term for a thought or concept held within the mind before it is spoken</note>—that is, the description of things to be created within the mind of God itself. This is interpreted either **as an idea** according to **Lucas Brugensis**, or **as a decree** as with **Rabbi Bechai** <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Jewish scholar</note>, or **as the will** considered intrinsically and in the abstract. This latter view is favored by **Theodoret**, **John Philoponus** in *On the Creation of the World* (chapter 22), the Arabic version of **Rabbi Saadia** <note>Saadia Gaon</note>, **Rabbi Moses Nachmanides** <note>also known as Ramban</note>, **Maimonides**, **Cajetan**, **Mercer**, **Hottinger**, and others. Others contend that the **uttered word** <note>original: *sermonem προφορικὸν* (*prophorikon*); the external expression or vocalization of a thought</note> is what is designated—not by the sound of an external voice, but through an effective **command** as if proceeding from God. Toward this view "sail" <note>a Latin metaphor for favoring an opinion</note> **Basil of Seleucia**, **Abraham ibn Ezra**, **Socinus**, **Matthias Flacius Illyricus**, **Hakspan**, **Mersenne**, **Pellicanus**, **Alting**, **Piscator**, and others, though we will immediately observe the different classes among them.

XI. A difficulty arises for all these men: although they laboriously gather a great crowd of Scriptural sayings—as **Witter** has attempted regarding this passage in Genesis after the efforts of others—they still produce none that is sufficient to prove that anywhere else...

<meta>catchword: At the re-</meta>

...whether the word <term>amar</term> <note>Hebrew: אמר; meaning "to speak" or "to say"</note> is used to describe actions of the pure mind. For those passages [cited by opponents] introduce either **God speaking** or **men**. Those which concern **God** either clearly introduce Him revealing His will through some **external word** (as in Genesis 24:51, compared with verse 40; Psalm 105:31, 34; and Jonah 2:11), or they involve the same mystery as our primary text <note>meaning Genesis 1, where "God said"</note>—for example, Psalm 33:9, 148:5, and 2 Corinthians 4:6. Therefore, citing those passages to prove their point is a case of "begging the question" <note>a logical fallacy where the premise of an argument assumes the truth of the conclusion</note>. This same reasoning must be extended to related expressions like <term>qara</term> <note>Hebrew: קרא; to call</note> and <term>dabar</term> <note>Hebrew: דבר; to speak</note>. Consult the notes we have already provided on this matter in the dissertation on Psalm 33:6, sections 10 and 11.

Furthermore, those passages in which they believe the word *amar* designates a **human will** or **precept** either make a clear distinction between a decree of the will and an external saying (as in Job 22:28), or they also presuppose and involve an external word (Numbers 14:10; 2 Samuel 21:16; Deuteronomy 17:14; Ephesians 1:17, etc.). In other cases, they include a clear clarifying phrase from which it is plain that the text is dealing with a speech still residing as a concept in the mind—specifically, when it is constructed with the word <term>leb</term> <note>Hebrew: לב; heart</note>, meaning "to say in one's heart" (Psalm 10:6, 14:1; Ecclesiastes 2:15, etc.). 

**Abenezra** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a renowned 12th-century Jewish scholar</note> observed, quite aptly, that if Moses had intended to describe a *command* from God, he would then have had to say *wayyomer Elohim lihyot* <note>original: ויאמר אלהים להיות; "And God said to be"</note>, because where the word *amar* occurs with the meaning of "commanding," it is usually constructed with the preposition *L* <note>the Hebrew letter Lamed, used to mean "to" or "for"</note>, as **Gousset** <note>Jacques Gousset, a 17th-century Hebraist</note> teaches. For this reason, **Mercer** and **Hottinger** <note>Prominent Reformed theologians and linguists</note>, in practicing their critique of Abenezra, ought to have refuted him with specific examples. If we wished to examine every single instance, we would wander too far afield.

XII. To ensure that no "crack in the door" <note>an idiom meaning to leave no room for doubt or counter-argument</note> remains, we add that certain passages are twisted toward this same purpose through a distorted interpretation, when they clearly point elsewhere. For example, in Genesis 26:9, it is translated: *How could you say, "She is my sister"? To which Isaac said, "I did it because I said [to myself], lest I die because of her."* 

It might indeed seem here that Isaac had not spoken the words aloud, but merely turned them over in his mind. But the text reads: *ki amarti pen amut aleha*, which should be rendered: *"Because I said* (namely, that she was my sister) *lest perhaps I should die because of her."* In this case, there is no "ellipsis" <note>omitted words assumed by the reader</note> remaining, which those who hold the opposite view are forced to assume. Likewise, **Hottinger** and **Witter** appeal to Psalm 104:7: *At the re-* <note>original: Ex incre-; likely referring to the "rebuke" of God's voice</note>

XIII. Let us grant, however, that this manner of speaking is not unusual in the sacred style; nevertheless, it is clear that it is far removed from the passage we are considering. Indeed, it argues against the **internal word** <note>Original Greek: *ἐνδιάθετον* (*endiathetos*); a philosophical term for "thought" or the "word within" before it is spoken.</note> that such a word does not actually differ from the **Decree of God**. Through such a decree, He makes the future occurrence of things possible while He views them as future, yet He does not, by that act alone, place them outside of Himself [into actual existence]. But Moses’ goal was not to describe God’s eternal decree regarding future things, but to explain how they were produced in a certain order according to that decree.

XIV. More probably, others flee to the **spoken word** <note>Original Greek: *προφορικὸν* (*prophorikos*); the "proffered" or externally spoken word.</note>, which they understand to be God's effective mandate for actual production. And in truth, nothing prevents "to say" from being used for "to command," provided that the nature of both the **subject** and the **object** allows it. We admit a suitable subject is present here—namely God, who possesses the power and authority to command. However, every command requires not only a **commander**, but also an **object** to which the command is directed. Let them teach us, then: what was that object in the first production of things? Was it the **Angels**, or **God** himself, or perhaps the **Creatures** yet to be produced? Those who embrace the first option hold that the **Angels** acted as either the partners or the witnesses of God in creation. **Philo** <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Jewish scripture.</note> and other more recent Jews easily admit the former. XVI. Therefore, there remain the creatures to be produced [as the intended audience of God's speech], an idea which pleases many. But who would think a divine command is directed toward an object devoid of all capacity to obey? Such was surely the state of matter: an undigested mass, a formless body both in its own nature and at the first origin of things—and even more so, a "work" before it actually existed. Or should it be thought that light contributed anything to its own production? Could light, in that first instant of its existence, be considered in any way as a *cooperating* cause, or at least a *second and subordinate* cause of its own existence? Rightly, therefore, has **MAIMONIDES** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher. XVII. XVIII. What the most learned man notes in the latter part concerns us little. For although it can be granted that matter existed before this word of God, it suffices for our purpose that those *individual Beings* did not yet exist, which were produced anew on each day when each received its form. But no small prejudice seems able to arise from the saying in Romans 4:17, especially since Interpreters wish that *to call* among the Hebrews is often the same as *to cause to exist*. ...if we followed the reading which **AUGUSTINE** has already rejected—*Who calls those things which are not, so that they may be*—we would hesitate not a little. XIX. Thus, for example, in Jeremiah 31:15, it is said of the Messiah with respect to the slaughter at Bethlehem: *because he was not* <note>Hebrew: *ki einennu*</note>, for which we read in Matthew 2:18: *because they are not* <note>Greek: *hoti ouk eisi*</note>—namely, **Rachel and her house**. Matthew preserves the Greek translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek version of the Old Testament.</note> because this was a necessary consequence. Therefore, those who have scraped together a hodgepodge of passages from Greek authors to prove that "not being" is equivalent to "being dead" have been far too laborious. They have not sufficiently grasped the emphasis of the citation, nor have they noticed that a notable impiety lurks under that phrase in pagan authors. Because of this, any perceived parallel between the sacred and profane pages regarding this phrase falls apart on its own.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on Romans 4:17, "God who calls things that are not as though they were," debating whether this refers to the act of creation out of nothing or the unfolding of God’s providential plan for his chosen people. The author is moving from a theological analysis of the Apostle Paul's words to a critique of "metonymical" interpretations of the creation narrative in Genesis.</meta>

# ON THE ORIGIN OF THE NAME LOGOS.
<sig>Bbb 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: singular</meta>

The Apostle says: *of the one who gives life and calls* <note>original Greek and Latin: *tou zōopoiountos kai kalountos* / *vivificantis & vocantis*</note>. Therefore, he is describing the work of divine Providence, and specifically a work that has a certain relationship to that *resurrection* of which the Apostle speaks. For this reason, the phrase *the things that are not* <note>original Greek: *ta mē onta*</note> here designates for us most directly those very benefits of grace which God uses as means to bring his plan for the elect into action. Although those means may be hidden from the eyes of the faithful, God nevertheless holds them in His account; He not only outlines them beforehand in His word as if they already exist, but also, according to His own pleasure, renders them effective even if they are inherently unsuitable. From this it is clear how little this passage has in common with our current subject <note>The author argues that Romans 4:17 is about God's plan for salvation, not a literal description of the physical creation of the world</note>.

XXI. Those who interpret the phrase *metonymically* <term>metonymy: A figure of speech where an effect is described by naming its cause, or vice versa; here, using "calling" to represent "creating"</term> focus on the manner in which the effect is produced by God, and especially on the wonderful *ease* with which it is established. This was the opinion of **CHRYSOSTOM** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching</note>, in addition to those cited above in section 8. The authors of the **ENGLISH ANNOTATIONS** <note>Likely the "Assembly's Annotations" (1645), a popular 17th-century English biblical commentary</note> are of the same opinion, suggesting that four aspects of Creation are implied: (1) *ease*; (2) the *Authority* of the Creator exercising dominion over every creature like a King; (3) the *Efficacy* in fully establishing the effect according to the decree; and (4) the *Freedom* of the Creator. However, the reason we do not rest easy with these explanations is that the sacred Historiographer <note>Referring to Moses, the traditional author of Genesis</note> would have expressed that manner much more clearly and effectively if he had said without such roundabout phrasing that all things were made by the sole will of the Deity. For the labor is not in *commanding*, but in executing. Therefore, alongside **PLACÆUS** <note>Josué de la Place (1596–1665), a French Protestant theologian</note>, we do not grasp how the mention of a preceding command or order helps to exclude labor, difficulty, trouble, or movement from the execution of the task. Nor do we see what can be strongly opposed to **AMYRALDUS** <note>Moïse Amyraut (1596–1664), a French Protestant theologian known for his theory of "hypothetical universalism"</note> when he contends that if Moses had wished to represent the efficacy of divine productive power through the likeness of physical things, he could have more conveniently written that all things were made by a single divine nod. This would be in the likeness of that famous line from **HOMER**: *He shook great Olympus* <note>original Greek: *Megan d' elelixen olympon*</note>, which **MARO** <note>The Roman poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro)</note> expressed in a successful imitation:

> -> He made all Olympus tremble with a nod. <-

# DISSERTATION
<meta>catchword: singular</meta>

...[singular] height of expression <note>original Greek: *Hypsos*, often translated as "The Sublime"</note> contained this formula of Moses. The passage is found in chapter IX of *On the Sublime*, § 18: *In this way, the Lawgiver of the Jews—no ordinary man—since he truly knew and declared the power of the divine according to its worth, wrote at the very beginning of his laws: "God said," he says. What? "Let there be light, and it was. Let there be earth, and it was."*

*In the same way (by this height of sense), the Lawgiver of the Jews, a man not at all to be looked down upon, captured an image of God's power worthy of Him, and spoke of it worthily. For at the very beginning of his Laws, he says: GOD SAID. What? LET THERE BE LIGHT: AND IT WAS MADE. LET THERE BE EARTH: AND IT WAS MADE.*

In this, **LONGINUS** <note>A Greek teacher of rhetoric (c. 213–273 AD) famous for his treatise *On the Sublime*</note> was stuck in the same opinion as those we are refuting—namely, that "the power of the divine according to its worth" <note>original Greek: *hē tou theiou dynamis kata tēn axian*</note> was designated by these words; it is in this that he places the "richness" <note>original Greek: *tēn hadrotēta*</note> of this phrase. And he seems to have drawn this not from an inspection of the original sources, but from other Jews whose teaching his Queen, **ZENOBIA** <note>The 3rd-century Queen of the Palmyrene Empire, who was a patron of Longinus</note>, had been enticed by. For the observations made regarding the emphasis of the Mosaic diction by both **ARISTOBULUS** (in **EUSEBIUS**, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book XIII, chapter 12) and **PHILO THE JEW** (in *On the Creation of the World*) agree with this; **TOLLIUS** provides their sayings in his notes. **WAYENUS** brings forward more from **PHILO** on this matter in his work on the *Word* <note>original Greek: *logō* (the Logos)</note> against **LE CLERC**, page 139 and following.

Despite this, **HUETIUS** <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar</note> rejected the opinion of **LONGINUS**. He defended his assertion from his *Demonstration of the Gospel* (Proposition IV, chapter 2, § 52) that nothing "sublime" was breathed here, but rather the simplicity of the Mosaic style, against the criticism of **BOILEAU** <note>Nicolas Boileau-Despréaux, the French poet and critic who translated Longinus</note>. The famous **LE CLERC** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a Genevan theologian</note> adds his vote to this. As far as I can see, there is quite a lot of "word-warring" <term>logomachy: A dispute about words; a semantic argument where both sides might actually agree on the underlying facts</term> in this controversy, and neither side has reached the far deeper sense actually hidden under this verbal envelope. I only urge that these most learned men are "cutting their own vines" <note>A Latin idiom (*sua vineta caedere*) meaning to damage one's own cause or provide arguments that can be turned against oneself</note> when they claim that Moses intended to designate the "effective operation of God." For by this hypothesis, it is actually acknowledged that the same "sublime" quality Longinus assigned to those words is indeed hidden within them. This is why **PHILOPONUS** <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570), a Christian philosopher and scientist</note>, in the place cited, although he remains within those same boundaries, tries to show from this phrase how much the sublimity of Moses exceeds **PLATO'S** narrative on the origin of things.

### ON THE ORIGIN OF THE NAME *LOGOS*.

<sig>Bbb 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: XXV.</meta>

...if the text is completely weakened by the interpretations listed above, what will become of the Holy Scripture when one considers such frequent repetition of the same phrase in the same context? Who would believe that in this shortest and wisest of histories—in which nothing is said or left unsaid in vain—roughly a third of the text signifies nothing, or expresses through obscure and unusual wordplay what could have been stated clearly in a single word? Is this that "simplicity of Mosaic style" <note>The author is referring to the scholarly debate over the literary style of Moses, the traditional author of Genesis</note> which those men who hold the leading positions in the Art of Criticism so studiously emphasize?

XXIV. We, however, recognizing in this passage the **Mystery of the Son of God**, the **Hypostatic Word** <note>original Greek: *Logou Hypostatikou*. In theology, "hypostatic" refers to the Word (the Son) as a distinct person within the divine essence</note>, are not only free from these difficulties, but we also rest upon a firm foundation. For first, the entire context supports us, in which **Elohim** <note>original Hebrew: *אלהים* (God)</note> *commanding* and **Elohim** *executing* the command are repeatedly distinguished. Thus, in verse 4, *God seeing the light to be good* and *God making a distinction between the light and the darkness* is differentiated from *God saying, "Let there be light."* Likewise, in verse 6, *God says, "let there be an expanse"*; and in verse 7, *God making the expanse* is introduced. So too in verse 14, *God said: "let there be lights in the expanse of the heavens to distinguish"* etc. Soon after, in verse 15, it is added: *And God made...* <note>original Hebrew: *Va-ya'as Elohim ve-go'* (ויעש אלהים וגו׳)</note> *two great lights*. (It is not, as **JUNIUS** <note>Franciscus Junius (1545–1602), a Reformed theologian and translator</note> rendered it with a completely discordant sense, "For God made.") 

The same construction returns between verses 24 and 25, as well as between verses 26 and 27. Therefore, **PISCATOR** <note>Johannes Piscator (1546–1625), a German theologian known for his biblical commentaries</note> objects to us without cause when he claims this exposition is inconsistent with the name *Elohim*, which he thinks should be understood here just as it was in verse 1. For the text itself lights our way, in which all things—concerning both the **Author** and the **Work**—are unfolded more specifically and part-by-part in relation to the earth from verse 2 onward, which had been treated more generally in verse 1 regarding the entire universe. Why, then, in this detailed account of the divine work, should a distinction of the persons not also be set forth more clearly, in an order fitting the divine essence? Certainly, this manner of narration is so clear and simple that anyone convinced of the plurality of persons in the divine essence cannot doubt that this most plain and frequently repeated distinction between God speaking (or *ordering*) and the one *executing* refers to that mystery; while those who doubt this mystery are already invited, on the very first page of Holy Scripture, to meditate more closely upon it.

<summary>The author argues that the repetitive structure of Genesis 1—where God speaks and then acts—is not a redundant literary device but a deliberate revelation of the Trinity. He identifies the "Speaking God" as the Father and the "Executing God" as the Son or Word (Logos).</summary>

### DISSERTATION

<meta>catchword: foundations</meta>

XXV. In the creation of man (2) we find even more manifest traces of the Son of God. For not only have others demonstrated that the famous phrase, *Let us make man*, pertains to the Trinity, but a distinction between the image of the one commanding and the one executing is clearly perceived in verse 27: *And God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him.* Indeed, we believe Moses teaches two things here: ($\alpha$) that the Son of God carried out the Father’s command regarding the production of man in such a way that he fashioned him most closely according to his own image, in accordance with the **Divine Economy** <term>Divine Economy (Oeconomia divina): The theological concept of how God manages the world and reveals Himself to humanity through specific roles for the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</term>. ($\beta$) Nevertheless, that image of the Son was not different from the image of the entire Holy Trinity because of the unity of the divine essence. In this way, we believe a refined and meaningful emphasis exists in the words of Moses. Therefore, it is clear that the more diligently and with due sobriety we compare the Mystery of the Trinity with the history of creation, the more any appearance of **tautology** <note>original: "tautologiae"; the author is arguing against the idea that the repetitive phrasing in Genesis is merely "saying the same thing twice" without deeper meaning</note> vanishes from our sight.

XXVI. But also (3) immediately after creation, the Mystery of the Son became known to the **First Parents** <note>original: "Protoplastis," referring to Adam and Eve</note>. For they rejoiced not only in familiar commerce with God, but also in external conversations; as appears from the *Blessing* joined immediately with the *Creation* in verse 28. Add to this chapter II:15 and following. If anyone should think that such things could have been revealed to the First Parents through an internal illumination of the mind, let him consider that the names called out by God himself were bestowed upon things in chapter I:5, 8, and 10, which could not have happened without the sound of an external voice. Since, moreover, in the Divine Economy the Son is consistently the one—in distinction to the Father—who explains the divine will to man (*Isaiah XLVIII:16*), from which foundation we are persuaded that *his goings forth from the days of eternity* (*Micah V:2*) are derived, why should we not judge that Moses specifically looked to him in this distinction of persons?

XXVII. Indeed, it is manifest (4) that Proverbs VIII:27–29 alludes to this, where **Eternal Wisdom** <note>original: "Sapientia aeterna"; in Christian tradition, the "Wisdom" described in Proverbs is often identified as the pre-incarnate Son of God</note>, the Son of God himself, is introduced as speaking: *When he prepared the heavens, I was there; when he set a compass upon the face of the deep: when he established the clouds above: when he strengthened the fountains of the deep: when he gave to the sea his decree, and to the waters, that they should not pass his commandment: when he appointed the foundations—*

# ON THE ORIGIN OF THE NAME LOGOS <note>The Word</note>

...foundations of the earth. For why would Wisdom declare that she was present not only for the entire work of Creation, but also for each of its individual parts, if not to emphasize more diligently that, of all things which have been made, *nothing was made without her* <note>original Latin: "nihil sine ipsa factum esse"; John 1:3</note>. Thus, she is that **Word** through whom each individual thing was produced according to the Father's command and in the order that Moses outlined.

XXVIII. This is the very thing (5) that the Apostle Paul recognizes whenever he explicitly testifies that God the Father produced all things, both whole and individual, through the Son. Ephesians 3:9: *God, who created all these things through Jesus Christ.* Hebrews 1:2: *Through whom also he made the ages* <note>original Greek: "Δι’ οὗ καὶ τοὺς αἰῶνας ἐποίησεν"</note>. Add also Colossians 1:16. The particle *through* <note>original Latin/Greek: "dia"</note> in this construction indicates a distinct relationship of the work to the Father and the Son as distinct causes, following one another in the order of operation. For this reason, the phrasing never switches. Although the word *through* is sometimes referred to the Father’s work when he is considered simply on his own without relation to the Son (as in Hebrews 2:10 and Revelation 4:11), it is never said that the Son created the world *through the Father*. We believe that this fact—that the order of the Persons never switches, even in the work of nature—is a very strong argument for the **Natural Generation of the Son** <term>Natural Generation: The theological belief that the Son is eternally and by nature "begotten" of the Father, rather than being a created being or a temporary role</term>. Those who have asserted a merely **Economic Generation of the Son** <term>Economic Generation: A view the author opposes, which suggests the Son's status as "Son" is only a temporary role assumed for the sake of managing (economy) creation and salvation</term> have not paid enough attention to the unbreakable strength of this argument. Is it even believable that this order, in the explanation of which Scripture is so constantly consistent, was completely ignored by Moses?

XXIX. Finally, (6) the analogy between the Old and the New Creation requires that the same order of operation among the Persons of the Holy Trinity recurs in both. Perhaps we will deal with this mystery more closely elsewhere. Here it is enough to have noted that Scripture, when explaining this, considers those specific parts of creation as a type or pattern of divine operations in Grace; in these, Moses made a distinction between God indicating his will by a **spoken word** and God executing that will. Let 2 Corinthians 4:6 <note>The text says VI. 6, but the quotation matches IV. 6</note> serve as an example: *For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, is the one who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.* Behold, God illuminates the hearts of the chosen in the same order as when he said, *Let there be light out of darkness!*

->XXX.<-

The author contends that this "order of operation" supports the doctrine of the Son's eternal, natural generation rather than a temporary role.</summary>

# DISSERTATION

XXX. But if one were inclined to wage battle using historical authorities (7), there has been no interpretation more ancient or more universal than this. Among the early Church Fathers, we find it in the works of **Justin Martyr**, **Athenagoras**, **Tatian**, **Theophilus**, **Irenaeus**, **Tertullian**, and **Origen** <note>These are prominent Christian thinkers from the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD who helped shape early doctrine</note>; these were followed in turn by **Ambrose**, **Augustine**, **Athanasius**, **Basil**, **Junilius**, **Rupert** <note>Rupert of Deutz, a 12th-century mystic</note>, **Rabanus Maurus** <note>A Carolingian scholar</note>, **Thomas Aquinas**, and others. The earlier of these writers, by applying this mystery somewhat incautiously, left an open flank to the **Gnostics** <term>Gnostics: A diverse group of early religious thinkers who combined Christian, Jewish, and Platonic ideas, often viewed as heretical by the early Church</term>. The Gnostics, following **Plato**’s imaginative theories about the creation of the world, believed they had found a similar structure in this "Economy of the Trinity," and thus mixed light with darkness in strange ways. Among more modern writers—besides those praised in Section 4 who treated this subject more formally—why should I mention **Luther**, **Calvin**, **Borrhaus**, **Cornelius a Lapide**, **Pareus**, **Cameron**, **Calovius**, and six hundred others? Our own **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius, the famous Dutch legal scholar and theologian</note> is of this same mind, as is clear from the evidence he gathered regarding John 1:3.

XXXI. Indeed, it is established that something quite illustrious regarding this history dawned upon the Jews as well. The author of the **Book of Wisdom** <note>Though the text cites Wisdom 16:14, the Greek quote actually matches Judith 16:14</note> in chapter 16, verse 14 says: *Let all your creation serve you (Lord), for you spoke and they were created; you sent forth your spirit and it built them* <note>original Greek: "Σοι (κυριε) δουλευσατω πασα ἡ κτισις σου, ὁτι ειπας και ἐγενηθησαν, ἀπεστειλας το πνευμα σου, και ᾠκοδομησε"</note>. In this passage, learned men have observed clear traces of the Trinity. No less relevant is this statement by **Rabbi Solomon Jarchi** <note>Commonly known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note>: *The throne of glory stood in the air and spread itself over the face of the waters through the Spirit of his mouth and his Word.* <note>original Latin translation of Jarchi: "Solium gloriæ stabat in aëre & expandebat se super faciem aquarum per Spiritum oris sui & Verbum suum."</note> Other materials on this subject, though they require careful selection, were collected by **Leidekker** in the work cited above on page 65 and following.

XXXII. We might also mention the most ancient philosophers and poets of the nations. Whatever sound truths they produced in their writings about the creation of the world were drawn entirely from Moses. From his narrative, they took the opportunity to distinguish a certain *personal word* in the production of things by God—even if we might demonstrate more fully at another time that they by no means grasped the true mystery. To this end, those verses of **Orpheus** are directed—whether they be his own or attributed to him by **Onomacritus** <note>A 6th-century BC Greek poet known for editing or forging Orphic poems</note>—which have been so often and so eagerly brought forward against the Gentiles:

*I swear by Heaven created by a great and wise God; I swear by the Voice of the Father, which he first established with his mouth, when he himself founded the whole world by his own counsel.* Yet we do not dwell too much on these or other similar passages, since it is certain that even the best Church Fathers were often deceived by the beautiful sound of such testimonies, and from them they forged "leaden weapons" <note>A Latin idiom, *plumbea tela*, referring to arguments that appear sharp but are actually soft or ineffective</note> against the Philosophers.

XXXIII. This task now remains for us: that we might help those whom we have persuaded that the mystery of the Son of God is contained within the phrasing of the Mosaic history to fully embrace it. This bursting forth of the divine voice, or the manifestation of the internal divine concept, is the Spirit of God’s manifestation and glorification. As soon as this voice, this almighty "Let it be!" resounded, whatever exists was made.*

This opinion must be deservedly rejected: 

I. Because it contradicts the <term>analogy of faith</term> <note>The principle that Scripture should be interpreted in a way consistent with established Christian doctrine</note> and too openly favors the <term>Socinians</term> <term>Socinians: A sect that denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ, viewing Him as a man rather than God</term>. Add to this that he expresses himself in such a way that the essence of the Son is defined as God's concept regarding future things (restricting it to the "future-ness" of things), while the essence of the Holy Spirit is restricted to the actual production of those things.
