## DISSERTATION
<meta>The catchword "tatio" from the previous page completes the word "interpretatio" (interpretation).</meta>

...interpretation is, and how feeble it is, is clear from what has been said. Therefore we rightly wonder why the most learned collectors of those "offerings" <note>Referring to the *Berlin Spontaneous Offerings* cited on the previous page</note> passed over this opinion without any note or censure, especially since they otherwise seem to seriously oppose **Socinianism** <note>A 16th-century theological movement that denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ</note>.

XXXIV. But even among the more orthodox, various views are brought forward by various people. The oldest opinion of the Fathers of the Church was that the Hebrew word <term>amar</term> <note>Hebrew: אמר; "to say" or "to speak"</note> was essentially the same as *to generate*, and thus the eternal **Generation of the Son** was described by Moses under that term. **JUSTIN MARTYR** <note>A 2nd-century Christian apologist</note> leans toward this in his *Dialogue with Trypho* (Jebbian edition, p. 183). For after he had recounted the more illustrious names of the Son of God, and among them the name **LOGOS** <note>Greek: ΛΟΓΟΣ; Word or Reason</note>, he adds: *He has the right to be called by all these names, both from the administration of the Father’s counsel and will, and from the voluntary generation from the Father.* "But is it not such a thing as we see happening in our own case? For in bringing forth some word, we generate a word, yet not by a cutting-off <note>original Greek: ἀποτομήν (apotomēn); a division or separation</note>, so that the word within us is diminished by being brought forth." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ οὐ τοιοῦτον ὁποῖον καὶ ἐφ’ ἡμῶν γενόμενον ὁρῶμεν; λόγον γάρ τινα προβάλλοντες, λόγον γεννῶμεν, οὐ κατ’ ἀποτομήν, ὡς ἐλαττωθῆναι τὸν ἐν ἡμῖν λόγον προβαλλόμενοι</note> **FULGENTIUS** inclines toward the same opinion in Book III of his work *To Monimus*, as do **GREGORY THE GREAT** in his commentary on Job 33:14, **THOMAS AQUINAS**, and a few others. Yet we cannot abide by that view, since it can appear rather dangerous, as it restricts the **Generation of the Son** by a certain reasoning to the actual work of Creation. For as for what some offer—that the Son is *perpetually generated* by the Father—it is not only <term>unwritten</term> <note>original Greek: ἄγραφον (agraphon); meaning a doctrine not explicitly found in the text of the Bible</note> but also obscure, since they do not explain what they mean by this "perpetual Generation." Meanwhile, we would easily grant this: that through the Mosaic phrase <term>wayyomer</term> <note>Hebrew: ויאמר; "And [God] said"</note>, reference is made to that eternal and essential relation between the Father and the Son (which is expressed through the metaphor of Generation) insofar as that relation was demonstrated through the order of Creation. But if the pious Fathers intended to indicate that, it must be admitted that they expressed themselves quite obscurely.

XXXV. Among those who speak more clearly, there are two main divergent paths. For they either judge that the Son is that very "speech" which God brought forth when he founded the world, or they consider him as the object of that speech...

It is clear that the Ancients <note>Referring to the early Church Fathers</note> already thought about both possibilities from that book of **AUGUSTINE** on the *Literal Interpretation of Genesis (Unfinished)*, chapter 5: *"It may be asked whether that which was said was spoken to the only-begotten Son, or whether the very thing that was spoken is the only-begotten Son."* Soon after, he embraces the latter opinion: *"Therefore, if this which was said—'Let there be Light'—both began and ceased to be spoken, this word was spoken to the Son rather than being the Son himself."* He has **ATHANASIUS** agreeing with this hypothesis in his *Third Oration against the Arians*, pages 401–402. I add **BASIL THE GREAT** in his *Hexaemeron* <note>A series of homilies on the six days of creation</note>, Homily III, pages 26–27, whose words are much to my liking: *"Scripture therefore outlines and paints him for us in a more expressive figure, not just to declare that God willed a creature to be made, but so that it might be brought forth through a certain 'fellow-worker' <note>original Greek: δια τινος συνεργου (dia tinos synergou)</note>. He certainly could have touched upon and recounted each detail in a similar style to how he began: 'In the beginning God made heaven and earth'; and continuing: 'He made the firmament.' But now, by introducing God as both commanding and speaking at the same time, he quietly includes the one whom He commands and with whom He discusses."*

XXXVI. Indeed, the former opinion—although among the moderns **RIVET**, **PLACAEUS**, and **SCHMID** openly follow it—suffers from a significant difficulty. For first, it differs little from the error of those who understand Moses as speaking of the Word as either "internal" <note>original Greek: ενδιαθετω (endiathetō); the unspoken word or thought within the mind</note> or "prolated" <note>original Greek: προφορικω (prophorikō); the spoken or uttered word</note>. For although they seem to laboriously try to distinguish their *Word* from that error, they offer no other perceptible definition of the **Logos** <note>original Greek: Λογου (Logou); Word or Reason</note> that does not strike against either the first rock (which is closer to the **Sabellians** <note>Followers of Sabellius, who taught that the Father, Son, and Spirit were merely different "modes" or masks of one person, rather than three distinct persons</note>) or the second rock (which is closer to the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that the Son was a created being, not co-eternal with the Father</note>). Thus, for example, **PLACAEUS**, who meditated more closely on this matter in order to define the personal distinction of the Most Holy **Trinity**, distinguishes between the *One who commands*, the *Command* itself, and the *One who executes*, without which a free external action cannot be conceived. But he does not explain how that *Command* is personally distinct from the *One who commands*; nor do I think he could have explained it even with greater twists of subtlety than the more than sufficient ones he provides.

XXXVII. Added to this is the inconvenience for this hypothesis that it leaves the literal sense of Moses’s words obscure and not demonstrated to adversaries...

Who could easily persuade a skeptic that these simple words—*And God said*—involve a "substantial Command" within God the Creator, which must be personally distinguished from the One Commanding, and through which the world was founded? Does the very nature of this phrase, which recurs hundreds of times in the Holy Scriptures, provide any foundation for such an interpretation? Do there not rather occur in this very context things that break it down? Compare, for instance, verse 26: *And God said: Let us make man*. Defenders of the Holy Trinity everywhere agree that here the Father addresses the other divine persons. XXXIX. Furthermore (2) this interpretation fits the whole context of Moses. We have already cautioned above that in that passage, God <note>original Hebrew: אלהים (Elohim)</note> as the speaker and God *executing what was said* are to be distinguished. Add to this that the Spirit of God <note>original Hebrew: רוח אלהים (Ruach Elohim)</note> is placed before these two in Verse 2 as the immediate cause of the effect brought into action. Since the Spirit is distinguished from both the speaker and the executor, there occurs right at the very entrance of Holy Scripture a clear testimony not only of the Mystery of the Trinity in general, but also of the personal distinction within it.

XL. And (3) this very order of working, which the Triune God observed while *founding the visible world*, returns in the production of the *rational world* or the Spirit of Man. For not only does God the Father, through his *word* in Verse 26, communicate his good pleasure regarding the creation of man—according to his eternal counsel—to the Son and the Holy Spirit; but the Son also, not without the Holy Spirit, executes this good pleasure in Verse 27 and following. This partnership of the third person is easily drawn out: *firstly*, from the creation of man in the image of God (which is the specific work of the Holy Spirit); *secondly*, from the Son's address to the <term>Protoplasts</term> <note>The "Protoplasts" refer to the first-created human beings, Adam and Eve.</note> in Verse 28 as the Interpreter of the divine will to humanity, through which he pronounces a *blessing* upon them (the fulfillment of which likewise belonged to the <term>Economy</term> <note>In theology, 'Economy' refers to the specific roles and actions of the Trinity in history.</note> of the Holy Spirit); and *thirdly*, from the manner of the soul's creation in Genesis 2:7, described more fully through the symbol of *breathing into* <note>original Latin: infufflationis</note>, which is a constant symbol of the Holy Spirit.

XLI. Moreover, (4) we are even more drawn to embrace this view because there is a singular agreement across all of Holy Scripture, though there is not enough space here to explain it more broadly. We leave two points here especially for the reflection of others. One is provided by those passages which introduce the Son of God directly as the *Shaper* of all creatures, and indeed specifically of light (Psalm 102:26; Isaiah 45:7; compare what was said regarding Psalm 33:6). The other point, which relates much more to our subject, is that the <term>Economy</term> of the Holy Trinity in the work of Redemption—which Holy Scripture considers as the <term>antitype</term> <note>An 'antitype' is the fulfillment or reality prefigured by an earlier symbol; here, the work of Christ (Redemption) is the fulfillment of the pattern established at Creation.</note> of Creation—functions in exactly the same way. It presents the Father as the primary Source of both the decree and its execution, speaking to the Son and *showing* him all things, [sending] him...

### DISSERTATION

...sending him; the Son, however, is the one *fulfilling the good pleasure of the Father, having been sent*, revealing His will, and doing so with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, as if through another *Legate, Interpreter, and Advocate* <note>original Latin: *Paracleto*</note>, through whom the Son performs all things. For this reason, in the realm of grace, the Spirit also returns as the cause that stands most closely to the finished effect.

XLII. Furthermore (r) our perspective excellently illustrates the true emphasis of the name **WORD** <note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΟΣ (LOGOS)</note>, whose origin we have been investigating here. We have presented a summary of this in our Commentary on John, Chapter 1, verse 1. For although we bring together several reasons for this name in that work, we nevertheless rest primarily on that <term>metonymical</term> <note>A figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it; here, the Son is called "the Word" because he reveals the Father's words.</note> meaning by which He is called the *Word of the Father*, because He is the *Revealer* of the divine will. He performs this office both in *words* and in *deed* itself as the highest and first **Archangel** <note>The author uses this term in its literal Greek sense of "Chief Messenger" to describe the Son's role, not to imply He is a created angelic being.</note>. This fits both the *name* and the *reality* of the matter. 

As for the *name*, the Son of God is not called <term>Amrah</term> <note>original Hebrew: אמרה (imrah/amrah), often referring to a spoken word or utterance</note> but <term>Dabar</term> <note>original Hebrew: דבר (dabar), which can mean both "word" and "thing/substance"</note> by the Psalmist. It appears from the nature of the Hebrew language that the root *Amrah* corresponds more to the external sounding of a word, whereas *Dabar* responds more precisely to the actual sense or meaning that lies beneath the external word. Therefore, the Holy Spirit did not wish to call the Son of God *Amrah*, lest anyone should stop at the mere derivation of the word from the verb "to say" <note>original Hebrew: אמר (amar)</note>. Instead, He preferred the name *Dabar*, both because its emphasis is greater, and because the name *Dabar* alluded not just to the action of speaking (ascribed here to God), but to the entire *discourse* which God the Father spoke to the Son, which the Son communicated to the Holy Spirit, and which He put into execution through the Spirit. 

As for the *reality* itself, the Son of God, according to this concept, already performed in the <term>Economy of Creation</term> <note>The "Economy" refers to the specific roles and actions the Persons of the Trinity take in relation to the world.</note> that which He provides for humanity in the Economy of Salvation. Doubtless He performed the same with respect to the good Angels themselves. However, Moses had his reasons for not dealing with the angels expressly. Therefore, Moses stopped at teaching that the Son exercised the office of the **WORD** <note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΟΥ (LOGOU)</note> in the work of Creation even in relation to the Holy Spirit. Thus it was established with greater certainty that this is the natural and unchangeable order of working among the persons of the Holy Trinity: that the Son further communicates the will of the Father—communicated to Himself in a way <term>worthy of God</term> <note>original Greek: Θεοπρεπως (Theoprepōs)</note>—to the third person, so that the entire Trinity is united in producing the final effect. It will suffice to have merely pointed this out for now, since we will, God willing, more fully illustrate the true emphasis of the name **WORD** at another time.

XLIII. We may, therefore, pause at this point. There is no need for us to proceed further with the famous **Leidekker** <note>Melchior Leydecker (1642–1721), a Dutch Reformed theologian</note>, who asserts that <insert>the Father spoke to the Holy Spirit in the Son</insert> at this moment. Regarding the evidence he brings for that hypothesis—namely, that the Holy Spirit also played His part in Creation—it provides him no real support. We grant that point with "both thumbs" <note>An ancient Roman expression meaning to give full or enthusiastic approval</note>. The only question is whether that idea is hidden within the phrase we are currently handling. This could be conceived in two ways: either that the *Son* is contained within the word **and He said** <note>original Hebrew: ויאמר (Vayomer)</note>, or within the word **God** <note>original Hebrew: אלהים (Elohim)</note>. We do not believe the former should be admitted, lest we fall back into the same disadvantage we already noticed in the **Placæan** opinion <note>Referring to Josué de la Place (1596–1665), a theologian who suggested the "Word" was merely a figurative expression for God's power</note>. For in that case, the sacred writer would be defining the person of the Son solely by the action of speaking. It would be better, then, to understand **God** <note>Elohim</note> as referring to the Father and the Son together speaking to the Holy Spirit. However, this is contradicted by the fact that the difficulty proposed in Section 37 would return: there would be no basis found in this saying for deriving the name **WORD** <note>original Greek: ΛΟΓΟΣ (LOGOS)</note>, which is proper to the Son alone. For if **Moses** <note>Traditionally regarded as the author of Genesis</note> joined both the Father and the Son in the same *act of speaking* through the single name *Elohim*, then no reason appears why the Son should be called the **WORD** any more than the Father.

...occurs, is clear not only from the fact that the obscurity of this or that passage cannot prejudice the clarity of Scripture. This is because the same truth which is found to be covered in those places by a veil of words is taught in other places with singular simplicity and evidence. This is the response of **EPISCOPIUS** <note>Simon Episcopius (1583–1643), a prominent Dutch Remonstrant theologian</note> to this objection, found in his *Theological Institutes*, book IV, chapter 18. But it is also because, wherever Scripture is obscure, the most wise Authors of the Divine Word established reasons why, in such circumstances, they preferred an enigmatic way of speaking over one that is open and plain. This especially occurred in the Lord’s conversations with the Jews. In these, although He brought forth things that would have been sufficient to convince them regarding the Redeemer of the world <note>original Latin: *Redemtore mundi*</note> who was expected at precisely that time, and regarding the divinity of His person and mission—unless their hearts had been filled with an insuperable hatred of the truth—He nevertheless, on account of this very perversity and their wild struggle against the light itself, by a just judgment hid many mysteries of the Kingdom of God <note>original Latin: *Regni Dei mysteria*</note> in parables, which were to be explained more fully to the disciples, as seen in Matthew 13:10 and following. Since He had such listeners, if anywhere, certainly in that conversation in which our words occur, who would have blamed the Supreme Wisdom if He had wished to profess what the matter was concerning Himself more covertly? This was especially so since *His hour had not yet come* <note>original Latin: *hora ejus nondum venisset*</note>, which would have made it untimely to expose His head to the most immediate danger of death through a blunt and explicit confession of His Deity and His mediatorial office, and to place an obstacle before the time in laying the foundations of His Kingdom through His teaching. However, that very obscurity was so tempered that the true sense of the Lord’s words was not impossible to perceive for those among the Jews who had "ears to hear," nor is it entirely hidden from those who bring the necessary attention within the Church established after the Lord’s departure. We shall attempt to demonstrate this matter in our passage, following others and specifically **CHAMIER** <note>Daniel Chamier (1565–1621), a French Reformed theologian</note> in his *Panstratia Catholica*, volume I, book XV, chapter XV, who argues this point against **BELLARMINE** <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Jesuit Cardinal and a central figure in the Counter-Reformation</note>.

### III.
The connection with the following verse has more merit. ### IV.

Then he reads <gloss>hoti</gloss> <note>meaning "that" or "because"</note> rather than <gloss>ho, ti</gloss> <note>meaning "what"</note>. His logic is: *"In the first place, many things must be said by me; many things must be prefaced regarding your defiance and unbelief, before I answer you as to who I am."* **SAUBERTUS** <note>Johannes Saubert the Younger (1638–1688), a German theologian</note> mentions in his posthumous work (page 32) that this same opinion was defended by **NORTON KNATCHBULL** <note>An English baronet and biblical critic (1602–1685)</note> in his *Paradoxical Annotations* on this passage. But anyone can see that the words "because I even speak to you" <note>original Greek: ὁτι και λαλω ὑμιν</note> hardly admit this interpretation. Furthermore, in the preceding verses, He had already said who He was.

,, pronounce and judge against you: but he who sent me is true*: it is necessary
,, that his oracles—which promised that I, upon coming, would refrain from 
,, judging and would devote my entire effort to the salvation of men—should
,, obtain their truth. ,, 

We admit that there is nothing forced in this construction, and it is easier than all the other opinions we have examined to produce a clear sense from words arranged in this way. For this reason, we would have gladly given Gousset our "thumb of approval" <note>original Latin: *pollicem addidissemus*, a reference to the Roman gesture of approval in the gladiatorial arena</note>, were it not that he left it obscure where that phrase *the beginning* <note>Greek: *την ἀρχὴν*</note> should be referred, and the connection with the preceding words is rendered more intricate by this hypothesis.

VII. Among those who consider our words as an independent statement in themselves, we deservedly recoil first of all from those who [treat the] Grammar...

<meta>This page continues the critique of grammatical interpretations of John 8:25. The previous page ended by noting how certain interpretations "disturb the rules of grammar" (maticæ regulas turbant). Here, the author specifically targets the Latin Church Fathers, led by St. Augustine, for their grammatical errors in translating the Greek text.</meta>

# REGARDING THE PASSAGE JOHN 8:25.
<page-num>395</page-num>
<sig>Ddd 2</sig>

...disturb the rules of grammar. The Latin Fathers are guilty of grammatical errors <term>solecisms</term> <note>A "solecism" is a grammatical mistake or an intentional breaking of linguistic rules, often seen by later scholars as a sign of poor translation</note> in this matter, led by AUGUSTINE in his *38th Tractate on John*, where among other things he says: "And those men, always having earthly wisdom and always hearing and responding according to the flesh, what did they say to him? ***Who are you?*** For when you said, 'unless you believe that I am,' you did not add who you were. Who are you, that we may believe? And he answered: ***The Beginning.*** <note>original Latin: *Principium*</note> Behold what it is to be. The Beginning cannot be changed: the Beginning remains in itself and renews all things: the Beginning is he to whom it was said: *But you are the same, and your years shall not fail.* [Psalm 102:27]" etc. What he adds next, in order to reconcile this interpretation with the rules of Grammar, we pass over here as trivial. Nor does he attempt to show the connection with what follows in a sufficiently suitable way. "And he added, ***because I also speak to you:*** <note>Augustine is interpreting the phrase "tēn archēn hoti kai lalō hymin"</note> that is, because I have been made humble for your sake and have descended to these words. For if the Beginning remained with the Father as it is, such that he did not take the form of a servant and speak as a man to men, how would they believe in him; since weak hearts could not hear the intelligible Word without a sensible voice? Therefore, he says, believe that I am the beginning, because, so that you might believe, I not only am, but I also speak to you." 

But these things might be excused, were it not impossible to construct the accusative phrase "**the beginning**" <note>original Greek: *τὴν ἀρχήν* (tēn archēn)</note> with the question of the Jews: "**Who are you?**" <note>original Greek: *Σὺ τίς εἶ;* (Su tis ei)</note>. For this reason, AUGUSTINE even judges that this question should be rendered as: *Whom do we believe you to be?* <note>original Latin: *Quem te credimus?*</note> as if it were written: *Whom do we believe you?* <note>original Greek: *τίνα σὲ πιστεύομεν;* (tina se pisteuomen)</note>; a construction which is clearly imagined "against the grain" <term>invita Minerva</term> <note>A Latin idiom meaning "against the natural inclination" or forced, suggesting the logic is being tortured to fit a theory</note> for the sake of his hypothesis. Nevertheless, following AUGUSTINE—who teaches the same thing in *The City of God*, book 10, chapter 24—were AMBROSE in the *Hexameron*, book 1, chapters 2 & 4; *On the Faith*, book 3, chapter 4; FULGENTIUS in book 2 *To Thrasymund*; PROSPER in his *Commentary on Psalm 109*; BERNARD in book 5 *On Consideration*; as well as the *Standard Gloss* <term>Glossa Ordinaria</term> <note>A standard collection of biblical commentaries used in the Middle Ages</note> and LYRANUS. Some have even ascribed this same opinion to CYRIL OF ALEXANDRIA—which one would not expect from a Greek Father—but they failed to notice that Book 5 and the three following books of Cyril's *Commentaries on John* belong to the supplement written by JODOCUS CLICHTOVÆUS <note>Josse Clichtove (1472–1543), a Flemish theologian who completed Cyril's unfinished works</note>, who followed AUGUSTINE here as he did in most matters.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the phrase "the beginning" (tēn archēn) in John 8:25. While the previous page critiqued the Latin Church Fathers like Augustine for their grammatical errors, this page examines more recent attempts by scholars to justify the phrasing as a mystical or linguistic allusion to the Old Testament.</meta>

# DISSERTATION
<page-num>396</page-num>

VIII. Yet there was a learned man among more recent writers who, writing under the initials J. W. d. N. in the "Spontaneous Offerings" <note>This refers to a contemporary scholarly journal published in German in Berlin</note> published in the vernacular in Berlin, attempted by another method to address this <term>solecism</term> <note>a grammatical error</note> while preserving the same hypothesis of the Church Fathers (Vol. II, p. 852 and following). He believed that Jesus, through the phrase "the beginning," <note>original Greek: *tēn archēn*</note> was alluding to the first word of Genesis, "In the beginning." <note>original Hebrew: *Bereshit*</note> The Chaldean <term>Aramaic Targum</term> <note>ancient Jewish translations and paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible</note> rendered this as "through wisdom" <note>original Aramaic: *be-chokhmetha*</note>; and so, in order for the allusion to be more evident, he argues the Savior wished to preserve the <term>oblique case</term> <note>a grammatical case other than the nominative, here referring to the accusative form used in the Greek text</note>. But several things stand in the way: first, that Jesus does not seem to have spoken Greek in the Temple; second, even if that were admitted, he would have likely said "In the beginning" <note>original Greek: *En archē*</note> as the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> does; and third, that the Chaldean version does not seem to have expressed the true mind of the sacred historian.

The author of this hypothesis might have fared better if he had simply stuck to the paraphrase with which he closed his study: *You are to look upon me as the Beginning,* <note>original Hebrew: *Reshit*</note> *because I have not only spoken from the beginning of the world until now; but because I still speak to you as the essential Word.* For the name "Beginning" <note>original Hebrew: *Reshit*</note> occurs among the names of the Son of God in Proverbs 8:22, Colossians 1:18, and Revelation 3:14. It could also have been added that among the <term>Kabbalistic</term> <note>referring to Jewish mystical tradition</note> names of God, he is called "Beginning" <note>original Hebrew: *Reshit*</note> based on that passage in Deuteronomy 33:21: *And he saw the beginning* <note>original Hebrew: *reshit*</note> *for himself*; as STOLBERGIUS observed from Marco Marini's *Noah’s Ark*. But the illustrious MEIER, in his *Mystery of the Trinity* (p. 60 and following), and DANZ, in his *Inauguration of Christ* (p. 188), have established this same point more extensively from the book of *Zohar* <note>the foundational work of Jewish Kabbalah</note> and other Kabbalistic writers. Nor is there any doubt that this flowed from ancient Jewish instruction, since PHILO <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher</note> already places that name "Beginning" <note>original Greek: *Archē*</note> among the mystical names of the Word <term>Logos</term> in his work *On the Confusion of Tongues* (p. 341). Hence, STEPHEN LE MOINE in his *Sacred Miscellany* (Vol. II, p. 452) also thinks that "the beginning" <note>original Greek: *archēn*</note> in our Evangelist [John] should be rendered as "The Beginning"; however, he believes it refers more to the passage in Proverbs 8:22. But even then, the <term>ellipsis</term> <note>a grammatical omission where words are understood but not stated</note> remains just as harsh in light of the Jews' question as the one we noted in AUGUSTINE.

IX. Perhaps the **VULGATE** <note>the standard Latin Bible translation</note> provided the handle for this error, which rendered our words as: *The Beginning, who also speaks to you.* In this version, two things are problematic: first, that "the beginning" <note>original Greek: *tēn archēn*</note> is rendered in the <term>nominative</term> case as *Principium*, and second, that "who" is put in place of "because." <note>The Greek word *hoti* can mean "because" or "that," but the Vulgate translated it as a relative pronoun *qui* (who)</note> The former was excused by ERAS- <meta>catchword: ERAS-</meta>

<summary>This page discusses various scholarly attempts to interpret Jesus's self-identification as "The Beginning" in John 8:25, exploring potential links to Genesis, the Kabbalah, and the Aramaic Targums. The author critiques the Latin Vulgate for contributing to a long-standing grammatical misunderstanding of the original Greek text.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of John 8:25, specifically investigating whether the Greek phrase "tēn archēn" should be interpreted as an adverb (meaning "at first" or "to begin with") rather than a noun ("the Beginning"). It moves from critiquing older theories to examining the views of major Reformation-era and Enlightenment scholars.</meta>

### ON THE PASSAGE JOHN 8:25.
->Ddd 3<-

IX. ERASMUS, believing that *the beginning* <note>original Latin: *principium*</note> should be taken adverbially. But others have countered that sufficient authority for this is lacking from the classic authors. For those exposing the <term>solecism</term> <note>a grammatical error or non-standard usage</note> of the Vulgate <note>the 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note>, one should compare STOLBERG in his *Exercise IV*, SAUBERT’s posthumous works (pages 31–32), and GATAKER. The latter argued against RAMIREZ DE PRADO—who had defended the Vulgate in his *Pentecost*, chapter 32—in his own *Posthumous Adversaria*, chapter 39. Nonetheless, LUTHER seems to have understood the Vulgate in this way and followed it in his own version: *Firstly he, who I speak with you.* <note>original German: "Erstlich der, der ich mit euch rede." Luther interprets the phrase as Jesus saying he is the one he claimed to be from the start.</note> The same view was held by LUDOVICUS VIVES in his commentary on Augustine's *City of God* (Book 10, ch. 25), giving this paraphrase: *In the beginning, I am he who speaks to you, using a mortal body as an instrument; no longer commanding through an angel, but through myself.* GROTIUS also joined this camp, although he tempers the meaning slightly differently, saying: *Christ says this because he could have proclaimed many other things about himself besides what he had said, but he is content with that for now.* But even if this defense were admitted, the sense would still be both weak and discordant, as it is not clear what that "firstly" would refer back to.

X. A different reasoning pleases NOLDIUS in his *Concordance of Particles* (n. 1350), who renders it: *In the beginning, was it not?* or *In the beginning certainly* (namely in verse 12, compared with Isaiah 49:6) *I already told you.* However, there are no available examples in which <term>the beginning</term> <note>original Greek: *tēn archēn*</note> is used to refer to a mode of elapsed time, nor should the present tense be rashly changed into the past.

XI. APOLLINARIUS clings to the same version of <term>the beginning</term> <note>original Greek: *tou tēn archēn*</note> as meaning "at first." An excerpt of his is preserved in the *Catena Patrum* <note>a "chain" of interpretations from Church Fathers</note> on this passage: *It was not necessary, he says, to speak to you at all at the beginning, but rather to grant this to those who were ready to receive my words gladly. He signifies the multitude of the Gentiles, and at the same time declares that he had spoken to the unworthy Jews themselves because of the promise made to the Fathers.* <note>original Greek: Εδει με, φησιν, ουχ υμιν ολως προσλαλησαι κατα την αρχην, εκεινοις δε μαλλον τουτο χαριζεσθαι, τοις ετοιμως μελλουσιν ασμενως τους εμους υποδεξασθαι λογους. Σημαινει δε των εθνων την πληθυν. Δεικνυει δε δια τουτων, οτι και τοις αναξιοις Ιουδαιοις ελαλει δια την προς τους Πατερας επαγγελιαν.</note> But regarding the ellipsis...

<meta>This page continues the philological investigation of John 8:25, specifically debating the meaning of the Greek phrase "tēn archēn" (the beginning) and the conjunction "hoti" (that/why). It critiques the theories of Ludovicus de Dieu and Suicerus regarding whether the sentence should be read as a question or an assertion.</meta>

# DISSERTATION

insolence; moreover, the fact that the "what" or "that" <note>original Greek: "to ho, ti, sive hoti"</note> is plainly neglected here easily leads us not to cling to this observation.

XII. But Ludovicus de Dieu thinks that "the beginning" <note>original Greek: "tēn archēn"</note> could mean *first* <note>original Latin: "primo"</note> here in a slightly different way. He notes that the Greek word "that" <note>original Greek: "hoti"</note> is equivalent to the Hebrew particle *ki* <note>Hebrew: כי</note>, which is well known to frequently serve a questioning purpose, as seen for example in Isaiah 29:16. From this, he fashions the following sense: *Do I even speak to you first?* <note>original Latin: "Primumne etiam loquor vobis?"</note> as if to say: "You ask me who I am, as if you had never been taught that by me before. Am I now addressing you for the very first time, such that you have a need to ask that now?" 

But since this most learned man easily sensed that he could be required to produce an example where "that" <note>original Greek: "hoti"</note> is placed precisely as an <term>interrogative</term> <note>a word that introduces a question</note>, he adds another observation: namely, that "that" <note>original Greek: "hoti"</note> sometimes signifies *really, certainly, indeed,* or *for my part* <note>original Greek: "ontōs"; original Latin: "revera, certe, utique, equidem"</note>. He adds an example of this usage from 1 John 3:20. From this, while preserving the questioning form, the following sense emerges: *Do I indeed even address you first?* Or, so that the definite article in "the beginning" is also accounted for: *Do I indeed even speak to you at this beginning?* That is, *is it only now for the first time?* 

Suicer, in his *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus* (Volume I, page 529), prefers this interpretation over all others. To illustrate it, he brings forward various passages from the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> and the Church Fathers, through which he tries to prove that "the beginning" <note>original Greek: "tēn archēn"</note> denotes *first*. However, most of those cases are such that "the beginning" does not mean *first*, but rather *in the beginning* or *from the beginning*. 

Whatever the case may be, using the word "that" <note>original Greek: "hoti"</note> to mean "certainly" is not only unusual, but it also does not fit in our specific passage and would be clearly redundant; hence, the distinguished author would have been more successful if he had stuck to his first explanation. For he himself, in his notes on Mark 9:28, proved from Homer that "that" <note>original Greek: "hoti"</note> is sometimes interrogative. Stolberg added examples of this from Herodotus in the work cited above (page 275). In all of these, however, it must be observed that "that" is never used in an absolute question, but only in an indirect one. But let that pass as well. If "that" were a question-word, shouldn't it have been placed at the very start of the sentence? And wouldn't the word "even" <note>original Greek: "kai"</note> also be superfluous here? Since this interpretation is somewhat forced from every angle, we will not be easily persuaded to change a statement of fact into a question for its sake.

XIII. Another opinion, which renders "the beginning" <note>original Greek: "tēn archēn"</note> as *as soon as possible*, will not detain us long. This is found in the commentary on this passage by Hunnius, who explains it thus:

<meta>This page continues the philological investigation of John 8:25, where Jesus answers the question "Who are you?" with the enigmatic phrase "tēn archēn ho ti kai lalō hymin." The author is currently evaluating various historical interpretations of "tēn archēn" (the beginning/at first).</meta>

proposes: *I shall speak to you as soon as possible, or soon, and reveal who I am, namely when I shall have been lifted up from the earth: for then you will know that I am he.* <note>original Latin: "Ego quamprimum seu mox id loquar vobis & patefaciam, quis sim, quando nimirum de terra fuero exaltatus: tum enim cognoscetis, quod ego sum."</note> This same view pleased **Brenz** <note>Johannes Brenz (1499–1570), a prominent Lutheran reformer</note>, who, to illustrate it, brings forward that in **Xenophon** <term>tēn tachistēn</term> <note>original Greek: την ταχιστην; a technical adverbial phrase meaning "most quickly"</note> means *most quickly*, and <term>tēn syntomōtatēn</term> <note>original Greek: την συντομωτατην</note> means *by a shortcut*. But these examples are neither fitting nor are they successfully applied to our passage, since they assume a harsh <term>enallage</term> <note>the substitution of one grammatical form for another</note> of the present tense for the future, and the facts of the matter themselves argue against it. For Jesus did not intend to say *soon* who he was, but in truth he had just said it, and had said it frequently already.

XIV. The interpretation of **Zwingli** <note>Huldrych Zwingli (1484–1531), leader of the Reformation in Switzerland</note> on this passage is also too vague: *First of all, what I am even speaking to you, I am. Or otherwise: The sum of those things which I say to you, I am. As if to say, I am that which I speak to you: for above he had said that he was the light of the world and that his flesh was food.* <note>original Latin: "Imprimis quod & loquor, quasi dicat, quod loquor vobiscum, ego sum. Seu aliter: Summa eorum, quae vobis dico, ego sum. Quasi dicat, id sum, quod loquor vobis..."</note> **Musculus** <note>likely Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563), a Reformed theologian</note> followed him in this.

XV. **Clarius Lightfoot** in his *Hebrew and Talmudic Hours* on this passage observed that in the Talmud <term>reisha</term> <note>Hebrew/Aramaic: רישא</note> is the same as *primarily*, as opposed to the distinct <term>seifa</term> <note>Hebrew/Aramaic: סיפא</note>, which denotes *secondarily*. From this he constructs the following paraphrase: *You ask, who am I! The <term>reisha</term> [The Beginning] is that thing which is primarily to be investigated, which I also speak to you; namely that I am the Light of the World, the Son of God, the Messiah etc. But what I do, what I teach, and by what authority, those are <term>seifa</term> [the end], matters of secondary inquiry: the primary thing is who I am.* <note>original Latin: "Quaeritis, quis ego siem! רישא Principium illud est... primariae est illud, quis siem."</note> But neither the words nor the matter itself favor this interpretation. Not the words, because a very unusual and gaping <term>ellipsis</term> <note>the omission of words needed to complete a grammatical structure</note> is assumed here. Nor the matter itself, both because the Savior did not wish to praise the Jews but to rebuke them, and because the first inquiry is most closely bound to the second; for attending to the teaching and works of Jesus was especially necessary so that they might be convinced by them that he was indeed the *Light of the World*.

XVI. Much greater appearance of truth is held by those who explain <term>tēn archēn</term> <note>original Greek: την αρχην</note> as <term>holōs</term> <note>original Greek: ολως</note>, meaning *altogether* or *entirely*, since it cannot be denied that this meaning is not infrequent among the Greeks. This had been proven with many good examples by **Erasmus**, **Camerarius** on this passage, and **Stolbergius** in the work cited, page 278; **Glassius** in *Sacred Philology*, Book III, Treatise V, Canon 17, page 473; and **Dilherrus** in his *Academic Disputations*.

<meta>This page continues the philological investigation of John 8:25, following the discussion of Johannes Brenz and Huldrych Zwingli's interpretations of the Greek phrase "tēn archēn." The author is listing various scholarly opinions that attempt to reconcile the Greek text with Hebrew linguistic patterns or specific grammatical figures like ellipsis.</meta>

# DISSERTATIO

...demonstrated. Volume I, page 285. **Colomesius** <note>Paul Colomiés (1638–1692), a French librarian and scholar</note> in *Opuscula*, pages 637, 638. **Fabricius** <note>Johann Albert Fabricius (1668–1736), a German classical scholar and bibliographer</note> in his notes on Sextus Empiricus, page 26. **Hammond** <note>Henry Hammond (1605–1660), an English New Testament scholar</note> on this passage. **Homberg** in *Parerga Sacra*, page 165. **Hottinger** <note>Johann Heinrich Hottinger (1620–1667), a Swiss philologist and theologian</note> also reconciles it with a Hebraism, producing the example of **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher</note>, who in *Hilchot Sabbath*, chapter 1, puts the Hebrew <term>l'chatchilah</term> <note>Hebrew: לכתחלה; meaning "from the start" or "initially"</note> in place of the Talmudic <term>legamre</term> <note>Hebrew: לגמרי; meaning "completely"</note> writing: *Behold, this is entirely permitted from the start.* <note>original Latin/Hebrew: "הרי זה מותר לכתחלה Ecce id omnino licitum est."</note> One may consult the *Heidelberg Primitives*, Dissertation III, page 81, and *On the Use of Hebrew Scripture in the New Testament*, edited by Rhenferd, page 400.

XVII. However, interpreters have not used this hypothesis in only one way. The <term>exegesis</term> <note>critical explanation or interpretation of a text</note> of **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), Archbishop of Constantinople</note> is plainly forced, as he defines it thus: *You are completely unworthy of even hearing words from me, let alone learning who I am, for everything you speak is to test me, and you pay no attention to anything I bring forward.* <note>original Greek: "του όλως ακουειν των λογων των παρ' εμου αναξιοι εστε, μητι γε και μαθειν όστις εγω ειμι, ύμεις γαρ παντα πειραζοντες φθεγγεσθε και ουδενι των παρ' εμου προσεχοντες."</note> This is also the opinion of **Theophylact** and **Euthymius** <note>Byzantine commentators on the Gospels</note>, although anyone can see that a very harsh <term>ellipsis</term> <note>the omission of words needed to complete a grammatical construction</note> is being established here, which is entirely without precedent. Furthermore, the word "that" [hoti] is exchanged for "who" or "whoever" [hos or hostis], an error we noted the Vulgate also committed.

XVIII. **Maldonatus** <note>Juan de Maldonado (1533–1583), a Spanish Jesuit theologian</note> presents another ellipsis devised by **Leontius** and some anonymous author under the hidden meaning of "entirely," in this sense: *For this reason you despise me, and for this reason you ask me contemptuously, "Who are you?" because I even speak with you at all. Or: you completely despise me for this reason, because I am accustomed to speaking with you. Wherefore you are unworthy for me to tell you who I am.* But since the same difficulties recur here, we shall dismiss this view as well.

XIX. More likely, **Flacius** <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575), a Lutheran reformer and scholar</note> writes in his *Key to the Scriptures*: *Furthermore, "tēn archēn" is a phrase containing a strict assertion. I am absolutely he himself, who speaks to you.* <note>original Latin: "Est autem την αρχην phrasis continens severam asseverationem. Prorsus ille ipse sum, qui loquor vobis."</note> And those whom we just cited in Section XVI—**Stolberg**, **Glassius**, and the rest—believe this opinion should be especially maintained. Add to these **Oecolampadius**, **Melanchthon** <note>Leading figures of the Protestant Reformation</note>, and **Johannes Schedius**, who supports it in a particular treatise (Wittenberg, 1688), which is reviewed in the *Acta Eruditorum Lipsiensia Supplement I*, pages 335, 336.

<meta>This page continues the philological investigation of John 8:25, specifically debating how to translate the Greek phrase "tēn archēn" (the beginning). It follows previous discussions of whether the phrase should be read as a noun or an adverbial expression.</meta>

### ON THE PASSAGE JOHN 8:25.

->Eee<-

...yet he suggests a doubt, both because such a formula of assertion is clearly distant from the Savior’s style—who was accustomed to corroborating His emphatic sayings with the word *Amen*—and because this statement is somewhat harsh: "*Altogether, that which I am also speaking to you*"; since the word *also* <note>original Greek: *το και* (to kai)</note> is entirely redundant here. Those who observe that "the beginning" <note>original Greek: *την αρχην* (tēn archēn)</note> does not merely assert but also intensifies, and therefore translate it as *plainly* or *altogether*, remove the first difficulty. Compare **Perizonius** <note>Jakob Perizonius (1651–1715), a Dutch classical scholar</note> in his notes on Aelian, book III, 14, and in the Index. Thus, the Lord’s meaning would be: "In all emphasis, I am that which I also speak to you." **Colomiés** <note>Paul Colomiés (1638–1692), a French scholar and librarian</note>, **Homberg** <note>Jakob Homberg, author of *Parerga Sacra*</note>, and **Elsner** <note>Jakob Elsner (1692–1750), a Prussian theologian</note> seem to lean toward this view. But such a meaning, besides the redundancy of the word *also*, does not fit the dispute with the Jews, who were not arguing about the emphasis of words, but about the reality itself.

XX. There was also someone who attempted to find a suitable construction in which the <term>accusative</term> <note>a grammatical case usually indicating the direct object of a verb</note> "the beginning" <note>original Greek: *την αρχην* (tēn archēn)</note> would be preserved as "The Beginning" <note>original Latin: *principium*</note>, namely Dr. **Sebastian Schmidt** <note>Sebastian Schmidt (1617–1696), a Lutheran theologian and Hebraist</note> in his paraphrase on this passage. This view is defended by the celebrated **Majus the Elder** <note>Johann Heinrich Majus (1653–1719), a German theologian</note> in *Prophetic Theology*, page 246, who cites a specific dissertation written on this verse. Schmidt maintains that Christ wanted to suggest His origin—which He had from above and from eternity—to the Jews in this way: "*The Beginning (of myself) even as I speak to you*"; as if He said: "It is indeed a wonder, O Jews, that you ask me who I am at the very time when I am speaking with you about my origin and my beginning; I am saying more to you than what you ask. For if I simply told you who I am—namely, GOD—you would not immediately grasp my origin. But when I reveal my beginning to you, I tell you both: for from the beginning, who I am becomes perfectly clear." It would have been pleasing if this dissertation had been available to me, especially since the praised Majus testifies that this sense fits excellently with what comes before, what follows, and the rest of the words and arrangement of the divine oracle itself, as he proves at length. This does not appear so clearly to us. For although we can grant that the connection is not much of an obstacle, one can easily see that both the construction and the <term>ellipsis</term> <note>the omission of words needed to complete a grammatical structure</note> supposed here are somewhat harsh, as is the unusual meaning attributed to the particle *that* <note>original Greek: *ὅτι* (hoti)</note>.

# DISSERTATION

XXI. The opinion of **Beza** <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major French Protestant theologian and scholar</note> comes very close to the true meaning of the Savior. He establishes that "the beginning" <note>original Greek: *την ἀρχην* (tēn archēn)</note> declares nothing other than "from the beginning" <note>original Greek: *ἐξ ἀρχης* (ex archēs)</note>. He argues this should be connected by a reversal of word order to the verb "I speak" <note>original Greek: *λαλῶ* (lalō)</note>. Furthermore, he suggests that "what" <note>original Greek: *ὁ, τι* (ho, ti)</note> should be written as a pronoun; then, the verb "I am" <note>original Latin: *sum*</note> must be understood <term>apo koinou</term> <note>a grammatical term where a single word is understood to apply to two different clauses</note>. Finally, he views the word "and" <note>original Greek: *το και* (to kai)</note> as a <term>pleonasm</term> <note>the use of more words than are necessary for the sense, often for emphasis</note> that is not only common in the Greek language but even elegant. From this, the following meaning emerges: *When the Jews asked who He was, Christ responded that He is exactly what He had told them from the beginning—that is, what He had already urged upon them so many times and in so many ways.* Nor is it without emphasis that the Evangelist uses the present tense "I speak" <note>original Greek: *λαλῶ* (lalō)</note>, as if He were saying: *I am that which I told you from the beginning, and which I am saying even now: namely, the Light, the Life, the Truth, etc.* 

Most versions, both ancient and modern, favor this interpretation. Thus, the **Syriac** has already rendered it: *Even that which I began to speak with you* <note>original Syriac: אפין דשרית דאמלל עמכון</note>. At the very least, this appears to us from the version of **Louis de Dieu** <note>Ludovicus de Dieu (1590–1642), a Dutch orientalist</note>, with which the **Schaaf** edition <note>Karl Schaaf, editor of the Syriac New Testament</note> agrees: *Even if I have begun to speak with you, I still have much to say about you.* Nor does the **Arabic** in the Erpenian Codex disagree, according to **Tarnovius's** translation: *I, and what I am, have already begun to say in speaking with you.* And **Nonnus** <note>Nonnus of Panopolis, a 5th-century poet who wrote a verse paraphrase of the Gospel of John</note>: 
> *Who are you? And Christ cried out: That which to you* 
> *I declared from the beginning.* <note>original Greek: Τις συ πελεις; και Χριστος ἀνιαχεν. Οττιπερ ὑμιν / Εξ ἀρχης ἀοριζον.</note> 

The **Modern Greek** version says: *That which I tell you from the beginning* <note>original Greek: Εκεινος ὁ που σας λαλω ἀπο την ἀρχην</note>. Most vernacular versions do not differ, including the **French**, **Spanish**, **English**, **Italian**, **Dutch**, **Piscator's** translation, and others. It has also gained no small number of supporters, among whom are **Jansenius of Ghent**, **Rivet**, **Chamier**, **Hammond**, **Hackspan**, **Saubert**, **Le Clerc**, **Elsner**, and many more.

XXII. Certainly, as far as the notion of the word "the beginning" <note>original Greek: *την ἀρχην* (tēn archēn)</note> considered in itself is concerned, no one will easily doubt that it can be used for "from the beginning" <note>original Greek: *ἐξ ἀρχης* or *ἀπ' ἀρχης*</note> if they weigh the examples produced on this matter by **Stolberg**, **Elsner**, and others. Nor can those things which **Louis de Dieu** [argues] against this opinion...

Indeed, as for the objections he raises, they all carry the same weight, as **Stolberg** <note>Balthasar Stolberg (1640–1684), a German philologist and professor</note> has proved at length against him in the work cited. However, there are two things that make us slower to agree. One concerns the *words*, the other the *subject* itself. No one is so blind that they do not see that the construction of the words according to **Beza's** <note>Theodore Beza, a major French Protestant theologian</note> hypothesis has a somewhat harsh tone. While one might consider the individual points he has sought, it is hardly acceptable that so many anomalies and so many ellipses <note>the omission of words that are understood from context</note> should occur at once in so few words. Furthermore, I cannot easily swallow either the phrase "the beginning" <note>original Greek: *το την αρχην* (to tēn archēn)</note> occupying the start of the speech according to this interpretation, nor the redundancy of the connecting word "and" <note>original Greek: *και* (kai)</note>. As for the subject itself, it is unclear which *beginning* Jesus was referring to. Was it, as it seemed to **Schlichting**, **Hemming**, and others, the beginning of His public preaching among the Jews? But Jesus did not have the same audience then, nor did He immediately manifest His divine glory to them in explicit words. Or was it perhaps the beginning of the rebuke against the Jews started primarily in Chapter 5, as **Bucer** <note>Martin Bucer (1491–1551), a German Reformer based in Strasbourg</note> thought probable? Or, which more pleases **Hammond**, **Le Clerc**, and **Wolzogen**, the beginning of this specific sermon, or at least of this conversation with the Jews? But who does not notice that this would be quite weak, and that "the beginning" properly ought to be translated as "just now" or "previously"?

XXIII. The opinion of **Calvin** <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the influential French Reformer</note> lessens these difficulties significantly. He thinks the words can be resolved this way: "According to the principle [beginning], that is, He of whom I have long since, and even now, as if anew, confirmed: or indeed, what I am now speaking is in conformity with the oracles of all ages, so that it might be a firm validation. In short, this response consists of two parts. For by the name of the 'Beginning,' He encompasses the continuous series of ages from the time when God's Covenant was established with the Fathers. When He says that He is also 'Speaking,' He connects His present teaching with the ancient prophecies and shows that it depends upon them." This hypothesis was polished by the famous **Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for 'Covenant Theology'</note>, who likewise understands this as *the beginning of speaking to the Jews or Israelites*, namely from the time the Son of God appeared to Moses in the burning bush and spoke from Mount Sinai; and he considers it a specific allusion to Isaiah 48:16, where the *Messiah is said not to have spoken in secret from the beginning*, as if to say: *I am He who from the*

"...*I spoke to Israel from the beginning.*" However, for the present-tense phrase "I speak" <note>original Greek: λαλῶ (*lalō*)</note>, he provides this reasoning: because He was still speaking and had always spoken to the people, and what He had promised He would be, He was now beginning to be in reality. From this, it is clear that the particle "and" <note>original Greek: καὶ (*kai*)</note> is by no means redundant here. For it signifies that both belong to Him: speaking from the beginning, so that the ancestors might place their faith in Him, and later, that this should come to pass in actual events and be discovered to be exactly what He had spoken. This opinion, being vigorous and full of substance, has deservedly found many followers among the students of that great man. Among these, we now name **J. H. Heidegger** <note>Johann Heinrich Heidegger (1633–1698), a Swiss Reformed theologian</note> in his *History of the Patriarchs*, Volume I, dissertation 3, sections 12 and 13; and **Cornelius Hase** <note>Cornelius Hase (1653–1710), a German theologian</note> in his work *On the Proto-Gospel*, Chapter I, section 6 and following, in the *Thesaurus of Theological Philology*, Volume I, page 70. These authors even extend the Lord's saying further, ascending to the very beginning of the created world, from which the **Word** <note>original Greek: ὁ Λόγος (*ho Logos*)</note> was heard speaking. Yet, all difficulty is not yet removed, since a rather harsh <term>metathesis</term> <note>the transposition or reordering of words from their natural grammatical sequence</note> remains in that version regarding the word "the beginning" <note>original Greek: τὴν ἀρχὴν (*tēn archēn*)</note>, which refers to the verb "I speak" and must be placed after the phrase "whatever." Among all the metatheses that **Stolberg** <note>Balthasar Stolberg, mentioned on the previous page</note> collects in the cited location, none is similar to this one of ours. Therefore, although we might rest content here regarding other matters, and though the mind inclines toward this most elegant opinion, we nevertheless shrink back—unwillingly—from a construction so unusual in prose.

XXIV. There remains, however, another opinion which seems to successfully address this difficulty, put forward by **Toletus** <note>Francisco Toledo (1532–1596), a Spanish Jesuit commentator</note>, who renders it: **FROM THE BEGINNING, WHAT I ALSO SPEAK TO YOU**, so that the phrase "From the beginning" makes sense by itself—namely: "From the beginning, I am." Here, he quite aptly compares the passage from **Psalm 93:2**: *From eternity You are* <note>original Hebrew: מעולם אתה (*me’olam attah*)</note>, in which pronouncement the substantive verb "to be" is likewise absorbed or understood. Very close to this is the view of the most elegant scholar **J. H. Majus the younger** <note>Johann Heinrich Mai (1688–1732), a German Hebraist and theologian</note>, who observes in his *Sacred Observations*, Book I, pages 69–70, that "the beginning" is used in place of "according to the beginning." He argues that this word should be construed not with "I speak," but with "I am" (which was to be repeated from the previous question of the Jews), in this manner: *(According to) the beginning (I am) what I also speak to you.* This translates to: **"Even before the beginning of all things, I was all that I have so far explained to you."** We do not see what could be greatly desired in this version,

## XXV.
Therefore, lest any doubt remain, and by applying only a very slight change—while gratefully acknowledging that we have been led so close to determining the true sense of the passage by most learned men—we substitute this translation: **IN THE BEGINNING I AM, THAT WHICH I EVEN NOW SPEAK TO YOU.** It is now our task to place in full light the fact that this version both fits the sacred phraseology most aptly and yields a most rich meaning, perfectly suited to the connection of the dispute in which Jesus was engaged with the Jews.

## XXVI.
Regarding the phraseology, we first preserve here the true and proper notion of the words. "Beginning" <note>original Greek: *Ἀρχὴ* (*archē*)</note> is taken by us not only in a convenient sense, but also precisely in the sense that is familiar to our Evangelist <note>The author of the Gospel, John</note>, in whose writings "beginning" <note>original Greek: *ἀρχὴ*</note> frequently occurs in reference to the origin of things, specifically when he is occupied in describing the eternity of our Savior in chapter 1, verses 1–2, and in his First Epistle, chapter 1, verse 1. For this reason, he also emphatically names Jesus "the one who is from the beginning" <note>original Greek: *τον ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς* (*ton ap’ archēs*)</note> in the First Epistle, chapter 2, verses 13–14. Other Evangelists speak more fully: "from the beginning of the world" <note>original Greek: *ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς κοσμου* (*ap’ archēs kosmou*)</note> in Matthew 24:21, or "of creation" <note>original Greek: *κτισεως* (*ktiseōs*)</note> in Mark 13:9. Add to this 2 Peter 3:4. Furthermore, we have shown what emphasis that word "beginning" <note>original Greek: *ἀρχὴ*</note> carries regarding the person of our Savior in the Commentary at the start of our Gospel.

## XXVII.
Furthermore, it is admitted by all that the oblique case "the beginning" <note>original Greek: *την ἀρχην* (*tēn archēn*)</note> indicates an <term>ellipsis</term> <note>the omission of a word or phrase that is understood from the context</note> of a preposition. We judge that the particle "according to" <note>original Greek: *κατα* (*kata*)</note> is to be preferred over the particles "from," "out of," or "in," <note>original Greek: *τῳ ἀπο* (*apo*), *ἐκ* (*ek*), or *ἐν* (*en*)</note> both because the accusative case especially requires it, and because it does not elsewhere reject the word "beginning" <note>original Greek: *ἀρχη*</note> when it denotes a start. Hence, "at the beginnings" <note>original Greek: *κατ’ ἀρχas* (*kat' archas*)</note> is found in Psalm 102:26 for the Hebrew word "formerly" <note>original Hebrew: *לפנים* (*lepanim*)</note> and in a contracted form "at the start" <note>original Greek: *καταρχας* (*katarchas*)</note> for the Hebrew word "from of old" <note>original Hebrew: *קדם* (*qedem*)</note> in Psalm 119:151 among the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX</note> interpreters. How frequent the ellipsis of the preposition "according to" <note>original Greek: *κατα*</note> occurs will be taught not only by **Pasor** <note>Georg Pasor (1570–1637), a noted lexicographer of New Testament Greek</note> regarding the New Testament, but also by **Lambert Bos** <note>Lambert Bos (1670–1717), a Dutch scholar of Greek philology</note> in his work *On Ellipses*, page 297 and following. From there, those who are about to apply it to our passage in the *Leipzig Acts of the Erudite* <note>original: *Acta Eruditorum Lipsiensia*, the first scientific journal of the German lands</note>, year 1713, page 367, use it, although it is brought forward by the author of the review there so that the opinion of those who explain "the beginning" <note>original Greek: *την ἀρχην*</note> as "entirely" or "at all" <note>original Greek: *ὁλως* (*holōs*)</note> may receive support.

# DISSERTATION

### XXVIII. 
But since the particle *kata* <note>A Greek preposition that can mean "according to," "throughout," or "at."</note> has many meanings, we do not without reason prefer the translation **IN**. For first, among those passages which have been excerpted by other learned men to prove that the phrase "the beginning" <note>original Greek: *την αρχην* (*tēn archēn*)</note> signifies "from the beginning," some occur which are more accurately translated as **IN THE BEGINNING**. 

Thus **HIPPOCRATES** <note>The famous ancient Greek physician, often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> at the start of his book *On Ancient Medicine*: "**IN THE BEGINNING** the medical art had not yet been found, nor was it sought." 

**HELIODORUS** in *Aethiopica*, Book IV: "The worsening disease indeed causes me pain, but even more so does the fact that I did not restrain the disease **IN THE BEGINNING**." 

**ISOCRATES** in his *Praise of Helen*, page 412: "And I fear lest I seem to some to labor more over this matter than over her whom I proposed **IN THE BEGINNING**." 

The same author in his *Praise of Busiris*, page 440: "For those who instilled this fear in us **IN THE BEGINNING** were the cause of our not living altogether like wild beasts toward one another." 

In these instances, just as we suppose in our specific passage, the author is speaking about the beginning of things. 

Furthermore, II. a point made by Keuchenius <note>Petrus Keuchenius (1654–1689), a Dutch theologian and philologist.</note> is relevant here: in Daniel 8:1, when the Prophet says he saw a vision after the one "which had appeared to him" **in the beginning** <note>Hebrew: *batchillah* (בתחלה)</note>, the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament, abbreviated as LXX.</note> rendered it as "after the one seen by me **at the beginning**" <note>Greek: *την ἀρχην* (*tēn archēn*)</note>. Yet in Daniel 9:21, where the Prophet says Gabriel appeared to him, "whom," he says, "I had seen in the vision **in the beginning**" <note>Hebrew: *batchillah*</note>, the same translators put "whom I saw in the vision **in the beginning**" <note>Greek: *ἐν τῃ ἀρχῃ* (*en tē archē*)</note>. 

Therefore, our opinion holds an advantage over other interpretations—especially over the popular one that explains "the beginning" <note>*την ἀρχην*</note> as meaning "wholly" or "at all" <note>Greek: *ὁλως* (*holōs*)</note>. This latter usage is found only in secular authors, and no example of it is found in either the New Testament or the Septuagint, whereas our interpretation corresponds perfectly to the sacred and Hellenistic <note>The Greek of the Bible and Jewish-Greek literature.</note> style. 

III. Moreover, Noldius <note>Christian Noldius (1626–1683), author of a famous work on Hebrew particles.</note> will show that the omission of the Hebrew letter *bet* <note>The Hebrew preposition meaning "in."</note> is very frequent. An example of this can be seen in Proverbs 8:28, where "in the east" <note>Hebrew: *be-kedem*</note> is used for "the east" <note>Hebrew: *kedem*</note>. 

IV. Added to this is the fact that, although we do not think the sense we examined in sections 5 and 6 refers to the beginning of Genesis, nevertheless...

### XXIX. 
Indeed, it is especially to be observed here that such an expression could not have been harsh or unusual to the ears of the Jews. For since Jesus was constantly in the habit of alluding to the prophecies of the Old Testament whenever he brought forth some illustrious testimony about his own person—in order to prove the agreement of his teaching with them—it is not at all to be doubted that he did the same in this precise declaration, which was so glorious for himself. Although the former opinion seems to have great patrons and well-grounded reasons, the latter is nonetheless supported by authorities of equal weight. For it is rendered this way in the **ENGLISH** version, as well as those of **LUTHER**, **PISCATOR**, **DIODATI**, and our own **BELGIAN** <note>The Dutch Authorized Version or Statenvertaling.</note> translation. To these are added philologists of great reputation, such as **GEJER**, **GLASS**, **MERCER**, **NOLD**, and others. Indeed, this interpretation was ancient and was undoubtedly not unknown in the very times of Christ. I could easily be persuaded that the authors of the **SEPTUAGINT** <note>The "Seventy," the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> used the word *beginning* <note>original Greek: *archēn*</note> adverbially to mean *at the start* or *in the beginning*, in the same way we use the phrase *the beginning* <note>original Greek: *tēn archēn*</note> in this passage. Certainly, the **CHALDEAN PARAPHRAST** <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation and commentary.</note> has: ***in the beginning of his creation*** <note>original Aramaic: *be-resh beriteh*</note>. The **SYRIAC** version has the same: ***in the beginning of his creation***. Add to this the **VULGATE**: *The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways.* <note>Proverbs 8:22. The author is linking the "Beginning" in John's Gospel to the figure of Wisdom in the Old Testament.</note> **NOLD** and **MAJUS** incorrectly count **AQUILA** <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek.</note> among those who think this way. The contrary is clear from the version of the full verse in the *Hexapla* of **MONTFAUCON**, expressed thus: *The Lord possessed me as the summit of his ways, from the beginning of his works.* In this case, the word *from the beginning* <note>original Greek: *archēthen*</note> corresponds not to the word *for a beginning* <note>original Hebrew: *le-reshit*</note>, as they thought, but to *from of old* <note>original Hebrew: *le-qedem*</note>.

### XXX. 
And the Lord had all the more occasion to lead his listeners here by the hand, since it was not entirely hidden from the ancient Jews that the **Messiah**, the Redeemer of the world, was the subject about whom Solomon spoke in the passage cited. We touched upon this briefly in our *Inaugural Oration on Supreme Wisdom*. It is worth adding a passage on this matter cited from the ancient **Kabbalists** <note>Jewish mystics who sought hidden meanings in the Torah.</note> by **RABBI MEIER Ben Gabbai** in the *Service of Holiness* <note>original Hebrew: *Abhod Hakkodesh*</note> and excerpted by **RHENFERD** regarding the style of the *Kabbalistic Apocalypse*. In this text, **Wisdom**, the **Glory of the Lord**, and the **SHECHINAH** <note>The Divine Presence or indwelling of God on earth.</note> are held to be synonyms, and the letter **B** <note>The Hebrew letter *Bet*, the first letter of the Bible.</note> in the word *In the beginning* <note>original Hebrew: *Bereshit*</note> is presented as the place of the house of the **Shechinah**. Add to this what is read concerning the **Shechinah** in the *Palace of the Lord* <note>original Hebrew: *Hechal Adonai*</note>: ***And this property (the SHECHINAH) is the PRINCIPLE, and the start of the entrance to knowing the divine emanations, moving from below to above; and there is no way to reach the Beginning except by acquiring this property, which is perfect Wisdom; and therefore she is called 'In the Beginning.'***

<summary>This page argues that interpreting Christ as "The Beginning" is supported by major Reformation-era Bible translations and ancient versions like the Targum and Vulgate. The author further connects this to Jewish Kabbalistic traditions that identify the Messiah and Divine Wisdom with the "Shechinah" (the Presence of God).</summary>

Neither is there any other way by which a man may advance his *entry* toward the **BEGINNING** [PRINCIPIUM], unless he has already acquired for himself this property, which is the **WISDOM OF SOLOMON**; for this very reason, it is also called the **BEGINNING**. Nor does a passage from **RABBI JOSEPH Ben Gekatilia** <note>Yosef Gikatilla (1248–1305), a Spanish Kabbalist; the work cited is likely the *Sha'are Orah* (Gates of Light).</note> differ much, as cited by **ALLIX** <note>Peter Allix (1641–1717), a French Protestant pastor who wrote on Jewish views of the Trinity.</note> in *Judgment of the Ancient Jewish Church against the Unitarians*, p. 138: *The Jews, having God angry with them, will be by far the most miserable, until the Messiah comes to earth to unite Wisdom with himself. When this happens, the Spirit of grace and mercy will emanate from the first sephira <note>In Kabbalah, the "Sephirot" are the ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite reveals itself. The "first sephira" refers to Keter, the Crown.</note>, and so—what is most important—he will compensate for the injury done to the violated Deity.*

XXXI. Regarding the omission <note>The technical term is *ellipsis*, where a word is left out because it is understood.</note> of the verb **I AM** <note>original Greek: *EIMI*</note>, there is no difficulty, since it is not only very frequent elsewhere, but is also very easily supplied from the preceding question of the Jews. Hence, even those who otherwise disagree with us on other points admit that this must necessarily be inferred. Furthermore, it follows that it must be understood in the present tense, both from the question being answered and from that custom by which Jesus—even when discussing the glory he once possessed—claims it for himself in the present (Compare John 3:13 and below in chapter 8:58). He did this to teach the immutability of his essence and divine glory, even while appearing in the form of a servant in his state of deepest humiliation <note>A reference to "kenosis" or Christ's self-emptying as described in Philippians 2:7.</note>.

XXXII. Concerning **THE WORD THAT** <term>to OTI</term>, certain things must likewise be noted. Whether it should be considered as one particle <note>meaning "because" or "that"</note> or split into two <note>meaning "that which" or "whatever"</note> is not easily settled from the Codices <note>Ancient manuscript books.</note>, since no punctuation exists in the oldest copies. Neither option is entirely out of place regarding the connection of the words. For if you read it as **because** <note>original: *hoti*</note>, the resulting sense will be: *I am the beginning, **because** I am even now speaking to you*, and through my words I prove that I am He, as one who has the power to testify of myself; or rather, I speak this to you with boldness <note>original: *parrhesia*, meaning frankness or plainness of speech</note> from my innermost consciousness; or **and yet** I speak this to you. For the word **that** <term>to hoti</term> sometimes seems to **NOLDIUS** <note>Christian Noldius (1626–1683), author of a famous concordance of Hebrew particles.</note> to be taken for "and yet." This would yield the easiest sense of all, were such usage not so rare. For this reason, we have preferred to separate the small words. But there is no end yet to these minutiae [fine details], which to neglect would be to leave something obscure in the text through lack of care. Namely—

<header>DISSERTATION</header>

The Greek phrase *to ho, ti* <note>original: το ὁ, τι</note> designates: **THAT WHICH**. It remains ambiguous and has been debated whether this very phrase "**that which**" should be separated by a comma or joined to the preceding words. In the former sense, the phrase **the beginning** <note>original Greek: την ἀρχην (tēn archēn)</note> does not form a complete thought on its own, but must be constructed with the following clause, as if to say: *I was already in the beginning that which I now constantly am, and what I now speak to you.* In the latter sense, the phrase **the beginning** constitutes a full statement in this manner: *I am the Beginning, which is the very thing that I currently assert to you regarding myself.* It matters little which of these two constructions is preferred, yet I lean more toward the latter, both because the meaning is straightforward and because it more clearly expresses the reality of the matter. For Jesus could not assert of himself with total emphasis that he was or had been everything "in the beginning" (or regarding the very beginning of all things) that he had testified about himself. For when he had said in verse 12, *I am the light of the world, etc.*, he then presupposed that the world had already been created. He had said *that he was from above, and not of this world* (verse 23), which pertained not to the first start of all things, but to his mission into the world. Other additions in verses 21 and 24 described his future glory. For this reason, I profess a slight disagreement in this part with the illustrious **Majus** <note>Johann Heinrich Majus (1653–1719), a German Lutheran theologian and orientalist.</note>, and I rest in the latter construction, which plainly agrees with the truth of the matter itself. For his claim to *be in the beginning*—in the same sense that the **Word** <note>original Greek: Λογος (Logos)</note> was said to be in the beginning in Chapter 1:1—is clearly included in these words, even if it is not contained **explicitly** <note>original: κατα ῥητον (kata rēton), meaning "according to the literal word."</note>. For he had not only claimed such attributes for himself as belong only to the true and eternal God, but also, when he declares in verse 14 *that he knows whence he came*, and in verse 23 *that he is not of this world*, he had sufficiently and evidently professed his own eternity. For while he asserts that he is from elsewhere than from this world, he distinguishes himself from the world, from all created things, and from the whole human race. Therefore, no measurement of his existence alongside time (which is proper to the world) or any generation from man was to be attributed to him; and no one will doubt that he who claims this for himself is ascribing absolute eternity to himself.

XXXIII. **Musculus** <note>Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563), a Reformed theologian and commentator.</note> notes a singular emphasis in this: that when the Jews asked *who he was*, he responded more with *what* he is than *who* he is. *This,* he says, *is useful and necessary...*
