...necessary knowledge of Christ, to hold firmly what he was appointed by the Father, and how and for whose sake he was sent. In this, it is better to exercise our faith rather than to dispute with curiosity and subtlety about the person of Christ and his **accidents** <term>accidents: in philosophy and theology, these are the qualities or characteristics of a person that are not part of their essential nature.</term>. I do not condemn the diligence of the ancient Church Fathers, by which they were forced to clarify the natures and glory of Christ's person against the triflings of heretics, but I warn that the curiosity of idle men should be avoided. This observation is not to be despised: although Jesus abundantly satisfies the question of the Jews, he nevertheless does not respond according to their frame of mind. For they desired to hear such things about the Lord's person which would either suit their carnal understanding or provide them with an opportunity for **cavilling** <term>cavilling: raising petty, annoying, or trivial objections to avoid the main point.</term>. Jesus, however, chiefly directs his effort toward this: that he might explain to them the reason for his office and the goal of his coming, upon which the hinge of all salvation turns.

XXXIV. Furthermore, we clearly have no need to remove the conjunction **and** <note>original Greek: καὶ (kai)</note> from this place. Nothing is more evident than that it designates **also** <note>original Latin: etiam</note>, just as the Hebrew letter **vav** <note>original Hebrew: ו</note> does. **Noldius** <note>Christian Noldius (1626–1683), a Danish theologian famous for his work on Hebrew particles.</note> teaches that it is sometimes used for **already** <note>original Latin: jam</note>. It can be constructed either with the verb **I speak** <note>original Greek: λαλῶ (lalō)</note> or with the pronoun **to you** <note>original Greek: ὑμῖν (hymin)</note>. In the first construction, it signifies that he continues even now to testify to the same truth which he had manifested to the Fathers through the Prophets. For frequently the Spirit of Christ had predicted through the Prophets in detail that he would be the same one who was in the beginning. The most evident testimony regarding this matter is that of Supreme Wisdom speaking of herself in Proverbs 8:22 and following. And thus also the saying compared to our passage by the celebrated **Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology" and study of biblical languages.</note> in Isaiah 48:6 pertains here. Add also Psalm 102:36. 

But the word **and** <note>original: τὸ καὶ (to kai)</note> can also be joined with the phrase **to you** <note>original: ὑμῖν</note> with significant emphasis. This would designate that Jesus is filled with such **long-suffering** <term>long-suffering: patient endurance and tolerance, especially in the face of provocation.</term> as well as confidence in his cause, that he does not cease, nor fear, to bring forth this truth even before them—even though they followed in the footsteps of their unbelieving fathers, to whom the same thing had been so often instilled, and even though he was attacked by them with deadly hatred because of this free confession. This latter sense is particularly favored by what follows immediately in verse 26: **I have many things to say and to judge concerning you. But he who sent me is true, etc.** <note>original Latin: Multa habeo, de vobis loquenda ac judicanda. Sed qui me misit, verax est &c.</note> as if to say: **I also grant this grace to you. For although you are clearly unworthy of it, since many things against you justly...**

XXXV. Finally, even the word **"I speak"** <note>original Greek: λαλαῶ (lalo)</note> has a fuller sense here, as it does throughout Greek literature. For not only does it often alternate with **"I say"** <note>original Greek: λεγω (lego)</note>—given that in the **Septuagint** <term>Septuagint: the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX.</term> it is very frequently used for the Hebrew word **"to speak"** <note>original Hebrew: דבר (davar)</note>—but sometimes it is even the same as **"to deliver a divine oracle"** <note>original Greek: χρηματιζω (chrematizo)</note>, as is clearly evident from Hebrews 12:25: **"See that you do not refuse him who speaks. For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth..."** <note>original Greek: Βλεπετε μη παραιτησησθε τον λαλουντα. Ει γαρ εκεινοι ουκ εφυγον, τον επι γης παραιτησαμενοι χρηματιζοντα κ. τ. λ.</note>. Compare this with Luke 1:70, Hebrews 1:1, Acts 3:21, 7:38, 7:44, and 28:25, in which places the word is used for divine oracles themselves. Sometimes it is also used to mean **"to testify solemnly."** Thus of Abel it is said: **"though he died, he still speaks"** <note>original Greek: αποθανων ετι λαλειται</note> in Hebrews 11:4. And in John 3:11: **"We speak of what we know, and we testify to what we have seen. And you do not receive our testimony"** <note>original Greek: ο οιδαμεν, λαλουμεν, και ο εωρακαμεν, μαρτυρουμεν. Και την μαρτυριαν ημων ου λαμβανετε.</note>. Both senses fit the present matter most aptly, where Jesus was both offering a public and solemn testimony about his own person before the Jews, and speaking with such authority as was fitting for a witness who was present from heaven—consistent with what he had asserted a little earlier in verse 14: **"Even if I testify about myself, my testimony is firm."**

XXXVI. Since it is abundantly clear from this interpretation of the words how much power they acquire, it must still be demonstrated that they harmonize with the connection and goal of the conversation in which Jesus brought them forth. For it is perceived not obscurely, both from what precedes and what follows, that the Savior labored to establish both his divine authority and, specifically, his eternity. He had established his divine authority to present himself as the source of life from the consciousness of his eternal **coexistence** <term>coexistence: the state of existing at the same time and in the same way as the Father, before the world began.</term> and communion with the Father, even before his birth from Mary, by saying in verse 14: **"Even if I testify about myself, my testimony is firm, because I know where I came from and where I am going."** He was testifying about himself, therefore, because he knew where he came from. Our words contain nothing other than an inversion of this pronouncement, while Jesus declares to them that he is that very thing, as far as the **Principle** <term>Principle: referring back to John 8:25, where Jesus calls himself "the Beginning" or "the Principle" of all things.</term> of things is concerned, which he was already testifying to those who did not know it. In the same way, in verse 23, he again **impressed** <note>catchword: incul- (inculcaverat)</note>

### I.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'L' featuring ornate foliage and a central figure, possibly a saint or biblical character, amidst the scrollwork.</image-desc>

The sojourn of Lazarus among the living—when he reclined at the banquet in Bethany after being *raised* by the Lord (John 12:2) and provided new fuel for the fury of the Jewish priests (verse 10)—has given us the opportunity to meditate seriously on the state of those whom God, at any time after death (which they truly underwent), commanded to return to life.

->### ON THOSE RAISED BY MIRACLE.<-

the number is not strictly defined, though it ought to be joined with those who emerged from their tombs at the resurrection of Jesus (Matthew 27:52–53).

### III.
But we do not hesitate to include *Moses* in this same category, even though his Resuscitation <note>original Latin: *Resuscitatio*</note> is not expressly recorded. First, he was seen in a true bodily form by the disciples on the mountain where Jesus was glorified (Matthew 17:3; Mark 9:4; Luke 9:30). Not only must one never rashly depart from the simplest sense of the words—especially in a historical narrative of actual events—but here one cannot depart from it without a violent distortion of the text. 

For either Moses was seen in a body belonging to someone else, assumed for a time; or that vision was not real but a phantasm; or the body Moses bore was his own, and thus resuscitated. The *first* option multiplies entities beyond necessity and paves the way for new complications. Nor is there any other example of the souls of the righteous, to whom God has granted their own body, appearing in the body of another. Add to this that Moses is joined to Elijah in a single breath. Since Elijah enjoys his own body in the heavens, why should the same not be presumed for Moses? 

The *second* option falls apart, not only because Moses and Elijah were seen while the disciples were fully awake <note>The author argues this was a physical event rather than a dream or "ecstasy" (a trance-like state).</note>, but also from the clear text of Luke: "And behold, two men were talking with him, who were Moses and Elijah, who, appearing in glory..." <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἰδοὺ, ἄνδρες δύο συνελάλουν αὐτῷ, οἵτινες ἦσαν Μωσῆς καὶ Ἠλίας, Οἳ ὀφθέντες ἐν δόξῃ &c.</note> The Evangelist expressly narrates not just what the disciples saw, but what actually happened in reality. Indeed, he describes the quality of the bodies they bore when he says they were seen "in glory," attributing glorified bodies to both, to Moses as much as to Elijah. Therefore, we rightly stand by the *third* option <note>That is, that Moses was physically raised in his own body.</note>.

### IV.
The testimony of Jude in the ninth verse concerning the *Body of Moses* favors the same hypothesis. It is well known that most people hunt for a mystical meaning here. Nor do we contend that the fact mentioned by Jude is devoid of a greater mystery. Nevertheless, while he narrates the fact as an example, the literal truth must be recognized above all. It is excellently defended by Danhawer, Hecht, and Tarnov <term>Tarnov: Johann Tarnow (1586–1629), a Lutheran theologian and biblical commentator.</term> in their commentaries on this passage, and by Witsius in his *Leiden Meditations* <note>original: *Meletemata Leidensia*</note> p. 443 and following. Nor is there a need for us to point out from where the Apostle—who enjoyed divine inspiration and who—received notice of that fact.

...and who <note>Referring to the Apostle Jude, the author of the Epistle of Jude.</note> had brought forth other things of this kind in this same epistle from immediate revelation. Therefore, the *Archangel Michael* truly disputed with the *Devil CONCERNING THE BODY OF MOSES*. But what was the matter of the dispute? Here a new harvest of conjectures arises. The opinion that has snatched the prize from the rest is that which many Church Fathers and more recent Interpreters hold: that the Devil attempted to prevent the hiding of *Moses'* body, which the Son of God had ordained for that purpose, lest the Israelites, or others, abuse the corpse of such a great Prophet for either idolatry or necromancy <note>The practice of communicating with the dead to predict the future.</note>. Regarding this opinion, we consider the greatest disadvantage to be that a miracle such as is supposed here would require greater purposes. Furthermore, since a clearly unusual honor would be considered shown to the *Body of Moses* through such a hiding, idolatry concerning *Moses* might not have been so much diminished by it as given a new pretext.

To me, indeed, no simpler cause for the struggle, nor one more suitable to the litigating parties, appears than that which asserts the Devil attempted to hinder the resuscitation of *Moses*. For the circumstances make it manifest that this whole *dispute* was both *verbal* in form and *legal* <note>original Latin: *de jure*</note> in matter—a right which the Devil claimed for himself. There is no foundation for such a right in the cause just mentioned <note>Referring to the theory about hiding the body to prevent idolatry.</note>, but in our view, the foundation is most evident. 

Since *Moses* seems to have been the first among those who returned to life, it was fitting for Satan to object that this effort of Michael's was contrary not only to the truth of the divine threat—by which man must return to dust—but also to God's justice, which required the price of redemption. And thus an analogy exists between this fight and that other one recorded in Zechariah 3:2. For although *Jude* attributes almost the same words to *Michael* that Zechariah recounts concerning Jehovah <note>referring to the phrase "The Lord rebuke you."</note>, it does not follow (as it seems to many) that the same history is being recorded in both places. The Apostle [Jude] deals with *an actual event*, whereas the Prophet [Zechariah] deals with a *vision*. Meanwhile, in a similar cause, the same Jehovah—who is at the same time the *Angel of the Lord* and the true *Michael*—pours forth similar words. The same Devil who once did not want the *Body of Moses* to be resuscitated, also did not want the *Body of the Jewish Commonwealth* <note>original Latin: *Corpus Reipublicae Judaicae*</note> to mystically revive through the restoration of the Priesthood. For the Israelite Church is called the *Body of Moses* by the same reasoning as the Christian Church is named <insert>the Body of Christ</insert>...

V. We consider that the history of the burial of Moses itself, which others think brings significant prejudice against our opinion, actually works in our favor if the text is properly examined. Thus, indeed, in Deuteronomy 34:6 <note>The original Latin text cites Chapter 24, which is a common early modern printing error for Chapter 34.</note>, the sacred Historian speaks: *And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, opposite Beth-peor: and no man knows his burial place to this day.* <note>original Hebrew: ויקבר אתו בגי בארץ מואב מול בית פעור ולא ידע איש את קבורתו עד היום הזה</note> Junius and Tremellius <note>Authors of a famous 16th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note> translate it: *Who buried him in the valley in the land of the Moabites, in the region of Beth-peor: nor has anyone known his sepulcher even to this day.* The Alexandrian Interpreters <note>The translators of the Septuagint, the Greek version of the Old Testament.</note> differ in two points, whom I would not wish to desert here without cause. This latter view seems to us the more acceptable, since it is not only frequent elsewhere among the Hebrews, but it is clear that it was used precisely regarding this verb from the passage in 2 Kings 21:26, which is the only one outside of ours that exhibits the root *qabar* <note>The Hebrew root for 'to bury'.</note> in the same form: *And he was buried in his sepulcher.* <note>original Hebrew: ויקבר אתו בקברתו</note> Here, for the same reason, the Septuagint has: *And they buried him.* <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἔθαψαν αὐτον</note> From this it appears on how light a foundation the opinion rests—to which a torrent of Interpreters leans—namely, that Moses was buried by Jehovah himself. I deflect from this opinion more easily here because, in this way, that harsher concept perishes, by which something humble beyond all example is attributed to the Lord of heaven and earth—something which could very easily have been performed by human hands. The second point is that they translate *Gai* <note>The Hebrew word for valley.</note> as *Gai* <note>original Greek: Γαὶ</note>, as if to imply it should be understood as a proper name, or at least for emphasis. VI. From the things observed, we conclude that nothing extraordinary occurred in the *burial of Moses*. But it causes all the more amazement that *the sepulcher of Moses has remained unknown unto this day*. For while a certain learned man thinks that the word <term>keburah</term> <note>Hebrew: קבורה (keburah). The author is debating whether this refers to the act of burial or the physical tomb.</note> should be rendered here not as *sepulcher* but as *burial*, suggesting that the manner of Moses's burial was something no one had grasped; although this is not inconsistent with the usage of the word, it nonetheless fits less with the added phrase: *until this day*. Therefore, we consider that the Sacred Historiographer added this section <note>original: "tmema," a Greek term for a segment or clause of a text.</note> to advise that this matter is of deeper inquiry: that Moses was buried in the ordinary manner; that his body was transferred from the mountain where he had died into a well-known valley, and precisely to a place opposite the Temple of Peor <note>original: "Templo Phegoris." This refers to Beth-Peor, a site associated with the pagan god Baal-Peor.</note>; that the lamentation of Israel, staying there for thirty days, followed; and that nonetheless the sepulcher was thereafter completely unknown. What other cause for this stupendous event could be thought of, except that the corpse had been taken away? Most wisely, however, the Secretary of the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Amanuensis Spiritus Sancti." A theological term for the human author of a biblical book, acting as an inspired scribe for God.</note>, whoever he finally was, *expressed something*, yet did not wish to add *everything*. He could not remain completely silent, lest it be twisted to the prejudice of the historical truth regarding the origins of the Israelite people—that the sacred Annals should describe the burial of the Founder and the place of the funeral so accurately, and yet no mortal ever afterward saw the monument itself, though it was located on the borders of Canaan. But nevertheless, led by the Spirit, he had to restrain his pen from saying more, because what precisely happened to the *Body of Moses*—sought so long in vain—was less advisable to reveal to the Israelite people, who were too stubborn <note>original: "craſſiori," literally "thicker" or "more dense," referring to their lack of spiritual perception.</note> and too prone to superstitious veneration of Moses; which is the very thing that **JOSEPHUS** <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), the Romano-Jewish historian.</note> indicates in the passage to be cited immediately.

### ON THOSE RAISED THROUGH A MIRACLE.

<center>Ggg 2</center>

Among Christians, the report is well known. Among the Jews, **JOSEPHUS** in *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book IV, Chapter 8, where he lengthily added various circumstances of the death of Moses from national tradition to the sacred text, describes his departure in section 48 as follows: *“While he was embracing both Eleazar and Joshua, and while he was still conversing with them, a cloud suddenly stood over him, and he disappeared into a certain ravine. But he wrote in the sacred books that he had died, fearing that, on account of the excellence of his virtue, they might dare to say he had departed to the Divine.”* <note>original: "Ἀσπαζομένου δὲ... τολμήσωσιν εἰπεῖν." This Greek passage from Josephus suggests Moses recorded his own death merely to prevent the Israelites from deifying him after his mysterious disappearance.</note> Others have extracted similar accounts from the **TARGUMIM**, the **MIDRASHIM**, from **SOTAH**, from the book **ZOHAR**, and from **SIPHRE** <note>These are foundational works of Jewish rabbinic literature and mysticism.</note>—to say nothing of more recent authors—which are such that I cannot lend my support to **LUDOVICUS CAPPELLUS**, who is of the opinion that this Jewish view was derived from the Gospel history of the Lord’s glorification on the mountain. <note>Cappellus argued that Jewish traditions about Moses' assumption were late copies of the Transfiguration of Jesus in the New Testament.</note>

Nonetheless, it has been proved by **CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA**, **ORIGEN**, **JEROME**, as well as from the entire apocryphal book *The Assumption of Moses* <note>original: "Ἀνάληψεως Μωυσέως" (Analepsis Moyseos)</note>—which has been very well known in the Church since the second century—and others, that Christians early on diverted this same tradition into their own channels. Besides various interpreters of Deuteronomy, this is noted by **GROTIUS** on the Epistle of Jude, verse 9; **EDWARD BERNARD** on the cited passage of Josephus; **ALLATIUS** in his notes on Eustathius' *Hexaemeron*, page 310; **HOTTINGER** in *Oriental Treasures*, page 458; **BARTOLOCCI** in the *Rabbinic Library*, Volume III, page 24 and following; and **FABRICIUS** in the *Codex of the Old Testament Pseudepigrapha*, Volume I, page 839 and following.

For this reason, it is less surprising that this opinion has been accepted by the best of the Christian interpreters. It is established that this was the mind of **JEROME** in his ninth Homily, section 6; **GREGORY OF NYSSA** in his *Life of Moses*; **AMBROSE** in Book I of *Cain and Abel*, chapter 2; and others. However, a suspicion arises from a closer inspection of their words: they may have determined that Moses was not so much *raised from the dead* as he was *renewed* without a preceding natural death, in the manner of Elijah. **ALSTEDIUS** inclines toward this opinion...

# DISSERTATION

**COCCEJUS** and others argue for a symbolic death, though the text is resistant to this view, since no example of the word *death* <note>original Hebrew: מות (*mavet*)</note> occurs with such a meaning, nor does the detailed description of the *burial of Moses* which immediately follows allow for it. For this reason, others more correctly determine, according to the tenor of the text, that Moses was taken up *after a real death had occurred*. This was the opinion of **THEOPHYLACT**, **HEIDEGGER**, **AMYRAUT** (*Salmurian Disputations* Vol. IV), and those who more explicitly defended the resurrection of Moses: **JOHANN BUXTORF** (*Catalog* no. CXXIV) and **JOHANN HULDRICH HEYDEN** in the *Disquisition on the Resuscitation of Moses* debated at Halle in 1723.

VIII. But those who grant that *the body was truly restored to Moses* inquire as to when it was restored. For some contend it happened shortly after the death of Moses, while others say it was before the glorification of Christ on the mountain <note>The Transfiguration, where Moses and Elijah appeared with Jesus.</note> and that it was done specifically for this purpose: so that he might increase the glory of the Lord with his presence along with Elijah. This latter view seems probable to **THEOPHYLACT**, **CALVIN**, **CALOVIUS**, **OLEARIO**, and **WITSIUS** (*Leiden Meditations*, Diss. VI, § 15) and others. They add a reason: *because Christ is the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep* <note>1 Corinthians 15:20. The theological argument here is that if Moses resurrected fully before Christ, Christ would not be the "first" to do so.</note>. However, this reasoning is weak, because on the same grounds, a translation into heavenly glory would have to be denied to bodies that did not properly *die*, but were *changed* <note>transformed without dying</note>, such as those of Enoch and Elijah. 

At least from my own hypothesis, it follows naturally that the corpse had already been taken away by the time the final chapter was added to Deuteronomy. Indeed, I believe this is the only reason why his grave could not be precisely described or shown. Added to this is the analogy of all those who returned to life. For none of them is found whose body was *reduced to dust through putrefaction*. Therefore, quickly and shortly after the burial, and at the most within the thirty-day interval of mourning, the body of Moses disappeared. For I do not think the search for Moses' grave was extended any longer than that. And yet the text declares it was known to no one afterward, which would not have been the case if the corpse had remained in the tomb *for a significant amount of time* and only then disappeared. By what means this removal of the body was accomplished, just like the taking up of Enoch, Scripture covers with a curtain of silence

<meta>This page continues the discussion on individuals miraculously raised from the dead, specifically addressing and refuting skeptical interpretations of the resurrections performed by the prophets Elijah and Elisha, as well as heterodox views on the nature of the soul after death.</meta>

<page-num>423</page-num>

# ON THOSE RAISED BY MIRACLE

<note>original header: DE RESUSCITATIS PER MIRACULUM</note>

**X.** ...he had to lie upon the boy for some time until he first grew warm and finally opened his eyes. This objection also strikes at the similar miracle performed by Elijah. Maimonides <note>The influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher Moses Maimonides.</note> in *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *More Nevoch.*</note>, Part I, chapter 42, will show that some among the Jewish Teachers held this view before him. But those who religiously place their faith in the sacred history will easily despise these claims; the history plainly testifies to the death of the boy in verse 20, and refers to this deed among the **great things** <note>original: הגדולות *magnalia*</note> of Elisha in 2 Kings 8:4. Furthermore, it is clearly ignorant of any natural causes sufficient for such a great effect. This is to say nothing of how the authority of the Apostle is practically trampled underfoot, who in Hebrews 11:35 affirms that these pious mothers **received their dead by resurrection** <note>original: ἐξ ἀναστάσεως *per resurrectionem recepisse*</note>.

**XI.** These same people will consider it no less than a "lead weapon" <note>An idiom for a weak or useless argument.</note> which Moses Cordubensis <note>Likely referring to the Jewish scholar Moses Cordovero.</note>—as noted by Drusius—fashioned against Elijah's miracle from the phrase occurring in 1 Kings 17:17: *and his sickness became so severe* **until no breath remained in him** <note>original: עד אשר לא נותרה בו נשמה *usque dum halitus in eo non remansit*</note>. For he considers this phrase to be equivalent to the one occurring regarding the **fainting** <note>original: λιποθυμίᾳ, a Greek term for swooning or loss of consciousness</note> of Daniel in chapter 10:17: **No breath was left in him** <note>original: נשמה לא נשארה בו *Halitus in eo residuus non erat*</note>. But this commentator <note>original: *verpus*, a derogatory term for a Jew in contemporary Latin polemics</note> is mistaken. For in the history of Elijah, the context reveals the phrase must be understood in its fullest sense, since the mother in verse 18 complains that the boy was taken by death; the Prophet confirms this in verse 19; and in verses 21 and 22, not only does **soul** <note>original: נפש *nephesh*</note> alternate with **breath** <note>original: נשמה *neshamah*</note>, but Elijah also testifies to his own powerlessness in restoring the son to life; and the return of the soul is joined with the boy's revival.

**XII.** Those who suffer from a **physical** concept of the essence of the soul do not sin with an equally profane spirit, but they believe that although some people have been seen after death, their bodies were not raised, but rather their souls alone appeared. Thus a certain anonymous heterodox writer, who favors the **Soul-Sleepers** <note>original: *Psychopannychitis*, referring to the Psychopannychia, the belief that the soul sleeps between death and the final judgment</note>, argues in his *Serious Inquiry into the State, Place, and Life of Souls* (a work expressly refuted by Bebel). This author **distinguishes the soul from the spirit and the body**, and based on this hypothesis, he believes that the soul of Moses appeared just as **incorporeal** <note>original: ἀσώματον</note> as the soul of Samuel. He even contends that the same happened to Christ; he attempts to extract from 1 Peter 3:18 that Christ was made alive according to the soul at that time when he was still dead in respect to his body, and descended to the underworld.

<summary>The author refutes skeptical Jewish and heterodox Christian interpretations of biblical resurrections, arguing that the miracles of Elijah and Elisha involved true physical death and restoration rather than mere fainting or spiritual appearances.</summary>

Related to these matters are the theories which Theophrastus Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous Swiss physician and alchemist.</note>, Helmont <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644), a chemist and physician who followed Paracelsian ideas.</note>, Wallis, and others have philosophized regarding the *Astral Spirit* or the *Sensitive Soul*. They claim that this spirit survives for a time after the coarser body has died and occasionally appears to the living. These concepts are vigorously opposed by Henry More <note>A 17th-century English philosopher and member of the "Cambridge Platonists."</note> in *On the Immortality of the Soul*, Book II, chapters 16 and following. However, More opposes them in such a way that he promotes a no less dissonant opinion held by the Platonists and Kabbalists <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah).</note>—an opinion which Windetus (in *On the Life of the Departed*, Section VII, pages 108–109) and Delrio (in the cited work) prove they held. These thinkers **assign a certain proper vehicle, both aerial and ethereal, to the soul, through which it may hear, see, remember, imagine, and move the body; they believe the soul preserves this vehicle even when separated from the body, so that it retains the power of appearing within it.** Even more absurdly, certain defenders of the doctrines of Purgatory and of Witches—along with Peter of Andlau—have attributed to the soul a natural power of taking on various shapes. Maresius <note>Samuel Maresius (1599–1673), a French Protestant theologian.</note> draws his pen against these ideas in his *System*, locus XIV, § 7. Before him, Johannes Wierus <note>A 16th-century physician and occultist who was among the first to argue against the persecution of witches.</note> in *On the Deceptions of Demons* (Apology, page 835 and following) had refuted Paul Scalichius, who taught the same thing. For us, being persuaded of the immaterial essence of the soul, it will suffice to have merely mentioned such "abortions" of human wit for the purpose of refuting them.

**XIII.** Regarding the *State of those Resurrected*, to those inquiring more closely, it occurs first of all to look into how their souls behaved during the interval of their separation from the body. As for their *natural state*, there is no reason to doubt here that the soul behaved in the same way as any souls separated from their bodies are accustomed to exist. For if they were truly *resurrected*, who could doubt that they were truly *dead*? The distinction brought forward by G. J. Vossius <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a highly influential Dutch classical scholar and theologian.</note> in *On Idolatry*, Book III, chapter 20, is far too subtle. He states that **the soul did not depart from the bodies of either Eutychus or the daughter of Jairus, but only that its bond with the body was dissolved.** Since the soul is "there" where it operates, it follows that when the operation upon the body ceases because the bond is broken, that *relation* by which the soul is said to be *in* the body ceases at the same time. As for the phrase in Matthew 9:24, where Jesus says **"the girl is sleeping, and is not dead,"** that can help that most learned man <note>original: *πολυμαθέστατον* (polymathéstaton) - a Greek term for a person of great and diverse learning.</note> very little. These words of the Lord are subject to various interpretations, among which—to mention this <note>original: *ἐν παρόδῳ*, meaning "in passing" or "as an aside"</note>—the interpretation of Clericus <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a Genevan theologian known for his critical approach to scripture.</note> pleases me least of all. The patrons of *Simulations* and *Equivocations* <note>Philosophical or theological justifications for misleading speech.</note> would pay a high price for such an example, but it results in a singular prejudice against both the highest Holiness—which shrinks from any use of unlawful means—and against inexhaustible Wisdom, which neither needs such aids nor ever performs *miracles* so obscurely that their truth could be justly called into doubt by the eyewitnesses <note>original: *αὐτόπταις*</note> themselves. The common opinion holds that the Savior spoke this way because of the ease of the imminent resurrection. This view is not burdened by any significant difficulty. However, the Savior's words gain a fuller emphasis if we suppose that the soul of the little girl had already actually returned at the Lord’s command, although the body was not yet fully restored until the Lord’s act of raising her occurred. This directly contradicts the hypothesis of Vossius <note>Gerhard Johann Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar and theologian.</note>, because in Luke 8:55 it is said that *her spirit returned* <note>original: *reverſum fuiſſe Spiritum ejus*</note>. This has been abundantly demonstrated by Jean d'Espagne <note>Jean d'Espagne (1591–1659), a French Reformed theologian who served in London.</note> in the Letter found at the end of his small works, page 451 and following.

XVI. Perhaps an opportunity will arise elsewhere, God willing, to examine this hypothesis more thoroughly when we deal generally with the state of souls separated from the body. However, I do not understand what the history of those raised from the dead contributes to asserting this theory. We have already addressed the example of Eutychus <note>A young man in Troas who fell from a window during a sermon by Paul and was raised from the dead (Acts 20).</note>. The meaning assigned to Paul’s words is clearly foreign to his purpose. For those words would have contained nothing to encourage the disciples in that present case if the Apostle had been speaking of the common state of the dead. The phrase used concerning the son of the widow of Zarephath <note>original: *Filius viduæ Sareptanæ* — the boy raised by the prophet Elijah, as recorded in 1 Kings 17.</note>, if explained according to the literal meaning—from which one should not depart without cause—clearly opposes the author's hypothesis. Nor does he gain more from the remaining passages. Thus, he does not argue from the words as they appear, but only by logical consequence, while pretending that the defenders of the contrary opinion multiply miracles unnecessarily. This is a groundless claim, since both sides agree that only *one* miracle is at issue—namely, the Resuscitation—and they only dispute the *manner* of it, which should be understood in a way consistent with the nature of the soul and body. Those who propose a different manner, entirely departing from the essence of things, involve themselves much more in this difficulty. But that is the very point of dispute. Furthermore, the foundation of this entire inquiry is twofold: *first*, that it is considered necessary for a certain and specific place to be assigned to separated souls; and *second*, that a connection with the body is claimed to be necessary for the soul's continued existence. Once these principles are overturned, all the difficulties that might arise regarding this matter vanish.

XIX. For when we proceed to inquire what happened to **those who were raised from the dead**, we encounter a new divergence of opinions. Some believe that either **all**, or at least **some**—though perhaps none of the fewer group—**tasted death again**. Praiseworthy men have vigorously championed the cause of the former: from the Lutherans, Bebel and Johann Friedrich Mayer <note>Johann Friedrich Mayer (1650–1712), a prominent Lutheran polemicist.</note> in his *Dissertation on the condition of those raised from the dead*, which is reviewed in the *New Baltic Literature* of 1702, page 325 and following; from our own side <note>The author identifies with the Reformed/Calvinist tradition.</note>, Comarinus <note>Georg Comarin (1605–1666), a Hungarian Reformed theologian.</note> and Jean d'Espagne <note>Jean d'Espagne (1591–1659), a French Protestant pastor in London; his name is Latinized here as Despagnius.</note> in a rather sharp letter written to a certain anonymous dissenter, found in his *Works*, Volume II, page 436 and following; and Jean Claude <note>Jean Claude (1619–1687), a famous French Protestant controversialist.</note> in *Letter XVI*, in his posthumous works, page 73 and following. **Jean d’Espagne’s** <note>Jean d’Espagne (1591–1659) was a French Protestant theologian who wrote on the "errors" of popular belief.</note> position on this passage is that he assumes we are arguing from the word *all*, which does not even appear in the text. The primary defense of our cause lies in the word **ONCE** <note>original Greek: *ΑΠΑΞ* (hapax)</note>, which we contend must be understood here in its fullest sense. For (1) we do not allow ourselves to be moved from the simplicity of the letter and the natural emphasis of the words without a compelling reason. (2) A limitation of the word **ONCE** is even less permissible because the very core of the comparison rests upon it—the comparison the Apostle Paul establishes between the single natural death of man and the single vicarious death of Christ. For it is not only used in the same way regarding Christ's offering and man's death, but it is also contrasted with the word *often* <note>original Greek: *πολλακις* (pollakis)</note> in verse 25 and *a second time* <note>original Greek: *ἐκ δευτερου* (ek deuterou)</note> in verse 28. If an exception were granted to the law by which *it is appointed for man to die once*, the Roman Catholics would find no small pretext therein for the repetition of the **sacrifice of the Mass** <note>original: *missatici*—referring to the theological debate over whether the Mass is a new sacrifice or a memorial of the one-time sacrifice of Christ.</note>. (3) Immediately following death is the **final judgment**, which has no place as long as another death of the body is still to be expected. Those who object that the Apostle is speaking of the *ordinary* law of nature should at least produce extraordinary examples to the contrary. As for their appeal to **Enoch** and **Elijah**, as well as those to be changed at the coming of the Lord mentioned in 1 Corinthians 15:51, this is **beside the point** <note>original: *extra rhombum*—a Latin idiom meaning "off the mark" or "irrelevant."</note>, since we are not seeking examples of those who were glorified without dying, but rather examples of those who died twice; for we have shown that the Apostle is not dealing with the general law of death, but specifically with the law of *dying once*.

XXI. Furthermore, we seize for our cause the fact that most people admit at least some were exempted from a new death. Regarding **Moses**, Scripture itself forbids any other conclusion, as it testifies that he was seen in glory <note>referring to the Transfiguration of Jesus, where Moses and Elijah appeared.</note>. ...those who carefully consider the matter realize that this is not about a change of *place* <note>original: *loci*</note>, but of *status* <note>original: *status* — referring to a theological state of being rather than a physical location</note>. Did the **rapture of Paul into Paradise** <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 12:2-4, where the Apostle Paul describes being caught up to the "third heaven."</note> or other ecstasies of the Saints require long physical distances? **Bebelius** <note>Balthasar Bebel (1632–1686), a Lutheran theologian known for his works on ecclesiastical history.</note> thinks the greatest difficulty lies in the fact that the souls of these deceased persons were not free from the stain of sin, and therefore could not be received into heaven. But this very point was exactly what was being questioned, since the state of heavenly bliss is, by definition, a state of perfect holiness. He who posits the former state necessarily implies the latter. At the very least, it was not right for him to accuse those souls of sin without manifest evidence, of which he produced none. We will soon demonstrate that we take an entirely different view regarding this circumstance.

XIX. **D’Espagne’s** <note>Jean d’Espagne (1591–1659), a French Protestant theologian.</note> position on this passage is that he assumes we are arguing from the word *all*, which does not even occur in the text. The primary defense of our cause lies in the word *ONCE* <note>original: *ΑΠΑΞ* (hapax) — a Greek term meaning "once and for all."</note>, which we contend must be understood here in its fullest sense. For (1) we do not allow ourselves to be moved from the simplicity of the letter and the natural emphasis of the words without a linguistic cause. (2) A limitation of the word *ONCE* is even less acceptable because it contains the "point of comparison" <term>tertium comparationis</term> <note>The specific point of similarity being compared between two things.</note> which the Apostle establishes between the single natural death of man and the single vicarious death of Christ. For it is not only used in the same way regarding Christ’s offering and man’s death, but it is also contrasted with "often" <note>original: *τῳ πολλακις* (tō pollakis)</note> in verse 25 and "a second time" <note>original: *τῳ ἐκ δευτερου* (tō ek deuterou)</note> in verse 28. If an exception to the law were granted, by which *man must die once*, the Roman Catholics <note>original: *Pontificiis*</note> would find no small pretext for the repetition of the **Mass-sacrifice** <note>original: *sacrificii missatici* — the author is arguing that if humans can die twice, it weakens the argument that Christ only needed to be sacrificed once.</note> from that point. (3) Immediately connected with death is the **final judgment** <note>original: *judicium peremtorium* — a decisive judgment that ends all debate</note>, which has no place as long as another death of the body is still to be expected. Those who object that the Apostle is speaking of the *ordinary* law of nature should at least produce extraordinary examples. Their appeal to **Enoch and Elijah**, as well as those to be changed at the coming of the Lord in 1 Corinthians 15:51, is *beside the point* <note>original: *extra rhombum* — a Latin idiom for being off-target.</note>, because we do not seek examples of *glorified* persons, but of those who *died twice*; for we have shown that the Apostle is not dealing with the *general Law of death*, but specifically with the *Law of dying once*.

If anyone thinks the distinction lies in the fact that the framework of the body had not yet been dissolved into dust through putrefaction, let him consider whether this would provide a reason to doubt whether the Savior Himself underwent a "peremptory" death? Could it not also be argued that some bodies might be preserved uncorrupted for entire generations? Would we not then make it plausible that Moses rose shortly after his burial? Was not the thief on the cross—on the same day he died—translated into Paradise, and therefore "peremptorily" dead and judged?

...death was accomplished through the words of the Lord in Mark 5:36 and Luke 8:50. Therefore, no one ever dared to ask for the resurrection of the dead from the Lord on their own, not even those Mothers mentioned by the Apostle in Hebrews 11:35: *Women received their dead by resurrection.* <note>original Greek: Ἔλαβον γυναῖκες ἐξ ἀναστάσεως τοὺς νεκροὺς αὐτῶν</note> For the fact that they received back their sons does not necessarily imply that they had requested them. Nor does Faith have a place where no divine revelation—through which it is established that such things will happen—has come before. But let us grant that Jesus wished to gratify the *weakness of the flesh* or a desire that was not entirely pure; did he not not only fulfill that desire but even exceed it, if he raised the dead friends to immortality, and if he granted them the ability to enjoy their presence in a far more perfect way for a suitable time in a fully sanctified body?

XXX. Nothing remains but for us to examine the manner of interaction of those raised with the few friends of the Lord who were still present. When this is considered externally, there was a unique case for **Moses**, who was already glorified. The disciples of Christ did not enjoy direct and immediate interaction with him. There seems to have been a greater familiarity between the disciples and the *Saints* <note>Referring to the "many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep" that were raised at Christ's resurrection in Matthew 27:52</note> at the time of the Lord’s resurrection. The greatest degree of interaction was with the others, whom the history of **Lazarus** and the **daughter of Jairus** shows to have reclined at the table, eaten, and performed other actions belonging to this life. But if anyone should ask whether that was done out of *natural necessity* or by *special dispensation* <note>term: dispensative (by special dispensation); meaning an exemption from the usual rules, where they ate not because they needed food to survive, but to prove they were truly present</note>? We profess our ignorance as to which to choose, being all the more uncertain because both modes of interacting with sinners occur in the history of **Christ** both before and after his resurrection. We remain equally hesitant regarding both the *time* and the *manner* of their assumption <note>Their final departure or being "taken up" into heaven</note>. That a different manner could have taken place in these resuscitated persons is clear from the history of **Enoch** and **Elijah**. Regarding the time, however, nothing precise is read in the sacred texts. It is clear from 2 Kings 8:5 that the boy raised by **Elisha** survived for a full seven years. Whether he or anyone else lived longer, who would dare to affirm?

XXXI. It seems, however, that antiquity promises us some assistance here, at least regarding those whom the history of the New Testament mentions among...

# 438

He situates those who were raised. We have already brought forward the testimony of **Quadratus** <note>Quadratus of Athens was a 2nd-century Christian apologist; his work is mostly lost except for fragments preserved by Eusebius.</note> regarding the truth of the resurrection of **Lazarus** and others from **Eusebius's** *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, Chapter 3, in our commentary on John 11:44, page 796. However, whether that same testimony is sufficient to prove that they survived for a long course of years after Christ’s departure is a matter requiring deeper investigation. *The works of our Savior,* he says, *were always visible, because they were true: both regarding those who were freed from diseases and those who rose from the dead; who were not only seen as healed and raised, but were also present afterward,* <note>original Greek: οὐδ' ἐπιδημοῦντος μόνον τοῦ Σωτῆρος, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀπαλλαγέντος, ἦσαν ἐπὶ χρόνον ἱκανόν· ὥς τε καὶ εἰς τοὺς ἡμετέρους χρόνους τινὲς αὐτῶν ἀφίκοντο</note> *not only while the Savior was staying among us, but also after his departure, they survived for a sufficient time; so much so that some of them even reached our own times.* A manifest ambiguity remains here in the words **SOME OF THEM**, because it is not necessary that the phrase be extended to both groups—the healed and the raised. For the truth of Quadratus’s words holds firm even if those "some" whom he mentions are restricted only to those who were healed of diseases. Nor is the testimony of **Epiphanius** <note>A 4th-century bishop known for his "Panarion" (Against Heresies); he is often cited by later scholars but sometimes criticized for his lack of historical rigor.</note> in *Heresies* LXVI, § 34 of greater weight, although he expressly names **Lazarus** and asserts that he lived for thirty years after his resurrection, and thus returned to the Lord by "falling asleep" <note>A common biblical euphemism for death.</note>. Not only is the reliability of Epiphanius—a writer who was credulous <note>Easy to convince or prone to believing rumors.</note> beyond measure—too "new" <note>original Latin: "mustea," literally meaning "like new wine" or unrefined; here suggesting the source is too late to be historically reliable.</note> in this matter, with no ancient author preceding him for over three centuries, but also, when he says that *we found these things in traditions,* he abundantly indicates that he suffers from a lack of suitable authors for such a significant claim.

XXXII. Furthermore, it should not be doubted that the task which the Lord wished to carry out on earth through such extraordinary ways and through such glorious instruments was a grand one. It is true of all [those raised] what is affirmed of Lazarus in John 11:4: these miracles were destined both to demonstrate the glory of God in general, *and specifically* <note>original Greek: ἵνα δοξασθῇ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ</note> *that the Son of God might be glorified.* In the example of that same man in verse 44 of the same chapter, we have abundantly shown how clearly such resurrections established the divinity and truth of the Gospel, and confirmed the hope of the promises of God made to the Church—

# 439

...they have affirmed. However, as certain as this is concerning the return of the pious to this life, so certainly must we conclude regarding the continued presence of those *living again* <note>original Greek: Παλιμβίων (*Palimbion*), referring to those who have returned to life.</note> among mortals, because that presence was intended for the further confirmation of *Faith*, through the testimony which these blessed inhabitants of Heaven then provided to the truth, both *in reality* and undoubtedly also through *words*.

XXXIII. Truly, the fact that these divine envoys stayed for some time among men most effectively demonstrated the truth of the divine omnipotence by which they had been restored to life. For, so that not even the slightest occasion for doubting their true resurrection might arise, they could be *seen, heard, and touched*, not once, but repeatedly, and not by a few, but by many, in close proximity. Thus, the boy himself was shown to the King as a witness of the great works of God performed through Elisha (2 Kings 8:3-5). <note>The original text cites "1 Reg. VIII," following an older naming convention where the books of Kings were numbered differently; this refers to the story of the Shunammite woman's son.</note> Thus, our Savior was able to direct the disciples of John to these witnesses (Matthew 11:5). Thus, no one could doubt that the doctrine brought forth by those through whom God performed such great wonders was truly divine. Not only was the doctrine in general proven, but also the equal truth and wonderful harmony of its individual parts—whether presented in the Old or New Testament, or through the Prophets or the Apostles—was established by this same kind of greatest miracles repeated at intervals. For it did not happen by chance that, besides God and his Son, only the two greatest Prophets after Moses, *Elijah* and *Elisha*, as well as the two chief Apostles, *Peter* and *Paul*, restored life to the dead.

XXXIV. Furthermore, the primary parts of the Gospel doctrine were illustrated and sealed by miracles performed on the deceased. Some were raised more *immediately* <note>Meaning directly by God’s power without a human intermediary.</note>, namely Moses and the Saints who accompanied Christ: the former was seen only *in glory* <note>A reference to the Transfiguration, where Moses appeared in a glorified state.</note>; the latter had only a brief interaction with men. By these examples, the hope of the highest glorification—to be provided immediately by the Lord for both Christ himself and for believers—was confirmed. In the others, who were raised more *mediately* <note>Meaning through the agency of a prophet or apostle acting as a middleman for God's power.</note> and lived among men for some time, there were simultaneously signs of the Church's liberation from various forms of spiritual death, and of its constant preservation, even in the most dismal times...

# 440

...exhibited for preservation. We do not examine every circumstance now, but we have shown how these can be investigated here by using the example of the companions of Christ's resurrection <note>Referring to the "saints who had fallen asleep" who were raised after Christ's resurrection in Matthew 27:52-53.</note> (*Bremen Library, in the place cited*) and *Lazarus* at *John 11:44*. We merely add here that those *Raised from the Dead* were not immediately consumed again by a fresh death; this in a remarkable way sealed both the eternity of heavenly glory, which is never to be interrupted again, and the constant preservation of the Church, which is gifted with the life-giving Spirit, according to *Revelation 20:6*:

> Blessed and Holy is he who has part in the first resurrection. Over these the second death has no power. Compare *Revelation 2:11*.

XXXV. Jean D’Espagne <note>original: "DESPAGNIUS"; a 17th-century French Protestant theologian.</note> doubts whether they also provided testimony to the truth *through the words of the Resurrected*, since nothing is read concerning their preaching. There is certainly a reason for doubt as to whether God wished to employ these witnesses for public testimony. For He wills His word to be set forth not through the dead, but through the living (*Isaiah 8:19, Luke 16:29, 30, 31*). We also gather from the "snatching up" of Paul that these individuals, returning from heaven, had discovered many things in the blessed *Vision of God* that are not to be rashly disclosed to mortals; in that state, he heard "unspeakable words" <note>original Greek: ἄρρητα ῥήματα (*arrhēta rhēmata*)</note> which "it is not lawful for a man to utter" <note>original Greek: ἃ οὐκ ἐξὸν ἀνθρώπῳ λαλῆσαι (*ha ouk exon anthrōpō lalēsai*)</note> (*2 Corinthians 12:4*). This is not because the memory of things perceived by pious souls in the state of separation <note>The state of the soul between death and the final resurrection.</note> perished for them like a dream—as Johann Musäus <note>A prominent Lutheran theologian (1613–1681).</note> argued in his first disputation *On the State of Separated Souls* (§ 47) following Martin Luther and Marc'Antonio de Dominis—but because God, according to His wisdom, deems those who still dwell in the body of death to be less capable of receiving such great mysteries. Indeed, we gather from their history, so far as it has been preserved, that they appeared sparingly before the world, and that their ministry looked not so much toward the conviction of the wicked (who are sent away to *Moses and the Prophets* in the place cited) as toward the confirmation of the pious. Certainly, the world was most unworthy of them (*Hebrews 11:38*). We have also declared at *John 12:2* that all the things told concerning the Apostleship of *Lazarus* are fabulous, as even the Papists <note>A common post-Reformation term for Roman Catholics.</note> themselves confess. Of no better quality are the stories which the Martyrologies <note>Books containing accounts of the lives and deaths of Christian martyrs.</note> fabulate concerning Maternus—the Youth of Nain—who was allegedly sent into the Western regions by Peter along with Eucherius and Valerius as the Apostle of the people of Cologne, Trier, and Tongeren; these stories are marked as spurious <note>original: "obelo confixa," literally "pierced with an obelus," a mark used by ancient critics to denote a passage as doubtful or false.</note>

XXXVI. I would not, however, for that reason, wish to render these precious instruments and pledges of divine Grace on earth entirely idle. If it was granted to the disciples of Jesus to perceive the words of the glorified Saints on the mountain <note>A reference to the Transfiguration, where Moses and Elijah appeared and spoke with Jesus (Matthew 17).</note>, and to be confirmed by those words in the faith of the prophetic doctrine concerning the *departure of the Lord*, why would others, who lived more familiarly and for a longer time among mortals, not have performed the same service for their friends? They were not among their own people as <term>κωφὰ πρόσωπα</term> <note>original Greek: "kopha prosopa"; literally "mute characters" or "silent masks," a term used in theater for actors who have no lines.</note>, but rather, though not *public* heralds, they were *private* forerunners in the praise of God. Just like the heavenly hosts appearing at the birth of the Lord, they stirred up their own people to give *Glory to God in the highest*, and prepared them for that blessed communion in heaven, in which every creature of God *will bring blessing and honor, and glory and power, unto Him who sits upon the throne, and unto the Lamb, forever and ever.*

# ON THE CEDAR.

<margin>1 Kings 4:33.</margin>
...it is often from those more frequent meditations returning that we shall gather what is to be put to the test, beginning now with the **CEDAR**, from which **Solomon**, the wisest of mortals in former times, likewise began his discourse on plants. <note>In 1 Kings 4:33, Solomon is described as speaking about plant life "from the cedar tree that is in Lebanon even unto the hyssop that springeth out of the wall."</note>

II. The proper name for this tree among the Hebrews is *Erez* <note>Hebrew: ארז</note>, which is also accepted in common use in the other Eastern languages by the Samaritans, Syrians, Chaldeans, and Arabs. Hence, the **Seventy** <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament from the 3rd century BCE.</note> constantly translate it as *cedar* <note>Greek: κέδρος (kedros)</note>; with four exceptions, however, which have *cypress* <note>Greek: κυπάρισσος (kyparissos)</note> instead of *Erez*: Job 40:12, Ezekiel 27:5, 31:3, and 31:8. For indeed, other ancient authors also sometimes confused Cedars and Cypresses because of the affinity that Cypresses and Cedars have between them, as will be indicated more extensively in the dissertation on the mystical Cypress. But this is the less surprising since not only do learned men harbor a just suspicion that the so-called version of the Seventy is the work of various men and times, but also the Alexandrian Jews who prepared it suffered from a manifold ignorance both of Jewish affairs and of the Hebrew language itself. A remarkable specimen of this is the great diversity and inconsistency that everywhere dominates among them in translating the names of Biblical plants and trees, which would not have occurred if they had thoroughly understood the proper meaning of those words. Thus, the help that someone might think they could hope for from such an ancient version in this category of subject matter is certainly quite meager. By a similar error, the **Seventy** twice make synonyms of the Cedar out of *Berosh* <note>Hebrew: ברוש; usually translated as cypress or fir</note> and once out of *Teashur* <note>Hebrew: תאשור; often identified as the box-tree</note>, even though they were different trees, albeit related. There are also learned men who hold *Gopher* wood <note>The wood used for Noah's Ark.</note>, and others who hold *Shittim* wood <note>The wood used for the Ark of the Covenant.</note>, to be synonyms for the cedar, but we shall see about these when we examine them more specifically. Following **AVENARIUS**, **MARTINIUS** in his *Lexicon* derives its etymology from the word *razah* <note>Hebrew: רזה</note>, because the tree is slender and tall. Regarding its height, it is indeed certain, but not regarding its slenderness, which is the most specific notion of that root. **URSINUS**, however, thinks it more appropriate to link it to the Chaldean word *Arza*, which designates a "mystery," and from which **BOCHART** derives the Greek word for "secret rites" <note>Greek: Ὄργια (Orgia)</note> in *Canaan* book 1, chapter 18, page 445. But this is more far-fetched. If I may add a new conjecture to the conjec-

### D I S S E R T A T I O
<meta>catchword: prefers.</meta>

...prefers. For although it is possible that the perhaps obsolete root *erez* <note>Hebrew: ארז</note> designated *being robust*, *firm*, or *powerful*. Among the Arabs, at least, the root *arara* <note>Arabic: ארר</note> designates that which is *firm* and *stable*. From this, they also call a robust camel *arar* <note>Arabic: ארר</note>, and they call a *place of refuge* or *asylum* a *maurar* <note>Arabic: מורר</note>. Am I mistaken, or is this the origin of the Greek *Ares* <note>Greek: $A\rho\eta\varsigma$, the god of war</note> and the Latin *Mars*, since it is easily granted that the idol of the nations was named for his strength? Compare the famous Schultens <note>Albert Schultens (1686–1750), a Dutch philologist who often used Arabic to explain difficult Hebrew words</note> in his *Observations on Job*, pages 199 and 200. To this same origin can also be referred *arsen* <note>Greek: $\alpha\rho\sigma\eta\nu$, meaning male or sturdy</note>, and *mas* <note>Latin for male</note> (with the 'r' removed), from which come *mares*, and *aros* <note>Greek: $\alpha\rho o\varsigma$</note>, which designates *utility* or *benefit* in Aeschylus’s *The Suppliants*. From this, Vossius <note>Gerardus Vossius, a 17th-century scholar of classical languages</note> derives the words for *art* <note>Latin: ars</note>, *virtue* <note>Greek: $\alpha\rho\epsilon\tau\eta$ (arete)</note>, and *best* <note>Greek: $\alpha\rho\iota\varsigma o\varsigma$ (aristos)</note>. Add to these *aries* <note>Latin for "ram"</note> and similar words. Thus, Cedars in the East would be called *erezim* <note>Hebrew: ארזים</note> just as among the Latins the oaks are called *robora* <note>Latin: *robur* means both "oak" and "strength"</note>. But perhaps we have already played too much with etymology.

III. According to the Jews, *erez* is the name of a certain entire genus of trees, which encompasses various species under it. The Rabbis count twenty-four species of Cedars in the *Bereshit Rabba* <note>A classic Jewish commentary on Genesis</note>, section XV. The authors of the Talmud, however, count only ten in the tractate *Rosh Hashanah*, folio 23, page 1; similar accounts are read in the tractates *Bava Batra* and *Taanit*. Rabbi Bechai, in his commentary on the Law, folio 173, counts only seven, as noted by Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf, author of a major 17th-century dictionary of Talmudic Hebrew</note> in his *Talmudic Lexicon*, page 212. Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar</note> supports this in his *Treatise on the Red Heifer*, chapter III. But all of these claims are beyond the scope of Scripture, which makes mention of only one species of *erezim*, to which all the biblical descriptions apply.

IV. The Greek word *kedros* <note>Greek: $\kappa\epsilon\delta\rho o\varsigma$</note>, which is also read in the New Testament in John 18:1, is derived in various ways. Those who seek its origin in the East derive it either from *qadar* <note>Hebrew: קדר, meaning to be dark or black</note> or from the Hebrew word *erez* itself. The latter theory pleased Vossius and Thomassinus, whether by inserting a 't', as the former suggests, or by changing the sound to a 't' <note>referring to how *erez* might morph phonetically into *kedros*</note>, as the latter notes. The same author shows that the Hebrew root survives in the Spanish *Al-erze* <note>likely referring to the Spanish word for larch or cedar, *alerce*</note>. It also corresponds to the Polish *Drzewo* <note>Polish for "tree"</note>. The *Etymologicon Magnum* <note>A famous 10th-century Greek dictionary</note> provides various etymologies from Greek writers: *Kedros* is named from *being easily laid down* <note>Greek: $\kappa\epsilon\iota\sigma\theta\alpha\iota \rho\alpha\delta\iota\omega\varsigma$</note>, or from *to prick* <note>Greek: $\kappa\epsilon\nu\tau\omega$</note>, because it is *thorny* <note>Greek: $\kappa\epsilon\nu\tau\rho\omega\delta\eta\varsigma$</note>. Or it is from *edos*, which signifies the *ground* <note>Greek: $\epsilon\delta\alpha\phi o\varsigma$</note>, with an added 'r', making *edros* and then *kedros*. It is also etymologized from *standing firmly* <note>Greek: $\epsilon\delta\rho\alpha\iota\omega\varsigma \iota\sigma\tau\alpha\sigma\theta\alpha\iota$</note>, or from *exuding moisture* <note>Greek: $\iota\delta\rho\omicron\upsilon\nu$</note> *while burning* <note>Greek: $\kappa\alpha\iota\epsilon\sigma\theta\alpha\iota$</note>, or from *keo* <note>Greek: $\kappa\epsilon\omega$, meaning to split or to burn</note>. Martinius <note>Matthias Martinius, a 17th-century lexicographer</note> prefers the last of these.

V. Furthermore, among secular authors, various kinds of Cedars are likewise enumerated. For they mention a "greater" and "lesser" kind, and they describe other diverse species of the latter which do not concern us here; it is very clear from nearly all the passages of Scripture dealing with Cedars that they refer to that most excellent kind of Cedar for which Phoenicia and Lebanon were especially famous. **BELON** <note>Pierre Belon (1517–1564), a French naturalist who traveled extensively in the Levant</note> provides the following description of this kind, and **DODOENS** <note>Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585), a Flemish physician and botanist</note> follows him: *The Great Cedar is an exceedingly large and tall tree, not only surpassing other resin-bearing and cone-bearing trees, but also exceeding all other trees in its vast size: its trunk is frequently so thick that, according to Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note>, the arms of four men cannot encircle it. The bark of the lower part, which extends from the ground to the first branches, is quite rough; the rest, however, is smooth and hairless, visible between the branches. The branches emerge from almost the bottom and not far from the ground all the way to the top, gradually becoming smaller and shorter as they climb higher, so that the tree reflects the shape of a pyramid. These surround the trunk in a circle and are arranged in such an alternating order that one can climb by these to the very summit, as if by a ladder. The leaves are hair-like, like the pine, but shorter and not at all prickly. The cones are much shorter and thicker than those of the fir, composed of soft, not hard, scales; these do not hang downward but stand upright on the branches, to which they adhere so stubbornly that they cannot be pulled away without a piece of the branch. The wood is a very hard material and experiences neither rot nor old age; its core is fragrant and reddish. A resin flows from this tree, similar to that of the fir, fragrant, and of a very sticky substance; indeed, if chewed, it sticks so firmly to the teeth that it can only be removed with difficulty. At first it is more liquid and whitish, but by the heat of the sun it hardens and becomes dry.*

Cedars grow high, yet with branches extended in a circle parallel to the ground, creating nearly a complete solar parasol <note>original: "umbellam solarem"</note> with their circuit. But when snow falls, because it would accumulate in great quantities upon them, and they could not endure such a weight pressing for so long without a certain risk of breaking, nature—the provident mother of all things—granted them a defense: as winter approaches and snow falls, the branches immediately rise upward and, joined together, form a sort of cone, so they may better protect themselves from the coming enemy. For it is a truth of nature itself that any strength, when united, is rendered stronger.

VII. From this description, the testimony of Pliny regarding Cedars can be exceptionally illustrated, and it can be determined to which species of the Cedars mentioned by him those praised in the Holy Scriptures should be referred. Thus he writes in his *Natural History*, Book 13, Chapter 5:

> The Phoenicians have a tree similar to the juniper, and also a smaller Cedar. There are two types of that genus, the Lycian and the Phoenician, differing in their leaves: for that which has a hard, sharp, and prickly leaf is called the Sharp-Cedar <note>original: "Oxycedros"</note>, being branchy and troubled with knots; the other excels in its scent. They bear fruit the size of a myrtle berry, sweet in taste. And there are two types of the larger Cedar: the one that flowers does not bear fruit; the fruit-bearing one does not flower; and in it, the new fruit takes the place of the preceding one. Its seed is similar to the Cypress. Some call it the Cedar-fir <note>original: "Cedrelaten"</note>. From this, a most praised resin is obtained. Its wood is indeed eternal; therefore they even used to make images of the Gods from it. There is a Cedar statue of Apollo Sosianus in a shrine in Rome, brought there from Seleucia <note>The Apollo Sosianus was a famous statue in the Temple of Apollo Medicus, likely brought to Rome by Gaius Sosius in the 1st century BCE</note>.

There is no doubt that the two larger Cedars described by Pliny are of the same species as the Cedar of Lebanon, and that the tree he calls the Cedar-fir—as if to say "Cedar-fir"—is the one referred to by way of emphasis as the "Cedar" in the Holy Scriptures. For those who have treated the Cedars at greater length, one may consult Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a famous Italian physician and botanist</note> on Dioscorides, Book 1, Chapter 89, whose description comes very close to that of Larroque which we just cited; Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585), a Flemish physician and botanist</note>, *Herbal*, Part 4, Book 30, Chapter 17; Johannes Bodaeus à Stapel on Theophrastus’s *History of Plants*, Book 3, pages 197 and following; and J. H. Ursinus, *Biblical Trees* <note>original: "Arbor. Bibl." refers to Ursinus's 1663 work Silva Theologiae Symbolicae</note>, Chapter 19. VIII. The principal quality for which Scripture frequently praises the Cedar is its height and loftiness, as seen in Isaiah 2:13, 37:24, Ezekiel 17:22–23, and Amos 2:9. To this theme is referred the fact that the Cedar and the <term>Hyssop</term><note>A small, bushy plant often contrasted with the mighty cedar to represent the scale of creation from the largest to the smallest.</note> appear to be placed in opposition, as in 1 Kings 4:33, where Solomon is said to have spoken of plants, from the Cedar that is in Lebanon even unto the hyssop *that grows out of the wall*. 

Juan de Pineda, in his work *On the Deeds of Solomon* (Book III, Chapter 12), observes that the Cedar and Hyssop cannot be considered the two absolute extremes in terms of physical size among all plants. Just as the hyssop does not seem to be the smallest of herbs, so the Cedar is not the tallest of all trees. Indeed, Theophrastus suggests that the Juniper grows taller than the Cedar, and writers describing the New World mention other trees so thick that eight men cannot encircle them. From this, Pineda infers that Solomon’s comparison was not based on a single physical trait like size, but on many factors, as the Cedar can be regarded not only as the largest, but also as the most precious and useful. 

However, there is no need for such roundabout arguments, since the matter here undoubtedly concerns those specific trees of which Solomon spoke. The text does not say he spoke of *all* plants in existence. Among those he discussed, the Cedar was the greatest and the Hyssop the smallest. Why Solomon restricted himself to these trees and the types in between them remains a matter of debate. Most scholars believe he intended to treat precisely those plants that are most prominent in medicine and human utility. Others—following Josephus—feel that Solomon used the trees as an occasion for allegories; these scholars, along with Sanchez <note>Caspar Sanchez (1554–1628), a Jesuit commentator known as Sanctius.</note>, seek the reason in the ritual law of the Israelites, which, as we shall see, joined the Cedar and the Hyssop together <note>Cedar and hyssop were used together in the ritual cleansing of lepers and houses in Leviticus 14.</note>. 

Furthermore, the height of the Cedar gave Pliny an occasion, in the passage previously cited, to use the name *Cedrelates* <note>original: "Cedrelatem"; likely a Greek-derived term meaning 'fir-cedar' or 'tall cedar'</note> for the larger Cedar that excels in fruit. Compare the same author in Book 24, Chapter 5. Although Pliny seems to have erred in the name—perhaps reading or hearing the term *kedrelaton* <note>original: "κεδρελατον"</note> in the Greek source he was copying instead of *kedrelaion* <note>original: "κεδρελαιον"; cedar oil</note>, as Salmasius <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), a renowned classical scholar.</note> argues in his *Hylas Iatricus*, Chapter 103—he was by no means wrong about the physical reality of the tree. Thus, Dioscorides says in Book I, Chapter 105: *The Cedar is a great tree* <note>original Greek: "Κεδρος δενδρον ἐστι μεγα"</note>. Theophrastus, in his *History of Plants*, Book V, Chapter 9, writes: *For where the lotus grows, there also the cedar becomes wonderful, just as it is in the region of Syria.* <note>original Greek: "Ενθα μεν γαρ λωτος, ἐνθα δε κεδρος γινεται θαυμαση, καθαπερ και περι Συριαν."</note>

To note this in passing: a considerable difficulty arises in this testimony because **Maundrell** differs so much in defining the thickness of the Cedar from **La Roque** <note>Jean de La Roque (1661–1745), a French traveler who also visited Lebanon and described its cedars.</note>, whom we heard from in Section VI. Thus, one of two things must be concluded: either they came across Cedars planted in different locations, or one of the two erred in memory or with the pen. The former seems more likely, because **Maundrell's** Cedars flourish on the highest peak of Lebanon covered in snow, whereas **La Roque** saw his on a certain slope on the side of the mountain. Hence, the latter also seems to have been too quick to believe those asserting that no Cedars survive anywhere else on the whole mountain of Lebanon except those he visited. ### DISSERTATION

**Diodorus Siculus** <note>A 1st-century BC Greek historian known for his monumental universal history.</note> in Book II concerning *Arabia* writes: "In the mountains there are not only silver fir and pine, but also cedar and juniper, etc." <note>original Greek: "Ἐν δὲ τοῖς ὄρεσιν οὐ μόνον ἐλάτη καὶ πεύκη ἀλλὰ καὶ κέδρος καὶ ἄρκευθος."</note> Regarding *Cyprus*, we shall hear from **Pliny** below. **Meursius** <note>Johannes Meursius (1579–1639), a Dutch classical scholar who wrote extensively on Greek antiquities.</note>, in his work *Creta*, Book II, chapter 8, proves that cedars are specifically attributed to *Crete*. I suspect, however, that in some of these locations, the Cypress has been confused with the Cedar.

XII. Furthermore, it is suggested in Numbers 24:6 that cedars love water; this should especially be understood as referring to those cedars which, through human cultivation, were planted in gardens along riverbanks to provide pleasant shade. The valley of *Kidron* might be mentioned here, if it indeed took its name from cedars—a point we note as not improbable in our commentary on John 18:1, comparing it with what we will soon teach regarding the use of cedars on the Mount of *Olives*. The mountains themselves are reservoirs of water, which is particularly true of Lebanon, the parent of many rivers. Hence it is considered like a miracle when, in Isaiah 41:19, God promises that He will provide *cedars in the desert*—"into the waterless land" <note>original Greek: "εἰς τὴν ἄνυδρον γῆν"</note> as the **Septuagint** <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> puts it. And in Ezekiel 31:10, it is said of the Cedar of Lebanon that the waters nourished it.

We gather that **Solomon**, at least in his pleasure gardens and groves which he created (Ecclesiastes 2:9), also took account of cedars. This is because he not only alluded to them in Song of Songs 5:14 and spoke of them in 1 Kings 4:33, but it is also proclaimed of him that he *made cedars as plentiful as sycamores in the lowlands* <note>Referring to 1 Kings 10:27; the "lowlands" or Shephelah was a region in Israel where sycamore-figs were abundant.</note> because of their great number. To this same context I would refer the *House of the Forest of Lebanon* (1 Kings 7:2, 10:17; 2 Chronicles 9:16); that is, a "house of cooling" according to the **Chaldean Paraphrase** <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation and expansion of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. This was built not on Mount Lebanon itself, but in the vicinity of Jerusalem, to enjoy the pleasant shade during the summer season under trees from Lebanon (among which the cedars are preeminent) planted there, as I intend to show in another place when discussing sacred groves. Compare 2 Chronicles 9:27 and Isaiah 9:10. 

We have little doubt that this was achieved through planting and cultivation, because the method of propagating cedars by means of shoots plucked from the tops of branches is explicitly described in Ezekiel 17:4, and even more clearly in verse 22: *“Plucking a tender twig from the top of its young branches, I will plant it upon a high and lofty mountain.”* Yet, this seems to depart from the natural behavior of the cedar, and is thus "mysterious" <note>original Greek: "μυστηριῶδες" — implying a symbolic or allegorical meaning rather than just a botanical one.</note>.
