->### ON THE CEDAR<-

it is granted that the branch was plucked from the summit. For if the crown is damaged or removed, the Cedar dies. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a 1st-century Roman naturalist</note> in Book XVII, chapter 24, writes: *The same logic applies to the removal of the crown in the cypress, the pine, and the Cedar; for these perish if the summit is removed or scorched by fire.* **Theophrastus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> noted this same fact before Pliny in his *History of Plants*, Book IV, chapter 19, as did **Jerome** in the location previously cited.

XIII. The Holy Scriptures record various uses for Cedars, whether natural or those sought through human craft. To the former belongs the shade which they provide for birds. Hence, Ezekiel 17:23 says: *All birds of every wing shall dwell under it; in the shadow of its branches shall they dwell.* Specifically, they place their nests there, according to Jeremiah 22:23 and Psalm 104:17. We shall shortly provide an example concerning doves.

XIV. *Among the uses sought through craft, the Sacred uses stand out.* First, we refer here to the fact that cedar wood was employed to make the <term>aspergillum</term> <note>A brush or branch used for sprinkling holy water in ritual purifications</note> used in the purification not only of lepers in Leviticus 14:6, but also of houses infected with leprosy in verses 51 and 52 of the same chapter. Those who seek natural causes for this ritual observe that cedar wood possessed a unique healing power to expel the most foul contagious diseases, among which <term>Elephantiasis</term> <note>A severe skin disease often grouped with leprosy in antiquity</note> (a species of leprosy) must be included. Indeed, **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and pharmacologist</note> in Book I, chapter 105, testifies that it *also benefits those suffering from elephantiasis* <note>original Greek: "ὠφελεῖ καὶ ἐλεφαντιῶντας"</note>. **Pliny** notes the same in Book XXIV, chapter 5. **Quintus Serenus** <note>A Roman medical writer</note> writes in chapter XI concerning the repelling of elephantiasis:
> Against this, there shall be juice from the bark of the Cedar.
However, I would be reluctant to rely on this reasoning alone. For a dry stick made of cedar wood used for sprinkling a leper has nothing in common with cedar juice, just as leprosy itself has nothing in common with elephantiasis.

XV. Cedar wood was required not only for the sprinkler but also for the preparation of the <term>lustral water</term> <note>Water used for ritual cleansing</note> itself, which was to be burned according to the precept in Numbers 19:6. The Rabbis indicate that a considerable amount of that wood was used; they state that cedar wood was especially required for building the pyre of the <term>Red Heifer</term> <note>A sacrificial cow whose ashes were used for ritual purification</note>. Thus **Maimonides** <note>A preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and scholar</note> writes concerning the Red Heifer in chapter III: *The commandment was that there be arranged there cedars, oaks, firs, and smooth fig trees, and they would make the wood-pile like a tower.* <note>original Hebrew: "מצות מסודרים היו שם ארזים ואלונים וברושים ועצי תאנה חלקה ועושין מערכה כמין מגדל"</note>

> *...and in her proud halls*
> *She burns scented Cedar for light through the night.*

From a confusion of these passages, learned men derive the error of **PLINY**, who in his *Natural History*, Book XIII, chapter 16, cites as from **HOMER** concerning Circe that which had been said of Calypso. For this reason, Cedars were also used for funeral pyres, as mentioned in Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book XI, line 137. Aelian also notes this in his *Various History*, Book V, chapter 6. However, Bartenora <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro, a 15th-century Italian rabbi and commentator on the Mishnah</note> and Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides, the influential medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> believe that a certain specific type of Cedar—well known to the Arabs at that time and called *al-sāfan* <note>original: אלסאפן</note>—was used for the burning of the red heifer. We believe this goes against the literal word of the Law, which simply commanded the use of Cedar. We also do not believe that Pine has a place here, as Zeller suggests, since it was a tree of an entirely different kind. Thus, Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle, often called the "father of botany"</note> clearly distinguishes between Cedar and Pine in Book V, chapter 8: *Those who inhabit Syria and Phoenicia use Cedar (for ships), for they lack Pine.* <note>original Greek: Οἱ δὲ κατὰ Συριαν καὶ Φοινικην, ἐκ κεδρου, σπανιζουσι γαρ πευκης.</note> Pliny noted in Book XIII, chapter 1, that through the "perverse imitation" <term>cacozelia</term> <note>A term used by Christian scholars to describe how pagan rituals were thought to be distorted imitations of biblical truths, often attributed to the influence of the devil</note> of Satan, Cedar wood was also burned in the sacred rites of the pagan nations. He wrote that in the times of the Trojan War, it was the custom that they did not worship the Gods with Frankincense or costum <note>An aromatic root used in ancient perfumes</note>: *They knew only the thick smell, rather than a fragrance, of Cedar and citrus wood—their own local shrubs—enveloped in the smoke of their sacrifices.*

XVI. Furthermore, a huge quantity of Cedar was used for the construction of the Temple. Josephus confirms the same regarding the first Temple in *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book VIII, chapter 2, and regarding the second Temple in Book XI, chapter 4. Specifically, the paneled ceilings, the roof, and the walls of the Temple consisted of Cedar (1 Kings 6:9, 10, 15), as did the porticoes (1 Kings 7:11, 12). As much as we have learned from the monuments of antiquity, they crafted the statues of the Gods from these woods: ebony, cypress, cedar, oak, smilax <note>a type of woody vine</note>, and lotus. ### XVIII.
Furthermore, cedar was extensively used for the palaces of Kings and Princes. Hence the Royal Palace of David is named the **House of Cedars** <margin>House of Cedars <note>Hebrew: *Beit Arazim*</note></margin> in 2 Samuel 7:2 and 1 Chronicles 18:1. Cedar paneling of palaces is mentioned in Jeremiah 22:14. Thresholds covered with cedar boards occur in Zephaniah 2:14. But it is also taught that the **beams** <note>Hebrew: *qorot*</note> of houses were made of cedar in Song of Solomon 1:17. Thus it was customary in the East. Homer <note>the legendary Greek poet</note> says in the *Iliad*, Book 24, line 191:
> *He himself descended into the fragrant chamber, cedar-built and high-roofed.* <note>original Greek: Αυτος δ' ες θαλαμον κατεβησετο κηωεντα Κεδρινον, υψοροφον</note>
The Scholiast <note>an ancient commentator</note> on the cited passage says: *(Cedar-built, high-roofed)* Made from cedar woods, having a high roof. See also Euripides in *Orestes*, Act V. Polybius, in his *Histories*, Book X, chapter 24, says regarding the royal palace in Ecbatana:
> *For since all the woodwork was of cedar and cypress, none of it was left bare: instead, the beams, the coffered ceilings, and the columns in the porticos and peristyles <note>courtyards surrounded by columns</note> were encased in plates, some of silver and others of gold.* <note>original Greek: Ουσης γαρ της ξυλιας απασης κεδρινης και κυπαριστινης ουδεμιαν αυτων γεγυμνωσθαι συνέβαινεν... κ.τ.λ.</note>
Virgil, in the passage cited above, calls cedar "useful for houses." -># DISSERTATION #<-

For the Athenians, there is also the theater built for Regilla, with a roof constructed of cedar—a wood that is also highly valued for sculpture. <note>original Greek: Ἀθηναίοις καὶ τὸ ἐπὶ Ῥηγίλλῃ θέατρον...; this refers to the Odeon of Herodes Atticus at the base of the Acropolis.</note> Furthermore, Herodes <note>Herodes Atticus, a wealthy Greek aristocrat and Roman senator</note> built this theater for the Athenians in memory of his wife, Regilla, with cedar-paneled ceilings; the material was elegantly worked even for statuary.

### XIX.
It is also well established that various vessels and precious furniture were crafted from cedar. Treasures enclosed in cedar chests or boxes by Tyrian merchants are mentioned in the version of **JUNIUS** <note>Franciszek Junis, a 16th-century theologian</note> at Ezekiel 27:24. That cedar chests were not unknown to the ancients is clear from these lines of **EURIPIDES** <note>a famous Greek tragedian</note> in *Alcestis*, line 158:

> Taking garments from the cedar chambers,
> She adorned herself in fitting splendor.
> <note>original Greek: Ἐκ δ᾽ ἑλοῦσα κεδρίνων δόμων...</note>

By "cedar chambers," the poet means chests or boxes. However, nothing of the sort appears in the standard Hebrew text, because the words "And cedars in your marketplace" <note>original Hebrew: וארזים במכלתך</note> can be separated from the preceding words, as if presenting a distinct kind of merchandise. For this reason, **JEROME** <note>the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note> rendered these words as: *They also had cedars in your trading.* Certainly, cedar wood was of the highest value, as it was employed for any works requiring elegance and long-term preservation. Thus, images of ancestors were fashioned from cedar, according to **VIRGIL** in the *Aeneid*, Book VII, line 178. Tombs were also constructed from cedar, as noted by **EURIPIDES** in *Alcestis* (line 365) and *The Trojan Women* (line 1141), as well as by **PLINY** <note>a Roman naturalist</note> in Book XXIV, chapter 5. Compare also **KIRCHMANN** in *On Roman Funerals*, Book I, chapter 8. Ornaments for doors made of cedar are mentioned in the Song of Solomon 8:9, and **SAGITTARIUS** <note>Caspar Sagittarius, a 17th-century historian</note> in *On Ancient Doors*, chapter XXIII, concludes that cedar was often used for the doors themselves. Although he does not cite a specific author, he bases this on the fact that cedar not only resists rot but also does not naturally warp or crack, according to **PLINY**, Book XVI, chapter 40.

### XX.
In the construction of ships, and specifically for the mast, cedar was used, as indicated in Ezekiel 27:5: *They took cedar from Lebanon to make a mast for you.* <note>original Hebrew: ארז מלבנון לקחו לעשות תרן עליך</note> However, there seems to be a counter-argument: cedar begins to divide into many branches not far from the root, which makes it less suitable for a mast, as judged by **MEIBOMIUS** <note>Marcus Meibom, a scholar of ancient music and technology</note> in *On the Construction of Triremes* <note>ancient warships with three banks of oars</note> in the *Treasury of Roman Antiquities*, Volume XII, page 647. <meta>This page continues the discussion of cedar wood’s practical applications, specifically focusing on its use in maritime engineering and its legendary durability in ancient architecture.</meta>

-># ON THE CEDAR #<-

The description of Lebanon, which we provided above, remains relevant. However, it can be observed from those meager remains <note>referring to the surviving cedar groves in Lebanon during the author's time</note> that it cannot be definitively concluded that no Cedars ever enjoyed such a height that a mast could be fashioned from them. According to the testimony of **PLINY** (Book XVI, 40), it is recorded that in Cyprus, a cedar was cut down for the eleven-banked galley <note>A massive warship with eleven rows of oarsmen</note> of **DEMETRIUS** <note>Demetrius Poliorcetes, a Hellenistic king and famous naval innovator</note> that was one hundred and thirty feet long, and of such thickness that it required the embrace of three men to span it. But the Prophet <note>Ezekiel 27:5, discussing the maritime power of Tyre</note> also indicates something that was less obvious and a sign of singular luxury. **ABARBANEL** <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish commentator and statesman</note> notes that Cedar from Lebanon was the most suitable material for a ship's mast, and for this reason, the Prophet deliberately placed "Cedar" in the singular number, while placing "firs" in the plural. We admit the latter grammatical point, though we do not think the former—that it was common for masts—was so universal. Meanwhile, although the trunk of a Cedar was ordinarily not tall enough, or perhaps too thick to be easily used for masts, it is abundantly clear from what was observed in sections 6 and 9 that its branches could fulfill this use.

It is certain, however, that Cedar was employed for other parts of ships. Thus **DIODORUS SICULUS** (Book I, chapter 57) recorded of Sesostris <note>a legendary king of Egypt</note>: *Furthermore, he constructed a cedar vessel 280 cubits <note>approximately 420 feet</note> long, covered in gold on the outside and silver on the inside. This he dedicated to the God whom the Thebans worshiped most religiously.* Add also the passage from Book XIX, 58 cited above. **PLINY** (Book XVI, 40) writes: *But in Egypt and Syria, kings are said to have used Cedar for their fleets because of the lack of fir.* Compare **THEOPHRASTUS** (IV, 6) in the passage cited above, as well as Book V, chapter 8: *Fir, pine, and Cedar, to speak simply, are most suitable for shipbuilding.* <note>original Greek: Ἐλάτη μὲν καὶ πεύκη καὶ κέδρος, ὡς ἁπλῶς εἰπεῖν, ναυπηγήσιμα.</note> So too **ATHENAEUS** (Book V, chapter 9) tells of the prodigious vessel of [Ptolemy] Philopator, which was called the *Thalamegus* <note>literally "the room-carrier," a massive floating palace</note>: *The greatest part of it consisted of split Cedar and Milesian cypress.* <note>original Greek: Κατεσκευάσθη δ' αὐτοῦ τὰ μὲν πλεῖστα ἀπὸ κέδρου σχιστῆς καὶ κυπαρίσσου Μιλησίας.</note>

XXIII. The analogy between the Cedar in general and the Messiah is multifaceted, concerning both its nature and its use. Regarding its nature, the Messiah King is compared to an *excellent and distinguished Cedar* above others for several reasons: I. Because of the invincible strength of his Kingdom: "For He is the eternal King" (Jeremiah 10:10). V. Because of the most pleasant fragrance of the gifts of the Holy Spirit with which he is filled and which he shares with others (Isaiah 11:2). VI. Mount Lebanon <note>The traditional home of the finest cedars</note> is sometimes a symbol in the Holy Scriptures for the Temple and the Jewish State, and sometimes for the Roman Empire. Both are under the Messiah's dominion. At the very least, the mountains and hills of the world are to be subjected to his Kingdom (Song of Solomon 2:8; Isaiah 2:2, 13, 14; 5:12).

For, if the Scripture wished to make a comparison with a Palm, why is a Cedar also added? Or if it wished to make a comparison with a Cedar, why is the Palm added? Clearly, if the comparison had been made with the Cedar alone, excluding the Palm, I might have thought: just as the Cedar produces no fruit, so too the pious man produces no fruit; therefore, to prevent this thought, the mention of the Palm is also introduced. Furthermore, because of his firmness and his security in good things, he is likened to the Cedar in Lebanon. For the Cedar is rot-resistant and very dense, while the Palm is always flourishing and has a "heart" that turns upward. Moreover, the righteous man, like the Cedar, has many branches, since many people find salvation through him.*

It is particularly worthy of note that the symbol of the **Cedars of Lebanon** applies most strongly to the faithful, not only from among the Jews but also from the Gentiles, and specifically from the Roman world. *Even if Lebanon, because of the fruitlessness of its Cedars, stands as a mark and symbol of the Nations <note>In a biblical context, "the Nations" or "the Gentiles" refers to non-Jewish people.</note>, nevertheless, the justice of God is multiplied among the Nations as well. For though many Prophets, many Patriarchs, and other God-bearing and righteous men arose from Israel, the number of those has been surpassed by the Martyrs who came forth from the Nations, in whom the justice of God has advanced into a great multitude.* <note>original: "Ἐι και των ἐθνων ὁ Λιβανος δια την ἀκαρπιαν των κεδρων χαρακτηρ ὑπαρχει και συμβολον..." / "Etsi Libanus propter Cedrorum infructuositatem, Gentium nota symbolumque existit..." This passage explains that while Cedars do not bear edible fruit (unlike the Palm), they represent the vast "planting" of the Gentile church and its many martyrs.</note>

The fact that Solomon specifically held these Cedars in high value, planted them, and employed them for various uses—chiefly sacred ones—likewise indicates the care which the **celestial Solomon** <note>A common metaphor for Jesus Christ.</note> exercises toward the Church gathered from the nations. **D'OUTREIN** <note>Johannes d'Outrein (1662–1722), a Dutch theologian known for his work on biblical symbols.</note> treated this symbol more extensively in the vernacular in his *Sacred Emblems*, Volume I, pages 190 and following.

XXIX. Thirdly, the Cedar depicts the **MAGISTRATES** and **PRICES** among the **PEOPLE OF GOD**, such as the Davidic Kingdom in *Ezekiel 17:2 and following*, and the King of Israel in *2 Kings 14:9* and *2 Chronicles 25:18*. We understand these same Kings of the people of God through the phrase **"Cedars of God"** in *Psalm 80:11*. This is not because this phrase generally indicates the tallest or most excellent Cedars—for we do not recognize such a use, or rather abuse, of the name <term>Elohim</term> <note>original: אלהים. In Hebrew, adding the name of God to a noun often creates a superlative, meaning "mighty" or "greatest." The author here argues for a more literal theological connection rather than just a linguistic habit.</note> in the sacred texts—but because of the special relationship these Kings had to the God of Israel. Since they were exalted by Him, they acted in His place, sailed toward His honor, and finally served as a prelude to His spiritual Kingdom.

Balaam also understood the succession of these illustrious Kings through the image of Cedars in *Numbers 24:6*. For he adds in the following verse: *His King shall rise above Agag, and his Kingdom shall be exalted.* Furthermore, the Nobles of Judah are named in this way in *2 Kings 19:23, Zechariah 11:1–2, Jeremiah 22:7,* and *Ezekiel 31:15.* Hence Simeon and his brothers are compared to Cedars in *Sirach 50:13.* The celebrated **VITRINGA** <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a leading expert in the interpretation of the Prophets.</note> notes at great length that *Isaiah 10:33* refers to the same concept. From here, this emblem passed to the more illustrious Princes in the Church of the New Testament in *Isaiah 41:19.*

# ### DISSERTATION

*“They shall set in the desert the Cedar, the most choice Cedar.”* <note>A reference to Isaiah 41:19, where God promises to plant trees in the wilderness to provide shade and beauty.</note> Add to this Psalm 148:9. Nor do I interpret Psalm 104:16 differently: *“The trees of the Lord are satisfied, the Cedars of Lebanon which he planted.”* By using the name **Jehovah** <note>The personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible, often associated with his faithfulness to his promises.</note> in this emphasis, the text says He planted them—not because that phrase indicates nothing more than that they grow spontaneously (as the famous **Le Clerc** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a prominent theologian and biblical critic who often favored naturalistic explanations for biblical phenomena.</note> explains in his commentary on the Book of Numbers), but because, as Isaiah speaks in the preceding passage, *God placed them*. That is to say, through His grace, He raised up **Princes** in the world to provide a defense for His people. In this very benefit, He demonstrated the power of the name Jehovah: His faithfulness, His truth, and His all-sufficiency. Among the Arabs as well, the word <term>ארז</term> <note>Erez: the Hebrew and Arabic word for Cedar.</note> metaphorically designates a "pillar of the people." 

Under this symbol, those Princes deserve to be displayed in whom the same virtues shine forth for which individual believers are compared to Cedars; yet in these leaders, those virtues radiate even more splendidly because they have been elevated to a higher dignity above others. In a full sense, they are the **Anointed of the Lord**, whose beauty, placed in a higher position, is an object of admiration and veneration to many, and whose "good odor" <note>An allusion to the fragrant resin of the cedar, symbolizing a leader's good reputation and influence.</note> spreads further to refresh the people of Jehovah. It belongs to them specifically to protect others with their shadow, and to provide the beams and roofs for the building of the Church. In this way, they express the royal virtues of Christ not only through general virtues, but specifically in the governance of the people of God. The special mention of the **Cedars of Lebanon** bids us think once again of the Princes of the Roman Empire who were to be brought to the faith of Christ.

XXX. XXXI. Fourthly, the **LAWS** of the Kingdom of the Messiah, contained within the word of truth, are compared to Cedar tablets in Song of Songs 8:9: *If she is a door, we will fashion upon her a tablet of Cedar.* <note>original Hebrew: אם היא דלת נצור עליה לוח ארז</note> We believe this should be translated as: *“If she is a door, we will fashion upon her a Cedar tablet.”* For the word <term>צור</term> (*tsur*) here signifies not so much "to fortify/enclose," as most interpreters suggest, but "to form" or "to fashion." It borrows this meaning from the root <term>יצר</term> (*yatsar*), in the same way as seen in 1 Kings 7:15: *And he fashioned two columns.* <note>original Hebrew: ויצר את שני העמודים</note> Indeed, the word *upon her* <note>original Hebrew: עליה (*aleha*)</note> indicates an ornament placed above a door, as does the analogy with the ornament of the *wall* described immediately before. Such an ornament is best represented by an elegant tablet placed above a door, bearing an inscription of either a **name** or a **Law**. Both were customary in the temples of the ancients. 

The former is evident from **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote a famous biography of Pythagoras.</note> in Book I of the *Life of Pythagoras*, Chapter 3: *“He built a temple to Apollo, inscribing it with the name PYTHIAN.”* <note>original Greek: ἱερον ἐδείματο Ἀπολλωνι, ΠΥΘΙΟΥ ἐπιγραψας</note> The latter is seen in the inscription of the Delphic Temple, *“Know Thyself,”* <note>original Greek: γνωθι σεαυτον (*gnothi seauton*)</note> concerning which **Plato** writes in his *Charmides*, using the version by **Marsilio Ficino** <note>The influential Italian scholar (1433–1499) who first translated Plato's complete works into Latin.</note>: *“For I consider this very thing to be temperance: to know oneself. I agree with him who inscribed this precept on the Temple of Apollo itself. In this way, God addresses men entering the Temple with a singular sentiment, greeting us differently than men do, as he intended, in my judgment, who wrote the inscription, etc.”* 

In the following sections, he narrates that others added different precepts, such as *“Nothing in excess,”* and similar sayings. ->centered text<- I.

When the prophets, moved by God, revealed the order of future events to the Jewish people, they were sometimes commanded to join the use of the voice with actions that would serve as symbols of things to be done. Jeremiah bound his neck with a yoke, and sent the same to neighboring kings, to signify that they would all soon go into the servitude of the Babylonian Empire (Jeremiah 27). One may also look to Ezekiel, who sketched the siege of Jerusalem on a brick (Chapter 5), prepared for himself the gear of an exile and migrated through a hole dug in the wall (Chapter 12), and set out a boiling pot filled with meat (Chapter 24). Agabus binding Paul in Acts 21:11, and others who appear in no small number, serve as witnesses to demonstrate this same practice. Indeed, lest anything be left untried by the Impure Spirit <note>Referring to the Devil or demonic influence.</note> to win for itself a reputation for divinity, we find the same thing practiced by false prophets. Truly, that "son of a lie," Zedekiah *son of Chenaanah*, had made for himself horns and said: *“Thus says the Lord: With these you shall gore the Syrians until you have consumed them”* (1 Kings 22:11). In the same manner, responses were given at the oracle of Ammon <note>A famous ancient oracle in the Libyan desert associated with Zeus or Amun.</note>. Strabo, in Book 17, says: *Not as at Delphi and Branchidae, where prophecies are given through words, but for the most part through nods and **SYMBOLS**, as also in Homer: "He spoke, and with his dark..."*

# CONCERNING ISAIAH NAKED AND BAREFOOT

...the son of Cronus <note>Zeus</note> nodded with his brows. <note>original Greek: ὀφρυσι νευσε Κρονιων</note>. When the prophet takes on the role of Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus</note>, this is intended to say expressly to the king that he was the son of Jupiter. That is: *the responses are not given in words, as they were at Delphi or Branchidae <note>Famous locations of Greek oracles where prophecies were spoken aloud</note>, but for the most part by nods and signs, just as in Homer:*

> He spoke, and the nourishing father nodded with his dark blue brows,

*with the seer, of course, imitating Jove. Moreover, he expressly said this to the King: that he himself was the son of Jove. From this, the ancient grammarian Dionysius Thrax correctly pronounced regarding the ancients:* Some indicated actions not only through speech, but also through SYMBOLS. <note>original Greek: Εσημαινον οὐ δια λεξεως μονον, ἀλλα και δια ΣΥΜΒΟΛΩΝ ἐνιοι τας πραξεις.</note>

## II.
In the inventory of prophecies joined with SYMBOLS, I place the act of Isaiah stripping and going barefoot at the command of God. *Isaiah 20:2:* Go and loosen the sackcloth from your loins, and pull off your sandal from your foot; and he did so, walking naked and barefoot. <note>original Hebrew: לך ופתחת השק מעל מתניך ונעלך תחלץ מעל רגלך ויעש כן הלך ערום ויחף</note> *The simple interpretation of which is this: Go and open that sackcloth from your loins, and draw off your shoe from your foot; and he did so, walking naked and barefoot.* You have the subject matter here, Reader, in which we shall exercise our strength to arrange and illustrate it. So that this may be done more distinctly, we will consider the WORDS OF GOD COMMANDING in the first place, and then the DEED OF ISAIAH OBEYING, in such a way that we may attach the elegant LIKENESS and harmony of this SYMBOL WITH THE THING SIGNIFIED, in which this entire discussion will end.

## III.
*God commands: Go, and open that sackcloth from your loins, and draw off your shoe from your foot.* The command is twofold: that he should open the sackcloth, and that he should draw off the shoe. It is preceded by a particle, or if you prefer, an imperative: "Go." <note>original Hebrew: לך (lech)</note> For there is little difference; under the sense in which it occurs here and in many other places, it can be counted among the particles. For it designates not so much motion to a place or from a place, as the prompt undertaking of the work being commanded, with the adverbial force of an exhortation. This is very frequent in the Scriptures. Compare the passages: *Isaiah 6:9; 21:7; 22:15; Jeremiah 36:19; Hosea 1:2;* and many others. It is exactly as it is among the Latins. *Claudian, The Rape of Proserpine, Book I, where Pluto says to Mercury:*

# DISSERTATION
<meta>Catchword: ילבש (He shall wear)</meta>

> Go, cleave the swift South winds. <note>original Latin: I, celeres proscinde Notos. From Virgil’s Aeneid.</note>
> And Jupiter to the same in *Aeneid* IV:
> GO, come now, son, call the West winds and glide on your wings. <note>original Latin: VADE, age, gnate, voca Zephyros & labere pennis.</note>

God therefore wishes Isaiah to execute his commands without delay and with eagerness, the second of which is: *Open that sackcloth from your loins.*

IV. The command concerns the SACKCLOTH, in which Isaiah was clothed. For the Hebrews, the word *Saq* <note>Hebrew: שק</note> has a double meaning. In general, it refers to whatever is fashioned from a rougher cloth to contain any object; that is, a sack. See Genesis 42:25, 27. For what is called a *sack* there is also called *amtachat* <note>Hebrew: אמתחת - a pouch or baggage-sack</note> in verses 17, 28, and chapter 44:1, 8, 12, etc., which is rendered by the Greeks as *marsippos* <note>Greek: ὁ μάρσιππος - a bag or purse</note>. The same meaning occurs in Joshua 9:4 and Jonah 3:8. And since this word has been granted "citizenship" <note>adopted</note> into almost all other languages by a sort of common consent, it has mostly preserved this meaning in them as well. However, the second meaning—that of a *garment*—has almost vanished; we shall explain this more extensively as it is appropriate to this passage. It might seem doubtful to some whether the *sackcloth* should be placed among the category of garments, because it seems to be clearly distinguished from them in Leviticus 11:32: *...whether it be a garment, or a skin, or a sack.* <note>original Hebrew: או בגד, או עור, או שק</note> Where the Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> has: *...either a garment, or a hide, or a sack.* <note>original Aramaic: או לבוש, או משך, או שק</note> The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> has: *...either of a garment, or of a skin, or of a sack.* <note>original Greek: ἢ ἱματίου, ἢ δέρματος, ἢ σάκκου.</note> But we believe that in this passage, by a <term>metonymy</term> <note>A figure of speech where the material is used to represent the finished product</note>, the material is put for the object made from it. Thus, *garment* <note>Hebrew: בגד / beged</note> does not signify all clothes so much as specifically those which were made neither from leather nor from sackcloth: such as those which seem to be more precious, like those consisting of wool or linen in 1 Kings 1:1. Hence, in a specific sense, *beged* is a cloak in Genesis 39:12, Ezekiel 26:16, etc., which the famous Braunius <note>Johannes Braun (1628–1708), a theologian famous for his work on Hebrew priestly clothing</note> declared was usually made from those materials. <margin>a) Braun, Sacred Vestments, Section 408.</margin> Maimonides followed this distinction in *The Recitation of the Shema*, Chapter 3, Paragraph 17: *It is forbidden to recite a prayer in the presence of naked skin; let him not recite while he is naked until he covers his nakedness. If there was a belt of cloth or sackcloth upon his loins...* <note>original Hebrew: אסור לקרות כנגד עורתו לא יקרא כשהוא ערום עד שיכסה עורו. היתה החגורה של בגד או שק על מתניו.</note> Willem Vorst <note>A 17th-century Dutch Hebraist</note> translates it: *It is a sin to recite a prayer in the presence of uncovered skin: let him not pronounce it while he is naked, or before he has covered his nakedness and applied a piece of a garment or a sack to his loins.*

V. Since, therefore, the sackcloth was neither linen or wool (*beged*), nor skin (*or*), from what material was it finally woven? Kimchi <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), a preeminent medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator</note> in the *Book of Roots*: *The sack is a garment of wool or a belt of wool...* <note>original Hebrew: השק הוא לבוש צמר או אזור צמר</note>

<summary>This page analyzes the Hebrew word 'saq' (sackcloth), distinguishing its common use as a container from its specific biblical use as a rough garment worn by prophets like Isaiah. The author uses linguistic evidence from the Septuagint, Targum, and Maimonides to define the sackcloth as a distinct category of clothing from leather or fine linen.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological investigation into the nature of the "sackcloth" (Saq) mentioned in the previous page. Having established that it functions as a garment, the author now debates whether it was made of wool or coarse animal hair.</meta>

<page-num>475</page-num>
<header>ON ISAIAH NAKED AND BAREFOOT.</header>

<term>A man wears it upon his flesh, and it is cheap, thick, and hard; for in a time of distress and mourning, a person wears it or girds it.</term> <note>original Hebrew: ילבש אדם אותו על בשרו והוא פחות ועבה וקשה כי בעת הצער והאבל ילבש אדם אותו או יחגור</note> *A sackcloth is a woolen garment, or a woolen belt, which one is accustomed to gird upon the flesh, and it is lowly, rough, and hard: for in a time of distress and mourning one is clothed in it or girded by it.* Either Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a prominent 12th-13th century Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator</note> is mistaken, or he is misusing the meaning of <term>wool</term> <note>Hebrew: צמר, *tsemer*</note>, as frequently happens among the Rabbis when they transfer a word that properly denotes sheep's wool to the hair of other animals as well. According to the opinion accepted by the illustrious men Aria Montanus, Pellican, Menochius, Heinsius, Meursius, Casaubon, Bochart, and others, it denotes *cilicium* <note>hair-cloth, typically used for penitential garments</note>. Hair-cloth is both a garment and anything made primarily from goat hair. It took its name from the region of Cilicia, where it is certain that goats—and the best of them in great numbers—were commonly shorn. This custom then passed to many peoples of the East. Pliny, in Book VIII, chapter 50, states: In Cilicia and around the Syrian regions (others say *Scyros*, but the illustrious Braunius, along with Bochart, embraces the former) *they are clothed in shorn hair*. Compare Aristotle, *History of Animals* VIII. 22. Aelian affirms the same regarding the Lycians in XVI. 30; Varro regarding the Phrygians in *On Agriculture* book 2; Virgil regarding the Cinyphians in *Georgics* 3; and even Festus Avienus regarding the Spaniards. And that sackcloth consisted of this same material was already a matter of common knowledge among the ancients. Alcimus Avitus, writing on the sackcloth of the Ninevites in Book IV:

> *Soft garments cast away, the bristles of the Cilicians provide the coverings.*

And on the same subject, Prudentius in his hymn for those fasting:

> *The darkened fathers stand in disarray with loosened robes,*
> *And the mourning crowd takes up woven bristles;*
> *The maiden, her hair uncombed, is covered in the shaggy hair of beasts.*

Furthermore, Jerome, in his *Life of Hilarion* near the end, uses "sackcloth tunic" and "hair-cloth tunic" interchangeably. Rabbi Solomon Jarchi <note>also known as Rashi, a premier medieval commentator</note> also favors this view, along with many Jews, in the volume *Sabbath*, chapter 6: <term>There it is made from the hair of goats.</term> <note>original Hebrew: שם הוא עשוי מנוצה של עזים</note> *Sackcloth is fashioned from the coarse hair of goats.* The same is defended by comparing Isaiah 50:3 and Revelation 6:12.

<page-num>476</page-num>
<header>DISSERTATION</header>

For what the prophets called <term>the Saq</term> <note>Hebrew: שק, the term for sackcloth</note> is rendered by the Apostle as <term>a sackcloth of hair</term> <note>Greek: σάκκος τρίχινος, *sakkos trichinos*</note>, which is to say, made of hair-cloth. Hence the conjecture of the most celebrated <margin>Bochart, *Canaan*, Book I, chapter 42.</margin> Bochart is not displeasing: that the French word *sagum* <note>a coarse military cloak</note> is derived from *saccus* (sack), because it was woven from the same kind of material. And garments of this sort were usually shaggy and hard. Yet they were not always so. Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Jewish scholar</note> in the *Gate of Moses*, page 300, writes: <term>Hair-cloth is that which is woven from hair, whether it be thin or very thick, like that from which sacks are made, since it is universally called a sack.</term> <note>The original Arabic text is here translated into English via the author's Latin version: "Cilicium autem est illud, quod contexitur è pilis..."</note> Pococke <note>Edward Pococke, a 17th-century English Orientalist</note> translates it thus: *“Hair-cloth is that which is woven from hair, whether it be finer or coarser, like that from which sacks are made, since it is universally called a sack.”* That the color was mostly black is proven from Revelation 6:12, where <term>the sun became black as sackcloth of hair</term> <note>Greek: ὁ ἥλιος ἐγένετο μέλας ὡς σάκκος τρίχινος</note>. And Jerome <note>An early Christian theologian known for the Vulgate Bible translation</note> joins together "dark clothing" and a "sackcloth belt" in his *Letter to Eustochium*. Hence the "dark-clad Fathers" in the work of Prudentius <note>A Roman Christian poet</note> mentioned in the cited place are those clothed in sackcloth. This fits the custom of using the sack in mourning, in which it is well known that not only the Gentiles, but also the Jews, were <term>dressed in black</term>.

VI. As for what the form of the sackcloth was, it is more difficult to determine, since there are no descriptions of this matter among the ancient monuments of writers. It is sufficient that it was fitted to the body in the manner of ordinary clothes. See Esther 4:1-2, Psalm 35:13, Psalm 69:12, Jonah 3:5. It was an inner garment, placed, as far as is known, <term>upon the flesh</term> <note>Hebrew: על בשרו, *al besaro*</note> as seen in 1 Kings 21:27 and 2 Kings 6:30, or <term>upon the skin</term> <note>Hebrew: עלי גלד, *ale galed*</note> as in Job 16:15. Such was that shaggy toga of the older Romans, much desired by the poet Lucan:

->- - - *And the precious garment*<-
->*The shaggy toga he put on over his limbs in the manner of a Roman citizen.*<-
->- - -<-

Hence those who were overwhelmed with grief used to tear their other garments, and as a sign of this, they wore the sackcloth beneath (Genesis 37:34, 2 Samuel 3:31, 1 Kings 21:27, 2 Kings 6:30, Esther 4:2, Isaiah 37:1). For this reason, they were also accustomed to be girded with it, for only inner garments were typically girded according to the custom of the ancients, a matter discussed in Section IX.

VII. The Prophet [Isaiah] was therefore girded with such a garment when the command of God came to him. Here, indeed, there is a dispute among the learned as to what the occasion was that caused Isaiah to wear a garment that was less <meta>catchword: customary</meta> outside of mourning—

It concludes by beginning an investigation into why the Prophet Isaiah was wearing such a garment when he received God's command.</summary>

<header>CONCERNING ISAIAH NAKED AND BAREFOOT.</header>
<sig>Ooo 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: prophets</meta>

...as was customary, he would go out into public dressed. There are those who feel <margin>a) Piscator on this passage; Grotius; Cocceius; Forerius; Sanctius; Alvarez on this passage; Bochart, *Canaan*, Book I, chapter 42 and *Hierozoicon*, Book I, chapter 2; Drusius on Zechariah; Molinaeus in *The Prophet*, chapters 10, 14.</margin> that this happened according to the common custom of the prophets, and to support this opinion they cite the passages 1 Kings 19:13, 2 Kings 1:8, Zechariah 13:4, Matthew 3:4, and Hebrews 11:37. 

But if I may be permitted to modestly disagree with these most eminent men, I do not see how it can be deduced from these sayings by any reasoning. For truly (1) it cannot be clearly demonstrated from any passage that sackcloth <note>the coarse hair-cloth used for mourning</note> was ever used by another prophet; (2) in those very passages, different characteristics appear which clearly prevent anyone from understanding it as sackcloth, such as we have described it. 

Let us examine the individual cases. In 1 Kings 19, it is read of Elijah: *And it was so, when Elijah heard it, that he wrapped his face in his* <term>toga</term> <note>original Hebrew: באדרתו, *be-adereto*, meaning a mantle or cloak</note>, as Junius translates. The Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> uses <term>melote</term> <note>original Greek: μηλωτη, a sheepskin</note> as usual. Cocceius translates it as "cloak." The Chaldean translation has <note>original: בשפיחא, *be-shaphicha*</note>, which signifies sometimes "cloak" and sometimes "toga," neither of which can fit the description of sackcloth, which is certain to be an undergarment, and thus also unsuitable for wrapping around the face. 

The term <term>melote</term> <note>original Greek: Μηλωτη</note> both here and elsewhere among the Greek interpreters, and in Hebrews 11, designates a sheepskin according to the genuine meaning of the word. The same word <term>aderet</term> <note>original Hebrew: אדרת, a mantle</note> occurs in Zechariah 13, where it says against the false prophets: *And it shall come to pass in that day, that the prophets shall be ashamed every one of his vision, when he hath prophesied; neither shall they wear a* <term>hairy mantle</term> <note>original Hebrew: אדרת שער, *aderet se'ar*; Latin: *toga villosa*</note> *to deceive.* The same reasons hold here, and it can be added that nothing prevents us from understanding this as a garment made of skin. And perhaps the prophet was referring to the custom of the pagan seers, who delivered their oracles either dressed in skins or, very frequently, while spread out upon a skin. 

Nor does the fact that Elijah is called in 2 Kings 1 a <term>hairy man</term> <note>original Hebrew: איש בעל שער, *ish ba’al se’ar*</note> denote anything else than that he was dressed in a shaggy garment, made of skin or coarse hair, whether it was an outer or inner garment. 

As for John, there are those who, based on Matthew 3—*he had his raiment* <term>of camel’s hair</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τριχων καμηλου, *apo trichon kamelou*</note>—would have it that John walked about dressed in skins. This may be held without penalty, as nothing stands in the way, yet it remains doubtful. Camero, citing Sozomen on page 51, says: *In his way of life, John the Baptist was similar to Elijah; for both had the same clothing, the same food, and both delighted in the same kind of dwelling, which was not done without mystery.* For the Prophets...

prophets were accustomed to displaying symbols of the doctrine they preached, even in external matters. Therefore, since both were preachers of repentance—the symbols and signs of which are cheap and despised clothing, food that is easily obtained and neglected, and likewise solitude—those symbols were for that reason adopted and employed by both. Heeserus, in his work, derives the garment of John from the <term>Nazirite vow</term> <note>a set of ancient Jewish ascetic practices including refraining from cutting hair and drinking wine</note>, specifically the <term>Addereth</term> <note>Hebrew: אדרת, a mantle or cloak often associated with prophets</note>. This much is certain: nothing definite can be concluded from this regarding sackcloth. And even if we were to grant that, what then? What is the connection? Because John the Baptist used sackcloth, does it follow that sackcloth was the ordinary clothing for the prophets of the Old Testament, and among them Isaiah?

### VIII.
Since, therefore, this opinion was supported by no probability, others have more correctly held that Isaiah was clothed in sackcloth because he was mourning the sins of his people and the impending hardships resulting from them. Jerome says on this passage: *The sackcloth tunic was the prophetic garment of one mourning the sins of the people.* Clement of Alexandria, in the *Pedagogue*, book II, page 237 (Potter edition), says of Isaiah: <note>original Greek: πολλακις δε και σακκον ημπιχετο, ταπεινοφροσυνης ενδυμα</note> *And often he also wore sackcloth, which is a garment of humility.* Rabbi David Kimchi writes: <note>original Hebrew: ומה שאמר לו יפתח השק לפי שהיה לובש שק על גלות השבטים ומתאבל עליהם</note> *And why does he say to him: "and open the sackcloth"? Because he was wearing sackcloth on account of the exile of the tribes and was mourning for them.* Although Kimchi may intend a different cause for the mourning, he nevertheless agrees on the fact itself. Notably among others, a) Calvin says: 

*Some think that it was his ordinary dress, because prophets were accustomed to being clothed in a mantle, as Zechariah testifies (13:4). But that conjecture is too weak and carries little weight. It is more credible that he was clothed in sackcloth to present the appearance of a mourner. For so great was the complacency in Judea that although they saw their brothers miserably afflicted and scattered, they were not moved, nor did they think that misery pertained to themselves. Meanwhile, they thought they were out of range of the arrows, and they even insulted the prophets themselves when they threatened and announced destruction. Hence Micah also complains that no one mourns the calamity of Israel (1:13).* 

b) Munster, Spanheim, Lightfoot, Noldius, and others agree with these views. I now add: this [garment] of Isaiah...

this garment was most appropriate, both so that he might mourn calamities—whether the past hardships of the captive tribes, the present ones of their stubborn persistence, or the impending ones of the captivity of Judah—and so that he might intercede with God for the future. Indeed, it is well established that this clothing was used for such purposes many times, as seen in Isaiah 3:24, where the phrase <note>original Hebrew: מחגרת שק, machgoret sak</note> "girding of sackcloth" is poorly translated as "a belt of sackcloth." The <term>Chaldean Paraphrase</term> <note>the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> translates it more accurately as: "he shall gird himself with sacks" <note>original Aramaic: יסרון קקין</note>, as do the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>: "he shall gird on sackcloth" <note>original Greek: περιζώσῃ σάκκον</note>. Brissonius <margin>a) Brisson, *On Persian Matters*, p. 257.</margin> noted that the Persians followed the same custom. Indeed, what is remarkable is that in the entirety of the Scriptures, no other occasion occurs for using sackcloth among the Jews except for these two: mourning and fasting. Wagenseil—following <term>Maimonides</term> <note>a famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note> in the *Laws of Fasting*, chapter 4, sections 1 and 2—teaches that people wore sackcloth during fasts. Compare also Barth’s *Adversaria* 42.7, pages 1879–1880, and Grotius on Matthew 11:21. For this reason, I am reluctant to see even the most learned scholars depart from the consistent patterns found throughout Scripture unless it is absolutely necessary. We add one further point which we found noted in the <term>Genesis Rabbah</term> <note>an ancient Jewish commentary on the book of Genesis</note>: that this practice was only customary among the higher classes. Here are the words:

->*Rabbi Aibo said: Because our father Jacob took hold of sackcloth <note>Genesis 37:34, upon hearing of Joseph's presumed death</note>, it has never departed from him, nor from his sons, nor from his grandsons until the end of all generations; yet it is the custom only among great men. David, as it is said (1 Chronicles 21:16): "David and the Elders fell down, covered in sackcloth." Ahab (1 Kings 21:27): "He put sackcloth upon his flesh." Joram (2 Kings 6:30): "And the people saw, and behold, he had sackcloth upon his flesh." Mordecai (Esther 4:1): "And he dressed in sackcloth and ashes."*<- <note>The author provides the original Hebrew text followed by a Latin translation, both of which are rendered here in English.</note> Regarding this passage, see the notes recorded in that same book. **VIII.** Since, therefore, this opinion was supported by no probability, others have more correctly held that Isaiah was clothed in sackcloth because he was mourning the sins of his people and the hardships that were imminent because of them. Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> says on this passage: *The sackcloth tunic was the prophetic attire of one mourning the sins of the people.* Clement of Alexandria <note>a prominent 2nd-century Christian theologian</note> in *The Instructor*, book II, page 237 (Potter edition), says of Isaiah: *and often he was also clothed in sackcloth, which is a garment of humility* <note>original Greek: πολλακις δε και σακκον ημπιχετο, ταπεινοφροσυνης ενδυμα</note>. Rabbi David Kimchi <note>a medieval Jewish commentator known as Radak</note> wrote: *And as for what He said to him: "and open the sackcloth"? It was because he was wearing sackcloth on account of the exile of the tribes and was mourning for them* <note>original Hebrew: ומה שאמר לו יפתחה השק לפי שהיה לובש שק על גלות השבטים ומתאבל עליהם</note>. In this, although he may intend a different cause for the mourning, they nonetheless agree on the fact itself. Among others, Calvin <margin>a) Calvin on this passage.</margin> explains excellently: *Some think that this was his ordinary garment, because prophets were accustomed to be clothed in a mantle, as Zechariah testifies (13:4). For there was such a sense of security in Judea that even when they saw their brothers wretchedly afflicted and scattered, they were not moved, nor did they think that misery concerned them. ### DISSERTATION

prophets used to exhibit symbols of the doctrine they preached, even in external matters. Therefore, since both were preachers of repentance—the signs and symbols of which are cheap and despised clothing, easily obtained and neglected food, and solitude—those symbols were used and adopted by both. *Heeser*, in his discussion on the <term>mantle</term> <note>Hebrew: אדרת (adderet), a cloak or mantle often associated with prophetic office</note>, derives the clothing of John the Baptist from the lifestyle of a Nazirite. This much is certain: nothing definite regarding sackcloth can be drawn from this comparison. And even if we were to grant that point, what follows? What is the connection? Does it follow that because John the Baptist used sackcloth, it was therefore the ordinary garment for the prophets of the Old Testament, and for Isaiah among them?

VIII. Since this opinion was supported by no probability, others more correctly concluded that Isaiah was clothed in sackcloth because he was mourning the sins of his people and the hardships that were imminent because of them. *Jerome* says on this passage: *The sackcloth tunic was the prophetic attire for one weeping over the sins of the people.* *Clement of Alexandria* in *The Teacher* (Book II, page 237, Potter edition) says of Isaiah: <note>original Greek: πολλάκις δὲ καὶ σάκκον ἠμπίχετο, ταπεινοφροσύνης ἔνδυμα</note> *But often he also wore sackcloth, which is a garment of humility.* *Rabbi David Kimchi* writes: <note>Hebrew: ומה שאמר לו יפתח השק לפי שהיה לובש שק על גלות השבטים ומתאבל עליהם</note> *And why does it say to him: "and open the sackcloth"? Because he was wearing sackcloth on account of the captivity of the tribes and was mourning for them.* While he may suggest a different specific cause for the mourning, they nonetheless agree on the fact itself. Excellently among the others, a) *Calvin* states: *Some think that it was his ordinary attire, because prophets were accustomed to being clothed in a mantle, just as Zechariah testifies (13:4). ### DISSERTATION

*Open the sackcloth.* Translators vary here. The <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translates it as: <note>original Greek: αφελε (*aphele*)</note> *take away.* The <term>Syriac</term> <note>A dialect of Aramaic used in early Christian translations</note> version says: *lay aside.* The actual force of the word does not seem to suggest this. These versions were born from a specific hypothesis, which we discuss below. The <term>Targum of Jonathan</term> <note>An ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> renders it: <note>original Aramaic: תיסר סקא (*taysar sakka*)</note> *shut the sackcloth.* This was improvidently translated by the editor of this version in the *English Polyglot Bible* as: *loosen your sackcloth.* Jarchius <note>The medieval Jewish commentator Rashi</note> noted this paradoxical version: <note>original Hebrew: ופתחת השק מעל מתניך ח' ותיסר סקא בחרצך והדברים מוכיחי' שהרי עד עכשיו לא ציוהו לחגור שק שהוא אומר ונעלך תחלוץ זהו סימן לאבלים ופירוש ופתח' כמו מפוחתו</note> i. e. *Open the sackcloth from your loins*

*Jonathan translates it: "and close the sackcloth around your loin." And the facts demonstrate it. For until now, God had not commanded him to gird himself with sackcloth, which is why He says, "and take off your shoe"—this is a sign for mourners. And the explanation of the word* <note>original Hebrew: פתחת (*patachta*)</note> *is, just as it is said in Exodus 39:6, "engraved with the engravings of a seal," suggesting he should gird the sackcloth as if it were engraved into his very flesh.*

He says: *For why? What if you say, as happens elsewhere very often, that here also one word is placed for two for the sake of brevity, so that it is said "loosen the sackcloth" instead of "put on the sackcloth and loosen it"?* By this reasoning, he thinks the question is easily solved: how did Isaiah walk naked? I truly do not know what Schmidt saw in this opinion that pleased him so much. Why did he depart from the simple sense of the words, which we believe should not be changed without necessity? Specifically, the inner garments or tunics of the ancients were usually girded.

# ON ISAIAH NAKED AND BAREFOOT.
### PPP
<meta>catchword: cinctu-</meta>

<margin>See Gonfalio to Peter, page 54 and following; Braun, *On the Vestments of Priests*, Book II, chapter 3.</margin>

According to the most learned men—Stukius, Ferrari, Rubenius, Brisson, Gonfalio, Braun, and others—just as a garment is closed when a belt is wrapped around the loins, so too do you "open" it when you remove that belt. Indeed, a thing is opened when it has been either closed or bound. In this sense, the Hebrew word <term>patach</term> <note>original: פתח; meaning "to open" or "loosen"</note> is used very frequently in Scripture. Compare Job 12:18, Isaiah 5:27, 41:1, Jeremiah 15:1, 40:4, and others. Now, Isaiah was indeed girded. Among the Jews, sackcloth was tied with a belt, as seen in 2 Samuel 3:31, Isaiah 15:3, 22:12, Jeremiah 4:8, 6:26, 49:3, Ezekiel 7:18, 27:31, and Joel 1:8. This was because it was an inner garment, fitted to the skin—a tunic—which, according to the custom of the ancients, had to be belted. 

Hence, you will find the phrase <note>original Greek: χιτων ζωσος (*chiton zosos*)</note> "a belted tunic," and in Homer’s *Odyssey* (Book 14), "he bound the tunic with a belt" <note>original Greek: ζωστήρι συνέεργε χιτῶνα (*zosteri syneerge chitona*)</note>. In Plato’s *Hippias*, one finds "the belt of a small tunic" <note>original Greek: ζώνην χιτωνίσκου (*zonen chitoniskou*)</note>, and in Tertullian, the phrase "a tunic caught up by a belt" <note>original Latin: *Tunicam cingulo correptam*</note>. Compare Revelation 1:13 and Isaiah 22:21. When a toga was worn over a tunic, it was the tunic that was belted, not the toga. One may read in the first book of the <term>Theodosian Code</term> <note>A compilation of Roman laws</note>, in the section *On the dress that is proper in the city*: "Indeed, one must observe that the inner garment be properly belted." Therefore, Isaiah was belted over his sackcloth, and he was commanded to remove this belt. Compare Psalm 30:11, "You have loosed my sackcloth" <note>original Hebrew: פתחת שקי (*patachta sakki*)</note>. The words that immediately follow prove that this is about a belt: "and you have girded me with gladness."

<margin>a) Fessel, *Sacred Observations*, V. 9.</margin>

X. Isaiah’s sackcloth was to be opened "from his loins" <note>original Hebrew: מעל מתניו (*me'al motnav*)</note>, or "from his waist," as the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> renders it <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς ὀσφύος αὐτοῦ (*apo tes osphyos autou*)</note>. Fessel (a) translates this as "kidneys" <note>original Latin: *renes*</note>. Kimchi <note>A famous medieval Jewish commentator</note> translates the Hebrew word <note>original: חלצים (*chalatzim*)</note> as "loins," which is also the meaning of the Aramaic word <note>original: חלץ (*chalatz*)</note>, and this is the most frequent usage. Otherwise, the ancients were not infrequently accustomed to belt themselves around the chest; hence that line from Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*: "and garments belted at the breasts," and in his third book of *The Art of Love*: "A narrow band around the slender chest." 

Tertullian, in his work *On the Pallium* (Chapter 1), mentions "dividing the folds of the garment with a belt." Ancient coins and marbles, which are found everywhere among lovers of antiquities, lead us to this same conclusion. Compare Revelation 1:13 and 15:6. Even the High Priest "is bound at the chest" <note>original Greek: κατα στερνων δειται (*kata sternon deitai*)</note>. The *Etymologicon Magnum* <note>An influential medieval Greek dictionary</note> provides the reason for this style of belting: "To gird <note>original Greek: ζωννυειν (*zonnyein*)</note> is from the word 'to live' <note>original Greek: ζην (*zen*)</note>, because we are belted in that place where the heat of the body, or the heart, is located." There are many disputes among the Rabbis regarding the exact placement of the belt—

*"Open the sackcloth."* <note>original Latin: *Aperi faccum*; referring to the command in Isaiah 20:2</note> Interpreters vary on this. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translates it as "Take it away" <note>original Greek: ἄφελε (*aphele*); Latin: *aufer*</note>. The Syriac version says: "Lay it down" <note>original Latin: *depone*</note>. However, the literal force of the word does not seem to imply this. These versions were born from a specific hypothesis, which we will discuss below. The Targum Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> renders it: "Bind the sackcloth" <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: תיסר סקא (*teisar saqa*); Latin: *claude faccum*</note>. This was carelessly translated by the editor of this version in the English Polyglot Bibles as: "Loosen your sackcloth" <note>original Latin: *solve faccum tuum*</note>. The medieval commentator Jarchi <note>Also known as Rashi</note> noted this paradoxical version:

"And you shall open the sackcloth from your loins" <note>original Hebrew: ופתחת השק מעל מתניך</note> (Jonathan translates: "and bind the sackcloth around your loins"). The facts demonstrate this: for until now He had not commanded him to gird himself with sackcloth so that he might say that. "And you shall take off your shoe"—this is a sign of mourners. The explanation of the word "opened" <note>original Hebrew: *pethachtah*</note> is like the phrase "engravings of a seal" <note>original Hebrew: *pittuchei chotham*, citing Exodus 39:6</note>; it means he was to bind the sackcloth so tightly that it was like it was engraved into his flesh.

This is that remarkable reasoning, though I would wish that the theologian of the Augsburg Confession, Sebastian Schmidt <note>A prominent 17th-century Lutheran scholar</note>,—otherwise a learned interpreter of Scripture—had not attributed too much to it *a)*, even if he differs slightly in his hypothesis. For he says: "What if we say that, as often happens elsewhere, it occurs in this place too—that one word is placed for two for the sake of brevity? Thus, 'loosen the sackcloth' is said instead of 'put on the sackcloth and loosen it.'" By this reasoning, he thinks the question of how Isaiah walked "naked" can be easily solved. 

I truly do not know what Schmidt saw in this opinion that pleased him so much. Why would he retreat from the simple sense of the words, which we believe should not be changed without necessity? Why would he do away with a clear expression to make room for an ellipsis <note>a grammatical omission</note> that, while used occasionally elsewhere, here seems entirely gaping and broken? Why does he think the difficulty concerning Isaiah’s nakedness is best solved by this method, when that could be achieved while preserving the original hypothesis—as we do in section 17? 

The most celebrated interpreter *b)* <note>referring to Johannes Cocceius</note> says: "The Prophet is commanded either to tear a part of his garment, or even to lay aside his toga." We approve of neither of these, as long as nothing stands in the way of the simplest use of this word. Specifically, the inner garments or tunics of the ancients were usually belted. This custom was accepted by the Romans, the Greeks, and the peoples of the East. This has been proven *c)* by many.

### ->CONCERNING ISAIAH NAKED AND BAREFOOT.<-

<margin>Gonfalio's *Notes to Peter*, page 54 and following. Braun, *On the Dress of Priests*, Book II, chapter 3.</margin>
To the most learned men Stuckius, Ferrarius, Rubenius, Brisson, Gonfalio, Braun, and others, it appears that just as a garment is closed when a belt is wrapped around the loins, so when you take that same belt away, you open it. For a thing is "opened" whether it was previously closed or bound. And it is in this sense that the word *open* <note>original Hebrew: פתח (*patah*)</note> is most frequently used in Scripture. Compare Job 12:18, Isaiah 5:27, 41:1, Jeremiah 15:1, 40:4, and others. Now, Isaiah was indeed girded. For sackcloth was belted by the Jews, as seen in 2 Samuel 3:31, Isaiah 15:3, 22:12, Jeremiah 4:8, 6:26, 49:3, Ezekiel 7:18, 27:31, and Joel 1:8. Since it was an inner garment <note>term: *tunica* (tunic); the basic garment worn next to the skin in the ancient world</note> fitted to the flesh, it had to be girded according to the custom of the ancients. Hence you will find the "belted tunic" <note>original Greek: χιτὼν ζωστός (*chiton zostos*)</note> in Homer's *Odyssey* (Book 14), "he fastened the tunic with a belt" <note>original Greek: ζωστήρι συνέεργε χιτῶνα</note>; in Plato’s *Hippias*, "the belt of the small tunic" <note>original Greek: ζώνην χιτωνίσκου</note>; and in Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from North Africa</note>, "the tunic pulled in by a belt." Compare Revelation 1:13 and Isaiah 22:21. And when a <term>toga</term> <note>the formal outer wrap of a Roman citizen</note> was worn over the tunic, it was not the toga, but the tunic that was girded. We read in the first law of the Theodosian Code, *On the dress which is required in the city*: "but observe the inner garment especially with belts." Isaiah, therefore, was belted over his sackcloth, and he was commanded to remove this belt. Compare Psalm 30:11: "You have opened my sackcloth" <note>original Hebrew: פתחת שקי (*pitathta saqqi*)</note>. That this refers to the belt is proved by the words that immediately follow: "and you have girded me with gladness."

<margin>a) Fesselius, *Sacred Notes*, V. 9.</margin>

Tertullian, in his work *On the Mantle* (Chapter 1), mentions "dividing the folds with a belt." Ancient coins and marbles, found everywhere among lovers of antiquities, lead us to the same conclusion. Compare Revelation 1:13 and 15:6. Even the High Priest "is bound at the chest" <note>original Greek: κατὰ στέρνων δεται</note>, that is, tied around the breast. The *Etymologicon Magnum* <note>A large Greek grammatical and historical encyclopedia from the 12th century</note> adds a reason for this type of girding: "to gird <note>original Greek: ζώννυειν (*zonnyein*)</note> is derived from 'to live' <note>original Greek: ζῆν (*zen*)</note>, because we are girded in that place where the heat of the body, or the heart, is located." Indeed, many passages of Scripture are available: Jeremiah 13:11, Isaiah 45:1, Exodus 12:2, 2 Kings 1:8, Isaiah 5:27, Ezekiel 23:13, Ephesians 6:15, and 1 Peter 1:13. Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a prominent medieval Jewish scholar and grammarian</note> in his *Book of Roots* says: "Your loins: these are otherwise the *Chalizim* <note>term: *chalizim*; a Hebrew word for the loins or the part of the body where strength resides</note>, the place where they are girded." <note>original Hebrew: מתניו הם החלצים מקום שחוגרין עליו</note> The same is found in other authors. Homer, in the *Odyssey*, Book 5, line 230:

> But the Nymph herself put on a great silver robe,
> fine and graceful, and she cast a belt about her loins.

Specifically, this was the "girdle of Diana," by which the garment was pulled back as far as the knees, which Callimachus <note>A noted Greek poet and scholar of the 3rd century BCE</note> describes as "to gird the fringed tunic as far as the knee." <note>original Greek: ἐς γονυ μεχρι χιτωνα ζωννυσθαι λεγνωτον</note> In his *Hymn to Diana*, line 11. Here it is worthy to observe that the belt of the huntresses who served Diana was double: one around the chest, and the other around the loins. For coins represent them thus, especially those that Spanhemius <note>Ezechiel Spanheim, a 17th-century diplomat and expert on ancient coins</note> illustrated for this purpose in his work on Callimachus, page 134. By this very fact, it is clear what those lines of Claudian <note>A 4th-century Latin poet</note> mean in *The Rape of Proserpina*, Book 2, line 33:

-><note>original Latin: Duo cingula veſtem / Crure tenus pendere vetant.</note><-

Compare Apollonius, Book 4, line 949. Hence, for Aeschylus <note>The ancient Greek tragedian</note>, the belt around the chest is called a *strophos* <note>term: *strophos*; a band or cord worn under the breast</note> while the one around the loins is called a *zona* <note>term: *zona*; a standard belt or girdle</note>, as in *The Suppliants*, line 446. Cresconius Philippus <note>Likely referring to the 6th-century poet Corippus</note>, Book 2:

->*A shining belt girt the master's loins.*<-
-><note>original Latin: Baltheus effulgens lumbos præcinxit heriles.</note><-

For the same reason, the prophet also had his sackcloth girt about his loins, which he was commanded by God to open. That the sackcloth was indeed girded around the loins is clear from Genesis 37:34, Jeremiah 48:37, Amos 8:10, Judith 8:5, and other places.

# CONCERNING ISAIAH NAKED AND BAREFOOT.

XI. We subjoin the second command: *Take off your shoe from your foot.* There is mention here of the <term>SHOE</term> <note>original Hebrew: *na’al* (נעל)</note>. This is the only word the Hebrews have to designate footwear. Consequently, there is a more difficult investigation regarding its form. There are some who think it ought to be distinguished from sandals. However, Antonius Bynæus <note>A 17th-century Dutch theologian and expert on ancient Hebrew customs; his work *On the Shoes of the Hebrews* is the primary reference here</note>, that most successful craftsman of the ancient Hebrew shoe *a)*, did not think their reasons were significant enough to prevent him from concluding the opposite. Since I have nothing to add to his findings, I refer the reader to them, sparing myself the trouble of a lengthy description. The fact that the Scripture uses the singular number should trouble us very little. I confess, we read that the ancients sometimes used only one shoe. This is certain regarding the Ætolian soldiers <note>A people of central Greece known for their distinctive military habits</note>, who were for that reason called <term>single-booted</term> <note>original Greek: *monokrepides* (μονόκρηπιδες)</note>, and Virgil says of the Hernici <note>An ancient Italic tribe</note> in *Aeneid, Book VII*:

> *They set the naked tracks of the left*\
> *foot; a raw hide boot covers the other.*
> <note>original Latin: *Vestigia nuda sinistri / Instituere pedis, crudus tegit altera pero.*</note>

Furthermore, sorceresses would loosen the binding of one foot in their magical rites, which others have noted from *Aeneid, Book IV*, Ovid's *Metamorphoses, Book VII*, and Seneca’s *Medea, Act IV*. "Single-booted" is an epithet of Mercury found in Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>: and Philostratus, in his *Epistle to a Barefoot Youth*, relates that Jason was usually depicted wearing only one shoe. See also *Hyginus, Fable 12* and *Macrobius, Dream of Scipio, Book 5, chapter 18*. These examples, however, contribute little to our case. *b)* It is a mere <term>enallage</term> <note>A grammatical figure where one grammatical form—in this case, the singular number—is substituted for another</note> of number, the use of which in the Hebrew language is passed down by grammarians.

XII. *The Prophet is commanded to REMOVE THE SHOE FROM HIS FOOT*, continuing the grammatical shift. Isaiah was wearing shoes according to the custom of the Eastern peoples and especially his own. This is contrary to the opinion of *c)* *Schmidius* <note>Sebastian Schmidt, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian and prolific commentator</note>, who says: *He is said to "strip off" or "remove" something who was not wearing it. Thus, in this place, Isaiah seems to be commanded to strip off his footwear, that is, so that he might not wear it. However, if it is preferred that he did have them on, but had not yet removed them, it will not harm the interpretation of the sackcloth mentioned earlier.* To be honest, this modest man admits that there is no probability in this explanation of his, and that it was devised to defend a hypothesis which we shattered in Section IX. Thus, it is hardly necessary to labor over matters that are refuted on their own merits and are suspected even by their own inventor. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> translates this as *to loosen* <note>original Greek: *hypolysai* (ὑπολῦσαι)</note>. Not badly. From—

This is the nature of the Greek language. Plato says in his *Symposium*: "Boys, untie Alcibiades' shoes." <note>original Greek: ὑπολύετε, παῖδες Ἀλκιβιάδην</note>. Aeschylus says in *Agamemnon*: "Let someone loosen the boots quickly." <note>original Greek: ὑπαί τις ἀρβύλας λύοι τάχος</note>. This fits the reality of the object described. Among the Hebrews and other nations, shoes were fastened with straps. In addition to many authors, this is confirmed by coins, statues, and ancient monuments. Compare Genesis 14:23, Isaiah 5:27, John 1:27, etc. In Latin, we use the word <term>to pull off</term> <note>original Latin: *detrahere*</note>; for this word is naturally suited to explain both the Hebrew term, which occurs in the same sense in Deuteronomy 25:9-10, and the action itself. Compare Tibullus, Book I, Elegy 5:

->And he himself will pull the bindings from the snow-white foot.<-

And Terence in *The Self-Tormentor*, Act I, Scene 1: *Slaves run up, they pull off the light shoes.*

XIII. God has commanded this much. Let us now see the obedient Isaiah: **And he did so** <note>original Hebrew: וַיַּעַשׂ כֵּן (*vaya’as ken*)</note>. The <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX</note> deviates here, saying: *and do so*, as if the command were being narrated as a continuous instruction throughout the whole verse. Unless there is an error in the text, they go against all the rules of the grammarians, which I do not have time to argue here. We more rightly note the singular obedience of Isaiah. He indeed, since he did not yet know the reasons for the command, humbly stopped inquiring into them; and before God’s plan was revealed to him, **HE DID SO**, as God had ordered, walking naked and barefoot. He preferred to undergo conditions that were shameful in the eyes of the world, rather than step outside the boundaries within which—would that men often confined their itching reason. He believed no other role was given to him than that of submission. Come then, let us accompany the prophet for a little while as he walks in this unusual manner, but by God’s command.

XIV. HE WALKED **NAKED** <note>original Hebrew: עָרוֹם (*arom*)</note>. Interpreters disagree here. Some ancient writers think this refers to total nakedness. Jerome <note>The 4th-century scholar and Bible translator</note> says on this passage: *Just as Isaiah walked naked and showed his foulness with naked buttocks to those watching, so all Egypt and Ethiopia would become naked when the Assyrian devastated them, and nothing at all would remain in the land.* And a little later: *At the same time we learn the obedience of the prophets; for a noble man—as the Hebrews relate, Isaiah was the father-in-law of Manasseh, the son of King Hezekiah of Judah—was not ashamed to walk naked. Instead, judging nothing more honorable than God’s commands, he laid aside his sackcloth*

after throwing this off, he would have been naked, having previously had only one tunic, and that one made of sackcloth. Ambrose, in Book VI, Epistle 36, strives to prove at length that Isaiah was stripped not in a shameful manner but in a most glorious one in the sight of the people coming to meet him, as one who was echoing the oracles of the Lord with his own mouth. The great <margin>a) Calvin on this passage.</margin> Calvin took up the defense of this same opinion and, among other things, softens and defends it for two reasons: (1) because he thinks the prophet was clothed at home, and even in public, and was not naked except when he wished to go out to teach; (2) when an objection is made regarding the heat and cold to which the prophet would have been exposed, he appeals to the omnipotence of God. Nor, to tell the truth, are there any better things that can be said for this position. For they gain nothing from the use of the word <note>the Latin *nudus* or Hebrew *arom*</note>, since it is <term>polysemous</term> <note>original Greek: πολυσημος; having many meanings</note>. For this reason, very learned men later departed from these views; they refuted their arguments, brought forward contrary ones, and thought of a new meaning. To be brief, the command about removing the shoe from the foot would lack its proper emphasis if God had commanded total nakedness for the seer in the prior phrase. For a man is not naked in every part if he still has his feet covered with shoes; nor is it necessary, where a general stripping is commanded, that a special mandate should forbid him from being shod in shoes. Furthermore, it seems something harsh, unusual, and dishonorable to have prescribed for a man of gravity, descended from the royal family <note>Isaiah was traditionally considered to be of royal blood, the nephew of King Amaziah</note>, if that interpretation is admitted. Indeed, since there is absolutely nothing to prevent us from softening the meaning, who would not think that a milder path should be taken? Finally, there would be more in the execution than in the command itself, which I feel should not be easily admitted without any necessity.

XV. Efforts have been made in the opposite direction in various ways. There are some among the Hebrews who side with <term>Jonathan</term> <note>Referring to the Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Prophets</note>, who renders "naked" <note>original Hebrew: ערום (*arom*)</note> as *pocheach* <note>original Hebrew: פחיח</note>. Solomon Jarchi <note>Also known as Rashi, a preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator</note> translates this word as: *in torn and worn-out clothes, but not actually naked* <note>original Hebrew: בבגדים קרועים ובלואי ולא ערום ממש</note>. So too Barthenora <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro, a 15th-century Italian rabbi</note> on the Book of Megillah, Chapter 4, Mishnah 6: *Pocheach: one whose arms are visible and his clothes are torn* <note>original Hebrew: פותח : זרועותיו וקרועים בגדיו</note>, *and he appears naked and barefoot; we translate this as "pocheach" and barefoot.* <note>original Hebrew: ונראים ערום ויחף מתרגמינן פתח ויחף</note> For these words, "Naked and barefoot," are translated in the <term>Chaldean</term> <note>Aramaic</note> as: *Pocheach* and barefoot. In the Massefchet Sopherim <note>A minor tractate of the Talmud concerning the work of scribes</note>, chapter 14: *Pocheach is one whose legs are exposed or whose clothes are tattered...* <note>original Hebrew: פחיח שקראו כרעיו או בגדיו פרומים</note>
