# DISSERTATION

...naked in such a way that either his legs are visible, or his garments are torn. <margin>a) Buxtorf, p. 1181.</margin> If you take the word in the first way, it could to some extent be reconciled with the opinion we are preparing to defend. Not at all, if you take it in the latter way. For in that case, it would have been necessary for the prophet both to strip off his sackcloth and to be dressed in some other kind of rag, which cannot be imagined, since Isaiah could not have known this from the divine command, nor does the meaning of the word <term>arom <note>Hebrew: ערום; naked</note></term> allow for it.

XVI. Therefore, the majority of interpreters have concluded this: *Isaiah* (the words are <margin>b) Glassius, Rhetorica Sacra, Tract 1, chapter 16.</margin>) *walked naked by the command of God, not because he was entirely stripped of clothing, but because he laid aside his outermost garment, and thus, having removed his cloak, he walked in his undergarments, dressed in the manner of those who are usually taken into captivity, so that the reality would match the sign.* And indeed, they have argued their case with plausible arguments thus far. (1) The Prophet could have been a sign to the people even in this way, if he simply appeared dressed differently than he was accustomed to. If he had been seen entirely naked, he would indeed have been <term>arom</term>, but it would not have been fitting for <note>The author argues that total public nudity would undermine the respectability required for a religious leader.</note> prophetic dignity; it would have been nearly a disgrace and an insult to natural modesty. Whatever seems harsh in this matter is softened when this word is understood as referring only to the removal of some upper garment. In this way, the seer neither sinned against the rules of decency, nor did he fail to satisfy the divine command. (2) This is supported by the comparison of the sign with the thing signified <note>The "signified" refers to the Egyptian and Ethiopian captives who would soon be led away stripped of their outer finery.</note>, which brings about a sufficiently fitting harmony. (3) This is also consistent with the style of Scripture, where a person is called "naked" who lacks part of their clothing. Thus, in 1 Samuel 19:24, the "nakedness" of Saul is understood as the removal of his military attire. Compare also Micah 1:8. In the same way, Aelian says of Gelon in his *Miscellaneous History*, Book VI, chapter 11, that he "came into the marketplace naked" <note>original Greek: ἐλθὼν εἰς τὴν ἀγορὰν γυμνὸς</note>, which is explained in Book XIII, chapter 37: "Behold, then, I stand before you in a small tunic, naked of weapons" <note>original Greek: Ἰδοὺ τοινυν ὑμῖν ἐν χιτωνισκῳ γυμνὸς τῶν ὅπλων παρεστηκα</note>. And Herodian, in Book II, chapter 13, writes: "Lest through fear of being wounded, being naked (of armor), they might not dare to fight against those who were armed, and being few against many" <note>original Greek: Ὡς δέει τοῦ τρωθῆναι, γυμνοί τε πρὸς ὡπλισμενους καὶ ὀλιγοι πρὸς πολλους μὴ μαχοιντο</note>. Compare also Book III, chapter 14. Nor should Peter in John 21:7 be thought to have been naked in every part, yet he is called <term>naked <note>original Greek: γυμνὸς (gymnos); Hebrew: ערום (arom)</note></term>, he who...

### CONCERNING ISAIAH NAKED AND BAREFOOT.

...who is poorly dressed, as seen in Job 22:6, 24:10, Matthew 25:36, 43, and James 2:15. Hence the word <term>gymneteuein <note>Greek: γυμνητεύειν; to be poorly clad or to go naked</note></term> is correctly translated as being naked, or being poorly dressed and not sufficiently protected against the harshness of the weather (against which we are normally shielded by clothing), as in 1 Corinthians 4:11. <margin>a) Grotius on John 21:7; Roa, *Singularia* II. 4. 1; Cuper, *Observations* Book I, ch. 7; Pitiscus on Suetonius’s *Augustus*, etc.</margin> Men most skilled in these matters—such as Grotius, Roa, Cuper, Pitiscus, and others—have noted that this usage was also common among classical authors. Juvenal, in *Satire V*, line 163, writes:

->*For who is so naked, that he*<-
->*would endure him twice.* - - - -<-

In this context, "naked" refers to one who is poor and destitute, following the example of Horace in his *Satires* (Book II, Satire 5) and *Odes* (Book III, Ode 17). Compare also Caesar’s *Gallic Wars* I. 25, Aristophanes’s <term>Ecclesiazusae <note>Greek: ἐκκλησιάζουσαι; The Assemblywomen, a comedy by Aristophanes.</note></term> line 37, Apollonius Book 3, line 1281, and Virgil’s famous line: *Plow naked, sow naked.* The author of *On Illustrious Men* says of <term>L. Q. Cincinnatus <note>Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus (c. 519–430 BC), a Roman statesman and hero famous for his humility and returning to his farm after serving as dictator.</note></term> that the legates sent to him found him "naked" while he was plowing across the Tiber. However, I read in the work of the most celebrated Gisbert Cuper, in the location already cited, that it has been explained from a coin of P. Seguinus that they actually plowed while wearing a single garment. <margin>b) Wolfius on *Philosophy of Origen*, page 158.</margin> From this, the renowned Wolfius suspects that the <term>Gymnosophists <note>Greek: γυμνοσοφισταί; literally "naked philosophers," a group of ancient Indian ascetics known for their detachment from material goods.</note></term> and the "naked" philosophers of the Egyptians were not entirely destitute of all clothing, but perhaps were only girded with the bark of trees. 

And thus far, this opinion has stood upon these arguments and has been defended by <margin>c) Gataker, *Miscellaneous Adv.* Book 9; Pellican, on this passage; Forerius, on this passage; Glassius, in the cited location; Witsius, *Miscellanea* Vol I, Book I, ch. 12, § 3; Noldius, *Concordance*, page 917.</margin> very learned men. Yet if I may be allowed to disagree with them without penalty, I confess that I still find something lacking in each of the reasons offered. (1) It is not likely that Isaiah threw off his outer garments while keeping his inner ones, since he only possessed one: a sackcloth tunic worn against his skin. Isaiah could not have put aside an outer garment which he did not have, nor his inner garment, if he wished to maintain the respectability for which they argue. # DISSERTATION

...set apart from the point of dispute, you will more fortunately inquire into the mind of the Holy Spirit and find it more easily. Furthermore, it is shown in Section 2 that even if the hypothesis is changed, that most wise harmony remains. (3) The passages of Scripture compared here do not exclude another interpretation that is no less consistent with the Scriptures: sometimes they serve a specific hypothesis, but do not prove what they ought. Concerning secular authors, we remain silent; they illustrate those points, but they do not explain them.

XVII. Finally, however, I see that I must reveal what I think. I would believe—so long as the reason for any objection remains hidden to me—that Isaiah was nothing but stripped of his outer belt, and that by the same <term>synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part of something is used to represent the whole, or vice versa (e.g., "hired hands" for workers).</note></term> which others defend, the Hebrew word <term>arom <note>original Hebrew: ערום; traditionally translated as "naked," but here interpreted as "undressed" or "lightly clad."</note></term> means the same as "unbelted." There is an initial doubt regarding the reasoning behind this word. And to frankly profess what is true, in all the writings of the Old Testament, there is no passage that makes this specific meaning strictly necessary. Yet, as the following arguments show more clearly, it should be inferred in this instance. Nor would I wish to be so bold as to invent a definition for this word against all authority—a meaning it never holds in the sacred pages. I mean this only regarding the Bible, for various passages exist in Rabbinic writings that support my view. But since these prove nothing, I will not use them to defend myself. To preserve the proper beauty of the speech of this most elegant prophet, I do not flee from figurative language, but rather I appeal to it. 

Nor should you think, Reader, that the biblical text is being distorted here. To see how great a use <term>synecdoche</term> has in the sacred writings and how widely it applies, consult *a)* Glassius, who learnedly explained everything pertaining to this <term>trope <note>A figurative or metaphorical use of a word or expression.</note></term>. Thus, I believe I am committing nothing absurd, nor am I unfairly twisting the Scriptures to fit a hypothesis. Indeed, the Holy Spirit himself seems to lead the way in John 21:7. There, the disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter: "It is the Lord." When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, <note>original Greek: τον επενδυτην διεζωσατο (ην γαρ γυμνος); "he girded his tunic (for he was naked)"</note> he tucked in his tunic (for he was naked) and threw himself into the sea. There is no one who would deny that a synecdoche is present here. I affirm the same, but I explain it differently—namely, as being "unbelted"—and, as I think, this is most consistent with the simple arrangement of the words.

### ON ISAIAH NAKED AND BAREFOOT. 489

...very clearly, concerning which anyone who reads this without prejudice may judge. Indeed, a person is considered "naked"—and quite indecently so—not only in the greatest part but also when walking with their clothing open; I have shown in the appropriate place that this sign served to signify that very thing. By a similar <term>trope <note>A figurative or metaphorical use of a word or expression.</note></term>, the Luperci <note>Priests of Lupercus in ancient Rome who ran through the streets during the Lupercalia festival.</note> seem to be called "naked" by ancient authors, even though they were covered with the skins of goats—"wearing the skins of goats" <note>original Greek: τα δερματα των αιγων κατανεμοντες</note>, as found in Plutarch’s *Life of Romulus*—yet they were naked in that part where men are normally girded. See examples in the same author's work, as well as in his *Life of Julius Caesar*; Livy, Book I, Chapter 5; Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book VIII; Festus under the entry *Capros*; and others. To these may be added the passage from Aelian which we cite in Section II, § 7, where "naked" <note>original Greek: γυμνος [gymnos]</note> is clearly used to mean "unbelted" <note>original Greek: αζωσος [azosos]</note>. 

(2) Since, therefore, the very meaning of the word does not prevent us from departing from the commonly accepted opinion, it seems improper to us that more should be contained in Isaiah’s obedience than in God’s command. To add anything to a command, just as to take away from it, ought to have been a <term>piaculum <note>A sin or a crime requiring atonement; a violation of divine law.</note></term> for a prophet. God commanded: *"Loosen that sackcloth from your loins."* We think it is clear that by these words God intended for Isaiah to be unbelted (See Section IX). We add now that He intended nothing more. If indeed God intended more by that phrase, then let it be proven from any passage of Scripture that "to loosen" <note>original Hebrew: פתח [pathach]</note> is the same as "to strip bare." If that were proven, I would lose the great force of this argument, though not the entire argument, let alone the whole case. Surely, in precepts of this kind, God always uses the simplest possible language, where even ambiguous phrases have no place unless they are explained—or need to be explained—by other circumstances. 

(3) When God commanded that future events be explained to His people through symbols, He seems to have always employed a most wise proportion according to the nature of the matters at hand. Thus, the more the future disasters pertained to the Jews themselves, the more difficult the tasks often undertaken by the prophets, who served as signs and symbols to the attentive observer through their actions. Conversely, it is believable that the less the calamities concerned the immediate fate of the Jews, the milder the condition the prophets underwent in foreshadowing them. The symbol we are discussing belongs to this latter class <note>The author suggests that because Isaiah's sign concerned foreign nations like Egypt and Ethiopia rather than the immediate destruction of Jerusalem, the physical toll on the prophet was likely less extreme.</note>. I would not wish, therefore, for Isaiah to have been literally naked, but others disagree with me. Yet these same people, even when they do not intend to, strip the prophet of his clothes because they assume he had only one garment, which, if removed, would leave him instantly naked. XVIII. But the prophet also complied with the second command. He walked *BAREFOOT* <note>original Hebrew: יחף [yachaph]</note>. I remember reading this word five times in the text of the Old Testament: in this chapter of Isaiah (verses 2, 3, and 4), as well as in 2 Samuel 15:30 and Jeremiah 2:25. Therefore, with his shoes removed, Isaiah went barefoot, contrary to the custom of the Jewish nation. Those examples that are cited elsewhere describe a clearly unique rite, undertaken either for religious reasons or some other specific occasion. Hence, the celebrated *b)* Morin labors in vain to uphold Bochart's opinion. Let whoever wishes to inquire into these matters at greater length read the praised book by Bynaeus. That task has not been assigned to us at present.

David Kimhi <note>A celebrated 12th-13th century French rabbi and Hebrew grammarian, often called the Radak.</note> on Isaiah: <note>original: "ויעש כן וגו'" – "And he did so, etc."</note> *This matter cannot be explained according to its literal meaning, as if God commanded the prophet to go naked and barefoot. Münster <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a pioneering German Hebraist and cartographer.</note> seems to have accepted this opinion, as does Clarius <note>Isidore Clarius (1495–1555), a Benedictine scholar and editor of the Vulgate Bible.</note>, who often describes it word-for-word.

XX. Now, these arguments are of such a nature that they can be refuted with little effort. They bring forward almost nothing to support their case except certain parallel passages of Scripture which, if the gods please, seem to agree with that same opinion. But in truth, anyone who reads attentively easily perceives how few passages should actually be explained according to that hypothesis, and how those very examples have no analogy with our text; how many are miserably twisted to assert the exact opposite; and how others are highly controversial. We shall not go through every single one. Those which argue for the opposing side in Section I will suffice. But even if we grant all their points, nothing further follows except that God, in His wisdom, sometimes revealed future events to His prophets through symbols in a prophetic vision. 

However, there is another point that they could have pressed more forcefully, and which Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the most influential medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> touched upon: <note>original: "הנה יקשה מאד למה צוה השם יתברך לנבאיו דומים למשוגעים ולשוטים"</note> *Behold, there is a very great difficulty as to why God, blessed be He, commanded His prophets to act in ways similar to the insane and fools.* Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and commentator who frequently argued for the literal reality of biblical events.</note> cited these words from him; since Abarbanel is almost the only one taking the opposing side, he occupies himself at great length only in refuting the first argument, leaving this specific point almost untouched. 

Yet even that argument easily falls. For being <term>discinctum</term> <note>Literally "un-girt," meaning appearing in one's undergarments or tunic without the formal outer cloak or belt.</note> or barefoot is not so far removed from decent customs that one is permitted to twist the Scripture—against its own will—into a preconceived hypothesis. It was perhaps more unusual to be dressed in sackcloth while "un-girt" than while fully dressed; but was it truly something to be ashamed of for a prophet who was promptly obeying divine commands and foretelling something incredible—at least to the minds of the Jews? 

And what of being barefoot? Were shoes worn by those who entered the Temple? Or by the priests who ministered in sacred matters? Or by those who publicly professed penance on the Feast of Expiation <note>Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, when wearing leather shoes is traditionally forbidden.</note>? If it is worth your while, look at the tractate *Berachot* <note>A section of the Talmud dealing with blessings and prayers.</note> chapter 9; the *Gemara* <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis.</note> in *Yevamot* chapter 1; and the aforementioned *Berachot*; Gregory of Nyssa <note>A 4th-century Christian theologian and Church Father.</note> in his *Second Homily on the Song of Songs*; the tractate *Yoma* chapter 8; the *Arba Turim* <note>A landmark code of Jewish law by Jacob ben Asher.</note> in the laws of the Day of Atonement; and the collections of more recent authors such as Braun, Sheringham, Bynaeus, Sagittarius, and others—then you will think differently. I will say nothing of how common this was in certain sacred rites among the Gentiles, which writers highly skilled in these matters have long since noted.

# DISSERTATION

The things we note in the following section will bring more light. But here we add the wise words of Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508) was a Jewish statesman and philosopher who preferred historical and literal explanations of the Bible over purely allegorical ones.</note> speaking thus:

> *Therefore I say, that to reach the true truth of the matter, a general rule should be established: namely, that in those matters which are possible in themselves, as things that could have been done, and concerning which Scripture testifies that they were indeed done, we should not depart from the literal sense when explaining them, nor offer a figurative explanation, nor distort the text from its proper meaning.*

XXI. I consider that arguments which carry more weight—just as the others were lighter—must be briefly touched upon, since they rest on their own significant gravity. You will already find these among the ancients: Cyril, Jerome, Origen, Ambrose, and Procopius. Among more recent scholars, there is almost no one who does not defend the same view with unanimous consent. I note only the following points. 

(1) Not only is Isaiah commanded to strip himself, but he is recorded as having actually done so: **AND HE DID SO.** <note>Isaiah 20:2. The author argues that the simple statement of the act confirms its physical reality.</note> These words are so simple that unless an absolute necessity stands in the way, anyone who dares to make an exception would act recklessly—I might even say impiously. However, we have already proven that nothing stands in the way. 

(2) God shows this act of Isaiah to the people as a symbol of a future event that would be visible to everyone's eyes. Read the following verse:

> *And the Lord said: Just as my servant Isaiah has walked [naked and barefoot] for three years, etc.* <note>Isaiah 20:3.</note>

Could anything clearer even be conceived? Either there is no emphasis in these words, or the preceding parts must be understood as referring to the actual deed of Isaiah himself. 

(3) I see no way that the phrase *for three years*, found in the third verse, could be applied to the opinion we have refuted without some distortion. There are some, I know, who refer this to a <term>sign and a portent</term> <note>original Hebrew: *ot u-mofet* (אות ומופת). In biblical Hebrew, these terms often refer to miraculous or symbolic acts meant to prove a divine message.</note>, as if Isaiah being naked and barefoot foreshadowed either a calamity lasting three years or one that would happen three years later. Neither explanation is pleasing. Not the latter, because the fulfillment of the prophecy must be referred to the much more distant times of Nebuchadnezzar <note>The King of the Neo-Babylonian Empire who eventually conquered Egypt and Ethiopia, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy.</note>; and not the former, because that affliction by Nebuchadnezzar did not remain within such brief limits. I therefore necessarily refer the "three years" to Isaiah's own actions. And in this, the Septuagint <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> and the Chaldean <note>The "Chaldean" refers to the Targum, the ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> have led the way. No differently from Jerome, Cyril, and Procopius did Origen (who is older than them) argue in *Against Celsus*, Book VII, page 336, and in the *Philocalia*, chapter 26. But by what color of reasoning can it be said that he was in a prophetic vision for three whole years? Or at least that those events, though described as a three-year span, [were contained in]

...that they all represented themselves to his imagination at one and the same time? (4)
Our excellent prophet suffered the same fate here that was also the lot of other prophets. These men were indeed frequently mocked by the common people and regarded as little short of insane. Boys pursued Elisha with shouting, mocking his baldness (2 Kings 2:23). I will not press the examples of Moses, Jonah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, for they are too well known. Our Isaiah truly says of himself: *Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me are for signs and for portents among the Israelites (Chapter 8:18).* As Origen rightly says in *Against Celsus*, Book VII: <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar. Here he defends the prophets against the philosopher Celsus, who mocked their strange behavior.</note> "For the Word chooses such to be the prophets of the God over all, who showed the endurance of Antisthenes, Crates, and Diogenes to be a mere plaything." <note>original Greek: "Τοιουτους γὰρ καὶ ὁ λόγος αἱρεῖ δεῖν εἶναι τοὺς τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσι Θεοῦ προφήτας οἵτινες παίγνιον ἀπέφηναν τὴν Ἀντισθένους καὶ Κράτητος καὶ Διογένους εὐτονίαν"</note> That is to say: *For the Word chose such Prophets of the greatest God, that when compared to them, the rigid austerity of Antisthenes, Crates, and Diogenes would seem ridiculous.* <note>Antisthenes, Crates, and Diogenes were famous Greek "Cynic" philosophers known for their extreme poverty and disregard for social norms. Origen argues the prophets' divinely mandated hardships were even more impressive.</note> (5)
In this symbolic display, Isaiah is presented to the people as a *portent* <term>mopheth: מופת - a sign or wonder intended to catch the eye</term>, that is, an unusual thing which, by striking the eyes in an unaccustomed way, stirs up wonder in those who do not expect it. I prefer to emphasize this using the words of the great <margin>a)</margin> Cocceius: <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian and famous Hebraist.</note> *In a* <term>mopheth</term> *one does not always look for admirability in terms of power (from which "miraculous works" are called* <term>niphlaoth: נפלאות - supernatural miracles</term>*) but rather in terms of custom and decency; that which is unusual strikes the eyes and creates wonder in the spectators as to why and for what purpose it is done (Ezekiel 12:6).* *For I have given you as a* <term>mopheth</term> *(portent) to the house of Israel (verse 11). I am your* <term>mophethkem</term> *(your portent): by which you may be stirred to think about what is going to happen to you. See also Ezekiel 24:24, 27; Isaiah 20:3; Psalm 71:7: "I have been as a portent to many"; and Zechariah 3:8. For* <term>anshei mopheth</term> *(men of portent) are those in whom something wonderful or unusual happens, by which people are stirred to think about my promises, etc. Thus far his words.*
Compare Wagenfeil's *Fiery Darts of Satan*, pages 385, 386. <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil (1633–1705) was a German Hebraist. His book title "Tela Ignea Satanae" refers to anti-Christian Jewish polemics he was refuting.</note>

### I.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' featuring architectural scrollwork and foliage.</image-desc>Having inquired into the analogy between the thing signified and the sign—which we have explained according to the <term>pshuto: פשוטו - the literal or plain meaning</term>—it is now necessary to agree upon the **SIGNIFIED REALITY** or the **OBJECT OF THE SIGN**. The Holy Spirit leads the thread of this inquiry, but it is a thin thread and not easily traced except by one who pays the closest attention. We learn from verse 3 that there was to be a <note>original Hebrew: "אות ומופת על מצרים ועל כוש" (ot u-mopheth 'al mitsrayim ve-'al kush)</note> *sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush*. Therefore, whatever was signified by that garb of Isaiah pertained, in terms of its fulfillment, to the Egyptians and the Cushites <note>The term "Cush" traditionally refers to the region of the Upper Nile, including ancient Nubia and Ethiopia.</note>. The calamities which Isaiah announced as coming were to be feared by them. But were they ever fulfilled? We do not think one should rashly doubt a matter whose fulfillment seems to serve the manifestation of God’s glory and truth. Nor does anything occur to us that might move us to think otherwise. Yet if they were fulfilled, when was it? If I were to say I did not know, I would be committing nothing beneath my strength or the expectations placed upon me. Nevertheless, let me be permitted to search timidly, if any truth may be granted to be known.

# DISSERTATION

<margin>a) Marsham, *Chronological Canon*, p. 515.</margin>
...situated on the furthest borders, it was not captured, but merely besieged for a short time; soon it was abandoned, and nothing else was attempted. All these facts prove that the expedition was a source of regret for the Assyrians and Egyptians rather than a success. Furthermore, if the conjecture of a) Marsham <note>Sir John Marsham (1602–1685) was an English chronicler famous for trying to synchronize Egyptian history with the Bible.</note> holds weight—and he was often most successful in untangling chronological difficulties—the timing itself cannot be made to agree. For he identifies *Sargon*, mentioned in verse 1, as the same person as *Esarhaddon* (or *Sarchedon*, as appears in Tobit Chapter 1, verse 21), the son and successor of Sennacherib. Therefore, the prophet could not have predicted as a future event something that had already occurred.

III. Others have therefore judged it more cautious to postpone the fulfillment of the prophecy to the era of Nebuchadnezzar <note>original Latin: *Nabuchodonosori*</note>. As their arguments are more probable, they easily earn my trust. This view is favored by (1) the consensus of Scripture itself and the harmony of the various prophecies. The matter is quite clear. Compare, if you please, Jeremiah 25, 44, and 46, as well as Ezekiel 29–32. Many of these passages will appear again below, so we will refrain from excerpting them here. It is also favored by (2) the reliability of secular writers. Josephus, in *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 10, chapter 11, writes:

*For in the fifth year after the destruction of Jerusalem, which is the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar's reign, he brought war to Coele-Syria. Having subdued it, he fought against the Ammonites and Moabites; and once these nations were made subjects, he invaded Egypt to overthrow it. He killed the king who was then reigning, and having appointed another, he again took the captive Jews who were there and led them to Babylon.* <note>original Greek: "Τῳ γαρ πεμπτῳ της ἱεροσολυμων πορθησεως ἐτει..."</note>

Berosus <note>Berosus was a Babylonian priest and historian whose works are mostly lost but were quoted by other ancient writers.</note>, as cited in Eusebius’s *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 9, chapter 40, says:

*But when Nebuchadnezzar heard, after a short time, of his father's death, having arranged matters in Egypt and the rest of the country, and having commanded certain of his friends to bring the captives of the Jews, Phoenicians, and Syrians from the nations within Egypt to Babylonia, he himself arrived there.* <note>original Greek: "Αισϑομενος δε μετ' οὐ πολυν χρονον την του πατρος τελευτην..."</note>

V. It was a sign (II) of **humiliation**, especially the act of going barefoot, as seems can be proven from 2 Samuel 15:30 <note>This verse describes King David fleeing Jerusalem and weeping with his head covered and his feet bare.</note>. Thus Berenice <note>Berenice (28 AD – after 81 AD), the daughter of Herod Agrippa I and sister of King Agrippa II</note> is described by Josephus in *The Jewish War*, Book II, Chapter 15: *Barefoot before the tribunal, she entreated Florus* <note>original Greek: Γυμνόπους προ του βήματος ἱκέτευσε τον φλωρον; Berenice was petitioning Gessius Florus, the Roman procurator, to stop the slaughter of Jews in Jerusalem.</note>. Regarding the pagans, Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–240 AD).</note> writes in his book *On Fasting*, Chapter 16: *When the heavens are closed and the year is parched, barefoot processions are proclaimed.* Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian apologist (c. 100–165 AD).</note> thinks in his *Second Apology* that they learned this rite from Moses. But it is not permitted to linger longer on this custom, because it has for a long time been illustrated by the care of most learned men. If you have the time, consult the works of Hospinian, Gyraldus, Morinus, Larroquanus, Lomejer, Braun, Bynaeus, etc. <margin><a> Hospinian, *On Festivals*, Vol II, p. 132; Gyraldus, *Various Criticisms*, Dialogue 10; Morinus, *Dissertation IV*; Larroque, *Adversaria* II. 19; Lomejer, *On Lustrations*, ch. 34; Braun, *On Sacred Vestments*, Book I, ch. 3; Bynaeus, *On Hebrew Footwear*, Book II, ch. 2, etc.</margin> Furthermore, those nations were to be humbled who, puffed up by the success of their affairs, "carried their crests high," namely the **Ethiopians** and **Egyptians**. Thus concerning the Egyptians in Ezekiel 29:15: *It shall be the lowliest of kingdoms; neither shall it exalt itself any more above the nations: for I will diminish them, that they shall no more rule over the nations.* He depicts the same thing in the whole of Chapter 31 under the elegant emblem of a cedar tree. Who nevertheless had them marked with **chalk**. This proves both points, and refutes Dempster <note>Thomas Dempster (1579–1625), a Scottish scholar.</note>, who thinks it was the shoes that were chalked, and not the feet...

# DISSERTATION

...as Caspar Sagittarius <note>Caspar Sagittarius (1643–1694) was a German historian and educator</note> asserts in *On the Barefootedness of the Ancients*, chapter I, section 27. See also Balduinus <note>Benoît Baudouin (d. 1632), a French scholar known for his work on ancient footwear</note> in *On Ancient Shoes*, chapter XXIII. However, Balduinus was mistaken when he claimed that slaves always walked with bare feet, since Leone <note>likely a reference to an antiquarian work on monuments</note> in *On Monuments* (IV. 2. §. 5) has confirmed with examples that they were often shod in wooden clogs <note>original: *sculponeis*; heavy wooden shoes typically worn by slaves or peasants in ancient Rome</note>. That captives were kept ungirded and barefoot by the ancients is proven by Saint Luke in Acts 12:8, where the Angel, about to free Peter from prison, says: *Gird yourself and put on your sandals* <note>original Greek: *Περίζωσαι, καὶ ὑποδησαι τὰ σανδαλια σου*</note>. Juvenal also mentions this in *Satires* VIII, verse 129:

> ->*How great a reward will you carry off for such a dire crime,*<-
> ->*Since Marius has recently stripped the thin Africans.*<-
<note>Juvenal refers to the stripping of provincial subjects by corrupt governors; "stripping" here implies removing their belts/girdles as a sign of degradation.</note>

In the works of Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century Church Father</note>, Volume II, he writes: *The nakedness and barefootedness of captives indicates their status* <note>original Greek: *ἡ δὲ γυμνοτης καὶ ἀνυποδησια το των αἰχμαλωτων σχημα δεικνυει.*</note>. Hence, the Roman Emperors, when leading captives in a triumph, wore purple shoes as a supreme sign of their great deeds and of the nations they had subdued. On a stone monument dedicated to the memory of Gaius Marius, which Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a renowned classical scholar</note> cites, the inscription reads: FROM THE SPOILS OF THE CIMBRI AND TEUTONES, THE VICTOR BUILT THIS TEMPLE TO HONOR, IN TRIUMPHAL DRESS AND PURPLE SHOES <note>original: *DE MANUBIEIS CIMBRICEIS ET TEUTONICEIS AEDEM HONORI VICTOR FECIT VESTE TRIUMPHALI CALCEIS PUNICEIS*</note>. Corippus <note>Flavius Cresconius Corippus, a 6th-century Latin poet</note> adds the reason for this in Book II, chapter 3:

> ->*It is fitting for the Emperors alone to use this finery,*<-
> ->*Under whose feet lies the blood of kings.* - - -<-

Those who believe this custom can be traced back to the age of Abraham are convinced it is a very ancient practice. Indeed, we read in Genesis 14:23 that Abraham, speaking to the King of Sodom upon his return from battle, said: *If I take even a thread* <term>ועד שרוך נעל</term> <note>Hebrew: *ve-ad serok na'al*</note> *or a sandal strap, or indeed any thing that is yours.* It is most certain that this was already a custom in the time of Isaiah, as seen in 2 Chronicles 28:15: *They took the multitude of captives, and clothed all the naked among them from the spoil; and when they had clothed them and SHOD THEM, and given them food and drink etc., they led them away.* It is also asked whether the words of Jeremiah 2:25 can be referred to this same practice: <term>מנעי רגלך מיחף</term> <note>Hebrew: *min'i raglek mi-yachaf*</note> *Keep your foot from being bare*, a translation preferred by the illustrious men <margin>a) Casaubon on Suetonius' *Life of Julius Caesar*, ch. 45. b) Castellio on this passage; Cocceius on this passage and in his Lexicon.</margin> Sebastian Castellio <note>Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563), a French theologian and Bible translator</note> and Johannes Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian</note>? Others, however, feel differently.

# ON ISAIAH NAKED AND BAREFOOT.

<margin>

b) Bynaeus, *On Shoes* p. 195 ff.
</margin>

...they feel. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page.</note> a) Fesselius paraphrases it thus: *“O Judean people, who until now have lived in the manner of a harlot, do not bare your foot—that is, your private parts, which ought to be covered—nor prostitute your body for sale to lust.”* <note>original Latin: "ô gens Judæa, quæ meretricium in modum hactenus vitam instituisti, ne pedem h. e. pudenda tua, quæ velata esse oportet, nudes, aut corpus tuum venale prostituas libidini." Fesselius (1606–1650) was a German theologian who often sought metaphorical or moralizing interpretations of scripture.</note> The celebrated b) Bynaeus <note>Anthony Bynaeus (1654–1698), a Dutch orientalist known for his exhaustive work on ancient footwear</note> follows the same opinion, in which he has the Chaldean <note>The Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> and many Hebrew teachers as his forerunners. And truly, this does not seem far from reason. 

But that is not our current concern. Rather, barbarian conquerors sometimes stripped captives entirely. This is hinted at in Ezekiel 16:39 and 23:29. This is also how we should understand Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian</note> in Book 22, chapter 6: *“With Maharbal giving his word—who had caught up with them at night with all the cavalry forces—that if they surrendered their weapons, he would allow them to leave with a single garment each; they surrendered themselves.”* <note>original: "Fidem dante Maharbale... si arma tradidissent, abire cum singulis vestimentis passurum; sese dediderunt."</note>

In Herodian <note>A 3rd-century Greek historian of the Roman Empire</note>, Septimius Severus addresses the captives in Book 2, chapter 13: *“I command the soldiers surrounding you to ungird you and strip you of whatever military clothing you are wearing, and to send you away naked.”* <note>original Greek: "Τοῖς τε περικειληφόσιν ὑμᾶς στρατιώταις κελεύω ἀποζῶσαί τε ὑμᾶς καὶ ἀποδυσάντας, εἴτινας περίκεισθε ἐσθῆτας στρατιωτικάς, γυμνοὺς ἀποπέμπειν."</note> And a little later: *“Then, having snatched away their belts, their clothes, and whatever military insignia they bore, they sent them away naked and dismissed from service to a man.”* <note>original Greek: "Τάς τε ζώνας, καὶ τὰς ἐσθῆτας, καὶ εἴ τι σύμβολον ἔφερον στρατιωτικόν, ἀφαρπάσαντες γυμνοὺς ἐξεπέμπον."</note>

Similarly, Achilles Tatius <note>A Greek novelist of the 2nd century</note> in *The Loves of Leucippe and Clitophon*, Book 3: *“But when they saw them both naked and in bonds, suspecting the truth, they received them within the ranks and, having sent them to the rear, allowed them to rest.”* <note>original Greek: "Ὡς δὲ εἶδον καὶ γυμνοὺς καὶ δεσμὰ ἔχοντας, ὑπονοήσαντες τὴν ἀλήθειαν, δέχονται τῶν ὅπλων εἴσω, καὶ ἐπ' οὐρὰν παραπέμψαντες εἴων ἡσυχάζειν."</note>

All these things were fulfilled according to the letter. The Cushites <note>Ethiopians</note> and Egyptians were led away into slavery by the victor Nebuchadnezzar, naked and deprived of the use of all things necessary for sustaining life comfortably. Isaiah 20:4: *“The King of Assyria shall lead away the captive multitude of Egyptians and the deported crowd of Ethiopians, young and old, naked and barefoot.”* <note>original: "Abducet Rex Assyriæ captivam multitudinem Ægyptiorum & deportandam turbam Æthiopum puerorum & senum nudam & discalceatam."</note> Also Jeremiah 46:25–26, and Ezekiel 29:9–12, and verse 19: *“Behold, I will deliver the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon, that he may take its multitude, and strip its spoil, and plunder its prey, to be the wages for his army.”* <note>original: "Ecce ego trado Nebucadnezari, Regi Babyloniæ terram Ægypti..."</note> Moreover, this captivity for forty years...

# DISSERTATION

...remained for forty years, as seen in Ezekiel 29:13: *“At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the peoples among whom they were scattered, etc.”*

VII. It was a sign (IV) of *ignominy and disgrace*. Such an appearance has been considered shameful and a vice among the Romans since ancient times. Asinius Pollio, in Cicero’s *Letters to his Friends* (X. 32), once criticized Balbus because, while overseeing a public execution, *“he walked about barefoot and in a loose tunic after lunch.”* <note>original: "pransus nudis pedibus, tunica soluta inambulaverit." In Roman culture, appearing in public without a belt or proper footwear, especially after a midday meal (prandium), suggested a lack of discipline and gravity.</note> Similarly, it was held against Nero that he sometimes went out in public *“without a belt and barefoot,”* according to Suetonius in *Life of Nero*, chapter 51. a) Hence, among military punishments, and indeed the most shameful ones, were being *“unbelted and unshod.”* <note>original: "discingi & discalceari"</note> Frontinus, in Book IV, writes: *“Piso ordered Titius, the Prefect of a cohort, to stand daily at the headquarters with the belt of his toga cut and his tunic loose and barefoot, because he had retreated before fugitives.”* <note>original: "Piso Titium Præfectum cohortis... cinctu togæ præciso, soluta tunica, nudis pedibus in principiis quotidie stare jussit."</note> Valerius Maximus, recording the same event in Book II, chapter 7, says: *“He afflicted the prefect with these types of disgrace: he ordered him to be present dressed in a toga with its fringes cut off, and in an unbelted tunic and bare feet.”* Compare this to Job 12:18. From this practice, those who voluntarily resigned their honors would cast aside their belt. A passage in Aelian’s *Various History* (VI. 11) regarding Gelon <note>Gelon was a 5th-century BC ruler of Syracuse known for his military prowess.</note> is noteworthy here: *“Having entered the forum naked, he said he was returning power to the citizens.”* <note>original Greek: ἐλθων εἰς την ἀγοραν γυμνος ἐφατο ἀποδιδοναι τοις πολιταις την ἀρχην. The author clarifies that "naked" here refers to being unbelted.</note> For *“naked”* is explained as *“unbelted”* in the same work (XIII. 27), where it is explicitly stated that *“a statue was erected to him in an unbelted tunic.”* This relates to the shameful rite of removing the shoe in the Law of the Levirate, <note>Under Mosaic Law (Deuteronomy 25:5-10), if a man refused to marry his deceased brother's widow, the woman would remove his shoe in public to shame him for failing to continue the family line.</note> which others have noted and about which one may consult Vatablus, Menochius, Bonfrerius on this passage, Schindler’s *Lexicon* under the word <term>נעל</term> <note>Hebrew: na'al, meaning "shoe."</note>, Delrio’s *Sacred Proverbs* (Vol. I, verse 73), Selden’s *On the Hebrew Wife* (Book I, ch. 13), and J. Clodius’s special dissertation. b) It is well known that Christians were sometimes subjected to the same kind of disgrace. George Codinus Curopalata, writing on the offices of the Court of Constantinople, says: *“What is now called a Diadem was once called a military belt, a badge of honor.”* Hence, tyrants *“would take away the belt and the neck-ring from the more honored martyrs who confessed Christ.”* Thus they would hand them over to the torturers as *“private citizens.”* The prophets threaten the Egyptians and the Cushites <note>The people of Ethiopia or the upper Nile region.</note> with that very disgrace as a companion to their other miseries. Hence, in verse 4 of our chapter, they are to be led away.

### CONCERNING ISAIAH NAKED AND BAREFOOT

<margin>a) Bochart, *Phaleg*, Book 4, chapter 2. b) Huet, *Commentaries on Origen*, page 49; *On the Site of Paradise*, chapter 13.</margin>

VIII. One thing I cannot conceal here: while everyone sees that these prophecies were elegantly fulfilled, no doubt can enter anyone’s mind regarding Egypt. But who are those Cushites, about whom secular history says nothing? Yet the same ruin predicted by both Isaiah and Ezekiel awaited them. It was the opinion of almost all the ancients that Ethiopians were meant. The Hebrews (nearly all of them), the Greeks, the Vulgate <note>The Latin version of the Bible common in the author's time.</note>, Philo, Josephus, the Arabic version, etc., have followed this view. This remained the case until the most celebrated man <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667) was a renowned French Protestant scholar of biblical geography and zoology.</note> *a)* Samuel Bochart attempted to assert with many arguments that we should always look to Arabia, and never to Ethiopia, when the text mentions "Chus." That great man certainly achieved this much: he forces one to admit, even if unwillingly, that at times Arabia cannot help but lie hidden under the name *Chus*. However, *b)* P. D. Huet <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar who debated the location of the Garden of Eden.</note> and others thought they would act more cautiously if they called all the inhabitants on both sides of the Red Sea "Cushites"—the Arabs on one side (who themselves are sometimes called Ethiopians) and the Ethiopians on the other. I confess, if there are passages that support the Arabs, there are no fewer that support the Ethiopians. Look only at two: Esther 1:1 and Jeremiah 13:23. If you explain these as referring to the Arabs, you must take care not to twist the Scripture.

IX. Indeed, the answer is more difficult for us because Nebuchadnezzar fought both the Arabs and the Ethiopians and conquered both, as is evident not so much from secular writers as from the prophecy of Ezekiel. A notable testimony is Ezekiel 30:5: <note>original Hebrew: כוש ופוט ולוד וכל ערב וכו</note> *Cush and Put, and Lud, and all Arabia, etc.*

But it also happened that, especially after the time of Solomon, they frequently entered into treaties with them, established friendships, and relied on their strength and help. This occurred at many other times, but most significantly during the period when this prophecy was both delivered and fulfilled. It was pronounced during the expedition of either Sennacherib <note>King of Assyria (reigned 705–681 BCE) who besieged Jerusalem.</note> or in the times immediately following. Here, the words of Rabshakeh <note>The high-ranking Assyrian official sent by Sennacherib to demand the surrender of Jerusalem.</note> in Isaiah 36:6 are noteworthy: *“Look, you are trusting in the staff of this broken reed, in Egypt, on which if a man leans, it will go into his hand and pierce it; so is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him.”*

### DISSERTATION

Compare Verse 9, 2 Kings 18:21, etc. This was fulfilled after the destruction of the city. Here, however, not only is Zedekiah frequently accused of violating the oath he had sworn to the Babylonians and placing his trust in Egypt—as seen in Jeremiah 37:5 and Ezekiel 17:13, 15, and 29:6–7—but even after the city was captured, the Jews were preparing to flee to Egypt with an obstinate spirit, despite all threats, exhortations, and advice. They viewed it as their sole hope and protection now that their affairs were desperate. See Jeremiah 42, 43, and 44. 

The exact nature of the commerce or relationship that existed between the Jews and the Cushites <note>Inhabitants of the kingdom of Cush, located south of Egypt in the region of modern-day Sudan and Ethiopia.</note> is not quite as certain. What is certain is that some interactions did occur, especially during the time when Sennacherib was threatening Jerusalem. For Tirhakah, King of the Cushites, undertook an expedition against him to divert the enemy from Judea (see 2 Kings 19:9 and Isaiah 37:9). On this matter, Josephus relates that a portion of the army was led against him by the Assyrian king, who, after restraining him and returning, found his own legions slaughtered and put to flight.

XII. I could stop my pen here, were it not for the fact that I must briefly touch upon those who, abusing the example of Isaiah and others, have imagined that such acts were intended for them to imitate. Is the wearing of haircloth sacks <term>cilicia</term> <note>Rough garments made of goat hair, traditionally worn as a form of penance or self-mortification.</note> a sign of the monastic pride of our times, or would you rather call it hypocrisy? This practice was learned from heretics, or at least from superstitious little men. Epiphanius, in his *Panarion* (Heresy 80), noted long ago that the Messallian heretics <note>A 4th-century sect that rejected the sacraments in favor of perpetual prayer and extreme asceticism.</note> affected the use of haircloth. He introduces them as <note>original Greek: σακκῳ προφανει ἐπερειδομενους</note> "leaning on visible sackcloth," and he rightly notes against them that <note>original Greek: ἀλλοτριον ἐσι της Καθולικης ἐκκλησιας σακκος προφανης</note> "visible sackcloth is foreign to the Catholic Church"—meaning a sackcloth that is intended to catch the eyes of others. 

Jerome, in his letter to Eustochium, writes: *There are those who dress in haircloth and with specially made hoods, so that they might return to infancy, imitating owls and night-birds.* The same author, in the *Life of Hilarion*, says: *He never washed the sackcloth in which he had once been clothed, saying it was superfluous to seek cleanliness in haircloth.* And again: *Thus, his limbs were covered only by sackcloth, and he wore a leather outer-garment <note>original Greek: ἐπενδυτην</note> which the blessed Anthony had given him as he was departing.* Rutilius Namatianus, in his *Travels* <note>A 5th-century Latin poem titled 'De reditu suo', which contains famous critiques of the early monastic movement.</note>, not without reason criticized this filthy habit of monks and the grime of their clothing:

->The wretched man thinks the heavens are fed by filth.<-

Paulinus of Nola <note>A 4th-century Roman senator who became a Christian bishop and poet, known for his ascetic lifestyle.</note> should be understood as referring to this same style of dress in his poem on the death of Celsus, verse 451:

> *If only a heavy sackcloth of rough covering*
> *Made from the offspring of goats might cover and goad you while you mourn.*

**Note:** *while mourning* <note>original: "lugentem"</note>) since a monk has the duty not of a teacher but of one who laments—one who mourns for himself or the world, and waits in fear for the coming of the Lord; as Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), a prominent Church Father known for his Latin translation of the Bible (the Vulgate) and his promotion of monasticism.</note> says in the place cited. *Offspring of goats* <note>original: "Caprigenum fetis"</note>) You have the material here: goats' hair, see Section I. §. 5. *Might cover and goad* <note>original: "Tegat & stimulet"</note>) The purpose of this habit is taught: to protect from the injuries of the weather, and to goad or restrain the flesh so that the soul might be more vigilant in prayer. And these are those "pale and humble ones" of whom Paulinus speaks in Letter 7: *Our fellow-servants and fellow-pale-ones, not proud with embroidered garments, but humble in bristling haircloth.* <term>cilicia</term> <note>Coarse garments made of goat hair (cilices) worn next to the skin as a form of penance.</note> Sulpicius Severus <note>A Christian writer best known for his biography of Saint Martin of Tours.</note> testifies that the same rule was kept by the disciples of Blessed Martin in his *Life of Martin*, chapter 7.

XIII. Nor did this superstition stop within these bounds. So that they might behave like Moses, Joshua, and Isaiah in other respects, some began to walk barefoot. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential theologians in Western Christianity.</note> writes in *On Heresies*, chapter 68: *There is another heresy of those who always walk with bare feet, because the Lord said to Moses (or to Joshua): "Remove the sandals from your feet." And because the Prophet Isaiah was commanded to walk with bare feet. Therefore, it is a heresy because they do not walk this way for the sake of bodily affliction, but because they misunderstand the testimonies in such a manner.* Philastrius <note>A 4th-century bishop and writer on heresies.</note> says in Heresy 80: *The "Barefoot Ones" <term>Excalceati</term> are a heresy which asserts that men ought to walk barefoot because, they say, it was told to Moses: "Remove your sandals," and because Isaiah walked thus for three years. These things are more of human and vain superstition than of the tradition of the Saints or the command and authority of the Lord Jesus Christ and His power.* Compare Honorius Augustodunensis at the end of his book *On Heresies*; and Isidore of Seville <note>A 7th-century scholar and bishop, author of the "Etymologies" (Origines).</note> in *Origins* VIII. 5. Jerome points these out in Letter 22 to Eustochium <note>A Roman noblewoman and one of the "Desert Mothers" mentored by Jerome.</note> with these words: *Shun also those men whom you see in chains, with feminine hair contrary to the Apostle, a goat’s beard, a black cloak, and feet bare in endurance of the cold. All these are the arguments of the Devil, etc.* Jerome paints those masks quite elegantly. From which it simultaneously appears, among other things, that the work of Epi— <note>The text cuts off here; "hypobolimaion" is a Greek term meaning "spurious" or "forged."</note> is spurious.

When Constantinople was shaken by earthquakes, Theodosius the Younger <note>Eastern Roman Emperor from 408 to 450 AD.</note> prayed to God with bare feet. John Malalas <note>A Byzantine chronicler from Antioch.</note> writes in his *Chronicle*, Book 14: <term>The Emperor himself offered prayers, along with the Senate, the people, and the clergy, barefoot for many days.</term> <note>original Greek: Οσις βασιλευς ἐλιτάνοσε, μετα της συμπλητου, και του ὄχλου, και του κληρου, ἀνυπόδητος ἐπι ἡμερας πολλας</note>. *The Emperor, therefore, along with the Senate, the people, and the entire clergy, prayed to God [barefoot] for many days.* 

It is established from Cassian <note>John Cassian (c. 360–435 AD), a monk and theologian who brought Eastern monastic traditions to the West.</note> (*On the Habit of Monks*, Book 1, Chapter 10) that certain Egyptian monks used no shoes. Francisco Álvares <note>A Portuguese missionary who provided one of the first detailed European accounts of Ethiopia.</note> (*Description of Ethiopia*, Chapter 12) testifies that Ethiopians always enter their churches barefooted. That our ancestors sometimes did the same while singing the Litany is evident from the <margin>b)</margin> Council of Mainz, held in the year 813 AD during the time of Charlemagne and Pope Leo III under Archbishop Richulf. Chapter 33 of that Council states: *It has pleased us that the Great Litany should be observed by all Christians for three days, just as we find in our reading and as the Holy Fathers established: not riding on horseback, nor dressed in precious garments [but walking], unless illness prevents it.* 

Wherefore President Fauchet <note>Claude Fauchet (1530–1601), a French historian and magistrate.</note> (Book 2, Chapter 49, *On the State of Religion under Clovis*) lists BAREFOOTEDNESS <note>original Latin: NUDIPEDALIA</note> among the many rites that flowed into the Church from the Gentiles and the Jews. They do so for:
(2) Hypocritical ostentation and boasting in their vows, as if they were those who, above other Christians, have undertaken to do more than God commanded.

God's gifts are to be used according to the condition and rank of each person, and for the glory of the Giver. Just as in the past pride shone through the torn cloak of the Philosopher <note>This refers to a famous anecdote about the Cynic philosopher Antisthenes; Socrates is said to have told him, "I can see your vanity through the holes in your cloak."</note>, so today it often shines through affected clothing. And just as neither the military cloak, nor the sword-belt, nor crowds of attendants harm a religious mind, so on the other hand, a cheap little cloak, a yellowish tunic, bodily filth, and feigned poverty profit nothing for a man who is either profane or a hypocrite, as Jerome well teaches to Salvina <note>A Roman noblewoman to whom Jerome wrote a letter regarding widowhood and the spiritual life.</note>.* That is all!

Paul responds to an objection regarding the difference in spiritual gifts by stating that everyone has received everything from the one Christ. He proves this in verse 8 by the authority of Psalm 68:19 <note>The author uses the Vulgate numbering, Psalm LXVIII. 19; in modern Bibles, this is Psalm 68:18.</note>. This statement is further explained in verses 9 and 10, where there is a contrast between the descent and ascent of Christ. Regarding verse 9, the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> observes two things. First, that the descent preceded the ascent: *“Now this, ‘He ascended’—what does it mean but that He also first descended?”* <note>original: Τὸ δὲ ἀνέβη, τί ἐστιν, εἰ μὴ, ὅτι καὶ κατέβη πρῶτον.</note> Second, that He descended into the lower parts of the earth: *HE DESCENDED INTO THE LOWER PARTS OF THE EARTH.* <note>original: ΚΑΤΕΒΗ ΕIC ΤΑ ΚΑΤΩΤΕΡΑ ΜΕΡΗ ΤΗC ΓΗC.</note> These are the very words upon which we now intend to test our analytical strength. To do this in an orderly fashion, we will first provide a brief <term>anaskeue: a rhetorical refutation of an opponent's argument</term> of those opinions we find inconsistent with the Apostle's meaning, before offering a more detailed <term>kataskeue: the confirmation or positive proof of one's own position</term> of the interpretation we accept.

II. We have observed six different schools of thought here in total. Those who err most crudely, whom we place at the forefront, are those who imagine Christ’s descent into hell in a literal sense. <note>original: κυρίως (kyrios), meaning 'literally' or 'properly speaking'.</note> The Roman Catholics <note>original: "Pontificii," referring to those loyal to the Pope.</note> err more harshly in this, while many of our Lutheran brothers err more mildly. Hence, there are two "horns" <note>A logical metaphor referring to the branches of a dilemma or argument.</note> of this opinion. The horn with which the Roman Catholics strike us is two-headed. For there are those who want the text to refer to the "Limbo of the Fathers" <term>Limbo of the Fathers: a theological concept of a place where the souls of the righteous who died before Christ's resurrection were held</term>, whom we feel no need to refute. Let them prove to us with more solid reasons than they have so far that such a "Limbo of the Nations" ever existed anywhere or at any time. Then, indeed, we will consider whether the Apostle was referring to it. There are others who fabricate a literal hell here; while many agree on the place, they fight tooth and nail over the purpose. Some think that there were new pains remaining for Christ to endure in hell. We demand of these: with what audacity do they dare—while all of Scripture is silent—to assign new pains to our Savior after His perfect completion of suffering on the cross? Others want it that Christ showed Himself a victor in hell, led out the Patriarchs, and bound the Prince of Darkness. To these, before we delve into their opinion, we propose they must prove: (1) that Hell exists in the center of the earth, where they quite recklessly place it; (2) that the Patriarchs, contrary to the clear faith of Scripture, were shut up in that place they designate until the time of Christ; (3) that the Savior [did this] by any means...

III. We come now to those theologians of the Augsburg Confession <note>A reference to Lutherans, who adhere to the 1530 Augsburg Confession</note> who, while speaking more modestly, yet still not quite correctly, assert that Christ descended into hell for these purposes: (1) that He might fulfill all things, (2) that He might show Himself as victor, (3) that He might institute a legal preaching <note>A formal proclamation of judgment</note> before the damned, and (4) that He might sing a victory song <term>epinicium: a hymn or song celebrating a triumph</term> based on Hosea 13:14 and 1 Corinthians 15:26. For besides the fact that Eusebius’s reliability is suspect in many matters, this concerns a story that is entirely false: namely, the miraculous healing of Abgar. With better justification, they cite Irenaeus's *Against Heresies* chapter 31; Tertullian's *On the Soul* chapter 55; Origen's *15th Homily on Genesis*, his *2nd Book Against Celsus*, and his *Commentary on the Books of Kings*; Cyril of Jerusalem’s *Catechism* 4 and 14; Ambrose’s *On the Paschal Mystery* chapter 4; and Jerome’s *Works*, Volume IX, *Commentary on this passage*, etc.

# ON THE DESCENT OF CHRIST TO HELL.

Let us examine these points individually; it is worth the effort. There are five in number. (1) The first is taken from the **Apostle’s** <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul</note> purpose. But truly, when he tries to bolster a false hypothesis here with other falsehoods, what truth can be established from it? He says, along with **Calovius** <note>Abraham Calov (1612–1686), a prominent Lutheran orthodox theologian</note>, that the **Apostle’s** purpose is to describe the triumph and majesty of Christ; but that is exactly what we deny. He wishes to establish from this, **(a) that the purpose of Psalm LXVIII is the same, from which the Apostle draws certain words.** But how this follows logically, let those with sharper eyes determine. Just as the **descent of Christ to hell** (to use the phrase in the sense they do) is a fable, so too is that "captivity of hell." I know, indeed, that even sensible <note>original: "cordatis," literally "having a heart," implying wisdom or sound judgment</note> theologians do not agree on the meaning of these words. ### ON CHRIST’S DESCENT INTO THE UNDERWORLD.

...and so on. Therefore, both premises are false, and the whole mass of these hypotheses will collapse if we demonstrate another goal of the Apostle in Section 26. The remaining arguments for this matter in Carpzovius are of such a kind that they can be easily struck down based on what has already been said.

V. He builds (2) his hypothesis from the opposition between *ascent and descent*. He argues that the *ascent is literal; therefore, the corresponding descent must also be literal*. <term>℞.</term> <note>original: "℞." stands for "Responsio," the author's reply to an opponent's objection.</note> The force of this argument by itself proves nothing conclusively (for it is not unusual among two opposite terms for one to be taken literally and the other figuratively). Thus, it might have some weight if joined with other points, were it not for the fact that the foundation on which it rests is wobbling. He tries to prove it (3) *from the opposition between "heaven" and the "lower parts of the earth."* But indeed, I believe I have more successfully reclaimed this point in Sections 21 and 22, to which I refer the reader. Here, I generally advise that one should not understand "the highest places" by the phrase *far above all heavens* <note>original Greek: ὑπερανω παντων οὐρανων (hyperanō pantōn ouranōn)</note>, nor the "lowest depths" by the *lower parts of the earth*. Carpzovius himself partially acknowledges the latter when, following the mind of Theophylact <note>Theophylact of Ohrid, an 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator.</note>, he teaches that this phrase is *not to be explained literally, but according to common opinion, likeness, and analogy*. I prefer to explain the former using the words of the great Wittichius <note>Christoph Wittich (1625–1687), a Reformed theologian who sought to reconcile Cartesian philosophy with scripture.</note> in his *Theological Exercises* II, Section 46: *Just as the words "far above all heavens" are not to be twisted as if the meaning were that Christ ascended to a place where there are no heavens—since it is clear that through the ascent Christ was raised into heaven—so too one should not fashion a "center of the earth" out of the "lower parts of the earth."* He asserts his point (4) *from the "filling of all things."* The words of the text, he says, flow thus: "He who descended is the same as he who also ascended, so that he might fill all things." *Behold! How the Apostle also makes the "filling of all things" the goal of the descent which he now describes.* Up to this point, that "Great Man" [Carpzovius] was tolerable, but by no means when he proceeds to fight with the weapons of Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a powerful Jesuit Cardinal and leading figure of the Catholic Counter-Reformation. For Christ wished to descend even to the true hell, just as he had descended into the lands, so that he might visit all parts of his kingdom, which is threefold, according to that passage in Philippians 2: "That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth." The "man in purple" <note>original: *Purpuratus*. (a) If he literally fulfilled all things, did he also penetrate the waters? VI. The second opinion is held by those who understand the *lower parts of the earth* <note>original Greek: κατωτέρα μέρη της γης (katōtera merē tēs gēs)</note> as the incarnation of Christ <note>Meaning Christ "descending" from heaven to take on human flesh on earth.</note>. Also Eusebius in *Demonstration* VI, chapter 2; Proclus in his *Epistle to the Armenians*; Basil in *Homily 25*; and Bernard in his *Sermon 1 on the Advent of the Lord*. Among more recent authors, they have been followed by Arias Montanus, Paul Fagius, John Cameron, Robert Bellarmine (though as usual he is hardly consistent with himself), Schindler, Georg Calixtus, Hunnius, Maresius, Arnold, and, though hesitantly, Theodore Beza and Johannes Piscator. They borrow a splendid argument from *Psalm 139:15*, where David says he was formed *in the lowest parts of the earth* <note>original Hebrew: בתחתיות ארץ (be-tachtiyyot aretz)</note>. Some think that in this passage, this phrase designates—not incorrectly—the dark and secluded place of the mother's womb, since it is familiar in the Scriptures to use the emblem of "earth" to foreshadow a notable darkness. But in truth, it can be objected: (1) it is one phrase to *descend into the lower parts of the earth*, and another to be *formed in the lowest parts*. (2) The opposition <note>The rhetorical contrast between ascending to heaven and descending to earth.</note> is not as evident as I believe must be urged, especially in this passage. Compare Section 21. Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a leading defender of Lutheran Orthodoxy.</note> in his *System of Theology*, vol. Therefore, he argues these things cannot be understood as Christ's descent into his mother’s womb. However, it quite frequently pleased the Holy Spirit to speak <term>synecdoche</term> <note>A figure of speech where a part of something is used to represent the whole, or the whole to represent a part.</note> and to affirm of the whole what is true only of a part.

# DISSERTATION

VII. The third place is occupied by those who simply understand the phrase as referring to the earth, so that one part of the earth is not compared with another, but rather the whole earth is compared with heaven. The sense, in their view, is that Christ descended from so high a seat into our deep abyss <note>original: *barathrum*. A term from Greek mythology for a deep pit or chasm, used here to describe the vast difference between heaven and earth.</note>. Most of the **Scholastics** <note>Medieval theologians who used logic and philosophy to explain Christian doctrine.</note> are of this mind, including **Anselm** in this passage, **Peter Lombard**, **Aquinas**, and **Lyranus**. Joining them are **Cajetan**, **Catharinus**, **Grotius**, **Calvin**, **Aretius**, **Hemmingius**, and others. **Bodius** claims that **Augustine** belonged to this same party, though I am not sure if he is entirely correct. However, all these men, while holding this opinion, satisfy neither the phrase "lower parts" <note>original Greek: *κατωτερα ΜΕΡΗ* (katōtera merē)</note>, nor the **analogy of Holy Scripture** <term>The principle that any interpretation of a specific verse must be consistent with the rest of the Bible</term>, nor, finally, the illustrious opposition between the ascent and descent of Christ.

VIII. Others approach this opinion closely and believe that *the Apostle signifies the supreme dejection of Christ*—these are the words of **Bochart** regarding this view in his *Letter to Tapinus, Works, Vol. I, page 985*—*by these words, which are opposed to that glory which he now enjoys above the heavens.* **Glassius**, **Brentius**, **Hakspan**, **Bullinger**, **Crocius**, **Schmidt**, and others agree with this. They frequently have on their lips that saying of **Theophylact** <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and influential Bible commentator.</note>: *It is clear that since he was in the highest places, he descended through the incarnation into the earth and through death into the underworld* <note>original Greek: *Δηλον ὁτι ἀνω ὡν κατεβη και σαρκουμενος εἰς την γην και θανων εἰς τον ἁδην*</note>. Why we do not agree with the first part of this opinion was explained in section VI; why we do not agree with the latter part will be stated in section IX. Meanwhile, arguments are offered in defense of the more distinguished scholars we are dealing with here. They bring forward (1) the analogy of Holy Scripture: *Psalm 139:1, "To cry out of the depths"* <note>The author likely intends Psalm 130:1, the "De Profundis."</note> and *Psalm 61:3, "To cry from the ends of the earth"* are the same as crying out from the deepest anguish of one's heart and profound temptation. They also cite *Job 30:8*, where it is said of the vilest of lowly men: *they are children of no name, they were driven out of the land* <note>original Hebrew: *בני בלי שם נכאו מן הארץ* (bene beli-shem nik’u min ha’aretz). The Latin translates this as "pressed down lower than the earth."</note>. From these and other similar passages, they conclude what has been said. But in response: (a) the entire phrase must be considered together if possible, not just one or two words; nor is the logical deduction valid that because *the depths of the earth*, *Sheol* <note>The Hebrew place of the dead.</note>, or *Tehom* <note>The primordial deep or abyss.</note> denote miseries and the deepest humiliation, therefore "descending into the lower parts of the earth" must mean being afflicted with these kinds of calamities. (b) Nor does this interpretation fit the context of all the passages they bring forward. (2) They think there is an opposition here...

here [comparing] the entire state of humiliation and exaltation among themselves. **Response** <note>original: *℞*, an abbreviation for *Responsio* (Response)</note>: It can be proven only with difficulty, since the "session at the right hand of God" <note>The theological concept of Christ taking his place of honor in heaven.</note> is also a degree of Christ's exaltation, yet it can be proven by no reasoning that it is alluded to here. (3) By the authority of **Chrysostom** (whose words see in the following section) and **Theophylact**, they assign a different goal to the Apostle here. They think that by presenting Christ as an example, he is warning us that, just as He did not refuse to descend, so we also should not refuse to lower ourselves through humility and condescend to others, or to be compliant. **Response**: From an inspection of the Text, it is most clearly evident that in the immediately preceding verses the Apostle is exhorting us not to humility, but to the unity of the Spirit. It is therefore false that Christ is being proposed as an example of humility. Add to this the points we have already opposed to the opinions of others at the end of the preceding section.

IX. A fifth line of battle is drawn up by those who claim that death is designated by Paul in the phrase we are explaining. This is the view of **Theodoret**, and **Photius**—who is somewhat inconsistent with **Theophylact** and **Oecumenius**. **Chrysostom**, a follower of the same opinion, presents their collected arguments in this place:

> *What he establishes in the epistle to the Philippians, he also does here. Just as there, when advising on humility of mind, he introduces Christ, so he does in this place also, from the fact that He descended into the lower parts of the earth. For unless this were so, that speech which he spoke there would be empty—namely, that He was made obedient even unto death. Indeed, he shows His descent from His ascent; he called death the "lower parts of the earth," and this from the assumption and opinion of men. Just as Jacob said: "You will bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the lower world" <note>original: *inferos*. Referring to the grave or the realm of the dead.</note>, and David in the Psalm: "I shall be like those who go down into the pit."*

But indeed, we charge this very Father—though he be "Golden-mouthed" <note>original Greek: *χρυσοῦ στόματος* (chrysou stomatos), the literal meaning of the name Chrysostom</note>—with inconsistency first of all. Behold his words from *Exposition on the Apostles' Creed, Homily 2*:

> *He descended to the lower regions, so that the miracle would not be absent there. For many bodies of the saints rose with Christ, who afterwards died. And again in "Demonstration of the Gospel against the Gentiles": Furthermore, He descended to hell, disturbed everyone, and destroyed the fortress filled with tumult and confusion; hear concerning this those making an uproar in the lower regions and saying: "Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, you everlasting doors" <note>A reference to Psalm 24, traditionally interpreted as Christ entering the gates of Hades.</note> etc.*

Nor am I surprised by this division <note>Or "divergence of opinion."</note> of the great man.

### ON THE DESCENT OF CHRIST INTO HELL.
### 519

here they connect the entire state of humiliation and exaltation to one another. <note>The symbol ℞ is used here as "Respondeo" or "Response" to an opposing argument.</note> **Response.** It is only with difficulty that this can be proven, since the "sitting at the right hand of God" is a degree of Christ’s exaltation, yet it can be proven by no reasoning that such an allusion is intended here. (3) On the authority of **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching.</note> (whose words see in the following section) and **Theophylact** <note>Theophylact of Ohrid (c. 1055–1107 AD), a Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator.</note>, they attribute a different goal to the Apostle here. They think that by presenting Christ as an example, Paul warns us that just as Christ did not refuse to descend, so we should not shrink from lowering ourselves through humility and condescending to others, or complying with them. **Response.** From an inspection of the Text, it appears most clearly that in the verses immediately preceding, the Apostle is exhorting us not to humility, but to the unity of the Spirit. It is therefore false that Christ is being proposed here as an example of humility. Add to these points those arguments which we have already opposed to the opinions of others at the end of the preceding section.

IX. A fifth line of battle is formed by those who argue that the phrase we are explaining was intended by Paul to signify **death**. This is the view of **Theodoret**, as well as **Photius**—who is somewhat inconsistent with himself—along with **Theophylact** and **Oecumenius**. **Chrysostom**, a follower of this same opinion, presents their collected arguments on this passage: *“What he asserts in the letter to the Philippians, he also does here. Just as there, when admonishing regarding humility of mind, he introduces Christ, so also in this place, he does so from the fact that He descended into the lower parts of the earth. For unless this were so, that discourse he spoke there would be empty—namely, that He was made obedient even unto death. From the ascent, however, he suggests His descent; he called the 'lower parts of the earth' death, and he did so based on the common assumption and opinion of men. Just as Jacob also said: 'You will bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the underworld,' <note>original: "ad inferos," referring to the grave or the realm of the dead.</note> and David in the Psalm: 'I will be like those who go down into the pit.'”*

But indeed, to this very Father, though he be of the <term xml:lang="grc">Golden</term> <term xml:lang="grc">Mouth</term> <note>original Greek: χρυσου ςοματος (chrysou stomatos). This is a pun on the name "Chrysostom," which means "Golden-Mouthed" in Greek, acknowledging his status as a great orator while still critiquing his logic.</note>, we first of all reproach his own inconsistency. Behold his words in his *Exposition on the Apostles' Creed*, Homily 2: *“He descended to the lower regions, so that there he might not be without a miracle. For many bodies of the saints rose with Christ, who afterwards died.”* And again in his *Demonstration of the Gospel against the Heathen*: *“Moreover, He descended to hell, disturbed all, and destroyed the citadel filled with tumult and confusion; hear concerning this those making an uproar in the lower regions and saying: 'Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, you infernal gates,' etc.”* Nor am I surprised at this disagreement of so great a man.
