->DISSERTATION<-

<page-num>520</page-num>

The weapon with which he fought, though three-pronged <note>original: "trisulcum"</note>, was nevertheless feeble. For indeed, (1) he attributes the same goal to the Apostle which we refuted in the preceding section. (2) He claims the opinion of men, that is, the common usage of the phrase, but he considers that usage (a) to be ambiguous and (b) looks at the phrase in isolation rather than in the joined connection of the words. (3) The passages of Holy Scripture which he brings forward we understand as referring to the burial with the same—perhaps even greater—justification than he understands them as referring to death. The remaining points which could be opposed to him in Sections VI and VII have already been so thoroughly executed that it is not necessary to add more.

### X.

The opinion which I have reserved for the sixth place is also my own. For in this passage, by the **descent into the lower parts of the earth** <note>original Greek: "κατάβασιν εἰς τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς"</note>, I understand nothing other than **the final stage of Christ's humiliation** (these are the words of the celebrated **Wittichius** <note>Christoph Wittich (1625–1687), a Dutch Cartesian theologian who sought to reconcile science and scripture.</note> in the work cited below) **by which it happened that he even willed to be hidden within the earth, and thus to enter the place of corruption, as the opposite to the highest degree of exaltation, by which he was raised above all visible heavens.** I know that the ancient Fathers of the early church went in entirely different directions. I have found few who would walk in step with this opinion. Among the rare traces of this view, I refer here to **Anastasius of Nicaea** <note>Likely referring to Anastasius I of Antioch (d. 599), sometimes called Anastasius of Nicaea, a prolific theological writer.</note>, who says in *Question 89*: *It is necessary to consider that time of the three-day burial, during which he was truly in the heart of the earth. Moreover, he was there after he breathed his last, when he had descended, as the Apostle says, into the lower parts of the earth.* And **Anastasius Sinaita** <note>A 7th-century Greek monk and abbot of Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai.</note> in *On the Dogmas of the Faith*, Book V: *The Savior rose after nearly three days and, having left behind the shackles of corruption in the sepulcher, he was established as the firstborn from the dead. For he descended into the lower parts of the earth, and entered into its heart.*

Truly, that perpetual disagreement of the Fathers has moved us very little—even though antiquity adds value to the learned explanations of the sacred pages, just as it does to perfumes and wines. The saying of **Lactantius Firmianus** <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine I.</note> fits here, not only regarding the first masters of pagan superstition, but also regarding any other teachers, in Book II of *On the Origin of Error*, chapter 8: *They strip themselves of wisdom who, without any judgment, approve the discoveries of their ancestors and are led by others in the manner of cattle.* And **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420), best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> on *Psalm LXXXVI*: *Although someone may be holy after the Apostles, and although he may be eloquent, he does not have authority.* The same most learned Father, with his usual modesty, says of himself in his *Apology against Jovinian*: *Concerning myself, whenever I do not interpret the scriptures, but*... <note>The text ends here, with the catchword "libere" (freely) indicating the start of the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of his specific interpretation of the "descent into the lower parts of the earth." ->CONCERNING THE DESCENT OF CHRIST INTO THE UNDERWORLD.<-

<header>ON THE DESCENT OF CHRIST TO THE UNDERWORLD</header>

*I speak my mind freely; let anyone who wishes rebuke me. Truly, antiquity was ignorant of many things that posterity has seen more clearly. Consider the same to be true of our own statement: that great men have finally dragged this matter out of the shadows and placed it in its proper light. The esteemed Cocceius* <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian famous for "Federal Theology."</note>*, both elsewhere and specifically in his work against Masenius's "Proofs of Scripture" (Chapter 1), argues this point: to prove that the "lower parts of the earth" are those things which are beneath the ground, where the corpses of men and the roots of trees are found. Compare this with Wittich's "Theological Exercises" II, § 46. Nor do those of the Augsburg Confession think otherwise, such as Calixtus* <note>Georg Calixtus (1586–1656), a Lutheran theologian who sought to find common ground between denominations.</note>*, or from our own tradition, Parker, Lavater, Drusius, Burman, Momma, Heidegger, and others. I would list more, if I thought this matter should be settled by a list of witnesses rather than by arguments. These arguments I shall now pursue more extensively.*

### XI.

The first argument I bring forward is from the **CLEAR SENSE OF THE INDIVIDUAL WORDS**, which, whether considered one by one or all together, correspond most suitably to our interpretation. First, we encounter:

(1) **TO DESCEND** <note>original Greek: "KATABAINEIN"</note>. I admit this word is frequently used for those who travel to "hell" <note>original: "infernum"</note> simply defined. It is a common phrase among the Rabbis: *they descend into Gehenna* <note>original Hebrew: "יורדין לגיהנם" (yordin l'gehinnom)</note>. However, even this can be easily explained in our favor based on their own hypothesis, since they establish a "double Gehenna"—an upper and a lower—and by the "upper," they understand the grave itself. The poet Virgil says in *Aeneid* Book VI, *The descent to Avernus is easy* <note>Avernus was a volcanic crater lake near Naples, believed by Romans to be the entrance to the underworld.</note>. Lucian elegantly paraphrases this in his *Dialogues of the Dead* (between Diogenes and Alexander): *Is it lawful for anyone to return who has once sailed across the lake and proceeded into the mouth of the cave?* <note>original Greek: "Θέμις ἀνελθεῖν τινα τῶν ἅπαξ διαπλευσάντων τὴν λίμνην, καὶ ἐς τὸ εἴσω τοῦ στομίου προελθόντων."</note> But these and similar examples, twisted from the fables of the pagans, move us very little.

Properly speaking, **to descend** <note>original Greek: "katabainein"</note> signifies a change from a higher place to a lower one, as is seen everywhere. Figuratively, it is transferred either to a human being who is humbled in any way, or to God, noting either a manifestation of God (whether gracious or coming for judgment) or the humiliation of Christ. Taken finally in this sense, the word can be attributed to Christ in two ways:

(a) Through the **Incarnation**, as he descended into the womb of Mary and onto this earth. Compare John 3:13, 6:33, 37, 41, 42, 50, 51, 58; 1 Thessalonians 4:16; James 1:17; and Isaiah 64:1. From this, some derive the name of **Jared** (who was the father of Enoch) from the word *to descend* <note>original Hebrew: "ירד" (yarad)</note>, because it might hint at the expectation of the descents of the Messiah. See Ursinus’s *Meletemata*, Book I, page 11, number 66. Indeed, many of the ancients were persuaded that all human souls [descended] from...

<header>DISSERTATION</header>

...sublime to descend into this world. To this refers what Celsus said in the works of Origen <note>Celsus was a 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of early Christianity; his works are known primarily through Origen's rebuttal, "Against Celsus."</note>: *that souls fell from the vaults of heaven* <note>original Greek: "apo tōn apsidōn tou ouranou"</note>: *for it happened that, being drawn down by a certain natural charm* <note>original Greek: "iungi tini physikē kataspōmenai"</note> *and leaning toward the inferior part, they drank from the river Lethe <note>In Greek mythology, the river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note> of the corruptible region even unto intoxication; and soon, forgetting themselves and suffering a loss of wings* <note>original Greek: "pterorrhuyēsin"</note>*, they slipped through the Northern Gate into the lower orb.* Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial and author.</note> has much on the same subject in his *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, Book I. Also, Clement of Alexandria <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 150–215 AD).</note> in *Stromata* I, quoting Plato, says: *Good souls, having left the super-heavenly place, endured coming into this Tartarus* <note>original Greek: "elthein eis tonde ton tartaron"</note>, *that is, to come into this worldly Tartarus.* The same author in *Stromata* III says regarding the Philosophers: *they lead down the soul, which is divine, into the world as if into a prison-house* <note>original Greek: "kathaper eis to kolastērion ton kosmon"</note>. Hence in Homer there are *two gates*, which are *descents for men* <note>original Greek: "kataibatai anthrōpōn"</note> by which humans may descend. And an oracle in Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher-bishop.</note> warns:

> *Do not lean down toward the dark-shining world.* <note>original Greek: "Mēde katō neusēs eis ton melanaugea kosmon"</note>

That is: *Do not incline downward toward a world lacking in light.* However, the Anabaptists <note>A radical Reformation group; the author here attacks their "celestial flesh" Christology, which claimed Christ's body was not made of human flesh from Mary but of heavenly substance.</note> are dealing in trifles when they assert, based on the nature of this phrasing, that Christ brought down his human nature from heaven—formed from the essence of the Father and the Holy Spirit, or from the dew of the eternal Divinity, or from celestial, starry, or elementary matter—and that he merely passed through Mary like water through a channel, or solar rays through glass.

(b) Our Savior *descended* in a far more illustrious way when he descended into the tomb. The word *to descend* <note>original Hebrew: "yarad" (ירד)</note> is very frequent in this sense in the Old Testament <note>referred to here as the "Old Instrument"</note>, with the Greeks almost always translating it as *to descend* <note>original Greek: "katabainein" (καταβαίνειν)</note>. See, if you please, Genesis 37:34, Exodus 15:5, Job 7:9, 17:16, Psalms 30:11, 55:16, 88:4, 106:26, 113:26, Ezekiel 31:15, etc. Hence the Hebrews say: *They descend into the depths of the grave.* <note>original Hebrew: "Yoredu be-ma’amake ha-keber" (יורדו במעמקי הקבר)</note> Rabbi Levi ben Gerson <note>A 14th-century Jewish philosopher and commentator also known as Gersonides.</note> on Proverbs 9: *To go into destruction.* <note>original Hebrew: "Yelek le-abaddon" (ילך לאבדון)</note> The Greeks say *to descend into Hades* <note>original Greek: "aidan katabainein"</note>, meaning to descend into the tomb. Sophocles in *Antigone*, line 816, uses *to descend* <note>original Greek: "katabainein"</note> simply to mean *to die*. In the *Greek Anthology*, Book 3: *to be beneath the earth* <note>original Greek: "einai hypo chthona"</note>. Pindar in the *Isthmians*: *to go down* <note>original Greek: "apienai katō"</note>. Euripides in *Hecuba*, line 418: *To sink into the multi-bedded Hades* <note>original Greek: "Dynai ton polykoinon hadan"</note>. Sophocles in *Ajax*, line 1264: *To walk the final road* <note>original Greek: "Tan neatan hodon steichein"</note>. Ibid, *Antigone*, line 804. The Latins: *to go to the lowest Tartarus* <note>original Latin: "ire ad imum Tartara"</note>. Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* Book VI: *to depart from here to the common place* <note>original Latin: "abire hinc in communem locum"</note>. Plautus in the prologue of *Casina*, line 19: *To enter the mound of the earth* <note>original Latin: "Tumulo succedere terrae"</note>.

<meta>This page continues the philological investigation into the term "descending." While the previous page addressed the philosophical idea of souls "descending" into bodies or the world, this section focuses on the linguistic connection between "descending" and the grave as an "eternal house" or a "dwelling of the dead."</meta>

<page-num>523</page-num>

<header>ON THE DESCENT OF CHRIST TO THE UNDERWORLD.</header>

Virgil, *Aeneid* Book XI: *To come to the shadows.* <note>original Latin: "Venire ad umbras"</note> Juvenal, *Satire* X, etc.

XII. A refined explanation for this figurative, yet very frequent, meaning can be provided. The Hebrews, Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans describe the tomb as a place enclosed by a fence, a house with its own gates and keys, into which it is permitted for the dead to descend. Thus, Job 17:13: *the grave is my house* <note>original Hebrew: "sheol beiti"</note>; *the gates of death* <note>original: "portae mortis"</note> in Job 38:17 and Psalm 107:18; and Psalm 49:12: *Their graves are their houses forever* <note>original Latin: "Sepulchra eorum domus eorum in seculum"</note>. In the Chaldee Paraphrase <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> for Isaiah 14:15 and Ezekiel 26:20, it is called the *house of destruction* <note>original Chaldee: "beit abdana"</note>, that is, the tomb or the pit; and in Ecclesiastes 12:4, it is the *house of burial* <note>original: "beit keburata"</note>. The Rabbis hold the same view regarding the passage in Proverbs 31:21: *She is not afraid for her household because of the snow*, as can be seen in the *Lekach Tov* <note>A midrashic commentary on the Pentateuch and Five Scrolls.</note> on Isaiah: for these same people, the tomb is the *house of his world* or *house of his eternity* <note>original: "beit olamo"</note>. For this reason, we also find in Revelation 1:18: *the keys of death and of Hades* <note>original Greek: "kleis tou thanatou kai tou hadou"</note>.

Regarding the Egyptians, there is an elegant passage in Diodorus Siculus <note>A 1st-century BC Greek historian.</note>, Book I: *The inhabitants of this region consider the time of life to be circumscribed by small limits, but they value most highly that which will have a famous memory of virtue after death. And they call the dwellings of the living "inns," as we inhabit them for a short time. But they call the tombs of the deceased "eternal houses," because they spend an infinite age in the underworld.* <note>The author quotes Diodorus in Greek first—"tous de tōn tetelutēkotōn taphous aidious oikous prosagoreuousin"—and then provides the Latin translation.</note> *Consequently, they are less concerned about the construction of houses, but they spare no effort regarding tombs.* 

In Homer, the phrase *the house of Hades* <note>original Greek: "dōm’ aidao"</note> is frequent in the *Odyssey* (Book 4 and 11) and the *Iliad* (Book 15). It appears as *the house of Hades* <note>original Greek: "Aidou dōma"</note> in Theognis (v. 1007 and 1117). Sophocles calls it an *ever-guarding dwelling* <note>original Greek: "Oikēsis aeiphrouros"</note> in *Antigone* (v. 885). Who has not said this? This is reflected in many Roman inscriptions. This appears on the Stone of Pola in Illyria in Gruter <note>Jan Gruter, a 16th-century scholar famous for his collection of ancient inscriptions.</note> (p. 804), which we provide here:

-> MANILIA PAULLA <-
-> FROM HER OWN PATRIMONY <-
-> FOR HERSELF AND <-
-> AURELIUS PAULLINUS <-

XIII. (2) The place into which Christ descended is first described generally as *PARTS*. <note>original Greek: "ΜΕΡΗ" (mere)</note> Regarding this word, we observe briefly: no small difficulty arises here for those who understand Paul’s statement <note>referring to Ephesians 4:9: "He also descended first into the lower parts of the earth."</note> as referring to hell. Truly, if Christ descended into a *part of the earth*, he did not descend into hell. For hell *is not a part of the earth*. Whatever is contained within a thing is not immediately a "part" of that thing which acts as the container. By the same logic, those who take this to mean a universal descent to the earth can be refuted. Christ descended into the *parts of the earth*. I see it could be objected here that Judea is a part of the earth into which Christ lowered himself. Those who feel this way should consider by what reasoning Judea could be called a *lower* part of the earth. For it is well known to be a very mountainous region, rising above others, which is why some think it was called the *navel of the earth* <note>original Hebrew: "tabbur ha-aretz"</note> in Ezekiel 38:12, the kind of places the Greeks call *breasts* <note>original Greek: "μαζοὺς" (mazous)</note> or *breast-shaped*. <note>original Greek: "μαζοειδεῖς" (mazoeideis)</note> From this same origin comes the fact that the ancients placed the center of the earth (specifically of our hemisphere, which was all that most ancients knew of) in Judea. See Caelius Rhodiginus, *Ancient Lessons*, Book XV, chapter 20; Casaubon, *Exercises against Baronius*, XVI, chapter 83, etc. Whatever the case may be, Luther was not satisfactory when he translated the Greek word for "parts" <note>original: "μέρη"</note> simply as: **Places**. <note>original German: "Oerter"</note> Truly, Christ descended (3) *INTO* <note>original Greek: "ΕΙC" (eis)</note> the parts, which is rightly translated as *WITHIN* the parts; since this meaning is very well known, we will not dwell on it long, but prepare ourselves for the remaining points.

# ON THE DESCENT OF CHRIST INTO THE UNDERWORLD.

**LOWER** *parts* <note>original Greek: "ΚΑΤΩΤΕΡΑ μερη"; original Latin: "inferiores partes"</note>. The comparative degree can be explained simply: they are "lower" parts in respect to others that are "higher." This is especially clear from our hypothesis. For just as a tomb is hidden beneath the earth, so it is lower than the surface. Furthermore, the Savior descended into the lower parts, *not the lowest* <note>original: "non infimas"</note>, or the center of the earth, where some fictitiously imagine hell to be. Although these points are true, the observation of the great Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note> is not unpleasing; he thinks Saint Paul had an eye on Psalm 68:9, which deals with the descent of God onto Sinai. According to his mind, when the law was being brought by the ministry of Angels, Christ descended from heaven to a "higher" earth, such as Mount Sinai was. His descent was "lower" by far when he descended into the tomb and the hidden parts of the earth. Meanwhile, the terms *the below* and *lower parts* <note>original Greek: "τα κατω" (ta kato) and "κατωτερα μερη" (katotera mere)</note> are generally a designation for any lower thing as opposed to a higher one. Thus in the Old Testament we see: <term>tachtonoth</term> <note>Hebrew: תחתנות; "lower parts," used for the depths of the earth or lower stories of a building</note> in Ezekiel 42:5, 41:7, and 40:18; <term>tachtonah</term> <note>Hebrew: תחתונת; "lowest"</note> in Isaiah 22:9; and <term>tachtith</term> <note>Hebrew: תחתית; "lower/underneath"</note> in Joshua 15:19. No less frequently are these words used to designate subterranean places. So the particle <term>tachat</term> <note>Hebrew: תחת; "under" or "beneath"</note> in Genesis 49:26, Exodus 20:4, and Job 18:6. To this exactly corresponds the positive Greek term *below* <note>original: "κατω" (kato)</note>, which is why the underworld among them is frequently called *the below*. Lucian, in his *Dialogue on Mourning*: *Bearing witness before the judges of the underworld.* <note>original Greek: "μαρτυρουντες παρα τοις κατω δικασαις"; original Latin translation provided: "Testimonium perhibentes apud inferni judices"</note> In the same work: *As those who will use and enjoy those things there in the underworld.* <note>original Greek: "Ως χρησομενοις ἐκει και ἀπολαυσουσιν ἀυτοις κατω"; original Latin: "Quibus fruuntur illic in inferno"</note> Hence the term *the gods below* in Diodorus Siculus, Book I. Aristophanes in *The Frogs*:
HERACLES: *Will you then descend into the lower Hades?*
DIONYSUS: *And by Zeus, yes, if there is anything even lower.* <note>original Greek: "HP. Ποτερον εἰς Ἀιδου κατω; ΔΙ. Και νη Δι’, εἰ τι γ’ ἐσιν ἐτι κατωτερω."</note>
Compare the same author in *The Pythagorista*. Specifically, the *tomb* is noted in Sophocles' *Ajax*, line 931:
*But the rest I shall tell to those below in the grave.* <note>original Greek: "Τα δ’ ἀλλ’ ἐν ᾅδου τοις κατω μυθησομαι"; here "Hades" is interpreted as the grave</note>
In the *Anthology*, Book III:
*How much better are the things below than those which Zeus possesses.* <note>original Greek: "Ωσῳ τα κατω κρειττω ’σιν ὡν ὁ ζους ἐχει"</note>
Euripides in *Hecuba*, line 418:
*O mother, O you who gave me birth, I am now going below.*
*And there in the grave I shall lie apart from you.* <note>original Greek: "Ω μητερ, ὦ τεκουσ’, ἀπειμι δη κατω. Ἐκει δ’ ἐν ᾅδου κεισομαι χωρις σεθεν."</note>

XV. I proceed. (5) THE EARTH <note>original Greek: "Η ΓΗ"; Latin: "terra"</note>: in a general sense, whatever is outside of heaven, or under heaven. There is no difficulty in this that I can see. I only note this: even if the other terms were omitted and the primary reasons converged, we would not be acting absurdly if we considered the burial of Christ to be indicated by the name of "the earth" alone. Indeed, among the Greeks and Romans, the designation of "the earth" <note>Greek: "του γη"</note> and "burial" <note>Greek: "ταφης"</note>—that is, earth and *tomb*—are very frequently conflated. "To commit to the earth" or "to commit to the ground" <note>Latin: "Terræ mandare, humo mandare"</note> stands for "the tomb." Nor is <term>Sheol</term> <note>Hebrew: שאול; the biblical place of the dead</note> itself inconsistent with this, which signifies mere "earth" in Numbers 16:30, 33 and, according to some, Psalm 139:7. For they call *Gehenna* by seven names: <term>שאול. צלמות. טיט. היון. דומה. באר שחת. גיהנם.</term> and <term>ארץ תחתיות</term>—*the Underworld* or *the tomb, the shadow of death, the muddy clay, silence, the pit of destruction, Gehenna, and the lower earth.* <note>The author provides a list of Hebrew synonyms for the grave or hell</note>. So too the Greeks and Latins in countless places. **Homer, in the Iliad**:

> *Deepest beneath the earth is the abyss,* <note>original Greek: Βάθιστον ὑπὸ χθονὸς ἐστὶ βέρεθρον</note>

> *As far as the upward view to the heavenly height of the sky.*

> *Here the house of the underworld opens the mouth of Dis,* <note>Dis is another name for Pluto, the god of the underworld</note>

> *a huge abyss lies open with vast jaws.*

But besides the fact that this fits the context, consider these lines from Seneca’s *The Trojan Women*:

> *and Cerberus, the guardian sitting at the threshold*
> *that is no easy entrance—*
> *these are empty rumors and hollow words,*
> *a story no different from a restless dream.*

The opinion of the Hebrews is no more at odds with those authors than it is with us, if you compare the notes at Section XI. Furthermore, among secular authors, these phrases generally describe the grave itself rather than the underworld of the damned. We must especially remember here the words of Diodorus Siculus in the fifth book of his *Library of History*: *It is said that Hades established the customs surrounding burials, funeral processions, and the honors given to the dead, since before that time there was no care given to them. XVII. Therefore, those who judge the <term>lower parts of the earth</term> <note>original Greek: κατωτερα μερη της γης</note> to be spoken of the grave, rather than of a local hell, act more correctly. Vatablus renders it "from the lower grave," along with Basil, Theodoret, and others. The same judgment should be made of Psalm 55:24, the <term>pit of destruction</term> <note>original Hebrew: באר שחת (be'er shakhat)</note>. Let this be compared with the Hebrew source. The phrase **the heart of the seas** <note>original Hebrew: לב ימים (*Lev yamim*)</note> is also found in Exodus 15:8, which Rabbi Don Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a prominent Jewish statesman and philosopher</note> explains as **concerning the interior space of the sea, which was between the heaps of water, a metaphor taken from the heart of a human existing within the body.** <note>original Hebrew: על אמצע הים שהיה בין הערמה</note> **Therefore, whatever is in the interior part is called the "heart."** <note>original Hebrew: כמשל לב האדם שהוא באמצע הגוף ולכן כל דבר שבאמצע יקרא לב</note> See his *Commentary on the Law*, folio 158, columns 1 and 2. See also Ezekiel 27:4 and 28:2, and Proverbs 30:19. **The heart of the seas** <note>original Hebrew: לב ימים</note>; and in 2 Samuel 18:14, **the heart of the oak** <note>original Hebrew: לב אלה</note>. It has been noted by those skilled in the Arabic language that the Arabs call the <term>meridian</term> <note>original Greek: το μεσουראνημα; the highest point reached by a celestial body</note> in their own tongue the **heart of heaven** <note>original Greek: καρδίαν οὐρανοῦ</note>. Theophrastus <note>a Greek successor to Aristotle</note> called the pith of trees the **heart of trees** <note>original Greek: καρδίαν δένδρων</note> and the **inner-heart** <note>original Greek: ἔγκαρδιον</note>; Aristotle named the interior part of a water-clock the **heart of the water-clock** <note>original Greek: καρδίαν κλεψύδρας</note>.

Therefore, Cardinal Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Jesuit theologian who argued for a literal local descent of Christ into a subterranean Hell</note> trifles miserably when he transfers these terms to a **literal** <note>original Greek: κυρίως</note> descent of Christ’s soul to the underworld. See, if you please, the subtle and truly learned book by Parker on the descent of Christ to the underworld, which we cited above (Book III, sections 41 and 44). Likewise, see Saubertus’s *Palæstra*, page 210 and following.

Since our Savior, when speaking of the **heart of the earth** <note>original Greek: καρδίᾳ τῆς γῆς</note>, intends an eye toward the whale that swallowed Jonah, the "heart" is rightly translated as the stomach or belly—a usage not uncommon among the Greeks. Suidas <note>the author of a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> states in his Lexicon: **The ancients called the stomach the "heart."** <note>original Greek: οἱ παλαιοὶ τὸν στόμαχον καρδίαν ἐκάλουν</note> Indeed, pains of the stomach were called **heart-aches** <note>original Greek: καρδιαλγια; literally "cardialgia," which we now associate with the heart, but originally referred to the upper stomach or "heartburn"</note>. See Pitiscus on Suetonius’s *Life of Claudius*, section 31.

Furthermore, it is very frequent among authors to use the grave as a <term>euphemism</term> <note>original Greek: ἀντίφρασιν; "antiphrasis," the use of a word in a sense opposite to its proper meaning</note> for the stomach or belly. These instances are too numerous to list here. You will find them collected in Kirchmann’s *On Roman Funerals* (Book III, chapter 10) and Gataker’s *Commentary on Marcus Aurelius’s Meditations* (Book IV). Especially elegant and relevant to this matter is a passage from Basil of Seleucia’s *Orations* (Orat. 12, Commelin edition, page 104):

> **Jonah was carried in a living tomb, dwelling in a swimming prison, tossed in a whirlpool; he inhabited the place of death, a lodging-house for the dead, not the living; he inhabited a womb that was the mother of death.** <note>original Greek: Ἦν Ἰωνᾶς ἐν ζῶντι τάφῳ φερόμενος... οἰκῶν γαστέρα θανάτου μητέρα</note>

(b) Philippians 2:10, where the buried are called **those under the earth** <note>original Greek: καταχθονιοι</note>, who are surely the same ones whom Isaiah 26:19 calls by the same meaning **dwellers of the dust**. <note>original Hebrew: שכני עפר (*Shokhne aphar*)</note>

...and David in Psalm 22:30: <note>original Hebrew: יורדי עפר (*Yordei aphar*)</note> **Those descending into the dust.** Indeed, besides the Orthodox <note>The author uses "Orthodox" here to refer to the established Protestant tradition of his time.</note> of our own age, Athanasius, Synesius, Augustine, Theodoret, and even Arias Montanus <note>Benito Arias Montano (1527–1598), a Spanish Orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible; though a Catholic, he was respected for his scholarship.</note> from the very school of our adversaries, have long held that this passage must be explained in this way. XVIII. The second argument is FROM THE SENSE OF THE COMBINED WORDS, as received by sound interpreters and confirmed by parallel passages. The Syriac <note>The Peshitta, the standard Syriac translation of the Bible.</note> reads: **He descended before to the lower parts of the earth.** <note>original Syriac: נחת לקדם לתחתיתא דארעא (*Nachet l’qedam l’tachtita d’ar’a*)</note> Luther translates: **He first travelled down into the lowest places of the earth** <note>original German: *Er ist zuvor hinunter gefahren in die unterste Oerter der Erden*</note>, or: **He was carried down before into the lowest places of the earth.** <note>original Latin: *Devectus est ante in infima loca terræ*</note> I note three things in this version. First, the little word **parts** <note>original Greek: μερη (*merē*)</note> is not satisfied, which the Syriac also did not express—though in that, the Syriac followed the idiom of the Orientals and especially the Hebrews, concerning which see the following section. Furthermore, that phrase **travelled down** <note>original German: *Hinunter fahren*</note>, which means to be carried downwards, does not quite please me, since it can arise from a very false hypothesis which makes the descent of Christ to the lower world a stage of his **exaltation** <note>Some theologians argued the descent was a triumphant entry into hell to liberate souls, rather than a state of humiliation/burial.</note>. Thirdly, I would wish that the great translator <note>Referring to Martin Luther.</note> had not used the superlative, which the Dutch have also retained: **He also first descended into the lowest parts of the earth.** <note>original Dutch: *Hy is ook eerst nedergedalt in de nederste deelen der aerde*</note> The French translate it better: **He had descended to the lower parts of the earth.** <note>original French: *Il estoit descendu aux parties les plus basses de la terre*</note> Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant reformer and successor to Calvin.</note> writes: **He descended first into the lower parts of the earth.** <note>original Latin: *Descendit prius in inferiores partes terræ*</note> So says the Vulgate itself and the majority of more discerning interpreters.

XIX. There are, as far as I know, four places in the Old Testament entirely parallel to ours, which must be explained in the same way. Indeed, there is no necessity urging us to explain this as that part of the earth which is around its center, according to the hypothesis of the Papists. # DISSERTATION

...compared with the Hebrew source. The phrase **heart of the seas** <note>original Hebrew: לב ימים (*leb yamim*)</note> is also found in Exodus 15:8, which Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel <note>A prominent Jewish statesman and theologian (1437–1508) who served the Portuguese and Spanish courts.</note> explains as **referring to the middle of the sea that was between the heaps of water, a comparison taken from the human heart which is in the middle of the body. Therefore, whatever is in the interior part is called the heart.** <note>original Hebrew: על אמצע הים שהיה בין הערמה כמשל לב האדם שהוא באמצע הגוף ולכן כל דבר שבאמצע יקרא לב</note> *Commentary on the Law*, folio 158, columns 1 and 2. See also Ezekiel 27:4 and 28:2; Proverbs 30:19, **heart of the seas**; and 2 Samuel 18:14, **heart of the oak** <note>original Hebrew: לב אלה (*leb elah*)</note>. 

Those skilled in the Arabic language have noted that the Arabs, in their own tongue, call the <term>meridian</term> <note>original Greek: το μεσουρανημα (*to mesouranēma*); the point where a celestial body crosses the highest point in the sky</note> the **heart of heaven** <note>original Greek: καρδιαν ουρανου (*kardian ouranou*)</note>. Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle, often called the father of botany.</note> called the pith or marrow of trees the **heart of trees** <note>original Greek: καρδιαν δενδρων (*kardian dendrōn*)</note> and **within-the-heart** <note>original Greek: εγκαρδιον (*enkardion*)</note>. Aristotle named the interior part of a <term>clepsydra</term> <note>An ancient water-clock used to measure time by the flow of liquid.</note> the **heart of the water-clock** <note>original Greek: καρδιαν κλεψυδρας (*kardian klepsydras*)</note>. 

Therefore, Cardinal Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a leading Jesuit theologian of the Counter-Reformation who argued for a literal descent of Christ into a physical underworld.</note> is wretchedly trifling when he transfers these terms to Christ's descent of the soul to the underworld, strictly so-called. See, if you please, Parker in his subtle and truly learned book *On the Descent of Christ to the Underworld*, which we have already cited above (Book III, § 41, 44). Likewise, see Saubert’s *Palaestra*, page 210 and following. 

When our Savior, speaking of the **heart of the earth** <note>original Greek: καρδια της γης (*kardia tēs gēs*)</note>, directs his eye toward the whale that swallowed Jonah, the "heart" is rightly translated as the stomach or belly, which is not unusual among the Greeks. Suidas says in his *Lexicon*: **The ancients called the stomach the heart.** <note>original Greek: οι παλαιοι τον στομαχον καρδιαν εκαλουν</note> Indeed, stomach pains were called <term>cardialgia</term> <note>Literally "heart-pain," though used historically for what we now call heartburn or gastric distress.</note>. See Pitiscus’s notes on Suetonius’s *Life of Claudius*, § 31. 

Furthermore, it is very common among authors to use the term stomach or **belly** to mean a grave, through the use of <term>antiphrasis</term> <note>A rhetorical figure where a word is used in a sense opposite to its literal meaning.</note>. There are too many instances of this to list here. You will find them collected in Kirchmann’s *On Roman Funerals*, Book III, chapter 10, and Gataker’s *Commentary on Marcus Aurelius’s Meditations*, Book IV. 

Especially elegant and relevant to this matter is a passage from Basil of Seleucia <note>A 5th-century bishop and writer known for his ornate rhetorical style.</note>, *Oration 12*: **Jonah was carried in a living tomb, inhabiting a swimming prison, moving in a chasm, dwelling in the seat of death, a lodging-house of the dead, not the living, inhabiting a belly that is the mother of death.** <note>original Greek: Ην Ιωνας εν ζωντι ταφω φερομενος, νηχομενον οικων δεσμωτηριον, εγκινουμενον φαραγγι, θανατου χωριον οικων, νεκρων πανδοχειον, ου ζωντων, οικων γαστερα θανατου μητερα</note> (b) See Philippians 2:10, where the buried are called **those under the earth** <note>original Greek: καταχθονιοι (*katachthonioi*)</note>, who are surely the same as those Isaiah calls in the same sense (Isaiah 26:19) **dwellers in the dust** <note>original Hebrew: שכני עפר (*shokhne aphar*)</note>...

# ON CHRIST'S DESCENT TO THE LOWER REGIONS.

...and David in Psalm 22:30: **Those who go down to the dust** <note>original Hebrew: יורדי עפר (*yorde 'aphar*); original Latin: *Descendentes in pulverem*</note>. Indeed, besides the Orthodox of our own time, Athanasius, Synesius, Augustine, Theodoret, and even Arias Montanus from the school of our adversaries <note>Arias Montanus was a Spanish Benedictine monk and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible; though a Catholic, he was respected for his linguistic scholarship.</note> have long since maintained that this passage must be explained in this way. These same are named in Revelation 5:13 as **creatures under the earth** <note>original Greek: κτισμα ὑποκατω της γης (*ktisma hypokatō tēs gēs*)</note>. Likewise, the dead are said to be **hidden beneath the ground** <note>original Greek: κατα χθονος (*kata chthonos*)</note>, as found in Sophocles' *Antigone*, line 23. From this it is clear why the Greeks and Romans called tombs **subterranean chambers** <note>original Greek: ὑπογαια (*hypogaia*); original Latin: *hypogæa*</note>, concerning which see Tertullian’s *On the Soul*, chapter 28; the *Lexicon* of Hesychius; Petronius’s *Satyricon*; Erhard’s *Symbols* on that work; Argoli on Panvinio’s *On the Games*, book 2, chapter 3; Meursius’s *Miscellaneous Observations*, book 3, chapter 20, etc.

### XVIII. THE SECOND ARGUMENT from the sense of COMBINED WORDS, as received by sound interpreters and confirmed by parallel passages.

Syriac version: **He gave himself previously to the lowest parts of the earth.** <note>original Syriac: נתת לקדס לתחתיתה דארעא</note>
Luther: **He previously traveled down into the lowest places of the earth** <note>original German: *Er ist zuvor hinunter gefahren in die unterste Oerter der Erden*; original Latin: *Devectus est ante in infima loca terræ*</note>. I note three things in this version. First, it does not satisfy the little word **parts** <note>original Greek: μερη (*merē*)</note>, which the Syriac also failed to express—though in that, the Syriac followed the idiom of the Eastern languages and especially the Hebrews, discussed in the following section. Next, that phrase **traveled down** <note>Luther's *hinunter fahren*</note>, which means to be carried downward, does not please me much, since it may have arisen from a very false hypothesis which makes Christ's descent to the lower regions a stage of his exaltation <note>The author argues here against the view that the descent was a "victory march" through hell, preferring to see it as part of Christ's humiliation (death and burial).</note>. Thirdly, I would wish that the great interpreter <note>referring to Martin Luther</note> had not used the superlative **lowest**, which the Dutch have also retained: **He also first descended into the lowest parts of the earth.** <note>original Dutch: *Hy is ook eerst nedergedalt in de nederste deelen der aerde.*</note> The French have done better: **He had descended to the lower parts of the earth.** <note>original French: *Il estoit descendu aux parties les plus basses de la terre.*</note> Beza: **He descended first into the lower parts of the earth.** <note>original Latin: *Descendit prius in inferiores partes terræ.*</note> So says the Vulgate itself and the greater part of prudent interpreters.

### XIX. There are, so far as I know, four passages in the Old Testament that are parallel to our text in every respect and must be explained by the same reasoning.

(1) Psalm 63:10. **Those who seek my life for destruction shall enter the lower parts of the earth** <note>original Hebrew: יבאו בתחתיות ארץ (*yabo'u betachtiyot eretz*)</note>, that is, they shall be thrust down to the place of death and corruption, which is below the surface of the earth. Indeed, there is no necessity urging us to explain this as that part of the earth which is near its center, according to the hypothesis of the Papists. For in verse 11, it is said of these same enemies of David that...

...they shall be a portion for foxes. Now foxes, so that they may hide more securely, have their dens in the very bowels of the earth. On this matter, Oppian writes in his *Cynegetica*, book 3:
->**And the clever one dwells in the deepest dens.**<-
<note>original Greek: Καὶ πινυτὴ ναίει πυμάτοις ἐνὶ φωλεοῖσιν (*Kai pinyte naiei pymatois eni phōleoisin*)</note>
Phaedrus also writes in Book IV, fable 19:
->**A fox, while digging its lair and turning up the earth,**<-
->**And having driven many tunnels deep down,**<-
->**Reached the deepest cavern of a dragon,**<-
->**Who was guarding hidden treasures.**<-
See more in Bochart’s *Hierozoicon*, Volume I, Book III, chapter 13, page 852; and Rittershusius on the passage from Oppian cited above. (2) Ezekiel 26:20: **And I shall make you go down** <note>original Hebrew: וְהוֹרַדְתִּיךְ (*ve-horadtikha*)</note> **with those who descend into the pit to the people of old, and I will place you in the lower earth** <note>original Hebrew: בְּאֶרֶץ תַּחְתִּיּוֹת (*be-eretz tachtiyot*)</note>. The Prophet is speaking here of the destruction of Tyre by Alexander the Great <note>Alexander the Great besieged and destroyed the island city of Tyre in 332 BCE.</note>, which was to fall into ashes, not descend into hell. (3) Ezekiel 32:18: **Son of man, wail for the multitude of Egypt, and command her to go down** <note>original Hebrew: וְהוֹרִדֵהוּ (*ve-horidehu*)</note>**, she and the daughters of the famous nations, into the lower earth.** With this agree (4) the words regarding the same matter in verse 24 of this chapter: **There is Elam and all her multitude surrounding her grave, all of them slain, who fell uncircumcised into the lower earth.** For in both places there is added: **Those who go down into the pit** <note>original Hebrew: יֹרְדֵי בוֹר (*yorde vor*)</note>; a phrase which signifies the deceased and the buried. Compare Section XVII. Furthermore, is not this entire chapter like a funeral dirge, sung by the Prophet for the King of the Egyptians and all his people? Finally, in verses 21, 23, 24, 25, and 26, there is open mention of the grave, especially in verse 27: **Who go down to the grave** <note>original Hebrew: אֲשֶׁר יָרְדוּ שְׁאוֹל (*asher yardu she'ol*)</note>. I translate *Sheol* <note>The Hebrew word *Sheol* is often translated as "Hell," but the author argues here it means a physical tomb.</note> in this way because it follows immediately: **with their weapons of war, their swords placed under their heads.** For the ancients were accustomed to hide weapons, and especially swords, in the biers and tombs of heroes. Arrian, in his *Expedition of Alexander the Great*, Book VI, where he describes the tomb of Cyrus <note>Cyrus the Great, founder of the Achaemenid Empire.</note>, says: **Therein were placed a robe, necklaces, and scimitars** <note>original Greek: Επειναι δὲ καὶ κανδυς... καὶ στρεπτοὶ καὶ ἀκινάκαι (*Epeinai de kai kandys... kai streptoi kai akinakai*)</note>. Diodorus Siculus, in his *Library of History*, Book XVIII, chapter 26, says of the casket of Alexander: **Over this was laid a magnificent purple cloth embroidered with gold...**

For which other formulas have *into Hades* <note>original Greek: εις ᾀδην (*eis hadēn*)</note>.

...others have guessed, phrases from the **Athanasian Creed** <note>A Christian statement of belief focused on the Trinity and Christology, traditionally attributed to St. Athanasius.</note> were written in the margin of the **Nicene Creed**, and from there they crept into the first text of the Nicene, and subsequently the **Apostles' Creed**. Once they have struck this out—though they never will—a new task will remain for them: to defend the meaning which men, blind to the point of stubbornness, manufacture. Nothing is indeed more evident to great men than that this phrase must be referred both to the burial of Christ, regarding the body, and to the infernal anguishes, regarding the soul. I refrain from praising every individual who has contributed to the Creed here or adding more on this matter, lest I seem, as they say, *to carry owls to Athens.* <note>original Greek: γλαυκας ες Αθηνας αγειν (*glaukas es Athēnas agein*); a Greek proverb meaning to do something completely unnecessary or redundant, like "carrying coals to Newcastle."</note>

XXI. My third argument is the emphatic and complete **OPPOSITION OF THE ASCENT AND DESCENT OF CHRIST** and, under that, the states of exaltation and emptying <term>exinanition; from the Latin *exinanitio*, referring to the concept in Philippians 2 where Christ "empties" himself of his divine glory to become human</term>. So that this may appear more clearly to the eye, we note a few things beforehand. (1) It is very common, especially in Holy Scripture, to set the humiliation and exaltation of our Savior in opposition to one another. This was already done in the prophecies under the Old Testament, as is clear from **Psalm 2**, where from verses 1 to 3 the uprisings of the nations and the rebellions of kings are opposed to the exaltation of the Savior described in verses 4–12. The same is observed in **Psalms 8, 40,** and **69**. **Psalm 110:7**: *He shall drink from the stream along the way; therefore he shall lift up his head.* **Isaiah 53:10**: *But the Lord willed to weaken him and made him sick; when his soul has made a payment of satisfaction, he shall see his offspring, who shall prolong his days, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand.* Also **Isaiah 49** and **50:6–9**. In order that the prophecies might have more certain credibility, the writers of the New Testament observed the same thing. Christ himself says in **Luke 24:26**: *Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and enter into his glory?* Paul says this most clearly in **Philippians 2:6** and following; compare this with **Romans 6:7, 8, 9; 4:25; 8:34; Hebrews 1:3;** and **1 Peter 1:11**. (2) The Orthodox theologians—who recognize in the present passage an opposition of these two states of Christ—wrongly fight for the opinion regarding his **Incarnation**, which we have already refuted in section VI. For although the most excellent Savior was "emptied" through other circumstances in the Incarnation, he was not humiliated by the mere fact of becoming flesh. And this is (a) because even in the likeness of man he remained exalted. (b) He is said to be emptied *for a little while* <note>original Greek: μικρὸν, βραχύ τι (*mikron, brachy ti*)</note>, or for a short time, for...

...a brief time *Psalm 8:6; Hebrews 2:7,* but he always retained his human nature. (c) *Paul in Philippians 2:7* distinguishes "being made in the likeness of men" <note>original Greek: γίνεσθαι ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων (*ginesthai en homoiōmati anthrōpōn*)</note> from "taking the form of a servant." <note>original Latin: *formam servi accipere*; referring to the Greek *morphēn doulou labōn* in the same passage.</note> And (d) God could have united to himself a human nature of the sort that possessed every proper perfection. (3) All those of the **Augsburg Confession** <note>Refers to the primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church; the author disagrees with their view that Christ's descent to hell was his first act of triumph (exaltation).</note> who wish for the descent of Christ into hell to pertain to his **exaltation** are in error. Surely, as long as Christ was in the tomb, he must be considered to have been under the dominion of death. If this is so, the descent into the tomb must be referred to his **humiliation**. But this point will perhaps be opened more fully in what follows.

XXII. With these points having been noted beforehand, I subjoin the reasoning for the opposition itself. In a certain respect, the **burial** is the lowest degree of Christ's **emptying** <term>exinanition; from the Latin *exinanitio*, the theological concept of Christ "emptying" himself of his divine status to take on human form</term>. Indeed, while in all the other degrees of his humiliation one may observe some spark of divinity, here there was either none at all, or it was extremely small. In the **incarnation**, the royal lineage, the wondrous birth from a virgin, the presence of angels, and the adoration of the Magi all contained illustrious elements. As a youth, he taught in the temple to the amazement of his listeners. I pass over his baptism, the angels ministering to him when he was tempted in the desert, his innumerable miracles, and his glory on the mountain [of Transfiguration]. Even while undergoing his **passion**, he was strengthened by an angel, he prostrated an entire cohort of treacherous men by the sound of his word, on the cross he promised paradise to the thief, and when near death he cried out with a loud voice; so many miracles accompanied his very passing. Is there anything similar to these in his **three-day burial**? Could he not seem to have been swallowed up by death and completely overcome? 

Conversely, the **ascension into heaven** was the most excellent degree of Christ's exaltation and glory, whence it is said "preeminently" <note>original Greek: κατ' ἐξοχήν (*kat' exochēn*)</note> that he entered into glory *Luke 24:26* and *1 Timothy 3:16,* "he was taken up in glory" <note>original Greek: ἀνελήφθη ἐν δόξῃ (*anelephthē en doxē*)</note>. I take nothing away from the other stages. I admit that his sitting at the right hand of God was the highest degree—not because the triumphal ascension of Jesus was lesser in itself, but because glory added to glory doubles the splendor. Among the ancient **Romans**, the honor of a **triumph** <note>A grand parade granted to successful generals; the author uses this as a metaphor for Christ's ascent.</note> was preferred even over the highest magistrates; a victor crowned with laurel ascended the Capitol more gloriously than a Consul dressed in a toga. If these points should still be less pleasing to someone, we bid him remain within the simple opposition of the places, which, since it is evident and emphatic, nothing...

...we shall not dwell on this for too long. A contrast is made between the highest place, to which Christ ascended—namely, heaven—and the lowest place, to which he descended—namely, the grave. This is not unusual for the Apostle Paul. For he says in Romans 10:6–7:
> *But the righteousness of faith speaks in this way: "Do not say in your heart, 'Who will ascend into heaven?'" (that is, to bring Christ down) or "'Who will descend into the abyss?'" (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).* <note>original Latin: *Justitia vero fidei ita dicit: ne dicas in corde tuo, quis adscendet in coelum? hoc est Christum deducere: Aut descendet in abyssum? hoc est Christum ex mortuis reducere.*</note>

The nature of our current project does not allow me to explain this difficult passage in full. I note only the harmony it shares with our current topic: *to ascend into heaven* and *to descend into the abyss*. The "abyss" is the same thing as the "lower parts of the earth," <note>original Latin: *inferiores partes terrae*; a reference to Ephesians 4:9, often debated as meaning either the earth itself or the grave.</note> which is to say, the grave. The Apostle himself indicates this when he adds: *to bring Christ up from the dead*. Therefore, he was among the dead while he was in the abyss.

### XXIII. Prefigurations from the Old Testament ###

Fourthly, the **TYPES OF THE OLD TESTAMENT** <term>Types; historical figures or events in the Old Testament seen as symbolic "shadows" or foreshadowings of Christ's life</term> align elegantly with our explanation. Here, I count four: Joseph, Elijah, Daniel, and Jonah. 

Joseph was of the same origin as his brothers, yet he was loved by his father in a special way. As a judge of his brothers' vices, he was sentenced to death by them, sold to the Gentiles for a price of 30 pieces of silver, and led away into Egypt. There, after suffering many insults and slanders, he was thrown into prison; having remained there until the third year (as one may gather), he was finally set free. 

In this way, he corresponds to our Savior coming in the body. Christ was made a sharer of human flesh, yet remained the beloved Son of the Heavenly Father; he was treated with insuperable hatred by those who were his "brothers according to the flesh." <note>original Greek: κατα σαρκα (*kata sarka*)</note> They bought him with silver pieces, and having deemed him worthy of death, they stood him before a Gentile judge. Here, treated in shameful ways, he is given over to death, is buried, and finally returns to life on the third day. 

Joseph—so that there might be faith in the predictions and dreams of Jacob—rose up, as it were, when he was brought out of prison. Moreover, in the royal chariot in which he triumphed, he foreshadowed the ascension into the heavens; and in his sharing of the power of reigning with Pharaoh, he foreshadowed Christ's sitting at the right hand of God. 

As we pass over the other details quickly, we should observe nothing here except that three-year stay in prison. I have no doubt that this prison was underground. Nothing was more common among the ancients. Such was the *Treasury of the Messenians*, which Plutarch, in his life of *Philopoemen*, calls "an underground chamber that receives neither air nor light from outside." <note>original Greek: οικημα καταγειον ουτε πνευμα λαμβανον ουτε φως εξωθεν (*oikēma katageion oute pneuma lambanon oute phōs exōthen*)</note> Another example is the *Kaiadas* among the Spartans, which was noted by Strabo and Pau- <meta>catchword: fanias,</meta> <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the name of the geographer Pausanias on the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Old Testament "types" or prefigurations that symbolize Christ’s descent into the state of death and the grave. The author is finishing the discussion of Joseph’s imprisonment as a symbol for the tomb before moving on to Elijah, Daniel, and Jonah.</meta>

# ON THE DESCENT OF CHRIST TO THE LOWER REALMS #

...Pausanias, Thucydides, Suidas, etc. For this reason, excavations <note>original Greek: *orygmata*</note> are simply called "prisons," and specifically <note>original Greek: *kyriōs*</note> the name for the place in Athens where criminals were punished. I need not even mention the *Barathrum* at Athens <note>a deep pit or fissure into which condemned criminals were thrown</note>. Whether the *ceadas* <note>original Greek: *keōdas*; a similar pit at Sparta</note> differs from it—which Suidas likewise says was "a deep place where criminals were cast"—I leave to those more skilled in these matters to decide. It does not give me pause that Joseph’s prison in his history is called the *Beth ha-Tsohar* <note>Hebrew: "house of the roundness," likely referring to a domed or circular building</note>. This is simply the idiom of the Hebrews and Chaldeans, by whom a prison is sometimes called *Beth asurim* <note>Hebrew: "house of the bound"</note> and sometimes *Beth matara* <note>Hebrew: "house of custody"</note>. Furthermore, grand and royal prisons were often laboriously built to look like houses or towers, yet they nevertheless sloped down into a depth where the captives were held. This was the case with the *Latomiae* of Syracuse <note>ancient stone quarries used as prisons, famously described by Cicero</note>, about which Cicero writes in *Against Verres*, Book V; the *Tullianum* at Rome <note>the lower, subterranean dungeon of the Mamertine Prison</note>; and other places for restraining defendants, about which writers on antiquity say more. Therefore, the three-day descent <note>original Greek: *katabasis*</note> of Christ "into the lower parts of the earth" <note>original Greek: *eis katōtera merē tēs gēs*</note> could not be more elegantly foreshadowed than by this subterranean house of Joseph, where he remained for three years.

XXIV. In **Elijah**, some recognize a type of the Savior; hence they want his being snatched up alive into the heavens to be an emblem of Christ’s ascension. Those who feel this way should step back a little and observe the humility previously depicted in 2 Kings 2. I refer to Elijah’s passage through the **Jordan**, in whose likeness Christ passed through the waters of death—but he only passed through. For although he descended to the lower realms <note>original Latin: *descendit ad inferos*; referring to the phrase in the Apostles' Creed</note>, he did not remain there. Just as **Daniel** was a type of the Savior, he fits the present matter most elegantly: for he was cast before the lions in Daniel 6, in a subterranean place which is repeatedly called the "den of lions" <note>Aramaic: *legob aryata*</note> and in the Apocryphal text titled *Bel and the Dragon*, verses 31 and 32, the "pit of lions" <note>Greek: *lakkos leontōn*</note>. Hence in verse 42: "And he drew him out, but those who were the cause of his destruction he cast into the pit." The most illustrious type of this matter, by the Savior's own confession in Matthew 12:40, was **Jonah**. We leave aside the rest. We only point with a light finger to those things which seem to pertain to Christ's descent "into the lower parts of the earth." # DISSERTATION #

...my argument gains further clarity if one compares the phrases by which the history of Jonah (Chapter II) describes that **living tomb** <note>original Greek: *zōnta taphon*</note> (or the **belly of the whale** <note>original Greek: *koilian tou kētous*</note>, compared with the **heart of the earth** in Section XVII). In verse 3, it is called the **belly of the grave** <note>original Hebrew: *sheol beten*</note> and in verse 4, the **heart of the sea** <note>original Hebrew: *lebab yamim*</note>. In verse 6, it is said: **The abyss surrounded me** <note>original Hebrew: *tehom yesobebeni*</note>, and in verse 7: **I went down to the roots of the mountains; the earth with its bars was about me forever** <note>original Hebrew: *lekitsbe harim yaradti ha’aretz bericheha ba’adi le’olam*</note>. Christ had truly descended as if into the **clefts of the mountains** <note>original Greek: *schismas*</note> when he was placed in the tomb **which he had hewn in the rock** <note>original Greek: *ho elatomēsen en tē petra*</note> (Matthew 27:60).

XXV. Fifthly, the **FREQUENT HARMONY OF PROPHECIES** adds strength to this view. When these prophecies discuss the future burial of Christ, they often use similar phrases. Psalm 16:10 says: **You will not leave my soul** *to the grave* <note>original Hebrew: *lish’ol*</note>. Indeed, **Sheol** <note>the Hebrew term for the realm of the dead or the grave</note> designates both the sepulcher and subterranean places (Compare Numbers 16:30, 33). Psalm 88:7: **You have laid me in the lowest pit, in dark places, in the depths** <note>original Hebrew: *bebor tachtiyot*</note>. Isaiah 44:23: **Sing, O heavens, for the Lord has done this; shout, you lower parts of the earth** <note>original Hebrew: *hari’u tachtiyot aretz*</note>. The great Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology"</note> elegantly **paraphrases** <note>original Greek/Hebrew hybrid: *periphrazei*</note> this passage in his *Lexicon* (p. 970): *“When Christ was returned from the lower parts of the earth, those places seemed to shout and rejoice that they were being liberated—and were yet to be liberated—from this bondage of vanity.”* Finally, Lamentations 3:53: **They have cut off my life in the pit** <note>original Hebrew: *bebor*</note> **and cast a stone upon me.**

XXVI. Finally, the **PURPOSE OF THE APOSTLE** <note>Paul</note> supports my case. This purpose is partly general and partly specific. The general purpose can be gathered from the analysis given in Section I. Indeed, since he exhorts them to unity in the faith in the first seven verses, in the ten following verses he subjoins a silent **prolepsis** <note>a rhetorical device where an author anticipates and answers an objection before it is raised</note>, which we noted then. This does not create any **digression** <note>original Greek: *parekbasin*</note> by the Apostle from his purpose, but rather strengthens it. The proposition of Paul’s response is laid down in verse 7 and proven by the word of Scripture in verse 8. I include the two following verses in a parenthesis, and I believe they can be understood this way: Saint Paul was taking care lest a doubt arise among the Ephesians as to whether those words of the Psalm were correctly applied to Christ. In this, he followed the example of his teacher in John 3:13. To remove this doubt at the root, he added the words we read in verses 9 and 10, and thus we define it: **“But this”** <note>original Greek: *To de*</note>, namely that word...

-># ON THE DESCENT OF CHRIST TO THE LOWER WORLD #<-
->Yyy 2<-

**He ascended** <note>original Hebrew: *alah*; original Greek: *anebe*</note>—of which it is said in the Psalm: **What is "he ascended" except that he also first descended?** <note>original Greek: *ti estin, ei mē hoti kai katebē prōton*</note>. Does this not indicate with all possible force one who descended before he ascended? He descended **into the lower parts of the earth** <note>original Greek: *eis katōtera merē tēs gēs*</note>, a place diametrically opposite to that height to which he ascended. Indeed, since this "ascending" implies one who previously descended, that descending person can be no one else but he who was then carried up by his own power above all the heavens: **The one who descended is the same one who also ascended far above all the heavens** <note>original Greek: *ho katabas autos esti kai ho anabas hyperanō pantōn tōn ouranōn*</note>. You Ephesians will easily conclude from his works that this is Christ, and thus the very one spoken of in the Psalm. For it is not true of everyone who ascends that they first descended. Moses ascended the mountain and afterward descended, because **he was from below** <note>original Greek: *ek tou katō ēn*</note>. But if Christ ascended, he first descended, because **he is from above** <note>original Greek: *ek tou anō estin*</note> (John 8:23, John 3:31; see also John 3:13).

Nothing could be more elegant or appropriate for the Apostle than to demonstrate the Ascension more illustriously by contrasting it with the lowest descent. Whether others prefer to say the Apostle wished to explain or merely illustrate the prophetic word, whatever goal you assign to him, you fight on our side. And these are the six points which, when collected together, prevent me from doubting further the opinion once accepted.

XXVII. However, while other interpretations face so many difficulties, I see only one objection raised here, and it is of such a kind that it can easily be struck down. The great **Carpzovius** <note>Johann Benedict Carpzov II (1639–1699), a prominent Lutheran theologian</note> cast it into a **syllogism** <note>a logical argument consisting of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion</note>, having drawn it previously from Book IV of **Bellarmine's** <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Cardinal and influential Catholic controversialist</note> *On the Soul of Christ*. He says:
> *Christ's descent in this passage should not be explained as referring to one who was not in the lower parts of the earth. But Christ’s tomb was not in the lower parts of the earth. Therefore [the conclusion follows]. The major premise is not universally true.*

That phrase—*the lower parts of the earth*—could be understood by analogy or figuratively. Yet, what makes his argument more suspicious than it is damaging is that, to resolve it more successfully, we expressly deny his **minor premise** <note>the second part of the logical argument: that the tomb was not in the "lower parts"</note>. If we follow **Salmasius** <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), a French classical scholar</note>, the matter is already clear. He maintains that the tomb was dug out, not merely cut out, in the manner of crypts (Pliny, *Exercises*, page 851). But since there are great men who have asserted the contrary with solid enough arguments and proven it was cut from rock, another response is ready at hand. From **Strabo** <note>an ancient Greek geographer</note>, **Jerome** <note>the 4th-century church father</note>, and the journals of more recent travelers, we know that the soil of Jerusalem and the surrounding regions is extremely rocky...

# DISSERTATION

...this was proved by the famous Huetius in his *Evangelical Demonstration*, Book IX, chapter 142, section 4, following Casaubon in his *Exercises*, XVI, chapter 122. In such soil, Christ’s tomb was carved out, yet it remained subterranean according to the custom of the inhabitants, who carved out not only tombs but also chambers and houses in underground rocks to escape the heat. Eyewitnesses declare that Christ’s tomb was of this form. *Johannes Phocas* <note>A 12th-century Byzantine pilgrim who wrote a famous account of the Holy Land.</note> says of it in his travelogue: *The cave which served as the tomb for the Lord’s body is double, and in one part lies the stone that was rolled away, etc.* <note>original Greek: Το δὲ εἰς ταφον χρηματισαν σπηλαιον τοῦ δεσποτικοῦ σώματος ἐϛὶ διπλοῦν καὶ ἐν μὲν τῷ ἑνὶ ἐπίκειται ὁ ἀποκυλισθεὶς λιθος &c.</note> What he calls a "cave" here, another ancient writer of a Jerusalem Travelogue found in the works of *Salmasius* <note>Claude Saumaise, a renowned 17th-century classical scholar.</note> calls a "crypt"; and an *Anonymous* writer in the collection of *Allatius* recorded that from the temple built over the tomb, one ascended to Mount Golgatha by fifteen steps: *To the left of the sanctuary of the Holy Tomb, one goes up 15 steps and enters into Golgatha* <note>original Greek: Ἡ δὲ ἀριϛερὰ τοῦ βήματος τοῦ ἁγίου τάφου ἀναβαίνει σκαλόνια ιε καὶ σεβαίνει εἰς τὸν γολγοθᾶ</note>. Here *Huetius*, by comparing other sources, prefers the reading to be *eighteen steps*, which supports our case even more—though we consider the matter of the tomb being a "lower part" of the earth to be already clearly established.

XXVIII. Therefore, we break our thread here. Since we have led the best Savior of the world to his tomb, we shall write an inscription—not the kind needed now, after the one who descended *into the lower parts of the earth* <note>original Greek: εἰς κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς</note> has ascended *far above all the heavens* <note>original Greek: ὑπερανω τῶν οὐρανῶν</note>, but such as Joseph of Arimathea might have written, had a three-day burial required any title at all.

# DISSERTATION

...was proved by the celebrated Huetius <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar who wrote the *Demonstratio Evangelica*.</note> in his *Demonstratio Evangelica*, Propos. IX, chapter 142, section 4, following Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a renowned classical scholar.</note> in *Exercitationes* XVI, chapter 122. In such soil, the tomb of Christ was carved out; nevertheless, it remained underground according to the custom of the inhabitants, who used to excavate not only tombs but also chambers and houses in the subterranean rocks to avoid the heat. Eyewitnesses declare that the tomb of Christ was of this form. Johannes Phocas <note>A 12th-century Byzantine pilgrim who wrote a famous account of the Holy Land.</note> says of it in his itinerary: "The cave which served as the tomb for the Lord’s body is double, and in one part lies the stone that was rolled away, etc." <note>original Greek: Το δ' εις ταφον χρηματισαν σπηλαιον του δεσποτικου σωματος εστι διπλουν και εν μεν τω ενι επικειται ο αποκυλισθεις λιθος &c.</note> What he here calls a <term>cave<note>original Greek: σπηλαιον (*spēlaion*)</note></term>, another ancient writer of a Jerusalem Itinerary—found in the works of Salmasius—calls a "crypt." Furthermore, an anonymous author in the works of Allatius <note>Leone Allacci (1586–1669), a Greek scholar and librarian at the Vatican.</note> recorded that from the church built over the tomb, one ascends fifteen steps to Mount Golgatha: "To the left of the sanctuary of the Holy Sepulcher, one ascends 15 steps and enters into Golgatha" <note>original Greek: Η δ'ε αρισερα του βηματος του αγιου ταφου αναβαινει σκαλονια ιε και σεβαινει εις τον γολγοθα</note>. In this passage, Huetius, by comparing other sources, prefers the reading of seventeen or eighteen steps, which supports our cause even more—though we consider our case to be already clearly established.

XXVIII. We break the thread of our discourse here. Having led the world’s greatest Savior to the tomb, we now write an inscription—not of the kind needed now, after He who had descended "into the lower parts of the earth" <note>original Greek: εις κατωτερα μερη της γης (*eis katōtera merē tēs gēs*), a reference to Ephesians 4:9.</note> has ascended "far above all the heavens" <note>original Greek: υπερανω των ουρανων (*hyperanō tōn ouranōn*), from Ephesians 4:10.</note>, but such as Joseph of Arimathea might have written, had a three-day burial required any inscription at all.

<header>DEFENSES.</header>
<sig>Zzz 3</sig>

To the best of my ability, I need not regret those things which I had publicly defended after casting them onto paper, even though I was then just a youth and poorly equipped with the resources that usually recommend a writer; nevertheless, I have held back my hand from rewriting. First, because I preferred to hide away for a time in that most pleasant solitude I was enjoying in the **territory of Cleves** <note>original: "agro Clivensi," referring to the Duchy of Cleves in the modern-day German Rhineland.</note>, rather than stepping out into the public light to argue with that *Lucius*, whose identity has remained obscure to me until now. I knew well that whatever smells of these kinds of disagreements—cooked and re-cooked so many times by the theologians of both sides—is written on **Sibylline leaves** <note>In Roman mythology, the Sibyl wrote prophecies on leaves that were easily scattered by the wind; the author implies the controversy is fleeting and unimportant.</note>, soon to be carried away by any wind, and rightly so. Added to this was my belief that my time could be spent more usefully than in refuting writings of this sort, which will not survive the test of time on their own, and contain nothing that a good cause should fear. Finally, I had resolved that at a more advanced age and with more mature judgment, I would eventually **re-lick** <note>A classical metaphor (often applied to bears "licking" their cubs into shape) for revising and perfecting one's early, unformed work.</note> this offspring of my early youth, and, joining it with other materials that lie begun among my papers, commit it to public judgment. At that time, I could conveniently mention the *Carpzovian Defenses* and recall them for examination in their proper place.

But when I emerged from my "hermitage" a few weeks ago and stopped over with you in **Bremen**, I was surprised by nothing more than the fact that there are those who—prone to interpreting everything unfavorably—boasted of my silence as if it were the most certain proof that I had abandoned the cause. Although I easily allowed them to enjoy their own inclinations, I nevertheless decided to demonstrate in a few words how little I value them now and shall value them in the future, so that their freedom to speak ill might be restrained. Truly, I see as clearly as the blindest among them what "light" they find in this effort of *Lucius*. Allow me, meanwhile, to briefly run through the *Defenses of the Carpzovian Dissertation on the Descent of Christ into the Underworld concerning Ephesians 4:9–10*, directed—**if it please the gods** <note>A sarcastic classical idiom (original: "si Dîs placet") used here to mock the pretentiousness of the opponent.</note>—against **Dr. Cornelius Hase** <note>Cornelius Hase (1653–1710) was a Professor of Theology at Bremen and the father of Theodor Hase, to whom this letter is written.</note>, the theologian of Bremen. I shall run through it, I say, for I will not—not even now—pour myself out into a long refutation, holding to the same plan I just mentioned, if the powers above favor me.

...as much as I could, nor were those things to be regretted which I, though still a youth and poorly equipped with the qualities that can recommend a writer, had cast onto paper and defended in public; yet I withheld my hand from writing back. Finally, my plan stood to eventually, at a more advanced age and with more mature judgment, **lick into shape** <note>original: "relambere," an allusion to the ancient belief that bear cubs are born as formless lumps and must be licked into shape by their mothers.</note> this offspring of my early youth and, joining it with other materials currently lying among my drafts, commit it to public judgment; at which time I could conveniently address the *Carpzovian Defenses* and recall them for examination in their proper place.

But when, a few weeks ago, I emerged from my "wilderness," so to speak, and turned aside to see you in **Bremen** <note>A major center of Reformed learning where Theodore’s father, Cornelius Hase, was a prominent figure.</note>, I was surprised by nothing more than the fact that there are those who are prone to interpreting everything in the worst possible light. These people gloried in that silence of mine as if it were the most certain evidence of a betrayed cause. Though I was happy enough to let them indulge their own nature, I nevertheless decided to demonstrate in a few words—so that their freedom to speak ill might be restrained—how little I value them now and shall value them in the future. Truly, I see as well as the blindest of men what "light" they find in this effort of *Lucius*. I will run through them, I say, for even now I will not pour myself out into a lengthy refutation, holding fast to that same plan I just mentioned, if the powers above favor me.

<header>E P I S T O L A</header>

...[judging] <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page: "even for one judging..."</note>, even though I have not found it in the collection of Carpzov's <note>Johann Benedict Carpzov II (1639–1699), a famous and staunch Lutheran theologian and professor at Leipzig.</note> disputations, nor does he aptly enough name the Carpzovian dissertation in the title of his *Vindications*—of which he himself is the author. However, the fact that he names your most celebrated father, **CORNELIUS HASE**—a man whose merits in the Church and the School others could chatter about to you more freely than I, to say nothing of myself—as the author of the disputation in question, makes him quite injurious toward both your venerable father and me. Toward him, because he attributes such a premature attempt—which displays evidence of its own insignificance everywhere—to a man from whom the public has seen nothing that does not **taste of bitten nails** <note>original: "morsos sapit ungues," a classical idiom from Horace meaning a work that has been painstakingly polished and refined.</note>. Toward me, because he maliciously strives to deprive me of whatever praise my labor might deserve. I was unconcerned about myself; but I considered it a **sin** <note>original: "piaculum," implying a religious or moral transgression.</note> to allow my most illustrious father to be so unworthily misrepresented any longer. This, I frankly confess, is the primary reason I have committed these words to print. "I, I am the one; here I am, I did it; let him turn his pen against me!" <note>Hase is quoting Virgil’s *Aeneid* (9.427): "Me, me, adsum qui feci."</note> The disputation is worthy of me, which he would have easily seen from the title if his mind had not been skewed, or if he had not thought it beneath his **Super-attendant dignity** <note>original: "Superattendentali supercilio," a biting pun on the office of "Superintendent," a high-ranking Lutheran official. Hase is mocking Lucius's perceived arrogance.</note> to cross swords with a beginner.

§. III. He thinks that Carpzov was not treated by me with enough honor; if that were true—which it is not—the saying of the Poet would apply to him: **Whatever word you speak, such a word you shall hear in return.** <note>original Greek: Οπποῖον δ' εἴπῃσθα ἔπος, τοῖον δ' ἐπακούσαις; a quote from Homer's Iliad, 20.250.</note> Truly, though he was a good and learned man, he was—I am not ashamed of the word—**most envious** <note>original: "lividissimus," literally "most leaden-colored" or "bruised," meaning spiteful and malicious.</note> toward our side <note>Hase refers to the Reformed/Calvinist tradition.</note>. Whoever doubts this should read his writing, full of black bile and an unrestrained spirit, *On the Hopelessness of a Union of Religions* <note>original: "de non speranda religionum unione," a polemical work arguing against the reconciliation of the Lutheran and Reformed churches.</note>; God, the judge of spirits, knows by what spirit he was inspired to write it.

§. VI. VII. Lucius cites theologians from our side who are, as he thinks, more modest on this issue: as if the contest were for the prize of modesty and not for the prize of truth; or as if modesty deserves praise when it hinders the pursuit of truth.

§. VIII — XII. He points out **divisions** <note>original: "divortia," literally "divorces" or "separations."</note> among our theologians in explaining the article **concerning the descent into hell** <note>original: "de descensu ad inferos."</note>. But what wonder is it that they struggle over its meaning, when a sound one can hardly be given? To such an extent did these words creep into the **Creed** <note>original: "symbolum," referring to the Apostles' Creed. This specific clause—"He descended into hell"—was a point of intense theological debate between denominations.</note> through the oversight of a former age; we, striving for mutual charity and edification, have preferred to interpret them as conveniently as possible rather than to cast them out entirely.
