# APOLOGETICS.

§. XIII--XVI. *He attempts to prove in two places that Christ really and properly descended to the* <margin>place</margin> <note>original: "ποῦ" (pou) – a Greek philosophical term referring to "location" or "where-ness."</note> *of the damned. The first is 1 Peter 3:19, where it is said of Christ that he preached to the* **spirits in prison** <note>original: "τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασι" (tois en phylakē pneumasi).</note>. *Even a schoolboy could respond to this. It is clear from the context that the Apostle is dealing with the spirits of the men who perished in the flood. Christ preached to them. But where? In hell? And when? In the time that elapsed between his death and resurrection? Kephas* <note>The Apostle Peter.</note> *says* **not a single word** <note>original: "γρύ" (gry) – a Greek idiom for the smallest possible sound or "a grunt."</note> *about that. How did he go? With spirit and body together, as Lucius holds in his thesis? Not at all; he went* **in spirit (alone)** <note>original: "ἐν πνεύματι (μόνῳ) πορευθείς" (en pneumati [monō] poreutheis).</note>. *Who, then, even while dreaming, could extract this thesis from that passage? Our scholars acknowledge that Christ preached to those spirits (who were in the prison of hell when Peter was writing these things)—namely, in the time of Noah, when the spirit of Christ contended with the men of that age, as seen in Genesis 6:3. I will not dwell on the fact that these words allow for no other explanation if the purpose of the Apostle is to be satisfied—a purpose which Lucius himself has laid out well enough. Let him, however, state the reason why they cannot be understood in this convenient way. But if no such reason can even be imagined, what audacity it is to forge from this a new and unheard-of dogma, contrary to both a sound mind and the analogy of faith, which Scripture has taught in no other part?*

As for the second passage, Ephesians 4:9, which he strives to claim for this cause in section 17 and following against me: nothing could be proved from it as long as it remained a matter of controversy. First, he is entirely occupied with trying to shatter the exceptions I made against the arguments of Carpzov. How successfully he does so, let others judge; we shall see in our own time, if God wills. Meanwhile, I safely leave all those matters in their place, as long as the dogma itself lacks a foundation. It ought to have been proved more solidly beforehand: first, that the **location** <note>original: "τὸ ποῦ" (to pou).</note> of the damned is indubitably, if not in the center of the earth, then at least in the lower parts of the earth; and second, that Christ descended there. Only then could the third point be looked into with greater profit: namely, whether the Pauline passage aims at this descent.

I will say it as it is: Those men were human; I am human. We are both able to err, and we do err. If he does not know it, I love the precept of the Stoics:* **Do not use the opinion of outsiders for...** <note>original Greek: "Τῇ δόξῃ τῶν ἐκτὸς μὴ κέχρησο πρὸς..." — The sentence is interrupted by the page break.</note>

...your own judgment, but for yourself and for your superiors. Which is the same as saying, to the truth. <note>original Greek: "την σεαυτου κρισιν, ἀλλα σαυτῳ και τοις κρειττοσι. §. XXX. and following. He <note>Lucius, the opponent</note> strives at great length to overthrow my arguments, by which I had attempted to explain the Pauline passage <note>A reference to a text by the Apostle Paul, likely concerning the theological meaning of Christ's burial in Romans 6:4 or Colossians 2:12</note> concerning the burial of our Savior. I do not have the leisure now to examine every single fallacy. However, it will be helpful to note these few things in general. 

First, the "middle term" <term>middle term (medius terminus): a technical term in logic for the word or concept that connects two premises in a syllogism</term> I have established lies in the combined strength of all the collected arguments. Hence, the question is not whether the arguments prove the point individually, but whether they do so when joined together? If the individual parts are true, then they prove the case when joined. 

Next, I had mixed in many things, digressing here and there for the sake of wit—not to serve the argument, but to show those who cared for my progress that I had cultivated fine literature <term>bonas literas: classical scholarship and the humanities</term>, as is often done with impunity and quite frequently at that young age. Therefore, friend, restrain your laughter when you read how he labors to force the philological <note>Literary or linguistic</note> digressions I sprinkled here and there into the form of those "Barbara" or "Celarent" <term>Barbara, Celarent: mnemonic names used by medieval and early modern scholars to remember valid types of logical arguments (syllogisms)</term>; perhaps he is not more skilled in elegant learning, but merely more obsessed with logical sophisms. Consequently, from a spiteful inversion of my words, he often extorts monstrous consequences and conclusions of which I had never even dreamed. 

Meanwhile, I do not deny that certain trifles fell from my pen here and there; although I could show at the proper time that they contain nothing absurd, I would have more safely spared them now that my judgment has been strengthened by the years. But what face—or what "eyebrow of Cato" <note>original: "Catonis supercilium" – an allusion to Cato the Censor, an ancient Roman known for his rigid, severe moral judgment</note>—would not indulge such things in a youth exercising himself in the "scholastic dust" <note>original: "pulvere scholastico" – a metaphor for the training ground of academic debate</note>? And how inglorious it would be to achieve victory in such a contest, where the highest praise would be to have snatched the palm of erudition from a youth not yet twenty years old?

Meanwhile, I could leave everything aside and, as it were, concede that no demonstration is contained in the entire pile of my reasonings. What then? Would he dare to assert that the words cannot have the meaning I gave them? If they can, what difficulty remains, since they confirm the truth upon which the "hinge" of our religion turns? But even if they were to support the sense that Lucius has falsely attached to them, and if that were proven by long "flasks" <note>original: "ampullis" – a rhetorical term for bombastic, inflated language</note> of syllogisms, of what use would it be? For as long as the thesis to which this passage is applied is judged by those of sounder mind and counsel—I will not say among things being judged... <note>original Greek: "κρινομενας" (krinomenas), referring to matters under judicial or scholarly review</note>

It is now nearly two years since I, having been freed from scholastic dust, was able to proceed securely to higher matters. I—whom the will of my father (now among the saints <note>original Greek: "ἐν ἁγίοις" (en hagiois). And so, at that time, I felt I should follow the lead of my own natural disposition...

...than I had thought. For to speak the truth of the matter, besides that internal dictator <note>Referring to his own conscience or inner drive.</note>, I had no one to urge me on. And indeed, a kind of fated inclination of my nature grew along with the work itself; nor did I stop until I believed I could offer some public specimen of my labors. 

Therefore, this subject of Cymbals fell to me—a matter which, as far as I know, has been treated in full by none of the antiquarians <term>Antiquarian: A scholar who studies ancient artifacts, customs, and texts.</term>. For whatever has been said on this matter by Caelius Rhodiginus, Turnebus, Scaliger, Passerat, Pignorius, Salmasius, Meursius, Barth, Rubenius, Spon, and others, could be called mere gaps <note>original: "lacunæ." As soon as I began to publish the plan of my design, I seemed to have earned the general applause of the men whom I have held in my sight and heart with due respect. I had nothing to boast of regarding a lavish collection <note>original: "supellectile." To you, **GERHARD MEIER**, **MATTHIAS BOOT**, **CORNELIUS HASE**, and **JOHANN HEINRICH EGGELING**—the great luminaries of the city of Bremen, the guardians of fleeting learning—I credit whatever I have attempted. Lest you be unaware, Reader—for I shall conceal nothing—my bold efforts would have been in vain had I not drawn a great deal from their generosity. But even supported by such great pillars, I easily perceived that I could not yet safely trust my own talent, due to the tenderness of my years and the rawness of my judgment. 

It pleased me, therefore, before I stepped onto the stage, to send ahead these rough outlines of this little work; like the unformed offspring of bears <note>According to ancient folklore, bear cubs were born as shapeless lumps and their mothers had to "lick them into shape." Come then, O men whose hearts are stirred by a higher Phoebus <note>A poetic reference to Apollo, the god of light, music, and knowledge.</note>, men whose spirit it is to help with a serene countenance those striving toward noble things; wherever I have hesitated, advise me kindly; if I have omitted anything, suggest it gently; if I have erred in any way, correct it rightly. Just as I have always looked up to the venerable faces of distinguished men, so too those who have received me, though undeserving, with their kindness, and who encourage me as I hasten toward greater [things...]

<header>ON CYMBALS.</header>

### AT THE AGE OF 17.

### MAY IT BE HAPPY, FAVORABLE, AND PROSPEROUS.
<note>original: "Q. F. F. F. Q. S." — an abbreviation for the traditional Roman formula *Quod Felix Faustum Fortunatumque Sit*.</note>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicting a landscape or architectural scene with figures.</image-desc>

Deciding to speak about the Cymbals of the ancients, I have determined to complete the entire matter in three sections or, as it were, books. The first will explain the names *and types*, both Greek and Latin. In the second, you will find a fuller history of the origin and progress of Cymbals; finally, the Cymbals themselves—namely their *material, form, and manner of use*. You may seek their various *uses* among different foreign <note>original: "Barbaras." In this context, it refers to any non-Greek or non-Roman people.</note>, Greek, and Roman peoples, etc., and whether those uses were sacred or profane, from the final part.

### BOOK I.

CYMBAL <note>original: "ΚΥΜΒΑΛΟΝ" (Kymbalon).</note>, a Greek word, was later transferred to the Romans: grammarians differ regarding its etymology <term>Etymology: The study of the origin and historical development of words.</term>. Some derive it *from a hunch* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυφος" (apo tou kyphos); referring to a curved or bulging shape.</note>; others from a certain cup, which the Greeks called *Kypellon* <note>original: "Κυπελλον."</note>; the wiser scholars derive it more closely from *kymbos* <note>original: "κυμβος."</note>, meaning hollow. It designates a musical instrument, hemispherical, hollow, and sounded by striking them together, as I discuss in the second book. Rubenius, following Nonnus, thought that another instrument was described under the name of a Cymbal, which produced sound from double iron pipes packed together. He was mistaken. (2) *Ardaniai* <note>original: "Ἀρδανιαι."</note> or jars, which the Greeks used to place filled with water before the doors of the deceased, were called cymbals by others. Tertullian <note>A prolific early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD).</note> called them *bronze sandals*, for the sandals themselves are named from their *clashing* <note>original: "crepitu."</note>, because they used to be reinforced with bronze underneath. To the Glossator...

(3) In a Greek and Roman proverb, talkative **declaimers** and **Grammarians** are called **Cymbals**, while those who are scurrilously garrulous are called "the highest cymbals" <note>original: "κυμβαλα ἀκροτητα" (kymbala akrotita)</note>. In the Middle Ages, the bell by which Monks were summoned to the refectory and to burial was named the **Cymbal of the refectory**. Sometimes you may read this word in a corrupted form, with "Symbol" <note>original: "Symbolum"</note> substituted for "Cymbal." There were also **Cymbal-like temples** <note>original: "Κυμβαλικοι ναοι" (Kymbalikoi naoi)</note>, buildings roofed in the shape of a Cymbal, which were called "double-cymbals" or "triple-cymbals" <note>original: "βικυμβαλα, τρικυμβαλα" (bikymbala, trikymbala)</note> according to the number of dining couches they contained.

(4) **THE CROTALUM** <note>original: "ΚΡΟΤΑΛΟΝ" (Krotalon). A type of clapper or rattle.</note>. This is the "cross" <note>A metaphor for a torturous puzzle or difficulty.</note> of the most learned men, such as Scaliger, Valerianus, Bulengerus, etc., who, while they thought they were bringing some sound reasoning to the matter, fell into wretched error. Furthermore, the ancients themselves disagree wonderously. To one person, the *crotalum* is a **bronze ring struck by an iron rod** to the sound of a pipe, which the Greeks call a "rhombus" <note>original: "ῥομβον" (rhombon)</note> and the Latins call a "hoop" <note>original: "Trochum"</note>. To others, it is a **vessel made of shell, or wood, or bronze that is held in the hand**—that is, a rattle, a clapper, or a cymbal. A third group describes it as **sonorous little spheres** which, with certain grains placed inside, produce various sounds according to their size and the type of metal. Someone else describes it as an instrument **used during applause**. (5) The common opinion is this: A **Crotalum** is properly a **split reed**, which is manufactured specifically so that it makes a sound if someone shakes it with their hands, producing something like a "clap" <note>original: "κροτον" (kroton)</note>. It is an instrument not far removed from the Cymbal, both in use and in the method of playing, which is why it is confused by everyone. The etymology is manifest: from *krotos*, meaning **applause**. (6) In Athenaeus, the narcissus flower is called a "Crotalum," and others, imitating the Latins, have called **sandals** by this name; nor is anything more common than to call a talkative, eloquent, and shrewd man a "crotalum," or to name the delivery of a pathetic oration a "clap" <note>original: "κροτον" (kroton)</note>.

(7) **THE KROUMA** or *krousma* <note>original: "ΚΡΟΥΜΑ seu κρουσμα"</note>, such as Jacob Spon <note>A 17th-century French physician and archaeologist.</note> believes he can show on an ancient statue. It is an instrument of the Phoenicians and of the people of Gades <note>Modern-day Cádiz.</note> in Spain. It signifies the **breath of a flute, the plucking of a lyre, and the sound of a rustic reed**; finally, it can mean an unusual **whirlwind** of the mind or a **stirring of the emotions**. (8) That passage in Hesychius <note>An ancient Greek lexicographer.</note> has caused great difficulty: "The *Dipli* [Double] is a type of dance, or a *krouma*." Meursius <note>Johannes Meursius, a Dutch classical scholar.</note> placed the *Dipli* among the Tragic dances based on Pollux and Aristophanes, and to others, the *Dipli* is a figure which—

...a kind of triangle in comedies: But how is it a **type of rhythmic beat** <note>original Greek: εἶδος κρούματος (eidos kroumatos)</note>? Truly, "I am Davus, not Oedipus" <note>A Latin proverb from the playwright Terence meaning "I am a simple man, not a solver of riddles."</note>. Among more recent Greeks, this term is used for the striking of bells, which were wooden boards and iron plates intended to be struck together with an iron hammer. John of Genoa, a writer of the later Latin period <note>original: "infimæ Latinitatis"</note>, explains the word *cruma* <note>a rhythmic beat</note> as *crumena* <note>a purse or money-bag, likely a linguistic error by the medieval author</note>.

(9) **THE CLAPPER** <note>original Greek: ΠΛΑΤΑΓΗ (Platage)</note>. A *crotalum*, or an instrument very similar to a *crotalum* <note>a type of rattle or clapper</note>, usually made of bronze or boxwood, which produces a loud noise. It can also refer to a talkative man; in this sense, the character *Platagidorus* in the plays of Plautus was a boastful, loud-mouthed man. Aretinus was in error when he interpreted *Platage* as a small writing tablet in his commentary on Aristotle.

(10) Its diminutive form is:
**THE LITTLE CLAPPER** <note>original Greek: ΠΛΑΤΑΓΩΝΙΟΝ (Platagonion)</note>. This was a common **rattle used as a child’s toy**. According to the lexicographer Suidas, the term applies to anything that has width. Specifically, it refers to **poppy and anemone leaves**, which lovers used to test whether their sweethearts were faithful: they would place the leaves between the thumb and index finger and strike them together, divining the truth of their love from the sound of the pop.

(11) **THE VINEGAR BOWL** <note>original Greek: ΟΞΥΒΑΦΟΝ (Oxybaphon)</note>, also called an *acetabulum*, a vessel similar to a Cymbal. It was struck together to elicit a musical sound; to make the sound fuller, it was manufactured from several metals melted into one. The inventor of this instrument was Diocles. Otherwise, the *oxybaphon* was a specific type of drinking cup. To others, it was a vessel used for holding sauce <note>original: "embammati"</note>, which they were accustomed to use in the game of **Cottabus** <note>A popular Greek party game where players threw wine dregs at a target, often trying to sink small floating bowls</note>. Since there were various types of Cottabus, they called this one simply "the little Cottabus played with vinegar bowls" <note>original Greek: κοττάβιον δι’ ὀξυβάφων (kottabion di’ oxybaphon)</note>. Others called these vessels *oxides* or *ketheia*.

(12) **THE CUP** <note>original Greek: ΚΟΤΥΛΗ (Kotyle)</note>. It is clear from the writings of Athenaeus and Eustathius that the **Cymbal** was called by this name; and this is not surprising. For among the ancients, every hollow object was called a *kotyle*. It was most especially a cup of a certain measure, which Latin translators call a *hemina* <note>about half a pint</note>, and the scholar Casaubon calls the eighth part of a *choenix*. Such a cup was attached to the ritual branch called the *eiresione* <note>An olive or laurel branch wrapped in wool and hung with fruits and small jars, used in the festivals of Thargelia and Pyanepsia</note>. The cavity of the hip, the shoulder, and even the palm of the hand is called a *kotyle*: hence the game among the Athenians called "in the cup" or "in the hollow of the arm" <note>original: "ἐν κοτύλῃ seu ἀγκοτύλῃ" (en kotyle seu anktyle)</note>. Long ago, Demophon had written a specialized treatise on these *kotylae*.

(13) **THE WHIRLER** <note>original Greek: ΡΥΜΒΟΣ (Rymbos)</note>. This is identified as a **Cymbal** by the commentator on Apollonius. Other commentators, along with the author of the *Etymologicum*, read the word as *rhombus* <note>a spinning ritual instrument</note>, though I give little credit to them. Hesychius explains it as a *dinos* <note>a spinning vessel or whirlpool</note>. Now, the *dinos* is a vessel so similar to a Cymbal,

(14) **KREMBALA** <note>original Greek: ΚΡΕΜΒΑΛΑ</note>. These were rattles made of bronze, shell, or stone, sometimes gilded, which produced a clatter with the movement of a finger. "To strike with the *crembala*" <note>original: *Crembalis pulsare*</note> is expressed by the Greek terms *krembaliazein* <note>κρεμβαλιαζειν</note> and *kongchyliazein* <note>κογχυλιαζειν - literally "to play the shells"</note>. The term *krembaliastēs* <note>κρεμβαλιαστης</note> is used in Homer for one who uses them. "Double-yoked bronze" <note>original Greek: ΔΙΖΥΓΟΝ ΧΑΛΚΟΣ (dizygon chalkos)</note> is a poetic way of describing a *crotalum* <note>a type of clapper or castanet</note>.

(15) **BAKTYLIA** <note>original Greek: ΒΑΚΤΥΛΙΑ</note>. Identified as **cymbals** by Suidas, Hesychius, and the manuscript lexicon of Charles du Fresne. They are called *donakes* <note>original Greek: ΔONAKEΣ - literally "reeds"</note> in the works of Pollux. *Lekides* <note>original Greek: ΛEKIΔEΣ</note> were instruments shaken to produce a clash, according to Nicomachus, unless perhaps the text should be read as *lekanides* <note>small basins</note>. *Stromboi* <note>original Greek: ΣTPOMBOI</note> were **shepherds' rattles** used to gather the herd, mentioned in Plutarch; these were perhaps made of shell, as Aristotle uses the word *strombos* for a spiral conch shell.

(16) **ACETABULA**. These were the *oxybapha* <note>original Greek: Οξυβαφα - literally "vinegar cups"</note> of the Romans: they were cast from various metals and gave off a **sweet ringing sound** when struck. They were very commonly used by performers of sleight-of-hand, who were called *acetabularii* <note>cup-players or jugglers</note> because of them. Through speed of hand and by placing several cups on a table, they would make a pebble that you thought was hidden under one cup appear under another. The Greeks called these vagabond performers *psēphopaiktas* <note>stone-players</note>, *psēphokleptai* <note>stone-stealers</note>, or *klēropaiktas* <note>lot-players</note>.

(17) Latin interpreters of the **Books of Moses** <note>The first five books of the Bible</note> frequently mention these *acetabula*, which are explained in ancient glossaries as: "round vessels where wine is kept near the altar." However, learned men disagree on this, and it is not my place to settle such great disputes.

(18) Properly speaking, they were **vessels intended for vinegar**, as authors commonly agree; although the name is also transferred to a unit of measure which contains "the fourth part of a *hemina*" <note>roughly 0.06 liters</note>. Writers of a later age pronounce the word as *Acitabulum*, *Acetaforum*, or *Acetallum*.

(19) **TESTÆ** <note>literally "shells" or "tiles"</note>. These were cymbals made of baked clay that imitated the sound of clapping hands. They were used by those who did not have a supply of better instruments. Such shells, which boys used to place in their mouths and blow into, were called *lopadas* <note>original Greek: λοπαδας - literally "platters" or "flat shells"</note>.

(20) **IMBRICES** <note>literally "roof-tiles"</note>. These were **stone cymbals**, the sound of which people produced by clapping. The ancients were accustomed to imitating musical modes in their applause, especially the rhythm of cymbals.

(21) **CREPITACULA**. Also called *crepitacilla*, these were **infant rattles** or *crotala*. The word *crepundia* <note>toys/rattles</note> is derived from their rattling sound (*crepitu*); although *sistra* <note>loop-shaped Egyptian rattles</note> are also sometimes named this way...

<header>ON CYMBALS.</header>

...are used. **NAVLIA** <note>original: *Navlia*</note> were a type of cymbal mentioned in Ovid, as learned men believe. (22) Thus far we have discussed true cymbals; I now add those that are misidentified or false.

**KALYBE** <note>original Greek: ΚΑΛΥΒΗ</note> is incorrectly explained as the clanging of bronze vessels. As has already been noted by others, *calybae* are actually **booths** <note>original: *pergulas*</note> such as those set up in rented taverns; likewise, they are **small shrines** <note>original: *aediculas*</note> in the inner part of temples which held the statues and sacred couches of the gods. For this reason, a *calybita* <note>a dweller in such a booth</note> is correctly explained as a **shrine-attendant** <note>original Greek: θαλαμηπόλος (thalamēpolos)</note>, not a **percussionist** <note>original Greek: κρουματίσης (kroumatistēs)</note>.

(23) **SISTRON** <note>original Greek: ΣΗΣΤΡΟΝ; Latin: *Sistrum*</note>. The *sistrum* <note>a rattle used in ancient Egypt, especially in the worship of Isis</note> was placed among the cymbals by the ancients; modern writers have followed them eagerly but without much thought. Bochart’s interpretation of Isaiah 18:1, "The cymbals of the borders" <note>original: *Cymbala orarum*</note>, which he thinks refers to sistrums, presents great difficulties.

(24) **SCABILLA**. These might be called **foot cymbals** <note>original: *Cymbala pedum*</note>. Augustine directly called them cymbals, as did various glossaries after him. But this should be understood loosely and with caution. **TYMPANA**. A great Spanish scholar <note>likely referring to the scholar Covarrubias</note> was miserably mistaken when he confused these with cymbals; he even dared to cite a coin as evidence for this, though the coin shows not a single trace of a cymbal.

(25) **NACARIAE** <note>also called *nacchere* or *nacare*</note>. A rattle of the Middle Ages, which the learned men of the Accademia della Crusca interpret sometimes as a drum and sometimes as a *crotalum* <note>a type of clapper</note>. Both are wrong. It was an iron or wooden plate that was usually struck with a rod or hammer. Among the Greeks and Saracens, it took the place of a bell, and the earlier Franks adopted it from them.

## BOOK II.

I come now to the history of Cymbals—a matter that is, if anything is, extremely intricate. Cymbals are older than all other musical instruments, if what authors say is true: that music originally began from the tinkling of bronze. They were invented by the **Idaean Dactyls** <note>mythological craftsmen and healers associated with the Great Mother goddess in Phrygia</note> in Phrygia. (2) They were called "Dactyls" after the discovery of the *dactyl* <note>a metrical foot consisting of one long syllable followed by two short ones</note>, unless perhaps they were better named for "strength," which is often symbolically represented by fingers and hands <note>The word *daktylos* means "finger" in Greek</note>. They were the most ancient **original inhabitants** <note>original Greek: αὐτόχθονες (autochthones)</note> of Phrygia, whom Clement of Alexandria places in the 73rd year after the Great Flood. They should not be confused with the "Idaean Dactyl" stone, which takes its name from another source. (3) From them [others] learned...

...this music to the **Corybantes** <note>armed and rhythmic dancers who worshipped the goddess Cybele</note>, who were named, according to the opinion of Vossius, "because they move with butting heads." <note>original Greek: ὅτι κορυπτοντες βαινοιεν (hoti koryptontes bainoien)</note>. J. G. Grævius, a distinguished man and the glory of his own age—as he will be the wonder of those to follow—suggests that they were brave men and the bodyguards of the first Kings of Phrygia. **Wisely** <note>original Greek: Σοφῶς (Sophōs)</note>. To these men were later given the same sacred rites as the Mother of the Gods and Attis; their priests were called **Anactotelestæ** <note>original Greek: Ἀνακτοτελεσταί; priests who performed initiations for the "lords" or "kings"</note>. (4) Those authors are in error who claim they were in Crete, confusing them with the more ancient **Idaean Dactyls** <note>mythical metalworkers and magicians of Mount Ida</note>; for it was the latter, not the Corybantes, who traveled to Crete with Rhea and there also made cymbals common. (5)

The matter happened thus: Jupiter, the most ancient King of the Cretans, took as his wife Idaea, the Queen of Phrygia, who gave her name to two mountains. When she set out to join her husband, she took certain Idaean Dactyl nobles with her. During the journey, they called at Rhodes; there, the **Telchines** <note>mythological smiths and sorcerers</note>, who were refugees from the Peloponnese, had arrived. Idaea easily took them under her protection and brought them with her to Crete. It seems, however, that they later left Crete and settled in Cyprus. (6) Jupiter fathered ten **Curetes** <note>armed youths who protected the infant Jupiter</note> by Idaea, who were entrusted to the education of the Idaean Dactyls and were confounded with them by later generations. The eldest of them, Cres, reigned, and after him his daughter, who was married to **Ammon** the Egyptian <note>referring to the syncretism of the Greek Zeus and the Egyptian Ammon</note>. He fought a heavy war with foreigners, whom the myths call **Saturn** and the **Titans**. (8)

Meanwhile, the Idaean Dactyls passed away. The Curetes, being resentful of Ammon—a foreigner who nevertheless held the kingdom—abandoned him and easily persuaded his granddaughter Rhea, Ammon’s wife, to set out for Phrygia with them and her young son Jupiter. Nevertheless, the name of the Curetes remained attached to the whole island. (9) Thus the cymbals were carried back into Phrygia with the Curetes, who settled there among the Corybantes and raised Jupiter; they bestowed divine honors upon the deceased granddaughter **Rhea** and her mother **Idaea**. (10)

Among the Corybantes, three were especially conspicuous in authority; two of them killed the third brother and, fleeing because of the deed into Etruria <note>ancient Italy</note>, they carried over the sacred rites of Attis. There they were called **Cabiri** <note>mysterious deities of the underworld and fertility</note>. (11) Among these was also the **Phrygian Hercules**, who, while a fugitive with his brother, was harassed by certain insects as he passed through Arcadia; later generations called these the **Stymphalides** <note>usually described as man-eating birds in the labors of Hercules</note>. He put them to flight with the clatter of **crotala** <note>clappers or rattles used in ancient percussion</note>. (12) The worship of the Idaean Mother and Rhea passed from Upper Phrygia to the neighboring Trojans, and soon also that of the Idaean Dactyls, whose ministers...

-> # ON CYMBALS. <-

They were the **Cadmilli**, perhaps named after Cadmus, who was the most famous among them. These later became known to the Romans themselves, among whom some called them *Gods*, others *Samothracian fingers* <note>A reference to the Idaean Dactyls; "dactyl" is the Greek word for finger</note>, and others *Camilli*—servants who were summoned <note>original Latin: "extorto," possibly implying they were drawn out or recruited for service</note>. *I do not know how these conjectures will be received; nevertheless, relying on the credibility of the authors, they will easily reconcile most of their views. For there is no hope of restoring total harmony among all: such is the darkness caused by the Greek lust for lying.*

(3) **THE GALLI** <note>the eunuch priests of the goddess Cybele</note>, frenzied men. As servants of the Idaean Mother and Attis (or rather Jupiter), they not only frequently used cymbals, but even castrated themselves to the clashing of the instruments in the Phrygian musical modes.

(4) **THE PHOENICIANS** learned to play the cymbals from the Phrygians. And did the **JEWS** as well? I certainly have no historical authority on the matter, but it could easily have happened. Then Cadmus brought the frenzied cult of Cybele with cymbals to **THEBES**, where the name of Attis or Jupiter was lost, and another name—that of the "frenzied one" or **Bacchus**—took its place. (15) Nor were cymbals unusual in the rest of **GREECE**, where those who played them were called *cymbalists* <note>original Greek: κυμβαλισαι</note>, *temple-beaters* <note>original Greek: κροταφισαι</note>, *rhythm-makers* <note>original Greek: κρουματοποιοι</note>, and so on. Even **ERATO** herself, among the Muses, was a cymbal-player, for she was placed in charge of matters relating to harlots and lovers. Playing the cymbals was particularly characteristic of women of this sort, though you may read that it was occasionally not foreign to more honorable women. (16) Certainly the **MAGODI** <note>itinerant performers of mime and low comedy</note> should be recorded here; acting the parts of men while wearing female dress, they would sing of the miracles and powers of the magi amidst the noise of cymbals.

(17) Since **SPAIN** was frequently occupied by Phoenician colonies, among which were Gades <note>modern-day Cádiz</note> and Tartessos, it received the same cymbals and has preserved them through a very long series of ages even until now. From this come the famous female dancers of Gades or Tartessos mentioned by the ancients, who danced naked with obscene movements at banquets; they are wrongly confused with female harpists by Bulenger <note>Julius Caesar Bulenger, a 17th-century scholar of ancient customs</note>.

(18) I come at last to the **ROMANS**, among whom cymbals were likewise used. **Hercules** first brought them when he traveled through Italy on his return from Spain—the Theban Hercules, that is, not the Phrygian one, for both the facts and the dates align better. The Corybantes [practiced] this music; according to the opinion of Vossius <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a renowned Dutch scholar and humanist</note>, they were so named because they walked with their heads bowed <note>original Greek: ὅτι κορύπτοντες βαίνοιεν</note>. J. G. Grævius <note>Johann Georg Graevius (1632–1703), a leading German classical scholar</note>, a man of distinguished character, the glory of his own time and the wonder of those to follow, suggests they were brave men and the bodyguards of the first kings of Phrygia. Wisely <note>original Greek: Σοφῶς</note>. Subsequently, they shared the same sacred rites with the Mother of the Gods and Attis: their priests were called *Anactotelestae* <note>term for "initiators of the kings" or those who performed royal mysteries</note>. (4) Those authors are mistaken who claim they were in Crete, confusing them with the older Idaean Dactyls; for these—not the Corybantes—set out with Rhea for Crete and made cymbals common there. (5)

The matter proceeded thus: Jupiter, the most ancient king of the Cretans, married Idaea, the queen of Phrygia, who gave her name to two mountains. As she was setting out to join her husband, she took certain Idaean Dactyls—who were nobles—with her. In the meantime, they landed at Rhodes: there the *Telchines* <note>mythological craftsmen and sorcerers associated with Rhodes</note>, who were fugitives from the Peloponnese, had arrived. Idaea easily took them under her protection and led them with her to Crete. However, they seem to have left Crete later and settled in Cyprus. (6) Jupiter fathered ten *Curetes* <note>younger warrior-priests</note> by Idaea; these were entrusted to the education of the Idaean Dactyls and were later confused with them by posterity. The greatest of them, Cres, reigned, and after him his daughter, who married the Egyptian Ammon. He had a serious war with foreigners, whom the myths call Saturn and the Titans. (8)

Meanwhile, the Idaean Dactyls passed away. The Curetes, resenting Ammon because he was a foreigner though he held the throne, abandoned him. They easily persuaded his niece Rhea—Ammon’s wife—to set out with them and her young son Jupiter for Phrygia. Nevertheless, the name of the Curetes remained with the entire island. (9) Thus cymbals were brought back to Phrygia with the Curetes, who settled there among the Corybantes and raised Jupiter. They honored their deceased niece *Rhea* and her mother *Idaea* with divine honors. (10) Among the Corybantes, three were especially distinguished in authority; two of them killed the third brother and, fleeing because of the deed to Etruria <note>modern-day Tuscany, Italy</note>, brought over the sacred rites of Attis: there they were called the *Cabiri* <note>mysterious deities of the underworld and fertility</note>. (11) Among these was also the Phrygian Hercules, who, as a fugitive with his brother, was passing through Arcadia and was harassed by certain insects—which posterity called the Stymphalian birds <note>original: Stymphalidas</note>—and drove them away with the clanging of rattles. # ON CYMBALS.

### Aaaa 2
<meta>catchword: of Augustus</meta>

They were the **Cadmilli**, perhaps so named after Cadmus, who was more distinguished than the others. These later became known to the Romans themselves, among whom some called them *Gods*, others *Samothracian fingers* <note>original: *digitos Samothracios*</note>, and others *Camilli* <note>Attendants or young ministers of a sacrifice</note>. I do not know how these conjectures will be received; nevertheless, since they are supported by the authority of ancient authors, they will easily reconcile most of these views. Indeed, one cannot even hope to restore total harmony among all sources, for there is such darkness caused by the Greek passion for fabrication.

(3) **GALLI**, frenzied men. As ministers of the Idaean Mother <note>Cybele</note> and Attis (or more accurately, Jupiter), they not only used cymbals frequently, but also castrated themselves <note>original: *se exsecarunt*</note> amidst the clashing of these instruments in the Phrygian modes.

(4) The **PHOENICIANS** learned to play the cymbals <note>original: *cymbalissare*</note> from the Phrygians. Did the **JEWS** also? I certainly have no definitive authority on the matter, but it could easily have happened. **CADMUS** then brought the frenzied cult of Cybele to **THEBES** along with cymbals; it was there that Attis (or Jupiter) lost his name, and in his place came another name for a frenzied god: Bacchus. (15) Nor were cymbals unusual in the rest of **GREECE**, where those who played them were called <term>kymbalisai</term> <note>cymbal-players</note>, <term>krotaphisai</term> <note>those who strike rhythm instruments or clappers</note>, <term>kroumatopoioi</term> <note>composers or players of percussion</note>, and so on. Even the Muse **ERATO** herself is depicted as a cymbalist, for she was placed in charge of the affairs of courtesans and lovers. Indeed, playing the cymbals was particularly characteristic of women of that sort, although you may occasionally read of more respectable women playing them. (16) Certainly, the **MAGODI** <note>wandering performers or mimes</note> should be mentioned here; they were men who performed in women's clothing, singing of the miracles and powers of the Magi amidst the noise of cymbals.

(17) **SPAIN**, being frequently occupied by Phoenician colonies—among which were Gades <note>Cádiz</note> and Tartessos—received these same cymbals and has preserved them through a very long series of ages even to this day. Hence the famous Gaditanian or Tartessian dancers mentioned by the ancients, who danced naked with obscene movements at banquets; these are incorrectly confused with female harpists by Bulengerus <note>Jean-César Boulenger (1558–1628), a Jesuit scholar who wrote on ancient Roman and Greek customs</note>.

(18) I come finally to the **ROMANS**, among whom cymbals were likewise used. Hercules first brought them when he traveled through Italy upon his return from Spain. This was the Theban Hercules, of course, not the Phrygian one, for both the circumstances and the timeline align more closely. But they were later neglected and, it seems, only adopted again much later, perhaps alongside the art of dancing, which...

# DISSERTATION

### Aaaa 2
<meta>catchword: (25) MO-</meta>

Authors testify that they were finally introduced in the times of Augustus. (19) A distinguished man <note>Likely referring to a contemporary scholar like Isaac Vossius or a similar figure</note> then attempts to prove from **Augustine** that musicians <note>original: *Symphoniacos*</note> used cymbals; however, I have already advised above that these should be understood as *scabilla* <note>foot-clappers used by ancient conductors to beat time</note>. Furthermore, the statue he brings forth from **Rubenius** <note>Albert Rubens, a scholar of Roman dress</note> depicts, in my opinion, a **choir leader** <note>original: *MESOCHORUM*</note> rather than a musician, for those instruments are more suitable to the former. (19) Cymbals were the common delights of Roman prostitutes, whom they consequently called *Cymbal-players* <note>original: *Cymbalistrias*</note>, and **Sponius** displays them in three statues. Slightly different from these, though not by much, were the **castanet-players** <note>original: *crotalistriae*</note>, whom the same author depicts in an elegant figure. (20) The **tavern-maids** <note>original: *Copae*</note> were undoubtedly among the castanet-players, of whom you find traces in **Virgil** and **Suetonius**. It is debated whether they appear in **Cicero's** *Against Piso*; the greatest critics say no, but I affirm it. What they actually were is discussed variously among writers such as **Turnebus, Torrentius, Scaliger, Casaubon, Salmasius, Barth**, and others. I agree with those who assert they were women who managed taverns and were accustomed to offering their bodies to guests. As for the claim that they were old women because the poets ascribe a *mitra* <note>a type of headband or turban</note> to them, that is a very weak argument; for the *mitra* was common among prostitutes and foreign women. Having thus untangled the history of cymbals, I shall now describe the cymbals themselves more diligently.

(21) Their **SHAPE** was semi-round, as depicted by **Pignorio** and others. Some compare it to *acetabula* <note>small vinegar cups or sockets</note>, others to the leaves of the *cotyledon* plant, others to the hip-socket, and others to various other things. (22) The reason for the comparison to *acetabula* is easily established. The *cotyledon* is a herb with a concave leaf, and by a reciprocal way of speaking, **Dioscorides** calls it a <term>kymbalion</term> <note>original Greek: κύμβαλιον, meaning "little cymbal"</note>. Some wish this same plant to be called "Venus’s navel," a claim which **Salmasius** strongly refutes. Elsewhere, *cotyledones* referred to the "cups" of an octopus—the hollow parts on an octopus’s tentacles, which others call <term>plokamous</term> <note>original Greek: πλοκάμους, meaning "tentacles" or "twined locks"</note>. The *Coxendix* herb is either the same or not very different. The Fathers of the ancient, and even the medieval, Church frequently compare them to lips.

(23) They were **HANDLED** in more than one way: some by long metal plates, others by a convexity ending in a sharp point, and some in the form of a cross.

(24) Their **MATERIAL** was mostly bronze <note>original: *aes*</note>, and for that reason, "bronzes" <note>original: *aera*</note> is used simply to mean "cymbals" by countless authors. However, they were occasionally made of gold, silver, gilded metal, and so on.

# ON CYMBALS

(25) They were set in motion by clashing, which the ancient writers called *flictum* <note>A Latin term for a "striking" or "clashing" together</note>. For the verb *fligere* means the same as "to strike together," though it was more common among older authors than more recent ones. For this reason, cymbals were **PAIRED**. However, there were some who believed that Cymbals produced sound by a small mallet <note>original: *malleolus*</note> striking the convex part and hitting the concave part against the air, in the same way they write about the bronze of **Dodona** <note>The Oracle of Dodona featured bronze vessels that would ring when struck</note>, and as we have mentioned more than once regarding medieval bells.

(26) **Cassius Hemina** <note>An early Roman historian</note> used the word *cymbalissare* <note>to play the cymbals</note> for clashing Cymbals together. Others used the word *crepare* <note>to rattle or crack</note>, though improperly: for castanets <note>original: *crotala*</note> rattled, not Cymbals. The Greeks, however, imitated this and used the words *krotein* and *krotalizein* <note>Greek: κροτεῖν and κροταλίζειν, meaning to rattle or clap</note> for any kind of striking, but especially for Cymbals.

(27) The most common Greek term here is *krouein* <note>Greek: κρούειν</note>, which an old Lexicon explains as: *To strike, To hit, To beat*. This verb is derived from every kind of **collision of bronze**, but especially applied to Cymbals. It was often metaphorically applied to the **striking of the lyre**, the **beat of oars**, the **beat of feet** while walking, and even to **weaving** <note>original: *textrinam*</note>; hence garments were called "beaten" <note>original: *crustae*</note> because they were well-struck <note>referring to the process of beating the fabric to tighten the weave</note>, which others called *spathemata* <note>Greek: σπαθήματα, from the "spatha" or batten used in weaving</note>. Later writers sometimes used *krouzein* <note>Greek: κρούζειν</note>, and this is commonly applied to bells.

(28) Cymbals struck in this way produced a *Psophos* <note>Greek: Ψόφον, a general word for a sound or noise</note>, that unique sound. The Romans called it a **RINGING** <note>original: *TINNITUM*</note>. If you take the word broadly, it was applied to almost all musical instruments: flutes, drums, trumpets, rattles <note>original: *sistra*</note>, small bells, etc.; indeed, to every striking of bronze. To the Greeks, it was an *alalagmos* <note>Greek: ἀλαλαγμός, a loud shout or clanging</note>, an *echos* <note>Greek: ἦχος</note>, etc. A medieval writer uses the phrase *Cymbal-like voices*. For the term *voice*, though properly belonging to a living creature, is often transferred to inanimate things like flutes, trumpets, lyres, and here to Cymbals.

(29) That ringing expressed various SOUNDS, such as the syllables *kum, kar, ken, re, kre, ke, tri, chtha*, as found in the *Etymologicon* <note>An ancient Greek dictionary</note>. Also worthy of note is the account by **Borel** <note>Pierre Borel, a 17th-century scientist and physician</note> in his supplement to the life of **Peiresc** <note>Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc, a famous French scholar and collector</note> on page 285: *“I must not omit that I saw a bronze cymbal of wonderful elegance coming from the same Museum (of Peiresc): its shape was spherical, like an orange, hollow inside and divided into two portions like small cups; from the bottom of these, another cup emerged, attached to the former not at the edges but only at the point of contact. This second cup was pierced with small parallel holes from the top downward, as if by so many vents. If it were shaken even by a light hand, it emitted a harmonic sound continued for nearly twenty minutes* <note>original: *sesquiquadrantem*, literally a quarter and a half-quarter of an hour</note> *and a multiplying echo from the reflected air—”*

## BOOK III.

That cymbals were employed in the worship of the true God among the Jews is gathered from 2 Samuel 6:5, 1 Chronicles 13:8, Nehemiah 12:27, and Psalm 150:5. In these places, the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> uses the term *kymbala* <note>original Greek: κύμβαλα</note>, followed by almost all the Church Fathers and many more recent scholars. I also learn from Venantius Honorius, Geoffrey, and others, that cymbals were even struck in Christian churches during the Middle Ages. But it is not my purpose to pursue these matters here. (2) I move on to the gentiles <note>Pagan or non-Jewish nations</note>, where nothing is more common. First, barbarian deities were worshiped with this noise; Lucian is a witness regarding the Paphlagonians. I learned from a commentary <note>original: *Schol. ejus*</note> that a certain type of wooden cymbal was used in the human sacrifices to Saturn in Sardinia. (3) Who does not know of the cymbals used in the Phrygian rites of the Mother Goddess? <note>Cybele, often associated with loud music and ecstatic worship</note>. Besides countless authors, this is proven by the marble reliefs in Gruter’s collection; *the Attis in the Circus in Panvinius; two bronze hands, one from Pignoria and the other from Tomasini*, and other excellent relics of antiquity. The same was in use among the people of Cyzicus and others; however, among the Cretans and Scythians, they were not even admitted. (4) They provide various reasons for this custom. Phurnutus <note>Also known as Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher</note>, since he understands Rhea <note>The Mother of the Gods</note> to represent rains and storms, so *he wants the thunder to be represented by the mixture of drums and cymbals*. According to Augustine, citing Varro, *the sound of cymbals signifies the clashing of iron tools, hands, and the ringing of bronze in the cultivation of a field. These tools were made of bronze, because the ancients cultivated with bronze before iron was discovered.* Certainly:

*The use of bronze was known before that of iron.* <note>A quote from the Roman poet Lucretius on the history of technology</note>. Mythologists say the practice was instituted in memory of the hiding of Jupiter <note>Zeus</note> under a din of bronze <note>The Kuretes clashed shields and cymbals to drown out the infant Jupiter's cries so his father Saturn would not find and eat him</note>, a fable which we have already partly dismissed above, and partly restored to a more sensible meaning. Lucian <note>A 2nd-century Syrian-Greek satirist</note> remains silent, however, on where this took place. (6) The Egyptian rites of Isis and, finally, those of the Syrian Goddess were also celebrated with cymbals. (7) Cymbals were most frequent in the festivals of Bacchus, and especially in the triennial ecstatic rites <note>original: *trietericis orgiis*; these were festivals held every three years</note>. Besides countless authors, the *Gem* of *Casaubon* <note>Isaac Casaubon, a renowned Renaissance scholar</note>, the *Marble Vase of Spon* <note>Jacob Spon, a pioneer of archaeology</note>, and other items prove this abundantly. (8) Were cymbals also used in certain rites of Jupiter? I have found few traces, yet some exist. I believe that the infant Jupiter, that son of Rhea later called Attis, was considered to be Bacchus by the people of Thebes. Indeed, cymbals were struck for both of them. Prudentius <note>A Roman Christian poet</note> alone expressly mentions the cymbals of Jupiter. Additionally, I have found it most common to move cymbals in almost all Greek ecstatic rites. (9) To prove this more clearly, I thought I should dwell on this material for a moment.

"Ecstatic rites" <note>original Greek: *Όργια* (*Orgia*)</note> are to me what are elsewhere called "mysteries" <note>original Greek: *μυστηρια* (*mysteria*)</note>, and writers commonly use the terms this way. Servius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note> attempts in vain to apply the term to all sacred rites, for other authorities protest. Orpheus had already sung of these in his time, and they were customary in these sacred rites: 1. Primarily those of Bacchus, which are simply called "Orgies"; they seemed to be named either *from being performed in his passions* <note>original Greek: δια το ἐν ταις ὀργασιν αὐτου ἐπιτελεισθαι</note>, or *from the act of being moved by divine frenzy*, or *from the word for "reaching out" or "desiring."* 2. Those of Cybele. 3. Those of Proserpina and Ceres. 4. Those of Cotytus. But, you ask, were cymbals used for her as well? I do not know for certain, though I suspect so. The commentator on Juvenal certainly says, *Following the example of Cotytus, the rites of Isis are said to be celebrated*; and who is ignorant of cymbals in the rites of Isis? Additionally, Cotytus was a deity of shameful and meretricious matters; for this reason, Phurnutus <note>Also known as Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher</note> identifies her with Cupid. Achilles Tatius also mentions her ecstatic rites. She was a goddess of the Thracians, from whom the Athenians had received her; according to Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note>, she was the *overseer of shameful things*, hence the proverb "a soft man is a companion of Cotytus." (10) I return to Jupiter, whose *ecstatic celebration* <note>original Greek: ὀργιασμον (*orgiasmon*)</note> Strabo and others report; hence he was also called Sabazius. [these goddesses] are themselves the same as Cybele. 4. **Cotyto**. Here again I proceed by conjecture: and just as I previously equated him with Cupid, I now find him not unrelated to **Bacchus**. Cotytos was worshiped by the Thracians, and was the same as Bacchus—specifically **Sabazius** <note>A Phrygian and Thracian deity often identified by the Greeks with Dionysus/Bacchus</note>—as the Commentator on Aristophanes <note>original: *Schol. Aristoph.*</note> declares. Cotytos presided over shameful matters—and who would deny that of Bacchus? (11) I find that **cymbals** were used primarily in three festivals at Rome: regarding the **Saturnalia** <note>The mid-winter festival of Saturn</note>, **Statius** testifies; regarding the **Palilia** <note>A festival for the goddess Pales, involving the purification of flocks</note>, **Athenaeus**; regarding the **Suovetaurilia** <note>A major Roman sacrifice of a pig (*sus*), sheep (*ovis*), and bull (*taurus*)</note>, a most elegant marble in the collection of **Spon** <note>Jacob Spon, a 17th-century pioneer of archaeology</note> bears witness, with which the poet **Tibullus** seems to agree.

(12) So much for sacred uses; profane <note>secular or non-religious</note> uses follow. It was a common opinion among the ancients that the Moon suffered an eclipse due to the wickedness of Thessalian witches. They believed the Moon could be aided by the clanging of bronze and basins, and the blaring of horns and trumpets. I was unsure whether to include cymbals in this category due to the instrument's small size; but are not bells, if not smaller, certainly no larger in this custom? Absolutely. And **Juvenal** says so explicitly. Nor could the phrase from **Tibullus**, "beaten bronze" <note>original: *æra repulsa*</note>, or **Statius**, "bronze rattles" <note>original: *æra crepant*</note>, or **Martial**, "hands strike the bronze" <note>original: *æra verberant manus*</note>, be better explained. It should be noted, moreover, that they rarely used any equipment except bronze to recall the Moon. For they believed something divine and medicinal resided in bronze. Hence you may read that heroes rarely used anything but bronze weapons; herbs were cut with bronze sickles by witches, etc. (13) **Pliny** said that in his time **bees** delighted in the clapping and clanging of bronze; hence, cymbals were used to call them back so they would not fly too far in a swarm. However, this sound must have been sweet and rhythmic, because **Ammianus Marcellinus** reports they are driven away by turbulent noise, and adds the reason: a swarm of bees was an unlucky omen among the Romans, a fact to which historians testify everywhere. **Pliny** certainly records that "echoes with their rebounding sound" <note>original: *echum resultanti sono*</note> are hostile to bees. (14) Those who describe the equipment of dancers by no means omit the noise of cymbals; and authors report that cymbals were usually struck especially in banquet dances, and even wedding dances. Female cymbal-players <note>original: *Cymbaliſtriæ*</note> were also brought to the sick, for **Celsus** <note>A Roman medical writer</note> is the authority that in certain diseases "orchestral music, cymbals, and noises are beneficial." **Suetonius** tells something similar about the Emperor **Claudius**. For the ancients were persuaded that musical instruments possessed a certain power of healing, especially for those suffering from fevers...

(15) Cymbals were also danced to by beggars and vagabonds; these people, in order to more easily gain the pity of men, would carry with them some image of a deity—especially the *Syrian Goddess* <note>Atargatis, often identified with the Great Mother Cybele</note>—which is why they were commonly called <term>Metragyrtai <note>original: $\mu\eta\tau\rho\alpha\gamma\acute{\upsilon}\rho\tau\alpha\iota$; literally "mother-beggars," wandering priests who collected alms for the goddess Cybele</note></term>. **Chrysostom** testifies that in New Rome <note>Constantinople</note> such poor people were accustomed to strike cups and drinking vessels together like cymbals for the amusement of the wealthy. **Spon** <note>Jacob Spon, the archaeologist mentioned on the previous page</note> records something similar about his own countrymen; nor is it unusual in our own regions. (16) It is certain that among the toys of infants there were rattles, though these were more likely *crotala* <note>clappers or castanets</note> than cymbals; nurses used these when they desired to soothe crying and induce sleep. Both boys and girls later kept these *crotala* for their games. (17) The priests of the *Berecynthian Mother* <note>Another name for Cybele, after Mount Berecynthus in Phrygia</note> drank from the cymbal, although **Nemesianus** testifies that this was also done elsewhere—unless you prefer to believe that these "cymbals" were actually specific types of vessels intended for drinking and were named so due to their similar shape. (18) Even those who have not yet reached the age of public life <note>original: "nondum ære lavantur," an idiom likely referring to those not yet using the public baths or bronze coins</note> are aware of the water-organ (*Hydraulica*). **Vitruvius** <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer</note> places the cymbal within these instruments. I believe he does so improperly. For these organs otherwise consisted of pipes or channels—which others call flutes, trumpets, reeds, or hemlock-stalks as they please—filled with water, which, when moved in a particular way, produced a very sweet sound similar to cymbals. (19) This chapter will explain military uses. Were cymbals used in war among the Romans? A glossary seems to suggest so: "*Brass-players: <term>Cymbal-players <note>original: $\kappa\upsilon\mu\beta\alpha\lambda\omicron\kappa\rho\omicron\upsilon\sigma\alpha\iota$</note></term>*." Now, among the Romans, *Æneatores* <note>brass-players</note> were horn-blowers. But take care not to be deceived. I take "brass-players" here to mean anyone who uses any kind of bronze instrument. That good man **Alexander ab Alexandro** <note>A 15th-century Italian humanist</note>—though his scholarship is not to the taste of our age—attributes cymbals to the *Indians* in war. However, I think he rests on no authority, unless perhaps he is alluding to the drum of the *Parthians* which **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist</note> describes as being full of bells inside, which made a horrific sound when shaken. However, the primary battle-signal of the *Arabs* consisted of cymbals, and it is clear from **Eustathius** that the *Pygmies* used cymbals in their battles against the cranes (if you believe such people existed anywhere). (20) I will gather here a collection of various accounts. Before *Egypt* was reduced to the form of a province, there appeared in the clouds the noise of cymbals along with the sound of weapons. In

*Britain* was once said to be a cave in which, if the wind blew into it, the clashing of **cymbals** could be heard. I wish the distinguished gentleman had added a drawing of the object; and if it should be hidden away anywhere, I would earnestly ask learned men to share it with me. It could also simply be a sign for a <term>crotalistria</term> buried there. However, I do not deny that the traditions of the ancients regarding the delights of *Elysium* were wondrous. We Christians are nurtured by a more certain hope, and may God grant that it be more than just a hope. May the day come when we possess far more fully whatever we have been able to imagine regarding the joys of the life to come.

# ON THE MYRTLE

...this thesis, by which they judged that mountains planted with myrtle groves were signified, is where the idea originated. I am all the more inclined toward this view both because of the different forms of the letters and because they interpret the following word *metzulah* <note>original: מצלה; usually translated as 'the deep' or 'a hollow'</note> not as a valley, but as the shadow of the mountains, "between the shaded mountains" <note>original: ἀνὰ μέσον τῶν ὀρέων τῶν κατασκίων</note>. **Aquila** and **Symmachus** <note>Translators of the Old Testament into Greek in the 2nd century AD</note> translate this as "a myrtle grove" <note>original: μυρσινεων</note>. The origin of the word is hidden. **Martinius** <note>Matthias Martinius (1572–1630), a German lexicographer</note> in his *Lexicon* doubts whether it comes from the Hebrew *gahah* <note>to heal</note> and the Chaldean *asa*, because it offers medicine; or from the Greek *hedys*, meaning "sweetness"? The former is elegant, but the latter is jarring, since *hedys* and *hedone* <note>pleasure</note> undoubtedly stem from the Hebrew *eden* <note>original: עדן; meaning delight or paradise</note>. Perhaps its root was *asa* <note>original: אסא</note>, which is known to designate the myrtle among the Chaldeans, as seen in the *Paraphrast* <note>A term for the Aramaic translations/commentaries of the Bible known as Targums</note> regarding Esther 2:7, cited below. Among the Arabs, the myrtle is also called *As*.

The myrtle is a shrub of modest size, though through cultivation it sometimes grows into the appearance of a small tree. Its wood is so firm and strong that the Ancients fashioned missiles and spears from it. Hence **Virgil** says in *Georgics*, Book II:
> *Willows are fertile in twigs, elms in foliage;*
> *But the myrtle for sturdy spear-shafts— — — —*

It has flexible and compliant branches, and leaves that, although not very large, are always green; hence it is called the "green myrtle" by **Athenaeus** in the *Deipnosophistae* <note>The 'Banquet of the Learned,' a 3rd-century Greek work</note> XV. 6, by **Ovid** in *Fasti* IV. v. 139, and by **Horace** in Book I of his *Odes*, Ode 4. It is "green with everlasting foliage" according to **Pliny** in his *Natural History* XVI. 19. 20. For both of these reasons, it was used for crowns on various occasions, as **Paschalius** <note>Carlo Pasquale (1547–1625), author of a famous treatise on crowns and wreaths</note> extensively teaches in *On Crowns*, Book VII, Chapter XVIII and following. The fragrance of its branches joins the myrtle to the laurel in **Virgil's** *Eclogues* II. 54:
> *And you, O laurels, I shall pluck, and you, neighboring myrtle,*
> *Since, thus arranged, you mingle sweet fragrances.*

Add to this **Martial** III. 64 and **Cassianus Bassus** in the *Geoponica* XI. 7. Its flowers are white, and just like the leaves, they have a sweet

**Martial**, Book IV, Epigram 13, line 6:

**Matthiolus** <note>Pier Andrea Mattioli, a 16th-century physician and botanist</note> in his commentary on **Dioscorides** <note>The primary Greek authority on herbal medicine</note> Book I, chapter 128, notes that myrtles clearly shrink away from mountains. Therefore, when Nehemiah 8:15 <note>The text cites verse 16, but the instruction is in 15</note> says that branches of myrtles were sought from the mountains, it seems this should not be understood as if there were a notable abundance of myrtles on the mountains themselves, but rather that where there were mountainous areas, there was also a yield of myrtles in the adjacent valleys.

There can be no doubt that Judea, just like Asia, Egypt, and other regions of the East, nurtures myrtles and myrtle groves. It seems to **Bochart** <note>Samuel Bochart, a French Protestant biblical scholar</note> in his work *Canaan* that the city of Edessa in Syria received its name from myrtle groves <note>The Hebrew name for myrtle is *hadas*, similar to the root of the city's ancient name</note>; the reason is that these shrubs require warmer locations and cannot survive in cold places. **Theophrastus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle in the Peripatetic school</note> says in the place cited: <note>original Greek: Των δὲ ἡμερουμένων ἡκιστα φασιν ἐν τοις ψυχροις ὑπομενειν δαφνην καὶ μυρρίνην. They offer as proof that on Mount Olympus there is much laurel, but no myrtle at all; while in the whole region of Pontus, neither is found, even though people try to plant them with the greatest zeal and every skill for the sake of religious ceremonies.* **Virgil** says in *Eclogues* VII:

The Jews believe the first point should be affirmed based on Leviticus 23:40: *And you shall take for yourselves on the first day the fruit of a beautiful tree, fronds of palms, and the branch of a thick tree, and willows of the brook, and you shall rejoice before the face of Jehovah your God for seven days.* For in that place, they maintain that "thick tree" <note>original Hebrew: עץ עבת (*etz avot*)</note> is a synonym for the myrtle. > *Understand "the branch of the tree of thick foliage" mentioned in Scripture to be a branch from a tree of the kind whose leaves are so dense that they almost cover the tree itself. Such a tree is the myrtle, which is uniquely suited in this way, and besides which no other good or beautiful species is found whose habit is usually like this. Furthermore, what was said regarding "thick foliage" is to be understood in this way: specifically, when at least three leaves emerge from a single twig—that is, when three equal leaves emerge in a circle on one stem, so that one of them is no lower than the other. When they are seen thus, then they certainly cover the entire circuit or circumference of the tree, and then they can indeed have the name of "thick foliage." But if there are only two equal leaves on one stem, one facing the other, while the third leaf stands out higher or is lower than the rest, it is not called*

<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether the "thick tree" mentioned in Leviticus is specifically the myrtle, moving from linguistic arguments to historical and sectarian interpretations of the Feast of Tabernacles.</meta>

-># ON THE MYRTLE<-

it can be dense, but then it will rather *deserve the name of a spurious myrtle*.

I confess that among more cultivated myrtles, some are found which cover their branches with their thick leaves. However, I do not allow myself to be persuaded by this reasoning alone—that "thick trees" and "myrtles" are synonyms. Firstly, because in the cited passage of Nehemiah <note>Nehemiah 8:15, which lists both myrtle and "leafy trees."</note>, where they are distinguished from myrtles, a clear tautology <note>Needless repetition of the same idea in different words.</note> would occur. Secondly, because the word <term>עבות</term> <note>Hebrew: *avot*, meaning "thick," "leafy," or "interwoven."</note> is of more general use; it does not designate a specific species, but rather a category of certain trees that recommend themselves by the density of their foliage. For this reason, it is also used to describe taller trees in Ezekiel 6:13 and 20:28. Therefore, the Legislator <note>Referring to Moses and the Mosaic Law.</note> permitted any foliage of thick trees for the Feast of Tabernacles <note>Also known as Sukkot, a Jewish festival commemorating the dwelling of the Israelites in the wilderness.</note>. Consequently, Ezra and his colleagues established nothing outside the Law of Moses when they enjoined the people to seek branches, both of *myrtles* and of *oil-producing trees*, since these species and many others were included under the name of "leafy trees," as the famous Vitringa the Younger <note>Campegius Vitringa (1693–1723), a Dutch theologian and professor.</note> teaches in his first *Dissertation on the Feast of Tabernacles*, section 5.

Regarding the second question, there is a great conflict between the Rabbinites <note>Followers of traditional Rabbinic Judaism.</note> and the *Karaites* <note>A Jewish sect that recognizes only the written Tanakh (Hebrew Bible) as authority, rejecting the Oral Law/Talmud.</note>, whom Aben-Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish rabbi and scholar.</note> refutes according to his custom under the name of *Sadducees* in his commentary on the passage in Leviticus. It is very evident from Nehemiah 8 that these branches served the construction of the tabernacles <note>The temporary huts or "booths" used during the festival.</note> themselves. But the former group <note>The Rabbinites.</note> added that these branches were also used for bundles of foliage to be carried *in the hand*. It cannot be denied that this ritual was already practiced among the Jews during the time of the Second Temple. Hence, Josephus <note>Titus Flavius Josephus (37–c. 100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> follows the common interpretation of "thick tree" <note>Hebrew: *etz avot*</note> in his *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book III, chapter 10. Describing the solemnity of the Feast of Tabernacles, he says they celebrate *carrying in their hands a branch of myrtle and willow made with a palm frond* <note>original Greek: φέροντας ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν εἰρεσιώνην μυρσίνης καὶ ἰτέας σὺν κράδῃ φοίνικος πεποιημένην; the Latin text also provides a translation: "gestantes in manibus ramum myrti & salicis cum ramo palmæ facto"</note>. He even provides an example of such a celebration under the Ptolemies in *Antiquities*, Book XIII, chapter 21. For this reason, it is less surprising that Plutarch <note>Greek historian and essayist (c. 46–119 AD).</note> in his *Table Talk*, Book IV, Question 5, attributes the celebration of the Bacchanalia <note>Rites of Bacchus/Dionysus, the god of wine and ecstasy.</note> to the Jews, since the *myrtle* was also frequently used in Bacchic sacred rites. The same Plutarch, in *Table Talk*, Book I, Problem 1, mentions that drinking songs in honor of Bacchus were sung *after receiving a branch of myrtle and passing it to others by hand*. He records in the same place that this branch was called an *aisakon* <note>original Greek: αἴσακον; a branch, usually of laurel or myrtle, held by guests at a banquet while singing.</note>.

ATHENAEUS <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the 'Deipnosophistae' or 'The Banquet of the Learned.'</note> provides a reason in *The Banqueters*, Book XV: namely, because myrtle wards off and binds the fumes of wine. Other pagan rituals were also celebrated using leafy branches from sacred trees, which they called <term>verbenae</term> <note>original: "verbenas"; a Latin term for sacred boughs like laurel, olive, or myrtle used in religious ceremonies.</note>. Among these, myrtles held a distinguished place, as SERVIUS <note>A 4th-century grammarian known for his commentary on Virgil.</note> noted from MENANDER in his commentary on the *Aeneid*, Book XII, line 120: *We now call all sacred foliage "verbenae," such as laurel, olive, and myrtle.* TERENCE says: *Take the "verbenae" from the altar here; for Menander, from whom Terence translated, testifies that it was myrtle.* In the rituals of the Lares <note>Roman guardian deities of the household.</note>, TIBULLUS mentions myrtle branches and garlands in Book I, Elegy II, lines 27–28; on this point, let BROUCKHUSIUS <note>Jan van Broekhuizen (1649–1707), a Dutch classical scholar.</note> be consulted. However, all these things do not prove that this rite was of divine institution.

But ABARBANEL <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a prominent Jewish statesman and philosopher.</note> persuades himself that he can prove it using arguments drawn from the text of Leviticus itself. Let us briefly hear his brief arguments. *The first is: If those words "And you shall take for yourselves on the first day" <note>Leviticus 23:40.</note> simply indicate the construction of the tabernacles <note>The temporary booths or huts built for the festival of Sukkot.</note>, the Scripture is not free from tautology <note>Needless repetition of the same idea.</note>.* The Karaite <note>original: "Karraeus"; a member of the Karaite sect of Judaism, which interprets the Hebrew Bible literally and rejects the Oral Law of the Rabbis.</note> could retort that there is no trace of tautology here, since the "first day" indicates the time when the tabernacles must be erected. The same will suffice for the second reason, where he asks: *how could they explain this regarding the work of the tabernacles, since the festival for the Lord lasts seven days, and not only the first day?* Namely: because they were to be erected on the first day, but were to be inhabited for seven days. Third, he asks: *how can the words "And you shall take for yourselves" be explained as referring to the structure of the tabernacles?* The Karaite will respond by comparing it to the passage in Ezra. But ABENEZRA <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note> insists that Ezra is dealing with a different matter because he omits something—namely, the "fruit of the most beautiful tree"—and adds something—namely, willows. The Karaite will reply again that in the history of Ezra, the Law of Moses is too evidently invoked, and reasons for the differences can be given. *Beautiful fruits were more for decoration than for the structure of the huts. But willows were required in their own right, since from them, without doubt, the beams*

ABENEZRA <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note> adds another objection which, since it specifically concerns our myrtle, we shall add in his own words: *“When, however, in Ezra mention is made of myrtle foliage and branches of a thick tree, this in no way contradicts our ancestors. The reason for using myrtle branches in that Festival could be twofold. The *first* is that the use of myrtle branches generally pertained to increasing joy and festivity. To this we may also refer the fact that myrtle strewn in the road was a sign of public joy and the greeting of Princes. For this reason, HERODOTUS <note>A 5th-century BCE Greek historian, often called the "Father of History."</note> in Book VII, after a bridge was built by Xerxes to join the Hellespont to the continent, introduces the Persians <note>original: "μυρσίνῃσι στορνύντες τὴν ὁδὸν"</note> strewing the road with myrtle. Add that the same author in Book VIII records this among the signs of the Persians' joy over the capture of Athens. 

Additionally, the myrtle was specifically a symbol of sociality, love, and concord. To this belongs the passage in PLINY’S <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 CE), author of the encyclopedic 'Natural History.'</note> *Natural History*, Book XV, chapter 29: *“Indeed, it is recorded thus: with myrtle boughs the Romans and Sabines, when they had wished to fight because of the abducted maidens, laid down their arms and were purified in that place which now holds the statues of Venus Cluacina.”* For the ancients used the word <term>cluere</term> <note>original: "cluere"; an archaic Latin verb meaning to cleanse or purify.</note> to mean "to purify." And in that tree, too, a kind of incense is found. It was chosen then because Venus presides over union, and she presides over this tree. Likewise, in the final chapter of the same book, concerning the laurel: *“It is not because it is evergreen, nor because it is a sign of peace, that it is to be preferred above the myrtle and the olive, but because it is most distinguished on Mount Parnassus.”* This con—

In the Sacred Scriptures, the members of the true Church are portrayed as myrtles. This applies both to the Jewish Church as it was being redeemed from Babylon—to which the myrtles in the "deep" (or in Babylon, as the <term>Targum of Jonathan</term> <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew prophets.</note> translates it) refer in Zechariah 1:8, where a man stood among them riding a red horse—and to the Church that was to be spread among the nations. In the latter case, God promises that *he will plant the myrtle* (Isaiah 41:19) and that the *myrtle* should grow in place of the brier (Isaiah 55:13). The branches of myrtle required for the Festival of Tabernacles <note>Also known as Sukkot, a Jewish harvest festival commemorating the wandering in the desert by building temporary booths.</note> also seem to express this later symbolism, as that entire Festival specifically pointed toward the expansion of the Church’s "tabernacles" among the gentiles.

That the "righteous" are to be understood by the "myrtles" is evident from the <term>Chaldean paraphrase</term> <note>Another term for the Targum, the Aramaic translation of the Bible.</note> on Isaiah 55:13, which the celebrated <term>Vitringa</term> <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent Dutch theologian and expert in Hebrew studies.</note> cites in his commentary on that passage. The authors of the <term>Talmud</term> <note>A central text of Rabbinic Judaism containing legal and philosophical discussions.</note> acknowledge the same thing in the tractate *Sanhedrin*, section *Chelek*, where they gloss the cited passage from Zechariah as follows: *“There are no myrtles except the righteous, as it is said (Esther 2:7): 'And he was the foster-father of Hadassah (that is, the myrtle), she is Esther.'”* <note>original Hebrew: "אין הדסים אלא צדיקים שנ' ויהי אומן את הדסה היא אסתר"</note> Citing this passage in his work *The Dagger of Faith* <note>original: "Pugio Fidei", a 13th-century anti-Jewish polemical work by Raymond Martini.</note> (Part III, Dist. 3, Ch. 16, § 8), **Raymundus** understands these myrtles to be the women standing near the cross of Christ—an interpretation we leave to its own merit. 

Regarding Esther, she might have received the name *Hadassah* because myrtles were generally considered emblems of beautiful women in ancient times. Hence the phrase *virginal myrtles* <note>original Greek: "παρθενια μυρτα"</note> in Aristophanes’ *The Birds*. It is also believable that the myrtle was sacred to Venus to such an extent that the name *Myrtle-Venus* <note>original: "Venus myrtea"</note> in Pliny's *Natural History* (XV. 29) originated from it. Beyond **Brodaeus** and **Paschalius**, this fact is explained at length by **Pierio Valeriano** in his *Hieroglyphics*, **Meursius** in *Sacred Trees*, **Junius** in *On the Painting of the Ancients*, and **Spanheim** in his notes on Callimachus, as well as by a comparison with a gemstone in which Cupid appears with a crown of myrtle, as shown in **Beger's** *Brandenburg Treasury*.
