### ON THE MYRTLE.

In the Hebrew manner, parents wished to express their hope and prayers that their daughters might flourish like a myrtle in the garden of the Church. The <term>Chaldean Paraphrase</term> <note>Also known as the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and expansion of the Hebrew Bible.</note> agrees with this sentiment regarding Esther 2:7: *“They called her Hadassah because she was righteous; for the righteous are those who are compared to the myrtle.”* <note>original Hebrew/Latin: "vocabant autem eam Hadassa, eo quod esset justa, justi vero sunt, qui assimilantur myrto."</note> One may compare what <term>Ursinus</term> in *Biblical Trees*, <term>Buxtorfius</term> in his *Talmudic Lexicon*, and <term>Carpzovius</term> in his *Introduction to the Old Testament* have written regarding this name. Some scholars even argue that the name *Esther* itself signifies a "black myrtle" among the Persians. In this view, the name would be a synonym for *Hadassah*, retaining the same botanical meaning while merely adopting a Persian linguistic form.

It is certain that, among the ancients, myrtles served as a symbol for distinguished persons. <term>Buxtorfius</term> indicates that in the <term>Bava Batra</term> <note>A tractate of the Babylonian Talmud.</note>, the firstborn are compared to myrtles. Antiquity also compared illustrious heroes to *myrtles*; at times, the brows of victors were wreathed in *myrtle*, as taught by <term>Meursius</term> in *Sacred Trees*, <term>Coelius Rhodiginus</term>, and others—though <term>Pierius Valerianus</term>, in his *Hieroglyphics*, believes the coins of Papyrius should be interpreted differently. These accounts follow the well-known writings of <term>Pliny</term> in his *Natural History*. The most ancient mention of this practice is found in <term>Pindar’s</term> *Isthmian Odes* (Ode 8):

> *Let one of his peers weave a delicate crown of myrtle for Cleander, in honor of his victory in the pancratium.* <note>original Greek: "Αλικων τῳ τις άβρον / Αμφι παγκρατιου κλεανδρω / Πλεκετω μυρσινας / Στεφανον." The pancratium was a famous and grueling ancient Greek athletic competition combining boxing and wrestling.</note>

Consult what <term>Erasmus Schmid</term> notes on that passage. For the same reason, the people of Antiquity decorated the tombs of princes with myrtle. <term>Euripides</term> writes in his play *Electra* (line 323):

> *The tomb of Agamemnon has been dishonored; it has never yet received libations or a branch of myrtle...* <note>original Greek: "Αγαμεμνονος δε τυμβος ητιμασμενος / Ου πωποτ’ ου χוας ουδε κλωנה μυρσινης / Ελαβε."</note>

It should also not be overlooked that, among the ancients, the *myrtle* served as an emblem of both lowliness and nobility in the same subject. <term>Achmetes</term> <note>An 8th- or 9th-century author on the interpretation of dreams.</note> in *The Interpretation of Dreams*, chapter 151, writes: *If someone dreams that they possess a myrtle tree, they will be joined to a man who is noble but poor, because of the fragrance of the tree, and they will share in his joys.* <note>original Greek: Εαν ἰδῃ τις, ὅτι μυρσινην δενδρον ἐσχεν, ἐυγενει μεν ἀνθρωπῳ, πτωχῳ δε προσκολληθησεται δια το ἐνωδες του δενδρου και συγχαρησεται ἀυτῳ.</note>

With how much better a right—on account of a manifold fittingness—will pious and precious souls claim this emblem for themselves, having been planted in the garden of the Church. ## FRAGMENT OF A DISSERTATION
### ON THE
# <term>BEROSH</term> <note>Hebrew: ברוש; a tree frequently mentioned in the Bible, often associated with Lebanon.</note> OR CYPRESS.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' with floral scrollwork and architectural elements within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>Among the various interpretations of the word *Berosh*, the one most commonly held among recent scholars is that it is believed to designate the **FIR** <note>Latin: *abies*</note>, since most of the characteristics that occur in the Sacred pages can be demonstrated in the Fir tree. Although I myself once held this opinion, these difficulties have arisen for me upon more careful meditation on the matter:

**I.** That Firs are not found in Syria is testified by **PLINY** in Book XVI, Chapter 40: *“But in Egypt and Syria, because of a lack of fir, kings are said to have used cedar for their fleets.”* This was drawn from **THEOPHRASTUS** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and the 'father of botany.'</note> in Book V, Chapter 8, where the same thing is affirmed regarding the fir and the pine: *“Some even build triremes <note>Ancient warships with three banks of oars.</note> [out of pine] because they do not have an abundance of fir. Those who inhabit Syria and Phoenicia use cedar, for they also lack pine.”* <note>Original Greek: Ἔνιοι δὲ καὶ τὰς τριήρεις, διὰ τὸ μὴ εὐπορεῖν ἐλάτης. Οἱ δὲ κατὰ Συρίαν καὶ Φοινίκην ἐκ κέδρου, σπανίζουσι γὰρ πεύκης.</note> The translator correctly says: *“they also lack”*; for Theophrastus had just stated that the Fir is superior to the Pine for building triremes. Therefore, if the Syrians had possessed the Fir, they would not have used cedar in place of pine. Yet we shall see from the Sacred Scriptures how abundant and frequent the *Berosh* was on Mount Lebanon.

**II.** In other regions of the East as well, the Fir is an exile, being a tree belonging to the West and the North...

...from the silence of the authors, we conclude that it is more characteristic of the northern regions. <note>original: "trioni magis propriam" referring to the 'Septentrio' or the North.</note> **III.** Nor does any reason remain as to why the **Fir** <note>Latin: *Abies*</note>, a most common tree, would be so consistently joined with the cedar—a most famous tree—since it is neither found in the same locations as the cedar, nor (if you set aside its height, its somewhat similar leaf shape, and its evergreen nature) does it deserve to be compared or ranked with the Cedar in terms of its pleasant scent, its longevity, or its value. This is because **VITRUVIUS** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a Roman architect and engineer whose works were the standard for construction in the Renaissance.</note> in Book VII, Chapter 3, expressly states that the beams of ceilings should not be made of fir, because they are quickly corrupted by decay and age. **IV.** Much less is anything found in the fruit of this tree that corresponds to such a grand emblem <note>The author refers to the symbolic imagery of the tree in scripture.</note> as we find in **Hosea 14:8**. **V.** Furthermore, a tree of greater excellence was required for the magnificence of the Temple's structure and for the luxury of the Tyrians in constructing the decks of their ships.

Among the remaining interpretations, hardly any seem worthy of examination. It will suffice to mention only that of **AVENARIUS** <note>Johannes Avenarius (1516–1590), a German professor and Hebraist.</note> here, who translated it as **ASH** <note>Latin: *Fraxinus*</note>, not because it recommends itself by any particular appearance over the others, but because it has found a great patron in the celebrated **VITRINGA** <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent Dutch theologian.</note>, who prefers it to the others in his commentary on Isaiah 14:8. Yet he mentions no other argument than one sought from the similarity of the Hebrew and Latin names. That, however, is trivial in itself, especially since **URSINUS** <note>Johann Heinrich Ursinus, author of *Arboreti Biblici*, a famous 17th-century study of biblical plants.</note> shows that the Latin etymology is to be preferred from the word for "crashing" <note>Latin: *fragor*, suggesting the wood splits or makes noise.</note>, and in our opinion, which we shall soon present, it does not enjoy that prerogative any less. It should be added that the similarity of certain letters is not enough to counter the arguments for which we have no regard for the ash tree here. For it is itself also a common tree, not evergreen, not notable for its fruits, not used for magnificent works, nor in any other qualities at all comparable to the Cedar.

To me, the opinion of those who judge the <term>Berosh</term> <note>Hebrew: ברוש</note> to be the **CYPRESS** seems to come closest to the truth. Their opinion is favored, first, by the authority of **JOSEPHUS** <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian.</note>, who in his history of the Temple, where the Sacred Scriptures join "timbers of *Beroshim*" <note>Hebrew: עצי ברושים</note> with cedar woods, mentions that they were "made of cypress" <note>Original Greek: *Kyparissinon*</note>. So too, in the letters of Hiram to Solomon in *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book VIII, Chapter 2: *"For I have cut many and great timbers of both cedar and cypress."* <note>Original Greek: Τεμων γαρ ξυλα πολλα και μεγαλα κεδρου τε και κυπαρισσου.</note> That **EUPOLEMUS** <note>An early Jewish historian who wrote in Greek, circa 150 BCE.</note> is an author of the same matter is gathered...

### XXV.
## FRAGMENT OF A DISSERTATION
### CONCERNING
# *BEROSH* OR THE CYPRESS.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial 'I' set within a square frame featuring ornate floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>

Among the various interpretations of the word *Berosh* <note>Hebrew: ברוש; a term often found in the Old Testament describing precious wood used in the Temple.</note>, the one most widely circulated among modern scholars is that which believes it designates the **FIR** <note>Latin: *Abies*</note>, since most of the attributes that occur in the Sacred Pages can be demonstrated in the Fir tree. Although I once held this opinion myself, more careful meditation on this matter has given rise to these difficulties:

**I.** That Fir trees are not found in Syria is attested by **PLINY** <note>Pliny the Elder, a famous Roman naturalist whose "Natural History" was a primary source for early modern scholars.</note> in Book XVI, 40: *But in Egypt and Syria, because of the lack of fir, kings are said to have used cedar for their fleets.* <note>original Latin: "At in Ægypto & Syria Reges inopia abietis cedro ad classes feruntur usi."</note> This was drawn from **THEOPHRASTUS** <note>Theophrastus, an ancient Greek philosopher known as the father of botany.</note> in Book V, 8, where the same thing is affirmed regarding the fir and the pine: <note>original Greek: "Ενιοι δ᾽ ε και τας τριηρεις, δια το μη ευπορειν ελατης. Οι δ᾽ ε κατα Συριαν και Φοινικην εκ κεδρου, σπανιζουσι γαρ πευκης."</note> *Some also build triremes <term>triremes: ancient warships with three banks of oars</term> [out of pine] because they lack fir. Those who inhabit Syria and Phoenicia use cedar, because they even lack pine.* The translator rightly says: *even lack*; for Theophrastus had just stated that the Fir was superior to the pine for building triremes. Consequently, if the Syrians had possessed the Fir, they would not have used cedar in place of pine. Now, indeed, we shall see from the Sacred Scriptures how abundant and frequent the *Berosh* was in Lebanon.

**II.** In other regions of the East as well, the Fir is absent, being as it were a tree belonging to the west and the north <note>The Latin text ends with "septentrioni," referring to the North. The catchword "trioni" indicates the continuation of this word on the following page.</note>

<meta>catchword: trioni</meta>

...we conclude this more specifically from the silence of the authors. **III.** Nor is there a sufficient reason why the Fir, a very common tree, should be so consistently joined with the Cedar, a most renowned tree, since it is neither found in the same locations as the cedar, nor—unless you consider its height, the similar shape of its leaves, and its perpetual greenness—does it deserve to be compared or ranked with the Cedar in terms of its pleasant scent, its longevity, or its value. This is supported by **VITRUVIUS** in Book VII, Chapter 3, who explicitly states that the beams of ceilings should not be made of fir, because they are quickly spoiled by decay and old age. **IV.** Much less is there anything found in the fruit of this tree that corresponds to such a grand emblem as we find in Hosea 14:8. <note>The passage in Hosea compares God to a "green fir tree" (or berosh), producing fruit, which the author argues does not fit the botanical profile of a common fir.</note> **V.** Furthermore, the magnificence of the Temple's structure and the luxury of the Tyrians required a more excellent tree for constructing the planks of their ships.

Among the remaining interpretations, hardly any seem worthy of examination. It will be helpful here to mention only that of **AVENARIUS**, who translated the word as **ASH** <note>Latin: *Fraxinus*</note>; not because it recommends itself above the others by any particular appearance, but because it found a great patron in the celebrated **VITRINGA**, who prefers it over the others in his commentary on Isaiah 14:8. However, he mentions no other argument than one sought from the similarity between the Hebrew and Latin names. That in itself is a weak point, since **URSINUS** shows that the Latin etymology from "crashing" <note>Latin: *fragore*; referring to the sound of the tree breaking or perhaps its use in spears.</note> is to be preferred; and in our opinion, which we shall immediately present, our choice enjoys no less a prerogative. It must be added that the similarity of a few letters is not sufficient against the arguments for which we have no reason to consider the ash tree here. For the ash is also a common tree, it is not evergreen, it does not recommend itself by its fruit, it is not used for magnificent works, nor is it in any other qualities comparable to the Cedar in any way.

To me, the opinion of those who judge the *Berosh* <note>Hebrew: ברוש</note> to be the **CYPRESS** seems to approach the truth most closely. Their opinion is favored first by the authority of **JOSEPHUS**, who, in his history of the Temple—where the Sacred Scriptures join "timbers of *Berosh*" <note>Hebrew: עצי ברושים</note> with cedar wood—mentions **cypress wood** <term>Kyparissinon</term>. Thus, in the letters of Hiram to Solomon in *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book VIII, Chapter 2: **"For I have cut many and great timbers of both cedar and cypress"** <term>Temon gar xyla polla kai megala kedrou te kai kyparissou</term>. **EUPOLEMUS** <note>A Hellenistic historian who wrote about the kings of the Jews.</note> is also an author on this same matter...

-> DISSERTATION <-

...is evident from his words in the *Dissertation on the Mystical Cedar*, in the section cited. The **Alexandrian Interpreters** <note>The translators of the Septuagint, the ancient Greek version of the Hebrew Bible.</note> also in most places translate *beroshim* <note>Hebrew: ברושים</note> as **cypresses** <note>Greek: κυπαρίσσους</note>. They are not, indeed, entirely consistent with themselves; for instance, they once render it as **fir** <note>Greek: ἐλάτη; Latin: abies</note>, and more frequently as **pine** <note>Greek: πεύκη; Latin: pinus</note>. Since the pine is a tree closely related to the fir, quite common, and does not grow natively in Phoenicia and Syria, the same arguments we brought against the fir will also hold against the pine. Nor does the notable inconsistency of the **Seventy Interpreters** <note>Another name for the authors of the Septuagint.</note> in translating the names of trees delay us, since it is not necessary to assume they were particularly knowledgeable in natural history—especially that of Syria and other eastern regions. Furthermore, the hypothesis of those who maintain that the Alexandrian version was not the work of a single age or man, but of many different people, is quite probable.

Nor are the etymological reasons opposed to our view; for the word *Berosh* <note>Hebrew: ברש</note>, especially if the prefix *B* is added, lies hidden within the word **cypress** <note>Greek: κυπάρισσος</note>. We shall also see below that the name *Berot* <note>Hebrew: ברות</note> survives in the Greek words *brady* <note>βραδυ</note> and *borathos* <note>βοραθος</note>, which designate a certain species of cypress. **Ursinus**, however, prefers to derive the word *kyparissos* from *kopher* <note>Hebrew: כפר</note>, meaning "to cover with bitumen," and *rishon* <note>Hebrew: ראשון</note>, meaning "first," because the resin of this tree is considered almost of the first rank. But the resin of the **Terebinth** and the **Lentisk** <note>The mastic tree.</note> is much preferred over it, according to **Pliny** in Book XIV, Chapter 20. Thus, this is no less a play of wit than that of the Greeks, who derive the name from the phrase "to bring forth equals" <note>Greek: κυειν παρισους</note>, because it produces branches, foliage, and fruits that are equal to one another.

It can be added that it is scarcely credible that a tree so celebrated, which comes closest to the Cedar and made Syria more famous than other regions, should not be mentioned in the sacred pages. For although **Fuller** in *Sacred Miscellany*, Book IV, Chapter 5, and **Bochart** in *Phaleg*, Book I, Chapter 4, understand the Cypress to be the **Gopher wood** from which Noah's ark was built, and **Ursinus** in *Biblical Botany*, Section II, Chapter 7, interprets it as the *Tirzah* <note>Hebrew: תרה</note> occurring in Isaiah 44:14, these terms are themselves <term>hapax legomena: words that appear only once in the entire Bible</term> and admit other explanations, as will be taught in their proper place.

This much is certain: whatever the Scripture records concerning the *Berosh*, it can be shown with little effort to apply to the **Cypress**. In general, the Ancients understood it to be a wild tree, tall, and evergreen...

<page-num>577</page-num>

# ON THE CYPRESS #

...fragrant, which **Servius** describes not ungracefully in his commentary on the *Aeneid*, Book 3, line 64: *“It is a tall tree with a long, straight trunk, evergreen foliage, and a powerful scent. There are two kinds: the one that is sterile is called the female, coiled into the shape of a cone at the top.”* Because of this, it is called by the specific epithet **cone-shaped** <note>original Greek: κωνοειδής</note>. *“In contrast, the male spreads its branches more widely and bears cones not unlike pine nuts, though smaller. It has a marvelous fertility among trees, being thrice-bearing, with fruit ripening in January, May, and September; however, these are useful for nothing—indeed, they are rather harmful, just like the tree itself, whose very shade is believed to be poisonous.”*

Scripture clearly hints at the nature of the Cypress by so often and so consistently joining it with the **Cedar** in most places where it is mentioned: 1 Kings 5:8, 10; 9:11; 2 Kings 19:23; 2 Chronicles 2:7; Psalm 104:17; Isaiah 14:8; 37:24; Ezekiel 27:5; 31:5; and Zechariah 11:2. Who would not conclude from this that the **Berosh** <note>Hebrew: ברוש</note> is the tree occupying the place right next to the cedar and is very closely related to it? For this reason, the Jewish scholars do not neglect to count it among the species of cedars, and the **Seventy** <note>The translators of the Septuagint, the ancient Greek Bible.</note> themselves quite often rendered **cedars** <note>Hebrew: ארזים (*erezim*)</note> as **Cypresses**, as I showed in the *Dissertation on the Mystical Cedar*. And certainly, there is a great affinity between these trees, both in their characteristics and their uses.

**Hosea**, in Chapter 14, verse 8, implies that the **Berosh** is evergreen, just like the foliage of the Cedar. For this reason, in the *Geoponica* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine collection of agricultural lore.</note>, Book 11, Chapter 1, it is numbered among the **evergreen trees that never shed their leaves in winter** <note>original Greek: δένδρα ἀειθαλη και μηδέποτε φυλλοῤῥουντα ἐν χειμωνι</note>. For this reason, it seems to be called the **“happy cypress”** <note>original Latin: *læta cupressus*</note> by **Virgil** in the poem *Culex*:

> *The trees of Mount Ida, both the dark species and the happy cypress.*

**Martial** also mentions the "living Cypress" below. **Plutarch** provides the reason in his *Symposiacs*, Book 3, Question 2: *“The olive, the laurel, and the cypress are preserved as evergreens by their oiliness and heat”* <note>original Greek: Ελαιαν δε και δαφνην, και κυπαριττον ἀειθαλη διαφυλάσσει το λιπαρον, και το θερμον</note>.

That the Cypress is nearly equal to the Cedar in height is suggested in Psalm 104:17. Hence, it is described in **Ovid’s** *Metamorphoses*, Book 10:

> *To gaze at the starry sky with its slender peak.*

In **Theocritus's** *Idyll 1*, "slender cypresses" <note>original Greek: *ῥαδιναὶ κυπάρισσοι*</note> occur, meaning "tall cypresses" <note>original Latin: *procerae Cupressi*</note>. **Ennius**, in a fragment from Book 7 of the *Annals* preserved by **Servius**, writes:
-> - - - - - - - And tall cypresses <-
-> Stand with upright leaves - - - - - - <-

In **Pausanias's** *Description of Greece* (Book 8, "Arcadia"), mention is made of the cypresses around the tomb of **Alcmaeon** <note>A hero in Greek mythology; his tomb was located in the city of Psophis.</note>, which had grown "to such a height that even the mountain overlooking Psophis was shaded by them" <note>original Greek: *ἐς τοσοῦτον ὕψος, ὥστε καὶ τὸ ὄρος τὸ πρὸς τῇ Ψωφιδι κατεσκιάζετο ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν*</note>. **Plutarch**, in his *Life of Phocion*, records: "Your words, young man, are like cypresses; for although they are large and tall, they bear no fruit" <note>original Greek: *οἱ λόγοι σου ὦ μειράκιον ἔοικασι κυπαρίττοις, μεγάλοι γαρ ὄντες καὶ ὑψηλοὶ καρποὺς οὐ φέρουσι*</note>. "Your speech," said **Phocion** <note>An Athenian statesman and general known for his dry wit.</note>, "is like the cypress trees: for these are grand and lofty, but they bear no fruit." The same author derives a reason for the sterility of cypresses from their great size in *Table Talk* (Book 2, Question 6), writing: "Just as those who are heavy with a mass of flesh usually do not produce offspring—the nourishment being consumed by the body itself so that no reproductive residue is left—so trees of this kind, consuming all nourishment within themselves, grow to an ample size but bear no fruit, or only small fruit that ripens slowly."

The pleasing appearance of cypresses is also commended. Hence **Aristaenetus**, in his description of a lover's paradise, joins the cypress to other beautiful trees in Book 1, Epistle 3: "Vines of great length wind themselves around very tall cypresses" <note>original Greek: *Ἄμπελος παμμηκεις σφόδρα γὲ ὑψηλαὶ περιελίττονταὶ κυπαρίττους*</note>. And in **Apuleius's** *Metamorphoses* (Book 5), **Cupid**, about to speak to **Psyche**, summoned this tree and addressed her from its high summit. Because of this, cypresses appear in the description of a most pleasant place in **Petronius's** *Satyricon* (Chapter 131):
> And Daphne crowned with berries and tall cypresses.
> Among these a foaming river played with wandering waters,
> and turned the pebbles with a complaining dew,
> a place worthy of love - - - - - -

And when **Philostratus** recounted the fable of **Cyparissus** <note>A youth in Greek mythology who was transformed into the tree that bears his name.</note>, the Assyrian youth changed into a tree, in his *Life of Apollonius* (Book 1, Chapter 16), he adds: "And the beauty of the plant confirms the transformation" <note>original Greek: *Καὶ πισουται τὴν μεταβολὴν ἡ ὥρα τοῦ φυτοῦ*</note>: And the...

# ON THE CYPRESS. 579.

...which the beauty of the tree contributes to the transformation. **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian (64 BC – 24 AD).</note> in *Geography*, Book 16, mentions the "cypresses in the groves and paradises in Babylonia" <note>original Greek: *τῶν ἐν τοῖς ἄλσεσι καὶ τοῖς παραδείσοις ἐν τῇ βαβυλωνίᾳ κυπαρίττων*; original Latin: *Cupressorum in lucis & Paradisis Babyloniæ*</note>, which were used for the construction of ships when other material was lacking. **Democritus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher; here cited via the *Geoponica*, a Byzantine collection of agricultural lore.</note>, according to **Didymus** in the *Geoponica*, Book 11, Chapter 5, recommends planting cypress between walls, "so that they might serve both for delight and for fortification" <note>original Greek: *ἵνα κατ' ἀμφότερα εἰς τέρψιν καὶ περιφραγὴν γένηται*</note>. And how successfully the cypress is still cultivated in the Paradises <note>The word "Paradise" here refers to the Persian *pairidaeza*, a grand, walled garden or hunting park.</note> of the Persians is shown by the most learned **Engelbert Kaempfer** <note>A German naturalist and physician (1651–1716) who traveled extensively in Russia, Persia, and Japan.</note> in *Exotic Pleasures* <note>original Latin: *Amoenitates Exoticae*</note>, Fascicle 2, Relation 7, § 1, when describing **Shiraz**, or "New Persepolis," where he writes among other things:

*Indeed, the greatest ornament and magnificence of the gardens and the city comes from the cypresses, as the spirit of the earth uniquely favors their vigor; for, planted in very dense rows, they everywhere rise with a rapid and equal growth to the height of a musket shot, maintaining a stubborn beauty with their very straight trunks and foliage governed by a cone-shaped law. I dare to affirm that nowhere else on earth does there exist either such a great multitude of cypresses in one place, or any that flourish with such high peaks and such joyful and harmonious elegance.* And a little later: *From above, we look down upon so many dense rows of cypresses, planted both along the sides of the roads and through the margins of the gardens, which present to our imagination a kind of ineffable magnificence, like troops of spearmen serving as guards; a sight than which art and nature, with their combined efforts, could produce nothing more elegant.* Hence, the Persian poetic vein praises **Shiraz**, calling it the "eye of the empire," its own delight, and "Paradise": a place where the Gods themselves would fix their seat, if they were to descend to earth to live among mortals.

Furthermore, it is numbered among the scented trees just like the **Cedar**. Because of this, **Varro** <note>A prolific Roman scholar and writer (116–27 BC).</note> mentions that the cypress was placed around funeral pyres so that it might soften the stench of the corpse with the pleasantness of its own scent, according to **Servius** <note>A 4th-century grammarian known for his commentary on Virgil.</note> in his notes on the *Aeneid*, Book 5, line 216. In **Homer's** *Odyssey*, Book 5, line 64, it is called the "sweet-smelling cypress" <note>original Greek: *εὐώδης κυπάρισσος*</note>. From this, it is clear from **Aelian's** *Various History*, Book 5, Chapter 6, that cypresses were employed at tombs alongside Cedars. **Theocritus** <note>The creator of ancient Greek pastoral poetry.</note> also calls it "sweet-smelling" in his *Epigrams*. For this reason, it is so often joined with other fragrant foliage, such as laurel, myrtle, and cedar.

# DISSERTATION 580

Because of its particular hardness and strength, the **Cypress** is certainly to be equaled with, if not preferred over, the **Cedar**. **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 371–287 BC) often called the "father of botany."</note> explicitly gives it first place in Book 5, Chapter 5: "Cypress, cedar, ebony, lotus, etc., are naturally resistant to rot... but among these, cypress seems to be the longest-lasting" <note>original Greek: *Ασαπη δὲ φυσει κυπαρισ- σος, κεδρος, εβενος, λωτος κ. τ. λ. τουτων δὲ χρονιωτατα δοκει τα κυπαριττινα ειναι.*</note>. See also the passages from **Pliny** <note>Roman author of *Natural History*.</note> and **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome, known for his Latin translation of the Bible.</note> in the *Discussion on Cedars*. To these, add **Virgil** in *Aeneid*, Book 2, line 713:

> For those who have left the city, there is a mound and an ancient temple
> of abandoned Ceres, and nearby is an ancient Cypress,
> preserved through many years by the religious devotion of our Fathers.
> <note>original Latin: *Est urbe egressis tumulus, templumque vetustum Desertæ Cereris, juxtaque antiqua Cupressus, Relligione Patrum multos servata per annos.*</note>

**Martial** <note>A Roman poet (c. 40–104 AD) famous for his epigrams.</note> in Book 6, Epigram 49 writes:

> But born from living Cypress;
> Which fears neither a hundred centuries past,
> Nor the decay of long old age.
> <note>original Latin: *Sed viva generata de Cupresso; Quæ nec secula centies peracta, Nec longæ cariem timet senectæ.*</note>

And in Epigram 73:

> — — — In everlasting Cypress that shall never die.
> <note>original Latin: *Perpetua nunquam moritura Cupresso.*</note>

**Vitruvius** <note>A Roman architect and engineer (1st century BC) whose work heavily influenced the Renaissance.</note>, writing on the Cypress and the Pine in Book 2, Chapter 9, adds the reason: *They are preserved into old age without defects because that liquid <term>sap</term> which is deep within their bodies has a bitter taste; due to its pungency, it does not allow rot to penetrate, nor those little creatures that are harmful. Therefore, works constructed from these types of wood remain for an eternal duration.* Compare this with **Fuller** <note>Nicholas Fuller (1557–1626), an English scholar of sacred texts.</note> in *Sacred Miscellany*, Book 4, chapter 5, and **Bochart** <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant scholar who wrote on biblical geography and animals.</note> in *Phaleg*, Book 1, chapter 4. **Gyraldus** <note>Lilio Gregorio Giraldi (1479–1552), an Italian scholar and poet.</note> provides a singular example of this hardness in his small book *On Ships*, chapter 7.

Add to this that the Cypress loves the same locations as the Cedar. Among those trees that love the peaks of mountains, it is numbered by **Theophrastus** in *Inquiry into Plants*, Book 4, chapter 1, to such an extent that it does not even reject snow-covered summits: "Indeed, in Crete they say that on the Idaean mountains and on those called the White Mountains, on the very peaks where snow never fails, the cypress is found. For there is more of this wood both in the mountains and throughout the island in general" <note>original Greek: *Εν Κρητη γουν φασιν ἐν τοις Ιδαιοις ὀρεσι και ἐν τοις Λευκοις καλουμενοις ἐπι των ἀκρων, ὁυπερ ουδεποτε ἐπιλειπει χιων κυπαριττον ειναι. Πλειον γαρ ταυτης της ὑλης και ἐν τοις ὀρεσι, και ὁλως ἐν τη νησω.*</note>. *And so they affirm that on the island of Crete, in the Idaean mountains and those called the White Mountains, on the summits where snow is never absent, the cypress is found. For that kind of forest is most abundant both in the mountains,*

And it is found throughout the entire island. However, Scripture suggests that the cypress loves waters and rivers and is not easily found in completely arid places in Isaiah 41:19, naming the *Berosh* <note>The Hebrew term *berosh* (בְּרוֹשׁ) is traditionally translated as cypress, though sometimes as fir or pine.</note> among the trees to be produced by a miracle in the desert—but only after the desert has been changed into a pool of water. Besides the previously cited passage from **PETRONIUS**, **PHILOSTRATUS** teaches the same in the *Life of Apollonius*, Book 1, chapter 16, regarding the river Ladon. And **DIDYMUS** <note>Referring to the *Geoponika*, a collection of agricultural lore attributed to Didymus of Alexandria.</note> in *Geoponica*, Book 11, chapter 5, says: "It delights rather in moist and sheltered places." <note>original Greek: *χαίρει δὲ μᾶλλον καθύγροις καὶ σκεπηνοῖς τόποις*; original Latin: *Gaudet autem humidis magis & opacis ac umbrofis locis.*</note>

The Cypress grows especially in Lebanon, joined with the Cedar, as seen in 1 Kings 5:8, 2 Kings 19:23, Isaiah 37:24, 60:13, and 2 Chronicles 2:7. Hence **DIODORUS SICULUS** <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC.</note> in Book 19, chapter 58, mentions that Lebanon is full of "cedar and cypress woods, marveling at both their beauty and size." <note>original Greek: *ξύλων κεδρίνων καὶ κυπαρισσίνων θαυμάζων τό τε κάλλος καὶ μέγεθος*; original Latin: *lignis cedrinis & cupreffinis, tam quoad pulcritudinem quam magnitudinem.*</note> Mount Senir is also named in Ezekiel 27:5, which is the same as Mount Hermon and is connected to the Lebanon range. Even in more recent times, it is clear from **THEOPHANES** <note>A Byzantine chronicler (c. 758–818 AD).</note> in the *Life of Anastasius* that cypresses in Syria were sought after for building ships: *"When he learned that the Saracen fleet was hurrying from Alexandria to Phoenicia to cut down cypress wood and prepare it for the use of ships."* <note>original Latin: *Cum didiciffet, claſſem Saracenorum ab Alexandria in Phœnicem properare ad ligna cupreſſina incidenda, eademque ad ufum navium comparanda.*</note> 

Besides Syria, the regions most fertile in cypresses are Babylonia, according to **ARRIAN** in *The Campaigns of Alexander*, Book 7, and **STRABO** in Book 16; as well as Lycia, Rhodes, and Crete according to **THEOPHRASTUS**, Book 4, chapter 6—especially Crete. Compare **BODÆUS** <note>Johannes Bodaeus a Stapel, a 17th-century physician and botanist who commented on Theophrastus.</note> on Theophrastus in the cited place, **SPANHEIM** on Callimachus, pages 159–160, and **MEURSIUS** in *Creta*, page 105. In Phocis <note>A region in central Greece.</note> there was also a city called Kyparissos <note>meaning "Cypress"</note>, which **HOMER** already mentions in the *Iliad*, Book 2, lines 519 and 593, and which according to the **SCHOLIAST** <note>An ancient commentator or annotator of classical texts.</note> took its name from this tree. In the Peloponnese, Mount Lycone, especially renowned for its cypresses, appears in **PAUSANIAS'S** *Corinthian* (or Book 2, page 129); he mentions noteworthy cypress groves elsewhere in Greece as well. The Milesian cypress is praised above others in **ATHENÆUS'S** *The Banquet of the Learned*, Book 5, chapter 10. But there is no need to linger on these details.

Regarding its uses, Scripture likewise diligently joins the Cedar with the *Berosh* <note>cypress</note>...

# DISSERTATION

Just as those trees are a dwelling for birds, so this tree is equally a home, especially for storks, according to Psalm 104:17. For although storks commonly nest in towers and on the rooftops of houses, their natural habit, before houses were built, was undoubtedly to place their nests in trees, as observed by **THOMAS BROWNE** <note>Sir Thomas Browne (1605–1682), an English polymath and author of *Miscellany Tracts*.</note> in *Miscellaneous Dissertation I: On the Plants of Holy Scripture*, section 33. Compare the passages on this matter collected by **BOCHART** <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar known for his work on animals in the Bible.</note> in *Hierozoicon*, part II, book II, chapter 29, page 330. Among these, the most relevant to us is that of **BELON** <note>Pierre Belon (1517–1564), a French naturalist who traveled extensively in the Levant.</note>, in which the mountains of Syria are considered among the primary refuges of storks: *Storks, which are in Europe during the summer, spend a great part of the winter not only in Egypt, but also around Antioch and near Mount Amanus.* **HOMER** also affirms that larger birds love cypresses and nest in them in the *Odyssey*, Book 5, verse 63:

> A wood had grown flourishing around the cave,
> Alder and poplar and sweet-smelling cypress,
> There also birds with long-extended wings used to sleep,
> Owls and hawks and long-tongued crows.

The Latin text also provided a translation: *Sylva autem ſpecum circumcreverat vireſcens, Alnus, populuſque & bene odorata cypreſſus, ibi quoque aves extenſas alas habentes nidulabantur, aſiones accipitreſque, lataſque linguas habentes cornices.*</note>

In the construction of the Temple, the use of Cypress was as widespread as that of Cedar (1 Kings 5:8, 9:11). Specifically, the <term>floor</term> <note>original Hebrew: *karqa* (קַרְקַע)</note> of the house was adorned with cypress (1 Kings 6:15), as were the walls (2 Chronicles 3:5) and the doors (1 Kings 6:34). A similar decoration was used in the celebrated Temple of Diana at Ephesus. **THEOPHRASTUS** <note>Greek successor to Aristotle, often called the "father of botany."</note> says in Book 5, chapter 5: *In Ephesus, the cypress wood from which the doors of the new Temple were made had been kept for four generations.* For in Ephesus, the cypress timber from which the folding doors of the newly built Temple of Diana were made had lain in storage for four ages. **PLINY** followed him in Book 16, chapter 40: *The folding doors are of cypress, and although the material is nearly four hundred years old, it all remains like new.* However, **BODAEUS** <note>Johannes Bodaeus à Stapel, a 17th-century commentator on Theophrastus.</note> shows that Pliny poorly expressed Theophrastus’s meaning, but that controversy does not concern us. Indeed, **HOMER** describes the posts of Odysseus’s palace as being magnificently crafted from cypress in the *Odyssey*, Book 17, verse 340:

> Leaning against a cypress post, which once a craftsman...

"He planed it skillfully and straightened it by the line." <note>original Greek: Ξέσσεν ἐπισταμένως, καὶ ἐπὶ στάθμην ἴθυνε. It is no wonder that Cypress was employed for magnificent works, not only because of the hardness of the material but also its luster. **THEOPHRASTUS** <note>The "Father of Botany," a successor to Aristotle.</note> in the cited work says: "This tree alone also receives a luster; therefore, they are accustomed to make the more elegant of their works from it." <note>original Greek: μονα δε και στιλβηδονα δεχεται, διο και τα σπουδαζομενα των ἐργων ἐκ τουτων ποιουσι.</note> This tree alone accepts a shine, and for this reason, they were accustomed to build the more sumptuous works from it. **PLINY** expressed it thus in the cited passage:

> *The cypress is naturally fragrant and does not admit rot; it is suitable for all technical craftsmanship, being smooth, harmonious, and well-suited for the adornment of engravings.* <note>original Greek: Εὔπνοει φυσι- κῶς ἡ κυπάρισσος, καὶ σηπεδόνος ἐστὶν ἀπαράδεκτος καὶ πρὸς πᾶ- σαν τεκτονικὴν φιλοτεχνιαν ἐπιτηδείως ἔχει, λεία τε γενομένη, καὶ ἐναρμόνιος, καὶ πρὸς τοῦτο διὰ τῶν γλυφίδων καλλωπισμοὺς ἐπι- τηδείος.</note>

...that it is suitable, as **COLOMESIUS** <note>Paul Colomiès (1638–1692), a French scholar and librarian.</note> correctly noted in his *Minor Works*, page 300; this is abundantly clear from the passages already cited.

As for what now concerns the symbolic nature of this tree, many have held the opinion that it expressed something deadly and hateful, specifically because of its frequent use in funerals. **VIRGIL**, *Aeneid* VI. 216:

> — — — — *They place*
> *funeral cypresses before [the pyre]* — — — —

**HORACE**, *Odes*, Book II, Ode XIV:

> — — — *Nor shall any of these trees which you tend*
> *follow you, their short-lived master,*
> *except for the hated cypresses.*

**SILIUS ITALICUS**, Book X:

> *But a deadly honor, the mournful cypresses*
> *at the funeral pyres* — — — —

**STATIUS**, Book V, *Silvae* I. line 135:

> — — — *Now is the time to set aside your leaves,*
> *O Phoebus, and to doom your hair with the mournful cypress.* <note>Phoebus Apollo was usually associated with the laurel; wearing cypress signaled deep mourning.</note>

Whoever desires more passages on this matter should consult **PASCHALIS** on *Crowns* IV. 17; **GUTHERIUS** on *The Law of the Dead* I. 19; **KIRCHMANN** on *Roman Funerals* I. 14; **NICOLAUS** on *Greek Mourning*, Chapters V & XIII; **ARINGHI** in *Subterranean Rome* VI. 42; **SAGITTARIUS** on *Doors*, Chapter XXXI; and **VAN DER WOUWER** on *Petronius's Satyricon*, Chapter 120. Indeed, the cypress was all the more "hated" because of the dark interpretations attached to it. **FESTUS** <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note> writes: *Cypresses were placed at the homes of the dead for this reason: because a tree of this kind, once cut down, does not grow back; just as there is no longer anything to be hoped for from the dead. For this reason, it was thought to be under the protection of Father Dis.* <term>Dis Pater: The Roman god of the underworld, equivalent to the Greek Hades or Pluto.</term> **PLINY**, Book XVI, chapter 33: *Difficult to grow, useless in its fruit, grim in its berries, bitter in its leaf, violent in its scent; not even pleasant in its shade, and sparse in its wood—almost like an unproductive species—it is sacred to Dis, and therefore placed at houses as a sign of a funeral.* Many things are asserted here by **PLINY** in a distorted way and contrary to the truth, simply to make the symbolism of the cypress all the more sorrowful—such as the claims he makes about its sterility, its heavy scent, and the scarcity of its wood, where he says...

->### DISSERTATION ###<-

he says, and these points can be partly refuted from what has been said before. Add to this the commentary of **SERVIUS** <note>Maurus Servius Honoratus, a 4th-century grammarian known for his commentary on Virgil.</note> on *Aeneid* III regarding those words:

> *The high forest of Jupiter, and the grove of Diana:* <note>original: "Sylva alta Jovis, Lucusque Dianæ"</note>
> *[They are called the forest] of Jupiter, because of the oak; and of Diana, because of the cypress. For she herself is also Proserpina <note>The Roman goddess of the underworld, identified with the Greek Persephone.</note>. Therefore, cypresses are treated as belonging to the underworld, either because they do not grow back once they are cut down, or because among the Athenians, a house in mourning is veiled with the foliage of this tree.*

It seems no less clever to me that **FULLER** <note>Nicholas Fuller (1557–1622), an English Hebraist and philologist.</note> in his *Sacred Miscellany* IV. 5, argues that this omen of the cypress should be traced back to **Noah's Ark** itself. He believes the Ark was built of cypress and served as a kind of "tomb for the living" for a long enough time. I find this unconvincing, not only because the hypothesis is nothing more than conjecture, but also because Noah's ark was intended for salvation, not for death.

Therefore, none of these arguments persuade me that those who, in the most ancient times, decided the cypress should be used around the dead, assigned such a "deadly" emblem to this tree. Since this tree so often appears among the joyful and favorable ones—consecrated to the "upper" gods such as Jupiter, Apollo, and others—I would certainly judge that a different reason lay behind it. I have no doubt that the durability of the wood served as a symbol of eternity among the gentiles <note>Here referring to the non-Christian peoples of antiquity.</note>. After a funeral, the ancients attributed this eternity to their dead in two primary ways: either through <term>apotheosis</term> <note>The process of a human being elevated to divine status, often after death.</note>, or through the everlasting memory of their noble deeds. I gather that this was their intention because antiquity used to surround only the monuments of illustrious men and heroes with Cypress trees or groves. Hence that line from **LUCAN**, Book III, verse 442:

> *And the cypress, witnessing mourning that is not for commoners.* <note>original: "Et non plebejos luctus testata Cupressus." This implies the cypress was a mark of status for the elite dead.</note>

**KÆMPFER** <note>Engelbert Kaempfer (1651–1716), a German naturalist and traveler who documented Persia and Japan.</note> narrates in the location previously cited that such a cypress grove, surrounding the magnificent tombs of most famous men, still stands in the "New Persepolis," and he provides a drawing of it. Furthermore, a cypress crown served as a prelude to deification according to **SPARTIANUS** <note>Aelius Spartianus, one of the authors of the *Augustan History*.</note> in his life of the Emperor Severus:

> *While he was pondering what omen might meet him, a certain Ethiopian from the military ranks—of famous reputation among the jesters and always celebrated for his jokes—met him with a crown made of cypress. When the Emperor, angry, ordered him to be removed from his sight—troubled both by the man's color and the omen of the crown—the man is said to have said to him as a joke: "You have been everything, you have conquered everything."* <note>original: "Totum fuisti, totum vicisti." This implies the completion of a glorious life.</note>

-># ON THE CYPRESS #<-

...now let God be the victor. Therefore, the ancients wished to honor their dead with the cypress and to claim immortality for them.

But another reason could also be added: namely, that the most ancient peoples, from whom the Romans borrowed this custom, enclosed the bodies of the dead in cypress chests <note>The author refers to "cistis cupressinis," essentially cypress coffins.</note>, specifically so that they might preserve them for a longer time against corruption. **THUCYDIDES** <note>A prominent Athenian historian (c. 460–400 BCE) known for his "History of the Peloponnesian War."</note> in his *History*, Book II, Wechel edition, page 120, writes:

> When the day for the funeral procession arrives, wagons are brought, which carry chests made of cypress, one for each tribe. In these are the bones of each tribe, to which the individuals belonged. <note>original Greek: "Επειδαν δε και η εκφορα η, λαρνακας κυπαρισσινας αγουσιν αμαξαι φυλης εκαστης μιαν. Ενεστι δε και τα οστα, ης εκαστος ην φυλης."</note>

**CEDRENUS** <note>George Kedrenos, an 11th-century Byzantine historian.</note> reports that the body of the Emperor Michael was also placed "in a cypress chest" <note>original: "ἐν κυπαρισσινῳ λαρνακι"</note>; and **LAERTIUS** <note>Diogenes Laertius, a 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> will mention a "cypress coffin" <note>original: "σορου κυπαρισσινης"</note> in a passage to be cited shortly. This was done for the same reason that books intended for long-term preservation were stored in cypress boxes. **HORACE** <note>The famous Roman lyric poet (65–8 BCE).</note> in his *Art of Poetry*, line 331, says:

> *We hope poems can be crafted*
> *Worthy of being smeared with cedar oil and kept in smooth cypress.*

Regarding this, an ancient commentator notes: *Cypress is a species of cedar, from which small boxes are usually made, in which the writings of poets were placed to protect them against moths.*

Among the sacred emblems <term>emblemata; symbolic representations used in art or literature to convey a moral or religious truth</term> of the cypress, the first is that God Himself promises to show Himself similar to it in Hosea 14, in the second to last verse: *Ephraim, what have I to do anymore with idols? I have answered and I will look upon him; I am like a green cypress; from me is your fruit found.* <note>original: "אני כברוש רענן" (Ani ke-berosh ra'anan). The Hebrew "Berosh" is often translated as cypress, fir, or juniper.</note> The **CHALDEAN** <note>The Targum, or Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, the **SYRIAC**, and the **VULGATE** <note>The standard Latin Bible translation.</note> consider the cypress (or fir) here as a symbol of Israel being restored to a happier state. They assume an ellipsis <note>A grammatical omission where words are implied but not stated.</note>, as if it were said: *I will establish him like that fir tree.* **GROTIUS** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch legal scholar and theologian.</note> also follows this interpretation. However, because this requires a somewhat forced ellipsis, we prefer to stick to the accepted opinion and understand the cypress as referring to **Jehovah** Himself, the God of Israel, and specifically to the **Messiah**, whom the Aramaic translator in the preceding verse thought was indicated by the "scent of Lebanon." **KIMCHI** <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), a medieval Jewish rabbi and grammarian.</note> expresses the reason for the comparison in this way:

> *I will be to you like a green cypress; just as they bend its top down toward its roots, so I [bend down to you]...* <note>original Hebrew: "אני אהיה לך כמו הברוש רענן שכופפין ראשו אצל שרשיו כן אני"</note>

*I dwell in the high and holy place, and with the contrite and humble spirit* <note>original Hebrew: "מרום וקדוש אשכון ואת דכא ושפל רוח" — Isaiah 57:15</note>; *I will be to you like a green cypress* <note>original Latin: "Ego ero tibi velut Berofch viridis" — a reference to Hosea 14:8</note>. This genus of tree inclines its top toward its roots; thus, "I dwell on high and in holiness, yet also with the contrite and humble spirit." **Jarchius** <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says in a similar way: "I will bend down to him to hold his hand, for like a green cypress that bends to the earth so that a man might take hold of its branches, so I will be found by him" <note>original Hebrew: "אני לו נכפף להיותו אוחזו ידו כי כברוש דענן נכפף לארץ: שאדם אוחז בענפיו כלומר' אהיה מצוי לו"</note>. *I will lower myself to him, so that his hand can grasp me; just as the green cypress bends itself to the ground, so that a man may grasp its branches; so that the meaning is: I may be easily found by him.*

This interpretation seems to us to be a bit far-fetched. There are others, therefore, who think we should look instead to the shade of this tree, especially since the preceding verse refers to the shade of the trees of Lebanon: *Those who dwell in its shade will rest.* It does seem to conflict, however, with what **PLINY** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (23–79 CE), the Roman author of Natural History.</note> says in the cited passage—and from him, no doubt, **SERVIUS** <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil.</note>—who declare the shade of the cypress to be "unpleasant" <note>original Latin: "ingratam"</note>. But that it was pleasing to the ancients is clear from its frequent use in groves and gardens.

Yet we should not stop at this comparison, as I think we should look even more toward the image of constancy which the cypress possesses, following **ABARBANEL** <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and philosopher.</note>, who gives this paraphrase of the phrase: "I do not change, for I am like a green cypress, enduring and standing without change" <note>original Hebrew: "דאין אני משתנה כי אני כברוש רענן קיים עומד מבלי שנוי"</note>. *But I shall never be torn from this purpose: for I am like the green Berosh <term>Berosh: the Hebrew word for cypress</term>, lasting and subsisting without any change.*

And so the likeness involves what constitutes the essential prerogative of this tree over others: its nearly invincible hardness. This indicates the reason why the "green cypress" is mentioned—namely, because it never loses its vigor. Under this representation, the unbroken strength of divine power and the never-interrupted vigor of His faithfulness are most elegantly shadowed forth. This same idea agrees with the "shade of immortality" which we have shown the cypress to bear.

Added to this is the saying of **Pythagoras** <note>The famous Greek philosopher and mathematician.</note> regarding the cypress scepter of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>. **DIOGENES LAERTIUS** <note>A biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> in Book VIII, chapter 10, says of the Pythagoreans: *They also abstained from a cypress coffin, because the scepter of Jove was made from it, as Hermippus says in the second book on Pythagoras* <note>original Greek: "Ἀπείχοντο δὲ καὶ σοροῦ κυπαρισσίνης, διὰ τὸ τοῦ Διὸς σκῆπτρον ἐντεῦθεν πεποιῆσθαι, ὡς φησὶν Ἑρμιππος ἐν δευτέρῳ περὶ Πυθαγόρου."</note>. **JAMBLICHUS** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> in his *Life of Pythagoras*, among his proverbs in chapter 155, records this: *Cypress...*

But every doubt will be removed if it is noted—something the interpreters have overlooked—that the God of Israel here opposes himself to the *idols* which Ephraim worshiped. For they possess this unique quality: they produce cones three times a year, and these are filled with the smallest seeds, from which a great multitude of such tall trees can be born with wonderful fertility. From this, the fruiting of the cypress becomes an elegant emblem of the spiritual seed of Christ. Though this seed seemed most contemptible and thin at the beginning, it was destined to grow into a prodigious multitude by the power of Christ’s Spirit. Indeed, the preceding points also look toward this increase of mystical offspring. And this is undoubtedly the meaning of the name *Ephraim* <note>The name Ephraim (אֶפְרַיִם) is derived from the Hebrew root meaning "to be fruitful."</note>, placed with singular emphasis at the start of our verse.

Nevertheless, a doubt could remain as to why the God of Israel preferred to use the Cypress as his symbol, not only over the more noble Cedar but also over so many trees that bear sweet, pleasant, and useful fruits. But all doubt will be removed if it is noted—something the interpreters have neglected—that the God of Israel here opposes himself to the *idols* that Ephraim worshiped. Now it is well known that idols, in whose worship the Israelites once...

# DISSERTATION

<page-num>590</page-num>

[the Israelites] had been defiled, were sought from Syria. Indeed, the idolatry of Syria especially favored the Cypress. For instance, Antioch, a city of Syria, was adorned with a cypress grove dedicated to the Sun. Philostratus, in his *Life of Apollonius* <note>Philostratus (c. 170–250 AD) was a Greek scholar; his biography of the philosopher Apollonius of Tyana is a major source for 1st-century religious life.</note>, Book I, Chapter 16, describes the Temple of Apollo at Daphne:

> <note>original Greek: "Κυπαρίττων τε ὕψη ἀμήχανα περιέστηκε κύκλῳ τὸ ἱερόν, καὶ πηγὰς ἐκδιδῶσιν ὁ χῶρος ἀφθόνους τε καὶ ἠρεμούσας, αἷς τὸν Ἀπόλλω, φασί, ῥαίνεσθαι; Ἐνταῦθα κυπαρίττου τε ἔρνος ἡ γῆ ἀναδέδωκεν, ἐπὶ κυπαρίττῳ, φασίν, Ἀσσυρίῳ."</note> *Cypresses of immense height surround the temple in a circle, and the region brings forth abundant and calm springs, in which they say Apollo is washed. Here the earth also gave forth a sprout of cypress, for the sake of Cyparissus, as they say, the Assyrian.* <note>original Latin: "Cupressi quoque immensæ proceritatis Templum circulo ambiunt, & fontes aquis uberes placidosque regio profert, quibus Apollinem lavari perhibent. Hic & Cupressi germen terra edidit, propter Cyparissum, ut ajunt, Assyrium."</note>

The poet Ovid tells this fable more extensively in his *Metamorphoses*, Book X, line 105 <note>Ovid recounts the myth of Cyparissus, a youth beloved by Apollo who was transformed into a cypress tree after accidentally killing a sacred stag.</note>. This same grove is described by Priscian of Caesarea <note>A 6th-century Latin grammarian.</note> in such a way that the Cypress is named first among various trees:

> Here the woody places of Daphne grow green, the lofty Cypress
> Is raised up, and the fragrant laurel intertwines its branches.

The historian Libanius <note>A 4th-century Greek rhetorician from Antioch.</note> confirms its sanctity in his *De vita sua* [On His Own Life], pages 76 and 77, warning: <note>original Greek: "μὴ ἐπιφέρειν κυπαρίττοις σίδηρον"</note> *that iron [axes] must not be brought against the cypresses,* and <note>original Greek: "ὡς οὐ παροζυντεον τὸν Ἀπολλω διὰ τῶν κυπαρίττων"</note> *that Apollo must not be provoked on account of the cypresses.*

It is clear from coins that in other cities of Syria, cypress groves were sacred to Jupiter or the Sun. One such example is found in Jean Vaillant’s *Coins of the Emperors* <note>Jean Foy-Vaillant (1632–1706) was a pioneering French numismatist.</note>, Part II, page 181, regarding the Temple of Heliopolis <note>Modern-day Baalbek in Lebanon.</note> (the stupendous ruins of which were described by Jean de La Roque). It shows a Cypress in the middle, a tree sacred to the sun, whom they worshiped under the name of the "Syrian Jupiter." Without a doubt, the same tree is seen for no other reason on the coins of the people of Damascus in the same work, pages 161 and 222.

One might also perhaps suspect whether the Syrian idol **Baal Berith** <note>Mentioned in the Book of Judges; usually translated as "Lord of the Covenant." The author here speculates on a linguistic connection between "Berith" and "Berosh," the Hebrew word for cypress.</note> derived his name from this. At the very least, it will now be easily clear that since the Israelites—who received the worship of Baal along with groves and high places from the Syrians—undoubtedly also learned from them to adorn their own groves with Cypresses, the God of Israel took this as a timely opportunity. In direct contrast to the idols, He likened Himself to a "green cypress," as if to say He alone provides true and constant shade and fruitfulness, which was expected in vain from the idols worshiped in cypress groves.

# CONCERNING THE CYPRESS

Secondly, Scripture likens the faithful—those who are especially illuminated by the gifts of the Holy Spirit—to Cypresses. These people are truly the fruits of the "mystical Cypress," a title we have just shown applies to the Messiah. The cypress-wood walls of the Temple likewise point to this same truth. To this end, one should look at Psalm 104:17, Isaiah 41:19, and 55:13, and particularly Isaiah 60:13, which refers to the magnificent members of the Church in the end times. It should not be overlooked here that in the work cited previously, Philostratus cleverly introduces Apollonius comparing men who have been changed for the better to the cypresses in the grove of Apollo. <note>Philostratus was a 3rd-century biographer of the philosopher Apollonius of Tyana. How the "reborn" <note>Referring to the spiritually "born again" or baptized.</note> can be likened to cypresses is taught by Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397 AD), a hugely influential Bishop of Milan.</note> in his commentary on Psalm 118: *This genus of tree never loses its greenness; in winter just as in spring and summer, it nourishes its foliage, nor is it changed by a different color. This is the only tree that the wind never despoils of its honor; it alone is never stripped of its old garment nor clothed in a new blossom. In the same way, the grace of the Apostles knows no failing, but flourishes in its own beauty. Therefore, the soul that thrives with flourishing merits and always sustains the heights of justice and other virtues with patient magnanimity does not know how to be corrupted. It does not fall away or drop off, because there is nothing in it that is cracked or loose, nothing unstable, nothing slippery—nothing that could be poured out of it by a vice of speech.*

Gregory the Great <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604 AD), known for his extensive writings on the Bible.</note> says in his commentary on the Song of Songs, Chapter 1: *Cedar and Cypress are said to be rot-resistant woods; all the elect are well represented by these because, while they pursue worldly things with no desire, they become eternal by fixing their minds on eternal things.* Furthermore, the pious can be compared to Cypresses because of their height—ascending in a straight line toward heaven—their pleasant appearance, the scent they spread widely, and their shining luster. Various uses of the wood can also be applied to the faithful. Just as cypress wood, shaped by the hand of a craftsman, provides a singular ornament, so these faithful are the work of the Holy Spirit: vessels made for glory. ...stones or beams for decorating and completing the sanctuary of the Lord. The strength of the Holy Spirit within them makes them fit for spiritual armor. Through them also, the "Hallelujah" of the celebration of His name rings out in the house of the Lord. For this reason, **ARINGHIUS** <note>Paolo Aringhi (1600–1676) was a Roman priest and archaeologist famous for his study of the catacombs.</note> in his *Subterranean Rome* (Book VI, chapter 42), teaches that the graves of Christians were sometimes marked with Cypresses, and he presents a stone as a witness to this practice.

Thirdly, the Cypress specifically depicts Christian Princes. The pairing of cypresses with myrtles and lowlier trees in *Isaiah 41:19 and 55:13* <note>These verses describe the desert blooming with majestic trees as a sign of God's blessing.</note> teaches us that those passages refer chiefly to them. Nor would I think the cypress walkways mentioned in *Song of Songs 1:17* pertain to anything else. The tall stature of this tree, extended upward like a column, allows it to be seen from afar. The former [its height] denotes the singular prerogative to which God has raised them above the lot of other men—those who bring their own glory into the heavenly Jerusalem. The latter [its visibility] teaches that the work of the Lord is most conspicuous in such people; placed in a higher position, they spread abroad the beautiful appearance and fragrance of Christian virtues. The fruitfulness of Cypresses fits them well, because "the whole world is shaped after the example of the King." <note>original Latin: "Regis ad exemplum totus componitur orbis" — a famous maxim by the poet Claudian suggesting that subjects follow the behavior of their leaders.</note>

And because Lebanon is fertile with these trees, this again pertains to the Roman Empire, which would one day produce such defenders of the Church. Nothing is more pleasant to the sight than to look upon Cypresses standing out in elegant order among smaller shrubs. Thus, nothing is sweeter than when Princes and subjects are driven and joined by the same vital Spirit of God. Just as Cypresses receive and break the gusts of winds and storms, shielding smaller trees from them, so the power of Christian Princes drives away many storms of persecution from the Church. In the tops of such Cypresses, the "mystical storks" build their nests, and they promote the work of the Church's fruitfulness, at least externally. <note>An allusion to Psalm 104:17: "The birds make their nests; as for the stork, the cypress trees are her house." ## ON THE CYPRESS
<page-num>593</page-num>

Fourthly, Great Men and Princes are sometimes compared to Cypresses, quite apart from any consideration of the utility they provide to the Church. This is seen in the Kings of Israel in *Ezekiel 31:15*, the Princes of the Jews in *Zechariah 11:2* and *2 Kings 19:23*, and *Isaiah 37:24*. Other worldly powers are described this way in *Isaiah 14:8*. In a similar vein, the flourishing state of the Roman Empire is depicted by **VIRGIL** <note>The famous Roman poet (70–19 BC).</note> in his first *Eclogue* (line 25):

> *But this city has raised its head as far above other cities,*
> *As cypresses are wont to do among the bending osiers.*
> <note>original Latin: *Verum hæc tantum alias inter caput extulit urbes, Quantum lenta solent inter viburna Cupressi.*</note>

The rising again of a Cypress tree was also seen to foreshadow the rise of the Vespasian family to imperial power, as recorded by **SUETONIUS** <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus was a Roman historian who wrote the *Lives of the Twelve Caesars*.</note> in *Life of Vespasian*, chapter 5: "A cypress tree on the ancestral estate, which had been torn up by the roots and laid low without any force of a storm, rose again the following day greener and firmer than before." To this we might add the words of **ACHMET** <note>Achmet son of Seirim was a medieval author known for a popular Greek treatise on the interpretation of dreams (*Oneirocritica*).</note> from his *Interpretation of Dreams*, chapter 151: "If anyone seems to see a palm or a Cypress tree growing inside his house (a dream which cannot occur to a person of low or poor condition, but only fits the most eminent and great men), the Cypress is judged to represent the status of a King because of the elegance and fragrance of its scent, and because it neither withers nor loses its leaves." <note>original Greek: ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις, ὅτι δένδρα, φοινῖξ ἢ κυπάρισσος, ἀνέφυ ἔνδον τοῦ δώματος αὐτοῦ... (if anyone sees that trees, a palm or a cypress, have grown within his house...)</note>

**ALCIATUS** <note>Andrea Alciatus (1492–1550) was an Italian jurist who created the "Emblem" book genre, combining images with moralizing poems.</note> records an elegant symbolic reason for this, which deserves to be included here as a healthy warning for Great Men. In his *Emblem 198*, he places this couplet beneath an image of a Cypress:

> The image of the cone and the name of the Cypress
> Indicate that his subjects are to be treated with equal condition.

To this, the famous commentator **Claude Mignault** <note>Often referred to as Cl. Minos, Mignault was a 16th-century scholar whose commentaries on Alciatus’s emblems became standard.</note> adds this explanation: "Many say the name *Cyparissus* is derived from the Greek phrase for 'conceiving and bearing equal branches and fruit,' <note>original Greek: διὰ το κυειν και φερειν παρισους κλαδους τε και καρπους (because of the bearing and carrying of equal branches and fruits)</note> because of the equality of its fruit and the branches it produces. For indeed, the Cypress rises from the root to the summit with a straight trunk, and it extends all its limbs with equal symmetry into the shape of a cone at the top. In this way, the Magistrate and the Prince are warned that they must maintain and protect equality within the Republic and the provinces subject to them."

> *As cypresses are wont to do among the pliant shrubs.*

Beneath the illustration of a Cypress in Emblem 198, he provides this couplet:

> *The image of the goal-post and the name of the Cypress*
> *Show that his subjects must be treated with equal standing.*

To which the famous **MINOS** <note>Claude Mignault (1536–1606), a French scholar whose commentaries on Alciato's emblems became standard.</note> adds this explanation: "Many say that it is called *Cyparissus* <note>The Greek-derived name for Cypress.</note> because it conceives and bears equal branches and fruits <note>original Greek: *dia to kyein kai pherein parisous kladsous te kai karpous*</note>, due to the equality of the fruits and the branches it produces. For indeed, the Cypress rises from the root to the summit with a straight trunk, and extends all its arms with equal symmetry into the shape of a cone toward the peak. By this, a Magistrate and Prince can be warned to maintain and protect equality in the Republic and the provinces subject to him."

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'L' featuring an ornate border with several figures engaged in an activity, possibly representing a classical or historical scene.</image-desc>To measure a fair price for human longevity is a task only for a refined reason—one that weighs the worth of things on an accurate scale. For we of the mortal race are split into such contrary opinions on this matter that not only does one person add exactly as much as another takes away, but even individually we are not a little at odds with ourselves. As long as old age seems to be far off, it is sought after by almost universal prayers and desires; yet once it has dawned, everything rings with complaints about its discomforts. Whenever the year returns to its start in the cycle, everyone is generous and eloquent in forming vows for a life extended to a late age—whether out of genuine affection or so as not to seem lacking in their duty. But if the inexorable Law of death has rendered those vows void, the scene changes and the style of speaking changes; and those whom we were predicting would be happy if they had lived longer, we immediately pronounce blessed because they have passed away. Either view would be correct enough, if held with enough sobriety and consideration. He who considers a longer span of life to be a great part of happiness in itself seems to have cast out from his mind the memory of the troubles that accumulate with the years, the care for eternity itself, faith in divine promises, and finally, all hope and desire for a better life.

# ON THE DEATH OF THE CONSULAR WIDOW ASCHENIANA. <note>The term "Consular Widow" (original: *Vidua Consularis*) refers to the widow of a Consul—at this time, a high-ranking civic leader or magistrate, such as a mayor or city councilor. <image-desc>A large ornamental initial 'L' featuring an engraved scene of a human figure in a pastoral landscape with trees.</image-desc>Measuring the fair value of human longevity is a task only for a purified reason—one that weighs the worth of things on an accurate scale. For we mortals are so split into contrary opinions on this matter that not only does one person subtract as much as another adds to its value, but we even find ourselves frequently wavering in our own judgments. As long as old age <note>original: *senectus*</note> seems far off, it is sought after by almost everyone with common prayers and zeal; yet once it has dawned, the world rings with complaints about its hardships. Whenever the year comes around in its circle, everyone is generous and eloquent in offering vows for a life to be extended to a late age—whether out of true affection or so as not to seem lacking in their duty. But if the inexorable Law of death <note>original: *Lex mortis*</note> makes those vows void, the scene changes and the tone of our speech shifts: those whom we predicted would be happy if they had survived longer, we immediately pronounce blessed because they have passed away. Both perspectives would be right enough, if only they were held with enough sobriety and consideration. He who considers a longer span of life to be a great part of happiness in itself seems to have cast aside the memory of the troubles that pile up with the years, the concern for eternity itself, faith in divine promises, and all hope and desire for a better life.

This is the true and solid prerogative of the new age: that believers long to be released from the bonds of this body, sigh for its redemption, and repeat with the Spirit and the Bride: COME, LORD JESUS! Who would recklessly wish for long wanderings at sea for a sailor, or a long absence from home for a traveler, or a slow release from chains for a prisoner? *Who would not*—to use the pen of CYPRIAN <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), an early Christian bishop and martyr.</note> here from his book *On Mortality*—*hasten to better things? Who would not desire to be changed and reformed to the likeness of Christ, and to come more quickly to the dignity of heavenly grace?* However this may be, even more advanced years have something that frees from blame those who piously and sincerely pray for them for their own sake. Old age itself can never come as a burden to those who love God, because all things work together for their good. If even in the judgment of SOPHOCLES <note>The famous Greek playwright of the 5th century BC.</note>, the *old age is not heavy* for those <term>ἐν οἷς ὁ νοῦς Θείᾳ ξυνεσιν ἡμερα τεθραμμενος</term> <note>Greek: "whose mind is nourished by divine understanding/light."</note>, how much more should this be felt of those whom the heavenly light of Grace has irradiated? Yet I would judge that a Christian <term>Macrobion</term> <note>original Greek: *Maκροβιον*, meaning "one who lives a long life."</note> gains more for others than for himself. If God commands those by whose protection both Christian and Public affairs flourish to remain for a long time, no one will doubt that this should be regarded as a most great benefit. But it is also in the interest of others rather than themselves that persons of whatever sex or condition leading a private life should remain longer in the race-course of piety. #### II.

### ON THE DEATH OF

# H. D. BUREN

## JURIST OF BREMEN.

Those who have exaggerated the poverty of the Holy Tongue <note>A traditional term for the Hebrew language.</note> beyond what is right have either admitted or claimed that it lacks a native word that denotes ETERNITY in its own proper and original sense. Who could easily persuade themselves of such a thing regarding a language whose Teacher for man was the same one who was the Founder of the tongue—that it would lack a term for the highest perfection of divine and human life, the goal of all desires, the reward of virtue, and finally the [inter-] <note>The text cuts off here; "inter-" likely begins a word meaning "intercourse" or "communion" such as "intercursum".</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Hebrew word for eternity (OLAM), finishing the question of whether the language is deficient in expressing this concept. It then transitions into a philosophical meditation on the nature of eternity itself, contrasting it with finite time.</meta>

<page-num>600</page-num>
# PROGRAMS

...of designating the ultimate end between God and man, has labored under a deficiency? Even if there are theologians and philologists of no small reputation <note>literally "not of the lowest bench"</note> who hold this erroneous view, the opposite is apparent from the name *OLAM* (עולם) and its common use in the Sacred Pages. For it is used so frequently, sometimes in an absolute sense for Eternity, and sometimes applied to immortal subjects—*to God, His Decree, Law, Covenant, and Kingdom*, and finally to the *lot* <note>original: "forti," likely a variation of "sorti" meaning fate or portion</note> of the *pious* and the *wicked* after this life—that it is easily noticed that whenever it seems to breathe a lesser emphasis, it must be understood only figuratively. 

The very nature of the word agrees with this most common usage. For its root is a verb signifying "to be hidden," and how perfectly this hits the mark <note>original: "ad rhombum veniat," an idiom for hitting the target or being relevant</note> is plainly evident. For what, I ask, lies more hidden—as if immersed in the proverbial well of Democritus <note>The philosopher Democritus famously stated that truth is hidden at the bottom of a well, far from human perception.</note>—than the solid concept of endless Eternity? 

We do not even pause over that inexhaustible ocean of most absolute Eternity in God Himself, of which only flashes shine forth in the immortality of created minds. Who can gaze without awe upon these very flashes—this very immortality <note>original: "ἀθανασία" (athanasia)</note>—for which conscience intimately convinces everyone who consults the dictates of Reason that they were made and destined? While everything we see, experience, or represent to ourselves in thought consists of number and measure, here every art of numbering and measuring vanishes. Whichever way we turn, we can scarcely, or not even scarcely, reach the first vestibule of Eternity in our thoughts. It would be easier to calculate how many leaves the forest holds, how many grains of sand the shore, how many drops the sea—nay, even by how many mathematical points a line passing through or surrounding the celestial spheres (however many they are conceived to be) or how many atoms the structure of this universe consists of—than to count how many thousands upon thousands of years and ages make up the mere beginning of Eternity. 

*For whatever*, as Censorinus <note>A 3rd-century Roman grammarian and author of "De Die Natali" (On the Birthday).</note> most excellently says in *On the Birthday*, Chapter 16, *has no end, does not admit a comparison of measure; therefore, I shall not attempt to measure an age either by the number of years or centuries, nor finally by any module of finite time: for these things, compared to infinite age, are not even* ***LIKE A SINGLE HOUR IN WINTER.*** <note>In the ancient world, hours were often unequal; a "winter hour" was the shortest possible division of time.</note> Nor is it only the limits of Eternity extended into infinity, but also whatever she [holds] in her vast bosom...

what it encompasses, a thick night presses. An ignorance of that moment from which that innumerable flow of moments will begin keeps those who fix their mind's eye upon it suspended between hope and fear throughout their entire lives. Indeed, what fate awaits individuals in this whirlpool—alas!—it is hedged in by such great darkness. Antiquity imagined this to be the Kingdom of Shadows, where dark shadows flit about, and certainties mixed with uncertainties hold minds in distraction. 

Hence that wavering cry of the Emperor Hadrian: *Little soul, wandering and charming, guest and companion of the body, into what places will you now depart?* <note>original: "Animula, vagula, blandula, Hospes comesque corporis, Quæ nunc abibis in loca?" This is a famous poem attributed to the dying Emperor Hadrian, reflecting on the uncertainty of the soul's fate after death.</note> Is it any wonder? For even Socrates himself, while drinking the hemlock—if we trust Plato—confessed his blindness before his judges, saying: *Which of us goes toward a better state is hidden from everyone, except for God.* <note>original: "ὁπότεροι ἡμῶν ἔρχονται ἐπὶ ἄμεινον πρᾶγμα, ἄδηλον παντὶ, πλὴν ἢ τῷ Θεῷ." This quote appears at the conclusion of Plato's *Apology*.</note> Is it any wonder? For even those upon whom the light of the Gospel has shone often stumble in that same night. With what sweet dreams the sinner here deludes himself! By what great waves the faithful are sometimes tossed in the darkness of temptations! 

Even those who see something through a lattice <term>lattice: original "trasfenna," referring to a window screen or grate that allows only a partial view of what lies beyond</term>, how little it is they see! To whom is a mind or tongue sufficient to either grasp or express the weight of eternal misery as well as eternal blessedness, in a manner worthy of its majesty? To represent this darkness overwhelming those meditating on Eternity, as Horapollo records, the Egyptians used to paint a *Basilisk* <note>original: "Basilisicum." Horapollo was an author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs; early modern scholars often used his work to interpret symbols. Here, the basilisk—or perhaps the Ouroboros serpent—represents the infinite.</note> *whose tail lay hidden beneath the rest of its body.* <note>original: "ἔχοντα τὴν οὐρὰν ὑπὸ τὸ λοιπὸν σῶμα κρυπτομένην."</note> 

This Eternity is that vast and unknown cave which Claudian skillfully depicted toward the end of his second book *In Praise of Stilicho*: *Far off, unknown, and impassable to our mind, scarcely accessible even to the Gods, the unkempt mother of years, the cave of immense age, which brings forth times from its vast bosom and calls them back again.* 

What is most to be grieved here is that a matter so hidden in itself becomes daily more obscure through the sluggishness and stupidity of men. The mind, entangled in fleeting trifles, despises eternal things and almost mocks them. This has reached such a point that the closer we approach Eternity, the more it seems to hide itself from the sight and senses of mortals. And yet, what could be more important for them than, by meditating in this very abyss...
