...expounded. To such an extent that he deserves to be proposed to all the priests of divine Justice <note>A poetic term for judges and legal scholars, common in the early modern period.</note> as an example most worthy of their emulation through all the ages of the world, especially since he did not fear to assert of himself in the fourteenth verse of the same chapter: **I PUT ON JUSTICE, AND IT CLOTHED ME: MY JUDGMENT WAS LIKE A ROBE AND A CROWN.** Those who are not strangers to the holy language <note>Hebrew</note> cannot be unaware of the very frequent conjunction of the names *Mishpat* and *Tzedek* <note>original: משפט & צדק</note>, that is, **JUSTICE AND JUDGMENT**. By the former, that Virtue is designated which is the sole guiding star <term>Cynosure|The North Star, used here metaphorically as a guiding principle.</term> for administering the Law; by the latter is designated the very administration of the Law according to its dictates. 

Furthermore, the struggle of this most holy man in this field is most elegantly compared to the putting on of a garment. Indeed, it has been observed by the most learned interpreters—**Pineda**, **Schmid**, and others—that according to a very ancient custom, those who sat before the Tribunal appeared in the forum adorned with certain insignia of dignity and clothing suitable for inspiring veneration in those standing by. Traces of this custom can be found in the words of the seventh book of the *Aeneid*: 

*This was the attire of Priam, when he gave laws to the assembled peoples in the customary manner* - - - 

Alluding to this, the truly divine guardian of the Laws among the Arameans <note>Referring to Job.</note> wished to present both the most holy inclination of his mind in declaring the Law, and its public demonstration, through a most pleasant allegory using two types of clothing. He compared Justice itself to the inner garment. For unless this first possesses the mind and lies closely against it, the shameful nakedness and defect of everything required of a judge will easily show through. But when a Judge has associated Justice with himself by a constant purpose of mind, as the director and inseparable companion of all his counsels and efforts, then he himself shall be clothed and adorned by her. 

Regarding this, **Epictetus** gives excellent advice in **Stobaeus**, *Sermon XLIV*: *If you propose to consecrate certain ornaments for the city, first clothe yourself with the most beautiful ornament of gentleness, justice, and beneficence.* <note>original Greek: Ει προκειταί σοι την πολιν ἀναθημασι κοσμειν, σεαυτῳ πρωτον ἀναθες το καλλιστον ἡμερότητος και δικαιοσυνης και εὐποιας ἀναθημα.</note> Upon this inner garment, the outward practice, which breathes the highest majesty and glory, is placed over it.

<header>P R O G R A M S.</header>

From the shoulders a *Robe* flows down; a *Diadem* encircles the brow. Both types of clothing, since they look more toward decoration than to any specific practical use for the body, have been the attire of leading men since the most ancient times. For no other reason did the God of Israel command the *High Priest* to be dressed in both, more so than the common priests, than so that he might be taught through these insignia that he was appointed not only as a leader of sacred rites, but also as the highest judge of the people of God. To that end, he was equipped with the majesty of God himself as His representative—acting as the supreme King in Israel. 

This custom easily grew strong throughout the whole East. It has been observed by **Brisson** <note>Barnabé Brisson (1531–1591), a French jurist and scholar of Persian history.</note> and other researchers of antiquity that the Kings of the East—especially in Persia, which neighbors "Happy Arabia" <note>Arabia Felix, a historical name for the fertile southern Arabian Peninsula.</note>—wore a *Robe* or *Kandys* <note>original: *Candyn*; a Persian sleeved tunic or cloak.</note> over a floor-length Persian stole, and encircled the head with a *Cidaris* <note>original: *Cidari*; a royal Persian headdress or turban.</note> or *Diadem*. **Dionysius of Halicarnassus** records in his third book that the ambassadors of the Etruscans—a people descended from the Phoenicians—offered to Tarquinius, among other symbols of leadership <note>original: συμβολα της ἡγεμονιας (symbola tēs hēgemonias)</note>, a wrap or *purple variegated robe*, such as the Kings of the Lydians and Persians used to wear. 

I will not dwell now on the *short, purple wool robe*, shining with divine brilliance in the Temple of Jupiter Capitoline, which **Vopiscus** recorded in his *Life of Aurelian* <note>One of the authors of the *Augustan History*.</note> as a gift from the King of the Persians (who had obtained it from the inner Indians) to the Emperor Aurelian. And who has not heard the story <note>The author uses the Latin idiom *Cui non dictus Hylas?* (To whom has Hylas not been spoken of?), a reference to Virgil meaning a "well-worn tale."</note> of the *diadem*, which was common not only to other Kings of Armenia and Asia, but also to the Greeks and Romans along with the Persians? It is common to such an extent that learned men (not of the common sort) have judged that an argument for the royal dignity of the man Job is supplied by this very phrase. 

Yet Job boasts not that he ever wore a physical *robe* and *diadem*, but rather that the *judgment according to the norm of Justice* which he administered was to him in place of a *robe* and a *diadem*. Just as he preferred this praise to all the treasures of the world, so he equated it to royal honor. If the *robe* hanging from the shoulders of Princes is a sign of a "decorous burden"—a weight that presses upon the defenders themselves so that they may provide protection to others—does it not deserve profound veneration? For like Atlas, they place their shoulders under a world threatening to ruin through the injustice of men; through the incorruptible course of judgment, they provide solace to the oppressed and terror to the rebellious...

...asserted, what do they deserve? But the diadem, distinguished from the robe, and placed on the head—as if in the highest citadel of human prudence—what could it more aptly express than the very bond of the most sacred Laws? This bond sits before the eyes of a just Judge like a headband, restricting all his deliberations so that he decrees or defines nothing except that which most accurately accords with their tenor. This symbol was confirmed for the Israelites by the authority of God himself, who commended his Law to his people <gloss>as frontlets</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: לטוטפת (totafot)</note> in Exodus 13:16 and Deuteronomy 6:8. To this very day, the Jews have not entirely forgotten this, although they cling perhaps too much to the literal surface of the text; they bind to their foreheads, like a diadem, **phylacteries of the head** <note>original Hebrew: תפלין של ראש (tefillin shel rosh)</note>, which are leather boxes containing parchment strips inscribed with certain sections of the Mosaic Law. For this reason, nothing is more frequently discussed by the pens of the Hebrew Teachers than the *Crown of the Law*, distinguished from the *Crown of Kingship* and the *Crown of Priesthood*. In the Talmudic Book **Yoma**, Chapter 7, Rabbi Jochanan compares this to the crowning rim of the Ark of the Covenant, in which the tablets of the Law were stored. Nor is that saying of **Pythagoras** <note>A famous Greek philosopher and mathematician (c. 570–495 BCE).</note> far removed from this comparison: *The crown is not to be plucked*, which **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 CE) who wrote a biography of Pythagoras.</note> interprets in his *Life of Pythagoras* (Chapter 42) as follows: *That is to say, the laws are not to be violated, for they are the crowns of cities.* So it truly is. If the *power of the Judge* is foreshadowed by the robe spreading wide from the shoulders, the *diadem*, gently encircling the head—the throne, as it were, of the soul—will serve as a reminder of the legal bonds in which his counsels must be entwined, lest he abuse that power. Far from this restriction casting any shadow over the majesty of the Judge, it rather places it in the fullest light. If nothing is more wholesome for human society than the rigid observation of Justice and the administration of the Laws according to its prescription; if I may use the phrase of **Pindar** <note>An ancient Greek lyric poet (c. 518–438 BCE).</note> (*Olympian Odes* 13.7): *Justice is the firm foundation of cities*; if **Hesiod** <note>A Greek poet (c. 700 BCE) often cited for his moral and agricultural wisdom.</note> (*Works and Days*, line 261) rightly counts among the plagues of the earth and the hatreds of heaven *those who, devising baneful things, turn justice aside, speaking crookedly...*

What is the splendor of those whose highest honor is placed in the unsullied worship of Justice, if not a ray of divine Majesty itself? Is it not the radiance <note>original Greek: ἀπαύγασμα (apaugasma), a term often used in theology to describe Christ as the "brightness" of God's glory</note> of the Sun of *Justice* himself—the Son of God—to whom the Prophet assigns *Justice* as a belt for his loins? <note>A reference to Isaiah 11:5.</note> O diadem, truly scattering its rays and full brightness in every direction from on high; yet placed upon a difficult height! For in order *that one might render to man what is his own, it is necessary to offer to GOD WHAT IS HIS* above all else. 

If the goal toward which every public and civil matter is rightly directed is the promotion of divine worship and glory; if the highest principle of all Justice is the most holy and immutable Will of the supreme God himself, who wishes States to be formed and preserved in the world so that they may serve the Counsel of His Grace; if no one weighs this rightly except the one whose eyes celestial illumination has opened; if no one will establish the true price for *Justice and Judgment* except he who has been cleansed from the filth of innate iniquity through effective Grace; who does not notice that the path which can raise one to that peak of highest dignity which Job occupied is difficult and trodden by few? With a solemn speech concerning the **RELIGIOUS LEGAL CONSULTANT**, he has arranged to begin it this coming Thursday, May 12th, following the conclusion of divine services. With what success he was imbued with the discipline of the men flourishing at that time, he gave public testimony in a Valedictory Dispute on the *Power and Efficacy of the Supplementary Oath* <note>original: *Jurisjurandi suppletorii*. serves, with a marvelous consensus, the Ecclesiastical Writers **ORIGEN**, **BASIL THE GREAT**, **GREGORY NAZIANZEN**, and **CHRYSOSTOM**, <note>These are prominent early Christian "Church Fathers" from the 3rd and 4th centuries.</note> to say nothing of those who followed in their footsteps, have judged that this emblem refers to the **TURTLE-DOVE**. The incomparable **BOCHART** <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant scholar famous for his work on the animals of the Bible.</note> (*Hieroz. Lib. I. cap. 5.*) wonders why this was done. However, it would not have been so difficult to guess the reason if that most learned man had observed that their leader was **ORIGEN**. He was the one who, in his second Homily, noted the following while illustrating the praise of the Turtle-dove—which divine Solomon, surpassing all the wise men of the Egyptians in his higher skill of Sacred Enigmas, presents in his prophetic Song: *“They say the nature of the Turtle-dove is such that neither does the male approach any female other than his one mate, nor does the female suffer more than one male; so that if it happens that one is lost and the other survives, the love of physical union is extinguished for the survivor along with the spouse.”* <note>original: *“Turturem ferunt hujusmodi naturam esse... pariter cum conjuge extinctus sit ei concubitus amor.”*</note> Accordingly, the likeness of the Turtle-dove is fittingly applied to the Church, either because she knows no marriage to another man after Christ, or because a multitude of people, like turtle-doves in their self-restraint and modesty, fly within her.

Now, if it can be proven that **ADAMANTIUS** <note>A nickname for Origen, meaning "Man of Steel," referring to his indomitable spirit.</note> did not stray far from the mark in either his review of the emblem or his attached explanation, it will be clear that other writers quite rightly followed in his footsteps. Whether that is truly the nature of **Turtle-doves**, as writers show from **Horus the Nilotic** <note>Referring to Horapollo, the supposed author of a 5th-century treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, I leave for the investigators of natural things to explore. Certainly, regarding **Doves**, a bird dedicated to Venus, no one besides our author has asserted such a thing. Indeed, **ULYSSES ALDROVANDUS** <note>Ulisse Aldrovandi (1522–1605), a renowned Italian naturalist and "father" of modern natural history.</note> (*Ornithol. Lib. XV.*) has established with no small amount of evidence that the much-celebrated chastity of doves, spoken and written of by many, is not entirely without blemish. 

However, the best authors proclaim Turtle-doves to be chaste by definition. Hence **AELIAN** (*Hist. Anim. Lib. III. c. 44.*) prefers wood-pigeons as well as Turtle-doves over common Doves in the praise of chastity. And **CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA** (*Stromat. Lib. II.*), reviewing various species of birds preeminent for chastity, omitted common doves and named *“the wild pigeons, the wood-pigeons, and the turtle-dove genus.”* <note>original Greek: *τας πελειαδας και τας φασσας και το τρυγονον γενος*</note> Surely the love of solitude belongs to Turtle-doves above all other kinds of pigeons...

Indeed, **ARISTOTLE** teaches in his *History of Animals (Book V, 17)* that the turtle-dove is also to be classified under the *peristeroeides genos* <note>original Greek: $\pi\epsilon\rho\iota\sigma\tau\epsilon\rho\text{o}\epsilon\iota$-$\delta\epsilon\varsigma$ $\gamma\epsilon\nu\text{o}\varsigma$, the dove-like genus</note> or dove-like family. Whatever the case may be, this solitary bird—most chaste, sacred to God, a messenger of spring, and one who invites her mate with a hoarse throat whether she is calling him in his absence or mourning his loss—presents a most elegant shadow of the **Heavenly Bride** <note>The "Bride" is a traditional metaphor for the Church or the individual human soul in relation to Christ.</note>. For the first care of the soul betrothed to Christ will be to withdraw itself from the world; abhorring the world's ruined ways, the soul passes its life in the greatest crowd of men as if in solitude, mindful of that saying: *he who has hidden well, has lived well* <note>original Latin: "bene qui latuit, bene vixit," a quote from the Roman poet Ovid suggesting that a private life is a good life.</note>.

Next, it is necessary that she preserve the untainted faith she pledged to her divine Spouse. She must repay His eternal love—which is invincible even against Death and Hell—with the purest, most intense, and most constant affection. She must value nothing but Jesus and the seraphic delights of spiritual union with Him, desiring nothing and judging nothing worthy of her prayers or deepest care except to be drenched in those delights in secret, to be immersed in them, and to taste in them the first-fruits of future glory. Nevertheless, the soul that is becoming accustomed to the Lord does not rashly overlook the opportunities and signs of the times that invite her to come forth from her hiding places and to raise her voice. When the winter of afflictions ceases and the new light of divine Grace rises upon the Church; when the heat of the **Sun of Righteousness** <note>A biblical metaphor for Christ.</note>, tempered by the rain of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, makes the field of the spiritual Canaan fertile; when the face of Emmanuel’s Earth is renewed like a smiling Spring through the budding seed of the Gospel and the hope of a joyful harvest turning green in the blade; then, above all, the voice of the mystical Turtle-dove is heard (*Song of Solomon 2:12*), she being not ignorant of that time *in which she must return* (*Jeremiah 8:7*). This voice is heard not as a mere sound, but as a most longed-for sign. You ask, my [Christian...]

O lover of Christ? Furthermore, since those virtues of souls acting as widows in this land during Christ's absence—which the image of the Turtle-dove expresses—are the same as those which the Apostle in **1 Timothy 5:5** <note>"Now she that is a widow indeed, and desolate, trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day."</note> wishes to shine forth in every Christian widow, it is plainly evident how much these things apply to the present matter. If, after the manner of the Egyptians, it were permitted to paint this funeral on this very day according to the mind of those to whom the virtues of the Deceased were known, this page would show nothing but a **BLACK TURTLE-DOVE** on white paper.

->V.<-

## ON THE DEATH OF
# H. MEYER,
### CANDIDATE OF LAW.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'H' featuring elaborate foliate designs with leaves and swirling vines.</image-desc>As we return somewhat late to the delights of the gardens—after a most stubborn winter has barely been conquered—the inexorable command of Morta <note>original: "Morta," the Roman goddess of death and one of the three Fates</note> repeatedly interrupts our joy. Having poured out from our enclosures into the milder air, we were grieving here for an aged tree that was unequal to enduring such great cold; there, for a sapling of great promise not yet strong enough against the harshness of the North Wind <note>original: "Aquilo"</note>; and elsewhere, for a war declared upon the very buds and blossoms by an innumerable army of caterpillars.

Truly, however anxious we may be to repair our losses, the funerals of the old and young mixed together so often interrupt us that whoever is not completely blind may easily perceive that this lot is common to the human race as well as to plants. Therefore, those pious souls among the people of God most wisely established a custom: so that they might temper the delight perceived from the most pleasant greenery with the meditation of death, they became accustomed to build monuments for themselves and their kin in the very places established for the relaxation of the soul. The first traces of this most holy custom are found in the history of Abraham... <note>The text likely continues to discuss Abraham purchasing the cave of Machpelah in a field as a burial site</note>

...history shows. Who is unaware that the cave of Machpelah (Genesis 23:17), purchased from the Hittites with silver and made famous by the tombs of the Patriarchs, was situated in a field planted with trees? Who does not know that Deborah was buried under an oak tree in Bethel (Genesis 35:8), or that Samuel was entombed in his own house (1 Samuel 25:1)? For this must be understood as referring to the Garden which was adjacent to the house; both the ritual immunities <note>The author refers to the Jewish laws of ritual purity; a corpse inside a dwelling-house would render the building and its inhabitants "unclean," so "in the house" is interpreted by scholars as the attached private garden.</note>—the greatest of which would have been brought into the house by a corpse according to the Law—and a comparison with 2 Chronicles 33:20 teach us this. For when Manasseh, King of the Jews, is likewise said here to have been buried in his house, 2 Kings 21:18 records that this was done *in the garden of his house, in the garden of Uzza*, where later the bones of Amon (2 Kings 21:26) were also laid to rest. Thus, what Piety once commanded gradually also became a sign of *Dignity*. Following this custom, Joseph of Arimathea—a man illustrious for the splendor of his office, but even more for the praise of his justice and hope in the Kingdom of God—prepared that tomb for himself in a garden (John 19:41), which provided rest to the Savior of the world after the work of Redemption had been completed. 

The same method of honoring the dead soon spread to the gentiles. Plutarch, in his most elegant little book *On Isis and Osiris*, mentions the ancient monument of Metis <note>Likely referring to a site associated with Egyptian mythology or a specific Hellenized Egyptian figure</note> on the island of Nistitane among the Egyptians, which was shaded by a plant that exceeded the size of any olive tree. We believe Arrian (Book 6, chapter 29) and Strabo (Book 15) when they say that *at Pasargadae, in the royal paradise <note>original: "ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ τῷ βασιλικῷ," referring to a Persian "paradeisos" or walled pleasure-garden</note>, was the tomb of Cyrus, and around it a grove of all kinds of trees had been planted <note>original: "ἄλσος ἐμφυτεῦθαι δένδρων παντοίων"</note>, and it was a grove irrigated with water <note>original: "καὶ ὕδατι εἶναι κατάῤῥυτον"</note>.* Among the institutions of the ancient Etruscans, this Law is recorded in the Fragments of Book 3: *If anyone does not have their own tomb, let them be buried in a leafy forest.* And although Plato in *Laws* (Book 12) prohibited *taking any part of a cultivated field, or one that could be cultivated, for a tomb, so that no one, living or dead, might diminish the land which can produce crops and, like a mother, supply us with food*—to use Cicero’s interpretation here from his second book *On Laws*—nonetheless, the same custom recommended itself to the Romans. This is evident from the woods which Augustus added to his Mausoleum, as Suetonius records in chapter 100, and from many other examples provided in abundance by Kirchmann <note>Johann Kirchmann (1575–1643), a German philologist known for his work "De Funeribus Romanorum" (On Roman Funerals)</note>...

One thing only is to be lamented: that this practice, which seemed so commendable for the sanctity of its purpose, turned for the worse—first through luxury, and soon through the impious superstition of the Pagans. For when foolish descendants began to bestow divine honors upon their ancestors, the woods that surrounded their tombs were transformed into "sacred groves" <note>The Latin term *lucus* refers specifically to a grove dedicated to a deity, often viewed with suspicion by Judeo-Christian writers as a site of idolatry.</note>. Sacred history itself shows traces of this impiety. Josiah destroyed the tombs along with the grove profaned by idolatry, as recorded in 2 Kings 23:15–16. For this reason, the Prophet Isaiah (65:3–4) joins together those *who sacrifice in gardens and dwell among the tombs*. Hence, according to Book III of the *Aeneid* (line 302):
*Before the city, in a grove by the stream of a false Simois,*
*Andromache was offering libations to the ashes and calling the spirits*
*to Hector’s mound.*
Likewise, in Book V of the same *Aeneid* (line 760): *A priest and a widely sacred grove were added to the tomb of Anchises.* From this, [Cicero] says in his *Oration for Milo*: *You, I say, Albanian mounds and groves, you I implore and call to witness.* Therefore, [John] Spencer, in *On the Laws of the Hebrews*, Book II, chapter 16, believes it follows from this that these sacred groves often consisted of Cypress trees, since the cypress was a tree associated with death and had become almost consecrated to the ceremonies of the dead through long usage. To follow this practice further—as it has been abundantly illustrated by Paschalius <note>Carlo Pasquale (1547–1625), an Italian diplomat and scholar who wrote *De Coronis* (On Crowns).</note> in *On Crowns*, Book IV, chapter 5 and following; by Kirchmann in the work already cited; by Faesius in his commentary on Gyraldus’s *On Burial*, page 740 and following; and by others—the narrowness of this page does not permit. Truly, for holier meditations, the contemplation of a tomb standing out among the flowerbeds smiling with a thousand colors and the rows of trees arranged with wondrous art opens a freer field. Here, it will never be unhelpful to remember that Garden planted by the hand of God Himself <note>The Garden of Eden.</note>, which sealed for the first man both the hope of eternal life and, when that hope was neglected, brought forth the curse, hardship, and death itself. Here, plants and flowers of every kind—rising only to fall—foreshadow the inconstancy of temporal goods, the fleeting nature of life, and the most diverse types of death that press upon every age. Some seem to be led to a certain maturity of very brief duration; most are gnawed by little worms within this limit, now scorched by the cold, now by the heat of the sun, or withered by a lack of sap, or infected by a malignant dew, or cast down by the inclemency of the winds. For this reason, it was a custom not only in the sacred pages of Job 14:2 and Psalm 103:15, but also among the Poets of the Heathen, to compare the life of men to a *flower*. *For the swift little flower of our narrow, miserable, and very short portion of life hastens to run out—* <note>original: "Festinat enim decurrere velox Flosculus angustæ miseræque brevissimæ vitæ Portio"</note> as Juvenal writes in *Satire IX*, verse 126. And the epigram about the Rose, which is attributed to Virgil, ends thus: *Gather roses, maiden, while the flower is new and youth is fresh: and be mindful that your age hastens even so.* <note>original: "Collige virgo rosas, dum flos novus & nova pubes: Et memor esto, ævum sic properare tuum." This poem, "De rosis nascentibus," is now often attributed to Ausonius.</note> Indeed, man is taught that there are as many heralds of mortality as there are leaves, by being compared to a *driven leaf* in Job 13:25. Thus the race of men, one part grows and flourishes, another ceases to be.* <note>original: "Nil ortus noster foliorum distat ab ortu, Quæ ventus modo fundit humi, modo denique sylvis Multa renascuntur formosi tempore veris. On medical advice in the year **1728**, during the month of June, he bid farewell to Belgium to drink the **Pyrmont mineral waters** <note>original: "Acidulas Pirmontanas." Bad Pyrmont was a famous spa destination for the European aristocracy and scholarly class in the 18th century.</note> directly from the spring. Relieved for a short time by their use, he sought out Halle in Saxony <note>Hala Saxonum</note>, and committed himself to the instruction of those most illustrious men, **JUSTUS HENNING BÖHMER** and **NICOLAUS HIERONYMUS GUNDLING**, who were professing the Law there with great renown. However, noticing that **Hygeia** <note>The Greek goddess of health; a poetic way of saying his health was not returning.</note> was not yet reconciled to him, and with his doctors urging him, he turned his journey back toward his fatherland. About a two-month period passed from the time he returned to the embrace of his family. Yet, Providence, the divider of human affairs, did not wish this joy to be long-lasting. For by a slow **consumption** <term>Tabes: a wasting disease, often referring to tuberculosis.</term>, the strength of his weakened little body was gradually so exhausted that all care and medical art failed. This alone was to be considered a gain of the highest order: that a sound mind remained in a body that was anything but sound, and that divine Grace significantly comforted him as he lay ill. To this grace alone must it be attributed that, standing in the very **springtime of his life** <note>original: "in illo vitae vere"</note>, he resigned himself entirely to the divine will; that he considered it a great blessing to be warned of the imminent danger and to be prepared for eternity through pious conversations and prayers; that with a broken heart he seriously grieved the failings of his heedless youth; that he ardently fled to the Father reconciled to the sinner in Christ; and finally that he founded all his hope and trust solely in the Lord, renouncing any presumption of his own righteousness. Intent on these spiritual exercises and anticipating the expectations of his family, he delivered his soul into the hands of his Creator and Savior, peacefully breathing his last this past Saturday after three in the afternoon, having completed **24** years of age, exactly ten months, and as many days. The hour of **1:00** this afternoon has been appointed for the escorting of the funeral, which we now announce, and for laying him to rest in **St. Ansgari’s Church**.

### VI.
## ON THE DEATH OF THE
# HAVIGHORST WIFE.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'A' featuring foliage and decorative patterns.</image-desc>

The enigmatic Alphabet of Womanly Praises <note>The author refers to Proverbs 31:10–31, which in the original Hebrew is an acrostic poem where each verse begins with a successive letter of the alphabet.</note> was placed as a crowning achievement in the Proverbs of the wisest of Kings, Solomon, by those who collected them under the guidance of the heavenly Spirit. Among those verses, the one marked with the letter **ד** <note>Daleth, the fourth letter of the Hebrew alphabet.</note> especially displays this: that the *diligent woman’s* <note>original: "strenuæ Mulieris"</note> LAMP IS NOT TO BE EXTINGUISHED AT NIGHT. It differs not a little from the customs of our own delicate age—which is nearly broken by every kind of softness—that a Royal Wife, such as this prophetic model represents, is introduced as industriously urging on her work deep into the night by the light of a lamp, having driven away sleep. Truly, this is not at all contrary to the ancient simplicity, even that of noble women. Hence, **OVID** in his first *Epistle* introduces **Penelope** writing thus to her husband, the King of Ithaca:

> *Lest the hanging loom weary my widowed hands*
> *as I seek to pass the long night.* <note>original: "Nec mihi quærenti spatiosam fallere noctem / Lassaret viduas pendula tela manus." From Ovid's Heroides, Penelope to Ulysses.</note>

And according to the same author in the second book of the *Fasti* (line 741), when Tarquinius rushed in late at night, **Lucretia** was spinning:

> *Before the bed were the baskets and the soft wool:*
> *By a small light, the handmaidens were drawing out their assigned tasks.* <note>original: "Ante thorum calami lanaque mollis erat: / Lumen ad exiguum famulæ data pensa trahebant." Lucretia was a legendary model of Roman female virtue.</note>

However, we do not think that the "use of the lamp" refers only to the labor of a woman’s work, but at the same time to that which a Wife shows while waiting for the arrival of her Husband. In this way, we have no need for the **hyperbole** <term>Hyperbole: a literary device using exaggeration for emphasis.</term> that **MERCERUS** <note>Jean Mercier, a 16th-century French scholar of Hebrew.</note> and others establish here. For while hardly anyone would praise a wife because she spends the best part of the night in labor rather than rest, no one would blame her because she waits for her Husband by staying awake and remaining intent on good work. But greater things lie hidden beneath this shell. Many interpreters, both ancient and modern, openly acknowledge that those who think nothing but a eulogy for a diligent Mother of a household is contained in this passage fall short of the majesty of the Divine Word. Who would believe the Holy Spirit intended nothing but **household rules**,

As for Saint Genevieve of Paris and Gudula, the patroness of Brussels—concerning whom those who worship saints <note>original: "Hagiolatræ"</note> imagine that their extinguished candles were relit at night by Angels through the favor of heaven, and for that reason the title *Her lamp shall not be extinguished in the night* <note>original: "Non extinguetur in nocte lucerna ejus"</note> is usually applied to their images—we leave them in their place. Those who, along with **CORNELIUS À LAPIDE** <note>A famous Jesuit biblical exegete (1567–1637).</note>, invoke the Blessed Virgin herself here, sell even more inept nonsense; they claim she alone kept the faith while the other Apostles failed during Christ’s passion, and for that reason she is called an *inextinguishable lamp* <note>original: "lampas inextinguibilis"</note> by **CYRIL** in his sermon against Nestorius. To us, **Night** represents any unhappy times of the Church, whether through the thickening darkness in doctrine and morals, or through the storms of afflictions. The **Lamp**, however, represents both the truths of doctrine and the likeness of the Witnesses who preserve and defend them; this is proven alone by the eulogy our Savior offers to John the Baptist in John 5:35, when He calls him a *burning and shining lamp* <note>original: "λύχνον καιόμενον καὶ φαίνοντα" (lychnon kaiomenon kai phainonta)</note>. Its preservation from being extinguished can be seen partly as a duty to be fulfilled by the pious, and partly as a benefit promised to the Bride of the Lamb <note>The Church.</note>. Following the former concept, **AUGUSTINE** in his 45th sermon on various subjects exhorts: *Let our lamp burn all night. And because He who speaks the word to us daily pours in the oil, lest the lamp be extinguished; therefore daily let us hear...*

...let us hear the word, let us take up the oil, let us sustain the burning lamps, as the Lord teaches: *And let your lamps be burning in your hands,* <note>original: "Et lucernæ ardentes in manibus veſtris"</note> Luke 12:35. For in this way we shall imitate the example of this virtuous woman. I would prefer, however, to understand these words as a promise, not only because they are joined in the same sentence with another benefit in a single sequence, but also because they are expressed in the future tense, so that a perpetual good that will never cease might be designated. Add to this that among the most serious threats, the "extinguishing of a lamp in darkness" is recorded as a proverbial way of speaking in Proverbs 20:20; hence, its opposite takes on the form of a most magnificent promise. Therefore, the pious and heaven-inspired Mother of Lemuel <note>Lemuel is traditionally identified as King Solomon; his mother is Bathsheba.</note> sensed that the Lamp of the Church—whether through the ferocity of storms or through a Night weighing down longer than hoped—would be brought into the greatest danger of extinction, and yet would overcome every violence of temptation.

Therefore, I would consider the interpretation of **RABBI SOLOMON JARCHI** <note>Also known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval French rabbi and author of comprehensive commentaries on the Talmud and Tanakh.</note> to be not at all contemptible; he suggests that this refers to the Night of the Israelites' liberation from Egypt, in which the light of the Pillar of Cloud—which he regards as a figure for the Divine Law—illuminated and protected them. Meanwhile, more closely, the same Mystery was foreshadowed by the light of the golden Lampstand <note>The Menorah in the Temple.</note>, which can be viewed as a ray flashing forth from that sacred fire initially appearing from the Pillar, whose perpetual splendor has been celebrated by the pens of the Pagans themselves. For **HECATAEUS OF ABDERA** <note>A Greek historian and skeptic philosopher who lived in the 4th century BCE.</note>, whose remarkable excerpt concerning the Jews was preserved by **EUSEBIUS** <note>The "Father of Church History" (c. 260–339 CE).</note> in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 9, chapter 4, calls its light *unquenchable by night and by day* <note>original: "φῶς ejus ἀναποσβετον καὶ τὰς νύκτας καὶ τὰς ἡμέρας"</note>. From this, **DIODORUS SICULUS** <note>A 1st-century BCE Greek historian.</note> in Book 34 noted that the Lampstand itself *was called the immortal lamp by the Jews* <note>original: "immortalem lucernam à Judæis dictum fuiſſe" / "ἀθάνατον λύχνον"</note>. **KIMCHI** <note>David Kimchi, or Radak (1160–1235), a medieval rabbi and grammarian.</note>, among other Jewish Teachers, contends on 1 Samuel 3 that *at least the middle lamp of the golden Lampstand was never extinguished, even if it happened that some of the others went out.* In this way, under this shadow, the God of Israel gave his word for the perpetual preservation of the Gospel Light. This relates most significantly to what is promised concerning the Messiah in Isaiah 42:3: *A bruised reed he shall not break,* or, as seems more fitting, *he shall not remove.*

These virgins, with lamps lit and abundantly supplied with oil, awaited the arrival of the heavenly Bridegroom at night, although they did not wait by keeping watch as they ought, but by sleeping. 

Since the allegory of our Prophetess <note>Referring to the mother of Lemuel, the presumed author of the "virtuous woman" passage in Proverbs 31.</note> recurs in these Virgins, a most effective sense emerges when compared with our passage: *The wife of the heavenly Solomon* <note>An allegorical reference to the Church or the pious soul as the bride of Christ (the "New Solomon").</note> *who applies herself strenuously to promoting the work of the Lord, shall not only taste the fruit of her labors when the evening of sadder times falls, but, being equipped with the never-failing oil of the Holy Spirit, her Lamp of the Word of Truth shall be illuminated until the Husband arrives; finding her vigilant, He shall lead her with Him into the heavenly bridal chambers.* 

Such great hope for the Church is sealed through the manifold experience of individual believers who live in the Night of worldly security, calamities, temptations, and finally death itself. Although the souls of the pious sit in Darkness, the Lord is their Light. The light of divine promises dissipates the clouds gathered by the waves of doubt, by pains, by diseases, by the long duration of sufferings, by the assaults of the Prince of Darkness, and finally by the terrors of imminent death. The most noble and excellent woman **METTA CAPPELIA** surely tasted this goodness of Jehovah while confined to her bed and at the very threshold of death. She was the most beloved wife of the Greatly Reverend and Most Learned Man, Mr. **JOHANN HAVIGHORST**, Ordinary Professor of Sacred Theology and Eloquence, most celebrated Librarian and Head of the Paedagogium, most worthy member of the Royal Prussian Society of Sciences, who has served our Gymnasium and School most excellently for twenty-three years, and our most honored colleague. He was not present without an *Angel Precursor* <note>original: "Angelo Præcursore"; referring to John the Baptist as the messenger who prepares the way for Christ.</note>, who publicly testified to lowering the mountains, raising the valleys, and removing all obstacles. How much more illustrious will be that second arrival for which we wait? Instead of one Precursor, an entire army of *Angels* will appear. By their ministry, not just certain stumbling blocks, but *all* of them <note>original: "omnia"</note>, as many as have hitherto been placed in the way of the progress of the Kingdom of Heaven, will be removed. Thus they will carry out what was commanded through Isaiah (62:10):

The boundaries of the prophetic scene as well as the phrasing prove that the best Savior aimed for this battle-cry. To the ears of refined Greece, the word <term>scandalon<note>original: "του Σκανδαλου" (tou Scandalou). In ancient Greek, this originally referred to the trigger-stick of a trap, but in the Bible, it came to mean a "stumbling block" or "offense."</term> was hardly heard, but among the Hellenists <note>Greek-speaking Jews who lived in the Mediterranean world.</note> it was quite common. This has been noted abundantly by Vorstius, Heinsius, Martinius, G. J. Vossius, Ekhard, and other <term>philologists<note>Scholars who study the history and structure of languages.</note></term>; it indicates any kind of stumbling block for the feet. Thus it accurately agrees with the etymology, which is *skazein* <note>Greek: "σκαζειν", meaning to limp.</note>, "to limp"; and thus with the Hebrew word to which it usually corresponds, *mikshol* <note>Hebrew: "מכשל"</note>, "a stumbling block" or "impediment." By the diligence of Henry Hammond—whom G. Olearius excerpted—three kinds of stumbling blocks, known as *scandalon*, were observed:

> *For it signifies either a "pagis" <note>Greek: "παγιν", a snare or trap.</note>—a trap or noose placed at the feet to entangle them; or stakes, sharpened wood, and tangles of branches which, when scattered along the road, hinder the step of a soldier—even if he is not "bronze-greaved" <note>original: "χαλκοκνημιδος" (chalkoknemidos); a famous description from Homer's Iliad of the well-armored Greek warriors.</note> as the Achivi <note>The Greeks of the Heroic age.</note> are depicted by Homer; or finally, whatever may be cast into the way by any chance, especially stones, which can injure the unwary.*

Under these emblems, the *Holy Spirit* most wisely outlines all kinds of *offenses* <note>original: "offendicula"</note>, whether through *doctrine*, or through *life*, or through external *members of the Church*, or through its *enemies*—both given and received—which stir up some prejudice against the Cause of the Lord and the Kingdom of Heaven. ...to mean *Scandals* <note>original: "Scandala"; from the Greek *skandalon*, meaning a stumbling block or offense.</note>, as is established by the example of Peter (Matthew 5:23) and of Christ himself (1 Corinthians 1:23, 2 Peter 2:7). Is it any wonder if, through their immense number, the hope of the pious is all but cut off, their prayers are rendered void, and darkness prevails in place of the desired light, while Hell boasts and the flock of the Lord laments? Yet more precisely, our faithful Teacher <note>likely referring to Christ or a specific Church Father mentioned in the surrounding context.</note> wished to warn us about *Scandals* arising from the very bosom of the corrupted Church through both the *adulteration* and the *distortion* of true doctrine. Indeed, the most celebrated interpreters, such as **JOHANNES MELCHIOR**, **CAMPEGIUS VITRINGA**, and others, understand the deceptive fallacies of Antichristian doctrine here. ...do they continue to obscure? Why should I mention how, on one hand, under the pretext of an irrevocable decree <note>A reference to the doctrine of absolute predestination, which the author suggests can lead to fatalism.</note>, a fatalistic order of things is encouraged, sin is downplayed, and the form of faith is overturned? Or how, on the other hand, under the plausible title of more abundant Grace, our native corruption is minimized, and Grace itself is rendered weak, uncertain, and changeable? On both sides, however, a cushion is spread for the **mind of the flesh** <note>original Greek: "τῷ φρονήματι τῆς σαρκὸς"; see Romans 8:6.</note>, which is the fertile mother of so many errors. What shall I say of the delusions of *False Mystics* brought back from the cloisters of monks by Fanatics? What of the most obstinate love for superstitious rituals? What of the prejudices of human authority, the affectation of Hierarchy, and the proscribed liberty of prophesying? Are not these, and many others of the same kind, the snares by which the unwary are deceived? Are they not led either to embrace these same errors or to form the worst possible conceptions of our most holy Confession <term>Confession<note>Refers to a formal statement of religious doctrine, such as the Augsburg Confession.</note></term>, thereby harassing, nitpicking, and belittling it? Are these not the obstacles that entangle the steps of the slow-moving, and—unless their feet are shod **with the readiness of the Gospel of peace** <note>original Greek: "ἐν ἑτοιμασίᾳ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου τῆς εἰρήνης"; see Ephesians 6:15.</note>—hinder the growth of the Kingdom of Christ? Do they not present many troubles to be swallowed by those who ardently long for His coming? Are these not the stones of offense upon which the profane and the hypocrites stumble to their own destruction, while the true members of the mystical body are often exposed to the gravest temptations, or at least are affected by the sharpest pains of a wounded and broken heart? Who would not acknowledge that *Angelic Wisdom*, strength, and zeal are required to remove these impediments from the way of the Lord? O sweet consolation in the dregs of our age, that Angels sufficient for this *Herculean* labor will be provided at the right time! How great a thing it is, then, that those men have not yet entirely passed away who perform the duty of divine ambassadors among us—men who, by their prayers, their efforts, and their preparation of the youth for such great hope, play a prelude to so great a work! Among these, as he has already enrolled his name before, so he shall from this time forth more solemnly profess it:

->THE MOST REVEREND AND ILLUSTRIOUS MAN<-

## LORD NICOLAUS NONNEN,

->Doctor of Sacred Theology, and Preacher in the St. John's Church of this city.<-

...that these manifestations are called *Stumbling Blocks* <note>original: "Scandala"</note> is established by the example of Peter (Matthew 16:23) <note>The OCR cites Matthew 5:23, but the context of Peter and stumbling blocks refers to Christ's rebuke of Peter in Matthew 16.</note> and of Christ himself (1 Corinthians 1:23; 2 Peter 2:7). Yet our faithful Teacher <note>Referring to Jesus Christ.</note> wished to warn us more precisely about *Stumbling Blocks* arising from the very heart of the corrupted Church, through both the *adulteration* and the *distortion* of true doctrine. <note>original Latin: *temnere* (catchword from previous page). The opening sentence refers to a scholar despising or disregarding the dangers of doubt once they have reached safety.</note>...to despise them, once the rocks have been sailed past, and it is permitted to emerge from the waves of doubt and finally fix a firm foot upon the shore. If it were not for this [certainty], how would the human race excel over the animals that crawl prone upon the earth? What would the Schools and Lyceums <note>Ancient Greek institutions of learning, here used to mean universities.</note>—illustrious for the commerce of Wisdom—be, if not caves of ignorance or stables of despair? For we know no more than what we know for certain. To define other matters that rest upon opinion or conjecture, or to wish to deduce something certain from the uncertain, is the nearest path to stupidity. A man begins to act as a human, and thus to use his reason, only when he ceases to doubt with reason. *The resolution of a difficulty is the discovery of truth* <note>original Greek: "Η λυσις της ἀποριας, εὑρεσις ἐστι της ἀληθειας". From Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII, Chapter IV.</note> (as Aristotle witnesses). Let all those who aspire to the very citadel of true Wisdom strive toward this goal. The prize is placed in the center. For no one will presume anything of the Best, Wisest, and most Truthful Being [God] other than that he himself was created for an end consistent with his nature, and was equipped with faculties suitable for attaining that end. From this, it is as impossible for a person to be deceived in the right use of those faculties as it is impossible for God to wish to deceive, or to be unwilling to reach the goal He Himself established. Who, then, would dare to doubt the will of the Creator here, who has abundantly provided the human race with sufficient means to obtain this end? 

By His favor, infallible ways are at hand—though they are little known and even more rarely traveled. These guides are *Conscience*, or if you prefer, *Anticipation*, *Prolepsis* <term>Prolepsis: A Stoic philosophical term for a "preconception" or an innate idea that allows us to understand basic truths without prior instruction.</term>, or *Preconceived Knowledge*. Without this, as Cicero defines it (*On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I), *nothing can be understood, nor sought, nor discussed.* It is the storehouse of ideas implanted in the mind, drawing every attentive person into agreement by a light inherent in these principles from the outset <note>original Latin: *à priori* (from what is before). This refers to knowledge gained through deduction and innate reason rather than observation.</note>. The second guide is *Experience*, which, through the service of the senses, examines the sensible effects of things from what follows <note>original Latin: *à posteriori* (from what comes after). This refers to knowledge gained through observation and physical evidence.</note>; by comparing these effects, it proceeds step by step toward an infallible judgment regarding their nature and causes. The more these clearest fountains of all truth are observed to agree with one another, the more the fear of deception is cast aside. Upon these two "witnesses," as it were, all faith—both divine and human—rests. They perform the role of two lights which, when joined together, detect objects more strongly and more certainly; for if anyone were to despise either one...

...to despise it and wish to deny its authority would be just as if he were to tear out one of his own eyes. For this reason, while the school of Epicurus made use of "Anticipations" <note>original Latin: *Anticipationum*. This refers to the Epicurean concept of *prolepsis*, or innate "pre-conceptions" that allow us to categorize new experiences.</note> and the school of Plato proscribed the Senses, those from the school of the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> seem to have judged most wisely of all. Concerning them, **SEXTUS EMPIRICUS** (in Book I of *Against the Dogmatists*) asserts that they admitted a double <term>criterion|a standard or test by which something is judged</term>: *sense-perception for things sensed, and intelligence for things understood; but that which is common to both, as Theophrastus said, is self-evidence.* <note>original Greek: "αἰσθησιν μεν αἰσθητων, νοησιν δε των νοητων, κοινον δε ἀμφοτερων, ὡς ἐλεγεν ὁ Θεοφραστος, το ἐναργες".</note> This is the experience of the senses regarding sensible things, and the intelligence regarding intelligible things; and according to Theophrastus, that which is common to both is what is evident. 

God established the very certainty of heavenly mysteries upon these pillars, although—in order to raise that certainty above all human certainty—He instilled in them a stronger power to compel faith through the supernatural operation of the Heavenly Spirit. For by this celestial light, ***Conscience***, and by a taste of the first-fruits of eternal life, ***Experience***—armed as if with a clear crystal—they lead one so far toward acknowledging the pure truth of the most hidden things (even absent and future things) that the mind would be ready to undergo a thousand deaths rather than cloud or betray the truthfulness of God with new doubts. And this is so true that **EURIPIDES** judged that this certainty should be sought nowhere except in divine matters, when he declares (in *Helen*, lines 1164–1165):

> *I do not have anything clear as to what exists among mortals. I have found the word of the Gods to be true.* <note>original Greek: "οὐδ’ ἐχω τι το σαφες, ὁτι ποτ’ ἐν βροτοις. Το Θεων ἐπος ἀλαθες εὑρον."</note>

I would not wish, however, for the Sun of ***Certainty*** to be confined within these boundaries. For although human sciences do not strive toward that great measure of Certainty in which alone Christian Faith glories, a person who diligently and attentively consults those two most praised Witnesses will by no means complain that the path to it is closed. In moral truths, the ***Testimony of Conscience***, and in historical and physical matters, ***Experience***, abundantly hold out the torch. In both cases, however, one witness <note>original Latin: *pollicem premens*. Literally "pressing the thumb," a Roman idiom meaning to express favor or support, derived from the gestures of spectators at gladiator matches.</note> supporting the other persuades more fully. For on one hand, whatever is drawn from the very *principles* of knowledge innate to the mind in metaphysical and moral sciences is wonderfully confirmed by the external help of the senses; thus *invisible things are more certainly known from visible things*...

...to be known, or "that which is known of God" <note>original Greek: *το γνωστον του Θεου* (*to gnoston tou Theou*). This is a reference to Romans 1:19, regarding God’s visibility through creation.</note> being understood through His handiwork, teaches abundantly. Nor is strength less added, on the other hand, to physical experiments if they are applied to *abstract ideas*—ideas which the mind does not create within its own depths but rather finds there. Without these ideas, the mind could form no argument, weave no logical sequence, nor derive any judgment comparing equals to equals; indeed, it could not even imagine a distinction between truth and falsehood, or between certainty and uncertainty. When applied to these ideas, experiments are found to harmonize wonderfully. We therefore owe immortal thanks to God that He has not yet allowed the hope of finding the true and the certain to fail us—as we might have deserved—amidst the darkness of our age and of a mind obscured by so many prejudices.

We do not count it among the least signs of the patience, long-suffering, and benevolence which the most merciful Deity shows toward the human race, that through His provident care those sciences have been cultivated, promoted, and esteemed thus far, through which we can emerge toward that divine **CERTAINTY**, that point and center of all <term>Philomathia|The love of learning or knowledge</term>. Among these sciences, it is easily gathered that **MATHEMATICS** <note>The author uses the term *Mathesis*, which in this period referred broadly to the mathematical sciences as a path to certain knowledge.</note> raises its head because of the remarkable light with which it shines, and which it simultaneously ignites in other disciplines. 

It becomes manifest how little Mathematics, when properly cultivated, needs to fear any clouds of prejudice, since it derives truths belonging to its domain from a few—yet most simple and evident—principles. It does so by a method so plain and clear that if someone should stumble through a lack of attention, the error is very easily detected. Nor would anyone easily call this praise of ***Certainty*** in ***Mathematics*** into doubt, unless he were inclined to rave alongside Democritus, Aristippus, or Epicurus. According to the testimony of **CICERO** (in *Academic Questions*, Book IV. 33), Epicurus most impudently pronounced that Geometry and the other mathematical arts could not be true, since they proceeded from beginnings that were not true. For it is this very thing that Mathematics counts as its own special property: that it admits no "probable" reasons, but only <term>demonstrations|absolute proofs</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀποδείξεις* (*apodeixeis*)</note>. By their evidence, these proofs strike even the unwilling, dragging everyone into agreement, and for that reason, Mathematics is immune from disputes, dissent, and heresy. Hence, there is nothing that renders the mind so <term>unshakeable|impossible to be knocked down or altered</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀμετάπτωτον* (*ametaptoton*)</note> as Mathemati-

It positions mathematical clarity as a divine gift that allows humanity to overcome the darkness of prejudice and dissent.</summary>

...Merchant, and **Segerina Lommia**, a matron distinguished by the virtues that adorn her sex, and the daughter of **Johannes Lommius**, formerly a most skillful negotiator. After the foundations of the **humanities** <note>original: *humaniorum literarum*, referring to the study of classical language, literature, and rhetoric</note> were laid with the highest praise in his home **Academy** <note>original: *Athenaeo patrio*; likely the Gymnasium Illustre of his native city</note> in the year 1723, he chose the **University of Utrecht** <note>original: *Almam Trajectinam*</note> as the seat for his Muses. There, he watered his growing talents from the clearest fountains of both Philology and Philosophy, utilizing those most celebrated teachers: **Mr. Charles Andreas Duker**, **Mr. David Mill**, and **Mr. Jacobus Ode**. Being thus excellently prepared, he passed into the camp of **Theology**, and in that field, alongside the most renowned **Mr. Johannes Ensius**, he chose the same **Lampe** <note>Friedrich Adolph Lampe (1683–1729), a highly influential German-Dutch theologian</note> as his guide. It must now happen most joyfully that, within a few weeks, Lampe is able to introduce another of his former pupils—now among a few most esteemed men—into this illustrious **Lyceum** <note>the school or academy</note>, and may hereafter enjoy him as a most longed-for colleague. Regarding this honor, he congratulates himself all the more deeply because our subject has produced such a brilliant proof of a mind most devoted to this teacher of his. 

For when Lampe was recalled from the Netherlands to his fatherland two years ago, Lommius did not hesitate to follow him. This was after he had received his well-merited highest honors in Philosophy, having most solidly written an inaugural dissertation **On the Immortality of the Soul** and defended it most successfully before a publicly applauding circle of learned men. However, since he burned with a singular desire for the **Philosophical** as well as **Mathematical** sciences, and having maturely weighed his reasons, he noticed the nod of Divine Providence in this insurmountable instinct of his nature and affection; he thus gave himself over entirely to the deeper examination of these studies. In order to reach the goal he had set for himself more surely, he went to **Leiden** <note>original: *Lugdunum Batavorum*</note>. There, aided by the instruction of those men most celebrated in these arts, **Mr. Willem Jacob 'sGravesande**, **the Great** <note>original Greek: *τοῦ Πάνυ* (*tou Pany*), a title of high honor for a preeminent scholar</note>, as well as **Mr. Jacob Wittich**, he penetrated into the very inner shrines of those disciplines. Meanwhile, the man's erudition and virtue had gained him such high esteem in this city of ours that our most splendid leaders—rightly weighing how much honor would accrue to our school from a solid handling of **Mathematics**—decided to appoint him to teach it publicly...

Seguinus <note>Pierre Séguin, a 17th-century scholar of ancient coins</note> shows a coin of Trajan carrying a *Stag* in his left hand, and in another coin of Balbinus, the Sun holding a *Stag* in his right hand (Select Coins, p. 131 ff.); while Vaillant (Imperial Bronze Coins, II. 150) displays the Hercules of the Tyrians carried in a chariot drawn by four *Stags*. Drawing its origin from the strength of the Hebrew *Ayil* <note>original: איל; meaning a ram or a stag, often associated with power or leadership</note> with which they designate the *Stag*, and which perhaps gave birth to the Greek *Ellos* <note>original: Ελλὸς; a young deer</note>, it denotes a singular strength not only of the horns, but also of the limbs and their function. Joined with this is a beauty of distinguished form, providing a most pleasant image of both insurmountable constancy and the heavenly beauty with which the Son of God shines. 

Furthermore, since it was a "hieroglyph" of longevity in the Egyptian tradition <note>referring to the Renaissance belief that Egyptian hieroglyphs were a system of symbolic wisdom</note> because of the prodigious number of years it lives—which those searching the secrets of nature have long observed—it reflects the perennial fountain of immortal life in the supreme Prince of Life. I will now pass over briefly <note>original: *sicco pede*—literally "with a dry foot," an idiom for touching on a subject without lingering</note> its role as a model of purity, vigilance, gentleness, its legendary battle with serpents <note>Early modern natural histories often claimed stags hunted snakes by blowing air into their burrows</note>, and other virtues. How nature painted these qualities in *stags* has not been neglected by Aringhius (Subterranean Rome, Book VI, ch. 33), Cyprian (in his Commentary on Franzius’s History of Animals, Part I, ch. XV), Pierius Valerianus (Hieroglyphics, the entirety of Book VII), and others. 

For we think this imagery better suits the *affection of the Bride* <note>In this context, the Bride represents the Church or the individual soul longing for Christ</note>. That the force of the most intense love stands out in *Stags* was already noted by Oppian (Cynegetica, Book II, line 187). He says, "A very vehement love belongs to the Stags" <note>original Greek: Τρηχὺς, δ’ αὖτ’ ἐλάφοισιν ἔρως</note>. To more effectively demonstrate and consummate that love toward the Church, she seeks with her warmest prayers that He be present. And just as love makes these sighs take wing, so she urges with the most fervent impulse that the Groom, by fleeing, might accelerate the progress that has been long delayed. 

For we take for granted how much the *Stag and the Young Fawn* excel in speed, as has been abundantly proven by Bochart (Hierozoicon, Part I, Book III, ch. 17), Gesner (History of Animals, Book I), and others. This relates especially to the present matter, in proving which Ulysses Aldrovandus (On Cloven-hoofed Quadrupeds, Book I, ch. 27) is particularly thorough: that the swiftness of *Stags* is demonstrated specifically in flight. The Muse of Maro <note>The poet Virgil</note> expressed this graphically, for whom (Aeneid IV, line 153):

...the open fields *they cross in their course, and the herds of stags gather their dusty columns in FLIGHT, and leave the mountains behind.* <note>A quotation from Virgil’s Aeneid, Book 4, lines 154–155, describing a hunt.</note> For this reason, ALCAEUS <note>Alcaeus of Messene, a poet known for his biting epigrams</note> (as cited by PLUTARCH in his *Life of Flaminius*) did not hesitate to attribute to Philip, King of Macedon, a flight "swifter than deer" <note>original Greek: ἐλάφων ἐλαφροτέραν</note>. This is precisely the reason why the Bride compares the arrival of her Beloved to a fleeing Stag. For this reason, we find it difficult to depart from the well-known and customary meaning of the word *barach* <gloss>Hebrew: to flee</gloss>, as some learned men have done.

We do not deny, however, that this allegory breathes something of a paradox when we hear the arrival of the Lord compared to a *flight*. Since one who arrives turns his face toward us, while one who flees turns his back, how will these two things fit together? Interpreters would have untied this knot more successfully if they had observed that not just a "Stag," but a "Fawn of the Stag" <note>a young deer</note> is brought into the comparison. For XENOPHON teaches in his *On Hunting* <note>original: Cynegeticus</note> that *the speed of fawns is plainly incomparable, especially when they are struck by greater fear due to the absence of their mother hinds.*

With this agree the accounts brought forward by PLINY (*Natural History* VIII. 32) and SOLINUS (*Collection of Remarkable Things*, chapter 19), that *hinds train their fawns in running, and they become accustomed to practicing flight and leaping over steep places.* This is conveniently applied to our case, since the chief desire of the mystical Bride here is to lead her betrothed Friend with her into the innermost chambers of *her Mother*, which is evident from the second verse of our chapter <note>Song of Solomon 8:2</note>.

Therefore, there appears before us here the most holy Shulammite <note>the Bride in the Song of Solomon</note>, rejoicing with her Brother-Groom in the same Mother—namely, the Israelite and Apostolic Church. She beholds Christ *leaping upon the mountains*, so that he might traverse the kingdoms of the nations with a swift course. Truly, she grieves greatly because he has not yet entered his Mother's house to finalize the marriage with her sister; for before the final conversion of the Jews, the promises made to the Fathers are not yet fulfilled. But she also senses at the same time the new attempts of enemies. To escape these, and to take refuge from them in a secure hiding place—so that, having fully renounced and rejected those ungrateful ones, he might carry his Bride away with him into the heavenly bridal chambers, and to that end make her feet also *like those of hinds* (Habakkuk 3:19)—this is the sum of her prayers and sighs. He saw something here through the lattice <note>original: per transennam, an idiom for a partial or fleeting glimpse</note>, who—

# P R O G R A M S.

...whoever he was, the **CHALDEAN PARAPHRAST** <note>Referring to the Targum, an Aramaic translation and expansion of the Hebrew Bible known for its allegorical interpretations.</note> of the Song of Songs says: *At that time, the elders of the assembly of Israel, explaining the text, shall say: Flee for yourself, my Beloved Ruler of the age, from this unclean earth, and let your majesty dwell in the high heavens.* <note>original: "In illo tempore, exponens, dicent senes cœtus Israëlis: Fuge tibi, Dilecte mi Dominator seculi, de terra hac immunda, & habitet majestas tua in cœlis excelsis."</note> **HONORIUS** <note>Honorius of Autun, a 12th-century theologian and prolific writer.</note> did not stray far from this line of thought when he said: *The Beloved flees from the wicked when he leads his Bride from the hardships of the world to the joys of heaven.* To him we may add **LYRANUS** <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a Franciscan teacher whose literal and moral commentaries were highly influential.</note>, who understands this swift flight as the *transfer of the Bride with the Groom to the heavenly realms.*

However, while many Church Fathers interpret our passage as referring to Christ’s Ascension into heaven forty days after his resurrection, they were mistaken in their reasoning. They applied words to the first event which properly look toward the second—referring both to the preparation (**Daniel 7:13**) and the completion (**1 Thessalonians 4:15, 17**) of the being "caught up" into heaven. This is that **FLIGHT** that bursts through every barrier, prefigured by that most powerful exit of the Israelites breaking out from Egypt—even if they were technically fugitives. 

Is it any wonder that all those who love the appearing <note>original Greek: τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν (tēn epiphaneian), referring to the Second Coming of Christ.</note> of the Lord become accustomed to this sweetest sigh? That they delight in it? That they repeat it until the very last breath of this fragile life? That they die into it? That they testify to how sweetly their bones rest in this hope through their very funeral markers? For the ancient Christians were accustomed to this, as shown by their subterranean chambers <note>the catacombs</note> and sepulchral lamps frequently adorned with the image of a Stag, an engraving of which **ARINGHIUS** <note>Paolo Aringhi (1600–1676), an archaeologist who documented the art of the Roman catacombs.</note> provided for contemplation in the place cited.

Among these chaste souls, intoxicated by heavenly love, we may without hesitation include that Distinguished Maiden, snatched from human affairs by an untimely death, **GESA MARGARETHA KLUGKIST**. While she lived, she was an ornament both to her sex and the choir of young women, and especially to her own home, which she found to be most splendid. Her father is the Most Noble, Distinguished, and Expert Mr. **DIEDERICH KLUGKIST**, an excellent Legal Consultant and a well-deserving Senator of this city; all good people pray that he may long continue to grace the city with his most healthy counsel. Her mother is that excellent and most choice Matron, **ELISABETH BALTZER**. She was born in our city on the day before the Kalends of June <note>May 31st</note> in the year **1709**.

That upright character and those beautiful gifts of both mind and body, which our deceased inherited from her most brilliant lineage through divine generosity, were so refined by a diligent education that from a soul imbued with the knowledge of truth from a tender age, a great harvest of virtues sprouted most abundantly—and among them, the queen of the rest: sincere Piety. # P R O G R A M S.

an intermittent fever seized her at her suburban estate and compelled a hurried return to the city. Although the disease seemed to remit for a few days, it soon returned with greater ferocity. The continuous fever was accompanied by a difficult <term>peripneumonia: An archaic term for inflammation of the lungs or severe pneumonia.</term>, a distressing cough, and the sharpest pains in her right side; then, as a massive pulmonary abscess ruptured, the condition degenerated into a lethal <term>phthisis: A historical term for pulmonary tuberculosis or any progressive wasting disease of the lungs.</term>. This was the long-awaited <term>colophon: Traditionally the finishing stroke or final imprint of a book; here used metaphorically for the "final chapter" or conclusion of a life.</term> of a difficult struggle, yet one most beautifully fought through Christian faith and patience, as we may piously hope. For one could observe not only the signs of her preparing herself for flight with her Beloved away from the murky mire of worldly affairs—the vanity of which she had already recognized while healthy and sound—but also the extraordinary traces of one seriously longing for that path.

Why then, Parents, Brothers, Sisters, Relatives, and Friends, do you gaze sadly from behind at her soul as it flees into the eternal palaces? Why do you delay her flight with empty prayers? Rather, My Reader, why do we ourselves delay? While we play, while we are entangled in trifles, whether we are at leisure or occupied with difficult nonsense, <note>original: "fugit irreparabile tempus," a famous phrase from Virgil’s *Georgics* meaning "irreparable time flies."</note> time flies beyond recovery, life flows away like water, and the Judge flies toward us. Come then, let us rather hasten, so that we ourselves may escape from the snares of sin and death; and before we must migrate from here, let us be seriously concerned with finding a refuge that does not fail. When we may hope that we have attained this, even while we are afflicted and struggling, weary of the soil that keeps us bound, let us repeat this one thing a thousand times a thousand:

<header>ON THE ETERNITY OF PUNISHMENTS</header>

...guise of piety <note>This completes the sentence from the previous page: "...under the distinguished guise of piety."</note>, a crop of those sponsoring an error that is both contrary [to truth] and most pleasing to the flesh is growing strong, especially throughout Germany, and invites our attention. We could add the imprudent detractions of certain Lutheran brothers that prick our ears—as if that opinion concerning the end of infernal punishments could not be unwelcome to the Doctors of our Church <note>Lampe is referring to the Reformed/Calvinist Church</note>, as a certain theologian of great name among them has very recently maintained—if they were of such great importance.

II. However, since those with whom we enter the arena here demonstrate, by the very bitterness and insolence of an intemperate style, how far they have truly cast off love and mercy toward their neighbor (the impulse for which they feign), we shall by no means follow in their footsteps in this regard. Instead, insisting solely on the stronghold of the cause, we shall begin from the defense of our own opinion, proceeding thereafter to the examination of the opposing errors. In the first part, we shall proceed in such a way that we will first defend both the truth and the holiness of the dogma itself; then, as if by way of extra weight <note>original: "superpondii loco"</note>, we shall show the consensus of witnesses, both domestic and external, regarding it. *Scripture* shall teach the former [the truth], purified *Reason* the latter [the holiness], and *History* the final [the consensus].

III. The testimonies of Scripture which extend the eternity of punishments into infinity—since their number is remarkable—we assign to various classes, so that the strength of each may appear more clearly. The *first* place is occupied by those very frequent sayings which expressly call the punishment of Hell *eternal*. For it is called *eternal fire* in Isaiah 33:14, Matthew 18:8, and 25:41; *eternal disgrace* in Daniel 12:2; *eternal destruction* in 2 Thessalonians 1:9; *eternal chains* in Jude verse 6; and *eternal darkness* in verse 13.

IV. The objection drawn from the different meanings of the terms <term>olam</term> <note>Hebrew: עוֹלָם; a word that can mean a long duration, an age, or eternity depending on context</note> and <term>aion</term> <note>Greek: αἰὼν; similar to the Hebrew "olam," it refers to a period of existence or eternity</note>, based on the diversity of the subject, does not affect us. For:
A. It is certain that our detractors cite many passages in a weaker sense <note>i.e., meaning a limited time</note> which require a fuller one <note>i.e., meaning absolute eternity</note>. To this, for example:
α) The "eternity" quite frequently ascribed to certain legal statutes in relation to their eternal antitype can be referred here. <note>In 18th-century theology, an "antitype" is the permanent spiritual reality—usually in Christ—prefigured by temporary Old Testament "types" or laws.</note>
β) I would refer to the same place those passages in which <term>olam</term> <note>Hebrew: עוֹלָם</note> is combined with <term>dorot</term> <note>Hebrew: דּוֹרֹות; "generations"</note>. Thus, in *Genesis 9:12: The rainbow shall be established as a sign* <term>for eternal generations</term> <note>original: "in generationes seculi" / "le-dorot olam"</note>. Add Exodus 12:14, 17; 27:21. In Exodus 40:15, a priesthood is promised to the sons of Aaron...

<header>PART I. DOGMATICS.</header>

...priesthood <note>This completes a sentence likely referring to the Aaronic or Levitical priesthood</note> as a <term>perpetual priesthood throughout their generations</term> <note>original: לכהנת עולם לדורותם (*le-khunat olam le-dorotam*)</note>. For since "generations" designates human successions, it introduces a clear limitation. In the same way, we judge that $\gamma$) the eternity of the earth (Ecclesiastes 1:4), of the heavenly bodies (Psalm 148:6), and of the Son remaining in the house (John 8:35 <note>The text cites verse 30, likely a printer's error for verse 35</note>), etc., are restricted without any [valid] reason. Whether the first two imply full eternity, Eternity itself will teach us; at the very least, Scripture is entirely silent regarding their total destruction. In the latter case, however, it undoubtedly deals with the absolute Eternity of the Son of God himself. $\delta$) Also to be entirely excepted are those passages dealing with divine judgments—though they may be temporal—which express their limit through the word <term>olam</term> <note>The Hebrew word typically translated as "forever" or "world," which universalists argued only meant an "age" or a specific period</note>. This is considered to happen because those judgments are joined with the eternal punishments of the rebellious. See Jeremiah 25:9, 51:39. 

There are $\epsilon$) furthermore certain sayings which are touted as "Achilles-arguments" <note>An "Achilles" argument is one considered unassailable or the strongest point in a debate</note>, and yet they clearly require a metonymic <note>Metonymy is a figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it; here, the "sign" of the covenant is called the "covenant" itself</note> meaning. Such is Genesis 17:13: *My covenant shall be in your flesh* as a <term>perpetual covenant</term> <note>original: לברית עולם (*le-berit olam*)</note>. Here Petersen <note>Johann Wilhelm Petersen (1649–1727), a radical Pietist and leading proponent of the "Restoration of All Things" (Universalism) in Germany</note> and others explain this *olam* as referring to the Old Testament. But this distortion is removed when, according to sacramental custom, we interpret these words as follows: *The sign of my covenant shall be in your flesh as a sign of the Eternal Covenant*, that is, of the Covenant that will last forever, by which God (in verse 7) had pledged that *He would be their God*. Add Numbers 18:19. 

A restriction is also $\zeta$) made by the word *choq* <note>Hebrew for "statute" or "decree"</note> in the frequently recurring phrase <term>perpetual statute</term> <note>original: חקת עולם (*chuqqat olam*)</note>, since it is established that this is used in a specific way for ceremonial statutes, which were transitory by their very nature. $\eta$) I think it should not be left unsaid that even learned men sometimes "nod" <note>An allusion to the Roman poet Horace's line that "even the great Homer sometimes nods," meaning even experts make mistakes</note> here, and concede more than was right or necessary. Take, for example, Huet <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar</note> in his *Origeniana*, Book II, Question 11, Section 26, where:

> " he wants to prove from Luke 1:33 that <term>aion</term> <note>The Greek equivalent of the Hebrew *olam*</note> designates not an infinite, but an indefinite time: *And he shall reign over the house of Jacob forever* [Greek: *eis tous aionas*]. For, he says, if that phrase expressed an unending space of time, why would it be added: *And of his kingdom there shall be no end*? Therefore, this is what Luke (or rather the angel Gabriel) means: *he shall indeed hold a long-lasting kingdom in the house of Jacob, one that will lack no end.* "

As if this interpretation did not suffer from a much greater tautology <note>Needless repetition of the same idea</note>! However, that can be clearly refuted for two reasons. First, in those words...

<summary>Lampe continues his linguistic defense of eternal punishment by arguing that while the Hebrew word 'olam' can sometimes refer to limited periods (like ceremonial laws), this is due to specific context and does not invalidate its meaning as 'absolute eternity' in other contexts. He critiques the universalist Petersen and the scholar Huet for using verses about Christ's kingdom to suggest that 'eternity' only means a long duration.</summary>
