--- Page 758 ---
<meta>This page continues the philological defense of the word "eternal" against universalist interpretations, moving from the Hebrew "olam" to the Greek "aion." It argues that while these words can occasionally mean a limited age, their primary and emphatic meaning is "endless," especially when referring to immortal subjects.</meta>

<page-num>4</page-num>
<header>ON THE ETERNITY OF PUNISHMENTS</header>

By adding those words: *and of his kingdom there shall be no end* <note>original Greek: και της βασιλειας αυτου ουκ εσται τελος; quoting Luke 1:33</note>, the conjunction "and" <note>original: *kai*</note> can be considered explanatory or causative to explain the true nature of the Messiah's Kingdom, which had been obscured by the distortions of the Jews. Furthermore, since the angel Gabriel alludes to many passages of the Prophets and wishes to show their imminent fulfillment, I do not doubt that these two phrases are joined so that various sayings of the Prophets might be recalled to mind. Some of these predicted an *eternal Kingdom* <note>original: *Regnum aeternum*</note>, such as Psalm 45:6-7, Daniel 2:44, and Daniel 7:14, 27; others predicted a *Kingdom without end* <note>original: *Regnum sine fine*</note> for the Messiah, such as Isaiah 9:7.

B. Even if it is granted that "eternal" sometimes means nothing more than "long-lasting," this does not harm our position because: 1. we should not rashly abandon the more *emphatic* <note>The "emphatic" meaning here refers to the strongest possible sense: absolute eternity.</note> meaning; 2. especially when that meaning is *more frequent*, as is clear regarding these controversial words (besides the Lexicographers and Concordances) from the *Sacred Observations* of **Andreas Fessel** <note>original: **FESSELII** *Advers. Sacr.* III. 2; a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note>. Finally, 3. no trace of limitation occurs in the cited passages.

V. Add to this that even among our opponents <note>The "Antagonists" or Universalists, who argued for the eventual salvation of all</note> it is admitted that *eternity always and everywhere denotes the duration of a thing for as long as it ought to exist, or that being "eternal" means the same as lasting as long as the thing is meant to last*. These are the words of the illustrious **Aepinus**, accepted by **Ludwig Gerhard** in his *System of Restoration* <note>original: *Systemate Αποκατας.* (Apokatastasis) §. 165. The term "Apokatastasis" refers to the universalist belief in the final restoration of all souls to God.</note>. Thus **Siegvolck** <note>The pseudonym for Georg Klein-Nicolai, a prominent 18th-century Universalist author</note> admits an eternity consistent with the nature of the thing (p. 56). The celebrated **Gousset** brilliantly illustrated this thesis regarding the word <term>olam</term> <note>original: עולם; the Hebrew word for an age, a long time, or eternity</note>. The logic is the same for the word <term>Aion</term> <note>original: Αιων; the Greek equivalent for "age" or "eternity"</note> in the New Testament, which must be explained according to the nature of the Hellenistic style. This is even more the case since its etymology—which according to **Aristotle** (*On the Heavens*, Book 1) and others is derived from "always being" <note>original: *αει ων* (aei on)</note>—agrees with this. Therefore, although it was later used more loosely, as taught by **Windet** (*On the State of the Dead*, X), **Huet** (cited above), **Masson** (*Critical History*, III, p. 145), etc., this does not concern us, who follow the Sacred Writers. From what has been conceded, we infer that since the *things* or *subjects* to which "Eternity" is attributed in the cited passages are by their nature *immortal*, an equally far-reaching Eternity is assigned to their condemnation.

VI. We have not begun a full list of all examples to illustrate this rule, as a comparison of them can easily be made.

# PART I. DOGMATICS.

established. However, one point remains where some might hesitate, which **Alardus de Raat** <note>A 17th-century Dutch theologian</note> identifies in his *Defense of the Truth* (page 240) as the most famous example in this matter: namely, Exodus 21:6. There, speaking of a Hebrew servant who chooses to stay with his master, it says: *and he shall serve him forever* <note>original Hebrew: ועבדו לעלם (*ve-avado le-olam*)</note>. Many interpreters, both Jewish and Christian, believe that "forever" <note>original: *le-olam*</note> here designates the time until the Jubilee; they compare this to the Law in Leviticus 25:10, 40, 41, where God *ordered everyone to return to their own possession and family in the 50th year, and that a servant should serve only until the Year of Jubilee.* Against this "torrent" of opinion—following **Piscator** <note>Johannes Piscator (1546–1625), a German Reformed theologian</note>, who interprets it as *to the end of life*, and **Ainsworth** <note>Henry Ainsworth (1571–1622), an English nonconformist clergyman</note>, who interprets it as *until the death of the Master*—**Gousset** <note>Jacques Gousset (1635–1704), a French Hebraist</note> argued that when a servant declared his will to undergo servitude "forever" <note>original: *le-olam*</note>, he did not go free at the Jubilee, and therefore this refers to a different case. In support of this, he points out that in the same chapter, Leviticus 25:46, "forever" <note>original: *le-olam*</note> is contrasted with the term of the Jubilee. Although he provoked the criticism of **Ernst Georg Goelitz** in his *Dissertation on the word "Le-olam"* because that latter passage refers to Gentile servants (whose servitude ended only by death, not by the Jubilee), this does not invalidate the point. The contrast between the term of the Jubilee and "forever" <note>original: *tou le-olam*</note> remains clearly evident, which is sufficient for our purpose. Indeed, it is even more helpful to embrace Gousset’s opinion because the Year of Jubilee cannot be what is intended in Exodus 21:6. For: 1) since it could happen that a Hebrew servant offered himself for voluntary servitude in a Sabbatical year which was only seven years away from a Jubilee, the word "forever" <note>original: *le-olam*</note> would then mean a mere seven-year period—a sense that is completely contrary to the nature of the word. 2) Furthermore, the Year of Jubilee had not yet been instituted at that time. The commands in Exodus 20–23 were given before the Sinai Covenant, whereas those in Leviticus were only delivered after the *worship of the Golden Calf* <note>original Greek: μοσχολατρειαν (*moscholatreia*)</note>.

VII. The Socinians <note>A rationalist Christian sect that denied the Trinity and often argued against the traditional view of eternal hellfire</note> attempt to weaken the force of this argument in another way. Among them, **Wolzogen** <note>Johann Ludwig von Wolzogen (1594–1661), a Socinian commentator</note> says regarding Matthew 18:8:

> *An eternal fire is not called such because the thing thrown into it is burned eternally and never consumed, but because it burns and consumes the thing in such a way that it is never restored to its whole state, or because it burns as long as is necessary until that thing is plainly and entirely burnt up.*

Truly, these are the most strained figures of speech...

# ON THE ETERNITY OF PUNISHMENTS

With these words added: *and of his kingdom there shall be no end* <note>original Greek: καὶ τῆς βασιλείας αὐτοῦ οὐκ ἔσται τέλος (*kai tēs basileias autou ouk estai telos*)</note>, the conjunction "and" <note>original: *kai*</note> can be considered explanatory or causal. It serves to explain the true nature of the Kingdom of the Messiah, which had been obscured by the distortions of the Jews. Furthermore, since Gabriel alludes to many passages from the Prophets and wishes to show their imminent fulfillment, I do not doubt that both these phrases are joined so that various sayings of the Prophets might be recalled to mind. Some of these had predicted an *eternal kingdom*—such as Psalm 45:6-7, Daniel 2:44, and Daniel 7:14, 27—while others, such as Isaiah 9:7, predicted a *kingdom without end* to be given to the Messiah.

B. Even if it were granted that "eternal" sometimes means the same as "long-lasting," this does not hinder our argument because: 1. one should not rashly depart from the more *emphatic* meaning of a word; 2. especially when that meaning is more *frequent*, as is clear from lexicographers and concordances regarding the controversial words, and from **Andreas Fesselius** in his *Sacred Adversaria* (Book III, Chapter 2). Finally, 3. no trace of limitation or "cutoff point" occurs in the cited passages.

V. Add to this that it is admitted even by our opponents that *eternity always and everywhere denotes the duration of a thing for as long as it is able to exist, or that "eternal" signifies the same as lasting as long as the thing itself is meant to last.* These are the words of the illustrious **Johann Aepinus** <note>A 16th-century Lutheran theologian</note>, which were accepted by **Ludwig Gerhard** in his *System of Restoration* <note>original Greek: Ἀποκατασ. (*Apokatastasis*); refers to the doctrine that all forerunners of creation will eventually be saved</note>, section 165. Likewise, **Paul Siegvolck** <note>Pseudonym of Georg Klein-Nicolai, a universalist author</note> (page 56) admits an eternity appropriate to the nature of the thing. The celebrated **Jacques Gousset** excellently illustrated this thesis under the Hebrew word *olam* <note>original Hebrew: עולם, often translated as "world" or "eternity"</note>. The logic of the word *Aion* <note>original Greek: Αἰών, meaning "age" or "aeon"</note> in the New Testament is the same, and must be explained according to the character of the Hellenistic style of Greek. This is all the more true since its etymology—which according to **Aristotle** (*On the Heavens*, Book 1) and others is derived from "always being" <note>original Greek: ἀεὶ ὢν (*aei on*)</note>—is in agreement. Although the term was later used more loosely, as taught by **James Windet** (*On the State of the Dead*, Chapter X), **Pierre-Daniel Huet**, **Jean-Philippe Masson** (*Critical History*, Vol. III, p. 145 ff.), and others, this does not affect us, as we follow the Sacred Writers. From what has been granted by our opponents, we infer that since the "subjects" (the souls or beings) to which Eternity is attributed in the cited passages are immortal by their very nature, Eternity must be assigned to their condemnation with an equally infinite scope.

VI. We have not undertaken a full listing of every example to illustrate this rule, since a comparison of them can be easily made by the reader.

**F.** Furthermore, this phrase is equivalent to the Hebrew *forever and ever* <note>original Hebrew: עולם ועד (*olam va-ed*)</note>. Some more recent writers follow these tracks, to whom it seems that this is asserted not merely "perhaps," but most truly. However, since these ideas do not please others from their own circle, and the reasons already brought forward are sufficient, we shall not dwell on this matter. A more frequent phrase in the parallel doxologies of the Old Testament is *from eternity to eternity* <note>original Hebrew: מעולם ועד-עולם (*me-olam v'ad-olam*)</note> from 1 Chronicles 16:36, 29:10; Nehemiah 9:5; Psalm 41:14; and Psalm 106:48. I have shown the equivalence of this in my *Vernacular Sermon VIII on Psalm 41, page 366 and following*.

**G.** From these comparisons, it also appears that our opinion preserves a notion of the phrase that is simple and consistent with common usage, while those who disagree must call upon foreign and discordant interpretations for support. For the *ages of ages* are the ages of the future life, extended beyond the times of the present life and stretching themselves out in an infinitely perpetual succession. In this way, not only is the phrase itself fully satisfied, but the same consistent notion—one suited to the nature of the subject—is preserved. Those who disagree, however, are tossed about through various "vortices of <term>Aeons</term>," <note>Referring to the theory that time moves in immense cycles or "Ages" (Aeons), and that punishment might only last for one such cycle.</note> by which all things are supposedly restored successively—some in this age, others in the following. It is unnecessary to track their footsteps here, since most of their points are coldly assumed **without scriptural basis** <note>original Greek: ἀτερ γραφης (*ater graphēs*)</note>.

# PART I. DOGMATIC.

...requires. It is clear from a review of all given passages that no example of this same phrase exists elsewhere. Regarding parallel phrases, some are presented as equivalents which simply cannot be considered as such. These are the instances in which the small word *unto* <note>Hebrew: עד (*ad*)</note> does not follow, but rather precedes the phrase *forever and ever* <note>Hebrew: לעד לעולם (*le-ad le-olam*)</note> as in Psalm 148:6, 111:8, 10, and 104:5; as well as *in the generation of generations* <note>Hebrew: בדור דורים (*be-dor dorim*)</note> in Psalm 102:25, 100:5, 145:13, and 33:11. Although even in these specific places, nothing prevents us from understanding an **Eternity without end**, given the nature of the subject being discussed. 

The passages in Jeremiah 7:7 have more of an appearance of [a finite duration]: *“I will dwell with you in this land, which I gave to your Fathers”* **from age to age** <note>Hebrew: למן עולם ועד עולם (*le-min olam ve-ad olam*)</note>. Yet this does not particularly hurt our case, because such an "Eternity" is understood as is appropriate for the promised land; furthermore, the restoration of its possession in the "latter days" is hinted at by other Prophets. 

However, we do not think it should be overlooked that in both places, these words *from age to age* are separated from the preceding words by the **Athnach** accent <note>A Hebrew musical and grammatical mark that functions like a semicolon or colon, creating a logical pause</note>, so that they constitute a separate sense—at least, they do not immediately cling to what comes before. Furthermore, in the commonly accepted interpretation, the prefix **L** <note>The Hebrew letter *Lamed* (ל), often meaning "to" or "for"</note> would be entirely redundant. Yet **Noldius** <note>Christian Nold (1626–1683), a Danish theologian famous for his exhaustive concordance of Hebrew particles</note> has abundantly proved that this prefix can sometimes signify *indeed, or rather*, and sometimes *up until*. From either option, a very full meaning arises. For whether you translate it: *“I will dwell with you in this land; indeed (I will dwell with you) from age to age”*; or thus: *“I will dwell with you in this land up until [the time] from age to age”*—that is, until the consummation of the age, when full Eternity shall arise—absolutely no violence is done to the words. The former sense is both fuller and more consistent with the nature of the **Divine Covenant**, which is why we primarily rest our case upon it.

**X.** Consequently, **Ludovicus Gerhardus** <note>A 17th-century theologian known for defending "Universalism," the idea that all will eventually be saved</note> was anxious for new support for his views. He believed he had found it in the fact that in passages concerning the *ages of the blessed*, the word **all** is sometimes added. Three examples are produced for this: Ephesians 3:21, *“unto all generations of the age of ages”* <note>Original Greek: εις πασας τας γενεας του αιωνος των αιωνων</note>; and the Epistle of Jude, verse 25, *“now and unto all the ages”* <note>Original Greek: νυν και εις παντας τους αιωνας</note>. To complete the triad, Psalm 145:13 is added from the **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>.

### ON THE ETERNITY OF PUNISHMENTS
<meta>catchword: requires.</meta>

...will He not demonstrate Himself as one who lives forever and ever <note>original: *in secula seculorum*</note> even through the infliction of His Wrath? Indeed, how could He demonstrate this through the outpouring of His Wrath, unless that very application of Wrath were extended **forever and ever**?

F. Furthermore, this phrase is equivalent to the Hebrew *forever and ever* <note>Hebrew: עולם ועד (*olam va-ed*)</note>. This is clear, both because the **Chaldean Paraphrast** <note>A reference to the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> renders it as *ages of ages* <note>Aramaic: עלמי עלמין (*almi almin*)</note> in Psalm 45:7, which coincides exactly with the Greek expression, and because it is used in the **doxology** <note>A short hymn of praise to God.</note> of God in Psalm 145:1–2, to which the phrasing in the Book of Revelation seems to allude. I have taught more extensively in *Exercise VI on Psalm 45, § 7* that this same phrase likewise indicates an Eternity **without end**. 

And so, the observation of **Origen** <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) who famously speculated that all beings, including the damned, might eventually be reconciled to God.</note> falls apart by itself; to him, that phrase *unto the age and beyond* seemed to show something more than *the age and the ages*, perhaps even more than *the ages of ages*—namely, a time when all things are no longer in "an age," but rather **God is all in all** <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 15:28, often used by those who believe in universal salvation.</note>. Some more recent writers follow these tracks, to whom it seems that this is asserted not merely *perhaps*, but *most truly*. However, since these ideas do not please others from their own circle, and the reasons already brought forward are sufficient, we shall not dwell on this matter. A more frequent phrase in the parallel doxologies of the Old Testament is *from age to age* <note>Hebrew: מעולם ועד־עולם (*me-olam ve-ad-olam*)</note> from 1 Chronicles 16:36, 29:10; Nehemiah 9:5; and Psalms 41:13 and 106:48, the equivalence of which I have shown in my *Vernacular Sermon VIII on Psalm 41*, page 366 and following.

G. From these comparisons, it also appears that our view preserves the simple notion of the phrase, consistent with its common usage, whereas the dissenters call upon foreign and absurd interpretations for support. For the **ages of ages** are the ages of the future life, extended beyond the times of this present life and destined to extend themselves in an infinite, perpetual succession. In this way, not only is the phrase itself fully satisfied, but the notion remains consistent and appropriate to the nature of the subject. The dissenters, however, are spun around by various **vortices of Aeons** <note>The author is mocking the complex, cyclical theories of time used by opponents to argue that "eternity" actually consists of finite cycles or "Aeons."</note>, through which all things are supposedly restored successively—some in this Aeon, others in the following. It is unnecessary to follow their tracks here, since many of these things are coldly hypothesized **without Scripture** <note>original Greek: ἄτερ γραφῆς (*ater graphes*)</note>.

IX. The main objection that can be raised here is the introduction of passages in which the same or a parallel phrase requires a limited sense.

### PART I. DOGMATICS
<header>PART I. DOGMATICS.</header>

...requires. It is manifest from a review of all the relevant passages that no example of this same phrase exists <note>The author is arguing that the specific phrasing used to describe eternal punishment is unique and not used for temporary things</note>. Certain phrases are offered as parallels, but they simply cannot be regarded as such. These include those where the particle **until** <note>original Hebrew: *ad* (עד)</note> does not follow but rather precedes, as in *unto the age, unto eternity* <note>original Hebrew: *la-ad le-olam* (לעולם לעולם)</note> in Psalm 148:6, 111:8, 10, and Psalm 104:5; as well as *in the generation of generations* <note>original Hebrew: *be-dor dorim* (בדור דורים)</note> in Psalm 102:25, 100:5, 145:13, and 33:11. Although even in these very places, nothing prevents us from understanding an **Eternity** that is without end, according to the nature of the subject.

The passages in Jeremiah 7:7 carry more weight: *I will dwell with you in this land, which I gave to your Fathers* **from age to age** <note>original Hebrew: *le-min olam ve-ad olam* (למן עולם ועד עולם)</note>. The same is predicated of the same subject in chapter 25:5. We admit that the best interpreters concede that a long duration is meant here. This does not particularly hinder our cause, because such an "Eternity" is understood as is appropriate to the promised land, and its restoration in the final days is hinted at by other prophets. However, we do not think it should be overlooked that in both places, these words (*from age to age*) are separated from the preceding words by the **Athnach** <note>A Hebrew musical and grammatical accent that functions like a semicolon, indicating a major pause in the verse.</note> in such a way that they constitute a separate sense, or at least do not cohere immediately with what comes before. Furthermore, the prefix **Lamed** <note>The Hebrew letter *L* (ל) used as a preposition</note> is entirely vacant in the commonly accepted interpretation; yet **Noldius** <note>Christian Nold (1626–1683), a scholar famous for his exhaustive study of Hebrew particles</note> has abundantly proved that it sometimes signifies *indeed, or even*, and sometimes *even unto*. From either option, a very full sense arises. For whether you translate it: *I will dwell with you in this land; indeed (I will dwell) from age to age*; or thus: *I will dwell with you in this land even unto (the time) from age to age*—that is, until the consummation of the age, when full **Eternity** shall arise—no violence is done to the words. The first sense is fuller and more consistent with the nature of the Divine Covenant; thus, we primarily rest upon it.

**X.** Therefore, **Ludwig Gerhard** <note>A 17th-century theologian who advocated for "Universal Restoration," the idea that all will eventually be saved</note> was anxious for new support. He believed he had found it in the fact that in passages concerning the "ages of the blessed," the word **all** <note>original Greek: *pantes* (πάντες)</note> is sometimes added. Three examples are produced for this: Ephesians 3:21, *unto all generations of the age of ages* <note>original Greek: *eis pasas tas geneas tou aionos ton aionon*</note>; and the Epistle of Jude, verse 25, *now and unto all the ages* <note>original Greek: *nyn kai eis pantas tous aionas*</note>. To complete a group of three, Psalm 145:13 from the **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> is added: *Thy* [Kingdom...]

-># ON THE ETERNITY OF PUNISHMENTS<-

"...thy kingdom is a kingdom of all ages," <note>original Greek: βασιλεια σου βασιλεια παντων των αἰωνων</note> in place of the Hebrew "all ages." <note>original Hebrew: כל־עולמים (kol-olamim)</note> Before him, Petersen <note>Johann Wilhelm Petersen (1649–1727), a theologian famous for advocating the "restoration of all things," or the idea that hell is not eternal</note> had already observed this in his *Dialogues*, Volume I, page 27, where he also insists on the importance of the definite articles <note>original Greek: τους & των (tous & ton)</note>, which he believes indicate certain fixed and determined Ages. This is a trivial point, as it is well known in the common schools of grammar that such articles are frequently used simply for emphasis. 

Regarding the passages he cites: the first is not very fitting because it does not speak of "all ages" <note>original Greek: παντες αἰωνες</note> in the abstract, but rather "all generations" <note>original Greek: πασαι γενεαι</note> living in the age of ages. Furthermore, since this specific phrase appears only once in the text <note><term>hapax legomenon</term>: a word or phrase that appears only once in a body of writing, making its interpretation more dependent on context</note>, we can understand it through the Apostle’s goal of proving the union of all the earth's nations in Christ. He refers to all the families of the elect who are to be joined together in the possession of the eternal inheritance, not one after another, but all at the same time. In the other two cases, the word "all" should be seen as explanatory. Since the text mentions simply "ages" rather than "ages of ages," the Holy Spirit intended to fill this grammatical gap <note><term>ellipsis</term>: a literary device where a word is omitted because it is understood from the context</note> by adding the word "all." Therefore, our mocking opponent has gained nothing so far, unless by searching through his reference books again he can find a passage where "all the ages of the ages" actually appears.

### XI.

The third class of evidence consists of passages that explicitly deny an end to punishments. These are the ones that name the fire of hell as **unquenchable fire** <note>original Greek: πυρ ἀσβεστον (pyr asbeston)</note>. This was done not only by John the Baptist in Matthew 3:12 and Luke 3:17, but even more forcefully by the Savior himself in Mark 9:43–44: **into Gehenna, into that unquenchable fire, where their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched.** <note>original Greek: εἰς την γεενναν, εἰς το πυρ το ἀσβεστον, ὁπου ὁ σκωληξ αὐτου οὐ τελευτᾳ, και το πυρ οὐ σβεννυται</note>. 

It is clear that if human language were to describe a punishment that has no end, nothing more eloquent or forceful could be produced to overcome all disbelief. For not only is the word **unquenchable** <note>original Greek: ἀσβεστος</note> used by the most ancient Greek authors to mean a fire *not currently extinguished*, but also one that *cannot be extinguished*. The descriptive phrase <note><term>periphrasis</term>: using a longer, descriptive phrase in place of a shorter one; here, the "worm" and "fire" description</note> which the Savior took from Isaiah 66:24 proves this abundantly; He correctly explained it as referring to the punishments of the future life, a fact even admitted by the most ancient Jewish interpreters. This point is even more binding because the Prophet uses the future tense: "For their worm [shall] not..." <note>original Hebrew: כי תולעתם לא (ki tolatam lo)</note>

# PART I. DOGMATICS.

"For their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished, and they shall be an abhorrence to all flesh." <note>original Hebrew: לא תמות ואשם לא תכבה והיו דראון לכל בשר</note> <note>original Latin: quoniam vermis eorum non morietur, & ignis eorum non extinguetur, & erunt opprobrium omni carni</note> The pairing of the "worm" with "fire" also teaches us that this is not about a temporary, purifying fire <note>referring to the concept of Purgatory</note>, but rather a punishment that exists alongside the persistent guilt of a wicked conscience. Indeed, the torments of a restless conscience—which is always receiving new fuel from new sins—are as aptly represented by a worm perpetually feeding upon the soul as by that famous vulture devouring the liver of Tityus <note>In Greek mythology, the giant Tityus was punished in the underworld by having two vultures eternally feast on his liver</note> daily. Regarding this, Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman philosopher whose commentary on the "Dream of Scipio" was a standard textbook in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> writes in *The Dream of Scipio*, Book I, Chapter 10: *By the vulture pecking at the immortal liver, they wish nothing else to be understood than the torments of an evil conscience; it searches the inner vitals which are subject to crime, and tears at the very life-organs with the unwearied reminder of the wickedness committed.* It should not be overlooked that the Hebrew word *tola* <note>original: תולע</note> specifically designates a small red or crimson worm, as has been abundantly proven by Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant scholar of biblical animals</note> in *Hieroz.* Part II, Book IV, Chapter 27, and Braun <note>Johannes Braun (1628–1708), an expert on the vestments of Hebrew priests</note> in *On Sacred Clothing*, Book I, Chapter 15. Sins are compared to such a worm in Isaiah 1:18, with respect to the guilt and the "stain of blood." For the elect, this guilt was transferred to Christ, the "worm" of Psalm 22:7; but for the reprobate <note>those destined for damnation</note>, this worm "shall not die." Since the guilt remains eternally, any limit or end to the punishment is expected in vain. Furthermore, the possessive pronouns in the phrases *their fire* and *their worm* imply that the subjects themselves endure eternally within those punishments; this excludes any possibility that the "material" could run out, whether by the total destruction of the person <note><term>Annihilation</term>: the belief that the wicked eventually cease to exist entirely rather than suffer forever</note> or by the sin being "burnt away." This is the natural meaning that immediately strikes the mind of any reader—a meaning which our Savior not only does not restrict in any way, but seriously hammers home by repeating it three times, thus taking great care that no one should dare to diminish the weight of this most grave threat.

XII. The more clearly these points strike home, the more subtle are the loopholes sought by opponents. Along with the Socinians <note>A rationalist Christian sect often accused of denying eternal torment</note>, Burnet <note>Thomas Burnet (c. 1635–1715), an English theologian who questioned the eternity of hell</note>, in *On the State of the Dead and the Resurrection*, page 248, and other critics of that same ilk, flee to the idea of "Accommodation" and "Hyperboles" <note>the theory that God uses exaggerated language to scare people, rather than describing literal truth</note> accepted by proverbial use. But we judge these men—who offer a manifest insult to the majesty of the sacred style and the simplicity of the Divine Lawgiver—as not even worthy of a response. Those who patronize the <term>Apocatastasis</term> <note>the doctrine of the "restoration of all things," which suggests everyone, including the devil, will eventually be saved</note> enjoy a greater appearance of validity. For they demand *first*: "that a passage be produced in which it is said in round words..."

# ON THE ETERNITY OF PUNISHMENTS

...it is said, *Punishments are not to be ended.* But who would dare to prescribe to God which words He ought to use? If it pleased Him to bring forth a truth of such great moment—not plainly, but for the sake of greater emphasis—through metaphors <note>original: "tropos," referring to figurative language</note> that are clear and powerful, does that not require all the more attention? Is it not even more unjust to demand plain language, since these opponents frequently twist even "improperly" used words to suit their own case? Even if we were to fulfill their condition for plainness, they would immediately arm themselves against the light of truth with some new exception.

XIII. Second, they gather a heap of passages in which things are said to *have no end*, which nevertheless must certainly come to a finish. Thus, in Isaiah 2:7 and Nahum 2:10, it is said that *their treasures have no end*. Add to this Job 22:5: *Your iniquities have no end*. The same is asserted regarding labor in Ecclesiastes 4:8, regarding company in verse 16, and regarding books in Ecclesiastes 12:12. Similarly, in 1 Timothy 1:4, we find *genealogies having no end*. However, these things are compared contrary to wisdom <term>original: "invita Minerva," a Latin idiom meaning to do something against one's natural inclination or against common sense</term>. It is one thing when things are said to lack an end in relation to men, because humans cannot reach the end by counting; it is quite another when God Himself, in the Decree of His Law, denies an end to either Rewards or Punishments in formal terms. Furthermore, in the present life, *treasures, sins, and books* are rightly said to have no end because they are currently continuing, and thus have not yet reached a conclusion. Everyone can see that there is a vast difference between this and the fact that God, who is most truthful, simply declares that Punishments will never be ended in the future.

XIV. They cling more closely to certain sayings in which subjects are said to be *not dying*, which nevertheless are not destined for everlasting life. Revelation 9:6: *And in those times men will seek death, and will not find it; and they will desire to die, and death will flee from them.* Also, Deuteronomy 33:6: *Let Reuben live and not die.* Regarding the first passage, it would be superfluous to dwell on it, because a sufficiently manifest limitation is present: 1) since it says *in those times* this shall happen, which implies a certain measure of judgment circumscribed within a defined track of time; 2) because it does not imply every kind of death, but specifically that death which they *will seek and desire* so that they might be liberated from heavier judgments. <header>PART I. DOGMATICS.</header>

*...in one and the same sentence [the Lord] said: "These will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life." <note>A quotation of Matthew 25:46, frequently cited by St. Augustine in his work *The City of God* (21.23) to argue this exact point.</note> If both are "eternal," then surely both must be understood as either lasting for a long time with an end, or both as perpetual without an end. For they are related as equals. To say, in this one and the same context, that eternal life will be without end, but eternal punishment will have an end, is quite absurd.*

XVIII. **LUDWIG GERHARD** <note>Johann Ludwig Gerhard (1680–1738), a German theologian who was a prominent defender of "Universalism"—the belief that all people, and even the devil, would eventually be saved.</note> exhausts every storehouse of subtlety here to the point of nausea, "so that he might direct that rule against us, by which the students of Logic <note>original: *Logicorum filii* (literally "sons of logicians")</note> know that *the reasons and consequences of opposites are opposite.*" From this he concludes that the eternities of punishment and life are also opposite [in nature], and he seizes an opportunity for mockery against those who appeal to a different Logical Rule: *the reason of opposites is the same.* This purely sophistical <note>term: sophistical (using clever but false arguments)</note> war will be easily settled if it is observed that the truth of both Rules can exist at the same time in different respects. For *the reason of opposites is opposite* regarding their opposite attributes, but it is *the same* in the "third point of comparison" <note>term: *tertium comparationis* (the specific quality that two different things share when being compared)</note>. Therefore, in our text, one must distinguish well between what is properly opposed and what is compared. That **PUNISHMENT** and **LIFE** are opposed, but the **ETERNITY** of both is being compared, is demonstrated clearly enough by the sound of the words themselves and the repetition of the same adjective without any mark of distinction.

XIX. We shall dispatch the remaining evasions in a few words.
A. It is objected "that opposites ought to be equals. Now, however, the Eternity of life is agreed upon by both sides, but the Eternity of punishment is still disputed." But, I ask you, does that dispute bring about an inequality in the things themselves? Ought it not suffice for recognizing the equality of these things that God Himself testifies that they are equals by such an evident declaration in His word? Especially when dealing with matters whose equality was not known by nature, and yet contains nothing contradictory in itself. Is it not unfairly demanded that this equality be proven from other arguments beforehand, when it is declared clearly enough by this very saying?
B. Certain passages of Scripture are objected "which seem to imply an equal reasoning of opposites just as evidently, and yet do not." As a hypothesis, Romans 5 is brought forward for this purpose...

**D.** **Siegvolk** <note>Paul Siegvolk, pseudonym for Georg Klein-Nicolai (1671–1734), author of "The Everlasting Gospel," a foundational text for the doctrine of Universal Restoration.</note> argues in another way, though from a similar principle. For, he claims, so the matter stands with eternal salvation; for that, or the glorious Kingdom of God, was in God and with him without beginning, etc. 

**Response 1.** The passages we use clearly deal not with *past* eternity but with *future* eternity. Therefore, we rightly do not extend the comparison beyond its third limit <note>A logical term meaning the comparison only applies to the future duration, not the origin.</note>. **2.** We are considering here the eternity that falls upon creatures. Anyone who mixes this with the Eternity of God confuses the Creator with the work of his hands, and attributes the necessity of existence to contingent things, thus Deifying the world. We leave this impiety to the Atheists with loathing. **3.** It is absurd to conceive of the Kingdom of God as actually existing without subjects. If subjects began to exist in time, the Kingdom of God also has a beginning. **4.** The Kingdom of God could not have been from eternity except eminently in His idea and decree. In that way, however, evil also existed from eternity, because God foresaw it and willed to permit and punish it before the foundations of the world were laid.

**XX.** We must not omit here the saying in John 3:36, which pertains simultaneously to this and the preceding class, and is rightly numbered among the clearest: *Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. Whoever is disobedient to the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.* Here, not only is all hope of life negatively cut off from the unbeliever, but also the "remaining wrath" <note>original: *ὀργὴ μένουσα* (orgē menousa)</note> is set in opposition to eternal life. I find that three primary objections are woven against this most evident declaration.

A. "The word 'to remain' is often attributed to subjects that have a finite duration. Therefore, unless we wish to beg the question <term>beg the question: a logical fallacy (petitio principii) where the conclusion is assumed in the premise</term>, we must prove from elsewhere that the Wrath of God is infinite." **Response.** We do not argue based solely on the definition of the word *remain* <note>original: *μένειν* (menein)</note>, but from its connection with the preceding threat that eternal life shall not be seen. The Wrath of God, which remains in opposition to eternal life in such a way that this life is not to be seen in the future, extends into infinity.

B. "This threat is restricted to the unbeliever. However, if damned men are at some point converted, they are no longer unbelievers, and thus the Wrath of God no longer remains upon them." 
**Response 1.** Based on this hypothesis, a restriction is violently forced upon a text that speaks in the most general terms. 
2. This threat is extended into the future, while the sin itself is expressed in the present: *He who is now an unbeliever, shall not see life in the future.* 
3. A person is called "unbelieving" either in opposition to *historical faith* or to *living faith*. <note>In the theology of this period, "historical faith" meant merely accepting the Bible as factually true—a state even demons share—while "living faith" was a transformative, heart-felt trust in God.</note> The former is held even by the Demons, though they tremble while expecting the fulfillment of the threat. The latter is the very beginning of that life which the unbeliever shall not see. How shall he believe, who remains in death?

**Response.** It is quite obvious that this passage does not concern the eternal death of the future life, but rather the spiritual death of the present life. This is clear because not only is the present tense used, but it is immediately preceded by: *we know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brothers.*

XXIII. Nor can the strength of this argument be broken by the **"invention of a middle-ground,"** <note>original: *figmento temperamenti*</note> by which the sinner would pay in part through his own person, while that which remained to be paid would be wiped away through the grace of God and the **merit of Christ**. However, since they maintain that no sin deserves punishment without end, they contend that after such a blasphemer has paid every deserved penalty without any forgiveness, grace must nevertheless be granted to him."

XXIX. From where, then, would the *hope of the Forgiveness of sins* shine forth, since that requires the *shedding of blood* (Hebrews 9:22), and likewise that unique sacrifice of Jesus Christ, from which the reconciliation of all those to be saved is derived forever (Colossians 1:20, Hebrews 10:14)? But now, the effect of that sacrifice expires once the limit of grace has passed (Hebrews 10:26, 27). *If we sin willfully after receiving knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a fearful expectation of judgment and a fury of fire that will consume the rebels.* To those for whom the only means of salvation is denied, nothing remains but judgment and consuming fire to be expected forever; how then could their sins be forgiven? 

Nor do the cruder Universalists <term>Apocatastatici: Those who believe in the *Apocatastasis*, or the eventual restoration of all souls—including the damned and the devil—to a state of holiness and union with God</term> have anything to reply, except that such people are to be set free without the Forgiveness of sins after they have endured all the *degrees* of Punishments, through which, at last, all their malice will be burned away. To them, the "consuming *fire*" is a fire that burns away and purifies whatever is rebellious—a claim than which nothing more meager could be said. For the metaphor is taken from the fire of the altar, which does not purify the sacrifices but consumes them, prefiguring the *vicarious punishment* <term>Vicarious punishment: The doctrine that Christ suffered the punishment for sin in the place of humanity</term> to be inflicted upon the Surety <note>original: *Sponsori*; Christ acting as the legal guarantor who pays the debt of another</note>, who offered himself as a sacrifice for us (Leviticus 9:24, 1 Kings 18:38, compared with Psalm 69:5). 

This same sacred *fire* was also sometimes used for divine punishments <term>original Greek: *theēlatous*; punishments sent or driven by the hand of God</term>. Hence the term is used when judgments sent by God through fire are described (Leviticus 10:2, Numbers 16:35) and whenever the prophet depicts terrible demonstrations of divine wrath (Isaiah 5:24, 9:18, 30:27). However, a *burning* fire <note>in the sense of a refining fire that cleanses a person</note> has more the character of a blessing (Isaiah 4:4, Malachi 3:2, 3). Moreover, these thinkers are barely mindful of the sinner's inability to endure the punishments of sin (Isaiah 33:14), upon which the necessity of reconciliation through the blood of Christ depends; and they ignore the precise hope of eternal Renewal, which we are now about to demonstrate.

### C. Scripture denies all causes of Conversion and Salvation to the damned.

5) **The <term>Accidental Cause</term> is divine judgment.** <note>In scholastic logic, an "accidental cause" (causa accidentalis) is a factor that contributes to a result without being its primary or essential source; here, it refers to how God’s punishment indirectly leads to further sin.</note> It is gathered from the effects of temporal judgments—especially those that stand out for their severity—that such judgments do not, of themselves, soften the heart, but rather harden it and ignite a frenzy for sinning. For if temporal punishments can make the souls of sinners so fierce, how much more should this be expected from punishments that are harsher and more lasting?

For since a vessel for honor is there called *sanctified and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work*, on the contrary, a vessel for dishonor will be an impure vessel from which no fruit returns to the Lord, being unfit for producing any good work. Indeed, to say nothing of the fact that those speaking here are introduced as looking more to present than future misery, it cannot be established by any suitable foundation that the Savior is looking only to temporal punishments.

G. And why should the Conversion of the future age not be denied, when even in this life the Conversion of certain people is declared impossible? **Hebrews 6:4–6**: *It is impossible for those who were once enlightened, etc., to be renewed again to repentance, since they crucify the Son of God anew and expose him to mockery.* The reason for this impossibility is not physical but moral; it is not derived from a decree of God (in which case this situation would have nothing unique compared to others), but from His own decency and holiness, since those who have mocked the Son of God himself, and thus the supreme God, deserve this...

<meta>This page continues the theological debate against "Apocatastasis" (Universal Restoration). Having previously argued that the biblical descriptions of Judas's fate imply a permanent state, the author now transitions into a logical and moral argument: if the damned could stop sinning or love God, their punishment would logically have to end, but their intense suffering only produces further blasphemy rather than repentance.</meta>

# ON THE ETERNITY OF PUNISHMENTS

and the Savior of the world, through a new apostasy to Judaism they exposed him to the same reproach as the Jews, and thus fell into the same crime as them. As long as this cause lasts, so long the same effect remains.

H. If the damned did not sin, or at least were able not to sin, their state would be far preferable to the state of sinners in this life. For ***moral evil is weightier than physical evil.*** <note>In traditional theology, "moral evil" refers to sin or the rebellion of the will, while "physical evil" refers to suffering or pain. The author argues that being a sinner is worse than being a sufferer.</note> From this it follows that a lesser degree of sinfulness is more miserable than the greatest punishments. What kind of condemnation would it be in which the damned would actually gain something <note>i.e., by being freed from the ability to sin</note>?

I. A damned person acts either ***badly*** or ***well***. There is no middle ground. He who acts well acts out of the Love of God according to His Law for His Glory. Therefore, one cannot conceive of anyone being immune from sinning unless they are filled with a sincere desire and love for God. But how could the punishment of hell <term>gehenna: a biblical term for the place of fiery judgment</term> subsist even for a single moment with such a disposition of the soul? Is the damned person not separated from God? But does that separation not cease as soon as one begins to sincerely love God? Or will God not love in return the one who loves Him? Will He not approve of being loved? Will He not reward those who seek Him?

K. So great is the evidence of this matter that even among the universal Restorationists <term>Apocatastatics: from the Greek 'apocatastasis', referring to those who believe all souls, including the damned and the devil, will eventually be saved</term> there are those who yield on this point. Explicitly, LUDWIG GERHARD <note>Ludovicus Gerhardus (1680–1738), a German theologian who famously defended the doctrine of universal salvation</note> *in chapter III, section 422, acknowledges it as settled that the damned in hell will curse the day of their birth thousands upon thousands of times, and as long as the punishment is intolerable, they will very often blaspheme their Creator for bringing them forth from nothing.* Nevertheless, what they 

,, give with one hand, they take away with the other, while they consider this very 
,, atrocity of Punishment as a means through which the free will of the 
,, sinner must eventually be filled with hatred for sin, and thus finally 
,, be healthily humbled under the hand of the Judge. ,, 

These things are plainly **inconsistent** <term>ἀσύστατα (asystata): a Greek term for arguments that are logically incompatible or "do not hold together"</term>. For from where would a sinner, dead in his sins, obtain the faculty of pursuing hatred of sin sincerely—that is, out of Love for God and His Holiness? And if the very atrocity of the Punishment elicits the Blasphemy of the most holy divine Name above all else, does it not follow from this that the more intolerable the Punishments are, the more monstrous a hatred of God must be produced by them?

### PART I. DOGMATIC THEOLOGY.

<meta>catchword: copam</meta>

XXXII. The sixth class of evidence consists of those passages which cut off any hope of Restoration for the evil *Angels*. <note>The author refers to the "fallen angels" or demons, debating the controversial theory of "Apocatastasis"—the idea that even the Devil might eventually be reconciled with God.</note> *Genesis 3:14* is most correctly referred to here, where it is said to the Serpent: *Because you have done this, cursed are you above every beast and above every wild animal of the field; on your belly you shall go and dust you shall eat all the days of your life.* We must assume here that by the "Serpent," we are to understand not a mere animal, but the Seducing Spirit himself. This is for several reasons: 1) The address to one and the same subject <note>The symbol $\dot{\psi}$. is used throughout the text to denote "verse."</note> in verse 15 continues without any sign of the slightest distinction. This is even more evident because these verses are joined by a prefix, and the suffix for the second person remains constantly the same. Therefore, whatever arguments are brought forward to apply the fifteenth verse to the Devil also serve for the preceding verse. 2) That "Serpent" must be understood as the one who committed the act. What he did is indicated in verse 13: *The Serpent*, Eve says, *deceived me and I ate.* Therefore, this Serpent is guilty of fraudulent seduction—a rational action—which does not apply to a mere beast. 3) He truly sinned, because a *curse* is pronounced upon him, which likewise cannot be reconciled with the nature of a beast. <note>In traditional theology, animals are considered "amoral" and cannot sin; therefore, a formal curse implies a being with a will and conscience.</note> 4) Learned men have shown that the literal sense holds more difficulty than is commonly thought. For instance, there are many species of reptiles besides snakes; furthermore, the idea that the food of snakes is "dust" smacks of a Jewish fable. ARISTOTLE, in book 8 of his *History of Animals*, chapter 4, asserts that snakes are *all-eaters and the most gluttonous of animals* <note>original Greek: παμφαγοι & λιχνοτατοι των ζωων</note>, devoted to delicacies above all other living things. Since *there is no nourishment in dust*, it is hardly likely that any animal could live on it. Even BOCHART <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a famous scholar of biblical animals.</note> confesses in his *Hierozoicon* <term>Hierozoicon: a 17th-century encyclopedia of animals mentioned in the Bible</term>, part I, book 1, chapter 4, *that dust is assigned as food to the serpent not as if it eats only dust, but because it swallows dust into its mouth along with its other food.* Finally, there is great plausibility in the opinion of those who claim that the Serpent used as the instrument of Seduction was from a species of "dragons" that did not constantly crawl, but stood with an upright body, gaped, flew, and lay in wait for birds—though we will not deal with that now.

[They] resolve the passage, and explain the following clause regarding a literal serpent, with whom our *Restorationists* <note>original: "Apocataftatici"—those who believe in *Apocatastasis*, the doctrine that all beings, including the Devil, will eventually be saved and restored to God.</note> would not wish to be compared; or they explain the whole section first *literally* and then *mystically*, a hypothesis that is not entirely opposed to ours. After Calvin, Rivet, Cregut, Grotius, and others, this cause was vigorously defended by the celebrated Cornelius Hase—my former teacher, whom I must not mention without a preface of honor—in his very learned treatise on the *First Gospel* <term>Protevangelium: traditionally referring to Genesis 3:15, the first prophecy of a Savior who would crush the serpent's head.</term>, chapter 2 and following. However, there are also some very learned men who divide our verses, either applying verse 14 to both the Devil and the Serpent (as Hunnius does) and verse 15 to the Devil alone, or (like Geier, Calovius, Frischmuth, and Pfeiffer) adapting the first clause only to the Serpent and the second clause only to the Devil. But those who understood our verse as referring to the Devil alone have "pierced the eyes of the crows" <note>original: "cornicum oculos confixerunt"—a Latin idiom meaning to have outwitted the experts or solved a very difficult problem with superior insight.</note>: Sebastian Schmidt in his *Biblical College*, Part I; J. H. Majus in his *Theological Topics*, section 7; Gousset in his *Triple Treatise against the Jews*; Witsius in *The Economy of the Covenants*; Momma in *The Economy of Times*; Salomon van Till in his commentary on *Genesis*; Cocceius and Witter in their respective works on the Law of Israel; and those who treated this matter more specifically, the illustrious Johann Christoph Ortlob in his essay *On the Serpent Not Punished with Satan* (Leipzig, 1708), as well as Schlosser and the younger Vitringa in their specific dissertations on the seducing Serpent. Truly, the reasons of those who think otherwise are flimsy <note>original: "ficulneæ," literally "made of fig-wood," a metaphor for something weak or useless.</note>, since there is nothing that compels us to force a literal sense onto the fourteenth verse; rather, an allegorical sense—and the continuation of that allegory through the following clause—as well as a comparison of parallel phrases (such as those occurring in Psalm 44:26 and Isaiah 65:25) demands and confirms it.

XXXIV. If the Serpent is the seducing Spirit himself, then the curse imposed upon him here will endure for all eternity. For that which continues "all the days of his life" will only cease when his life ends. However, since his life is immortal, it is manifest that the punishments involved in that curse will be equally immortal. Indeed, Rivet, in his commentary on Genesis, correctly exhausted the emphasis of our phrase in this way.

### PART I. SYSTEMATIC THEOLOGY

*Exercises on Genesis, XXXV*. No small amount of prejudice is stirred up against our opinion by those who interpret these same words as an indication of the time when the punishment should end. For this reason, we cannot ignore that the highly acclaimed Hase—who is now among the saints <note>original: "τὸν νυν ἐν ἁγίοις" (ton nyn en hagiois). > "But neither is this perverse delight of the Devil and his power of any kind over the dust destined to last forever; rather, once that certain and determined span of time has flowed past—which circumscribes that power like a boundary—it is destined to expire. For we hear him being ordered to eat the dust for all, and indeed only, the days of his life. These will end with the *consummation of the age* <note>original: "συντελεια του αἰωνος" (synteleia tou aionos), referring to the end of the world.</note>, when that great day of judgment shall shine forth, for which the sinful Angels are kept, bound by chains of eternal darkness (Jude v. 6)."

This same opinion, following Fagius, Cocceius, and others, is held by the celebrated Nicolaas Schiere in *Doctrine of the Testament*, book II, chapter I, sections 5 and 6; Salomon van Till in the passage cited; and Johannes Marckius in *History of Paradise*, book IV, chapter 3. Yet these views do not undermine our interpretation. For:

1) We cling to the received definition of 'life.' Those who disagree ought to provide a reason why they restrict 'all the days of the Serpent’s life'—which is a universal phrase—to the present age. *He lost his moral life <note>In this context, "moral life" refers to a state of holiness or spiritual communion with God.</note> immediately at the Fall; however, he will preserve his physical life in the eternal fire itself through the immortality of his nature.*

2) We admit this restriction even less because the eating of the dust itself will continue into eternity. We readily grant that his power over carnal sinners is described by this allegory. *For dust is an emblem of the ungodly (Isaiah 5:24, 65:25). What is chaff, if not dust, which represents the same people? (Psalm 1:1, Matthew 3:12).* The Teachers of the Hebrews <note>The Rabbis</note> looked to this when they commanded that the foreskin be cast into the dust during circumcision, and they derived the reason for their command from this very curse: *namely, so that the foreskin, wrapped in the dust, might be yielded to the Serpent as food, as is shown by the many passages brought forward by Eisenmenger in "Judaism Unmasked," Part I, pp. 683 ff.* <note>Johann Andreas Eisenmenger (1654–1704) was a German orientalist whose work "Entdecktes Judenthum" cataloged Jewish traditions and laws, often with a polemical intent.</note> Will his power over this dust end with the Day of Judgment? *Not in the least!* For he will be the perpetual inflictor of infernal punishments, and will take those fully into his power, around whom...

### ON THE ETERNITY OF PUNISHMENTS

...those against whom his power was more limited as long as they were the object of divine long-suffering.

XXXV. So far is it from being the case that this phrase opposes our hypothesis, that it rather involves the eternity of the punishment of the wicked in another way. For if, *as long as the Seducer <note>original: "Seductor", a common epithet for Satan.</note> lives, he eats dust*, and if by *dust* we are to understand the *wicked*, then it follows that the wicked will serve as his food through all the days of his life—and thus for eternity. This, however, cannot be fulfilled in any other way than through the torments and tortures to be perpetually inflicted upon them. 

It does not, of course, escape my notice that the most eminent interpreters here simultaneously understand by *dust* the bodies of the faithful, which are to be destroyed in their own time and reduced to dust through bodily death. This death is the "bite of the Devil" originating from sin; hence, Satan "eats their dust" because he holds this right through sin, an exercise in which he delights. But those very authors who assert this usually hold this sense to be only secondary. 

It would be better to abandon that view entirely, since it is surely by <term>catachresis</term> <note>a figure of speech in which a word or metaphor is used in a strained or paradoxical way</note> that he is said to "swallow" by *eating the dust of the bodies* which the faithful have temporarily laid aside. It suggests he brings entirely into his power those over whom only a shadowy, temporary power is actually granted. Nor does he have any cause for delight in it, since that dust is in reality the "cast-off garments" of souls who, having been freed from his assaults, now celebrate a triumph over his Kingdom. Add to this that such a "bite" belongs rather to the *bruising of the heel of the Woman's Seed* <note>A reference to the prophecy in Genesis 3:15.</note>, which is clearly distinguished from the *eating of dust*.

XXXVI. Our interpretation is shed with further light from Isaiah 65:25, where there is an open allusion to our passage. There, *dust, the food of the Serpent*, is directly contrasted with the true members of the Church: 

> "*The wolf and the lamb shall feed together; and the lion shall eat straw like the ox; and as for the Serpent, dust shall be his bread. They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain,* says *Jehovah*." 

The most celebrated interpreter of this Prophet, Campegius Vitringa <note>A famous 17th-century Dutch theologian known for his commentary on Isaiah.</note>, sides here with those who, setting aside the symbolism of the *dust*, wish the phrase to indicate nothing other than the most abject and degraded state of Satan. This view also pleased Rivetus <note>André Rivet, a French Huguenot theologian.</note> regarding the passage in Genesis, when compared with the phrase in Micah 7:17: "*They shall lick the dust like a serpent.*"

...of the serpent. But it is one thing to <term>lick</term> <note>Hebrew: <term>לחך</term> (*lāḥak*), meaning to lick up or lap like a dog</note>, and another to eat for the sake of nourishment—indeed, to eat it like bread or customary food. The wording of Micah indeed seems to bring something natural to the serpent into the comparison, even though VITRINGA <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a famous Dutch theologian and commentator on Isaiah.</note> himself previously noted on this passage that serpents, by their nature, *do not eat dust*. And the logic of allegory requires that the food of the serpent be explained through metaphor just as much as the food of the Wolf and the Lion. Nor does the objection usually raised against our hypothesis hold weight:

> „If what the Prophet describes were granted to Satan at this time, what consolation would remain for him? This very thing is the food by which he is nourished. For what would he work in them, except to incite them against the Church? But the Kingdoms of the World are supposed at this time to be subject to God and his Son.”

However, it is clear from Revelation 21:8, 27 and 22:11 that even in that glorious state of the Church, the wicked will not be lacking, and they will become the food of Satan. We admit this would be a miserable consolation, especially since he will try in vain to use them to harm the Church; hence it provides no more true nourishment than dust does to a serpent. Yet this consolation suits the nature of the Seducer <note>original: "Seductoris", a title for Satan.</note>, even if it is nothing other than what he will keep for eternity—namely, having companions in his evils. 

Since this is the case, it will now be abundantly clear that *dust* here designates the wicked, in contrast to all the inhabitants of the holy mountain. Since the infernal Dragon will no longer bring any harm to those inhabitants in the future Kingdom of Christ, this very thing will be a sign of victory over him: that all his power is to be restricted only to the wicked, who stir up vain and powerless rages against the people of God, and who even then *were an object of contempt to all flesh* <note>original: "opprobrium erant omni carni"</note> as in Isaiah 66:24. In this way, our prophecy describes a new stage in the fulfillment of the Paradisiacal threat <note>The curse of the serpent in Genesis 3:14–15.</note> and a new prelude to the eternal punishment of Satan and his angels, which will be maintained in a similar manner.

> ...because of you, in sorrow you shall eat of it all the days of your life; which likewise must be understood not of Adam's life in general, but of his life in the state of corruption, as is conceded on both sides.

We reply, however: 1) That it is the nature of the name <term>Chayyim</term> <note>Hebrew: <term>חיים</term>, the word for "life."</note> to primarily designate physical life, which is still included even when moral life is simultaneously alluded to. Eminent theologians consider this to be the true **reason for the dual form** <note>In Hebrew, the word for "life" is grammatically dual or plural, which scholars often interpret as signifying the two-fold nature of life: both physical and spiritual.</note>. One must not rashly depart from the customary meaning of the word. 2) Indeed, the saying in verse 17 works greatly in our favor, since Adam's physical life is certainly hinted at there, such as was appropriate to his mortal nature. From which 3) by the added condition of this mortality in verse 18, this threat is immediately limited, whereas such a limitation is plainly absent from our passage. 4) Even though the nature of such a solemn threat would especially require it. 5) Rather, the contrary appears to be the case, since if this hypothesis were to stand, new obscurities would be encountered. For this threat itself involves the continuation of *corrupt life* or rather *spiritual death*. From which this sense would result: *as long as you continue to sin, so long will you continue to seek nourishment suitable for sin—that is, to heap sins upon sins.* Who does not perceive that not only is an absurd tautology <note>A logical error where the same thing is said twice in different words without adding meaning.</note> introduced into the formal words of the sentence of the Supreme Judge, but also that those who argue this way are **cutting down their own vineyards**? <note>A Latin idiom (*propria vineta caedere*) meaning to damage one's own cause or provide the arguments for one's own defeat.</note> For how could any end to sinning appear, if the sinner by sinning deserves this, and gathers this curse upon his own head—that he should continue to sin and obtain all his nourishment from the sins of others? Or will any remission regarding the severity of the punishment take place as long as the sinner continues to fill the measure of his guilt, or rather to become more obstinate in sin day by day?

# PART I. DOGMATIC THEOLOGY.

,, ...but as one who is fully destined to die through the crushing of his head. ,, <note>This refers to the "Protoevangelium" or "First Gospel" in Genesis 3:15, where God declares that the offspring of the woman will crush the serpent's head.</note> But this objection vanishes because: 1) even according to this very hypothesis, the "crushing of the Head" exists simultaneously with the "days of life" assigned to the Serpent. XXXIX. But from where could any Salvation shine forth for the fallen Angels, since the causes from which it must be derived are denied to them? To which point that passage in **Hebrews 2:16** strongly applies: *For surely he does not take hold of angels.* <note>Original Greek: *Ου γαρ δηπου αγγελων επιλαμβανεται* (Ou gar dēpou angelōn epilambanetai).</note> For he does not vindicate Angels at all. Learned men have established that the verb *to take hold of* <note>Greek: <term>επιλαμβανεσθαι</term> (epilambanesthai)</note> corresponds here to the Hebrew word **Goel** <note>Hebrew: <term>גאל</term>, referring to a "Kinsman-Redeemer" who has the right or duty to rescue a family member or their property.</note>. One may consult **BRAUNIUS** and **D’OUTREINIUS** <note>Johannes Braun (1628–1708) and Johannes d'Outrein (1662–1722) were influential Dutch Reformed theologians.</note> on this passage, as well as **CRAMER**'s work *On the Goel*, book II, chapter 2, where it is most clearly shown that the entire connection of the Apostolic allegory requires this version. The explanatory particle *for* shows that the Apostle is here giving the reason why the purpose of His **Incarnation** was to destroy the Devil and to free the believing Israelites from the fear of death that had filled them under the Old Testament Economy. The reason for this different outcome is this: that he was the **Vindicator** and **Redeemer** <note>Latin: <term>Assertor</term> and <term>Redemtor</term></note>—the *Goel*—*not of Angels*, but of the *Seed of Abraham*. Thus, the Angels are clearly excluded from all hope of salvation through Christ. And that phrase *surely not* <note>Greek: <term>ου δηπου</term> (ou dēpou)</note> has a particular force here, which we render as *not at all* or *in no part*; lest anyone should object that, although he might not redeem **Angels** in the same way as the **seed of Abraham**, some other way of redeeming them might nonetheless lie open. Thus every crack is sealed shut, and all the more so because this **Vindicator** is at the same time the true God. Since, therefore, there is no salvation outside of God, from where would it shine upon the evil Angels?

Who does not perceive that not only is an absurd tautology introduced into the specific words of the Supreme Judge’s sentence, but also that those who maintain this are undermining their own argument? <note>Original Latin: *propria vineta... cædi*, literally "cutting one's own vineyards," an idiom for self-sabotage or proving oneself wrong.</note> For how will any end to sinning dawn if the sinner deserves it by sinning, and heaps this curse upon his own head—to continue sinning and to obtain all his nourishment from the sins of others? ...to **take hold of angels** <note>Original Greek: *ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι ἀγγέλων*</note> is as much as to say **to assume human nature.** Here they <note>The opponents of the author's orthodox view</note> complain that "concrete terms are being rashly changed into abstract ones; indeed, nothing prevents **good Angels** from being understood here, whom Christ is not said to 'take hold of' because he does not admit them as Brothers or as sharers in his Kingdom." But when it is assumed that **to take hold of** <note>Greek: <term>epilambanesthai</term></note> here necessarily signifies *to claim* or *to liberate*, then these arguments collapse of their own accord. For from this it is established that we understand not an "angelic nature" in the abstract, but actual persons. And only evil angels can be understood, since Redemption does not apply to the good ones. Add to this that our words contain the logic of the Judgment described against the Devil in verses 14 and 15. Indeed, if the opponents' hypothesis were admitted, then it would simultaneously have to be proven that the future condition of the **Seed of Abraham** will eventually be more illustrious than that of the **good angels** themselves. Meanwhile, each side has certain exceptions which, lest they cause delay, must be resolved in a few words.

### XLI. 
Those who wish to argue that **evil angels** are being discussed here reason as follows:

A. ,,From the fact that it is said in the present tense that Christ *does not take hold of Angels*, it does not follow that he will never *take hold of them* in the future.,,

Response: It certainly does follow. For the **taking hold** <note>Greek: <term>Epilepsis</term></note> is a work also related to the **Seed of Abraham**, which the Savior began in this age, but will continue and complete in the age to come. However, just as full and eternal redemption is granted here to the Seed of Abraham, so by the power of opposition, eternal redemption is denied to the Angels.

B. They add: ,,even if it is granted that Angels are not redeemed through Christ, nothing prevents God from looking after the salvation of the fallen angels by some other means.,, 
Response: 1. We believe in God that there is no salvation outside of Christ. 2. The very dissenters themselves pretend that the angelic world was reconciled through Christ (citing Ephesians 1:10, Philippians 2:10, Colossians 1:20, etc.), and they even want to claim he interceded for the Angels in Luke 23:34. # PART I. DOGMATIC THEOLOGY.

> „ He <note>The opponent whose views the author is refuting</note> wishes the name *Angels* to be used only for *good* angels, unless it is explicitly restricted. „ Response: We accept this observation, since the context clearly demonstrates such a restriction.

> „ He considers the *Taking up of the Seed of Abraham* <note>Referring to Christ becoming human as a descendant of Abraham</note> as a benefit, through which the faithful are received into a certain most excellent level of Glory—one that even the Angels cannot achieve—so that this Glory of the Seed of Abraham is to be raised far above the dignity of the Angels. He locates this Glory in the fact that the world to come is to be made subject not to Angels, but to Christ and the members of his mystical Body, according to Hebrews 2:5 and following. From this, he derives the idea that Angels are nowhere called the *Bride* or *Brothers* of Christ; nowhere is the *sitting on the Throne* of Christ or a Priestly Kingdom attributed to them. Instead, they are regarded merely as *ministering spirits* <note>Original Greek: *λειτουργικα πνευματα*</note> as seen in Hebrews 1:14. To this same point belongs the *Judgment of the saints over the Angels* from 1 Corinthians 6:3. Indeed, he thinks the angelic nature itself demands this, as it only involves a part of the world—specifically, the spirits of air and fire—which is why they appear as spiritual winds and flames of fire in Psalm 104:4. Man, however, is everything. For in man is found not only the spirits of air and fire, but also water and earth; thus, the innermost or *fifth essence* <note>Original Latin: *quintam essentiam*, the "quintessence" or purest element that binds all others</note> of all created things is found in man in its highest excellence. For this reason, he believes man is the most suitable instrument for God to use in the governance of all things. This is why, even in this life, Angels offer service to humanity (Hebrews 1:8), and even entire armies of Angels are ready to serve a single person (Genesis 32:1-2; 2 Kings 6:17). „

Response: Many absurdities <term>atopa</term> <note>Original Greek: *ἄτοπα*, meaning things that are logically "out of place" or irrational</note> are gathered here to prop up a false hypothesis in whatever way possible. The idea that the Glory of the chosen ones is superior to that of the Angels is a mere fiction. We leave it to God’s free will to decide whether and to what extent He wishes to distribute specific levels of eternal Glory. However, the arguments brought forward here do not hit the mark. 1) Hebrews 2:5 and the following verses do not concern a distinction between the divine plan of this age and the age to come, but rather the difference between the Old and New Testaments. Furthermore, the *world to come* <term>oikoumenē mellousa</term> <note>Original Greek: *οἰκουµενη µελλονσα*</note> does not refer to the physical structure of this world being subjected to the saints. Instead, it refers to the body of the saints itself, which will no longer be submitted to *Angels*—who were treated like *fictitious gods* <note>Likely referring to the belief that the Old Testament law was administered by angels</note>—but will henceforth be submitted to Christ alone.

# ON THE ETERNITY OF PUNISHMENTS

2) The names **Bride and Brothers** refer to the specific way the **Redemption** of the chosen among humans is carried out, while the phrases about **sitting on the throne and the Kingdom** focus on certain circumstances in the application of salvation. If these specific terms were set aside, nothing would prevent the titles of **Bride and Co-heirs** from being applied to the Angels because of their bond of friendship with the Triune God <note>The Holy Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</note>, or the title of **eternal Priesthood** from being given to them because of the perfection of their divine worship. However, Scripture is more sparing in describing the Glory of Angels because it was written not for the sake of the Angels, but to attract and strengthen our own faith. 

3) When *Hebrews 1:14* calls them **ministering spirits** <note>Original Greek: *πνεύματα λειτουργικὰ* (*pneumata leitourgika*)</note>, this very term grants them a **spiritual Priesthood**. Their **service** <note>Original Greek: *διακονία* (*diakonia*)</note> is not performed for humanity, but subjects them to God alone. I should also mention that those who provide a Priestly Ministry by promoting the salvation of others are performing a most glorious work. 

4) The **Judgment over Angels** mentioned in *1 Corinthians 6:3* concerns only the Evil Angels; for such a judgment does not apply to the chosen angels, who were confirmed in goodness at the time the rest of them fell. 

5) The arguments put forward concerning a universal "fifth essence" <term>Fifth essence: Also known as the "quintessence," an ancient and medieval idea of a fifth element (ether) that makes up the celestial bodies, distinct from earth, air, fire, and water</term> of sensible things are **of a bad character** <note>Original Greek: *πονηροῦ κόμματος* (*ponērou kommatos*), a phrase meaning "of a bad stamp" or "suspicious quality"</note>. Not only is something bodily attributed to the Angels, but their spiritual nature is supposedly changed into a subtle body of fire and air. Such ideas do not even deserve to be refuted. Even if they were proven true, it still wouldn't prove that the Angels will have a lesser Glory than humans in the world to come. It is not clear why "thicker" bodies (which have some earthly or watery element mixed in) would have a greater capacity for celebrating God than "subtle" ones. Not to mention how foolish it is to make God's free Grace in rewarding us dependent on some unknown physical bodily circumstances. 

6) Finally, the fact that armies of Angels are at hand for the faithful even in this life does not imply a lower degree of Glory—unless one wants to make the most absurd claim that believers are already more excellent than Angels in our present state. In such appearances, the Angels are not the attendants of the believers themselves, but rather of the **Archangel** <note>The author likely refers to Christ here as the "Chief Messenger" or leader of the heavenly host</note> who is present. Compare *Luke 2:9, 13*.

For the merit of satisfying justice must be equal to the merit of the punishment. If, therefore, Justice is eternal, then it is necessary that Punishment also be eternal.

VII. 25. It is clear that these passages deal specifically with those saved in this life, *both* because the Apostle speaks in the present tense throughout the entire passage, *and* because in verse 26 he immediately applies these words to himself and his contemporary believers: *For such a High Priest was fitting for us, etc.* <note>Original Latin: *Talis enim nos decebat Sacerdos summus*. XLV. Eighth, let those sayings close the line of argument which attribute the entire cause of righteousness and salvation solely to the Merit of Christ, excluding every other price <note>See 1 Corinthians 1:30, Ephesians 1:3–8, and Colossians 1:9, 20.</note>. Hence the Church preserves that word **freely** <note>The author provides the term in Hebrew: *חנם* (*khinnam*) and Greek: *δωρεαν* (*dōrean*), both meaning "as a gift" or "without cost."</note> as a sacred anchor, offered and emphasized in Isaiah 55:1 and Revelation 22:17. The rope of this anchor is cut with rash daring by all those who prattle on about the damned paying their punishments *down to the last farthing* <note>A reference to Matthew 5:26, often used by universalists to suggest a debt can eventually be paid off.</note>, claiming that once this is paid, a way to escape will lie open to them.
