> “...pretending that the punishments of the damned will only be *purifying* <term>Purifying: translated from *expurgatoria*, suggesting a temporary 'cleaning' process like Purgatory</term>, 
> “but not *expiatory* <term>Expiatory: translated from *expiatoria*, referring to the actual atonement or payment for sin</term>. From this they conclude that, even if 
> “they were to be tortured for a thousand other Ages, they would never escape 
> “by the power of these sufferings, *unless* the merit of Christ's 
> “obedience was added to them.”

### VII. 25. 
It is clear that these passages deal specifically with those saved in this life, *both* because the Apostle speaks in the present tense throughout the entire passage, *and* because in verse 26 he immediately applies these sayings to himself and his contemporary believers: *For such a High Priest was fitting for us, etc.* 3) This is equally clear in Hebrews 10, where in verse 10 he speaks in a similar manner: *In which we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ made once for all;* and in verse 14: *He has perfected forever* <note>original Greek: τους ἁγιαζομενους</note> *those who* (in the present) *are being sanctified*. Therefore, it is clearer than the midday sun that these passages concern the eternal salvation and perfection not of those who are to be converted after this life, but of those who have already been converted.

### XLV. 
Eighth, let those passages close the line of argument which attribute the entire cause of justice and salvation solely to the **Merit of Christ**, excluding any other price (1 Corinthians 1:30; Ephesians 1:3–8; Colossians 1:9, 20). Hence, the Church preserves—as if it were a sacred anchor—that word <note>original Hebrew: חנם (khinnam); Greek: δωρεαν (dorean)</note> **"freely"** or **"gratis"**, which is offered and emphasized in Isaiah 55:1 and Revelation 22:17. Those who rashly cut the rope of this anchor are all those who drone on about the damned having to pay their penalties *down to the last penny*, and who want a way of escape to lie open for them once that debt is fully paid. They sometimes flee to this refuge:

> "...pretending that the punishments of the damned will only be **cleansing** <term>expurgatoria: punishments intended to purge or 'wash' the soul of sin</term>, but not **expiatory** <term>expiatoria: punishments intended to pay the legal debt or 'ransom' for sin</term>. From this they conclude that even if they were further tortured for a thousand other **Ages** <term>Aeons: vast cycles of time or world-epochs</term>, they would never escape by the power of these sufferings *unless* the merit of Christ's obedience were added."

This is certainly the position **Petersen** <note>Johann Wilhelm Petersen (1649–1727), a prominent German theologian and mystic who famously defended the "Apokatastasis" or the eventual restoration of all souls to God.</note> takes in Volume III, pages 78 and following. But the **worthlessness** <note>original Greek: οὐδενεια</note> of this hiding place is manifest. For: 
1) This itself is an insult to the blood of Christ, because the power of cleansing from sins is being attributed to Punishments, a power which Scripture claims entirely for the Blood of Christ (1 John 1:7, etc.). 
2) Every concept of punishment perishes when the power of expiation <note>the legal payment for wrongdoing</note> is taken away from them. 
3) They become guilty of an evident contradiction, because elsewhere they are accustomed to attack us from this stronghold: that sins committed in time can have no proportion to eternal punishments.

### XLVI.

...[he] presumes; partly from the effects <note>original: "a posteriori"; reasoning based on observed consequences rather than first principles.</note>, he teaches that the Revelation of this Eternity is easily reconciled with the Fitness of God, and indeed that it illustrates His Glory in a wondrous way, which we shall demonstrate in a few words below.

XLVIII. We assume that along with the Law of God, its Sanction <note>The binding force of a law that provides for reward or punishment.</note> is implanted in the conscience of every individual through the very act of creation. That Sanction encompasses both *Rewards* and *Punishments*. The Eternity of Rewards is a point of general agreement. From this, however, the Eternity of Punishments follows naturally. For if those who act according to the Law rightly hope for eternal Rewards, those who violate it also rightly fear eternal Punishments. Let those who resist this show why the merit <note>In this context, "merit" refers to the moral desert or weight of an action, whether for good or for ill.</note> of those who act well and those who act poorly should be *unequal*. If that *inequality* existed, it would be grounded either in the *Nature of God* or in the *nature of the free actions* of the rational creature. Reason knows nothing of either. 

If the foundation of *inequality* existed in the *Nature of God*, it would then have to be shown that it is more contrary to some known Perfection of God to punish the damned eternally than it is to save the godly eternally. What Perfection would that be: *natural* or *moral*? If *natural*, then the Lawgiver <term>Legislator: God as the author of moral law.</term> would not be as powerful to destroy as He is to save, which is a contradiction. If *moral*, then it would conflict with His *Holiness*—not His *essential* holiness, which is not the issue here, but His *relative* holiness, which encompasses both His *Justice* and His *Kindness*. If the *Justice* of God stood against eternal Punishments, then one would have to say that evil actions deserve eternal Punishments less than good actions deserve Rewards. This will be dismantled in the following section. Therefore, only the Kindness or Goodness of God remains. But what can an enemy of God, a denier of His supreme Lordship—and indeed of all His Perfections—hope for from that? Will it be a slight against God’s Goodness that He does not show indulgence to a creature who despises it?

XLIX. Furthermore, we establish that the foundation for this alleged *inequality* does not exist in the *free actions* of the creature either. If God were to reward good actions eternally and punish evil ones only for a limited time, then it would follow that the merit of good actions exceeds the merit of evil ones by an infinite degree. For any length of time, even if it is extended for many thousands of years, is—when compared to Eternity—nothing but a point, a moment, a num[ber]— <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence, likely continuing with "numberless" or "numerical trifle" on the next page.</note>

# PART I. DOGMATIC THEOLOGY #

page 45

...and of a progression into infinity there is scarcely a beginning. But how absurd it would be to establish this is manifest when the gain and the loss are well calculated—those which actions cause either in relation to God, or in relation to ourselves, or in relation to others.

L. In **relation to God**, it follows that nothing less than this kind of inequality should be admitted from the fact that the virtue of a creature profits God just as little as vice harms Him. He is raised equally high, immutable, and uniquely blessed <note>original: "solus beatus"; referring to God as the only source of perfect happiness, unaffected by external changes.</note> above both. Our obedience adds nothing to His happiness. Our disobedience brings no detriment to His peace. If, therefore, sins are a small evil in relation to the supreme **Lawgiver**, will rightly performed deeds be a greater good? Do they not continue to be "useless servants" <note>An allusion to Luke 17:10: "So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, 'We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.'"</note> who fulfill even all the precepts of so great a Lord? Why then do those who so easily persuade themselves that God wishes to reward such a small good with an eternal prize, so with such difficulty admit that He will also punish the evil of sin—which they judge to be so small—with eternity?

LI. But if we **contemplate ourselves**, we certainly acquire a huge gain by acting rightly. For **virtue is its own reward**. Our perfection consists solely in holiness, and the exercise of it embraces the entire activity of a blessed life. But is the loss caused by sin not equally inestimable, since by its very nature it utterly destroys all this beauty of the rational creature and introduces the opposite foulness?

LII. Not even in **relation to other creatures** does any inequality of gain and loss occur. Concerning rational creatures confirmed in goodness <note>Referring to the "church triumphant"—angels and souls already in Heaven.</note>, their lot is placed in safety and can suffer nothing through sin, nor can it be aided by the holiness of others. However, regarding those who are conceived to still be in a changeable state <note>Humans currently living on Earth.</note>, their conversion is hindered just as strongly by a bad example as it is promoted by a good one. The remaining creatures, which are subject to the use of rational beings, are equally corrupted through sinful abuse as they are perfected through lawful use.

LIV. This presumption acquires a singular strength because **Reason** perceives within its own heart no way through which any end to **Punishments** could be expected. For an end would have to be imposed on Punishments either through *Annihilation* <note>The theological theory that the souls of the wicked are eventually deleted from existence rather than suffering forever.</note> or through the *Restoration* of the sinner to a state of integrity. There is no third option <note>original: "Tertium non datur"; a reference to the logical Law of the Excluded Middle, stating there is no middle ground between two opposites.</note>. Whichever you choose, you must concede that a notable benefit would be shown to the sinner. The latter—restoration—is certainly the greater gift. However, even through *Annihilation*, a favor is shown to the wretched. The end of existence would simultaneously end the misery. Those placed in great torments sometimes consider it better to end them by a voluntary death; and they at least acknowledge the acceleration of death as a grace from the Judge, even then, when Eternity remains, in which they do not yet have their final lot determined. But from where shall an enemy of God, filled with hatred for Him, promise himself even the slightest of His favors? But let us examine each point.

LV. **Reason** finds plainly no occasion to expect *Annihilation*. For why would God destroy His own work? Or why would He have instilled *immortality* into the minds of the wicked if He did not wish to preserve them in that state? Was He unaware that they were going to sin? Could He fail in His purpose, or feel regret <note>original: "poenitentia agi"; literally "to act with repentance," though here referring to God changing His mind about His creative acts.</note> for having created man? All other things, both the **Omniscience** and the **Omnisufficiency** of the Lord, suggest otherwise. Add to this that no example of **Annihilation** occurs in the visible Kingdom of God. Much less should it be presumed in the invisible Kingdom, which is governed toward more excellent ends.

LVI. The possibility of *Restoration* appears far smaller. It is of such a great burden <note>original: "Tantae molis"; a phrase suggesting immense effort or difficulty, famously used by Virgil in the Aeneid.</note> even in the present age that it exceeds every edge of **Reason**. Much thicker darkness surrounds this when Reason investigates the *means* through which a *Restoration* to wholeness would be obtained in the future age. Especially when it considers the connection and relationship that the future age has to the present, from which it appears that the Judgment of the actions of this life is deferred to the future life. Whence Reason rightly concludes that if it pleased God for some...

LVII. **Reason**, once imbued with these grave predispositions, easily and without resistance admits the **Eternity of Punishments** once it notices that **Revelation** explicitly teaches it. Not only that, but **Reason** also supplies the weapons to defend the *Equity* <note>The fairness or moral justice of a punishment fitting the crime.</note> of those punishments. Who would dare deny that God most justly leaves the sinner to himself and separates him as far as possible from His face? Moreover, a sinner left to himself cannot help but sin. To create a new heart is the work of God alone. But since this is the greatest benefit and is joined with eternal salvation, on what grounds shall the most just Judge be obligated to provide that to a transgressor of His Law? As long as he continues to sin, God rightfully continues to punish.

LVIII. Furthermore, to God as the supreme **Legislator** belongs the *Right* to sanction His Law with eternal **Punishments**. Nothing in the *nature of God* nor in the *nature of the finite mind* contradicts this. This *Right* is consistent with the **nature of God**, because His Dominion—which the transgressor denies—extends into eternity; and thus, by the same right that He dispenses eternal **Rewards**, He dispenses eternal **Punishments**. It is also consistent with the **nature of the created mind**, which through its immortality is capable of eternal **Punishment**. If, therefore, God rightfully threatens eternal **Punishments** in His Law, then He also executes them most justly. Otherwise, the threat itself would have been unjust. This **Right** is redoubled because, as I may here adopt the words of the most celebrated **Roellius** <note>Hermann Alexander Roëll (1653–1718), a prominent Dutch theologian known for emphasizing the role of reason in theology.</note> on Question IV of the *Heidelberg Catechism*, page 99: *one who transgresses a law sanctioned by eternal punishments falls into the guilt of eternal punishment by his own will and fault; and when God proposes to man eternal life and death, eternal good and evil, eternal blessing and curse, He does no injury if He inflicts eternal evil upon the one who chooses it over the good.*

LIX. This point especially pleads for the supreme **Right** of God in this cause, which our **Palatine Catechism** <note>The Heidelberg Catechism (1563), originally published in the Palatinate region of Germany; a foundational document for Reformed Protestantism.</note> urges, namely Ju-

...that the Justice of God <note>original: "justitiam Dei"</note> demands that what is committed against the supreme Majesty of God should also be paid for with the highest—that is, eternal—punishments of both the soul and the body. LX. The very Freedom of Mercy, which God exercises toward those who are to be saved, confirms this Right of His. For Grace would not be offered to the chosen sinner out of God's mere good pleasure if God could not justly punish for eternity. He would instead be bound by His own holiness to eventually relent from punishing. However, not only the Word of God, but also the deep-seated conscience of every sinner regarding their own merit <note>meaning the "merit" or "deservingness" of punishment</note>, abundantly teaches that the case is otherwise.

LXI. And how could that be unworthy of God which manifests the *Glory of His Perfections* in such a singular way? His *Independence* <term>Independentia: The theological concept that God is entirely self-sufficient and does not need His creation to be happy.</term> from every creature is made evident by this: it demonstrates that nothing is lost from His supreme blessedness through the eternal rejection of a rational creature. His *unlimited power* is seen in this: that He is able not only to make one eternally happy, but also to exclude one from true blessedness, to render all the efforts of the creature to the contrary vain, and to demonstrate His sufficiency in continuing the torments not only of the body, but also of the soul and the hidden stings of conscience forever. What makes His *Majesty* more to be feared than that the injury against it is so severely avenged? What demonstrates His inviolable *Holiness* <note>original: "Sanctitatem"</note> more effectively than that He excludes the sinner from His communion forever? Even the *Kindness* which He exercises toward believers is intensified by the exercise of this Right. ...is extolled, in that God wishes to deliver the sinner from eternal Punishments. LXII. For the sanction of the Law through eternal Punishments strikes a holy fear into those who are obedient, and sharply incites them to vigilance; it is a saving means for those who must be converted, so that they may be awakened from the sleep of security; and it places a bridle upon those persevering in sin, driving them so that they do not—by their wantonness in sinning increasing beyond measure—exacerbate those Punishments from which no redemption is to be expected for eternity.

The general fruit of this doctrine, which distributes itself to all, is this: that it overturns all **boasting of the Flesh**, and demonstrates that the entire Glory of **Redemption** belongs fully to the most free Grace of God alone. For by this very fact, that the sinner has deserved eternal Punishments, the horrendous filthiness of sin shines out; the absolute impossibility of escaping from misery through any powers of our own or of any other creatures is recognized; and the necessity of divine omnipotence to abolish the guilt of sin and to break the chains of hell is made manifest.

And just as the greatest weight is added to the merit of sin <note>In this context, "meritum" refers to "demerit" or what sin justly deserves</note> through this Eternity, so the proper weighing of it is a most healthy means to melt the heart through such an exuberant fervor of divine Love, to value the inestimable price of Christ’s blood above a thousand worlds, and to bring honor to God into all Eternity—of which every single moment renews this benefit. LXIII. It is, however, usually objected "that experience teaches the opposite, since that saving effect is not observed among those to whom the **Eternity of punishments** is emphasized. For it appears that some are rendered more stubborn in sinning; indeed, they are driven by this very doctrine to greater impiety, since, despairing of **divine Grace** and with all hope of **repentance** cut off, they give themselves over entirely to the pursuit of evil desires." We reply, however: I. The number of those who abuse this doctrine to increase their profanity is small; nor does their impiety proceed from the actual tenor of the doctrine itself, but rather from a most foul distortion of it. For although we deny an **End to Punishments**, we nevertheless recognize such **Degrees** of those punishments that, for this reason alone, it would be beneficial for a sinner to flee the more atrocious vices as much as he is able. For as great a difference as occurs in the rank of service between a Gentile living in some way agreeably to the light of nature and a Christian of abandoned life, so much more atrocious will the punishments of the latter be. Nor is there any handle for despair as long as this life lasts. Therefore, it would be a sign of the greatest madness if someone in this life wished to break through all the restraints of sinning simply because no **Restoration** <term>Restitutio: referring to 'Apocatastasis,' the theological theory that all beings, including the damned, will eventually be restored to God</term> is to be expected in the eternal life. That this means is fruitlessly applied to many for their salvation is according to the purpose of God, *who has mercy on whom He will, and hardens whom He will.* <note>A reference to Romans 9:18</note> And it is enough that it attains a better effect among some according to the good pleasure of God. It is indeed true, as some continue to urge against us, "that the proclamation of Punishments alone is not in itself a sufficient means to promote **Conversion**." Nevertheless, its momentum is significant when joined with the preaching of **Grace**. For we have already proven how much it exalts Grace itself. And just as two spurs applied from both sides incite more strongly, so the efficacy of persuasion is greater when it is fortified on one side by promises and on the other by the gravest threats. Hence the wisdom of the **Lawgiver** <note>God</note> fortified the Law on both sides with this two-part Sanction. And this agrees with the perpetual **practice** of all the messengers of God. III. The same may be said concerning the Preaching of Grace and Love...

LXV. Persuaded by these and similar reasons, the Christian Church of every age has enjoyed a singular unity of faith regarding this truth. Testimonies on this matter have been collected in great number by **Johann Gerhard** in his *Commonplaces*, Volume 9, "On Hell," paragraph 59 and following; **Natalis Alexander** in his *History of the Third Century*, dissertation 27; **Matthieu Petitdidier** in Volume 2 of his *Annotations on the Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*, page 403 and following; and **Dionysius Petavius** in his *Dogmatic Theology*, Volume 3, "On the Angels," book 3, chapters 4 and 8. **Th. Alethinus** (or **Jean Le Clerc**, the editor of Petavius's works who hides under this name) wonders that this most learned man piled up so many passages on a matter which is well known to have been accepted by all, except for the **Origenists** <term>Origenists: followers of the 3rd-century scholar Origen, some of whom taught that all souls, including the devil, would eventually be saved</term>.

But I would have also desired a better selection in that hodgepodge of source citations. For various passages are brought forward which, although no suspicion of heresy falls upon the writers themselves, nevertheless do not clarify their true meaning, and are therefore quite "wide of the mark." <note>original: "parum ad rhombum". A Latin idiom meaning to miss the point or fail to hit the target.</note> Nevertheless, we believe that the principal testimonies—those which prevail due to their antiquity, and especially those called into doubt by our antagonists—should not be passed over with a "dry foot." <note>original: "sicco plane pede". An idiom meaning to pass over something quickly or without due attention.</note>

LXVI. If the fragment of **CLEMENT OF ROME** <note>Clement of Rome (c. 35–99 AD) was one of the "Apostolic Fathers," considered the first successors to the Apostles.</note> cited from **JOHN OF DAMASCENE** (*Eclogues*, book φ, Title 1) were genuine, we would have a testimony of an Apostolic man dating back to the first century. For it reads as follows: *All souls are immortal, even those of the ungodly. For them, it would have been better not to be incorruptible. For, being punished by unquenchable fire with an endless penalty, and not dying, they can find no end to their own misfortune.* <note>original Greek: "Αθανατοι πασαι αἱ ψυχαι και των ἀσεβων...". This quote emphasizes that the soul's immortality becomes a burden when coupled with eternal punishment.</note>

LXVII. More certain witnesses from the second century are at hand, and these are of the greatest weight: **JUSTIN MARTYR** (*Apology I*), **IRENAEUS** (*Against the Heretics*, Book IV. 47 & V. 27), **TATIAN** (*Against the Greeks*), **THEOPHILUS OF ANTIOCH** (*To Autolycus*, at the end of Book 1), **TERTULLIAN** (*Apology*, chapters 13 & 45; and *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter XIV; as well as in the poem *On the Judgment of the Lord*, chapter 9).

LXVIII. **GROTIUS** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a famous Dutch jurist and theologian; the author here critiques his interpretation of history.</note> certainly attempts to snatch away the greater part of these testimonies in his notes on Matthew 25:46, while he claims that **JUSTIN**, **THEOPHILUS**, **TATIAN**, and **IRENAEUS** believed in an end to punishments. **HUET** <note>Petrus Daniel Huetius (1630–1721), a French scholar known for his work on the early church father Origen.</note> does the same in his work *Origeniana* (Book II, page 158, 159). However, he will not easily obtain what he wishes. There exists a passage of **JUSTIN** in his *Dialogue with Trypho* where he says: *Those souls which have appeared worthy of God do not die any longer; but the others are punished as long as God wills them both to exist and to be punished.* <note>original Greek: "αἱ μεν ἀξιαι του Θεου φανεισθαι, οὐκ ἀποθνησκουσιν ἐτι...".</note> Furthermore, it is abundantly established that **JUSTIN** is doing this to teach that souls are not [naturally eternal]...

### PART I: DOGMATICS

...that the <note>original: "mas", likely the end of "animas" (souls) from the previous page.</note> souls of the ungodly would at some point cease to exist, but rather that by the will of God, and not by any necessity of their own existence, they would live forever. This is demonstrated not only by the clear passage of **JUSTIN MARTYR** that we have noted, but also by the entire context of the present argument. For in it, he aims to dismantle the kind of **immortality** <note>original Greek: *ἀθανασία* (athanasia)</note> that certain Platonists taught—one in which the soul lives **through itself** <note>original Greek: *δι᾽ αὐτῆς* (di' autēs)</note> or by its own inherent power. And so, lest anyone think he might be admitting to the mortality of souls in this way, he explains himself immediately before our cited words, saying: *Indeed, I do not say that all souls die; for that would truly be a stroke of luck for the wicked.* <note>original: "Ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐδὲ ἀποθνήσκειν φημὶ πάσας τὰς ψυχὰς ἔγω. ἕρμαιον γὰρ ἦν ὡς ἀληθῶς τοῖς κακοῖς." Justin is arguing that if the soul simply vanished after death, the wicked would escape punishment, which he finds illogical.</note> Compare **NATALIS ALEXANDER** <note>A 17th-century French Dominican theologian and church historian.</note> (Century II, dissertation 6, § 6), **NICOLAUS LE NOURRY** (*Apparatus to the Library of the Fathers*, Century II, dissertation II, § 19), and **SAMUEL JEBB** in his notes on the cited passage of Justin.

LXIX. **HUGO GROTIUS** <note>A towering figure in 17th-century law and theology.</note> cites **IRENAEUS** (*Against Heresies*, Book II, ch. 64) regarding the same matter, where it reads: *Since God, therefore, grants both life and perpetual endurance, souls—which previously did not exist—receive the ability to persevere, since God willed them both to exist and to subsist. For the will of God ought to hold the first place and rule over all things; everything else must yield and be subject to it.* But the similarity between these words and those of **JUSTIN** easily persuades us that they should be understood in the same way, especially since the other passages we have cited explicitly attribute immortality to souls. From the preceding context, it is also clear that **IRENAEUS** wants to refute those who say *that souls, which began to exist only a short time ago, cannot endure for a long time, but must either be uncreated to be immortal, or, if they have a beginning through birth, they must perish with their bodies.* Against them, he asserts that souls endure and are extended through the length of ages according to the will of God the Creator, and thus not by the power of an innate nature, nor through their own selves. See **PETAVIUS** <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a Jesuit theologian.</note> (*Dogmatic Theology*, Vol. III, book I, ch. 5) and **LE NOURRY** (loc. cit. dissertation 6, ch. 9, § 1), and especially **MASSUET** (preliminary dissertation on Irenaeus, III, Article IX). The famous **DEYLING** <note>Salomon Deyling (1677–1755), a German Lutheran theologian known for his "Observationes Sacrae."</note> also comes forward to oppose the distortions of **DODWELL**, <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), a scholar who controversially argued that the soul is naturally mortal and only becomes immortal through a gift of God administered via baptism.</note> who tried to use this passage of Irenaeus to support his error regarding souls being naturally mortal.

# ON THE ETERNITY OF PUNISHMENTS

<meta>catchword: to claim (vindicare)</meta>

in Irenaeus’s *Evidence for the Truth of the Gospel*, section 42. **LE NOURRY** <note>Nicolas Le Nourry (1647–1724), a French Benedictine scholar known for his "Apparatus" to the Library of the Fathers.</note> also dispels the suspicion that might be raised against **TATIAN** in his fifth dissertation, section 3. Nor should one harbor ill thoughts regarding **THEOPHILUS** on this point, according to the explanation given in the same work (Dissertation 4, chapter 3, section 2). To this may be added the illustrious **WOLF** <note>Johann Christoph Wolf (1683–1739), a German theologian and scholar of Greek.</note> at the end of his recent edition, pages 448 and following, where he refutes the attempts of **DODWELL** <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), an influential but controversial theologian who argued that the soul is not naturally immortal but made so by baptism.</note> concerning this passage.

LXX. Just as no one among the Orthodox Fathers before **ORIGEN** <note>Origen (c. 185–253 AD) was a hugely influential theologian whose ideas about the eventual salvation of all beings—including the devil—were later declared heretical.</note> called the eternity of punishments into doubt, so too in the following centuries hardly anyone is found in the Church who dared to attack it. The testimonies of **MINUCIUS FELIX** and **CYPRIAN** at the end of his book *To Demetrianus* are well known from the 3rd Century. In the 4th Century, an entire army comes forth: **HILARY**, **GREGORY OF NYSSA** and **GREGORY OF NAZIANZUS**, **CYRIL OF JERUSALEM**, **AMBROSE**, **JEROME**, **CHRYSOSTOM**, and **AUGUSTINE**. There is no need to recount how the teachers who followed stood in their footsteps, as it can be abundantly proven from these writers what the general faith of the primitive Church was regarding this article of faith.

LXXI. Some recent proponents of **Universal Restoration** <term>Apocatastatici: from "Apocatastasis," the belief that all sentient beings will eventually be reconciled to God</term> have attempted to deceitfully snatch some of these Fathers away from us to avoid the unpopularity of their "new-wine" error. **PETERSEN** <note>Johann Wilhelm Petersen (1649–1727), a radical pietist who was one of the most famous proponents of universal salvation in the 17th century.</note> boasts, for example, that **HILARY** supports him in his *Testimonies of the Truth* (which he added to the second volume of his larger work), basing this on certain obscure phrases that actually favor **Chiliasm** <term>Chiliasm: the belief that Christ will reign on earth for a literal thousand years before the final judgment</term> rather than a supposed Restoration of all things. Hilary's own assertion is clear enough to the contrary, as is his solid demonstration in Canon 5 on Matthew, where he says:

> *Therefore, no rest shall be given to the nations, nor shall rest be granted by the shortcut of death, as they desire. But a bodily eternity shall be destined for them as well, so that there may be eternal matter for the eternal fire within them, and in all the everlasting ones, an everlasting vengeance.* <note>original: "Igitur requies nulla gentibus, neque mortis, ut volunt, compendio quies dabitur. Sed corporalis & ipsis æternitas destinabitur: ut ignis æterni sit in ipsis æterna materies & in universis sempiternis ultio sempiterna."</note> *If, therefore, a bodily eternity is granted to the nations only so that they may soon be destined for the fire of judgment, how profane it is for the saints to doubt the glory of eternity, when for the wicked, the work of eternity is provided for punishment.*

*Compare what the Benedictine Fathers, the editors of Hilary, have noted in their Preface, chapter VI.*

LXXII. But they also try to claim **GREGORY OF NYSSA** for themselves...

### PART I. DOGMATICS.

They [the proponents of universal restoration] are accustomed to cite him, as in his *Catechetical Oration* (chapter 26), his book *On Creation* (chapter 22), his *Treatises on the Psalms* (I and II), as well as in his book *On the Soul and the Resurrection*, where he clearly teaches that all evil must one day be entirely removed from nature, and that wicked men and demons are to be purged of their malice and subjected to the dominion of Christ. **PETAVIUS** <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a highly influential Jesuit theologian known for his work on the history of dogma.</note> supports them in this (chapter 7 of the work cited). However, an excerpt by **PHOTIUS** <note>Photius the Great (c. 810–893), Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar.</note> from the book by **ST. GERMANUS** <note>Germanus I of Constantinople (c. 634–733), who defended the church against iconoclasm.</note> titled *The Requiter and the Lawful* (Code 233), strips this witness away from them. In that work, it is observed that the writings of **GREGORY OF NYSSA** were shamefully corrupted by the frauds of the Origenists, <note>Followers of Origen who held to the doctrine of "apokatastasis" or the eventual restoration of all things, including the salvation of the devil.</note> *partly through false additions, and partly by violently twisting sound arguments*. **NICEPHORUS** <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos (c. 1256–1335), the last of the Greek church historians.</note> observed the same in his *Ecclesiastical History* (Book II, chapter 19). This view is all the more to be accepted because otherwise **NYSSA** would be at immense odds with himself; for in his oration *On Those Who Delay Baptism*, he denies all hope of salvation to those who die without it, *contrasting them with those who fall into new sins after baptism: For a sin may perhaps obtain pardon or mercy, for which there is great hope among the good*, <note>original: "Nam peccatum quidem veniam fortasse consequetur, aut clementiam, cujus magna spes est apud bonos"</note> but for the latter [those without baptism], salvation is altogether forbidden by a fixed decree: <note>original Greek: "το δὲ παντάπασιν ἀπηγορευμένην ἔχει τὴν σωτηρίαν ἐξ ἀποφάσεως ὡρισμένης"</note> *salvation is entirely denied to the other by a certain and defined sentence*. Compare this with **NATALIS ALEXANDER** <note>Noël Alexandre (1639–1724), a French Dominican theologian and church historian.</note> (3rd Century, Dissertation 27), where he simultaneously clears **GREGORY OF NAZIANZUS**, **AMBROSE**, and **JEROME** from the suspicion of this error, which the patrons of "Restoration" have pinned upon them.

LXXIII. The Protestant Church followed these footsteps immediately upon departing from the communion of the Papal assembly, declaring in the **AUGSBURG CONFESSION** (Article XVII): *Also they teach that Christ will appear at the consummation of the world for judgment, and will raise up all the dead; He will give to the godly and elect eternal life and everlasting joys, but ungodly men and the devils He will condemn to be tortured without end.* <note>original: "UT SINE FINE CRUCIENTUR"</note> It soon adds: *We condemn also the Origenists, who imagined that there would be an end to the punishments of the devils and the damned.* It is abundantly clear that the authors of the **HEIDELBERG CATECHISM** held the same mind from Question 11, and that the Fathers of the **SYNOD OF DORT** conspired in the same view from Article 37.

70. Just as none of the Orthodox Fathers before **ORIGEN** <note>A famous 3rd-century theologian whose views on the eventual salvation of all souls, including the devil, were later condemned.</note> called the eternity of punishment into doubt, so in the following centuries hardly anyone is found in the Church who dared to oppose it. > *Therefore, no rest is given to the nations, nor will the shortcut of death provide them with repose, as they desire. Instead, a physical eternity will be destined for them as well, so that there may be eternal fuel for the eternal fire within them, and in all those everlasting [beings], an everlasting vengeance. If, therefore, a physical eternity is granted to the nations only for this reason—so that they may soon be destined for the fire of judgment—how profane is it for the saints to doubt the glory of eternity, when an eternal labor is provided to the wicked for their punishment.*

Sed corporalis & ipſis æternitas deſtinabitur: ut ignis æterni ſit in ipſis æterna materies & in univerſis ſempiternis ultio ſempiterna. Si igitur gentibus idcirco tantum indulgetur æternitas corporalis, ut mox igni judicii deſtinentur, quam profanum eſt ſanctos de gloria æternitatis ambigere, cum iniquis æternitatis opus præſtetur ad pœnam."</note>

Having previously addressed the Church Fathers and their responses to Origenist views, the author now pivots to examine the "consensus of the nations," looking at how pagan poets, philosophers, and Jewish traditions have historically viewed the duration of punishment in the afterlife.</meta>

<header>ON THE ETERNITY OF PUNISHMENTS</header>

LXXIV. Distinguished men have handed down the consensus of the Pagans <note>Latin: *Gentilium*; referring to non-Christian peoples of antiquity, specifically Greeks and Romans.</note>, both poets and philosophers, regarding the eternity of punishments, aligning their views with the faith of the Church. **MINUCIUS FELIX** <note>Marcus Minucius Felix (c. 2nd–3rd century AD), one of the earliest Latin Christian apologists.</note> appeals to this when disputing with the Pagans in his *Octavius, § 35*: *And yet men are warned by the books and poems of the most learned poets of that river of fire and of the heat of the Stygian marsh <note>The Styx was the mythological river forming the boundary between Earth and the Underworld.</note> that frequently encircles them—torments which, prepared for eternal torture and known through the disclosures of demons and the oracles of the Prophets, they have handed down. And therefore, among them, even King Jupiter himself swears religiously by the torrents, the banks, and the black abyss. For, foreknowing the punishment destined for himself and his worshippers, he trembles with dread. Nor is there any measure or end to these torments. There, a wise fire <note>original: "sapiens ignis"; a concept where the fire "knows" to punish without destroying, often found in early Christian descriptions of Hell.</note> burns and restores the limbs, consumes and nourishes them; just as the fires of lightning strike bodies but do not consume them, and as the fires of Etna and Vesuvius and of burning lands everywhere blaze yet are never exhausted, so that penal fire is not fed by the destruction of the guilty, but is nourished by the undiminished tearing of their bodies.* **HUETIUS** <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and influential scholar.</note> (*Alnetanae Quaestiones*, Book II, chapter 24) and **PFANNER** <note>Tobias Pfanner (1641–1716), a German theologian who wrote on the "theology of the Gentiles."</note> (*Theology of the Gentiles*, chapter XX, § 16) stand in support of this same opinion. Nevertheless, we admit that these witnesses are not above all exception. For as far as the poets are concerned, the hyperbolic style of speaking which they love renders them less suitable as witnesses. Moreover, among the philosophers, they primarily follow **PLATO**, and it is not entirely explained whether he assigned any souls to hell without any hope of emerging.

LXXV. Regarding the Jews, there is no lack of traces among them of the instruction of the Fathers <note>Refers to the ancient Jewish patriarchs or sages.</note> who thought correctly about the eternal state of the damned. To this end, if I am not mistaken, belongs that saying in the *Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer* <note>A midrashic work on the Torah traditionally attributed to the 1st-century sage Eliezer ben Hyrcanus.</note>, chapter 43: *There is no repentance except until death.* <note>original Hebrew: "אין תשובה אלא עד המיתה"</note> And a passage from the Talmud in *Rosh Hashanah* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning the New Year and judgment.</note>, Chapter I, is excellently suited to this, in which the **School of Shammai** <note>One of the two major schools of Jewish thought in the 1st century BC, known for its more rigorous and strict interpretations compared to the School of Hillel.</note> remarkably defends this same truth, as cited by **WINDET** (*On the State of the Dead*, Section VI). **RABBII ABARBANEL** <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and philosopher.</note> adheres to the same opinion in his commentary on *Numbers XV:30*, as does **RABBII MANASSEH BEN ISRAEL** <note>A Portuguese rabbi and author (1604–1657) who founded the first Hebrew printing press in Amsterdam.</note> (*On the Resurrection of the Dead*, Book II, chapter 8), and others whose words were recorded by the celebrated **JOHANNES A LENT** (*On Modern Jewish Theology*, chapter XIX, § 18). But since they are few in number and authority, and have obscured this truth with other errors, we do not rely upon them too heavily.

->Uprooting and destroying false opinions.<-

<image-desc>A large, ornate drop-cap initial letter 'Æ' decorated with intricate woodcut-style floral patterns and curling foliage.</image-desc>The number of opponents and their various arrows, shot from many directions—which easily terrify the unwary by their appearance—require us to vigorously defend the **Eternity of Punishments**, now that it has been established by suitable reasons, against the force of those who assault it. We do not linger here on those who, having removed the distinction between the Mind and the Body, wish for everything that exists to be nothing more than certain modifications of matter. From this, they maintain that souls, whether wicked or holy, must gradually be resolved back into those principles from which they are composed, and thus they overturn the hope of Rewards along with the fear of Punishments. We now dismiss these ignoble spirits, who trample upon their own glory <note>The "glory" here refers to the inherent dignity and immortality of the human soul, which materialists deny.</note>, along with **SPINOZA** <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a philosopher often accused of atheism or pantheism in this period for his views on the nature of God and substance.</note> and **HOBBES** <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), whose work *Leviathan* contained controversial views on the state of the soul and the duration of hellfire.</note> (the latter of whom deliberately mocked the eternity of punishments). Instead, we shall listen only to those who acknowledge that the nature of souls is free from matter and death, yet nevertheless contend that punishments will have an end. However, since these men do not all fight from a single citadel, two distinct camps must be identified among them. For although they all contend that hellish punishments will have an end, those who—

...tain people, however, contend that it [the end of punishment] must be achieved by *Annihilation*, while others argue for the *Restoration* of the damned. <note>The author is distinguishing between those who think the wicked cease to exist (annihilation) and those who think the wicked are eventually saved (restoration or 'apocatastasis').</note>

II. The leaders of the first group in the early Church were the **Gnostics** <note>A broad term for early mystical religious groups who often held dualistic views of spirit and matter.</note>, as **TERTULLIAN** <note>An influential early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD).</note> testifies in his work *Against Valentinus*, Chapter 32: *And the soul among them is mortal, unless it has found salvation through faith.* <note>original: "Et anima mortalis apud illos, nisi quæ salutem fide invenerit."</note> This error arose from another, which TERTULLIAN critiques in the same work, chapter 29, where that worst of heresiarchs <note>A leader of a heretical sect; here referring to Valentinus.</note> distinguished three types of humans: *Spiritual, Soulish, and Material*. <note>original: "Pneumaticum, Psychicum & Hylicum." These terms describe a hierarchy of human nature in Gnostic thought.</note> He claimed the first and second were equipped with a good soul; to the third, he assigned a bad soul. These last ones were destined for destruction; the first were "perfect" and could therefore rush into any disgrace with impunity; those in the middle would either earn salvation through good works or be annihilated in the slime of matter.

III. The Gentile philosophers—whose writings he [Valentinus] plundered—gave occasion for this way of thinking, particularly those of the **Stoa** <note>The Stoics, a school of Hellenistic philosophy.</note> who followed **CHRYSIPPUS**. While some of the Stoics followed **Panaetius** in believing that all souls die with their bodies, others followed **Cleanthes** in believing that all survive at least until the universal conflagration <note>The Stoic belief that the universe is periodically destroyed and reborn in fire.</note>. Indeed, they almost all agreed with what **CICERO** taught in *Tusculan Disputations, Book I*: *they say souls will remain for a long time, but they deny they remain forever.* <note>original: "diu mansuros ajunt animos, semper negant"</note> Those whom **PLUTARCH** discusses in *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* (IV. 7), as well as **ARIUS DIDYMUS** (quoted in **EUSEBIUS's** *Preparation for the Gospel*, XV. 20) and **THEODORET** in *The Cure of Greek Afflictions* (Book X), dealt with this same group. For these made a distinction between *wise* and *foolish* souls, and held that *the souls of the foolish (whom Plutarch calls "uninstructed") and of irrational animals perish together with the bodies.* <note>original Greek: τὰς τῶν ἀφρόνων (ἀπαιδεύτους PLUTARCHUS nominat) καὶ ἀλόγων ζώων ψυχὰς συναπολλύσθαι τοῖς σώμασι</note> Compare **JAKOB THOMASIUS** in *Dissertation on the Stoic Burning of the World*, 15. Truly, their opinion suffers from a notable stain of impiety, because they thought that even the wise souls would last longer but would eventually burn up with the world—as **MÉNAGE** has abundantly proven in his notes on *Diogenes Laërtius's Lives of the Philosophers* (pages 325-326).

IV. To some, it seems that the **Valentinians** adopted this dogma from the **Jews**, because some of their Teachers <note>Referring to Rabbinic authorities.</note> early on brought it into their...

...also seem to have accepted this view. Whether this error of theirs is so ancient, I have my doubts. Certainly among more recent thinkers, **MAIMONIDES** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), one of the most influential Jewish philosophers and Torah scholars of the Middle Ages.</note> held this view in his *Treatise on Repentance*, chapter 8: 

> *Whoever does not deserve to live this life, he dies and never lives again, but is cut off in his impiety and perishes like a beast, etc.* <note>original: "Quicunque non meretur, ut vivat vitam istam, ille moritur, & nunquam reviviscit, sed exscinditur in impietate sua & perit, ut jumentum, &c."</note>

**R. MOSES NACHMANIDES** <note>Also known as Ramban (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar and mystic.</note> followed the same opinion. Many more passages on this subject were excerpted by **JOHANNES A LENT** in his *Jewish Theology*, chapter 19, section 18. Hence they conclude that a part of the infernal fire—which they claim was created on the second day—is to be annihilated; but that Gehenna <note>A term often used for Hell, derived from a valley near Jerusalem.</note>, which was created before the six days of creation, is to be purified and changed into Paradise. This is taught from the *Yalkut Reuveni* (item 2) and other places by **EISENMENGER** in *Judaism Revealed*, Part II, Chapter 6, page 360. <note>Johann Andreas Eisenmenger (1654–1704) was a German orientalist whose work "Entdecktes Judenthum" is a massive, though highly controversial and polemical, collection of Jewish traditions.</note>

V. In the Christian Church, this same error was embraced at the end of the 3rd century by **ARNOBIUS** <note>Arnobius of Sicca (died c. 330 AD), an Early Christian apologist.</note> in his work *Against the Heathen*, Book II: 

> *Although cruel death may seem able to extinguish souls and, having reduced them to nothing, destroy them with an unreturnable abolition.* <note>original: "Quamvis (animas) mors sæva posse videatur extinguere & ad nihilum redactas irremeabili abolitione delere."</note>

And thereafter: 

> *They are made and vanish, reduced to nothing by the failure of perpetual destruction. For they are of a middle quality, as has been discovered on the authority of Christ: they are such that they can perish if they remain ignorant of God, and be freed from destruction if they apply themselves to His threats and mercies.* <note>original: "faciuntur & ad nihilum redactæ interitionis perpetuæ frustratione vanescunt. Sunt enim mediæ qualitatis..."</note>

The origin of this error was a false concept regarding the bodily essence of souls. He thought that because souls were material, they would be gradually consumed by the torments and pains of a very long time; however, he believed that what is truly immaterial could not be subjected to any agonizing punishments. Whether any other Church Fathers drank in this error, we do not know. This one witness, however, is of less importance because the books he wrote *Against the Heathen* while still a <term>Catechumen</term> <note>A person receiving basic instruction in Christianity before being baptized.</note> prove his ignorance of Christian theology in every respect. He was certainly more successful as an attacker of the Pagans than as a defender of the Christians, as **DU PIN**, **NATALIS ALEXANDER**, **CAVE**, and others have observed. <note>These were famous 17th-century historians and bibliographers who cataloged the works of the Church Fathers.</note>

To this group belong those who think that although God threatened those punishments in His word, it remains entirely within His power as the Supreme Lawgiver to dispense with their execution and to apply some moderation, even if unknown to us. I gather from the words of **JOHN CHRYSOSTOM** <note>Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople (c. 347–407), known for his powerful preaching.</note> in his *Homily on the Resurrection* that people holding such views already existed in his age:

> "From where shall I persuade you?" he says. "When I say, *their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be extinguished* <note>A reference to Mark 9:44.</note>; when I say, *they will go into eternal fire*; when I place before you the rich man already wailing in the flames, you say, 'at least these are only threats.' This is a satanic word, making the Grace given to you useless and making you lazy."

Augustine, in *The City of God*, Book 21, Chapter 24: *“This also applies against those who, pleading their own cause, try to oppose the words of God with a supposedly greater mercy: arguing that these things are true precisely because men deserve to suffer what He said they would suffer, not because they actually will suffer them.”* <note>original: "Hoc autem & adversus eos valet..." > "Threats do not produce the same obligation as promises, because he who threatens takes on the role of a *Creditor*, while he to whom the threat is made takes on the role of a *Debtor*. Conversely, he who promises makes [the other person] a *Creditor*. Now, it is within the Creditor's power to waive a debt, whereas the Debtor is bound to everything he has promised." <note>This legalistic argument suggests that if God promises Heaven, He owes it to the person; but if He threatens Hell, He is the 'owner' of that punishment and can choose to 'cancel the debt' without being unfaithful.</note>

This opinion does little harm to our cause. For it assumes that the *eternity of punishments* is consistent with the decency and justice of God. Otherwise, He could not have even threatened them. Furthermore, once it is granted that God most justly threatened *eternal punishments*, it follows at least that it is right to fear them as long as it is not clear from another Revelation that God will grant a dispensation from them. Therefore, those who strive to release the human race from this fear disrupt the very calculations of divine Governance. Much less should one attack this fear with such flimsy arguments <note>original: "stramineis argumentis," literally "arguments made of straw."</note>. **Augustine**, in the place cited above, has already responded to the example of *Jonah*. One might investigate whether Jonah joined a proclamation of repentance with the threat of destruction, or whether he at least should have joined it by divine command. However, there should be no doubt that any threats made in public proclamation assume a silent condition: that the person continues in sin. The reason for this is that the "Time of Grace" has not yet expired—a reason which ceases to exist in the future life. Indeed, threats are put forward for this very end: that some might be saved *through fear*...

<summary>This page discusses the theological "Tillotsonian" argument that God's threats of eternal punishment might be mercifully remitted, using the legal analogy of a creditor forgiving a debt. The author refutes this by arguing that such threats are just and necessary for divine governance, noting that the example of Jonah's Nineveh does not apply to the afterlife where the "time of grace" has ended.</summary>

THEODORE CAMPHUYSEN <note>Dirck Rafaelsz Camphuysen (1586–1627), a Dutch poet and teacher associated with the Arminians or Remonstrants, a group that broke from strict Calvinism.</note>, famous for his sacred songs among the Arminians, asserts in a letter joined to them that he was prone to abandoning all religion until he happened upon those books which taught that perpetual fires and eternal torments were nothing. VII. HENRY DODWELL <note>An influential but eccentric English theologian (1641–1711) who argued that the soul is not naturally immortal.</note> gave another form to this error, defending the idea that souls are mortal by nature; in this, his assertion is not far removed from the assertion of THOMAS HOBBES in *Leviathan*, chapter 44. However, he added this peculiar point: he feels that souls are rendered immortal by the Spirit conferred by the hand of a Bishop in Baptism, as he argued in an epistolary discourse published in English in 1706. Various back-and-forth writings <note>original: *amœbea* — referring to "amoebaean" verse or dialogue, implying a literary volley or debate</note> regarding this paradox broke out between DODWELL and his various defenders and antagonists. One may consult ZACHARY GRAPIUS regarding these in *Recent Theological Controversies*, Part II, chapter 4, question 2, page 106 ff., where the sufficient sources for a refutation are also opened. Add to this PFAFFIUS in *History of Theological Literature*, Book III, pages 289–290.

VIII. Furthermore, regarding those who believe that the *Restoration* <note>original: *Restauratio* — often called "Apocatastasis," the belief that all damned souls and even the devil will eventually be saved.</note> of the damned is to be hoped for: some of them more modestly wish to determine nothing regarding its method. To this group belong those who think that although God threatened those punishments in His word, it remains entirely within His power as the Supreme Lawgiver to grant a dispensation regarding their execution and to apply some mitigation, even if unknown to us. I gather that people thinking this way already existed in the age of CHRYSOSTOM <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching.</note> from his words in the *Homily on the Resurrection*:

> *With what shall I persuade you?* he says. *When I say, "their worm will not die and their fire will not be extinguished," when I say, "they will go into eternal fire," when I set before you the rich man already wailing in the flames, you say these are merely threats. This is a Satanic word, making the Grace given to you useless and making you sluggish.*

Augustine in *The City of God*, Book XXI, Chapter 24: *“This, however, also prevails against those who try to plead their own causes against the words of God, as if with a greater mercy: so that they are true for the reason that men are worthy to suffer what He said they would suffer, not because they will suffer it.”* <note>original: "Hoc autem & adversus eos valet, qui suas agentes causas contra Dei venire verba velut misericordia majore conantur: ut ideo videlicet vera sint, quia ea, quæ dixit homines esse passuros, pati digni sunt, non quia passuri sunt."</note> Add Chapter 18. Among more recent authors, the same idea pleased **John Tillotson** <note>John Tillotson (1630–1694), Archbishop of Canterbury, whose sermon on the "eternity of hell-torments" suggested God had the right to remit punishment despite His threats.</note> in *Sermon XXX*, where he specifically brings forward the example of the Ninevites to illustrate his hypothesis. For although God threatened them with destruction in specific words, He nevertheless granted remission from the predicted punishment to the ungrateful Prophet [Jonah]. Nor does **Jean Le Clerc** <note>A renowned Arminian scholar and theologian (1657–1736).</note> show himself to be difficult in his review of this in the *Bibliothèque Choisie*, Volume VII, page 307 and following. **Anthony Collins** <note>A prominent English deist and freethinker (1676–1729).</note> mentions in his *Discourse on Free-Thinking*, Section 2, that **Henry More** <note>A leading member of the Cambridge Platonists (1614–1687).</note> and other Englishmen conspired in this same hypothesis, led primarily by this argument, that:

> "*Threats do not produce the same obligation as promises, because he who threatens takes on the persona of a **Creditor**, while the one threatened takes on that of a **Debtor**. On the other hand, he who promises constitutes a **Creditor**. Now it is in the **Creditor's** power to remit the debt, since the **Debtor** is held to all that he promised.*"

This opinion does little harm to our cause. For it supposes that *the eternity of punishments is consistent* with the decency and justice of God. Otherwise, He could not even have threatened them. However, once it is granted that God most justly threatened *eternal punishments*, it follows at least that it is right to fear them as long as it is not clear from another Revelation that God will dispense from them; and therefore, those who contend to release the human race from this fear take it upon themselves to disturb the accounts of divine government itself. Much less should this fear be attacked with such flimsy <term>straw-man</term> <note>original: *stramineis* — literally "made of straw," meaning weak or unsubstantial</note> arguments. Augustine, in the place cited above, already responded to the example of Jonah. It can be investigated whether Jonah joined the proclamation of repentance with the threat of destruction, or whether he at least should have joined them by divine precept. Regarding this, there is no doubt: whatever threats are made in public preaching assume a silent condition of [the people's] perseverance in sin. The reason is that the time of Grace has not yet expired, which is a reason that ceases in the future life. Indeed, threats are proposed for the end that some *through fear might be saved—* <note>The text ends mid-sentence with the catchword "salven-", likely from the Latin *salventur* (might be saved).</note>

IX. The remaining [opponents] more audaciously not only deny that the eternity of Punishments is taught in sacred writings, but even conceive various modes of the *Restoration* <note>original: *Restaurationis*, referring to the concept of "Apocatastasis" or the ultimate reconciliation of all beings (including the damned and the devil) to God.</note> of the damned. Here we rightly assign the first degree of absurdity to the **Pseudo-Mystics**, who emerged chiefly from the school of the masked **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of esoteric writings (Hermetica) that influenced Western mysticism.</note> and **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>The pseudonym of an influential Christian theologian and Neoplatonist of the late 5th to early 6th century.</note>; they asserted that all creatures emanated from the divine essence and would eventually return to it. There are indeed those who write apologies in their defense. Among these, the Jesuit **Sandæus** <note>Maximilian Sandæus (1578–1656), a Jesuit author known for his works on mystical theology.</note> stands out in *Mystical Theology*, Book II, Commentary 6, Exercise 8. Nevertheless, things occur in their writings which cannot be excused. Hence **Jean Gerson** <note>Jean Gerson (1363–1429), the influential Chancellor of the University of Paris, known for his efforts to distinguish true mysticism from heresy.</note> candidly confesses, according to his custom, in *Mystical Theology*, Consideration 41, *“that there were those who said that the rational spirit, while it is carried toward God in perfect love, fails entirely from itself and returns into its own idea, which it had immutably and eternally in God, according to that [passage] of John 1: What was made was life in him;”* <note>original: *Quod factum est in ipso vita erat*. This refers to a specific punctuation of the Vulgate Bible (John 1:3-4) often used by mystics to suggest that all created things have an eternal, living existence within God.</note> *he adds that they affirmed that such a soul loses itself and its own being and receives true divine being: so that now it is a true creature, yet it sees and loves God not through a creature, but as God Himself, who is also seen and loved.* However, those holding such views are usually divided into two parts. Those guilty of a coarser <term>Apotheosis</term> <note>The process of being deified or "becoming God."</note> alongside **Spinoza** <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), the philosopher who argued for a form of monism where God and Nature are the same substance.</note> are those who think that what emanates is of the same essence as the starting principle. A more subtle view must be assigned to those who indeed distinguish the world from God, but nevertheless claim that particles of the divine essence are infused into the individuals of which the world consists, which must therefore eventually return to God. The origin of this dogma seems to be traced back to the school of pagan Philosophers, both the **Pythagoreans** and the **Stoics**. Compare **Thomasius** <note>Christian Thomasius (1655–1728), a prominent German jurist and philosopher.</note> in the place cited, Dissertation XIV, §. 62 and following, and the whole of XXI; and **J. Fr. Buddeus** <note>Johann Franz Buddeus (1667–1729), a Lutheran theologian and philosopher.</note> in *Historical-Philosophical Analysis on the errors of the Stoics*, Exercise I, §. 3. From there it flowed into the Kabbalah of the Jews, of whose...

The famous **Buddeus** <note>Johann Franz Buddeus (1667–1729), a prominent Lutheran theologian and philosopher.</note> provides a summary of the opinions of these men concerning this chapter in his *History of Hebrew Philosophy*, page 395:
> Their philosophy, he says, seems to come down to this: that the first being, or the **Ensoph** <note>original: *Ænsoph*, from the Hebrew *Ein Sof*, meaning "the Infinite" or "the Boundless." In Kabbalistic thought, this is God prior to any self-manifestation.</note>, contains all things within himself, and that in him there is always the same quantity of entity in the universe, whether it exists in a created or uncreated state. Hence, in the created or "pre-world" state, God is simply all things, but this world finally exists only when God unfolds and evolves himself through emanations and outflows from the highest to the lowest, by which the diverse forms and orders of created things are established. Therefore, they frequently speak of vacuums, of vessels and small containers—as if to receive these outflows—and of flowing rays, and of the channels through which they run down and are propagated. Finally, when God withdraws and re-absorbs these rays, they say the external world perishes, and all things become God once again.

It is well known that the **Gnostics**, among whom the Council of Braga <note>A church council held in 561 AD in what is now Portugal, primarily directed against the Priscillianist heresy.</note> specifically names the **Manichaeans** and **Priscillianists**, held similar views. *Eutychianism <note>A 5th-century Christological heresy which claimed that Christ's divine and human natures were blended into a single nature.</note>, by asserting a confusion of divinity and humanity into the same nature, provided a "midwifery hand" <note>A metaphor for assisting the birth or development of an idea.</note> to this same error.* Furthermore, **Amalric of Bena**, a doctor of Paris, is believed to have been its promoter above others at the beginning of the 13th century—unless his opposition to the Roman See (which he regarded as Antichristian) and his conspiracy with the **Albigensians** <note>A dualist medieval religious sect in southern France, also known as Cathars.</note> on various articles of Faith gave cause for his reputation to be spitefully torn apart after his death. This was all the more easily done because among the Fathers and Doctors of the Church themselves, not a few are encountered who rendered themselves suspect by phrases that, at least, sound the same. It must be admitted, however, that the excuse applies to them which **Vossius** <note>Gerardus Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch scholar and theologian.</note> uses in *On Imitation*, Chapter IV, § 8, to mitigate the imprudent sayings of more recent writers on this matter: *The Christian religion does not acknowledge any **offshoots, or segments, or parts of the soul of the whole**.* <note>original Greek: *ἀποσπάσματα, ἢ τμήματα, ἢ μόρια τῆς τοῦ παντὸς ψυχῆς*.</note> Nevertheless, one may see many excellent men today speaking in this way: not because all of them actually feel this way, but more often because they do not sufficiently consider what they read or write. However, it cannot be denied that the **Enthusiasts** <note>A term often used pejoratively in the 17th and 18th centuries for mystics who claimed direct, personal inspiration from God.</note> foster something of a monster here when they defend the essential union of souls with God. Consult on this matter **Colberg’s** *Platonico-Hermetic Christianity*, Part II, chapter 12.

X. In another way, those who teach the *transmigration of souls* <note>original: *transmigrationem animarum*, the belief more commonly known today as reincarnation or metempsychosis.</note> into other bodies overturn the eternity of punishments. How widely this error had already pervaded Egypt and the entire East even before Pythagoras, and was disseminated among the Gentiles and Jews alike, is shown by the authors cited by the famous Christian Wolff in *The Philosophy of Origen*, page 36 and following, and by Elswich in *Philosophers Rashly Afflicted with Holy Men*, sections 16 and 22. Those who taught that souls pass through the bodies of various living creatures established that evil souls are thrust down into inferior bodies, and that this itself takes the place of punishment; however, they believed that these same souls, having been repeatedly released and purified from those bodies by a continuous revolution, eventually return to the higher powers. 

We dismiss the impious way in which Christoph Sandius <note>Christoph Sand (1644–1680), an Arian historian who sought to find precedents for his heterodox views in early church history.</note>—along with certain other Jews—attributed this stain to the Patriarchs and Moses in his work *On the Origin of the Soul*, page 100. Furthermore, he seeks support from the ancient Church in vain. We do not envy him his association with Simon Magus, Basilides, or Carpocrates, those impure Gnostics. On page 136, he adds **Clement of Alexandria**, whom he attempts to prove taught the transmigration of souls <note>original: *metempsychosis*</note> in his books of *Outlines* <note>original: *hypotyposes*, a lost work of Clement known primarily through summaries by later writers.</note>, citing Photius in *Codex 109*. However, Noël Alexandre, Nourry, and others have abundantly proved that those books were greatly corrupted by the fraud of heretics; for this reason, Photius himself, in the passage cited, attributes the errors excerpted from those books to Clement only with great hesitation.

XI. Regarding Clement’s disciple **Origen**, it is more certain that he was lured too much by the charms of Platonism in the school of Alexandria. It is particularly appropriate to set forth his opinion clearly here, since the more recent teachers of the *Restoration of All Things* <note>original: *Restitutionis omnium*, or *Apocatastasis*, the doctrine that all created beings—including the damned and the devil—will ultimately be saved.</note> count Origen among their chief leaders, lest they appear entirely destitute of any support from antiquity. In this matter, we would gladly oblige them, were it not that the difference between the Origenist system and the *Petersenian* system <note>Referring to Johann Wilhelm Petersen (1649–1727), a prominent contemporary proponent of universal salvation whose views the author is refuting.</note>—both in its argument and in the origin and method of the error—is far too manifest. It should suffice to show this in just a few words, since one may already read most extensively about this notable error of Origen in Huet’s *Origeniana*, Book II, chapter 2, question 11, and in Pierre Halloix’s *Life of Origen*:

XII. However, despite the diligent effort spent by so many distinguished men in excavating and explaining this dogma of **ORIGEN**, a precise account of his teaching cannot be expected. For it has been the constant opinion of all ages that his works were interpolated and corrupted by heretics and enemies of Origen alike. Nor are there few instances in which he so evidently contradicts himself that it appears either that he repeatedly changed his opinion, or that violent hands were laid upon his writings. Therefore, we must rely on the more general points in which **ORIGEN** is consistently similar to himself and where other ecclesiastical writers agree.

XIII. From this, however, one may conclude that **ORIGEN** did indeed conspire with modern **Apocatastatics** <note>Those who believe in *Apocatastasis*, or the "restoration" of all things, implying that eventually everyone—even the damned—will be saved.</note> on this point: he called into doubt whether the punishments of both demons and the impious are eternal. However, when our modern thinkers judge that all *Aeons* <note>original: *Aeones*; here meaning vast cycles of time or "ages."</note> of both life and eternal punishment must end and be absorbed into a different kind of "quiet eternity"—which they claim will no longer be subject to any change—they find **ORIGEN** by no means supporting them. For although he acknowledges that all things must be restored at the coming of Christ, he imagines other orders of new worlds following this world’s "economy," through which perfected spirits, if stained by a new fall, might slide back down into these lower realms. This doctrine is clearly enough revealed in his books <term>On First Principles <note>original Greek: *peri archon*; Origen's most famous and controversial work of systematic theology.</note></term>, and specifically in Book III, where among other things it is asserted:
> *From which we believe—since the soul is indeed immortal and eternal—that it is possible for it to descend from the highest good to the lowest evils and to be repaired from the ultimate evils to the highest goods, through many and endless spaces across immense and diverse ages.* (A little earlier he had said: *so that it might even be made equal to wickedness and the opposing powers.*)

**AUGUSTINE** explains this dogma most fully in his book *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeum:
> *There are also other dogmas of Origen which the Church does not receive: in which she does not falsely accuse him, nor can he be excused by his defenders; especially concerning the purga-*

...restoration and liberation, and again after a long time the return of the entire rational creation to those same evils. *For what Catholic Christian, whether learned or unlearned, would not vehemently shudder at that which he calls the "purgation of evils"? etc. And again, after very long periods of time, all who were liberated fall back and return once more to these evils: and these alternating cycles of happiness and misery for the rational creature have always been and will always be.* <note>original: "restitutione... semper fore." This is a summary of Origen's perceived errors regarding the "revolving door" of heaven and hell, likely quoted from Augustine’s *City of God*.</note> Consistent with this are the arguments he brings forward in the *City of God*, Book XXI, chapter 17. And it is according to this hypothesis that we must understand the <term>metensomatosis: the theory of the soul entering a new body, which Origen distinguished from the more common "reincarnation"</term> defended by **ORIGEN**. By this, he did not mean that souls released from the chains of this body immediately return into other bodies. That would have been <term>asystaton: inconsistent or logically incompatible</term> with the Doctrine of the degrees of Punishments and Purgations after this life. Instead, he judged that only after ages spent in supreme bliss, souls—through the abuse of free will—fall back into other bodies and subsequently measure out a new order of purgation. Hence, **PHOTIUS** in his *Library*, Code 8, reviewing **ORIGEN’S** books *On First Principles*, says: *He relates other things that are excessively absurd and full of impiety. For he talks nonsense about the migrations of souls and the stars being living beings.* <note>original Greek: "Μετεμψυχώσεις τε γὰρ ληρώδεις, καὶ ἐμψύχους τοὺς ἀστέρας" (Metempsychoseis te gar lerodeis, kai empsychous tous asteras).</note>

XIV. This will be made clearer when we consult the murky sources of this Error. Its external origin was, without a doubt, an excessive love of **Platonism**. Enticed by this, **Origen**, along with other teachers and students of the **Alexandrian School**, strove to reconcile **Plato** with Christian doctrine—especially in those parts where **Plato** appeared to have transformed the doctrine of **Pythagoras** into a better form. This study was fueled by the fact that the dogmas of **Pythagoras** had been drawn from **Egypt**, and they still flourished there during the beginnings of Christianity, being taught by the **Gnostics** <note>Early mystical groups often considered heretical for their complex views on spirit and matter.</note> to deceive Christians. Therefore, while the **Gnostics** taught a "cruder" <term>Metempsychosis: the transmigration of souls, specifically the idea that a human soul could inhabit an animal</term> alongside the followers of **Pythagoras**, which overthrew all the foundations of Christianity, **Origen** plainly rejected it. Hence, he says expressly in *Against Celsus*, Book V: *We do not in any way say that there is a re-embodiment of the soul and its descent even to the level of irrational animals; clearly then, unlike Pythagoras, even if we sometimes abstain from animals, we do not use their flesh for that reason.* <note>original Greek: "Οὐδαμῶς μέντοιγε λέγοντες μετενσωμάτωσιν εἶναι ψυχῆς καὶ κατάπτωσιν αὐτῆς μέχρι τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων..." (Oudamos mentoige legontes metensomatōsin einai psychēs...). Origen argues here that while he believes in cycles of the soul, he rejects the idea that humans can become animals.</note> In no way...
