# PART II. DOGMATIC THEOLOGY. 67

*...namely, saying that the migration of the soul occurs from body to body and its descent even into brute cattle; certainly not in the way of **Pythagoras**, for even if we occasionally abstain from animals, we shall not use their flesh.* <note>original: "scilicet dicentes... non utemur." This quote argues against the Pythagorean idea that souls can inhabit animals, which led to strict vegetarianism.</note> And in Book V of the *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*: *But* **BASILIDES** <note>A prominent early Gnostic teacher in Alexandria who taught that suffering was a punishment for sins committed in a past life.</note> *not noticing that this should be understood as the natural law, dragged the Apostolic discourse into the Pythagorean doctrine—that is, that souls are poured from one body into another—and attempts to build this claim from the words of the Apostle.* Therefore, **ORIGEN** deemed it better to side with **Plato** here. Although **Plato** admitted the passage of the soul from one human body to another (from the terrestrial to the celestial), he did not acknowledge the specific migration of the human soul into the body of a beast; and when he seemed to speak of it, it should be understood in a metaphorical sense regarding beast-like behaviors. Thus, when **ORIGEN** disputes against <term>metensomatosis: the Greek term for the soul's migration into new bodies</term>, which he does very frequently, he is attacking the error of the Pythagoreans that was adopted by the Gnostics.

XV. However, although he sides more with **Plato** here, he by no means agrees with him in every respect. Hence, in his work *Against Celsus*, Book IV, he says:

> *If* **Celsus** <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and the first major intellectual opponent of Christianity.</note> *had understood what follows the soul in the eternal life to come, and what should be thought regarding its substance and principles, he would not have so mocked the immortal soul entering a mortal body—not according to the <term>metensomatosis</term> of Plato, but according to another, more sublime contemplation.*

In this at least, he did not agree with **Plato**, if **SERVIUS** <note>A late 4th-century grammarian known for his commentary on Virgil’s Aeneid.</note> correctly understood Plato's mind in his commentary on *Aeneid* III: *that Plato says the soul is perpetual, and makes a transition to different bodies immediately according to the merits of its prior life.* For it does not appear that **ORIGEN** imagined other returns of souls into new terrestrial bodies, except those that were to be expected in those *new worlds* destined to succeed our own. Furthermore, in this very structure of new worlds, although he seems to approach **Plato’s** "Great Year" <note>The 'Great Year' or 'Platonic Year' is the time it takes for all the planets and stars to return to their original positions, often associated with the world repeating its history.</note>, a significant difference occurs between him and **Plato**. For he never taught—to use the words of **MEISNER** <note>Balthasar Meisner (1587–1626), a Lutheran theologian known for his "Physiologia Divina."</note> in the cited work, section 34—that equal revolution of all things which depends on an unchangeable fate after the passing of a determined space of time; rather, he refuted it more than once. Indeed, he purposefully disputes against this very idea with **Celsus**, and in Book 2 of *On First Principles*, [he argues that] not by some [fixed] course...

<header>ON THE ETERNITY OF PUNISHMENTS</header>

"...someone," he says, "souls are driven, having been revolved back into the same circles after many centuries, so that they either do or desire this or that; but wherever the freedom of their own nature aims, they direct the course of their actions there." <note>original: "aliquo, ait... dirigunt cursum." This quote refers to Celsus’s view of fate, which Origen rejects.</note> But **ORIGEN’S** cycle is different; it is variable based on the condition of the different use of free will, and it is not fixed to any certain span of time.

XVI. And so we slide gradually toward the internal origin of this error and the <term>fundamental falsehood: original: "πρῶτον ψεῦδος," referring to the primary error in a line of reasoning</term>, which was the idol of free **Will**. It is a constant complaint of the Church Fathers that **ORIGEN** paved the way all too much for the **Pelagians** <note>Followers of Pelagius (c. 354–418 AD), who emphasized human free will over divine grace—a view the early Church declared heretical.</note>. For he was of the opinion that all things capable of reason possess a perpetual use of liberty (or rather, an equilibrium regarding good and evil). Compare **JANSENIUS** <note>Cornelius Jansen (1585–1638), a Dutch bishop whose study of St. Augustine led to the Jansenist movement which emphasized predestination over free will.</note> in *Augustinus*, Volume I, Book VI, 13 and following; **NORISIUS** <note>Enrico Noris (1631–1704), an Augustinian cardinal and prominent historian of theology.</note> on the *Fifth Synod*, chapter 12; and the venerable elder, **J. JAC. HOTTINGER** <note>Johann Jakob Hottinger (1652–1735), a Swiss Reformed theologian and church historian.</note> in *History of Grace*, Book I, § 19 and following. Once this foundation is laid, nothing else follows except that the powers to turn oneself toward the better always remain intact for a rational creature, and that even those established at the very peak of happiness remain subject to the danger of sinning. **ORIGEN**, along with other Fathers of that age, undoubtedly fell into this Charybdis <note>In Greek mythology, a dangerous whirlpool; here used to represent an extreme theological error.</note> while they were avoiding the opposite Scylla <note>A multi-headed sea monster; here representing the opposite error of fatalism or predestination.</note> of the **Gnostics** and **Valentinians**—specifically their teaching regarding two equally necessary principles and the resulting fatal necessity of both good and evil. **HUETIUS** <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar who wrote the "Origeniana," a definitive study of Origen's life and thought.</note> noted this best in *Origeniana*, Book II, page 155: 

> *Finally, an excessive desire to crush the Valentinian heresy offered Origen a cause for error. For since they believed that those who were of a spiritual nature could not be damned, and those of an earthly nature could not be saved—and they counted the Devil among the latter, and Angels among the former—Origen, going in the opposite direction, stumbled, asserting that Angels could be damned and that some are indeed damned at times; and that the Devil could be saved, and in truth would sometimes be saved.* <note>original: "Postremo nimium... aliquando iri."</note>

The supreme rashness in defining things which these [modern] men display is diametrically opposed to his [Origen's] fluctuation and timidity. Hence, in Book I of <term>On First Principles: original: "περὶ ἀρχῶν," Origen's foundational work on Christian theology</term>, chapter 6, at the beginning, concerning the punishments of the damned and...

...about to discuss related dogmas, he introduces them thus: *These things are indeed spoken by us with great fear and caution, as those discussing and investigating rather than establishing things as certain and defined.* <note>original: "Quæ quidem à nobis cum magno metu, & cautela dicuntur, discutientibus magis & pertractantibus, quam pro certo ac definedo statuentibus."</note> **JEROME** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Vulgate, who was initially an admirer of Origen but later became one of his harshest critics.</note> himself acknowledges this modesty of **ORIGEN** in Letter 59 to Avitus, chapter 1. Indeed, Origen does not even think it advisable that these matters be made public, since they could easily foster <term>carnal security: the dangerous spiritual state of feeling "safe" from judgment, leading to a lack of moral effort</term>, writing in his *First Homily on Ezekiel*: *It was necessary to hide these things and not bring them into the open, but—<note>Note well</note>—the heretics compel us to bring things that should be concealed into the public eye: because they are usefully covered among those who are still children according to the age of the soul, who need the fear of teachers and must be corrected with threats so that they may be able to attain goodness, and through bitter remedies finally desist from the wounds of their sins.* No one is unaware of how greatly these words differ from the arguments of those who claim to be his followers. Moreover, these remarks deserve to be noted all the more because they simultaneously make it clear that this error was previously unknown in the orthodox Church before **ORIGEN**.

XVIII. It is clear from the refutations of the Fathers and the formal condemnations of the orthodox that this error wandered through the Church for a long time. **PHOTIUS**, **NICEPHORUS**, and **CEDRENUS** <note>Three important Byzantine historians and scholars who documented the history of the early Church and its councils.</note> provide evidence that it was condemned in the **Fifth Ecumenical Council** <note>Held in 553 AD in Constantinople; it officially condemned "Origenism," including the doctrine of the pre-existence of souls and the final restoration of all things.</note>. The riots of the monks on **ORIGEN’S** account, especially in Palestine, demanded this remedy; concerning these, one may consult **EVAGRIUS**, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 38. **HUETIUS** <note>Pierre-Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar who wrote "Origeniana," a definitive study of Origen's life and thought.</note> weaves together the history of others in the Greek Church who both defended and followed Origen’s party in *Origeniana*, Book II, chapter 4. They were also divided into factions, among which the names of the *Philoponians* and the *Canonites* became especially well-known, as is established from **TIMOTHY THE PRESBYTER’S** work *On the Reception of Heretics*, found in Cotelerius’s *Monuments of the Greek Church*, Volume III, pages 416 and following. Certain more recent "Enthusiasts" have recalled this error from the underworld, as it were. ### XIX.
We now arrive at the *final class* of thinkers. These are the ones who maintain that after various levels of punishment have been endured—corresponding to the variety of each person’s merits—and after the strict demands of divine justice have been satisfied, everyone will be restored. They believe that all human sinners, and even the devils themselves, will be gradually boiled out and purged <note>original: "excoctum atque expurgatum"</note> of all corruption by the very punishments inflicted upon them. They claim that at last, after certain orders of **Aeons** <term>Aeons: vast cycles of time or "ages of ages" used in ancient philosophy to describe the passage of cosmic history</term> are completed, or after all the "ages of ages" have been exhausted, these souls are to be joined in the same communion of highest happiness with the Blessed, who in the meantime have already begun to be clothed in heavenly glory. Together with them, they are to spend a full and peaceful Eternity, which will finally begin after those various levels of the "ages of ages" have passed. They attribute the immediate cause of such an excellent transformation to the restoration of **Free Will** <note>original: "Arbitrii"</note> to its original state of liberty, once whatever was sinful has been purged away by the fire of the punishments themselves. Yet they do not wish to seem to completely exclude the merit of Christ; they argue that He obtained salvation for all men and all angels alike, although they are quite confused, obscure, and inconsistent when defining the actual fruit of the Lord’s death, as is clear from what we noted in the preceding dissertation, sections 24 and 45.

### XX.
This is that *Eternal Gospel* <note>original: "Evangelium illud æternum"</note>, the announcement of which they claim has been specifically reserved for themselves. Nevertheless, they "turn every stone" <note>An ancient idiom meaning to try every possible means.</note> to win some protection from antiquity for their cause. Indeed, they realize without difficulty that it would be damaging to them if a doctrine of such weight—which they categorize among the primary and fundamental articles of Christianity—had been either ignored or rejected by the **Orthodox Church**. However, we have already dispersed a great part of these mists, both in the preceding dissertation (section 64 and following) and in the sections just prior, while we were discussing **ORIGEN** himself. He is the primary hero in whom they exult, although...

<header>PART II. DOGMATICS.</header>

Their claim to orthodoxy is rightly and deservedly called into question; we have snatched it away from them. **PETERSEN** <note>Johann Wilhelm Petersen (1649–1727), a radical Pietist who famously advocated for the "Restoration of All Things."</note> also dared to boast about Origen’s teacher, **CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA**, both near the end of his second volume (pages 47 and 48) and in his third volume (page 10). Yet, he brings forward no passage in support of this, except for one from the *Stromata* <note>Clement's major work, the "Miscellanies."</note>, Book VI. There, Clement deals only with Christ’s **Descent into Hell** <note>original: "Christi ad inferos Descensu"</note> according to a false concept that was already becoming prevalent among many of the Church Fathers at that time. While I would readily grant that this opinion provided a convenient handle for the Origenists to put forward their own views more confidently, and for many to think more mildly of them, it is clear that this idea has no inherent connection to the doctrine of the **Restoration of All** <term>Restoration of All: Known in Greek as "Apokatastasis," the belief that eventually everyone—even the damned and the devil—will be saved and returned to God.</term>. The same must be observed regarding the citations of other passages heaped together from various Fathers who speak awkwardly about the same *Descent* or about the *flames* that purge souls after this life. Furthermore, those passages added from **MACARIUS**, **PSEUDO-DIONYSIUS**, and others are either serving a hypothesis for free or are twisted by force <note>original: "per fidiculas," literally "by the torture-strings," meaning to interpret something in a strained or forced way</note> to support this matter, or they refer to that universality of calling and Grace which certain Fathers believed obtained in this life.

### XXI.
Perhaps more support might be found in the opinion of the **Merciful Brothers** <note>original: "Fratrum misericordium," a group within the early church who struggled to accept the doctrine of eternal damnation.</note>, against whom **AUGUSTINE** drew his pen, were it not for the fact that a difference in the system they followed is evident from the same source. For in Book XXI, Chapter 17 of *The City of God*, he writes:

> *Now I see that I must deal and peacefully argue with our merciful ones, who refuse to believe that eternal punishment will be the lot of either all those men whom the most just Judge will judge worthy of the punishment of Gehenna <note>original: "gehennae supplicio"</note>, or some of them; but they think they must be delivered from there after certain limits of time, longer or shorter according to the magnitude of each one's sin.*

In this matter, **Origen** was surely more "merciful," for he believed that even the Devil himself and his angels—after suffering more severe and lasting punishments according to their merits—would be plucked out of those torments and joined with the holy angels. And indeed, in the same work (Chapter 23), Augustine proclaims this particular error of **Origen** to be intolerable in the Church compared to the other, stating that he could not bear the arguments of men who promised purgation or indulgence even to the Devil after the greatest and most long-lasting punishments.

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion of Eriugena.</note> ...specially <note>original: "cialiter," likely completing "specialiter"</note> received, was done, and in the future will be generally perfected in all things. Therefore, let no one think it a small thing that the Word of God became human <term>inhumanation: a literal translation of the Latin "inhumanatio," referring to the act of the Word taking on human nature; usually called the Incarnation</term> and, as it were, saved human nature alone; rather, let him firmly believe and most purely understand that through the becoming-human of the Son of God, every creature in heaven and on earth was made safe. The first is that he wants it to be seen that he received this system not from men, but from God himself. Hence, in the same work on page 225, he says: *Regarding the return of human nature, and of all other things in it and because of it, into the eternal reasons from which they proceeded, and their restoration to their former dignity, I have neither read nor heard of anyone having written yet, although such a form of doctrine frequently shines forth here and there in the divine books and the teachings of the holy Fathers.* From this, it is clear both that the primary propagator of this error leaned too much toward Enthusiasm <note>In a historical theological context, "Enthusiasm" refers to the belief that one receives direct, private revelations from God outside of scripture or church tradition.</note>, and that before him, this doctrine had not yet been accurately or thoroughly dealt with in the Church.

For thus it reads on page 242 of the same work: *Furthermore, universal nature will be joined to the Creator and will be one in him and with him. And this is the end of all visible things, when all visible things shall pass into intelligible things, and the intelligible into God himself, by a wonderful and ineffable union; not, however, as we have often said, by a confusion or destruction of essences or substances.*

XXIV. Those who acted as midwives to this error after the Reformation offer little reason for pride to its supporters. *First*, it was revived by certain **Anabaptists**, a group of people as turbulent as any at that time; their names are listed by **ABRAHAM CALOVIUS** in his *System of Theology* (Volume XII, part VI, chapter 3, question 1). Among their leaders as early as 1525 was **HANS DENCK**, whose followers were called **Denckians**, although it is established from the *Annals* of **ABRAHAM SCULTETUS** (decade 1) that he was led by **Oecolampadius** to sing a palinode <term>palinode: a poem or statement in which the author retracts something said in a previous work; a formal recantation</term>. However, it is presumed from **JOHANN HEINRICH HOTTINGER’S** *Ecclesiastical History* (Volume VI, page 435) that this was only done for show. **VIRET** (in book II, *On the Ministry of the Word*) mentions the **Libertines** in France who held the same view. From the same flock, **STANISLAUS PANNONIUS** published a work on *divine philanthropy* <note>In this context, "philanthropy" refers to the Greek "philanthropia," meaning God's love for mankind</note> to defend this cause. *Second*, some who were infected with the poison of the **Socinians** <note>Socinians were a sect that denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ, often leaning toward rationalist interpretations of scripture</note> stood for this opinion, among whom we count **CAELIUS SECUNDUS CURIO** in his book *On the Greatness of God's Kingdom*, and **ERNEST SONNER**, a philosopher and physician from Altdorf. *Third*, many clothed in **Enthusiastic** principles leaned toward the same; to this group we refer **ABRAHAM VON FRANCKENBERG**, **FRANCESCO GIORGIO** (a Minorite friar), **PETRUS SERARIUS**, **JANE LEADE**, **JOHN PORDAGE**, and others. Even **JAKOB BÖHME** is understood this way by some who hold him in high esteem. Yet there is little doubt that many of these conceived even worse ideas in their minds, hiding **Deification** <note>the mystical belief that the human soul can become one with the divine substance</note> itself—if not the **resolution** of matter into its first principles—beneath phrases suspicious for their obscurity. *Fourth*, they increase the number of their witnesses by the addition of unconventional minds <note>original: "ingeniorum heteroclitorum," referring to eccentric or non-conformist thinkers</note> who lean significantly toward profanity. Such was **GUILLAUME POSTEL**, who defended this error in his *Key to Hidden Things*, although the famous **ITTIG** notes in his *Supplement* to the dissertation on Postel (Addendum 3) that he revoked it elsewhere.

<header>PART II. POLEMICAL.</header>

To the same category belongs that drunkard **ALEXANDER DE RAAT**, **THOMAS BURNET**, and—though more indirectly—**PIERRE BAYLE**, who, under this guise, exposes the "naked side" of Religion to the Manichaeans <note>followers of Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that struggled with the origin of evil</note> by teaching such things regarding the permission of moral evil from which the eternal damnation of most men follows. However, men of this sort are usually more inclined to attack the opinions of others than to frankly admit their own. Perhaps no one has exhausted more labor in assembling this opinion into a formal system than **JOHANN WILHELM PETERSEN**, who, in three volumes published in the vernacular <note>original Latin: *vernacule*; referring to German</note> on the *Mystery of the Universal Restoration* <note>original: *Mysterio Apocatastaseos*</note>, compiled his own reflections and those of others on this subject. These volumes gave rise to many responsive writings, the review of which we shall omit. Among our own countrymen, this matter has been treated more explicitly by the most illustrious men **HEINRICH HORCH**, **WALDSCHMIDT**, and **CLASSEN**.

XXV. It is now appropriate to finally approach the arguments that the *Neo-Origenists* <note>Modern followers of Origen of Alexandria, who famously theorized that all beings, including the devil, would eventually be saved</note>—whom we especially strive to defeat—bring forward in favor of their cause. Here, they first attempt to overwhelm us with a cloud of Scriptural sayings, but when these are weighed according to the rules of legitimate interpretation, they offer no protection. This will become clear from a brief review of those we have encountered.

1) Genesis 3:15. From this passage, **STURM** argues as follows: *The person whose head is crushed has had their life and essence taken away. Through Christ, the Head of the Serpent is to be crushed. Therefore, his essence—which consists in his malice—will be removed.* **Refutation.** There is a double flaw in the major premise. First, it plays with the ambiguous term *essence*. Second, the conclusion wavers. For in symbolic Theology, the *Head* is not an emblem of *essence* but of *power* <term>power: specifically, authority or legal dominion</term>. We can even invert the argument: The crushing of the Serpent’s head denotes something that already happened in the death and exaltation of Christ (Hebrews 2:14; Revelation 12:9, 10, 11). Yet, through that event, it was not the *malice* but the *power* of the Serpent that was broken.

2) Leviticus 25:8 and following. 3) **Psalm LXVI** [66] is referred entirely to the final Restoration of all things by **CHRISTOPH SEBACH** <note>Christoph Sebach (1650–1701), a German theologian who held views leaning toward universalism</note>, but on no other probable foundation than that in verses 1 and 4, "all the earth" is understood to include all the impious and earthly men, and because in verse 7 their conversion is predicted. 5) **Psalm LXXXIX:48** [89:47]. *Why would you have created all the sons of men in vain?* <note>Often cited as: "Remember how short my time is: wherefore hast thou made all men in vain?"</note> From this it is gathered that "since God does nothing in vain, and yet He would have created them in vain if they perish eternally, such a thing is not to be expected from God." **Response:** The Psalmist is not dealing with eternal punishments, but with the destruction of the **Davidic Kingdom**. If that had happened, the entire human race would have been sustained so long in vain through the long-suffering of God; indeed, all the promises and all the hope of Israel would have been empty. Furthermore, it cannot be said that all the sons of men are created in vain when some of them—while the rest are saved—manifest the rigor of divine justice for eternity.

6) **Psalm CXLV:9–10** [145:9–10]. *The Lord is good to all, and his mercy is over all his works. All your works shall praise you, O Lord, etc.* They wish this passage to be among the primary ones, since it is manifest that even the wicked and the evil Angels belong to the "Works of the Lord."

<meta>This page continues the logical refutation of universalist arguments, specifically focusing on the linguistic analysis of the Greek term "Apokatastasis" (Restoration) used in the New Testament to argue that it refers to the fulfillment of prophecy rather than the salvation of all souls.</meta>

# PART II. REFUTATIVE.

The term **Restoration** <note>original Greek: *Apokatastasis*</note> by no means supports their position. For even if it were granted that **Restoration** is the same as a **reinstatement to the original state** <note>original Latin: *Restitutio in integrum*</note>, as the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> seem to use this word in Genesis 11:13, 41:13, Job 8:6, and Jeremiah 23:7, it does not follow that this "Restoration" extends any further than the application of the salvation won by Christ, which is established until the end of the age. However, this word also admits other meanings, which the celebrated **WOLF** <note>Johann Christoph Wolf (1683–1739), a German theologian and Hebraist</note> recounts in his *Philological Observations* on this passage, while simultaneously citing many authors who deserve to be consulted here. Among others, he brings forward these points from **RAPHELIUS** in his notes on the New Testament from Polybius (p. 314): "Others take **Restoration** to mean the **fulfillment** <note>original Latin: *impletio*</note> of those things which the Prophets foretold. So say the **SYRIAC** version and **OECUMENIUS**; and among the more recent scholars, Knatchbull and Karlius in the *Bremen Library*, Class VI, p. 1112. And thus **HESYCHIUS** <note>An ancient Greek lexicographer</note>, perhaps with respect to this passage, interprets **Restoration** as **perfection** or **completion** <note>original Greek: *teleiosis*</note>, not inaptly, provided an example of that meaning can be demonstrated from ancient Greek literature." We, however, are not delayed by this, since it is sufficient a) that our word is used by the Hellenistic writers in a similar or related sense. **LIGHTFOOT** <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and Rabbinical scholar</note> indeed observes beautifully on this passage that not only does the **ARABIC** version interpret it as **consummation**, but also the Rabbis' term **completion** or **establishment** <note>original Hebrew: *hitqammemut* or *qayyamut*</note> corresponds to it. Furthermore, he notes that the prefix **from** <note>original Greek: *apo*</note> does not properly have the force of **back** or **again** <note>implying a return to a previous state</note>; finally, when it is said of Elijah in Matthew 17:11 that he **shall restore all things**, this is to be understood not as a restoration to a former state, but as the **completion** of all things. Regarding the same matter, **LUDOVICUS DE DIEU** <note>A Dutch orientalist</note> on this passage and the celebrated **ROELL** in his preface to Nemethus on Zechariah have observed that the verb **to restore** <note>original Greek: *apokathistanai*</note> is used by the Seventy to translate Hebrew words meaning **he placed**, **he caused to remain**, **he established**, or **he supported**. Thus, it is the same as bringing it about that a thing is in its proper state and place. Hence **SUIDAS** <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist</note> also defines it: **Restoring: giving, granting.** And as an example, he adds Psalm 16:5, where the Seventy place: *You are the one who restores my inheritance to me*; which he interprets as: *That is, returning the kingdom of the nations and the former dominion.* And in truth

### ON THE ETERNITY OF PUNISHMENTS

This notion is more consistent. For the sentence flows far more easily in which it is said, *until the confirmation, or the completion of all things, of which God spoke through the mouth of all his holy Prophets, namely through the fulfillment, etc.*; than if this sense were substituted: *Until the restoration of all things, whether of times or of matters, into their original state, of which God spoke, etc.* For either "of all things" <note>original Greek: *pantōn*</note> refers back to "times" <note>original Greek: *kairous*</note>, or it designates the matters themselves in the neuter gender. If you choose the former, times are not "restored," because once they have passed, they never return. If the latter, the Prophets do not speak so much about the objects themselves as they do about the **Restoration**. And furthermore, it is agreed among the debating parties that we should expect not only a Restoration to an original state, but also a transformation into a far more excellent state. 

b) Since the word "of all things" <note>original Greek: *pantōn*</note> is directly connected with the words, "which God spoke" <note>original Greek: *hōn elalēsen ho Theos*</note>, Peter hints at the specific presentation of those things individually about which all the Prophets spoke. Now, however, from the examination just conducted on the sayings which the **Opponents** <note>The "Antagonists" or universalists who argued that hell is temporary</note> are most accustomed to produce, it is clear that such a Restoration as they imagine for themselves was unknown not just to one or two, but to all the Prophets. 

c) The boundary point receiving the **Restoration** <note>original Greek: *Apokatastasin*</note> is the Return of Christ from the heavens. However, the dissenters claim that this return must be expected long before that restoration. For they bid us expect the **Final Judgment** either before the "Ages of Ages" <note>A biblical phrase for eternity</note> of the future life, or while they are flowing away together, whereas they claim the **Restoration** is only to be expected after those ages are finished. 

d) The Apostle immediately adds examples of the matters he was aiming at, which were all the **Benefits of Grace** promised through the coming of the **Great Prophet** <note>A reference to the Messiah, as foretold in Deuteronomy 18:15</note>, which have already begun to be displayed and are to be continued step by step, until *all the families of the earth have received a blessing through the Seed of Abraham.* 

e) If the "times of refreshing" <note>original Greek: *kairoi anapsyxeōs*</note>, which are mentioned in verse 19, are the same as the "times of restoration" <note>original Greek: *chronois apokatastaseōs*</note>, as it seems quite fitting to many, it is manifest that the reference is not to Ages to be expected at a long interval after the Coming of the Lord. Rather, it refers to those times to be completed *with* His coming, in which relief will be given from the heat of the afflictions of the humbled Church, and for which the seed of Israel ought to be prepared through sincere conversion in this present life. 

Compare **GULICHIUS** <note>Abraham Gulichius (1642–1679), a Dutch theologian known for his work on the prophetic books</note> in his *Sacred Hermeneutics*, latter part, section 61 and following.

## PART II. CRITICAL REFUTATION.

22) **Romans 5:18.** This passage is placed by **Ludovicus Gerhardus** <note>Ludwig Gerhard (died 1738), a controversial theologian who argued for universal salvation</note> at the very forefront as his strongest argument <note>literally "his Achilles," referring to an "Achilles' heel" or primary strength</note>. However, he explicitly admits in section 470 that it should be regarded as such only in controversies with Lutherans, but not with the Reformed <note>Calvinist theologians</note>, since the latter must first be convinced from elsewhere that God wills all men to be saved. We leave the task of extricating themselves from this conflict to them. We rest in the resolution of our own theologians, for whom **all men placed under Condemnation are all those among men who perish in Adam; to these are opposed whichever men become sharers of the Justification of life in Christ.** The reasons why we cast our vote for this interpretation are:

a) Because there is no difficulty in the translation. For our rendering of "all" <note>original Greek: *pantes*</note> as "whichever" or "all types" fits the character of the Scriptural style. 

b) Because there is a manifest ellipsis <note>an intentional omission of words</note> in our verse, which the particle "consequently then" <note>original Greek: *ara oun*</note> indicates must be supplied from the immediately preceding verses; for this particle here signifies "and so." The Apostle often uses it in this sense in this epistle, such as in chapter 7:3, 25 and 8:12, even with a similar ellipsis in Romans 10:17 and Romans 9:16. Now, in the preceding verse, **all these justified people are described as** "those receiving the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness" <note>original Greek: *hoi tēn perisseian tēs charitos kai tēs dōreas tēs dikaiosynēs lambanontes*</note>, "who will reign in life through that one man, Jesus Christ." It is most evident, then, that this is a description of those who, under the Economy of the New Testament, enjoy the more abundant measure of Justification. 

c) The "**all**" over whom **condemnation** <note>original Latin: *katakrima*</note> rules through Adam are not here every single individual human being. For they are those "**many**" who actually died by the fall of one man (verse 15), without distinction of sins or age (verse 14). And condemnation is abolished for those who are in Jesus Christ (Romans 8:1). Therefore, the law of opposition requires that by "**all men**" who are justified, we understand not **every individual**, but whichever ones [are in Christ]. 

d) It has also been abundantly observed by others that it favors us that in verse 19, the word "many" <note>original Greek: *polloi*</note> occurs instead of "all" <note>original Greek: *pantes*</note>.

23) **Romans 11:32.** This contributes nothing to this matter, a) because it is clear from the context that the "**all**" upon whom God wills to have mercy are not **every individual** but **all groups**, both Jews and Gentiles. b) Furthermore, it is plainly evident that this concerns the Mercy to be exercised in the last days through the conversion of both groups.

24) **Romans 11:36.** It is falsely assumed that all things cannot be "unto God" <note>original Greek: *eistheon*</note> unless they return into Him through a Universal Restoration. 25) **1 Corinthians 3:13–15.** They <note>the Universalists</note> claim "that the **fire of hell** is to be understood here, by whose purifying power they wish for a man who has done evil works (compared to wood, hay, and stubble) in this life to be finally saved." 
**Response:** 
a) This is not a discussion of just any sinner, but specifically of a Teacher <note>Latin: *Doctor*, referring here to a minister or theologian</note>, whose "work" is his doctrine. Nor is just any Teacher implied, but one who clings to the foundation of faith, even if he imprudently mixes in the "wood, hay, and stubble" of human doctrines that foster disputes, while keeping the foundation safe. 
b) For this reason, it cannot designate the fire of hell, but rather the fire of temptation and trial in this life. 
c) Nor does it say that he is saved simply through fire, but comparatively "as through fire" <note>original Greek: *hōs dia pyros*; implying a narrow escape or a difficult process rather than a literal purifying fire in the afterlife</note>.

26) **1 Corinthians 15:22.** **All those who will be made alive through Christ** are immediately called "those who are Christ's" <note>original Greek: *hoi tou Christou*</note> in the following verse (23). Thus, it does not refer to all men, but to those who are His own special possession, as the entire context demonstrates. Furthermore, this passage deals with the Resurrection of the dead, which our opponents themselves grant will precede the **Restoration** <note>original Greek: *Apokatastasin*</note> by many thousands of years.

27) **1 Corinthians 15:24–28.** This provides various weapons for our opponents, but they are made of lead <note>an idiomatic way of saying the arguments are weak or ineffective</note>. Therefore: 
a) In vain do they wish that the "death to be abolished" in verse 26 be understood as the **second death** <note>The OCR reads *mors fecunda* (fruitful death), but contextually this is almost certainly an error for *mors secunda* (the second death), the state of eternal punishment mentioned in Revelation</note> in which the damned lie. For from a comparison with verse 25, it is clear that this Death is considered as the **last from the number of those enemies** whom the Father wished to place at the feet of the Son as He sat at the Father’s right hand. Thus, the abolition of this enemy had to occur at the end of His sitting upon the Father’s throne. That reign, however, was to be terminated with the coming of the Son for Judgment. This is even more evident because the **end** is joined with this abolition...

(c) But also, *God will be all in all* immediately after the end of this administrative Kingdom. Therefore, it is all the more certain that *all* here refers to the same people discussed in verse 22.

34) 1 Peter 3:19, 20 compared with 4:6 does not constrain us at all, as we reject the *local descent of Christ into hell* <note>The "Local Descent" refers to the literal belief that Christ's soul physically entered the underworld between his death and resurrection to preach to the damned.</note>; and we judge that the "preaching" mentioned there refers to what Christ instituted in the days of Noah for the conviction of those who died in the flood. These things, however, are very far removed from the eternity which we attribute to the damned.

XXIX. The <term>Antagonists</term> <note>original: "Antagonistæ"; referring here to the Universalists or those who argued against the doctrine of eternal damnation.</note> are accustomed to spend their greatest effort in exaggerating the *Goodness* or *Love of God*. ,,Since God is *pure Love*,, [they argue] ,,it follows that Love is the foundation of all His perfections and the principle of all His actions; and this Love must exclude *eternal punishments*.,, Lest we stumble here right at the threshold, it is necessary to agree upon our terms. A double ambiguity can lie hidden here unless carefully distinguished: one in the concept of *Divine Love*, the other in the concept of those *Punishments* which are said to be contrary to it. To avoid the former, we note that these words designate either an *essential* or a *relative* perfection in God.

*Essentially*, the very *Holiness* of God is called by this name. Concerning this, we concede that it is the basis and source <note>original: "scaturigo"; literally a spring or fountainhead.</note> of all divine virtues and operations. But that Holiness has no object except God Himself. He is *Best* through His Holiness, because through it He cannot act otherwise than *well*—that is, in a manner consistent with His own perfections. He is entirely Love because, turned toward Himself, He approves of Himself, delights in Himself, and is most effectively and constantly active regarding Himself; He does all things for His own sake, and has—and can have—no other end for His working than His own glory. From this most absolute concept of God's Goodness, the Antagonists gain nothing. This is because He *acts well* when He separates Himself as far as possible from every object contrary to His perfections; and because He most evidently demonstrates that He loves Himself when He punishes the sinner who denies Him. This effect is truly one of *Love*, but of love scorned and violated, which makes its contemnor feel how great a *Good* <note>original: "Bonum"; here referring to God as the Supreme Good.</note> he has trampled underfoot.

On the other hand, *relative Goodness* and the *Love of God* designate nothing but His inclined will, by which He promotes the good of the <term>Creature</term> <note>In 18th-century theology, "Creature" refers to anything created by God, including humans and angels.</note>. This virtue cannot be viewed as the *primary* source of divine actions. For the exercise of this goodness is just as contingent and free as the creature itself is contingent <note>"Contingent" here means something that does not have to exist by necessity, but exists only because God chose to create it.</note>, which is the object of this relationship. Hence, just as He dispenses the degrees of this Goodness indifferently—since it is entirely within His power to make a creature more or less perfect at His pleasure, and to grant some perfection either to such an extent

...or to deny it to them entirely; thus it is indifferent to Him whether that creature be blessed or miserable, provided that through it He attains His own purpose. Furthermore, this <term>relative Goodness</term> <note>God's kindness directed toward created beings, as opposed to His "essential goodness" which is His own internal holiness.</note> is founded upon the essential Goodness. Hence, He loves nothing except Himself in that creature, and He loves it only insofar as He has placed a certain vestige or image of His own perfections within it. Therefore, since this image of God is nowhere more lacking than in a sinner, it follows that as long as He does not wish to restore that image, one cannot conceive how He would love a creature in whom no object suitable for Divine Love is found. 

However, by affecting that creature with a worthy punishment, He displays the rays of His relative Love in more than one way: first, regarding those who are punished, because this Love prevents Him from exceeding the limit in punishing—never punishing more than the creature deserves—which is why various degrees of punishment arise; second, regarding those who are liberated from those same punishments, who all the more acknowledge and admire the riches of His incomprehensible love shown to them beyond all merit.

> "For since *God* is pure *Love*,
> "hence *Love* is the foundation of all His perfections,
> "the principle of all His actions; and that this [Love] excludes *eternal*

Lest we stumble right at the threshold here, it is necessary to agree on terms. However, unless a careful distinction is made, a double ambiguity can lie hidden here: one in the concept of *Divine Love*, the other in the concept of those *Punishments* which are claimed to be contrary to it. To avoid the former, we note that these terms designate either an *essential* or a *relative* perfection in God. *Essentially*, the very *Holiness* of God is so named. Regarding this, we grant that it is the basis and source of all divine virtues and operations. Truly, that [Holiness] has no object except God Himself. He is *Best* through His *Holiness*, because through it He cannot act otherwise than *well*, that is, in accordance with His perfections. He is total *Love*, because having turned toward Himself, He approves of Himself, delights in Himself, and is most effectively and constantly active toward Himself; He does all things for His own sake, and neither has nor can have any other end for His work than His own glory. From this most absolute concept of God's Goodness, the <term>Opponents</term> <note>original: "Antagonistæ"</note> gain nothing, because He acts *well* when He separates Himself as far as possible from every object contrary to His perfections; and because He demonstrates most clearly that He loves Himself when He punishes the sinner, who denies Him. This effect is indeed one of *Love*, but of a love spurned and violated, which makes its despiser feel how great a *Good* he has trampled underfoot. *Relative Goodness and the Love of God*, however, designates nothing but His inclined will by which He promotes the good of the <term>Creature</term> <note>original: "Creatura"; any created being, such as a human or angel.</note>. This virtue cannot be viewed as the *primary* source of divine actions. For its exercise is just as contingent and free as the creature is contingent, which is the object of this relation. Whence, just as He dispenses the degrees of this Goodness indifferently, since it is entirely within His power to make a creature more or less perfect at His pleasure, and [to grant] some perfection either in such a degree...

XXXI. **BURNET**, in *On the State of the Dead*, page 244, takes another path, claiming "that the strictest application of the law is often called the greatest injustice <note>original: *summum jus, summa injuria* — a legal proverb suggesting that justice applied without equity becomes an injury</note>, or at least it does not harmonize with goodness and mercy; and yet God would be using the strictest Law while punishing with the most exquisite and eternal torments." It is in a Prince's interest to punish only a few of his subjects and seek to reform the others by preserving them, so that he does not rule over an empty palace. ### XXXIV. The **Justice of God** seems to conflict with the Eternity of Punishments on two main grounds:

> 1) because it does not appear that there is any **Proportion** between a finite or momentary fault and an eternal punishment;
> 2) because, in this way, all inequality of Merit would be removed, since all offenses would have to be judged as **equal**—following the view of the **Stoics** <note>The Stoics were ancient philosophers who famously argued that all sins were equal in gravity, a view the author here rejects</note>—if all are atoned for by eternal punishments.

Those who separate themselves from our view dwell most especially on this argument. Among them should be numbered a certain author in **Simon Episcopius** <note>A Dutch Remonstrant theologian (1583–1643) known for his more liberal views on dogma</note> (*Response to Question LXII*), **Tillotson** <note>John Tillotson (1630–1694), Archbishop of Canterbury, who suggested in a famous sermon that God might not actually carry out the threat of eternal punishment</note> in the work cited, **Ernst Sonner** <note>A German physician and Socinian philosopher (1572–1612) who argued against the eternity of hell on rational grounds</note>, and others who have dealt with this matter quite subtly. To us, however, this argument is not at all binding.

**A.** Because we would be defining the **Proportion** between sins and punishments recklessly, as long as our concept of the supreme Majesty of God—which is the foundation of this proportion—suffers from such great obscurity. And Reason itself rightly acknowledges with Paul that the Judgments of God are **unsearchable** <note>original Greek: *ἀνεξερεύνητα* (anexereunēta); a reference to Romans 11:33 regarding the inscrutable nature of God's decisions</note>. For if it is within the right of an earthly King to establish punishments for certain crimes which, although they may seem harsh, nevertheless agree with his own hidden reasons and those of his Kingdom, how much more does that Power belong to the **King of Ages**?

**B.** Even in a human court, the Proportion between crimes and punishments is not measured according to *time*. Many crimes committed in a tiny moment of time are punished with perpetual infamy, exile, imprisonment, or even the death penalty. This last punishment not only eternally strips one of the use of the present life, but also, among most people, cuts off forever all means of Conversion <note>The process of turning back to God/repentance</note> to escape the torments of Gehenna <note>A biblical term for Hell</note>.

**C.** Even if God has commanded Punishments to be equal in terms of *duration*, there remain other factors that involve a most equitable proportion—not only between the crimes and the punishment, but also between greater and lesser sins. These are the **DEGREES OF PUNISHMENT**, which Reason demands and about which Revelation commands us to be so certain, that it would be impious to deny faith to God who so solemnly witnesses to it. This certainty regarding the Degrees of Hell bids us to calmly wait...

> "If individual sins are infinite, how will God's justice be satisfied?

**D.** There is certainly something in the nature of crimes that corresponds to the Eternity of punishments: *first*, that the damage caused by them is irreparable forever by any powers of a creature; *second*, that the sinner *will not cease* from sinning for eternity, as was proven more extensively in the previous disputation (§ 30. 31.).

### XXXV.

It has a greater appearance of truth that in *Luke 16:24 and following*, good impulses of reverence toward Abraham and Lazarus and mercy toward brothers seem to appear in the Rich Man. But the Savior here is sketching the state of souls before the resurrection, which has not yet reached the highest degree of either Punishment or Despair.

*On the State of the Dead*, page 242: "God will not take away the power or liberty of leaving behind vices from one in whom He implanted the power—or rather the weakness—and the liberty of falling into vices. But, you will say, God does not take away this power or liberty from those wicked ones, but it arises from their own will that they persist, immovable and inflexible, in evil. I respond: But according to your hypothesis, God has so constructed their nature that they cannot help but be inflexible and irrecoverable once they have departed from this life or descended into their torments." 

**Response:** It is clear where these arguments tend: namely, that the "Helen" <note>original: *Helena* — a rhetorical reference to Helen of Troy, used here to describe a seductive but dangerous idea that people fight over</note> of **Free Will** <term>Free Will: *Liberum Arbitrium*, the capacity of agents to choose between different possible courses of action unimpeded</term>, which the patrons of **Universal Restitution** <term>Universal Restitution: *Restitutio universalis*, the belief (also known as Apocatastasis) that all created beings, including the damned and the devil, will ultimately be saved and restored to God</term> love so dearly, may be promoted. 

Furthermore, the disputant ought not to have torn apart those things which we join together in the origin of **Eternal Hardening** <note>original: *Induratio æterna* — the theological concept that the heart becomes permanently calloused against God's grace</note>: 
1. The **Meritorious Cause**, which is *spontaneous sin*, by which man renders himself unworthy of the divine Help necessary for perseverance in the good; 
2. The **Impulsive and Permitting Cause**, which is the *Justice of the Heavenly Judge* declaring the sinner to be henceforth unworthy of this Help; 
3. And finally, the **Efficient Cause**, which is within man himself. This is both *physical*, according to the Laws of divine Concurrence <note>The doctrine that God's power cooperates with every secondary cause in its action</note> with free actions (both bad and good), and *moral*, namely that very malice which, by its own nature, necessarily continues once the obstacle has been removed. 

These Causes, joined in this way, produce such an inevitable necessity of sinning that the sinner cannot be converted except by a miracle, and yet it cannot be doubted that God acts justly. This is all the more true because He most justly established a "non-losable" righteousness as the reward for obedience. From this, the law of opposition—where it is established that the merits of good and evil actions are equal, as was proven in the previous disputation (§ 48 and following)—requires that the abandonment of the wicked in their evil be just as constant as the confirmation of the righteous in their goodness. Thus, the same help which was promised for eternity as a reward is denied to transgressors for eternity.

**BROTHER FRANCESCO GIORGIO** <note>Francesco Giorgio (1460–1541), a Venetian Franciscan friar and Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, *Problems in Sacred Scripture*, Volume VI, Section 7, *On the World and Nature*, problem 252, asserts "that everything exists only insofar as it is good; but when goodness is removed, it returns to nothing, according to that celebrated saying of **Plato**, and afterwards...
"

<summary>The author argues that eternal punishment is a result of "Eternal Hardening," where a sinner's own malice and the withdrawal of divine grace make their state irreversible. He refutes the idea that this violates Free Will, claiming that God's justice requires an eternal abandonment of the wicked just as He provides an eternal reward for the righteous.</summary>

### PART II. REFUTATORY.

->"...however, according to *Aristotle*, EVIL DESTROYS ITSELF."<-

**Petersen** <note>Johann Wilhelm Petersen (1649–1727), a prominent German theologian and advocate for the restoration of all things</note> greatly praises this reasoning in the Appendix to Volume II, pages 13 and 14, and compares it with the Church Fathers who fell into the same opinion—namely, that evil has no root of essence. 

But how hollow this is is clear. For: 
1) Those who follow the decrees of the Gentile Philosophers—who were ignorant of the gravity of **Moral Evil** <term>Moral Evil: *Malum morale*, sin resulting from the intentional actions of free agents</term>—and consider sin as "non-being," ought to weigh carefully that *there are no properties of a non-being*, and therefore it *cannot even destroy itself*. 
2) If sin, by its very nature, destroys itself, then it ought to perish immediately after its birth. 
3) In that case, there would be no need for **Atonement** <term>Atonement: *Satisfactio*, the doctrine that Christ's suffering paid the debt for human sin</term>, not even *on Christ's part*; 
4) Nor, as our antagonists would have it, *on the part of the damned*. 
5) So far is sin from destroying itself that it instead gradually grows stronger like a gangrene, hardens the heart, and renders the sinner more incurable and worse because of the evil, as experience no less than Scripture teaches. 
6) If *Evil* destroys itself, then *Good* would arise of its own accord, since a rational creature is never in a state of equilibrium, but is either good or evil. 
7) Anyone who weighs the sayings of the Church Fathers will discover that they were driven into the opposite extreme partly by their hatred of the **Manichaeans** <term>Manichaeans: Followers of a dualistic religion that viewed evil as a physical substance rather than a corruption of good</term>, and partly that they denied—**unphilosophically** <note>original: *ἀφιλοσόφως* (aphilosophōs)</note>—not so much the *inclination to sin* as the *opportunity and actual crimes* in the damned, since they would have no rest from their punishment; as if the consciousness and sensation of punishment alone could not have vice mixed within it.

**C.** And from this, another pretext falls away by itself: the idea that "through punishments, the lust for sin is extinguished." For that lust is never extinguished; rather, it is merely poured into another form because the objects of desire have changed. Although the sinner cannot lust after earthly goods in the same way (as they were taken away with the world), he nevertheless lusts *against God*, his Preserver and Judge.

**D.** It is added—if not by the **Neo-Origenists** <term>Neo-Origenists: 17th-century thinkers who revived Origen of Alexandria's 3rd-century theory that hell is temporary and all will be saved</term>, then at least by those who argue from our own hypothesis: "Where there is no **Law**, there no transgression of it takes place; but there is no place for the Law [in hell], both because the space for performing it is not granted due to the atrocity of the punishments, and because the end of the Law cannot be attained in those whom God does not wish to be converted, but only to be subjected to perpetual..."

<meta>catchword: "...punishments."</meta>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Name" of the Holy Spirit, transitioning from the introductory title on the previous page into a specific scholarly debate regarding whether the name "Holy Spirit" is used exclusively for the Third Person of the Trinity or if it was occasionally applied to the Son (Jesus Christ) in early Christian writings.</meta>

# CONCERNING THE NAME
<meta>Catchword: Spiritu (Spirit)</meta>

is a matter of controversy. Regarding this, two questions can be raised: **A.** Whether the name is so unique to Him by way of title <note>original: "antonomastice," referring to the use of a descriptive phrase as a proper name</note> that it is never attributed to the other Persons? **B.** What specific emphasis or significance does the name carry?

II. The first question is called into doubt by certain learned men, who believe that even from the time of the Fathers of the primitive Church, *the Son of God was designated by the term "Holy Spirit."* For this reason, they appeal to the *Shepherd of Hermas* <note>A popular 2nd-century Christian literary work</note>, where in Book III, Similitude V, § 5, it is said: *Moreover, the Son is the Holy Spirit*; **George Bull** <note>A prominent 17th-century English theologian</note> contends that these words refer to the Second Person [the Son] in his *Defense of the Nicene Faith*, Section II, chapter 2. **J. Ernst Grabe** tries to excuse this most learned man from a charge of negligence in his notes, and he also finds agreement from **Comenius** in his *Admonition to Irenaeus Irenicus*, pages 100–101, and **Ittig** in his work on the first century, Chapter 3, Section 3, § 7, page 161. However, the context suggests something entirely different. For a certain parable had been proposed in which the *Master of the Estate*, his *Son*, and a *Servant* are clearly distinguished. This is applied to the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity as follows: *The Master of the estate is shown to be He who created and finished all things, and gave power to them. Moreover, the Son is the Holy Spirit. But that servant is the Son of God.* It is very clear here that the *Son*, who is called the *Holy Spirit*, is none other than the "son of the family" proposed in the parable. But if anyone decides that it is less than fitting for the Second Person to be proposed under the figure of the *servant* and the Third Person under the figure of the *son of the family*, it is all the same to me, since one might as well count this distorted parable among the most tasteless absurdities of Hermas. By the grace of God, our holy faith does not stand in need of such defenders. Other Fathers have also been called to support this view by **Grotius** in his notes on Mark 2:8, **Raupach** in his *Sacred Observations from the Apostolic Fathers*, and **Schoettgen** in his work on the <term>invocation</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπικλήσει (epiklēsei), referring to the calling upon or naming of a deity</note> of the Holy Spirit. However, I notice that no passage is brought forward by them in which the Second Person is <term>expressly</term> <note>original Greek: κατὰ ῥητὸν (kata rēton), meaning literally or according to the written word</note> called the *Holy Spirit*. They all stop at calling Christ *Spirit, Immaculate Spirit,* or *Spirit of God*, which is not the question here. For although **Grotius** praises **Cyprian** <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage</note> for writing in *On the Vanity of Idols*: *The Holy Spirit puts on flesh*, nevertheless, the best manuscripts are unaware of that reading, and in the printed copies it is read as: *The flesh...*

### CHAPTER I. ON THE HOLY SPIRIT
<note>original: "SPIRITUS SANCTI CAP. I."</note>

**IV**
<meta>catchword: rests,</meta>

...with the Holy Spirit cooperating, he is clothed. With better justification, certain ancient and more recent interpreters are brought into this discussion who have applied some passages of Scripture, in which mention of the Holy Spirit is made, to Christ; **Campegius Vitringa the Younger** <note>A Dutch theologian (1693–1723) known for his work on the early church</note> set out to argue their cause in a specific, professional dissertation.

III. The entire case rests upon the testimony of Holy Scripture, in which, however, we rightly require such passages that preserve the complete phrase **HOLY SPIRIT** without any alteration. For this reason, we set aside:
*   **Romans 1:4**, where the phrase "spirit of holiness" <note>original Greek: πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης</note> is used.
*   **Mark 2:8**, **1 Timothy 3:16**, and **1 Peter 3:19**, where simply "spirit" <note>original Greek: πνεῦμα</note> is mentioned.
*   **1 Corinthians 15:45**, where "life-giving spirit" <note>original Greek: πνεῦμα ζωοποιῶν</note> is used.
*   **Hebrews 9:14**, where "eternal spirit" <note>original Greek: πνεῦμα αἰώνιον</note> is recorded.

The clear change of terms in these places can rightly be seen as intended to more specifically direct our meditation toward the <term>Second Person</term> <note>referring to God the Son, or Jesus Christ</note>.

IV. The most significant passage, therefore, which comes into consideration here, is **Luke 1:35**, where the Angel says to Mary: *The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee.* Following **Justin Martyr** (*Apology 2*), **Tertullian** (*Against the Jews*, chapter 13, and *Against Praxeas*, chapter 26), and **Ambrose** (on Romans 1:4), certain more recent theologians—and most notably the celebrated **Johannes Cocceius** in various places, which the famous **Bynaeus** <note>Anthony Bynaeus (1654–1698), a Dutch theologian</note> transcribed and refuted in *On the Nativity of Jesus Christ*, Book I, chapter 1, § 40—have striven to claim this passage for Christ. We do not, however, grant them our approval <note>original: "Pollicem tamen illis non premimus," a Latin idiom for showing favor</note>, since a fundamental reason would have to intervene for us to depart from the constant usage of the phrase in this one saying alone—a reason which does not appear here. It is pointed out, indeed, that according to the accepted hypothesis, this passage can be less successfully urged against the <term>Socinians</term> <note>A group that denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ</note>. But aside from the fact that the right to demand the truth cannot be taken from the <term>Anti-Trinitarians</term> just because we do not deviate from the accepted meaning for the sake of a hypothesis, the celebrated **Cocceius** himself has abundantly taught that the greatest strength of this passage remains even if we stick to the customary notion. Therefore, concerning the cited passage of Luke, he argues as follows: *that the Holy Spirit, insofar as it signifies the third person, cannot be said to come into any mother so that the Son being born is called the Son of God, unless the Son of Man is also the Son of God. For he who is the Son of God is such because the Spirit of the Father and of the only-begotten Son of God rests upon him from the beginning of conception,*

### VI.

*...rests, he is necessarily and truly the only-begotten and eternal Son of God.*
This is even more compelling when, through the "Power of the Most High," the power of the Son of God himself is understood to be occupied in building for himself this **Tabernacle of humanity** <note>A metaphorical way of describing the Incarnation, where God "pitched his tent" in human flesh</note>. See, in addition to the authors cited by the distinguished **Wolf** <note>Johann Christoph Wolf (1683–1739), a German Hebraist and theologian</note> on this passage, the celebrated **Cremer** in his *Theological Exercises on the Firstborn Son of God*, dissertation VI, § 4 and following.

V. Furthermore, there are some who maintain that in **Matthew 12:31**, the *Holy Spirit*—against whom blasphemy is declared unforgivable—should be understood as the Divinity of Christ. The distinguished **Olearius** <note>Gottfried Olearius (1672–1715), a philologist and theologian</note>, in his *Observations on Matthew* (XLVI), lists the passages from the Church Fathers cited for this view. However, it is not clearly evident from those cited examples that this was their actual meaning. As an example, take a testimony that seems more evident than the rest, from **Cyprian** <note>Bishop of Carthage and early Christian writer (c. 210–258 AD)</note> in *Epistle 16*. When he was discussing how pardon should not be easily granted to the "lapsed" <note>Christians who renounced their faith under Roman persecution</note>—that is, those who denied Christ—he adds the passage we are discussing:

> *All sins and blasphemies shall be forgiven the sons of men. But whoever shall blaspheme the Holy Spirit shall not have forgiveness, but is guilty of eternal sin.*

From this, **Rigaltius** <note>Nicolas Rigault (1577–1654), a French classical scholar</note> concludes that Cyprian felt that blaspheming the Holy Spirit was exactly the same thing as denying Christ. However, that does not follow at all. It was sufficient for Cyprian to bring forward that saying in this case if he merely judged that the formal nature of that sin—which is called blasphemy against the Holy Spirit—consists in the rejection of the Son of God; thus, an apostate is guilty of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit through their hatred of the truth, which rests upon the testimony of the Holy Spirit. This was certainly the understanding of that sin held by the Fathers of that age, such as **Origen**, **Clement of Alexandria**, and others. More to the point <note>original Latin: "ad rhombum," an idiom meaning "hitting the mark" or "getting to the point"</note> are the things **Suicer** <note>Johann Caspar Suicer (1620–1684), author of a famous dictionary of Greek Church Fathers</note> brings from **Athanasius**, **Photius**, and others in his *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus* (Vol. I, p. 699). Nevertheless, the arguments brought by **Fell** and **Zorn** in favor of this hypothesis are of no great weight, since the nature of this sin is such that it is most directly an injury against the <term>Third Person</term> <note>The Holy Spirit, distinct from God the Father and God the Son</note>, as will be explained in its proper place. Compare the arguments **Lilienthal** discusses against Zorn in the *Appendix to the dissertation on the sin against the Holy Spirit*.

# CHAPTER I: THE HOLY SPIRIT

### VI.

But the distinguished **Schoettgen** <note>Christian Schoettgen (1687–1751), a German biblical scholar known for using rabbinic literature to explain the New Testament</note> in the place cited (§ 3), regarding **Luke 4:1, 14**, maintains that the divinity of Christ is expressly called the **Holy Spirit**, since Christ himself, full of this Spirit, went into the desert to endure temptation. The words of the Evangelist are: *Jesus, being full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan, and was led by the Spirit into the desert* <note>original: "Jesus autem plenus Spiritu Sancto revertit à Jordane; και ήγετο ἐν πνευματι εἰς την έρημον"</note>, which is rightly rendered as: *And he was led by the same Spirit into the desert.* Indeed, there appears to be no reason why we should follow the distinguished **Homberg** <note>Andreas Homberg (1653–1710), a legal scholar and theologian</note> in understanding the "Spirit" mentioned in the second instance as the Spirit of Christ’s own Divinity, nor why we should deny that the Spirit who inhabited, filled, and led Christ was the Third Person of the Trinity.

### VII.

In the pages of the Old Testament, the complete name "HOLY SPIRIT" does not occur in this exact construction. However, there are closely related phrases, such as **Spirit of His holiness** <note>original Hebrew: רוח קדשו (*ruach kodsho*)</note> in **Psalm 51:11** and **Isaiah 63:10, 11**, as well as the Aramaic <note>The text refers to this as "Chaldaicum," an older term for the Aramaic language used in the book of Daniel</note> in **Daniel 4:8, 9, 18** <note>original Aramaic: רוח אלהין קדישין (*ruach elahin kaddishin*), usually translated as "the spirit of the holy gods"</note>, **Spirit of the Holy Gods**. The **Targum** <note>An ancient Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> imitates this in **Psalm 143:10**, writing **Your good holy Spirit** <note>original: רוח קודשך טבא (*ruach kodshak taba*)</note>. There is no doubt that the New Testament refers back to these passages, all the more so because the **Septuagint** <note>The influential Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX</note> renders them as *the holy spirit of God* <note>original: το πνευμα Θεου το άγιον</note>. From this, it became customary among the Jews themselves to call it the **Holy Spirit** <note>original Hebrew: רוח הקדוש (*Ruach Ha-Kodesh*)</note> in their own dialect. Nevertheless, the interpretation of this name should not be sought solely from Jewish sources, as **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and Hebraist</note> incautiously argued in his *Harmony of the Evangelists* on **Luke 4:1**; for the following pages will show just how much the Jews drifted from the correct faith of the Fathers regarding the Holy Spirit.

### VIII.

For those investigating the true emphasis of this characteristic name, it will easily become clear that one must necessarily depart from its common meaning. I do not wish to wander here into the **multiple meanings** <note>original: πολυσημιαν (*polysemia*), referring to a word having many different senses</note> of the word **SPIRIT**. On that matter, besides the lexicographers, one may consult **Vorstius** <note>Johannes Vorstius (1623–1676), a scholar of "Sacred Philology"</note> in his *Philologia Sacra* (Part I, p. 130 ff.) and, more accurately than others, **Christian Ludovici** <note>Christian Ludovici (1663–1732), a philosopher and theologian</note> in *On the Spirit of Moses* (§ 9 ff.). # I. ON THE NAME

...motion, and therefore nothing but an accident <note>In philosophical terms, an "accident" is a property that does not exist by itself but only within a substance, like color or movement</note>. Which of these notions holds priority in antiquity is not a matter of such great importance. And no danger of **Hobbesianism** <note>Referring to the philosophy of Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), whose mechanical view of the world was often accused of leading to atheism or materialism</note> is to be feared from this, even if someone should judge that <term>ruach</term> <note>original Hebrew: רוח, meaning wind, breath, or spirit</note> properly designates "wind," as I see was objected to **WITTER** by **GRAPIUS** in *Theology of Recent Controversies, Part I, p. 73*, and by others. It is enough that a remarkable analogy exists between motion and a "thinking essence." For motion in bodies constitutes their life, in a way, just as thinking does in minds. Whatever the case, we must not stop at either notion here. Not in the notion of *breath* [or wind], because the spiritual essence of the Third Person is not subject to physical motion. Nor in the more sublime notion of a *thinking substance*. For perfect Thought, just like Holiness, constitutes the essence of the entire divine nature so absolutely that it applies to each divine person in equal degree. 

**DIDYMUS** <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398), an Alexandrian theologian and author of a famous treatise on the Holy Spirit</note> says in *On the Holy Spirit, Book III*: *The terms "sanctification" and "goodness" refer equally to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; just as the title "Spirit" does. For the Father is called Spirit, as in the passage "God is a Spirit"; and the Son is called Spirit, as when it says "The Lord is his Spirit." However, the Holy Spirit is always designated by the title "Holy Spirit"; not because he is placed alongside the Father and Son merely through a shared name, but because one nature possesses one name.* <note>original Latin: "Sanctificationis bonitatisque vocabulum & ad Patrem & ad Filium & ad Spiritum Sanctum æque refertur..."</note> Add to this the passages collected on this matter by **PETAVIUS** <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a French Jesuit theologian and key figure in the history of dogma</note> in *On the Trinity, Book VII, ch. 10, § 9*. We must therefore move to a more figurative sense, which can be understood here in two ways: one *metonymical*, the other *metaphorical*.

IX. Those who explain our name through *metonymy* <note>A figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it, such as "the crown" for the king</note> borrow the reasoning for the name from the works of the Holy Spirit, while looking toward the notion of a *thinking substance*. He can indeed be forcefully called **SPIRIT**, both because the primary object and stage (so to speak) of His works is the spirit of the elect; and because He is the Author of that new nature in the elect, which is usually contrasted with the "flesh" under the name of "Spirit" (*John 3:8*), since it encompasses spiritual qualities and constitutes the true perfection and life of created minds.

For Scripture frequently employs these symbols to foreshadow the operations of the Holy Spirit, who is the immediate author of every *motion* in the Kingdom of nature and of grace. It was therefore fitting that a symbol most suited to foreshadowing the whole character of the Third Person’s economy <note>In theology, "economy" refers to God's management or arrangement of the world and the plan of salvation</note> should provide an occasion for His characteristic name. Between these two metaphors, however, the Church Fathers have generally preferred the latter, because the *breathing of breath* seemed more convenient to them for foreshadowing the mystery of the *Procession of the Holy Spirit* <note>The "Procession" is the technical term for the eternal relationship of the Holy Spirit to the Father and the Son</note>. **PETAVIUS** <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a French Jesuit theologian renowned for his work on the history of dogma</note> has collected passages on this matter in the place cited, section 1 and following.

XI. For He is called *Holy in Himself* because the *Sanctification* of the sinner—which demonstrates the perfect holiness of its Author—is His peculiar work in the economy of salvation. No less fittingly is He the *Spirit of the Holiness of God*, or what amounts to the same thing, the *Spirit of the holy God*, because that work is such that it reveals the *Holiness* of both the *Father* and the *Son* in an illustrious manner.

It is *exchanged* with others whenever it indicates His more specific relations, whether to the other persons of the Godhead, to the subjects upon whom He works, or to the operations themselves. The first occurs whenever He is called the *Spirit of Jehovah*, the *Spirit of God*, the *Spirit of the Father*, or the *Spirit of Christ*. The second is seen in the passage of **2 Kings 2:9**, where He is called the *Spirit of Elijah*. That this was indeed the *Holy Spirit* is clear from a comparison with **Luke 1:15, 17**. Closely related to this is what is read concerning the *Spirit* that was upon Moses in **Numbers 11:16, 25**. Regarding the third, this occurs whenever He is called the *Spirit of knowledge, truth, faith*, and so on, after the gifts with which He enriches the soul. # ON THE NAME

...indicate that the subject being discussed is the one who is distinguished by this name through excellence <note>original: *per excellentiam*—a logical term meaning a name is used for the most supreme example of a category, e.g., calling the Holy Spirit "The Spirit"</note>.

XIII. Moreover, this characteristic name has a peculiarity compared to the names of the other Persons <note>Referring to the Father and the Son in the Trinity</note>, in that it sometimes seems to be applied through <term>metonymy</term> <note>A figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something closely associated with it, such as using "the Spirit" to mean "the gifts of the Spirit"</note> to **spiritual gifts**. Our theologians are quite willing to grant this hypothesis; but perhaps they are sometimes too willing, interpreting certain passages as referring to the gifts of the Holy Spirit while excluding His Person. For to those who examine these passages more diligently, it will be clear that not only is the Person of the Holy Spirit assumed in them, but—such is the richness of the sacred style—He is simultaneously *involved*; indeed, He is the primary one designated, albeit considered in relation to those gifts. We shall illustrate this with a few examples, which will serve as a beacon for the rest.

XIV. Generally, this refers to phrases in which it is said that the Spirit *rests upon someone, comes into them, is poured out, is in them, dwells in them*, etc. A very large part of the passages that are explained as referring to the **Gifts** rather than the **Person** of the Holy Spirit can be assigned to this category. This interpretation is often made without sufficient cause: 1) because these phrases express the very operations of the Holy Spirit using highly appropriate metaphors. For what, for example, is *outpouring* <note>original: *effusio*</note>, if not His very *mission* <note>The theological concept of the "sending" of the Spirit into the world</note> represented through the symbol of pouring? What is *indwelling* <note>original: *inhabitatio*</note>, but the constant and effective guidance of the faithful? Now, if these words outline the actions of the Holy Spirit, and action is a quality of a **Person** rather than a **Gift**, who can doubt that all such passages designate the **Person** of the Holy Spirit more than the **Gifts**? Add to this 2) that these metaphors are drawn from types and symbols representing the Person of the Holy Spirit Himself. *Outpouring* alludes to the symbol of **water**; *indwelling* to the presence of the Holy Spirit with the other Persons in the **Sanctuary of the Old Testament**. 3) Indeed, in those very allegorical passages, the Spirit is frequently distinguished from His Gifts. Thus, in **Isaiah 44:4**, the divine *blessing* (encompassing all spiritual goods) is mentioned alongside the *Spirit*. Likewise, in **Zechariah 12:10**, while the *outpouring of the Spirit of grace and supplication* is promised, undoubtedly *grace and supplications* encompass the sum total of heavenly gifts. What, then, does "the Spirit" designate here, if not their Author?
