# CHAPTER I. ON THE HOLY SPIRIT

XV. It will be no less appropriate to apply this rule to other passages as well. Indeed, all those err who interpret the *seven Spirits* in Revelation 1:4 as merely the gifts of the Holy Spirit. For they are considered here as the fountainhead of Grace and Peace, and thus of all heavenly Gifts, from which the Apostle prays for those blessings. And when it is said in Acts 2:38, *“You shall receive the Gift of the Holy Spirit,”* the third person of the Trinity is called the *Gift of God* by the same right that the second person <note>referring to Jesus Christ</note> is in John 4:10. Certain passages seem to favor the opposing view more—those where God is said to give *from his spirit* <note>original Greek: *ἐκ του πνευματος αὐτου*</note> (1 John 4:13) and a portion *of the spirit* <note>original Hebrew: <term>ב רוח</term> (*be-ruach*)</note> of Elijah (2 Kings 2:9), which is translated everywhere as being "of the Spirit." But since the particles "from" <note>the Greek *ek*</note> and "of/in" <note>the Hebrew *be*</note> also indicate the origin from which a divine office or gift is derived, the opponents gain no advantage from these phrases either. And so the definition of the concept of the Holy Spirit remains consistently uniform.

XVI. However, we shall not linger here at the threshold over the distorted interpretations of the enemies of the truth <note>referring to groups like the Socinians who denied the Trinity</note>, through which they pretend He is called now *love*, now *divine power*, now the *Gospel*, or even *Angels* or the *souls of the godly*. We shall instead undertake a formal examination of these claims in the Refutation <note>original: *Elencho*—the standard academic term for the section of a treatise dedicated to disproving opposing arguments</note> itself.

# ON PERSONALITY <note>original: DE PERSONALITATE</note>

...the same should be taught concerning the Holy Spirit. Thus, in Matthew 28:19, **Baptizing in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit** is prescribed. From this it is clear that the "name" belongs to the Holy Spirit in the same sense as it is held by the Father and the Son. The use of the singular number indicates this forcefully, as **AMBROSIUS** <note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397), an influential Bishop of Milan and defender of Trinitarian theology</note> beautifully observes in *On the Holy Spirit*, Book I, Chapter 4: *“He said ‘in the name,’ not ‘in the names.’”* <note>original: In nomine dixit, non nominibus</note> Therefore, the **name of the Father**, the **name of the Son**, and the **name of the Holy Spirit** is nothing other than **one God**. Furthermore, that "name" can designate either the **authority** by which Baptism is conferred, or the **honor** toward which Baptism is directed; both of these certainly presuppose something personal. For **authority** has no place except in a person who possesses the power of commanding, nor is anyone capable of **honor** except a person who demands, deserves, receives, and approves it. No less significantly, in 2 Corinthians 13:13, the Spirit is added alongside the **Lord Jesus Christ** and God the Father as the Author of a particular benefit—namely **Communion** <note>or Fellowship</note>—which is derived from Him in the same way that **Grace** comes from the Son and **Love** from the Father. It is equally evident in 1 John 5:7 <note>This refers to the "Johannine Comma," a passage traditionally used to support the Trinity</note> that He is joined to the Father and the Word as a **third Witness**. From this it flows that just as the testimony of the Father and the Son is a personal testimony, so also the testimony of the Holy Spirit must be regarded as personal.

They also cite how Christ Himself says in Revelation 3:12: *“I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God,”* even though that city is not a person. But this is beside

### CHAPTER II: ON THE HOLY SPIRIT
<meta>Signature: P</meta>
<meta>Vol. II. catchword: VI.</meta>

...of the Saints, of which the Holy Spirit is the author, or which the Spirit exercises.

IV. Regarding **1 John 5:7** <note>This verse, known as the "Johannine Comma," states: "For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one." It was a central proof-text for the Trinity in the early modern period.</note>, a) an objection is raised that in the verse immediately following, three witnesses are likewise established on earth, *who nevertheless are not personally distinct.* We respond: $\alpha$) *Although the witnesses on earth are not personally distinct, they are nonetheless distinguished in reality as diverse witnesses.* $\beta$) The reason they are not personally distinct is that the subjects (water and blood) are not persons. However, in our verse, it is manifest from the names of the *Father and the Son* that personal subjects are encountered. $\gamma$) One and the same name used for several subjects in the same statement must be interpreted in the same sense regarding them. Since, therefore, the Father and Son are designated as Witnesses in the proper sense of the word, the same must be concluded regarding the Holy Spirit.

b) The nonsense <note>original: $\phi \lambda \upsilon \rho \iota \alpha$ (phlyaria); meaning idle talk or babble</note> of **SERVETUS** <note>Michael Servetus (1511–1553), a radical reformer famously executed in Geneva for denying the Trinity</note> is hardly worth mentioning: he claims that *one and the same person, the Father, is called "three witnesses" because He testified through the Word (the Son) that He is his Son, and because He sealed this Word with various works and gifts of His Spirit.* What could be more absurd than to take a witness—who brings forth his testimony both by mouth and confirms it with certain signs—and for that reason divide him into three witnesses? Or, if anyone thought God wished to use such a weak <term>catachresis</term> <note>A figure of speech in which a word is used in an unconventional or strained way</note>—lacking any precedent—to refer to different modes of bringing forth testimony as if they were different witnesses, would not a total of only two such fictional witnesses result from it at most?

V. Secondly, we call upon a whole forest of other passages in which the Holy Spirit is combined with other personal subjects in such a way that it cannot be doubted that He also constitutes a personal subject. Thus, in **Isaiah 48:16**, He is coordinated with the Son. The same occurs in **Matthew 12:31-32**, which carries even greater emphasis because there the Holy Spirit is opposed to Beelzebub, the Prince of Demons, as a person against a person. Similar pairings are provided by passages in **2 Samuel 23:2-3**, **Haggai 2:4-5**, and others. The Apostles also, in **Acts 15:28**, joining person to persons, say: *It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.* Furthermore, the joint testimony <note>original: $\sigma \upsilon \mu \mu \alpha \rho \tau \upsilon \rho \iota \alpha$ (symmartyria)</note> of the Holy Spirit with our spirit is preached in **Romans 8:16**. Compare also verse 26.

# ON PERSONALITY #

->IV.<-

VI. *Thirdly, the Holy Spirit is joined to the remaining Persons in such a way that He is simultaneously distinguished from them as a distinct Person, as in John 14:16: I will pray the Father, and He will give you ANOTHER ADVOCATE, that He may remain with you forever.* In my commentary on this passage, following others, I have shown that the word <term>ἄλλος</term> <note>allos; Greek for "another," typically meaning "another of the same kind"</note> not only distinguishes the Holy Spirit from the Son as one person from another, but also substitutes the Spirit for the Son as one person for another. **WOLZOGENIUS** <note>Johann Ludwig von Wolzogen (1591–1661), a Socinian theologian who argued against the Trinity, claiming the Spirit was just God's power</note> objects, claiming that the Savior chose this comparison between Himself and the Spirit of Truth for the sake of rhetorical elegance, in a similar way to how David in Psalm 119, when saying that Princes consulted against him, called the divine statutes his "men of counsel" or "counselors." However, beyond the fact that the Lord is using a formal doctrinal style here, many other markers of personality are piled up, among which the pronoun <term>ἐκεῖνος</term> <note>ekeinos; a masculine demonstrative pronoun meaning "That One" or "He"</note> stands out (compare John 15:26, 16:8, 13, 14). This is all the more compelling because John very frequently uses this demonstrative to indicate personal subjects. Additionally, in the cited passage of the Psalm, there is no comparison, but rather an opposition. For opposition is often established even between subjects of a different nature. However, subjects that are compared to one another, and are so similar that one succeeds the other in the same task, ought to be of the same nature.

VII. *A fourth argument we draw from personal attributes and faculties which belong to rational subjects. For all these are attributed to the Holy Spirit. Intellect* is ascribed to Him in Nehemiah 9:20, Isaiah 11:2, 1 Corinthians 2:10, 12:11, John 14:26, and 16:13. *Will* is ascribed in John 3:8, 1 Corinthians 12:11, and Acts 15:28. *Power* is ascribed in Isaiah 11:2, Micah 2:7, 2:8, and Ephesians 3:16.

VIII. *Fifthly, personal offices are frequently ascribed to the Holy Spirit.* Such are the offices of *Advocate* <note>original: Paracleti</note>, *Teacher*, and *Judge*, and especially the *Angel of Jehovah*, the specific emphasis of which relationships we shall examine in their proper place.

IX. *Sixthly, our theologians have extracted a complete and lengthy catalog of personal operations from the sacred pages.* To this belongs the fact that He *works* as He wills (1 Corinthians 12:11); that He *searches* the depths of God (1 Corinthians 2:10); that He *convicts* <note>original: arguat; also translated as "reproves" or "convinces"</note> (John 16:8); that He *strives* <note>original: litiget; meaning to contend or plead a case</note> (Genesis 6); and that He *speaks* (Acts 28)...

### CHAPTER II. THE HOLY SPIRIT ###

...the Spirit receives. Acts 13:2. <note>original: "accipiat"</note> That He acts upon or impels the children of God. Romans 8:14. That He *intercedes for them.* Romans 8:26. That He leads into truth and announces things to come. John 16:13; 1 Peter 1:11. That He teaches. Luke 12:12; John 14:26. That He appoints *Bishops* <note>original: "Episcopos"; meaning overseers or leaders in the early church</note>. Acts 20:28.

X. Related to the seventh point is the fact that passive affections—emotions or experiences that can only happen to a person—are also predicated of the Holy Spirit. To this we refer the facts: that He is tempted (Acts 5:9); that a lie is committed against Him (Acts 5:3); that He is embittered <note>original: "exacerbetur," sometimes translated as 'grieved' or 'vexed'</note> (Isaiah 63:10); that blasphemy is committed against Him (Matthew 12:31); and that He is affected by sadness (Ephesians 4:30).

XI. A general prejudice is raised against these four arguments based on the claim that all these expressions can be explained through mere <term>prosopopoeia</term> <note>A rhetorical device where an abstract quality or inanimate object is represented as a person; personification.</note>. But to blow away this "smoke" which they are selling <note>A Latin idiom meaning to offer empty or deceptive arguments</note>, it is enough to observe the following:

A. No example of a personification so constant and so dominant throughout the entirety of Scripture can be produced.

B. When such things that only apply to a person are predicated of certain qualities, clear criteria are usually available from which one can gather that the subject is not actually a person, and that personification can and should be admitted. In those cases, it can either be proven from the nature of the thing itself that personal traits conflict with its nature (and must therefore be understood figuratively); or, within the context and other sayings, traces will not be lacking which make it clear through comparison that the Holy Spirit is speaking through a figure of speech; or it will be established from reliable authors that such a way of speaking is common. However, none of these conditions occur in the present case.

C. The majority of the passages we have produced are of such a nature that they can only be understood as referring to a person. For: 1) Most of these expressions occur not in a *poetic, allegorical,* or *parabolic* style of speaking, but in one that is *plain, historical, and dogmatic*. 2) The personal properties predicated of the Holy Spirit are linked with a personal human being <note>likely referring to the Spirit's interactions with the apostles</note>. 3) *Emphatic* adjectives and pronouns are frequently added to the names, which call us away from any interpretation of personification.

But what prevents Him from being a person, even if He is said to pray and sigh because He produces these effects in the reborn?

BASIL the Great praises a similar saying of the same author in *On the Holy Spirit, chapter 29*: <note>original Greek: Ζῇ ὁ Θεὸς, καὶ ὁ Κύριος, Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς, καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον.</note> *God lives, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit.* From where Clement might have drawn this is unknown, as COTELERIUS <note>Jean-Baptiste Cotelier (1629–1686), a famous French scholar of early Christian texts</note> noted in his commentary on the cited passage.

-># CHAPTER II. ON THE HOLY SPIRIT #<-

...RIUS <note>Likely a reference to a specific heretical author or a variant reading.</note>. Grabe <note>Johannes Ernst Grabe (1666–1711), a scholar known for his editions of the Church Fathers.</note> also points out in *Spicilegium SS. Patrum* Vol. I, p. 301, that this does not lack suspicion of spuriousness <note>original Greek: νοθείας, referring to a "bastard" or forged text</note>.

**XVII.** At the dawn of the second century, **Ignatius** in his *Letter to the Philadelphians*, §. 5, writes as follows: *Just as the Pseudo-Prophets and Pseudo-Apostles drew upon one and the same evil spirit, deceitful and a seducer of the people; so too the Prophets and Apostles received one and the same Holy Spirit—good, principal <note>original Greek: ἡγεμονικὸν, meaning "guiding" or "sovereign"</note>, and true, a Teacher—from God through Christ. For there is one God of the Old and New Testaments. One mediator between God and men, for the craftsmanship of the intelligible and sensible creation and for a providence that is useful and suited to things. And there is one Paraclete <note>An Advocate or Comforter</note>, who worked in Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles.* The words he has in his *Letter to the Philippians* are in agreement with this.

**Irenaeus** also reviews the catalog of the personal operations of the Holy Spirit, both in the short formula of faith found in Book I, chapter 2, and in the review of his various offices in Book III, chapter 19: *The Holy Spirit descended upon the Son of God who became man: so that he might grow accustomed to dwelling within the human race; and to resting among men; and to working the will of God in them; and to renewing them from their old state into the newness of Christ. Likewise: to adopt men for God.* Indeed, he says the Holy Spirit was given for this reason: *so that, because the Devil was thrust down from heaven, we might have a Paraclete <note>Advocate</note> there where the Devil is our accuser.* 

Nor do we doubt that this was also the faith of **Athenagoras**, who wrote in his *Embassy for the Christians*, chapter 10: *Although we say that the Holy Spirit himself, acting in the Prophets, flows out from God and is reflected back to him, just as rays emitted from the Sun are reflected back. Who then would not wonder that we, who preach God the Father, and God the Son, and the Holy Spirit, in such a way that we explain the power of their union and the distinction of their order, are called impious and godless men?* The words he has in chapter 22 point to the same thing. How unfairly these were twisted by **Petavius** and **Sandius** to charge Athenagoras with Sabellianism <note>A heresy that claims Father, Son, and Spirit are only roles or "masks" of one person, rather than three distinct Persons.</note> will be shown by **Wormius** in *History of Sabellianism*, chapter 8, § 1 and following, after **Bull** in *Defense of the Nicene Faith*, chapter 5. Add also **Nourry** in *Writings of the Second Century*, Dissertation chapter 5. Furthermore, nothing is more explanatory than the dispute **Tertullian** formally undertook *Against Praxeas*, where among other things he says: *The Spirit is the third*

**XVIII.** The consensus of the Fathers of the Third Century is also manifest. Regarding **ORIGEN**, he is so far from the suspicion of denying the personhood of the Holy Spirit that he is rather thought to have paved the way for the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that the Son and Spirit were created beings rather than co-eternal with the Father.</note> and to have taught an essential difference of the Holy Spirit from the Father and Son. **XIX.** Finally, we do not doubt that this truth was acknowledged in the ancient instruction <note>original Latin: *Catechesi*</note> of the Jews. This is assumed by the sermons of John the Baptist, the Savior, and the Apostles. Hence, the Jews are not said to "deny" the Holy Spirit, but to "blaspheme" him, to "resist" him, and so forth. This doctrine is not entirely exiled from the older monuments of the Jews. Specifically relevant is the fact that the **Shechina** <note>original Hebrew: שכינה, the "Indwelling" or Divine Presence</note>—that is, the symbol of the divine presence—and the **Holy Spirit** <note>original Hebrew: רוח הקדש, *Ruach HaKodesh*</note> are frequently used interchangeably for the same subject. The celebrated **VITRINGA** has established this with suitable examples against **BUXTORF** in *Sacred Observations*, Book I, chapter 4, §. 4, as has **DANZ** in *The Initiatives of Christ*, page 191. Nevertheless, they call the *Shechina* an "Angel," or even a "Mediator and Advocate" <note>original Hebrew: סרסור ומליץ, *Sarsur u-Melitz*, terms for an intermediary or spokesperson</note>...

**XXI.** It could more easily be granted that the Sadducees did not acknowledge the Holy Spirit, as is argued by **EPIPHANIUS** in *Heresies* XIV, **GREGORY NAZIANZENUS** <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers" known for defining Trinitarian theology.</note> in *Oration XXXVII: On the Holy Spirit*, and **PHILASTRIUS** in his entry on Dositheus, whom **PETAVIUS** follows in *Dogmatic Theology: On the Trinity*, Book I, chapter 14, § 1. However, even this point is not properly proved. They do indeed appeal to Acts 23:8: *For the Sadducees say there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit: but the Pharisees confess both.* In this saying, some interpret the word "spirit" <note>original Greek: πνεῦμα (pneuma)</note> in a general sense, as denoting any substance lacking a body. In this way, the Sadducees would have been purely theoretical atheists of the crudest sort, which is not clear, as the celebrated **PEARSON** <note>John Pearson, a 17th-century English theologian and Bishop of Chester, famous for his "Exposition of the Creed."</note> also observes in the location cited. Others explain "spirit" specifically <note>original Greek: κυρίως (kyrios)</note> as referring to the Third Person of the Trinity. These people favor our argument to the extent that, according to their opinion, the Pharisees would have believed in the Holy Spirit. We would not hesitate to agree with them, were it not clear from the context that the discussion concerns the doctrine of the resurrection, to which faith in the existence of the Holy Spirit does not relate so directly. Therefore, "spirit" is more correctly understood as the soul surviving after the death of the body, comparing this with **JOSEPHUS** <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> (*Jewish Antiquities* XVIII. 2), who teaches that the Sadducees denied the "permanence of the soul" <note>original Greek: ψυχῆς τὴν διαμονὴν</note> along with rewards and punishments. Despite this, the words in verse 9 uttered by the Scribes of the Pharisaic sect—*But if a spirit or an angel spoke to him* <note>original Greek: εἰ δὲ πνεῦμα ἐλάλησεν αὐτῷ ἢ ἄγγελος</note>—can be referred to the Holy Spirit, to whom those Scribes attribute a personal work. Nor is it necessary to use the word "spirit" in the same sense in both places. For Luke intended one thing, and these Scribes intended another.

# LIST OF ADVERSARIES

The Holy Spirit is often substituted with Prophecy. For this reason, **EPIPHANIUS** <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD), a bishop known for his fierce defense of orthodoxy against early heresies.</note> in *The Anchored One* §. 118, calls the Sabellians "second Jews" <note>original Greek: *deuterous Ioudaious*</note>. This provided the occasion for **JEROME** in his 65th Letter to Pammachius to charge **LACTANTIUS** with the "Jewish error." Jerome says: *Lactantius, in his books, and especially in the letters to Demetrianus, entirely denies the substance of the Holy Spirit, and by a Jewish error, says he is either referred to the Father or the Son, and that the "Sanctification" of each Person is merely demonstrated under his name.* **VINCENT OF LÉRINS** <note>A 5th-century monk best known for his "Canon" on how to identify true Christian doctrine.</note> likewise in his *Reminder against Heresies*, chapter 17, notes that Photinus, *in the Jewish manner, denied the fullness of the Trinity, and did not believe there was any Person of the Holy Spirit.* Indeed, **ATHANASIUS** in his *Oration against the followers of Sabellius*, and **BASIL** in his 64th Letter, assert that Sabellianism <note>Sabellianism: The heretical belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three distinct persons, but three different "modes" or masks worn by a single God.</note> is "Judaism under the mask of Christianity" <note>original Greek: *Ioudaismon en proschemati Christianismou*</note>. Consequently, the Church Fathers considered Sabellianism to be *Judaism*, and the opposing error of Arianism <note>Arianism: The belief that Jesus was a created being, not co-equal with God the Father.</note> to be a subtle form of *Paganism*. **THEODORET** in his work *Against Sabellius* (found in Baluzius's *Miscellanies*, Volume IV, page 3) writes: *Look, therefore, how Sabellius, while fleeing Arius, became a Jew; and how Arius, while fleeing Sabellius, became a pagan.*

IV. Among Christians, those who have attacked the personal substance of the Holy Spirit can be reduced to five main classes. For they claimed the Holy Spirit was either:
1. Simply **one and the same "Triple-named" person** with the Father and the Son,
2. Or **a certain part of the divine essence**,
3. Or **a specific way of thinking within God**,
4. Or **the power of God**,
5. Or **His peculiar gift**.

These ideas agree in their foundation, yet they developed so that later hypotheses illustrated the first. For those who held the Holy Spirit to be a mere name had to explain why that name appeared so often in Holy Scripture. Some derived this cause more distinctly from a *cruder concept of parts of the divine essence*; others from the *internal mode of divine operation, which they called love*; others from the *divine operation effective from the outside, which is the power of God*; and others from the *effect itself of the divine operation, which was the gift of God*. Thus, one and the same root divided into four branches of error.

V. Therefore, the foundation of this multifaceted vanity was laid by those who, along with Praxeas, Noëtus, Sabellius, Photinus, and others, held the Holy Spirit to be one...

Indeed, **IRENAEUS** testifies in *Against Heresies*, book 1, chapter 10, that Simon claimed to have descended in Samaria as the Father, in Judea as the Son, and to the remaining nations as the Holy Spirit. However, **AUGUSTINE** disagrees in *On Heresies*, chapter 1, reporting that Simon boasted he gave the Law to the Jews on Mount Sinai in the person of the Father; that in the time of Tiberius he appeared supposedly in the person of the Son, and afterwards he came upon the Apostles in tongues of fire as the Holy Spirit. All these points lead back to this: in what sense did that foul impostor, according to **JEROME** on Matthew 24, say: *I am the Word of God, I am the beautiful one, I am the Comforter, I am everything of God?* Did he seriously establish some system of doctrine? Or, mocking the nations out of a perverse imitation <note>original Greek: *κακοζηλία* (kakozēlia), meaning a failed or distorted imitation of another's style or ideas.</note> of the Christians, did he ascribe to himself with unrestrained license whatever they attributed to the Son and the Holy Spirit?

VI. It would have been desirable if the Church Fathers who wrote against Praxeas <note>A 2nd-century monarchian who taught that the Father and Son were not distinct persons.</note> and his followers had more clearly explained how those heretics interpreted both the other names of God and specifically the name of the "Holy Spirit." If we listen to **EPIPHANIUS** in *Heresies* 62, the Sabellians understood the Spirit as a certain "part" of the Deity. For he writes in section 1:
> Their opinion is this: that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the same, such that three titles apply to the same person <term>hypostasis</term> <note>hypostasis: a technical term for the distinct "personhood" of the Trinity; the Sabellians used it to mean a single individual with three names.</note>. Or just as body, soul, and spirit exist in one man: so that the Father is like the body, the Son like the soul, and finally the Holy Spirit is held to be like the human spirit within the Divinity itself. They also illustrate this with the analogy of the Sun; in which, while there is one substance, there is nonetheless a triple action: namely, the power of illuminating, the power of heating, and the circular shape. And indeed, that heating power—that is, the heat and warmth—corresponds to the Spirit; the power of illuminating to the Son; and finally the Father is, as it were, the form of the entire substance.

Although something seems to be expressed here, very different concepts are nonetheless confused. For placing "parts outside of parts" within the divine essence is in itself a fatal error, ascribing something corporeal to God, from which

those who understand a certain power in God—for example, the power of illuminating and warming—through the Son and the Holy Spirit, are very far from the truth.

VII. Those who have organized the matter more subtly substituted certain **modes of thinking** in God. Among their number are those whom **AUGUSTINE** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers.</note> describes in *On Faith and the Creed*, book 1, chapter 19:

*Some, however, have dared,* he says, *to believe that the very communion of the Father and the Son, and (so to speak) the Deity—which the Greeks call* <note>original: θεότητα (*theotēta*)</note> *theotēta—is the Holy Spirit: so that since the Father is God and the Son is God, the Deity itself, by which they are joined to one another—the former by begetting the Son, and the latter by adhering to the Father—is made equal to Him by whom He was begotten. They say that this Deity, which they also want to be understood as the mutual love and charity of both toward each other, is called the Holy Spirit, etc.*

Immediately after, he adds the laboriously chosen words of Scripture which those who hold this view employ. Not only does he hardly refute this opinion, as **PETAVIUS** <note>Dionysius Petavius (1583–1652), a French Jesuit theologian known as the "father of the history of dogma."</note> notes in *On the Trinity*, book VII, chapter 12, section 5, but even in section 20 he proposes the arguments of the dissenters quite coldly. Indeed, he hints that those arguments are not particularly significant, and finally leaves the whole matter undecided, adding: *Wherefore, whether that opinion be true, or something else, the faith must be held unshaken.* There are also passages in his books *On the Trinity* that are quite clear, revealing that the Bishop of Hippo <note>Augustine</note> himself leaned in that direction. 

However, although this opinion cannot be reconciled with the **personal subsistence** <term>subsistentia: the distinct, individual existence of a person within the Trinity</term> of the Holy Spirit—since love is a certain inclination of the will, and thus nothing but a certain "mode of thinking" which is attributed to each of the divine Persons indiscriminately—the authority of **AUGUSTINE** nevertheless drew many into the same mindset, as **PETAVIUS** teaches in the place cited. Indeed, introduced into the Christian schools through **THOMAS AQUINAS** and **PETER LOMBARD** <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1100–1160), whose "Sentences" became the standard textbook of medieval theology.</note>, it took firm root. 

Yet it cannot be denied that this opinion has been considerably softened by the **Scholastics** <note>Medieval theologians who emphasized logic and Aristotelian philosophy.</note>, especially the more recent ones. For they contend that **AUGUSTINE** himself implicitly retracted it, and they want the Holy Spirit to be called "Love" only insofar as He is the *product* of the love of the Father and the Son through His eternal **spiration** <term>spiratio: "breathing forth," the theological term for the way the Holy Spirit originates from the Father and the Son</term>; as can be seen in the works of **BECANUS**, **VALENTIA**, and others who twist themselves into various positions here...

### CHAPTER III: ON THE PERSON OF THE HOLY SPIRIT

...one may see the following coils <note>The author uses "coils" (spiras) metaphorically to describe the winding, complex paths of theological reasoning.</note> of thought. Two things in particular acted as "midwives" to this concept: first, the fact that the disputations against the Donatists <note>A schismatic Christian group in North Africa that argued for the purity of the church and the invalidity of sacraments performed by "traditores" (those who had surrendered scriptures during persecution).</note> and the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that the Son of God was a created being, subordinate to the Father.</note> drove many Doctors of the Church to lean into the opposite extreme more than was right; second, that this very idea was thought to elegantly reconcile Platonic philosophy with the Christian faith. It is well known how closely the things which the ancient Egyptians and Orphics recorded concerning *Love* <note>original: *Amore* (referring to Eros)</note> agree with the Holy Spirit as the Creator of the World; **TRIBBECHOVIUS** <note>Adam Tribbechov (1641–1687), a German theologian and historian.</note> provides a summary of this in *On the Creation of the World* in **CRENIUS**, volume I, page 291 and following. **HUETIUS** <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar who sought to demonstrate that all pagan wisdom derived from Moses.</note> acknowledges in *Alnetan Questions*, book II, chapter 3, that the things **PLOTINUS** <note>The OCR reads "Photinus," but the context of the Enneads (VI.8.15) refers to Plotinus, the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> brought forth concerning this *Love* in *Ennead* VI, book 8, chapter 15, are very close to the faith regarding the Holy Spirit. To this pertains what **CLAUDIANUS MAMERTUS** <note>A 5th-century Gallic theologian and philosopher.</note> wrote in *On the State of the Soul*, book II: after he had stated in chapter 6 that *the Holy Spirit is love*, <note>original: "Spiritum Sanctum amorem esse dixisset"</note> he sought to reconcile that with the doctrine of Plato in chapter 7. Others may see how successfully he did so. For our part, it certainly does not please us that in the preceding sections he establishes a double image of the Trinity in man: regarding the *body, through measure, number, and weight*; regarding the *soul, through memory, counsel, and will*. Hence he says in chapter 5 that the *weight* of the soul is the *will*, which is more properly called *Love*, and is compared with the Holy Spirit. On this same opinion, the oration of **CAMPANI** on the Holy Spirit, published with notes by the illustrious **BUNEMANN**, deserves to be read.

VIII. Of those who judged that the *Holy Spirit* should be understood as some kind of divine *Power*, the crowd of Gnostics leads the march. Regarding Cerinthus, <note>A 1st-century Gnostic teacher who was a contemporary of the Apostle John.</note> that testimony of **EPIPHANIUS** <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD), a prominent heresiologist.</note> is well known, from *Heresies* XXVIII, section 1: *He taught that after Jesus grew up, having been born from the seed of Joseph and Mary, the Christ—that is, the Holy Spirit—descended into him from that highest God in the form of a dove at the Jordan; and then he revealed the Parent, who was unknown to him, and through him to posterity. And for that reason, as soon as that heavenly power poured itself into him, he performed wonders and miracles.* And perhaps those who, according to Ignatius in his *Letter to the Trallians*, utterly denied the Holy Spirit, belong to this class. **IRENAEUS** has similar accounts in book I, chapter 26, as does **THEODORET** in *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, book II.

# LIST OF OPPONENTS

### CHAPTER 3.

From this it is clear that Cerinthus <note>A late 1st-century Gnostic teacher who was a contemporary of the Apostle John; he often distinguished between the human Jesus and a divine "Christ" spirit.</note>—for whom **TERTULLIAN** <note>Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155–220 AD), a prolific early Christian author from Carthage.</note> substituted *Valentinus* in *Against Praxeas*, chapter 37—foreshadowed Sabellio <note>Sabellius (fl. c. 215), the priest and theologian who taught "Modalism," the idea that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are merely different modes or "faces" of a single divine person.</note> by confusing Christ with the Holy Spirit as well as with the Father; at the same time, he regarded the Spirit as that power by which Jesus, once filled, performed miracles. That these tracks were followed by the rest of the Gnostic crowd is clear from that excerpt of **THEODOTUS** found in **CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA**, section 16: *"Moreover, a bodily dove was seen, which some call the Holy Spirit, and those who side with Valentinus call 'the spirit of the Father's reflection, making its descent into the flesh of the Word.'"* <note>original Greek: "το πνευμα της ενθυμησεως του Πατρος, την κατελευσιν πεποιημενον επι την του Λογου σαρκα." The term "Enthymesis" refers to a thought or reflection, often personified in Gnostic cosmology.</note> I do not wish to compare the remaining parts of those excerpts regarding this cause, lest we cause too much delay at the threshold. To this same group I would refer those who dreamed of two or three Spirits or "Paracletes" <note>A term from the Gospel of John meaning "Advocate" or "Helper," usually identifying the Holy Spirit.</note>, such as those mentioned in the *Apostolic Constitutions* VI.11 and *Apostolic Canon* XLI; see Cotelerius <note>Jean-Baptiste Cotelier (1629–1686), a French scholar who edited the works of the Apostolic Fathers.</note> on these passages. 

**MARCELLUS OF ANCYRA** <note>A 4th-century bishop whose opposition to Arianism led him to an extreme view that some saw as Sabellianism.</note> must have revived this error, if **THEODORET** correctly expressed his opinion in *On Heretical Fables* II.10, where, after he had said that according to him a certain extension of the Father's divinity came into Christ, he adds: *"He says the Holy Spirit is an extension of an extension, and that this was given to the Apostles."* These things are of an even worse sort if, following the Gnostics, he understood that extension of divine power as a kind of material emanation. Furthermore, a learned man, **J. G. GERRET**, attempts to clear *Lactantius* <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250–325), an early Christian advisor to Constantine known as the "Christian Cicero."</note> from the suspicion of a similar error in *An Examination of the Theology of Lactantius*, Question III. 

Closer to this view were the Bogomils <note>A medieval dualist sect that emerged in the 11th-century Balkans, often accused of radical heresies.</note>, appearing in the 11th century, about whose monstrous errors **EUTHYMIUS** reports, among other things, in *Panoply*, Title XXIII: *"that they deceived the simple by saying they believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but in reality they attributed three names to the Father; and they raved that He, endowed with a bodily form, emits two rays from two membranes of the brain—one of the Son, the other of the Holy Spirit, etc."*

It was noted under the preceding title that it is primarily the **Sabellians** <note>Followers of Sabellius (fl. c. 215 AD), who taught "Modalism"—the idea that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three persons, but three modes or "masks" of one single God.</note> who deny the Holy Spirit; they are said, according to the traditions of the ungodly, to call Him a *gift* rather than the *giver*. They claim authority for this evil view by misusing sacred testimonies, especially because He is recorded as being "given" and "received," as when the Savior spoke to the Apostles: *“And breathing on them, he said: Receive the Holy Spirit, etc.”* <note>John 20:22. The argument was that if the Spirit is something "given," He must be an object or a power rather than a person.</note>

**LUC D'ACHERY** <note>Luc d'Achery (1609–1685), a French Benedictine scholar who published a massive collection of primary sources titled *Spicilegium*.</note>, who published this book in the first volume of his *Spicilegium of the Fathers*, notes in his preface that our author was hallucinating <note>A common, though sharp, scholarly term in this period for being mistaken or deluded.</note> in his description of the Sabellian heresy, since he attributes to Sabellius what actually belongs to **Macedonius** <note>Macedonius I (died c. 362), associated with the "Pneumatomachians" or "Spirit-fighters," who denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note>. But I fear that he himself, as well as his defender **WORM** <note>Likely referring to the Danish scholar Ole Worm (1588–1654) or a contemporary theologian.</note> in the seventh chapter of the work cited, did not sufficiently grasp the Macedonian dogma, which—along with the Semi-Arians—admitted the personal subsistence <term>subsistence: a theological term referring to the distinct, individual existence of a person within the Godhead</term> of the Holy Spirit. 

It was certainly common for certain **Sabellians**, wishing to bring some account of the concept of the Holy Spirit into the open, to stoop to calling Him a *gift* or some *effect* of God in humans. This is exactly what seems to have happened with the followers of **PAUL OF SAMOSATA** <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Antioch whose teachings were condemned as heresy; he viewed Jesus as a man and the Spirit as an impersonal power of God.</note>, who drank in errors similar to the Sabellians. Among these, **LEONTIUS** <note>Leontius of Byzantium (c. 485–543), a key figure in the Christological debates of the early Church.</note> records in *On Sects*, Article 3, that Paul named the Spirit as that "grace" which came upon the Apostles. This was a more serious error because, along with the personality of the Holy Spirit, it also took away His Deity.

X. In the more recent era after the Reformation, others drank from these impure fountains, adopting now these and now those concepts indiscriminately. Before others, the earlier **Anabaptists** <note>A "Radical Reformation" group often persecuted by both Catholics and other Protestants; they were frequently accused of various heresies beyond their views on baptism.</note> were made suspect of denying the personal subsistence of the Holy Spirit; but more recent ones have cleared themselves of this charge in their Confessions. This prejudice arose partly from the excessive stubbornness of certain individuals regarding the word *person* at the **Colloquy of Frankenthal** <note>A 1571 debate between Reformed theologians and Anabaptists in the Palatinate.</note> and the **Emden Colloquy**, and partly from the confusion of the more crude **Enthusiasts** <note>From the Greek *enthousiasmos* ("possessed by a god"); a term used dismissively for those who claimed direct, private revelation from the Spirit over scripture.</note> with the Anabaptists. For it is evident that the former [Enthusiasts] revived that "monster of emanations" <note>original: "monstrum emanationum." A reference to Gnostic theories where various powers flow out from God like ripples in water.</note> from the divine essence, which was once cast out by the Gnostics. Nor shall we act unfairly if we count the infamous **MICHAEL SERVETUS** <note>The Spanish physician executed in 1553 in Geneva; he remains the most famous historical critic of the traditional Trinity.</note> among their first leaders. For although in his *On the Errors of the Trinity*, Book II, page 59 and following, he declares his opinion on the Holy Spirit in such a way that he appears to understand by Him nothing but internal operations in the souls of those being sanctified, nevertheless he reveals his **Enthusiasm** more clearly—

...a confusion of vain aspirations and most urgent, extremely excruciating restlessness. <note>This continues the critique of Westphal from the previous page, who viewed spiritual experiences as mere psychological disturbances.</note> He compares these properties in God with the faculties of the soul in the following sections, and teaches that the image of the Father exists through justice in **Conscience**, that of the Son through **Truth** in **Intelligence**, and that of the Holy Spirit through **Love** <note>original: "Caritatem"</note> in the faculty of loving. However, this is easily reconciled with the system of that sharp "philosopher from the common folk" <note>A likely reference to Baruch Spinoza, who was often disparagingly called a "common" or "lay" philosopher because he was a lens-grinder by trade.</note>, in which created spirits themselves are nothing but modifications of a certain universal **Thought**.

### XII. ###

Many of the Papists <note>original: "Pontificiis"</note> have entangled themselves more subtly in this error, twisting **Augustine's** concept in various ways. An example is that description of the Holy Spirit which **Friedrich Nausea** <note>Friedrich Nausea (c. 1496–1552), the Bishop of Vienna and a Catholic reformer.</note> presents in his *Explanation of the Apostles' Creed, page 118*:

> *He is nothing other than God borne into his own essence through a reciprocal love proceeding from the Father and the Son.* <note>original: "Est nihil aliud quam Deus latus in suam essentiam per amorem reciprocum à Patre Filioque procedentem."</note>

Meaning, of course, that because God the Father loves his own essence, and the Son likewise loves the same, it follows that this "bearing" of love—taken passively, i.e., *that the Father and Son are borne toward their own essence through a single love*—becomes a substance. Those who became known under the name of **Deists** or **Naturalists** struck the same rock. Thus, for **Arthur Bury** <note>An Oxford theologian whose book *The Naked Gospel* (1690) was burned for its allegedly Socinian/Arian tendencies.</note> in *The Latitudinarian Orthodox, page 63*, the Holy Spirit designates **Power, Activity, and Grace**, just as the Father designates **Eternity and Goodness**, and the Son **Wisdom, Truthfulness, and Justice**. Certain theologians, who otherwise think correctly and piously, were not sufficiently cautious here. **Jacob Alting** <note>A 17th-century German-Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> in *Heptad VI, dissertation 5*, follows the lead <note>original: "pollicem... premit"; an idiom meaning to support or favor.</note> of **Augustine** and others who, following the dictates of the philosophers, understand the Holy Spirit as Love. Presenting Understanding, Will, and Power as the image of the Holy Trinity, he assigns the Holy Spirit to the last of these <note>i.e., to Power</note>. **Herman Deusing** <note>Herman Deusing (1654–1722) was a Dutch physician and theologian known for his highly allegorical and often controversial interpretations of the Trinity and the Bible.</note>, having been enticed far too much by a zeal for allegories, says in his *Dissertation on the Mystery of the Trinity*, III, § 124: "The Holy Spirit is the will of the Father and the Son, by which the Father wills and loves the Son—that is, his own truth—and the Son loves himself." Yet he does not simply understand the will of God through the Holy Spirit, but specifically that will which has been displayed in the New Testament through his pouring out and spiritual quickening; in this way, he does not even understand the Holy Spirit as an essential mode of thinking, but as a mere mode of outward operation. He strives to illustrate this opinion more fully in what follows.

XIII. The **Socinians** <note>A non-trinitarian movement following Fausto Sozzini, which denied the pre-existence of Christ and the personality of the Holy Spirit, viewing the latter as a power or gift from God.</note> everywhere wish to bundle together the errors of those who call the Holy Spirit a "power" <note>original: "virtutem"</note> and those who call him a "divine gift." This is obvious to the eye from the distinction made by **Volkelius** <note>Johannes Volkelius (d. 1618), a leading Socinian theologian and author of "On True Religion."</note> in *On True Religion*, book V, chapter 14, where he says:

> The Holy Spirit is considered in two ways: either insofar as he belongs to God and Christ and flows forth from them, or insofar as he is communicated to man and thus resides in him. In the first way, those things are ascribed to him which properly belong to God and Christ, and which he effects through his Spirit; in the second way, those things which are accomplished by man through his power and impulse.

Generally, indeed, for them, according to the **Racovian Catechism** <note>The primary confession of faith for the Socinians, first published in 1605 in Raków, Poland.</note>, section VI, chapter 6:

> The Holy Spirit is a power or efficacy <note>original: "virtus seu efficacia"</note> flowing from God into men and communicated to them, by which he separates them from others and consecrates them to his own uses; they consider this power to be common to both Father and Son and existing in both—in the Father by nature, but in the Son by the benefit and grace of God.

However, they argue among themselves whether by that "power" a mere gift and effect of God is indicated—and thus something created—which **Socinus** <note>Fausto Sozzini (1539–1604), the movement's namesake.</note> leaves undecided in his work against Wujek <note>Jakub Wujek (1541–1597), a Polish Jesuit who defended the Trinity against Socinus.</note>, chapter 10; or whether it is a certain divine quality, and thus an essential property in God, which **Smalcius** <note>Valentin Schmalz (1572–1622), a prominent Socinian polemicist and rector of the Racovian Academy.</note> acknowledges in his writing against Grawer <note>Albert Grawer (1575–1617), a Lutheran champion of orthodoxy.</note> on the Holy Spirit; or whether both notions should be joined, which **Ostorodt** <note>Christoph Ostorodt (d. 1611), an influential figure in the early Socinian movement.</note> and his followers tend toward; or finally, whether it designates something intermediate between God and a created thing. This last view is defended by **Crellius** <note>Johannes Crellius (1590–1633), a German-Polish Socinian theologian whose works were widely read in the 17th century.</note> in his *Treatise on the Holy Spirit* and *On God*, chapter 22; for him, the Holy Spirit is not a power naturally residing in God, but... <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword for the next page is "certain" (quædam).</note>

# THE PERSON OF THE HOLY SPIRIT: CHAPTER III

...a certain quality flowing from that very power residing in God and acting as a sort of intermediary between the power itself in God and the more manifest effects proceeding from it. In this way, he falls into the very abyss of "emanations" <note>The Gnostic idea that various beings or powers flow out from the divine source like ripples in water.</note> of the Valentinian <note>Followers of Valentinus, a 2nd-century Gnostic teacher who proposed a complex system of divine emanations called Aeons.</note> and Enthusiastic <note>A term often used by 17th and 18th-century writers to describe radical religious groups who claimed direct, personal revelation from the Spirit, often bypassing traditional scripture.</note> schools. This is clear to the eye from the analogies which he uses in Book I of *On the One God the Father*, Section 3, Chapter 9:

> *There is,* he says, *an immense abundance of the Spirit with God, which resides in Him as if in its own fountain, but proceeds and flows from Him whenever and to whatever extent He wills, not unlike light from the Sun, or that force which they call "influence" from the stars, or as heat from a fire into objects placed near it.*

Since, however, that power of God introduces itself through various effects, they argue from this that certain more specific divine gifts are called the "Holy Spirit" in a stricter sense. This is the reason why **Smalcius** <note>Valentinus Smalcius (1572–1622), a notable Socinian theologian and co-author of the Racovian Catechism.</note> contends that there is not just one Holy Spirit, but many, and indeed unequal in dignity, in his *Examination of 157 Errors*, error 137. He and others speak in such a way that they seem to concede that a richer knowledge of divine things, the hope of eternal life, and finally the Gospel itself have been named "the Holy Spirit." Following in these footsteps, the author of *Platonism Unveiled*, **Souvereinius** <note>Michel Le Vassor published "Du Platonisme dévoilé" in 1700 under the pseudonym Souverain, arguing that the doctrine of the Trinity was a corruption of Christianity influenced by Greek philosophy.</note>, in Part I, Chapter 3, likewise understands by "Spirit" nothing but the energy <note>original: ἐνέργειαν (energeian)</note> or efficacy of God, which coincides with the Word <note>original: *Verbum*</note>, except that the *Word* refers more to outward operation and the *Spirit* to inward. However, he subtly distinguishes between the *Spirit of God* and the *Holy Spirit*. By the former, he understands the divine efficacy visible in all the works of God; by the latter, the communication of extraordinary gifts, which was given to the Prophets and especially to Christ. More recently, **Isaac Watts** <note>Written as "J. Wats" in the text. Isaac Watts (1674–1748) was a famous English hymn-writer and theologian whose later writings on the Trinity sparked controversy for their perceived leanings toward non-traditional views.</note> published a new Socinian system of the Doctrine of the Trinity in English, adding certain dissertations to illustrate it, the fifth of which deals specifically with the Holy Spirit. He thinks indeed, in Section 2, page 126, that he should be distinguished from Socinus, Schlichting, and Crellius <note>Jonas Schlichting and Johannes Crellius were major figures in the development of Socinian theology.</note> in that he regards the Holy Spirit as a *power in God that is not accidental, but essential or substantial*. Yet he does this in such a way that he does not believe this notion holds constantly everywhere. For more often, along with the coarser Sabellians <note>Followers of Sabellius (3rd century), who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not distinct persons but merely three different "modes" or "faces" of the one God.</note>, he defends the idea that the Holy Spirit is God Himself (pp. 130 ff.).

# A REVIEW OF ENEMIES
-> <note>original: "ELENCHUS HOSTIUM"</note> <-

XIV. But enough of their forces. Let us now examine their weapons—both those with which they generally attack the **Personality of the Holy Spirit**, and those with which the principal leaders of individual factions defend their own positions. To the former belong all those arguments by which a **Personal** distinction within the divine essence is entirely abolished in general. We set those aside for now, intending to examine only those which specifically oppose the **Personality of the Holy Spirit**.

XV. The **RACOVIAN CATECHISM** <note>The defining statement of faith for the Socinians, a group that denied the Trinity and the divinity of Christ.</note> vigorously brings forward the first and strongest "battering ram" in Section VI, Chapter 6. It contends *that many things attributed to the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures do not fit a person at all. These include: that it is given from him, and that either according to a measure or without measure; that he himself is poured out, and that something is poured out from him; that men drink of him, and are baptized with or in him; that he is given in double portion, distributed in parts, and that there are certain "first fruits" of him; that he himself is taken away and something is taken from him; that at one time he did not exist; and finally, that he is extinguished, etc.* To these, others add: *that it is a gift of God, that the Apostles gave the Holy Spirit, that he is given through breathing, that he is said to be in God himself, that we are sealed by him, that Christ is said to be anointed with the Holy Spirit, and so on.*

XVI. It is possible to blow all these away with a single breath, since A) it is sufficient that the Holy Spirit can be considered in all such passages in relation to his gifts. There is nothing in this that deviates from common figures of speech, where something is predicated of the cause which actually belongs to its effect. This **Metonymy** <note>A figure of speech where a thing or concept is referred to by the name of something closely associated with it—here, using the "Spirit" to mean the "gifts of the Spirit."</note> has its foundation not only in the usage of language, but in the reality of the matter itself. For whatever is the cause of a cause is also the cause of the result. Therefore, what is characteristic of an effect is also conveniently attributed to the cause. If this were not the case, it would be the end of all "affections" and **anthropopathisms** <note>original: "ἀνθρωποπαθείαις" — the attribution of human emotions or physical traits to God, such as God "changing his mind" or having "hands."</note> which are very frequently attributed to God himself in the sacred writings. Let the adversaries, therefore, offer a reason why a *soul* is ascribed to God, or a *shortness of soul* <note>A Hebrew idiom for impatience or grief.</note>, or *pain, repentance, ignorance, and remembrance*; or why He is said *to receive consolation, to rest, to breathe again, and so forth.* Just as such things are said improperly <note>In a non-literal or metaphorical sense.</note> of God, so too the sacred style can improperly attribute things to the Person of the Holy Spirit which do not, in themselves, apply to a person.

<header>ON THE PERSON OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAP. III.</header>

XVII. Add (B) that the examples produced contain nothing which is at all foreign to the nature of a *person*. (1) There are very frequent instances in which the Holy Spirit is said *to be given*. But is a person not given when we are admitted into his fellowship in such a way that we can not only enjoy his goods, but also consider his virtues and actions as our own, insofar as they are expended for us and assigned to us as a personal possession? Is a groom not given thus to a wife, a bride to a husband, a son to a father, a *King* to a people, a *Teacher* to disciples, and so on? Is not the Son of God, whom they admit to be a Person, very frequently considered as *given* by the Father? Is not the same one who is said to be gifted described elsewhere as the author of spiritual gifts? (1 Corinthians 12:11).

XVIII. Lest they should still cling to the manner in which the Spirit is sometimes said *to be given*, there is nothing in it that is inconsistent with a person. 
a) It is said in 1 John 4:13 that God *has given to us of his Spirit*. But "of" <note>original: "ex"</note> here denotes the efficient cause, and thus nothing else is designated but that he gave those gifts which have the Spirit as their author, and which are also called "gifts from God" <note>original: "charismata ek Theou"</note> in 1 Corinthians 7:7. Add, that the phrase in Revelation 21:6 clearly corresponds: "I will give from the fountain of the water of life" <note>original: "Dōsō ek tēs pēgēs tou hydatos tēs zōēs"</note>. For here the "fountain" is a symbol of a divine Person, as in Jeremiah 2:13 and Psalm 36:8. And for a similar reason, the Holy Spirit stands in the place of a fountain in relation to his gifts. However, the exception of CRELLIUS <note>Johannes Crellius (1590–1633), a leading Socinian theologian and critic of the Trinity.</note> is vain, while he pretends that this phrase alternates with the phrase in 1 John 3:24. For there it is simply said that God gave *the Spirit himself*; but here, the focus is aimed more specifically at the fruits of this given Spirit, and particularly at that "love" <note>original: "agapēn"</note> so highly commended in verse 12, which occupies the first place among them in Galatians 5:22.

b) The same Spirit is said to be given *not by measure* (John 3:34). We have dealt extensively with the meaning of this phrase in the Commentary. What, however, prevents the Holy Spirit from being a Person, even if by him here the most ample measure of his gifts is understood? And why should we not conclude that his Person itself is involved here? For those words most conveniently admit this sense: that the Spirit himself—whether to Christ or to the believers of the New Testament—is *given* or ad-

is said to be given as a personal possession <note>original: "peculium"; a Roman legal term for property held by a subordinate but managed as their own</note>, with this power and condition: that he might flood first Christ, and then his people, with the most generous stream of his gifts. Add to this that the Manna of old, divided *according to measure*, was a figure of the person of Christ as the Savior who is sufficient for all.

c) As for the fact that *it is given in double portion*, this refers to *2 Kings 2:9* <note>the request of Elisha for a double portion of Elijah's spirit</note>, which we explained in Chapter I, Section 15.

d) *It is most false to say that the Apostles gave the Holy Spirit.* For although the faithful in the Apostolic Church received the Holy Spirit *through the laying on of hands* <note>original: "χειροθεσία" (cheirothesia)</note>, this *laying on of hands* was not the cause of the giving of the Holy Spirit, but merely a kind of moral medium or external seal. This is clear because:
*α)* it was preceded by *prayers to God for others, that they might receive the Holy Spirit* (Acts 8:15). 
*β)* because sometimes the Holy Spirit was given without that laying on of hands (Acts 9:7, 11:15). 
*γ)* because the command and declaration of God regarding the giving of the Holy Spirit preceded it (Acts 9:7, 13:2 and following). 
*δ)* because those by whose ministry the Spirit was distributed to others lost nothing of the Spirit themselves.

e) That *the Holy Spirit was given by the breath of Christ* cannot be twisted out of *John 20:22* by any instrument of torture <note>original: "fidiculis"; literally "little strings/chords" used for torture, here meaning a forced interpretation</note>. For, just like the laying on of hands, it was nothing but an external symbol elegantly sketching the manner of the administration <note>original: "oeconomiae"</note> of the Holy Spirit and sealing the certainty of his mission. This is clear because: 
*α)* the Apostles did not receive the gift of the Holy Spirit immediately, but on the fiftieth day after this appearance of the Lord. 
*β)* That quality which is assigned to the disciples here cannot be given through a breath. *The authority of forgiving and retaining sins required infallibility*, even concerning facts. What does that have in common with a breath? 
*γ)* The gift of infallibility supposes a Person teaching and warning inwardly regarding those cases in which infallible judgment was to be exercised.

XIX. We shall resolve the remaining points just as easily. 2) It has already been noted in Chapter I, Section 14 *that the outpouring of the Holy Spirit designates his very mission.* What appears distorted in that symbol? Do not *rivers* as well as *fountains* bear the emblem of *Teachers*, and thus of persons? What, then, prevents us from considering the Supreme Teacher as an *outpoured river*?

### CHAPTER III: THE PERSON OF THE HOLY SPIRIT

...[consi]der? What is distorted in the fact that the faithful are given to drink from this *river*? Is it any more absurd to represent a person as a drink than as food? Is not Christ himself the bread, and the *spiritual* food as well as drink (1 Cor. 10:3, 4) from which the Fathers ate and drank? Must not the flesh of Christ be eaten and his blood be drunk (John 6:53, 54)? Is not Christ himself that *Manna* which was to be eaten (John 6:49, 50; Rev. 2:17)? This argument is not shaken by Peter's citation in Acts 2:17: *I will pour out of my Spirit* <note>original: "ἀπὸ πνεύματός μου" (apo pneumatos mou)</note>. For here he followed the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> who rendered it this way, whereas in Joel 2:28 it was stated simply: *I will pour out my Spirit*. Peter did not wish to correct this version, since the word "of" <note>Greek: "ἀπὸ" (apo)</note> can be understood here in the same sense as "in" <note>Greek: "ἐν" (en)</note>, which we explained in the preceding section.

XX. 3) Related to this is the allegory of *Baptism* in the Holy Spirit <note>original: "ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ" (en Pneumati hagio)</note>, mention of which is made in Matt. 3:11, Mark 1:8, Luke 3:16, and John 1:33. For it regards the same emblem of a *river* or *water*, which is why this Baptism is contrasted with Baptism in water <note>original: "ἐν ὕδατι" (en hydati)</note>. And union with the Person of the Holy Spirit, and his personal operation, is required not only for the satisfaction but also for the purification of souls.

XXI. A 4) more significant point <note>original: "Major species"</note> occurs in those passages which seem to suggest a *distribution* of the Holy Spirit. To this category—besides 2 Kings 2:9, Acts 2:17, and 1 John 4:13, which we have already resolved—people usually refer to Num. 11:17, Heb. 2:4, and Rom. 8:23. From these, VOLKELIUS <note>Johannes Völkel (d. 1618), a leading Socinian theologian who argued against the Trinity</note> argues as follows: *No person can be given to multiple persons, especially those located at a great distance from one another, at the same time.* Thus he is blind in the very light. For is not a *King* given to many subjects at once? Is this not much more applicable to a divine Person, who by the very perfection of his essence is present everywhere? Is this not the true reason why the Holy Spirit is compared to a *river* spreading its waters far and wide, namely to foreshadow that he is sufficient for many? The citations added to the contrary are nothing but smoke.

a) In Psalm 51:11 <note>original: "Ps. LI. 13"; numbering differs in the Vulgate/Hebrew</note>, David prays that the Spirit of Jehovah's holiness not be taken from him. But persons are also "taken away" when they die (Isa. 41:16). And more relevantly here, those whose sweet companionship we are deprived of are said to be taken from us (Ezek. 24:16). Thus Christ himself, as the bridegroom, was to be taken away from the disciples (Matt. 9:15, Mark 2:10).

# REFUTATION OF ENEMIES

b) However, there is another explanation for the passage in Numbers 11:17, where Jehovah says: <note>original Hebrew: "ואצלתי מן הרוח אשר עליך ושמתי עליהם" (ve-atzalti min ha-ruach asher aleika ve-samti aleihem)</note> *And I will take of the Spirit that is upon you, and will put it upon them.* This promise is recorded as being fulfilled in verse 25. Truly, these words would be awkwardly understood as referring to mere spiritual and prophetic gifts, since Moses did not lose what was granted to the Seventy Elders <note>The group of leaders chosen to assist Moses in governing the Israelites</note>. Moses' subsequent life teaches us this, for in it he displayed illustrious examples of that same Spirit dwelling within him. Therefore, the Syriac version <note>The Peshitta, an ancient Syriac translation of the Bible</note> renders it *I will diminish, I will shorten from your Spirit* without foundation; although Calvin <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the influential Reformation theologian</note> agrees with it, maintaining that something was taken away from Moses as a punishment. Everything flows correctly if we conclude that the Person of the Holy Spirit is hinted at here, whom Jehovah promises would operate in those Seventy in the same manner as He had operated in Moses. The Holy Spirit is surely a *Fountain* in his own right, which does not run dry even if many drink from it, and He is a *Lamp* whose light does not fail even if other *torches* are lit from it.

c) Furthermore, what is more manifest than that in Hebrews 2:4, by the *distributions of the Holy Spirit* <note>original Greek: "μερισμοὺς Πνεύματος ἁγίου" (merismous Pneumatos hagiou)</note>, it is not *passive* distinctions of the Holy Spirit into parts that are designated, but the *active* distributions of spiritual gifts <term>charismata; special abilities granted by the Holy Spirit</term> which the Holy Spirit established? For it is immediately added, *according to his*—that is, the Holy Spirit's—*will* <note>original Greek: "κατὰ τὴν αὐτοῦ θέλησιν" (kata ten autou thelesin)</note>. To this Spirit, in the parallel passage of 1 Corinthians 12:4 and following, the *distributions* <note>original Greek: "διαιρέσεις" (diaireseis)</note> of gifts are attributed as to their Author, *just as he wills* <note>original Greek: "καθὼς βούλεται" (kathos bouletai)</note>.

d) The *Firstfruits of the Holy Spirit* <note>original: "Primitiæ Spiritus S."</note> in Romans 8:23 are even less relevant here. For—not to mention that there were firstfruits which served as a type or model for persons—Paul mentions not so much the "Firstfruits" that are the Holy Spirit himself, but rather the *Firstfruits* which the Holy Spirit, as the source of all good things, graciously bestows.

XXII. Furthermore, 5) from the fact that it is said the *Spirit was not yet* <note>referring to John 7:39, "the Spirit was not yet given"</note>, nothing can be gathered against his personality. For persons are said *not to be*, even if they truly exist, when they are not noticed through their operations. Thus God himself is said *not to be* where he does not manifest himself in a certain way, as in 1 Kings 19:11–12 <note>The story of Elijah where God was not in the wind, earthquake, or fire</note>. Thus Christ says he *is no longer* in the world in John 17:11, because he was ceasing to manifest himself in the world through his works.

XXIII. Regarding 6) the fact that the Holy Spirit is said to be *quenched* in 1 Thessalonians 5:19.

->### THE PERSON OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER III.<-

V. 19. <note>original: "non infringit ejus personalitatem"</note> ...does not undermine His personality. For even persons are said to be *extinguished* who have spread a singular light from themselves. Hence we read concerning David, *lest the lamp of Israel be extinguished* (2 Samuel 21:17). Furthermore, to be *extinguished* among good authors is equivalent to "dying." Indeed, entire armies are *extinguished*, just as fuel is extinguished, when they are so utterly destroyed that nothing more of their fire is to be feared (Isaiah 43:17).

XXIV. Argument 7) is based on the passage in 1 Corinthians 2:11, from which Volkelius <note>Johannes Völkel (d. 1618), a leading Socinian theologian who argued against the traditional doctrine of the Trinity</note> argues as follows:
> *That which is determined to be in God in the same way that a man's spirit is in a man. From this it is concluded that the Holy Spirit is not a person, unless we wish to say that one person exists within another person, and certainly not interchangeably or vice versa (for God is not said to be in His Spirit), which can happen in no way at all.*

**Response:** a) The alleged comparison between the Spirit of God and the spirit of man actually works in our favor. For the spirit of a man is an intelligent substance <note>The author argues that since a human spirit is a "thinking thing," comparing the Holy Spirit to it supports the idea of the Spirit being a "Person" rather than just a force</note>. b) If the "point of comparison" <note>term: "tertium comparationis" - the specific quality shared by two things being compared</note> is placed in the way the Spirit is in the man, it proves too much, because the spirit of a man is a *part* of him <note>which would imply God has parts, a concept orthodox theology rejects</note>. Therefore, the analogy refers only to the act of "knowing," which is a personal operation. c) To prevent us from using those phrases in which the *Son is said to be in the Father* and the *Father in the Son*, our opponent cleverly notes that it is not said that God is interchangeably in the Spirit. However, since the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are *one* in the same way (1 John 5:7), it follows naturally that by the same reasoning that the Father is in the Son, the Father and Son are in the Holy Spirit. Thus, Jehovah was present to Elijah in the "thin whisper" representing the Holy Spirit (1 Kings 19:12).

XXV. Argument 8) comes from the passages in which we are said to be *sealed by the Holy Spirit* (Ephesians 1:13, 4:30; 2 Corinthians 1:22). This is pushed by Smalcius <note>Valentin Schmalz (1572–1622), a Socinian writer known for his polemics against the deity of Christ and the Spirit</note> in this way: "No one is sealed by a person, but rather a person is the one who is sealed, while men are sealed by an object." **Response:** Nothing prevents us from considering a Person as a Seal. For *to be sealed* is metaphorically the same as "to be confirmed." Now, we are indeed confirmed by Persons; for example, when a guarantee <note>original: "vas"</note> is offered to a creditor. Children, too, are the "pledges" of marital love. Thus, in the writings of Aulus Gellius <note>A 2nd-century Roman author known for his "Attic Nights," a collection of notes on grammar, philosophy, and history</note>, hostages are called a *pledge* <note>term: "arrhabo" - a down-payment or earnest money given to ratify a contract</note> (Attic Nights, XVII, 2). Hence, in the sacred writings, the emblem of a seal occurs in reference to persons (Song of Solomon 8:6; Haggai 2:23; Jeremiah 22:24). And ABARBANEL <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a prominent Jewish statesman, philosopher, and biblical commentator</note>

Furthermore, 2) the better interpreters judge that this does not concern a physical sealing, in which the Holy Spirit is the seal, so much as it concerns that which the Holy Spirit is the author of. For in Ephesians 4:30 it is said *by whom you were sealed* <note>original Greek: ἐν ᾧ ἐσφραγίσθητε</note>, where the word *in* <note>original Greek: ἐν (en)</note> here, as very often, corresponds with the Hebrew *in/by* <note>original Hebrew: ב (bet)</note>. Nor is it an obstacle that the word *in* is omitted in Ephesians 1:13, because any verb allows for a dative of cause, as the Grammarians teach.

XXVI. Regarding the *anointing* <note>note 9 in original</note> which is mentioned in Acts 10:38 concerning the Holy Spirit—where God is said to have *anointed Christ with the Holy Spirit and power*—there is nothing in this that is a misuse of language. If the adversaries think that either "Power" itself is designated by a *hendiadys* <note>term: hendiadys - a figure of speech where two words joined by "and" express a single complex idea, e.g., "power and Spirit" meaning "spiritual power"</note> or His gifts are designated, why do they judge it more acceptable to attribute "anointing" to a *Power* or to *gifts* than to a *Person*? Since this metaphor supposes that a Person is compared to *oil* or *ointment*, why should that be harsher than the emblem of *water*, which we showed in section 16 applies to the Holy Spirit, or the metaphors of *clothing*, *salt*, etc., which are used regarding persons?

XXVII. They defend their own views with equal lack of success. We set aside those who, considering the Holy Spirit as a "particle" or a "degree of divine emanation," overturn the concept of simplicity and spirituality in God; they shake the very foundations of truth known through nature itself. We will offer only a few counter-arguments to those who consider the Holy Spirit to be either *God in action*, or a certain *mode of thinking*, or some *divine Power*, or who think various notions should be combined as the occasion arises.

XXVIII. So that ISAAC WATTS <note>Isaac Watts (1674–1748), the famous English hymn-writer, who also wrote theological treatises exploring the nature of the Trinity, sometimes leaning toward "Arian" or "Sabellian" views that contemporary orthodox writers challenged</note> might make his *first hypothesis* seem probable, he observes: "1) that often the 'spirit of a man' in the phrasing of Scripture expresses the man himself. **Response:** Scripture cannot contradict itself. Therefore, since there exist passages in which the Holy Spirit is distinguished from the other Persons <note>The author refers back to the distinctions established in Chapter 2, Sections 1 and following</note>, we must not depart from this understanding without a very weighty reason. Such a reason does not occur in the sayings brought forward. 

1) In the style of the New Testament, the *Mind* is considered to consist of *Spirit* and *soul*. This is evident from 1 Thessalonians 5:23 and Hebrews 4:12. In the first passage, *soul* aptly expresses the appetitive and sensory faculties, while *Spirit* expresses the purely spiritual ones. In the latter passage, *soul* <note>original Greek: ψυχή (psychē)</note> refers to the qualities of *nature*, while *spirit* <note>original Greek: πνεῦμα (pneuma)</note> refers to the qualities of *grace*, which are the effects of the Holy Spirit. Following this distinction, which we prefer, the Apostle exhorts the faithful to continue pushing the work of renewal by means of that grace of the Holy Spirit which has fixed its seat in their *mind*. Furthermore, in Colossians 1:22, the *body of Christ’s flesh* is distinguished from *His glorified body*.

2) The very thing in question is being assumed as true when it is claimed that the names of "God" and "Holy Spirit" are used interchangeably; in the very passages cited, they are clearly distinguished. Meanwhile, there is a most serious reason why that which is ascribed to the Holy Spirit is also predicated in other sayings about God or the other Persons. For this is required both by the unity of the Persons in their outward works, and by that divine order in which the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son in His operation.

3) The *Soul of God* does not designate God Himself in a redundant sense, but *anthropopathically* <note>term: anthropopathically - a figure of speech where human feelings or passions are attributed to God to make a divine concept easier for humans to understand</note> to describe the intimate inclination and affection of His will.

## II. Among the NAMES, the name Yahweh <note>original: "יהוה" (YHWH), the sacred tetragrammaton or personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible</note> excels, which we claim for the Holy Spirit:

A. From the direct application of certain passages in the New Testament to the Holy Spirit, which in the Old Testament use the name Yahweh <note>original: "יהוה"</note>. Compare Hebrews 3:7, 9 with Psalm 95:7, 8 and Exodus 17:1, 7; Hebrews 9:7, 8 with Leviticus 16:1, 2; and Hebrews 10:15, 16 with Jeremiah 31:31.

## III. B. From those sayings of the New Testament in which the name Lord <note>original: "Κυριος" (Kyrios)</note> is so attributed to the Holy Spirit that it is clear it should be regarded as a translation of the name Yahweh <note>original: "יהוה"</note>.

Thus in the words of 2 Corinthians 3:17, *Now the Lord is that Spirit*, the name *Lord* corresponds to *Yahweh* <note>original: "τῷ Jehova"</note>, because it is clear from verse 16 that the matter concerns that *Lord* to whom Israel must one day be converted when the veil of Moses is removed. Moreover, it is manifest even from Hosea 3:5 that this Lord is *Yahweh*. Nor is it an obstacle that *Lord* seems to be the subject of this statement, a view toward which Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), a champion of Trinitarian theology against Arianism.</note> (in *On the Trinity*, book 2) and Basil <note>Basil of Caesarea (330–379), one of the Cappadocian Fathers who defined the divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note> (in *Against Eunomius*, book 3) have already inclined—the former understanding God in general by the term "Lord," and the latter understanding specifically the second person [the Son]. And no one would doubt that the Spirit of the Lord is the Holy Spirit.* The same opinion was held by Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius. Nor does any reason appear why Hammond, Grotius, Leclerc <note>original: "Clericus"</note>, and Whitby should concede to the Socinians <note>A group of non-Trinitarian Christians who denied the pre-existence of Christ and the personality of the Holy Spirit; the author views their interpretations as a threat to orthodoxy.</note> by thinking that Christ is pointed out here by the word "Lord."
