# ON THE DEITY. CHAPTER IV.

[in this] chapter <note>original: "capite," completing the word from the previous page</note> occurring more frequently, it designates nothing other than the third Hypostasis <note>term: Hypostasis — a Greek theological term referring to a distinct person within the Trinity, as opposed to the shared "substance" or essence of God</note>, and our verse easily admits this same notion; we rightly adhere to it.

IV. The most learned WHITBY <note>Daniel Whitby (1638–1726), an English theologian known for his commentaries on the New Testament</note> observes two points to the contrary.
> 1) He claims that Christ is called *Spirit* by metonymy <note>term: Metonymy — a figure of speech where a concept is called by the name of something associated with it, like saying "the crown" to mean "the king"</note> in the same way He is called *the Way, the Life, the Resurrection*, etc., because He is the Cause and Giver of the Holy Spirit and his operations.

But it is not permitted to argue from those abstract words to a personal and characteristic name. Who, I ask, would undertake to defend that the *Father* is anywhere called *Christ*, simply because He is the first source of his mediatorial office and thus of all his benefits?
> 2) He presses the final words of verse 18: *from the Lord the Spirit* <note>original: "ἀπὸ Κυρίου Πνεύματος" (apo Kyriou Pneumatos)</note>, which he thinks should be rendered *from the Lord of the Spirit*, and not indeed *from the Spirit of the Lord*, as it seems to many, because otherwise, according to the constant usage of the sacred style, it ought to have been read in the inverse order: *from the Spirit of the Lord* <note>original: "ἀπὸ Πνεύματος Κυρίου" (apo Pneumatos Kyriou)</note>.

We admit that this reasoning is sharp enough to refute those who, through the latter version, could also snatch this phrase away from us. But since it is likewise plainly unusual for the Son to be called the *Lord of the Holy Spirit*, we seize upon this observation for our own cause; and we are all the more persuaded because those words are to be distinguished thus: *from the Spirit, the Lord* <note>original: "ἀπὸ Πνεύματος, Κυρίου"</note>, or *who is the Lord*. And so a new example offers itself to us here, in which the Holy Spirit himself is called *Lord* <note>original: "Κύριος" (Kyrios)</note>.

Triados"</note> will easily allow the sayings in Numbers 6:26, Deuteronomy 6:4, Joshua 22:22, and Psalm 50:1 to be referred to it, in which the name *Yahweh* occupying the third place is without doubt to be understood as the Holy Spirit. Add the six hundred places in which *Yahweh* is said to have spoken through the mouths of the Prophets, and they appeal to the word or saying of *Yahweh*, since it is manifest that the *Holy Spirit* was in them and spoke through them (2 Samuel 23:2, 3; Acts 1:16; 1 Peter 1:11; 2 Peter 1:21). Nor should it be neglected that in Deuteronomy 32:12, *Yahweh alone is named the Leader of Israel*, and nevertheless in Isaiah 63:14...

The same [divine status] should be ascribed to the *Spirit of Holiness* of the Lord. For the objection—that *subordinate leaders*, such as Moses and the Angels were (Exodus 23:20, 21), are not excluded here—is easily refuted; rather, it is the *coordinate* leaders, and specifically the idols of the Gentiles, that are excluded. For the *leading* which is praised here is not *ministerial* <note>meaning service-oriented or acting on behalf of another</note>, but *principal* <note>meaning primary or originating from the source</note>, as is evident from the context, as well as from Psalm 143:10, where this same leading of the Holy Spirit is alluded to. Moses himself was merely the instrument of this supreme *Leader* (Psalm 77:21). Furthermore, when the *Angel* in whom the *Name of Jehovah resides* is considered as the *Leader of Israel*, it designates none other than the *Son of God*, that *Shepherd of Israel*. Add to this the manifest passage of Isaiah 28:5, 6: *In that day the Lord of hosts will be*, etc., <note>original Hebrew: לרוח משפט ליושב על המשפט</note> *for a spirit of judgment to him who sits in judgment*. For although better interpreters wish for the Messiah to be designated here by the name *Jehovah*, nothing of the strength of our argument is lost. Since the *Spirit of judgment* through whom judgment is administered (Isaiah 4:4) is distinguished from Him, yet here is so closely joined that He is, as it were, united with that Spirit, it is most clearly indicated that the Son and the Holy Spirit are so intimately united in essence and in work that the name *Jehovah Zebaoth* <term>Jehovah Zebaoth — "The Lord of Hosts," a title emphasizing God's military-like command over the celestial armies and all creation</term> is appropriate to both.

VI. We also attribute the name *Adonai* <note>original Hebrew: אדני; a title meaning "Lord" or "Master," often used by Jews as a substitute for the tetragrammaton Jehovah</note> to the Holy Spirit based on a comparison of *Acts 28:26* with *Isaiah 6:9*. For the Spirit, according to Paul's testimony, spoke the very things that the Prophet testifies were spoken by *Adonai*. Nor does it stand in the way that the Apostle says the Holy Spirit spoke *through Isaiah*, while in Isaiah 6 the words of the Lord are directed *to Isaiah*. For the Apostle implies both: that the words he recites were made *through Isaiah* and *to Isaiah*, since he adds: <note>original Greek: Λεγον, πορευθητι κ. τ. λ.</note> *Saying, Go, etc.* From this it is clear that they are brought forward just as *Adonai* spoke to Isaiah, demanding at the same time that he carry the same words to Israel. We are all the more persuaded because *Adonai*, repeated for the third time at the end of the prayers in Daniel 9:19, designates the *Holy Spirit*. To say nothing of the fact that the same one who is called *Adonai* in this verse is called *Jehovah of Hosts* in verse 3, to which *the Lord God, the Almighty* <note>original Greek: Κυριος ὁ Θεος, ὁ Παντοκρατωρ</note> corresponds in Revelation 4:8.

...could [one become the temple of the Father], who has not believed in Him? *What if [he is the temple] of Christ?* Nor could he become the *Temple of him who denies that Christ is God. What if [he is the temple] of the Holy Spirit? Since the three are one, how can the Holy Spirit be at peace with one who is an enemy of either the Father or the Son?* This is even more compelling because that **God** <note>original Greek: *Theos*</note>, whose **fellow workers** <note>original Greek: *synergoi*</note> the Apostles are said to be in verse 1, is the Holy Spirit himself, as **PLACÆUS** <note>Josué de la Place (1596–1665), a French Protestant theologian known for his work on the Trinity</note> notes against **CRELLIUS** <note>Johannes Crellius (1590–1633), a leading Socinian theologian who argued against the traditional doctrine of the Trinity</note> in Volume II, page 1118.

X. Moreover, it is clear that these Names are attributed to the Holy Spirit with full emphasis, since the entire perfection and glory of the most absolute Deity is predicated of him. Relevant here, in a general sense, is that he is said to be *One with the Father and the Son* in 1 John 5:7 <note>A reference to the "Johannine Comma," a passage traditionally used to support the Trinity</note>; that he is commemorated in the same order with the Father and the Son in those places where the association of a mere creature has no place, namely in Isaiah 48:16, Matthew 28:19, 1 Corinthians 12:4-6, and 2 Corinthians 13:13. These passages have already been defended in Chapter II, section 1 and following. Furthermore, it is asserted that he is in God just as *the spirit of a man is in the man* in 1 Corinthians 2:10-11. For one may infer from this that, just as the *spirit of a man* pertains to the essence of a human being, so the *Spirit of God* constitutes the divine essence itself by the same Necessity of Nature as the Father and the Son. But this will become *more distinct* from the fact that Scripture attributes to him both truly divine Attributes and their manifestation—both *active* through **Works** requiring divine all-sufficiency, and *passive* through the admission of religious **Worship** <note>original Latin: *Cultus*, referring to the honor and devotion due to God alone</note> which belongs to God alone. No one can demand anything further to defeat all doubts regarding the divine Glory of the Holy Spirit with any appearance of fairness.

XI. Since all **DIVINE ATTRIBUTES** are contained within the Idea of a most perfect Life, one must certainly be recognized as God who possesses everything pertaining to that life in the most perfect way. Whatever constitutes a most perfect life is accomplished by a most perfect intellect and will. The former corresponds to the *omniscient* Spirit, the latter to the *omnipotent* Spirit. He possesses both in the most perfect manner, being the Possessor of such great excellence through absolute Eternity, and thus through the very Necessity and Independence of his Nature. The sacred pages provide us with such a vast and sublime concept of the Deity of the Holy Spirit.

# ON THE OMNISCIENCE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT #

XII. OMNISCIENCE includes an adequate knowledge of God Himself and of all created things. *The Apostle clearly ascribes both to the Holy Spirit in 1 Corinthians 2:10–11. For here, first, the most universal object of His knowledge is established—namely, **all things**, not even excluding the depths of God <note>original Greek: "ta bathe tou Theou"</note>. Furthermore, it is evident that the manner of this knowledge is adequate, both because there is nothing within God outside of His depths, and because this knowledge is denied to every creature: "The things of God no one knows, except the Spirit of God."*

XIII. To wrest away this "club" <note>A metaphorical reference to a powerful argument, like the club of Hercules</note> from us, our adversaries commit various fallacies, such as arguing: *that the Holy Spirit is distinguished from God here; that men have "received" Him; that He is said to be "from" God; and that it cannot be said that He alone knows the things of God, since the Father and the Son know the same things besides Him; and similar points.* We have already dealt with some of these in Chapter III, Section 24, and others will coincide with our review of His Relations. More specifically regarding this matter:

> A. “That **searching** the depths of God is inconsistent with divine omniscience.”

The Church Fathers responded to this difficulty in two ways. Some judged that what is attributed to the Holy Spirit is meant in an absolute sense regarding what He does in *the faithful*, whom He impels to search the depths of God <note>original Greek: "ta bathe tou Theou"</note>. **SCHLICHTINGIUS** <note>Jonas Schlichting (1592–1661), a Polish Socinian theologian</note> and **CLARKE** <note>Samuel Clarke (1675–1729), an English clergyman accused of Arianism for his views on the Trinity</note> seize upon this same point for their own purposes. However, this cannot be admitted, *partly* because the words breathe a greater emphasis, since our Apostle teaches in Romans 11:33 that the depths of God are "unsearchable" <note>original Greek: "anexereunēta"</note> even to oneself <note>meaning, to any finite mind</note>; and *partly* because from the force of the opposition in verse 11, it is clear that it speaks of the Spirit of God *who is in God*. Many note that "to search" <note>original Greek: "to ereunan"</note> indicates not ignorance, but—through <term>anthropopatheia</term> <note>Attributing human characteristics or actions to God to make a concept understandable to humans</note>—a most accurate knowledge. **SUICERUS** <note>Johann Caspar Suicer (1620–1684), author of the "Thesaurus Ecclesiasticus," a dictionary of Greek Church Fathers</note> provides references under this word. We rest in this latter response, not only because such a figure of speech is very frequent, but also because "searching" <note>original Greek: "ereunan"</note> occurs explicitly with this meaning in Revelation 2:23. Similarly, the Hebrew word *chaqar* <note>original Hebrew: "חקר"</note>, which the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translates as "searching" <note>original Greek: "ereunan"</note> in Job 28:27, is attributed to God. And the context confirms this interpretation, because those things which the Holy Spirit is said to *search* in verse 10, He is asserted to *know* in verse 11.

XVI. That the **HOLY SPIRIT IS ETERNAL** is established from those passages which teach that he was present not only at the beginning of Creation (*Genesis 1:3* <note>original: "Gen. I. 3."</note>) but that he pre-existed in the eternal Decree and Counsel itself. For it is clear from comparing *Isaiah 40:13* <note>original: "Jes. XL. 13."</note> that the *mind of the Lord* designates *his Spirit* in *Romans 11:34*. And in *Proverbs 8:23*, the eternal *Anointing of Wisdom* implies the *Oil of the Holy Spirit*.

Neither the Father nor the Son undertook anything, nor brought anything *into action*, of which he [the Spirit] was not a partner. That he was a part of the divine *Decree* and was the *Creator of the World* is established at the same time from the passages just cited. The latter is confirmed by *Job 26:13, 33:4* and *Psalm 33:4*. But he is also active in the *Preservation* and *Renewal* of the world (*Psalm 104:29, 30; 147:18*); indeed, he is the Author of miracles, which deviate from the order of this visible world and thus have the character of a New Creation (*Matthew 12:28, Acts 2:4, 1 Corinthians 12:4–11*). Added to these are all the Operations of *Grace*, especially those concerning the application of Salvation—*both* by reason of the Son of God himself, who, notwithstanding the all-sufficiency of his own Deity, willed to be *filled* and led by this Spirit (*Isaiah 61:1, 2; Matthew 3:16; 4:1; 12:28; Luke 4:1*), *and* by reason of the universal Church and each of the elect, whom he effectively brings to life, converts, preserves, and will finally raise up and glorify. Hence, whatever can be referred to him [God] is attributed to the Holy Spirit. Its highest peak consists in **ADORATION**. Whether examples of prayers directed to the Holy Spirit are available is a matter of controversy. We concede that they are somewhat rare, and we derive this from the nature of the divine Economy, according to which he himself is the *Spirit of prayers* (*Zechariah 12:10*). XIX. These examples enjoy all the greater weight the more evidently such things are attributed to the Holy Spirit which suppose or involve the duty of *Adoration*. This is clear, firstly, from the PETITIONS <note>original: "VOTIS"; in this context, the solemn intercessory prayers or benedictions of the biblical authors.</note> of the *Saints*, who pray for truly divine Benefits from the Holy Spirit. For petitions of this kind are nothing other than a testimony of that which we earnestly request in Prayer from Him whom we consider as the Fountain of such Goods. Among such *Petitions* we include the *Priestly Blessing* of Numbers 6:25, where it is prayed by "Jehovah" (appearing third in the sequence) that *He lift up His face* and *grant peace*, as well as the *Pauline Blessing* in 2 Corinthians 13:13, and that of John in Revelation 1:4, in which he prays for <term>grace and peace</term> <note>original Greek: "charin kai eirēnēn"</note> <term>from the seven spirits who are before His throne</term> <note>original Greek: "apo tōn hepta pneumatōn, ha estin enōpion tou thronou autou"</note>. The exceptions to which this passage seems liable more than others will easily vanish once we have proven, *firstly*, that the explanations of those who understand the "seven Spirits" to be something other than the third Person of the Deity contain nothing plausible; and *secondly*, that there are foundational reasons why the Apostle wished to designate only the Holy Spirit under the name of the *seven Spirits*.

->## ON THE DEITY. CHAPTER IV. 163 ##<-

XX. Those who strive to weaken the demonstrative force of this passage contend that these *seven Spirits, or sevenfold Gifts and Operations*, should be considered abstractly, or—as most are inclined to believe—*that they signify as many principal Angels from the heavenly household.* Against the *former* [those who see them as abstract qualities], we counter that the name used is personal; it is mentioned in the middle position between the Persons of the Father and the Son; and the source of the blessing being prayed for is distinguished from the blessing itself. Nor does the <term>Hendiadys [a figure of speech where two words express a single complex idea]</term> which <term>Grotius</term> <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a prominent Dutch jurist and theologian who often sought rationalist or philological explanations for scripture.</note> puts forward have any place here—as if "peace from God and the seven Spirits" were merely peace from God operating in seven modes. This is because *Hendiadys* is not only extremely rare in the sacred scriptures, but it has absolutely no place regarding personal names, especially those occupying a middle position between preceding and following personal names.

Against the *latter* [those who see them as angels], the fact stands that nowhere else in the passages of Scripture is this honor attributed to Angels—namely, that divine gifts should be sought from them. *This also does not suit them because "Grace and Peace" contain the sum of all Good things, as included in the solemn Blessing of both the Priests in Numbers 6 and the Apostles in nearly all the beginnings of the Pauline Epistles.* Furthermore, it is very difficult to conceive that *Angels would occupy a middle place between the Father and the Son*. Finally, *these Seven Spirits in chapters IV and V* [of Revelation] are not numbered among the creatures offering honor to God, but are immediately joined with the description of the Throne itself and thus with the object of the subsequent <term>Doxologies [hymns of praise]</term>.

It is indeed objected that *to stand before the throne is only for subjects waiting to receive commands.* However, the text does not read *that they stand*, but that they *are before his throne*, and in the same place as the Lamb, and thus *in the middle of the throne (Revelation 5:6).* Nor is that passage they urge, 1 Timothy 5:21, useful <term>for distinction</term> <note>original Greek: πρὸς διάκρισιν (pros diakrisin), meaning a point of comparison or differentiation.</note>. *For to establish Angels as witnesses, and to pray for divine Gifts from Angels, are actions as different as the whole of heaven.* Therefore, it is not surprising that almost all the ancient and the better modern Interpreters agree with such consensus that the *Holy Spirit* is understood here. Even <term>Pererius</term> <note>Benedictus Pererius (1535–1610), a learned Jesuit commentator.</note> himself, despite the leanings of the <term>Pontiffs</term> <note>The author is referring to Roman Catholic authorities/theologians.</note>, acknowledged in his 7th Disputation on the Apocalypse *that this opinion is almost universal among Interpreters, so much so that he does not dare to completely reject a view put forward by so many and such great men.* And it is all the more troublesome that certain...

A cloud of objection is raised. For even through prayers directed generally toward God, the Holy Spirit, who is *in God*, is honored at the same time; and that efficacy which He exerts when He renders the elect fit for the Worship of God is a work so glorious and truly divine that, for this reason, He is to be glorified by them for eternity. However, so that some specific examples may be seen to exist, we appeal to the *Trisagion* <note>original: τρισάγιον; the "thrice-holy" hymn "Holy, Holy, Holy" found in Isaiah 6:3, which theologians often interpreted as a reference to the Trinity.</note> in Isaiah 6:3, which is shown to pertain also to the Holy Spirit from what was noted in section 7. From this, its parallel in Revelation 4:8 must be extended to the same degree. To this may be added the passage cited from Daniel 9:19. In the New Testament as well, Matthew 9:38 contains the command for the *Adoration of the Holy Spirit*, as is established by comparing it with Acts 13:1–4 <note>In Acts 13, the Holy Spirit speaks directly to the leaders of the church in Antioch, saying "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul," which the author views as an exercise of divine authority requiring prayerful obedience.</note>. Nor does an example seem to be lacking in Acts 4:24–25, since it is manifest that the one *who spoke through the mouth of David* was the Holy Spirit—both from the person speaking in Psalm 2:1, who is distinguished from Jehovah and *his Anointed*, and by comparison with Acts 1:16. Furthermore, Simeon in Luke 2:29 adores that Lord who had predicted to him that he would see *Christ*; it is taught in verse 26 that this person was the Holy Spirit.

XIX. These examples enjoy all the more weight because those things which suggest or involve the duty of *Adoration* are so evidently attributed to the Holy Spirit. This is clear, first, from the *VOWS of the Saints*, which pray for truly divine benefits from the Holy Spirit. For *Vows* of this kind are nothing other than a testimony of that which we earnestly demand in prayers from Him whom we consider the Fountain of such Goods. Moreover, among such *Vows* we number the <term>Priestly Blessing</term> <note>Found in Numbers 6:24–26, this blessing is structured in three parts; the author identifies the third part—granting peace—specifically with the Holy Spirit.</note> in Numbers 6:25, where it is vowed by Jehovah, who is third in the order, that *he might lift up his face and grant peace*; as well as the *Pauline Vow* in 2 Corinthians 13:13, and that of John in Revelation 1:4, in which he prays for grace and peace from the seven spirits, which are before his throne <note>original: χάριν καὶ εἰρήνην precatur ἀπὸ τῶν ἑπτὰ πνευμάτων, ἅ ἐστιν ἐνώπιον τοῦ θρόνου αὐτοῦ.</note>. The exceptions to which this passage seems liable more than others will easily vanish once we have proven, *first*, that the explanations of those who understand the "seven Spirits" to be anything other than the third Person of the Deity contain nothing plausible; and *second*, that fundamental reasons exist as to why the Apostle wished to designate the Holy Spirit alone under the name of the *seven Spirits*.

# ON THE DEITY. CHAPTER IV. #

XX. Those who strive to weaken the demonstrative force of this saying contend that these *seven Spirits* signify either abstract *Gifts* and *sevenfold Operations*, or—as most are inclined to believe—an equal number of principal *Angels* from the heavenly family. Against the *former* group, we object that the name is personal; that it is commemorated in the middle position between the Persons of the Father and the Son; and that the source of the benefit being prayed for must be distinguished from the benefit itself. Nor does the *hendiadys* <term>hendiadys: a figure of speech where two words joined by "and" express a single complex idea, such as "grace and peace" meaning "peaceful grace"</term> that GROTIUS <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a prominent Dutch theologian and jurist often criticized by more orthodox writers for his linguistic interpretations of scripture.</note> pretends have a place here—as if *peace from God and the seven Spirits* were merely *peace from God through seven operating modes*. This is because hendiadys is not only extremely rare in the sacred scriptures, but it has no place at all in personal names, especially when occupying the middle position between preceding and following personal names.

*Against the latter group* [who favor the Angel interpretation], the fact stands that *nowhere* in other passages of Scripture is this honor attributed to *Angels*, such that divine gifts should be sought from them. Furthermore, such an honor *does not suit them*, because *Grace and Peace* contain the sum of all Goodness, included in the solemn Blessing both the Priestly one in *Numbers 6* and the *Apostolic* one found in nearly all the openings of the Pauline Epistles. It would also be *most difficult to conceive* of *Angels* occupying the middle place between the Father and the Son. *Finally, these Seven Spirits* in chapters 4 and 5 are not counted among the creatures offering honor to God, but are immediately joined with the description of the Throne itself and are thus the direct object of the following Doxologies <term>doxology: a short hymn or formula of praise to God</term>.

It is indeed objected that *standing before the throne is nothing other than the posture of attending subjects* who wait to receive commands. However, the text does not read *that they stand*, but that they *are* before his throne, and in the same place as the Lamb—and therefore *in the midst of the throne* (Revelation 5:6). Nor is that passage they urge, 1 Timothy 5:21, relevant <note>original: "προς Διονυσον" (pros Dionyson); a Greek idiom meaning "to the point" or "pertinent to the matter."</note>. For to appoint Angels as *Witnesses* and to pray for divine Gifts from Angels are *actions* as different as the entire sky. Therefore, it is no wonder that almost all the ancients, and the better among the modern Interpreters, understand the Holy Spirit here with such consensus that even PERERIUS <note>Benedict Pererius (1535–1610), a Jesuit scholar whose commentary on Revelation was widely read even by Protestants.</note> himself, to the displeasure of the Roman Catholics, acknowledged in his 7th disputation on the Apocalypse that this opinion is almost universal among *Interpreters*, so much so that he does not dare to completely reject an idea put forward by so many and such great men. XXI. However, so that interpreters—at least those positioned outside the partisan fray—may be rendered more favorable to us, we must observe more accurately what the Apostle was looking back to in his greeting. The hypothesis of those who, along with AUGUSTINE, COCCEIUS, GRELOT, and VITRINGA, believe an allusion is made to Isaiah 11:2, does not exhaust the matter. For the attributes ascribed there to the Spirit of Jehovah do not make up a *sevenfold* group, but a *sixfold* one. <note>Isaiah 11:2 lists six qualities: wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, and the fear of the LORD. While some traditions count the "Spirit of the LORD" as a seventh, the author argues the list itself is sixfold.</note> Therefore, nothing else can be elicited from there regarding Him than what is not unusual in sacred phraseology: to distinguish different properties of the same divine Spirit as if they were different spirits. This also occurs in Romans 8:15, where the *Spirit of slavery* and the *Spirit of adoption*, though they are the same Person, dwell together as distinct ones.

Therefore, those who think the *symbol of the Golden Candelabrum* <note>The Menorah of the Tabernacle and Temple.</note> should be considered strike closer to the mark: *either* looking to the *seven lamps* of the continuous work proceeding from the lampstand itself, as the celebrated WITSIUS does in the cited location, section 31; *or* with others, looking to the oil channeled through the seven <gloss>original Hebrew: מוצקות (*mutzakot*)</gloss> *tubes* or *funnels* of Zechariah 4 into its bowl; *or*—which seems most likely to me—to the *Sacred Fire* itself, which burned in this Candelabrum divided into seven flames. For it is from this that these seven Spirits are called <gloss>original Greek: ἑπτα λαμπάδες πυρος καιόμεναι ἐνώπιον του θρόνου (*hepta lampades pyros kaiomenai enōpion tou thronou*)</gloss> *seven lamps of fire burning before the throne* in Revelation 4:5. And they are so joined with <gloss>original Greek: ἀσραπαις (*astrapais*)</gloss> *lightnings* proceeding from the throne (comparing Daniel 7:10), that it should not be doubted that the same *Fire* which *issued from the throne like a river* was divided in these <gloss>original Greek: λαμπάσι πυρος (*lampasi pyros*)</gloss>—that is, *lamps*—which were entirely nothing but *fire*, though they kept the shape of lamps, to form just as many rays or bright horns of fire above the head of the *Lamb* in Revelation 5:6. Therefore, the matter here was the same: one body of fire divided into seven gleaming flashes. And this was analogous to that phenomenon of the same Fire, shadowing forth the same Spirit of God, but distinct in the shapes of flaming tongues in Acts 2:3.

...[should] arise, because this unusual and enigmatic naming of the *Holy Spirit* occurs in the *Apostolic Greeting* <note>The greeting in Revelation 1:4–5: "Grace to you and peace... from the seven spirits who are before his throne."</note>, which seemed to require a simpler style, we consider that three things must be observed. *The first is* that the entire description of the Holy Trinity, which John addresses in his prayer, is fashioned from the enigmas of the visions that follow. This was done most wisely, because in this way the path was paved to understanding the mystery of the visions themselves—and especially the representations of the Holy Trinity—in a manner worthy of God <note>original Greek: *θεοπρεπῶς* (*theoprepōs*); meaning in a way that befits the divine nature.</note>. Therefore, this description presents the *Holy Spirit* not as He is in His essence, but as His depiction appeared both in the *Vision* and in that *Type* <term>Type: In biblical interpretation, a "type" is a person, object, or event in the Old Testament (like the Tabernacle) that symbolically foreshadows a greater reality in the New Testament.</term> of the Sanctuary from which that Vision was drawn. For this reason, those who judge our interpretation to be inconvenient are ignorant of the logic of Typological discipline, in which the same personal subject is frequently represented under divided forms in relation to His various operations or objects. Thus, the two Altars, the sacrifices multiplied at the same time, the drops of blood divided by a sevenfold sprinkling, and so on, all foreshadowed the same Sacrifice of Christ—indeed, the same Christ—and His various relations and applications.

XXIII. *Secondly*, we emphasize this above all: that the Greek phrase "the seven spirits" <note>original: *τα επτα πνευματα* (*ta hepta pneumata*)</note> is here more rightly rendered as *seven Winds* than *seven Spirits*. For it is clear from the passages cited in *Revelation 4 & 5* that these *spirits* were visible. Yet the word *spirit* <note>The Greek word *pneuma* can mean spirit, wind, or breath.</note> is never applied to any visible body. But if you ask in what form these *Winds* could have appeared? Surely in no form more fit than streaks of fire which, ignited by the speed of their movement in the air and driven by them, fly around most swiftly and divide themselves most widely, just as usually happens in the greatest storms and tempests which are often mixed with lightning. Hence, *Winds and flames of fire* occur as joined emblems of the same subjects in *Psalm 104:4*. Indeed, the *Holy Spirit* Himself was poured out under the combined phenomena of a mighty wind and tongues of fire in *Acts 2:2–3*; and thus He is emphatically called the *Spirit or Wind of burning* <note>original Hebrew: רוח בער (*ruach ba'er*); see Isaiah 4:4.</note>. XXV. Furthermore, for the same *Honor of Adoration*, point B argues:
That a TEMPLE is assigned to the Holy Spirit in 2 Corinthians 3:16 and 6:12. <note>The author likely intends 1 Corinthians 3:16 and 6:19, which are the foundational texts describing the believer as a temple of the Holy Spirit.</note> Now, a Temple is the House of God, and specifically one destined precisely for his invocation, as in Isaiah 56:7. The speech of AUGUSTINE in Book I *Against Maximinus*, number 11, is clearly moving here:

> Would we not be cursed by the truth of Christ and by the Church of God if we made a temple of wood and stones to some most excellent holy Angel? This is because we would be exhibiting to a creature that service which is owed to God alone. If, therefore, we would be sacrilegious by making a temple for any creature, how is he not the true God, for whom we do not make a temple, but are ourselves his Temple?

Nor do I think I shall wander outside the bounds <note>original: *extra oleas*; a Latin idiom meaning to go off-topic or exceed the proper limits of a discussion</note> if I refer here to those phrases by which the Holy Spirit is said to *rest* upon the Prophets and Illustrious Men of the Old Testament (Numbers 11:25; 2 Kings 2:14), upon the Messiah (Isaiah 11:2), and upon the faithful of the New Testament (1 Peter 4:14). D. Furthermore, **BAPTISM** in his name (Matthew 28:19) is an honor fitting for God alone (1 Corinthians 1:13). > But also, when the Lord commands that the Nations be baptized in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, it is most clear that the Holy Spirit is not a creature. This is evident either from that very partnership which he has together with the Father and the Son, or because the Lord never commanded that anyone be baptized in the name of a creature. And it is well that he used a single "name," saying: *In the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit*; so that one primary authority of the indivisible and perfect Trinity might be believed.

E. Add to this that we are bound to **FAITH** in the Holy Spirit, and indeed with the same emphasis with which we must believe in the Father and the Son. Hence, believing and being baptized are joined in relation to the whole Trinity in Matthew 28:19. And the Testimony of the Holy Spirit, just like that of the other persons, must be received through Faith as the Testimony of God (1 John 5:7, 9, 10). **DIDYMUS** <note>Didymus the Blind, a 4th-century Alexandrian theologian.</note> in Book II of *On the Holy Spirit* does not do badly to compare this with Ephesians 4:5: *One Lord, one Faith, one Baptism.* For here, not only are Faith and Baptism joined, but Unity is assigned to both, specifically because Faith is occupied with the Holy Spirit in one and the same way as it is with the Father and the Son. From this it follows that if Faith in the Father and the Son involves Adoration, Faith in the Holy Spirit extends just as widely. Furthermore,

F. he declares *himself to be the goal of the entire Gospel Ministry* in Acts 13:2, commanding: *Separate FOR ME Barnabas and Saul.* Therefore, the Apostles were devoted to the service of the Holy Spirit, even though they wished to be regarded as nothing but servants of the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:23).

# ON THE DEITY. CHAPTER IV.

...to direct prayers, and to seek either the same or certain different benefits from him individually? <note>original: "preces dirigere, atque aut eadem aut diversa quaedam beneficia ab illo sigillatim petere?"</note> JOHN FORBES <note>John Forbes of Corse (1593–1648) was a prominent Scottish Episcopalian theologian.</note> at least, in his *Historical-Theological Instructions*, Book I, chapter 23, judges that it is not a suitable mode of worship if the three Persons are invoked separately, as if in a continuous series of three distinct acts of worship. As far as we are concerned, we think the examples we have brought forward are more than enough to settle this matter; those who admit them will also acknowledge that the Holy Spirit has been addressed by the saints separately, both for the same and for different benefits. Nor should it be feared that by this method something divided in the Divine Essence will appear to the one praying, provided only that they are convinced of the Unity of that Essence. For whoever asks for the same benefit from the Three Persons distinctly, confesses that His glory belongs to each individual Person. And whoever prays for different benefits has that order before his eyes according to which those Benefits—separate as to their effect and the nature of the object, but intimately connected to each other as to their nature—are desired from those Persons who, according to the teaching of Scripture, have the closest relationship to them. The renowned ZACHARY GRAPIUS <note>Zacharias Grapius (1671–1713) was a Lutheran theologian and professor at Rostock.</note> treated this matter more extensively in his *Theology of Recent Controversies*, Part I, pages 178 and following.

XXVIII. Finally, just as clearly as Holy Scripture asserts the Divine Honor of the Holy Spirit, it just as plainly condemns any offense against him, and threatens a **VENGEANCE** so atrocious that it can only belong to the supreme Majesty of God. On this point, it is sufficient to note that *Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is declared to be unforgivable* <note>original: "Blasphemia contra Spiritum Sanctum pro irremissibili"</note> in Matthew 12:31, 32. For the foundation from which the weight of such a punishment flows—one that is not to be forgiven for eternity—cannot be anything other than the infinite dignity of the Person against whom this sin is committed.

# ON THE HOLY SPIRIT

...why *Blasphemy against the person of the Holy Spirit is more unforgivable than against the person of the Son. But because the works of the Holy Spirit are the most effective means for the conviction of men, for that reason the rejection of them is the greatest aggravation of guilt.* <note>original: "cur Blasphemia contra personam Spiritus Sancti magis sit irremissibilis..." This refers to the "unforgivable sin" mentioned in Matthew 12:31-32.</note> **Response 1.** Just as Blasphemy against the Son pertains to his person, the same must be established regarding Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. **2.** *Blasphemy* is properly a vice that has a *person* as its object, not a thing, since it is in reality a most atrocious kind of slander. **3.** We invert the argument. For a certain preeminence of dignity cannot be attributed to the work of the Holy Spirit in the present case—which dealt with miracles—since those miracles were the works of the Son as much as the Holy Spirit. **4.** The circumstances provide another very clear reason. For the Majesty of the Son was up to this point hidden <note>This refers to the "State of Humiliation," where Jesus lived as a common man, making his divine nature less obvious to observers.</note>, but the Majesty of the Holy Spirit struck the eyes and the mind. **5.** Those very works which CLARKE <note>Samuel Clarke (1675–1729) was an influential English clergyman and philosopher whose views on the Trinity were often accused of leaning toward Arianism (the belief that the Son and Spirit are subordinate to the Father).</note> concedes to the Holy Spirit were divine.

**C.** He adds, *that it is not sin in general, but specifically Blasphemy against the Spirit that is declared unforgivable, not because of this single Act, but because of an incorrigible Habit, of which such an Act was the Sign; hence also in the following verse 33, this likeness is applied: that a bad tree is known by its bad fruit.* <note>Referencing Matthew 12:33, "Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad."</note> **Response.** We easily admit the first part of this observation. However, we deny **1)** that "incorrigible" and "unforgivable" are synonyms. The latter is the foundation of the former. The most obstinate sinner does not resist the will of God except insofar as he is left to himself and excluded from the efficacy of the merit of Christ. **2)** The consequence is also void; for whether a *Habit* <term>Habitus: a settled disposition or character trait</term> or an *Act* <term>Actus: a specific deed or performance</term> of sin is hinted at, it is all the same to us, as long as it has not been refuted that the exaggeration of the sin in this passage is derived from the dignity of the object <note>The "object" here is the Holy Spirit himself; the author argues the sin is great because the Spirit is God.</note>.

**XXX.** Against the weight of so many arguments, the *Ante-Nicene* <term>Ante-Nicene: Referring to the era of the Christian Church before the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.</term> Church itself rose up from the very beginnings of Christianity. Vain are the efforts against this truth by CRELLIUS <note>Johannes Crellius (1590–1633), a Polish-German theologian and leading figure in Socinianism, which denied the Trinity.</note>, SANDIUS <note>Christoph Sand (1644–1680), an Arian historian who argued that the early Church did not believe in the Trinity.</note> and WHISTON <note>William Whiston (1667–1752), an English theologian who was famously expelled from Cambridge for his Arian views.</note>, the latter of whom proceeds with such boldness in his *Account of the Primitive Faith*, Article XX, page 369 and following, as to assert that not before the middle of the 4th Century was the Holy Spirit either directly called *God* or invo— <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "invoked" (invocatum).</note>

He asserts this with the same degree of reliability with which, shortly thereafter, he praises **Petavius** <note>Dionysius Petavius (1583–1652) was a French Jesuit theologian and a foundational figure in the history of dogma.</note> as being of the same opinion, citing his words from *Dogmatic Theology, Volume II, Book I, Chapter 14*, in which he says, *most Christians did not dare to openly profess the Holy Spirit as God; and furthermore, that the first of all the Synod of Alexandria in the year 362 decreed that the Holy Spirit must be held as God.* For it is manifest that **Petavius** is dealing there only with those Fathers who, in the 4th century, were fighting against the **Arians** <note>Arians: Followers of Arius who taught that the Son and Spirit were created beings, not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> and **Macedonians** <note>Macedonians: Also known as 'Pneumatomachi' (Spirit-fighters), a sect that denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note>. He notes, however, that the "dissimulation" <note>Dissimulation: Here meaning a strategic silence or concealment of the full truth for the sake of unity.</note> of the 4th-century Fathers arose from a desire for peace and concord. XXXI. And how truly we may claim the Antiquity of the Church for our side is shown by that most ancient **Doxology** <note>Doxology: A short hymn of praise. The author is referring to the "Glory be to the Father..."</note>, already used by **Polycarp** and the Church of Smyrna, which is directed to the Holy Spirit equally with the Father and the Son. For although the Ancients asserted that the Father and Son should be glorified indiscriminately, sometimes "with" the Holy Spirit and sometimes "in" the Holy Spirit, they nevertheless abundantly proved—after others, **Dionysius Petavius** in *Dogmatic Theology, Part II, Book II, Chapter 6*, **George Bull** <note>George Bull (1634–1710) was an English Bishop famous for his defense of the Nicene Creed.</note> in *Defense of the Nicene Faith, Section II, page 55 and following*, and **Johann Friedrich Burgius** in his *Dissertation on the Glorification of the Holy Spirit, debated at Leipzig, 1711*—that the latter phrasing is to be understood "economically" <note>Economically: Referring to the 'Economy of Salvation,' or the specific roles the persons of the Trinity take in relation to humanity, rather than their internal essence.</note> and is to be explained by the former. Whiston believed they were written by the Apostles themselves, a view modern scholars (and the author of this text) reject.</note> to explain how that matter stands. As if any light could be expected for the writings of **JUSTIN MARTYR** from a spurious work that belongs to the times of the Arians!

But it is also clear that **ATHENAGORAS** <note>An early Christian philosopher and apologist from Athens, writing around 177 AD.</note> honors the Holy Spirit with the name of GOD, as is evident from the passage cited in Chapter 2, section 17; to which one should add what he says in the same place, section 22: *We assert God, and His Son the Word, and the Holy Spirit, to be united in power*. We also join **IRENAEUS** <note>Bishop of Lyons (c. 130–202 AD) and a key early theologian against heresy.</note> from Book 4, chapter 12, who discourses in this way on the passage from *Isaiah* 57:16, *The Spirit shall go forth from me, and I have made every breath*: *assigning the Spirit specifically to God, which in the last times He poured out through the adoption of sons upon the human race: but showing the breath to be common in the creation and a thing made. Now, that which is made is one thing, and He who made it is another. The breath, therefore, is temporary, but the Spirit is eternal.* 

For while he says, *setting the Spirit specifically upon God* <note>original: "τὸ πνεῦμα ἰδίως ἐπὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ τάξας"</note>, which the translator renders as *assigning the Spirit specifically to God*, he acknowledges that the Holy Spirit belongs to the uniqueness <note>original: "idioteta" (ἰδιώτητα)</note> of the divine essence, and on this foundation he places Him above all creatures and attributes eternity to Him from before time began. Compare **MASSUET** <note>René Massuet (1666–1716) was a Benedictine scholar famous for his definitive edition of Irenaeus’s works.</note> in his dissertation on Irenaeus, Book 3, Article 5, section 63. 

What, moreover, is clearer than that passage of **TERTULLIAN** <note>The first major Christian author to write in Latin (c. 155–220 AD); he coined many theological terms used today.</note> in *Against Praxeas*, chapter 2? *He thinks that the one God is not to be believed in any other way than if He says that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are the selfsame: as if one were not thus also all things, through the unity of substance, and nonetheless the mystery of the economy* <note>original: "oikonomias" (οἰκονομίας). In early theology, 'economy' refers to how the three persons of the Trinity relate to one another and to the world.</note> *is preserved, which disposes the unity into a Trinity, directing the three: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Three, however, not in status but in degree; not in substance but in form; not in power but in aspect; yet of one substance, and of one status, and of one power: because it is one God, from whom these degrees, and forms, and aspects are assigned in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.*

XXXIV. Regarding the fact that some babble that the honor of the Holy Spirit was not even provided for by the *Council of Nicaea* <note>The First Council of Nicaea (325 AD) focused primarily on the nature of the Son.</note>, this was long ago addressed by **AMPHILOCHIUS** of Iconium <note>A 4th-century bishop and cousin of Gregory of Nazianzus.</note> in a *Synodal Letter* found in **COTELERIUS’S** *Grecian Monuments*, Vol. II, page 101:

> *It was necessary then for the Fathers to describe more extensively the dogma of the Only-Begotten Son, since they were striving to cut out the Heresy of Arius which had recently arisen at that time. And since at that time the question regarding the Holy Spirit was not being raised, they therefore added nothing further. However, to those who read prudently, the doctrine concerning the Spirit contained in that faith will seem sufficient. For they taught that just as we must believe in the Father and the Son, so also must we believe in the Spirit: neither introducing any other nature into the divine and blessed Trinity, nor cutting anything away from the Trinity in that exposition of faith.*

Ever since the error of the Semi-Arians <note>A group that attempted a middle ground between Nicaea and Arianism, often questioning the full divinity of the Spirit.</note> grew strong, the honor of the Holy Spirit has been abundantly provided for by entire Councils—not only local ones in Alexandria, Illyricum, and Rome, but also by the Second Ecumenical Council of Constantinople <note>Held in 381 AD, this council expanded the Creed to include a fuller description of the Holy Spirit.</note>—through a new clause added to the Nicene Creed. We do not deny that some of the Post-Nicene Fathers were more scrupulous than was strictly necessary regarding the attribution of the name *GOD* to the Holy Spirit. However, they frequently declare that this arose primarily because they did not think the name of God should be attributed *directly* to the Third Person <note>The Holy Spirit.</note>, which must be attributed to their fear of misinterpretation <note>original: "παρερμηνείας" (parermēneias)</note>; otherwise, they manfully defended His divine essence. ### ON THE DEITY. CHAPTER IV.

...and a suspicion remains that some of them used a certain dissimulation <note>original: "dissimulatione," meaning a strategic concealment of their full beliefs</note>, lest they exasperate the **MACEDONIANS** <note>The Macedonians, or Pneumatomachians, were a 4th-century sect that accepted the divinity of the Son but denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note>, whom they initially thought were united with them against the **ARIANS**. In this matter, if they suffered from any human frailty <note>original: "si quid humanius passi sunt," a polite idiom for making a mistake or showing weakness</note>, they later noticed that their hopes had been mocked, and they thereafter fought quite candidly and strenuously for the Deity of the Holy Spirit.

XXXV. In the writings of the Jews themselves, such passages exist from which it is clear that they were not averse to recognizing the Deity of the Holy Spirit. To this point look the words in the *Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer*, Chapter XXXIII:

*Rabbi Phineas says: Twenty years after everyone was killed in Babylon, the Holy Spirit rested upon Ezekiel and led him out to the Valley of Dura, and showed him very many dry bones... He [the Holy Spirit] said to him: "Is there power in me to revive them?" And he should have replied: "Lord of the world, there is power in You to do much more than these"; but instead he said: "Lord God, You know this," as if he did not believe. Therefore, his bones were not buried in a pure land, as it is said: "And in an impure land you shall die and be buried."* <note>original Hebrew: "רבי פנחס אומר לאחר כ׳ שנה...". This midrashic story interprets Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones, suggesting the Holy Spirit speaks with divine authority and power.</note>

The same is confirmed by the name **SHEKHINAH** <note>Hebrew: שכינה, referring to the "Divine Presence" or "In-dwelling" of God</note> attributed to the Holy Spirit, as we noted in Chapter II, Section 19. For the name *Shekhinah* is considered among the divine names by the Jews, as is abundantly clear from the passages excerpted by **BUXTORF** in *History of the Ark*, Chapter XIV; **CRAMER** in *Theology of Israel*, Part II, p. 343ff; **RHENFERD** in *Dissertations*, p. 19ff; **EISENMENGER** in *Judaism Revealed*, Part I, Chapter VI, p. 268, and others. It is also clear from the synonymy that exists for <term>the <note>original Greek: τῷ</note></term> *Shekhinah* among the Jewish Masters with the phrase **KAVOD YHWH** <note>Hebrew: כבוד יהוה, meaning "The Glory of the LORD"</note>, which was most learnedly investigated by the most celebrated **TH. HASE**—my own pride, and that of his country and the Church—in his dissertation on Haggai 2:8ff, cited above. Yet we do not cling to these arguments excessively, since from what we noted in Chapter III, Sections 1 and 2, it is clear that under a confession of the Deity of the Holy Spirit, the poison of **SABELLIANISM** <note>Sabellianism was a heresy that claimed the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons, but merely three different "modes" or "masks" of a single person.</note> may lurk.

## CHAPTER V.
# VINDICATING THE DEITY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT AGAINST ADVERSARIES.

->I.<-

If the things recorded by **EPIPHANIUS** <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403), a Church Father known for his "Panarion," a massive work refuting various heresies.</note> concerning the **HELCESAITES** are true, they were the most ancient enemies of the Deity of the Holy Spirit, dating back to the very times of the Apostles. For he says in *Heresies 19, section 4*, that their author, whom he names *Helxai*, or *Jelxai*, associated himself with a certain Jewish sect called the *Ossenes* around the time of the Emperor Trajan. He claimed that *the Holy Spirit is female in gender and similar to Christ, standing like a statue above a cloud and between two mountains.* He adds in *Heresies 53, section 1*, that *they confess Christ in word only, but think him to be a created being who appears repeatedly: first, he himself fashioned the body of Adam, and then he put it on again whenever it seemed right to him. They believe the Holy Spirit is his sister in a female form; both Christ and the Holy Spirit are said to be ninety-six miles high and twenty-four miles wide.* But we read here nothing but monstrous riddles, which their very name indicates these men affected <note>original: "affectasse," meaning they deliberately cultivated or imitated this obscure style</note>. For Epiphanius's own explanation shows that it was not so much the name of a person as the name of a sect, which he translates as *hidden power* <note>original Greek: δύναμιν ἀποκεκαλυμμένην; the author is interpreting this as "hidden" rather than "revealed" based on the following etymology</note>, because *Hel* <note>Hebrew: יאל (*Y'al*)</note> signifies *power*, and *Esai* <note>Hebrew: כסיי (*Kassay*)</note> signifies *hidden*. I certainly rest in this derivation alongside **PETAVIUS** <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a prominent Jesuit scholar of the early Church</note>, as it is much simpler than the ones proposed by **Scaliger** or **Rhenferd**. I have little doubt that they were an offshoot of the **Gnostics**, since Jewish, Christian, and Pagan dogmas were combined in their confession; they borrowed the appearance of the greatest mysteries through the obscurity of their words, and they rejected all martyrdom. For this reason, these very things they prattled on about regarding Christ and the Holy Spirit I would relate to the masculine and feminine <term>Syzygies</term> <note>Syzygies were divine "pairs" of beings in Gnostic cosmology, representing the balancing of male and female principles within the divine realm.</note> of the Gnostics, through

II. A blasphemy of no less importance is attributed to **MONTANUS** by **CYRIL OF JERUSALEM** in *Catechesis XVI*, section 4, asserting that this almost insane and demented man dared to claim that he himself was the Holy Spirit. **THEODORET** recorded the same about him in *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, Book III, chapter 2, as did **PSEUDO-AMBROSE** <note>An anonymous author whose works were traditionally but incorrectly attributed to St. Ambrose of Milan.</note> on 1 Thessalonians 5. Nevertheless, there were various sects among the Montanists: one claimed the Paraclete dwelt more fully in *Montanus* than in the Apostles, while another taught the error of <term>Sabellianism|the belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three distinct persons, but three different modes or "masks" of a single God</term> at the same time. This latter point is clear from the words of **JEROME** in his *Letter to Marcella*, in which he testifies that the Montanists say that because God could not save the world through two stages (*in Moses and Christ*), He finally descended through the Holy Spirit into *Montanus*, *Prisca*, and *Maximilla* <note>Prisca and Maximilla were two women who accompanied Montanus and claimed to be prophetesses receiving direct revelations from the Spirit.</note>, whom he calls "insane women." ## DEFENDING THE DEITY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT AGAINST ADVERSARIES.

->I.<-

If what **EPIPHANIUS** <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD) was a bishop known for his *Panarion*, a massive work detailing and refuting early Christian heresies.</note> reports regarding the **ELCESAITES** is true, they were the most ancient enemies of the Deity of the Holy Spirit, dating back to the very times of the Apostles. He allegedly claimed that the *Holy Spirit was female in sex and similar to Christ, appearing like a statue above a cloud and standing between two mountains.* He adds in *Against Heresies, Book LIII, § 1* that they confess Christ in words only, though they believe him to be a created being who appears repeatedly; specifically, that he first fashioned the body of Adam and then, whenever he pleased, would put it on again. He further claimed that the Holy Spirit was Christ's sister in female form, and that both Christ and the Holy Spirit were ninety-six miles in height and twenty-four miles in width. <note>These bizarre, massive dimensions are characteristic of the mystical and often "monstrous" allegories found in early heterodox groups.</note>

III. In the same category, I would include others who are reported to have attributed the name of the Holy Spirit to themselves or to other mere men. This seems to have been the intention of the **HIERACITES** <note>Followers of Hierax of Leontopolis, a 3rd-century Egyptian ascetic.</note> when, as **EPIPHANIUS** records, they asserted that *Melchizedek* <note>The mysterious priest-king mentioned in Genesis and the Epistle to the Hebrews.</note> *was the Holy Spirit*, understanding a celestial power through him. The **Author of Questions on the Old and New Testaments** (Question 109) leans toward the same opinion. **CYRIL** also, in the place cited, accuses **MANI** <note>The founder of Manichaeism.</note> of the same crime as Montanus, even though it is clear from other sources that the Manichaeans spoke of the Holy Spirit as a distinct entity. For the same reason, the **Muslims** claim that Muhammad is that *Paraclete* <note>original: "Paracletum"; a Greek term for "Advocate" or "Comforter" used in the Gospel of John.</note> or Spirit of Truth whom Christ promised; **MARACCI** investigates the origin of this title in his *Introduction to the Alcoran*, part 2, page 26 and following. Regarding **GUGLIELMA OF BOHEMIA** <note>A late 13th-century religious figure in Milan whose followers believed she was an incarnation of the Holy Spirit.</note> at the end of the 13th century, **JEAN MABILLON** likewise records in his *Italian Museum*, Volume I, pages 19–20, that she was regarded as the Holy Spirit incarnate. The same author notes that this same impiety was attributed to a certain **DOLCINO OF VERCELLI** in the *Chronicle of Nangis* for the year 1306.

IV. **ORIGEN** <note>One of the most influential early Christian theologians, whose complex views on the Trinity later became a source of major controversy.</note> is considered the first to have more openly denied the Deity of the Holy Spirit, teaching that the Spirit is as much inferior to the Son as the Son is to the Father; he argued that while the Spirit is of the substance of the Son, He was nevertheless made by Him. In this matter, he even misused the passage from John 1:3, asserting that the Holy Spirit *was made* through the Word, because it is written universally: *All things were made through him*. This error was abundantly refuted against the admirers of Origen by **PETAVIUS** in *On the Trinity*, Book I, chapter 14, section 8 and following, and by **HUET** in his *Origeniana*, Book II, Question 2. These authors did not fail to note how the same error passed into Origen’s disciples: **Dionysius of Alexandria**, **Gregory Thaumaturgus**, **Pierius the Presbyter of Alexandria**, and finally **Eusebius of Caesarea**.

V. Those who spoke more incautiously than Origen were those who, striving to reconcile Platonic philosophy more closely with Christianity, held the Platonic *World Soul* <note>original: "Animam Mundi"; the concept that the universe possesses a living soul.</note> to be the Holy Spirit. For it is well known that just as the Stoics wished the *World Soul* to be God himself, so the Platonists

### OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER V.

The Platonists taught that she <note>The "World Soul."</note> was born from God, and although she was certainly a god of a certain rank, she was nonetheless merely secondary. Nevertheless, **CHALCIDIUS** in his *commentary on the Timaeus*, **CYRIL OF ALEXANDRIA** in *Book II of Against Julian, at the end*, **JEROME** in *Book II of his Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians*, and others, have attempted to represent Plato as favoring the Christian school here. Perhaps there would be no need to mention this, had this error not broken out more forcefully in subsequent times. For **HONORIUS OF AUTUN** in *On the Philosophy of the World, Book I, 15* says: *The World Soul, according to some, is the Holy Spirit.* And it is clear that the mind of **ABELARD** <note>Peter Abelard (1079–1142), the influential and often controversial medieval philosopher.</note> was disturbed by this concept, as seen in his *Christian Theology*, which is included in **MARTÈNE’S** *Collection of Anecdotes, Volume V, Book I, Chapter 5*, although his error may be excusable to the extent that he softens Plato's pronouncements on the *World Soul* <note>original: "Anima Mundi"</note> with a kindly interpretation.

VI. I shall not dwell now on **APOLLINARIS** <note>Apollinaris of Laodicea (c. 310–390), whose attempts to explain the Incarnation led to his views being declared heretical.</note>, who is blamed by some because he asserted the Holy Spirit was lesser than the Son, and the Son lesser than the Father. But while this distinguished man suffered many indignities and was exposed to the envy of many in his time because of the gifts bestowed upon him, this accusation is the most unworthy of all. This is apparent even from the passage in **THEODORET’S** *Compendium of Heretical Fables, IV, 8*, where in one breath he is accused of both this subordination and of Sabellianism <note>The belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not distinct persons but merely three modes or "masks" of a single God.</note>, even though those positions are <term>inconsistent</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀσύστατα" (asystata); things that cannot logically stand together.</note>. Add to this that, according to the **SUDA** <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note>, he was among the principal <term>champions</term> <note>original Greek: "προμάχοις" (promachois); literally those who fight in the front rank.</note> of the doctrine of <term>consubstantiality</term> <note>original Greek: "του ὁμοουσίου" (tou homoousiou); the orthodox belief that the persons of the Trinity share the "same substance."</note> against the Arians, to such an extent that historians affirm that *Athanasius*—and how great a man he was!—could be <term>judged as a child</term> <note>original Greek: "ὡς παῖδα κριθῆναι" (hos paida krithēnai).</note> *compared to Apollinaris*. Greater suspicion falls upon **ARIUS** himself. For although no mention of the Holy Spirit occurs in his remaining writings, nor in the letters of Alexander concerning him—which is why the Council of Nicaea established nothing against his error regarding the Holy Spirit—nevertheless, once the Deity of the Son was shaken, the Deity of the Holy Spirit could not be preserved either. And according to **AUGUSTINE** in *Heresies, 49: The Arians wished the Holy Spirit to be a creature of a creature; that is, created by the Son himself.* Their opinions on this matter were quite divided: some maintained the Holy Spirit was a creature, others a God of an inferior order, and others declared they did not know to which class he should be assigned, as is evident from **GREGORY NAZIANZEN**—

### DEFENSE OF THE DEITY
<meta>catchword: NASIUS</meta>

...of **GREGORY OF NAZIANZUS** <note>original: "ZIANZENI," referring to Gregory’s *Oration 37*</note> in his *Oration XXXVII*. Indeed, one might conclude from the examples of **Eustathius**, **Eudoxius**, and **Eunomius** <note>Influential figures in the 4th-century Arian controversies</note> that the coarser **Arians** at one time followed more closely in the footsteps of **Origen**, while the **Semi-Arians** spoke more modestly regarding the Holy Spirit, were it not necessary to shorten our sails <note>A metaphorical way of saying "to be brief."</note>.

VII. It was truly from the flock of the **Semi-Arians** that the famous **MACEDONIUS** emerged, whose followers specifically retained the name of **PNEUMATOMACHI** <note>From the Greek *Pneumatomachoi*, meaning "Spirit-fighters."</note>. This name undoubtedly arose because these people seemed to hold more correct views than the coarser **Arians** regarding the person of the Son, and thus they had this peculiar trait: they excluded only the person of the Holy Spirit from communion with the supreme Deity. For this reason, **AUGUSTINE** describes their error in *On Heresies, chapter 52*, as follows:

> The Macedonians are named after Macedonius, Bishop of the Church of Constantinople; the Greeks also call them *Spirit-fighters* <note>original Greek: Πνευματομαχους</note> because they contend regarding the Holy Spirit. For they hold the correct view regarding the Father and the Son, believing that they are of one and the same substance or essence; but concerning the Holy Spirit, they refuse to believe this, calling him a creature. Some prefer to call these people "Semi-Arians," because in this question they are partly with us and partly with them. Although it is maintained by some that they say the Holy Spirit is not God, but the Deity of the Father and the Son, and has no distinct substance of his own.

From these words, it is clear that it is not entirely explained what the mind of **Macedonius** actually was. It is not credible that they only denied the personality of the Holy Spirit while admitting his Deity—as those later writers wished to claim, whom **AUGUSTINE** mentions, and whom the **AUTHOR OF THE PREDESTINATED** <note>An anonymous 5th-century work, *Praedestinatus*, which catalogs heresies.</note> records in chapter 52 (doubtless following Augustine, though he names **Philastrius**), just as we noted in chapter III, section 9. For this is contradicted by the constant consensus of antiquity and the very name "Spirit-fighters" branded upon them by the *First Canon of the Council of Constantinople*; we have already shown in the place cited that the cradle of that error is far older. However, with the passage of time, the name of **Spirit-fighters** also stuck to those who sided with **Sabellius** <note>Who taught that the Father, Son, and Spirit were merely different "modes" or roles of one person.</note>, as is clear from **JOHN OF DAMASCUS** in *On Heresies, number 74*. Nor is it settled that **Macedonius** held the correct view regarding the Son and only abandoned the orthodox faith in his concept of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, **PHILASTRIUS** asserts this in *On Heresies, chapter 67*... ATHA- <note>Catchword referring to Athanasius on the following page.</note>

### OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER V.

**ATHANASIUS** <note>The OCR reads 'NASIUS', but this refers to Athanasius of Alexandria</note> in his *Letter I to Serapion, sections 1 and 2*. **RUFINUS** in *Book I, chapter 28*. **RATRAMNUS** <note>A 9th-century monk known for his treatises on the Eucharist and predestination</note> in *Book 2 against the Greeks, chapter 2*. For Origen had taught that the Spirit was made only from the substance of the Son, but these men maintained that he was created out of nothing.

VIII. What kind of creature the Holy Spirit was according to **Macedonius** is more difficult to determine. **PETAVIUS** <note>Denis Pétau, a prominent 17th-century Jesuit theologian</note> left this untouched, as did the most learned **GOETZIUS**, who commented specifically on the Macedonians and whose dissertation is included in **VOGT'S** *History of Heresiology, Volume I, Part I*. According to **RUFINUS** in *Ecclesiastical History, Book I, chapter 25*, "*Macedonius taught that the Holy Spirit is a power created by God, which is implanted in created things through a division of essence.*" But this reeks of the Platonic *World Soul* <note>original Latin: Animam mundi</note> and even of the system of **Origen**, from which it is established by many testimonies that **Macedonius** had separated. **PHILASTRIUS** says that he *preached that the Spirit was made and created.* From others, however, it appears that he considered this created Spirit as a kind of excellent Angel. Hence he is not only spoken of poorly by **GREGORY OF NAZIANZUS** in *Oration XLIV* for having made the Spirit *of a fellow-servant status* <note>original Greek: ὁμοδουλον (homodoulon)</note> to himself, and by **PHOTIUS** in his *Letters, page 6*, because *he ranked His sovereign and supreme lordship among the servants and ministers* <note>original Greek: εἰς δουλους, και ὑπηρετας την δεσποτικην και ὑπερκειμενην αὐτου συνεταττε κυριοτητα</note>; but **SOZOMEN** also openly states in *Ecclesiastical History IV. 27*: He asserted that the Holy Spirit was devoid of the same honor and dignity (with the Father and the Son): *Calling Him a servant and a minister, and saying whatever else someone might say concerning the divine angels without being in error.* <note>original Greek: Διακονον και ὑπηρετην καλων, και ὁσα περι των θειων ἀγγελων λεγων τις, οὐκ ἀν ἁμαρτοι</note> In the same direction tend...

# DEFENSE OF THE DEITY

...that of **EPIPHANIUS** in *Heresies, 74, § 8*: *Neither like the rest of the spirits is the Spirit of Truth something created or made; nor is that Angel of Great Counsel <note>A title for Christ derived from the Septuagint translation of Isaiah 9:6</note> called an "angel" in the same manner as the others.* And **ATHANASIUS** <note>The influential 4th-century Bishop of Alexandria and defender of orthodoxy</note> clearly states in *Letter 1 to Serapion, § 1*: *It was not without grief that you informed me that some, while detesting the impious Arian heresy against the Son of God and having indeed withdrawn from them, nevertheless hold perverted views regarding the Holy Spirit. They contend that He is not only a created thing, but even that He is one of the ministering spirits, differing from the Angels only in rank.* From these words, it appears how incautiously **GOTTFRIED ARNOLD** <note>A radical Pietist historian known for his "Impartial History of the Church and Heresy," which often sympathized with those labeled as heretics</note> took up the defense of Macedonius and his followers in his *History of Heresies, Part I, Book 4, Chapter 8, § 26 and following*. For this reason, the most learned **THOMAS ITTIG** <note>A Lutheran theologian and professor at Leipzig</note> rebuked him with sharp criticism in his *Theological Works, page 408 and following*. Furthermore, as for the fact that **BERNARD OF CLAIRVAUX** and **ABBOT WILLIAM** <note>William of Saint-Thierry</note> claimed this error was spread by **PETER ABELARD**, this undoubtedly arose because they did not grasp his meaning. It appears clearly enough from his writings that he approached closer to the camp of the **Sabellians** <note>Those who believed that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were merely different "modes" or "masks" of one single person, rather than three distinct persons</note> than the Arians; on this matter, one may consult the excerpts which **NATALIS ALEXANDER** <note>A French Dominican theologian and church historian</note> provides in his work on the *12th Century, Dissertation 7, Article 6*.

IX. Among more recent figures, **VALENTINO GENTILE** <note>An Italian Antitrinitarian executed for heresy in 1566</note> followed primarily in the footsteps of Origen. He claimed that the Holy Spirit, just like the Son, is so distinct from the Father by nature itself that the Father is the "essentiator" <note>the giver of essence or being</note> of the Holy Spirit, while the Spirit is the one who receives essence from Him. This is evident from his *propositions* found at the end of the Works of **CALVIN**, specifically *8, 10, 22, 24, 36, and following*. Likewise, in the *Short Admonition to the Polish Brethren* found in the same place, he reveals that many in Poland at that time were already infected with the same poison. But this error was revived much more significantly by **WILLIAM WHISTON** <note>An English theologian and successor to Isaac Newton, famously expelled from Cambridge for his Arian views</note>, who followed the footsteps of **RICHARD BROCKLESBY**, as is clear from Articles 19 and 21 of his Confession, which he himself published in his *Response to the Observations of Allix*:

> *The Holy Spirit of God is a divine person, made under the supreme God through our Savior, or (in the proper sense) proceeding from the Father and the Son; entirely different from the Son of God in perfections and offices, and in nature and attributes [superior] to all subordinate creatures.*

# THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER V.

...superior to all else, but inferior to the Father and the Son, and subordinate to them in the creation and governance of things; the inspirer of the Prophets and Apostles, the worker of miracles, the Advocate of the Church, the great author of sanctification in all the godly, and the chief witness of the Savior. 

->XXI.<-
->**The supereminent dignity of the Holy Spirit must be admitted and asserted, and a fitting degree of divine worship must be rendered to Him.**<-

X. The error of **SAMUEL CLARKE** <note>An influential English philosopher and cleric (1675–1729) whose work "The Scripture Doctrine of the Trinity" was accused of Arianism</note> is more subtle, as he does not wish to acknowledge that the Holy Spirit is a "thing made" or a creature of God. However, he does acknowledge Him to be a substance so distinct from God the Father from all eternity that He is simultaneously subordinate to Him, depending on His will both for His Essence and His Power. This is found in his *Scripture Doctrine of the Trinity, Part II, Proposition 40 and following*. Consequently, certain "amoebean" <note>original: "amœbea"; a term for alternating or back-and-forth dialogue</note> writings between him and **WHISTON** <note>William Whiston, a scientist and theologian who was expelled from Cambridge for his Arian views</note> emerged. Many others in our time have stumbled over this same stone—a certain natural subordination, which is usually called the *Platonic Trinity* <note>A view suggesting a hierarchy of divinity, similar to the "emanations" in Plato's philosophy</note> or "milder Arianism." Some conceive of this more subtly than others, among whom **GEORGE BULL**, **RALPH CUDWORTH**, **JOHN WALLIS**, and other most learned men in England should be counted. I will not mention the *Arminians* <note>Followers of Remonstrant theology who were often accused of leaning toward Subordinationism</note>, who sometimes declare a mind too inclined toward this error, such as **EPISCOPIUS**, **LIMBORCH**, and others. Indeed, the latter, in his *Christian Theology, Book II, Chapter 17, § 21*, says: *There is a certain supereminence of the Father with respect to the Son, and of the Father and Son with respect to the Holy Spirit, by reason of dignity and power: for it is more dignified to beget than to be begotten, to breathe out than to be breathed forth.* <note>original: "spirare, quam spirari"; these are technical terms for the "procession" of the Holy Spirit from the Godhead</note>. But the famous **ADRIAAN VAN CATTENBURGH** <note>A Dutch theologian who defended Remonstrant views against charges of heresy</note> "refused him his thumb" <note>A metaphor from Roman gladiatorial games meaning he denied him his approval</note> and refuted him in his *Gleanings of Christian Theology, Book II, Chapter 17*.

XI. **JOHN BIDDLE**, a Master of Arts from Oxford, approached more closely to the **MACEDONIANS** <note>A 4th-century sect that claimed the Holy Spirit was a created being</note>. In other matters, he was of the "same opinion" <note>original: ὁμοψῆφος (homopsēphos)</note> as **SOCINUS** <note>The father of Socinianism, which denied the Trinity</note>, and he established that the Holy Spirit is a created person and the Prince of the Angels. He gained followers for himself in meetings held in London, who were called *Biddellians*, as **CHRISTOPHER SANDIUS** relates in his *Anti-Trinitarian Library, page 159*. **CHRISTOPH MATTHÄUS PFAFF** lists his books in his *History of Theological Literature, Book III, pages 328–329*. Among our own thinkers, **CLOPPENBURG** refuted him expressly...

### OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER V.

...exceed the nature of a Creature <note>original: "naturam Creaturæ"</note>, which is why some have explained it as the **Providence of God**; we rightly reject this diligence as dangerous. Much more abominable is the "Enthusiastic" Impiety which confuses the doctrine of Moses concerning the **Holy Spirit** with whatever the Chemists have devised regarding the **Spirit of the World** <note>original: "Spiritu Mundi"</note> and the **Archeus** <note>In alchemy and early medicine, the *Archeus* was thought to be the vital force or "internal chemist" that governs the body</note>, or whatever the Philosophers have commented regarding the **Universal Intellect**, the **Hylarchic Principle** <note>A term used by the Cambridge Platonists to describe a spirit that governs and organizes matter</note>, or **Plastic Nature** <note>An intermediate power between God and the material world that carries out the physical formation of things</note>. XIV. But there is also a recurring error among some who apply the name of the Holy Spirit to mere human beings. **SANDIUS** <note>Christopher Sand (1644–1680), an Arian historian</note> acts as a midwife to these views in the place cited, contending that at least sometimes the "Holy Spirit" designates the **sanctified mind of a human**. Those who, with **BRENDELIUS** and others, call the **Spirit of God** that **particle of the divine breeze** <note>original: "divinæ auræ particulam"</note> which they place within individual souls, sin more directly. **JOHANN BELLA**, author of *Innocent Religion* (1714, page 751), reports that it is taught within Popery that Joseph, the spouse of the Blessed Virgin, was the Holy Spirit incarnate. Not far from this fiction is the heresy of **FRANCESCO GIUSEPPE BORRI**, who **claimed that the Blessed Virgin was the Holy Spirit incarnate in the womb of Anne**, as is clear from the *Analects* on his history, which were published by the renowned **SCHELHORN** in *Literary Amenities*, Volume V.

...are inserted.
