**XV.** So manifold a battle-line of adversaries has come forth in this recent age against the Holy Spirit that, in order to defeat them by relying on the help of the Spirit, we must first dissolve the petty arguments <note>original: "ratiunculae"</note> with which they collectively dispute against us; thereafter, we shall easily destroy, one by one, the foundations of the particular hypotheses which some among them have adopted.

**XVI.** Among the petty arguments opposed to us, let the first be: *that the Holy Spirit is never directly called God.* We have, indeed, abundantly proved the contrary in Chapter IV, Section 7 and following. However, since there are those who admit this premise—among whom may be numbered **GREGORY OF NAZIANZUS** <note>One of the Cappadocian Fathers (4th century); in his *Oration 37*, he discusses the divinity of the Spirit and the linguistic hesitancy of some earlier writers</note> in his *Oration XXXVII*, and **ERASMUS** in his *Ecclesiastes* <note>Erasmus's manual on preaching</note>, as well as the silence of **HILARY** and **BASIL** <note>Hilary of Poitiers and Basil the Great, who were sometimes criticized for not using the explicit word "God" for the Spirit to avoid unnecessary conflict with heretics</note>—it can be added out of an abundance of caution that the conclusion does not follow. For, in the first place, it is sufficient that other equivalent names and truly divine attributes are assigned to a subject for it to be recognized as divine, even if the name "God" does not occur in so many letters. Furthermore, most who use this argument admit that the Son of God is sometimes called God. But if they are unwilling to be convinced of his Deity from this name being directly given to him, they demand of us fruitlessly that we prove this name is given to the Holy Spirit in order to establish His Deity.

**XVII.** Secondly, they appeal to passages "in which mention is made of the Father and the Son, but there is silence regarding the Holy Spirit." **Response:** It is sufficient that He is commemorated in the same rank with the Father and the Son in such circumstances as exclude all fellowship with a creature. Add to this that the omission of one or another person does not exclude them, because one is in the other; and that according to the **Economy of Salvation** <note>original: "Oeconomiam salutis" — the theological concept of how the three Persons of the Trinity work in distinct but unified ways in human history</note>, certain more specific works pertain more to one person than to another...

This page focuses on how Scripture distinguishes the Spirit from "God" without denying the Spirit's divine nature.</meta>

->### CHAPTER V. ON THE HOLY SPIRIT<-

...for they must be referred back <note>This continues a point from the previous page regarding how divine actions are attributed to different persons of the Trinity</note>; and just as the operation and glory of the Father are not excluded when the Son joins himself with the Holy Spirit (for example, in Matthew 12:28, 31, 32), so also neither the operation nor the honor of the Holy Spirit is excluded when Christ speaks of himself and the Father exclusively <note>original: "privative"</note> in John 5:17, 23.

**XVIII.** Thirdly, they <note>the adversaries of the doctrine of the Trinity</note> argue in various ways from the distinction of the Holy Spirit from God himself. For they say:

A. "*He who is distinct from God is not God. But that the Holy Spirit is distinguished from God is clear from 2 Corinthians 13:13, Ephesians 4:4–6, etc.*" 

**Response:** By the name **God**, Scripture understands either the very Nature of God, or the three persons considered together, or the person of the Father or the Son viewed **economically** <term>Economically: referring to the "Divine Economy," the specific roles or "offices" that the Father, Son, and Spirit take on in relation to the world and salvation, rather than their shared inner essence</term>. Now, the argument does not hold unless the Adversaries produce a passage in which the Holy Spirit is presented simply as distinct from the **Nature of God**. This they cannot do, because all the disputed sayings are to be understood in the second or third sense <note>meaning they distinguish the Spirit from the Father or the Trinity as a whole, not from the divine essence itself</note>.

B. "*He who gave the Holy Spirit is Jehovah alone. For to the one of whom it is said in Nehemiah 9:6: 'You alone are Jehovah'; it is also said in verse 20: 'You gave your good Spirit to instruct them.'*" 

**Response:** We deny 1) the premise. For in verse 6, the text speaks generally of God as the Creator of the World, and thus the Creator Holy Spirit himself is included; while in the following verses, including verse 20, the more specific operations of the individual Persons, distinguished according to various **economies**, are enumerated. 2) The conclusion is flawed because the phrase **Jehovah alone** is not considered in opposition to the Holy Spirit, but in opposition to the idols of the nations, to whom the glory of Creation does not belong.

C. "*If the Holy Spirit has an intellect and will distinct from God, he is not God. But the premise is evident from 1 Corinthians 2:10, 12, etc.*" 

**Response:** We stand by the response already given to the first objection. For in these passages, the intellect and will of the Holy Spirit are not essentially distinguished from the Nature of God itself; rather, such things are predicated of both faculties that involve the highest perfection, as was shown in the preceding Chapter, Section 12 and following.

...they want to apply to the Holy Spirit, which would imply that he is lesser than the *Father and the Son*. Thus, for example, when the Savior says in Matthew 12:28, *If I cast out demons in the Spirit of God*, they interpret the preposition *in* <note>original: "in"</note> as indicating an instrument or an assistant. 

**Response:** 1) In John 3:21, it is said of the works of the faithful themselves that they are *done in God*. 2) The little word *in* <note>original Greek: ἐν (en)</note> is often equivalent to *with* <note>original Greek: σὺν (sun)</note>, and therefore can designate a partnership in the divine work with the Son.

**XX.** *Fifthly*, they hit closer to the mark when they try to attribute certain things to the Holy Spirit that overturn the very idea of supreme perfection.

**A.** They derive an *ignorance* attributed to the Holy Spirit regarding the *Father and the Son* from Matthew 11:27, because it is said there, *no one knows the Father except the Son, nor the Son except the Father*. As if it were not manifest that the *Father and the Son* are not being opposed here to the Holy Spirit, but rather to the "wise men of this age," from whom Jesus wished to pull his disciples away to bring them into his own teaching. Even more absurd is that some infer from 1 Corinthians 2:10 that because the Holy Spirit "searches" the deep things of God, he must lack knowledge of them. We have already established the contrary from this passage in Chapter IV, Section 13.

**B.** *For the contingency* <note>referring to being a created or dependent being</note> of the Holy Spirit, they cite John 1:3, *all things were made through the Word*, arguing that the Holy Spirit should not be excluded from "all things." We have already shown extensively in the commentary on this passage how the Macedonians <term>Macedonians: A 4th-century heretical group, also called Pneumatomachians or "Spirit-fighters," who denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit, claiming he was a creature or a servant</term> once abused this text by using a corrupted punctuation. Once this is rejected, the quibbles of the heretics collapse on their own, since according to the genuine sense of the words, the latter part of the phrase restricts *all those things* to *those things which were created*. Even more frivolous is the argument brought from Amos 4:13, where the Lord is called <term>bore ruach</term> <note>original Hebrew: בורא רוח</note>. The context shows this must not be rendered as *creating the Spirit*, but as *creating the wind*.

**C.** To undermine the *Omnipresence* of the Holy Spirit, they distort the fact that he *changes location*; for this, they point to the Holy Spirit *descending from heaven in a bodily form* in Luke 3:21–22. D. ,,*Finally, they attempt to build a case for the **dependence of the Holy Spirit** from a heap of various passages; for example, that he is sent by God, that he does not speak of himself but from God who sent him, that he receives from another, and that he prays to God, etc. Isaiah 48:16, John 16:7, 13, 14, Romans 8, Revelation 22:17.*,, Although all these citations form a significant cloud of arrows if they are counted separately, we blunt them with a single stroke. ,,deduce this from **Acts 19:2**.,, However, not only is it not established whether those men were truly believers at that point, but the passage there does not deal with an ignorance of the *person* of the Holy Spirit. B. ,,They urge that the Son of God commanded us to 
,,adore the Father in his name, without any mention 
,,of the Holy Spirit: **John 14:13, 14; 16:23**.,, But we counter this: first, because no exclusion of the Holy Spirit occurs here; second, because the Holy Spirit is adored within the Father; and third, because the goal of the passages cited is by no means to discuss the *object* of prayer. Instead, it is only to indicate the difference between the *manner* of praying in the Old and New Testaments. This difference consists in the fact that now, through the completed work of the **Savior of the World**, believers can approach the throne of grace by the merit of his service, which previously had not been permitted. Therefore, these sayings do nothing to cast doubt on the arguments we have produced for the **Adoration of the Holy Spirit**.

XXVI. How great a harvest of absurdities <note>original Greek: *άτοπων* (atopōn)</note> flows from this assertion is easily apparent. For not only does it contradict everything that has been set forth concerning the *divine* and *unique* essence of the Holy Spirit, but also what Scripture teaches regarding the nature of *Angels*. Indeed, Scripture attributes various imperfections to them, which are plainly incompatible <note>original Greek: *άσυσταται* (asystatai)</note> with the perfections ascribed to the Holy Spirit. Most relevant to this is that their holiness is subject to change, as seen in Job 4:18.

XXVII. As for those who dream that the Holy Spirit is the *Soul of the World* <note>original: *Animam mundi*; a philosophical concept suggesting a spiritual force animates the entire physical universe</note>, it is only right that they first prove the existence of such a *universal created spirit*. However, this cannot be expected from them, since this dogma is an insult to God himself—attributing divine operations to a creature. At the same time, it is contrary to Scripture, which clearly ignores this "intermediate cause" of natural phenomena. It would be easy to demonstrate that all actions attributed to this "soul" are actually derived from a power implanted individually in the creatures themselves by the Creator and preserved within them. But these thinkers even more audaciously trample upon the glory of God when, by mixing the *Spirit of God* itself with this chimera <note>An illusion or fabrication of the mind</note> of their own invention, they make God himself the Author of sin. Against such powerful weapons, they have nothing to oppose except certain passages of Scripture in which various divine operations, relating to the Power and Governance of God in Nature and Grace, are attributed to the Spirit of the Lord. Examples include Genesis 1:4 <note>Likely a reference to Genesis 1:2, where the Spirit hovers over the waters</note>, Job 27:3, 33:4, Psalms 104:29-30, 147:18, Isaiah 40:7, and Ezekiel 37:5, 14. Truly, since nothing prevents us from concluding that the divine Spirit itself is being celebrated in those verses, there is no need for us to dwell on them.

XXVIII. Furthermore, the confusion of the divine spirit with the human spirit, which we mentioned in the last place, can be easily cleared up. Those who transform the Soul into a *divine particle* <note>The idea that the human soul is a literal piece of God's essence</note> are refuted in another place by the same arguments used against the *Spinozist Deification of the World* <note>original: *Spinoſiſtica Mundi Apotheoſis*; referring to Baruch Spinoza’s philosophy that God and the material universe are the same thing</note>. Those who attribute an Incarnation to the Holy Spirit do not directly attack his Deity, but rather suffer from excessive boasting about themselves or presumption regarding others. Finally, those passages which mention whatever minds...

The more foolish these petty arguments <note>original: *ratiunculae*</note> are, the more clearly the splendor of the Deity in the Holy Spirit breaks through all these clouds.

### I.

Now that the divine Person of the Holy Spirit has been considered in himself, his RELATIONS, both *Natural* and *Economic* <note>In classical theology, "natural" refers to God's internal existence (the Trinity), while "economic" refers to God's external actions in the world and human history</note>, must be thoroughly examined. The former [Natural relations] involve his essential and necessary respect toward the Father and the Son...

...are necessary; **these** <note>referring to the Economic Relations</note> contain all those operations attributed to the Holy Spirit in the **Economy of Salvation** <term>Oeconomia Salutis: God's plan and external actions for the salvation of humanity throughout history</term>. **Those** <note>referring to the Natural Relations</note> are the foundation of these, while these are like sketches of infinite divine wisdom, distributed in a measure suitable for **wayfarers** <term>viatorum: a traditional theological term for human beings on their earthly pilgrimage toward heaven, as opposed to "comprehensors" who have already reached God</term>. Since those natural relations are entirely unknown to human Reason and incomprehensible by their very nature, they would have remained immersed in deep darkness had not an opportunity to meditate on them been offered to us through the revelation of these economic works. Therefore, we know only as much about the natural relations of the Holy Spirit to the Father and the Son as can be gathered from this image, as if **through a mirror, dimly** <note>original Greek: *δι' ἐσόπτρου ἐν αἰνίγματι* (di' esoptrou en ainigmati), a reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12</note>. The majesty of the Mystery itself requires that we cut away whatever else human philosophy and terms smelling of **scholastic dust** <note>A dismissive reference to the overly complex and dry academic terminology used by medieval university theologians</note> might suggest.

### II.

Just as it is right for us to confine ourselves within these boundaries set by the Holy Spirit himself, so on the other hand, we contend that whatever is drawn out by logical consequence from the Holy Spirit’s **Economic** order to establish his **natural** order rests on a firm footing. For it is certain that as God has demonstrated himself in his works, so he truly is in his essence; since the goal for which God most freely decided to produce works outside of himself was precisely to manifest his virtues in the most fitting manner. While this is true regarding all divine works, it is to be expected in a special way from the **Work of Grace**, because God wished to establish it as the most excellent theater of his perfections, and through it to reveal himself more evidently as **Triune**. That we are following in the footsteps of the most excellent men in this mode of arguing will be clear from the points presented later in sections 24 and 27.

### III.

But so that this comparison may be properly established, it must first be noted that those things which concern the divine relations are everywhere in the sacred pages wrapped in a curtain of most wise emblems; this is so that faith may have a space in which to exercise itself, and that a desire for the **heavenly Academy** <note>A metaphor for the state of knowledge in heaven, where believers will finally understand divine mysteries</note> might be kindled. In that Academy, divine wisdom—proceeding by degrees in revealing itself—has reserved the unraveling of these riddles. Therefore, with cautious circumspection and sober meditation through the fear of the Lord...

...caution is needed, lest in examining the metaphors of sacred phrasing we proceed beyond the **point of comparison** <term>tertium comparationis: the specific quality or detail that two things being compared actually have in common, beyond which a metaphor should not be pushed</term>. This will happen most effectively if we firmly assume that whatever casts even the slightest shadow upon the concept of supreme and divine Perfection must not be brought into the comparison.

### IV.

With these preliminary warnings, we begin with those Names by which the Orthodox Church from ancient times has designated the natural Relation of the Holy Spirit to the Father and the Son. The words *Spiration* <note>original Greek: Πνεῦσις</note> and *Procession* <note>original Greek: Ἐκπόρευσις</note> are most prominent here. I notice that many consider these to be *synonyms*. However, they seem to me rather to be *correlates*. *Spiration* is the beginning of *Procession*, while *Procession* is the consequence of *Spiration*.

This is illustrated significantly through the relationship of the metaphors. For since *spiration* is predicated of both the wind and the *breath of the mouth*, the verb "to go out" <note>original Greek: ἐκπορεύεσθαι (ekporeuesthai)</note> is used for the departure of speech from the mouth, which happens by means of the breath, as in Matthew 4:4 and 15:11. For the same reason, it occurs in the mention of the *two-edged sword* coming out of the mouth of the Son of God, which is an *emblem of the word of God* in Revelation 1:16, 19:15, and 19:21. The **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> uses the same word regarding the movement and progress of the wind in Ecclesiastes 1:5 and Jeremiah 25:32. 

Other words used by the Church Fathers to designate this mystery—such as *projection* <note>original: προβολὴ</note>, *going out* <note>original: ἐκφοίτησις</note>, *blowing* <note>original: πνοὴ</note>, *to go forth* <note>original: προϊέναι</note>, *to step forward* <note>original: προκύπτειν</note>, *to be poured out* <note>original: προχεῖσθαι</note>, as well as *breathing out* <note>original: ἔκφυσις</note> and *budding forth* <note>original: ἀναβλάστησις</note>, which **PETAVIUS** <note>Dionysius Petavius (1583–1652), a Jesuit scholar known as the "father of the history of dogma"</note> reviews in *The Trinity*, Book VII, chapter 10—we shall now pass over, since they are neither drawn from Scripture nor do they offer us even the slightest light. 

Nor will we dwell on the terms *manifestation* <note>original: ἐκφάνσεως</note> and *effulgence* <note>original: ἐκλάμψεως</note>, which **MICHAEL LEQUIEN** <note>Michel Le Quien (1661–1733), a French Dominican historian and scholar of the Eastern Church</note> noted as being frequent among the Greek Fathers on this subject in his *Dissertation on Damascene* I, page 3. Although these are not unsuitable by that name, since the *illumination of the Holy Spirit* <note>original: φωτισμὸς</note> is compared with the *shining forth of light* <note>original: λάμψει φωτὸς</note> out of the darkness in the creation of the world. 

The word *emanation* has pleased others; although it was made suspect through the corruption of the **Gnostics** <term>Gnostics: early religious groups whose complex mythologies described spiritual beings "emanating" or flowing out from a distant God</term>, it nevertheless agrees with the phrasing of Sacred Scripture insofar as it alludes to the *emblem* of a river flowing from a source. **SUICERUS** <note>Johann Caspar Suicer (1619–1684), a Swiss theologian famous for his lexicon of Greek ecclesiastical terms</note> adds the words *sending out* <note>original: ἐκπέμψις</note>, *progression* <note>original: πρόοδος</note>, and *to come forth* <note>original: προέρχεσθαι</note> in his *Exposition of the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed*, chapter 14, pages 308–309.

# OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER VI.

### V.
The term **Spiration** <note>original: *Spirationis*; the "breathing forth" of the Spirit from the Father and the Son</note> is drawn from the very name that characterizes the Third Person of the Trinity. It aligns with the metaphors of **Blowing**, **Wind**, and **Breath** which the Spirit himself frequently uses when describing his own Relations. Furthermore, there is a unique kinship between this name and the name *Logos* or **the Word** <note>original Greek: Λογος</note>. In 1 John 5:7, this "Word" alternates with the name "Son," and therefore belongs to his personal character. For the Spirit is the **Breath of the mouth** <note>original: *Spiritus oris*</note>, and without breath, a "Word" that has been conceived and formed cannot be spoken aloud. Hence, we find the **Word of the Lord** and the **Breath of his mouth** joined together in Psalm 33:6: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth.* However, this terminology displeased **Amyraldus** <note>Moïse Amyraut (1596–1664), an influential and sometimes controversial French Protestant theologian</note> in his *On the Mystery of the Trinity*, dissertation 6, page 377. His objections are as follows:

**A.** "He believes that **essential Spiration** <note>The internal, eternal "breathing" of the Spirit within the Godhead</note> is unknown in Scripture. For although Wisdom is said by Solomon to have been **begotten**, he argues that we never read that the third person was **spirated** <note>breathed out</note>." 
But beyond the fact that the opposite is clear from the passages already cited, it is sufficient to say that the name **Spirit** contains within itself the concept of **Spiration** by the same logic that the name **Son** contains the concept of **Generation**.

**B.** He insists that "the name **Son** necessarily implies some kind of **Generation**, whatever that may be; but the name **Spirit** does not necessarily signify that kind of **Spiration**." 
Yet, where things are similar, the logic should be similar. Furthermore, he contradicts himself when, a little later, he uses the analogy of these names as the foundation for that **Economic Spiration** <term>Economic: referring to God’s actions in the world and salvation history, rather than his internal essence</term> by which he believes the third person is named. For he says: *Just as the Son of God is so named not because he made others sons of God (for our adoption in Christ is a different matter), but because he has within himself the reason why he is so named—namely, **Sonship** <note>original Greek: την υιοτητα</note>—so the Third Person should be called the Spirit of God because he has within himself the reason why he was so named.*

**C.** Finally, he adds: "The word for 'begetting' is suited to the production of the second person because through Generation a nature is shared, and the one begotten is like the one who begets. Spiration, however, is a concept that does not seem well-suited to describe the production of the third person, whatever that production may be. For the air that we breathe out differs so much from the nature of the one breathing that it has nothing in common with it; whereas the nature of the Holy Spirit differs in no way from...

<meta>This page continues the argument against Moïse Amyraut’s objections to the term "Spiration." <page-num>198</page-num>
-> THE MYSTERY OF PROCESSION <-

> "...the nature of the other two persons. And since both the **Generation** of the Son and the **Procession** of the Holy Spirit are works that occur within the divine nature, every 'spiration' [breathing] emits a breath outside of the one breathing."

But this dispute is empty. **Spiration** is just as much a metaphor as **Generation**. The "point of comparison" <note>original: *tertium comparationis*; the specific quality that links a metaphor to the reality it describes</note> regarding this term is shrouded in just as much darkness as it is regarding the former. It is agreed upon among the Orthodox that the metaphor of Generation is to be understood not according to every physical or human sense it might imply, but in a **manner becoming of God** <note>original Greek: $\Theta\epsilon o\pi\rho\epsilon\pi\omega\varsigma$ (*theoprepōs*)</note>, so that no violence is done to the concept of the highest Perfection. We hold the same, therefore, concerning the metaphor of **Spiration**. Hence, if anyone wished to derive from it some idea contrary to the essence of a most perfect Being, it would be more advisable to frankly profess ignorance of the "point of comparison" than to admit such a thing.

### VI.
Meanwhile, it should be noted that since the term **Spiration** can be understood in both an **active** and a **passive** sense, nothing prevents it from being used in either way regarding the Holy Spirit. For:

**A.** Scripture employs it in both ways. **Passive Spiration** <note>the Spirit being "breathed out" by the Father and Son</note> occurs in John 20:22, where the Savior **breathed on** <note>original Greek: $\epsilon\nu\epsilon\phi\upsilon\sigma\eta\sigma\epsilon$ (*enephysēse*)</note> the disciples and said: *Receive the Holy Spirit.* For that physical breathing was a sign and seal of the mission or "coming out" of the Holy Spirit from the Son, which was then imminent. We read an example of **active Spiration** <note>the Spirit himself acting as a breath or wind</note> in John 3:8: *The Spirit breathes <note>or blows</note> where he wills* <note>original Greek: $\tau\grave{o}\ \pi\nu\epsilon\tilde{\upsilon}\mu\alpha, \text{ὅ}\pi o\upsilon\ \theta\acute{\epsilon}\lambda\iota, \pi\nu\epsilon\tilde{\iota}$</note>.

**B.** Such is the nature of the metaphor that it permits both meanings. For **spiration** is a certain motion or impelling of air. Now, not only does a produced motion repeatedly produce another, but also the motion which breathing forms is reciprocal. In breathing, we breathe back. <note>The author uses the physical act of respiration to illustrate the "back and forth" relationship within the Trinity.</note>

**C.** This kind of reciprocity occurs in those operations which Scripture attributes to the Holy Spirit. For he conducts himself **passively** in relation to the Father and the Son, by whom he is **spirated**. He conducts himself **actively** in relation to external objects, upon which he mystically breathes while giving them life. Indeed, a certain faint shadow of **active spiration** in relation to the Father and the Son might even be seen to exist in that reciprocal operation of the Holy Spirit toward the Father and the Son, by which he promotes the glory of both.

### VII.
The term **PROCESSION** is more commonly used in practice, taken from the very words of the Savior in John 15:26, by which He declared that the Holy Spirit **proceeds from the Father** <note>original Greek: *παρα του Πατρος εκπορευεσθαι* (*para tou Patros ekporeuesthai*); Latin: *à Patre procedere*</note>. However, it should be noted that the force of the Latin word falls short of the Greek. For the Greek term *ekporeuesthai* carries a greater emphasis than the Latin *procedere* [to proceed]. The concept of **Procession** does not necessarily involve a "point of origin" <note>original: *terminum à quo*</note> in the same way that the concept of **Egress** <note>literally "a going out"</note> does. 

For the rest, I have explained my thoughts on this phrase in my Commentary on that passage, granting that these words certainly suppose a *natural* relation to the Father and an **Order** within the divine essence, but in such a way that they primarily look toward a certain **Economic Order** <note>term: <term>Economic Order</term>; this refers to the "Divine Economy," or the way God manages the world and reveals Himself through history, rather than His internal, eternal nature in itself</note>, through which divine Wisdom wished to illustrate this secret and venerable **depth** <note>original Greek: *βαθος* (*bathos*)</note> of the divine Essence. I have previously shown that great names in our Church felt the same way, including **BEZA**, **CALVIN**, **GUALTHER**, **COCCEJUS**, and **ALLINGA**. 

To these, as further weight, I now add **MOÏSE AMYRAUT** in his *Dissertation on the Mystery of the Trinity*, VI, p. 391, who openly defends the same hypothesis with arguments that deserve attention; also **HENRI HULSIUS** in his *Typus*, Chapter II, section 22; **WILLEM MOMMA** in his *Theological Lectures*, p. 143; **NICOLAAS GURTLER** in his *Institutes of Theology*, Chapter III, section 250; and **JOHANN HEINRICH HEIDEGGER** in his *Body of Theology*, Location IV, section 74. But even among the ancients, **BEDE** <note>The Venerable Bede (672–735 AD), an English monk and scholar</note> explained the phrase in the same way in his Homily for the 8th day after the Ascension of the Lord:

> *When the grace of the Holy Spirit is given to men, the Holy Spirit is surely sent by the Father, and sent by the Son, because His very mission is that **Procession** by which He proceeds from the Father and the Son.*

From this, the opportunity arose for the Scholastics <note>medieval university theologians who used logic to explain Christian doctrine</note> to distinguish between the **eternal** and the **temporal** procession of the Holy Spirit. So did **PETER LOMBARD** in Book I, Distinction 14. So did **THOMAS AQUINAS** in Part I, Question 43, articles 2, 3, and 8. Since their orthodoxy was never stained by any hint of suspicion because of this interpretation, I thought I could be safe from the slander of others on this point. However, it pleased a certain troublesome...

Hence, already in the creation itself, he is called the **Spirit of God** in Genesis 1:2 and the **Spirit of the mouth of the Lord** in Psalm 33:6 and Job 33:3. This mystery, since it is inexplicable, we deeply venerate; and where Scripture is silent, we do not wish to obscure it, if not defile it, with **scholastic terms** <note>Technical jargon developed by medieval theologians, which the author feels can sometimes complicate simple biblical truths</note>. In the meantime, we believe the latter [the Economic relation] is principally intended."

I have deemed it necessary to transcribe these words here, since I will have to appeal to them repeatedly, and it must be shown from them with what [bad] faith this Antagonist deals with me.

<meta>This page continues the logical and theological defense of the "Order" within the Trinity, specifically focusing on why the Holy Spirit is considered the third person based on how He exists and how He acts.</meta>

# THE MYSTERY OF PROCESSION #
<meta>catchword: Holy</meta>

**A.** From the granted **Order of acting**. For every active being operates in a manner consistent with its nature. Therefore, the constant Order of acting assigned to a subject reflects its <term>Order of subsisting</term><note>The "Order of subsisting" refers to the internal way a person of the Trinity exists in relation to the others, while the "Order of acting" refers to how they work in the world.</note>. This is especially true when one acts for the purpose of revealing oneself to others and displaying a specimen of the virtues of one's essence through one's works. Furthermore, in the concept of a rational subject, "acting" and "subsisting" differ only by reason. For its essence consists in thinking, and to think is the same as to live and to be active; thus, the idea of operation involves the idea of the existence of the thinker, and vice versa.

**B.** From those metaphors of both *Spiration* <note>original: *Spirationis*; the "breathing" or "out-breathing" of the Spirit</note> and *Procession*, by which the characteristic difference of the third Person is indicated. For the breath of the mouth, which is breathed out, always presupposes a breather in our concept, and that which proceeds presupposes that from which it goes forth.

**C.** From the fact that the Holy Spirit occurs in the same order when Scripture describes the works of nature, as we have already declared using the words cited above in section 8.

**D.** From the analogy of the characteristic names *Father* and *Son* or *Word*. Since these bring about an Order of existing—such as that of the Son to the Father, or the Word to the speaker—it is right to interpret the characteristic of the Third Person similarly regarding the Order of existing. This is all the more so since the metaphor of *Spirit* has a manifest relation to the metaphor of the *Word*, and constitutes a single allegory with it, as shown in section 5.

**E.** This double order is illustrated significantly by comparing the names used to express it. For the emblem of *Spiration* seems to represent the order of existing, whereas *Procession*, or rather *Egression* <note>original: *Egressionis*; a going out or departure</note>, represents the order of acting. Just as Spiration precedes Egression, so the order of existing is the foundation for the order of acting. And just as *Spiration* is a **passive** attribute in relation to the Holy Spirit <note>Meaning the Spirit is the one being "breathed out."</note>, while *Egression* is an **active** attribute; so the Order of existing includes something passive, while the Order of acting includes something active.

**XXIII.** We recognize this distinction all the more because we further confess that this Order of existing involves the Holy Spirit...

### OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER VI. ###

The Holy Spirit, in his subsistence and in his operations, is **not from himself, but from the Father and the Son**. Here again, we rejoice in Scripture as our guide.

**A.** In **John 16:13**, it is declared that the Spirit **will not speak of himself** <note>original: *non loquuturum eſſe à ſemetipſo*</note>; a passage which <term>Gualtherus</term> <note>Rudolf Gualther (1519–1586), a Swiss Reformer and influential biblical commentator.</note> and other excellent interpreters have taught aims, through the use of the future tense, at a specific immediate demonstration of that order. I have not, however, fixed my feet in their opinion, but in my **Commentary on this passage, page 317**, I have expressly taught that the <term>natural Order</term> <note>The inherent, eternal relationship between the persons of the Trinity, rather than just their roles in human history.</note> of the Holy Spirit toward the other persons is simultaneously hinted at. Nor did I assert this unless I was inwardly convinced of this truth. For:

1) This predicate, **not to speak of himself**, is extended very widely to **whatever he shall hear** <note>original Greek: *ὅσα ἂν ἀκούσῃ*</note>; those things, moreover, are the same as what he just now called **all the truth**. For although here there is respect only for the saving truth to be revealed in the <term>economy of the New Testament</term> <note>The "economy" refers to God's specific plan and actions in human history for the salvation of mankind.</note>, it nevertheless extends most broadly. The very **depths of God, which eye has not seen and ear has not heard**, and thus whatever is knowable concerning the perfections and ways of the Triune God through the **Light of Reason and Faith**, are included under it. In all these things, moreover, **to speak nothing of himself** involves a constant order of operating from another.

2) There is also the analogy between the operations of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, which is manifest from a comparison with **John 5:19**, where the Son testifies of himself with greater emphasis: **"Amen, Amen, I say to you: the Son cannot do anything of himself."** This passage must be extended to the natural relation of the Son to the Father in all his works—both of **nature** and of **grace** (and thus both internal and external, both essential and free). I have so clearly declared this in my **Commentary, page 35**, and so strongly proved it, that the shameless quibbles of certain people against me are bound to strike the fair reader with amazement. Let us now tighten the knot <note>i.e., bring the logical argument to its conclusion</note>. Those divine persons who, regarding all their personal operations, are **not from themselves**, are also, regarding their personal subsistence, **not from themselves**. The premise is predicated not only of the Son with the greatest weight of words, but also of the Holy Spirit using the same phrase by the same supreme Master. Therefore, the conclusion is true.

# THE MYSTERY OF THE PROCESSION #

**XXIV. B.** Furthermore, this is confirmed by the nature of the metaphors of both *breathing* <note>original: *spirationis*</note> and *outgoing* <note>original: *egressus*</note>. For that which is *breathed* is, by a certain logic, from the one breathing; and that which goes out from someone is—at least in its operation—from the one from whom it proceeds.

**C.** In this way, a new harmony between the name of the *Son* (or the *Word*) and the name of the *Holy Spirit* is observed. For in the concept of the "Son," it is included that he is *from the Father*; and for that reason, if the metaphor applied to the Holy Spirit is so constructed that it involves being *from the Father and the Son*, that likewise must be admitted.

**D.** We should not overlook the argument that <term>Amyraut</term> <note>Moïse Amyraut (1596–1664), an influential French Protestant theologian.</note> derives in his *Dissertation on the Trinity VI*, page 398, from the frequent title *Spirit of the Father and of the Son*. 

> *Just as,* he says, *the fact that the Son is called "of the Father" clearly demonstrates that the person of the Son depends on the person of the Father in such a way that the Father exists as some kind of cause—an incomprehensible one, to be sure, but a cause nonetheless—of his subsistence; so from the fact that the Spirit is called the "Spirit of both," one may undoubtedly conclude that he holds that same mode of subsistence from both and—which is the same thing—that both concur so that the Spirit possesses the divine essence equally with them in his own proper way.* 

I fully agree with this reasoning.

**E.** Likewise compelling is what is drawn on page 400 from the same source, from the statements in which the Holy Spirit is said to be *given* and *sent* by the Father and the Son. From this it is established that he depends on both in the manner of his subsistence. 

> *For although,* he continues, *it was done <term>Economically</term> <note>The "Economy" refers to God's external actions in human history for salvation, as opposed to His internal nature.</note>—plainly for our own understanding—that the Father should send the Son, and the Spirit should be sent by both; nevertheless, that external Economy, which pertains to the procurement of our salvation, is founded on the internal Economy, according to which the <term>relationships</term> <note>original Greek: *σχέσεις* (schesis), referring to the eternal, internal relations between the persons of the Trinity.</note> of the persons themselves are referred to one another. And just as it was fitting for that internal Economy that the Father should send the Son, but not the Son the Father; so it was consistent with the same that the Spirit should not send the Father and the Son, but be sent by them.* 

The famous <term>Hulsius</term> <note>Antonius Hulsius (1615–1685), a Dutch Reformed theologian and professor.</note> successfully uses the same kind of reasoning in his *Model*, Chapter 2, Section 22: 

> *From the mission of the Spirit by Christ, the foundation of whose right in acting does not exist except through a natural dependence in being, without which this authority used in operation [would be] a denial...*

### OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER VI. ###

*it would be a matter of equality.* Add MOMMA in his *Theological Lectures*, page 142: *The mission of the Spirit, which is attributed to the Father and the Son, is not indeed that eternal procession itself, but belongs to the Economy of Ministry <note>The "Economy" refers to the way the three persons of the Trinity act in human history and the work of salvation, as opposed to their eternal inner relationship.</note> of the three Persons in the work of our salvation; nevertheless, from that distribution of roles, the order and logic of the Procession of the Holy Spirit is rightly gathered. Just as the Father is sent by no one, because he is from no one; and the Son is sent by the Father, because he was begotten by him; so the Spirit is sent by both, because he proceeds from both. If the Spirit did not proceed from the Son—since the Spirit himself is God, just as much as the Son—what right would the Son have to send the Spirit, or to act and work through him? An equal has no authority over an equal, nor does one of equal rank have authority over another of equal rank.*

XXV. This point must be held precisely here: that this Order is attributed to the Holy Spirit not only in relation to the Father, but also to the Son, and for the same reason.

A. This follows from the metaphor of Breathing <note>original: *Spirationis*</note>, which refers not only to the Father but also to the Son. Thus, in the words of Job 33:4, *The Spirit of the strong God <term>אל</term> <note>Hebrew: El</note> made me: and the breath of the Almighty <term>שדי</term> <note>Hebrew: Shaddai</note> gave me life;* one may understand the Father through "God" and the Son through "the Almighty." At the very least, in relation to the Son, he is called "the Spirit of the mouth of the Lord" in Psalm 33:6. The Son also grants the Spirit to the disciples by *breathing* upon them, and thus confirms this truth through a symbolic act <note>original: *sacramento*</note>.

B. The symbol of Outgoing <note>original: *Egressionis*</note> likewise looks toward the Son, as is established from Revelation 22:1, where *from the Throne of the Father and the Lamb proceeds a river of water of life.* Hence, the orthodox Fathers <note>The "orthodox Fathers" refers to early Christian theologians who defended the established creeds.</note> have correctly used for their cause those passages in which the Son is compared to a Fountain and the Holy Spirit to living water. See ATHANASIUS <note>A 4th-century bishop of Alexandria and a chief defender of Trinitarianism.</note> in his book *On the Human Nature Assumed*.

C. Hence, the Holy Spirit is third in order, since he has the foundation of his personal existence <note>original: *subsistentiæ*</note> and operation not only from the Father, but also from the Son.

D. *The Son is declared to be one with the Father* in John 10:30, specifically in relation to the work of preserving the faithful, which is most directly perfected through the Holy Spirit.

E. Add to this that the "Spirit of the Father" and the "Spirit of the Son" are so often used interchangeably; and that the Spirit is not only from the Father, but also, as has just been proven—

XXVI. Nevertheless, despite this equality of relation which the Third Person <note>The Holy Spirit</note> has toward the First <note>The Father</note> and Second <note>The Son</note>, it is concluded from the following reasons that a certain difference in the manner of this relation must be admitted.

A. Although most phrases used regarding this Mystery are interchangeable, they are not all interchangeable. *The Son sends the Spirit from the Father*; but no one would dare to say that the Father sends the Spirit from the Son. Supreme Wisdom <note>A traditional title for Christ, the Word of God.</note> from eternity *was anointed through the Spirit by the Father* (Proverbs 8:23). But who would contend that the Spirit is anointed through the Son by the Father? Or that the Father is anointed through the Spirit? In the same way, the Son receives the Spirit from the Father to be bestowed upon and poured out into the Church, but the Spirit does not receive the Son to be given in a similar manner.

B. This same point is confirmed by that Order according to which the Son is the Second Person of the divine essence. Now indeed, there is a difference between the relation which the third has to the second, and that which he has to the first.

C. Certain things in the Order of operating—both natural and Economic <note>The "Economy" refers to the way the three Persons of the Trinity act in human history and the work of salvation, as opposed to their eternal inner relationship.</note>—are common to the Holy Spirit and the Son, which are not common to them and the Father. Thus the Savior says of himself and the Holy Spirit in John 3:11, *we testify to what we have seen*, in distinction from the Father. Similarly, the Father sends the Son and the Holy Spirit (Isaiah 48:16). However, it cannot be proven that the Holy Spirit sends the Son (at least according to his divine nature), as will be shown in its proper place. From this it follows that the Procession <note>The eternal "coming forth" of one person of the Trinity from another.</note> of the Holy Spirit from the Father is of a different nature than his Procession from the Son.

XXVII. However this difference may stand, the chief attribute of this entire Relation of the Third Person to the First and Second consists in this: that it is ESSENTIAL. By this expression, two things can be indicated.

A. The primary point <note>original: *Palmarium*</note> is that this Relation belongs to the divine *Essence* itself...

1) From the connection between the **Economic and natural Relation** <note>The "Economic" relation refers to how the Trinity acts toward creation in history, while the "Natural" relation refers to the internal, eternal relationship between the Father, Son, and Spirit.</note>, which we assumed in § 1, and for which the orthodox theologians have fought most strongly for this truth. The First Person is never called the Father of the Spirit, nor is the Second Person called the Son of the Spirit.

### THE MYSTERY OF THE PROCESSION

4) We have already established that the Holy Spirit was active in Creation itself in a manner consistent with this relationship. For it is rightly concluded that the relationship of the divine Persons to one another—which recurs in all His works, not excluding the works of nature—is truly immutable, and thus pertains to the very essence of God.

XXVIII. B. Furthermore, we assert that this relationship is **Essential** <note>Meaning it belongs to God's very nature, not just a temporary role He plays.</note> because it contains nothing except what exactly agrees with the idea of the most perfect Essence of God. He is **from the Father and the Son** in such a way that neither the Unity and Simplicity of the entire divine Essence, nor the most absolute equality of the highest Perfection with the Father and the Son—which we demonstrated in the preceding chapters that the Holy Spirit possesses—is obscured by even the slightest cloud. We set aside the former point here, as it concerns the demonstration of the Mystery of the Holy Trinity in general. By the latter point, we attribute to the Holy Spirit Independence, Eternity, Necessity of Existence, and in a word, the most perfect <term>Self-Divinity</term> <note>original: "Αυτοθεοτητα" (Autotheoteta); a technical term for being God in and of oneself, rather than having a "derived" or "lesser" divinity.</note>, as attributes that constitute the idea of highest perfection in such a way that if they were removed, this idea would be overthrown and disappear at the same time. This also proves the equality of the Holy Spirit here: that this dependence, if any is to be attributed, is mutual. For although the Father may seem to exert the power of the divine essence more immediately, and the Son and the Holy Spirit more mediately, it nevertheless follows from the unity of their essence that the Father and Son cannot work more inseparably from the Holy Spirit than He can from them. No person is capable of an operation that excludes the third, if you set aside certain personal and relative operations toward one another.

XXIX. Here the adversaries move a "battering ram" <note>A metaphor for a strong or forceful argument.</note> that should not be thoughtlessly disregarded, when they object that the idea of absolute independence and the order of subsisting and operating from another are <term>incompatible</term> <note>original: "ἀσύστατα" (asystata); logically inconsistent or things that cannot exist together.</note>. However, so that we may successfully resolve this, we believe a distinction must be made between *dependence regarding the essence viewed in general*, and *dependence regarding a certain order of subsisting and operating within that essence.* The celebrated **Witsius** <note>Herman Witsius (1636–1708), a renowned Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> speaks acutely on this matter in *Sacred Dissertations on the Creed*, VII, § 20: *Scripture teaches a distinction of order, which, since*

### CHAPTER VI. OF THE HOLY SPIRIT

Since it is only a matter of personal order, it implies no superiority or inferiority—qualities which belong to essence. This is the same sentiment held by the most celebrated theologian of the Zurichers, *J. H.* Hottinger <note>Johann Heinrich Hottinger (1620–1667), a famous Swiss theologian and philologist</note>, who was appointed to the Chair at Leiden, in his *Course of Theology, Topic III*: *“The ambiguity of the word <term>autotheos</term> <note>original: αὐτόθεος; meaning 'God of Himself' or 'God in His own right'</note> is removed by a distinction. **Absolutely**, only the **Father** is <term>autotheos</term>, because he is not from another in respect to either essence or person, as one who is simply God of himself. **In a certain sense**, the **Son** and **Holy Spirit** are also <term>autotheos</term>; not by reason of their person, but in regard to their essence, which existed from eternity of and through itself.”* It would be easy to illustrate with examples from created things how a certain order of existing and acting can coexist with an absolute equality of essence. However, we prefer not to press those examples, lest anyone take the opportunity to compare human things to divine, or finite to infinite—as easily happens—beyond what is proper. And we maintain silence here all the more safely because, since it is clear that the inner nature of this order has not been manifested to us, there is no need for us to fully resolve every doubt that might arise. For that which is revealed ought not to be denied on account of that which is obscure. Nor can any contradiction be justly charged against us, as long as there is not equal evidence for the opposing views.

XXX. This, therefore, is the boundary which God himself has fixed for our meditations upon this immense and venerable Mystery. No further definition can be given of the order of existing and acting that belongs to the Holy Spirit. If anything else has been brought forward by some regarding the <term>why</term> <note>original: τὸ διότι (to dioti); a philosophical term referring to the underlying reason or cause of a thing</note> of it, we safely leave it aside as something spoken beyond the Scriptures. Whether posterity, shining with a clearer light of the Holy Spirit, will advance these boundaries, time will tell. For our part, we prefer to measure ourselves by our own reach <note>literally: "measure ourselves by our own foot"</note> rather than defile these sacred matters with the scholastic dust of meaningless words. Why is it necessary for brothers, who wish to be regarded as Ministers of the Spirit, to provoke one another with words which the most gentle Spirit does not teach? If God has revealed more to them, we do not envy them that glory. We prefer to humbly profess our ignorance, and in this matter, to follow in the footsteps of those theologians who fear the **Word of the Lord**.

...so that through their authority at least, a safe silence might be granted to us. **FRANCIS TURRETIN** <note>Francis Turretin (1623–1687) was a central figure in Reformed Scholasticism.</note>, in his *Elenctic Theology, Topic III, Question 31, Section 3*: *"It cannot be denied that the **Procession** <note>The term for how the Holy Spirit 'comes forth' from the Father and Son, distinct from how the Son is 'begotten.'</note> differs from the **Generation** of the Son, because they exist as distinct persons who have a mutual relationship of origin to one another. Before him, **SIMLER** <note>Josias Simmler (1530–1576), a Swiss theologian.</note> offered similar thoughts regarding the Holy Spirit in Book IV, page 319: *"We know that **Generation** and **Procession** differ; yet, since their formal distinction is not explicitly stated in Holy Scripture, we frankly confess our ignorance."* This is something that most learned theologians before us have likewise admitted.

**POLANUS** <note>Amandus Polanus von Polansdorf (1561–1610), a refined systematic theologian.</note> in Book III, Chapter 6, confesses *“that the manner of the Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, by way of an eternal and internal breathing, is to us **incomprehensible** <note>original: ἀκατάληπτος</note> and **unutterable** <note>original: ἄρρητος</note>.”*

**CLOPPENBURG** <note>Johannes Cloppenburg (1592–1652), a Dutch theologian.</note> in his *Theological Exercises, Topic III, Disputation 2, Section 16*: *"The manner of the Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son is distinct in itself, but it is a secret and ineffable mystery, no less so than the manner of the Son’s Generation. However, certain points serve to indicate the fact of this distinction <note>original: τοῦ ὅτι; referring to the 'that-ness' or the fact of the matter as opposed to the 'how.'</note>:"*

1.  *"That the term **Procession** <note>original: ἐκπορευσις; the 'out-going' or proceeding</note> is attributed specifically to the Holy Spirit in **John 15:26**, which can also be actively called 'Spiration' <note>From the Latin 'spiratio,' meaning breathing.</note> based on the external sign used by Christ when he said, 'Receive the Holy Spirit' in **John 20:22**."*
2.  *"The order of the Persons, by which the Holy Spirit is the third and final person of the Deity; before him is the Son, the second person, who is the Only-Begotten of the Father alone. It is from the Father and the Son that the Holy Spirit, in his third manner of existence, has his origin."*

**DANAEUS** <note>Lambert Daneau (c. 1530–1595), a French Reformed theologian.</note> speaks boldly in his *Questions on the First Book of Lombard’s Sentences*, when examining the procession of the Holy Spirit: *"To what end,"* he asks, *"does this **Vain Talk** <note>original: Ματαιολογια</note> lead? To what end does this curiosity—or rather, this madness—tend, that it should so audaciously cast its eyes into the inner sanctuary known to the Trinity alone, just as those men of **Bethshemesh** <note>A reference to 1 Samuel 6:19, where the people were punished for looking into the Ark of the Covenant.</note> looked into the sacred Ark of the Lord? All these questions (which are **limitless** <note>original: ἀπέραντοι</note>, as Paul says, and therefore ought to be entirely cut off by true theologians rather than nourished or increased)—all these questions, I say, have arisen from the fact that this ineffable and indescribable emanation of the Divine Persons has been subjected to the grasp of human intellect. Those things which were said by the pious Church Fathers merely to illustrate such great obscurity in passing have been treated too severely and at too great a length by the following age."* And after a few more words: *"Although..."*

The previous page established that while these two acts are distinct, their internal nature is a divine mystery. This page reinforces that stance by advocating for "religious ignorance" over "rash subtlety."</meta>

# OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER VI.

...which we grant to **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent medieval Scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note>, *that the **Divine Persons** are distinguished from one another by relations alone, and that the Son and the Holy Spirit (each of whom proceeds from the Father) proceed in a different manner. Indeed, even to our human reasoning, there is some order to be understood regarding this origin; yet, who has revealed these unsearchable secrets of God to these men—secrets which not even the blessed Angels are capable of grasping?* **PAULUS CAROLUS** and **ANTHONY GARISSOLIUS** <note>Professors at the Protestant Academy of Montauban in France.</note>, Professors, in their *Explanation of the French Catechism, Section XIV*, about to discuss the **Procession of the Holy Spirit** <term>Procession: The theological term for the way the Holy Spirit "comes forth" from God the Father (and the Son), distinguished from the "Generation" of the Son.</term>, begin in this way: *"It is safer to adore this Procession with awe than to scrutinize it more curiously and deeply than the revealed Word of God allows."* And after some points made with a refined judgment, they interject: *"But how much wiser were the ancients, who, not daring to rashly scrutinize the depth of such a mystery, openly confessed their ignorance."*

**ATHANASIUS** <note>Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373), a central figure in the development of Trinitarian theology.</note> in *Dialogue I on the Trinity*: *How God generates the Son and how He sends forth the Spirit, I do not busily investigate, but I believe that both the Son is generated and the Spirit proceeds in an unutterable and passionless way.* <note>original Greek: "Πως γεννᾷ τον Υἱον ὁ Θεος και πως ἐκπεμπει το Πνευμα, οὐ πολυπραγμονεῶ, ἀλλὰ πιστευῶ, ὁτι και ὁ Υἱος γεννηται και το Πνευma ἐκπορευεται ἀρῥητῶς και ἀπαθῶς."</note> That is, I do not curiously inquire how God generates the Son and how He sends the Holy Spirit, but I believe that the Son is generated and the Holy Spirit is sent.

And **DAMASCENE** <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), an influential monk and systematician of the Eastern Church.</note> in *Book I, Chapter 10*: *That there is a difference between **Generation** and **Procession**, we have learned. But what the manner of that difference is, we have not learned at all.* <note>original Greek: "Ὁτι μεν ἐστι διαφορα γεννησεως και ἐκπορευσεως μεμαθηκαμεν. Τις δε ὁ τροπος της διαφορας μηδαμως."</note> That is, we have learned that there is a difference between the **Generation** of the Son and the **Procession** of the Holy Spirit. But where that difference lies, we have nowhere learned.

**AUGUSTINE** <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430), the most influential of the Latin Church Fathers.</note> in *Book III against Maximinus, Chapter 14*: *"Who can explain what the difference is between being born and proceeding? Not everything that proceeds is born, although everything that is born proceeds; this I know. But how to distinguish that **Generation** and that **Procession**, I do not know, I am not able, I am not sufficient."*

Therefore, imitating their modesty, we frankly confess that we do not know the difference between *Divine **Generation** and **Procession**.* *In these most hidden matters, which surpass our understanding, a religious ignorance is far better than a rash subtlety.* **DANIEL TILENUS** <note>Daniel Tilenus (1563–1633), a Protestant theologian noted for his systematic works.</note> in *Theological Syntagma, Part I, Disputation 18, Sections 18 and following*: *"To scrutinize the mutual Relations of the three Persons, within and among themselves, more deeply and curiously than the boundaries of the revealed Word allow, is the mark neither of a Christian theologian nor of any sane man at all."* Because

<meta>This page continues the argument that the inner workings of the Trinity are a divine mystery. While the previous page cited Athanasius and early Church Fathers to emphasize "religious ignorance" over rash speculation, this page draws on more recent Reformed theologians like Louis Cappel, Johannes Cocceius, and Willem Momma to warn against the logical "audacity" of the Scholastics.</meta>

### THE MYSTERY OF THE PROCESSION

We must carefully guard against the intemperance and most unhappy audacity of the **Scholastics** <note>Medieval theologians (c. 1100–1500) known for using philosophy and logic to categorize every detail of faith; the author here critiques them for being overly speculative.</note>, whom this abyss swallows up as they investigate, through their complex disputes, *the mode and nature of the difference between the **Generation of the Son** and the **Procession of the Holy Spirit**.* It is better for the pious to soberly hold to the **fact that it is** <note>original Greek: *to hoti*, referring to accepting a truth because it is revealed, without needing to know "how."</note> and religiously adore it, than to perilously seek the **reason why** <note>original Greek: *to dioti*, referring to the underlying cause or logical explanation.</note> and rashly define it. Since nothing can be worthily uttered concerning divine matters due to their majesty, we must at least take care not to think too unworthily of them. And therefore, in neither Procession (namely, of the Son and of the Holy Spirit) should we dream of anything like what occurs in natural things that fall under our grasp—in which we observe a process occurring from the imperfect to the perfect, from place to place, or **FROM CAUSE TO EFFECT**. For that mode in divine things is plainly *unutterable and incomprehensible* <note>original Greek: *arrhētos kai akatalēptos*</note>. **LOUIS CAPPEL** <note>A famous 17th-century French Protestant theologian at the Academy of Saumur.</note>, *Theses of Saumur*, Volume I, pages 175–176. However, we believe the mode and nature of both the Generation of the Son and the Procession of the Holy Spirit to be *incomprehensible* <note>original Greek: *akatalēpton*</note> not only to the minds of men but even to the intellect of Angels; nor should it be investigated or defined where Scripture is silent. Yet the distinction between the Generation of the Son and the Procession of the Spirit is at least manifest to us from Holy Scripture in this: that the Generation of the Son is from one alone, namely the Father, while the Procession of the Spirit is from two, the Father and the Son, and so forth. The most solid **COCCEIUS** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian.</note> in *Summary of Theology*, Chapter XI, Section 68, explains the **spiration** <term>Spiration: From the Latin "spiratio" (breathing); the traditional term for the way the Holy Spirit "breathes forth" from the Father and the Son.</term> from the Son such that the Holy Spirit exists in an **INEFFABLE WAY** because the Father and the Son are [His source].

His genuine disciple, **WILLEM MOMMA** <note>A 17th-century Dutch theologian and follower of Cocceius.</note>, *Theological Lectures*, page 142: *"The mode and nature of the Procession of the Holy Spirit is incomprehensible to the minds of both men and Angels, nor should it be investigated when Scripture remains silent. God judged that this should reach our conscience insofar as it pertains to our salvation."* The same author later on page 150, having brought forward the opinions of others regarding the mode of Generation and Procession, concludes thus: *"Yet because Scripture has expressed no mode for this Mystery, it is perhaps safer to remain silent and define nothing. Let neither knowledge nor tongue proceed further than the boundaries of the Word of God extend. Let us leave the knowledge of God to God. For He alone at last, as **Hilary** says, is a fit witness to Himself, who..."* <note>Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), a bishop known as the "Hammer of the Arians" for his defense of the Trinity.</note>

### OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER VI.

...is an idea that is anything but clear and distinct stirred up by such a definition?

**XXXV.** Examining the antiquity of the Church, we find little support for the <term>Procession</term> <note>The theological term for the way the Holy Spirit "proceeds" or originates from the Father (and, in Western theology, the Son).</note> of the Holy Spirit as we have described it, but yet nothing stands as an obstacle against our view. The Pre-Nicene centuries <note>The period of Christian history before the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.</note> barely mentioned those questions on which the heart of the matter now turns. It is clear from the note added to John 16:13 that certain passages from **CLEMENT**, **HERMAS**, **TERTULLIAN**, and **ORIGEN** neither help nor hinder us. If any of them were to be taken into account, **TERTULLIAN** should not be neglected. But who will explain the mind of that African to us, or who would dare add a finishing touch to his argument in *Against Praxeas*, chapter 8, where he flourishes so much in his usual manner? 

*For the Spirit is third from God and the Son, just as the fruit from the bush is third from the root; and the stream from the river is third from the source, and the point of light from the ray is third from the sun. Yet nothing is alienated from the matrix from which it draws its properties. Thus the Trinity, running down from the Father through intertwined and connected stages, does not conflict with the Monarchy <note>original: "Monarchiæ"; the concept of God as a single, unified principle or ruler.</note> and protects the state of the Economy <note>original: "oikononomias"; the "management" or "arrangement" of how God reveals Himself as Father, Son, and Spirit in history.</note>.* 

In the Creeds of those times, including the Nicene Creed itself, there is profound silence regarding the Procession of the Holy Spirit. But if we wished to adorn ourselves with forged testimonies, we would appeal to the letter of **MARTIAL** to the people of Bordeaux, from which the **MAGDEBURG CENTURIES** <note>A massive 13-volume history of the Church published in the 16th century by Lutheran scholars.</note> (Century II) brought forth an excellent passage that expresses our view perfectly. However, even the Catholic writers have long recognized its spuriousness <note>original Greek: "notheian", meaning a work is a forgery or illegitimate.</note>. 

No less to our point is **JUSTIN MARTYR** in his *Exposition of the Faith*: *The unbegotten, the begotten, and the proceeding do not declare the essence, but signify the subsistences.* <note>original Greek: "To agenneton kai genneton, kai ekporeuton, ou ousias delōtika, semantika de tōn hypostaseōn estin." Justin is arguing that these terms describe the relationships between the persons of the Trinity, not what God is made of.</note> But the authenticity of this writing is by no means clear, as the famous **SALIGIUS** established after others in *On the Eutychians before Eutyches*, chapter 4, although the orthodoxy of that writing has been highly valued until now. Hardly anything more explicit about this mystery occurs in that whole interval, unless you turn to the words of **DIONYSIUS OF ALEXANDRIA**, whose fragments **ATHANASIUS** preserved in his *Letter on the Opinion of Dionysius* in the first volume of his Works.

**XXXVI.** Nor will we make much progress through the post-Nicene Fathers <note>The influential Christian theologians writing after the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.</note>. During that fairly long period, the Fathers of both the Greek and Latin Churches agreed that a certain relationship and "Essential order" of the Holy Spirit to the Father and the Son must be recognized. XXXVII. This liberty to disagree concerning the mode of subsisting <term>subsisting: the way in which a person of the Trinity exists as a distinct individual substance</term> was supported by the conviction they held regarding the venerable depth of this mystery, which they often expressed graphically. ## CHAPTER VII.
### AN EXAMINATION OF THE PRINCIPAL ERRORS IN THE DOCTRINE OF THE PROCESSION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT.

->I.<-

As many as foster erroneous concepts regarding both the *Person of the Holy Spirit* and his *Deity* <term>Deity: his nature as God</term> also suffer from false prejudices concerning his Procession <term>Procession: the theological term for the way the Holy Spirit originates within the Trinity</term>. Indeed, it is superfluous to enter into a full listing of them here, since once the fortress of their error has been stormed, all its consequences collapse at once. Nevertheless, it should not be assumed that those who have judged correctly regarding those two articles [the Person and the Deity] have necessarily held correct views regarding the Procession of the Holy Spirit. There have certainly been those—especially since the Church was torn into many parts through various concepts concerning the subordination of the Persons—who imagined that the Son and the Holy Spirit came forth *through out-flowing* <note>original: per effluxionem</note>; there were those who imagined it was *through expansion* <note>original: per dilatationem</note> of the divine substance; some dreamed they were produced *through the intellect alone*, others *through the will alone*. The *Anomoeans* <note>A 4th-century radical Arian sect that claimed the Son was "unlike" the Father in essence.</note> specifically boasted that the modes of production of the Word and the Holy Spirit were perfectly known to them. Mention of these is made by **ATHANASIUS** in *Oration III against the Arians*, **NAZIANZEN** <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note> in *Oration XXXV*, and **AUGUSTINE** in *Book III against Maximinus*, chapter 14. However, the greatest contention regarding this article arose with the Greek Church, a matter treated more fully by **PETAVIUS** in *On the Trinity*, Book VII; **NATALIS ALEXANDER** in his discussion on the 9th and 10th Centuries, Dissertation XVIII; **LEQUIEN** in his dissertation on Damascene, I; **MONTACUTIUS** in his notes on the *Second Letter of Photius*; and **HEINECCIUS** on the *State of the Greek Church*.

<summary>The author introduces the history of "errors" regarding the Holy Spirit’s Procession, noting that even those who believe in the Spirit's divinity have disagreed on the "mode" of his origin. He cites early Church Fathers and more contemporary scholars to highlight the long-standing conflict between the Western and Greek (Eastern) Churches on this doctrine.</summary>

<header>EXAMINATION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER VII.</header>

In Part II, chapter 2, we will briefly touch upon the main points of the highest importance regarding both the history and the error itself.

II. The spark from which such a great fire arose was lit, as far as is known, by THEODORE OF MOPSUESTIA around the beginning of the 5th Century. He composed a Creed <note>Theodore was a prominent bishop and theologian, though his works later became controversial during the Nestorian debates.</note>, which was included in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus (Act VI), in which he asserted concerning the Holy Spirit: *But neither do we consider him to be the Son, nor to have received his existence through the Son.* <note>original Greek: οὔτε δι' Υἱοῦ τὴν ὕπαρξιν εἰληφός</note> However, since several things in this Creed seemed to be crude and foreign to the faith of the Church at that time, THEODORE did not hesitate to correct them out of a desire for peace, as we know from a letter of JOHN OF ANTIOCH to Nestorius, preserved in the same Acts (Part I, chapter 15). Thus, with THEODORE having died in the communion of the Church and leaving behind a great reputation for learning and doctrine, this dispute would have remained dormant, had not the "Anathemas" <term>Anathemas: formal curses or denunciations of heresy</term> of CYRIL, prematurely hurled against Nestorius, stirred the fire from the embers. For in his ninth Anathema, Cyril had thundered thus:

> If anyone shall say that the Lord Jesus was glorified by the Spirit, using the Spirit’s power as if it were a foreign power, and that he [Jesus] received from him [the Spirit] the power and efficacy to work against unclean spirits and to perform divine miracles among men, and does not rather confess that the Spirit, through whom he performed divine signs, was his own, let him be anathema.

To this, THEODORET—who was once a fellow student of Nestorius under Theodore and thereafter his strenuous defender—opposed the following: *That the Spirit is the Son’s own, in the sense that he is of the same nature with him and proceeds from the Father, we shall jointly confess and receive as a pious expression; but if [it is meant] as having existence from the Son or through the Son <note>original Greek: εἰ δὲ ὡς ἐξ Υἱοῦ, ἢ δι' Υἱοῦ τὴν ὕπαρξιν ἔχον</note>, we reject this as blasphemous and impious.*

III. Nevertheless, the matter did not break out into a public schism at that point. For on one side, THEODORET interpreted CYRIL’S words in a negative light due to excessive fervor, as is evident from his letter (inserted into the fifth session of the Fifth General Council), in which he declares that the poison of Macedonius and Apollinaris <note>Macedonius denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit; Apollinaris was a heretic who taught that Christ had a human body but a divine mind.</note> lurked beneath those words. On the other side, the words of THEODORET were not [marked] with a public brand of...

...established. For although the Fathers of the Council of Ephesus in the year 431, under the presidency of CYRIL, condemned the Creed of THEODORE OF MOPSUESTIA in a general sense, they made no mention of the error regarding the Procession of the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, JEAN GARNERIUS <note>Jean Garnier (1612–1681) was a learned Jesuit theologian and church historian known for his editions of early Christian writings.</note>, in his notes on Marius Mercator regarding the Nestorian controversy (Dissertation I, chapter 6), clearly proves that NESTORIUS himself did not provoke the Church's censure upon himself because of this particular adopted opinion, as some have claimed. Therefore, regarding the distinction between the *Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son*, individual judgment was left sufficiently free for a long time afterward. And if by chance one or two of the Fathers professed their disagreement in this matter, no public definition by the Church intervened. 

In this regard, there is a notable passage by MAXIMUS <note>Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662 AD), a monk and theologian who sought to bridge the gap between the Roman and Byzantine churches.</note> in his Letter to Marinus, a Presbyter of Cyprus, in which he wrote that the Greeks and Romans agree on the heart of the matter regarding this controversy, even though there was some dissonance regarding the words: *For they know,* he says, *that the one cause of the Son and the Holy Spirit is the Father—one by way of generation, the other by way of emission <note>original: "emissionem" (sending forth)</note>: but in order to suggest that the Spirit goes forth through the Son, and by this (namely, the word "and the Son" <note>original: "Filioque"</note>), they demonstrate the communion and indivisibility of their substance.* 

Looking at this passage, ANASTASIUS THE LIBRARIAN <note>Anastasius Bibliothecarius (c. 810–879 AD) was the chief archivist of the Roman Church and a key translator of Greek works into Latin.</note> candidly testifies concerning MAXIMUS: *He teaches both us and the Greeks that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son according to one sense, and does not proceed according to another: thus highlighting the difficulty of expressing a specific property from one language into the property of another. In the same way, the holy Athanasius once used a similar pious interpretation to unite the Easterners and Westerners who were at odds over the name for "subsistence" or "person" <term>subsistence: the Greek term "hypostasis," which Romans often translated as "substance," leading to confusion until Athanasius clarified the terms</term>, while he taught that both sides believed and held the same thing in their understanding, even if they confessed it differently due to the variation of language and were raging in restless contentions.*
