And in Section 48, dealing with those who admitted nothing but a *temporal* procession <note>A "temporal" procession refers to the Holy Spirit being sent into the world at a specific time (like at Pentecost), as opposed to an "eternal" procession from the nature of God himself.</note>, he appeals to the Confession of Macarius of Antioch, a Monothelite <term>Monothelite: A 7th-century theological position claiming that Christ had two natures but only one will; it was eventually declared heretical.</term> heretic, in which it is read concerning the Holy Spirit: *And in the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and appearing through the Son, clearly to men* <note>original Greek: "καὶ δι' Υἱοῦ πεφηνὸς δηλαδὴ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις"</note>, or "shining forth through the Son, namely to men." From this, he further guesses that the exposition of the Faith by **GREGORY THAUMATURGUS** <note>Gregory "the Wonderworker" (c. 213–270 AD), a famous early Christian bishop known for his missionary work and miracles.</note> was falsified by the Monothelites by adding those two words, *clearly to men*, which never appeared in the ancient translation by **RUFFINUS** <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410 AD), a monk and historian famous for translating Greek Church Fathers into Latin.</note>. 

But the Learned Man is mistaken. In no Synods or public Acts were the Monothelites ever accused of heresy regarding the Holy Spirit. Although perhaps a few among the Monothelites might have established something different from the faith of the Orthodox East, it cannot be imputed to the entire sect. The case of **MACARIUS OF ANTIOCH** was aired widely and most fiercely in the Sixth Ecumenical Council <note>The Third Council of Constantinople (680–681 AD), which condemned Monothelitism.</note>, and his Confession was rigidly examined; yet, not even a tiny bit was noted against that particular phrase. 

Regarding the Exposition of **GREGORY THAUMATURGUS**, the arrangement is useless, as the whole thing is a fabrication and a substitution, though by a man of which party, it is unknown. But even if it had that same author, there is no reason why it should be denied that such an expression flowed from his pen. He was not as *wondrous* <note>original Greek: "Θαυμασιος" (Thaumasios), a play on his title "Thaumaturgus" or Wonderworker.</note> in his words as he is said to be in his deeds. Hence, he is believed by some to have been a precursor to Eutychianism <note>Eutychianism was the belief that Christ's divine nature swallowed his human nature; it was condemned at the Council of Chalcedon in 451 AD.</note>. The phrase itself was not infrequent in **CYRIL** and others. 

However, in the Synodal letters of **MARTIN** <note>Pope Martin I (reigned 649–653 AD), who was martyred for his opposition to Monothelitism.</note>, which are inserted into the Acts of the Lateran Council of the year 649 AD, I have sought such an expression in vain. If it did exist, it would surely exhibit the first public testimony for the Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. For so far, that expression has not appeared *literally* <note>original Greek: "κατὰ ῥητόν" (kata rhēton), meaning "word for word" or "explicitly."</note> in the Acts of the Church.

**VI.** From here, it gradually passed into other Western Churches, aided by the favor shown to the *Athanasian Creed* <note>A statement of Christian belief focused on the Trinity and the nature of Christ, traditionally attributed to St. Athanasius but now generally thought to be of later Western origin.</note>, which, it seems probable to me, was fabricated from the decrees of Toledo around these very times. I would not judge these to have been drawn from the *Athanasian Creed*, but rather that they represent its rough drafts, which were later more precisely refined in Gaul <note>The region corresponding mostly to modern-day France.</note>. Those who attribute a greater age to the Creed lack sufficient reasons. The distinguished **SALIG** <note>Christian August Salig (1692–1733), a German historian known for his work on the history of the Augsburg Confession.</note> reviews the differing opinions on this matter in *Eutyches before Eutyches, Chapter XV*, from which it can be seen that nothing is brought forward that carries us beyond that era, and the manuscripts do not go back further than the 8th century. Recently, the distinguished **DANIEL WATERLAND** <note>Daniel Waterland (1683–1740), an English theologian and Master of Magdalene College, Cambridge.</note> left no stone unturned in his *Critical History of the Athanasian Creed* (published in Cambridge in the English language) to push back the composition of this Creed to the beginning of the 5th century, even trying to prove that **HILARY OF POITIERS** <note>A 4th-century bishop and theologian who was a staunch defender of the Trinity against Arianism.</note> was its author. For it does not specifically strike at **APOLLINARIS**, nor would it follow, even if that were admitted, that the Creed must be referred back to his age, since it is enough that some remnants of his followers remained in Gaul when this Creed was being composed. Nor are his testimonies sought from antiquity any more valid. Among the citations before **ABBOT REGINO** <note>Regino of Prüm (c. 840–915 AD), a Benedictine abbot and chronicler.</note>, who flourished in the year 760, there is none earlier than the Canon of a certain *Council of Autun* held in 670, the meaning and authenticity of which are not yet entirely free of doubt. ...[Greeks], unless their spirits had been further provoked by the pride of the Roman Pontiffs, especially in the case of **Photius** <note>Photius the Great (c. 810–893 AD), Patriarch of Constantinople, whose conflict with Rome contributed to the East-West Schism.</note> and the disputes over the Bishopric of the **Bulgarians** <note>A major point of contention between Rome and Constantinople was which church had jurisdiction over the newly converted Bulgarian people.</note>, in the 8th century. > *In addition to the mentioned absurdities, they attempted to adulterate the holy and sacred Creed—which is confirmed by the votes of all the Ecumenical Councils and possesses invincible force—with spurious meanings and counterfeit words, which was the height of their audacity. Oh, diabolical machinations! They have invented a new custom that the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Father alone, but also from the Son.* <note>original: "Spiritum Sanctum novo more comminiscebantur non ex solo Patre, sed etiam ex Filio procedere." This refers to the "Filioque" clause.</note>

What did the Romans say to this? For a long time, they ignored this reproach to such an extent that we read of no formal opposition to it; indeed, even **Pope John VIII** <note>Reigned 872–882 AD.</note>, in a letter produced by **Photius**, wrote to him in these words:

> *It has seemed reasonable to us that no one should be violently forced by us to omit that addition by which the Creed was enlarged; but rather, that they should be prepared with prudence and gentleness, gradually advising them to turn away from the blasphemy.* <note>original: "ἀποστῆναι τῆς βλασφημίας" (apostēnai tēs blasphēmias). This refers to the controversial "Filioque" addition as a blasphemy in the context of the Greek perspective.</note>

VIII. Roman writers cannot stomach this, and for that reason, they cry out that these letters were forged by **Photius**, whom they insult as a most foul villain. **Baronius** <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607), a Cardinal and historian who wrote the *Annales Ecclesiastici* to defend the Roman Catholic Church.</note> dealt with this matter extensively under the year 879 AD. To this argument, they also add that the Pope, in his own ordination, had repeatedly confessed the very thing that is here traded as "blasphemy." Truly, we have no greater faith in the "parasites of the Roman Court" <note>A derogatory term for the scholars and officials who defended the Pope's interests.</note> than we do in **Photius**, whom we consider to be the most learned man of his age and one who deserved well of the Church. The Pope had the weightiest reasons for changing his opinion, even if he had professed another previously: **Basil**, the Emperor of the Greeks <note>Basil I (reigned 867–886 AD), the Byzantine Emperor.</note>, had promised—as a reward for reconciliation with **Photius**—the submission of both the Bulgarians and **Photius** himself to the Roman See, as well as a powerful army and fleet against the **Saracens** <note>Medieval term for Arab Muslims who were then invading Southern Italy.</note> who were pressing upon Italy. The word "blasphemy" also more clearly points to the act of adulteration regarding the Creed...

Baronius is criticizing Pope John VIII for being too lenient toward Photius for political reasons.</note>

IX. Whatever the case may be regarding John VIII, his successors abstained from the use of the "adulterated" <note>The author uses "adulterated" to refer to the version of the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed that included the *Filioque* ("and the Son") clause.</note> Constantinopolitan Creed. **MICHEL LEQUIEN** <note>A French Dominican theologian and historian (1661–1733).</note> proves against **VOSSIUS** <note>Gerardus Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch humanist and theologian.</note> and others in his *Dissertations on Damascene II, § 23 and following*, that the public reception of it was hardly attempted before **MICHAEL CERULARIUS** <note>The Patriarch of Constantinople during the formal Great Schism of 1054.</note>—that is, the middle of the 11th century—although he remains doubtful as to which of the Pontiffs who succeeded from Benedict VIII to Leo IX it should be attributed. This is consistent with what **WATERLAND** <note>Daniel Waterland (1683–1740), an English theologian known for his history of the Athanasian Creed.</note> makes manifest in the place cited: namely, that the **Athanasian Creed** <note>A statement of Christian doctrine traditionally attributed to St. Athanasius, which explicitly includes the *Filioque*.</note> was likewise not used in Rome before the year 1050. This was undoubtedly done for the same reason: because through that Creed, the use of the term *Filioque* was more firmly established.

X. Roman Catholic writers have busied themselves with obscuring the controversy, which has been more sharply debated since that time, in various ways. They cast the blame for the contention onto **CERULARIUS**. They claim he was the "torch and the trumpet" <note>A metaphorical way of saying he was the primary instigator and voice of the conflict.</note> of the strife. Yet it is clear that **HUMBERT** <note>Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida, the papal legate who famously excommunicated the Patriarch in 1054.</note>, the Legate of Leo IX, began the fatal schism by hurling the bolt of excommunication against Cerularius and his associates in the city of Constantinople itself. I cannot wonder enough that the entire College of Sorbonne Doctors <note>The theological faculty of the University of Paris.</note>, in order to induce **Peter** <note>Peter the Great (1672–1725), Tsar of Russia, who had dealings with Western theologians regarding church union.</note>, the recent Monarch of Great Russia, to a reconciliation with the Roman Church...

...and from that same time, they began to debate more intensely not only about the wording but even about the reality itself. For since it could not be denied that the ancient Greek Fathers—though they had consistently rejected the phrase *Procession from the Father and the Son* <note>original: "Processionis à Patre Filioque"</note>—had nevertheless acknowledged a *Procession from the Father through the Son*, they explained this in two ways. 

Some plainly denied that any relational quality existed in this phrase, maintaining that nothing else was expressed by it except the **shared essence** <term>original: "τὸ ὁμοούσιον" (to homoousion). The foundational Christian doctrine that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of the same "substance" or "being."</term> with the Son, or that he is of the same essence as the Son and descends from the same source with him. This opinion, although already admitted among the ancients, began to be less tolerated after it was more explicitly defended by **GREGORY PALAMAS** <note>A 14th-century monk and Archbishop of Thessaloniki known for defending the distinction between God's essence and His "energies."</note> in his *Refutation of Beccus* <note>John XI Bekkos, a Patriarch of Constantinople who briefly favored union with the Roman Catholic Church.</note>, Chapter 1, and by others. And this is what **LE QUIEN** <note>Michel Le Quien (1661–1733), a French Dominican theologian and historian.</note> in the place cited, section 48, especially undertook to prove: namely, that as many as wrote in favor of the schism, at least from the time of **CERULARIUS** until **BECCUS**, almost unanimously asserted no Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father through the Son, except for that temporal manifestation or granting of spiritual gifts. This is confirmed by the writings of **MICHAEL PSELLOS**, **NICETAS OF NICOMEDIA**, **GEORGE OF CYPRUS**, and others.

Hence, following others, **THOMAS SMITH** in *The Present State of the Greek Church*, page 133 (of my copy), states that no...

XIV. It is easily perceived that both sides have erred here in various ways. It will not be a cause for regret to set forth as an example this "saw of contention" <note>An idiom for a repetitive, back-and-forth argument that achieves nothing.</note> which has been so spiritedly pushed back and forth through so many centuries. From this, one may learn how many monsters are birthed by vain disputes over terms invented by men. In the Latins [the Roman Church], we certainly condemn: 1. That they dared to change anything in the Formula of Faith <note>The Nicene Creed.</note> established by common authority through their own private audacity. 2. That by their addition [of the *Filioque*] they added something not contained in the **literal word** <note>original: "κατα το ῥητον" (kata to rhēton)</note> of Scripture, which is to that extent ambiguous and suspect, because it gave no handle for making a distinction between the Procession from the Father and that from the Son.

**XV.** The Greeks are no less to be blamed: 1. Because they have raised so much dust <note>A Latin idiom (*pulveris suscitarint*) meaning to create a great deal of commotion or confusion.</note> over words that were capable of a more gentle interpretation, and because they have frequently exceeded the Romans themselves in the harshness of their speech. 2. Because, while they wish to appear to follow the footsteps of the Church Fathers closely, they have put forward new interpretations that were either unknown to the Fathers or not universally accepted; in this way, they have made the gaping wounds of the Church even wider in these latter days. Nevertheless, regarding the importance of the question, I subscribe to the moderate judgment of the celebrated **HEIDEGGER** <note>Johann Heinrich Heidegger (1633–1698), a prominent Swiss Reformed theologian known for his work on the Helvetic Consensus.</note>, following other theologians, in his *Body of Theology, Topic IV, Section 74*:

> The remaining disagreement over words is to be tolerated as a weakness, not to be hounded as a heresy.

**XVI.** However, the principal arguments by which the Greeks attack the essential Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son must be refuted in a few words.

**A.** "In John 15:26, it is simply declared that the Holy Spirit *proceeds from the Father*, with no mention of the Son added, by whom he is said only to be sent in time." **Response:** 1. There is no indication here that a going forth from the Son is excluded. Therefore, since this is also taught in other places (as we showed more extensively in the preceding chapter), those passages must be compared with this saying. 2. Scripture often attributes to individual Persons what belongs equally to all three. The Son is called the "True Light"; the Father is called "the only true God" <note>original Greek: *ho monos alēthinos Theos*</note>, and so forth. 3. Even if the Son had not expressed the going forth of the Holy Spirit *from himself* as explicitly as he did *from the Father*, it would not be a problem. For as long as he lived in his state of humiliation on earth, he went about asserting the Father's honor more explicitly than his own. For he had come to glorify the Father. Thus, for example, he commanded us to pray to the Father, yet he did not exclude himself from that same honor. 4. We easily grant that this saying deals most directly with the temporal Mission <note>The "Mission" refers to the Holy Spirit being sent into the world at a specific point in time (like at Pentecost), rather than his eternal origin within God.</note> of the Holy Spirit. Truly, I have taught no less clearly in my commentary on this passage that the Economic <term>The "Economic" Trinity refers to God’s actions and roles in the world and human history, as opposed to the "Ontological" Trinity, which refers to God’s eternal internal nature.</term> going forth of the Holy Spirit from the Father is also understood here. Just as it has been demonstrated that the Economic relation of the Holy Spirit to the Father is founded in the essential relation, so the same must be concluded regarding his relation to the Son.

**XVII.** **B.** "If the Holy Spirit has his existence from the Son as much as from the Father, then there are two Principles <note>In Trinitarian theology, a "Principle" (*Principium*) refers to the source or origin of a Person's existence.</note>, and with these, two Essences...

# ERRORS CONCERNING THE PROCESSION

> "...are predicated in one God."

**Response 1.** The term *Principle* <term>Principle: In Trinitarian theology, a "principle" (Latin: *principium*) refers to a source or origin. The Father is the principle of the Son; the Father and Son together are considered the "single principle" of the Holy Spirit in Western theology.</term> is obscure and ambiguous when it is used concerning the Order of the divine Persons. No definition of it borrowed from the schools <note>Referring to the "Schoolmen" or Scholastic philosophers who used precise logical definitions.</note> fits this case, because no other example of such a *Principle*—through which the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son—occurs anywhere in the universe. Whatever this distinct Principle may be, it is of such a nature that it wages no war against the Unity of Essence of the Father and the Son. It is sufficient to embrace this by faith according to the Scripture. Moreover, no one will be able to demonstrate against us a conflict between these two truths: that the principles of the Procession <note>The "Procession" is the way the Holy Spirit originates within the Trinity.</note> of the Holy Spirit are distinct, and yet those principles subsist in one essence; for we declare that we are ignorant of the manner of that distinction.

**2.** If the Persons themselves can be distinct while the Unity of the divine essence remains intact, nothing prevents us—according to the testimony of Scripture—from conceiving of their relations and the manner among them by which one person is from another as distinct, while that same Unity is preserved. As long as that Principle remains inexplicable, it cannot be demonstrated that the joining of two Principles implies a difference of Essences.

**2.** <note>The author repeats the numbering "2" in the original text.</note> Just as, according to the Greeks <note>The Eastern Orthodox theologians.</note>, the divine Essence is not multiplied when they distinguish between the Principle and the Principiate <term>Principiate: That which has a principle; the "originated" person (the Son or Spirit) as opposed to the "originator" (the Father).</term>, so also such a multiplication of essence should not be attributed to us when we distinguish "Principle" and "Principle" according to two different modes of Relation.

### XVIII. C.
> "The Father is the Fountain of the Deity"

**Response 1.** The metaphor of the "Fountain" implies the same thing as the word *Principle*. Therefore, the same response applies. 

**2.** If nothing prevents the Father from being called the "Fountain of the Deity" in relation to the subsistence <note>The state of existing as an individual person within the Trinity.</note> of the Son and the Holy Spirit, then nothing can be brought forward to prevent the Son from also being called the "Fountain of the Deity" in relation to the subsistence of the Holy Spirit.

### XIX. D.
> "Either the production by which the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father is perfect, or it is not. The latter is impiously asserted. If the former is true, then production from the Son is superfluous."

**Response 1.** This argument also relies on a prejudice regarding "two divided Principles" in the Godhead, a charge with which they burden us. 

**2.** The concurrence of the remaining Persons with the Father in effecting the same work hinders nothing...

### EXAMINATION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER VII.

...it hinders its perfection, and is necessary because of the unity of the divine essence. Otherwise, by similar reasoning, we could argue about the creation of the world: *Either the act of the Father in producing the world was perfect, or it was not, etc.* <note>The author is using a "reduction to absurdity" argument: if the Father's action in the Trinity required no "help" from the Son, one could wrongly argue that the Son had no role in Creation either, which contradicts the Gospel of John.</note>

XX. "If the Father alone is the cause of the Son, but is not alone the cause of the Holy Spirit; then he is more the cause of the Son than he is of the Holy Spirit." 
**Response 1.** As long as we remain ignorant of the specific manner in which the Father is the cause of the Son and the Holy Spirit, it is not permitted to argue based on the nature of that causality. 
**2.** We acknowledge a difference in the relationship between the Father and the Son from that which exists between the Father and the Holy Spirit, yet it is of such a kind that it introduces no inequality. 
**3.** Since "cause" <term>Cause: In this theological context, "cause" (Latin: *causa*) does not mean a creator making a creature, but the eternal source or origin within the Godhead.</term> here denotes the same thing as "principle," the response returns to this: that the Spiration <note>original: "Spiratio"; the theological term for the "breathing forth" of the Spirit.</note> of the Father and the Son is one single and undivided principle. Thus, the objection falls apart which some add, saying: "That which comes from two is never equal to that which comes from only one. But the Spirit comes from two, while the Son has his birth from the Father alone. Therefore, the Spirit is not equal to the Son, but is either greater or lesser." For this only affects those who defend two principles that are not only divided but also subordinate to one another.

XXI. "Since the Holy Spirit descended from the Father upon the Son when Christ was baptized at the Jordan, it is necessary that he proceed from the Father alone. For if he also proceeds from the Son, there would have to be two Sons: one who sends the Spirit, and another upon whom he is sent." 
**Response.** From this, it does not follow that there are two Sons or two persons, but only two natures. Therefore, Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius (c. 296–373), a central Church Father who defended the divinity of Christ.</note>, in his book *On Human Nature*, says that *the Holy Spirit descended from Christ into Christ* <note>original: "Spiritum S. à Christo in Christum descendisse"</note>, which is to say, *from his divinity into his same human nature.*

XXII. "Finally, they appeal to the ancient faith of the Church." 
**Response.** They will gain very little from this, because: 1) They cannot prove that this dispute was decided by public Church authority. The Creeds <note>original: "Symbola"</note>, which express only the *Procession from the Father*, do not by that fact immediately reject every *Procession from the Son*. The Latins <note>Referring to the Western/Roman Church.</note>, even while adding the phrase "and from the Son" <note>original: "Filioque"</note>, have often testified to their tolerance regarding this article. 2) If one descends to the authorities of the Doctors of the Church, their true opinion is so obscured by the tangled complexity of their terms...

-># ERRORS CONCERNING THE PROCESSION<-

...it is permitted to argue in either direction, and it has been so argued, so that they will achieve nothing by this route either. 3) Add to this that they join other interpretations of their own making which were unknown to the Church Fathers.

XXIII. Moreover, the things which the Scholastics <term>Scholastics: Medieval theologians who used Aristotelian logic to explain Christian doctrine, most notably Thomas Aquinas.</term> devise in defining the "mode" of the Procession of the Holy Spirit are no less absurd; it will be helpful to bring forward some of their fictions, if perhaps they might restrain the rashness of others who strive to be wise in this matter beyond and above what is written in Scripture. Thus, **Thomas Aquinas** in *Summa Theologica*, Part 1, Question 27, Article 1, asserted *that the Catholic faith posits that, just as the Procession of the Son is through the operation of the intellect, so the Procession of the Holy Spirit occurs through the operation of the will.* <note>Aquinas argued that the Son is the "Word" (Intellect) and the Spirit is "Love" (Will).</note> **Hieronymus Zanchius** rightly pronounces this opinion rash in his work *On the Three Elohim* <note>original: "de III. Elohim"; Elohim is a Hebrew name for God.</note> Part I, Book III, final chapter. For this reason, Zanchius was poorly treated by **Gregory de Valentia**, who defended the opinion in *Disputation* II, Question I, point 3. Yet Valentia brings nothing else to support it than the error of **Augustine** examined above in Chapter III, in which he contends that the Holy Spirit *is Charity* <note>original: "Charitatem"; here meaning divine Love.</note>; from which Valentia infers: *Charity and love surely proceed from nowhere else but the will.* Various absurdities <note>original: "ἄτοπα" (atopa)</note> converge here, such as: that an error is used as a foundation which turns the divine persons into mere "modes of thinking" and destroys the actual personality of the Holy Spirit; that the most perfect intellect and will in God are "torn apart" as if they were separate functions; that a distinct operation is attributed to each person in opposition to the others; and finally, that the very necessity of the three persons in one divine essence is destroyed by this concept. For if the Father produced the Son naturally through his intellect, and produced the Holy Spirit naturally through his will, there is nothing to stop the Son from generating another Son through *his* intellect, and another Holy Spirit through *his* will, and so on forever.

XXIV. The more these theories become entangled on all sides, the more it is to be lamented that many of our own theologians have adopted the same opinion. Above others, **Samuel Maresius** defends it explicitly—and not without his usual sharp "sting"—in his *System of Theology*, Locus III, section 28. He appeals to "a thousand celebrated theologians of great name" who are not displeased by this distinction between Intellect and Will, and he even declares that those who hiss at this opinion are doing the work of the **Socinians**. <note>Socinians: A radical 16th/17th-century group that rejected the Trinity and the deity of Christ; calling someone a Socinian was a severe theological insult.</note> I indeed, who so...

->### EXAMINATION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER VII.<-

...I should think those who hold these views are not at all to be hissed off the stage, but rather tolerated; though it often makes one wonder how tolerance for certain opinions liable to very grave consequences can sometimes be extended so widely by those who seethe with such implacable feeling against opinions of much less importance. Indeed, it is clear that this fabrication—notwithstanding the authority of **Augustine**—wanders as far from reason as it does from Scripture, and is weighed down by the gravest consequences. **Maresius** <term>Samuel Des Marets (1599–1673): A leading French Reformed theologian known for defending orthodoxy against both Catholicism and radical rationalism.</term> says:

> "What difficulty or danger is there in establishing that God the Father, by understanding Himself, begets His Son and rouses an image of Himself within Himself, just as our mind, by understanding itself while it reflects upon itself, rouses an idea and image of itself within itself? But if the Generation of the Son and of the *Word* <note>original Greek: "του λογου" (tou logou)</note> can be traced back to the divine intellect—as is done by all who do not wish to explain this name of the *Word* <note>original: "Logou"</note> in the Socinian <term>Socinianism: A rationalist Christian movement that denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ, viewing "Word" as a mere title or metaphor.</term> manner—why should the origin and Procession of the Holy Spirit not be traced back to the will of God, not as a free or indifferent act of His, but as a necessary and natural one? Certainly, not even the slightest obscurity would remain here if, just as the name *Image* is certainly attributed to the Son, the name *Love* were also attributed to the Holy Spirit—which, however, people commonly wish to gather from 1 John 4:8."

But what then? Does no obscurity remain in a concept that builds so many absurdities <note>original Greek: "ατοπα" (atopa)</note> upon such a light foundation? The *foundation* seems to be drawn from Scripture, but it does so by supposing things that an accurate interpreter <term>Hermeneuta: A scholar focused on the rules and methods of biblical interpretation.</term> will never admit. For example: that unless you wish to explain the name *Word* <note>original: "Logos"</note> in a Socinian way, you must conclude that the Generation of the Son through the *intellect* is contained within it; or that the same is clear from the name *Image of God* used for the Son—as if there were no other kind of image than that which is formed through ideas of the intellect, or as if the Son were not the *Image of the Father* in a completely different way than an idea is an image of the mind. Another assumption is that the Procession of the Holy Spirit through the *will* flows automatically from the granted Generation of the Son through the *intellect*, or that the word "Love" in 1 John 4 refers specifically to the person of the Holy Spirit. On this fabulous foundation, many things are put forward unphilosophically <note>original Greek: "αφιλοσοφως" (aphilosophōs)</note>. Such as the idea that God rouses an idea of Himself in Himself according to the likeness of our mind—as if He did not already have that idea present by the power of His most perfect intellect, and as if this presence of the idea of Himself and of

# ERRORS CONCERNING THE PROCESSION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT, ETC.

...[of all attributes] does not belong to the nature of the most perfect intellect, which is common to the Son and the Holy Spirit along with the Father: that the Generation of the Son is nothing other than the production of an idea, which materially is the thinking mind itself, but formally nothing but a certain mode of thinking—and the rest of the points we have already touched upon. **Mornay** <term>Philippe de Mornay (1549–1623): A prominent French Protestant statesman and theologian known for using philosophical reason to defend Christian doctrines.</term> is no less laborious in bringing forward "little arguments" for this concept in *On the Truth of the Christian Religion*, Chapter 5; however, we do not wish to follow him any further through those types of thorny thickets.

XXV. **Durandus** <term>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334): A medieval Scholastic philosopher and theologian known as the "Resolute Doctor" for his independent and often controversial views.</term> proceeds by another path in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book I, Distinction 6, Question 2), where he derives this Procession *from the fecundity of nature*, or as others put it, *from the notional property of the person alone, through a certain other communicative act of the divine nature, prior to the acts of will and intellect*. But here mere "smoke" is being sold <note>The author uses the idiom "vendi fumos" (to sell smoke), meaning to offer empty, worthless, or deceptive talk.</note>; by devising new phrases, they not only require a new definition, but also—insofar as they are even understandable—they breathe more than one absurdity. For who would allow himself to be persuaded that there is something in God different from His intellect and His will, preceding both, and acting as the starting point for certain operations? What exactly is that *fecundity of the divine nature*? Or if it is a property of the divine nature, why would it belong any less to the Son and the Holy Spirit than to the Father? Does not the entire divine nature, and whatever is proper to it, belong by equal right to all three persons? Anyone who desires more of the various scholastic "sword-clashings" <note>original: "digladiationes" — sharp academic disputes.</note> should consult **Vásquez** <term>Gabriel Vásquez (1549–1604): A Spanish Jesuit theologian famous for his meticulous and often critical commentaries on Thomas Aquinas.</term> in his *Disputations on Thomas*, Question 27, Disputation 111 and following.

XXVI. Let the paradox of **Vitus Besoldus** (a Saxon Pastor, around the year 1638) close the ranks. He proposed a view in which he defends that the Holy Spirit proceeds from Christ even according to His human nature—and indeed, this relates not only to His "economic" mission <note>The "Economic Trinity" refers to how God reveals Himself and acts in the world (e.g., Jesus sending the Spirit to the disciples), whereas the "Immanent Trinity" refers to God's eternal internal nature.</note> but even to His personal character. **Höpner** <term>Johann Höpner (1582–1645): A Lutheran theologian at Leipzig who defended traditional orthodoxy.</term> examines this controversy in a certain letter found in the *Innocent Reports* <note>original: "Relat. Innoc." likely referring to the *Relationes Innocentis*, a collection of theological reports or news.</note> of 1704, page 232 and following. A slippery path to this error is certainly opened by those who extend the "communication of divine attributes" <term>Communicatio idiomatum: The doctrine that the properties of Christ's divine nature (like omnipresence) are shared with His human nature because they are united in one Person.</term> granted to the humanity of Christ further than is right. But since that error, as far as is known, died out with its author, there will be no need to dwell on its refutation.

THERE REMAIN now those RELATIONS of the Holy Spirit which are called **ECONOMIC** <term>Economic (from the Greek 'oikonomia'): In theology, this refers to God’s "household management" or the way He acts in human history to bring about salvation, rather than His internal, eternal nature.</term>, because they concern that most wise administration which God directed toward rational creatures for His own Glory and for their salvation. The sacred pages <note>The author refers here to the Bible.</note> deal with these far more abundantly than with His natural relations; this was to be expected, since the Scriptures were recorded for the very purpose of recounting the way in which God wills to be glorified in the sinner. We have established two classes of these Relations, based on the twofold and very different objects of the Holy Spirit’s operations. For He is active in one way toward the Father and the Son, with whom He constitutes the unity of the Godhead <note>original Greek: "το εν της Θεοτητος" (to hen tēs Theotētos), meaning the unity of the Divinity</note>; and in another way toward creatures, which are His own work.

### THE ECONOMY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT IN RELATION
<meta>catchword: -sion</meta>

II. Continuing now with the first mode of operation, we observe that two types of Economic works <term>Economic works: Actions performed by God in relation to the created world and the plan of salvation, rather than His internal existence.</term> are ascribed to the Holy Spirit in relation to the Father and the Son. Some of these regard God’s eternal *Decree*, while others regard its *Execution* in time.

III. That the Holy Spirit, along with the Father and the Son, was the *Author* of the eternal Decree itself follows from the unity of the divine Essence. We conclude the same from the roles which the Holy Spirit has constantly fulfilled in the entire Covenant, both of Nature and of Grace. For those roles are so excellent and constant, and are so closely linked together by an intimate bond, that He could not have failed to be a principal part of the Counsel itself, upon which all its events and ends depend. Hence, the will of the Holy Spirit is regarded as the source of all His operations in 1 Corinthians 12:11. He is also said to "search"—that is, to know intimately, as we explained this phrase in Chapter 4, § 12—"the depths of God" <note>original Greek: "τὰ βάθη τοῦ Θεοῦ" (ta bathē tou Theou)</note> in 1 Corinthians 2:10. That these "depths of God" are understood to be His decrees is shown both by the use of the phrase in Romans 11:33 and by the context of this passage. For what the Apostle called in verse 7 "the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the ages for our glory," and what he referred to in verse 9 as "the things which God has prepared for those who love Him," he now calls "His depths." The Holy Spirit also provided a sample of this intimate knowledge of God’s Decrees through all the revelations and inspirations by which He manifested those things long before they happened, which needed to be predicted for the certainty of faith.

IV. More directly relevant to this point is the passage in Isaiah 40:13: *Who has accurately weighed the Spirit of the Lord?* We prefer this reading with Forerius <note>Franciscus Forerius (1523–1581), a Portuguese Dominican theologian and linguist.</note> and others, rather than "helped" as in the Vulgate <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note>, "directed" with Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent Dutch theologian.</note>, or "fitted" with Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology."</note>. Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius (1510–1580), a Jewish convert and leading Hebraist.</note> agrees with us, rendering it as "weighed out"; Piscator <note>Johannes Piscator (1546–1625), a German Reformed theologian.</note> translates it as "measured" <note>original German: "abgemessen"</note>. The phrase designates a most accurate knowledge, by which not only the workings of the Holy Spirit but even their "momenta" <term>Momenta: Here meaning the importance, weight, or moving forces behind an action.</term> are weighed—that is, the reasons and ends are explored and recognized as fitting for the dignity of God. This concept agrees with our word in Proverbs 24:12, 1 Samuel 2:3, and Ezekiel 18:25. Therefore, we rightly adhere to it, since even the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX.</note> renders it with "knew" <note>original Greek: "ἔγνω" (egnō)</note>, which ver-

It is to this **fellowship** <note>original Greek: κοινωνιαν (koinōnian)</note> of divine decrees that Genesis 1:26 undoubtedly refers, where the Holy Trinity is said to have spoken—namely, in that eternal purpose: *“Let us make man,” etc.*

V. Nor did the Scripture completely neglect to remind us what relation the Holy Spirit held toward the other Persons in that same eternal Testament. In this regard, He is joined with the Son in John 3:11, because He has seen the Father working. *“The things we have seen,”* the Savior says—meaning, *“I and that breathing Spirit who blows where He wills”*—*“we testify.”* We have previously noted in our commentary on this passage that this expression, common to the Second and Third Persons, refers to that order of operation according to which the Father willed to be recognized as the first fountain of the eternal counsel for saving the sinner.

VI. This is made manifest by Peter’s testimony in Acts 10:38: *God anointed Him* (namely, Jesus of Nazareth) *with the Holy Spirit and power.* <note>original Greek: ἔχριϲεν αὐτον ὁ Θεος Πνευματι ἁγιῳ και δυναμει (echrisen auton ho Theos Pneumati hagiō kai dynamei)</note> We have touched upon this matter at greater length in our commentary on Psalm 45, Exercise 6. -># THE DISPENSATION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT IN RELATION<-

[Gregory] Nazianzen, John of Damascus, Titus of Bostra, and others, who understood the **hypostatic union** <term>hypostatic union: The theological doctrine that in the person of Jesus Christ, a human nature and a divine nature are perfectly joined in one single "hypostasis" or individual existence.</term> through this anointing. *Therefore, the anointing of the Son from eternity* <note>original: "Unctio ergo Filii ab æterno"</note> teaches us that even then, the Father assigned the Holy Spirit to the Son—and indeed, the Spirit most freely consented to this purpose—to be His companion in the acquisition of salvation, to furnish His human nature with the necessary gifts, and to carry out every will of the Son. From this principle, the Holy Spirit is the most significant part of that inheritance which was established for the Son, the *Heir of all things*, by virtue of the eternal Testament. And this is that very *sanctification of the Son* which is considered the foundation of His mission into the world in John 10:36.

VII. In accordance with this pact, the Holy Spirit demonstrates Himself in actual deed. This demonstration is such that a certain *dependence* <note>original: "dependentia"</note> of the Holy Spirit upon the Father and the Son in His working can be observed, yet at the same time, the highest *spontaneity and liberty* appear in His acting. Instances of both qualities are most wisely woven together, so that from the former it may be proved that the Holy Spirit, even in His subsistence <term>subsistence: In Trinitarian theology, this refers to the distinct manner of being of each person within the one divine essence.</term> in a certain respect, is not *from Himself*, but *from the Father and the Son*; yet from the latter, the most absolute **self-divinity** <note>original Greek: $\alpha\upsilon\tau\omicron\theta\epsilon\acute{\omicron}\tau\eta\varsigma$ (autotheotēs); the quality of being God in and of Himself.</note> of the Godhead itself is equally and undoubtedly revealed. We shall show in a few words how the Scripture teaches each point. It establishes the *dependence* of the Holy Spirit's operations in two ways: first, by teaching that their *principle and norm* is the will of the Father and the Son, and second, that the *glory of the Father and the Son* is the *end* <note>In this context, "end" means the ultimate goal or purpose.</note> of those same operations.

VIII. We have already reviewed the passages that prove the first point in Chapter VI, Section 23 and following. The series of those same operations which the Holy Spirit exerts in creatures, to be enumerated by us, will confirm this. For such are those works as they ought to be according to the Pact of the Father and the Son. Hence, He works effectively toward salvation in no one except in the *elect* chosen by the Father and redeemed by the Son. This is the chain of the work of salvation, in which the *sanctification of the Spirit* is subordinated to the *foreknowledge of the Father and the sprinkling of the blood of Christ* (1 Peter 1:2). Paul maintains the same order in Ephesians 1 in his list of the *spiritual blessings of the New Testament*, deriving them from the *election of the Father* (verses 4-5) and *redemption through the blood of Christ* (verse 7), from which he also derives the *sealing* in verses 13-14—

[likewise] subjoins [perfection] through the *Holy Spirit*. Nor can this matter be otherwise, given the most perfect union of the Most Holy Trinity. For if the Holy Spirit were effective for the salvation of those whom the Father *did not enroll in the book of life*, and whose names the Son did not wish *to carry in His own mouth*, there would be a manifest discrepancy of will between Himself and the remaining Persons. Add to this that in such a case, the Glory resulting from this work would pertain not to the Father and the Son, but to the Holy Spirit alone; and both the purpose of the Father and the propitiation <term>propitiation: An act that appeases divine justice, specifically referring here to Christ's sacrifice.</term> of the Son would have been superfluous. IX. From this order, all those passages which imply a dependence of the operations of the Holy Spirit derive light. Some of these teach a dependence on the *Father* alone; others on both the *Father and the Son*. The former prevails in those operations whose object is the *Son*; both prevail in those whose objects are *other creatures*.

X. To the first class of the Holy Spirit's operations belong those passages in which the Holy Spirit is considered as *given or bestowed* by the Father upon the Son. This bestowal has its own stages and periods. Its prelude was more obscure in those ages which preceded the coming of the Son in the flesh. For although explicit testimonies of this act of the Father do not occur, it is nevertheless clear from the effects. The host of the heavens *was made by the Spirit of the mouth of Jehovah* (Psalm 33:6). The *Bereshit Rabbah* <note>A foundational collection of ancient Jewish interpretations (midrash) on the Book of Genesis.</note> itself says regarding *Genesis 1:2*: *“The Spirit of God hovering over the surface of the waters—this is the Spirit of the Messiah.”* <note>original Hebrew: רוח אלהים מרחבת פני מים זו רוח של משיח</note> The Holy Spirit, testifying in the Prophets and acting through them, was even then the *Spirit of Christ* (1 Peter 1:11). Nor should it be doubted that the Jehovah whose Spirit contended with the corrupt world (Genesis 6:3) was the *Son of God*, if you compare it with 1 Peter 3:20.

This prerogative is involved in the *Name of Jehovah*, which was bestowed upon the Son as the *Angel of the Lord* <note>original: "Angelo Jehovæ," a reference to the divine messenger in the Old Testament often identified by theologians as the pre-incarnate Christ.</note>; especially since the violation of it [provoked] the same punishments...

But whatever the case may be regarding the errors of Nestorius, we do not doubt that the *Anointing* of Christ, in its total complexity, pertains to His <term>God-man<note>original Greek: Θεάνθρωπον (Theanthrōpon); a term describing Jesus as a single person who is simultaneously fully God and fully man.</note></term> person. For not only is *anointing* attributed to Him from eternity in the passage from **Proverbs** cited in section 6, but also the manner in which He received the promise of the Holy Spirit after His exaltation, with full power to send and distribute Him, was so illustrious that it would not be fitting unless for the <term>God-man<note>original Greek: Θεανθρώπῳ (Theanthrōpō); the dative form of the previous term.</note></term> person. The origin of the error of those who restricted His anointing to the human nature of Christ seems primarily to have been that they did not attend to the broader significance that this phrase has in the Scriptures, and they judged only the *sanctification* of the human nature of Christ—both at His birth and His Baptism—to be called His *anointing*. Although not even in this way should the *Deity* of Christ have been excluded. ## THE ECONOMY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT IN RELATION TO THE SON

...to be imbued, and to possess such great power to produce whatever miracles through the Holy Spirit by the mere nod and command of his will, and other similar things, are prerogatives that suppose more than mere humanity.

XIV. *The manner in which the Holy Spirit was given to the Son was different according to the various stages of Christ's anointing at His coming. We establish the first stage, certainly, at the Lord's Incarnation. The second at His Baptism. The third at His Session at the Right Hand of the Father.* The [Church] Fathers omit the last one, except that GREGORY OF NYSSA <note>A 4th-century bishop and theologian, one of the "Cappadocian Fathers" who shaped early Christian doctrine.</note> considers those same three stages as *three first-births* in CORDERIUS’s *Catena on Luke 3:22* <note>A "Catena" (Latin for "chain") is a form of biblical commentary made up of strings of passages from earlier theologians.</note>. Regarding the first and second [stages], these same Fathers argue, and they fight everywhere for the former, undoubtedly carried away by partisan zeal against NESTORIUS <note>A 5th-century Archbishop of Constantinople whose views on the separation of Christ's human and divine natures were declared heretical.</note>, who seemed to admit only the second stage of Anointing while excluding the first. Those who compare the passages that PETAVIUS <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a Jesuit theologian known for his massive work on the history of dogma.</note> compiled in the cited work, Chapter 9, will easily notice that this is the case. Yet, all these things can be elegantly subordinated and distinguished.

XV. That the Father bestowed the Holy Spirit upon the Son immediately from the *Incarnation* is clear from **Luke 1:35**, in which we proved in Chapter 1, §4, that the name *Holy Spirit* is to be understood personally. Hence, the *sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit* are joined in one breath in **Isaiah 48:16**, so that you may know that both must be initiated from the same starting point. Therefore, since the sending of the Son began from His incarnation, the Holy Spirit was present with the Son from then on. And in **Isaiah 11:2**, immediately with the rising of the *shoot from the stump of Jesse, the resting of the Spirit of Jehovah upon him is joined.* For Christ ought not be lesser in this respect than His Precursor [John the Baptist], of whom it is said in verse 15: <term>he shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb</term> <note>original Greek: Πνευματος ἁγιου πλησθησεται ἐτι ἐκ κοιλιας μητρος αὐτου</note>. Indeed, the Lord’s excellence over His minister is manifest, *firstly* because John’s conception in the womb precedes his being filled by the Holy Spirit, whereas in Mary’s womb the <term>coming upon</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπιλευσις (epeleusis); referring to the Spirit coming upon Mary in the Annunciation.</note> of the Holy Spirit precedes the conception itself; *secondly* because God’s extraordinary dispensation regarding John tended toward this end: that the Holy Spirit might exhibit a clear testimony to the Son of God from his very conception through the Spirit's miraculous movement <note>Refers to John the Baptist "leaping" in Elizabeth's womb upon the arrival of the pregnant Mary.</note> within the womb itself.

### TOWARD THE DIVINE PERSONS. CHAPTER VIII.

XVI. Furthermore, various functions of the Holy Spirit concerning the *incarnation* of the Lord can be distinguished. For:

A. In the miraculous *production* of the most holy fetus, the Spirit so exerted His power that He can be considered the <term>immediate efficient cause</term> <note>In traditional philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the agent or force that actually brings something into being.</note> for that reason. Hence, in Matthew 1:18, Mary is said to be "with child BY THE HOLY SPIRIT" <note>original Greek: *en gastri echousa ek pneumatos hagiou*</note>. And the Angel in verse 20 asserts: "that which is conceived in her is FROM THE HOLY SPIRIT" <note>original Greek: *to en autē gennēthen ek pneumatos hagiou estin*</note>. Moreover, through this production—which is considered a *new creation* in Jeremiah 31:22—distinguished gifts and faculties, even physical ones, were instilled into the humanity of the Son of God. Through these, He not only excelled among all the sons of Adam, but also possessed an instrument fit for the immense work of Redemption. Thus, the Spirit was equally occupied in the formation of the "second Adam" <note>A theological title for Jesus, contrasting him with the first Adam of Genesis.</note> as He was in the first. And since the performing of miracles is the Spirit's peculiar work, the greatest miracle of all had to be produced by His power.

B. Since *Sanctification* pertains most directly to the "Economic" <note>The "Economy" of God refers to the different roles the Father, Son, and Spirit play in human history and salvation.</note> operations of the Holy Spirit, who could doubt that the things required to sanctify the Lord's humanity even in the womb were performed by the efficacy of the Holy Spirit? Therefore:

1. He *preserved* the *mass* <note>The "mass" (*massa*) refers to the physical matter or "stuff" of the human body.</note> from which the divine Redeemer's body was fashioned from all contagion of Original Sin. Regarding this preservation, a long dispute flourished among the <term>Scholastics</term> <note>The "Scholastics" were medieval university theologians known for their highly technical and logical debates.</note> and other theologians. Some maintained that *that mass was only purified from all inherent stain and sin by the Holy Spirit at the moment of Christ’s conception*; others, however, asserted that *that mass had already been in the loins of Abraham, and indeed Adam, and was kept pure through all those generations mentioned by Luke in chapter 3:23 and following, all the way to Mary*. Let anyone who wishes read JOHANNES FECHT’S <note>A prominent Lutheran theologian (1636–1716) known for his works on the state of the soul and Christology.</note> *Dissertation on the preserved mass from which Christ was born*, section 13 and following. For us, it is a matter of religious caution to search too curiously into these mysteries, which Scripture does not reveal and which depend not a little upon physical hypotheses that have not yet been sufficiently brought to light.

2. Since the fetus, as long as it lay hidden in the Mother's womb, had to draw nourishment from her substance, and since the body of a sinful woman [is subject to] confused movements of the blood and <term>animal spirits</term> <note>In early modern medicine, "animal spirits" were believed to be subtle fluids in the body that controlled movement and sensation.</note> and

...to be imbued, and to possess such great power for performing any miracles whatever through the Holy Spirit—produced at the mere nod and command of His will—and other similar things, are prerogatives that suppose more than mere humanity.

XIV. The manner in which the Holy Spirit was given to the Son was diverse, corresponding to the different stages of Christ’s anointing during His arrival. We fix the **first stage** certainly in the Lord’s **Incarnation**. The **second in His Baptism**. The **third in His Sitting at the Right Hand of the Father** <note>This refers to the "Session," the theological term for Christ taking his throne in heaven after the Ascension</note>. The Church Fathers omit this last stage, except for Gregory of Nyssa <note>A 4th-century bishop and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers" who shaped early Christian doctrine</note>, who considers these same three stages as three "first-births" in Corderius's *Chain of Commentary on Luke 3:22* <note>Balthasar Corderius was a 17th-century Jesuit who compiled "Catenas," or chains of quotes from ancient Greek Fathers</note>. Regarding the first and second stages, these same authors disagree and generally fight for the priority of the first; they were undoubtedly carried away by partisan zeal against Nestorius <note>A 5th-century Archbishop of Constantinople whose views on the separation of Christ's divine and human natures were declared heretical</note>, who seemed to admit only the second stage of Anointing while excluding the first. Those who compare the passages collected by Petavius <note>Denis Pétau, a 17th-century Jesuit theologian known for his work on the history of dogma</note> in the cited location, chapter 9, will easily notice that this is the case. Nevertheless, all these stages can be harmoniously organized and distinguished.

XV. It is clear from Luke 1:35 that the Father bestowed the Holy Spirit upon the Son immediately from the **Incarnation**; we proved in Chapter 1, § 4, that the name **Holy Spirit** in that passage is to be understood personally <note>Meaning it refers to the Person of the Spirit, not just a generic "divine power"</note>. Hence, the **sending of the Son and the Holy Spirit** are joined in a single breath in Isaiah 48:16: "The Lord God and His Spirit have sent Me," so that you may know both missions begin from the same point. Therefore, since the mission of the Son began from His incarnation, the Holy Spirit was present with the Son from that moment forward. Also, in Isaiah 11:2, the **resting of the Spirit of Jehovah upon Him** is joined immediately to the **emergence of the shoot from the stump of Jesse**. For in this regard, Christ ought not to be lesser than His own Forerunner [John the Baptist], of whom it is said in verse 15: "He will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb" <note>original Greek: *Pneumatos hagiou plēsthēsetai eti ek koilias mētros autou*</note>. Indeed, the excellence of the Lord over His Minister is manifest: *firstly*, because John’s conception in the womb precedes his being filled by the Holy Spirit, whereas in Mary’s womb, the "coming upon" <note>original Greek: *epeleusis*</note> of the Holy Spirit precedes the conception itself; *secondly*, because God’s extraordinary arrangement regarding John tended toward this end: that the Holy Spirit, through His miraculous stirring within the very womb, might exhibit a clear testimony to the Son of God from the moment of His conception.

XVI. Furthermore, the various functions of the Holy Spirit regarding the **incarnation** of the Lord can be distinguished. For:

A. In the miraculous **production** of the most holy fetus, He so exerted His power that He could be considered the proximate efficient cause for that reason. XVII. A. The solemn testimony which the Holy Spirit gave to the Savior in the form of a dove, so that it would be publicly established that He was truly that **Anointed One** <note>original Latin: "Unctus," the literal translation of the Hebrew 'Messiah' and Greek 'Christos'</note> so long expected by Israel according to the word <note>literally: "the mouth"</note> of the Prophets.

To this end, the perpetual suggestions of arguments drawn from the "counsel of peace" <note>A theological term referring to the eternal agreement between the Father and the Son for the salvation of humanity.</note> revealed through the Prophets served most of all, as well as the testimonies of paternal favor and love issued internally, and other spiritual emotions in which the most holy soul of the Lord experienced something analogous to other believers.

C. The joining of the efficacy and power of the Holy Spirit with the preaching of Christ, not only in the hearts of the listeners but also in the gift of miracles. For this power did not appear in Him before the Baptism of Christ. Whatever is brought forward concerning the *miracles of Christ's infancy* by apocryphal authors is of dubious faith <note>original Latin: "sublestæ est fidei," meaning the stories are unreliable or lack historical credibility</note>. And the relationship which miracles have to the word of truth makes it hardly credible that the Savior would have wished to perform them before He exercised the office of a public Teacher in the Church. Nor would Scripture have been entirely silent about them. Moreover, that this power of performing miracles ought to be considered as a charismatic gift of the Holy Spirit with which Jesus was anointed, the Savior Himself asserts in Matthew 12:28: *If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, the Kingdom of God has already come to you.* Wherefore He also holds the Pharisees, who blasphemed these miracles, guilty of *blasphemy against the Holy Spirit* in verses 31 and 32. It was indicated in verse 18 of the same chapter that this pertained to the fulfillment of Isaiah 42:1. Thus the Holy Spirit exercised the same function regarding the prophetic office of Christ as He did regarding the Prophets of the Old Testament and afterwards in the Apostles. And this seems to be the foundation of the distinction between the **Holy Spirit** and **power** <note>original Greek: "Πνευμα Ἁγιον & δυναμιν"</note>, which are joined in the Anointing of the Messiah in Acts 10:38. For here *the Holy Spirit* is best referred to the general, sanctifying, and preparatory gifts with which the Messiah was already imbued from birth; **power** <note>original Greek: "δυναμις" (dynamis)</note>, however, refers to that accumulation of miraculous and heroic gifts with which He, being filled, undertook and completed the work of Redemption itself. This distinction is especially favored by the familiar use of the word **power** <note>original Greek: "δυναμις"</note> in describing extraordinary charismatic gifts <term>charismatic gifts: From the Greek 'charismata,' referring to supernatural abilities granted by the Holy Spirit for the benefit of the community.</term>.

XIX. From these points, it is clear how empty is the dispute which certain interpreters, following the Church Fathers, have started regarding the beginning of the Lord's Anointing <note>Anointing (Latin: *Unctio*) refers to being set apart by God for a holy purpose; it is the root meaning of the titles "Messiah" and "Christ."</note>: whether it should be traced back to his Birth or to the Baptism of the Lord? In reality, these were merely different degrees of a single anointing. The Grace conferred upon the Lord from his very conception was simply given a new expansion when he took up his public office. To settle this dispute, the words of **RUPERT** <note>Rupert of Deutz (c. 1075–1129) was a famous Benedictine theologian and mystic.</note> in his *Commentary on John*, Book II, where he discusses the passage in Luke stating that *Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan*, are especially fitting:

> *He was indeed full, but not because he then for the first time received the Holy Spirit; for he was conceived by the operation of the same Spirit from the very beginning of his humanity. What then happened now, for it to be said that he returned from the Jordan "full of the Holy Spirit"? Doubtless, the fullness which was already in him spread itself to the surface—that is, to his very outward actions—so that we might all receive from it. It is as if the fullness of living and unfailing water, which is in a very deep well, were to rise up to the surface of the opening, so that the ability to draw or drink might be given even to small children. In this way, the fullness he held within spread to the exterior, and grace was poured upon his lips, so that its abundance—with which he was full of grace and truth—might be heard in his words and seen in his miracles.*

XX. A third and most illustrious degree of the Lord's Anointing was added through his **Exaltation** <note>The "Exaltation" refers to Christ's Resurrection and Ascension to heaven.</note>. This is specifically hinted at in Psalm 2:6 and 45:8. Psalm 68:19 also pertains to this: <note>original Hebrew: לקחת מתנות באדם</note> *You have received gifts for man.* The sense of this very simple version is expressed by the citation in Ephesians 4:8: <note>original Greek: ἔδωκε δόματα τοῖς ἀνθρῶποις</note> *He gave gifts to men.* For he who received from the Father an overflowing measure of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, not for his own sake but for the sake of man, it was fitting for him to distribute what he had received to those for whom they were intended. Hence it is clear that Peter provides a paraphrase <note>original Greek: παραφρασιν</note> of the Psalm in Acts 2:33, saying: <note>original Greek: Τῃ δεξιᾳ οὐν του Θεου ὑψωθεις. την τε ΕΠΑΓΓΕΛΙΑΝ ΤΟΥ ἉΓΙΟΥ ΠΝΕΥΜΑΤΟΣ ΛΑΒΩΝ παρα του Πατρος, ἐξεχεε τουτο, ὁ νυν ὑμεις βλεπετε και ἀκουετε</note> *Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this which you now see and hear.*

# ON THE DIVINE PERSONS. CHAPTER VIII.

Ii 3

The effects of the Holy Spirit, which demonstrated that the Prince of Salvation <note>The "Prince of Salvation" refers to Jesus Christ as the leader or author of the faith.</note> was now perfected through sufferings, had reconciled the Father, and had occupied the Throne of Glory. Hence, the Holy Spirit is said *not yet to have been present* <note>original: *nondum adfuisse*</note> because Jesus was not yet glorified (John 7:38). For the outpouring of the Holy Spirit was an effect of his glorification, through which his cause was fully established. Compare John 16:7. This testimony given by the Holy Spirit to the Son is described in Hebrews 2:4, where it says concerning the word of the Gospel revealing such a great acquired salvation, that *God bore witness with him* <note>original: *Deus illi contestatus fuerit*</note> by signs and wonders and various powers, and distributions of the Holy Spirit, according to his own will <note>original: σημείοις τε καὶ τέρασι καὶ ποικίλαις δυνάμεσι, καὶ Πνεύματος Ἁγίου μερισμοῖς, κατὰ τὴν αὐτοῦ θέλησιν</note>. To this point, following **THEODORET** <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457 AD) was an influential theologian and bishop in early Christian Syria.</note>, many excellent interpreters refer that passage in 1 Timothy 3:16: *He was justified in the Spirit* <note>original: ἐδικαιώθη ἐν πνεύματι / *justificatus est in Spiritu*</note>, or through the Spirit. For although others have preferred to understand this as the *Spirit of the Deity of Christ*, their arguments do not overturn the preceding view. They have nothing to appeal to except the opposition that appears here between "flesh" and "spirit," which they illustrate by comparing Romans 1:4 and 1 Peter 3:18. However, an opposition also remains in our passage, albeit for a different reason. And the passages they cite are not parallel at all. In those verses, the subject is named "the Son of God" and "Christ"; but here, simply "God." By the word "God" <note>original: Θεὸς</note>, the Deity of Christ is already indicated plainly <note>original: ἁπλῶς</note>. If, therefore, nothing but the Deity of Christ were also indicated by "Spirit," *then the Deity would be said to be justified by the Deity—that is, by itself.* 

Hence the famous **COCCEJUS** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian who emphasized the "Covenants" between God and humanity.</note> did not wrongly join the two together. For in truth, the Spirit of the Deity of Christ and the Holy Spirit were never separated, not only because of the personal union but also because of the partnership in mission according to the Covenant of Salvation <note>original: *Pactum salutis*</note>. Nor, however, is this justification through the Holy Spirit to be restricted only to this final stage, although it was perfected in it. Wherefore the famous **RICHARD KIDDER** <note>Richard Kidder (1633–1703) was the Bishop of Bath and Wells and a prominent English theologian.</note> in his *Demonstration of the Messiah*, published in English, Part I, chapter 5, includes under that phrase that he *became justified through the Spirit*: 

1. When he was conceived by the Holy Spirit, before God and men. 
2. Before the Devil, *when through the Spirit* he did not... <note>The text continues on the next page.</note>

Before the world: in *Baptism*, in the proclamation of the *Gospel*, in miracles, in the *resurrection*, and in the *inspiration, exaltation, and mission of the Apostles*, so that through them the *Christian Religion could be transmitted to following centuries*. 4. B. The *bestowal* <note>original: *addictionem*</note> and communication of the Holy Spirit was made in an ineffable way from the Father to the Son, so that through His power and effective operations He might found the heavenly Kingdom, take possession of the inheritance <note>original: *peculium*—literally a small private property, here referring to the people of God</note> given to Him by the Father, and subject His enemies to Himself. This kind of bestowal occurs in Psalm 2:8–9: *Ask of me, and I shall give You the nations for Your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for Your possession. You shall rule them with a rod of iron; You shall break them in pieces like a potter's vessel.* For the "rod of iron," which is promised here to the Son by the Father, is the Holy Spirit Himself joined with the proclamation of the word. In this same respect, it is said that *Jehovah*, that is the Father, *will send the Rod of the Messiah's strength out of Zion* (Psalm 110:2).

XXII. The prophecy of Isaiah 11:2 seems to show us these three stages of the Lord's *Anointing* in an elegant connection: *And the Spirit of Jehovah shall rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Jehovah.* Interpreters have tried in various ways to distinguish the seven attributes <note>original: *prædicata*</note> of the Spirit to be conferred upon the Messiah which are joined here. The celebrated **VITRINGA** <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a famous Dutch theologian known for his commentary on Isaiah.</note> has applied his diligence here more than others. However, the present matter requires that we also add our own meditation. The Hebrew accentuation <note>Refers to the system of "te'amim" or cantillation marks in the Hebrew Bible, which serve as musical notation and punctuation, indicating how phrases are linked or separated.</note> not without reason separates the first attribute more strongly from the remaining six, because that first one concerns the *source* of the communication of the Holy Spirit, while the six following concern its *effects*. 

Hence I pay little heed to the opinion of those who—in order to distinguish seven specific "gifts"—either carve out a seventh gift from verse 3 along with the **GREEKS** <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, which often lists seven gifts.</note> and **JEROME** <note>Saint Jerome, whose Latin Vulgate translation influenced the traditional Catholic list of the "Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit."</note>—which the illustrious **ABICHTIUS** <note>Johann Georg Abicht (1672–1740), a specialist in Hebrew grammar and accents.</note> shows (in *On Accents*, chapter 24, section 10), following **AMAMA** <note>Sixtinus Amama, a 17th-century Dutch Hebraist.</note>, **FRISCHMUTH** <note>Johann Frischmuth, a German Orientalist.</note> and others, to savor of gross ignorance of the language—or, like the **CHALDEAN** <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, explain the *Spirit of Jehovah* as the *Spirit of Prophecy*, although they do not prove that the name *Jehovah* designates a prophetic gift. XXIII. To derive our analysis from a firmer foundation, certain things overlooked by other interpreters must be noted in advance.

1. The three pairs of attributes are recited in such a way that in each pair, the former is more theoretical, while the latter is more practical. *Wisdom*, *Counsel*, and *Knowledge of Jehovah* pertain primarily to the intellect; however, *Prudence* <note>often translated as understanding</note>, *Might*, and the *Fear of Jehovah* relate more directly to the will. The famous **ALTING** <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679), a prominent Dutch theologian</note> suspected this, although otherwise he is not sufficiently accurate.

2. The first and third members almost coincide. For true wisdom is perfected by knowledge, and true prudence by the fear of Jehovah. Compare **Job 28:28.** Thus, unless a notable distinction appears from circumstances beyond the literal meaning of the words, tautology <note>original Greek: *tautologia*—the redundant repetition of the same idea</note> can hardly be eliminated from this saying. It pleased the famous **COCCEIUS** and **VITRINGA** <note>Leading 17th-century biblical scholars</note> to include His Love under the *Knowledge of Jehovah*. But, not to mention that the phrase "fear of Jehovah" already involves Love, this contradicts the very elegant structure we already noted in point 1.

### XXIV. Having weighed these matters well, everything bestowed upon Christ through the Holy Spirit is presented here in the most suitable order.

I. **Gifts**, which may be called **immanent**, since they encompass the qualities bestowed upon his very person. These are expressed by our Prophet through the first and second pairs, because they are of a dual nature.

A. **Common** gifts, which a human nature perfectly clothed in the divine image requires, and which to that extent belong to the Messiah along with all the elect and the saints, though in a different measure.
1. Regarding the intellect: **Wisdom**, consisting in the true knowledge of God, of oneself, and of other things according to their nature and relation.
2. Regarding the will: **Prudence** <note>In this context, *Prudentia* refers to practical wisdom or the ability to apply spiritual truth to daily actions</note>, directing judgment and all actions according to the light of the intellect, and thus encompassing **all holiness**.

B. **Special** gifts, which were appropriate for a divine person preparing himself in an extraordinary way for the work of mediation.
1. Regarding theory: **Counsel** indicates, in part, the intimate knowledge of the divine decrees and especially of the *Council of Peace* <note>The "Council of Peace" refers to the eternal agreement between God the Father and God the Son regarding the salvation of humanity</note>; in part, the arguments deduced from the tenor of this eternal Council—

XXVI. This same dependency of the works of the Holy Spirit occurs in those **Economic** <term>Economic: from "oeconomia," referring to the "Divine Economy" or the way God manages and acts within human history and creation, as opposed to His internal, eternal nature</term> operations which he exercises concerning other creatures, both in the Realm of **Nature**, and especially in the Realm of **Grace**. Indeed, I have already explained in Chapter 6, sections 9 and following, to what extent I am persuaded that the natural procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son is intended by that phrase. Here, however, the order of treatment requires that I clear those most eminent men—along with myself—from the suspicion of **heresy**, who have judged that in this passage our Savior chiefly intended the Economic operation of the Holy Spirit. For although this controversy might seem of minor importance to fair-minded judges—hardly worth such sharp debate—and although I am not so self-satisfied <note>original: *suffenus*; a reference to Suffenus, a Roman poet famous for his vanity</note> that I cannot tolerate those who disagree with me, nevertheless, my Censor’s incurable **itch for reviling** <note>original: *cacoëthes*; a Greek-derived term for a bad habit or uncontrollable urge</note> compels me to show briefly that the interpretation I have embraced harbors nothing **absurd**, much less any **MONSTER** or **HERESY LONG CONDEMNED BY THE CHURCH**.

XXVIII. My opinion consists of two main parts. The first is that our Savior chiefly refers to the **Economic Procession of the Holy Spirit**; in this, I have followed the footsteps of men who have served the orthodox Church with great distinction. The second is that this **Procession** from the **Father** can be distinguished from the **Mission** <term>Mission: the "sending" of a divine Person into the world for a specific purpose</term> of the Holy Spirit through the **Son**, in such a way that it refers most closely to those Economic operations which he has performed **up to this point**, whereas the "Mission" belongs to the subsequent Economy of the New Testament. However, since this meditation was born on my own ground <note>meaning: it was his own original thought</note>, I have brought it forward only with great modesty.

3.) The connection of the present passage, which analysis sufficiently illustrates.
