For my case, it is indeed sufficient that "to proceed" <note>original Greek: *το ἐκπορεύεσθαι* (*to ekporeuesthai*)</note> is recognized as being of such a character that it necessarily involves a **manifestation toward the outside**. For this alone is what is being disputed: since we are in perfect agreement regarding the **point of origin** <note>original Latin: *termino à quo*</note>, the question is whether that word denotes not only the point of origin, but also the **point of destination** <note>original Latin: *terminum ad quem*</note> to which the going forth is directed? Since my Antagonist grants this to me, and most firmly confirms it by adding—out of an abundance of caution—the examples of Matthew 15:11, 18; Mark 7:21, 23; Luke 4:22; and Revelation 20:1 (all of which describe a **going forth toward the outside**), the strength of my first argument remains unshaken through the very generosity of my Critic.

XXXI. I have searched in vain through the preceding sections for what was brought forward to refute the *second reason*. I believe, therefore, that his memory failed him here, and that the man, occupied with something else, stopped short of the attempt. So far, then, he has spared me the trouble of defending it. Nor has he actually achieved more, although he seems to have done something, to defeat the *third reason*, which I brought forward following the celebrated **Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian known for "Covenant Theology," which emphasized the historical unfolding of God's plan</note>. For his position consists in this: that, having granted the analysis I presented, he tries to prove that **natural procession** <note>the eternal, internal "breathing forth" of the Spirit within the Godhead</note> is not excluded in it; since I grant this wholeheartedly <note>literally "with both thumbs" (*utroque pollice*); a Roman idiom for total approval</note>, he gains nothing against me. If he had wished to refute my argument, he would have had to prove that the extension of this phrase to demonstrate natural procession through the works of the Economy is diametrically opposed to the connection of the words.

XXXII. The remaining reasons produced by me are examined more closely. The *fourth* was this:
> "Because the term 'to proceed' <note>Greek: *ἐκπορεύεσθαι*</note> itself, whenever 
> "it is applied to the Holy Spirit, always has respect to his work in the **Economy** 
> "**of salvation**. Compare Revelation 1:16, 4:5, 19:15, 21, 22:1. Add the **Septuagint** 
> <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> on Daniel 7:10, 
> "where the 'river of fire proceeding' is an emblem of the Holy Spirit in the 
> "same way as the river of living water in Ezekiel and in Revelation."

Both the premise and the conclusion of this argument are denied. Yet nothing is brought forward to prove the denial of the premise, even though producing just one or two passages to the contrary would have fundamentally drained the strength of my argument...

XXXIII. Fifthly, I proceeded as follows:
> "If we were dealing here with the natural Procession of the Holy Spirit, it would have to be derived not only from the Father, but also from the Son, since there is no reason why the Father alone should be commemorated in this relation to the Holy Spirit. And to this extent, the **Greek Church** <note>The Eastern Orthodox Church, which historically argued that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, unlike the Western Church which added "and the Son" (*Filioque*)</note> judged correctly that 'Procession' in our passage denotes, in a restrictive sense, the relation of the Holy Spirit to the Father."

In this "wedge" <note>An argumentative tactic or sharp point</note>—which was used individually following **Amyraut** and **Cocceius** by the celebrated **Allinga** in his *Inquiries*, page 29, and more incidentally <note>original Greek: *ἐν παρόδῳ* (*en parodō*)</note> by the celebrated **Sibersma** in his vernacular *Commentary* on this passage—one must labor harder to repel it.

> **A.** "It is countered that in the Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father, His Procession from the Son is also involved. To make this appear probable, an appeal is made to **John 5:26**, from which it is deduced that the Divine Essence was given to the Son from all eternity through eternal Generation, along with the power and right of communicating that essence to the Holy Spirit. And for that reason, the Son testifies that He and the Father are one (**John 10:30**), and that He is in the Father, and the Father is in Him (**John 10:38; 14:10**)."

But even if all these points are granted, it does not yet follow from them what was to be proven: namely, that precisely in this passage, under the phrase "Procession from the Father," a "Procession from the Son" is simultaneously understood. For the reasoning that the mention of one Person sometimes involves another is not sufficient here. For, 1) that rule can indeed be valid when dealing with properties that are common to several Persons, but not when dealing with **personal characteristics**...

# THE ECONOMY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT RELATIVELY

,,therefore if the Mission is Economic, the same must also be established regarding the Procession.,, 

While I was merely arguing *ad hominem* <note>An argument directed against the person one is debating rather than the subject itself.</note> here, I could have safely bypassed this argument, especially since he again twists my words into a completely foreign sense. For he argues against me as if I were attacking the strength of that argument by which the Spirit's *Procession* is established from his *Mission by the Son*, which is most false. 

Nor does he rest there; he furthermore takes an objection—which the Distinguished ROELLIUS, <note>original: "ὁ νυν ἐν ἁγίοις" (ho nyn en hagiois), a Greek honorific meaning "who is now among the saints," used for the deceased.</note> could have formed against his reasoning—and cites it in the same series as if it were my objection, while suppressing that man's name. The objection is: *that the Holy Spirit, in the Council of Peace, finally subjected Himself of His own accord to the Father, to go forth from Him according to His word and mandate.* <note>The "Council of Peace" (Consilium Pacis) refers to a Reformed theological concept of an eternal pact made between the persons of the Trinity regarding the salvation of mankind.</note> 

Then, he attacks this opinion with excessive violence and imprudence, as if it were a patron of the foulest *Polytheism* <note>The belief in multiple gods; a serious charge in a Trinitarian debate.</note>. Does this not again breathe a spirit of deceiving the public and persuading the unwary that I am in agreement with the Distinguished ROELLIUS on the article of the *Procession of the Holy Spirit*? 

May God forgive him this deceit as well. A fairer reader, however, will not allow a film to be placed over his eyes, provided he observes that in the words cited, I am looking solely at the dispute between the Latin and Greek Churches. 

The Greeks contend that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, according to the *literal word* <note>original: "κατα το ῥητον" (kata to rhēton)</note> of our Savior. The Latins, indeed, recognizing that the *literal word* <note>original: "το ῥητον" (to rhēton)</note> which the Greeks urge favors them not a little, think it advisable to derive the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son not from that phrase, but from the following phrase regarding his *Mission*. They argue from the **Economic** relationship to the **natural** relationship. <term>Economic vs. Natural: "Economic" refers to how God acts in history (sending the Spirit), while "Natural" or "Essential" refers to God’s internal, eternal nature (the Spirit's origin).</term>

It is open to the Greeks to reply here that the Latins ought to provide a reason why they believe the Savior, in the same context, spoke in different ways—teaching a natural Relation to the Father directly, but to Himself only by consequence. The Latins will not fully resolve this to the conviction of the Greeks unless they acknowledge that the prior phrase is also **Economic**, and that one must argue from the Economic to the essential regarding the **Procession** in the same method as one does for the **Mission**. For thus it will be clear that Jesus, in instructing us about the mysteries of the adorable Holy Trinity, constantly keeps to the same path.

# XXXV.
Having thus defended the primary part of my opinion concerning our phrasing, I can be confident about the other part. In the first part lies the foundation, and once that is admitted, what we intend here contains nothing discordant. For we do not force upon anyone that distinction between the <term>Economic Procession</term><note>The "Economic" Procession refers to the Holy Spirit’s role within the "economy" or historical plan of salvation, as opposed to the "Ontological" Procession, which refers to the Spirit's eternal, internal relationship within the Trinity.</note> from the Father and the **Mission** through the Son from that same Father, although we consider that the difference in time, just as much as the matter itself, supports it to no small degree. Whether, however, that distinction departs so greatly from either the emphasis of the words or from the truth itself, we shall examine in few words.

# XXXVI.
> He [the Censor] claims that I violate the proper usage of words because I trace the **Procession** from the Father back to the decrees themselves, or at least to the creation and the preceding ways of God in the Church, while nevertheless in the text the present tense, "goes forth," <note>original: "ἐκπορεύεται" (ekporeuetai)</note> occurs. If I am unwilling for the future tense to be included under the present here, then (he argues) I have no right to understand the past under the same. Moreover, [he claims] the present tense best encompasses the remaining tenses when God is being discussed, in whom only a *perpetual present* has a place.

To this point, in summary, return the things which the censor disdainfully repeats twice in different places. But 1) why I cannot admit the Censor’s hypothesis in interpreting this phrase, the reason is this: because I have been convinced thus far that it refers primarily to an **Economic** going-out. As long as I stick to that opinion, that "always present today" of the divine essence cannot be understood by me here. As for the fact that I joined the *past* with the *present*, I shall easily obtain pardon for it. For I wished to extend the emphasis as broadly as the nature of the phrase and the context permitted. The nature of the phrase considered in itself would even have admitted the *future*, but the context fought against it, because the *future* relation of the Holy Spirit is expressed by a specific phrase. Nothing, however, stands in the way of the *past* being involved. When an action is described which, although it began in the past, nonetheless continues in the same way even now, is it not fitly set forth in the present? But let us leave that to the benches and bandages of children <note>A Latin idiom ("scamna ac serperastra") referring to elementary or schoolboy matters.</note>. This one thing I warn again: that the Censor attacks me too hastily once more for this reason—that I referred the Promise of the Holy Spirit in the **Council of Peace** <note>The "Consilium Pacis" is a Reformed theological concept describing an eternal agreement between the Father, Son, and Spirit regarding the salvation of humanity.</note> simultaneously to His **Economic Procession**; which he falsely [ascribes] to me...

# XXXVII.
However, to prove that I am an enemy to the *truth*, the Censor renews a dispute that the "Brethren" <note>This likely refers to the "Voetians," the theological opponents of the Cocceian school in the 17th-century Netherlands.</note> often raised against the followers of **Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian who emphasized that God's relationship with humanity changed across different periods of biblical history.</note>. Regarding the **Procession** <note>The "going forth" or sending of the Spirit.</note> under the Old Testament as being from the Father alone, I laid down this foundation:

> "that the Son did not possess the full right to the Spirit as the **SCEPTER OF HIS STRENGTH** <note>original: "SCEPTUM ROBORIS"</note> until he was perfected through his sufferings, through which he was meant to specifically acquire the Spirit."

To understand these words, the Reader should observe what the Censor has hidden—though it should be obvious to anyone’s eyes from the words I emphasized in a different typeface. Specifically, the issue here is not the Son’s *natural right* <note>The right Christ has eternally as God.</note> regarding the Holy Spirit, but only his **Economic right** <term>jus Oeconomicum</term><note>The legal or functional authority granted to Christ specifically within the "economy" or historical plan of salvation.</note>. Because of this, the Censor changes the entire state of the controversy; he fights for the "natural right," a point I would never dispute, as I acknowledge and revere it just as much as he does.

Furthermore, even regarding the **Economic right**, I was not disputing the Son's full right to the Holy Spirit and His works within the plan of salvation viewed generally. Rather, I was speaking of "the Son’s full right to the Spirit, viewed as the **Scepter of his strength**." This phrase, taken from Psalm 110:2 <note>The text cites Psalm 110:3, following a different verse numbering common in some older Latin Bibles.</note>, clearly refers to that most abundant measure of the Holy Spirit expected in the Kingdom to be taken up by the Messiah after he sat down at the right hand of the Father, as was already noted in Section 21.

Therefore, I was speaking only of that **authority** <term>ἐξουσία</term><note>original Greek: exousia, meaning right or delegated power.</note> which Christ acquired for himself through his completion [his death and resurrection] and which he demonstrated in the pouring out of the Holy Spirit after taking his seat at the Father's right hand, along with the effects that followed. 

Since the Censor's arguments are directed only against my earlier thesis, there is no need for me to defend myself further against his attacks—even though the harshness of his style and his logic has stirred up a great deal of dust. ### ON THE DIVINE PERSONS. CHAPTER VIII. 269

I believe it is established from the Word of God that there is a difference in the **economies** <note>The historical arrangements or stages of God's plan for humanity.</note> of the Holy Spirit when viewed in relation to the Father, according to the different eras of the Church. I do not do this for the sake of an opponent who mixes up the highest and lowest things here, but so that I may calmly pursue the thread of my own treatment from this point forward, which I will attempt to explain as best I can.

# XXXVIII.
Sacred Scripture speaks of the *operations* of the Holy Spirit in such a way that it is clear that both *saving* works—given to the **elect** <note>Those chosen by God for salvation.</note>—and other *extraordinary* works—given to whoever was necessary for the salvation of the Church and its individual members as seemed sufficient to divine wisdom—were granted from the beginning of the world, even before the coming of Christ. Meanwhile, those meditating on the source of this Grace will discover that the Holy Spirit, according to these operations, then depended more on the Father than on the *Son*. For that reason, up to that point, the Son did not possess **full right** <note>original: "plenum jus"</note> over the Holy Spirit in a certain sense.

# XXXIX.
This results *firstly* from the very connection of divine operations in the business of salvation according to the **eternal covenant** <note>The "Pactum Salutis," an agreement within the Trinity to save humanity.</note>. For divine operations "ad extra" <note>Actions of God directed toward the created world, rather than the internal relationships of the Trinity.</note> have a double foundation: a *remote* one in His very essence (which we will not touch upon here), and a *proximate* <note>The immediate or direct cause.</note> one in the **Decree** <note>God's sovereign plan.</note>, in which both their *Goal* and an *Order* appropriate to that goal are established. 

This Order is the origin of the connection through which, in the execution of the plan, these operations depend on one another. Thus, if a certain operation must go first to pave the way for a following one, the first can be considered the *proximate* foundation of the second, and the second as depending on the first. According to this connection, it can be asserted that a certain Person of the Holy Trinity does not enjoy **full right** to operate in a certain way and in certain circumstances, as long as something else remains to be done according to the divine Decree by which that right was to be acquired. Indeed, even if He legitimately exercises that right *by anticipation* <note>Acting in advance of the legal requirement being met, based on a future certainty.</note>, the full right is nonetheless not fully realized until all the prerequisite acts have preceded it. 

Therefore, the **full right** to send the Spirit into the very hearts of the elect could not belong to the Son of God except after his completion through **sufferings** <note>The Passion and crucifixion of Jesus.</note>, since that <term>ransom</term> <note>original Greek: λύτρον (lytron), the price paid for redemption.</note> had not yet been fully paid; although, notwithstanding this, by virtue of his **suretyship** <note>original: "sponsio," a legal pledge or guarantee to pay a debt.</note> he [protected] all the elect from the beginning of the world in...

XLII. There remain those **Operations of the Holy Spirit** which indicate a dependence on the Father and the Son at the same time. Not a few traces of this dependence occur even before the arrival of the Lord. For although he finally used this right by full authority after his exaltation, he nevertheless most effectively exercised that right—which belonged to him as **Sponsor** <note>original: "Sponsori." In this context, Christ is viewed as a legal guarantor or "Surety" who ensures the salvation of the elect even before his physical sacrifice.</note> over the Holy Spirit, and which was suitable for his elect who were to be saved in that state of affairs; on this matter, let the passages collected in sections 9 and 10 be weighed. There are various phrases by which the Prophets are accustomed to express this dependence of the Operations of the Holy Spirit. Sometimes they speak more properly of his **giving**, which I illustrated regarding John 14:16. Quite often, however, they employ metaphors, among which four stand out. 

The first is of **Mission** <note>Sending</note>, the emphasis of which I indicated regarding John 14:26. The second, of **Breath** <note>original: "Flatus"</note>, was illustrated at John 20:22. We touched upon the third, of **Effusion** <note>Pouring out</note>, at John 4:10 and 7:37 and following. More implicit is the metaphor of **effulgence** <note>Shining forth</note>, such as that of light, fire, or lightning struck from the clouds. Now, all these acts, through which the heavenly gifts of the Holy Spirit were to be granted to the New Testament Church, are very rarely attributed to the Father alone in the prophetic word. Most frequently they are attributed to **Jehovah** in general—and thus to the Father and the Son together, without any note of the Son's exclusion—and sometimes they are expressly attributed to the Son. 

The **mission** mentioned in Isaiah 48:16 and Psalm 110:2 does indeed look to the Father alone, yet in such a way that through this mission the Spirit was joined to the Son and, as it were, committed to him for promoting the glory of the Kingdom to be established. The **giving** of the Holy Spirit is ascribed to **Jehovah** without distinction in Ezekiel 36:27 and 37:14. In the same way, his **Effusion** is promised by **Jehovah** in Isaiah 44:3–4 and Joel 2:28. Zechariah 9:12 can be referred to the Son alone. XLIV. How these actions of the Father and the Son concerning and through the Holy Spirit exist within the divine essence itself is a height our sharpest intellect cannot reach. What are these expressions but riddles and metaphors <note>original Latin: "ænigmata atque figuræ"</note> through which God wished to exercise our faith and humility? It is helpful for us to be careful only that we do not imagine anything under the shadow of these words that would contradict the perfect *simplicity* <term>Simplicity: The theological concept that God is not composed of different parts or properties, but is a single, indivisible essence.</term> as well as the *unity* of God. 

Regarding unity: while in other contexts the "sender" and the "sent" are separate persons, here, through their union—or rather their essential unity—they are within one another in such a way that the existence of one necessarily involves the existence of the other. This natural bond is not broken by that *sending* <note>original: "missio"</note> or *outpouring* <note>original: "effusio"</note>; this is clear because whatever the Holy Spirit works, the other Persons of the Trinity also work. Their works are attributed to them as *distinct* but not *disjoined*. 

But we must also keep the honor of the divine *simplicity* safe and intact; therefore, these "Economic" <note>Relating to the "Economy of Salvation," or how God reveals Himself and acts within human history.</note> relations should not be torn too far apart from the "natural" relation of the Holy Spirit. For although distinguished men have separated the *Natural and Economic Outgoing of the Holy Spirit*, it does not follow that two separate types of "Outgoing" or "Procession" <term>Procession: The theological term for the way the Holy Spirit originates eternally from the Father (and the Son).</term> actually exist. Instead, the latter is considered by us to be a demonstration of the former—what we usually call *Breathing*, *Sending*, *Outpouring*, or *Giving*. 

On this matter, we should not ignore the argument of Michael Caleca <note>A 14th-century Greek theologian and convert to Catholicism known for his defense of Western Trinitarian views.</note> in his work *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, chapter 5, where he writes: *From this it is clear that there are not two Processions of the Holy Spirit, one outside of time and another within time. First, because none of the Saints ever said this. Second, because if that were granted, many absurdities would arise. ### ON THE DIVINE PERSONS. CHAPTER 8.

*...the Holy Spirit proceeds. However, when created beings came into existence and were deemed suitable to receive the knowledge or illustration of such a Procession, he is said to proceed to them, to shine forth, to be poured out, and to be given through the Son. At that point, what is eternal in itself happens to those creatures within time. For that Procession is indeed one and eternal. Nothing new ever happens to God, because of His supreme simplicity* <term>Simplicity: The theological idea that God is not made of parts, but is a single, unchanging essence.</term> *and perfection. But to creatures, this same Procession seems to be, and is called, temporal; not because a temporal condition is added to God, but because it is added only to those who come to know or receive it within time. Hence, if the source from which the Spirit comes is considered, the Procession is one; but if the destination he reaches is considered, it appears as two. For the Holy Spirit proceeds singularly from the Father through the Son: yet in such a way that, proceeding into his own hypostasis* <term>Hypostasis: A Greek term used to describe a distinct person within the Trinity who shares the same divine essence.</term> *from the Father through the Son as if from a single principle, he is said to go forward according to one and simple Procession. But when the creature is added—whom he is said to go forth to sanctify—then he is understood as proceeding from the Father through the Son, and being sent, supplied, and dispatched from the Father through the Son. That entire Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father through the Son toward the creature is called a "mission," which occurs in time for the sake of the creature who becomes a participant in time; thus, this temporal condition is attributed to us, not to God. And indeed, it is a single reality, but it differs in how we reason about it. We are not permitted to call that reality "temporal" just because we receive it in time (thereby transferring our own human experience onto God), any more than we would say a sunbeam or light only just began to go forth from the sun simply because a blind man, having now recovered his sight, has begun to enjoy its rays. For it is clear that even before the man received it, the light and the ray existed in the same way in the Sun; and in the same way, the ray had already reached the eyes.*

This allegory is especially to be observed, since we advised in Chapter 1, Section 10, that the very emphasis of the characteristic name of the Third Person is to be drawn from there. ### THE ECONOMY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT IN RELATION
<meta>catchword: those</meta>

Compare those things which were previously noted concerning the limit of **Spiration** <term>Spiration: From the Latin 'spiratio' (breathing); the theological term for the way the Holy Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father and the Son.</term> in Chapter VI, § 5. However, a clearer light is shed upon this when we understand *the Son* through the *Mouth* and *Jehovah the Father* [as the speaker], as has been done by various interpreters, both Jewish and Christian. For in this way, the various properties of the source of the Holy Spirit's operations are illustrated, since from this it appears:

1) That all three Persons concur in operations toward the outside <note>In theology, "external operations" refers to God’s actions in creation and history, as opposed to the internal relationships within the Trinity.</note>.
2) That the Spirit works from both the Father and the Son.
3) That the relationship of the Holy Spirit in these operations is one way toward the Father and another toward the Son. He considers the former as the *remote* and *first* source, and the latter as the *near* and *second* source.
4) That he has a singular and most immediate relation to the Son, through whom he is considered the *Word of the Lord* or **Logos** <term>Logos: A Greek term meaning Word, Reason, or Discourse, used to describe the Second Person of the Trinity.</term>, and the manifestation of the divine will through the external preaching of the divine word as well. For he is that *breath of the mouth* which is gathered through the formation of the voice in the mouth and comes forth with its speaking.
5) That he is the one who brings the good pleasure of the Father, confirmed through the Son, most closely to creatures, especially rational ones.

XLVI. The second phrase, *the Light of the Face of Jehovah*, which occurs in Psalm 4:7 and 89:16, has no less emphasis. Nor would I doubt that the Son is designated here by the *Face of Jehovah*, and that through an allusion to the symbolic presence of God in the typical Sanctuary <note>The "Sanctuary" refers to the Tabernacle or Temple where God's presence was said to dwell among the Israelites.</note>, which is very frequently called the *Face of God*. From this, whoever flocked to that place where the **Ark of the Covenant** <term>Ark of the Covenant: The sacred chest representing God's throne and his legal agreement with Israel.</term> was located, as the typical throne of God, were said to appear before the *Face of the Lord*. Therefore, just as the *Light* of this *Face* according to the literal sense was that *splendor* which normally burned in the lampstand as well as on the altar, and sometimes flashed forth extraordinarily, by which both the Priests and the Israelites celebrating the Feasts typically *walked in the light*; so in the mystical sense, the *Light of the Face of Jehovah* are those illustrious operations of the Holy Spirit, through which he so illuminates the hearts of the elect and the entire Church, that its true members, as if *walking in...*

XLVII. Just as the Holy Spirit works so consistently from the *Father and the Son*, so also His works are directed toward the *Son and the Father*. That the *Glory of the Son* is promoted through Him is clear from the anointing of the Son by the Spirit and specifically from the Testimony which was exhibited to the Son by the Holy Spirit, which we discussed above in § 21. 1) That the Holy Spirit works from the Father and the Son:
> For he will not speak on his own, but whatever he hears, he will speak, and he will announce the things to come (namely, according to the Covenant of the Father and the Son) to you.
2) That the same Spirit directs His work toward the Son:
> He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you.
We refer the reader here to our Commentary; adding only that just as the Father is glorified through the glorification of the Son, so also the Holy Spirit, by glorifying the Son, directs all things toward the Glory of the Father as the ultimate end. This is confirmed by all the gracious effects He has in the hearts of the elect and the believers. In them, He not only teaches the faithful to call Christ "Lord" (1 Corinthians 12:3) and is the guarantee <term>guarantee: original "arrhabo," a legal deposit or down payment ensuring the full inheritance to come.</term> of their inheritance to the praise of the glory of Jesus Christ (Ephesians 1:14), but also through Him they cry out, "*Abba, Father*" <note>original: "Abba, Pater"; "Abba" is an Aramaic term for father conveying deep intimacy, often paired in the New Testament with the Greek "Pater."</note> (Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:6). The Apostle reinforces this excellently with his prayer in Ephesians 1:17 and following, directed to the Father of Glory, that He might give the Spirit of wisdom and revelation...

Meanwhile, I would not doubt that the former interpretation <note>The interpretation of Origen: that the Father sent both the Son and the Spirit.</note> is the truest, because it not only agrees perfectly with the *structure* of the words but also duly expresses *the matter itself*.

-># THE ECONOMY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT IN RELATION<-
<meta>catchword: -retur</meta>

...would have been fitting, both for the order of the persons of the Holy Trinity and for the custom of the sacred style, for it to be constructed with the prefixed letter *bet* (ב) <note>original: "ב"; the Hebrew preposition meaning "by" or "with"</note>, as in Psalm 33:6. Nor is the observation of **DAVID KIMCHI** <note>A famous medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator (1160–1235) often cited by Christian scholars of this period.</note> in his *Michlol* (page 15, column 3) for nothing, noting: *There is a "vav" (ו) used in place of a "bet" (ב), as when it is said: "The Lord God sent me and his Spirit," that is, "with his Spirit" or "by his Spirit."* <note>original Hebrew: יש ו׳ במקום ב׳ כמו יהוה אלהים שלחני ורוחו. Kimchi argues that the "and" in Isaiah 48:16 actually means "by means of," suggesting the Spirit is the instrument of the mission, not a co-sender.</note> For the Jewish scholar rightly noticed that if it were to be translated in the nominative case <note>i.e., as "The Spirit sent me"</note>, it would be unusual, unless "vav" were used instead of "bet." He only ought to have proved by suitable examples that this use of "vav" occurs elsewhere in the Holy Scriptures. However, **HACKSPAN** <note>Theodor Hackspan (1607–1659), a Lutheran theologian and orientalist known for his work on Hebrew grammar.</note> shows in this place that Kimchi did not provide such proof.

L. Nevertheless, the argument of the matter itself invites us more strongly to follow this opinion. Certainly, Scripture nowhere teaches that the **Son** was sent or is being sent by the **Holy Spirit**. To be sure, appeal is made to Isaiah 61:1 (compared with Luke 4:18 <note>The text reads Luke 4:11, likely a printer's error for 4:18, where Christ quotes Isaiah 61.</note>), where likewise two "senders" are thought to be presented: the Lord Jehovah and His Spirit. But the text itself resists this. For when it is said: *The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me, etc.* <note>original Hebrew: רוח אדני יהוה עלי יען משח יהוה אותי וגו׳</note>, these words, according to the <term>accents</term> <note>The Masoretic cantillation marks in the Hebrew Bible, which serve as musical notation and punctuation to clarify the sentence structure.</note>, ought to be constructed thus: *The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me: Because the Lord has anointed me, he has sent me to preach the gospel to the poor.* From this it is clear that the words *The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me* form a complete sentence by themselves; however, the words *Because the Lord has anointed me* pertain not to the preceding part, but to the following member, and they derive the reason for the Son’s <term>mission</term> <note>The theological term for the "sending" of a person of the Trinity into the world.</note> from his <term>anointing</term> <note>The ceremonial act of pouring oil on a king or priest, here symbolizing the Holy Spirit being given to Christ.</note>. For anointing is truly the inauguration and preparation for a mission: but the *Mission* is the purpose of the *anointing*. And thus, the one who is said here to send the Son is the same as the one who anoints him. But the **Anointer** is **Jehovah**, who is clearly distinguished here from the **Spirit of Jehovah**. Nor, according to Scripture, can the Spirit be the *anointer*, since He is constantly compared to the oil of anointing, and as such is said in our very passage to be *upon the Messiah*. Add to this that with this mission in verses 2 and 3, such benefits are joined which were not to be distributed except after the sitting of the Messiah at the right hand of the Father. No one would easily say that the Son is sent by the **Holy Spirit** even after his glorification.

[...established] so that the personal properties of the Holy Trinity <note>original: "SS. Triadis"</note>, which are otherwise constantly distinguished, would not be confused with one another and wrapped in new obscurity. For in that relationship, the Holy Spirit would not be the third person, but the second. From this, no small amount of strength would be added to the faith of the Greek Church <note>A reference to the "Filioque" controversy. The Western Church teaches the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; the Eastern/Greek Church teaches the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. The author suggests that if the Spirit "sent" the Son, it would imply the Son is subordinate to or proceeds from the Spirit.</note>, since it would follow from this relationship that, far from the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Son, the Son would rather, in a certain way, proceed from the Holy Spirit. 

And this becomes even more complicated if that rule acknowledged by many Fathers stands: *the mission of a divine person in time is the manifestation of their eternal procession* <note>original: "missio personæ divinæ in tempore est processionis æternæ manifestatio." This is a fundamental principle in Trinitarian theology: how the Persons of the Trinity act in human history (their "mission") reveals their eternal relationship to one another (their "procession").</note>. This rule is used by **GREGORY NAZIANZEN** in *Oration 37*; **ATHANASIUS** in Volume I of his works, in the *Letter to Serapion*; **AUGUSTINE** in Book IV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 20; **JOHN OF DAMASCUS** <note>original: "DAMASCENUS"</note> in Book IV of *On the Orthodox Faith*, chapter 19; and others. 

Now, since this principle has held true thus far—because economic relations <note>term: "Economic relations" refers to the roles the Father, Son, and Spirit play in the history of salvation (the "Economy" of God's plan), as opposed to their internal, eternal nature.</note> are founded upon natural relations, as established above—it would follow that if the Son were sent by the Holy Spirit, the Son would then proceed from the Holy Spirit just as much as the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. However, so that it may appear more fully how much this interpretation deviates from the true order of the divine Persons, both those who make the *Divinity* <note>original: "Deitatem"</note> [of Christ] and those who make the *Humanity of Christ the object of this mission* must be refuted individually.

### LII.
Several Fathers embrace the former opinion [that the Spirit sent Christ's Divinity]. But if that were the case, *the mission of Christ’s Divinity would have to be derived either from the necessity of nature or from a covenant*. The first concept is contradicted by the third order of existence <note>original: "subsistendi"</note> and operation which is attributed to the Holy Spirit. For we conceive of the sender as being "before" the one who is sent. The latter concept [a covenant] is likewise complicated, both because that covenant is founded on the natural order of the persons, and because we have proved above that in the execution of the Eternal Covenant, the operations of the Holy Spirit depend on the operations of the Son, and not the other way around. For as the execution of the divine counsel is, such also was its first constitution.

### LIII.
Let us hear, nonetheless, with what weapons they defend themselves.
A. **AUGUSTINE**, in *On the Trinity*, Book II, chapter 5, argues: *He could not have been sent by the Father without the Holy Spirit: not only because the Father is understood [to be the sender] when He sent Him, that is, made Him from a woman, which was certainly not done without His own Spirit...*

Matthew 1:18.</note> However, we rightly reject this minor argument, both because it has nothing to do with a "mission" <note>In theology, a "mission" refers specifically to a Divine Person being sent into the world for the work of salvation.</note>, and because this operation of the Holy Spirit properly had only the humanity of the Lord as its object, and because the mission of the Son is the personal work of the Father.

B. **AMBROSE** <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), Bishop of Milan and a foundational figure in Western theology.</note> in Book III of *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter I, thinks that the divine honor of the Holy Spirit hinges on this very point, writing: *Whom, as you hear, the Spirit also sent: lest when you read that the Son sends the Spirit, you might believe the Spirit to be of inferior power. If therefore the Son and the Spirit send each other, just as the Father sends, it is not an insult of subjection, but a matter of common power.* <note>original: "Quem, ut audis, & Spiritus misit... Si ergo se invicem Filius & Spiritus mittunt... non subjectionis injuria, sed communis potestatis est."</note> Against these words, it is enough to advise that even if personal operations—especially in the Economy of salvation <note>term: Economy of salvation (Oeconomia salutis). The divine plan for the redemption of humanity as it unfolds in history.</note>—do not alternate, no inequality of the persons arises from that fact. Just as the Father sending the Son does not make the Son unequal to the Father (even though the Father is not sent by the Son); so the fact that the Son sends the Holy Spirit, and not vice versa, does not make the Holy Spirit unequal to the Son.

LIV. Others, especially among more recent writers, prefer the view that Christ was sent by the Holy Spirit according to his Humanity. However, it is enough to oppose these with the celebrated **VITRINGA** <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a famous Dutch theologian known for his commentary on Isaiah.</note> on this passage; for although this might be more easily admitted insofar as Christ as a man was *driven* by the Holy Spirit, nevertheless in our current context the Son of God does not speak as a man. He not only ascribes divine attributes and works to himself, but also presents himself as one who existed long ago and has already taught the people through the Prophets.

LV. Yet I would think that we should not rely too heavily on this latter argument, provided there are sufficient reasons that are usually brought forward in favor of the literal text of the received Version. **HAKSPAN** and **HABICHHORST** <note>Theologians and Hebraists; Habichhorst was a specialist in the system of Hebrew accents.</note> in the place cited note the following on this matter:

> A. "If *Jehovah* <note>The Hebrew Tetragrammaton יהוה.</note> were in the Accusative case [the object of the verb], then because of the connection with the suffix *-nu* [me] in *shlachani* [he sent me], this word should not have been marked with the distinctive accent *Tipcha*, but with the conjunctive accent *Merca*." <note>term: Tipcha and Merca. These are "accents" in the Hebrew Bible (cantillation marks). A "distinctive" accent like Tipcha marks a grammatical pause or separation, whereas a "conjunctive" accent like Merca joins words together. The author argues that the punctuation proves "the Spirit" is not part of the subject.</note>

<header>TO THE DIVINE PERSONS. CHAPTER VIII.</header>

This is most common, since minor dividers are very frequently used for the sake of emphasis, so that things which are distinct by their nature may also be considered distinctly. Here, however, not only were the subjects to be accurately distinguished, but also two different missions, differing from each other in their beginning, nature, and purpose; and so the *Tipcha* <note>A Hebrew musical and grammatical accent that functions as a minor pause or separator within a verse, often used to signal a nuance in the text's meaning.</note> excellently warns us here that we should pause in meditation between the mission of the Son and the mission of the Holy Spirit.

B. “If the name *Yahweh* <note>original: יהוה</note> were to be rendered in the Accusative <note>The grammatical case indicating the direct object of a verb—the person or thing being acted upon.</note>, then to remove ambiguity, the particle *et* <note>original: את; a Hebrew marker often used before a definite direct object.</note> should have been placed before it, since the preceding verb *sent me* <note>original: שלחני (*shilchani*)</note> does not allow an accusative here without the particle *et* intervening.” This argument likewise wavers, both because the omission <term>ellipsis: the leaving out of a word that is understood from context</term> of the word *et* is frequent in the sacred writings; and because, where different subjects occur, the *et* is usually placed before each one. Therefore, according to this hypothesis, it should have been said: *He sent me and His Spirit* <note>original: שלח אתי ואת רוחו (*shlach oti ve-et rucho*)</note>, which would nonetheless have been less fitting here. For in such a construction, the *et* separates the subjects at the same time, and thus indicates separate individuals, which has no place regarding the Persons of the **Most Holy Trinity** <note>original: **SS. Triados**</note>.

C. As for what **HACKSPAN** <note>Theodor Hackspan (1607–1659), a Lutheran theologian and expert in Oriental languages.</note> adds—"that the word *Yahweh* with this prefix and suffix occurs only three times according to the **MASORETIC** <note>The Masora refers to the traditional system of notes and rules intended to preserve the precise text of the Hebrew Bible.</note> notation, and indeed always in Isaiah, namely in this place and chapter 30:28 and 34:16"—it contributes nothing to this matter. For the conclusion formed from this—that because in the two other places it does not allow the meaning of an accusative, it should likewise not be admitted in the present place—is rightly rejected. For whether it marks an accusative does not depend on prefixes or suffixes, but solely on the construction with the verb by which it is most closely governed. The remaining points that **HABICHHORST** <note>Andreas Daniel Habichhorst (1634–1704), a German theologian.</note> mentions are either already addressed or are so trivial that they do not deserve to be weighed.

**LVI.** Although certain **Socinians** <note>A group of 16th- and 17th-century thinkers who denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ, often using grammatical technicalities to support their views.</note> have praised **CASTELLIO'S** <note>Sébastien Castellio (1515–1563), a French theologian and translator known for his humanist approach to the Bible.</note> version for the purpose of wringing from it an argument against the Deity of the Holy Spirit, nothing of its value is lost thereby. For what they claim—that *the Mission of the Holy Spirit is contrary to His Deity*—is quite empty, as we have already warned in Chapter V, Section 20, number **D.** And very strongly from this very interpretation...

<header>THE ECONOMY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT IN RELATION <note>original: *Oeconomia Spiritus S. Relate*; referring to the "Economic Trinity," the theological concept of how the Father, Son, and Spirit act in relation to the world and salvation history.</note></header>

...[interpreta]tion <note>The Latin text begins mid-word with *-tione*, likely the end of *interpretatione* (interpretation) or *argumentatione* (argumentation).</note> of our passage, we fight for the Deity of the Holy Spirit. For he who is joined in the same order of *Mission*, without any sign of distinction, with a divine person—which is surely the case for the one speaking here—must himself be regarded as such. Compare Chapter IV, §. 10. Truly, those who defend the received version <note>Referring to the standard translations of the Bible common in the 17th and 18th centuries.</note> bring more darkness to this passage (which deservedly should be numbered among the more illustrious for the Mystery of the Trinity), as is clear not only from the Jewish but also from the Christian interpreters, among whom were **LUTHER** and **CALVIN**. For they were confirmed by that version in the prejudice that not the Messiah, but Isaiah the Prophet, sent by the Holy Spirit, should be considered as the person speaking in our text. However, even among the Jews themselves, the **MIDRASH TEHILLIM, R. SAADIA GAON, R. DAVID KIMCHI, and R. ABARBANEL** <note>These are prominent medieval Jewish scholars and commentators; the author is pointing out that even non-Christian sources sometimes support a "Messianic" reading of this verse.</note> concede that it is the Messiah who speaks, and to that extent, they have been much more clearsighted than certain Christian interpreters.

**LVII.** Just as it is clearly evident from what has been cited how the sacred pages subordinate the "Economic" operations <term>Economy: in theology, this refers to God's external actions and the specific roles of the Father, Son, and Spirit in history.</term> of the Holy Spirit to the operations of the Father and the Son, it is equally indubitable from the same sources that he enjoys equal independence and freedom of action with the Father and the Son. This follows:

A. From all the arguments that Holy Scripture brings forward for his supreme Deity. For the concept of supreme perfection necessarily involves the concept of independence in acting.

B. This flows especially from the divine attributes of *Omniscience, Omnipotence, and Eternity*, which we have claimed for the Holy Spirit. He who is *omniscient* is independent in his actions. For if he acts according to the light of knowledge—which must be established regarding the wisdom of the Holy Spirit—then it follows that, unless he depends on something else for his knowledge, he is also independent in his actions. Now indeed, he who depends on something else for his knowledge *is not* absolutely omniscient, because he does not *know all things* by his own nature, but by the will of another, by which it could have happened that he *might not have known all things*. Furthermore, he who is *Omnipotent* likewise depends on no one. For omnipotence admits no limits, except those which the omnipotent being places upon himself by his own will. *Finally, and Eter-* <note>The text breaks here; the catchword *nitas* completes the word "Eternity."</note>

# ON THE DIVINE PERSONS. CHAPTER VIII.

[Divi]nity <note>The text begins with the suffix "-nitas," most likely completing *Divinitas* (Divinity) or *Unitas* (Unity).</note> in its absolute sense involves independence. For that which is Eternal has nothing that exists before it, and exists by the necessity of its own nature; thus, it owes its existence to nothing except its own perfections. Moreover, he who exists by the necessity of his own nature—since his existence and his activity differ only in our mental concept—acts according to that same necessity of his nature, just as he wills.

**C.** In describing the <term>Economic</term> operations <note>The "Economy" of God refers to the distinct roles the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit take on in relation to the world and the plan of salvation, as opposed to their eternal essence.</note> of the Holy Spirit, active and passive words and phrases alternate. The word itself, <gloss>which is active</gloss> "proceeds" <note>original Greek: ἐκπορεύεται (*ekporeuetai*)</note>, is active, and thus denotes not a determination—much less a production—from the Father, but a spontaneous and most free departure from him. Hence he is not only said to be "sent," but also to "come" (John 15:26, 16:7, 13); not only to be "placed upon" someone, but also to "rest and remain" (Isaiah 11:2, John 14:17); not only to be "given," but also to work himself (1 Corinthians 12:11).

**D.** Whatever the Father and Son are said to work through the Holy Spirit in these passages, the Holy Spirit himself effects in other places. Not only were all things created through him, but he himself is also the Creator of man (Job 33:4). And for this reason, he is considered the Author of every blessing of Grace and the supreme Giver, both in the Priestly blessing (Numbers 6:26) and in the prayers of his people (Revelation 1:4).

**E.** This is also added by **JOHN GUYSE**, a London theologian, who piously and solidly set forth the doctrine of the <term>Deity</term> <note>The nature of being God; Godhood.</note> of the Holy Spirit in the English language in the year 1721 (page 39). He notes that it is often said that the Spirit is *sent* by the Father and the Son, but no mention is ever made of any command given to the Holy Spirit, or of obedience performed by him. Concerning Christ, indeed, with respect to his humanity, we read that *he received a command from the Father* (John 10:18), and that *he became obedient* (Philippians 2:8). But nothing similar occurs regarding the Holy Spirit. The reason for this difference is that Christ, by the <term>hypostatic union</term> <note>The theological term for the union of Christ's divine and human natures in one person.</note>, joined to himself an inferior nature, in which he became the *Servant of Jehovah* <note>original: *Servus Jehova*; a title for the Messiah used in the book of Isaiah.</note>, who could receive commands and subject himself to them. That, however, has no place in the third person, since he enjoys no other nature than the perfectly divine. It might indeed seem that something like a command is contained in it when the Spirit is said to be sent by the Father in the name of the Son. But in the name of anyone...

**F.** The same Most Learned Man <note>This likely refers to a contemporary theologian or commentator the author frequently cites, possibly Vitringa or Cocceius.</note> refers to this: that the Holy Spirit in Psalm 51:12 is called <note>original Hebrew: רוח נדיבה (*ruach nedivah*)</note> *the Spirit of spontaneity* <note>Commonly translated in English Bibles as "a free spirit" or "willing spirit."</note>. It is indeed true that this <gloss>spontaneity</gloss> is not so much an attribute of the Holy Spirit as it is an effect which he produces in those who, casting off the slavery and yoke of sin, offer themselves to God with a ready and cheerful mind as a <term>sacrifice of praise</term> <note>A biblical concept where prayer and thanksgiving are offered to God as spiritual alternatives to animal sacrifices.</note>. Nevertheless, one may argue from this effect back to the cause. If it is certain that, *he who planted the ear, must himself hear; and he who formed the eye, must himself see* (Psalm 94:9), then he who is all-sufficient not only for creating free and spontaneous minds, but also for making a sinner ready to willingly subject himself to the Law—which by nature was most hateful to him—must himself be most free in his own operations.

<header>THE ECONOMIC RELATIONS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT</header>

[They] chiefly enjoy him as their head, and through deep experience, they are conscious of the primary operations that are to be discussed here. This knowledge was necessary, for without it, they could not recognize the magnitude of the divine Benefit bestowed upon them through the gift of the Holy Spirit, nor could they return due thanks to the Triune God <note>The Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note> for such a treasure given to them. Furthermore, without this awareness, they could not draw sufficient comfort from the feeling of his operations, nor act prudently in distinguishing his guidance from any other impulse, nor guard themselves carefully enough against offending him or the very dangerous stifling of his work. In the meantime, not even everything here is so straightforward that the sharpness of our intellect does not grow dim at many things. Nicodemus was ignorant not only of *where this heavenly breath comes from, but also where it goes* (John 3:8). We must now weigh this ourselves as we undertake to investigate, modestly and reverently, *where the Holy Spirit goes*, by considering the effects his operations produce in both the *Kingdom of Nature* and the *Kingdom of Grace*.

II. Before we descend into more specific details, we rightly assume that a certain analogy exists between the government of the Kingdom of *Nature* and the Kingdom of *Grace*. For the relationship of the Holy Spirit to the Father and the Son is the same in the Kingdom of Nature as it is in the Kingdom of Grace. This is especially true because these two kingdoms are linked by mutual ties, so that the latter [Grace] is in a way the goal and <term>antitype</term> <note>A fulfillment or spiritual reality that corresponds to an earlier symbol or "type."</note> of the former [Nature]. For this reason, distinguished men focused on deep meditation have sought to illustrate the harmony between these two kingdoms. All who relate the Mystery of Creation to the Work of Redemption rely on this foundation. From this, the famous Horchius <note>Christoph Horch (1652–1718), a German theologian known for his mystical and Cartesian leanings.</note> in *The Invisible Things of God* deduces a perpetual communion between the works of Nature and Grace—between the governance of physical movement <note>original: "motuum extensionis," referring to "extension," the Cartesian term for physical matter occupying space.</note> and the thoughts of the mind. That this is not out of place is shown by two of the primary operations of the Holy Spirit in the Kingdom of Nature, which appear even more clearly in the Kingdom of Grace.

# ON THE KINGDOM OF THE WORLD. CHAPTER IX.

For he flows effectively and almost immediately into individual effects, so that they follow according to the Will of the Father and the Son with an outcome that is never in doubt and never fails. This is what those assume who wish to call the Holy Spirit, by way of emphasis, *Power* <note>original Greek: *Δυναμιν* (Dynamin)</note> or the *Virtue of God*. For this reason, he is surely called the "Scepter of Jehovah’s strength" in *Psalm 110:2*. Hence the Church Fathers—whom Suicerus <note>Johann Caspar Suicer (1619–1684), a Swiss theologian known for his dictionary of Greek ecclesiastical terms.</note> cites under the word *hand* <note>original Greek: *χειρ* (cheir)</note>—believed the Holy Spirit was sometimes foreshadowed by the symbol of the *Hand of God*. To this, I would especially refer the symbolic name of *Gabriel*, which designates the *Strong Man of God*, and we have proven in Exercise III on *Psalm 45, § 12* that this name expresses the Holy Spirit.

IV. Second, these are the roles of the same Holy Spirit: to direct and lead whatever effects, and specifically the operations of secondary causes <note>In classical theology, "secondary causes" are the natural laws, human choices, or physical forces that God (the First Cause) uses to achieve his goals.</note>, to a suitable goal. He does this while subjecting them all to the divine decree and ensuring that the Glory of God is revealed through them by a necessary connection. Therefore, we believe that whatever is presented in Scripture as a peculiar operation of the Holy Spirit can be included under the same general name of SANCTIFICATION. Indeed, this does not stray from the common use of the word, since whatever is in any way established as an instrument or evidence of divine Glory, and is adapted to illustrate it, is said to be *sanctified*. See *Isaiah 13:3* and *Jeremiah 51:27, 28*. Nor does the reality of the matter fit any less. In this way, we adhere to the emphasis of the characteristic name which the Third Person of the Trinity bears. Thus, we reserve the *third* or *final* place for his operations, since the consummation or perfection of creatures consists in this kind of sanctification, which places the finishing touch, as it were, upon divine works. In this way, he works constantly in other creatures just as it was proven in the preceding chapter (§ 16) that he worked in the humanity of the Son of God. Thus, we follow in the footsteps of the Fathers, who held *Sanctification* to be as much a characteristic of the third person as *Fatherhood* <note>original Latin: *Paternitas*</note> is of the first and *Sonship* <note>original Latin: *Filiatio*</note> is of the second. Hence Basil <note>Basil of Caesarea (330–379 AD), a central figure in defining the doctrine of the Trinity.</note>, in *Letter 391*, intending to point out the distinct *characteristics of each individual person* <note>original Greek: *τους αφωρισμενους περι εκαστον χαρακτηρας*</note>, names them *Fatherhood, Sonship, and Sanctification* <note>original Greek: *πατροτητα, και υιοτητα, και αγιασμον*</note>. He does the same in *Letter 349* and in *Book V against Eunomius*. It is also explicitly stated by EULO-

# THE ECONOMY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT [IN RELATION TO CREATION]

...GIUS, Bishop of Alexandria, as quoted in PHOTIUS, *Bibliotheca* Codex 230:
"God is thus perceived by us as both One and Three, being the fountain of incomprehensible wisdom and sanctifying power. Therefore, he is one God, Lord, and King—the Father himself, his perfecting wisdom <note>original Greek: *ἡ τελειοποιὸς σοφία* (hē teleiopoios sophia); Latin: *perfectrix ejus Sapientia*</note>, and his sanctifying power. For the Father is indivisible from his own wisdom and from his sanctifying power, being worshipped as a single nature." <note>original Latin: *Deus à nobis consideratur & unus & trinus; qui fons incomprehensæ Sapientiæ & Virtutis sanctificæ...*</note> We also add CYRIL OF ALEXANDRIA from his *Thesaurus*, Book 34: "We say that the Holy Spirit is that very sanctifying power proceeding naturally from the Father, which bestows perfection upon those things that are incomplete." <note>original Greek: *...δύναμιν ἁγιαστικὴν τὴν τοῖς ἀτελέσι τὸ τέλειον παρεχομένην...*</note> More on this can be found in PETAVIUS, *On the Trinity*, Book 7, chapter 13.

V. Furthermore, we rightly extend this work of **Sanctification** to all the works of Nature. Regarding rational beings <note>Such as humans and angels who possess intellect.</note>, there is no difficulty, for their perfection—or the fulfillment of their moral faculties intended for the praise of the Creator (that is, the <term>Divine Image</term> itself, which is planted by nature in Angels and Men alike)—is completed by this gift of the Spirit. Thus, BASIL, in chapter 9 of his book *On the Holy Spirit*, when recounting the creation of the Angels, teaches that their perfection consists in the "sanctification of the Spirit." 

But why should we not also extend this work to irrational and brute creatures? For just as they are *sanctified in an improper sense through legitimate use* (1 Timothy 4:5) and were *sanctified symbolically at times through their relation to the earthly Sanctuary* (Hebrews 9:10), they are also, in a more proper sense, sanctified through the works of nature by divine action. This occurs when **form** is bestowed upon them, or when they are so adorned and connected to one another in a most beautiful order that the observation of them stirs rational creatures to recognize the "fingerprints" of the Maker in the work of his hands and to celebrate him. It is through these things that they might more happily fulfill <note>original Latin: *defungantur* (to perform or discharge a duty)</note> this duty...

**VI.** Generally, the emblem of the **Divine Finger** most elegantly outlines this truth. For it appears that this term is applied to the Holy Spirit when one compares Exodus 31:18 <note>Where the stone tablets are written by the "finger of God."</note> with 2 Corinthians 3:3 <note>Where the "Spirit of the living God" writes on hearts.</note>, and Luke 11:20 <note>"If I by the finger of God cast out demons..."</note> with Matthew 12:28 <note>"If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God..."</note>. From this, Psalm 8:5 <note>Reference to the heavens as the "work of your fingers."</note> is also aptly referred to the Spirit, to which others add Exodus 8:19 and Daniel 5:5. That the Church Fathers recognized this emblem has been abundantly proven by Delrio in *Adagia* I. 69, Valeriano in *Hieroglyphica* XXXVI. 1, Bochart in *Hieroz.* II. Book IV, chapter 18, and Suicer under the word *daktylos* <note>original Greek: *δάκτυλος* (daktylos); meaning "finger."</note>. However, they did not so clearly notice the <term>Tertium Comparationis</term> <note>The specific point of similarity in an analogy.</note>, which should undoubtedly be placed in this: that the *works of the fingers* usually exhibit greater accuracy and *ornament* <note>original Latin: *ornatum*</note>, which is typically added through the skillful exercise of the fingers. Hence, *fingers* designate by metonymy works elaborated with singular art, providing testimony to the Author’s power and, most especially, his wisdom. That such a role belongs to the Holy Spirit in the divine works will become clear from a perception of them.

**VII.** Scripture teaches that the Holy Spirit was already active in **Creation** itself, both regarding the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "great world" or the entire universe.</note> in general, and regarding **Man** in particular. As for the Macrocosm, both the *heaven* and the *earth* are his work. Regarding heaven, Psalm 33:6 says that *by the Spirit of the Mouth of Jehovah all the host of the heavens was made.* <note>The Hebrew word *Ruach* can mean both "Spirit" and "Breath" or "Wind."</note> When the Psalmist speaks here of EVERY host of heaven, he seems to wish to include both the literal and the *mystical* hosts in the broadest sense. For just as there are *mystical* heavens, so also there are *mystical* hosts—namely the Church, both **militant** <note>The Church currently on earth struggling against sin.</note> and **triumphant** <note>The Church in heaven having achieved victory.</note>, which constitutes the *Kingdom of Heaven*. All the elect follow the standards of this host, as the "seed of Abraham" compared to the stars in Genesis 15:1; hence they are explicitly called so in Daniel 8:10. However, although the prophetic tenor of our Psalm does not exclude this sense, we understand in the first place the more literal hosts of the heavens, both the *corporeal* and the *intellectual*. For the *Stars* are called so in 2 Chronicles 23:5 <note>Likely a citation error in the original for 2 Kings 23:5 or 2 Chron 33:5, regarding the worship of the "host of heaven."</note>, Jeremiah 33:22, and 2 Kings 17:16. To illustrate this phrase, consult DELRIO’s *Adagia* I. 1; VORSTIUS’s *Sacred Philology* Chapter 23; CAPPELLUS on Genesis 2:1; and BYNÆUS’s *On the Birth of Jesus Christ*, Book I, chapter 4, section 16. Furthermore, it is possible to derive from the **metaphor of the Host** itself what may most closely be considered the work of the Holy Spirit. For it is well known that the formal meaning of the name <term>Tsaba</term> <note>original Hebrew: צבא (*tsaba*); usually translated as "host" or "army."</note> expresses whatever commends itself by a neat and beautiful order, or **any well-ordered multitude**. From this, the term was transferred to mean **an army**, in which nothing should be more prioritized than the most accurate order, upon which its entire strength depends. Hence, the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> rightly renders this word as *kosmos* <note>original Greek: κόσμον (*kosmon*); meaning "world" or "orderly arrangement."</note> in Genesis 2:1, Deuteronomy 4:19, Deuteronomy 17:3, Isaiah 24:21, and Isaiah 40:26. Following them, the Vulgate <note>The Latin Bible translation.</note> translates it as **adornment** <note>original Latin: *ornatum*</note>. At the very least, in relation to the creation of the Angels, the notion of an **ornately established order** fits the word *Tsaba* better than the notion of an "army," since at that time neither evil nor enemies existed.

But what is "order" in any given thing, if not the relationship of those things to one another—the bond placed between them by the Creator for the purpose of providing mutual aid toward a universal end, namely, to manifest the Glory of the Creator’s Wisdom? What, then, is the **Angelic Order** but the manner in which they have communion with one another under the Sovereignty of God for His Glory? This manner involves both the holy faculties with which each individual Spirit was equipped from the beginning, and their most sweet harmony with one another in glorifying God. This, therefore, was the work of the Holy Spirit regarding Heaven: to clothe Heaven and its inhabitants with that form through which it could become a heavenly Sanctuary—a theater of the perfections and, especially, of the Wisdom and Holiness of God.

# THE DISPENSATION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT IN RELATION TO THE WORLD
## CHAPTER IX.

->The goddesses of heaven feared him, and by his command he slew the dragon.<-
<note>original Greek: ϑεα ουρανου δεδοικασιν αυτον προσαγματι δ᾽ εϑανατωσε δρακοντα. This appears to be a variation of the Septuagint's rendering of Job 26:13.</note> The first segment of this verse is most unfortunately expressed in that version. Instead of **by his spirit** <note>Hebrew: *be-rucho* (ברוחו)</note>, through a common oversight in the Greek version, it was read as **bars** or **bolts** <note>Hebrew: *beriach* (בריחי)</note>. But regarding the word **shaphrah** <note>Hebrew: שפרה (*shaphrah*), translated as "garnished" or "adorned."</note>, perhaps he wished to paraphrastically express the **SYRIAC VERSION**, in which it is read: *By his spirit he governs the heavens.* For it is observed at the end of that book that our Greek version of Job was formed from the Syriac. However, that interpretation is beside the point, since the word *shapar* denotes "to adorn" or "to make beautiful." This term is used so broadly that, regarding our current subject, it encompasses not only external beauty but also internal cultivation. Aside from this passage, it occurs only once more, namely in the simple *Kal* form in Psalm 16:6, where it is used concerning the spiritual **beauty of the Lord's inheritance**. 

Much more so, the intensive *Pihel* form in our current passage indicates a **greatly adorned heaven**. This suggests not only the most pleasant sight of the sky—whether clear or distinguished at night by so many stars set like gems—but also, according to **THOMAS AQUINAS**, it involves the Angels, who are the heaven's rational inhabitants. The author of that adornment is the Lord through **his Spirit**. It is He who disposed the celestial bodies in such a neat and stupendous order, and so composed their motion, that they have become a fit theater for the Glory of God. It is He who gave inhabitants suitable to this most majestic palace, who shine with the beauties of perfected holiness, and who observe and celebrate the traces of the Creator's Glory from close at hand. Unless this were added, the heaven could not be called **greatly adorned**. Therefore, this emphasis is not to be passed over lightly.

IX. In this hypothesis, we are confirmed by the second segment of the verse, which the Greek interpreters rendered plainly to our liking. In our view, those who understand the **crooked serpent** <note>Hebrew: *nachash beriach* (נחש בריח)</note> as either a **Crocodile**, or a **Whale**, or at least some marine monster—as do **MERCER**, **DRUSIUS**, **BOCHART**, **COCCEIUS**, and **GOUSSET**—make too headlong a leap from the heaven into the sea. Those who think of the stars strike closer to the mark: **ABENEZRA** rendering it as the **celestial Dragon** <note>The constellation Draco.</note>, and **RABBI LEVI** (joined by **VATABLUS** and **CODURCUS**) as the **Milky Way**, while **BEZA** translates it as the **coils of the heavens**. # THE DISPENSATION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT IN RELATION TO THE WORLD
## CHAPTER IX.

[The interpreter] wants to substitute some *star* of ill omen. But I fear that a suspicion might arise from this: that Job intended to favor a superstitious distinction between auspicious and inauspicious stars. Among those who defend the literal meaning, no one hits the mark more closely than **PINEDA** <note>Juan de Pineda (1558–1637), a Spanish Jesuit known for his extensive commentary on the Book of Job.</note>, who believes it refers to *lightning*. I admit this more easily because its emission is an emblem of the fleeing Devil in Luke 10:18 <note>Jesus says, "I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven."</note>. To me, however, nothing so far appears more to the point than understanding it as the *Devil* himself.

This hypothesis is favored by:

1) The *meaning of the words*. The root **chul** <note>original: חול (*chul*)</note> signifies "to inflict pain" much more than "to form." Especially relevant here is the passage that **NACHMANIDES** <note>Moses ben Nahman (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note> has already compared, Isaiah 51:9: *Was it not you (O arm of the Lord) that cut <term>Rahab</term> <note>A primordial sea monster or a symbolic name for Egypt, representing chaos and pride.</note> in pieces, and wounded the <term>dragon</term>?* <note>original: תנין מחוללת (*tannin mecholat*)</note>. Here, the allusion to our passage, when compared with the preceding verse 12, is manifest. No one will doubt that both the name and the emblem of the *serpent* denoted the Devil among the most ancient peoples of the East. Furthermore, the word **beriach** <note>original: בריח (*beriach*)</note> properly means *to flee*, and thus to leave one's place and home; but in **ARABIC**, it also means *to fail* or *to defect*, which is why in 1 Samuel 12:10, the *defection* from the Lord himself to *Baalim and Ashtaroth* is expressed by this root. It is clear, therefore, that nothing is simpler than our version.

2) The *context* agrees. Job's goal was to impress upon **BILDAD**, that unjust insulter, the power of God—not just in general, but especially in the administration of justice. As an example, he brings forward the power God exercised over the ungodly in verse 5, and which He holds over Hell itself in verse 6. This is illustrated by examples of both His power (verses 7–8) and the Lord's majesty (verses 9–12). Therefore, nothing was more fitting than to conclude with that first judgment which He exercised against the Angels who excelled in power.

3) Furthermore, the *allegorical style*, which is familiar to Job, is used most especially in this context, as is clear from the description of the *divine throne* in verse 9.

4) Add to this that it is customary for Job to touch more explicitly upon the governance of the Angels whenever the opportunity arises.

5) Finally, Isaiah's allusion to our passage fits well, when in chapter 27:1 he likewise names the **mystical Leviathan**—who exercises tyranny in the darkness of the Antichristian Kingdom—as the **fleeing serpent** <note>original: נחש בריח (*nachash beriach*); Greek: ὄφιν φεύγοντα (*ophin pheugonta*)</note> according to the **SEPTUAGINT** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, since he was cast down from the celestial heights by the infernal Spirit...

...the apostate is being discussed; in the same style of speech by which, in Revelation 12:9, the "red dragon" of the Roman Empire is itself called the "ancient Serpent," the "Devil," and "Satan." Thus, I no longer dwell on the assessment of the Syrian and Arabic [translations], nor on that of other Church Fathers.

X. Truly, to return to our path, let us turn our attention from heaven to earth, and consider how the Spirit also exercised the office of the Sanctifier in the creation of the world. His roles in the visible world are indicated clearly in Genesis 1:2: <gloss>The Spirit of God moved</gloss> <gloss>over the face of the waters.</gloss> *And the Spirit of God made a powerful movement over the face of the waters.* We trust we have sufficiently proven elsewhere that the third person of the Holy Trinity is introduced here. Here, therefore, we consider only the nature of his work, which was *motion*—and indeed, as the <term>Piel form</term> <note>A Hebrew verb structure typically used to express intensive or repeated action; here, it suggests a vigorous "vibrating" or "brooding" motion.</note> requires, a *most powerful* one. This motion was stirred up *over the face of the waters*, and thus in the aerial region, while the earth itself was held as if submerged in the abyss of waters. Therefore, while the *production of matter* was assigned to the Holy Trinity in general, the glory of imparting the first *motions* is given to the Holy Spirit—which we have proved in the same place to have spread even to the Gentile philosophers <note>The author suggests that ancient Greek and Roman philosophers' ideas about a "world soul" or "prime mover" were actually distorted echoes of this biblical truth.</note>. Moreover, it is clear that this action of the Holy Spirit serves as a kind of *earthly sanctification* for two reasons:

1) Because the *form* of visible things depends on motion; without this, no beauty would appear in them, no effect would be produced through them, and thus matter would lie inert and destitute of everything. 2) Because through this motion, both the <gloss>waste</gloss> <note>Hebrew: *Tohu*. Usually translated as "formless" or "chaos."</note>—a *frozen solitude*, devoid of life and any living inhabitants—and the <gloss>void</gloss> <note>Hebrew: *Bohu*. Usually translated as "empty."</note>—the *lack of all appearance and ornament* which rendered the earth unfit for habitation—were gradually removed. Through the "waste," we recognize the Glory of God [by its absence], while in the "void," the very traces of this Glory were missing. The Holy Spirit sought to remedy both evils by stirring our terrestrial globe from above with a most powerful and penetrating motion.

XI. But we hasten to the rational inhabitant of the earth, *Man*, in whose sanctification we are taught in Genesis 2:7 that the Holy Spirit was already occupied from the very beginning of his existence, where we read: <gloss>And he breathed into his nostrils the breath of lives.</gloss> *And he breathed into his nostrils the breath of lives.* By <gloss>the breath of lives</gloss> <note>Hebrew: *Nishmat Chayim*. The plural "lives" is often interpreted by theologians to mean both physical life and the immortal soul.</note>, the mind is designated—which, though created, yet enjoys a life more excellent than all other creatures...

XIII. Nor do slight reasons favor this opinion. For:
