**POIRET** in *Divine Economy*, Book I, chapter II, renders it: *through the nostrils* or *through his face*, and believes the *Son of God* is intended here. In this way, the entire mystery of the Holy Trinity would be contained in our phrase, were it not for the objections raised by the Illustrious **LILIENTHAL** in the section cited above (§ 15). There are those who, along with **WITTER**, wish to claim the sacred style suffers here from a "frigid pleonasm" <note>A pleonasm is the use of more words than necessary. Witter suggests the phrase is merely repetitive and lacks deeper meaning.</note>. Nor was the usual sharpness of **JEAN D'ESPAGNE** successfully deployed here, who in his work *Shibboleth* (page 246) intending to destroy the popular error that the soul of a dying person exits through the mouth, thinks it should rather be established that it exits through the nostrils, because *it entered through the nostrils*. This is not far from the almost jocular error of **FRANCISCUS MERCURIUS VAN HELMONT** <note>Van Helmont (1614–1698) was an alchemist and physician known for his unconventional theories on the human soul and anatomy.</note>, who in his *Observations on Man*, contends from our passage to prove that the seat of the soul is to be located *in the nostrils of man*. Many find satisfaction in the Septuagint version <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> with the word *prosopon* (face), for which the **VULGATE** <note>The standard Latin Bible translation.</note> has *facies* (face). Nor does the reason proposed by **PHILO** <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE) was a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> displease them: that God is said to have breathed upon the face of man because it encompasses the primary organs of the senses. I confess, however, that this *synecdoche* <note>A figure of speech where a part (the face) represents the whole (the person).</note> seems to me not only poorly suited to the common use of the word, but also somewhat <term>catachrestic</term> <note>original Latin: *catachresticam*. Catachresis refers to a strained or paradoxical use of a metaphor.</note> in this context, and it does not fully exhaust the meaning of the phrase itself.

XV. What then? What if we consider that the word *be-appayim* <note>original Hebrew: באפים, literally "in the nostrils."</note> for "nostrils" is used here metonymically for the *breath* or *respiration* itself, of which the nostrils are the organ? This is all the more easily granted because the circumstances require that we understand here not just the clay-like shape of the nostrils, but the nostrils already warm and *breathing*. Add to this what the formal definition of the word demands. Since, according to the almost universal consensus of Grammarians, the word *aph* <note>original Hebrew: אף, nose or nostril.</note> comes from *anaph* <note>original Hebrew: אנף, meaning to breathe or blow through the nose.</note> (*to breathe*, or *to blow through the nostrils*), by the force of this origin, it denotes nothing other than nostrils impregnated with the vital breath. This being admitted, behold the animal body, which before this act of the Divine Spirit is already presented to our concept as if *breathing* and respiring. Thus, that which God *inspires* [breathes into] is clearly distinguished from that breath *already breathing* in the nostrils of man, and is shown to be of a most different kind from it. For upon these breathing nostrils, God, through the Spirit of His mouth, adds something more excellent: namely, the *nishmat chayyim* <note>original Hebrew: נשמת חיים, "the breath of lives." The author argues this refers to a higher spiritual life added to physical animation.</note> [the breath of lives].

### TOWARD THE KINGDOM OF THE WORLD. CHAPTER IX.

**XVI.** Now you ask, what do the nostrils—swelling with that recently instilled breath—have to do with this matter, such that the *Breath of lives* <note>original: "Halitus vitarum"</note>, or the *Rational soul*, is said to be instilled and, as it were, infused directly through them? Well, then! Is not *respiration* the first and the last of all animal movements that provide evidence of animal life? Is this not clear from the connection that exists between the nostrils, the brain, and the heart? Through this connection, odors can be carried via the sense of smell to both of these innermost chambers of the human body faster than a moment, and can revive exhausted strength. Is it not through the nostrils that the bodies surrounding us are most easily noticed and distinguished, since the sense of smell is the most acute of all senses? Is it not from this continuous draught of air—which impels both the blood and the fluid of the nerves—that motion is stirred and preserved? Is it not for this reason that *to breathe* is the same as *to live*? Is this not what James implies in chapter 2, verse 26, saying: *the body without the spirit is dead* <note>original Greek: "τὸ σῶμα χωρὶς πνεύματος νεκρὸν ἐστίν"</note>? For here, according to the literal sense, the "spirit" <note>original Greek: "πνεῦμα"</note> clearly designates the *power of breathing*. Therefore, since the goal here is the union of the immortal mind with the mortal body—so that by moderating the body's respiration, which is its life, the mind may use it as a fit instrument for the Glory of the Creator—nothing more wise could be said than that God willed, through His Spirit, to join and set a spirit equipped for a far more perfect life specifically to the most powerful organ of respiration.

**XVII.** And thus it is clear that in this same phrase more than one meaning is folded, as **BORRHAUS**, **MERSENNE**, and others acknowledge: namely, that the first man received not only an *immortal* soul, but also a *holy* one, clothed in the image of God. This is designated 1) by the plural word itself, *lives* <note>original Hebrew: "חיים" (chayyim)</note>. **GERHARD** <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a leading Lutheran orthodox theologian.</note> teaches this in the passage cited, writing: *Some more correctly establish that a twofold life of man is signified: the bodily and the spiritual, the temporal and the eternal.* For just as the "tree of life" is called *the tree of lives* <note>original Hebrew: "עץ חיים" (etz chayyim)</note> because it was able to preserve man for this life and for eternal life, so the soul is called the *breath of lives* <note>original Hebrew: "נשמת חיים" (nishmat chayyim)</note> because it was created not only for this life, but also for eternal life. Add to this that this plural form designates a life that is both most excellent and all-encompassing, whence it is to be extended as widely as the nature of the subject...

...as nature and circumstances permit. For although the *breath of life* <note>original Hebrew: נשמת חיים (*nishmat chayyim*)</note> is sometimes used to refer to the soul alone, excluding any reference to the image of God, nothing here prevents that image from being included. And from this 2) it is undoubtedly certain that the word *breath* <note>original Hebrew: נשמה (*neshamah*)</note> is used in a more sublime sense to refer to that more excellent *breath* proceeding from the Holy Spirit itself and set over the entire *breathing* of man—that is, the sanctified soul. Thus, in Job 27:3, that holy man emphatically testifies: *As long as* my breath <note>original Hebrew: נשמתי (*nishmati*)</note> *is in me, and the Spirit of God is in my nostrils, my lips shall not speak iniquity.* It appears that he is alluding here to the original formation of man. And the words that immediately follow indicate that Job is declaring things about himself that he would not have dared to assert unless he were relying on the beginnings of Grace and the help of the Holy Spirit. He describes here not his animal life, but his spiritual life, both in its presence in him (when he calls it his *breath*) and in its origin (which he assigns to the Spirit of God). He testifies that the Spirit is *in his nostrils* because it is that supreme Breath of the eternal Father, whose own *breathing* was the cause of the *breath of lives*, which was intended to holily moderate the movements of animal *respiration*. The word *breath* <note>original Hebrew: נשמה (*neshamah*)</note> has this same force in Proverbs 20:27 and Isaiah 57:16. Whether Isaiah 2:22 might also be of deeper inquiry, I do not think anything stands in the way. Add to this that the Holy Spirit itself is so clearly called by this name in Job 32:8 and 33:4. From this it is clear that *breath* <note>original Hebrew: נשמה (*neshamah*)</note> is analogous to the *spirit* <note>original Greek: πνευμα (*pneuma*)</note>, and therefore that passage from John 3:6 is rightly applied here: *That which is born of the Spirit is spirit.* <note>original Greek: Το γεγεννημενον ἐκ του πνευματος, πνευμα ἐσι.</note> The word *breath* <note>original Hebrew: נשמה (*neshamah*)</note> therefore has this unique quality: it often indicates a *holy soul*. When we then add 3) that this passage concerns a certain "economic" <note>In theology, "economy" refers to God's management or arrangement of the world and the plan of salvation.</note> work of the Holy Spirit; 4) that the governance of life and respiration in the human body could only have been entrusted by God to a holy soul; and 5) that the formation of man is repeated here and delineated more carefully to reveal what kind of subject it was that God wished to place over the Garden of Eden and unite with Himself in a covenant of friendship; then we are fully persuaded that the production of a soul that is not only *immortal*, but also equipped with *holiness of truth* <note>original Greek: ὁσιοτητι της ἀληθειας (*hosiotēti tēs alētheias*)</note> is what is being narrated here.

# TO THE KINGDOM OF THE WORLD. CHAPTER IX.

...wished to describe its circumstances and manner in such a way that its relation and fitness for a special communion of God with man would be made clear. For various truths pertaining to this matter are illustrated by our statement, such as: 1) That the soul of man, *produced* immediately by God, must acknowledge that it owes everything it is and possesses—its entire *being and well-being*—to Him alone. 2) That since it has an origin different from the body, is devoid of all matter, and has *nothing in common* by its essence with the earth, it was bound to set its mind on things above the dust. It should not place its happiness in any earthly good, nor promise itself anything from such a good as a necessary means for acquiring the highest good apart from the will of God; rather, it was obligated to consider all such things as being placed beneath itself. 3) That it did not *pre-exist* before the body, but was breathed into it once the body was already formed; being unaccustomed to any action produced separately from the body, it could view the body as a part of its own existence, from which it was never to be separated except by the intervention of sin. 4) That it was right for the soul to know and revere its God in covenant as *Triune* <note>The author refers to God as "fœderatum," reflecting "Covenant Theology," which views God's relationship with humanity through a series of divine agreements or covenants.</note>, who exhibited a clear example of the distinction of persons and the order of their existence through the very production of the human mind. 5) That it was fitting for the soul, considering itself in a peculiar way to be the *work of the Holy Spirit*, to surrender itself to His instinct and guidance.

1) First, He undoubtedly arranged the BODY so that it would simultaneously give an illustrious proof of God's glory to those contemplating it, and be obedient to the holy governance of the soul. Wherefore:

a) Those *Ideas* <note>Ideas: Here referring to innate concepts or fundamental truths that the author believes were placed in the mind by God at the moment of creation.</note>, which were to be the sole principles of all cognition and truth with which the *intellect* was to be equipped—along with the ease of drawing them out and combining them, and their legitimate order from the very first beginning of particular thoughts—were His work.

That *Light* by which man, once inspired, immediately knew God, himself, and his relation to God, and that *Law* which was already present in his heart while he was being created—the former was kindled by the Holy Spirit, and the latter was inscribed by the same. From this we easily conclude that the most majestic *Idea* of all, which presented the Creator Himself to Man, was among the first—indeed, was the very first of all—to be present to the intellect in its first moment of existence.

c) The strength of the same Spirit so disposed the *will* through its very production that its first act was not only holy, but also a sufficient principle for all holy actions. Therefore, if the first thought presenting itself to the intellect was of God, the first definition of judgment was that God exists and is lovable, and the first act of the determined will was the *Love of God* <note>original: "Amor Dei"</note>.

XXII. It must be admitted, however, that most of the Fathers stop at the point of understanding the *breath of life* <note>original: "spiraculum vitæ"</note> as referring only to the immortal soul considered in its barest sense. **THOMAS AQUINAS** <note>The influential 13th-century theologian and philosopher.</note> argues their case in Part I, Question 91, Article 1, even adding an argument that deserves attention, writing:

> Some have proposed that when it is said, "God formed man," it should be understood as the production of the body at the same time as the soul. But what is added—"and he breathed into his face the breath of life"—is understood to refer to the Holy Spirit, just as the Lord breathed upon the Apostles, saying: "Receive the Holy Spirit" <note>John 20:22</note>. But this exposition is excluded by the words of Scripture. For there is added to the aforementioned: "And man was made into a living soul." Which the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 15 refers not to spiritual life, but to natural life <note>original: "vitam animalem"; here meaning "soulish" or physical life governed by the soul, rather than the Spirit.</note>.

To this reasoning, we observe in advance that the Fathers, in making this distinction between the soul and the work of the Holy Spirit within it, did not sufficiently weigh the fact that the soul was created at the same time as the image of God, and was already holy from the first moment of its existence. This is the reason why, in our hypothesis, we do not distinguish between these two divine works, but by the *breath of lives* <note>The author uses "vitarum" (plural) to reflect the original Hebrew "nishmat chayyim," implying multiple types of life (natural and spiritual) given at once.</note> we understand, in a concrete sense, the *holy soul*. This being granted, nothing in the added effect of this formation contradicts us. For through this breath, man was made into a *living soul*—namely, with all emphasis, not only through a merely natural life, but also a spiritual one. For the very nature of the vastly different subject indicates that this phrase must be taken in a more excellent sense than that in which it is used in Genesis 1:19, 20 <note>Where "living soul" refers to animals.</note>. # ON THE KINGDOM OF THE WORLD. CHAPTER IX.

...tends toward assigning to Man a *life* held in common with the beasts, it is a view too feeble for us to cling to. If, however, we are compelled to admit a more sublime sense, why do we shrink from that one which the character of the phrasing permits, and the nature of the subject and its connection requires? Especially since those passages that apply this phrase to man also demand it, such as Genesis 9:16 and Ezekiel 47:9. Furthermore, the Pauline citation <note>Referring to 1 Corinthians 15:45: "The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit."</note> does not hinder our hypothesis, but rather illustrates it. Certainly, without cause would one restrict that "living soul" <note>original Greek: "ψυχην ζωσαν" (psuchen zosan)</note> with **THOMAS** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> to the merely natural soul. For it stands in the way that the whole context concerns the glorious bodies of the faithful, with which they will be clothed in the heavenly life after the resurrection. Therefore, if the rational soul is to be understood, then it must be understood as it is in the reborn, having been renewed through the sanctification of the Spirit.

XXIII. There are, however, many other interpreters—and not of the common sort—who maintain that by "living soul" the Apostle understood nothing but the *material* or *sensitive soul*. Thus argue **ESTIUS** <note>Willem Hessels van Est (1542–1613), a Dutch Catholic commentator.</note> and **GROTIUS** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), the famous Dutch jurist and theologian.</note>, and even among our own, **CALVIN**, **MUSCULUS** <note>Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563), a Reformed theologian.</note> and others. But the entire coherence of the passage opposes them. To make this clear, we observe that the words of verse 45 are a confirmation of the thesis proposed at the end of the preceding verse: "There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body" <note>original Greek: "Εστι σωμα ψυχικον, και εστι σωμα πνευματικον"</note>. In these words, however, we must be careful not to understand—along with **ORIGEN**, **ISIDORE** <note>Isidore of Pelusium (d. c. 449).</note> (Book II, Epistle 42), **THEOPHYLACT**, **HAMMOND**, **LE CLERC**, and **WHITBY** <note>A group of prominent patristic and early modern commentators including Henry Hammond (1605–1660) and Daniel Whitby (1638–1726).</note>—the "natural body" <note>original: "σωμα ψυχικον" (sōma psychikon)</note> as a body of *coarser matter*, and the "spiritual body" <note>original: "πνευματικον" (pneumatikon)</note> as something *more subtle*. For although the natural body is indeed *coarser* than the spiritual body, the adjective "natural" <note>original: "ψυχικον" (psychikon), derived from "psyche" or soul</note> does not designate "coarse," nor can the adjective "spiritual" be translated as *subtle*. This notion will never be confirmed by any examples. Furthermore, everyone sees that the opposition between the natural body and the spiritual body relates to the distinction that the Apostle often makes between "soul" and "spirit" <note>original: "ψυχην" (psuchen) and "πνευμα" (pneuma)</note> in 1 Thessalonians 5:23 and Hebrews 4:12—not as multiple souls, but as different states, aspects, and modes of operation of the same soul: the weaker through the "soul," the stronger through the "spirit"...

### THE ECONOMY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT

...signify. This distinction also underlies the opposition established between the **natural** <note>original Greek: ἀνθρωπον ψυχικον (*anthrōpon psychikon*)</note> or **fleshly** man and the **spiritual** <note>original Greek: πνευματικον (*pneumatikon*)</note> man in 1 Corinthians 2:14–15 and 3:1. Therefore, in our passage, the **Soul** <note>original Greek: Ψυχὴ (*Psyche*)</note> designates for the Apostle the soul of the faithful as it exists in its struggle with the hardships of the present life. Accordingly, the *natural body* <note>original: *corpus ψυχικὸν*</note> *is a body* that serves as an instrument for the soul while it possesses only the first beginnings of Grace in this life. **Spirit** <note>original Greek: Πνεῦμα (*Pneuma*)</note>, however, denotes the *mind* perfected in heaven once the contest of faith is finished; consequently, the *spiritual body* <note>original: *corpus πνευματικὸν*</note> *is the glorified body*, which shall be the eternal dwelling of the Blessed Spirits. Thus, in substance, these descriptions coincide with the descriptions of **heavenly bodies** <note>original Greek: σωμάτων ἐπουρανίων</note> and **earthly bodies** <note>original Greek: σωμάτων ἐπιγείων</note> occurring in verse 40. For the thesis is the same regarding the difference between bodies established by God according to the nature and purpose of each subject—a point the Apostle had explained and illustrated from verse 37, and which he repeats at the end of verse 45 with slightly different words to pave the way for a closer confirmation in the following verses.

XXIV. The confirmation of this thesis is constructed in such a way that the greatest distinction between these kinds of bodies is derived therefrom (verses 45–49): since, just as the faithful are like the first Adam in the former body, so they shall be like the second Adam in the latter. The Apostle handles this argument in the following order:

I. He compares the two supreme examples of the two different states of the rational soul—the first and the second Adam—with one another in verses 45–47. This comparison is two-fold, pertaining both to the *soul* and to the *body*; and both parts rest upon the text of Genesis 2:7, in which both the *production of the soul* and the *formation of the body* are described. In this matter, one should not overlook that the citation formula we read at the beginning of verse 45—**so it is also written** <note>original Greek: οὑτω καὶ γέγραπται</note>—refers not only to the words immediately following: **the first man Adam was made into a living soul**, but also (after a brief illustration) to those added in verse 47: **The first man is of the earth, earthy.** For these latter words are not to be confused with the preceding ones, but must be distinguished from them, as they clearly refer to the first part of Genesis 2:7, in which it is said that *God formed man* **from the dust of the ground.** <note>original Hebrew: עפר מן האדמה (*aphar min ha-adamah*)</note>

*...dust from the earth;* <note>original: *pulverem ex terra*</note> which is clearly the same phrase.

**A.** The first part of the comparison, concerning the different states of the **rational soul** <note>original: *animae rationalis*</note> in verses 45 and 46, is presented first; and rightly so, since the difference between those states is the cause of the difference occurring between the bodily organs. Here:

1. The comparison itself is established, showing how great the diversity is between the state of the mind of the first Adam and the second Adam <note>The "first Adam" refers to the biblical first man, while the "second Adam" is a title for Jesus Christ.</note>. This diversity is suggested in two ways: first, through different names, when **soul** <note>original Greek: ψυχη (*psyche*)</note> is attributed to the former and **spirit** <note>original Greek: πνευμα (*pneuma*)</note> to the latter; and second, through different qualities, when the former is called **living** <note>original Greek: ζωσα (*zōsa*)</note> and the latter **life-giving** <note>original Greek: ζωοποιουν (*zōopoioūn*)</note>. 

In the names themselves, we already observe an opposition. For **soul** is the proper word for a soul governing a natural or "animal" body, but **spirit** usually designates a more excellent state, such as that of the angels and the blessed in heaven. Therefore, this name is most aptly used for the *soul* of the Savior after He has entered into Glory. Indeed, we cannot understand anything else by this **spirit** than the human soul of the Lord itself, but in its glorified state, unless we wish to strain the connection and force of the opposition and obscure the Apostle’s entire reasoning. 

Furthermore, the opposition in the attributes is even clearer. For it is a far greater thing to **give life** <note>original: *ζωοποιεῖν*</note> than merely to **live** <note>original: *ζᾶν*</note>. Thus, the first Adam indeed enjoyed the excellence of being established as a **living soul** <note>original: *animam viventem*</note> in a manner suited to his earthly state. However, this Glory was very small if it is compared to that with which the human mind of the second Adam shines after His exaltation into heaven. For that glory is so great that He can be called a **Life-giving Spirit**. 

For this is that most holy soul which, having been placed as a **guilt offering** <note>original Hebrew: אשם (*asham*); see Isaiah 53:10</note> in **Isaiah 53:10**, earned life for the world when He subjected Himself to the curse on behalf of souls as a **ransom** <note>original: *lytrum*</note> for sin. Hence, by the power of His merit, **just as all die in Adam, so also in Christ shall all be made alive** <note>1 Corinthians 15:22</note>. This seems to us to be the primary reason for this title, although it is often overlooked. For it almost entirely explains it; and although this ransom that acquires life was provided through the humble nature of Christ, nothing—

Hence we clearly do not agree with those who claim that He is called *Lord from heaven* here according to the incarnation itself and a "heavenly origin" of Christ's human nature <note>This refutes the idea that Christ's physical body was brought down from heaven rather than being truly human and born of Mary</note>. 2) That, although that phrase "Lord from heaven" encompasses the whole heavenly glory of Christ, it nonetheless refers more directly and strictly to *His glorified body*. Indeed, the entire heavenly Kingdom which He governs manifests Him as the *Lord from heaven*. As such, He sent forth the Spirit from the heavenly Zion; from heaven He governs the affairs of the world and the Church; from heaven He hears and fulfills the prayers of His people. But precisely in relation to His *body*, He is the *Lord from heaven*, a) because that body shines with heavenly brightness, for which reason He is called the *heavenly* <note>original Greek: *epouranios*</note> Lord. <margin>A.</margin> Generally, it is certain that just as that first man made of dust conducted himself, so also those made of dust *must be*, as long as they live in an earthly state during the course of this life. The faithful themselves bear this image as long as they are clothed in a body composed of coarser elements. This is due to the similarity of functions and duties—such as physical nourishment, the cultivation of society with others, and the propagation of the race—which are required of them just as they were of the first Adam. From this, however, a more certain hope shines upon them: since they are grafted into Christ as the "second Adam" through faith, they know that when they are eventually translated into heaven, they will rejoice in a glorious body like the body of Christ (Philippians 3:21). For once the spirits of the Blessed are admitted into full union with Christ, they will be occupied with Him in the vision of the heavenly Father's face and in His eternal praise; for this purpose, to carry out such a glorious work, they will also enjoy a similar organ <note>The author uses "organ" here to mean the physical instrument of the soul: the body.</note>.

# TO THE KINGDOM OF THE WORLD. CHAPTER IX.

All the Semi-Arians <note>A 4th-century theological group that held the Son was of "similar" essence to the Father, rather than the "same" essence. The author is accusing his critic of leaning toward this heresy.</note> push this point. For it is manifest that such a mode of "production" <note>original: *productionis*. In this context, it refers to how one person of the Trinity originates from another.</note>, although not properly described here, is nonetheless uniquely supposed. However, whoever fosters even the slightest shadow of "production" in their intellect when speaking of the personal communication of essence, I rightly part ways with them, along with the Orthodox Church. 

But perhaps that is not the Author's <note>Referring to the critic or "Censor."</note> intention, and no idea of "production" is directly observed by him. We are certainly inclined to trust his words, by which he declared a little earlier that when **Spiration** <term>Spiration: The theological term for the way the Holy Spirit "proceeds" or "breathes out" from the Father (and/or Son).</term> is used concerning the third person, then every imperfect thing must be separated from that concept of breathing. 

But what, then, does our passage <note>Likely referring to Genesis 2:7, where God breathes life into man.</note> contribute to this matter? If you take away every imperfect thing from Moses's phrasing, what remains that can be used as a "third point of comparison" <note>original: *tertium comparationis*. A logical term for the specific quality two different things have in common when being compared.</note> to illustrate the eternal Spiration through the communication of essence? Nothing is shown here except a contingent work and a production suitable to the imperfection of a creature. Nor is anything brought forward by the Censor in which the power to illustrate the present matter is shown to be located in our passage. 

Unless, perhaps, it is obscurely indicated by a comparison with the passage in **Acts 17:28**, where a communication of this kind is asserted to be hinted at, because of which man is called the *offspring of God*. For this observation of the Censor agrees with his definition of divine **Generation** and **Procession** <note>Generation refers to the Son; Procession refers to the Holy Spirit.</note>, which to him is a communication of **SIMILAR** essence; although that definition labors under many difficulties. 

For he attempts to establish a term hitherto unheard of in the Church by his own private authority; and he confuses the characteristic marks of **Generation** and **Procession** as if they designated one and the same thing, contrary to the nature of the language and the phrasing; and by placing such a great diversity between the divine persons as exists between **SIMILAR** things, he comes too close to that very Polytheism <note>The belief in multiple gods. The author argues that saying the Trinity is made of "similar" essences rather than "the same" essence implies there are three separate gods.</note> into which he tries to draw others under suspicion.

This diversity of bodies, suited to the different states of the inhabiting mind, was the very thing that the Apostle <note>Likely referring to St. Paul's discussion of natural vs. spiritual bodies in 1 Corinthians 15.</note> had undertaken to demonstrate.

XXVI. It was therefore shortsighted of my **Censor**, who repeatedly makes a fresh clamor over nothing <note>original: *novos ex pelvi strepitus*; literally "new noises from a basin," a metaphor for making a loud, empty fuss over trivial matters.</note>—to dispatch him here in three words—when he thought he could illustrate his own hypothesis in this particular passage. In that hypothesis, he asserts that the ***spiration of the third person designates the communication of a SIMILAR essence***. For in order to prove that the ***Spiration of God*** denotes the ***communication of a spiritual essence***, he appeals to our passage <note>Genesis 2:7, regarding the breath of life.</note>, and claims it describes that communication of the mind with man ***on account of which man is called the offspring of God*** (*Acts 17:28-29*). That he did not pay enough attention to the true emphasis of the phrase is easily recognized from what has been observed. For the supreme Author of Scripture did not simply wish to declare, through the ***breathing of the breath of lives into the nostrils of man***, that God created the soul, but *how*—namely, through a certain peculiar operation of the third person <note>The Holy Spirit.</note>, as indicated in sections 18 and 19. And quite discordantly, he transfers this passage—which so excellently illustrates that order of operation (which I recognize is included in the natural Spiration of the Third Person)—to the illustration of his own hypothesis, which he thought must be defended against my "monstrous heterodoxy" as if fighting for "altars and hearths" <note>original: *tanquam pro aris ac focis*; a proverbial expression meaning to defend one's most vital interests or most sacred beliefs.</note>.

XXVII. Meanwhile, in waging war against me, he will have no triumphs; rather, he has offered an open flank to the enemies of the supreme Deity of the Holy Spirit. For indeed, he could hope for no protection, no light for his definition of the ***Spiration of the Third Person***—which he attempts to dictatorially thrust upon the brothers with such arrogance—from this scriptural saying, unless he conceived of a ***communication of essence*** here that happens through the ***production of a new essence***, which is dependent, imperfect, and most different from the divine essence; of the kind that the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arius, who believed that Jesus and the Holy Spirit were created beings, not of the same substance as God the Father.</note> and...

### TO THE KINGDOM OF THE WORLD. CHAPTER IX.

All the **Semi-Arians** <note>original: *Semiariani*; a 4th-century group who believed the Son was of a "similar" substance to the Father, rather than the "same" substance.</note> press this point. For it is manifest that such a mode of production <note>original: *productionis*; the way in which one divine person originates from another</note>, although not specifically described here, is nevertheless uniquely assumed. However, I rightly separate myself from the **Orthodox Church** and from anyone who harbors even the slightest shadow of "production" in their understanding when speaking of the personal communication of essence. 

But perhaps that is not the Author’s intent, and no idea of production is directly observed in his work. We are certainly inclined to trust his words, in which he declared a little earlier that when <term>Spiration</term> <note>original: *Spiratio*; the theological term for the "breathing" or procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and/or Son.</note> is used in reference to the third person of the Trinity, then every imperfection must be separated from that concept of breathing. But then, what does our passage contribute to this matter? If you take away every imperfection from the phrase used by **Moses** <note>Referring to Genesis 2:7, where God breathes life into Adam.</note>, what remains that can be used as a "third point of comparison" to illustrate <term>eternal Spiration through the communication of essence</term>? Nothing is shown here except a contingent work and a production suited to the imperfection of a creature. 

Nor is anything brought forward by the **Censor** <note>The critic challenging the author.</note> to show that the power to illustrate the present subject is found in our text. Unless, perhaps, it is obscurely indicated by comparing the passage in **Acts 17:28** <note>"For in him we live, and move, and have our being... For we are also his offspring."</note>, where a "communication" of this sort is asserted to be hinted at, because of which man is called the "offspring of God" <note>original: *genus Dei*</note>. For this observation by the Censor matches his definition of **Divine Generation and Procession**, which to him is the "communication of a SIMILAR essence"; though that definition suffers from many difficulties. 

For one, he attempts to establish a term previously unheard of in the Church by his own private authority. Secondly, he confuses the defining characteristics of **Generation** <note>the Father begetting the Son</note> and **Procession** <note>the Spirit proceeding from the Father</note> as if they designated one and the same thing, which goes against the nature of the language and the phrasing. Finally, by placing as much diversity between the divine persons as exists between things that are merely SIMILAR, he comes too close to that same **Polytheism** <note>the belief in multiple gods</note> of which he tries to make others suspect.

XXVIII. I noticed in passing, while looking through his most recent booklet, that he tries to fortify the definition he has brought forward with the agreement of certain theologians. Truly—to say nothing of the fact that canonical authority is in no way granted to this term by citing them—these quoted words only represent the private opinions of certain men concerning this mystery, about which, until now, people have disagreed without punishment...

This was something entirely new and clearly unusual in the Church. **XXIX.** While he declares that he bore these consequences I raised with great difficulty, let him learn from his own example and confession what a "pleasant" service he performed for me when, of his own accord and never provoked by any reason, he strove with all his skill to burden me with suspicions of the same kind. But I have by no means brought myself to return like for like and thus avenge an injury—however unfairly inflicted—with another injury, which would be against the duty of a Christian, let alone a theologian. I only wanted to demonstrate that I would not lack weapons if I wished to fight him with equal arms. Others, however, had to be warned **in passing** <note>original: *ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ*</note> about the danger into which the Faith of the Church is brought if words plucked from the [theological] schools are pressed too hard, lest we consume our strength against each other over ambiguous terms while facing common and open enemies. I deplore these unfortunate shifts in the Church of our time in my heart. 

Meanwhile, the fact that the **Censor** is moved by no repentance for the injury inflicted on me has been abundantly proven—not only by the stings (though sometimes dipped in honey) with which his new little book swarms, but also by the very harsh judgment of those whom he has, with marvelous skill, made to conspire against me. By this very act, he has granted me leisure from any further response. As long as he wanders about playing this same tune, the reasons I have publicly declared for why I abstain from a stricter way of dealing with him remain intact. It is right that little books of this kind should rot with the **Annals of Volusius** <note>original: *Volusianis annalibus*; a reference to the Roman poet Catullus, who used this phrase to describe worthless, poorly written literature destined for the trash.</note>. Let him enjoy his ferocity in insulting me while God permits it. Let him proceed to **buffet** <note>original: *κολαφίζειν*; to strike with the fist or treat with indignity.</note> me hypocritically with his followers. I will consider it my part to offer the other cheek as well.

# CHAPTER IX. IN RELATION TO THE KINGDOM OF THE WORLD.

**XXX.** As we now close this unpleasant parenthesis, it is a pleasure to continue the sweetest bond of the Holy Spirit's operations. This is done so that if the unhappiness of our litigious age has cast any clouds over the serenity of the mind, the brilliance of the most radiant theater, which we have begun to open, may dispel them. Truly, this same supreme witness of **God’s Holiness** manages the manifestation of that holiness through various effects—both **ordinary** and **extraordinary**—not only in **Creation**, but also in the **Preservation** and **Governance** of the world.

**XXXI.** To the **ordinary** effects belong the perpetual vigor of the Laws of nature established by the Creator concerning the changes of things, the propagation of species, and the birth and death of individuals; this is considered a continued creation. **Psalm 104:29-30**: *You hide your face, they are dismayed; you take away their spirit <note>original: "Spiritum"; in this context, the breath of life.</note> (of the living creatures), they expire and return to their dust. You send forth your Spirit (the Chaldean <note>Refers to the Aramaic Targum, an ancient Jewish translation and paraphrase of the Bible.</note> rightly translates: your Holy Spirit), they are created, and you renew the face of the earth.* **Psalm 147:18**: *He shall send forth his Spirit, and the waters shall flow.* **Isaiah 40:8**: *The grass withers, the flower falls, because the Spirit of Jehovah blew upon it.* For although these passages describe the Ways of the Lord most directly within the Church, yet since this is done through "hieroglyphics" <note>Used here in the sense of sacred symbols or metaphors drawn from the natural world.</note> drawn from the Kingdom of nature, the <term>operation</term> <note>original: *ἐνέργεια* (energeia); the active power or working.</note> of the Holy Spirit, which He exerts in governing this Universe, is without doubt presupposed in them. It was indeed fitting that He who glorified the Father and the Son should provide, through His omnipotence, a suitable home and theater for rational creatures to recognize the virtues of God. This is even more the case because the **Preservation** of the visible world rested upon the **Counsel of Peace** <note>A theological term for the eternal agreement between the Father and the Son for the salvation of humanity.</note>, and upon the **Suretyship** and **Merit of Christ**. The Holy Spirit could not promote the execution of this plan, nor distribute its fruits, unless the System of this World continued to subsist in the same order that was instilled in it from the beginning. Thus, in truth, that glory which the **Platonists** and other philosophers mistakenly attributed to a **Universal World Spirit** <note>original: "Spiritui Mundi"; a philosophical concept of a soul connecting all living things.</note> belongs to the **Spirit of Jehovah** alone.

**XXXII.** Furthermore, since the most immediate object of that **Counsel** was **Man** himself, the same Holy Spirit is occupied in the formation of every individual, even from the womb. Elihu acknowledged this in **Job 33:4**.

# THE ECONOMY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT IN RELATION TO THE WORLD

*“The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the All-Sufficient gave me life.”* <note>original: "Spiritus Dei me fecit, & Flatus omnisufficientis vivificavit me." A quote from Job 33:4.</note> I would not suggest that these words refer to the first creation of the world, but rather to the person of the Buzite <note>Elihu, one of the speakers in the Book of Job, is identified as a "Buzite."</note>, aiming at both his birth according to the **Law of Nature** and his **Regeneration** through **Grace**. For by alluding to Genesis 2:7, Elihu considers the Holy Spirit as the author of his rational life in the first phrase, and of his *spiritual* life in the second. The celebrated Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian known for "Covenant Theology."</note> has already abundantly proven against Enjedinus <note>György Enyedi (1555–1597), a Socinian theologian who denied the Trinity; the author is defending the orthodox view here.</note> that the third person of the Most Holy Trinity is indicated here, and that the entire mystery of the Trinity is respected in this passage. 

I only profess a disagreement with Cocceius on this one hypothesis: that he refers "making" only to the body, and "giving life" only to animal life viewed in general, and for that reason, "to make" is for him the same as "shaping from clay," while "to quicken and breathe the breath of life" <note>original: "vivificare ac inspirare spiraculum vitæ"</note> he understands as corporal life. Truly, I would rather judge that Elihu, intending to win authority for his words, boasted that he was not only fashioned by the Holy Spirit into a rational creature, but also renewed to a spiritual life, and thus has the right to speak through faith. This fits his purpose more closely, and the most celebrated Interpreter <note>Referring again to Cocceius.</note> was himself almost led to this view earlier, when, illustrating our text with this paraphrase to show the connection, he wrote:

> *I know that of myself I can do nothing: the Spirit made me. The same gives me life, and all my actions, my good thoughts, all knowledge, all uprightness and sincerity of mind is from him. I take diligent care that, unless he moves me, I do and say nothing.*

And surely I would not dare otherwise (compare Romans 15:18), because my life and salvation depend upon him.

**XXXIII.** However, it is right to distinguish here between the *general* operation of the Holy Spirit regarding all humans being born, and the *special* operation regarding the elect. The former consists in the faculties of the mind, which he stirs up, and in the union of the mind with the organic body. The latter renders those faculties such that they can be preserved from the danger of hardening and irremissible sins, and in due time be led into the Kingdom of God. For by nature we are all *children of wrath*. No soul is already sanctified from the beginning of its existence. **Regeneration**, without which no one enters the kingdom of God, presupposes generation. Having been born

# THE KINGDOM OF THE WORLD. CHAPTER IX.

*...that which is born of the flesh precedes that which is born of the Spirit.* <note>The author is quoting the principle that physical life must exist before spiritual regeneration can occur.</note> Nor does the example of John the Baptist stand in the way, concerning whom Gabriel had foretold in **Luke 1:15** that *he would be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb.* <note>original Latin: "adhuc ab utero matris suæ implendus esset Spiritu Sancto"</note> And the fulfillment of the promise appeared soon after in **verse 44**, when the infant in his mother's very womb, as Mary visited Elizabeth, *leaped for joy.* <note>original Greek: "ἐσκίρτησεν ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει"</note> For the Holy Spirit dispensed this in an extraordinary and miraculous way, so that a clear testimony might be shown to the Son of God while He was still hidden in His mother’s womb.

Even so, John's conception in sin preceded this. For without a doubt, even before this leaping, the Baptist's soul was produced in a corrupted little body and was thus stained by <term>original sin</term> <note>original: "labe originali"; the theological concept that all humans inherit a state of sin from birth.</note>. Aside from John, no one else is found who is known to have been filled with the Holy Spirit from the very beginning of the union of the soul with the body before birth. Indeed, it is difficult to conceive how the Holy Spirit can erect a Sanctuary for Himself in a soul as long as the faculties necessary for believing and acting out of faith are plainly lacking. Notwithstanding this, a certain preliminary operation of the Holy Spirit may be admitted, which is consistent with the purpose for which He knows the souls of the elect are destined.

XXXIV. Furthermore, it is clear from the example of **Bezaleel** <note>Bezaleel was the chief artisan of the Tabernacle, endowed by God with special skills (Exodus 31).</note> in **Exodus 31:3** that natural talents and skill regarding the exercise of various arts are the work of the Holy Spirit: *I have filled him with the Spirit of God: in wisdom and in prudence and in experience, and in every kind of craftsmanship.* In these words, there is no need for a "pleonasm" <note>the use of more words than necessary</note> as **Vatablus** <note>François Vatable (d. 1547), a French humanist and Hebraist.</note> allows, nor for a "tautology" <note>redundant repetition</note> as **Drusius** <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant Old Testament scholar.</note> and others maintain—provided that one observes the flow of the accents. Moses asserts generally at the outset that Bezaleel was filled with the Spirit of God; and thereafter he breaks down that assertion into parts, so that he first enumerates the more sublime gifts of Grace and of prophecy itself with which that Man of God was adorned. Therefore **Cartwright** <note>Thomas Cartwright (1535–1603), an influential English Puritan theologian.</note> rightly notes that it appears that whatever wisdom, intelligence, or knowledge Bezaleel possessed, he had it from a singular inspiration of the Holy Spirit. For nothing was more fitting than that this Man of God—who was to build the typical Sanctuary according to the pattern shown to Moses—

He added this reasoning because the word **Spirit** <note>original Hebrew: "Ruach"</note> in the Sacred Scriptures often designates "a gift of God, art, and industry in difficult and ingenious matters." We must not indulge the Socinians <note>A rationalist theological movement that often denied the personhood of the Holy Spirit, viewing it instead as God's power or human talent.</note> in this without cause, as their claimed examples are lacking, and this saying should draw light from that other passage in **Exodus 31:3**, which we have already explained. The Jews were more discerning here, as excerpted by Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf, a prominent Christian Hebraist.</note> in his *Sacred Exercises* (I, chapter 2) and Bartolocci <note>Giulio Bartolocci, author of the "Bibliotheca Rabbinica."</note> in his *Hebrew Library* (Volume I, page 689 and following), from which many truths mixed with falsehoods regarding the more divine knowledge of Bezaleel may be drawn.

# CONCERNING THE KINGDOM OF THE WORLD. CHAPTER IX. 319

...who nevertheless, according to verse 5, *did not know him, yet was moved by an impulse*, for the Lord is said to have stirred up his Spirit to release Israel from captivity, and who by his edict gave such an outstanding testimony to the God of Israel, though unknown to him? Ezra 1:1–4.

XXXVI. The power of the same Holy Spirit is manifested in divine judgments, by which the enemies of the Church are destroyed. This is taught in Job 15:30: *The flame dries up his branch, and he will wither by the Spirit of his mouth.* The **Chaldean** <note>Referring to the Targum, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> rightly rendered the final part: *by the Spirit of the mouth of God* <note>original Aramaic: "be-rucha de-pumeh de-Alaha"</note>. Hence, concerning the expeditions of the Messiah, through which he is to break all the barriers of his Kingdom, it is said in Isaiah 11:4: *And he shall strike the earth with the Rod of his mouth, and by the Spirit of his lips he shall slay the wicked.* The first part seems to refer to God's judgment on the Jews, while the latter part refers to the *utter destruction* <note>original Greek: "panolethrian"</note> of Antichristian forces. This is also clearly applied in 2 Thessalonians 2:8. Other passages also harmonize here, declaring that both judgments are to be carried into effect not without the Holy Spirit. Indeed, the destruction of Jewish pride in Isaiah 40:7 and the thwarting of Antichristian efforts in Isaiah 59:19 are attributed to the Spirit of Jehovah.

XXXVII. The *extraordinary effects* which the Holy Spirit presents in the visible world are Miracles. We have seen from Matthew 12:28 (Chapter 8, Section 18) that *our Savior cast out demons by the Spirit of God*. Therefore, the Spirit's efficacy in the other signs shown by Jesus Christ produced the effect according to the will and command of the Lord. Furthermore, the miracles performed by the Apostles and the other founders of the New Testament Church are numbered among the <term>charismata</term> <note>Spiritual gifts or divine empowerments.</note> of the Holy Spirit in Acts 2:4 and 12:4–11. The miracles performed by the Prophets of the Old Testament are to be derived from the same source. Thus, the stupendous works of Samson *are asserted to have been done when the Spirit of Jehovah came upon him*, as seen in Judges 14:6, 19 and 15:14.

XXXVIII. Moreover, if the Holy Spirit displayed miracles mediately through men, why should those things which proceeded more immediately from God not also be his work? Thus, the *Spirit of the holiness of Jehovah* manifested his presence in the Sanctuary from the beginning through miracles; especially since that *sacred fire*, whether falling from heaven or breaking forth from the inner sanctuary, was a symbol of the Spirit himself, as we taught in Chapter 4, Section 31.

-># THE ECONOMY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT<-

XXXIX. In all of these matters, the singular glory of the *sanctifying Spirit* appears. For here we may assume that through miracles, it is not so much the underlying essences of things that are altered, but rather their accidental properties <note>In traditional philosophy, "accidents" are qualities like color or motion that can change without changing what a thing fundamentally is.</note>; no new matter is created, but instead a different form is brought upon things that already exist. Now, the immediate cause of "form" is *motion*. Since this motion was the work of the Holy Spirit during the creation of the world, why should he not also be active in any notable movement that goes beyond the Laws fixed from the beginning—whether by suspending those laws or accelerating them? We indicated in paragraph 10 how much weight motion has for the *sanctifying of the name of Jehovah*. Indeed, extraordinary motion is much more relevant here than ordinary motion: *firstly*, because it more clearly demonstrates the greatness of that power which regulates uniform motion at its own pleasure and preserves it even under those anomalous impulses; *secondly*, because it shakes off human sluggishness and makes a person more attentive to the ways of God; and *thirdly*, because every such deviation from the laws of nature is subordinated to the divine plan for the salvation of the sinner—it strengthens the word of the Lord, confirms faith, fills the enemies of the Church with terror, and commands us to hope for things from the all-sufficiency of God that seem impossible to human flesh.

XL. The final work attributed to the Holy Spirit in the Kingdom of the World is the *Resurrection of the dead*. For this reason, when Ezekiel was about to foreshadow the mystical Resurrection of the people of God under the image of a literal Resurrection in Chapter 37:9–10, he wrote:

> *And he said to me, Prophesy to the Wind (the Spirit): Prophesy, Son of Man, and say to the Spirit, thus says the Lord Jehovah: from the four winds, come Spirit; and breathe upon these slain, and they shall live. And I prophesied as he commanded me: and the Spirit came into them and they lived.*

It is acknowledged by **Jerome**, **Theodoret**, **Lyra**, **Sanchez**, <note>These are prominent biblical commentators: St. Jerome (4th c.), Theodoret of Cyrus (5th c.), Nicholas of Lyra (14th c.), and Caspar Sanchez (17th c.).</note> and others that *Wind* or *Spirit* <note>original Latin: "Spiritus" can mean wind, breath, or spirit.</note> here does not strictly refer to a movement in the air, although they stop at the idea that it refers only to a *vital spirit* (the force of life). However, this is quite inconvenient and unphilosophical <note>original Greek: "aphilosophon," meaning contrary to sound reasoning.</note>. We maintain, therefore, that it must be understood as the Holy Spirit himself. This is clear: 1) from the fact that it is distinguished from the *four winds*, a number which includes all types of winds in our atmosphere. 2) ...

From the effect itself, since no external or physical breaths contribute anything to the production of the *vital Spirit* in man.
3) From the distinction of the Spirit produced in man through this Wind from mere bodily motion, which was already present, and yet *there was no spirit in them* <note>original Hebrew: ורוח אין בהם (*ve-ruach ein ba-hem*); this refers to the vision of the dry bones in Ezekiel 37:8.</note>, according to verse 8. In this phrase, a remarkable analogy also occurs with the saying in Genesis 2:7, which we have previously illustrated; it quietly reminds us that in the same way the bond between soul and body was established at the beginning of things, it will be restored in the resurrection of the dead. Related to this is what is read concerning the mystical resuscitation of the two witnesses of the Apocalypse in Revelation 11:11: *The Spirit of life from God entered into them* <note>original Greek: Πνευμα ζωης ἐκ του Θεου εἰσηλθεν ἐπ' αὐτους (*Pneuma zōēs ek tou Theou eisēlthen ep' autous*)</note>. *The Spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet*; where again there is an allusion to that which, in the resurrection, will be analogous to the first formation of man.

XLI. More directly, the Apostle promises that the Holy Spirit will be occupied in the resuscitation of the godly in Romans 8:11: *But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you* <note>original Greek: δια του ἐνοικουντος αὐτου πνευματος ἐν ὑμιν (*dia tou enoikountos autou pneumatos en hymin*)</note>. It is not hiddenly implied here that the very resuscitation of our Savior was performed by the Father through the Holy Spirit. Now, it is well known that the preposition *through* <note>original: *dia*</note> denotes both "by means of" and "on account of." Both meanings are excellently joined here. For he who will one day raise believers by means of this Spirit dwelling in them will also do it *on account of* this Spirit—namely, so that the Holy Spirit may consummate the work he himself began, not only in souls but also in bodies. From this, without a doubt, arises the fact that *vivification* <term>Vivification: the act of giving life or making something alive, used here to describe both the physical resurrection and the spiritual awakening of the soul.</term>, both literal and mystical, is considered the proper work of the Holy Spirit in John 6:63 and 2 Corinthians 3:6.

->I.<-

The Kingdom of Grace <term>Kingdom of Grace</term> <note>In traditional theology, the "Kingdom of Grace" refers to the spiritual realm where God rules over the hearts of believers through the Gospel and the Holy Spirit, distinguished from the "Kingdom of Nature" (physical world) and the "Kingdom of Glory" (heaven).</note> now invites us to itself, for it is the proper field of the Operations of the Holy Spirit through the *Application of Salvation* <term>Application of Salvation</term> <note>Known in Latin as *applicatio salutis*, this is the process by which the benefits of Christ's death and resurrection are actually brought to and made effective in the life of a believer.</note> acquired by the Son according to the eternal Good Pleasure. We divide these Operations into two classes. For some are more *extraordinary*, while others are *ordinary*. Through the former, the *Word of the Lord*, as the primary instrument of the dispensation of divine Grace, was handed down to the universal Church as the rule of faith; through the latter, Grace itself is [offered/conferred] to individual persons, especially—

—especially to the elect, and is dispensed in various ways. *Apparitions and Inspirations* belong to the former class <note>The "extraordinary" operations mentioned on the previous page.</note>. The latter class includes those operations which are *common* to all the elect, as well as those *peculiar* to certain individuals. To the common operations, we attribute those saving works which are strictly usually understood under the name of *Grace*. These are themselves distributed in certain degrees according to the various **Economies of the Church's Eras** <term>Economies</term> <note>From the Greek 'oikonomia,' referring to the different ways or "house rules" by which God managed his relationship with humanity at different times in history.</note>—being less perfect under the Law <note>The Old Testament period.</note> and more perfect under the Gospel. However, those operations which belong *specifically* to certain persons encompass the *ordinary Gifts of the Ministers of the Word*.

->II.<-

From this catalog, it is manifest how great a part of Theology is made up of the study of the Operations of the Holy Spirit. However, lest we spread ourselves too thin, we have decided for now to fix our feet only upon the **Apparitions of the Holy Spirit** <term>Apparitions</term> <note>In this context, visible or sensible manifestations where the Spirit was perceived by the senses, such as the dove at Jesus’ baptism or the tongues of fire at Pentecost.</note>. The remaining topics are usually inserted under other theological headings: *Inspirations* are referred to the section on Sacred Scripture; *Saving Operations* to the treatment of Grace; and the *Ordinary Gifts of Teachers* to the chapter on the Ministry of the Church. Additionally, since the Apparitions of the Holy Spirit are all symbolic and significant, they are such that they contain the most elegant "pictures" of the remaining Operations and provide a general introduction to the knowledge of them.

->III.<-

There is no small harvest of *Apparitions of the Holy Spirit*, even if we strike from the list various ones that are numbered among them by certain learned Interpreters. I will pass over those who contended in the ancient Church that **Melchizedek** <note>The mysterious "King of Righteousness" who met Abraham in Genesis 14.</note> was the Holy Spirit, as mentioned in Chapter V, § 3. Friedrich Niehenk** in his *Dissertation on the Three Men Appearing to Abraham* (1707). The latter, however, expressly refutes those who believe the Trinity appeared to Abraham. This was also achieved by the famous **Doutrein** in his commentary on Hebrews 13:2. Their arguments prevail with me, *both* because Abraham showed divine honor to only one of the three, *and* because in two of their number—

Nor is it inconsistent for a created Angel to provide strengthening to the person which our Mediator sustained at that time. Therefore, I think little weight should be given to this conjecture.

IX. Furthermore, I would not easily subscribe to the hypothesis of the renowned Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian who developed "Covenant Theology."</note> and Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent Dutch Reformed theologian known for his commentaries on Isaiah and Revelation.</note>, by which they judge the figure in Revelation 10:1–7 to represent the Holy Spirit. We have already discussed the primary foundation drawn from the analogy of the man clothed in linen in Daniel 10:5–6 in Section 6. Furthermore, nothing prevents us from determining that the Man swearing above the waters of the river in Daniel 12:7 was none other than Michael himself, or the Son of God, a pattern which is clearly alluded to in our passage of Revelation. For four persons appear here: I. *The swearing man* or *Michael* standing for the children of his people above the waters. II. *The man speaking to Daniel*, or *Gabriel*, who addresses Michael in verse 6. III. & IV. Two others distinct from these standing on either bank, whom Cocceius rightly considers as those "expecting the Kingdom of God." The renowned Vitringa adds that he is called *Another Angel* here, distinct from both the *Trumpeting Angels* and the *Priestly Angel* in Chapter 8:3. But not only is a different scene presented here, in which the same person could appear under a different form; it will also become probable below that the *Priestly Angel* represents the Holy Spirit.

However, they fall into the other extreme with Niehenck <note>Georg Friedrich Niehenck (1714–1795), a Lutheran theologian who wrote on theophanies.</note> (Dissertation Section 6), who—despite the consensus of the Fathers, Augustine, Epiphanius, Athanasius (in book 3 of *On the Trinity*), and other Fathers—believes that the Holy Spirit is never introduced in the Sacred Code as an *Angel*. Since they appeal to the "silence of Scripture," the opposite will become clear through a list of the apparitions of the Holy Spirit which we hold to be genuine, among which even angelic forms occur.

And this was undoubtedly the mind of the Hebrews in the **Bereshit Rabba**: <note>Genesis Rabbah, an ancient collection of Jewish homilies and interpretations of the Book of Genesis.</note> *Wherever Michael appears, the Glory of the Shekhinah is there.* <note>original Hebrew: כל מקום שמיכאל נראה שם הוא כבוד השכינה. XII. Furthermore, we shall easily establish that the Column in which the Angel of the Covenant dwelt represented something divine. For the name **Glory of the Lord** is sometimes given to this entire phenomenon considered as a whole, as in 1 Kings 8:10–11, 2 Chronicles 5:11, 13–14, and especially Ezekiel 1:28. And in relation to the <term>antitype</term> <gloss>the New Testament fulfillment of an Old Testament pattern</gloss> of the entire Holy Trinity in the Kingdom of Grace, it is called "Glory" in Isaiah 6:3. Sometimes this name designates one or another principal part of the vision specifically; for example, when the Angel of the Covenant alone, appearing in human form, is called so—which is then transferred by way of fulfillment to the Son of God in Isaiah 40:5, 2 Corinthians 3:18, and Hebrews 1:2. But also quite frequently, that bright Cloud by which the Angel of Jehovah was surrounded—and most strictly the Fire shining within it—is distinguished by the same name. # OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER X.

*...a consuming fire on the peak of the mountain in the eyes of the Children of Israel.* <note>Exodus 24:17</note> In the preceding clause, we understand the **Glory of God** to be the **Angel of the Covenant** <note>original: "Angelum Foederis"</note> dwelling within the Column and calling Moses from it. But in the latter clause, that fiery phenomenon <note>original: "meteoron," referring to an atmospheric or celestial appearance</note> is designated—the one which primarily surrounded the Angel and was seen alone by the people. See also Exodus 16:10. **Buxtorf** <note>Johannes Buxtorf the Younger (1599–1664), a famous scholar of Hebrew and Jewish tradition.</note> has argued this with many examples, though not all of them are equally compelling, in his *History of the Ark of the Covenant*, Chapter 13. However, I do not believe we should agree with him in this: that he refuses to allow the name **Glory of the Lord** to be applied to the Cloud, but instead restricts it specifically to the Fire. For sometimes both are clearly joined together, as in Ezekiel 10:4: *And the Glory of the Lord rose up from the Cherub to the threshold of the House; and the House was filled with the Cloud, and the courtyard was filled with the brightness of the Glory of Jehovah.* That is, the brightness that proceeded from the Cloud that was filling and covering the House. Add Ezekiel 1:4 compared with verse 28. Sometimes the phrase precisely designates the **Cloud** itself, as is established from 2 Chronicles 7:2–3: *And the priests could not enter that House, because the Glory of the Lord had filled the House of the Lord, and all the Children of Israel saw the Fire descending* <gloss>and the glory of the LORD was upon the house</gloss> <note>Hebrew original: "v'kevod Yehovah al ha-bayit"</note> *and the Glory of Jehovah upon the House.* Here, it is apparent from a comparison with 2 Chronicles 5:13 that the phrase "the Glory of the Lord filled the House" alternates with "the Cloud filled the House." Furthermore, the **Glory of the Lord upon the House** seen by all Israel was undoubtedly the Cloud itself, distinct from the Fire filling the House internally, as is suggested in Exodus 40:34–35. And it is asserted in 2 Peter 1:17 that the voice heard **from the cloud** <note>Greek: "ek nephelēs"</note> in Matthew 17:5 proceeded **from the Majestic Glory.** <note>Greek: "hypo tēs megaloprepous doxēs"</note> Thus, although the Hebrews everywhere understand the "Glory of the Lord" most strictly as a fiery splendor—as demonstrated with many authorities by **Danz** <note>Johann Andreas Danz (1654–1727), a theologian and Hebraist at the University of Jena.</note> in his *On the Inauguration of Christ*, section 50, page 177 and following, and by **Majus** <note>Johann Heinrich Majus (1653–1719), a German theologian known for his work on the Shekhinah.</note> in his specific *Dissertation on the Shekhinah*, section 8—nevertheless, these same authors admit along with **Abarbanel** <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a prominent Jewish statesman and Bible commentator.</note> regarding Exodus 40: <gloss>The Glory was never present without the Cloud.</gloss> <note>Hebrew original: "lo hayah kavod mibli anan"</note> From this source, the Gentiles undoubtedly drew their ideas, leading them to invent stories of Gods appearing in a bright cloud and manifesting their Glory to mortals. That famous passage in **Horace**, Book I, Ode 2, verse 30 and following, is well known.

XIII. We are persuaded that the **Holy Spirit** was specifically represented through this **Column** for the following reasons:

A. Since this Column figured some divine subject distinct from the **Son** (who was represented by the human and fiery appearance of the Angel), it follows that it must be referred either *to the Father* or to the *Holy Spirit*. However, it does not pertain to the Father, because it was the outer part of the magnificent Phenomenon <term>original: "Meteori." In this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric or celestial appearance, including clouds and lightning, rather than just falling stars.</term>, the brilliance of which was like the reflection of the fiery form in which the Angel of the Covenant himself shone. We do not deny that this visible **Glory of the Lord** was a shadow of the Glory of the entire Trinity, as follows even from the Trisagion <term>Trisagion: The "thrice-holy" hymn found in Isaiah 6:3 ("Holy, Holy, Holy"), often interpreted as a reference to the three persons of the Trinity.</term> in Isaiah 6:3. Yet, nothing occurs in it that expresses the Father hypostatically <term>hypostatically: Relating to the distinct "personhood" or individual subsistence of one member of the Trinity as opposed to the shared divine essence.</term> in this figure; for the Glory of the Father is not recognized immediately by a sinner, but through the Work of the Son and the Holy Spirit. Where the Glory of the Son and the Holy Spirit is, there is the Glory of the Father. The divine virtues which they reveal are the virtues of the Father himself, according to whose good pleasure the entire dispensation of salvation proceeds. And on this ground, *the form of the Father was also seen by the Jews*, even if not perceived, as in John 5:37; namely, insofar as the fire in the cloud represented the total holiness of God, but demonstrated through the fiery Angel of Jehovah and through the fiery Column. Compare what we have noted regarding the cited passage in the Commentary.

# ON DIVINE MANIFESTATIONS

Immediately, the generous promise of rain is joined with the fearsome majesty of the divine manifestation on Mount Sinai. And from this, the opportunity arises to illustrate the very phrase of the "outpouring of the Holy Spirit" found in the Prophets through an allusion to the Cloud that once expanded over the whole of Israel, dripping with plentiful waters. Indeed, the saying in Joel 3:1 <note>In English Bibles, this is Joel 2:28: "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh."</note>, when considered in its context, is not inappropriately referred to here—both because of the symbols occurring in verse 3, and because a finger is pointed at the same time to the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the seventy Elders under the sign of the descending Cloud, which is described in Numbers 11:25–26. 

From this, it also becomes clear why the Apostle says all the Israelites were "baptized by the Cloud and the Sea" in 1 Corinthians 10:2; namely, because a plentiful dew descended from that Cloud upon the Israelites. In terms of symbolic significance, this can be compared with the Sea in such a way that the Sea expresses the righteousness of Christ flooding every kingdom of darkness, while the Cloud expresses the Grace of the Holy Spirit. In this way, a most elegant analogy exists between that Legal <note>referring to the Mosaic Law</note> Baptism and the Evangelical <note>Gospel-based</note> Baptism. Compare the things already noted in the Commentary on John 1:33.

XVI. D. But the very *connection* <note>original Greek: συνάφεια (*synápheia*), meaning a close union or binding together</note> of the figure with the thing it represents also greatly favors our argument, as must be shown in a few points.

1) *The substance of the Pillar was composed of Fire and Cloud; the former being an emblem of Holiness, the latter of divine Goodness and Mercy.* The illustrious <term>Vitringa</term> <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a prominent Dutch theologian known for his work on biblical symbolism.</note> in his *Sacred Observations* V. 16, follows those who believe the *Cloud foreshadows the incomprehensibility of God.* It is certain that the pagans <note>original: *gentiles*</note> intended this when they veiled their appearing gods in a cloud, as is evident from <term>Majus's</term> <note>Johann Heinrich Majus (1653–1719), a German Hebraist and theologian.</note> *Observations* book IV, page 67. However, I do not think that is the focus here. For our Pillar did not display a dark cloud, but a *bright and transparent Cloud.* Without it, even the fiery splendor could not have been beheld without harm. When *God is said to dwell in unapproachable light* (1 Timothy 6:16), this pertains as much to the *Fire* as to the *Cloud*, or rather, even more to the *Fire*. Hence, the oracle of the Colophonian Apollo in <term>Lactantius</term> <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325 AD) who often quoted pagan sources to support Christian truths.</note> book I, section 7, describing the incomprehensible God, says:

-> *A name not even contained by reason, dwelling in fire.* <-
<note>original Greek: Οὔνομα μηδὲ λόγῳ χωρούμενον, ἐν πυρὶ ναίων.</note>
*Whose name surpasses every grasp of reason, who dwells in fire.*

Furthermore, among the pagans, a visible Cloud was held as a symbol of *Grace* and divine protection, as is evident from that passage in <term>Euripides'</term> *Heraclidae*, Act IV:

-> *For the twin stars, standing beneath the equestrian yokes, covered the chariot in a murky cloud.* <-
<note>original Greek: Δισσὼ γὰρ ἀστέρ’ ἱππικοῖς ὑπὸ ζυγοῖς / Σταθέντ’ ἔκρυψαν ἅρμα λυγαίῳ νέφει.</note>
*For the twin stars, having glided down and standing over the horse-yokes, enveloped the chariot in a dark cloud.*

This is surely the "Two-horse Chariot" <note>original: *Biga*</note> of virtues which God, in the work of Salvation, especially wished to establish as the object for the celebration of His name. This is what the colors of the *Rainbow* suggest. This is observed in the titles of the Saints in prayers directed to God. This is breathed forth by the mixture of *white and red* colors occurring throughout. Therefore, the conjunction of two seemingly contrary elements, *Fire and Water*, illustrates the balance <note>original: *temperamentum*</note> that is brought to the *Holiness* of God through His *Mercy* in saving the sinner; or rather, the way in which God wished to manifest the inseparable bond of both virtues. XVII. The man **clothed in linen** (Ezekiel 9:2 ff.) has appeared to most interpreters to be a divine person. And not without reason, since six angels, the executors of divine judgments, obey Him as their Prince and depend on His direction. Additionally, there is an analogy between this vision and the visions in the Book of Revelation <note>original: *Apocalypticis*, referring to the visions of St. John</note> (chapter 7:2 and 8:3 ff.), which we will explain below. Nor is this contradicted by the obedience that the Man testifies He performed at Jehovah’s command in verse 11. This is easily explained by the way the operations of the Holy Spirit depend on the operations of the Son, which we explained in Chapter 8, especially §39 ff. Nevertheless, the Church Fathers everywhere—and among them **Irenaeus**, **Jerome**, **Gregory the Great**, and **Rupert** <note>likely Rupert of Deutz, a prominent 12th-century theologian</note>, followed by many more recent authors cited by **Cornelius a Lapide** and **Calovius** <note>Abraham Calovius, a leading 17th-century Lutheran theologian; a Lapide was a contemporary Jesuit commentator</note>—maintain that the Son of God is meant here. They use a weak argument, namely that the *linen garments* <note>original Hebrew: בדים (*badim*)</note>, or **priestly linen garments**, are attributed to Him. However, there is no necessity to restrict the term *linen* to priestly garments, even though other subjects
