However, the greatest opposition to this hypothesis <note>The "hypothesis" that the man in linen is merely a regular angel or a different manifestation of Christ</note> is that he is sent by the *Glory of Jehovah*, and in *verse 11* he expressly declares that he has carried out His commands. For since He who appeared to Ezekiel with the *Glory of Jehovah*—sitting in the appearance of a Man upon a fiery Throne in *chapter 1:27, 28*—was the Son of God, this Man was certainly distinct from Him. Appeal is often made to the various relations <note>original: *scheses*</note> of the same person being depicted through different symbols. But a personal distinction cannot be more clearly expressed than it is in this passage. Two rational subjects are not only distinguished, but one is *commanding* and the other is *obeying*. Such an example does not occur elsewhere, and if it did, the argument we usually seek from symbolic apparitions to prove the distinction of the persons of the Holy Trinity would be rendered useless. Therefore, the celebrated Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology"</note> and his followers—among whom, after the famous Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a theologian and Hebraist</note>, I myself once counted my name in my second exercise on Psalm 45, section 14—rightly preferred that the *Holy Spirit* be introduced here. In Him, at least, all the attributes that occur here, both regarding his *personal appearance* and his *actions*, harmonize perfectly.

### XVIII. *The following pertain to his personal appearance.*

1) *The singular human appearance of the Man*, which is an emblem of wisdom and strength, and is frequently proposed in the following passages as an image of the Holy Spirit, especially when those works of His are displayed which are brought forth through the ministry of men, who are His instruments, vessels, and temples.

2) *The clothing: a) linen*, which according to Cocceius signifies those *whom the Spirit carries and holds joined to Himself, in whom He dwells and works.* It is simpler to maintain that *linen* remains the customary symbol of purity, from which the Spirit receives the title *Holy*. Hence, common *linen* was used for the priests not only in the rituals of the true God, but also in the most ancient sacred rites of the Gentiles, as well as for a covering of sacred things. Apuleius <note>A 2nd-century Roman writer and philosopher</note> in his *Apologia* says, among other things: <note>original: "Mundissima lini seges, inter optimas fruges terrae exorta, non modo indutui & amictui sanctissimis Aegyptiorum Sacerdotibus, sed opertui quoque inde rebus sacris usurpatur."</note> *“The cleanest crop of linen, arising from among the best fruits of the earth, is used not only for the clothing and garments of the most holy Egyptian priests, but also for the covering of sacred objects.”* And the white color of linen, and especially of *fine linen* <note>original: *byssini*</note>, which was most in use by the Priests, increases the emphasis of the emblem.

There was attached to his *loins* a <term>scribe’s ink-horn<note>original Hebrew: *qeset ha-sofer*</note></term>, as is commonly held by the <term>Chaldean Targum<note>The Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note></term> and the <term>Vulgate<note>The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note></term>; although <term>Castell<note>Edmund Castell (1606–1685), an English orientalist.</note></term> and <term>Michaelis<note>Likely Johann David Michaelis, a prominent 18th-century biblical scholar.</note></term> prefer, following the <term>Septuagint<note>The Greek Old Testament.</note></term>, to translate *qeset* as a *belt* or *girdle*. They do so not only because the loins are an unsuitable place for an ink-horn, but also because the "sealing" of the faithful was performed not so much by writing as by the impression of a *signet-ring*. Castell, however, incautiously followed them by translating the phrase "scribe’s ink-horn" as *made of sapphire*, as if the Hebrew text read *ha-sappir* <note>meaning "the sapphire"</note> instead of *ha-sofer* <note>meaning "the scribe"</note>. Without doubt, however, that belt was of the more ornate kind, for it was such as befitted a Royal Scribe, a Princely Person with intimate access to the King, and the Keeper of his Seal. Perhaps such belts were so constructed that the King’s *Seal*, or some other badge of high office, was attached to them. Indeed, that a Seal should be counted among this man’s equipment is clear from comparing the <note>The Hebrew letter 'Tau'</note> in verse 4. We have previously presented the Holy Spirit under the emblem of a Scribe in our second exercise on Psalm 45, sections 11 and following. I would merely observe here that the Holy Spirit is depicted in such a way that he is active not so much in himself, but through his ministers and their word. Thus, the *linen garment*—*white* and *priestly*—exhibits those very virtues and that dignity with which these instruments of Jehovah's glory are adorned by the Holy Spirit. They are the *Scribes* or <term>Amanuenses<note>Secretaries or artistic assistants who write down the words of another.</note></term> of God, as I taught in the cited work on pages 88 and 89. The *Belt* befits them because the Majesty of the heavenly King shines through them and is maintained through their discipline. The *Ink*—or, if you prefer, the *Oil*—represents the very gifts of the Holy Spirit which are conferred upon others through them. For the *ointment* of the Holy Spirit is contrasted with *ink* in 2 Corinthians 3:3 <note>The author cites 3:2, but the comparison of ink vs. Spirit is in 3:3.</note>. And we have taught at John 6:27 that the *Seal*, insofar as it exists on a Royal ring, foreshadows the Holy Spirit.

*...take righteous coals, and throw them over the city.* This is an image of the Holy Spirit, insofar as He is the *Spirit of judgment and of burning <note>original: "Spiritus judicii & exustionis"</note> in Isaiah 4:4*, intended not only for the purification of the Church, but also for the consumption of hypocrites. XX. Furthermore, it is not uncommon, at least in prophetic visions, to represent the *Holy Spirit* under the appearance of a *River*. To this we must refer the *waters flowing out from under the threshold of the house in Ezekiel 47:1 and following*, to which a *life-giving power* is assigned in verse 9 with such emphasis that it is appropriate only to the Divine Spirit. Whether one looks to the *waters drawn from the Rock*, or to the *channels of the Temple leading water into the brook Kidron*, this emblem became familiar to the Prophets. To this point belongs especially *Isaiah 44* and *Zechariah 14:8.* Nor do I fear to compare that vision which was offered to *Daniel in Chapter 7:10*, namely of a fiery Throne, *with a river of fire flowing from his presence.* That this river of fire represented the Holy Spirit is acknowledged by **RUPERT OF DEUTZ**, **COCCEIUS**, and other more recent interpreters. **WILHELM LYSER** illustrated this in a special *Pentecostal Program*, which **CALOVIUS** inserted into his *Commentary on this passage*, and it deserves to be examined here. Rightly indeed are the *baptism of fire in Matthew 3:11* and the procession <note>original: "ἐκπόρευσις" (ekporeusis), the theological term for the Holy Spirit's origin or "flowing out" from the Father.</note> of the Holy Spirit, as well as the *river of the water of life in Revelation 22:1 proceeding from the Throne of God and the Lamb*, compared with this description. For we do not conceive of the river here as being truly ignited, after the likeness of *Phlegethon* <note>In Greek mythology, the Phlegethon is one of the five rivers of the underworld, consisting of fire rather than water.</note>, celebrated in the fables of the Poets, but as a river rolling living waters, and thus the same as that which was shown to Ezekiel, since the same renewal of the Church is being considered. It is called, however, a *river of fire* because the fire of the Throne and of its wheels shone back in it: in the same manner as in *Revelation 15:2, a glassy sea mixed with fire* is presented, on account of the fire of either the Throne itself, or...

# CONCERNING APPARITIONS

...of the altar of burnt offerings, as it seemed to some, shining within it.

XXI. The richness of this symbolic image <note>original: "emblematis"</note> is extraordinary. *Living waters* are a figure for the gifts of the Spirit, which are pure and eternal by their very nature; as for their fruits, they quench the soul's thirst, provide refreshment to the conscience, heal its diseases, and make the banks of the Church fertile. A *river* of such waters depicts the abundant measure of these same gifts, which are destined to pour themselves out far and wide, gradually overwhelming the entire earth, as it were. These are the same waters that the fountain possesses and that the river carries along; but first they are in the fountain, and then in the river, though by being carried forth they are eventually adapted for many different uses. In this way, the Spirit applies the same gifts that the Son acquired. *The acquisition is assumed as the foundation, but the application ensures that those gifts reach their intended purpose in the chosen ones.* Just as the waters in that vision were more effective at reflecting the glowing splendor of the fiery Throne like a mirror the more pure and crystalline they were, so the gifts of the Grace of the *Holy Spirit* are the medium through which the brilliance of divine holiness and the rigor of His justice are recognized and demonstrated in the Church.

XXII. This comparison of Daniel with the Apocalypse <note>the Book of Revelation</note> rests on an even surer foundation because, in that same vision, something is immediately added that John's Apocalypse repeated from it: namely, the Son of God coming to the *Ancient of Days* <note>original: "permanentem dierum"</note> <term>עִם־עֲנָנֵי שְׁמַיָּא; with the clouds of heaven</term>. For that must certainly be compared with Revelation 14:14, where a bright white Cloud appears—that is, a cloud heavy with fire shining through it—upon which sits one like the Son of Man. This bright white Cloud undoubtedly coincides with the <term>θρονω λευκω μεγαλω; great white throne</term>, the *Great and spacious White Throne upon which He sits, from whose face heaven and earth flee*, in Revelation 20:11. For it is clear from a comparison with verse 12 that the vision of Daniel is alluded to there as well. Indeed, the Son of God established the Cloud filled with fire as a perpetual sign of His glorious presence. This is evident from the history of His birth, baptism, transfiguration <note>original: "glorificationis in monte"</note>, ascension, and the appearances made to Stephen and Paul. The predictions regarding His future coming, which is to be expected in certain stages, confirm this. To the citations just mentioned, Matthew <note>likely referring to Matthew 24:30 or 26:64</note> deserves to be added...

XXIII. From this foundation, I have asserted in the *Bremensis Library* <note>original: "Biblioth. Brem. Class. For that Jewish tradition is well known—which learned men consider older than the Talmud itself, since it appears on every page in the *Midrashim*, in *Bereshit Rabba* <note>an ancient commentary on Genesis</note>, and similar monuments, and is cited in the Babylonian Gemara in the tractate *Sanhedrin*—specifically, how they reconcile those two sayings from Daniel 7 (*Behold, he comes in the clouds of heaven*) and Zechariah 9 (*He will come poor and riding on a donkey*): <note>original Hebrew: "זכו עם ענני שמיא לא זכו עני ורוכב על חמור"</note> *If the Jews are worthy, the Messiah will arrive in the clouds of heaven; if unworthy, he will appear poor and sitting on a donkey.* Following others, the illustrious Carpzov <note>Johann Benedict Carpzov II, a prominent 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> illustrated this tradition extensively in his *Academic Disputations* VII and especially IX, sections 5 and following.

# ON APPEARANCES

I was convinced by two arguments, which it will be helpful to set down and explain here.

**A.** First, because the name *Gabriel*, just like *Michael*, fits created angels neither *literally* nor *symbolically*. It does not fit *literally* because angels do not use human language, nor does Scripture mention any of their names anywhere except for these two which are under discussion. This undermines the opposing arguments brought forward by Bynaeus <note>Anthony Bynaeus, a 17th-century Dutch theologian</note> in *On the Nature of Jesus Christ*, Book I, chapter 1, section 3. It does not fit *symbolically* because the name contains nothing except what is common to all angels, as the illustrious Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a famous federal theologian</note> acknowledged; he admitted that this name belongs to all the holy myriads, of whom *one speaks* for the rest—though this seems a forced explanation. 

On the other hand, those who arrange the <term>hierarchical orders of angels</term> <note>the traditional ranking of angels into nine "choirs" such as Seraphim, Cherubim, etc.</note> in their own imaginations have devised various theories regarding the name's meaning. For instance, Jerome says: *Because the vision concerned battles and the struggles of Kings, indeed even the successions of Kingdoms, Gabriel—who is placed in charge of battles—is assigned to this duty.* 

This gave rise to "sword-fights" <note>intellectual duels or heated debates</note> among the Roman Catholic theologians themselves as to which order of angels they should assign Gabriel. Some, following the system of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, whose writings defined the celestial hierarchy</note> more strictly, relegated him to the lowest order. Others, fearing this might seem insulting to his mission to Mary, the <term>Mother of God</term> <note>original Latin: "Deipara", the God-bearer</note>, placed him among the highest angels and assigned him the second place after Michael. Cornelius à Lapide <note>a prominent Jesuit biblical commentator</note> reviews these opinions in his commentary on Daniel 9:21. Most thinkers find it better to seek the reason for his naming in his "fortitude" or strength. But even though they stick closer to the literal meaning of the name <note>Gabriel is traditionally translated as "Strength of God" or "Man of God"</note>, they offer nothing that distinguishes one specific angel from another. Compare this with Psalm 103:20.

Others attempt to extract a more impressive argument from this name regarding Gabriel's mission. For example, Proclus, Archbishop of Constantinople, in his *Second Oration on the Incarnation* (found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume VI, page 590), writes: *What indeed should you interpret "Gabriel" to mean? Prick up your ears and learn: "God and man." Therefore, because He whom the angel announced was both God and man, the angel anticipates the miracle of the event by the significance of his name, so that he might more easily persuade us of the divine plan.* 

However, nothing unique appears here that would distinguish this angel not only from the <term>Angel of the Covenant</term> <note>a title often used for the pre-incarnate Christ in the Old Testament</note> in the Old Testament, but even from the angel who appeared to Joseph. Salmero <note>Alphonso Salmeron, a Jesuit theologian and one of the founders of the Society of Jesus</note> (Volume III, chapter 3) imagines that "Gabriel" is the same as *My man is God*, in order to signify the birth of Him who would be born of a Virgin,

<meta>This page continues the author's analysis of the name and identity of the angel Gabriel. # THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER X.

*...she might bring forth, and instead of a Man, have God—that is, the Holy Spirit—who would effect this conception.* <note>original: "pareret, ac pro Viro Deum, id est, Spiritum Sanctum, qui conceptum hunc operaretur, haberet."</note> Thus, in a convoluted way, the name which would have been suitable for Mary is assigned to the Angel. And what, I ask you, does this have to do with the Angel who appeared to Daniel, and just now to Zechariah? It is strange, however, that the Roman Catholics <note>referring to "Pontificios" or papists</note> did not think it better, for the sake of amplifying the honor shown to Mary, to classify Gabriel among the uncreated Angels. Indeed, some among the Jews are not far from this view, though they have other intentions. Thus we read in the *Bemidbar Rabbah* <note>A classic Jewish midrashic commentary on the Book of Numbers</note>, section 2: 
*Gabriel stands before the presence of the Lord at the banner of the tribe of Judah, next to Moses and Aaron toward the East.* Why was his <margin>Gabriel</margin> <note>original Hebrew: גבריאל</note> name so called? Concerning *Judah* it is written: *For Judah prevailed* <note>original: "gavar," the root of Gabriel</note> *over his brothers* (1 Chronicles 5:2). Furthermore it is written: *And his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God* <note>original: "Pele Yoetz El Gibbor" (Isaiah 9:6). The author is linking "Gabriel" (Man of God/Strength of God) to the "Gibbor" (Mighty) of the Messiah.</note> (Isaiah 9:6). Behold, from this comes the name <margin>Gabriel</margin> <note>original Hebrew: גבריאל</note>.

The emphasis of the name is therefore more fully exhausted when we apply it to the uncreated Angel <note>a term used by some theologians to refer to the second or third persons of the Trinity when appearing in the Old Testament</note>. Various translations of it can be obtained, depending on the consideration of the inserted *Yod* <note>The Hebrew letter 'i' or 'y' between the roots 'Gabar' and 'El'</note>. For we do not dwell on Maimonides <note>A famous medieval Jewish philosopher</note>, Hiller, and others who translate it as *Man of God*, because a mere appearance as a *Man* was not a sufficient reason for imposing the name on the Angel. If it is taken as a pronominal suffix <note>i.e., the 'i' meaning 'my'</note>, this sense results: *My strength* or *My victory is the mighty God*, as Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a prominent 17th-century theologian</note> prefers; or *My strength is of the mighty God.* If the letter is merely epenthetic <note>a connector letter with no meaning of its own</note>, then it means *Strength of the Mighty God*, or *The Mighty God is Strength.* This latter is the simplest of all, because it is most frequent in the formation of names of this type. Thus, for example: <margin>Channiel</margin> <note>original Hebrew: חניאל</note> *Channiel, Grace of God;* <margin>Adriel</margin> <note>original Hebrew: עדיאל</note> *Adriel, Flock of God;* <margin>Abdiel</margin> <note>original Hebrew: עבדיאל</note> *Abdiel, Servant of God*, etc. Add to this that the Apostle <note>the author of the Book of Hebrews</note> seems to have considered the name *Melchizedek* <note>original Hebrew: מלכיצדק</note> in this same way, rendering it: *King of Righteousness* <note>original Greek: "Basileus dikaiosynes"</note> (Hebrews 7:2). Since this name, whatever it may be, certainly has God as its Author, it follows that it must be taken in its full emphasis. This occurs when it is ascribed to that divine Person through whom God most powerfully demonstrates His Strength. Hence we have considered him as the *Sceptre of Jehovah’s Strength* from Psalm 110:2, in Chapter 8, section 37. Compare Chapter 9, section 3.

XXVI. B. It is added that there are attributed to Gabriel those things which belong to the person...

But other signs of Divinity also appear. XXVII. Most of the objections that can be raised against our hypothesis have already been addressed through these observations. One might perhaps dwell on the objection raised by Maracci <note>Ludovico Maracci (1612–1700), an Italian orientalist and translator of the Quran</note>—following other Catholic writers—against Gelaleddin <note>Jalal al-Din al-Mahalli, a famous commentator on the Quran</note> (in his notes on Sura II, note 87 of the Quran) and other interpreters of the Quran who understand the Holy Spirit to be Gabriel. Maracci objects that Gabriel promised the most Holy Virgin Mary that the Holy Spirit would come upon her—who was someone other than Gabriel himself—and that this same Gabriel predicted concerning John the Baptist that he would be filled with the Holy Spirit, as if with someone distinct from himself. However, it is clear that this argument has no force, given the very constant custom by which divine persons speak of themselves in the third person. Our Savior himself especially imitates this in the Gospel history, so often instituting a discourse concerning the *Son of Man* as if speaking of some third person.

XXVIII. Nor is there more weight in what the renowned Witsius <note>Herman Witsius (1633–1708), a Dutch theologian</note> especially urges in his *Sacred Miscellanies* (Book I, chapter 6, § 12): that before this is admitted, it must be shown that the Holy Spirit has exhibited himself elsewhere in a prophetic vision to be seen in the form of some majestic Angel. For since there can be no doubt regarding the truth that the Holy Spirit, together with Christ, undertook the office of a Messenger sent by God in the <term>Economy of Salvation</term> <note>The theological term for God’s plan and management of the world, specifically regarding human redemption</note>, nothing prevents us from judging that this relationship of the Holy Spirit was represented enigmatically there, where the connection of the entire vision openly favors it. Although, even here, other emblematic representations tending toward the same conclusion are not lacking.

Interpreters prefer, and wish all these things to be attributed to the *Man standing among the myrtles* <note>Zechariah 1:8</note>, whom the Jews themselves cannot deny is a divine person, and whom the best commentators grant is the Son of God, as **CALOVIUS** <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a leading Lutheran orthodox theologian</note> demonstrates more extensively on this passage. However, **GROTIUS** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian known for his historical-linguistic approach to the Bible</note> conceives here, just as in Daniel, a dialogue between two Angels, Michael and Gabriel; following in his footsteps, the celebrated **COCCEJUS** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian who emphasized the "covenants" of the Bible</note> added that two divine persons, the Son and the Holy Spirit, are conversing. **HOEKIUS**, **NEMETHI**, and others seem to have rightly followed him. For unless you wish to obscure the plain construction of the text without cause, you must admit that the *Angel speaking to the Prophet* in verse 9 is different from the *Man standing among the myrtles* described in verse 8. This is even more compelling when, according to **TARNOVIUS** <note>Johann Tarnow (1586–1629), a Lutheran theologian</note>, the words <note>original: המלאך הדובר בי</note> are translated: *The Angel speaking in me*. Nor is it less manifest in verse 13 that a distinction is made between *Jehovah*, and the *Angel speaking to the Prophet*, and that he brought forth *good words, words of consolation* to him, which are the words in verse 14 and following, announced to Zechariah by the Angel. The tenor of these words is such that the Son of God is introduced as the speaker. We conclude, therefore, that the Angel bringing forth the words of the Son of God as the words of a person distinct from himself was different from the Man standing among the myrtles who represented the Son of God. Since those words of Jehovah contain comfort directed at the complaint in verse 12, I would not doubt that the words of verse 12 are also the words of the same Angel who was speaking to the Prophet. For there was no need for the famous **COCCEJUS** to refer these to the Son of God, since the Holy Spirit is also the *Advocate* and *Intercessor* <note>original: "Advocatus atque Interpellator"</note> of the faithful. Thus two figures are presented here, both called the *Angel of the Lord* <note>original: "Angelus Jehova"</note> without distinction, equal in dignity. Those who allow the former to be the Son of God have no reason to deny that the latter designates his perpetual companion, the Holy Spirit.

XXXI. We have already mentioned another emblem of the Holy Spirit appearing in Zechariah 3:9, compared with chapter 4:10, in our earlier discussions in Chapter 4, § 24. Likewise, insofar as he is the *Spirit of faith* in the Church, the Spirit looks forward through the Church constantly across the seven ages toward the unique object of all faith, love, and obedience.

I believe that the assembly of the Lord's disciples mentioned in Acts 1:15 gathered on the day of Pentecost in the usual place of divine worship. While they were there awaiting the fulfillment of the Lord’s promise, a great storm arose. Out of a condensed cloud and a wind from heaven, the whole house was filled—just as had occurred long ago at the dedication of Solomon’s Temple—not shaking the building, but filling it. Then, a magnificent fiery phenomenon appeared, much like a flash of lightning. I gather from the present participle **"dividing"** <note>Greek: *διαμεριζόμεναι* (diamerizomenai)</note> that this presented a single mass of fire from the beginning, but it gradually divided itself into many flames. These were not called "**tongues of fire**" <note>original: *linguae ignis*</note> merely through a Hebrew idiom (as those who compare this to Isaiah 5:24 would suggest), but—as the word **"as if"** <note>Greek: *ὡσει* (hōsei)</note> explicitly teaches and the purpose of the vision required—they actually had the appearance of **tongues**. The term is not accurately translated as "distributed," but rather "**which were dividing**," or in the middle voice, "**which divided themselves**." Meanwhile, this fiery meteor, whose ends were divided into the shapes of fiery tongues, spread out not only over the whole group but also over the heads of each individual—not only of the Apostles, but also of the rest of the disciples, *as many as were present*. That is to say, not even one was excepted (so there is no need to assume any exaggeration here). It then "**settled upon them**," or rested for a short while. For the word **"to sit"** <note>Greek: *καθίζειν* (kathizein)</note> is equivalent to **"to remain"** <note>Greek: *μένειν* (menein)</note> as seen in Luke 24:49 and Acts 18:11, a term attributed to the symbol of the Holy Spirit's presence in John 1:32.

Thus, a singular analogy can be observed between this outpouring of the Holy Spirit and that distribution among the **70 Elders** found in Numbers 11:25–26. For when the Lord descended to Moses in the Cloud of Glory—or the **Divine Presence** <note>Hebrew: שכינה (Shekinah), the visible manifestation of God's glory</note>—and took some of the Spirit that was upon Moses and placed it upon them, it is immediately added that the Spirit **"rested"** upon those seventy Elders, and they straightway **"prophesied."** It appears most likely to me that a certain visible expansion of the fiery Cloud from the head of Moses over the heads of the Elders is being described there as well. However, whether that fire settling upon the heads of the Apostles had the appearance of many individual fiery tongues, or whether it was one continuous phenomenon resting upon them all at once, I would not determine rashly—though I lean toward the latter opinion. The matter would be different if the reading of the **Canterbury Codex** <note>Also known as Codex Bezae, a famous 5th-century manuscript of the New Testament held at Cambridge</note>...

XXXIV. Once again, therefore, a Sign appears here that alludes to the Pillar of Cloud and Fire, the Mystery of which we have just explained in relation to the Holy Spirit. In this way, our Savior more than satisfied the demand of the Jews—mentioned in section 21—that he should show a *sign from heaven*. He used the same sign to establish the Law in Zion as had once been used to confirm the Law on Mount Sinai. Indeed, I am almost persuaded that some similar visible symbol of the Holy Spirit is hinted at when, on certain extraordinary occasions, the Holy Spirit is said to have *fallen* (like *Fire* gliding down from heaven) upon certain individuals, as recorded in Acts 8:16, 10:44, and 11:15. Only one less common detail is added here: namely, the shape of the ignited Tongues, as if flashing forth and *divided* from that Fire. Nothing quite like this has been observed before in the form of the sacred and mystical Fire of the Old Testament. Some writers, such as **HENRY MORE** in *The Mystery of Godliness, book V, chapter II*, stop at the idea that these *divided tongues* were merely an external symbol of that internal faculty granted to the Apostles to speak in various languages, even though they had never learned them. However, such an explanation does not fully exhaust the mystery. For the *Gift of Tongues* <term>Gift of Tongues: The miraculous ability to speak in foreign languages previously unknown to the speaker, known as glossolalia or xenoglossy</term> was immediately and externally joined to this visible sign by actual experience; therefore, it did not require such a representation for its own sake. Rather, the gift itself should be numbered among the Miracles that illustrated and confirmed other heavenly Mysteries. Furthermore, this spiritual gift did not remain in the Church for long, nor did it seem to involve a permanent knowledge of languages; instead, it appears to have been an immediate Operation of the Holy Spirit that manifested only on specific occasions. In this regard, the observations made by **SCOTANUS** in *Miscellaneous Disputations, VII* are not to be dismissed. It is more probable, therefore, that the Lord intended to foreshadow something even higher.

...[the authors] wish to express the hypostatic <note>Refers to the personal relationship between the distinct persons of the Trinity</note> relationship of the Holy Spirit to the Son and His kinship with the *Substantial Word*, as **Gregory of Nazianzus** puts it. **Wegner** has collected several of their passages in the work cited, from which we provide here only the words of **Gregory the Great**: *He was shown in tongues because the same Spirit is co-eternal with the Son, and the tongue has the greatest kinship with the word. For the Son is the Word of the Father. And because the substance of the Spirit and the Word is one, the same Spirit ought to be shown in a tongue. Or certainly because the Word proceeds through the tongue, the Spirit appeared in a tongue; for whoever is touched by the Holy Spirit confesses the Word of God—that is, the only-begotten Son of God—and is unable to deny the Word of God, because the Holy Spirit now possesses his tongue.* These are pious thoughts and by no means to be despised, although they cannot be forced upon anyone.

XXXVI. However, I would primarily refer this imagery to the *effects* of the Holy Spirit, which He intended to exert through the tongues—both concerning the Apostles and the entire Church of the New Testament.

A. The *appearance of the tongues* in general signified that the Holy Spirit would constantly animate the tongues of His people in a wondrous way: both through the public preaching of extraordinary and ordinary Teachers <term>Doctorum: specifically referring to learned theologians and leaders of the church</term>, and through the perpetual testimony, confession, and celebration of individual believers learning the "new song" from them. *Every tongue shall now swear to Christ* (Isaiah 45:23). Hence, a perpetual *conjunction of the Spirit and the Word of Jehovah placed in the mouth* is promised in Isaiah 59:21.

B. The *fiery appearance of the tongues* designates several things: first, their origin from the heavenly Fire kindled through Christ—because of which we noted (at Psalm 45 and Exodus 4, § 4) that the lips of the Ministers, animated by the Spirit, are called the "Lips of the Messiah." Second, the *subject matter* in which these tongues are occupied, which is the praise of the Holiness of Jehovah (Isaiah 6:3). Third, the *accompanying* heavenly zeal of love, which inflames the tongues confessing Jesus. Finally, it portrays the *effect* of illuminating and inflaming others—which assumes the speaker himself is on fire—and even of consuming those who are rebellious. To this I would refer the fire proceeding from the mouth of the two witnesses in Revelation 11:5. Hence, **Philo**, in his work *On the Decalogue*, attributes to the Law a twin power of fire: "the one to illuminate, the other to burn" <note>original Greek: το μεν φωτιζειν, το δε καιειν (to men phōtizein, to de kaiein)</note>, resulting in the twin effects of salvation and destruction.

### ON THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER X.

C. The fact that the tongues share a single mass of fire as their base—with which they remain united even when they are divided—expresses a testimony that is distributed across various languages and nations, yet remains always the same through the most gentle union of the Spirit, repeatedly setting others ablaze. We read all of this condensed into a single phrase in **Zephaniah 3:9**: *I will return to the peoples a pure lip, so that they may all call upon the name of Jehovah.* <note>original: "Vertam ad populos labium purum..." This refers to God promising to restore "pure speech" or "pure lips" to the nations. The author treats "lip" as a metaphor for both language and the organ of praise.</note> For here we have: 
1) *The lip of Jehovah Himself;* 
2) *A lip that is pure and shining like fire;* 
3) *A lip divided among the nations, yet one in substance;* 
4) *A lip that rouses the lips of others, so that they too may call upon the name of Jehovah.* 
From this arises an elegant analogy between the Judgment of the Confusion of Tongues at Babylon and the Blessing of the Union of divided Tongues. **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note> notes on this passage: *The punishment of languages scattered mankind (Genesis 11). The gift of languages gathered the scattered back into one people.* Not far from this is the excerpt from the **Zohar** <note>The primary work of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah)</note> (page 55, column 1) cited by learned men: *The confusion of languages will be taken away in the days of the Messiah.*

XXXVII. In addition to the symbols of the Holy Spirit appearing as seven lamps, as well as the seven horns and eyes of the Lamb in **Revelation 4:5** and **5:6** (which we anticipated in Chapter 4, section 21 and following), the **Book of Revelation** presents to us in **Chapter 6:2** <note>The description that follows—an angel with a seal from the east—actually appears in Revelation 7:2. The author or printer likely made a citation error here.</note> an *Angel ascending from the rising of the Sun and holding the Seal of the living God.* We are persuaded, along with the distinguished **Cocceius** and **Vitringa** <note>Johannes Cocceius and Campegius Vitringa, influential 17th-century biblical scholars</note> through a comparison with the Vision of **Ezekiel Chapter 9**, that this represents the Holy Spirit. The learned men we have praised have concluded that a Divine Person appears here. Those who believe the *Son of God* appears here acknowledge the same thing in great numbers; **Calovius** <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a leading defender of Lutheran orthodoxy</note> provides a catalog of these authors. However, since they offer no other reason for disagreeing with us than their opinion that the form of an "Angel" is less fitting for the Third Person [of the Trinity]—an argument we have already overturned in previous sections—we see no reason to ignore the most elegant parallel in Ezekiel.

Thus, the common opinion of interpreters is that the Son of God is figured there. However, we prefer [to see] the Holy Spirit

<header>ON APPARITIONS</header>

...they wish to express the hypostatic <note>The term "hypostatic" refers to the personal relationship between the three persons of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—who share one divine substance.</note> relationship of the Holy Spirit to the Son and his kinship with the substantial *Word*, as **GREGORY NAZIANZEN** <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and influential theologian</note> speaks of it. **WEGNER** <note>Likely Gottfried Wegner (1644–1709), a German Lutheran theologian</note> collected several of their passages in the work cited above, from which we provide only the quote from **GREGORY THE GREAT** here: *He was shown in tongues because the same Spirit is co-eternal with the Son, and the tongue has the greatest kinship with a word. For the Word of the Father is the Son. And because the substance of the Spirit and the Word is one, the same Spirit ought to be shown in a tongue. Or certainly, because the Word proceeds through the tongue, the Spirit appeared in a tongue; for whoever is touched by the Holy Spirit confesses the Word of God—that is, the only-begotten Son of God—and cannot deny the Word of God, because the Holy Spirit now possesses his tongue.* These are pious thoughts and by no means to be looked down upon, even if they cannot be forced upon anyone as absolute requirements of faith.

XXXVI. I would, however, primarily relate this imagery to the *effects* of the Holy Spirit, which He wished to exert most powerfully through the "tongues," both concerning the Apostles and the entire Church of the New Testament.

A. The appearance of *tongues* viewed in a general sense designated that the Holy Spirit would constantly animate the tongues of His followers in a wonderful manner—both through the public preaching of extraordinary and ordinary **Teachers**, and through the perpetual testimony, confession, and celebration of individual believers who learn the *New Song* from them. *Now all tongues shall swear by Christ,* as seen in **Isaiah 45:23**. Hence, the perpetual conjunction of the Spirit and the *Word of Jehovah placed in the mouth* is promised in **Isaiah 59:21**.

B. The *fiery* appearance of the tongues denotes their origin from the heavenly **Fire** kindled through Christ. Because of this, we noted (regarding **Psalm 45** and **Exodus 4, § 4**) that the lips of Ministers animated by the Spirit are called the *Lips of the Messiah*. It also denotes the *subject matter* in which these tongues are occupied: the praise of the *Holiness of Jehovah* (**Isaiah 6:3**). Furthermore, it signifies the *attribute* of heavenly **zeal** and love which sets ablaze the tongues of those confessing Jesus. Finally, it illustrates the *effect* of illuminating and inflaming others—which presupposes that the speaker himself is on fire—and even of consuming those who are stubborn. To this, I would relate the fire proceeding *from the mouth of the two witnesses* in **Revelation 11:5**. Following this line of thought, **PHILO** <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note> in his work *On the Decalogue* attributes a dual power to fire: *one to illuminate, the other to burn* <note>original Greek: "τὸ μὲν φωτίζειν, τὸ δὲ καíειν"</note>, comparing these to the dual effects of the Law in bringing both salvation and destruction.

<header>OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER X.</header>

C. Because they have a single mass of fire as their base, with which they remain united even when they are divided, this testifies to the fact that the Spirit is distributed through various languages and nations, yet remains always the same through the most sweet union of the Spirit, repeatedly setting others on fire. We read all these things comprised in a single phrase in **Zephaniah 3:9**: *I will turn to the peoples a pure lip, that they may all call upon the name of Jehovah.* <note>The Latin text uses *labium purum* (pure lip), which in many English Bibles is translated as "pure language" or "pure speech."</note> For here we have: 1) *The lip of Jehovah himself*; 2) *A pure lip*, shining like fire; 3) *A lip divided among the peoples*, yet one in substance; 4) *A lip awakening the lips of others*, so that they too might call upon the name of Jehovah. From this arises an elegant analogy between the Judgment of the Confusion of Tongues at Babylon and the Blessing of the Union of divided Tongues. **GROTIUS** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch polymath and influential theologian</note> says on this passage: *The punishment of languages dispersed men (Genesis 11); the gift of languages gathered the dispersed back into one people.* Not far from this is what learned men have excerpted from the **ZOHAR** <note>The foundational work in the literature of Jewish mystical thought known as Kabbalah</note> page 55, column 1: *The confusion of languages will be removed in the days of the Messiah.*

XXXVII. In addition to the emblems of the Holy Spirit occurring as the seven lamps, as well as the seven horns and eyes of the Lamb in **Revelation 4:5** and **5:6**—which we anticipated in Chapter 4, § 21 and following—the **Revelation** presents to us in **Chapter 6:2** <note>The author likely intends Revelation 7:2, which describes the angel with the seal; Chapter 6 describes the riders of the apocalypse.</note> an *Angel ascending from the rising of the Sun, and having the Seal of the living God.* We are persuaded, along with the celebrated **COCCEJU**S <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his "federal theology"</note> and **VITRINGA** <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent commentator on prophetic books</note>, that this figure represented the Holy Spirit, based on a comparison with the Vision of **Ezekiel, Chapter 9**. The learned men we have praised have concluded that a divine Person appears here. Those who believe the *Son of God* appears here acknowledge the same in throngs; **CALOVIUS** <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a leading Lutheran orthodox theologian</note> provides a catalog of them. However, since they generally offer no other reason for disagreeing with us than their belief that the form of an "Angel" is less suited to the Third Person—an argument we have already overturned in the preceding pages—there is nothing that induces us to neglect this most elegant parallel with Ezekiel.

XXXVIII. Furthermore, that Angel *with the Censer*, who in **Revelation 8:2** and following opens the scene of divine Judgments, so excels the Angels blowing the trumpets that you might easily suspect an uncreated Angel <note>In older theology, the "uncreated Angel" refers to a member of the Trinity (usually Christ) appearing in angelic form, rather than a created celestial being.</note> is being represented. Therefore, it is the common opinion of interpreters that the Son of God is figured there. We, however, prefer to see the Holy Spirit there...

<header>CONCERNING THE MANIFESTATIONS</header>

...also appear there. For 1) there is a clear allusion here to the *Man clothed in a linen robe* <note>Latin: *Virum talari indutum*; a reference to the figure in Ezekiel 9 and 10 who marks the faithful</note> in **Ezekiel 9 & 10**, both because he is present among the executors of God’s judgments and moderates them, and because a similar task is ascribed to him in verse 5. 2) The words of verse 3—*much incense was given to him, so that he might give it with the prayers of all the saints* <note>Original Greek: ἐδόθη αὐτῷ θυμιάματα πολλὰ, ἵνα δώσῃ ταῖς προσευχαῖς τῶν ἁγίων πάντων</note>—apply more to the Holy Spirit than to the Son. For it is permissible to suppose that *incense* serves as an emblem of the various virtues that make prayers pleasing to God, and thus represent the fruits of the Holy Spirit. These are given to this Angel by another, so that he may bestow them upon the prayers of the Saints. From this it becomes clear that the subject is not the Intercession of Christ, but rather the *intercession of the Saints for the Church*; for which they require the Holy Spirit as their Teacher to properly institute it. Here, however, he has obtained from the Son the power to imbue the Saints with these gifts, and he exercises it as he becomes in them the *Spirit of Grace and Supplication* (**Zechariah 12:10**). 3) Those *effects* mentioned in verse 5—*voices, thunders, lightnings, and earthquakes*—express the various operations of the Holy Spirit concerning the Church, and thus relate more closely to him than to the Son of God. 4) That *Angel* who descends from heaven in **Revelation 10:1** ff., when he is called *another Angel*, is distinguished both from the *Trumpeting Angels* and from the *Angel bestowing incense*. The famous **VITRINGA** <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent Dutch theologian and commentator on Revelation</note> correctly observed this, and was led by it to understand the Holy Spirit in that passage, despite the nature of the prophetic allusions. Since, however, we have already shown above that the attributes of the *Angel descending with the Rainbow* are attributed in the Prophetic Word to the Son of God, it will be better to understand the *Angel with the Censer* as the Holy Spirit. 5) Add to this that in this way we avoid a certain awkwardness that appears when the Son of God, after his consummation in heaven, is introduced as standing before the Father and interceding for the Church, whereas he performs his priesthood and intercession in heaven more properly while seated (**Zechariah 6:13, Romans 8:34**). 6) Nor does this symbol deviate from the custom of the Sanctuary, in which **BRAUNIUS** <note>Johannes Braun (1628–1708), a Dutch theologian known for his work on Hebrew ritual and priestly vestments</note> noted in *Selected Sacred Works*, Book II, chapter 6, § 76, that the one offering the incense did not himself take the spices from the container, but they were placed into his hands by another Priest from the chamber of Abtines <note>A specific room in the Second Temple where the incense was prepared by the House of Abtinas</note>.

XXXIX. As for why such a great crowd of Interpreters [considers] Christ...

<header>OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. CHAPTER X.</header>

The desire to designate Christ here arose from the common prejudice that this Angel, by **lighting the incense**, performed the primary duties of the Priest in the heavenly Sanctuary. However, this cannot be established from the context. For he himself is not said to have burned the incense, but only to have **given it to the Saints**, **for their prayers**, so that they might raise a pleasing aroma before the throne of God. These **Saints** are therefore properly the Priests performing the incensing. Our Angel merely supplies the incense to them. Hence, in **Revelation 5:8**, the twenty-four **Elders** appear with **golden bowls filled with incense**; and this interpretation is added: <note>Original Greek: αἱ ἐισιν αἱ προσευχαὶ τῶν ἁγίων</note> *which are the prayers of the saints.* Lest anyone object to verse 4 of chapter 8, its construction must be properly observed: <note>Original Greek: Και ἀνεβη ὁ καπνος των θυμιαματων ταις προσευχαις των ἁγιων ἐκ χειρος του Αγγελου, ἐνωπιον του Θεου</note> *And the smoke of the incense arose with the prayers of the saints from the hand of the Angel, before God.* Here, some editions place a comma after "saints," as if asserting that the smoke of the sacred incense **was ignited by the hand of the Angel**. But when that comma is removed, nothing else is asserted than that the incense was received **from the Angel’s hand**, and thereafter **the smoke of those things, ignited upon the altar of incense by the Saints or the twenty-four Elders, ascended before the Lord**. This is all the more likely because nothing is assigned to that Angel except a <term>libanotos<note>Original Greek: λιϐανωτος; usually meaning frankincense, but here referring to the vessel holding it</note></term> or **incense-box, a censer**, which did not hold fire, but only the **incense**. As <term>Braunius<note>Johannes Braun (1628–1708), a Dutch theologian known for his works on the vestments and rituals of Hebrew priests</note></term> taught in the cited work (§. 67 ff.), those who understand *libanotos* here as a <term>machtah<note>Hebrew: מחתה; a fire-pan or coal-pan used to carry burning coals from the altar</note></term> or **fire-vessel** (in which burning coals were taken from the Altar of burnt offerings) are in error, since it is designated only as a <term>kaph<note>Hebrew: כף; a spoon or shallow bowl</note></term>, a **small incense-bowl or box**. Furthermore, since that **censer**, contrary to the common custom of the Sanctuary, was to be filled with coals from the Altar of burnt offerings, those coals were not taken up until after the smoke of the incense had already ascended: so that you may know, of course, that the mystical pouring out of those coals onto the earth follows the incensing performed by the Saints.

XL. If, nevertheless, it should still seem that the Angel himself **burned the incense** in our Vision, even then there will be no need to return to the Son of God. For although our Savior admitted no partner in the primary function of the Priestly office—namely, the offering of the atoning Sacrifice—no one would doubt that the role of **Intercession** also pertains, in a certain order, to the Holy Spirit.

### X.
## THEOLOGICAL DISSERTATION,
### CONCERNING
# DIVINE INSPIRATION
<note>Original Greek: *THEOPNEUSTIA* (ΘΕΟΠΝΕΥΣΤΙΑΙ), literally "God-breathed."</note>
## Of the Sacred Authors.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting a landscape or architectural scene with floral motifs.</image-desc>
I. Among the extraordinary operations of the Holy Spirit through which the Word of the Lord was delivered to the Church, the most prominent place is occupied by INSPIRATION, or *Divine Breathing*, a term the Apostle elegantly uses in *2 Timothy 3:16*. This word is chosen because it designates not only a truly divine work, but also one that is perfected through a certain *breathing* <note>Original Latin: *spirationem*</note>, and thus by the mediation of the *Holy Spirit*. The **SYRIAC** translator recognized the emphasis of this word when he rendered the beginning of the verse as: *For all Scripture which is written through the Spirit.* The **ARABIC** translator followed the same path: *And every Scripture, savoring of the divine breath.* Hence, **PISCATOR** <note>Johannes Piscator (1546–1625), a German Reformed theologian known for his influential Bible translation.</note> is more emphatic with: *blown into* <note>Original German: *eingeblasen*</note>; more so than **LUTHER** and the **DUTCH** <note>The *Belgae*, referring to the Dutch Authorized Version or *Statenvertaling*.</note>, who simply use: *given* <note>Original German: *eingegeben*; Dutch: *ingeven*</note>. The **ZURICH BIBLE** <note>The *Tigurina*, a Latin and German version associated with the Reformation in Zurich.</note> is even more expressive: *en-spirited* <note>Original German: *eingegeistet*, suggesting a deep spiritual infusion.</note>.

II. This word was clearly not unknown even to secular <note>The author uses *profanis* to refer to classical Greek and Roman authors outside of the biblical tradition.</note> authors...

<header># CONCERNING DIVINE INSPIRATION <note>Original Greek: *THEOPNEUSTIAI*</note></header>

...was considered to be said concerning speech, which they believed was brought forth by a divine impulse. Thus **PHOCYLIDES** <note>An ancient Greek gnomic poet, though the work cited here is likely by a later Jewish-Christian author writing in his name.</note>, or whoever was the author of these verses, says:

> — — — — — Speech is a bulwark for men.
> But of **God-breathed** wisdom, speech is the best.
> <note>Original Greek: *logos d' erym' anthrōpōn. Tēs de theopneustou sophiēs logos estin aristos.*</note>

*Truly, speech is a defense for men. But furthermore,* DIVINELY INSPIRED wisdom's speech is the best. That the Gentiles ascribed such a "divine inspiration" <note>Original Greek: *theopneustian*</note> to their own philosophers is clear from that passage of **MARINUS** in his *Life of Proclus*, chapter 23: *He did not seem to exist without divine inspiration; and he poured forth words truly like snowflakes from that wise mouth, for his eyes seemed to be filled with a certain radiance, and the rest of his face partook of a divine illumination.* <note>Proclus was a major Neoplatonist philosopher. Marinus describes him here as if he were a prophet.</note> (In this, one may notice a <term>kakozēlia</term> <note>A Greek rhetorical term for a "clumsy imitation" or "perverse rivalry." The author suggests Marinus is poorly imitating the biblical account of Moses' face shining.</note> of Moses in *Exodus 34:29*) *and his face shone with divine light.* Yet this concept applied even more to the Poets—the most ancient of philosophers—so that their words, brought forth in verse, were derived from the impulse of a divine Spirit, which is everywhere called *epipnoia*, or **inspiration**. **DEMOCRITUS**, according to **CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA** (*Stromata*, Book IV, ch. 18), *affirms that Poets wrote with divine enthusiasm and a holy Spirit.* **OVID** seizes upon this in Book III of *The Art of Love*, verse 549:

->*There is a God within us, and we have commerce with heaven.*<-
->*That Spirit comes from the celestial realms.*<-

Many authors have gathered more on this matter, besides **MERIC CASAUBON** and **PETITUS**, who treated this subject specifically: **J. C. BULENGERUS** in *On Divination*, Book III, 1, 2; **EZ. SPANHEMIUS** in his *Notes on Julian*, p. 18; **J. B. CARPZOVIUS** in *Academic Disputations* XXVI, §. 40; and **V. E. LOESCHERUS** in *Stromatals*, Section XII. We do not excerpt them here. However, it seemed to us that this should not be entirely overlooked, so that some light might be shed upon the saying of the Apostle <note>Paul, specifically referring to 2 Timothy 3:16.</note>. For this persuasion [among the Greeks] seems to have flowed from the fame of the sacred books to the Gentiles; hence, what **Plato** stole from **Moses**, he equally unfortunately from...

<header>T R E A T I S E</header>

**PHILO THE JEW** <note>A Jewish philosopher from Alexandria who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with the Hebrew Bible.</note> adapted this concept from Plato to the *divine inspiration* <note>Original Greek: *theopneustian*</note> of the Sacred Writers in his book *On the Change of Names*, page 1077, and *On the Life of Moses*, book III, page 664. But more auspiciously, Paul reclaims this glory—which had been falsely peddled regarding the coldest utterances and most foolish poems—and by a "restoration of rights" <note>The author uses the Latin legal term *postliminio*, referring to the recovery of rights by a person returning from captivity; here, it suggests the word "inspiration" is being rescued from pagan use and returned to its proper home in Scripture.</note> vindicates it for the Sacred Scripture.

**III.** This INSPIRATION is, moreover, a particular work of the Holy Spirit, by which He imparted both the matters and the words to the enlightened minds of the Prophets, which they brought forth for the use of the Church in both speech and writing. According to this definition, we must briefly examine both the Author and the work itself.

**IV.** Although the honor of Inspiration also pertains to the Father (Romans 1:1, 2) and the Son (Luke 1:68, 70; 2 Corinthians 3:3; Romans 15:18), for which reason the testimony concerning the salvation of the sinner is attributed to each person of the Holy Trinity in 1 John 5:7, it is nevertheless more frequently assigned to the Holy Spirit. He is the Author of all prophecy (Numbers 11:25, 29): in Balaam himself (Numbers 24:2); in David (2 Samuel 23:2, compared with Acts 1:16); in Isaiah (Acts 28:25); in Paul (1 Corinthians 2:4). Indeed, it is asserted of all the Prophets in 1 Peter 1:11 that the Spirit of Christ was in them; and in 2 Peter 1:21, that they spoke *as they were moved by the Holy Spirit* <note>Original Greek: *pheromenoi hypo Pneumatos hagiou*</note>. No less was the Gospel preached in the Holy Spirit (1 Peter 1:12). Most holily indeed has God reserved this entire work for Himself, so that our faith might not depend on any testimony of men, but on Him who testifies to what He has seen and speaks of what He knows (John 3:11). No less wisely does the power of that divine Person shine forth here, to whom the application of the Salvation acquired through Christ most closely belongs. Since the Word of the Lord is the perpetual medium of all operations of Grace—through which the fruits of the Obedience and Death of Christ are applied in this life—it was fitting that He who would use this instrument should be occupied in preparing it.

**V.** The infernal spirit once attempted to snatch this glory from the Spirit of Jehovah, when he tried to counterfeit some appearance of Inspiration both in false prophets and in those possessed by demons. Thus, the inspiration of false prophets is attributed to him by divine permission in 1 Kings 22:20, 21. Although, since that entire vision is...

<header>ON DIVINE INSPIRATION.</header>

...parabolic, it is difficult to determine whether there was a mere impulse toward agreement in producing a lie, or whether Inspiration properly so-called intervened. Even if the latter is not clearly asserted, there would nevertheless have been nothing alien to the character of the Devil in it, who, "when he speaks lies, he speaks from his own nature" <note>original Latin: *de suo loquitur*</note> (*John 8:44*).

**VI.** This is even more audacious: that he dared to inspire truth as well. An example is the Spirit of Python <note>original: *Spiritus Pythonis*, *Πνευμα Πυθωνος*. ### III.
This **INSPIRATION** is the unique work of the Holy Spirit, by which He instilled both the matters and the words into the illuminated minds of the Prophets, which they then brought forth for the use of the Church, both in speech and in writing. Following this definition, we must briefly examine both the Author and the work itself.

### IV.
Although the honor of *Inspiration* also pertains to the Father (*Romans 1:1–2*) and the Son (*Luke 1:68, 70; 2 Corinthians 3:3; Romans 15:18*)—whence the testimony concerning the salvation of the sinner is attributed to each person of the Holy Trinity in *1 John 5:7*—it is nevertheless more frequently assigned to the Holy Spirit. He is the *Author* of all prophecy: in the case of Eldad and Medad in *Numbers 11:25, 29*; in **Balaam** in *Numbers 24:2*; in **David** in *2 Samuel 23:2* (compared with *Acts 1:16*); in **Isaiah** in *Acts 28:15*; and in **Paul** in *1 Corinthians 2:4*. No less was the *Gospel* preached in the Holy Spirit (*1 Peter 1:12*). Most holily indeed, God reserved this entire work for Himself, so that our faith would not depend upon any human testimony, but upon Him who "testifies to what He has seen and speaks what He knows" (*John 3:11*). No less wisely does the power of that Divine Person shine forth here, to whom the application of the Salvation acquired through Christ most closely belongs. Since the Word of the Lord is the perpetual medium of all operations of Grace—through which the fruits of the Obedience and Death of Christ are applied in this life—it was fitting that He who would use this instrument should be the one occupied in adapting it.

We easily add our agreement <note>original Latin: *calculum*, literally "pebble" or "voting stone"</note> to Tacutius, his commentator, and **Hammond** <note>Henry Hammond, a 17th-century English churchman and scholar</note>. **Jurieu** indeed, in his *History of Dogmas*, Part 3, Treatise 2, Chapter 5, argues to the contrary: that it does not appear that this slave girl used a thin, screeching voice coming from the belly, according to the custom of ventriloquists <note>original Greek: *εγγαστριμυθων* (engastrimythōn)</note>, but rather a resounding one, since she is introduced as *crying out*. The celebrated **Deyling** uses the same argument after him in *Sacred Observations*, Vol. II, p. 200 and following, as does the celebrated **Wolf** in his notes on this passage, contending that the term "Python" was applied to any other kind of divination. However, this point has not yet been established with suitable examples. Nor do we have much need of them, since the circumstances seem to suggest that this slave girl, outside of her paroxysm <note>a sudden attack or fit</note> and the usual madness of ventriloquists, may have uttered those words in ordinary speech which she had been taught during the demonic inspiration <note>original: *afflatu Diabolico*</note> itself.

### VIII.
It might more easily come to mind here: whether by attributing *Inspiration*, and indeed the inspiration of words containing divine truths, to the Pythonic Spirit, anything might be detracted from the honor of the **Holy Spirit**? On that point, however, we are at ease, because the infernal Spirit—having *transformed himself into an Angel of light* <note>2 Corinthians 11:14</note> through the most base hypocrisy—brings forth nothing new here, nothing that could not have been known to those paying attention, and nothing except what he himself had learned from the Holy Spirit. How great a thing is it, however, that driven by the force of his own conscience, he should offer testimony not only to the most excellent Savior himself (Mark 1:24, 3:11), but also in our present passage to His servant? And that, at the command of the divine Spirit, he is forced to leave this impure cavern of a body immediately? Hence, there was no need—as **Balthasar Bekker** does in *The Enchanted World* <note>original Latin: *Mundi Fascinati*; Bekker was a Dutch minister known for his skepticism toward witchcraft and demonic possession</note>, Book II, chapter 24, § 16 and following—to understand the "Spirit of Python" as a "Good Angel." There is no need to show how frivolous this idea is, following the work of **Van der Wayen** against Bekker (§ 1378) and **Knibbe** in his *Prophetic History*, IV. 10. § 5, 6. Furthermore, we judge that the *Inspiration* of prophecies of any kind should never be attributed to the Devil. For God has reserved the glory of predicting future things for Himself alone, and has established it as a sign of the prophets sent by Him (Deuteronomy 18:21, 22; Jeremiah 28:9; 1 Samuel 3:19, 20; Isaiah 44:25, 26).

...[we can], so that its nature may be rightly understood, before all else we must examine its *object*. Generally, this extends as much to *spoken words* as to *written ones*. For as the needs of the Church required, some things were spoken by Divinely-Inspired <note>original Greek: Θεοπνεύστοις (Theopneustois)</note> men and not *written*; some were *written* and not *spoken*; and some were first *spoken* and then later, by a specific command of the Lord, *written* down. X. It is established from various examples that the holy men very frequently enjoyed the immediate Inspiration of the Holy Spirit in those *spoken words* which they uttered. But others also, adorned with the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit, are introduced as *speaking in the Spirit of God* (1 Corinthians 12:3). <meta>This page continues the argument regarding divine inspiration, moving from the specific instances of spoken prophecy (like David and the elders mentioned on page 359) to a broader definition of how the Holy Spirit governed both the speech and the writing of the biblical authors. It transitions into a discussion on "verbal inspiration"—the idea that the Spirit chose the specific words, not just the general ideas.</meta>

-># DISSERTATION<-

...taking the word from him. <note>original Greek: μιν του λογου λαβων</note> *Tell me then, receiving the power of speaking from the Spirit.* Yet this inspiration was not constant, occurring whenever they pleased; rather, it happened when it seemed fitting to God to use their ministry for the unique confirmation of His Word and the building up of the Church. That they enjoyed this heavenly inspiration only at specific times is easily proven by the "clouds" and "blemishes" of both ignorance and prejudice that occasionally appeared in them. For this reason, the Lord's promise of inspiration was restricted to certain circumstances of time. This was most wisely arranged so that no infallible Tribunal concerning the way of salvation would be established on earth, through which men might be made subject in their conscience to other sinful men of equal status. Add to this that inspiration itself belongs to the miraculous works of God, which He did not wish to multiply beyond what the needs of the Church required.

**XI.** The biblical writers enjoyed this same benefit of inspiration while writing. This glory is clearly claimed for the Holy Spirit when Scripture—citing the passage in 2 Timothy 3:16—is called *divinely inspired* <note>original Greek: θεόπνευστος (theopneustos), literally "God-breathed"</note>; and when in 1 Peter 1:11 it is asserted that the *Spirit of Christ* was in the Prophets, who previously testified of the sufferings of Christ and the glories that followed. It is also expressly asserted in 2 Peter 1:20–21 that *no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation. For prophecy was not brought forth by the will of men, but those holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit.* It is clear from the context that the act of "speaking" <note>original Greek: Το λαλειν (To lalein)</note> here must be extended to include those things which they wrote. For this word is often used metaphorically for any declaration of Doctrine, even that which is set down in writing, as seen in Luke 1:70, 24:25; Acts 3:21, 26:22; Romans 3:19, and elsewhere. Moreover, what is asserted regarding all the Prophets is also established for each individual, whose tongue and pen alike were subject to the Holy Spirit. To this point we may apply not only the words of David cited from 2 Samuel 23:2, but also those of Psalm 45:1: *My tongue is the pen of a ready writer.* Hence it is preached concerning Isaiah *that the Holy Spirit rightly spoke through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers* <note>original Greek: ότι καλως το Πνευμα το άγιον έλαλησε δια Ησαιου του Προφητου προς τους πατερας ήμων</note> in Acts 28:25.

**XII.** Furthermore, that this Inspiration extended not only to the *matters* <note>The underlying concepts or facts</note> which they taught, but even to the very *words* and *phrases* themselves, is shown both—

<meta>This page continues the technical defense of "verbal inspiration"—the belief that the Holy Spirit provided the biblical writers with the specific words they used, not just the general concepts. ->### ON DIVINE INSPIRATION. <-

...can be established both by the testimonies of Sacred Scripture and by solid reasons. Regarding the specific words, the Apostle removes all doubt in 1 Corinthians 2:4, where he opposes his own speech to all "persuasive words of human wisdom" <note>original Greek: πειθοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις</note> and, in verse 1, to "excellence of speech or wisdom" <note>original Greek: ὑπεροχῇ λόγου ἢ σοφίας</note>. Indeed, in verse 13, he declares that he speaks not in "words taught by human wisdom, but in those taught by the Holy Spirit" <note>original Greek: διδακτοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις... διδακτοῖς Πνεύματος ἁγίου</note>. It appears the Apostle is referring here to the words themselves for four reasons:

1) Because his aim was to defend not only the **subject matter** he was treating, but also the **manner** of treating it, which was despised by those of a worldly mind. That this was necessary for him elsewhere is clear from 2 Corinthians 11:6. 2) Because he clearly distinguishes between the "excellence of speech" and "wisdom." For just as "wisdom" refers to the **matter**, "excellence of speech" must be referred to the **manner** of speaking. 3) Because he truly opposes those who, not only with sophistical arguments but even with "bubbles of words," were drawing the minds of the unwary to themselves. Such, specifically, were the Stoics, who recommended themselves through "speculation in words" <note>original Greek: θεωρίᾳ ἐν λόγοις</note> according to **DIOGENES LAERTIUS** (Book I, chapter 88) and through the "sharpness of words" <note>original Greek: τερθρείᾳ τῶν λόγων</note>, as the same author says in his Preface. Add here the notes that the famous **ALBERTI** excerpted for this chapter. 4) Because in verse 5 it is simply denied that our faith ought to rely on the wisdom of men; yet it would rely on it in some part if the choice of words had been left to the power of men. Therefore, when he asserts that the Holy Spirit taught these speeches, he clearly declares that the Spirit is the Author not only of the **doctrine**, but also of the **words**.

**XIII.** And this interpretation is best supported by what is added: "comparing spiritual things with spiritual" <note>original Greek: πνευματικοῖς πνευματικὰ συγκρίνοντες</note>. We certainly do not listen to **CAMERARIUS**, even if **LOUIS DE DIEU**, **ERASMUS SCHMIDT**, **CLERICUS**, and **STARKIUS** give him their support <note>The Latin "pollicem addant" literally means they "add their thumb," a Roman arena gesture signifying approval.</note>, when he interprets "spiritual" <note>original Greek: πνευματικοῖς</note> as referring to *men*. He suggests that the Apostle was claiming to offer or adapt spiritual things to the judgment of spiritual men. However, this definition of "comparing" <note>original Greek: συγκρίνειν</note> is less common. And the argument upon which this interpretation uniquely relies—that soon after in verse 15 the "spiritual men" <note>original Greek: πνευματικοὶ</note> seem to be the same as those called "mature" <note>original Greek: τέλειοι</note> in verse 6—is one that—

-> # DISSERTATION <-

The argument that the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> refers to those same people here because of the textual connection carries little weight. For, to say nothing of the fact that our words are separated from what follows by the adversative "but" <note>original Greek: δέ (de)</note>; the "spiritual man" <note>original Greek: πνευματικὸς ἄνθρωπος (pneumatikos anthrōpos)</note>, to whom the judgment of all things is attributed, are the Apostles themselves "comparing spiritual things with spiritual" <note>original Greek: πνευματικὰ πνευματικοῖς συγκρίνοντες (pneumatika pneumatikois synkrinontes)</note>. These are the very ones who possess the "mind of Christ" <note>original Greek: νοῦν Χριστοῦ (noun Christou)</note> according to verse 16—that is, when compared with Isaiah 40:3 <note>Likely a reference to Isaiah 40:13, "Who has directed the Spirit of the Lord?"</note>, they possess the Spirit of Christ. We agree with **BEZA** <note>Theodore Beza, a major 16th-century French Protestant theologian</note>, who, to avoid ambiguity, translates it as: *Comparing spiritual things with those things which are spiritual.* He explains this as: *that is, adapting the words to the matter, so that just as the things we teach are spiritual, and the sincerity of heavenly doctrine is not corrupted by any human commentary, so also our manner of teaching it should be spiritual.* In this way, not only the Church Fathers **CHRYSOSTOM** and **THEOPHYLACT**, but even those "from the opposite side" <note>referring to Socinian or heterodox scholars</note> such as **SCHLICHTINGIUS**, **BRENIUS**, **VORSTIUS**, and others, led by the clarity of the sense, have interpreted our passage.

XIV. Allow me to add just a few points to further illustrate this opinion. **A.** The first is that the phrase "with spiritual" <note>original Greek: πνευματικοῖς (pneumatikois)</note> is here best joined with the immediately preceding noun "words" <note>original Greek: λόγοις (logois)</note>. This was excellently observed by the **DUTCH** <note>referring to the Dutch States Translation / Statenvertaling notes</note>, who provide this paraphrase in their Gloss: *Just as the teaching is spiritual, so we also present it not with worldly but with spiritual words.* **B.** Furthermore, one must not overlook what **HEINSIUS** and **GROTIUS** <note>Famous 17th-century Dutch scholars</note> have already observed: among the translators of the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX</note>, the word "to compare/combine" <note>original Greek: συγκρίνειν (synkrinein)</note> is consistently rendered by the Hebrew *parash* <note>original Hebrew: פרש</note> or *pathar* <note>original Hebrew: פתר</note>, which corresponds to the Chaldean *pesher* <note>original Aramaic/Chaldean: פשר</note>, and signifies: *to explain*. From this arises the easiest translation of all: *Explaining spiritual (mysteries) with spiritual (words).* I congratulate myself on the agreement in this regard with the celebrated **ELSNER** (on this passage) and **J. H. MAJI** (*Christian Theosophy*, chapter 1, section 14). And thus, the Apostle's entire reasoning hangs together most fittingly. For, in order to teach the Corinthians why he used a method in teaching plainly opposite to "human wisdom"—as he had asserted in verses 4 and 5—he shows in verses 6–13 how much the nature of the doctrine requires it; and for that reason, he removes himself, as a "spiritual man" or one taught by the Holy Spirit himself, from any judgment by "natural men" <note>original Greek: ψυχικῶν ἀνθρώπων (psychikōn anthrōpōn), literally "soulish" or unspiritual people</note> in verses 14–16. In the first part, he proceeds so that—

<header>ON DIVINE INSPIRATION <note>original: DE ΘΕΟΠΝΕΥΣΤΙΑΙ (De Theopneustiai)</note>.</header>

I. Let him teach the loftiness of the mysteries which were proposed through the proclamation of the Gospel. Here:
a. The Apostle’s thesis is that the Teachers of the New Testament speak wisdom *among the perfect* <note>original Greek: ἐν τελείοις (en teleiois)</note>—that is, wisdom that was suited to the mature state of the New Testament faithful. (Verse 6, beginning).
b. This is confirmed by two arguments:
α. Because it was previously unknown. (Verse 6, middle, through Verse 9).
β. Because it was revealed to the Teachers of the New Testament directly through the Holy Spirit. (Verses 10–12).

B. From this, he deduces that they employed words appropriate for such great mysteries—words taught by the same Spirit who had revealed the mysteries themselves. In this way, it was granted to them to explain those spiritual doctrines, which the Holy Spirit had directly manifested, using spiritual words originating from that same Spirit as their author, and which were therefore the most fitting. Consequently, a vast difference necessarily arose between their method and the *words of persuasive human wisdom* <note>original Greek: πειθοῦς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγους (peithous anthrōpinēs sophias logous)</note>.

C. To heighten the emphasis of this phrase, it is also worth adding that by *spiritual words* <note>original Latin: logos pneumatikous</note>—that is, words taught by the Holy Spirit—he designates either such words as the Holy Spirit once taught the Prophets, or such as He was now teaching the Apostles themselves. The former fits the hypothesis of the celebrated **COCCEIUS** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian</note>, who notes on this passage that the Apostles hardly ever use words other than those already employed in the Old Testament. The latter interpretation, however, seems to provide a clearer and simpler sense. Whichever is chosen, it supports our case. For if the Apostles used the words of the Prophets with such great care, they did so for no other reason than that they were convinced of their *divine inspiration* <note>original Greek: θεοπνευστίᾳ (theopneustia)</note>. Yet, it is best to combine both views. For those words were entirely to be recognized as words of the Holy Spirit which He inspired both in the Prophets of old and now, once again, in the Apostles. From this it appears that, although our theologians usually use the term <term>comparison of spiritual things</term> <note>original Latin: syncrisin spiritualium</note> to signify diligence in comparing the words of the Prophets, the phrase, when understood in its full emphasis, denotes a certain special prerogative of the Apostles. For to them alone was this granted,
