so that in the explanation of spiritual mysteries they would produce not only the words of others, but even words *inspired* <note>original: *inspirata*</note> by the Holy Spirit for themselves.

XV. No less compelling are the frequent promises which the Lord gave to His Ministers concerning the *suggestion* <term>suggestio: the theological concept that God "suggests" or dictates the specific words to be used by biblical writers</term> of the words themselves. Thus, in Exodus 4:12, He says to Moses: *I will be with your mouth, and I will teach you what you ought to speak.* Both the occasion and the purpose of this promise prove that it refers to the very utterance of words; it was meant to reassure Moses, who was anxious because of his lack of eloquence <note>original: loquelae ineptitudinem</note>, as the even clearer repetition in verse 15 confirms. Others add Isaiah 51:16, 59:21, and Jeremiah 1:9, though these are not quite as distinct. The first two passages concern not so much the Prophet alone as the entire Church, in whose mouth *God has placed His words*, since the Church relies on the words of *Jehovah* both in public confession and in prayer. More relevant here is the reassurance given to Jeremiah: *Jehovah, stretching out His hand, touched my mouth; and Jehovah said to me: Behold, I have placed my words in your mouth.* For he too, in verse 6, had complained of his lack of skill in speaking. And that the nature of this phrase encompasses both the *matter and the words* is evident from comparing Exodus 4:15 and 2 Samuel 14:9 with verse 3. Even more evident is the Savior’s promise from Matthew 10:19–20 (cited above in § 10) and repeated in Luke 12:11–12, where Lucas of Bruges, Flacius Illyricus, and Price <note>Three prominent 16th-17th century biblical commentators: Lucas Brugensis (Catholic), Matthias Flacius (Lutheran), and John Price (Anglican).</note> rightly advised that the *how* <note>Greek: τὸ πῶς (to pōs)</note> refers to the *form* of the speech, and the *what* <note>Greek: τὸ τί (to ti)</note> refers to the *material* or content of the Apostolic discourse. And nothing is clearer than that passage in Luke 21:14–15: *Settle it therefore in your hearts, not to premeditate* <note>Greek: προμελετᾶν (promeletan)</note> *your defense. For I will give you a mouth and wisdom* <note>Greek: στόμα καὶ σοφίαν (stoma kai sophian)</note> *which all who oppose you will not be able to contradict nor resist* <note>Greek: ἀντειπεῖν οὐδὲ ἀντιστῆναι (anteipein oude antistēnai)</note>. Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Archbishop and influential Bible commentator.</note> elegantly teaches how "mouth" and "wisdom" are to be distinguished here: *Because they were common and unlearned men, lest they be troubled when giving an account before wise men, He says: "Let this be no concern to you. For you will then receive from me eloquence and wisdom, so that even if all your adversaries were gathered together in one place, they will not be able to resist you—neither in wisdom, that is, in the power of your thoughts, nor in your eloquence and the steadiness of your tongue"* <note>Original Greek translated: οὔτε κατὰ τὴν σοφίαν... οὔτε κατὰ τὴν εὐστομίαν καὶ τὸ τῆς γλώσσης ἀπρόσκοπον</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of divine assistance in speech, specifically how God promised to provide the very words (the "mouth") and the wisdom to use them for the Apostles and Martyrs, defending this against Socinian and Remonstrant interpretations.</meta>

<header>ON DIVINE INSPIRATION <note>original: DE ΘΕΟΠΝΕΥΣΤΙΑΙ</note></header>

For often a person possesses wisdom in their reasoning and logic, yet is easily thrown into confusion by a noisy crowd, and thus, in the hour when they must speak publicly, they lose their focus. Johann Gerhard <note>a prominent 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> follows this view in his *Harmony*, Part II, chapter 160, as does Rudolf Gualter and others. The context confirms this interpretation. For "premeditating beforehand" <note>original Greek: τὸ προμελετᾷν</note> is expressly forbidden. Those who claim that only "worried and anxious" premeditation is forbidden effectively weaken this command without reason, arguing that it is merely a warning to avoid the extremes of either too much confidence or too much doubt. However, while such a rule might apply to ordinary Ministers today, the situation was different for the Apostles and Martyrs. Hence, in the passage from Matthew, it is promised that what they are to speak will be *given to them in that same hour*; this carries even greater weight because the "hour" <note>original Greek: ὥρα</note> in such a construction does not designate a specific part of the day, but "the exact point of time" <note>original Greek: τὴν τοῦ χρόνου στιγμὴν</note>, as Salmasius proves in his *Plinian Exercises*, Volume I, page 459. Furthermore, even some of our own theologians inappropriately use a "hypallage" <term>hypallage: a figure of speech where the natural relations of two words are reversed</term> to combine *mouth and wisdom* as if it meant "a wise mouth," whereas the words "to speak against" <note>original Greek: ἀντιειπεῖν</note>, which refers to the *mouth* <note>original Greek: στόμα</note>, and "to resist" <note>original Greek: ἀντιστῆναι</note>, which corresponds to *wisdom* <note>original Greek: σοφίᾳ</note>, clearly teach a distinction between the two.

XVI. The **BATAVIAN PSEUDO-THEOLOGIANS** <note>likely referring to the Remonstrants or Arminians in the Netherlands</note> attempt to wrest this club from our hands in their arguments against Simonius with certain frivolous little exceptions. They believe this promise was restricted only to specific cases—namely, when they were to be led before Governors and Kings—but this concerns us little, since we believe that similar conclusions should be drawn from similar cases. It is worse that, using the weapons of the Socinians <note>a rationalist sect that denied the Trinity</note>, they want the *Holy Spirit* or the *Spirit of God* to be understood merely as "a certain disposition of the mind." Truly, that idea is destroyed by the same arguments we use to maintain that the Holy Spirit is a true Person. As for what Enjedinus <note>a Socinian writer</note> argues—that it sometimes happens that the "sender" (who is absent) is said to do what he does through the "messenger" (who is present)—this is "completely irrelevant" <note>original Greek: ἀπροσδιόνυσον, literally 'nothing to do with Dionysus'</note> here. For in this context, the messengers are clearly distinguished from the One sending them. Nor is this about a speech commanded beforehand, but one supplied at that very moment. Add to this that their view is contrary to the very personhood of the Holy Spirit, which the Socinian error attacks.

<header>D I S S E R T A T I O N</header>

XVII. Since, therefore, it is beyond doubt that the words of those speaking were the words of the Holy Spirit himself, how much more should the same be presumed regarding the words of those writing? For what they spoke was intended only for the use of their own age; but what they wrote, they brought forth as a standard for the universal Church of all subsequent times. The more illustrious this goal was, and the greater the danger of the Word being corrupted while being passed through the hands of so many people, the greater the care that can be expected from divine goodness, ensuring that nothing concerning this Word of His was left to human power.

XVIII. To that end, that the very **expressions** were **dictated** through the Holy Spirit as if to the pen of the Holy Writers <note>original: Hagiographorum; a term for the authors of the biblical books</note>, a clear command to write regarding certain principal parts of Scripture teaches us. Such is the command given to Moses in Exodus 34:27–28: *And the Lord said to Moses: Write for yourself these words, because according to these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel.* For even if someone wanted to restrict this command to the Ten Commandments alone, it would nonetheless appear from this how much care God has for the words themselves. And the added reason—that he made the covenant "according to these words" (properly "according to the mouth of these words" <note>original Hebrew: על פי הדברים האלה</note>)—extends by its very nature to the other parts of Holy Scripture as well, as many as contain the conditions of the divine Covenant. For it is right to conceive of the words of a covenant in such a way that they express the entire mind of the Author of the Covenant himself, and cut off any opportunity for evasion. But it is abundantly clear that these words of the text cohere with those immediately preceding them, and so all those things which God had spoken to Moses up to that point are taken into account.

XIX. A similar command was enjoined upon Jeremiah in chapter 30:2, and emphatically repeated in chapter 36:2: *Take for yourself a scroll of a book, and write in it* **all these words** <note>original Hebrew: את כל-הדברים</note> (with a double emphasis lying both in the particle *et* and the prefix *ha*) *which I have spoken to you against Israel, and against Judah, and against the nations, from the day I spoke with you, from the days of Josiah even to this day.* Everything here is plain. Mention is made of those words which the Lord <note>original: Jehova</note> himself had spoken to Jeremiah, and specifically *all* of them, without any omission; a precept for which Jeremiah’s memory would not have been sufficient, unless the dictating Holy Spirit had brought new assistance. In the same way, it is enjoined upon John,

...what should be written in Revelation 1:1 and what should not be written in Revelation 10:4.

XX. Since this was the case, they possessed a boldness in their language, expressed in writing in the sacred Songs, such that it should be considered the *pen of a ready writer* <note>original: stylum velocis Scribæ; a reference to Psalm 45:1</note>, or rather the pen of the Holy Spirit Himself, according to *Psalm 45:2*. Compare what I have said on this passage in *Exercise II, § 6*. Hence David also praised his own words as the words of the Spirit speaking through him in *2 Samuel 23:2*; and nothing is more familiar to the Prophets than that formula by which they remind us that their words are the <term>Oracle of Jehovah</term> <note>original Hebrew: נאם יהוה (ne’um Yehovah); often translated as "declares the Lord"</note>; or, that Jehovah has spoken in this way. This would have been a grossly improper use of language <note>original: catachresticum</note> unless they had intended to indicate that Jehovah Himself offered the very words they brought forth through their pen, and therefore that those words were to be venerated in every part as the words of Jehovah. And this is the reason why the things the Prophets wrote are often directly attributed in the pages of the New Testament to God speaking through them, as seen in *Luke 1:70, Acts 1:16, Hebrews 1:1, 1 Peter 1:10, 11, etc.*

XXI. What is established regarding certain divine writers must also be determined for the rest. For as Peter teaches, <term>no prophecy of Scripture</term> <note>original Greek: πασα προφητεια γραφης (pasa prophēteia graphēs)</note> is of one's own private interpretation. For prophecy was never brought forth by the will of man, but those holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit, according to *2 Peter 1:20, 21*. From this, it is concluded that the matter here concerns not only the prophetic subject matter, but also the very words and phrases themselves, because the right of "private interpretation" is taken away from men and granted to the Holy Spirit alone. Now, the object of interpretation is words, and every person is considered the best interpreter of his own words. If, therefore, for this reason, a man is permitted nothing regarding the words of Scripture unless he knows the mind or Spirit of the Lord (*1 Corinthians 2:16*)—because every prophecy was brought forth through the Holy Spirit—then it rests on the firmest foundation that one must ascribe those very words to none other than the Holy Spirit, as He is the best Interpreter of His own words. Furthermore, since that interpretation which is not drawn from one's own whim, but can be considered as the interpretation of the Holy Spirit Himself, requires the attentive and faithful care of a pious mind regarding the goal, the connection, and the comparison of parallel passages; it follows from this that not only those parts of prophetic Scripture which we are currently explaining, but also those which we compare them with, must be held as the direct utterance of the Holy Spirit Himself.

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of the absolute integrity of the Biblical text. Having previously argued that the Prophets' words were the very words of the Holy Spirit, the author now turns to the words of Jesus to prove that even the smallest strokes of the Hebrew letters are divinely preserved.</meta>

<page-num>368</page-num>

<header>DISSERTATION</header>

XXII. This truth is confirmed in no small measure by the assertion of our Savior himself in *Matthew 5:18*, stating that *until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota, nor one tittle shall pass from the Law.* <note>original Greek: ἰωτα ἑν, ἠ μια κεραια οὐ μη παρελθη ἀπο του νομου. The "iota" refers to the smallest letter, while the "tittle" or "apex" refers to the tiny strokes that distinguish one Hebrew letter from another.</note> Parallel to this is *Luke 16:17*, where it is declared that *it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away, than for one tittle of the Law to fall.* <note>original Greek: του νομου μιαν κεραιαν πεσειν</note> Here, the "iota" is omitted, because a conclusion can easily be drawn from the lesser to the greater. However, the point is made even more strongly here, as the "falling" of even a single tittle is declared impossible; in this way, the necessity of the very marks of Scripture is greater than that of heaven and earth. 

The famous <term>Wolf</term> <note>Johann Christoph Wolf (1683–1739), a noted German theologian and Hebraist.</note> shows at length how much disagreement there is among interpreters regarding this promise. A large part of that disagreement arose from a love for a particular hypothesis, by which some—fearing that the integrity of Scripture, even in its smallest details, might be too clearly confirmed—claimed that the Heavenly Teacher was merely using a proverbial or even a <term>hyperbolic</term> <note>an intentional exaggeration not meant to be taken literally.</note> way of speaking. We rightly do not listen to any of these people, both because the Savior, being occupied with teaching the common people, used a plain style, and because I shrink significantly from the opinion of those who dare to smear the divine promises themselves with the charge of hyperbole. 

There is no difficulty in the simplicity of the literal meaning, provided that one sheds the prejudice that Scripture is not fully inspired in every respect. The Savior designates by "iota" and "tittle" that which is a part of the Law or the Scripture of the Old Testament. Therefore, we leave the "little crowns" and "tips" <note>original: coronulas & apiculos. These refer to purely decorative flourishes added by scribes.</note>—which were usually added by the Jews for the sake of ornament—to <term>Cappel</term> <note>Louis Cappel (1585–1658), a scholar who famously argued that Hebrew vowel points were a later human addition rather than part of the original inspired text.</note>, <term>Le Moyne</term>, and others, because these ornaments do not constitute integral parts of the Law. 

But if by "iota" we understand the smallest of the consonants <note>referring to the Hebrew letter Yod (י)</note>, and by "tittle" we understand either the <term>vowel points</term> <note>the marks added to Hebrew consonants to indicate vowel sounds.</note>, or the accents, or both, then all the individual elements of the Hebrew letters—from whose composition and construction words are formed—are most elegantly encompassed here. From this it appears that if the Savior wished to assert that the integrity of the Prophetic Scripture would be constantly preserved to the end through the most accurate Providence of God in all its parts, it could not have been expressed more elegantly or more fully. Such great care for even the individual letters of the sacred Text clearly supposes that those very letters are necessary particles of the Word of God, of which...

# ON DIVINE INSPIRATION

...the writing [of the scriptures] proceeded not from any human whim, but from the Holy Spirit. For the reason for such accurate preservation of the entire Scripture is none other than that *it is the Word of God.* Since it rests upon the truth and constancy of God, it is impossible for it to be broken in any part. Therefore, what he had observed concerning these minute details, the Savior asserts concerning his own words in *Matthew 24:35, Mark 13:31, and Luke 21:33* <note>original: "Marc. XIII. 32" — The text likely intends verse 31, which parallels the Matthew and Luke passages regarding heaven and earth passing away.</note>. And for that reason, the words which *Jehovah put into the mouth* of his messengers shall not depart forever, because they are the words of *Jehovah* himself (*Isaiah 59:21*). It is manifest, therefore, that every single letter and every single stroke belongs to the Word of God. From this, even among the Catholic writers, <term>Melchior Cano</term> <note>Melchior Cano (1509–1560) was a Spanish Dominican theologian. The author cites him here to demonstrate that even "the Papists" (Catholics) agree that every "jot and tittle" of the Bible is divinely inspired.</note> says in his *Theological Commonplaces*, Book II, chapter 17: "*Scripture* is woven together with such care and by the breath of God's assistance that not only is there no word, but not even a single iota or a single stroke that was not supplied by the Holy Spirit."

XXIII. Whatever is attributed in these sayings to the Old Testament as a whole extends likewise to the New Testament. For we have noted not only that the same phrases regarding <term>divine inspiration</term> <note>original Greek: Θεοπνευστία (*theopneustia*), literally "God-breathed."</note> are applied to the writers of the New Testament as are read concerning the Prophets, but also that this was to be expected by much greater right from the more abundant measure of the Holy Spirit poured out upon them. And all the more so because God wished to present a more abundant and clearer rule of faith and life to his people through the New Testament. For this reason also, John the Baptist is declared greater than all the prophets, yet the least in the Kingdom of Heaven is greater than John (*Matthew 11:11*). Hence, the writers of the New Testament use the same, or at least equally valid, expressions to assert their divine inspiration. Just as the Prophets appeal to the "saying of *Jehovah*," so these [Apostles] appeal to the "*Word of the Lord*." *1 Thessalonians 2:13: You received the word of God not as the word of men, but (as it truly is) as the Word of God.* *1 Thessalonians 4:15: This we say to you by the Word of the Lord.* *Colossians 1:25: Of which Church I was made a Minister according to the stewardship of God which was given to me toward you, to fulfill the Word of God.* Add to this *Luke 3:2-3, Romans 16:25-26, 1 Corinthians 14:37, etc.*, and especially that formula from the Book of Revelation: *He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches (Revelation 2:7, 11, 17, 29, etc.).* And it appears from *1 John 5:6* that the Testimony of the Apostles is just as much the Testimony of the Holy Spirit as the Testimony of the Prophets.

# CONCERNING DIVINE INSPIRATION
<note>original Greek: ΘΕΟΠΝΕΥΣΤΙΑΙ (*theopneustiai*)</note>

<sig>Aaa 2</sig>

applies to the Pauline Epistles. Add to this, that he praises that Scripture which was able to make one wise for salvation. Moreover, in that era in which believing that Jesus Christ had come into the world was necessary for salvation, this could not be expected from the Old Testament alone without the contribution of the <term>Evangelical Scripture</term> <note>In this context, "Evangelical Scripture" refers to the New Testament, specifically the Gospels and Apostolic writings.</note>. Finally, those beneficial uses which are attributed to this Scripture could not have been obtained without comparing the books of both Testaments. One may consult those who have illustrated this passage more professionally: <term>Calovius</term> <note>Abraham Calov (1612–1686), a leading Lutheran orthodox theologian.</note> in his *Illustrated Bible* in a specific dissertation on this passage, and <term>Carpzovius</term> <note>Johann Benedict Carpzov (1639–1699), a German Lutheran theologian and professor.</note> in his *Academic Disputations*, number 27.

XXV. With these points established, it will be easy to conclude that the Inspiration of these books extends to the words and phrases themselves. For what is predicated of the *whole* must be asserted of its individual parts—the greatest and the smallest—considered both in their <term>material and formal</term> <note>A philosophical distinction: "material" refers to the content or substance, while "formal" refers to the structure or the specific words chosen.</note> aspects, unless it is established from elsewhere that this universality must be limited. These limits must be fixed either by a manifest declaration of God or by the nature of the matter itself. The former clearly does not occur. But if the nature of the subject required a limitation, that would have to be established either *a priori* <note>from first principles or theoretical reasoning</note> or *a posteriori* <note>from observation or experience</note>. If *a priori*, then it ought to be evident that something absurd or unworthy of God is involved if it is maintained that He is the author not only of the subjects, but also of the words occurring in the sacred texts. No one will easily take upon themselves the burden of proving that. Nothing remains, then, except that something be shown *a posteriori* to exist in the sacred texts whose inspiration would contain something contrary to divine wisdom or holiness. But on this side also we are secure, as will appear more clearly later when we discuss those things which are raised as objections by some. I will say nothing now of how the very name "Scripture" <note>original Greek: γραφῆς (*graphēs*), literally meaning "a writing"</note> leads us toward this conclusion. For the Apostle uses the specific word "Scripture" rather than the general "Word of God" undoubtedly for the purpose of establishing the writing itself as the object of divine Inspiration. This is so plain that it has even extorted agreement from the <term>Papists</term> <note>A historical term for Roman Catholics.</note> themselves. Among them, <term>Willem Estius</term> <note>Willem Hessels van Est (1542–1613), a prominent Dutch Catholic commentator.</note> on this passage says, *rightly and most truly, it is established from this place that all sacred and Canonical Scripture was written by the dictation of the Holy Spirit; in such a way, surely, that not only the sentences, but also every word and [of the words...]*

order, and the entire *arrangement* is from God, as if He were speaking or writing through Himself. For this is what it means for Scripture to be divinely *inspired*.

XXVI. Such constant testimony of Scripture is supported by *Reason*, both *from cause to effect* <note>original: à priori</note> and *from effect to cause* <note>original: à posteriori</note>; at least these arguments should not be rashly rejected by those who, with us, confess the divine origin of the content of Holy Scripture. The nature of the instruments which God willed to use to reveal His will to men **proves**, *from cause to effect*, the necessity of *Inspiration* regarding the words and phrases themselves. For:

A. Between *words* and the things they signify, there exists a bond as intrinsic and indissoluble as that between the body and our mind. Indeed, through the very union of the soul with the body, our mind is so accustomed to this mode of thinking that it can neither stir up any idea within itself, nor compare one with another, let alone communicate it to another, unless it is marked and distinguished by the specific character of a word through which it can be expressed and explained to others. Much less could it have grasped new ideas of more sublime things, unless God, in revealing them, had also joined the suitable words and phrases through which they might be both distinctly conceived and conveniently passed on to others.

B. This is required much more when the majesty of *mysteries* is so great that not only was <term>the fact of their existence</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ ὅτι (*to hoti*)</note> completely unknown before Revelation, but even where that fact is established, <term>the manner of their being</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ πῶς (*to pos*)</note> remains nevertheless shrouded in deep darkness. For from whom will they expect the words, if not from God Himself—those who speak of such sublime things that neither they themselves, nor other holy men living at the same time, could grasp their true nature, to which the words must be suited? Moreover, this is the case not only with metaphysical and supernatural truths, but also with many physical descriptions; these were described by the sacred Authors in such a way that it was only after many centuries had passed that they were found to be truly so through the experiments of more recent men, as <term>Nieuwentijt</term> <note>Bernard Nieuwentijt (1654–1718), a Dutch philosopher and mathematician who argued that scientific discoveries in the natural world confirmed the accuracy of the Bible.</note> teaches throughout his *Sacred Cosmotheology*.

XXVII. More evidence for this matter is available *from effect to cause* <note>original: à posteriori</note>.

To wish to spend so many sweats, so many vigils, so many sighs and prayers upon it further would be superfluous. Indeed, the bolder someone is in exercising the **Critical Art**, the better Interpreter of the divine Word he will be from then on.

XXVIII. That the gift of *Inspiration* was to be extended this far <note>That is, extending to the very words used, not just the general ideas.</note> was already the faith of the *Fathers* from the earliest beginnings of the Church. For this purpose, CLEMENT OF ROME, in his *Letter to the Corinthians*, section 45, names the Scriptures: <note>original: "τας αληθεις ρησεις Πνευματος του αγιου"</note> *the true utterances of the Holy Spirit*. And ATHENAGORAS, in his *Embassy*, chapter 6, insists upon <note>original: "το πιστευειν τω παρα του Θεου Πνευματι, ως οργανα κεκινηκοτι τα των Προφητων στοματα"</note> *believing in the divine Spirit, who moved the mouths of the Prophets like instruments*. He says elegantly in chapter 8 regarding the Prophets: <note>original: "οι κατ' εκστασιν των εν αυτοις λογισμων κινησαντος αυτους του Θειου Πνευματος, α ενηργουντο εξεφωνησαν· συγχρησαμενου του Πνευματος, ωσει και αυλητης αυλον εμπνευσαι"</note> *those who, being placed outside their own thoughts while the Divine Spirit moved them, spoke out whatever he worked within them; the Spirit used them just as a flute player is accustomed to blow into a flute*.

From this point on, the emblem of a wind instrument <note>original: "inflati organi Musici." The author refers to instruments played by breath, such as flutes or pipes.</note> became a familiar image for the Church Fathers in this matter, doubtless because in it there is a manifest allusion to the word "Spirit" <note>original: "Πνευμα" (Pneuma), which literally means breath or wind.</note> and the term "Inspiration" <note>original: "Θεοπνευσιας" (Theopneustias), meaning "God-breathed."</note>. This can be seen from HIPPOLYTUS in *On the Anti-Christ* (Fabricius edition, page 5), from MACARIUS in *Homily 47*, and others. TERTULLIAN also teaches this very thing in *On the Soul*, chapter 28: *No speech is divine unless it is from the one God, with which the Prophets, the Apostles, and Christ himself thundered.*

XXIX. From the third century, CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA is added to the ranks in *Stromata*, Book VI, chapter 18: <note>original: "Τους δε του Παντοκρατορος Προφητας Θεου ουκ αν τις καταπλαγειη, οργανα θειας γενομενους φωνης;"</note> *Would not anyone be amazed by the Prophets of the almighty God, who became instruments of the divine voice?* And especially ORIGEN insists upon this throughout his works. To pass over other examples, in his *Philocalia*, page 19, he asserts: <note>original: "Πρεπει γαρ τα αγια γραμματα πιστευειν, μηδεμιαν ΚΕΡΑΙΑΝ εχειν κενην σοφιας Θεου"</note> *For it is proper to believe that the holy writings do not have a single <term>tittle</term> <note>original: "ΚΕΡΑΙΑΝ" (keraian). In biblical Greek, this refers to the smallest stroke or serif in a letter, implying that even the tiniest detail of Scripture is divinely intended.</note> empty of the wisdom of God; for from the fullness...*

# ON DIVINE INSPIRATION.

<note>original: "ματος αὐτου λαβοντες οἱ Προφηται λεγουσι"</note> ...receiving from His Spirit, the Prophets speak. *It is necessary therefore to believe that there is no stroke of a pen in the sacred writings that is devoid of the wisdom of God, since the Prophets speak having received from His fullness.* The same author says vividly in **Homily 1 on Exodus**: *Believing the words of my Lord Jesus Christ regarding the Law and the Prophets, I do not think that even one iota or one stroke is empty of mysteries, nor do I think that any of these can pass away until all things are fulfilled.* <note>The author is quoting Origen, a 3rd-century scholar who emphasized that even the smallest markings in the Bible (the "iota" or the "apex/stroke" of a letter) were significant.</note> **CYPRIAN** says in his *Sermon on Almsgiving*: *The Holy Spirit was the Scribe; the Prophets were the pens <note>original: "calami," referring to the reed pens used for manuscripts.</note> with which the Holy Spirit dictated what was to be written.*

XXX. The persuasion of the Post-Nicene Fathers <note>The "Post-Nicene Fathers" are those writing after the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.</note> was the same. There are indeed some among them who are not entirely consistent with themselves in this matter, among whom **JEROME** and **AUGUSTINE** are to be counted; likely because they do not seem to have meditated maturely enough on this entire question. Others, however, precede us more clearly and consistently. **AMBROSE**, in his *Preface to Luke*, weighing the phrase *they have attempted* <note>Referring to Luke 1:1, where Luke mentions others who "undertook" or "attempted" to write the Gospel.</note>, declares that this phrase should not be applied to the sacred Secretaries <note>original: "Amanuensibus"</note> in this way: *For he who attempted to organize, attempted it by his own labor, and did not complete it without effort. For there are gifts and grace from God: into which He has poured Himself, He is accustomed to water them, so that the writer’s genius does not lack but overflows. Matthew did not "attempt," Mark did not "attempt," John did not "attempt," Luke did not "attempt"; but with the Divine Spirit providing the abundance of all WORDS AND THINGS* <note>original: "DICTORUM RERUMQUE"</note> *they completed what they had begun without any struggle.* We add **CHRYSOSTOM** in **Homily 1 on Genesis**: *I beseech you all, do not simply pass over those things contained in the holy Scriptures. For nothing is written here that does not contain many riches of meaning. Since the Prophets spoke being inspired by the Divine Spirit, those things written by the Spirit contain a huge treasure within them. And do not wonder that I promise to show you many and hidden riches of thoughts in this list of names. For there is not even a syllable or a little stroke <note>original: "apiculus"</note> in the sacred writings in whose depth there is not some great treasure. Therefore, it is necessary for us to be led by divine grace and, being illuminated by the Holy Spirit, to approach the divine words.* Let **GREGORY THE GREAT** close the line in his commentary on the first chapter of *Job*: *It is quite uselessly asked who wrote these things, when the Author of the book is faithfully believed to be the Holy Spirit...*

<meta>This page continues the argument for "verbal inspiration" by completing a discussion likely derived from Gregory the Great, who used the analogy of a "pen" to describe the human authors of the Bible. # 378
# DISSERTATION

...it should be believed. He Himself, therefore, wrote these things, who was both the inspirer of that work and who, through the voice of the writer, transmitted His deeds to us to be imitated. If we were to read the words of some great man upon receiving his letters, and we were to ask with what pen <note>original: "calamo," referring to the reed pen used in antiquity.</note> they had been written, it would certainly be ridiculous if we did not strive to know the author of the letters and to understand their meaning, but instead sought to investigate with what kind of pen their words were impressed. Since, therefore, we recognize the matter itself and hold the Holy Spirit to be the author of that matter, when we seek the writer, what else are we doing but scrutinizing the pen while reading the letters? **DAN. HENRICI** has collected more on this subject in *On the Author of Holy Scripture*, section 77 and following; as has **CHRISTIANUS LUPUS** in his *Scholia IX on Tertullian’s Prescription*; and **HEIDEGGERUS** in *Biblical Exercises, Dissertation II*, section 21.

XXXI. The Jews also everywhere think magnificently of the Scripture of the Old Testament in this regard. In the **LEKACH THOBH** <note>Also known as *Lekach Tov*, an 11th-century commentary on the Torah and Megillot.</note>, or their symbolic booklet, Article 8, these words occur: *That the entire Law in its entirety, from the first word: "In the beginning," <note>original: "Bereshith" (Hebrew: בראשית)</note> until the final words: "before the eyes of all Israel," Moses wrote entirely from the mouth of the Lord; and there is no difference between the verse: "I am the Lord your God" (Exodus 20:2) and the verse: "And Timna was a concubine" (Genesis 36:12) and the like; but all of it was equal, and all its verses and words are the voice and speech of the Lord.* <note>The author is illustrating that for these scholars, a minor genealogical detail is just as divinely inspired as the Ten Commandments.</note> Hence **KIMCHIUS** <note>David Kimhi, a medieval Jewish biblical commentator and grammarian.</note> himself does not hesitate to interpret the words of Ezekiel 3:4, "and speak with my words to them," as: *In the same language in which I speak to you, you shall speak to them.* <note>original: "בלשון אשר אני מדבר... לך כן תדבר"</note> Hence that famous saying <note>original: "πολυθρυλλητον" (polythryllyton)</note>: *There is no letter in the Law upon which great mountains do not hang.* <note>This refers to a Talmudic idea that every tiny stroke of a letter contains mountains of legal and spiritual meaning.</note> Hence the belief in the immutability of the Law, even regarding the letters and the decorative tips of the letters <note>original: "apices," referring to the small strokes or crowns on Hebrew characters.</note>, which **LIGTFOOTUS** <note>John Lightfoot, a 17th-century Hebraist who sought to explain the New Testament through Jewish tradition.</note> teaches in his *Hebrew Hours on Matthew*, using many gathered testimonies. Hence also the superstitious meticulousness <note>original: "ακριβεια" (akribeia)</note> in transcribing the Book of the Law, which **SCHICKARDUS** depicts in *On Royal Law, Part II*. For although they may take away with one hand what they gave with the other, the force of truth has nonetheless squeezed this confession from them.

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of "Theopneustia" (Divine Inspiration), moving from the general authority of Scripture to the specific mechanisms by which the Holy Spirit interacts with human authors. # ON DIVINE INSPIRATION. 379

XXXII. The work of *Inspiration* itself can be considered by us in two ways: either insofar as the Holy Spirit prepared the Divinely Inspired <note>original: "Theopneustous" (Greek: θεοπνεύστους), meaning "God-breathed."</note> men to manifest His will through them on earth; or insofar as He directed either their tongue or their hand in the very moment <note>Latin: "temporis articulo," referring to the specific point in time of the prophetic act.</note> in which they were prophesying.

XXXIII. *Preparation for Inspiration* was either remote or proximate. To the more remote can be referred, in the broadest sense, all the ways of divine providence through which those subjects, whom God freely destined for such a great work, were placed in those circumstances so that, in their own time, they might become fit to undertake God's Mission among men. More *strictly*, however, I would refer to this those operations of the Holy Spirit through which they were furnished with the necessary gifts. This preparation was instituted *early*, from the very womb, in Jeremiah chapter 1:5 and in John the Baptist, Luke 1:15, 80, and appeared from infancy. From the latter example, we also gather that this adaptation was made by a peculiar power of the Holy Spirit. Whence it is also described as a certain kind of sanctification in the former example. In other subjects, however, the history of the Apostles itself teaches that this matter was completed more quickly. Nevertheless, the greatest difference lies in the fact that in some, the bestowing of *ordinary and extraordinary gifts* was combined; in others, the former were clearly lacking. Thus we are taught through Balaam <note>original: "Bileamum," a prophet mentioned in the Book of Numbers who spoke God's words despite his own character.</note>, and also through those who, although gifted with the prophetic Spirit in the early days of Christianity, nevertheless remained devoid of saving grace. Let Matthew 7:22-23, 1 Corinthians 13:2, and Hebrews 6:4-5 be examined.

XXXIV. *Proximate preparation* took place when things to be spread for the use of others were represented, either through visions or through voices, offered to those who were awake—whether in ecstasy <note>A state of being "outside oneself" or in a trance-like spiritual vision.</note> or outside of it—or to those dreaming. One might wander through various kinds of prophetic Revelations here, were it not necessary to stick closer to the present purpose. For that which we properly call Divine Inspiration <note>original: "Theopneustian" (Greek: θεοπνευστίαν).</note> does not yet occur in all those modes. For through those [revelations] they themselves were merely taught, but through *Inspiration* they taught others. Whence revelations sometimes happened to them which they did not communicate to the Church; while at other times with-

Here, the author transitions into analyzing the specific linguistic terms used in Scripture to describe how the Holy Spirit moves a human author.</meta>

<header>DISSERTATION</header>

nor is it credible that they were driven to write by any more special preparation. The former occurs in the rapture of Paul, the latter in the sermons of Christ and the Apostles, as well as in the recording of sacred history.

### XXXV.
<margin>→</margin>In order that the mode of *Inspiration* itself may be correctly understood according to the testimony of Scripture, the phrases used to describe it must be examined. The very word *Theopneustia* <note>original: "Θεοπνευστίας" (Theopneustias), meaning "God-breathed."</note> suggests not only the *Holy Spirit* as the Author, but also a most effective act, which is compared to a *breath* <note>original: "flatus"</note>; and without a doubt, it was prefigured specifically through the breathing of the Lord. It is, moreover, the nature of *breath* to impart a new motion to the air and the surrounding bodies, by which they are carried toward that place to which the breath impels them. Ezekiel 1:12 transfers this to the operations of the Holy Spirit in the Apostles: *Wherever the spirit (or wind) was to go, they went; they did not turn as they went.*

### XXXVI.
Linked by a very close bond to this metaphor is the phrase in 2 Peter 1:21: *being carried by the Holy Spirit, they spoke* <note>original: "ὑπὸ Πνεύματος ἁγίου φερόμενοι ἐλάλησαν" (hypo Pneumatos hagiou pheromenoi elalēsan)</note>. This phrase is not unknown in the writings of the Old Testament, where false prophets lying about divine inspirations are likewise called "spirit-bearers" <note>original: "πνευματοφόροι" (pneumatophoroi)</note> in Hosea 9:8 and Zephaniah 3:5. Regarding spiritual quickening, the phrase "to bring the spirit of life" <note>original: "φέρειν πνεῦμα ζωῆς" (pherein pneuma zōēs)</note> occurs in a somewhat broader sense in Ezekiel 37:5. Various scholars have brought forward various interpretations to illustrate this. Some, comparing it with the work of Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant theologian.</note> on Hebrews 1:3, believe it is taken from those *who cause anything to be moved and transferred*. Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius (1500–1574), a German classical scholar.</note> says the word pertains to runners, based on Hebrews 6:1, where it says "leaving [the basics], let us be carried forward," where "leaving" alludes to the starting line or the stalls from which they began to run. I am most firmly convinced that it refers to the impulse provided by the wind. Hence, the same word is used for the *wind* that was the symbol of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost. For in Acts 2:2, there is mention of "a sound like a rushing mighty wind" <note>original: "ἦχος ὥσπερ φερομένης πνοῆς βιαίας" (ēchos hōsper pheromenēs pnoēs biaias)</note>. And in the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> version of Job 13:25, we read "grass driven by the wind" <note>original: "χόρτος φερόμενος ὑπὸ πνεύματος" (chortos pheromenos hypo pneumatos)</note>. Among the same translators, the Greek "to carry" <note>original: "φέρειν" (pherein)</note> corresponds to the Hebrew word *nadaph* <note>original: "נָדָף" (nadaph), meaning to drive away or dispel</note> in Leviticus 26:36, where a "driven leaf" <note>original: "φύλλον φερόμενον" (phyllon pheromenon)</note> is a *leaf impelled by the wind*. For this reason, Polybius calls the wind "carrying" <note>original: "φόρος" (phoros)</note>, as Suidas observes. Thus, this phrase is very parallel to the language of Paul, and the word "carried" <note>original: "φερόμενοι" (pheromenoi)</note> would rightly be rendered as "those blown upon" or "inspired."

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of Divine Inspiration by comparing Christian theology with classical Greek philosophy. The previous page explored the biblical metaphor of being "carried" by the Spirit; here, the author examines how pagan writers like Plato and Iamblichus used similar terms, before defining the Christian view of inspiration as an irresistible divine operation.</meta>

<page-num>381</page-num>
<header># ON DIVINE INSPIRATION</header>

**XXXVII.** In the sacred magical rites <note>original: "Theurgicis," referring to theurgy, a type of ancient ritual intended to invoke the presence of gods</note> of the Gentiles, the same symbols were accepted by those who, following Plato in the sixth book of his *Republic*, were accustomed to call their enthusiasms **divine inspirations** <note>original Greek: *theias epipnoias*</note> and **divine carryings** <note>original Greek: *theophorias*</note>. Regarding the former, some points have already been brought forward in section 2. The latter is shown by an ancient epigram cited by Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist</note>:

-> Wildly was his soul <-
-> Stirred by the harsh Spirit of the Divine Carrying. <-

*Indeed, his spirit was vehemently stirred by the breath of the Divinity.* This same concept was very familiar to Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note>. Among other places, in his *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*, Section III, chapter 7, he writes: *For the work of the **Divine Carrying** is not human, nor does its total authority rest in human parts or activities; rather, these things are otherwise subordinate, and God uses them as instruments.* This **Divine Carrying** (divine inspiration) is a work more than human, and it does not lean upon mortal faculties or operations; instead, this matter behaves quite differently, since God uses those people as instruments. He continues concerning the mode of this kind of inspiration, putting forward things that he undoubtedly compiled from the writings of Christians:

> *The entire work of prophecy is fulfilled through God, who operates by Himself, purely and separately from all others (with the soul and body contributing nothing). Hence, prophecies conceived in this manner are true. But if the soul should be disturbed before the inspiration, or be stirred up during it, or be confounded by the body, or interrupt the divine harmony, the prophecies turn out confused and deceptive.*

But these ideas are soon so perverted by other false concepts that nothing healthy can be extracted from them. Furthermore, Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism</note>, in his *Enneads* (Book II, lib. 3, c. 10), calls this state of mind **the carrying toward things above** <note>original Greek: *tēn pros ta anō phoran*</note>.

**XXXVIII.** Since, however, that **Inspiration** <note>original: "Afflatus," literally a "blowing upon" or "breath"</note> must be understood in a way consistent with both the nature of the Holy Spirit and that of holy men, it will undoubtedly designate a certain **extraordinary**, **effective**, and **irresistible** **operation, concurrence, and determination** of the Holy Spirit, acting upon both the **mind** and the **body** of those who were inspired. By this means, they were to be considered as bringing forth, speaking, and writing not their own words, but the words of the Holy Spirit Himself.

**XXXIX.** This operation, following the natural order of the soul's faculties, undoubtedly begins from the **Intellect** as the director of the Will,

### XXXV.
But so that the *mode of Inspiration itself* may be correctly understood according to the testimony of Scripture, the *phrases* used regarding it must be examined. The word **Theopneustia** <note>original: Θεοπνευστίας; literally "God-breathed"</note> itself suggests not only the **Holy Spirit** as the Author, but also such a most effective act, which is compared to a blowing <note>original: *flatui*</note>, and was undoubtedly prefigured individually by the *breath* of the Lord. Now, the nature of a *breath* is such that it imparts a new motion to the air and surrounding bodies, by which they are carried toward that place to which the *breath* impels them. This is transferred to the operations of the Holy Spirit in the Apostles in Ezekiel 1:12: *Wherever the spirit (or wind) was to go, they went; they did not turn as they went.*

### XXXVI.
Connected by the tightest bond to this metaphor is the phrase in 2 Peter 1:21: *carried by the Holy Spirit, they spoke* <note>original Greek: ὑπὸ Πνεύματος ἁγίου φερόμενοι ἐλάλησαν</note>. This phrase is not unknown in the writings of the Old Testament, where false prophets lying about divine inspirations are likewise called **spirit-bearers** <note>original Greek: πνευματοφόροι</note> in Hosea 9:8 and Zephaniah 3:5. Regarding spiritual quickening, the phrase *to carry the spirit of life* <note>original Greek: φέρειν πνεῦμα ζωῆς</note> occurs in a slightly broader sense in Ezekiel 37:5. To illustrate this, various scholars have brought forward different views. Some, comparing it with the theologian **Beza** <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major French Protestant reformer</note> on Hebrews 1:3, judge it to be taken from those *who cause something to be moved and transferred.* **Camerarius** <note>Joachim Camerarius (1500–1574), a German classical scholar and reformer</note> says the word pertains to runners from Hebrews 6:1, where it is said *leaving [the beginning] behind, let us be carried forward* <note>original Greek: ἀφέντες φερώμεθα</note>; he notes that "leaving behind" alludes to the starting stalls <note>original: *carceres*; the starting gates in a Roman racecourse</note> from which they began to run. I am most convinced that it refers to the impulse *by wind*. Hence the same word is used for the *wind* which was the symbol of the poured-out Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost. For in Acts 2:2, *a sound as of a rushing mighty wind* <note>original Greek: ἦχος ὥσπερ φερομένης πνοῆς βιαίας</note> is recorded. And in the **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> version of Job 13:25, we read *grass agitated by the wind* <note>original: χóρτος φερόμενος ὑπὸ πνεύματος</note>. In the same translators, the word "to carry" corresponds to the Hebrew word **nadaph** <note>original: נדף; to drive away or scatter</note> in Leviticus 26:36, where a *driven leaf* <note>original Greek: φυλλον φερόμενον</note> is a "leaf impelled by the wind." From this, the historian **Polybius** calls a favorable wind *phoros*, as the lexicographer **Suidas** observes. Thus, this phrase is quite parallel to the Pauline one, and the word *carried* <note>original: φερόμενοι</note> might deservedly be rendered as *those inspired by breath* <note>original: *afflatos*</note>.

### XXXVII.
In the sacred Theurgical <term>Theurgy: A system of ancient rituals intended to invoke the presence of gods or achieve union with the divine.</term> rites of the Gentiles, the same symbols were adopted by those who, following Plato in the sixth book of his *Republic*, were accustomed to name their enthusiasms "divine inspirations" <note>original Greek: θείας ἐπιπνοίας</note> and "divine carryings" <note>original Greek: θεοφορίας; the state of being possessed or "borne" by a god</note>. Regarding the former term, certain points have already been brought forward in section 2. Regarding the latter, an ancient poem cited by Suidas <note>Suidas (or the Suda) is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> demonstrates it:

-> And wildly his <-
-> Harsh spirit was cooled by the divine carrying. <-
<note>original Greek: Ἄγρια δ' ἀυτου / Ἔψυχθη χαλεπες Πνευμα Θεοφορίην. The author provides a Latin translation: *Vehementer autem Spiritus ejus Numinis afflatu concitatus erat*, meaning "His spirit was vehemently stirred by the breath of the Deity."</note>

This same concept was very familiar to Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on magic and ritual.</note>. Among other places, in *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*, Section III, chapter 7, he writes: *For the work of Divine Carrying <note>original: Theophoria</note> is not a human thing, nor does its total authority rest in mortal parts or actions; rather, these things are subject in a different way, and God uses them as instruments.* He continues regarding the manner of this kind of inspiration, putting forward ideas which he undoubtedly compiled from Christian writings: *The whole work of divination is fulfilled through God, who operates by Himself, purely and separately from all others (while the soul and body contribute nothing). Thus, prophecies conceived in this manner are true. But if the soul should be disturbed before the inspiration, or be stirred up during it, or be confused with the body, or interrupt the divine harmony, the prophecies turn out confused and false.* However, these ideas are soon so perverted by other false concepts that nothing sound can be extracted from them. Furthermore, Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism.</note> in *Ennead* II, book 3, chapter 10, calls this state of mind "the upward movement" <note>original Greek: την προς τα άνω φοραν</note>.

### XXXVIII.
Since that Inspiration <note>original: Afflatus; literally a "breathing upon" or "blowing"</note> must be understood in a way consistent with both the nature of the Holy Spirit and of holy men, it will undoubtedly designate a certain extraordinary, effective, and irresistible operation, concurrence, and determination of the Holy Spirit upon both the mind and the body of those who were being inspired. By means of this, they were to be judged as bringing forth, speaking, and writing not their own words, but the words of the Holy Spirit Himself.

This operation undoubtedly begins from the Intellect, acting as the director of the Will, in accordance with the natural order of the faculties of the soul,

[the prophet] began in a natural state, and [God] so disposed him that, being inspired, he might easily perceive the Spirit of God as if present. For it is not believable that God wished to reveal His will to men through the service of other men, unless He had first and above all convinced those primary messengers through the most evident signs that the Holy Spirit <note>original Latin: Spiritus Sanctus</note> had indeed been given to them and was working within them by His immediate activity <note>original Greek: ἐνεργεία (energeia), meaning active power or operation</note>. The more prone a person might be to fall into most ruinous error—whether through the weakness of judgment or various forms of fraud, which have nowhere been more frequent than in the pretense of divine Revelation—the more the Majesty of Religion and the nature of offering Worship from *true faith* (which assumes full *persuasion*) demands that it be established and founded by those who are most deeply persuaded that what they teach and do, they do with God witnessing, commanding, and impelling them. If it were otherwise, the consciences of men would be bound not by God testifying through them, but by human testimony—that is, by something uncertain and fallible. For however much their own certainty were to decrease, human authority would increase by that same amount; and since every man is a liar, this is a ruinous foundation for belief, hated by God, to whom alone belongs the highest right concerning sacred matters. 

That the sacred Authors were intimately persuaded of the truth of the Inspiration granted to them is shown by several things: the hundreds of times that phrase is repeated, "Thus says the Lord" <note>original Hebrew: כה אמר יהוה (Koh amar Yehovah) or נאם יהוה (Ne'um Yehovah), meaning the "Utterance of Jehovah"</note>; the rigid examination they had to undergo in the public declaration of their prophecy, whether by the Aaronic Priesthood or by other Prophets and Divinely-inspired men <note>original Greek: Θεοπνεύστων (Theopneuston)</note>; and the most constant sealing of the truth through frequent Confession and Martyrdom.

rather, it demonstrates the sincerity of the speaker, who confesses himself to be a man whose eye had been obscured. It was, however, of importance to the Church that *Balaam* <note>original Latin: Bileamus; referring to the prophet in the Book of Numbers who was called to curse Israel but blessed them instead</note> should provide this prologue, so that no one might doubt that what he brought forth was spoken through *divine inspiration*. If I say, I will not mention him, or speak any more in his name, then...”*

# DISSERTATION

...which is in my heart like a burning fire shut up in my bones; I am weary of holding it in, and I can no longer. (Jeremiah 20:9). Hence Amos 3:8: *The Lord has spoken, who would not prophesy?* <note>The Latin OCR cites Amos 3:6, but the quotation corresponds to Amos 3:8.</note> For this reason, the mouths of those must be stopped who mark with the "black coal of rashness" that great boldness <note>original Greek: παρρησία (parrhesia) — frankness or courageous speech</note> in speaking which holy men used, far removed from all favoritism <note>original Greek: προσωποληψία (prosopolepsia) — literally "respect of persons" or showing partiality based on status</note> or fear of Princes themselves. For that which rendered them so intrepid was a heavenly instinct, to which it was not right to throw up any barrier, since God was to be obeyed more than men. For this reason, Peter concludes: *We cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.* Acts 4:10, 20. Compare also 1 Corinthians 9:16.

**B.** Yet, nothing happened to them against their will or through violent coercion. Indeed, a sense of their own weakness sometimes rendered them fearful and hesitant when they realized they were destined for this Ministry of God, as is proven by the examples of Moses (Exodus 4), Isaiah (6:5), Jeremiah (1 and 20), and Jonah (1). But the grace of both the general call to an extraordinary office and, most importantly, the special mode of Inspiration itself, made them willing participants. For the prevailing power of Jehovah was preceded by His persuasion through that illumination of the intellect, which caused the greatest readiness, even in the midst of greatest dangers. Hence, in the passage cited from Jeremiah: <term>פתיתני יהוה ואפת</term> — *You have persuaded me, O Lord, and I was persuaded.* <note>original Hebrew: *pattitani YHWH wa-eppat*; Jeremiah 20:7</note> Without any necessity, some have interpreted the word <term>פתה</term> <note>original Hebrew: *patah* — to persuade, entice, or deceive</note> here in a bad sense as "seduction." And so, that which God willed to be said and written through them, they themselves also willed to say and write. Thus, not only is God said to have spoken through them, but they themselves, as secondary and subordinate causes, are said to have spoken and written. Luke 24:25; Acts 26:22; 28:25; 1 Corinthians 2:6, 13, etc.

**C.** Meanwhile, 2 Peter 1:20 declares that no right was left to their own will in the formation or delivery of prophecy, since *prophecy never came by the will of man.* We have already noted in section 10 that, for this to be manifest, holy men did not always possess the gift of Divine Inspiration <note>original Greek: Θεοπνευστίας (theopneustias) — literally "God-breathedness"</note>. Therefore, the availability of opportunities was not in their power, but depended solely on the determination of the Holy Spirit, who directed all their ways.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of divine inspiration, moving from the internal willingness of the prophets to the physical and external process of writing the sacred texts.</meta>

### ON DIVINE INSPIRATION

Whether physical manifestation had a place here is difficult to determine. Ecstatic movements <note>refers to the physical shaking or trances often associated with pagan "enthusiasm"</note> were sometimes present in **Prophetic Vision**, and for that reason, we have categorized them under the preparation of the prophet. However, it does not seem that they had a place in the actual act of **Inspiration** itself. The presence of mind required speech directed to others, and even more so, the recording of Revelation into writing. Since the Apostles themselves, in their own discourses, expressly dismissed any suspicion of ecstasy or enthusiastic movements—as seen in *Acts 2:15* and *26:25*—it was this very quality that distinguished them from the frenzied priests of the Gentiles; the same must be presumed regarding their writings. Therefore, the tongue and the pen were directed by a will that was indeed divinely impelled, but also fully conscious of itself. On this point, **ORIGEN**—commenting on the words of *Romans 10:16, 20*—correctly pronounces their opinion to be false who thought the Prophets did not know what they were saying, as if they had prophesied while out of their minds.

XLIII. Regarding the direction of the hand, however, **SERARIUS** <note>Nicolaus Serarius (1555–1609), a Jesuit theologian and exegete</note> in his *Biblical Prolegomena, Chapter 5, Short Question 17*, proposed this problem: How does God affect the hand of the Biblical writer? He answers by acknowledging that it is not necessary to attribute a specific miraculous skill for writing to the hand; yet, he did not wish to deny the assistance of God, by which He holds the hand, as it were, lest the writer put one thing for another, one little word for another, or one letter for another.

XLIV. Finally, it is asked whether that Inspiration extended also to the **Amanuenses** <term>Amanuenses — professional scribes or secretaries who wrote from dictation</term> whom the sacred authors sometimes employed? If we listen to **JEROME**, it seems this must be admitted in certain cases. For he says in *Letter 150 to Hedibia*:

> We have said several times that the Apostle Paul was a most learned man, educated at the feet of Gamaliel. Although he possessed knowledge of the Holy Scriptures and the grace of speech and various languages—whereof he himself glories in the Lord, saying: *I thank God that I speak in the tongues of all of you more than others*—he was not able to explain the majesty of divine meanings in worthy Greek speech. He had, therefore, **Titus** as his Interpreter, just as the blessed **Peter** had **Mark**, whose Gospel was composed with Peter narrating and Mark writing. Finally, even the two epistles attributed to Peter differ from each other in style, character, and word structure.

From this we understand that, out of necessity...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on whether the secretaries or scribes who physically wrote the biblical texts were also divinely inspired, or if they were merely instruments of the primary authors (the Apostles and Prophets).</meta>

->### DISSERTATION ON DIVINE INSPIRATION<-

...of things, that he used different Interpreters. It is a poor argument here that Paul, due to a supposed lack of skill in the Greek language, is thought to have used an Interpreter. Furthermore, the story of Mark recording Peter's words in his Gospel—though often seized upon by Roman Catholics in favor of Peter's authority—nevertheless raises an unfair suspicion regarding the Gospel's own authenticity. Indeed, it openly contradicts the older and more trustworthy testimony of **IRENAEUS** <note>Irenaeus (c. 130–202 AD), a Greek bishop and early Church Father</note>, who in Book III, Chapter 1, records that Mark was indeed the disciple and *interpreter* of Peter, but adds that the Gospel was not written until after the *death* <note>original: "excessum"</note> of Peter and Paul. And although **CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA** <note>Clement (c. 150–215 AD), a Christian theologian who taught at the Catechetical School of Alexandria</note>, as cited in **EUSEBIUS'S** *Ecclesiastical History* (VI, 14), wishes for this Gospel to have been written before the death of Peter, he nonetheless notes that Peter *neither prohibited it, nor incited that it be written.* Consult further arguments against the rash testimony of **JEROME** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), famous for translating the Vulgate Bible</note> in the work of **BASNAGE** <note>Samuel Basnage (1638–1721), a French Protestant historian</note>, *Annals*, at the year 66 AD, §. 13.

XLV. **EDWARD KELLET** <note>Edward Kellet (d. 1641), an English divine and author of "Miscellanies of Divinitie"</note>, in Book II of his *Theological Miscellanies*, Chapter 9, considers that **Tertius** was a certain other *Divinely Inspired Secretary*. For since we read in Romans 16:22: *I, Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord;* Kellet does not doubt that Tertius was directed by the Holy Spirit both in the transcription of the letter and in these added words. Having set aside what others have thought about these words, I consider it safest to establish, along with **CARPZOV** <note>Johann Benedict Carpzov II (1639–1699), a prominent Lutheran theologian and Hebraist</note> in his *Academic Disputations* (XXVII, Chapter 2, §. 10), that Tertius added these very words by the command of Paul. For the context seems to me to require this, as nothing but the words of the Apostle immediately precede and follow them.

XLVI. This is surely how we should think regarding the *Secretaries* of Divinely Inspired men: that they followed them word-for-word as they dictated through Inspiration. **ABARBANEL** <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and philosopher</note>, commenting on Jeremiah 36:4, 18, declares that Baruch received the words of Jeremiah in this manner, stating, *all those words were from his mouth, and not even one of them was from Baruch.* **CARPZOV**, in the place cited above, added the full passage. However, granted this, it follows that as long as nothing is revealed concerning the immediate inspiration of those *Secretaries*, no reason appears why they ought to have been more infallible—to use the words of the illustrious **GISBERTUS VOETIUS** <note>Gisbertus Voetius (1589–1676), a Dutch Reformed theologian known for his strict orthodoxy</note> in his *Disputations*, Vol. I, p. 47—*than the booksellers and printers who, from the time of the Apostles even to this day, provide Bibles to the churches.* **CARPZOV**, to be sure, does not approve of this comparison, 

,, because these [printers] commit many slips and errors, the likes of
,, which those Secretaries, writing *by divine inspiration* while in the presence 
,, of the Divinely Inspired Man in whose name they were writing, 
,, could not commit.

But what it means to write *by divine inspiration* as something distinct from the *state of Inspiration* itself, I do not grasp. Furthermore, no lapse was to be feared from those first *Secretaries*—who were certainly holy men and most attentive out of reverence for the Divine—because they wrote under the eyes of the Inspired authors; by whom, if the pen had stumbled anywhere, their error would have been corrected on the spot.

# ORATION
## INAUGURAL.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a scene with a figure or landscape motif surrounded by ornate foliage.</image-desc>
Whoever prepares themselves for any great and difficult work must, in the first place, carefully contemplate the final end at which they aim. The next step is to look ahead in time for those aids <note>original: "adminiculis," meaning supports or tools used to achieve a task.</note> which, when properly used, may carry them toward the desired harbor as if with full sails. When they realize they are suffering from a lack of these, they must either abandon the proposal in good time, or diligently cast about their mind's eye to see if any source <note>original: "scaturigo," literally a spring or bubbling up of water, used here metaphorically as a source of wisdom.</note> might present itself, from whose rich storehouse <note>original: "penu," a term for a larder or inner household store.</note> means suitable to the pre-established goal can be drawn sufficiently and safely. But if, under a lucky star, you should happen upon it, then at last it is right to lean into all oars, so that from the fountain itself may be drawn whatever it holds in its depths suitable for undertaking and pursuing the work. And thus, finally, one may hope for a good omen right from the start regarding its desired success and an outcome that will not disappoint.

You have, Most Honorable Listeners, in this brief sketch <note>original: "tabella," literally a small tablet or painting; here meaning a brief outline or description.</note>, the thoughts by which I have been especially occupied—and am occupied even now—ever since the soul-swaying <note>original: "flexanima," a powerful rhetorical term implying a force that can bend or move the heart.</note> force of divine providence led my mind to decide that I must comply with the highly honorable call of the most distinguished Leaders <term>Procerum: the city magistrates or high-ranking officials who oversaw the university.</term> of this city to undertake the ordinary Theological Professorship in this most splendid Academy. How great a weight this proposal carries is clearly apparent from its goal, which is by far the most noble of all goals toward which a mind endowed with reason can be directed.

Namely, that the hidden shrines <note>original: "adyta," referring to the innermost, most sacred part of a temple, inaccessible to the uninitiated.</note> of true Wisdom may be opened; that the flashing rays of Divine wisdom may be displayed in full light through so many miracles of both nature and grace; that the deceits <note>original: "fuci," literally the red dye or rouge used as makeup, here meaning "false colors" or "pretenses."</note> and pitfalls of the opposing folly—which, like a most foul harlot, turns the minds of so many men away from the royal road of Wisdom—may be uncovered; that the hearts of the youth dedicated to God may be filled with the knowledge, veneration, and love of heavenly Wisdom; and that these same youth may be made fit to sow the seeds of this Wisdom into the souls of others throughout the whole Christian world, wherever it extends, with the hope of the most abundant fruit. This is the hinge <note>original: "cardo," the pivotal point upon which everything else turns.</note> upon which all my effort, from this time forward...

# INAUGURAL SPEECH.

...there was an opportunity. For since he <note>Referring to King Solomon.</note> had been illuminated by the light of an admirable Wisdom beyond all other mortals, he was nevertheless not unaware that he, though raised to that peak of Wisdom of which a man on earth is capable, was nothing but a shadow and a prelude of the heavenly Solomon <note>A common theological title for Jesus Christ, suggesting Solomon was a worldly "preview" of Christ’s divine wisdom.</note>. For who would allow themselves to be persuaded that a King, most skilled in the <term>enigmatic science of the ancients<note>Refers to the tradition of "dark sayings" or riddles (*enigmas*) used by ancient sages to convey deep spiritual truths.</note></term>, was unable to solve this most eminent enigma? This was an enigma that closely concerned his own person—a meaning that was not hidden from David, his father and predecessor, and which was the foundation of the prophecies about the fate of the Church published by the Holy Spirit through Solomon.

Therefore, being well aware of this venerable mystery, he held nothing more important than setting a limit on the veneration that the whole world showed to his own Wisdom; he sought to direct all cultivators of <term>Sophia<note>The Greek word for Wisdom, often used in a personified or divine sense in these texts.</note></term> away from the lamp and toward the **Morning Star** <note>original: *Phosphorus*. In Greek, this means "Light-Bringer," referring to the morning star (Venus), but here used metaphorically for Christ as the source of all light.</note>, from the disciple to the Master, and from the stream to the Ocean.

# ORATION

That Solomon was occupied with these most holy thoughts when he was recording the prologue of his **Proverbs**, and was bringing **Wisdom** onto the stage, as it were, with the most elegant ornament of speech, will become more fully evident once we have brought into the open <note>original: *in aprico posuerimus*. A Latin idiom meaning to make something clear or manifest.</note> what he precisely indicated by this Wisdom.

Interpreters go their separate ways here. Those wander quite far from the line <note>original: *Longiuscule a linea aberrant*. A metaphor for missing the mark or deviating from the truth.</note> who think that this perfection of the mind, which is called **Wisdom**, is abstracted from every subject and introduced through some kind of "enthusiasm"—either poetic or not much different from the poetic. We admit, indeed, that not a few figures of this kind occur in the ancient monuments of Poets and Philosophers. For who is unaware of **Astraea** <note>The goddess of Justice in Greek mythology, said to be the last immortal to leave Earth as humanity became wicked.</note>, who returned to the heavens after leaving the lands she had inhabited during the Golden Age because of the corruption of subsequent ages? Or the **Hercules** of **XENOPHON**, that Marvel who was assailed by two young women, **Virtue** and **Pleasure**, but was persuaded by the former to follow her? Or all the vices and virtues—and among the latter, in the first place, **Knowledge** <note>original: *Scientia*.</note>—painted in the dress of women in the **Table of CEBES**? <note>A famous allegorical description of the path of human life, attributed to Cebes of Thebes, often used in Renaissance education to teach ethics.</note> Indeed, the very [writings] of profane <note>In this context, "profane" simply means "secular" or "non-sacred" authors from the Greco-Roman tradition.</note> authors, whether they used prose or rhythmic speech...

<meta>This page continues the speaker's critique of interpreting the "Wisdom" of Proverbs as a mere rhetorical device. He is arguing against those who view it as a poetic personification (prosopopoeia) rather than a reference to a literal divine person (Christ).</meta>

<page-num>399</page-num>

-> INAUGURAL [ORATION] <-

...[if they were to consider it], it will be clear to anyone consulting the laws of rhetoric that it is unusual and rather uninspired <note>original: *frigidiusculum*. In classical rhetoric, a "frigid" style is one that feels forced, overly artificial, or inappropriate for the gravity of the subject.</note> to use such a figure almost at the very beginning of a discourse, or among moral precepts, or to repeat the same **Personification** <term>Prosopopoeia: A rhetorical device where an abstract quality or inanimate object is represented as a person.</term> several times in the same short book. And since in the fiction of a persona something either impossible or at least false is contained, those who use them are accustomed either to preface, insert, or add in an epilogue such details as clearly show a fable is being told; yet nothing of this sort appears in the context of the **Royal Proverb-maker** <note>original: *Paroemiastae Regii*. A scholarly title for King Solomon, the traditional author of the Book of Proverbs.</note>.

Indeed, when we consult the sacred authors, although every instance of personification is not banished from their style, they use it quite rarely, without any affectation, and as if only in passing. They do this so that nothing is taken away from the majesty of divine speech, from which nothing is more abhorrent than an empty heap of meaningless words—which cannot be separated from such a lengthy introduction of a fictional character. 

Furthermore, it is the duty of a good interpreter not to admit figurative language unless there is no room for a literal meaning. Hence, it is not right to easily assume a personification unless neither the name of the speaker nor what is spoken fits an actual person. However, the following points will prove that this is not the case here.

<page-num>400</page-num>
<header>-> ORATION <-</header>

In these same arguments, we promise to demonstrate in advance that the **Wisdom** whom Solomon introduces attributes divine excellence to herself. This is a claim which—unless a divine person were actually speaking—would be clearly contrary to the principles of a most perfect and truthful **Deity** <term>Numen: A Latin term for divine power or a presiding divinity.</term>, who does not give His glory to another. Indeed, [to claim such excellence otherwise] would be a task full of the most dangerous risk. For what would have been more effective for instilling the poison of idolatry more deeply into the minds of the Jews—who were already far too prone to it—than the transformation of such Wisdom not only into a persona and a woman, but into a **Goddess**? Indeed, the philosophers of the Gentiles, by incautiously employing such **figures** <note>original: *schemata*. Rhetorical devices or patterns of thought.</note>, provided a kind of "midwifery" to unspeakable superstition. This superstition erected temples and altars to *Virtue*, *Piety*, *Faith*, *Justice*, *Clemency*, and even to **WISDOM** herself under the name of *Mind*—for "Mind also possesses divinity," as that man <note>The Roman poet Ovid.</note> says (a)—and thus gave birth to false gods. (b)

For the same reason, the misguided interpretation of those who certainly bind our **WISDOM** to a specific subject, but to such a one...

The Gospel, whether brought forth by mouth or recorded in writing, is understood here as distinct from the rest. How absurd it would be to agree with the Jewish fiction <note>original: "Judaico... figmento." The author likely refers to the Rabbinic tradition that the Torah (the Law) was created before the world and served as God's blueprint for creation.</note> and to establish it before the very cradle of the world—stating that it was not only *possessed* (a) <note>original: "possessum." What a strained hyperbole <term>Hyperbole|An intentional exaggeration for emphasis.</term> it would be to assert that through this "Word" (the Gospel), *Princes and all the Judges of the earth* (c) hold dominion, when it remains hidden from most of them—not only in Solomon's time, but even today? What a harsh catachresis <term>Catachresis|The use of a word in a way that departs from its traditional or literal meaning, often creating a strained metaphor.</term> it would suggest if not only human actions but even the tenderest of affections were ascribed to this same "Word"—such as, for instance, the *love* for those who love Wisdom (d).

We must, therefore, proceed by another path, so that the knot of Solomon’s enigma is not simply cut <note>A reference to the "Gordian Knot," meaning solving a problem by force or oversimplification rather than through careful reasoning.</note> but peacefully unraveled.

Therefore, to those for whom Wisdom provides counsel, they can hope for *tushia* from her—that is, a happy outcome, a durable good, the effect of wise counsel. (2) This is more evidently clear from Proverbs 2:7, where it is said not of Wisdom (as is commonly asserted, since in this place it concerns the virtue of wisdom, not her person) but of Jehovah giving Wisdom: *He has stored up success for the upright* <note>original: "recondidit rectis rem"</note>, which is most aptly explained as solid happiness and an abundance of all goods.
