# SPEECH #

...perhaps the occasion for this fable was given, if not by the dreams of the Gnostics whom we were just mentioning, then by the careless expressions of the Church Fathers <note>the early Christian bishops and theologians</note> who were too much enticed <note>original: "inescatorum," literally "hooked with bait"</note> by Platonic philosophy. Therefore, no other option remains except the second person of the Deity <note>referring to Christ, the Son</note>, on whose behalf all arguments fight. If there were nothing else, this alone would suffice: that she calls herself the **FOSTER-CHILD** and the delights of *Jehovah*. (a) For who could claim these words as his own with better right than that *Son* of LOVE (b) <note>original Greek: ΤΗΣ ΑΓΑΠΗΣ, "of love"</note> and the BELOVED <note>original Greek: ΑΓΑΠΗΤΟΣ, "beloved"</note>, *in whom the Father was well pleased*, (c) that *only-begotten* one, who is IN THE BOSOM... <meta>catchword: SINU</meta>

# INAUGURALIS #

*...because of the excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord (a).* To grow daily in this knowledge of SUPREME WISDOM and to be of use to others—this shall be the sum of my vows, and the very pinnacle of my happiness. These little sparks burning within my heart I attribute so entirely to that WISDOM herself, whom I celebrate, that I hold them as a pledge; for since *her gifts and calling are beyond regret (b)*, I trust that the light of her grace—which she granted me beyond all merit in my previous career <note>original: "curriculo"; refers to his earlier path of life or studies</note>—will not fail me in this new path I now enter.

Relying on this hope, MOST NOBLE LEADERS, Overseers of the City and the Academy, I most gratefully embrace your exceptionally remarkable kindness, by which you desired me—a foreigner and one undeserving—to be an interpreter of SUPREME WISDOM in so illustrious a Lyceum <note>original: "Lyceo"; a classical term for a place of higher learning or university, referencing Aristotle's school in Athens</note>, under your watchful eyes and protection. I willingly and gladly set my shoulders to this task, a duty so outstanding and enviable. May God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Deus O. M." (Optimus Maximus); a traditional honorific title for God</note>, command that this be auspicious and healthful for His Church, and especially for this celebrated sanctuary of divine and human Wisdom. Inundated by so generous a dew of your favor, [I offer] my loyalty to you,

->vene-<-

# ORATION #

The images of so many distinguished and most celebrated men, my predecessors, through whose efforts this Academy <note>the university</note> grew to such great honor, will be constantly before my eyes. There were those among them whose instruction and friendship I once enjoyed, as I recall now with a mindful heart. Now, with God’s help, I shall follow in their footsteps in such a way that whatever is lacking in the strength of my talent, my erudition, or my practical experience, I may fulfill through my diligence and my desire to serve well the study of heavenly Wisdom, this Academy, and this flower of youth <note>original: "juventutis hoc flore"; a traditional metaphor for the student body</note>.

# INAUGURAL [ORATION]

...we are tossed. We beseech You, kindle a light from Your light in our minds. Dispel all the darkness of ignorance and errors by which we are clouded. Overcome that sense of the flesh <note>original: *sensum carnis*; a theological term referring to worldly intuition or carnal reasoning that opposes spiritual truth.</note> which so often drives us astray from the path of truth and right. Open the eyes of our understanding through Your Spirit, so that we may rightly recognize Your beauty and be entirely carried away into love and obedience to You. Send forth Your light and Your truth; let them lead us to Your holy mountain and to Your dwellings <note>original: *tabernacula*; a reference to Psalm 43:3, symbolizing the presence of God or the sanctuary of truth.</note>.

You have commanded in Your word: *If any of you lacks Wisdom, let him ask of God, and it will be given to him* <note>original: *Si quis vestrum deficitur Sapientia, petat a Deo, & dabitur ei*; a direct quotation of James 1:5.</note>. Be mindful now of this Your truthful saying, and have mercy on Your most unworthy servant, who, obeying Your command, girds himself for the duty of a Teacher <note>original: *Doctoris*; specifically referring to his new status and responsibilities as a professor.</note> in this Your workshop <note>original: *officina*; a common Early Modern metaphor for a school or university as a place where minds and souls are "forged" or "worked."</note>. Wash away all his faults, and pour over him abundantly the oil of Your Spirit. Supply to his intellect sharpness and insight, to his judgment prudence and skill, to his will a love of truth and the constancy to defend it even unto the very ashes <note>original: *ad cineres usque*; a phrase meaning "until death" or "to the very end."</note>, and finally, strength to his body, so that he may rightly discharge all parts of his office to Your honor.

Deign, O most gentle Jesus, to grant Your most humble servant a closer fellowship <note>original: *commercio*; literally "commerce" or "exchange," but in this mystical/theological context, it refers to intimate spiritual communion.</note> with You. Show him Your glory, so that he himself, [illuminated] by its radiance—

## WHEN THE MOST CELEBRATED MAN
# FRIEDRICH ADOLPH LAMPE
### *Entered upon the office of Ordinary Professor of Theology;*

->JUNE 24th <note>original: "VIII. KAL. JUL."; the 8th day before the Kalends of July in the Roman calendar.</note><-

->On the very day of SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST,<-
->“He was the burning and shining lamp.” <note>original: "Ἐκεῖνος ἦν ὁ λύχνος ὁ καιόμενος καὶ φαίνων"; a Greek quotation from the Gospel of John 5:35.</note><-

### E P I G R A M

**I**t was night, with a shadow cast from pitch-black clouds,
And the crowd of Jerusalem <note>original: "Solyma"; a poetic abbreviation of Hierosolyma, the Latin name for Jerusalem.</note> lay hidden, destitute of joy;
Suddenly, the Dawn illuminated the lands with a solar <note>original: "Phoebaea"; referring to Phoebus Apollo, the god of the sun.</note> LAMP,
This was the very Forerunner of the Lord:
Soon the SUN radiated from the peak of the highest heaven,
And gleaming, sent a majestic beam from the heavens' axis.
NOW, where the twilight <margin>Isaiah 59:9, 10</margin> gleams beneath the fleeing Sun,
Or, if the night has gone <margin>Zechariah 14:7</margin>, yet the day has not yet risen;
When the LAMP <note>The poet plays on the subject's name, Lampe, which means "Lamp."</note> shines, flashing with ruddy splendor,
Hung in a famous seat by a powerful hand:
I prophesy: the final LIGHT approaches, carried on swift chariots,
The light promised to the pious in the evening of the world.

->Willingly and Deservedly. <note>original: "L. M. Q.," an abbreviation for "Libens Meritoque," a common Latin formula for a dedication.</note><-
->**ALBERT VOGET.**<-
->*Pastor at Heemstede.* <note>original: "V. D. M. Heemst."; V.D.M. stands for Verbi Divini Minister, or Minister of the Word of God.</note><-

It personifies Wisdom as a Queen who appoints Lampe as her servant, maintaining the central "Lamp" pun found throughout these inaugural documents.</meta>

<page-num>471</page-num>

Who is sent? For the land of peace <note>original: "השלומה" (Ha-Shluma); likely a Hebrew play on Utrecht’s name or "Solyma" (Jerusalem), suggesting a city of peace.</note> is full:
At the sight of it, this Queen <note>Wisdom is personified here as a Queen.</note> immediately descended
From her holy dwelling, and with a crown of her might
She confers honor: She extended the scepter of glory
To **Lampe**: <note>original: "ללאמפה"; the subject's name, Friedrich Adolph Lampe, is integrated directly into the Hebrew verse.</note> and she said, "Touch the head of my staff."
But he was terrified because of these
Words, and he fell before the feet of Wisdom,
And he pleaded that she might pass the cup of pains <note>A biblical allusion to the "cup" of suffering or heavy responsibility.</note>
And he confessed the poverty of his knowledge and her great power:
Then the Queen said: "Do not reject my covenant,
For I have raised you to be a pillar for me,
A High Priest, a light, and a **Lamp** <note>original: "מנורה" (Menorah); another play on the name Lampe.</note> to serve me
In my holy place: you are more precious to me than all things:
Behold, I will carry you and I will lead at your right hand
My love, my compassion, and my arm of glory:
And the tongue of the learned <note>Isaiah 50:4</note> given by the Lord I shall grant you:
The spirit within you I have placed, your law and my fear:
My light and my glory shall be established upon you:
The right hand shall save you, my soul shall support you
So that your **Lamp** <note>original: "נרך" (Nercha); again, a pun on the name Lampe.</note> shall rejoice <note>The Hebrew "שומח" (shomach) is likely a poetic variant or misspelling of "שמח" (samach - rejoicing) or "צומח" (tzomach - sprouting/growing).</note> upon the abundance of oil,
Always emitting rays of glory like my sun."

### To the honor of my lord, the man glorious in his wisdom,
### **Our Teacher, Friedrich Adolph Lampe,**
### On the day he was raised to the head of this academy. <note>original: "ישיבה" (Yeshiva); while this term usually refers to a Jewish school, Christian Hebraists of this period used it to refer to their own theological academies or universities.</note>

Many days ago, Wisdom <note>Wisdom is personified here as a divine architect and queen, drawing on imagery from the biblical Book of Proverbs.</note> established her seven pillars;
She saw smoke filling the house,
From the incense of her righteous ones rising up,
And with voices of thanksgiving they cry out; with the breastplate <note>original: "חשן" (Choshen); the ceremonial breastplate worn by the High Priest, symbolizing judgment and leadership.</note>
In awe they approached you, Great Queen:
"Build for us the wall of our academy;
Arise and answer us in its time of stumbling;
This task is under your hand, for you are the rock of our region."
But Wisdom remained silent, listening to the sound;
Thus the righteous waited in silence for the Queen.
They did not relent, and so her heart overflowed with tears;
She ascended her throne, setting out on her path:
"Come to the land known as the Palatinate; <note>original: "פ'אלץ" (Pfalz); Lampe had been a prominent pastor and professor in the Palatinate (specifically Heidelberg) before his move.</note>
There is a man of knowledge, the crown of the innocent congregation,
Whose heart desires to find favor for her in her distress."
But because the wicked there plunder the vineyard, <note>A metaphorical reference to the religious or political conflicts in the Palatinate that prompted Lampe's departure.</note>
He turned away from there, and directed his face
Northward, toward the city of **Bremen**; <note>original: "ברע'מה" (Bre'ama); a phonetic Hebrew rendering of the city's name.</note>
There the flock of her pasture rests by the flowing rock.

### ON THE REMEMBRANCE OF THE SAINTS
<meta>catchword: Easily</meta>

...events <note>original: "fata"</note> provide. If a praiseworthy desire arises to understand the proven truth of individual dogmas—tested by the very attacks made against them—or to know the origin and character of errors and heresies (whose smoke Hell has sought in vain to use to cloud the rays of the Church’s light), one will labor in vain to satisfy this desire unless they have a thorough account of the Church’s battles and conflicts. 

If, finally, we recall the immediate and proper goal of Theology, nothing can more genuinely teach the way to worship God, nor more effectively ignite the practice of sincere piety, than that divinely imprinted character of the Church: that **Holiness** which is the Church’s eternal ornament. 

This is the same **Holiness** that was prefigured by the glittering gold of the earthly Sanctuary, the radiance of the gems on the High Priest’s breastplate, and the entire elaborate arrangement <term>choragium; originally a Greek term for the production of a play, here meaning the complex preparation and equipment of religious ritual</term> of the Levitical <note>referring to the tribe of Levi and the complex priestly laws of the Old Testament</note> worship, with all its consecrations and sanctifications. 

This is that **Holiness of Jehovah**, whose image is expressed through the Spirit of sanctification in the Virgin Church—betrothed to the Son of God with pure love. It constitutes her essential and permanent mark, through which she is radiant and glorious within herself before God, and visible and venerable on the outside before all humanity.

->ORATION<-

You will easily notice, my most honored listeners <note>original: "AA. HH.," an abbreviation for "Auditores Honoratissimi," a formal greeting used in academic and religious speeches</note>, how great a harvest of praise would grow for me if I were inclined to go through every detail that might make this field I am entering appear commendable to everyone—and especially those things that might entice genuine cultivators of Theology toward the study of Sacred History. But lest I myself labor under an excessive abundance of arguments, and lest I weary the fixed attention of you all, a significant reason invites me to dwell for a moment on this final fruit, setting aside the rest. For anyone who does not most shamefully abuse their own reason will most willingly grant me that the dignity and value of all sciences and arts are measured by the momentum they provide toward promoting true human happiness and perfection; furthermore, that this perfection depends upon one's progress in true holiness. 

But whoever grants this will, by the same effort, concede that nothing can render the History of the Church more beautiful, nor increase its value more, than those *outstanding examples of true holiness*. Through these examples—far more effectively than any of the famous deeds preserved in the annals of the world <note>secular historical records or worldly chronicles</note>—History exhibits living images of virtue and piety. It invites us to follow them; indeed, it most strongly incites and draws us toward them.

### ON THE REMEMBRANCE OF THE SAINTS.

Therefore, I have decided to explain briefly, as the time and place allow, how a student of <term>Church History</term> <note>original: "Historia Ecclesiastica"</note> ought to engage correctly and profitably with the **REMEMBRANCE OF THE SAINTS** in order to promote their own holiness and that of others.

Since, however, this fruit is lost to many due to a twofold vice: first, on the part of those who, through the innate depravity of the heart, have become accustomed to treating nothing more *negligently* than that which pertains to the amendment of life; and second, on the part of those who, suffering from a warped concept of holiness, "embrace a cloud instead of Juno" <note>original: "pro Junone... nubem amplectuntur," a classical Greek proverb referring to the myth of Ixion, who tried to seduce the goddess Juno but was tricked into embracing a cloud. It refers to someone who pursues a foolish illusion instead of the truth.</note>—deluded by a *foolish* imagination—I will strive to steer the sails of my speech in such a way that I may offer a remedy for both of these diseases of the mind. To that end, I will first attempt to overcome the lazy negligence of some by establishing the duty of the *Remembrance of the Saints* through suitable arguments. Thereafter, I will note the difficulties that can cause delay in this pursuit, and I will bring forward certain precautions and rules for exercising *due prudence* in this labor, striving to provide whatever support I can.

You, most honored listeners <note>original: "AA. HH.," an abbreviation for "Auditores Honoratissimi," a formal greeting used in academic and religious speeches</note>, give me your open ears and minds while I run this course. The subject I have chosen requires both my care and your

Furthermore, is anything in itself more suited to awakening in us a similar image of true piety than the constant contemplation of such illustrious examples? If **THUCYDIDES** <note>Athenian historian (c. 460–400 BC)</note> rightly called history *philosophy through examples* <note>original Greek: "φιλοσοφιαν εκ παραδειγματων"</note> (k); if the ancient Romans—in order to leave deep-seated stings in the minds of their descendants—used to *sing the praises and virtues of famous men at banquets to the accompaniment of the flute* <note>original: "conviviis ad tibiam clarorum Virorum laudes atque virtutes decinebant"</note> (l); if Caesar groaned upon seeing the statue of Alexander the Great, as if weary of his own laziness; if Themistocles <note>Athenian general and statesman</note> was awakened from sleep by the trophies of Miltiades <note>the victor of the Battle of Marathon</note>; will the noble deeds performed for truth and religion by the Saints who preceded us provide any less a stimulus for a more sacred virtue? Noble and most honorable listeners <note>Latin: "AA. ---

$(m)$ The illustrious **MUHLIUS** <note>Heinrich Muhlius (1666–1733), a German Lutheran theologian</note> has excerpted excellent testimonies from **BASIL** <note>Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), one of the "Cappadocian Fathers" of the Greek Church</note> and **JOHN OF DAMASCUS** <note>c. 675–749, a Syrian monk known for defending the use of icons</note> on this matter in his *Historical-Theological Dissertation on the Martyrs of the Evangelical Church*, pages 399–400. To these deserves to be added the advice of **CASSIODORUS** <note>c. 485–585, a Roman statesman and monk who encouraged the preservation of literature</note>, a man of consular rank, in his *On Divine Readings*, chapter 32: *“Mindful of future blessedness, read constantly the lives of the Fathers, the confessions of the faithful, and the sufferings of the Martyrs, which you will undoubtedly find among other things in the Letter of Saint Jerome intended for Chromatius and Heliodorus; those who flourished throughout the whole world, so that holy imitation, calling you forth, may lead you to the heavenly kingdoms.”* That this true veneration is owed to the memory of the Martyrs, and that this effect is to be hoped for from its preservation, the Church of Smyrna testifies in its letter on the martyrdom of Polycarp <note>An early Christian bishop and disciple of the Apostle John, martyred in the 2nd century</note>, as recorded in **EUSEBIUS’S** <note>The "Father of Church History" (c. 260–339)</note> *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, Chapter 15: *“For him [Christ], as the Son of God, we adore; but the Martyrs we rightly love as **DISCIPLES AND IMITATORS OF CHRIST** because of their exceptional devotion to their King and Master; <note>original Greek: ὧν γένοιτο καὶ ἡμᾶς συγκοινωνούς τε καὶ συμμαθητὰς γενέσθαι</note> **OF WHOM MAY WE ALSO BECOME PARTNERS AND FELLOW-DISCIPLES!**”* This passage is urged and defended by **BASNAGE** <note>Jacques Basnage (1653–1723), a prominent French Protestant historian who argued against Catholic practices</note> in his *History of the Church*, Book XVIII, Chapter I, pages 1007–1008, among others who argue against the patrons of the idolatrous cult of the Saints. **SULPICIUS SEVERUS** <note>c. 363–425, a historian best known for his biography of Saint Martin of Tours</note>, in the first chapter of his *Life of the Blessed Martin*, after he had premised: *“What benefit did posterity gain by reading of Hector fighting or Socrates philosophizing?”* since to imitate them is not only folly, but not to oppose them most fiercely is madness, soon adds: *“Wherefore I think it will be worth my effort if I write down the life of a most holy Man, soon to be an example for others: by which certainly [they may be led] to true wisdom, and heavenly warfare, and divine [virtue]...”*

...of the learned, **JOSEPH JUSTUS SCALIGER** <note>1540–1609, a French religious scholar and one of the founders of modern historical chronology</note>, who asserts concerning the ancient and genuine *Acts of the Martyrs* that *the soul of the pious is so affected by reading them that it never departs from them satisfied: indeed, he adds, every person can feel this according to their own capacity and the state of their conscience. Indeed, Antiquity, being persuaded of this most certain benefit to be drawn from the records <note>original Latin: *monumentis*, meaning physical or written memorials</note> of the Saints, applied a singular diligence in preserving these treasures. Above all, by reading of the pious Martyrs'

virtue, readers will be inspired. **EPHREM THE SYRIAN** <note>c. 306–373, a prominent Syriac Christian deacon, hymnwriter, and theologian</note> raises us higher in his *Eulogy for All Saints*, Works page 740, beginning thus: *The memory of the Saints is always illustrious and deeply lovable to both Angels and men: so that we also might struggle with equal zeal and fervor and love God in imitation of them. # SPEECH

But perhaps Divine Wisdom <note>original Latin: *divina Sapientia*</note> judged it prudent—when this most holy practice began to degenerate into superstition—to set limits upon it. This was done to punish the recklessness of those who had begun to contaminate the pious **Memory of the Saints** <note>original: *Sanctorum Memoria*</note> with a type of honor greater than what is appropriate for created beings. These people were no longer striving to follow the **examples** <note>original: *exempla*</note> of the saints' lives, but were instead seeking their **merits** <note>original: *merita*; the idea that a saint's "extra" holiness could be applied to someone else</note> as a source of vain confidence, effectively purchasing for themselves a license to sin. This evil began to creep in as early as the third century after the birth of Christ, and it grew with such intensity that from the fourth century onward, and after the time of **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History"</note>, almost nothing remained in the lives and...

# CONCERNING THE MEMORY OF THE SAINTS

When one encounters the **Martyrdoms of the Saints** <note>original Latin: *Martyria Sanctorum*</note>, it is clear that nothing in the vast number of homilies <note>Sermons or religious discourses</note> of the Church Fathers—written to proclaim the praises of the Holy Martyrs on their **birthdays** <note>original: *natalitiis*; the early church referred to the date of a martyr's death as their "birthday" into eternal life</note>, for so they named the days on which the Triumphs of the Martyrs were celebrated—is found that is not sprinkled with some stain of this superstition. This contagion proceeded to spread even further, as there were added visits to tombs, the **translation of relics** <note>original: *transportationes reliquiarum*; the practice of moving the physical remains of saints to new locations</note>, the veneration of images, the most shameless fabrications of miracles and apparitions, and finally **Papal apotheoses** <note>term: *apotheosis*—the formal process of "making someone a saint" or elevating a human to a divine-like status</note>. I have neither the time nor the inclination to dwell on each of these individually.

Who would not grieve at the infernal frauds of the **Devil** <note>original: *Diaboli fraudes*</note>? By these, he strove to subvert the most healthy use the Church could expect from the **Memory of the Saints** <note>original: *Memoria Sanctorum*</note>. Pursuing the very name of those deceased with a deadly hatred, he endeavored to turn their sweetest fragrance into a foul stench. Yet, even so, the honor due to true **Holiness** <note>original: *Sanctitas*</note> remains untarnished. For those who superstitiously worship the **Saints** <note>original: *Sanctos*</note> under such a pretext are unknowingly venerating that very Queen of all Virtues which is most hateful to the flesh. While they often praise so laboriously in the dead that which in

# ON THE MEMORY OF THE SAINTS.

<center>Rrr</center>
<meta>Vol. II., catchword: tibus</meta>

I am confident, honored listeners <note>original: *A. H.*, likely abbreviating *Auditores Honoratissimi*</note>, that none of you will any longer deny that time and effort <note>original: *oleum*, literally "oil," referring to the lamp oil burned during late-night study</note> are spent with great benefit in cultivating and repeatedly renewing the **Memory of the Saints**. But lest we be cheated of the reward for our labor, Christian prudence must guide the reins of our diligence. If any part of history—this part which otherwise excels so greatly in dignity—is filled with darkness, trackless paths, brambles, and even most ruinous snares, it is this. It will be worthwhile to briefly reveal the chief sources of this calamity before we point out the way to block them off.

We find no other springs here than those from which all uncertainty in any history is derived. Remove the *will to deceive* in those passing it down, and *credulity* in those receiving it, and the clear, naked truth will appear at the bottom.

No one will easily deny that even the first Fathers of the Church, as early as the Apostolic age, suffered in no small measure from the disease of credulity. <meta>This page continues the speaker's polemic against the "pious frauds" of the medieval Church. # ORATION

How many catalogs of new Saints were produced by the mutual envy of monks? These men, the more they were of corrupt morals, the more they considered it to be to their advantage to win a greater appearance of holiness for their Order among the common people through numerous forged titles of Saints—if not actual persons. In this way, wagonloads of "Acts," "Lives," "Homilies," and "Eulogies" were gradually poured into the Church, as numerous as swarms of flies in the peak of summer heat. Thus, first the monasteries and then the libraries were filled with thick volumes, offering puerile and most frigid fictions—though encrusted with an appearance of affected piety—to the ignorant commoners, in order to cloak the errors of the Roman Church and promote the authority of the Antichristian Priesthood. Thus, through an impudence for lying, Jacobus de Voragine <note>original: *Jacobus de Voragine*; also known as Giacomo da Varagine (c. 1230–1298), the Archbishop of Genoa and author of the famous collection of hagiographies</note> (or as others prefer, *de Viragine*), earned immortality for his name with his *Golden Legend* <note>original: *Legenda Aurea*; a hugely popular medieval collection of the lives of the saints, often criticized by later scholars for its many historical inaccuracies</note>...

---

...as an inspection of the evidence shows. From this, it came to pass that—especially from the 9th Century onward—those who composed the history of the Church sought the approval of the Pope. This is demonstrated by the preface of Anastasius the Librarian <note>original: *Anastasius Bibliothecarius* (c. 810–879), a significant historian and translator in the service of the Papacy</note> preceding his *Life of John the Almsgiver* <note>John V of Alexandria (d. 619), a Patriarch known for his extraordinary charity</note>, Patriarch of Alexandria, addressed to Pope Nicholas; and from the introduction to the *Pantheon* <note>A universal chronicle written by Godfrey of Viterbo</note> by Godfrey of Viterbo <note>original: *Gotfridus Viterbiensis* (c. 1120–1196), a chronicler and notary to several Holy Roman Emperors</note> addressed to Urban III, as well as others cited there on page 63 and following.

<summary>This page critiques the medieval practice of forging saintly lives (hagiographies) to increase the prestige of monastic orders and argues that ecclesiastical history became a tool of the Papacy through required approvals and censorship starting in the 9th century.</summary>

### 514

[phi]losophy’s excessive love was a snare <note>original: "fraudi fuit," literally "was a fraud" or "a source of harm"</note> for cautious men; yet we believe we should pronounce nothing rashly or somewhat harshly, nor anything against the piety owed to our Forefathers. ### 515

As I bring forward the deliberations of the Doctors of the Church <term>Doctors of the Church: Influential theologians and teachers throughout Christian history whose writings are considered authoritative</term>, we should most willingly offer them the palm of honor.

We have already hinted at the hidden quicksands <note>original: "Syrtes," referring to the dangerous sandbanks off the coast of North Africa, used here as a metaphor for intellectual hazards</note> in this sea, which make it treacherous and bid us to navigate cautiously. We must now look toward the North Star <note>original: "Cynosura," the constellation Ursa Minor used by sailors for navigation</note>, which we present here in a brief summary contained within a few rules.

I. Above all, those who have clearly strayed from the foundation of truth should not be added to the Catalog of Saints. It is well known (o) that heretics often sought to spread their errors more widely under the guise of piety, and that heretics boasted of their own "Saints" and their own "Martyrs." We do not recognize a piety for which truth does not carry the torch. *The Devil himself transformed himself into an Angel of light.* (p) *A sincere zeal for truth is the inseparable companion—indeed, the essential part—of true Holiness.*

If we look at their origin, they are divine corrections intended to rouse the Church from its sluggishness and are thus suitable means for increasing sanctification <term>sanctification</term><note>The process of being made holy or purified from sin.</note>. Yet they do not contribute anything of their own nature, nor are they more suited to produce this effect than the preaching of the Gospel <note>original: *Evangelii præconium*</note>, which is often perceived more abundantly and accurately during peaceful times than during stormy ones. And, I ask you, do not those very people against whom we argue admit that the age in which the Apostolic Men <note>original: *Viri Apostolici*; leaders of the early Church who were believed to have been direct disciples of the original Apostles.</note> still survived had a great advantage in holiness over the following ages?

(z) To this point belong, among other things, AUGUSTINE’S *Retractations* <note>original: *Retractationes*; a work where St. Augustine revisited and corrected his earlier writings</note> as well as his *Confessions*, of which the tenth book deserves to be compared here especially. > I omit feigned flatteries, so that I do not rise for prayers; likewise trivial and less religious entries into the Church, deliberately sought delays, futile talk in assemblies, too much care in preparing feasts, wicked disparagements in sacred places, laziness in praying, negligence in singing psalms, eagerness in deceiving, craftiness in making profit, feigned conversations with pious little women and frequent rebukes, contempt for the needy, deference to the rich, defrauding of a loan received, anger against those not serving correctly, changing of promises, and how I demanded the benefits of friends—which ought to be obtained by prayers—as if they were debts. I am silent about the insatiable greed for receiving gifts, sharing in others' sins, useless counsels in the hope of catching greater gain, flatteries, dissensions, supplications, various commemorations, harmful contentions, useless fights, and inept conversations and habits. This is my life, brothers; these are my faults and infirmities. If you can help me against such a crowd of sins, you rightly pity me. If you have the strength to repress such a phalanx of my wicked thoughts, I beg you not to desert me as I struggle.

If, however, there are those who believe that certain things occur in EPHREM’S *Confession* which seem to be said too incautiously because of the way worldly men might twist them, let them consider: 

1) We are using mere translations of the works written in Syriac by EPHREM, and those not reliable enough, as TENTZEL <note>Wilhelm Ernst Tentzel, a German historian and numismatist</note> learnedly demonstrates in his *Selected Exercises*, p. 11 and pp. 282 following. 

2) The humility of this confession surpasses all the feigned piety of worldly men. 

3) There is no need for us to understand the most holy Father to be speaking of "perfected" <note>actualized or fully committed</note> sins. For this is the sincerity peculiar to the truly pious: that they recognize even the very beginnings of faults as abominable before God, and are more afflicted in secret because of them than worldly men are because of fully committed crimes. 

4) No one should seek a defense for their own flaws in these passages, unless they find in themselves the same <term>compunction <note>from the Latin *compunctio*, a "pricking" of the conscience; a deep sense of remorse for sin</note></term> of heart and the other virtues which it is admitted were excellent in Ephrem himself.

## UNIVERSITY OF UTRECHT
<page-num>539</page-num>

it is the reason why the Prophet, as if not yet satisfied with such a splendid designation as the **Sun**, wished furthermore to present Him as the **SUN OF RIGHTEOUSNESS**. The chests of learned antiquity have been shaken out in vain to illustrate this phrase. Monuments of the Phoenicians and Greeks have been brought into the light. Certain epithets of Jupiter and Phoebus <note>Apollo, the Greek sun god</note> were produced, (*d*) but they are too far removed for the divine waters to be moistened by these muddy streams. And I ask, why should we anxiously search abroad for what we find at home? Let everyone be fully persuaded in their own mind: to me it appears certain that with most elegant brevity Malachi wished to condense what Jeremiah had sung more broadly and abundantly regarding the **MAN BRANCH** <note>original: "VIRO ZÆMACH"</note>, whose name would be **THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS** <note>original: "JEHOVA JUSTITIA NOSTRA"</note>.

Those who have even tasted Hebrew letters with their lips know that the name <term>Zemach</term> <note>original Hebrew: צמח; literally "sprout" or "branch"</note> designates the <term>Anatole</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀνατολὴν; "rising" or "dawn"</note>, the **Rising**. It does not escape me that there is a dispute stirred up among the highest philologists <note>scholars of language and historical texts</note>, whether it means rather a brightness rising out of darkness, or rather [something] rising from the earth...

# SPEECH ON THE INSIGNIA

...this hieroglyphic "branchlet" might suggest this name of the Messiah. However, since the nature of the word itself, the comparison of the places in which it occurs, and Zacharias (the father of the Baptist) in his song—who alluded quite clearly to the same concept—as well as the older interpreters all strongly favor the former opinion, there appears to be no reason why we should not prefer a more emphatic emblem (*e*), or at least include it (*f*). Jeremiah, therefore, presents to us the one rising under the concept of <term>Tzemach</term> <note>Hebrew: צמח. Usually translated as "Branch" or "Sprout," but also carries the meaning of "Rising Light" or "Dawn."</note>.

---

(*e*) The esteemed Le Moyne preferred this, bringing forward arguments not to be despised in the work cited, chapter 11. Before him, Hakspanius already defended the same opinion in *Philological Notes*, Volume II, page 764 and following. Nor does Gregory disagree in *Biblical-Critical Observations*, inserted in Volume IX, chapter 11. We also followed in the same footsteps <note>original: "pedibus ivimus," a Latin idiom meaning to provide support or agree with a proposal.</note> in *On the Mystery of the Covenant of Grace*, Book III, chapter 12, section 4, and chapter 13, sections 6 and 7. We insisted on the same in the dissertation *On the Horn of Salvation* in the *Bremen Library*, Volume II, sections 10 and 11, page 702 and following, where we observed—for the sake of further illustration—that the words <term>Keren</term> <note>Hebrew: קרן. Meaning both "horn" (symbol of power) and "ray of light."</note> and <term>Tzemach</term> are synonymous when they refer to the Messiah, and that both allude to the symbol of the miraculous column <note>Likely the Pillar of Fire and Cloud that guided the Israelites in the Exodus.</note>.

(*f*) It is certain that this can be done conveniently, because the nature of the root <term>Tzemach</term>, just like the Greek <term>anatellein</term> <note>original: ἀνατέλλειν. Meaning to rise up, like the sun, or to spring forth like a plant.</note>, allows for it. For each term generally denotes whatever flashes or springs forth from a certain place, whether it be the rising Sun, a brilliance coming forth, or a plant budding out. Indeed, my most dear Vriemuthus observed in his dissertation *On Shiloh*, chapter V, that several roots of this kind occur. But whoever desires to see both emblems—of light and of a rising plant—joined in the description of the Messiah, let him compare Numbers 24:17 and Revelation 22:16.

# ORATION ON THE INSIGNIA

...line <note>Continuing the thought from the previous page regarding the "rays" of the divine sun</note>, since there is no part of solid learning which is not a kind of torch lit from this Sun? It would be appropriate here to rise beyond the times of the Noachic flood and to begin with **ADAM** himself, certainly a Prophetic man. More probable evidence is available from the period after the flood. It is asserted that *Noah* carried the sparks of all the sciences, preserved from the old world, into the renewed world. For this reason, he has been likened to *Prometheus*, about whom **AESCHYLUS** sang:

Those who must speak solemnly in a majestic and crowded assembly are accustomed to prefacing their remarks with much talk—more with elegance than with true sincerity—about their mental distress. # INAUGURAL DISCOURSE

I will seize this task, and I will briskly gird myself for the work. As I was arranging my thoughts, there came to mind that golden maxim, read and reread a hundred times since my youth, with which the pious founders of this school adorned the front of our **Podium**. These founders willed that this magnificent Hall—cleansed of the dust and grime of *Mars* <note>original: *Mavortio*; the Roman god of war, implying the space was once used for military purposes or "the dust of battle"</note>—be consecrated to Holy **Theology**, the *Mistress of Heavenly Peace*.

### DISCOURSE

...shining with splendor, made the **Breastplate** <term>Pectorale</term><note>A sacred vestment worn by the Hebrew High Priest, containing twelve gemstones representing the tribes of Israel.</note>. Into this, the most wise Legislator <note>Moses</note> ordered a most holy heirloom to be placed, to which he simultaneously assigned the name of the **URIM & THUMMIM** by divine authority. In translating these words, **AQUILA** and **THEODOTION** <note>two 2nd-century scholars known for their Greek translations of the Old Testament</note> have, more than other interpreters, stuck to the literal meaning; they rendered them as *illuminations and perfections* <note>original Greek: φωτισμοὺς καὶ τελειώσεις, transliterated as "phōtismous kai teleiōseis"</note>. Those who read *illuminations and perfections* <note>original Greek: φωτισμοὺς καὶ τελειότητας, transliterated as "phōtismous kai teleiotētas"</note> in **ORIGEN'S Hexapla** <note>a massive six-columned comparative edition of the Old Testament compiled by the scholar Origen in the 3rd century</note> provide the same meaning. (*a*) If you wish to express the concept of the words more accurately, the first should be translated as **LIGHTS**, and the second as **INTEGRITIES** or **PERFECTIONS** in the plural number. We will not linger now on how much this command has exercised the pens and wits of the most learned theologians as well as philologists <note>scholars of language and history</note>, so that we may gain space to explain our own opinion more fully. However, so that our discourse does not seem to you, **Most Honored Listeners** <note>original: *AA. HH.*, an abbreviation for *Auditores Honoratissimi*</note>, to be entangled in some part by obscurity, we set this path for ourselves: what we, among so many divisions of opinion, [think] concerning...

***

(*a*) **DRUSIUS** <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a famed Flemish scholar of Hebrew and the Bible</note> has already noted this regarding **AQUILA** and **THEODOTION** in his *Major Notes*. But in the *Hexapla* regarding **Exodus 28:30**, it is noted that all Greek interpreters—if you set aside the "Seventy" <note>The Septuagint, the standard Greek version of the Hebrew Bible produced by 70 scholars</note>—read *the illuminations and the perfections* <note>original Greek: τοὺς φωτισμοὺς καὶ τὰς τελειότητας</note>, which is further confirmed by an ancient Greek glossary added by the most learned **MONTFAUCON** <note>Bernard de Montfaucon (1655–1741), a French monk and pioneering scholar of ancient texts</note>.

...arguments support those who hold this view. In the sacred scriptures <note>original: *literis*</note>, the mention of the Gems alternates with the Oracle of the Urim and Thummim in such a way that one or the other is commemorated in different places; this is so that you might know that the Oracle consists of the gems, or that the gems are comprised under the name of the Oracle. ($f$) Furthermore, the same characteristics <term>predicates</term> are applied to both. *The gems are said to have filled the breastplate, while the Oracle was placed in the breastplate*, ($g$) descriptions which do not differ much from one another; both are said to have been *worn by Aaron over his heart*. ($h$) Add to this that the entirety of sacred history does not exhibit even a jot <note>original Greek: *γρυ* (gry), meaning the smallest scrap or a grunt</note> by which it might be established that the Urim consisted of anything different from the stones themselves, or what kind of thing that might have been.

### INAUGURALIS.

...could be gathered with any appearance of truth. (*i*) Nor indeed does the character of the words themselves disagree,

<note>
(*i*) We do not dwell on the reasons of those who disagree. BUXTORF <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a celebrated Hebraist</note> presents them in summary in the place cited, as does EDZARD <note>Ezra Edzard, a theologian known for his work on Jewish law</note> in his commentary on *Avodah Zarah* <note>original: "Avod. Sara.", a tractate of the Talmud concerning "Foreign Worship"</note>, Chapter II, page 202 and following.

**I.** That the Urim and Thummim, in their material, form, and manufacture, are not described in the command given to Moses, as the rest of the garments are; from which they argue that they were something divine and mystical.
**Response 1.** According to our hypothesis, this is certainly done, since the Gems themselves and the craftsmanship required for them are accurately described.
**Response 2.** If they were something mystical, they ought at least to have been known in their "type" <term>type: a physical foreshadowing of a spiritual truth</term> and described to such an extent that a mystical sense could be derived from them.

**II.** That in the divine command, mention of them is made immediately with a prefixed article, even though they were not mentioned previously. They claim this was done because of their divine excellence and superiority. 
**Response.** CARTWRIGHT <note>Thomas Cartwright (1535–1603), an influential Puritan theologian</note> has already very well shown that this argument works in our favor; because the prefixed letter *He* <note>original: "ה", the Hebrew definite article meaning "the"</note> points back to those Gems which had just been described.

**III.** That the command concerning them was directed to Moses, and not simultaneously to the other craftsmen, from which it seems to follow that the Urim <note>original Greek: "τὰ Urim"</note> were made not by their hands, but by the hand of God himself. 
**Response 1.** This assumes the very point in question: namely, that there was a difference between the Gems and the Urim.
**Response 2.** Nowhere is it expressly said that God made the Urim, as we read regarding the Tablets of the Law, or the garments of the first parents <term>Protoplastorum: referring to Adam and Eve, the "first-formed"</term>. Where the Word of God is silent, no extraordinary or miraculous works should be attributed to Him.

# ORATION

...it would not have been a breastplate. **Response:** Regarding the first point, God willed by order to first follow both the individual names of the gems and their setting, and then to more closely examine both the quality and the use of the *Breastplate* (Verse 29, 30). This is all the more manifest because otherwise, what is commanded of Aaron in Verse 29—to carry the names of the *Children of Israel* in that sacred *Breastplate of Judgment*—would also fall under criticism, since the engraving of those names had already been prescribed in Verse 21. Regarding the second point, we are even more surprised that those arguing this way do not take account of the very frequent use of synecdoche <term>synecdoche: a figure of speech where a part represents the whole, or the whole represents a part</term>, which recurs quite often in the description of the *Breastplate*. For not only is the term *Breastplate* used in its strict sense <note>original: "κυρίως"</note> for that doubled quadrangular fabric to which the stones themselves were to be attached (Exodus 28:15–17), but also in Verse 30, where the *Urim* and *Thummim* were to be inserted, it is called the *Breastplate of Judgment*. This likewise must be understood through *synecdoche* and *prolepsis* <term>prolepsis: describing a future event or state as if it currently exists</term>. For, speaking strictly, without the *Urim* and *Thummim*, it was not yet the *Breastplate of Judgment*.

**V.** That the *Breastplate* was doubled for the reason that something mystical could be placed within it. **Response:** I would rather judge that it was done for this reason: so that it would be more suitable for the insertion of the stones themselves and for their connection with the *Ephod* <term>Ephod: a decorative vest or apron-like garment worn by the High Priest</term>. For since the front part of the doubled cloth received the Gems, the back part could be fastened more smoothly and strongly to the chest and shoulders of the High Priest without the risk of tearing the fabric. What the famous Frischmuth <note>Johannes Frischmuth (1619–1687), a German scholar of Oriental languages and theology</note> noted on this matter in his *Disputation on the Priestly Attire*, Chapter 3, Section 2, deserves attention; there, after other points, he explains his opinion as follows: *"The Breastplate was composed of a double layer or plate; the upper one, skillfully pierced with twelve holes or settings at equal distances from one another, received the same number of gems; the lower part was flat and with no holes..."*

MARTINII, who conjectures that by the *Urim and Thummim*, a flat golden plate or something similar is indicated, inserted within the doubling of the *Breastplate*. But this is likewise not only unwritten <note>original: "$\alpha\gamma\rho\alpha\phi\text{ov}$" (unrecorded in Scripture)</note>, but is easily resolved by a consideration of the structure of the *Breastplate*. For this was not only a thicker weave, but also stiff with gold; its doubling made the *Breastplate* sufficiently suitable not just for carrying the gems—which was not so great a weight—but also for attaching the golden rings and chains to it. Add to this that the golden rings undoubtedly cohered with the golden settings themselves, which joined the gems together; in this way, the weight of the gems was suspended not so much from the fabric of the *Breastplate* as from the golden chains.

**VI.** That very different phrases are used when speaking of the *insertion of the stones*, "and you shall fill in it a filling of stone" <note>original Hebrew: ומלאת בו מלאת אבן</note>, and of the *Urim and Thummim*, "and you shall put into the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim" <note>original Hebrew: ונתת אל חשן המשפט האור' ואת ההת'</note>. **Response:** A certain difference certainly exists; for the first phrase designates the work of the High Priest, while the latter designates its application by Moses. Otherwise, the matter comes to the same thing. For insofar as the gems with their golden settings not only covered the entire square of the *Breastplate* on the outside, but were also woven inside within the doubling to the doubled fabric, when they were applied to the *Breastplate*, they filled it at the same time. And thus, that objection by EDZARDI is simultaneously wiped out—

This stems from the broad meaning of "truth" <note>Hebrew: אמת</note> among the Hebrews, which refers not only to doctrine and opinion but also to the very quality of one's heart and actions. For this reason, **PHILO THE JEW**, **ORIGEN**, **JEROME**, and others well-versed in Hebrew have been willing to accept this version. Therefore, an error crept into the Concordances of the **Septuagint** <note>The Greek Old Testament, often abbreviated as "the LXX" or "the 70"</note> when, in Deuteronomy 32:8, "truth" is read in place of "Urim." In that passage, the **Septuagint** merely inverted the order of the words. This could have sufficed to excuse the **VULGATE**; had **BELLARMINE** <note>Robert Bellarmine, a prominent Catholic Cardinal and theologian</note> stopped there, his ignorance would not have deserved the harsh criticism of **AMAMA**, **DILHERR**, and others. Furthermore, this agrees with our own interpretation, which particularly pleased **GROTIUS** <note>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch jurist and theologian</note> when he wrote on the passage in Exodus: *In a teacher, such as the High Priest ought to be above all others, two things are required: knowledge and purity of life.* **SPENCER** discussed this more fully in *On the Urim and Thummim*, chapter 8, section 1. See also **CORNELIUS A LAPIDE** on the cited passage in Exodus and **LORINUS** in his *Commentary on Leviticus* 8:8. There you will find a whole forest of allegories; yet, although many have applied this type to the Ministers of the Gospel, the way it refers specifically to the Apostles has been very little understood.

...the mystical [number] arises, the ranks of the mystery are to be considered no less involved in it, since the census of the Church has likewise very often been accustomed to be established through these numbers which are frequently encountered. The **number three** <term>ternarius: the grouping of three</term> is dedicated to the *Triune God* of Israel itself, while the **number four** <term>quaternarius: the grouping of four</term> is dedicated to the Church, which is to be expanded through the four parts of the earth. Both have entered into a sweet marriage, as it were, in the **number seven** <term>septenario: the grouping of seven</term>, which is also accustomed to measuring all the intervals of the Church. However, in order for the **number twelve** <term>duodenarius: the grouping of twelve</term> to arise from the **three** and the **four**, they must be multiplied by each other. 

Although the Church may be divided into four camps <note>original: "castra." This likely refers to the arrangement of the twelve tribes of Israel into four camps around the Tabernacle in the wilderness</note>, yet for each and every one there is one *Triune God*, the *thrice Holy* One of Israel, whose Name alone the four living creatures <note>A reference to the "four living creatures" (tetramorphs) described in the visions of Ezekiel and the Book of Revelation</note> celebrate with a perennial stream of praise. These things, which seem to us to be suggested—at least with great probability—by the hidden enigma of this most holy number, you may easily apply to the **Priestly Gems** <note>The twelve precious stones set in the breastplate of the Jewish High Priest, each representing a tribe of Israel</note>, insofar as they delineate the excellence of the **Apostolic Doctrine**. For not only is this doctrine the same as that which was first revealed to the Patriarchs and thereafter constantly instilled in the sons of Israel; but also its entire argument turns upon that pivot: to propose, explain, and illustrate those truths which we strive to see reflected in our **number twelve**.

...he therefore leaves the matter in the middle <note>original: *medio*; likely finishing a sentence from the previous page regarding an undecided scholarly opinion</note>, yet in such a way that he allows it to pertain to the mysteries of this book. It cannot be denied that the supreme Lawgiver of Israel <note>God, who gave the specific instructions for the Tabernacle and its vestments to Moses</note> carefully arranged the rows of the **Stones of the Breastplate**. Regarding this, no one doubts that the names of the individual Tribes of Israel, or of the individual Patriarchs, were engraved on individual **Gems** which were arranged in an order defined by God. Divine Wisdom itself persuades us that this was likewise not done at random.

In the meantime, the exact order in which the names of the Tribes were inscribed is unknown, and interpreters who examine this matter more closely are split into two main camps. For some assert that these names were engraved according to the sequence of their birth, while others claim they followed the order of their dignity or rank. However, the lists of the Tribes of Israel in the Bible differ so much that no single instance occurs where one might safely plant a foot <note>A metaphorical way of saying there is no "firm ground" or certainty on this point</note>. Lest we also be **contributors of nothing** <term>asymboloi: a Greek term for those who attend a feast without contributing their share; here meaning someone who adds nothing to the scholarly discussion</term> in this matter, we judge no list to be more convenient for establishing a closer comparison with the gems than that which occurs in Ezekiel 48:31–35. There, the names of the twelve Tribes are listed to be inscribed on the **Gates of the Holy City**, and indeed in such a way that they are divided into four rows according to the four sides of the city. Therefore, they are assigned as follows:

### PROGRAM
### INVITATION.

# THE RECTOR AND PROFESSORS OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS
# SCHOOL OF BREMEN
# SEND GREETINGS TO THE READER. <note>original: "Lectori S." — shorthand for "Lectori Salutem," a traditional academic greeting.</note>

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap initial letter 'B' contained within a square frame, embellished with intricate floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>

That the condition of Kingdoms and Republics is blessed when Wisdom reigns—by whose help the knowledge of the best things and the pursuit of virtue are implanted in the minds of men—is a truth taught not only by experience itself, but one which the ages of the past confirm through countless examples. For where the wretched darkness of barbarism occupies all things and weighs upon the mind, it is inevitable that the power of intellect grows old and dull, and that peoples are subjected to the rule of perverse desires. Indeed, they become foul through every cruelty and monstrousness, almost shedding their very humanity, being stripped of the defenses by which those inner monsters can be defeated. This fact did not escape the more refined nations, who displayed a singular love for wisdom; they discovered through experience that by it, spirits are softened and brought to a gentler nature. 

To this end belongs a story recorded by some: that in **Elymais** <note>original: "Elymaïde" — an ancient region in the Persian Empire, east of the Tigris</note> there is a temple of **Adonis** <note>a deity often associated in classical mythology with beauty and the cycle of nature</note>, and in it are tamed lions. These lions receive those entering the temple with fawning, as if they were being greeted; if they are called to food, they attend as if invited to a banquet; and whatever you offer them, once they have received it, they depart modestly and decently. Interpreters of symbols maintain that beneath this "veil" or allegory lies shadowed a certain power of **Wisdom** <note>original: "Sapientiæ"</note>, by which the harsh and austere manners of men are smoothed. Once their wildness is cast off, they are fashioned into the modesty of human refinement—before which, as the **Poet** <note>likely a reference to Virgil, describing the calming of a storm</note> sings, *the winds are stilled and the waves subside*, the more sluggish... <note>The text breaks off here at the catchword for the next page</note>

<meta>This page continues the official invitation from the Rector and Professors of the Illustrious School of Bremen. The previous page discussed the general civilizing power of wisdom and mentioned ancient Persian temples. Here, the authors transition to the specific mythological and historical origins of European learning, moving from Orpheus and the Greeks to the Reformation in Bremen.</meta>

<page-num>653</page-num>
<header>INVITATIONAL PROGRAM.</header>

The Hebrus river froze with its waters bound; gentle hounds cherished the safe hare, and the lamb offered its side to the neighboring wolf: the harmonious deer play with the striped tiger, and the stags did not fear the Massylian mane <note>original: "Massylam... jubam" — the Massylians were a North African tribe, so this refers to the mane of an African lion.</note>. I omit the fables of the ancients regarding **Orpheus** <note>a legendary Thracian musician and prophet in Greek myth, whose music was said to be so beautiful it could charm animals and even stones</note>, such as that well-known story sung by so many:

*Orpheus, the sacred interpreter of the Gods, deterred forest-dwelling men from slaughter and a foul diet; because of this, he was said to soothe tigers and swift lions.* <note>original: a quote from Horace's *Ars Poetica*, lines 391–393, describing the civilizing power of poetry and music.</note>

However, it seemed to many of the ancients that there was a man of the Thracians, whom antiquity celebrated, of the noblest talent and wisdom. Some of them believe that the sacred rites <note>original: τὰς τελετὰς (*tas teletas*) — refers to the initiatory rituals or "mysteries" of ancient religion</note> are owed to Orpheus, since he supposedly drew from the Egyptian Sages all knowledge of theological matters, as well as purifications, the Underworld, and poetry. Others imagine from this that Philosophy first came into **Thrace** <note>a region in Southeast Europe, north of Greece</note> to Orpheus and **Eumolpus** <note>a legendary figure who supposedly founded the Eleusinian Mysteries</note>, and that they then sent it forward into Greece, whose footsteps it finally followed there.

It is certainly established among the learned that the first sacred rites of the Athenians were summoned from the Thracians, and according to the opinion of the Greeks, the **Muses** <note>the nine goddesses of inspiration in literature, science, and the arts</note> in the most ancient times settled in that region of Thrace which Orpheus inhabited, from whose homeland they also received the names **Pierides** and **Libethrides** <note>surnames of the Muses derived from locations in Thrace/Macedonia</note>. Greece, watered by this fountain, raised its head among peoples excelling in the cultivation of the mind; it not only flourished in every skill of craftsmanship, but was especially considered the mother and nurse of letters and the best studies, and stood above other nations in its religions, even if they were of false Gods. 

Let so many temples built by them bear witness, so many established Academies and "workshops of a good mind"—those of the Athenians, Lacedaemonians, Rhodians, Corinthians, Cretans, and others—which propagated the light of doctrine and virtue far and wide to others and scattered it throughout the world. If indeed those or any other peoples anywhere possessed wisdom, the Christians later transferred all of it into their own schools, corrected and polished of its many blemishes and flaws. These schools, however, began to be raised to the peak of their glory most especially after—within the memory of our fathers—superstition and the foul errors of the Papacy were renounced, the darkness of former times was dispelled, and they were illuminated by the most clear light of the Gospel. Since our city of **Bremen** <note>a major Hanseatic city in Northern Germany</note> was the first among the cities of Lower Saxony to admit this light, through the kindness of the most merciful Divinity, there was simultaneously aroused [the zeal] of the Fathers...

<page-num>654</page-num>
# PROGRAM

<meta>catchword: noted</meta>

Through the piety of the fatherland, what had previously been the hideouts of a degenerate clergy—receptacles of ignorance, injustice, and laziness suited only for feeding "lazy bellies" <note>This is a likely reference to Titus 1:12, a common polemic against monks during the Reformation.</note>—have now been converted into **places of study** <note>original: φροντιστήρια (*phrontistēria*), a Greek term for a place of meditation or a "think-tank."</note> for the fine arts, and **venerable shrines** <note>original: σεμνεῖα (*semneia*)</note> of learning and virtue. A distinguished growth followed these most auspicious beginnings when a broader theater for the highest disciplines was opened here with the dedication of the **Illustrious Gymnasium** <note>The *Gymnasium Illustre* of Bremen, founded in 1528 as a center of Reformed learning.</note>. This institution, adorned by the industry and learning of most excellent Professors, quickly spread the fame of its name far and wide.

Public lecture halls, in which the most beautiful sciences were promised, were opened and elegantly and splendidly furnished. Among these is that most spacious hall, located next to the Republic’s armory. Previously, it was used for storing gunpowder match-cords <note>original: "funiculis pyriis" — cords used to ignite early firearms</note> and similar instruments belonging to military equipment; now, it is consecrated to heavenly doctrine and echoes with the voices of the Theologians. Its pulpit is seen marked with this memorable inscription: **LIGHT & INTEGRITY** <note>original: LUX & INTEGRITAS; this corresponds to the "Urim and Thummim" of the High Priest in the Old Testament, symbols of revelation and truth.</note>.

Indeed, it pertains to the safety of the Republic that both be joined: care should not be brought only to constructing **Arsenals and Armories** <note>original: Ἀρείοις καὶ Ὁπλοθήκαις (*Areiois kai Hoplothēkais*) — "places of Ares (war) and weapon-stores."</note>, but also to **Schools and Museums** <note>original: Ἀθηναίοις καὶ Μυσείοις (*Athēnaiois kai Mouseiois*) — "places of Athena (wisdom) and shrines of the Muses."</note>. From these, weapons may be readied against impiety and those pestilential errors that threaten destruction to the kingdom of Christ. By fighting for the most holy Truth within these walls, they bring glory to the divine name.

*“Neither walls, nor towers, nor bulwarks and fortifications of cities, but the wise opinions of wise men prevail most of all,”* as the wise man of Cos <note>Hippocrates, the famous Greek physician from the island of Cos.</note> truly said. This applies even more correctly to the divine books: *“The sacred page,”* says **Laurentius Justinianus** <note>St. Lorenzo Giustiniani (1381–1456), the first Patriarch of Venice, known for his mystical and ascetic writings.</note> skillfully, *“is the mirror of the Word of wisdom, the armory of divinity.”* From this, **Gregory the Great** <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604), a central figure in medieval theology.</note> adapts what is read in the *Song of Songs* regarding the **Tower of David**, which is celebrated as being built with bulwarks, from which a thousand shields hang, all the armor of the strong. For there, he says, are the commands of God and the examples of the righteous; as many commands as there are there, so many are the defenses for our hearts. In the voice of the sacred word, we seek a defense of virtue for anyone, and we find it; from there let us take our commands and our examples, through which we may be armed unbreakably against our adversaries.

Furthermore, that hall dedicated to the instruction of Theologians was surely established by wise counsel, being pre-marked with the motto we mentioned...

<header>INVITATION.</header>
<meta>catchword: noted</meta>

was noted, modeled after the ancient ornament of the Hebrew High Priest <note>A reference to the *Choshen* or Breastplate of Judgment, specifically the Urim and Thummim, which were believed to shine when God gave an answer.</note>, from whose chest sparkled an admirable brilliance. This most beautiful title indeed possesses something that those who hand down sacred things, as well as those who drink them in with eager ears, should perpetually keep before their eyes. It is necessary that he be for both groups—lest they should one day regret the labors of the undertaken work and the exhaustion they have endured—a Leader and Guardian, a Witness as well as a Judge, a Counselor, Author, and Helper; let him be the Rule and the Goal; let him be, as Basil says, a **living image** <note>original: εικὼν ἔμψυχος (*eikōn empsychos*). This concept from St. Basil the Great suggests that a teacher should be a breathing, personified example of virtue.</note> upon which they may gaze, and from which they may transfer into themselves the likeness of breathing Wisdom and Virtue. But there is no necessity to pursue these matters more diffusely or accurately here, since this illustrious subject has taken it upon himself to explain in this Speech:

->THE VERY REVEREND, MOST DISTINGUISHED, AND MOST LEARNED MAN,<-

# FRIEDRICH ADOLPH LAMPE,

Doctor of Holy Theology, and recently the most celebrated Ordinary Professor of the same and of Ecclesiastical History in the Illustrious Academy of Utrecht <note>The University of Utrecht in the Netherlands, a major center for Reformed theology in the 18th century.</note>, now returned by divine calling to our Fatherland, where he is destined—as we rightly predict—to elegantly adorn both the Church and the Lyceum. The city of Detmold, the capital of the County of Lippe and the seat of the Most Noble Counts, granted him his first light of birth on the nineteenth day of February, 1683. His father was the Very Reverend, Most Distinguished, and Most Learned Man, **HENRY LAMPE**—the firstborn son of the most respected and upright man **PETER LAMPE**, a most prosperous merchant of Bremen—who was first a preacher at Detmold, then at Frankfurt am Main, and finally the court chaplain at Konigsberg in Prussia. His mother was the most Noble and in every virtue most Excellent Matron, **CHRISTINA ELISABETH ZELLER**, the daughter of the venerable **JOHANN JACOB ZELLER**, who was formerly the supreme overseer of sacred rites in the County of Lippe, a position they call General Superintendent. When he had completed his academic studies with singular praise, he served the congregation in the Duchy of Cleves, first for a period of three years at Weeze, then for three years at Tecklenburg—

<page-num>656</page-num>
<header>INVITATION PROGRAM.</header>

...after a second period of two years <note>The Latin 'nio altero' likely completes 'biennio altero' from the previous page.</note>, having served as a faithful interpreter of the divine word, he followed our people of Bremen—specifically the citizens of St. Stephen’s Parish—who chose him as their preacher. Ten years later, with their unanimous will and consent, he held the position of Lead Pastor. After the fame of his outstanding learning and virtue had spread throughout the Netherlands, he was formally summoned from here the following year by the most noble and distinguished Leaders and Curators of the **University of Utrecht** <note>original: *Academia Trajectina*</note> to take up a Professorship of Theology. He performed that duty for seven years, serving the University with great distinction; he even successfully served as its Rector <note>original: *Magistratum*. In a university context, this refers to the Rector Magnificus, the head of the institution.</note> this past year. 

But since the memory of this most praised Doctor had never faded from the hearts of our people in Bremen, they dared to recall him here from Utrecht, offering him splendid and highly honorable conditions. Not only was he chosen by the votes of the St. Ansgar congregation to succeed that venerable and most celebrated theologian—and our most close colleague as long as fate allowed—**Gottfried Jüngst** <note>original: *Godofredo Jüngslio* (1672–1726), a significant Reformed theologian in Bremen.</note>, in the holy ministry of the Gospel; but he was also named by the Illustrious Leaders of our Country as the Ordinary Professor of Sacred Theology and, at the same time, Rector in alternating years (roles which had also been Jüngst’s). With such success, and fueled by a zeal to help his homeland to the best of his ability, he did not hesitate to exchange the University of Utrecht for the new office offered to him. 

On the 11th of this coming September, after the morning assembly is dismissed, he will begin his inaugural speech to illustrate the most noble motto <term>Lemma|A short phrase or motto used to define the character of an office or institution.</term> of our Theological Chair: 

->**LIGHT AND INTEGRITY**<- 
<note>original: *LUX & INTEGRITAS*. This is the Latin translation of the Hebrew 'Urim and Thummim' from the High Priest’s breastplate, symbolizing divine revelation and moral perfection.</note>

With God’s favor, he will hereafter unfold the riches of his talent and learning for the benefit of our flourishing youth. 

We ask and urge with all due respect and zeal that the **MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND WISE SENATORS** <note>original: *Conscripti Patres*. A formal title for the city's ruling council, modeled after the Roman Senate.</note>, as well as **MEN OF LEARNING AND SUPPORTERS OF WISDOM** from every place and rank, and the **MOST NOBLE ASSEMBLY OF STUDIOUS YOUTH**, grace these formal professorial proceedings with their presence and listen kindly as he is initiated into his new office.

Publicly announced on the 13th Sunday after Trinity, in the year 1727.
